->MAY IT PLEASE YOUR GRACE,<-

**T**HE Philosophy of Plato, from its native dignity, and the noble birth of its author, has a double claim to the patronage of nobility. To whom, therefore, can it so properly apply for protection as to a nobleman like your Grace, who deservedly stands at the head of the Peerage, and who can look back upon a long series of ancestors whose renown is unrivalled in the annals of English history.

It is a remarkable circumstance, my Lord, that the writings of Plato were first translated into Latin by Ficino <note>original: "Ficinus"; refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian scholar who led the revival of Neoplatonism in the Renaissance.</note>, under the auspices of the illustrious Cosimo de' Medici <note>original: "Cosmo de Medici"; the de facto ruler of Florence and a massive patron of the arts and learning.</note>, and his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent, and that the first complete translation of them into English is under the patronage of your Grace. But however great the merit may be of the support which was

# DEDICATION.

given by the Medici to the first translation of Plato’s Works into Latin, it certainly is not equal to that of your Grace in the aid which you have afforded to the following translation of them into English. For your Grace’s patronage commenced at that period of the last very calamitous war <note>Taylor refers here to the French Revolutionary Wars (1792–1802), which had caused great economic strain and social unrest in England just prior to this publication.</note>, which was of all others the most unfavourable to the encouragement of literature, and continued to the present eventful period; while that of the Medici began and ended in peace. The patronage likewise of the Medici was more confined than that of your Grace: for, by giving Plato to the public in a Roman garb <note>A metaphor for the Latin language.</note>, unattended with his Greek interpreters in the same garb <note>Taylor is critiquing earlier Renaissance translations for providing only Plato’s words without the specialized commentaries of the later Neoplatonic philosophers, which Taylor considered essential for understanding.</note>, they may be said to have acted like one who gives an invaluable casket, but without the only key by which it can be unlocked. This key, my Lord, in consequence of the handsome manner in which you have enabled me to publish my translation, I have presented to the English Reader; and in this respect also the support of your Grace is more noble, because more ample than that of Cosmo and Lorenzo. <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464) and his grandson Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492) were the primary patrons of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>

Whatever, therefore, my Lord, may be the merit, whatever may be the fate of my labours in this arduous work, the aid which your Grace has afforded to the publication of those labours will be applauded as it deserves by every man of intrinsic worth of the present day, and will be admired and celebrated by the latest posterity. # GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

“**PHILOSOPHY**\*,” says Hierocles ¹, “is the purification and perfection of human life. It is the purification, indeed, from material irrationality, and the mortal body; but the perfection, in consequence of being the resumption of our proper felicity <note>happiness or blessedness</note>, and a re-ascent to the divine likeness. To effect these two is the province of *Virtue* and *Truth*; the former exterminating the immoderation of the passions; and the latter introducing the divine form to those who are naturally adapted to its reception.”

Of philosophy thus defined, which may be compared to a luminous pyramid, terminating in Deity, and having for its basis the rational soul of man and its spontaneous unperverted conceptions,—of this philosophy, august, magnificent, and divine, *Plato* may be justly called the primary leader and <term>hierophant</term> <note>a priest who interprets sacred mysteries or esoteric principles</note>, through whom, like the mystic light in the inmost recesses of some sacred temple, it first shone forth with occult <note>hidden or secret</note> and venerable splendor ². It may indeed be truly said of the whole of this philosophy, that it is the greatest good which man can participate: for if it purifies us from the defilements of the passions and assimilates <note>makes us like</note> us to Divinity, it confers on us the proper felicity of our nature. Hence it is easy to collect

To evince <note>to prove or demonstrate clearly</note> that the philosophy of Plato possesses this preeminence; that its dignity and sublimity are unrivalled; that it is the parent of all that ennobles man; and that it is founded on principles, which neither time can obliterate, nor sophistry subvert, is the principal design of this Introduction.

To effect this design, I shall in the first place present the reader with the outlines of the principal dogmas <note>here meaning "established doctrines" or core principles of a school of thought</note> of Plato’s philosophy. The undertaking is indeed no less novel than arduous, since the author of it has to tread in paths which have been untrodden for upwards of a thousand years, and to bring to light truths which for that extended period have been concealed in Greek. # GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

Let us also, imploring the assistance of the same illuminating power <note>Likely referring to the Divine Intellect or the "Sun" of the mental world, which Plato uses as a metaphor for the source of truth</note>, begin the solitary journey.

Of all the dogmas <note>established doctrines or core principles</note> of Plato, that concerning the first principle <note>the ultimate source or origin from which all reality flows</note> of things as far transcends in sublimity the doctrine of other philosophers of a different sect, on this subject, as this supreme cause of all transcends other causes. For, according to Plato, the highest God, whom in the *Republic* he calls *the good*, and in the *Parmenides* *the one*, is not only above soul and intellect, but is even superior to being itself. Hence, since every thing which can in any respect be known, or of which any thing can be asserted, must be connected with the universality of things, but the first cause is above all things, it is very properly said by Plato to be perfectly ineffable <note>too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note>. The first hypothesis therefore of his *Parmenides*, in which all things are denied of this immense principle, concludes as follows: 

> " *The one therefore is in no respect.* So it seems. Hence it is not in such a manner as *to be* one, for thus it would be *being*, and participate of essence: but as it appears, *the one neither is one, nor is*, if it be proper to believe in reasoning of this kind. It appears so. But can any thing either belong to, or be affirmed of that which is not? How can it? Neither therefore does any name belong to it, nor discourse, nor any science, nor sense, nor opinion. It does not appear that there can. Hence it can neither be *named*, nor *spoken of*, nor *conceived by opinion*, nor *be known*, nor *perceived* by any being. So it seems."

And here it must be observed that this conclusion respecting the highest principle of things, that he is perfectly ineffable and inconceivable, is the result of a most scientific series of negations <note>a method of defining something by stating what it is NOT, often called "negative theology"</note>, in which not only all sensible and intellectual beings are denied of him, but even natures the most transcendently allied to him, his first and most divine progeny <note>the first levels of existence that emerge directly from the ultimate source</note>. For that which so eminently distinguishes the philosophy of Plato from others is this, that every part of it is stamped

In short, an unscientific perception of the ineffable nature of the Divinity resembles that of a man, who, on surveying the heavens, should assert of the altitude of its highest part, that it surpasses that of the loftiest tree, and is therefore immeasurable. But to see this scientifically, is like a survey of this highest part of the heavens by the astronomer: for he, by knowing the height of the media <note>the intermediate spaces or substances, such as the air and orbits</note> between us and it, knows also scientifically that it transcends in altitude not only the loftiest tree, but the summits of air and æther <note>the pure, upper atmosphere or the substance of the stars</note>, the moon, and even the sun itself.

# GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

naturally prior to the <term>indigent <note>literally "needy"; in this philosophical context, it refers to anything that lacks self-sufficiency and depends on something else for its existence or completion</note></term>. For that which is in want of another is naturally adapted from necessity to be subservient to that of which it is indigent. But if they are mutually in want of each other, each being indigent of the other in a different respect, neither of them will be the <term>principle <note>the first cause, ultimate source, or "starting point" of all things</note></term>. For the unindigent is most adapted to that which is truly the principle. And if it is in want of any thing, according to this it will not be the principle. It is however necessary that the principle should be this very thing, the principle alone. The unindigent therefore pertains to this, nor must it by any means be acknowledged that there is any thing prior to it. This, however, would be acknowledged, if it had any connection with the indigent.

Let us then consider body, (that is, a <term>triply extended substance <note>a physical object defined by the three dimensions of length, breadth, and depth</note></term>,) endued with quality; for this is the first thing <term>effable <note>capable of being described in words</note></term> by us, and is <term>sensible <note>perceptible by the senses, rather than just the mind</note></term>. Is this then the principle of things? But it is two things, body, and quality which is in body as a subject. Which of these therefore is by nature prior? For both are indigent of their proper parts: and that also which is in a subject is indigent of the subject. Shall we say then that body itself is the principle and the first <term>essence <note>the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note></term>? But this is impossible. For, in the first place, the principle will not receive any thing from that which is posterior to itself. But body, we say, is the recipient of quality. Hence quality, and a subsistence in conjunction with it, are not derived from body, since quality is present with body as something different. And, in the second place, body is every way divisible; its several parts are indigent of each other, and the whole is indigent of all the parts. As it is indigent, therefore, and receives its completion from things which are indigent, it will not be entirely unindigent.

Further still, if it is not one but united, it will require, as Plato says, the connecting one. It is likewise something common and formless,

<note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page regarding how the soul interacts with matter.</note> ...mental energies (that is, energies belonging to the soul) are put into action while mixed with physical bodies. They are not purely mental, but are also physical; for perception belongs to the "living body," or to a soul that has taken on a physical form, although in such perception the mental <term>idiom <note>a unique characteristic or specific nature</note></term> is more dominant than the physical. A thing of this kind cannot be the **principle** (the first cause).

Before we reach this level of existence, however, we see a certain form that is separate from any physical subject and is <term>converted to itself <note>the ability of a consciousness to reflect upon its own nature and existence, turning its gaze inward rather than outward</note></term>; this is what we call **rational nature**. Our soul, therefore, governs its own actions and is able to correct its own mistakes. This would not be possible unless it could turn its attention inward; and it could not turn inward unless it had an essence independent of the body. Thus, it is not dependent on things lower than itself. 

Shall we then claim that the rational soul is the most perfect **principle**? No, because it does not use all its powers and energies at once, but is always lacking the greater part of them. The ultimate **principle**, however, must have no needs at all. But rational nature is a form of existence that is "needy" of its own potential actions. Someone might argue that the soul is an eternal essence with never-failing essential powers, always moving itself and always alive, and is therefore self-sufficient and should be the **principle**. To this we answer that the whole soul is a single nature that is partly self-sufficient and partly needy; but the true **principle** must be perfectly self-sufficient. 

The soul, which performs changing or "mutable" actions, cannot be the most proper **principle**. It is necessary that there be something higher than the soul, which is unchanging in every way—in its nature, its life, and its knowledge—and in all its powers and actions. This is what we call an eternal and unchanging essence: the highly honored **Intellect**. <note>In this philosophical tradition, 'Intellect' (often translating the Greek *Nous*) refers to a divine, universal Mind that perceives all truths perfectly and simultaneously.</note> Aristotle, having reached this height in his reasoning, believed he had <meta>catchword: discovered</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the hierarchy of existence. Having previously discussed the "self-moving" soul and "other-moved" matter, the text now ascends to the "immovable" cause: the Intellect.</meta>

# GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

It would be illogical for there to be things that are only moved (such as a physical body) without there also being something that moves other things without being moved itself. It is clear that such a "mover only" must exist, as it represents a more excellent nature. Even a <term>self-moved <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the Soul, which initiates its own activity but still experiences change or "motion" in its thoughts.</note></term> entity is more excellent in its role as a "mover" than in its role as something "moved." Therefore, the <term>essence <note>The fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note></term> that moves while remaining <term>unmoved <note>Often called the "Prime Mover" or "Intellect"; a cause that initiates action without changing or losing any of its own power.</term> must be the first in rank. 

Just as that which is moved without being a cause of motion is the third (lowest) rank, the self-moved sits in the middle. We say that the self-moved requires the unmoved mover in order to begin its own motion. In short, if something is in motion, it does not remain stable in that state of motion; and if it moves something else, it must remain a "mover" to do so. Where, then, does it get the power to remain stable? From its own nature, it derives either the power to be moved only, or the power to be both stable and moved at the same time. Where does it get the pure power of stability? It must come from that which is purely stable—the <term>immovable cause</term>.

We must therefore admit that the immovable is prior to the self-moved. But is this immovable cause the absolute first principle? How could it be? The immovable contains a vast "multitude" of forms in a stable way, just as the self-moved contains a multitude in a moving way. Furthermore, a state of "immovable separation" must exist before a "self-moving separation" can occur. This unmoved nature is simultaneously "one" and "many"—it is both united and distinct at once. This kind of nature is called <term>Intellect <note>The Greek "Nous"; the level of reality consisting of pure, eternal thoughts or "Forms" that exist before the physical world.</note></term>. 

It is evident that the "united" aspect of this Intellect is naturally higher and more honorable than its "separated" aspect. Separation always depends on union, but union does not depend on separation. However, the Intellect does not possess union entirely free from its opposite (separation). For every intellectual form is <term>coessentialized <note>original: "eocssentialized" (printer's error). This means the forms are woven together into the very same substance or essence.</note></term> with separation throughout its whole being. ...requires that which is simply united. Anything that exists alongside another thing is <term>indigent <note>Dependent upon or lacking something in itself.</note></term> of that which exists purely by itself; and that which exists by <term>participation <note>Sharing in a quality or property that belongs primarily to another higher source.</note></term> depends on that which exists by its own <term>essence <note>Its fundamental nature; being the thing itself rather than just having a piece of it.</note></term>. For the <term>Intellect <note>In Neoplatonic thought, this is the divine Mind, the realm of pure thought and perfect forms.</note></term>, being self-caused <note>original: "self-subsistent"</note>, produces itself as both a unified whole and as something divided into parts. Therefore, it exists according to both these states. 

It is produced, then, from that which is purely and solely united. Prior to anything that has a specific "form" is that which is uncircumscribed and not yet distributed into different shapes. This is what we call "the united," and what the wise men of antiquity called *being*. It possesses the "multitude" of all things in a single, condensed point <note>original: "contraction"</note>, existing before the many separate things emerge.

Having arrived thus far, let us pause for a while and consider whether *being* is the ultimate principle of all things that we are searching for. For what is there that does not share in *being*? Yet, we might ask: if *being* is "the united," is it not secondary to **the One**? Does it not become "the united" only by participating in **the One**? 

In short, if we imagine **the One** to be something different from *being*, and if *being* were prior to **the One**, then *being* would not share in oneness. It would, therefore, be only "many"—and these would be an infinite series of infinities. But if **the One** exists alongside *being*, and they are either equal in rank or divided from each other, there will be two ultimate principles, which leads to the logical absurdity we mentioned before. 

Alternatively, they might share in each other as two basic elements. Or perhaps they are both parts of a larger whole. If that is the case, what is the power that leads them to join with each other? For if **the One** unites *being* to itself, then **the One** must act <note>original: "energize"</note> before *being* exists, so that it may call forth and turn *being* toward itself. Therefore, **the One** must exist by itself, perfect in its own right, prior to *being*. Furthermore, that which is more simple is always prior to that which is more complex. If, therefore, they are both equally simple, there will either be two...

Hence this is the principle of all things, and Plato recurring to this, did not require any other principle in his reasonings. For the arcane in which this our ascent terminates is not the principle of reasoning, nor of knowledge, nor of animals, nor of beings, nor of unities, but simply of all things, being arranged above every conception and suspicion that we can frame. 

Hence Plato indicates nothing concerning it, but makes his negations of all other things except **the one**, from **the one**. For that **the one** is he denies in the last place, but he does not make a negation of **the one**. He also, besides this, even denies this negation, but not **the one**. He denies, too, name and conception, and all knowledge, and what can be said more, whole itself and every being. <page-num>xxiii</page-num>

->GENERAL INTRODUCTION.<-

[Ad]mitted to be one, so far it will be coarranged with other things which are the subject of <term>position <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "position" refers to the specific rank or order an entity holds within the hierarchy of existence.</note></term>. For it is the summit of things which <term>subsist <note>To exist in a fundamental, primary, or underlying way.</note></term> according to position. At the same time there is much in it of the ineffable and unknown, the uncoordinated, and that which is deprived of position, but these are accompanied with a representation of the contraries: and the former are more excellent than the latter. But every where things pure subsist prior to their contraries, and such as are unmingled to the comingled. For either things more excellent subsist in the *one* essentially, and in a certain respect the contraries of these also will be there at the same time; or they subsist according to participation, and are derived from that which is first a thing of this kind. Prior to the *one*, therefore, is that which is simply and perfectly ineffable, without position, uncoordinated, and incapable of being apprehended, to which also the ascent of the present discourse hastens through the clearest indications, omitting none of those natures between the first and the last of things.

Such then is the ascent to the highest God according to the theology of Plato, venerably preserving his ineffable exemption from all things, and his transcendency, which cannot be circumscribed by any <term>gnostic energy <note>The power of knowing or intellectual activity; the capacity of the mind to perceive spiritual truths.</note></term>; and at the same time unfolding the paths which lead upwards to him, and enkindling that luminous summit of the soul, by which she is conjoined with the incomprehensible one.

From this truly ineffable principle, exempt from all essence, power, and energy, a multitude of divine natures, according to Plato, immediately proceeds. That this must necessarily be the case will be admitted by the reader who understands what has been already discussed, and is fully demonstrated by Plato in the *Parmenides* <note>One of Plato's most challenging dialogues, which Neoplatonists interpreted as a systematic map of the divine hierarchy.</note>, as will be evident to the intelligent from the notes on that Dialogue. <meta>This page continues the exploration of the highest principles of reality. <page-num>xxiv</page-num>

->GENERAL INTRODUCTION.<-

This doctrine, which is founded in the sublimest and most scientific conceptions of the human mind, may be clearly shown to be a legitimate dogma of Plato from what is asserted by him in the sixth book of his *Republic*. For he there affirms, in the most clear and unequivocal terms, that ***the good***, or the ineffable principle of things, is <term>superessential <note>Literally "above being." In this philosophy, the highest principle is so pure that it cannot be limited by the definition of "being" or "existence."</note></term>, and shows by the analogy of the sun to ***the good***, that what light and sight are in the visible, that ***truth*** and ***intelligence*** are in the intelligible world. As light therefore immediately proceeds from the sun, and wholly <term>subsists <note>To have a fundamental or primary existence.</note></term> according to a solar <term>idiom <note>A specific property or unique characteristic belonging to a particular nature.</note></term> or property, so ***truth***, or the immediate progeny of ***the good***, must subsist according to a superessential idiom. And as ***the good***, according to Plato, is the same with ***the one***, as is evident from the *Parmenides*, the immediate progeny of ***the one*** will be the same as that of ***the good***. But the immediate offspring of ***the one*** cannot be any thing else than <term>unities <note>Also called "henads" in Neoplatonism; these are the first, divine differentiations that proceed from the One before the creation of the intellect or the physical world.</note></term>. And hence we necessarily infer that, according to Plato, the immediate offspring of the ineffable principle of things are superessential unities. They differ however from their immense principle in this, that he is superessential and ineffable, without any addition; but this divine multitude is participated by the several orders of being, which are suspended from and produced by it. Hence, in consequence of being connected with ***multitude*** through this participation, they are necessarily subordinate to ***the one***.

No less admirably, therefore, than Platonically, does <term>Simplicius <note>A 6th-century philosopher and one of the last great pagan Neoplatonists who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle and Epictetus.</note></term>, in his *Commentary on Epictetus*¹, observe on this subject as follows:

Therefore, individual principles are established within that principle which acts as a whole, and they are contained within it—not as a divided multitude, but as parts within a whole, as a multitude within the one, and as number within the <term>monad <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, a monad is the primary 'unit' or 'oneness' that stands at the head of a specific series of things (like the 'monad of beauty' for all beautiful things).</note></term>. For this first principle is all things before all things exist; many principles are multiplied around the one principle, and within the one goodness, many goodnesses are established. This, too, is not just a specific principle like the others: for among those, one is the principle of beauty, another of symmetry, another of truth, and another of something else; but this is simply *principle* itself. Nor is it simply the principle of beings, but it is the principle of principles. For it is necessary that the nature of "principle," like all other things, should not begin from a multitude, but should be gathered into a single monad as a peak, which is the principle of all principles.

Those things which are first produced by the first good, because they are <term>connascent <note>Literally "born with"; things that are naturally united with their source from the moment of their origin.</note></term> with it, do not fall away from essential goodness. Because they are unchanging and immovable, they are eternally established in that same blessed state. They do not lack "the good," because they are goodnesses themselves. However, all other natures produced by the one good and the many goodnesses fall away from that essential goodness; they are not unchangeably fixed in the <term>hyparxis <note>A technical term referring to the "essential existence" or the very "summit" of a thing's being.</note></term> of divine goodness. For this reason, they possess the good only through <term>participation <note>The concept that lower things do not possess a quality (like goodness or beauty) inherently, but rather "participate" in or receive a reflection of that quality from a higher source.</note></term>.”

<page-num>xxviii</page-num>

# GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

-><meta>catchword: For</meta><-

fundamental existence, and were made divine by light flowing from *the one*. They likewise said that there is a multitude of <term>superessential unities <note>Divine powers or "gods" that exist above the level of "being" or essence, acting as the most direct expressions of the ultimate Source.</note></term>, who are not independent existences, but are unions with the deity that are granted to all existing things by the highest God. However, this theory is not consistent with the doctrine of Plato, as seen in his *Parmenides*, where he shows that *the one* does not exist within itself. (See volume 3, page 133). For as we have observed from <term>Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note></term>, in the notes on that Dialogue, everything which is the cause of itself and is <term>self-subsistent <note>Something that contains the reason for its own existence within itself, rather than depending on an external creator.</note></term> is said to be "in itself." Since a producing power always contains the essence of what it produces, it is necessary that whatever produces itself should contain itself as a cause, and be contained by itself as a result; it must be at once both the cause and the effect, the container and the thing contained. If, therefore, "existing in another" means—according to Plato—being produced by a higher and more excellent cause, then "existing in itself" must mean being self-begotten and produced by oneself. If *the one* is not self-subsistent (because it actually transcends even this mode of existence), and if it is necessary that *something* in the universe must be self-subsistent, it follows that this must be the defining characteristic of whatever comes immediately after the <term>ineffable <note>The "Ineffable" is the ultimate, nameless source of all reality that is beyond all human language and thought.</note></term> source. It is clear that something must be self-subsistent; otherwise, nothing would ever possess true self-sufficiency.

Besides, as <term>Damascius <note>The last head of the Platonic Academy in Athens (c. 458–538 AD), known for his work on first principles.</note></term> well observes, if something lower in the natural order is "self-perfecting" (such as the human soul), it is much more likely that a divine soul would be so. And if this is true of the soul, it must also be true of the higher <term>intellect <note>In this context, "Intellect" refers to the divine Mind or the realm of pure thought.</note></term>. If it is true of the intellect, it will also be true of the principle of life; if of life, then of being itself; and if of being, it must also be true of the unities that exist above being.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of self-subsistence, moving from the philosophical definition of "existing in oneself" to how this applies to the hierarchy of reality—from the ultimate Source (the One) down to the human soul and physical bodies.</meta>

<page-num>xxix</page-num>

->GENERAL INTRODUCTION.<-

For the quality of being self-perfect, self-sufficient, and established within oneself, exists much more in higher beings than in lower ones. If these qualities exist in the latter, they must also exist in the former—namely, the state of a thing existing by itself and having its being rooted in itself. Such things include <term>essence <note>The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note></term> and life, intellect, soul, and body. For even the body, though it does not originate from itself, still exists by itself; because of this, it belongs to the category of <term>substance <note>In philosophy, a "substance" is something that can exist on its own, whereas an "accident" is a quality (like "red" or "tall") that can only exist if it belongs to a substance.</note></term>, and is distinguished from an "accident," which cannot exist without a subject to hold it.

<margin>¹ See volume 3, page 500. See also an extensive account of the nature of <term>daemons <note>In Neoplatonism, daemons are intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans; they are not "demons" in the modern sense.</note></term> in the note at the beginning of the *First Alcibiades*, volume 1.</margin>

Therefore, those <term>superessential <note>Existing beyond or above the level of "being" or "essence."</note></term> beings that are self-subsistent are the immediate offspring of ***the one***—if it is even permitted to name them such. It would be more accurate to call them "indescribable revelations" shining out from the Indescribable; for the word "offspring" implies a cause that produces them, and ***the one*** must be understood as something even more excellent than a cause. From this divine group of self-perfect and self-producing powers, a series of self-perfect beings—namely, existences, lives, intellects, and souls—proceeds. According to Plato, the human soul occupies the last link in this shining chain. The soul is directly suspended from the order of daemons; for this order, as he clearly states in the ***Banquet***¹ <note>Also known as the *Symposium*.</note>, “stands in the middle rank between the divine and human, fills up the vacant space, and links together all intelligent nature.” 

And here, the reader who has not explored the depths of Plato’s philosophy will undoubtedly find it extremely paradoxical that any being could be said to produce itself and yet, at the same time, originate from a higher cause. The solution to this difficulty is as follows: “Essential production”—or the energy through which a being produces something else simply by the fact of its existence—is the most perfect way of creating. We see traces of this even in the lowest of things; for example, fire provides heat simply by being fire, and snow provides coldness simply by being snow.

And in short, this is a producing of that kind, in which the effect is that secondarily which the cause is primarily. As this mode of production therefore, from its being the most perfect of all others, originates from the highest natures, it will consequently first belong to those <term>self-subsistent <note>Refers to entities that have the principle of their own existence within themselves, rather than being mere reflections or effects of something else.</note></term> powers, who immediately proceed from the <term>ineffable <note>The "Ineffable" is the ultimate, indescribable source of all reality, often called "The One."</note></term>, and will from them be derived to all the following orders of beings. Hence, from that which subsists at the summit of self-subsistent natures, a series of self-subsisting beings will indeed proceed, but then this series will be secondarily that which its cause is primarily, and the energy by which it produces itself will be secondary to that by which it is produced by its cause. Thus, for instance, the <term>rational soul <note>In this system, the "rational soul" is the human capacity for reason, which sits between the eternal divine mind and the temporary physical world.</note></term> both produces itself (in consequence of being a <term>self-motive <note>The ability to initiate motion or change from within, rather than being pushed by an external force.</note></term> nature), and is produced by <term>intellect <note>Original: "Nous." In Neoplatonism, this is the Divine Mind or the realm of pure thought that exists above the soul.</note></term>; but it is produced by intellect *immutably*, and by itself *transitively*; for all its energies subsist in time, and are accompanied with motion. So far therefore as soul contains intellect by participation, so far it is produced by intellect, but so far as it is self-motive it is produced by itself. In short, with respect to every thing self-subsistent, the summit of its nature is produced by a superior cause, but the evolution of that summit is its own <term>spontaneous energy <note>The natural, unforced unfolding of a being's own potential.</note></term>; and through this it becomes self-subsistent and self-perfect.

In Greek philosophy, "well being" is not just happiness, but the state of living according to one's highest virtue and purpose.</note> confessedly ranks higher and is more excellent than *mere being*. Highly laudable indeed, and worthy the imitation of all posterity, is the veneration which the great ancients paid to this immense principle. This I have already noticed in the Introduction to the *Parmenides*; and I shall only observe at present in addition, that in consequence of this profound and most pious reverence of the first God, they did not even venture to give a name to the summit of that highest order of divinities which is denominated <term>intelligible <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the highest realm of reality, consisting of pure forms and truths that can only be grasped by the intellect, not the senses.</note></term>. Hence, says Proclus, in his manuscript <term>Scholia <note>Explanatory comments or annotations written in the margins of ancient manuscripts.</note></term> on the *Cratylus*, “Not every genus of the gods has an appellation: for with respect to the first Deity, who is beyond all things, *Parmenides* teaches us that he is <term>ineffable <note>Too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.</note></term>; and the first genera of the intelligible gods, who are united to *the one*, and are called <term>occult <note>Hidden, secret, or concealed from view; referring to divine principles that are not immediately apparent.</note></term>, have much of the unknown and ineffable. For that which is perfectly effable cannot be conjoined with the perfectly ineffable; but it is necessary that the progression of intelligibles should terminate in this order, in which the first effable subsists, and that which is called by proper names. For there the first intelligible forms, and the intellectual nature of intelligibles, are unfolded into light. But the natures prior to this being silent and occult, are only known by intelligence. Hence the whole of the <term>telestic science <note>The sacred art of religious initiation and mystical rituals intended to purify the soul.</note></term> energizing <term>theurgically <note>From 'theurgy,' meaning 'god-work.' A practice of rituals meant to invoke the presence of the gods or achieve union with the divine.</note></term> ascends as far as to this order. Orpheus also says, that this is first called by a name by the other gods; for the light proceeding from it is known to and denominated by the intellectual gods.”

With no less magnificence therefore than piety, does Proclus thus speak concerning the ineffable principle of things. “Let¹ us now if ever, <note>The Greek footnote is a fragment from Proclus's *Platonic Theology* (Book II, ch. 11): Ἄγε δὴ οὖν, εἴπερ ποτέ, καὶ νῦν τὰς πολυειδεῖς ἀποσκευασώμεθα γνώσεις... Finally, from all that has been established, I believe it must be immediately obvious to everyone whose mental eye is not entirely blinded that there can be no such thing as a "trinity" in the theology of Plato that is in any respect similar to the Christian Trinity. <note>The translator, Thomas Taylor, was a staunch advocate for ancient Greek polytheism and frequently argued that Christian doctrines were misunderstood borrowings from Platonic philosophy.</note> For the highest God, according to Plato—as we have shown at length using irresistible evidence—is so far from being a part of a <term>consubsistent triad <note>A group of three divine entities that exist together as one substance or essence.</note></term> that he cannot be categorized or counted alongside anything else. He is so perfectly free from all multiplicity that he is even beyond the concept of "being" itself; he so unspeakably transcends all relation and condition that language is actually defeated when speaking of him, and knowledge is turned back into a state of sacred ignorance. <note>This refers to the "Way of Negation," the idea that the supreme principle is so high that we can only say what it is NOT, rather than what it IS.</note> What that "trinity" actually is in the theology of Plato—which undoubtedly gave birth to the Christian version—will be clear to the intelligent reader from the notes on the *Parmenides* and the extracts from *Damascius*¹. <note>Damascius (c. 458–538 AD) was the last head of the Platonic Academy in Athens.</note> This concludes our discussion of Plato's doctrine concerning the first principle of things and its immediate offspring; the great importance of this subject will, I trust, be a sufficient apology for the length of this argument.

In the next place, using *Proclus* and *Olympiodorus* as our guides, <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato's works centuries after his death.</note> let us consider the method by which Plato teaches us mystical concepts of the divine natures. He does not appear to have used the same mode of teaching everywhere; sometimes he reveals the truth through a divinely inspired energy, and at other times he unfolds it <term>dialectically <note>Using logical discussion and the investigation of opposing ideas to reach a higher truth.</note></term>. Sometimes he announces the unspeakable characteristics of the gods through symbols, but at other times he reasons toward them from physical images, discovering the primary causes of the universe within them. For in the *Phaedrus*, being clearly inspired and having exchanged human intelligence for a better possession—<term>divine mania <note>From the Greek "mania," meaning a state of divine inspiration or "madness" where the soul is lifted beyond ordinary human reason.</note></term>—he reveals many secret doctrines concerning the *intellectual*, *liberated*, and *mundane gods*. <note>In the Neoplatonic hierarchy: Intellectual gods are associated with pure thought; Liberated gods exist between the higher realms and the physical world; Mundane gods are those associated with the physical cosmos and planets.</note>

But in *The Sophist* <note>original: "Sophista"</note>, while dialectically debating the nature of being and how **the One** exists above all beings, and while questioning the philosophers older than himself, Plato shows how all beings are suspended from their cause and the first being. He demonstrates that "being" itself participates in that unity which is set apart from all things; therefore, being is <term>passive <note>original: "passive". According to Plato, whatever participates in or receives a quality from something higher is said to be "passive" to it. These acts of participation are called "passions" or "undergoings."</note></term> to that unity, but is not **the One itself**. It is subject to and united to the One, but is not that which is primarily One.

In a similar way, in the *Parmenides*, he unfolds through logic the ways in which being "procedes" or flows from **the One**. He does this through the first "hypothesis" <note>In the *Parmenides*, a hypothesis is a logical starting point used to explore the consequences of a theory—in this case, "If the One is..."</note> of that dialogue, following the most perfect division of this logical method. 

Again, in the *Gorgias*, he tells the myth concerning the <term>three fabricators <note>These are traditionally the three judges of the dead—Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus—but Neoplatonists interpreted them as divine "craftsmen" who shape the destiny of souls.</note></term> and their creative assignments. But in *The Symposium* <note>original: "The Banquet"</note>, he speaks about the union of love; and in the *Protagoras*, he discusses how the gods distributed life to mortal animals. In these works, he uses symbols to conceal the truth about divine natures, only hinting at his meaning for his most sincere readers.

Again, if we must mention the teachings delivered through mathematics, or the discussion of divine matters using ethical or physical language—many examples of which can be found in the *Timaeus* and the dialogue called the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politicus"</note>, as well as scattered throughout other dialogues—the method will be clear to those who wish to understand divine things through images. Thus, for example:
*   The *Statesman* provides a "shadow-image" of how the heavens were crafted. 
*   The shapes of the five elements, described using geometry in the *Timaeus*, act as images representing the <term>idioms <note>Specific characteristics or unique properties.</note></term> of the gods who preside over the different parts of the universe.

Again, since Plato employs fables <note>In this context, "fables" refers to myths, allegories, and symbolic stories used to convey philosophical truths.</note>, let us in the first place consider why the ancients were induced to devise fables, and in the second place, what the difference is between the fables of philosophers and those of poets. In answer to the first question then, it is necessary to know, that the ancients employed fables, looking to two things, namely: nature, and our soul. They employed them by looking to nature, and the fabrication of things, as follows. Things unapparent are believed from things apparent, and <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Natures that do not have a physical body or material form.</note> natures from bodies. For seeing the orderly arrangement of bodies, we understand that a certain incorporeal power presides over them; as with respect to the celestial bodies, they have a certain presiding motive power. As we therefore see that our body is moved, but is no longer so after death, we conceive that it was a certain incorporeal power which moved it. Hence, perceiving that we believe things incorporeal and unapparent from things apparent and corporeal, fables came to be adopted, that we might come from things apparent to certain unapparent natures; as, for instance, that on hearing the adulteries, bonds, and lacerations of the gods, castrations of heaven, and the like <note>These shocking mythological events were often criticized by literal-minded readers; the Neoplatonists argued they were intended to be so strange that they forced the reader to look for a deeper, symbolic meaning.</note>, we may not rest satisfied with the apparent meaning of such like particulars, but may proceed to the unapparent, and investigate the true signification. After this manner, therefore, looking to the nature of things, were fables employed.

But from looking to our souls, they originated as follows: While we are children we live according to the <term>phantasy</term> <note>From the Greek *phantasia*; the faculty of the soul that deals with mental images and imagination.</note>; but the phantastic part is conversant with figures, and types, and things of this kind. That the phantastic part in us therefore may be preserved, we employ fables, in consequence of this part rejoicing in fables. It may also be said, that a fable is nothing else than a false discourse shadowing forth the truth:

In the next place let us consider what the difference is between the fables of philosophers<gloss>¹ The following excellent account of the different species of fables is given by the philosopher **Sallust** <note>Sallustius was a 4th-century Neoplatonist and a friend of the Emperor Julian; his work "On the Gods and the World" is a primer of Greek theology.</note>, in his book on the Gods and the World, **chapter 4.**

"Of fables, some are **theological**, others **physical**, others **psychical** (or belonging to soul), others **material**, and lastly, others are **mixed** from these. Fables are **theological** which employ nothing corporeal, but speculate the very essences of the gods; such as the fable which asserts that Saturn <note>original: "Saturnus" (Latin). In Greek mythology, this is Cronos.</note> devoured his children: for it obscurely intimates the nature of an intellectual god, since every intellect returns into itself. 

But we speculate fables **physically**, when we speak concerning the energies of the gods about the world; as when considering Saturn the same as **Time** and calling the parts of time the children of the universe, we assert that the children are devoured by their parents. 

And we employ fables in a **psychical** mode, when we contemplate the energies of soul; because the intellections of our souls, though by a discursive energy they proceed into other things, yet abide in their parents. 

Lastly, fables are **material**, such as the Egyptians ignorantly employ, considering and calling corporeal natures divinities; such as Isis, earth; Osiris, humidity; Typhon, heat: or again, denominating Saturn, water; Adonis, fruits; and Bacchus, wine. And indeed to assert that these are dedicated to the gods, in the same manner as herbs, stones, and animals, is the part of wise men; but to call them gods is alone the province of madmen; unless we speak in the same manner, as when, from established custom, we call the orb of the sun and its rays the sun itself.

"But we may perceive the **mixed** kind of fables, as well as in many other particulars, as in the fable which relates, that Discord at a banquet of the gods threw a golden apple, and that a dispute about it arising from the goddesses, they were sent by Jupiter to take the judgment of Paris, who, charmed with the beauty of Venus, gave her the apple in preference to the rest. For in this fable, the banquet denotes the supermundane <note>Existing beyond or above the physical world.</note> powers of the gods; and on this account they subsist in conjunction with each other: but the golden apple denotes the world, which on account of its composition from contrary natures, is not improperly said to be thrown by Discord,</gloss> and poets. For who, endued with intellect, would believe that Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter" (Latin). The Greek god Zeus.</note> was desirous of having connection with Juno <note>original: "Juno" (Latin). The Greek goddess Hera. This refers to a specific scene in Homer’s Iliad where the gods consort on the ground.</note>, and on the ground, without waiting to go into the bed-chamber. So that the <term>poetic fable</term> abounds, in consequence of asserting such things as do not suffer us to stop at the apparent, but lead us to explore the **occult truth**. But it is defective in this, that it deceives those of a juvenile age. Plato therefore neglects fable of this kind, and banishes Homer from his Republic; because youth, on hearing such fables, will not be able to distinguish what is allegorical from what is not.

Philosophical fables, on the contrary, do not injure those that go no further than the apparent meaning. Thus, for instance, they assert that there are punishments and rivers under the earth: and if we adhere to the literal meaning of these we shall not be injured. But they are deficient in this, that as their apparent signification does not injure, we often content ourselves with this, and do not explore the **latent truth**. We may also say that philosophic fables look to the energies of the soul. For if we were entirely intellect alone, and had no connection with <term>phantasy</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "phantasy" refers to the faculty of imagination that processes sensory images.</note>, we should not require fables, in consequence of always associating with intellectual natures. If, again, we were entirely irrational...

The Greek goddess Aphrodite.</note>. But of these species of fables, such as are theological, belong to philosophers; the physical and psychical to poets; and the mixed to the mysteries*; since the intention of all mystic ceremonies is to conjoin us with the world and the gods.”

...and lived according to the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The faculty of imagination or mental imagery.</note>, and had no other energy than this, it would be requisite that the whole of our life should be fabulous. Since, however, we possess <term>intellect</term> <note>Pure reason or the highest intuitive mind.</note>, <term>opinion</term> <note>Beliefs or judgments about the world.</note>, and <term>phantasy</term>, demonstrations are given with a view to intellect: and hence Plato says, that if you are willing to energize according to intellect, you will have demonstrations bound with adamantine chains; if according to opinion, you will have the testimony of renowned persons; and if according to the phantasy, you have fables by which it is excited; so that from all these you will derive advantage.

Plato therefore rejects the more tragical mode of mythologizing of the ancient poets, who thought proper to establish an <term>arcane theology</term> <note>Secret or hidden teachings intended only for the initiated.</note> respecting the gods, and on this account devised wanderings, castrations, battles, and <term>lacrations</term> <note>original: "lacrations" (likely a typo for "lacerations"), referring to myths where gods are torn apart, such as Dionysus.</note> of the gods, and many other such symbols of the truth about divine natures which this theology conceals;—this mode he rejects, and asserts that it is in every respect most foreign from <term>erudition</term> <note>Formal education and the cultivation of the mind.</note>. But he considers those mythological discourses about the gods, as more persuasive and more adapted to truth, which assert that a divine nature is the cause of all good, but of no evil, and that it is void of all mutation, comprehending in itself the fountain of truth, but never becoming the cause of any deception to others. For such types of theology Socrates delivers in the *Republic*.

All the fables therefore of Plato guarding the truth in concealment, have not even their externally-apparent apparatus discordant with our undisciplined and unperverted anticipations of divinity. But they bring with them an image of the <term>mundane composition</term> <note>The structure and arrangement of the physical universe.</note>, in which both the apparent beauty is worthy of divinity, and a beauty more divine than this is established in the unapparent lives and powers of its causes.

“The truth (says he) concerning the gods pervades, as I may say, through all the Platonic dialogues, and in all of them conceptions of the <term>first philosophy</term> <note>Also known as metaphysics; the study of the fundamental nature of reality and the first causes of things.</note>, venerable, clear, and supernatural, are disseminated, in some more obscurely, but in others more conspicuously;—conceptions which excite those that are in any respect able to partake of them, to the immaterial and separate essence of the gods. Besides, things of this kind are only delivered adventitiously in the Platonic dialogues <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BC) wrote his philosophy in the form of conversations, or "dialogues," between characters, most notably his teacher Socrates.</note>; as the fable in the *Protagoras* <note>A dialogue concerning the nature of virtue and whether it can be taught.</note>, which is inserted for the sake of political science and the demonstrations respecting it. And, in short, all the axioms of the theological science appear in perfection in this dialogue; and all the divine orders are exhibited subsisting in connexion. So that this is nothing else than the celebrated generation of the gods, and the procession of every kind of being from the ineffable and unknown cause of wholes¹. The *Parmenides* therefore enkindles in the lovers of Plato the whole and perfect light of the theological science. But after this, the aforementioned dialogues distribute parts of the mystic discipline about the gods, and all of them, as I may say, participate of divine wisdom, and excite our spontaneous conceptions respecting a divine nature. ...that is not comprehended in the essence of **intellect** <term>intellect</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "Intellect" (or *Nous*) refers to the divine, eternal Mind that contains the perfect blueprints for all of creation.</note>; but it always establishes in itself **ideas**, which are not different from itself and its essence, but give completion to it, and introduce to the whole of things a cause which is at the same time productive <note>The power that creates or brings things into being.</note>, **paradigmatic** <term>paradigmatic</term> <note>Serving as a "paradigm"—an eternal, perfect model or archetype from which physical things are copied.</note>, and final <note>The ultimate purpose or goal toward which things strive.</note>. For it energizes as intellect, and the ideas which it contains are paradigmatic, as being forms; and they energize from themselves, and according to their own exuberant goodness. And such are the **Platonic dogmas** <note>The established doctrines or core philosophical principles of Plato.</note> concerning ideas, which sophistry and ignorance may indeed oppose, but will never be able to confute.

From this **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal Forms, which can only be "seen" by the mind, not the physical eyes.</note>, replete with omniform ideas, this **sensible world** <term>sensible world</term> <note>The physical universe that we perceive through our five senses.</note>, according to Plato, perpetually flows, depending on its **artificer** <term>artificer</term> <note>Also known as the "Demiurge," this is the divine craftsman who shapes the universe according to eternal patterns.</note> intellect, in the same manner as a shadow depends on its forming substance. For as a deity of an intellectual characteristic is its fabricator, and both the essence and energy of intellect are established in eternity, the sensible universe, which is the effect or production of such an energy, must be **consubsistent** <term>consubsistent</term> <note>Existing together in time; here, it means the world exists simultaneously with its eternal cause rather than being created at a specific starting point in time.</note> with its cause, or, in other words, must be a perpetual **emanation** <term>emanation</term> <note>An "outflowing" or "streaming forth," like light constantly radiating from the sun.</note> from it. This will be evident from considering, that every thing which is generated, is either generated by art, or by nature, or according to power. It is necessary, therefore, that every thing operating according to nature or art should be prior to the things produced; but that things operating according to power should have their productions coexistent with themselves; just as the sun produces light coexistent with itself; fire, heat; and snow, coldness. If therefore the artificer of the universe produced it by art, he would not cause it simply to be, but to be in some particular manner; for all art produces form. Whence therefore does the world derive its being? If he produced it from nature, since that which makes by nature imparts something of itself to its productions, and the maker of the world is **incorporeal** <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Lacking a physical body or material substance; purely spiritual or mental.</note>, it would be necessary that the world, the offspring of such an energy, should be incorporeal.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page liv regarding the relationship between the divine mind (Intellect) and the creation of the physical world. It remains, therefore, that the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Demiurge" (from the Latin *demiurgus*) is the divine Craftsman or Artificer who shapes the physical world according to eternal, perfect patterns.</note> produced the universe by power alone; but every thing generated by power exists together with the cause containing this power: and hence productions of this kind cannot be destroyed, unless the producing cause is deprived of power. The divine intellect therefore that produced the <term>sensible universe</term> <note>The physical world that we perceive through our five senses, as opposed to the "intelligible world" of pure thought.</note> caused it to be coexistent with himself.

This world thus depending on its divine artificer, who is himself an <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of eternal truths and perfect forms that exists within the divine mind.</note>, replete with the <term>archetypal ideas</term> <note>The original, perfect "blueprints" for all things that exist in our physical world.</note> of all things, considered according to its corporeal nature, is perpetually flowing, and perpetually advancing "into a state of becoming" <note>original: "εν τῳ γιγνεσθαι" — this refers to the physical world's nature of always changing and never truly "being" in a fixed, eternal state.</note>, and compared with its <term>paradigm</term> <note>The eternal model or blueprint that the physical world copies.</note>, has no stability or reality of being. However, considered as animated by a divine soul, and as receiving the illuminations of all the supermundane gods <note>Divinities that exist above and beyond the physical world.</note>, and being itself the receptacle of divinities from whom bodies are suspended, it is said by Plato in the *Timaeus* <note>The *Timaeus* is a famous dialogue by Plato which provides a detailed account of how the universe was created and organized.</note> to be a blessed god. The great body of this world too, which exists in a perpetual dispersion of temporal extension, may be properly called a **whole with a total subsistence** <term>total subsistence</term> <note>A technical term for a complete, self-contained system that exists as a unified whole, like the entire universe or a planet.</note>, on account of the perpetuity of its duration, though this is nothing more than a flowing eternity <note>A poetic term for "Time," which mimics the stillness of eternity through its never-ending movement.</note>. And hence Plato calls it **a whole of wholes**; by the other wholes which are comprehended in it meaning, the celestial spheres, the sphere of fire, the whole of air considered as one great orb; the whole earth, and the whole sea. Such, according to **Plato**, are the flights of the true philosopher, such the august and magnificent scene which presents itself to his view. By ascending these luminous heights, the spontaneous tendencies of the soul to deity alone find the adequate object of their desire; investigation here alone finally reposes, doubt expires in certainty, and knowledge loses itself in the ineffable.

These therefore being terminated, there can neither be an infinite mutation, according to a right line, nor can that which is always moved proceed according to a finished progression. Hence that which is always moved will proceed from the same to the same; and will thus form a periodic motion. But every thing which is moved perpetually and participates of time, revolves periodically and proceeds from the same to the same. And hence the soul, from possessing motion and energizing according to time, will both possess periods of motion, and restitutions to its pristine state.

On this wall are seen men bearing utensils of every kind, and statues in wood and stone of men and other animals. And of these men some are speaking and others silent. With respect to the fettered men in this cave, they see nothing of themselves or another, or of what is carrying along, but the shadows formed by the fire falling on the opposite part of the cave. In Plato's philosophy, this is the type of thinking used in mathematics and logic, which serves as a bridge between physical observation and pure intellectual intuition.</note> objects, in the mathematical disciplines. For as the shadows in the cave correspond to the shadows of visible objects, and visible objects are the immediate images of <term>dianoëtic</term> forms, or those ideas which the soul essentially participates, it is evident that the objects from which these shadows are formed must correspond to such as are <term>dianoëtic</term>. It is requisite, therefore, that the <term>dianoëtic</term> power, exercising itself in these, should draw forth the principles of these from their latent retreats, and should contemplate them not in images, but as subsisting in herself in impartible involution <note>An archaic way of saying that the concepts are held within the mind in a unified, indivisible state, rather than being spread out or fragmented like physical objects.</note>.

In the next place he says, “that the man who is to be led from the cave, will more easily see what the heavens contain, and the heavens themselves, by looking in the night to the light of the stars, and the moon, than by day looking on the sun, and the light of the sun.” By this he signifies the contemplation of <term>intelligibles</term> <note>In Platonic thought, "intelligibles" are the ultimate, unchanging realities or "Forms" that can only be perceived by the intellect, not the senses.</note>: for the stars and their light are imitations of intelligibles, so far as all of them partake of the form of the sun, in the same manner as intelligibles are characterized by the nature of *the good*.

After the contemplation of these, and after the eye is accustomed through these to the light, as it is requisite in the visible region to see the sun himself in the last place, in like manner, according to Plato, the idea of *the good* <note>The "Form of the Good" is the highest principle in Plato's philosophy, representing the ultimate source of truth, existence, and beauty—often compared to the sun because it makes all other truths visible to the mind.</note> must be seen the last in the intelligible region. Hence it is necessary to pass rapidly from things visible and audible, to those which are alone seen by the eye of intellect. **Dialectic**, however, or the "summit" of the mathematical sciences, as it is called by Plato in his *Republic*, is that master discipline which particularly leads us up to an <term>intelligible essence</term> <note>A reality that exists beyond the physical world, consisting of pure ideas or "forms" that can only be grasped by the mind.</note>. Suffice it therefore to observe in this place, that dialectic differs from mathematical science in this, that the latter flows from a hypothesis, while the former is free of it <note>Plato argued that mathematicians take their starting points (like "number" or "angle") for granted as assumptions, whereas the Dialectician seeks the ultimate, un-assumed source of all things.</note>. That dialectic has a power of knowing universals; that it ascends to the "good" and the supreme cause of all; and that it considers the good as the end of its elevation; but that the mathematical science, which previously constructs for itself definite principles, from which it proves things following those principles, does not tend toward the primary cause, but toward a conclusion. Hence Plato does not expel mathematical knowledge from the number of the sciences, but asserts it to be the next in rank to that one science which is the summit of all; nor does he accuse it of being ignorant of its own principles, but considers it as receiving these from the master science, dialectic, and that possessing them without needing demonstration, it demonstrates from these its following propositions.

It likewise sometimes uses definitions and demonstrations, and prior to these the definitive method, and the divisive prior to this. On the contrary, the merely logical method, which is solely conversant with opinion, is deprived of the incontrovertible reasonings of demonstration.

admirable specimen in the speech of Diotima in the Banquet <note>Also known as the *Symposium*, a dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of love.</note>. For there he ascends from the beauty about bodies to the beauty in souls; from this to the beauty in right disciplines; from this again to the beauty in laws; from the beauty in laws to the **ample sea of beauty** <note>original: το πολὺ πέλαγος τοῦ καλοῦ (to poly pelagos tou kalou)</note>; and thus proceeding, he at length arrives at the beautiful itself.

The second species of analysis is as follows: It is necessary to make the thing investigated, the subject of hypothesis; to survey such things as are prior to it; and to demonstrate these from things posterior, ascending to such as are prior, till we arrive at the first thing, and to which we give our assent. But beginning from this, we descend <term>synthetically</term> <note>The process of "synthesis" here refers to building a logical conclusion step-by-step from established first principles, the opposite of analysis.</note> to the thing investigated. Of this species, the following is an example, from the *Phædrus* of Plato. It is inquired if the soul is immortal; and this being hypothetically admitted, it is inquired in the next place if it is always moved. This being demonstrated, the next inquiry is, if that which is always moved, is self-moved; and this again being demonstrated, it is considered whether that which is self-moved, is the principle of motion; and afterwards if the principle is unbegotten. This then being admitted as a thing acknowledged, and likewise that what is unbegotten is incorruptible, the demonstration of the thing proposed is thus collected. If there is a principle, it is unbegotten and incorruptible. That which is self-moved is the principle of motion. Soul is self-moved. Soul therefore (*i. e. the rational soul*) is incorruptible, unbegotten, and immortal.

Of the third species of analysis, which proceeds from the hypothetical to that which is unhypothetic, Plato has given a most beautiful specimen in the first hypothesis of his *Parmenides*. For here, taking for his hypothesis that *the one is*, he proceeds through an orderly series of negations, which are not <term>privative</term> <note>Meaning they do not simply "take away" or deny existence, but rather define the subject by what it transcends.</note> of their subjects, but generative of

In the first place, therefore, Providence, according to common conceptions, is the cause of good to the subjects of its care; and Fate is the cause of a certain connexion to generated natures. This being admitted, let us consider what the things are which are connected. Of beings, therefore, some have their essence in eternity, and others in time. But by beings whose essence is in eternity, I mean those whose energy as well as their essence is eternal; and by beings essentially temporal, those whose essence is always in generation, or becoming to be, though this should take place in an infinite time. The medium, therefore, must be that whose essence is eternal, but energy temporal. And the three orders which compose this first, middle, and last are, the <term>intellectual</term> <note>Pertaining to pure, divine mind or "Nous," which is entirely outside of time</note>, <term>psychical</term> (or that pertaining to soul), and <term>corporeal</term> <note>Relating to physical, material bodies</note>. For from what has been already said by us concerning the gradation of beings, it is evident that the intellectual order is established in eternity, both in essence and energy; that the corporeal order is always in generation, or advancing to being, and this either in an infinite time, or in a part of time; and that the psychical is indeed eternal in essence, but temporal in energy <note>The soul has an eternal nature, but its actions and thoughts unfold sequentially over time</note>. Where then shall we rank things which, being distributed either in places or times, have a certain coordination and sympathy with each other through connexion? It is evident that they must be ranked among <term>altermotive</term> <note>Literally "moved by another"; referring to things that do not possess the power of self-movement, such as physical objects</note> and corporeal natures. For of things which subsist beyond the order of bodies, some are better both than place and time; and others, though they energize according to time, appear to be entirely pure from any connexion with place.

Hence things which are governed and connected by <term>Fate</term> <note>The law of cause and effect that binds the physical world together</note> are entirely altermotive and corporeal. If this then is demonstrated, it is manifest, that admitting Fate to be a cause of connexion, we must assert that it presides over altermotive and corporeal natures. If, therefore, we look to that which is the proximate cause of bodies, and through which also altermotive beings are moved, breathe, and are held together, we shall find that this is nature, the energies of which are to generate, nourish, and increase. If, therefore, this power not only subsists in us and all other animals and plants, but prior to partial bodies there is, by a much greater necessity, one nature of the world which comprehends and is motive of all bodies; it follows, that nature must be the cause of things

For if there are beings—namely, all **intellectual natures** <note>Beings consisting of pure mind or spirit, existing beyond the physical world</note>—which are eternally established above the laws of Fate, and also those which are distributed under the cycles of Fate throughout the whole of their life, there must be a middle ground between them. This middle ground is that nature which is sometimes above and sometimes under the dominion of Fate. This is because the progression of **incorporeal natures** <term>Beings without physical bodies, such as souls</term> is more continuous and without gaps than the progression of physical bodies.

The **free will** <note>original: "proairesis"; Plato’s concept of a deliberate, rational choice</note> of man, according to **Plato**, is a rational power of choice. It desires both the **true good** <note>Eternal, spiritual reality</note> and the **apparent good** <note>Things that look good on the surface, like physical pleasures, but are fleeting</note>, and it leads the soul toward both. Through this power, the soul either ascends toward the divine or descends toward the material; it either errs or acts with **rectitude** <note>Moral correctness or right action</note>. Consequently, this elective power is the very thing that defines our essence as human beings. 

According to this power, we differ from both divine and mortal natures, for neither of those has this two-fold inclination. The divine nature, because of its excellence, is established in the true good alone. The mortal nature, because of its limitations, is established in the apparent good. **Intellect** <term>The higher, intuitive mind capable of grasping divine truth</term> characterizes the divine, while **sense** <term>Physical perception and bodily desire</term> characterizes the mortal. As the philosopher **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who expanded on Plato's teachings</note> says, the intellect is our king, but the senses are our messengers. 

We, therefore, are established in this power of choice as a middle ground. Having the ability to lean toward both the true and the apparent good, we follow the guidance of the intellect when we lean toward the former, and the guidance of the senses when we lean toward the latter. Therefore, the power within us is not capable of all things. A power that is **omnipotent** <note>All-powerful</note> is characterized by **unity** <term>The state of being one, whole, and undivided</term>; it is all-powerful precisely because it is one and embodies the form of **the Good** <note>In this philosophy, the "Good" is the ultimate source of all existence</note>. But the elective power of choice is "two-fold," and for this reason, it is not able to effect all things; because it fluctuates between true and apparent good, it falls short of that nature which exists before all things. My present discourse therefore is addressed to those who consider experiment as the only solid criterion of truth. In the first place then, these men appear to be ignorant of the invariable laws of **demonstration** <term>A logical proof that shows a conclusion must be true based on certain premises</term> properly so called, and that the necessary requisites of all demonstrative¹ propositions are these: that they exist as causes, are primary, more excellent, more specific, truer, and better known than the conclusions. For every demonstration not only consists of principles that come before others, but of such as are "first" in the highest sense; since if the assumed propositions can be proven by other assumptions, such propositions may indeed appear to come before the conclusions, but they are by no means entitled to be called "first" principles. Others, on the contrary, which require no proof but are obvious in themselves, are deservedly esteemed the first, the truest, and the best. Such truths that cannot be proven were called by the ancients **axioms** <term>Self-evident truths that require no proof, such as "the whole is greater than the part"</term> because of their majesty and authority, as the assumptions which constitute **demonstrative syllogisms** <term>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal)</term> derive all their force and efficacy from these.

In the next place, they seem not to be sufficiently aware, that **universal** <term>General; applying to all cases</term> is better than **partial** <term>Specific; applying only to some cases</term> demonstration. For *that* demonstration is the more excellent which is derived from the better cause; but a universal cause is more extended and excellent than a partial cause; since the difficult investigation of *the why* in any subject is only stopped by the arrival at universals. Thus if we desire to know why the outward angles of a triangle are equal to four right angles <note>In geometry, the sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon is 360 degrees, which is equivalent to four 90-degree "right angles."</note>, and it is answered, "Because the triangle is **isosceles**" <term>A triangle with two equal sides</term>; we again ask, "But why because it is isosceles?" And if it be replied, "Because it is a triangle"; we may again inquire, "But why because it is a triangle?" To which we finally answer,
