Hence it will follow that induction <note>Induction is the logical process of drawing a general rule from specific examples. The author argues here that induction doesn't "create" a rule, but acts as a trigger for the mind to remember a rule it already knows.</note> is no otherwise subservient to science, than as it produces credibility in <term>axioms and petitions</term> <note>"Petitions" refers to postulates, or assumptions required for a mathematical proof.</note>; and this by exciting the universal conception of these latent in the soul. The particulars, therefore, of which an induction is made in order to produce science, must be so simple, that they may be immediately apprehended, and that the universal may be predicated of them without hesitation. The particulars of the experimentalists are not of this kind, and therefore never can be sources of science truly so called.

Of this, however, the man of experiment appears to be totally ignorant, and in consequence of this, he is likewise ignorant that parts can only be truly known through wholes, and that this is particularly the case with parts when they belong to a whole, which, as we have already observed, from comprehending in itself the parts which it produces, is called a **whole prior to parts** <note>This is a fundamental Neoplatonic concept. It suggests that a perfect, unified blueprint of a thing (the Whole) exists in the realm of intellect before any individual versions of it (the parts) appear in the physical world.</note>. As he, therefore, would by no means merit the appellation of a physician who should attempt to cure any part of the human body without a previous knowledge of the whole; so neither can he know any thing truly of the vegetable life of plants,

Here then is the great difference, and a mighty one it is, between the knowledge gained by the most elaborate experiments, and that acquired by scientific reasoning, founded on the spontaneous, unperverted, and self-luminous conceptions of the soul. The former does not even lead its votary up to that one nature of the earth from which the natures of all the animals and plants on its surface, and of all the minerals and metals in its interior parts, blossom as from a perennial root. The latter conducts its votary through all the several <term>mundane wholes</term> <note>The major universal components of the physical universe, such as the spheres of the elements or the heavens.</note> up to that great whole the world itself, and thence leads him through the luminous order of incorporeal wholes to that vast whole of wholes, in which all other wholes are centered and rooted, and which is no other than the principle of all principles, and the fountain of deity itself.

That he did so is abundantly evident from the testimony of **Eunapius** <note>A Greek sophist and historian (c. 347–414 AD) whose "Lives of the Philosophers" is a primary source for Neoplatonism.</note>, who particularly commends his style, for its *clearness, purity,* and *grace.* "Hence," says he, "**Porphyry** being let down to men like a mercurial chain <note>The author uses "mercurial chain" to translate the Greek "Hermetic chain," a concept in Neoplatonism referring to a lineage of wisdom descending from Hermes (Mercury) to humanity.</note>, through his various erudition, unfolded every thing into perspicuity and purity ²." With respect to the style of **Proclus**, it is pure, clear and elegant, like that of **Dionysius Halicarnassus** <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric in Rome (c. 60–7 BC).</note>, but is much more copious and magnificent; that of **Hierocles** is venerable and majestic, and nearly equals the style of the greatest ancients; that of **Sallust** possesses an accuracy and a pregnant brevity, which cannot easily be distinguished from the composition of the **Stagirite** <note>A reference to Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note>; and lastly, that of **Damascius** is clear and accurate, and highly worthy a most investigating mind.

Others again have filled themselves with a vain confidence, from reading the commentaries of these admirable interpreters, and have in a short time considered themselves superior to their masters. This was the case with **Ficinus** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Florentine Academy who translated Plato's works into Latin.</note>, **Picus** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a Renaissance philosopher famous for attempting to harmonize all philosophies.</note>, **Dr. Henry More** <note>Henry More (1614–1687), a member of the Cambridge Platonists who sought to reconcile Platonism with Christian theology and modern science.</note>, and other pseudo-Platonists, their contemporaries, who, in order to combine Christianity with the doctrines of **Plato**, rejected some of his most important tenets, and perverted others, and thus corrupted one of these systems, and afforded no real benefit to the other.

# GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

But it is now time to present the reader with a general view of the works of **Plato**, and also to speak of the preambles, digressions, and style of their author, and of the following translation. In accomplishing the first of these, I shall avail myself of the **Synopsis of Mr. Sydenham** <note>Floyer Sydenham (1710–1787) was an English scholar who began a massive project to translate Plato; Thomas Taylor, the author of this introduction, completed and revised Sydenham's work.</note>, taking the liberty at the same time of correcting it where it appears to be erroneous, and of making additions to it where it appears to be deficient.

The dialogues of **Plato** are of various kinds; not only with regard to those different matters, which are the subjects of them; but in respect of the manner also, in which they are composed or framed, and of the form under which they make their appearance to the reader. It will therefore, as I imagine, be not improper, in pursuance of the admonition given us by **Plato** himself in his dialogue named ¹ *Phædrus* <note>A famous dialogue concerning the nature of the soul, love, and the art of rhetoric.</note>, and in imitation of the example set us by the ² ancient **Platonists**, to distinguish the several kinds; by dividing them, first, into the most general; and then, subdividing into the subordinate; till we come to those lower <term>species</term> <note>In logic, a species is a specific category that falls under a broader "genus."</note>, that particularly and precisely denote the nature of the several dialogues, and from which they ought to take their respective denominations.

---

¹ "Unless one is able to divide things according to their kinds, and to comprehend each one under a single idea, he will never be skilled in arguments, as far as is possible for a human." <note>original: "Εαν μη τις κατ’ ειδη διαιρεισθαι τα οντα, και μια ιδεα δυνατος η καθ’ ἑν ἑκαστον περιλαμβανειν, ουποτ’ εσται τεχνικος λογων περι, καθ’ ὁσον δυνατον ανθρωπῳ."</note> Whoever is unable to divide and distinguish things into their several sorts or species; and, on the other hand, referring every particular to its proper species, to comprehend them all in one general idea; will never understand any writings, of which those things are the subject, like a true critic, upon those high principles of art to which the human understanding reaches. **Plato’s** *Phaedrus*. We have thought proper, here, to paraphrase this passage, for the sake of giving to every part of so important a sentence its full force, agreeably to the tenor of **Plato**’s doctrine; and in order to initiate our readers into a way of thinking, that probably many of them are as yet unacquainted with.

<meta>This page continues the classification of Plato's dialogues, shifting from the general introductory framing to a specific taxonomy of his writings. It outlines the division between Sceptical (investigative) and Dogmatical (instructional) works, categorizing their various methods of inquiry and demonstration.</meta>

<page-num>xciv</page-num>

->GENERAL INTRODUCTION.<-

The most general division of the writings of **Plato**, is into those of the **Sceptical** <note>Derived from the Greek *skepsis*, meaning "inquiry" or "investigation." Here, it refers to dialogues that explore questions without asserting a final conclusion.</note> kind, and those of the **Dogmatical** <note>Referring to "Dogma" in its original sense: a settled opinion or doctrine. These dialogues explicitly teach or state philosophical truths.</note>. In the former sort, nothing is expressly either proved or asserted: some philosophical question only is considered and examined; and the reader is left to himself to draw such conclusions, and discover such truths, as the philosopher means to insinuate. This is done, either in the way of inquiry, or in the way of controversy and dispute. In the way of controversy are carried on all such dialogues, as tend to eradicate false opinions; and that, either indirectly, by involving them in difficulties, and embarrassing the maintainers of them; or directly, by confuting them. In the way of inquiry proceed those, whose tendency is to raise in the mind right opinions; and that, either by exciting to the pursuit of some part of wisdom, and showing in what manner to investigate it; or by leading the way, and helping the mind forward in the search. And this is effected by a process through opposing arguments ¹.

The dialogues of the other kind, the **Dogmatical** or **Didactic**, teach explicitly some point of doctrine: and this they do, either by laying it down in the authoritative way, or by proving it in the way of reason and argument. In the authoritative way the doctrine is delivered, sometimes by the speaker himself magisterially, at other times as derived to him by tradition from wise men. The argumentative or demonstrative method of teaching, used by **Plato**, proceeds in all the **dialectic** <note>The art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical discussion and the categorization of ideas.</note> ways, *dividing*, *defining*, *demonstrating*, and *analysing*; and the object of it consists in exploring truth alone.

¹ It is necessary to observe, that **Plato** in the *Parmenides* <note>A famously difficult dialogue concerning the nature of "The One" and the "Many," often seen as a masterclass in logical training.</note> calls all that part of his Dialectic, which proceeds through opposite arguments, an **exercise** and **wandering** <note>original: γυμνασια και πλανη (gymnasia kai plane)</note>.

The learned reader will observe the latter half of the dialogues, according to this scheme, to be described by metaphors taken from the gymnastic art: the dialogues, here termed **gymnastic**, being imagined to bear a similitude to that exercise; the **agonistic**, to the combat. In the lowest subdivision, indeed, the word *maieutic* is a metaphor of another kind, fully explained in Plato’s *Theætetus* <note>A dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge, where Socrates famously describes his role as an intellectual midwife.</note>: the **maieutic** dialogues, however, were supposed to resemble giving the rudiments of the art; as the *peirastic* were, to represent a skirmish, or trial of proficiency: the *endeictic* were, it seems, likened to the exhibiting a specimen of skill; and the *anatreptic*, to presenting the spectacle of a thorough defeat, or sound drubbing.

The philosopher <note>Referring to Plato.</note>, in thus varying his manner, and diversifying his writings into these several kinds, means not merely to entertain with their variety; nor to teach, on different occasions, with more or less plainness and perspicuity; nor yet to insinuate different degrees of certainty in the doctrines themselves: but he takes this method, as a consummate master of the art of composition in the dialogue-way of writing, from the different characters of the speakers, as from different elements in the frame of these dramatic dialogues, or different ingredients in their mixture, producing some peculiar genius, and turn of temper, as it were, in each.

Socrates indeed is in almost all of them the principal speaker: but when he falls into the company of some arrogant <term>sophist</term> <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric in ancient Greece, often depicted by Plato as valuing winning an argument over finding the truth.</note>; when the modest wisdom, and clear science of the one, are contrasted with the confident ignorance, and blind opinionativeness of the other; dispute and controversy must of course arise: where the false pretender cannot fail of being either puzzled or confuted. To puzzle him only is sufficient, if there be no other persons present; because such a man can never be confuted in his own opinion: but when there is an audience round them, in danger of being misled by <term>sophistry</term> <note>The use of clever but false arguments, especially with the intention of deceiving.</note> into error, then is the true philosopher to exert his utmost, and the vain sophist to be convicted and exposed.

course extending itself through the latter. <note>This text continues a sentence from the previous page regarding the "course" of a flawed classification system.</note> This error consists in dividing the <term>Didactic</term> <note>Intended for instruction or teaching a specific doctrine.</note> dialogues with regard to their subject-matter; while those of the <term>Inquisitive</term> <note>Investigative; dialogues that seek truth through questioning rather than asserting it.</note> sort are divided with respect to the manner of their composition. So that the subdivisions fall not, with any propriety, under one and the same general head. Besides, a novice in the works of <term>Plato</term> might hence be led naturally to suppose, that the dogmatical or didactic dialogues are, all of them, written in the same manner; and that the others, those of the inquisitive kind, by us termed <term>sceptical</term> <note>original: "sceptical"; derived from the Greek 'skeptikos', meaning to inquire or look about. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page xcvi regarding how Plato tailors the style of his dialogues to the specific character and intellectual level of the participants, shifting from the "disputatious" style used against sophists to the "inquisitive" and "demonstrative" styles used with better-intentioned students.</meta>

<page-num>xcvii</page-num>
->GENERAL INTRODUCTION.<-

In some dialogues Plato represents his great master <note>Socrates.</note> mixing in conversation with young men of the best families in the commonwealth. When these happen to have docile dispositions and fair minds, then is occasion given to the philosopher to call forth $^1$ the latent seeds of wisdom, and to cultivate the noble plants with true doctrine, in the affable and familiar way of joint inquiry. To this is owing the inquisitive genius of such dialogues: where, by a seeming equality in the conversation, the curiosity or zeal of the mere stranger is excited; that of the disciple is encouraged; and by proper questions, the mind is aided and forwarded in the search of truth.

At other times, the philosophic hero of these dialogues is introduced in a higher character, engaged in discourse with men of more improved understandings and enlightened minds. At such seasons he has an opportunity of teaching in a more explicit manner, and of discovering the reasons of things: for to such an audience truth is due, and all $^2$ demonstration possible in the teaching it. Hence, in the dialogues composed of these persons, naturally arises the justly argumentative or demonstrative genius; and this, as we have before observed, according to all the <term>dialectic</term> <note>The formal method of logical argument used to uncover philosophical truths.</note> methods.

But when the doctrine to be taught admits not of demonstration; of which kind is the doctrine of antiquities, being only traditional, and a matter of belief; and the doctrine of laws, being injunctional, and

---

$^1$ We require *exhortation*, that we may be led to true good; *dissuasion*, that we may be turned from things truly evil; <term>obstetrication</term> <note>Literally "midwifery." Socrates famously compared himself to a midwife because he helped others "give birth" to the ideas and truths already latent within their own souls.</note>, that we may draw forth our unperverted conceptions; and *confutation*, that we may be purified from two-fold ignorance.

$^2$ The Platonists rightly observe, that Socrates, in these cases, makes use of demonstrative and just reasoning (<note>original Greek: apodeiktikou</note>); whereas to the novice he is contented with arguments only probable (<note>original Greek: pithanois</note>); and against the litigious <term>sophist</term> <note>Professional teachers who used clever but often fallacious reasoning to win arguments for money.</note> often employs such as are (<note>original Greek: eristikoi</note>) puzzling and contentious. See Alcinous, *Introduction to the Doctrines of Plato*, Chapter 6 <note>original: "Alkin. Eisagog. Keph. 6." Alcinous was a 2nd-century philosopher whose handbook was used for centuries to teach Platonic thought.</note>.

the matter of obedience; the air of authority is then assumed: in the former cases, the doctrine is traditionally handed down to others from the authority of ancient sages; in the latter, is magisterially pronounced with the authority of a legislator $^1$.

Thus much for the manner, in which the dialogues of Plato are severally composed, and the cast of genius <note>In this context, "genius" refers to the inherent spirit, character, or distinctive nature of the writing.</note> given them in their composition. The form under which they appear, or the external character that marks them, is of three sorts; either purely dramatic, like the dialogue of tragedy or comedy; or purely narrative, where a former conversation is supposed to be committed to writing, and communicated to some absent friend; or of the mixed kind, like a narration in dramatic poems, where is recited, to some person present, the story of things past.

Having thus divided the dialogues of Plato, in respect of that inward form or composition, which creates their genius; and again, with reference to that outward form, which marks them, like flowers and other vegetables, with a certain character; we are further to make a division of them, with regard to their subject and their design; beginning with their design, or end <note>The "end" refers to the "telos" or ultimate goal and purpose of the work.</note>, because for the sake of this are all the subjects chosen. The end of all the writings of Plato is that which is the end of all true philosophy or wisdom, the perfection and the happiness of man. Man therefore is the general subject; and the first business of philosophy must be to inquire, what is that being called man, who is to be made happy; and what is his nature, in the perfec-

The dialogues of Plato, therefore, with respect to their subjects, may be divided into the **speculative**, the **practical**, and such as are of a **mixed** nature. <note>In a classical context, "speculative" refers to theoretical contemplation and the search for truth, while "practical" refers to ethics, action, and how one should live.</note> The subjects of these last are either **general**, comprehending both the others; or **differential**, distinguishing them. The **general** subjects are either **fundamental**, or **final**: those of the fundamental kind are philosophy, human nature, the soul of man; of the final kind are love, beauty, good. <note>The "final" subjects refer to the *telos*, or the ultimate purpose and goal of human life.</note> The **differential** regard knowledge, as it stands related to practice; in which are considered two questions: one of which is, whether virtue is to be taught; the other is, whether error in the will depends on error in the judgment. The subjects of the **speculative** dialogues relate either to **words**, or to **things**. Of the former sort are etymology, sophistry, rhetoric, poetry: of the latter sort are science, true being <note>This refers to "ontology," the study of the nature of existence and reality.</note>, the principles of mind, outward nature. The **practical** subjects relate either to **private conduct**, and the government of the mind over the whole man; or to his **duty towards others** in his several relations; or to the **government of a civil state**, and the public conduct of a whole people. Under these three heads rank in order the particular subjects practical; virtue in general, sanctity, temperance, fortitude; justice, friendship, patriotism, piety; the ruling mind in a civil government, the frame and order of a state, law in general, and lastly, those rules of government and of public conduct, the civil laws.

Thus, for the sake of giving the reader a **scientific**, that is, a comprehensive, and at the same time a distinct, view of Plato's writings, we have attempted to exhibit to him their just and natural distinctions;

# GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

And here it is requisite to observe, that as it is the characteristic of the highest good to be universally beneficial, though some things are benefitted by it more and others less, in consequence of their greater or less aptitude to receive it; in like manner the dialogues of <term>Plato</term> <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BC) was the foundational figure of Western philosophy and a student of Socrates.</note> are so largely stamped with the characters of sovereign good, that they are calculated to benefit in a certain degree even those who are incapable of penetrating their profundity. They can tame a savage sophist, like <term>Thrasymachus</term> <note>A character in Plato's *Republic* who aggressively argues that "justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger."</note> in the <term>Republic</term>; humble the arrogance even of those who are ignorant of their ignorance; make those to become proficients in political virtue <note>Practical excellence in civic life and social ethics.</note>, who will never arrive at theoretic virtue <note>The highest intellectual excellence, achieved through the contemplation of eternal, unchanging truths.</note>; and, in short, like the illuminations of deity <note>A Neoplatonic concept suggesting that divine intelligence shines like light, and our ability to understand it depends on our own mental "aptitude" or readiness.</note>, wherever there is any portion of aptitude in their recipients, they purify, irradiate, and exalt.

After this general view of the dialogues of <term>Plato</term>, let us in the next place consider their preambles, the digressions with which they abound, and the character of the style in which they are written. With respect to the first of these, the preambles, however superfluous they may at first sight appear, they will be found on a closer inspection necessary to the design of the dialogues which they accompany. Thus the prefatory part of the <term>Timæus</term> <note>One of Plato's most influential dialogues, dealing with the origin and structure of the physical universe.</note> unfolds, in images agreeably to the <term>Pythagoric</term> <note>Referring to Pythagoras; his followers believed the world was built on mathematical and harmonic principles.</note> custom, the theory of the world; and the first part of the <term>Parmenides</term> <note>A famously difficult dialogue exploring the nature of "The One" and the "Many," forming the basis of Neoplatonic theology.</note>, or the discussion of *ideas*, is in fact merely a preamble to the second part, or the speculation of *the one*; to which however it is essentially preparatory. Hence, as <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–120 AD) who interpreted Plato's works for a Roman-era audience.</note> says, when he speaks of <term>Plato</term>’s dialogue on the Atlantic island <note>Referring to the story of Atlantis, found in the *Timæus* and the *Critias*.</note>: 'These preambles are superb gates and magnificent courts with which he purposely embellishes his great [edifices]...' <note>original: "edifices" — the catchword at the bottom of the original page indicates the first word of the next page.</note>

He acts, as <term>Dacier</term> <note>André Dacier (1651–1722), a French classical scholar who published a well-known translation of several Platonic dialogues.</note> well observes, like a great prince, who, when he builds a sumptuous palace, adorns (in the language of <term>Pindar</term> <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet (c. 518–438 BC) famous for his victory odes; his work often emphasized the splendor and nobility of his subjects.</note>) the vestibule with golden pillars. For it is fit that what is first seen should be splendid and magnificent, and should as it were perspicuously announce all that grandeur which afterwards presents itself to the view.

With respect to the frequent digressions in his dialogues, these also, when accurately examined, will be found to be no less subservient to the leading design of the dialogues in which they are introduced; at the same time that they afford a pleasing relaxation to the mind from the labour of severe investigation. Hence <term>Plato</term> <note>The Athenian philosopher (c. 427–347 BC) who founded the Academy and wrote in the form of dialogues.</note>, by the most happy and enchanting art, contrives to lead the reader to the temple of Truth, through the delightful groves and vallies of the Graces. In short, this circuitous course, when attentively considered, will be found to be the shortest road by which he could conduct the reader to the desired end: for in accomplishing this it is necessary to regard not that road which is most straight in the nature of things, or abstractedly considered, but that which is most direct in the progressions of human understanding.

With respect to the style of Plato, though it forms in reality the most inconsiderable part of the merit of his writings, style in all philosophical works being the last thing that should be attended to, yet even in this Plato may contend for the palm of excellence with the most renowned masters of diction. Hence we find that his style was the admiration of the finest writers of antiquity. According to <term>Ammianus</term> <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–395 AD), a Roman soldier and historian who often praised the intellectual achievements of the Greeks.</note>, Jupiter himself would not speak otherwise, if he were to converse in the <term>Attic tongue</term> <note>The dialect of ancient Greek spoken in Athens, celebrated for its refinement and literary elegance.</note>. <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Plato’s most famous student, whose own style was later described as more dry and systematic.</note> considered his style as a medium between poetry and prose. <term>Cicero</term> <note>The Roman orator and statesman (106–43 BC) who modeled much of his own philosophical writing on Plato.</note> no less praises him for the excellence of his diction than the profundity of his conceptions; and <term>Longinus</term> <note>The traditional name given to the author of the Greek treatise *On the Sublime*, which analyzes the qualities of great writing.</note> calls him,

Hence he is considered by this prince of critics <note>Referring to Longinus (c. 213–273 AD), a rhetorician and philosophical critic whose treatise *On the Sublime* is a foundational work of literary criticism.</note>, as deriving into himself abundant streams from the Homeric fountain, and is compared by him, in his rivalship of **Homer**, to a new antagonist, who enters the lists against one that is already the object of universal admiration.

Notwithstanding this praise, however, **Plato** has been accused, as **Longinus** informs us, of being frequently hurried away as by a certain *Bacchic fury* <note>Named for Bacchus (Dionysus), the god of wine and ecstasy; it refers to a state of inspired, frenzied eloquence that transcends ordinary reason.</note> of words to immoderate and unpleasant metaphors, and an allegoric magnificence of diction ¹. **Longinus** excuses this by saying, that whatever naturally excels in magnitude possesses very little of purity. For that, says he, which is in every respect accurate is in danger of littleness. He adds, “and may not this also be necessary, that those of an abject and moderate genius, because they never encounter danger, nor aspire after the summit of excellence, are for the most part without error and remain in security; but that great things become insecure through their magnitude?” Indeed it appears to me, that whenever this exuberance, this *Bacchic fury*, occurs in the diction of **Plato**, it is owing to the magnitude of the inspiring influence of deity with which he is then replete. For that he sometimes wrote from divine inspiration is evident from his own confession in the *Phædrus* <note>One of Plato's most poetic dialogues, which explores the nature of the soul, love, and rhetoric.</note>, a great part of which is not so much like an orderly discourse as a <term>dithyrambic</term> <note>A style of poetry originally written for choral hymns to Dionysus, characterized by its wild, passionate, and irregular rhythm.</note> poem. Such a style therefore, as it is the progeny of **divine mania** <note>In Greek philosophy, *mania* refers not to insanity, but to a state of being "possessed" by a divine power or muse, which Plato argued was superior to mere human logic.</note>, which, as **Plato** justly observes, is better than all human prudence, spontaneously adapts itself to its producing cause, imitates a supernatural power as far as this can be effected by words, and thus necessarily becomes magnificent, vehement, and exuberant; for such are the characteristics of its source. # GENERAL INTRODUCTION.

Both ancient and modern critics agree that his style is generally graceful and pure, and that it is sublime without being reckless or overly rapid. It is indeed no less harmonious than it is elevated, and no less accurate <gloss>1</gloss> than it is magnificent. It combines the strength of the greatest orators with the beauty of the finest poets; and, in short, is a river to which those celebrated lines by **Denham** <note>Sir John Denham (1615–1669), an English poet known for his influential descriptive poem *Cooper's Hill*.</note> may be most appropriately applied:

-> Though deep, yet clear; though gentle, yet not dull; <-
-> Strong without rage, without overflowing full. <-

Having thus considered **Plato’s** philosophy, provided a general view of his writings, and made some observations on his style, it now only remains to speak of the following arrangement of his dialogues and the translation of his works. I will then close this Introduction with a few appropriate observations.

As no accurate and scientific arrangement of these dialogues has been passed down to us from the ancients, I found it necessary to adopt an arrangement of my own. I trust this method is not unscientific, however inferior it may be to the one that was undoubtedly made—though unfortunately lost—by the later interpreters <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists of late antiquity, such as Proclus or Iamblichus, who had specific "curriculums" for reading Plato.</note> of **Plato**. In my arrangement, I have imitated the order of the universe, in which, as I have already observed, **wholes precede parts**, and <term>universals</term> <note>General concepts or qualities that can be shared by many things (like "Beauty" or "Justice" itself) rather than specific, individual objects.</note> precede particulars. Consequently, I have placed those dialogues first which rank as "wholes"—meaning those that provide a complete system—and afterwards those in which these systems are branched out into specific details. Thus, after the *First Alcibiades*—

Hence, the reader who has successfully grasped his depth finds, with astonishment, that not one word could have been added without being extra, nor one word taken away without damaging the meaning. [Alci]biades <note>The translator refers to the *First Alcibiades*, a dialogue traditionally used in antiquity as the first text for new students of Plato because it focuses on self-knowledge.</note>, which may be called, and appears to have been generally considered by the ancients, an introduction to the whole of **Plato's** philosophy, I have placed the *Republic* and the *Laws*, which may be said to comprehend systematically the morals and politics of **Plato**. After these I have ranked the *Timaeus*, which contains the whole of his <term>physiology</term> <note>In this historical context, "physiology" refers to the study of the natural world and the physical universe (from the Greek *physis*), rather than just the functions of living organisms.</note>, and together with it the *Critias*, because of its connection with the *Timaeus*. The next in order is the *Parmenides*, which contains a system of his theology. Thus far this arrangement is conformable to the natural progress of the human mind in the acquisition of the sublimest knowledge: the subsequent arrangement principally regards the order of things. After the *Parmenides* then, the *Sophist*, *Phaedrus*, *Greater Hippias*, and *Banquet* <note>Commonly known today by its Greek title, the *Symposium*.</note>, follow, which may be considered as so many lesser wholes subordinate to and comprehended in the *Parmenides*, which, like the universe itself, is a whole of wholes. For in the *Sophist* **being itself** is investigated, in the *Banquet* **love itself**, and in the *Phaedrus* **beauty itself**; all which are <term>intelligible forms</term> <note>These are the "Ideas" or "Forms"—the eternal, unchanging patterns of things that can only be understood by the mind, not the physical senses.</note>, and are consequently contained in the *Parmenides*, in which the whole extent of the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and reality that exists beyond the reach of our physical senses.</note> is unfolded. The *Greater Hippias* is classed with the *Phaedrus*, because in the latter the whole series of the beautiful is discussed, and in the former that which subsists in soul. After these follows the *Theaetetus*, in which <term>science</term> <note>Here meaning *episteme*, or certain, demonstrable knowledge, as opposed to mere opinion.</note> considered as subsisting in soul is investigated; science itself, according to its <term>first subsistence</term> <note>The primary or highest level of existence for a concept (like Knowledge or Beauty) before it is reflected in the human mind or the physical world.</note>, having been previously celebrated by **Socrates** in one part of the *Phaedrus*. The *Statesman* and *Minos*, which follow next, may be considered as ramifications from the *Laws*: and, in short, all the following dialogues either consider more particularly the dogmas which are systematically comprehended in those already enumerated, or naturally flow from them as their original source. After the dialogues¹ follow the *Epistles* of **Plato**, which are in every respect worthy that prince of all true philosophers. They are not only written with great elegance, and occasionally with magnificence of diction, but with all the becoming dignity of a mind conscious of its superior endowments, and all the authority of a master in philosophy. They are likewise replete with many admirable political observations, and contain some of his most abstruse <term>dogmas</term> <note>In this historical context, "dogmas" refers to established philosophical doctrines or core tenets of the school.</note>, which though delivered enigmatically, yet the manner in which they are delivered, elucidates at the same time that it is elucidated by what is said of these dogmas in his more theological dialogues.

His translation however of other parts which are not so abstruse is excellent. In these he not only presents the reader faithfully with the matter, but likewise with the genuine manner of <term>Plato</term>. The notes too which accompany the translation of these parts generally exhibit just criticism and extensive learning, an elegant taste, and a genius naturally philosophic. Of these notes I have preserved as much as was consistent with the limits and design of the following work.

Of the translation of the <term>Republic</term> by <term>Dr. Spens</term> <note>Hary Spens (1713–1787), a Scottish minister who published the first English translation of the Republic in 1763.</note>, it is necessary to observe, that a considerable part of it is very faithfully executed; but that in the more abstruse parts it is inaccurate; and that it every where abounds with <term>Scotticisms</term> <note>Phrases or idioms specific to the Scots language that were often considered non-standard in 18th-century literary English.</note> which offend an English ear, and vulgarisms which are no less disgraceful to the translator than disgusting to the reader. Suffice it therefore to say of this version, that I have adopted it wherever I found it could with propriety be adopted, and given my own translation where it was otherwise.

Of the ten dialogues, translated by <term>Dacier</term> <note>André Dacier (1651–1722), a French classical scholar. His translations were often the basis for early English versions.</note>, I can say nothing with accuracy, because I have no knowledge whatever of the French language; but if any judgment may be formed of this work, from a

# EXPLANATION
### OF CERTAIN
# PLATONIC TERMS.

---

->**As** some apology may be thought necessary for having introduced, in the course of the following translation, certain unusual words of Greek origin, I shall only observe; that as all arts and sciences have certain appropriate terms peculiar to themselves, philosophy, which is the art of arts, and science of sciences, as being the mistress of both, has certainly a prior and a far superior claim to this privilege. I have not, however, introduced, I believe, any of these terms, without at the same time sufficiently explaining them; but, lest the contrary should have taken place, the following explanation of all such terms as I have been able to recollect, and also of common words used by Platonists in a peculiar sense, is subjoined for the information of the reader.<-

<term>ANAGOGIC</term> <note>original Greek: αναγωγικος, "anagogikos"</note>. Leading on high <note>This refers to the process of raising the soul from material concerns to spiritual or intellectual truths</note>.

<term>DEMIURGUS</term> <note>original Greek: δημιουργος, "demiourgos"</note>. Jupiter, the artificer <note>or "craftsman"</note> of the universe.

<term>DIANOETIC</term>. This word is derived from <term>dianoia</term> <note>original Greek: διανοια</note>, or that power of the soul which reasons scientifically, deriving the principles of its reasoning from intellect. Plato is so uncommonly accurate in his diction, that this word is very seldom used by him in any other than its primary sense.

**THE DIVINE**¹ <note>original Greek: το θειον, "to theion"</note>, is *being* subsisting in conjunction with *the one*. For all things except *the one*, namely essence, life, and intellect, are considered by Plato as suspended from and secondary to the gods. For the gods do not exist in, but prior to, these.

¹ <note>See Proclus, *On the Theology of Plato*, page 64.</note>

# EXPLANATION OF CERTAIN
### PLATONIC TERMS.

which they also produce and connect, but are not characterized by these. In many places, however, Plato calls the participants of the gods by the names of the gods. For not only the Athenian Guest <note>The main speaker in Plato’s *Laws*, often identified with Plato himself</note> in the *Laws*, but also Socrates in the *Phædrus*, calls a divine soul a god. “For,” says he, “all the horses and charioteers of the *gods* are good,” etc. And afterwards, still more clearly, he adds, “And this is the life of the *gods*.” And not only this, but he also denominates those natures gods, that are always united to the gods, and which, in conjunction with them, give completion to one series. He also frequently calls dæmons <note>In the Platonic sense, *daemons* are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> gods, though, according to essence, they are secondary to, and subsist about, the gods. For in the *Phædrus*, *Timæus*, and other dialogues, he extends the appellation of gods as far as to dæmons. And what is still more paradoxical than all this, he does not refuse to call some men gods; as, for instance, the Elean Guest <note>The "Eleatic Stranger," the primary speaker in the *Sophist*</note> in the *Sophista*. 

From all this, therefore, we must infer, that with respect to the word god, one thing which is thus denominated is simply deity; another is so according to union; a third, according to participation; a fourth, according to contact; and a fifth, according to similitude. Thus every superessential <note>Existing above or beyond the realm of "being" or "essence"</note> nature is primarily a god; but every intellectual nature is so according to union. And again, every divine soul is a god according to participation; but divine dæmons are gods, according to contact with the gods: and the souls of men obtain this appellation through similitude. Each of these, however, except the first, is, as we have said, rather divine than a god: for the Athenian Guest, in the *Laws*, calls intellect itself divine. But that which is divine is secondary to the first deity, in the same manner as *the united is to the one; that which is intellectual, to intellect; and that which is animated, to soul.* Indeed, things more uniform and simple always precede; and the series of beings ends in *the one* itself.

**DOXASTIC.** This word is derived from *opinion* <note>original Greek: δόξα, "doxa"</note>, and signifies that which is apprehended by opinion, or that power which is the extremity of the rational soul. This power knows the universal in particulars, as that *every man is a rational animal*; but it knows not the *why* <note>original Greek: διότι, "dioti"</note>, or *why* a thing is, but only the *that* <note>original Greek: ὅτι, "hoti"</note>, or *that* it is.

**THE ETERNAL**, *the eternal* <note>original Greek: τὸ αἰώνιον, "to aionion"</note>, that which has a never-ending subsistence, without any connection with time; or, as Plotinus profoundly defines it, infinite life at once total and full.

-># PLATONIC TERMS.<-

<term>THAT WHICH IS GENERATED</term>, <note>original: "to genēton"</note>. That which does not have the whole of its essence or energy existing all at once, without being spread out over time.

<term>GENERATION</term>, <note>original: "genesis"</note>. An essence that is composite and multiform, and connected with time. This is the literal meaning of the word; but it is used symbolically by Plato, and also by theologians older than Plato, for the sake of hidden meaning. For as Proclus beautifully observes in his *Manuscript Commentary on the Parmenides*: “Fables call the ineffable unfolding into light through causes, 'generation'.” “Hence,” he adds, in the Orphic writings, the first cause is named Time; for where there is generation, according to its proper meaning, there also is time.

<term>A GUEST</term>, <note>original: "xenos"</note>. This word, in its broader meaning in Greek, denotes a *stranger*, but properly implies one who receives another, or is himself received at a feast. In the following dialogues, therefore, wherever one of the speakers is introduced as a <note>original: "xenos"</note>, I have translated this word as *guest*, as it is more suited to the spirit of Plato’s dialogues, which may be rightly called rich mental banquets; consequently, the speakers in them may be considered as so many guests. Hence in the *Timaeus*, the people in that dialogue are expressly spoken of as guests.

<term>HYPARXIS</term>, <note>original: "hyparxis"</note>. The first principle or foundation, as it were, of the essence of a thing. Because of this, it is also the very summit of essence.

<term>IDIOM</term>, <note>original: "idiōma"</note>. The characteristic peculiarity of a thing.

<term>THE IMMORTAL</term> <gloss>1</gloss>, <note>original: "to athanaton"</note>. According to Plato, there are many levels of immortality, stretching from on high down to the very last of things; the final echo, as it were, of immortality is seen in the everlasting nature of the world’s whole bodies, which, according to the doctrine of the Eleatic Guest in the *Politicus* <note>The Statesman</note>, they receive from the Father of the universe. For both the being and the life of every body depend on another cause; since a body is not naturally suited to connect, or adorn, or preserve itself. But the immortality of individual souls, such as ours, is more obvious and more perfect than this immortality of the perpetual bodies in the universe; as is clear from the many proofs given of it in the *Phaedo*, and in the 10th book of the Re-

For the immortality of partial souls <note>A "partial soul" refers to an individual soul, such as a human soul, which is part of a larger cosmic order but retains its own identity.</note> has a more principal subsistence, as possessing in itself the cause of eternal permanency. But prior to both these is the immortality of dæmons; <note>In Platonic philosophy, "dæmons" are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings that bridge the gap between gods and humanity.</note> for these neither verge to mortality, nor are they filled with the nature of things which are generated and corrupted. More venerable, however, than these, and essentially transcending them, is the immortality of divine souls, which are primarily self-motive, and contain the fountains and principles of the life which is attributed about bodies, and through which bodies participate of renewed immortality. And prior to all these is the immortality of the gods: for Diotima in the *Banquet* <note>The *Banquet* is another name for Plato's dialogue, the *Symposium*.</note> does not ascribe an immortality of this kind to dæmons. Hence such an immortality as this is separate and exempt from wholes. For, together with the immortality of the gods, eternity subsists, which is the fountain of all immortality and life, as well that life which is perpetual, as that which is dissipated into nonentity. In short, therefore, the *divine immortal* is that which is generative and connective of perpetual life. For it is not immortal, as participating of life, but as supplying divine life, and deifying life itself.

<term>IMPARTICIPABLE</term>, <note>original: "to amethekton"</note>. That which is not consubsistent <note>Meaning it does not exist in the same shared substance or level of reality.</note> with an inferior nature. Thus imparticipable intellect is an intellect which is not consubsistent with soul.

<term>INTELLECTUAL PROJECTION</term>, <note>original: "noera epibolē"</note>. As the perception of intellect is immediate, being a darting forth, as it were, directly to its proper objects, this direct intuition is expressed by the term *projection*.

<term>THE INTELLIGIBLE</term>, <note>original: "to noēton"</note>. This word in Plato and Platonic writers has a various signification: for, in the first place, whatever is exempt from sensibles <note>Objects that can be perceived by the physical senses.</note>, and has its essence separate from them, is said to be intelligible, and in this sense soul is intelligible. In the second place, intellect, which is prior to soul, is intelligible. In the third place, that which is more ancient than intellect, which replenishes intelligence, and is essentially perfective of it, is called intelligible: and this is the intelligible, which Timæus in Plato places in the order of a paradigm <note>A "paradigm" is an ideal model or pattern from which other things are copied.</note>, prior to the demiurgic <note>The "demiurgic intellect" refers to the Divine Craftsman or Creator who shapes the physical world.</note> intellect and intellectual energy. But beyond these is the *divine intelligible*, which is defined according to divine union and hyparxis. <note>Hyparxis refers to the very summit or primary essence of a being's existence.</note> For this is intelligible as the object of desire to intellect, as giving perfection to and containing it, and as the completion of being. **SCIENCE.** This word is sometimes defined by Plato to be that which assigns the causes of things; sometimes to be that the subjects of which have a perfectly stable essence; and together with this, he conjoins the assignation of cause from reasoning. Sometimes again he defines it to be that the principles of which are not hypotheses; and, according to this definition, he asserts that there is one science which ascends as far as to the principle of things. For this science considers that which is truly the principle as unhypothetic <note>Meaning it does not rely on assumptions but on a self-evident first principle.</note>, has for its subject true being, and produces its reasonings from cause. **THE TELESTIC ART.** The art pertaining to mystic ceremonies.

**THEURGIC.** This word is derived from <note>original: θεουργια (theourgia)</note>, or that religious operation which deifies him by whom it is performed as much as is possible to man. <note>Theurgy literally means "god-work." It refers to rituals aimed at purifying the soul and uniting it with the divine.</note>

**TRUTH,** <note>original: αληθεια (aletheia)</note>. Plato, following antient theologists, considers truth multifariously. Hence, according to his doctrine, the highest truth is characterized by unity; and is the light proceeding from *the good*, which imparts purity, as he says in the *Philebus*, and union, as he says in the *Republic*, to intelligibles <note>Things that can only be understood by the mind/intellect, rather than the senses.</note>. The truth which is next to this in dignity is that which proceeds from intelligibles, and illuminates the intellectual orders, and which an essence unfigured, uncoloured, and without contact, first receives, where also the plain of truth is situated, as it is written in the *Phædrus*. The third kind of truth is that which is connascent <note>Born together or existing naturally within.</note> with souls, and which through intelligence comes into contact with true being. For the psychical light is the third from the intelligible; intellectual deriving its plenitude from intelligible light, and the psychical from the intellectual. And the last kind of truth is that which is in sensibles <note>Things perceived through the physical senses, like sight or touch.</note>, which is full of error and inaccuracy.

Dionysius he makes mention in his dialogue called **The Lovers**—that even Dionysius the school-master might not be passed over in silence by Plato. After him he employed the Argive Aristo, as his instructor in <term>gymnastic<note>In ancient Greece, this referred to physical education and athletics intended to train both the body and the character.</note></term>\*, from whom he is said to have derived the name of Plato; for prior to this he was called <term>Aristocles<note>Meaning "best glory." It was common Greek custom to name a first-born son after his grandfather.</note></term>, from his grandfather: but he was so called from having those parts of the body the breast and forehead broad in the extreme, as his statues every where evince. According to others, however, he was called <term>Plato<note>From the Greek word "platys," meaning broad, wide, or flat.</note></term> from the ample and expanded character of his style; just as they say <term>Theophrastus<note>A student of Aristotle whose name translates to "divine speaker."</note></term> was so called, from his divine eloquence, his first name being Tyrtamus.

For his preceptor in <term>music<note>In this context, music included poetry, rhythm, and all arts governed by the Muses, not just instrumental sound.</note></term> Plato had Draco, the son of Damon; and of this master he makes mention in his **Republic**. For the Athenians instructed their children in these three arts, *viz.* grammar, music, and gymnastic—and this, as it seems, with great propriety. They taught them <term>grammar<note>The study of letters, literature, and correct speech.</note></term>, for the purpose of adorning their reason; music, that they might tame their anger; and gymnastic, that they might strengthen the weak tone of desire. Alcibiades also, in Plato, appears to have been instructed in these three disciplines; and hence Socrates says to him, “But you were unwilling to play on the pipe,” &c. He was also conversant with painters, from whom he learned the mixture of colours, of which he makes mention in the **Timæus**.

After this he was instructed by the Tragedians, who at that time were celebrated as the preceptors of Greece: but he betook himself to these writers on account of the sententious and venerable nature of tragic composition, and the heroic sublimity of the subjects. He was likewise conversant with <term>Dithyrambic<note>A type of wild, emotional Greek hymn or choral song, originally sung in honor of Dionysus.</note></term> writers, with a view to the honour of <term>Bacchus<note>Also known as Dionysus, the god of wine, fertility, and theater.</note></term>, who was called by the Greeks the inspective guardian of generation: for

Anatolius the grammarian <note>A scholar of literature and language in late antiquity.</note>, once reciting this verse, very much pleased Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and craftsmanship. It is said, that when Socrates first intended to receive Plato as his disciple, he saw in a dream a swan without wings sitting on his bosom, which soon after obtaining wings flew into the air, and with the sweetness of its shrill voice allured all those that heard it. This was a manifest token of Plato’s future renown. <note>The swan was the bird of Apollo, the god of music and prophecy; this dream signified that Plato would become a great communicator of divine truths.</note>

After the death of Socrates he had another preceptor, the Heraclitean **Cratylus** <note>A follower of Heraclitus, who famously taught that all things are in a constant state of flux.</note>, upon whom he also composed a dialogue, which is inscribed *Cratylus*, or, Concerning the rectitude of names <note>This dialogue explores whether the names of things are natural or merely conventional.</note>. After he had been sufficiently instructed by this master, he again went into Italy, where finding **Archytas** re-establishing a <term>Pythagoric school</term> <note>A school of philosophy based on the teachings of Pythagoras, emphasizing mathematics, music, and the soul’s transmigration.</note>, he again had a Pythagoric preceptor of this name; and hence it is that he makes mention of Archytas. But since it is requisite that a philosopher should desire to behold the works of nature, he also went into Sicily for the purpose of viewing the eruptions of fire in Mount Ætna, and not for the sake of the **Sicilian table** <note>A common ancient idiom for luxury and gluttony, for which the Syracusan Greeks were famous.</note>, as you, O noble **Aristides** <note>Referring to Aelius Aristides, a famous 2nd-century rhetorician who criticized Plato.</note>, assert.

When he was in Syracuse with **Dionysius the Great**, who was a tyrant, he endeavoured to change the tyranny into an aristocracy <note>In the Platonic sense: a "rule by the best" or most virtuous citizens.</note>; and it was for this purpose that he visited the tyrant. But Dionysius asking him whom among men he considered as happy? (for he thought that the philosopher, employing flattery, would speak of him,) Plato answered, Socrates. Again the tyrant asked him, What do you think is the business of a politician?

Plato answered, "To make the citizens better." He [Dionysius] again asked him a third time, "What, then? Does it seem like a small matter to you to decide rightly in judicial affairs?" (for Dionysius was celebrated for deciding in such affairs with rectitude <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse prided himself on his reputation as a fair and capable judge, despite his status as an absolute ruler.</note>.) Plato answered boldly, "It is a small matter, and the least part of good conduct; for those who judge rightly resemble such as repair lacerated garments." <note>Plato’s point is that legal judgments only fix damage after it has occurred; a truly good ruler educates citizens so they do not commit crimes in the first place.</note> Again Dionysius asked him a fourth time, "Must not he who is a tyrant be brave?" Plato replied, "He is of all men the most timid; for he even dreads the razors of his barbers, lest he should be destroyed by them." <note>This refers to the legend that Dionysius was so paranoid he would not allow a barber to use a razor on his throat, preferring to have his hair and beard singed off with hot coals.</note> With these answers Dionysius was so indignant, that he ordered him to depart at sun-rise.

The following was the cause of his second journey to Sicily. When, after the death of Dionysius the tyrant, his son succeeded to the throne, who by his mother’s side was the brother of Dion <note>The family relationships here are complex: Dion was actually the brother-in-law of the elder Dionysius and the uncle of the younger Dionysius (Dionysius II).</note>, with whom Plato became acquainted in his first journey, Plato again sailed to Sicily, at the solicitations of Dion, who told him it might now be hoped that through his exertions the tyranny might be changed into an <term>aristocracy</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, an "aristocracy" is not just rule by nobles, but "rule by the best"—the most virtuous and wise citizens.</note>. However, as Dionysius had been told by some of his attendants that Plato designed to destroy him, and transfer the government to Dion, he ordered him to be taken into custody, and delivered to one Pollidis of Ægina, a Sicilian merchant, to be sold as a slave. But Pollidis, taking Plato to Ægina, found there the Libyan Anniceris, who was then on the point of sailing to Elis, for the purpose of contending with the <term>four-yoked car</term> <note>A chariot pulled by four horses, known as a *quadriga*, which was the most prestigious event in ancient Greek athletic games like the Olympics.</note>. Anniceris gladly bought Plato from Pollidis, conceiving that he should thence procure for himself greater glory than by conquering in the race. Hence Aristides <note>Likely Aelius Aristides, a famous Greek orator of the 2nd century AD who often wrote about the lives of philosophers.</note> observes, that no one would have known Anniceris, if he had not bought Plato.

The following circumstance was the occasion of Plato’s third journey to Sicily. Dion, being proscribed by Dionysius, and deprived of his possessions, was at length cast into prison. He therefore wrote to Plato, that Dionysius had promised to liberate him, if Plato would again visit him.

But Plato, in order to provide support to his companion <note>This refers to Dion, Plato’s close friend and student, who was exiled from Syracuse.</note>, readily undertook this third voyage. This concludes the account of the philosopher’s travels into Sicily.

Plato also traveled to Egypt to converse with the priests of that land, and from them he learned everything concerning sacred rituals. Because of this, in his dialogue the *Gorgias*, he says, "Not by the dog, who is regarded as a god by the Egyptians." <note>Original: "per canem". This was a famous oath used by Socrates. In Egypt, the dog (or jackal) was associated with the god Anubis, the guardian of sacred mysteries.</note> To the Egyptians, animals serve the same purpose as statues do for the Greeks; they are symbols of the various deities to which they are dedicated. Although he wished to consult with the <term>Magi</term> <note>The Magi were the priestly and scholarly class of ancient Persia, renowned for their knowledge of astronomy and theology.</note>, he was prevented by a war that broke out in Persia at that time. Instead, he went to Phoenicia, where he met with the Magi of that country and was instructed by them in their wisdom. Consequently, based on his dialogue the *Timaeus*, he appears to have been skilled in divination; for in that work he discusses the significance of the liver, the internal organs, and similar omens. These events, however, should have been mentioned before his journeys to Sicily.

When he returned to Athens, he established a school in the Academy, setting aside a portion of this <term>Gymnasium</term> <note>In ancient Athens, a gymnasium was a public space used for both physical exercise and philosophical debate.</note> to serve as a temple to the Muses. <note>The Muses were the patron goddesses of the arts, music, and intellect. By dedicating a temple to them, Plato framed philosophy as a divine, musical pursuit.</note> Here, even Timon the misanthrope <note>Timon was a legendary Athenian figure famous for his hatred of human society; that he chose to associate with Plato suggests the philosopher's exceptionally gentle or profound nature.</note> sought out Plato's company alone. Plato drew many people to the discipline of philosophy, even preparing women²—who wore male attire—to be his students. He proved that his philosophy was worthy of the greatest voluntary effort. He avoided <term>Socratic irony</term> <note>A technique where a teacher pretends to be ignorant to expose the flaws in another's logic.</note>, nor did he hold his conversations in the public marketplace or in workshops, nor did he attempt to trap young men with his arguments. Additionally, he did not adopt the solemn oath of the Pythagoreans, their habit of keeping their doors closed to the public, or their reliance on the <term>ipse dixit</term> <note>Latin: "He himself said it." This refers to the Pythagorean practice of accepting a teacher’s statement as absolute truth without further proof.</note>, as he wished to conduct himself in a more open and civic-minded manner toward all people.

When he was near death, he saw himself in a dream being transformed into a swan. This swan, by flying from tree to tree, caused great <margin>labour</margin> <note>The "swan" is a traditional symbol for Plato, representing his soul's harmony and his connection to the god Apollo. The dream is often interpreted as a sign that his philosophy would be sought after by many but difficult to fully grasp.</note>

# INTRODUCTION <note>The whole of this Introduction is extracted from the manuscript Commentary of Proclus on this dialogue, with some occasional explanations by the translator, Thomas Taylor.</note>

->---<-

**T**HE most peculiar and firm principle, says Proclus, of all the dialogues of Plato, and of the whole theory of that philosopher, is the knowledge of our own nature; for, this being properly established as an <term>hypothesis<note>A foundational assumption or starting principle.</note></term>, we shall be able accurately to learn the good which is adapted to us, and the evil which opposes this good. For, as the <term>essences<note>The fundamental "what-it-is" or core nature of a thing.</note></term> of things are different, so also are their proper perfections; and this according to a subjection of essence. For, whether *being* and *the good* proceed, as Aristotle says, from the same <term>Vesta<note>original: "Vesta" (Latin). Referring to Hestia, the goddess of the hearth, who in philosophical terms represents the stable, central essence or "fountain" of the universe.</note></term> and first fountain, it is certainly necessary that perfection should be imparted to every thing according to the measures of essence; or whether good proceeds from a cause more <term>antient<note>Archaic spelling of ancient.</note></term> and more characterized by unity, but essence and being are imparted to things from another cause; still, as every thing participates of being more obscurely and more clearly, in the same degree must it participate of good; first beings, in a greater and more perfect manner; but those that rank in the middle orders, secondarily; and the last of things according to an ultimate subsistence. For, how otherwise can things participate of <term>deity<note>Divine nature or the presence of the gods.</note></term> and providence, and a distribution according to their desert? For it must not be admitted that <term>intellect<note>Greek: *nous*. The higher faculty of the soul capable of direct intuition of truth.</note></term> can lead things into order, and impart to each a convenient measure, but that *the good*, or the ineffable principle of things, which is more antient than intellect, should make its communications in a disordered manner; <term>viz.<note>Short for "videlicet," meaning "namely" or "that is to say."</note></term> that it should impart to causes and things caused the same portion of goodness, and distribute to the same things according to being the perfections of more primary and subordinate natures. For it neither was lawful, says <term>Timæus<note>Referring to the character in Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*, who describes the creation of the cosmos by a divine craftsman.</note></term>, nor is, for the best of natures to effect any thing but that which is most beautiful and most <term>commensurate<note>Proportionate or in proper measure.</note></term>. But the same good is not most commensurate to first and secondary

# INTRODUCTION.

->---<-

natures; but, as the Athenian guest <note>The "Athenian guest" is the lead character in Plato's *Laws*, widely understood to represent Plato's own voice or a high-level philosopher-statesman.</note> says, a distribution of inequality to things unequal, and of equality to things equal, of the greater to such as are greater, and of the lesser to such as are lesser, is of all things the most musical and the best.

According to this reasoning, therefore, good is different in different beings, and a certain good is naturally co-ordinated to the essence of every thing. Hence the perfection of intellect is in eternity <gloss>For, the perceptions of intellect being intuitive, whatever it sees it sees collectively, at once, and without time.</gloss>, but of the rational soul in time: and the good of the rational soul consists in an energy <note>In Greek philosophy, "energy" (*energeia*) refers to the active state or "at-work-ness" of a thing, rather than just raw force.</note> according to intellect, but the good of body is in a subsistence according to nature; so that he who thinks that though the nature in these is different, yet the perfection is the same, has an erroneous conception of the truth of things.

According to every order of beings, therefore, essence ought to be known prior to perfection; for perfection is not of itself, but of essence, by which it is participated. Hence, with respect to the essence of a thing, we must first consider whether it belongs to <term>impartible essences<note>Natures that cannot be divided into parts, such as pure thoughts or divine minds.</note></term>, such as intellectual natures, or to such as are divisible about bodies, viz. corporeal forms and qualities, or to such as subsist between these. Likewise, whether it ranks among eternal entities, or such as subsist according to the whole of time, or such as are generated in a certain part of time. Again, whether it is simple, and subsists prior to composition, or is indeed a composite, but is always in the act of being bound with indissoluble bonds <gloss>This is the case with the sensible universe, considered as a whole.</gloss>, or may again be resolved into those things from which it is composed. For, by thus considering every thing, we shall be able to understand in what its good consists. For, again, it is evident that the good of those natures which are allotted an <term>impartible essence</term> is eternal, but that the good of partible natures is conversant with time and motion; and that the good of things subsisting between these is to be considered according to the measures of subsistence and perfection; viz. that such a nature is indeed indigent <note>Dependent upon or lacking in itself.</note> of time, but of first time, which is able to measure incorporeal periods. # INTRODUCTION.

->---<-

scientific boundaries, must, as we have said, be considered as the most proper principle of all philosophy, and of the doctrine of Plato. For, where is it proper to begin, except from the purification and perfection of ourselves, and whence the Delphic god <note>The "Delphic god" refers to Apollo, whose temple at Delphi was the center of Greek prophecy and wisdom.</note> exhorts us to begin? For, as those who enter the Eleusinian grove <note>The site of the Eleusinian Mysteries, ancient religious rites focused on the soul's journey and the afterlife.</note> are ordered by an inscription not to enter into the <term>adyta<note>The most sacred, restricted inner chambers of a temple.</note></term> of the temple, if they are uninitiated in the highest of the mysteries, so the inscription **KNOW THYSELF**, on the Delphic temple, manifests, as it appears to me, the mode of returning to a divine nature, and the most useful path to purification, all but perspicuously asserting to the intelligent, that he who knows himself beginning from the <term>Vestal hearth<note>Referring to Vesta (Hestia), goddess of the hearth; philosophically, this represents the stable, central point of the soul's essence.</note></term> may be able to be conjoined with that divinity who unfolds into light the whole of truth, and is the leader of a <term>cathartic life<note>A life focused on spiritual purification and the shedding of material distractions.</note></term>; but that he who is ignorant of himself, as being uninitiated both in the lesser and greater mysteries, is unadapted to participate the providence of Apollo. 

Hence then let us also begin conformably to the mandate of the god, and let us investigate in which of his dialogues Plato especially makes the speculation of our essence his principal design, that from hence we may also make the commencement of the Platonic writings. Can we then adduce any other writing of Plato except the *First Alcibiades*, and the conference of Socrates which is delivered in this dialogue? Where else shall we say our essence is so unfolded? Where besides are man and the nature of man investigated? To which we may add, that it is Socrates who engages in this first conversation with Alcibiades, and that it is he who says that the beginning of perfection is suspended from the contemplation of ourselves. For we are ignorant of ourselves in consequence of being involved in oblivion produced by the <term>realms of generation<note>The physical world of birth, decay, and constant change, which Neoplatonists believed caused the soul to forget its divine origins.</note></term>, and agitated by the tumult of the irrational forms of life. In the mean time, we think that we know many things of which we are ignorant, because we essentially possess innate reasons of things.

This dialogue therefore is the beginning of all philosophy, in the same manner as the knowledge of ourselves. Hence many logical and ethical theorems are scattered in it, together with such as contribute to the entire speculation of felicity <note>"Felicity" here refers to "eudaimonia" or true philosophical happiness/flourishing.</note>. It likewise contains information with respect to many things which contribute to physiology, and to those dogmas which lead us to the truth concerning divine natures themselves. Hence too the

# INTRODUCTION.

->9<-

<meta>catchword: mingled.</meta>

The divine Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who organized Plato's works into a structured curriculum for students.</note> assigned this dialogue the first rank among the ten dialogues in which he believed the entire philosophy of Plato was contained.

Of the specific details presented in this dialogue, some come before and others follow the main objective, which is the knowledge of ourselves. For the theory of **twofold ignorance** <note>Twofold ignorance occurs when someone is ignorant but is also unaware of their own ignorance; this was the condition of Alcibiades at the start of the dialogue, and it is considered a common human failing.</note>, the call to action, and similar themes come first. However, the proof of virtue and happiness, the rejection of common arts—as they are ignorant of themselves, of what belongs to them, and indeed of all things—and everything else of this nature follow in order. But the most perfect and primary goal of the entire conversation is the contemplation of our own essence. Therefore, one will not be mistaken in establishing the care and knowledge of ourselves as the ultimate purpose of this dialogue.

Furthermore, the <term>amatory<note>Relating to the "art of love" (Eros), which in Platonic philosophy refers to the soul's longing for beauty, truth, and the divine.</note></term> form of life is specifically highlighted by Socrates in this dialogue. The discussion begins from this point, and he continues to perfect the young man until he makes him a lover of divine care, which is the primary benefit of the amatory art. In short, throughout all the sections of the dialogue, he always maintains that which is suited to a life defined by philosophical love. 

Just as there are three sciences which Socrates claimed to possess—namely the <term>dialectic<note>The art of logical investigation and cross-examination to reach truth.</note></term>, the <term>maieutic<note>The "midwife" method; Socrates' technique of helping others bring their own latent ideas to birth.</note></term> (that is, **obstetric**), and the **amatory**—we will find the structure of the dialectic and the unique nature of the maieutic science in this dialogue, but the effects of the amatory science are the most prominent. For even when Socrates is drawing out the concepts of Alcibiades, he still acts in accordance with his role as a lover; and when he uses the dialectic science, he does not stray from the specific style of amatory arguments. 

This is much like in the *Theaetetus*, where he acts as a midwife and is characterized primarily by this role, proceeding as far as the purification of Theaetetus's false opinions. But, having achieved this, he dismisses him, as the young man is then able to know the truth for himself—which is the goal of the <term>maieutic science<note>The art of intellectual midwifery.</note></term>, as he himself states in that dialogue. In the same way, he first introduces the amatory science in this dialogue, with which both the dialectic and maieutic are <insert>mingled.</insert>

# INTRODUCTION.

->15<-

<meta>catchword: mingled.</meta>

mingled. For everywhere Socrates introduces discourses adapted to the subject persons. And as every kind of good pre-exists in a divine nature, which is variously possessed by different beings according to the natural aptitude of each, in like manner Socrates—who comprehends all sciences in himself—employs a different science at different times, according to the aptitude of the recipients. He elevates one through the <term>amatory science<note>The "art of love" (Eros), which Socrates uses to redirect a student's desire away from physical attraction and toward the pursuit of eternal beauty and truth.</note></term>; he excites another to the <term>reminiscence<note>The Platonic theory that learning is actually a process of "remembering" knowledge that the soul possessed before birth.</note></term> of the eternal reasons of the soul through the <term>maieutic science<note>Literally "midwifery." Socrates famously compared himself to a midwife because he did not "give birth" to wisdom himself, but helped others bring forth the ideas already latent within them.</note></term>; and he conducts another according to the <term>dialectic method<note>A process of rigorous logical questioning used to strip away false beliefs and reach certain knowledge of first principles.</note></term> to the speculation of beings. Some he conjoins to the beautiful itself, others to the first wisdom, and others to *the good itself*. For through the amatory science we are led to the beautiful; through the maieutic, by calling forth our latent reasons, we become wise in things of which we were ignorant; and through the dialectic science we ascend as far as to *the good*.

Lastly, it will be found by those who are deeply skilled in the philosophy of Plato, that each of his dialogues contains that which the universe contains. Hence, in every dialogue, one thing is analogous to *the good*, another to *intellect*, another to *soul*, another to *form*, and another to *matter*. In this dialogue therefore it must be said, that:

*   An assimilation to a divine nature is analogous to ***the good***; 
*   The knowledge of ourselves is analogous to ***intellect***; 
*   The multitude of the demonstrations leading us to the conclusion—and in short, everything <term>syllogistic<note>Relating to formal logical arguments where a conclusion is inferred from two or more premises.</note></term> in the dialogue—is analogous to ***soul***; 
*   The character of the diction, and whatever else pertains to the power of speech, is analogous to ***form***; 
*   And the persons, the occasion, and that which is called by <term>rhetoricians<note>Ancient teachers of public speaking and persuasion.</note></term> the <term>hypothesis<note>In this context, the specific circumstances or "setting" of a dialogue (the who, where, and when) rather than the general philosophical question being discussed.</note></term>, is analogous to ***matter***.

It also explains how the structure of a Platonic dialogue mirrors the layers of the universe, from physical matter to the divine "Good."</summary>
