Olympus <note>The legendary home of the Greek gods, used here to represent the highest divine realm.</note>. This middle rank of beings, considered according to a twofold division, consists of **daemons** and **heroes**, the latter of which is proximate to **partial souls** <note>Individual human souls, which are considered "partial" because they inhabit specific bodies rather than being universal.</note> such as ours, and the former to **divine natures**, just as air and water subsist between fire and earth. Hence whatever is ineffable and occult in the gods, daemons and heroes express and unfold. They likewise conciliate <note>Bring into harmony.</note> all things, and are the sources of the harmonic consent and sympathy of all things with each other. They transmit divine gifts to us, and equally carry back ours to the divinities. But the characteristics of divine natures are unity, permanency in themselves, a subsistence as an immovable cause of motion, transcendent providence, and which possesses nothing in common with the subjects of their providential energies; and these characteristics are preserved in them according to **essence, power and energy**. On the other hand, the characteristics of partial souls are, a declination to multitude and motion, a conjunction with the gods, an aptitude to receive something from other natures, and to mingle together all things in itself, and through itself; and these characteristics they also possess according to essence, power and energy. Such then being the peculiarities of the two extremes, we shall find that those of daemons are, to contain in themselves the gifts of divine natures, in a more inferior manner indeed than the gods, but yet so as to comprehend the conditions of subordinate natures, under the idea of a divine essence. In other words, the prerogatives of deity characterize, and absorb as it were by their powerful light, whatever daemons possess peculiar to inferior beings. Hence they are multiplied indeed, but unitedly—mingled, but yet so that the unmingled predominates—and are moved, but with stability. On the contrary, **heroes** possess unity, identity, permanency, and every excellence, under the condition of multitude, motion, and mixture; viz. the prerogatives of subordinate predominate in these over the characteristics of superior natures. In short, daemons and heroes are composed from the properties of the two extremes—gods and partial souls; but in daemons there is more of the divine, and in heroes more of the human nature.

Having premised thus much, the Platonic reader will, I doubt not, gratefully accept the following admirable account of daemons in general, and also of the daemon of Socrates, from the Manuscript Commentary of **Proclus** <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note> on this dialogue.

For it is always requisite that demonstrations should begin from things more universal, and proceed from these as far as to individuals. For this mode of proceeding is natural, and is more adapted to science. Daemons therefore, deriving their first subsistence from the **vivific goddess** <note>original: "Juno" (Hera). In Neoplatonism, Hera/Juno is often identified as the "Life-generating" or "Vivific" goddess who oversees the soul's entrance into the world.</note>, and flowing from thence as from a certain fountain, are allotted an essence characterized by soul. This essence in those of a superior order is more intellectual and more perfect according to **hyparxis** <note>original: "ὕπαρξις". This term refers to the "summit of essence" or the primary existence of a thing, its very foundation of being.</note>; in those of a middle order, it is more rational; and in those which rank in the third degree, and which subsist at the extremity of the daemonic—

Possessing therefore an essence of this kind, they are distributed in conjunction with the gods, as being allotted a power ministrant to deity. Hence they are in one way subservient to the **liberated gods** <note>original Greek: *apolytoi theoi*. These are deities who exist above the physical world and are not bound by its laws.</note>, who are the leaders of wholes prior to the world; and in another to the **mundane gods** <note>Gods who oversee the physical cosmos and the movements of the planets.</note>, who proximately preside over the parts of the universe. For there is one division of daemons, according to the twelve supercelestial gods, and another according to all the <term>idioms</term> <note>The unique characteristics or essential properties that define a specific type of divinity.</note> of the mundane gods. For every mundane god is the leader of a certain daemonical order, to which he proximately imparts his power; viz. if he is a **demiurgic god** <note>A deity involved in the 'demiurgy' or the practical crafting and ordering of the material world.</note>, he imparts a demiurgic power; if **immutable**, an undefiled power; if **telesiurgic** <note>Relating to 'telestic' or perfecting power—the ability to complete or initiate a soul into its highest state.</note>, a perfective power. And about each of the divinities there is an innumerable multitude of daemons, and which are dignified with the same appellations as their leading gods. Hence they rejoice when they are called by the names of Jupiter, Apollo, and Hermes, &c. as expressing the idiom or peculiarity of their proper deities. And from these, mortal natures also participate of divine influxions. And thus animals and plants are fabricated, bearing the images of different gods; daemons proximately imparting to these the representations of their leaders. But the gods in an exempt manner supernally preside over daemons; and through this, last natures sympathize with such as are first. For the representations of first are seen in last natures; and the causes of things last are comprehended in primary beings. The middle <term>genera</term> <note>The plural of 'genus,' referring to the various classes or types of beings.</note> too of daemons give completion to wholes, the communion of which they bind and connect; participating indeed of the gods, but participated by mortal natures. He therefore will not err who asserts that the mundane artificer established the centres of the order of the universe in daemons; since Diotima <note>A female philosopher mentioned in Plato's 'Symposium' who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love as a great daemon.</note> also assigns them this order, that of binding together divine and mortal natures, of deducing supernal streams, elevating all secondary natures to the gods, and giving completion to wholes through the connexion of a medium. We must not therefore assent to their doctrine, who say that daemons are the souls of men that have changed the present life. For it is not proper to consider a daemoniacal nature **according to habitude** <note>original Greek: *kata schesin*. This refers to a state or relationship a soul might temporarily enter into, rather than its permanent, essential nature.</note> as the same with a nature essentially daemoniacal; nor to assert that the perpetual medium of all mundane natures consists from a life conversant with multiform mutations. For a daemoniacal guard subsists always the same, connecting the mundane wholes; but soul does not always thus retain its own order, as Socrates says in the *Republic*; since at different times it chooses different lives. Nor do we praise those who make certain of the gods to be daemons, such as the erratic gods <note>The planets, which were called 'erratic' or 'wandering' stars in antiquity.</note>, according to Amelius <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note>; but we are persuaded by Plato, who calls the gods the rulers of the universe, but subjects to them the herds of daemons; and we shall every where preserve the doctrine of Diotima, who assigns the middle order, between all divine and mortal natures, to a daemoniacal essence. Let this then be the conception respecting the whole of the daemoniacal order in common.

> “In the next place let us speak concerning the **daemons** <note>In this context, 'daemons' refers to the Neoplatonic hierarchy of spiritual intermediaries that bridge the gap between the absolute 'Gods' and the material world of 'Men.'</note> which are allotted mankind. For of these daemons, which as we have said rank in the middle order, the first and highest are divine daemons, and who often appear as gods, through their transcendent similitude to the divinities. For, in short, that which is first in every order preserves the form of the nature prior to itself. Thus, the first intellect is a god, and the most ancient of souls is intellectual: and hence of daemons the highest genus, as being proximate to the gods, is uniform and divine. The next to these in order are those daemons who participate of an **intellectual idiom** <note>A specific characteristic or essential property belonging to the realm of pure Thought or Mind (Intellect).</note>, and preside over the ascent and descent of souls, and who unfold into light and deliver to all things the productions of the gods. The third are those who distribute the productions of divine souls to secondary natures, and complete the bond of those that receive **defluxions** <note>The 'flowing down' or emanation of divine influence and energy from higher levels of reality to lower ones.</note> from thence. The fourth are those that transmit the efficacious powers of whole natures to things generated and corrupted, and who inspire partial natures with life, order, reasons, and the all-various perfect operations which things mortal are able to effect. The fifth are corporeal, and bind together the extremes in bodies. For, how can perpetual accord with corruptible bodies, and efficients with effects, except through this medium? For it is this ultimate middle nature which has dominion over corporeal goods, and provides for all natural prerogatives. The sixth in order are those that revolve about matter, connect the powers which descend from celestial to sublunary matter, perpetually guard this matter, and defend the shadowy representation of forms which it contains.

> “Daemons therefore, as **Diotima** <note>A female philosopher mentioned in Plato's 'Symposium' who taught Socrates about the nature of Love and the hierarchy of spirits.</note> also says, being many and all-various, the highest of them conjoin souls proceeding from their father, to their leading gods: for every god, as we have said, is the leader in the first place of daemons, and in the next of partial souls. For the **Demiurgus** <note>The 'Craftsman' or creator deity who fashions the physical universe according to divine patterns.</note> disseminated these, as **Timaeus** <note>Referring to the character in Plato’s dialogue 'Timaeus' who describes the creation of the world.</note> says, into the sun and moon, and the other instruments of time. These divine daemons, therefore, are those which are essentially allotted to souls, and conjoin them to their proper leaders: and every soul, though it revolves together with its leading deity, requires a daemon of this kind. But daemons of the second rank preside over the ascensions and descensions of souls; and from these the souls of the multitude derive their elections. For the most perfect souls, who are conversant with generation in an undefiled manner, as they choose a life conformable to their presiding god, so they live according to a divine daemon, who conjoined them to their proper deity when they dwelt on high. Hence the Egyptian priest admired **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. This refers to a famous story where a priest attempted to evoke Plotinus's guardian spirit and found it was a 'god' rather than a standard 'daemon.'</note>, as being governed by a divine daemon. To souls therefore who live as those that will shortly return to the **intelligible world** <note>The higher realm of true reality and pure ideas, as opposed to the physical world of the senses.</note> whence they came, the supernal is the same with the daemon which attends them here; but to imperfect souls the essential is different from the daemon that attends them at their birth.

> “If these things then are rightly asserted, we must not assent to those who make our rational soul a daemon. And I find, that, though they have been numerous, and such persons too as <note>The text refers to the wealthy and influential suitors who pursued the young Alcibiades for his beauty and status.</note> thought highly of themselves, there is not one whom <meta>catchword: whom</meta> detains me.” <note>This concludes the sentence from the previous page: while other admirers have left now that Alcibiades is older, Socrates remains because his interest is in Alcibiades’ soul, not just his appearance.</note> But man is a soul using the body as an instrument. > “This also is evident from **Plato** in the ***Timaeus***, where he says that intellect has in us the relation of a <term>daemon</term>. But this is only true as far as pertains to analogy. For a <term>daemon</term> according to essence is different from a <term>daemon</term> according to analogy. For in many instances that which proximately presides, subsisting in the order of a <term>daemon</term> with respect to that which is inferior, is called a <term>daemon</term>. Thus **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> in **Orpheus** calls his father **Saturn** <note>The Roman name for Cronus.</note> an illustrious <term>daemon</term>; and **Plato**, in the ***Timaeus***, calls those gods who proximately preside over, and orderly distribute the realms of generation, <term>daemons</term>: ‘for,’ says he, ‘to speak concerning other <term>daemons</term>, and to know their generation, exceeds the ability of human nature.’ But a <term>daemon</term> according to analogy is that which proximately presides over any thing, though it should be a god, or though it should be some one of the natures posterior to the gods. And the soul through similitude to the dæmoniacal genus produces energies more wonderful than those which belong to human nature, and which suspends the whole of its life from <term>daemons</term>, is a <term>daemon</term> *according to habitude* <note>original: "κατα σχεσιν" (kata schesin). This refers to a relationship or proximity rather than being a daemon by nature.</note>, i. e. proximity or alliance. Thus, as it appears to me, **Socrates** in the ***Republic*** calls those, <term>daemons</term>, who have lived well, and who in consequence of this are transferred to a better condition of being, and to more holy places. But an essential <term>daemon</term> is neither called a <term>daemon</term> through habitude to secondary natures, nor through an assimilation to something different from itself; but is allotted this peculiarity from himself, and is defined by a certain summit, or flower of essence, (<term>hyparxis</term> <note>A Neoplatonic term for the very core or 'pure existence' of a being, its most fundamental reality.</note>,) by appropriate powers, and by different modes of energies. In short, the rational soul is called in the ***Timaeus*** the <term>daemon</term> of the animal. But we investigate the <term>daemon</term> of man, and not of the animal; that which governs the rational soul itself, and not its instrument; and that which leads the soul to its judges, after the dissolution of the animal, as **Socrates** says in the ***Phaedo***. For, when the animal is no more, the <term>daemon</term> which the soul was allotted while connected with the body, conducts it to its judge. For, if the soul possesses that <term>daemon</term> while living in the body, which is said to lead it to judgment after death, this <term>daemon</term> must be the <term>daemon</term> of the man, and not of the animal alone. To which we may add, that, beginning from on high, it governs the whole of our composition.

> “Nor again, dismissing the rational soul, must it be said that a <term>daemon</term> is that which energizes in the soul: as, for instance, that in those who live according to reason, reason is the <term>daemon</term>; in those that live according to anger, the irascible part; and in those that live <meta>catchword: according</meta>

according to desire, the desiderative part. <note>In Platonic philosophy, the soul is divided into three parts: the rational, the "irascible" (spirited/emotional), and the "desiderative" (appetitive/desiring).</note> Nor must it be said that the nature which proximately presides over that which energizes in our life, is a <term>daemon</term> <note>original: dæmon; a guardian spirit or intermediary being between gods and humans</note>: as, for instance, that reason is the <term>daemon</term> of the irascible, and anger of those that live according to desire. For, in the first place, to assert that <term>daemons</term> are parts of our soul, is to admire human life in an improper degree, and oppose the division of **Socrates** in the ***Republic***, who after gods and <term>daemons</term> places the heroic and human race, and blames the poets for introducing in their poems heroes in no respect better than men, but subject to similar passions. By this accusation, therefore, it is plain that **Socrates** was very far from thinking that <term>daemons</term>, who are of a sublimer order than heroes, are to be ranked among the parts and powers of the soul. For from this doctrine it will follow that things more excellent according to essence give completion to such as are subordinate. And in the second place, from this hypothesis, mutations of lives would also introduce multiform mutations of <term>daemons</term>. For the avaricious character is frequently changed into an ambitious life, this again into a life which is formed by right opinion, and this last into a scientific life. The <term>daemon</term> therefore will vary according to these changes: for the energizing part will be different at different times. If, therefore, either this energizing part itself is a <term>daemon</term>, or that part which has an arrangement prior to it, <term>daemons</term> will be changed together with the mutation of human life, and the same person will have many <term>daemons</term> in one life; which is of all things the most impossible. For the soul never changes in one life the government of its <term>daemon</term>; but it is the same <term>daemon</term> which presides over us till we are brought before the judges of our conduct, as also **Socrates** asserts in the ***Phaedo***.

“ Again, those who consider a partial intellect, or that intellect which subsists at the extremity of the intellectual order, as the same with the <term>daemon</term> which is assigned to man, appear to me to confound the intellectual <term>idiom</term> <note>A specific characteristic or property.</note> with the daemonical essence. For all <term>daemons</term> subsist in the extent of souls, and rank as the next in order to divine souls; but the intellectual order is different from that of soul, and is neither allotted the same essence, nor power, nor energy.

“ Further still: this also may be said, that souls enjoy intellect then only when they convert themselves to it, receive its light, and conjoin their own with intellectual energy; but they experience the presiding care of a daemonical nature through the whole of life, and in every thing which proceeds from fate and providence. For it is the <term>daemon</term> that governs the whole of our life, and that fulfils the elections which we made prior to generation, together with the gifts of fate, and of those gods that preside over fate. It is likewise the <term>daemon</term> that supplies and measures the illuminations from providence. And as souls, indeed, we are suspended from intellect,

Hence **Plato**, in the ***Phaedrus***, calls intellect the governor of the soul; but he everywhere calls a <term>daemon</term> the inspector and guardian of mankind. And no one who considers the affair rightly, will find any other one and proximate providence of everything pertaining to us, besides that of a <term>daemon</term>. For intellect, as we have said, is shared by the rational soul, but not by the body; and nature is shared by the body, but not by the <term>reasoning part</term> <note>original: dianoëtic part; the aspect of the soul that engages in logical, step-by-step thinking</note>. And further still, the rational soul rules over anger and desire, but it has no dominion over accidental events. But the <term>daemon</term> alone moves, governs, and orderly disposes, all our affairs. For he gives perfection to reason, measures the passions, inspires nature, connects the body, supplies things that happen by chance, accomplishes the decrees of fate, and imparts the gifts of providence. In short, he is the king of everything in and about us, and is the pilot of the whole of our life. And thus much concerning our allotted <term>daemons</term>.

“In the next place, with respect to the <term>daemon</term> of **Socrates**, these three things are to be particularly considered. First, that he not only ranks as a <term>daemon</term>, but also as a god: for in the course of this dialogue he clearly says, ‘I have long been of opinion that the *god* did not as yet direct me to hold any conversation with you.’

“He calls the same power, therefore, a <term>daemon</term> and a god. And in the ***Apology*** he more clearly demonstrates that this <term>daemon</term> is granted a divine excellence, even while being ranked within a <term>daemon-like</term> nature. And this is what we before said, that the <term>daemons</term> of divine souls, and those who choose a life of intellect and <term>upward-leading</term> <note>original: anagogic; referring to a spiritual path that leads the soul back to the divine source</note> power, are themselves divine, surpassing the whole of the <term>daemon</term> kind, and being the first participants of the gods. For, just as a <term>daemon</term> is among the gods, so also is a god among <term>daemons</term>. But among the divinities, the <term>essential existence</term> <note>original: hyparxis; the foundational reality or 'flower' of a being's existence</note> is divine; but in <term>daemons</term>, on the contrary, the <term>characteristic nature</term> <note>original: idiom</note> of their essence is <term>daemon-like</term>, but the relationship which they bear to divinity shows their essence to be godlike. For, because they surpass other spirits, they frequently appear as gods. With great propriety, therefore, does **Socrates** call his <term>daemon</term> a god: for he belonged to the first and highest spirits. Hence **Socrates** was most perfect, being governed by such a presiding power, and conducting himself by the will of such a leader and guardian of his life. This then was one of the illustrious privileges of the <term>daemon</term> of **Socrates**. The second was this: that **Socrates** perceived a certain voice proceeding from his <term>daemon</term>. For this is asserted by him in the ***Theaetetus*** and in the ***Phaedrus***. And this voice is the signal from the <term>daemon</term>, which he speaks of in the ***Theages***: and again in the ***Phaedrus***, when he was about to pass over the river, he experienced the accustomed signal from the <term>daemon</term>. What, then, does **Socrates** indicate by these assertions, and what was the voice through which he says the <term>daemon</term> signified to him his will?

For it is evident that reason, imagination, and sense, enjoy the same energy differently; and that each of our inward parts is passive to, and is moved by, the <term>daemon</term> in a peculiar manner. The voice, therefore, did not act upon **Socrates** externally with passivity; but the daemonical inspiration, proceeding inwardly through his whole soul, and diffusing itself as far as to the organs of sense, became at last a voice, which was rather recognized by <term>internal consciousness</term> <note>original: "συναισθησις" (synaisthesis); a type of inner awareness where the soul perceives its own states</note> than by sense: for such are the illuminations of good <term>daemons</term>, and the gods.

> “In the third place, let us consider the peculiarity of the <term>daemon</term> of **Socrates**: for it never exhorted <note>urged him forward to act</note>, but perpetually recalled <note>restrained or stopped him from acting</note> him. This also must again be referred to the Socratic life: for it is not a property common to our allotted <term>daemons</term>, but was the characteristic of the guardian of **Socrates**. We must say, therefore, that the beneficent and philanthropic disposition of **Socrates**, and his great promptitude with respect to the communication of good, did not require the exhortation of the <term>daemon</term>. For he was impelled from himself, and was ready at all times to impart to all men the most excellent life. But since many of those that came to him were unadapted to the pursuit of virtue and the science of wholes, his governing good <term>daemon</term> restrained him from a providential care of such as these. Just as a good charioteer alone restrains the impetus of a horse naturally well adapted for the race, but does not stimulate him, in consequence of his being excited to motion from himself, and not requiring the spur, but the bridle. And hence **Socrates**, from his great readiness to benefit those with whom he conversed, rather required a recalling than an exciting <term>daemon</term>. For the unaptitude of auditors, which is for the most part concealed from human sagacity, requires a daemoniacal discrimination; and the knowledge of favourable opportunities can by this alone be accurately announced to us. **Socrates** therefore being naturally impelled to good, alone required to be recalled in his unreasonable impulses.

> “But further still, it may be said, that of <term>daemons</term>, some are allotted a purifying and undefiled power; others a generative; others a perfective; and others a demiurgic <note>creative or world-building</note> power: and, in short, they are divided according to the characteristic peculiarities of the gods, and the powers under which they are arranged. Each, likewise, according to his <term>hyparxis</term> <note>the essential core or "flower" of a being's existence</note>, incites the object of his providential care to a blessed life; some of them moving us to an attention to inferior concerns; and others restraining us from action, and an energy verging to externals. It appears, therefore, that the <term>daemon</term> of **Socrates** being allotted this peculiarity, viz. <term>cathartic</term> <note>purifying</note>, and the source of an undefiled life, and being arranged under this power of **Apollo** <note>the Greek god of truth, prophecy, and healing, often associated with the purification of the soul in Neoplatonism</note>, and uniformly presiding over the whole of purification, separated also **Socrates** from too much commerce with the vulgar, and a life extending itself into multitude. But it led him into the depths of his soul, and an energy undefiled by subordinate natures: and hence it never exhorted, but perpetually recalled him.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Socrates’ address to Alcibiades. On the previous page, Socrates listed the worldly advantages—beauty, birth, and wealth—that have made Alcibiades arrogant. This page transitions into a deeper philosophical explanation of why we are attracted to such things, interpreting them as echoes of divine principles.</meta>

do on any other. Elevated as you are in your own mind on these accounts, you have looked down on your admirers: and they, conscious of their comparative meanness, have bowed their heads, and have retired.

But, assuming a more elevated opening, let us consider from what concepts souls become so much attached to beauty and magnitude <note>In this context, magnitude refers to "greatness" or "stature," both physical and social.</note> of body, to nobility, and power: for these are images extended to souls of realities themselves, which the intelligent despise, but the stupid embrace with greediness. We must say, therefore, that beauty and magnitude appear in the first of the divine orders;—the former rendering all divine natures lovely, and desirable to secondary beings; and the latter causing them to transcend worldly wholes, and to be exempt from their own offspring. For magnitude, according to Plato, considered as a divine idea, is that cause by which every where one thing transcends another. Of those two great principles likewise, *bound* and *infinity* <note>These are the Pythagorean and Platonic principles of "Limit" (the defining, ordering force) and the "Unlimited" (the expansive, raw potential of the universe).</note>, which are next in dignity and power to the ineffable principle of things, *bound* is the source of beauty, and *infinity* of magnitude. Hence the alliance of beauty to the former, as being the "form of forms," and as swimming on the light of all intelligible forms; but of magnitude to the latter, from its incomprehensibility, from its embracing all things and subduing all things. From the first principles, therefore, beauty and magnitude proceed through all the middle orders, as far as to the visible world, which, according to the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato regarding the creation of the universe.</note>, they perfectly render the greatest and the most beautiful of sensible gods <note>The "sensible gods" are the celestial bodies and the living universe itself, which can be perceived by the senses.</note>. Souls therefore, according to their spontaneous innate conceptions, assume beforehand that these shine forth in divine natures; and hence they admire beauty and magnitude in mortal bodies, as possessing a resemblance of their divine originals. However, through their ignorance of the true archetypes, they are held back by, and alone admire, the obscure and fleeting imitations of real beauty and magnitude.

In the second place, with respect to nobility, this also first exists in divine natures. For things which derive their existence from more elevated causes transcend according to their kind those which are generated in secondary ranks. This is also evident from Homer, who makes Juno say to Jupiter:

->....... thence is my race derived, whence thine :<-
<note>original: "ἔνθεν γένος ἐστὶν ἐμοί, ὅθεν σοί" - Iliad, Book 4. Juno (Hera) asserts her equal status to Jupiter (Zeus) because they share the same parentage (Cronus and Rhea).</note>

and in consequence of this she wishes to possess an equal dominion in the universe with Jupiter. According to this conception, you may also say that in us the rational is more noble than the irrational soul, because, according to Plato in the *Timaeus*, the creator of the universe gave existence to the former—but the junior gods, or those powers that preside over the celestial spheres, to the latter. Natural succession is the image of this nobility; to which when souls alone direct their attention, they become filled with vain conceptions, and are ignorant of what Plato asserts in the *Theaetetus*, that it is by no means wonderful, in the infinity of time past, if he who is able to count twenty-five noble ancestors, should find, by ascending higher in antiquity, that these progenitors were descended from as many slaves. But the stable and perpetual alliance of souls is suspended from divine natures, about which they are spread, and from divine powers under which they are arranged. For the attendants of more exalted deities are more noble, as likewise are those powers which are suspended from greater divinities, according to their assigned place in the universe.—T. <note>The "T." indicates Thomas Taylor, the translator and commentator.</note>

-># THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.<-

**ALC.** Certainly it must.
**SOC.** Consider thoughtfully now, and tell me, What is the end or aim of that which is done best in the making or the continuing of peace, and likewise in the going to war with those with whom it is proper?
**ALC.** Well, I do consider; but cannot think of what it is.
**SOC.** Know you not, when we go to war, what it is which both the parties accuse each other of during their military preparations, and what names they give to the causes of their quarrels?
**ALC.** I do. They accuse each other of deceiving, or of offering violence, or of taking away some of their possessions.
**SOC.** But observe: How do they say they have been thus treated? Try to tell me what difference there is in the manner of this treatment they give to each other.
**ALC.** Do you mean, whether they thus treat each other justly or unjustly?
**SOC.** This is the very difference I mean.
**ALC.** These different manners of ill treatment differ totally and entirely.
**SOC.** Well then. With whom would you counsel the Athenians to engage in war? whether with those who treat them ill unjustly, or with those who treat them as they deserve?
**ALC.** A question, this, of very serious import. For, if any man should entertain a thought of the propriety of going to war with such as act uprightly, he would not dare to own it.
**SOC.** Because it is not lawful, I suppose, to engage in such a war.
**ALC.** By no means is it so, neither seems it to be beautiful <note>In ancient Greek philosophy, the "beautiful" (*kalon*) often refers to what is morally noble, honorable, or fine, rather than just physical appearance.</note>.
**SOC.** With a view therefore to these things <gloss>1</gloss>, and to what is just, you will make your speeches to the people.

---

<gloss>1</gloss> *These things* evidently mean the *lawful* and the *beautiful*, mentioned immediately before. The sentence in the original, as printed, is this: "therefore, with a view to these things, you also will make your speeches concerning the just" <note>original Greek: προς ταυτ’ αρα και συ το δικαιον της λογες ποιηση</note>. In which the words *and you* are undoubtedly transposed <note>A "transposition" is a common error in copying ancient manuscripts where the order of words is accidentally swapped.</note>, and should be read *you and*. The transposition not being discovered by Stephens <note>Henri Estienne, also known as Stephanus, was a famous 16th-century printer whose edition of Plato's works became the international standard for page numbering.</note> obliged him to change the word *these things* into *this*, as belonging to *the just*, and therefore made to agree with it. This alteration supposes *lawful* and *beautiful*, to be words merely synonymous with *just*, consequently superfluous, and introduced to no purpose. The transposition must have been more ancient than any manuscript of Plato now remaining; for it has corrupted not only the oldest editions, but the oldest translations too; affecting of course all those which came after. — S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

**SOC.** I think that you would, if you had discovered it by yourself.
**ALC.** Are you then of opinion that I could not have discovered it by myself?
**SOC.** I am entirely of opinion that you might, if ever you had sought for it.
**ALC.** Do you presume, then, that I have never sought for it?
**SOC.** I should presume that you had, if ever you had thought yourself ignorant of it.
**ALC.** Was there not then a time when I so thought?

**SOC.** And how is it now on the subject of **justice**? Do you find the multitude agreeing one with another, or even the same person always of the same mind, concerning either men or actions—who are the honest, or what is just?

**ALC.** It is.

--- Page 181 ---
<meta>This page continues the logical progression of the dialogue from page 42. Socrates is using a simple mathematical analogy to prove a point of logic: that the person answering a question is the one actually making the claim, not the person asking it. This forces Alcibiades to admit that he has effectively confessed his own ignorance.</meta>

-># THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.<-

**SOC.** How much greater is it?
**ALC.** Greater by one.
**SOC.** Now whether of us is it who says that two is a greater number or more than one by one?
**ALC.** It is I myself.
**SOC.** Did not I ask the question, and did not you give an answer to it?
**ALC.** True: it was so.
**SOC.** On this subject, then, who appears to have made any assertion? Do I, who only asked a question? or do you, who gave the answer?
**ALC.** I.
**SOC.** And if I ask you how many letters compose the name of **Socrates**, and you tell me, which of us is it who declares how many?
**ALC.** I.
**SOC.** In a word, whenever any question is asked, and an answer to it is given, say, who is it that makes an assertion, the party that asks the question, or the party that gives the answer?
**ALC.** The party that gives the answer, in my opinion, **Socrates**.
**SOC.** Through the whole of our past discourse was not I the party that asked the questions?
**ALC.** You was. <note>In the 18th century, "you was" was a common grammatical form for the singular "you," though it sounds incorrect to modern ears.</note>

**Soc.** And such as have no opinion of their own knowledge in the affair resign it up to others to act for them.

**ALC.** How should they do otherwise?

**Soc.** Ignorant persons of this kind live therefore without committing errors, because they give up the management of those affairs in which they are ignorant into the hands of others.

**ALC.** True.

**Soc.** What kind of persons, then, are those who err and act amiss? for certainly they are not such as know how to act.

**ALC.** By no means.

**Soc.** Since then they are neither the knowing, nor those of the ignorant who know that they are ignorant, are any other persons left than of that kind who are ignorant, but imagine themselves knowing?

**ALC.** None other than these.

**Soc.** This kind of ignorance, therefore, is the cause of wrong doings, and is the only kind which is culpable. <note>culpable: deserving of blame or censure.</note>

**ALC.** Very true.

**Soc.** And where it concerns things of greatest moment, is it not in these cases the most of any mischievous and shameful?

**ALC.** By far the most so ¹.

**Soc.** Well then. Can you name any things of greater moment than those which are honest, and beautiful, and good, and advantageous?

**ALC.** Certainly none.

**Soc.** Is it not on these subjects that you acknowledge yourself to waver in your opinions?

**ALC.** It is.

-># THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.<-

**Soc.** And, if you are thus wavering, is it not evident from our past conclusions, not only that you are ignorant in subjects of the greatest moment, but that amidst this ignorance you imagine that you know them?

**ALC.** I fear it is so.

**Soc.** For shame, Alcibiades! What a condition then are you in! a condition which I am loath to name: but however, since we are alone, it must be spoken out. You are involved, my good sir, in that kind of ignorance which is the most shameful, according to the result of our joint reasoning, and according to your own confession. From this kind of ignorance it is, that you are eager to engage in politics before you have learnt the elements of that science. Indeed, you are not the only person in this sad condition; for in the same state of ignorance are the numerous managers of our civil affairs, all of them, except perhaps *Pericles*, your guardian, and a few more.

**ALC.** And, *Socrates*, to confirm this opinion of yours, *Pericles* is said to have become wise, not spontaneously or of himself: on the contrary, 'tis reported of him that he had had the advantage of enjoying the conversation of many wise men, particularly of *Pythoclides* and *Anaxagoras* ¹: and even at this time, old as he is, he is intimate with *Damon* for this very purpose.

**Soc.** But what? have you ever seen a man who was wise in any art whatever, and yet was unable to make another man wise in the same art?

***

¹ The character of *Anaxagoras*, or rather that of his philosophy, is well known to be this: That he applied himself chiefly, as all of the Ionic sect <note>The Ionian school of philosophy focused on the physical nature of the universe rather than ethics.</note> did, to the study of astronomy, and of the elements of outward nature. *Pythoclides* and *Damon*, both of them, were such as the old Sophists <note>Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece who specialized in using tools of philosophy and rhetoric to teach "excellence" or "virtue."</note> in polymathy <note>polymathy: wide-ranging knowledge or learning.</note> and extensive learning; but neither of them assumed the character of Sophist. Indeed, they were so far from making a public display of their general knowledge, like the Sophists, that, on the contrary, they endeavoured to conceal it under the mask of some other character, professing only skill in music. We learn this, so far as relates to *Damon*, from *Plutarch*, in his *Life of Pericles*; and with regard to *Pythoclides*, we are told the same by *Plato* himself in his *Protagoras*. But further, *Aristotle*, as cited by *Plutarch*, relates, in some of those works of his which are most unfortunately lost, that *Pericles* in fact became accomplished in music by studying it under *Pythoclides*. And *Plutarch* tells us, on his own authority, that *Damon* was the director and instructor of *Pericles* in politics, and that he was banished from *Athens* by the people, as a meddler and a friend of tyranny <note>original: ὡς μεγαλοπράγμων καὶ φιλοτύραννος</note>, as a person who busied himself in great affairs, meaning those relating to the constitution of the state, and as a friend to tyranny, meaning the arbitrary power of a single person. —S. <note>The "S." likely identifies the note as belonging to the translator, Thomas Sydenham.</note>

**SOC.** You offer an affront, not only to the regard which I have for you, but to the opinion too which you have of yourself.

**ALC.** How so?

**SOC.** In that you think of entering the lists to contend with these men here at Athens.

-># THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.<-

**ALC.** Whom then am I to contend with?

**Soc.** Does this question become a man to ask who thinks his mind to be great and elevated $^1$?

**ALC.** How do you mean? Is it not with these very persons <note>Referring to the typical uneducated Athenian politicians discussed on the previous page.</note> that I am to stand in competition?

**Soc.** Let me ask you this question;—Whether, if you had any thoughts of commanding a ship of war, would you deem it sufficient for you to excel the mariners who were to be under your command, in the skill belonging to a commander? or, presuming yourself qualified with this due excellence <term>præ-excellence</term> <note>A term for being superior to others or excelling them in rank or skill.</note>, would you direct your eye to those only whom you are in fact to combat against,—and not, as you now do, to such as are to combat together with you? For to these men certainly $^2$ you ought to be so much superior, that they should never be your associates in competition against any, but your inferior assistants in combating against the enemy;—if you really think of exhibiting any noble exploits worthy of yourself and of your country.

**ALC.** And such a thought I assure you that I entertain.

**Soc.** Is it then at all worthy of you, to be contented with being a better man than your fellow-soldiers $^3$,—and not to have your eye directed toward the leaders of those whom you have to struggle with, studying how $^4$ to become a better man than they, and employing yourself in exercises which are proper with a view to them $^5$?

***

$^1$ The printer Aldus <note>original: "Aldus Manutius," a famous 15th-century Venetian printer.</note> erroneously printed this sentence in the Greek original without a mark of interrogation; and in this error he was blindly followed by Stephens <note>original: "Henri Estienne," a renowned 16th-century scholar-printer.</note>. The Basel editions <note>Scholarly editions printed in Basel, Switzerland.</note>, however, both of them, are here rightly printed, in agreement with the translations by Ficino <note>original: "Ficinus," referring to Marsilio Ficino, who translated Plato into Latin in the 15th century.</note> and Cornarius <note>original: "Cornarius," referring to Janus Cornarius, a 16th-century German scholar.</note>, and as the sense evidently requires.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Thomas Sydenham.</note>

$^2$ Here again the two Basel editions are right in giving us "certainly" <note>original Greek: "δη που" (dē pou)</note>; where Aldus and Stephens have been so regardless of the sense as to print "it is necessary" <note>original Greek: "δει που" (dei pou)</note>.—S.

$^3$ In the Greek, as printed, we here read "soldiers" <note>original: "στρατιωτων" (stratiōtōn)</note>; but perhaps we ought to read "fellow-soldiers" <note>original: "συστρατιωτων" (systratiōtōn)</note>, so that the word may correspond with the one just before to which it refers, "fellow-competitors" <note>original: "συναγωνιστας" (synagōnistat).</note>.—S.

$^4$ In the Greek editions it reads "when" or "since" <note>original: "ὁποτε" (hopote)</note>: but we suppose the right reading to be "how" <note>original: "ὁπως" (hopōs)</note>.—S.

$^5$ All the Latin translators rightly presume this sentence to be a question: though in all the editions of the Greek it is carelessly made into a statement. The secret meaning of Socrates in what he here says, according to the spirit of all his philosophy, we understand to be this:—that we ought not to use the characters of any specific men, who are all full of imperfections like ourselves, as the standards for our moral conduct; but we should keep constantly in our view, so as to copy them, the ideal and perfect patterns of moral excellence.—S.

**ALC.** The opinion without doubt of their being formidable.

---

<gloss>1</gloss> We are astonished to find <term>pheses <note>original: "φησεις", which means "you will say"</note></term> here printed in all the editions of Plato. The sense evidently requires us to read <term>physeis <note>original: "φυσεις", meaning "natures" or "natural dispositions"</note></term>: and it appears also from the Latin translation made by Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin.</note>, and from that also by Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius (1500–1558), a German humanist and editor of Greek texts.</note>, that they read <term>physeis</term> in the manuscripts from which they made their translations.—Had Le Fevre <note>Tanneguy Le Fèvre (1615–1672), a French classical scholar known for his critiques of ancient texts.</note> been aware of this, he would have spared himself the trouble of writing a long note to prove that hereditary monarchs and great lords are not always the best of men.—Socrates here is not asking who probably are the best men, (for this would be to anticipate the conclusion of his reasoning, in the very beginning of it,) but, who probably have the best natural dispositions.—S. <note>"S." refers to the English translator, Thomas Sydenham.</note>

<gloss>2</gloss> With this agrees the opinion of Aristotle in his Politics, book 3. chapter 8. <note>original Greek: "Βελτιους εικος τους εκ βελτιονων· ευγενεια γαρ εστιν αρετη γενους."</note> *It is likely that from the best ancestors should spring the best men. For to be well-born is to be of a good or virtuous family, (that is, nobility is family-virtue.)* The reasonableness of this opinion the great master of all lyric poetry <note>The Roman poet Horace.</note> proves by analogy from brute animals in these verses of the 4th ode of his 4th book:

> ->*Brave men are born from the brave and good.* <note>original Latin: "Fortes creantur fortibus et bonis."</note><-
> ->*In steers and horses the virtue of their sires* <note>original Latin: "Est in juvencis, est in equis patrum / Virtus"</note><-

This heated paper we may compare to a certain relation of inferiors to superiors; and its approximation to the lamp, to the opportune use of things according to time, place, and matter. But the procession of fire into the paper aptly represents the presence of divine light, to that nature which is capable of its reception. Lastly, the inflammation of the paper may be compared to the **deification** <term>Deification: The process of a mortal or material nature being filled with and transformed by divine light.</term> of mortals, and to the illumination of material natures, which are afterwards carried upwards like the enkindled paper, from a certain participation of divine seed.

For sulphur purifies from the sharpness of its odour; but marine water on account of its fiery portion. Besides this, in the worship of the Gods, they offered animals, and other substances congruous to their nature; and received, in the first place, the powers of **dæmons** <term>Dæmons: In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</term>, as proximate to natural substances and operations; and by these natural substance they convoked into their presence those powers to which they approached. Afterwards, they proceeded from dæmons to the powers and energies of the Gods; partly, indeed, from dæmoniacal instruction, but partly by their own industry, interpreting convenient symbols, and ascending to a proper intelligence of the Gods. And lastly, laying aside natural substances and their operations, they received themselves into the communion and fellowship of the Gods.”

When those circulations, therefore, take place, during which the parts of the earth subsist according to nature, and which are justly called, by **Plato**, **fertile periods**, the powers of plants, animals, and stones, magically sympathize with superior natures; but during those circulations in which the parts of the earth subsist contrary to nature, as at present, and which Plato calls **barren periods**, those powers no longer possess a magic sympathy, and consequently are no longer capable of producing magical operations.—T. <note>“T.” stands for Thomas Taylor, the translator, who frequently added his own Neoplatonic defenses to the text.</note>

...given to your rivals, if the story were not too long; and besides this, the points already mentioned are sufficient indicators of those other qualities which they bring with them. But your birth, Alcibiades, your upbringing and education, or any other circumstances surrounding you—hardly any Athenian is concerned with them at all, unless there is some man who happens to have a special affection for you. 

Further; if you were to consider the treasures of the Persian kings, the lavish furnishings of their palaces and tables, their collections of clothing, the long trails of their robes, the scent of their perfumes, their massive groups of attendants, and the rest of their luxury, in comparing all this with what you have yourself, you would clearly see how far you fall short of them and would be embarrassed by the comparison.

<note>lords and masters; not unlike to tenants in villenage <term>villenage: a medieval system of serfdom where peasants were bound to the lord's land</term> under the feudal laws in after ages. To the like hard conditions did these Lacedæmonians, long afterward, subject their own kindred and neighbours of Messenia, at the end of many long struggles between them; on the Lacedæmonian side, for the conquest of a country better than their own; on the other side for the preservation of their lands and liberties. The Messenians, being thus reduced to the same state of vassalage with the Helotes <note>Helotes: Better known as Helots, the subjugated labor class of Sparta who worked the land.</note>, were often comprehended under this latter name; as appears from Pausanias, in book 3, page 201 of the Hanov. edition; as also appears from Thucydides, in book 1, page 101. The scholiast <note>scholiast: An ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes in the margins of manuscripts.</note> to this great historian informs us further, that the Lacedæmonians, "because of their being always at odds with the Helots" <note>original Greek: "διὰ τὸ ἀεὶ διαφόρως εἶναι εἵλωταις"</note>, (for so this last word ought to be read, and not "with one another" <note>original Greek: "ἀλλήλοις"</note>, as it is absurdly printed,) because of the hatred which they always bore to the Helotes, were used to call their slaves by that name, in the way of contemptuousness and contumely. But Plato in the passage now before us, uses more accuracy: for meaning to include all the vassals, by whose labour in the lands much wealth accrued to the Lacedæmonians, he calls them, not "Helots," but "those of the Helot-kind" <note>original Greek: "εἱλωτικὰς"</note>. Just as Pausanias, in book 4, page 259, means by "the Helot-state" <note>original Greek: "τὸ εἱλωτικὸν"</note>, such a vassal-state as that of the Helotes. Plato, by other slaves, means such as were acquired by purchase, or by conquest unconditional, them and their offspring; and of these, such as were not employed in domestic services, but were set to work in agriculture and other country-labour: for Socrates is here speaking only of the value of the Lacedæmonian estates in land arising from such labour. — S. <note>S.: Likely the translator Thomas Sydenham.</note></note>

<note> $^1$ The Lacedæmonians were abundantly supplied with all the necessaries of life from their own lands; and being by their laws restrained from all splendour and magnificence, from all delicacy and luxury, as well in their houses and the furniture of them, as in their apparel and the provisions of their tables, they could have no occasion to purchase for their own use any foreign trinkets or commodities. Indeed sumptuary laws <term>sumptuary laws: laws intended to limit private spending on food and luxury items</term> were almost unnecessary in their commonwealth, through the force and effect of another law, by which they were prohibited not only from using any coined money, whether of gold, silver, or copper, in their home-traffic, but even from having any such useless treasure in their houses. The only money permitted to pass current amongst them was of their own making; it consisted in pieces of iron, of a conoidical <term>conoidical: shaped somewhat like a cone</term> form, so peculiarly tempered as to be of no other use. These pieces, therefore, having no real value, and a nominal value nowhere but in Laconia, would not be taken by any foreigners in exchange for merchandise. enemies consider more prudently for us than we do for ourselves, what sort of persons we ought to be before we venture to attack such enemies? Hearken therefore, my good sir, to the advice which I give you, in agreement with the Delphic inscription, KNOW THYSELF <note>original: "gnōthi seauton". This famous maxim was inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and serves as the philosophical foundation for this dialogue.</note>: since your antagonists are to be, not those whom you imagine, but these whom I have told you of: and these you never can excel in any other point than skill and application <note>The term "application" here refers to diligent practice or care of oneself (*epimeleia*).</note>; in which articles if you are found deficient, you will fail of that reputation and renown, as well with Grecians as Barbarians <note>To the ancient Greeks, a "Barbarian" was simply anyone who did not speak the Greek language, specifically referring here to the Persians.</note>, which I think you long for with more ardour than any other man does for whatever is the object of his wishes.

**Alc.** Can you teach me then, O *Socrates*, what sort of application I ought to use? for you seem to be entirely right in all which you have spoken.

**Soc.** Something I have indeed to say upon that subject. But let us enter into a joint consultation, you and I, about the means of becoming, both of us, better men. For when I say, there is a necessity for instruction, I mean it of myself as well as of you: since only one difference there is between you and me.

**Alc.** What is that?

**Soc.** He who is my guardian is better and wiser than Pericles <note>Pericles was the most prominent statesman of Athens and the legal guardian of the orphaned Alcibiades.</note>, who is yours.

**Alc.** And who is yours, O *Socrates*?

**Soc.** A GOD <note>Socrates refers here to his "daimonion," a divine inner voice or sign that he claimed guided his actions and restrained him from errors.</note>, O *Alcibiades*! he who permitted me not before this day to enter into any discourse with you: he it is, on whose dictates to me I rely, when I am bold to say, that you will acquire the renown you long for, by no other means than through me.

**Alc.** You are in jest, Socrates.

**Soc.** Perhaps so: but I speak the truth however in good earnest when I say that we stand in need of instruction, or rather, that all men want it; but that you and I have very especial need of it.

**Alc.** In saying that I have need of it, you are not mistaken.

**Soc.** Neither am I, in saying that I myself have.

**Alc.** What then must we do?

**Soc.** We must not despair, nor give ourselves up to indolence, my friend.

# THE FIRST ALCIBIADES

->72<-

**ALC.** By no means, Socrates, does it become us so to do.

**Soc.** Indeed it does not. We must therefore consider of the affair, you and I together. Now then answer to my questions. We profess to be desirous of becoming as excellent as possible : do we not ? <note>The word "excellent" here refers to the Greek concept of *arete*, which means "virtue" or the highest fulfillment of a person’s purpose.</note>

**ALC.** We do.

**Soc.** In what kind of excellence ?

**ALC.** In that certainly which belongs to men of merit. <note>In this context, "merit" describes the qualities of a noble or distinguished citizen.</note>

**Soc.** Of merit in what respect ?

**ALC.** In the management of business and affairs, undoubtedly.

**Soc.** But what business do you mean ? The business of a jockey ?

**ALC.** Clearly not.

**Soc.** For then we should go for instruction to those who understand the management of horses.

**ALC.** Certainly we should.

**Soc.** Do you then mean of a mariner ?

**ALC.** I do not.

**Soc.** For in that case we should apply to those who understand navigation.

**ALC.** Certainly so.

**Soc.** But what business or affairs then ? and by what sort of men are these affairs managed ?

**ALC.** I mean such affairs as are managed by men of honour and merit amongst the Athenians. <note>Alcibiades is referring to the "business" of governing the city-state of Athens.</note>

**Soc.** Men of honour and merit do you call such as have understanding, or such as are void of understanding ?

**ALC.** Such as have understanding.

**Soc.** In whatever business a man has understanding, in that has he not merit ?

**ALC.** He has.

**Soc.** And in whatever business he is void of understanding, is he not in that void of merit ?

**ALC.** Without doubt.

**Soc.** Whether hath a shoemaker understanding in the business of making shoes ?

**ALC.** He certainly has.

<summary>Socrates begins his cross-examination of Alcibiades, leading him to agree that true "merit" or "excellence" in any field is inseparable from having a specific "understanding" or technical knowledge of that field.</summary>

**ALC.** He is so.
**Soc.** The same man therefore, according to this account, is at the same time void of merit and possessed of merit.

**Soc.** What kind of men then do you mean by the men of merit?

**Soc.** Not to govern horses, I presume.
**ALC.** No, certainly.
**Soc.** But to govern men.

**Alc.** The good government and safety of the commonwealth.

**Soc.** And what is it which the commonwealth enjoys when it is governed best and preserved in safety? and what is it from which it is then preserved? as, if you were to ask me this question, What is it which the body enjoys when it is best taken care of, and preserved in safety? and from what is it then preserved? I would say that then it enjoys health, and is preserved from disease. Are not you of the same opinion?

**Alc.** I am.

**Soc.** And, if you were to ask me further, What do the eyes enjoy when the best care is taken of them? and from what are they then preserved? I would answer in like manner as before, that they enjoyed their sight, and were preserved from blindness. So likewise of the ears; when they are preserved from deafness, and have their hearing perfect, they are then in their best condition, and are taken the best care of.

**Alc.** Right.

**Soc.** Well, now; what does the commonwealth enjoy, and from what is it preserved, when 'tis in its best condition, has the best care taken of it, and is best preserved?

**Alc.** It seems to me, Socrates, that the members of it then enjoy mutual amity <note>Socrates uses "amity" (friendship) as a political term meaning social harmony or "concord" (*homonoia*), which prevents civil war.</note>, and are preserved from enmity and factions.

**Soc.** By amity do you mean their being of the same mind, or of different minds?

**Alc.** Their being of the same mind.

**Soc.** Now through what science is it that different civil states are of the same mind concerning numbers?

**Alc.** Through the science of arithmetic.

**Soc.** Well; and is it not through that very science that private persons are of the same mind one with another?

**ALCIBIADES.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** And that any person too, by himself, continues always in the same mind, is it not through his possessing that science? <note>In the Platonic context, "science" (translating the Greek *epistēmē*) refers to a systematic and certain body of knowledge or a specialized craft, rather than modern experimental science.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** And through what science is it that a single individual is always of the same mind concerning a span and a cubit <note>A span and a cubit were standard ancient units of length. A cubit was approximately the length of a forearm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger; a span was the distance between the tip of the thumb and the tip of the little finger when the hand is fully extended.</note>, whether of the two is the greater measure? is it not through the science of mensuration? <term>mensuration: the branch of knowledge dealing with the measurement of lengths, areas, and volumes.</term>

**ALCIBIADES.** Without doubt.

**SOCRATES.** And is it not so too between different private persons and civil states?

**ALCIBIADES.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** And how concerning weights? does not the same hold true in this case?

**ALCIBIADES.** I agree it does.

**SOCRATES.** But now the sameness of mind <note>Original: *homonoia*. This Greek term implies a "oneness of mind" or "concord." It was considered a vital political virtue for preventing civil war and internal strife.</note> which you speak of, what is that? What is the subject-matter of it? and through what science is it procured? I ask you likewise whether the same science which procures it for the public procures it no less for private persons; and whether it operates that effect in a man considered by himself as well as between one man and another.

**ALCIBIADES.** Probably it does.

**SOCRATES.** What science or art then is it? Do not labour for an answer, but speak readily what you think.

**ALCIBIADES.** I think it to be such an amity <note>Original: *philia*. This is the Greek word for friendship or affection. Alcibiades is suggesting that social harmony is rooted in the same kind of love found in a family.</note> and sameness of mind, that which we are speaking of, as there is between a father and a mother in loving their child, and as there is between brother and brother, and between man and wife.

**SOCRATES.** Do you then think it possible, Alcibiades, for a man to be of the same mind with his wife on the subject of weaving, when he is ignorant and she is knowing in the art?

**ALCIBIADES.** By no means.

**SOCRATES.** Nor ought he neither. For 'tis a piece of knowledge belonging only to women.

**ALCIBIADES.** Certainly.

# THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.

**SOCRATES.** Well; and can a woman be of the same mind with her husband on the subject of fighting in battle among the infantry, when she has never learnt the art?
**ALCIBIADES.** Certainly she cannot.
**SOCRATES.** For the knowledge of this you would perhaps say belonged only to men.
**ALCIBIADES.** I should so.
**SOCRATES.** Some pieces of knowledge, therefore, properly belong to women; others to men according to your account.
**ALCIBIADES.** No doubt can be made of it.
**SOCRATES.** On those subjects therefore which are not common to both the sexes there is no sameness of mind, between husbands and their wives.
**ALCIBIADES.** There is not any.
**SOCRATES.** Neither then is there any friendship; if friendship consist in sameness of mind. <note>Socrates is using a common Greek definition of friendship (*philia*) as "concord" or "thinking the same thing." He is leading Alcibiades into a logical trap regarding the division of labor.</note>
**ALCIBIADES.** It appears there is not.
**SOCRATES.** So far therefore as women are attentive to their own business they are not beloved by their husbands.
**ALCIBIADES.** It seems they are not.
**SOCRATES.** Neither are men beloved by their wives,—so far as their minds are engaged in their own business.
**ALCIBIADES.** It seems they are not.
**SOCRATES.** Neither then do citizens live well¹ together in cities, when each of them minds only his own business. <note>The concept of "minding one's own business" is central to Plato’s philosophy; in his *Republic*, it is actually the definition of Justice. Here, Socrates uses it to create a paradox about social cohesion.</note>
**ALCIBIADES.** Nay, Socrates; for my part I imagine that they do,—so far as they are thus employed.
**SOCRATES.** How say you? What, without friendship between them, by means of which we said that civil states were in a happy condition, and without which we said they could not flourish?

**ALCIBIADES.** But it seems to me that friendship is on this very account produced between them, because every one gives his whole attention to his own business.

**SOCRATES.** It did not seem so to you just now. <note>Socrates is pointing out that Alcibiades is contradicting his earlier agreement that "sameness of mind" is the basis of friendship.</note> But how do you explain at present what you said,—that friendship was produced by sameness of mind? <note>original: *homonoia*. This Greek term implies a literal "oneness of mind" or concord between citizens.</note> Whether is it possible that fellow-citizens can be all of the same mind on subjects in which some of them are knowing, and others ignorant?

**ALCIBIADES.** It is not possible.

**SOCRATES.** And do they do their duty, and act as they ought, or not, when each of them attends to his own business?

**ALCIBIADES.** As they ought, undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** When the citizens then of any city act as they ought, and all of them do their duty, is not friendship produced between them?

**ALCIBIADES.** It must be so I think, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** What kind of friendship, or sameness of mind, do you then mean, in the procuring of which you say that wisdom and prudence <note>original: *sophia* and *phronesis*. Socrates distinguishes between theoretical wisdom and the practical wisdom required for civic life.</note> are requisite to make us men of virtue and merit? For I can neither learn from you what it is, nor what objects it regards. But sometimes it seems to regard the same objects, and sometimes not, according to your account of it.

**ALCIBIADES.** Now by the Gods, Socrates, I know not what I mean, myself. But am in danger of appearing to have been, of a long time, in a shameful state of mind, without being sensible of it. <note>This admission of ignorance is a classic moment in Platonic dialogues called *aporia*. It is the necessary first step in philosophy: realizing that you do not know what you thought you knew.</note>

**SOCRATES.** Now therefore you ought to take courage. For if fifty years of your life had elapsed before you had discovered the real state of your mind, an application of it to the care of yourself would have been a difficult task for you. But you are now at the very time of life in which such a discovery should be made, to be of any advantage to you.

**ALCIBIADES.** What then am I to do, Socrates, now that I am made sensible of my condition?

**SOCRATES.** Only to answer to the questions I shall put to you, Alcibiades. And if you will so do, you and I, by the favour of God, if any credit may be given to a prophecy of mine, shall both of us be the better for it.

**ALCIBIADES.** Your prophecy shall be accomplished, as far as the accomplishment depends on my answering to your questions.

## THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.

**SOCRATES.** Come on then. What is it to take care of oneself? That we may not falsely imagine, as we often do, that we are taking care of ourselves, and know not that all the while we are otherwise employed. And when is it that a man is taking that care? Whether when he is taking care of what appertains to him, is he then taking care of himself? <note>Socrates begins his famous inquiry into the distinction between the "user" (the soul) and the "instrument" (the body or possessions).</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** For my part I must own I think so.

**SOCRATES.** And when is it, think you, that a man is taking care of his feet? whether is it then when he is taking care of the things appertaining to his feet?

**ALCIBIADES.** <note>The OCR mistakenly attributed the following line to Socrates, but the context of the dialogue confirms this is Alcibiades responding.</note> I do not apprehend your meaning.

**SOCRATES.** Do you acknowledge something to be appertaining to the hand,—a ring, for instance? Or <note>original: η (eta). This Greek particle functions as a disjunctive "or."</note> does it appertain to any other part of the human body than a finger?

**ALCIBIADES.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** And does not a shoe appertain to the foot in like manner?

**ALCIBIADES.** It does.

**SOCRATES.** Whether then at the time of our taking care of our shoes are we taking care immediately of our feet?

**ALCIBIADES.** I do not quite apprehend you, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Do you acknowledge that whatever be the subject of our care, a right care of it may be taken?

**ALCIBIADES.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** I ask you then, whether you think that a man takes a right care of whatever is the subject of his care, when he improves it and makes it better?

**ALCIBIADES.** I answer Yes.

**SOCRATES.** What art <note>term: *techne* — This refers to a specialized craft, skill, or system of knowledge, such as medicine or carpentry.</note> now is that by which our shoes are improved and made better?

**ALCIBIADES.** The shoemaker's art.

**SOCRATES.** By the shoemaker's art therefore it is that we take a right care of our shoes.

**ALCIBIADES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** And is it also by the shoemaker’s art that we take a right care of our feet? or is it by that art by which we improve our feet and make them better?

**ALCIBIADES.** It is by this art. <note>Alcibiades is agreeing that a specific skill is needed to actually improve the body part itself, rather than just its equipment.</note>

**SOCRATES.** And do we not improve and make better our feet by the same art by which we improve and make better the rest of our body?

**ALCIBIADES.** I believe we do.

**SOCRATES.** And is not this the <term>gymnastic art</term>? <note>In ancient Greece, the "gymnastic art" referred to the overall system of physical education and athletic training used to strengthen and perfect the human body.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** By the gymnastic art therefore we take care of the foot, and by the shoemaker’s art we take care of what is <term>appertinent</term> to the foot. <note>Appertinent: an archaic term (related to "appurtenant") meaning something that belongs to or is an accessory of a more important thing.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** Exactly so.

**SOCRATES.** And in like manner by the gymnastic art we take care of our hands, and by the art of engraving rings we take care of what is appertinent to the hand.

**ALCIBIADES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** By the gymnastic art also we take care of our bodies; but ’tis by the weaver’s art and some others that we take care of things appertinent to the body.

**ALCIBIADES.** I agree with you entirely.

**SOCRATES.** By one kind of knowledge therefore we take care of things themselves, and by a different kind of knowledge we take care of things only appertinent to those things which are the principal.

**ALCIBIADES.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** You are not therefore taking care of yourself when you are taking care only of the appertinences to yourself.

**ALCIBIADES.** At that time ’tis very true I am not.

**SOCRATES.** For one and the same art, it seems, doth not take care of a thing itself, and of the appertinences to that thing besides.

**ALCIBIADES.** It appears to be not the same art.

**SOCRATES.** Now then, by what kind of art might we take care of ourselves?

**ALCIBIADES.** I have nothing to answer to this question.

**SOCRATES.** So much, however, we are agreed in, that it is not an art by which we improve or better any thing which is ours; but an art by which we improve and better our very selves. <note>Socrates here sets the stage for his final argument: that to "know thyself" is to care for the soul, which is the true self, rather than the body or wealth.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** I acknowledge it.

**SOCRATES.** Could we ever know what art would improve or amend a shoe, if we knew not what a shoe was?

**ALCIBIADES.** Impossible.

**SOCRATES.** Neither could we know what art would make better rings for the finger, if ignorant what a ring for the finger was.

**ALCIBIADES.** Impossible.

**SOCRATES.** Let me ask you, then, whether it happens to be an easy thing to know oneself; and whether he was some person of mean attainments in knowledge, he who put up this inscription in the temple at Pytho¹: or is it a piece of knowledge difficult to be attained, and not obvious to every one? <note>The "inscription" refers to the famous Greek maxim "Gnothi Seauton" or "Know Thyself."</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** To me, Socrates, it has often seemed easy and obvious to every one, and often too, at other times, a thing of the greatest difficulty.

**SOCRATES.** But whether in itself it be an easy thing or not, with respect to us, Alcibiades, the state of the case is this;—had we attained to that piece of knowledge, we should perhaps know what it is to take care of ourselves; but never can we know this so long as we remain ignorant of that.

**ALCIBIADES.** These are truths which I acknowledge.

**SOCRATES.** Come then. By what means might it be found what is the <term>very self</term> of every thing? <note>The "very self" (or *auto to auto*) refers to the essential nature or identity of a thing, independent of its external parts or possessions.</note> for so we might perhaps find what we ourselves are: but so long as we continue in the dark as to that point, it will be no way possible to know ourselves.

**ALCIBIADES.** You are certainly in the right.

->### THE FIRST ALCIBIADES<-

**SOCRATES.** Attend now, I conjure you in the name of **Jupiter**: With whom is it that you are at this present time discoursing? Is it not <note>The translator suggests a correction to the original Greek text here. The original reading asks, "Is it with any other person than with me?" (original: αλλω τινι η εμοι;). However, because Alcibiades answers in the affirmative, the text likely should read: "Is it not with me?" (original: αλλοτι η εμοι;).</note> with me?

**ALCIBIADES.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** And am not I discoursing with you?

**ALCIBIADES.** You are.

**SOCRATES.** It is **Socrates** then who is discoursing and arguing.

**ALCIBIADES.** Quite true.

**SOCRATES.** And **Alcibiades** is attentive to his arguments.

**ALCIBIADES.** He is.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not by <term>reason</term> that **Socrates** thus argues in discourse? <note>Socrates is establishing that the faculty of reasoning is the "tool" by which the person conducts a dialogue.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** And is not to argue in <term>discourse</term> the same thing as to reason?

**ALCIBIADES.** Quite the same.

**SOCRATES.** But is not the person who uses a thing, different from the thing which he uses?

**ALCIBIADES.** How do you mean?

**SOCRATES.** As a shoemaker, for instance, cuts his leather with the shears, and the paring knife, and other tools.

**ALCIBIADES.** Well; he does so.

**SOCRATES.** Is not then the shoemaker, who cuts the leather and uses those tools in cutting it, different from the tools which he uses?

**ALCIBIADES.** Without doubt.

**SOCRATES.** Are not, in like manner, the instruments on which a musician plays, different things from the musician himself?

**ALCIBIADES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** It was in this sense that just now I asked you whether you thought that, in all cases, the person who used a thing was different from the thing which he used.

**ALCIBIADES.** I think he is.

**SOCRATES.** Now then, to resume the instance of the shoemaker; what say we? Does he cut the leather with his tools only, or also with his hands?
