**SOCRATES.** He therefore uses also these.

**ALCIBIADES.** He does.

**SOCRATES.** And does he not use his eyes also when he is cutting the leather?

**ALCIBIADES.** He does.

**SOCRATES.** And we are agreed, that the person who makes use of any things is different from the things which he makes use of.

**ALCIBIADES.** We are.

**SOCRATES.** The shoemaker then, and the musician, are different from the hands and eyes with which they perform their operations. <note>Socrates uses these craft analogies to show that if we are the "users" of our body parts, we cannot be identical to those parts.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** It is apparent.

**SOCRATES.** And does not a man use also his whole body?

**ALCIBIADES.** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Now the user is different from the thing used.

**ALCIBIADES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** A man therefore is a being different from his body. <note>This is a pivotal moment in the dialogue where Socrates separates the "Self" from the physical form.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** It seems so.

**SOCRATES.** What sort of being then is man?

**ALCIBIADES.** I know not.

**SOCRATES.** But you know that man is some being who makes use of the body.

**ALCIBIADES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** Does any being make use of the body other than the <term>soul</term>? <note>In this context, "soul" (original Greek: psyche) refers to the seat of consciousness, intellect, and personality, rather than just a religious concept.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** None other.

**SOCRATES.** And does it not so do by governing the body?

**ALCIBIADES.** It does.

**SOCRATES.** Further. I suppose that no man would ever think otherwise than this.

**ALCIBIADES.** Than what?

**SOCRATES.** That a man himself was one of these three things.

**ALCIBIADES.** What three things?

**SOCRATES.** **Soul**, or **body**, or a **compound** of them both, constituting one whole.

**ALCIBIADES.** What besides could be imagined?

**SOCRATES.** Now we agreed that the being which governs the body is the man.

**ALCIBIADES.** We did.

**SOCRATES.** What being then is the man? Doth the body itself govern itself?

**ALCIBIADES.** By no means.

**ALCIBIADES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** The body, then, cannot be that being which we are in search of.

**ALCIBIADES.** It seems not.

**SOCRATES.** But does the compound being govern the body? And is this the man? <note>The "compound being" refers to the idea that a human is the simultaneous combination of both soul and body acting as one unit.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** Perhaps it is.

**SOCRATES.** Least of any of the three can this be so. For where there are two parties, one of which is the party governed, there is no possibility that both of them should govern jointly. <note>Socrates argues that since the body is clearly the "subject," it cannot be part of the "ruler." Therefore, the "Self" cannot be a mix of the two.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** Right.

**SOCRATES.** Since then neither the body, nor the compound of soul and body together, is the man, it remains, I think, either that a man's self is nothing at all, or, if it be anything, it must be concluded that the man is no other thing than the soul.

**ALCIBIADES.** Clearly so.

**SOCRATES.** Does it then need to be proved to you still more clearly, that the <term>soul</term> is the very man? <note>soul: Here referring to the intellect or the "rational soul" as the true identity of a person.</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** It does not, by Jupiter! <note>original: "per Jovem" - a common oath used in these dialogues to express firm agreement.</note> For the proofs already brought seem to me sufficient.

**SOCRATES.** If it be proved tolerably well, though not perfectly, it is sufficient for us. For we shall then perhaps—and not before—have an accurate knowledge of "man's self," when we shall have discovered what we just now passed by as a matter which required much consideration.

<margin>1 Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> rightly understands Plato here to mean the rational soul. For the arguments produced in this part of the Dialogue, to show that the soul is a man's proper self, regard the rational soul only. This soul alone uses speech, as the instrument by which it makes known to others its mind and will. This alone uses argumentative speech, as an instrument to teach art and science, to correct error, to refute falsehood, and demonstrate truth. This alone uses the organical parts of the body, especially the hands and eyes, as instruments by which it operates in all the performances of the manual arts. This alone employs the whole body in its service, as the instrument of its will and pleasure; and is the sole governing and leading power in man, whether it govern well or ill, and whether it lead in the right way, or in the wrong; for the rest of the man must obey and follow. It governs well, and leads aright, through knowledge of itself; if this knowledge leads to the knowledge of what is just, fair, and good, and if the knowledge of these things be the science of rational, right, and good government.—S.</margin>

<note>* The Greek of this passage, in all the editions of Plato, is absurdly printed thus: "Whoever then knows the things of the body, knows the things belonging to him, but has not known himself" <note>original: ὅστις ἄρα τῶν τοῦ σώματος γιγνώσκει, τὰ αὑτοῦ, ἀλλ’ οὐχ’ αὑτὸν, ἔγνωκεν</note>. The first member of which sentence being ungrammatical, Stephens, in the margin of his edition, supposes may be rectified, either by inserting the word "something" <note>original: τι</note> before "of the" <note>original: τῶν</note>, or by changing the "of the" <note>original: τῶν</note> into "the [things]" <note>original: τὰ</note>. In either of these ways indeed the grammatical construction is amended, but not the sense: for thus represented (and thus represented it is by the Latin versions of Cornarius and Serranus), it is inconsistent with the reasoning, which requires that the body itself should be intended, and not "the things" (or "something of the things") "of the body" <note>original: τὰ (or τι τῶν) τοῦ σώματος</note>, such as the garments and other external things, or any of them, which are only appertinent to the body. Le Fevre and Dacier seem to have been well aware of this, and have rightly therefore rendered it into French by these words—*his body* <note>original: son corps</note>. They were led thus aright by Ficinus, who, in translating this part of the sentence, uses only the word *body* <note>original: corpus</note>. Perhaps in the manuscript from which he translated, he found the right reading, which we conjecture to be this: "Whoever then knows his own body, knows what belongs to him, but has not known himself" <note>original: ὅστις ἄρα τὸ αὑτοῦ σῶμα γιγνώσκει, τὸ αὑτοῦ, ἀλλ’ οὐχ’ αὑτὸν, ἔγνωκεν</note>.—S.</note>

**Soc.** Neither then can any thing which is our own, be known by us to be our own, any other way than through the knowledge of ourselves.

**ALC.** How should we?

**Soc.** And if we know not that which is ours, neither can we know any of the <term>appertinences</term> <note>Things that belong to, relate to, or are legally associated with a person or their property.</note> to what is ours.

**ALC.** It appears we cannot.

**Soc.** We therefore were not at all right in admitting, as we did just now, that certain persons there were, who knew not themselves, but who knew what belonged to them, and was theirs. Neither can such as know not themselves know the appertinences to what is theirs. For it seems, that ’tis the province of one and the same person, and is from one and the same science, to know himself, to know the things which are his, and to know the appertinences to those things.

**ALC.** I believe it will be found so.

**Soc.** And whoever is ignorant of what belongs to himself and is his own, must be likewise ignorant of what belongs to other men and is theirs.

**ALC.** Undoubtedly.

**Soc.** And if he is ignorant of what belongs to other men, will he not be ignorant also of what belongs to the public, and to other civil states?

**ALC.** He must be so.

**Soc.** Such a man, therefore, cannot be a <term>politician</term> <note>In this classical context, a statesman or citizen skilled in the affairs of the city-state (the "polis").</note>.

**ALC.** Certainly he cannot.

**Soc.** Neither will he be fit to manage a family.

**ALC.** Certainly not.

**Soc.** Nor will he have any certain knowledge of any thing which he is doing.

**ALC.** He will not.

**Soc.** And will not the man who knows not what he is doing, do amiss?

**ALC.** Certainly so.

**Soc.** And doing amiss, will he not act ill, both as a private person, and as a member of the public?

**ALC.** No doubt of it.

**Soc.** And the man who acts ill, is he not in a bad condition?

<meta>the</meta>

# GENERAL INTRODUCTION

### TO

## THE REPUBLIC.

**T**HE design of Plato, says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato’s works, viewing them as a unified system of spiritual and political philosophy.</note>, in this dialogue, concerns both a <term>polity</term> <note>original: "politeia" — This refers to a form of government, a constitution, or the way of life within a city-state.</note> and true justice, not as two distinct things, but as one and the same. For what justice is in a single soul, that same justice is found in a well-ordered city as described by Plato. Indeed, the three classes that make up a state are analogous to the three parts of the soul: the **guardian** class, which deliberates and consults, corresponds to **reason**; the **auxiliary** class, which engages in war and defense, corresponds to **anger** <note>In Platonic philosophy, this is "thumos" or "spirit"—the part of the soul associated with courage, indignation, and the drive for honor.</note>; and the mercenary class, which provides for the physical needs of life, corresponds to the **desiderative** <note>The "desiderative" part of the soul is driven by physical appetites and basic desires.</note> part of the soul.

For, according to Plato, it is the very same habit of character that brings order to a city, a household, and an individual person. If the common people in a city represent the desiderative part in an individual, and the ruling council is analogous to reason—as Plato asserts in his *Laws*—then justice is the "polity of the soul," just as the best possible polity for a city is justice. If these principles are true, then anyone teaching about justice (if they teach it completely) will necessarily teach about the state, because they will see justice everywhere. Conversely, anyone speaking about an upright state will also be speaking about justice. This justice exists within a state and also organizes the "people" within our own souls through our auxiliary part, following the decisions of our governing reason.

That this was Plato’s opinion on these matters will be clear when we consider that, in moving from the investigation of justice to the discussion of a state, he says the transition is not being made as if moving between two naturally different things. Instead, it is like moving from small letters to letters that are large and clear <note>Plato uses this famous analogy in Book II of the *Republic*. He suggests that because a city is larger than a person, it is easier to "read" or observe justice in the grand structure of a state before looking for it in the smaller scale of the individual soul.</note>, and which manifest

<summary>This page introduces the core concept of the Republic: the parallel structure between the human soul and the political state. It explains that justice is the balanced "polity" of the soul, where reason rules over desire through the spirit.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Proclus, Republic, justice, soul, polity, reason, guardians, auxiliaries, tripartite soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of justice by explaining the analogy of "large and small letters"—suggesting that justice is easier to observe in the grand scale of a city (the polity) than in the internal life of an individual. It transitions from the philosophical definition of justice into an analysis of the literary style Plato uses to present his arguments.</meta>

->GENERAL INTRODUCTION<-

the same things. The matter therefore of justice and a <term>polity</term> <note>The word "polity" (from the Greek "politeia") refers to the internal constitution or the way of life of a city-state, often translated as "republic."</note> is different, in the same manner as that of small and large letters, but the form is the same. Hence the transition is from polity to polity;—from that which is beheld in one individual, to that which is beheld in many: and from justice to justice;—from that which is contracted to that which is more apparent. Nor ought we to wonder that Plato does not express the thing discussed in this dialogue by the name of justice, but by that of a polity, in the same manner as he signifies another subject of discussion by the appellation of laws. For it is requisite that inscriptions should be made from things more known; but the name of a polity or republic is more known, as Plato also says, than that of justice.

With respect to the form of the dialogue, it will be requisite to recollect that Plato himself in this treatise says that there are only three forms of diction, namely the **dramatic** and **imitative**, such as that of comedy and tragedy; the **narrative** and **unimitative**, such as is employed by those who write dithyrambics <note>A "dithyramb" was a passionate, choral hymn sung in honor of the god Dionysus.</note>, and the histories of past transactions, without <term>prosopopœia</term> <note>A rhetorical device where the writer speaks in the voice of another person or an inanimate object.</note>; and a third species which is **mixed** from both the preceding, such as the poetry of Homer; diversifying some parts of the poem by the narration of things, and others by the imitations of persons. Such being the division of the forms of diction according to Plato, it is necessary to refer the present treatise to the mixed form of diction, which relates some things as transactions, and others as discourses, and alone preserves an accurate narration of persons and things; such as are—descending to the <term>Piræum</term> <note>The Piraeus was the port city of Athens. The dialogue of the Republic begins with Socrates walking down to this port for a religious festival.</note>, praying to the goddess, beholding the festival, and the like. But in the several discourses it makes the most accurate imitation; some things being spoken in the character of old men, others fabulously, and others sophistically; and attributes a knowledge and life adapted to the different speakers. For to preserve the becoming in these particulars is the province of the highest imitation.

With respect to justice, the subject of this dialogue, such according to Plato is its universality and importance, that, if it had no subsistence, injustice itself would be sluggish and in vain. Thus, for instance, if a city were full of injustice, it would neither be able to effect any thing with respect to another city, nor with respect to itself, through the dissension <meta>catchword: dissension</meta>

<summary>This page explains why the dialogue is titled "The Republic" rather than "On Justice," arguing that the city-state serves as a larger, more readable model for the human soul. It also classifies the work's literary style as a "mixed" form that combines objective narration with the dramatic imitation of different characters.</summary>

...dissension arising from those that injure and are injured. In a similar manner too in an army, if it abounded with every kind of injustice, it would be in <term>sedition</term> <note>In this context, "sedition" refers to internal discord or civil war within a group or the self.</note> with itself; and being in <term>sedition</term> with itself, it must be subverted, and become <term>inefficacious</term> <note>Ineffective or unable to achieve its purpose.</note> as to the purposes of war. Thus too, a house in which there is no vestige of justice, as it must necessarily be full of dissension, will be incapable of effecting any thing, through the want of concord in its inhabitants. But that which is the most wonderful of all is this, that injustice, when inherent in one person only, must necessarily fill him with <term>sedition</term> towards himself, and through this <term>sedition</term> must render him more <term>imbecil</term> <note>This archaic term means "weak" or "powerless" rather than a lack of intelligence.</note> with respect to various endurance, and incapable of pleasing himself. Of necessity, therefore, every one who acts unjustly, if he is able to effect any thing whatever, must possess some vestige of justice; so inseparable is the union between power and justice.

From what has been said, the following <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two related premises.</note> arises. All injustice separate from justice is <term>imbecil</term>. Every thing separate from justice, being <term>imbecil</term>, requires justice to its possession of power. All injustice therefore requires justice in order to its possession of power.---Again, we have the following <term>syllogism</term>. All injustice requires justice, to be able to effect any thing. Every thing which requires justice to be able to effect any thing, is more <term>imbecil</term> than justice. All injustice, therefore, is more <term>imbecil</term> than justice. And this was the thing proposed to be shown. Hence it follows that, even in the worst <term>habit</term> <note>From the Latin "habitus," referring to a stable state of character or a "disposition" of the soul.</note> of the soul, in which reason is blinded and appetite perverted, such <term>habit</term> is indeed <term>inefficacious</term>, in consequence of justice being most obscure in such a soul, so as to appear to have no subsistence whatever; yet such a <term>habit</term> has a being in a certain respect, so far as it is impossible that <term>common conceptions</term> <note>The innate moral truths or "universal ideas" that all humans are thought to possess.</note> can entirely desert the soul, and especially in its desire of good. So far therefore as it is impelled towards good, it participates of justice. And if it were possible that the soul could be perfectly, that is in every respect, unjust, it would perhaps perish: for this is the case with the body when perfectly diseased. But that in such a <term>habit</term> there is a vestige of justice is evident. For it is unwilling to injure itself, and to destroy things pertaining to itself. As it therefore preserves that which is just towards itself, it is not alone unjust; but not know-

Through logical syllogisms, the text demonstrates that justice is the true source of power and that absolute injustice would lead to the total destruction of the soul.</summary>

-># GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE REPUBLIC.<-

...ing <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "...requires justice to its possession of power, and while it is considering how it should preserve itself..."</note> how it should preserve itself, it is unjust, attempting to preserve itself through such things as are not proper.

From hence we may also collect the following <term>porism</term> <note>A term used in ancient geometry and logic meaning a "corollary" or a secondary truth that becomes evident during the proof of another.</note>, or corollary, which was first perceived by Amelius <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> the fellow disciple with Porphyry <note>The scholar responsible for editing and publishing the works of Plotinus.</note> of Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism, a philosophy that synthesized Plato’s ideas into a mystical framework.</note>, that from a greater injustice lesser evils are frequently produced, but from a lesser injustice greater evils. For, when injustice perfectly subdues the soul, life is <term>inefficacious</term> <note>Ineffective or powerless to act.</note>; but, when justice is associated with injustice, a certain action is the result. Nor let any one think that this assertion is false because greater evils are produced from <term>intemperance</term> <note>A habitual state of excess and lack of self-control.</note> than <term>incontinence</term> <note>A state where one knows what is right but fails to do it because of temporary impulse.</note>: for intemperance is a vice, but incontinence is not yet a complete vice; because, in the incontinent man, reason in a certain respect opposes passion; so that on this account a lesser evil arises from incontinence, because it is mingled from vice and that which is not vice.

I shall only add further at present, that the *Republic* of Plato **pre-subsists**, or is contained causally, in an <term>intelligible nature</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, this refers to the realm of pure Ideas or the Divine Mind, which exists prior to the physical world.</note>,—subsists openly in the heavens,—and is, in the last place, to be found in human lives. As it therefore harmonizes in every respect with each of these, it is a <term>polity</term> <note>A structured system of government or a civil community.</note> perfect in all its parts; and may be considered as one of the greatest and most beneficial efforts of human intellect that has appeared, or ever will appear, in any of the infinite periods of time.

And truly, I said, *Cephalus*, I take great pleasure in talking with those who are very advanced in years. It seems right to me that we should learn from them, as if they were travelers who have gone before us on a road that we will likely have to travel ourselves—to learn whether it is rough and difficult, or smooth and easy. I would gladly learn from you, now that you have reached that time of life which the poets call the "threshold of old age," <note>original: "epi geras oudō." This is a recurring Homeric phrase used to describe the transition point between active life and the end of life.</note> what your opinion of it is: do you consider it to be a painful part of life, or how do you describe it?

I will tell you, *Socrates*, he said, what my opinion really is. Several of us who are about the same age often meet together, following the old proverb <note>This refers to the Greek proverb "age mates delight age mates," similar to the English "birds of a feather flock together."</note>. Most of us, when we gather, complain about our condition; we miss the pleasures of youth and call to mind the delights of love, drinking, feasting, and other things like them. They express anger as if they had been robbed of great treasures. In those days, they say, they lived well, but now they do not truly live at all. Some of them also complain about the lack of respect old age receives from their families, and for this reason, they lament that old age is the cause of so many of their troubles. 

But these men, *Socrates*, do not seem to me to be blaming the real cause. For if old age were the cause, then I too would have suffered these same things, as would everyone else who has reached this age. However, I have met many who do not feel this way. I was once with the poet *Sophocles* <note>Sophocles (c. 497–406 BC) was one of the three great ancient Greek tragedians, famous for plays like *Oedipus Rex*.</note> when someone asked him, "How do you feel, *Sophocles*, about the pleasures of love? Are you still able to enjoy them?" 

"Hush, friend," he replied; "most gladly have I escaped from them, as if I had escaped from some frantic and savage master." 

His answer seemed wise to me then, and no less so now. For certainly, old age brings a great sense of peace and freedom from such passions. When the appetites cease to be so violent and finally relax, it is exactly as *Sophocles* said: we are set free from many "insane masters" <note>This refers to the Greek idea that uncontrolled physical desires are like tyrannical rulers over the soul.</note>. "You say true," he replied, "they do not agree with me; and there is something in what they say; but, however, not so much as they imagine. "As to the business of acquiring wealth <note>original: "chrēmatistou," referring to the art of money-making.</note>, I am in a middle position between my grandfather and my father. My grandfather, who bore the same name as I do, was left almost as much wealth as I possess at present, and increased it many times over; but my father, Lysanias, reduced it to even less than it is now. I am satisfied if I leave my sons here not less, but perhaps a little more, than I originally received." 

"I asked you," said I, "for this reason: because you seem to me to love riches only moderately. Generally, those who have not acquired their own wealth act this way; but those who have earned it themselves are doubly fond of it. For, just as poets love their own poems, and as parents love their children, in the same manner, those who have enriched themselves value their riches as a work of their own, as well as for the practical benefits they provide—which is why riches are valued by others. You speak the truth," he replied. 

"It is entirely so," said I. "But further, tell me this: what do you think is the greatest good derived from the possession of great wealth?"

In order to provide for the body’s advantage, this art of medicine was established. Do you think I am speaking correctly when I put it this way?"

For example, eyes lack sight and ears lack hearing, and for these reasons they need a specific art to look after them and provide what is beneficial for those purposes. Is there, then, some flaw within art itself? Does every art stand in need of *another* art to determine what is beneficial for it, and that second art in need of a third, and so on to infinity?"

"I understand two of the rewards <note>The rewards previously mentioned were money and honor.</note>; but this punishment you speak of, and why you mention it in place of a reward, I do not know."

"Then you do not know," said I, "the reward of the best of men, which is the reason the most worthy people govern when they consent to do so. Or do you not know that to be ambitious and greedy is considered a disgrace, and truly is so?"

"I know it," he said.

"For those reasons, then," I said, "good men are not willing to govern for money or for honor. They do not wish to be called <term>mercenaries</term> <note>original: "misthōtikoi" — those who work only for pay.</note> by openly receiving a wage for governing, nor to be called thieves by taking secretly from those they rule. Neither are they willing to govern for honor, for they are not ambitious. Out of necessity, then, a penalty must be imposed on them so that they will consent to govern. This is why it has traditionally been considered dishonorable to seek a position in government willingly, rather than waiting until one is forced to by necessity. 

And the greatest part of this punishment is to be governed by a *base person* <note>Someone of inferior character or wisdom.</note>, if one is not willing to govern oneself. It is from a fear of this, I believe, that good men rule when they do. They enter into government not as if they were approaching something good, or something from which they will gain an advantage, but as a necessary task. They do so because they can find no one better than themselves, nor anyone equal to them, to whom they can entrust the state.

Indeed, it seems that if there were a city made entirely of good men, the competition would be to **avoid** office, just as now the competition is to **obtain** it. In such a case, it would be manifest that a true governor does not naturally aim at his own advantage, but at that of the governed. Therefore, every man of understanding would rather choose to be served by another than to take on the trouble of serving others. 

On this point, I will never yield to Thrasymachus's claim that 'justice is the advantage of the more powerful'; but we shall consider that later. What Thrasymachus says now seems to me of much more importance, when he says that the life of the unjust man is better than that of the just. You, then, Glauco, which side do you choose? Which seems more truthful to you?"

"I believe the life of the just," he said, "is more profitable."

"Have you heard," I asked, "how many 'good things' Thrasymachus just now listed as belonging to the life of the unjust?"

"I heard," he said, "but I am not convinced."

"Are you willing, then, that we should try to persuade him, if we can find any way to argue—" <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword indicates the next page begins with "arguments."</note>

And, a discourse afterwards falling in, that injustice was more profitable than justice, I could not refrain from moving to this from the other. So the result of the dialogue is that I now know nothing; for while I do not know what justice is, I shall hardly know whether it be some virtue or not, and whether he who possesses it be unhappy or happy.

# INTRODUCTION

->TO THE<-

## SECOND AND THIRD BOOKS OF THE REPUBLIC,

->CONTAINING<-

### AN APOLOGY FOR THE FABLES OF HOMER.

---

**As** a very considerable part both of the second and third books of The Republic consists in examining and reprobating <note>to strongly disapprove of or condemn</note> the assertions of the poets, and particularly the fables of Homer, concerning divine natures, it appeared to me that I could not more essentially benefit the reader than by presenting him with the following defence of Homer and divine fables in general, from the exposition of the more difficult questions in this dialogue, by that <term>coryphæus (the leader or head of a school of thought)</term> of all true philosophers, Proclus. For in this apology, Homer and Plato are so admirably reconciled, that the poetry of the one and the philosophy of the other are in the highest degree honoured by the expulsion of the former from the polity <note>the ideal state or political system</note> of the latter. In short, it will be found, however paradoxical it may appear, that the most divine of poets ought beyond all others to be banished from a republic planned by the prince of philosophers. Such readers, too, as may fortunately possess a genius adapted for these speculations, will find that the fables of Homer are replete with a theory no less grand than scientific, no less accurate than sublime; that they are truly the progeny of <term>divine fury (theia mania; a state of being inspired by the gods or the Muses)</term>; are worthy to be ascribed to the Muses as their origin; are capable of exciting in those that understand them the most exalted conceptions, and of raising the imagination in conjunction with intellect, and thus purifying and illuminating its figured eye <note>a metaphorical reference to the mind's eye or the capacity to perceive spiritual truths through symbols</note>.

Though I availed myself in this translation of the epitome made by Gesner <note>Johann Matthias Gesner, a German scholar known for his work on ancient texts</note> of this apology, who seems to have consulted a more perfect manuscript

<summary>This page introduces a defense of Homer's mythological stories, which are famously criticized in Plato's Republic. The translator argues that the philosopher Proclus successfully reconciles Homer's inspired poetry with Plato's philosophical requirements through a deeper, symbolic understanding of myth.</summary>

### I. CONCERNING THE MODE OF THE <term>APPARATUS (the symbolic framework or literary machinery)</term> OF DIVINE FABLES WITH <term>THEOLOGISTS (those, like Homer or Orpheus, who write about the nature of the gods)</term>.—THE CAUSES OF SUCH FABLES ASSIGNED; AND A SOLUTION OF THE OBJECTIONS AGAINST THEM.

Since Socrates accuses the mode of fables according to which Homer and Hesiod have delivered doctrines concerning the Gods, and prior to these Orpheus, and any other poets, who with a divine mouth <note>original Greek: "ei theio stomati"</note> have interpreted things which have a <term>perpetual sameness of subsistence (an eternal, unchanging state of being)</term>, it is necessary that we should in the first place show that the disposition of the Homeric fables is adapted to the things which it indicates. For it may be said, How can things which are remote from the good and the beautiful, and which deviate from order,—how can base and illegal names, ever be adapted to those natures whose essence is characterized by the good; and is <term>consubsistent (existing together in the same substance)</term> with the beautiful, in whom there is the first order, and from whom all things are unfolded into light, in conjunction with beauty and undefiled power? How then can things which are full of tragical portents and <term>phantasms (illusory appearances)</term> which subsist with material natures, and are deprived of the whole of justice and the whole of divinity, be adapted to such natures as these? For is it not unlawful to ascribe to the nature of the Gods, who are exempt from all things through transcendent excellence, adulteries, and thefts, precipitations from heaven, injurious conduct towards parents, bonds, and castrations, and such other particulars as are celebrated by Homer and other antient poets? But, as the Gods are separated from other things, are united with *the good*, or the <term>ineffable principle (the ultimate reality that cannot be described in words)</term> of things, and have nothing of the imperfection of inferior natures belonging to them, but are unmingled and undefiled with respect to all things, <term>presubsisting (existing beforehand)</term> uniformly according to one bound and order,—in like manner it is requisite to employ the most excellent language

Whoever therefore has divested himself of every puerile and juvenile habit of the soul, and of the indefinite impulses of the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" or imagination was often seen by Platonists as a source of distraction that must be mastered to reach pure intellectual thought.</note>, and who has established intellect as the leader of his life, such a one will most opportunely participate of the spectacles concealed in such-like fables; but he who still requires instruction, and symmetry of manners, cannot with safety engage in their speculation.

It follows therefore, according to Socrates himself, that there is a two-fold species of fables, one of which is adapted to the instruction of youth, but the other is mystic; one is preparatory to moral virtue, but the other imparts a conjunction with a divine nature; one is capable of benefiting the many, the other is adapted to the few; the one is common and known to most men, but the other is recondite and unadapted to those who do not hasten to become perfectly established in a divine nature; and the one is co-ordinate with juvenile habits, but the other scarcely unfolds itself with sacrifices and mystic tradition. If therefore Socrates teaches us these things, must we not say that he harmonizes with Homer respecting fables? But he only rejects and reprobates them so far as they appear unadapted to the hypothesis of his discourse, and the narration of the education of youth.

### CONTAINING AN APOLOGY FOR THE FABLES OF HOMER. 141

To those who are able to follow the most elevated contemplations, we shall not hesitate to refer the "precipitations" <note>This refers to the story of the god Vulcan (Hephaestus) being cast down from heaven to earth.</note> of Vulcan to the irreproachable science concerning the Gods, nor the Saturnian bonds, nor the castrations of Heaven <note>The castration of Uranus (Heaven) by his son Saturn (Cronus).</note>, which Socrates says are unadapted to the ears of youth, and by no means harmonize with those habits which require juvenile tuition. For, in short, the mystic knowledge of divine natures can never subsist in foreign receptacles. To those therefore that are capable of such sublime speculations we must say, that the precipitation of Vulcan indicates the progression of a divine nature from on high, as far as to the last fabrication in sensibles <note>The physical world that can be perceived by the senses.</note>, and this so as to be moved and perfected and directed by the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>From the Greek 'demiurgos', meaning a craftsman; in this context, the divine creator or "artificer" of the universe.</note> and father of all things. 

But the Saturnian bonds manifest the union of the whole fabrication of the universe¹, with the intellectual and paternal supremacy of Saturn. The castrations of Heaven obscurely signify the separation of the Titanic² series from the connective³ order. By thus speaking we shall perhaps assert things that are known, and refer that which is tragical and fictitious in fables to the intellectual theory of the divine genera <note>The various classes or categories of divine beings.</note>. For whatever among us appears to be of a worse condition, and to belong to the inferior coordination of things, fables assume according to a better nature and power. 

Thus, for instance, a bond with us impedes and restrains energy, but there it is a contact and ineffable union with causes. A precipitation here is a violent motion from another; but with the Gods it indicates prolific progression, and an unrestrained and free presence to all things, without departing from its proper principle, but in an orderly manner proceeding from it through all things. And castrations in things partial and material cause a diminution of power, but in primary causes they obscurely signify the progression of secondary natures into a subject order, from their proper causes; things first at the same time remaining established in themselves undiminished, neither moved from themselves through the progression of these, nor mutilated by their separation, nor divided by their distribution in things subordinate. These things, which Socrates justly says are not fit to be heard by youth, are not on that account to be entirely rejected. For the same thing takes place with respect to

these fables—a fate which Plato notes somewhere also befalls divine and most holy teachings. For while these seem ridiculous to the common crowd, they reveal to the few who are awakened to intellectual activity a deep connection with reality; and through sacred rites themselves, they gain proof that they possess a power born together with all that is divine. For the Gods, when they hear these symbols, rejoice and readily answer those who call upon them, recognizing their own natures within these signs, which are familiar and specifically known to them. 

The mysteries as well, and the greatest and most complete of sacred initiations <note>original: τελεταί (teletai), referring to the final stage of mystic rites</note>, derive their power from these symbols. They allow the initiates to see, through these, whole, steady, and simple visions—visions that a young person, due to their age and even more their character, is not yet ready to receive. 

Therefore, we should not claim that such fables fail to teach virtue; rather, those who criticize them must demonstrate that they do not align perfectly with the laws governing sacred rites. Nor should it be said that they create a poor likeness of divine natures through obscure symbols; instead, it must be proven that they fail to prepare for us an unutterable connection toward the participation of the Gods. 

For fables composed for the education of youth should be grounded in probability and maintain a sense of "fabulous decorum" in their outward appearance; they should be entirely free from names that suggest the opposite of virtue and should be linked to divine natures through a clear similarity of symbols. 

But those fables which concern a more divinely inspired state—which harmonize the lowest things with the highest through analogy alone, and which are composed with an eye toward the sympathy within the universe between effects and their creative causes—such fables, disregarding the common crowd, use names in every possible way to indicate divine matters. 

Similarly, regarding musical harmony, we say that one kind is "poetic," which uses melodies that inspire virtue to cultivate the souls of the young. But there is another "divine" harmony, which moves the listeners and produces a divine madness <note>A state of being "possessed" by a god; a higher form of inspiration above human reason.</note>, which we rank as something better than mere self-control. We accept the first kind as part of a complete education, but we reject the latter as being unsuited to the practical administration of a state. Does not Socrates, then, banish the <term>Phrygian harmony</term> <note>A musical mode associated in ancient Greece with religious excitement and the rites of Cybele and Dionysus.</note> from his Republic because it produces ecstasy in the soul, and for this reason separates it from other harmonies that serve the purposes of education?

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the argument that mythology serves two distinct purposes: one for the moral education of the young (which must be probable and "decent") and another for spiritual initiation (which uses strange or "monstrous" symbols to point toward hidden divine truths).</meta>

->### CONTAINING AN APOLOGY FOR THE FABLES OF HOMER. 143<-

Just as, therefore, harmony is twofold—with one kind being suited for general education and the other being entirely different from it—mythology is divided in a similar way. It is split into that which contributes to the proper instruction of youth, and that which is used for the sacred and symbolic invocation of divine natures. The first method, which works through straightforward images, is suited to those who practice philosophy in a sincere and natural way. The other method, however, which points to a divine essence through hidden <term>recondite (obscure or deeply hidden)</term> signs, is meant for the leaders of more advanced, mystical rites. From this second method, Plato himself makes many of his own specific teachings more believable and clear. 

For instance, in the *Phaedo*, he honors with a respectful silence that hidden assertion that we are confined in the body as if in a prison guarded by a sentry. He also testifies, in accordance with the mysteries, to the different assignments given to the soul when it is in a pure or impure state upon its departure to Hades <note>The "invisible" realm of the afterlife.</note>. Furthermore, he speaks of the soul's habits and the triple paths arising from its essence, following ancient sacred traditions. All of these are full of symbolic theory, including the ascent and descent of souls celebrated by the poets, the symbols of Dionysus <note>original: "Dionyſiacal ſigns"</note>, and what are called the errors of the Titans <note>Refers to the "Titanic" nature in humanity that must be purified.</note>, the "triple-ways" <note>original: "triviæ," referring to the crossroads of the underworld</note>, the wandering in Hades, and everything else of this nature. Thus, Plato does not entirely reject this style of myth-making; rather, he considers it unsuitable for the education of the young. For that reason, he provides models of theology that are appropriate for the character of those being instructed.

It also appears to me that whatever seems tragic, monstrous, or unnatural in poetic fictions actually serves to rouse the listener in many different ways to seek out the truth. These elements draw us toward hidden knowledge and do not allow us to rest satisfied with shallow ideas based on mere probability. Instead, they compel us to penetrate into the inner parts of the fables, to explore the hidden intentions of their authors, and to observe what natures and powers they intended to signal to future generations through such mystical symbols¹.

Since, therefore, fables of this kind stir those who are naturally of a more excellent disposition toward a desire for the hidden theories they contain, and—

¹ Such fables also call forth our natural, uncorrupted ideas of divine beings, in which they effectively establish us through sacred disciplines that are not taught by rote; in short, they bring the vital powers of the soul to perfection.

## II. WHAT THE DIFFERENT MODES OF THEOMACHY <term>Battle of the Gods (from the Greek "theos," god, and "mache," battle)</term>, OR, THE BATTLES OF THE GODS, ARE, AMONG THEOLOGISTS, AND AN INTERPRETATION OF THE OCCULT TRUTH WHICH THEY CONTAIN.

And thus much concerning those forms of fables according to which other poets and Homer have delivered mystic conceptions respecting the Gods, and which are unapparent to the vulgar <note>meaning the uninitiated or common people who take the stories literally</note>. After this, it follows I think that we should distinctly consider the several fables in the order in which they are mentioned by Socrates, and contemplate according to what conceptions of the soul Homer represents the Gods fighting, or doing or suffering any thing else, in his poems. And in the first place let us consider this *theomachy* as it is called, or battles of the Gods, which Homer devises, but Socrates thinks worthy of animadversion <note>criticism or censure</note>, as by no means adapted to the education of youth. For, that there is neither sedition, nor dissension and division, as with mortals, among the Gods, but peace and an inoffensive life, the poet himself testifies when he somewhere says concerning Olympus, that it is a substratum <note>underlying foundation</note> to the Gods, who possess every possible joy, and spectacles of immense beauty:

->The blessed Gods in joy unceasing live.<-

What discord and war then can find any entrance among those who are allotted eternal delight, who are perpetually propitious <note>favorably inclined or benevolent</note>, and rejoicing in the goods which they possess? But if it be proper that discourses concerning the Gods should regard as well their providence as the nature of the beings for whom they provide, I think we may interpret as follows their opposition to each other:

In the first place, the divided progressions of all things, and their separations according to essence, supernally <note>from a higher or divine realm</note> originate from that division of first operating causes <gloss>1</gloss> which is unknown to all things; and subsisting according to those principles which are expanded above wholes, they dissent from each other; some being suspended from the unifying monad *bound* <note>original: "peras," the principle of limit and order</note>, and about this determining their subsistence, but others receiving in themselves

->### CONTAINING AN APOLOGY FOR THE FABLES OF HOMER.<-

When it comes to physical and material things, we should not be surprised by the fact that they share names with higher divine realities. For every chain of being carries the name of its **monad** <note>A "monad" is the single, unified source or primary unit from which a specific series of beings or things originates.</note>, and individual spirits love to be called by the same names as the universal wholes they belong to. Because of this, there are many different types of Apollos, Neptunes, and Vulcans <note>Homer’s Greek names for these gods are Apollo, Poseidon, and Hephaestus.</note>. Some of these exist entirely apart from the physical universe; others are assigned to the heavens; others preside over the basic elements; and still others govern specific individuals. 

It is not strange, then, that a more "partial" or localized Vulcan—one belonging to the **dæmoniacal** <term>dæmoniacal: In ancient philosophy, "daimones" were not evil spirits but intermediary beings—messengers and administrators who bridge the gap between the high gods and humanity.</term> order—should have a protective rule over material fire here on earth, or that he should be the watchful guardian of the art of metalworking in brass. If divine providence extends down to the very last divisions of reality—flowing in an orderly progression from the unified, high causes down to the smallest details—then this "Vulcan-like" spirit will naturally work to protect what he has been assigned. He will also be "hostile" toward anything that threatens to destroy or corrupt that which he guards. 

In these lower levels of existence, we see divisions of various powers, instances of friendship and discord, a shared feeling with the things they govern, arguments, and even "revenge" through mockery. These things are very appropriately understood to take place at the outer edges of the divine orders. Therefore, when myths represent these powers as being in conflict or opposing each other because of the different things they protect, the stories are actually quite close to the truth. This is because the "passions" or changes in the things being governed are reflected in the spirits immediately responsible for them.

In short, we can see two ways of understanding the "battles" described by poets inspired by Phœbus <note>Phœbus is another name for Apollo, the god of prophecy and poetry.</note>. One view looks at the orderly division of divine ranks that come from the two primary principles of all things—which the *one*, the supreme cause of everything, produced. This view represents the Gods as acting in opposition to each other based on these two principles. Whether we call these first principles "bound and infinity," or the "**monad** and the **indefinite duad**" <note>In Pythagorean and Platonic thought, the "Monad" represents unity and limit, while the "Indefinite Duad" represents the principle of multiplicity and endless division.</note>, they appear to be opposite to one another, and the various orders of the Gods are separated accordingly. The second view arises from looking at the variety and conflict found in the lowest level of things, and attributing that discord to the spirits involved.

For parts are preserved by their containing wholes, as long as they subsist.

## III. IN WHAT MANNER AN APOLOGY IS TO BE MADE FOR THOSE DIVINE FABLES WHICH APPEAR TO MAKE THE GODS THE CAUSES OF EVIL.

In the next place let us consider how, since the Gods in the summit of their essence are particularly characterized by goodness, poetry makes them to be the authors of both evil and good, though it is proper to refer to them the principal cause of what is good alone. For this, Socrates, demonstrating that divinity gives subsistence to good alone, but to nothing evil, thinks worthy of animadversion <note>Criticism or censure.</note> in the poems of Homer. And it seems that he reprobates the battles of the Gods, as subverting divine union, but condemns what we now propose to investigate, as diminishing the goodness of the Gods. For,

> Two vessels on Jove's <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods.</note> threshold ever stand,
> The source of evil one, and one of good <note>original: "Iliad. lib. 24. ver. 527." — Homer's Iliad, Book 24, verse 527.</note>.

...the Gods themselves. For all things are divided by the dual principles <term>biformed principles</term> <note>original: "biformed principles"—referring to "Bound" and "Infinity," the two foundational roots of all existence in Pythagorean philosophy.</note> of reality: specifically, the ranks of the Gods, the nature of all beings, the different types of souls, physical forces, the orbits of the heavens, and the various types of material objects. Finally, human affairs and the fates assigned by justice receive a twofold origin from these principles. Of these, some are of a higher condition, while others are of an inferior state.

By this, I mean that the natural qualities of bodies—such as beauty, strength, and health—as well as those things that belong to the soul independent of the body—such as power, honor, and wealth—belong to the higher category. However, the habits and circumstances that are opposite to these belong to the inferior category. Because things are necessarily divided in this manner, the ancients used to immediately label those in the better portion as "good," while they called those in the opposing portion "evil." Yet, they did not use the word "evil" with the same meaning we use when describing an unjust or undisciplined soul. Instead, they viewed these things as "evil" because they act as obstacles to our activity, overshadowing our natural character and disturbing the soul’s calm management of human life. They admitted them to be "evil" in a sense, but a sense quite different from what we call the "evils of the soul" <note>In this philosophy, moral evil (vice) is distinct from natural "evils" like sickness or poverty, which are seen merely as the "lesser" side of a physical duality.</note>. In this same way, they were also accustomed to calling disease, physical weakness, and a lack of life's necessities "evils."

Why is it necessary to cite only poetry as proof of this terminology? The Pythagoreans also established twofold pairings <term>coordinations</term> <note>original: "coordinations"—the *systoichia*, or parallel columns of opposites used to categorize every aspect of the universe.</note> of things across every level of existence, and they did not hesitate to call one side "good" and the other "evil." However, how could anyone truly believe that "even numbers," "oblong shapes," or "motion" are evils in the sense of being a total lack of good? How can we say that the feminine gender, or the concepts of "difference" and "unlikeness," are contrary to nature? I believe it is entirely evident that, throughout the entire progression of reality, they called the subordinate series of things "evil" only because these things moved away from the primary series and were neither inherently beneficial, nor...

It is necessary, therefore, to connect these twofold categories of good and evil in the universe to the <term>demiurgic monad</term> <note>The "demiurgic monad" refers to the single, supreme creative intellect that serves as the source of all structured reality.</note>. For the divisions of the Gods, and of the classes of being that come after the Gods, depend on that first principle. Likewise, the cause of the good and evil which happen by fate, and which are assigned to souls during their time in the realm of generation <note>The world of physical birth and change.</note> according to justice, must be attributed to the governor of the universe, who also sends souls into this mortal region. 

For the effects of fate are suspended from the <term>demiurgic</term> providence, around which the order of justice also exists; fate follows the boundaries of this providence, being, as the <term>Athenian guest</term> <note>The "Athenian guest" is the primary speaker in Plato's *Laws*.</note> in <term>Plato</term> observes, the avenger of the divine law. The <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Demiurge" is the Divine Craftsman who shapes the material world according to eternal patterns.</note> and father of the universe has therefore established within himself the cause of everything good and evil—of both the more excellent and the lesser gifts, of prosperous events, and of those things that act as obstacles to the soul's activities in the external world. He governs all things according to intellect, distributing to every being such things as are fitting, and referring all things back to his own fatherly administration. For he distributes to souls, with an eye toward the good, both things of the better and of the inferior categories, looking in his distribution toward the ultimate perfection of those who receive them.

If these things are correctly stated, we must accept the <term>Homeric</term> arrangement, which places in the <term>demiurgic</term> intellect of <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Jupiter is used here for Zeus, the king of the Gods.</note> twofold primary causes for the goods and the ills which he grants to souls. For, among all the intellectual kings, the <term>duad</term> <note>The "duad" refers to the principle of duality or "two-ness."</note> especially belongs to the <term>demiurgus</term> of the universe: since, according to the <term>Oracle</term> <note>This likely refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a text of great authority in Neoplatonism.</note>, "the duad is seated with him; and, by his governing all things, and disposing every thing in its proper place, he shows virtue to be victorious, and vice to be vanquished in the universe." 

For what difference is there between stating these things and comparing the <term>demiurgus</term> to a person playing at chess, sending souls into lives adapted to their respective natures? ### IV. HOW THE POETRY OF HOMER SEEMS TO REFER A VIOLATION OF OATHS TO THE GODS:—THE TRUTH RESPECTING THIS UNFOLDED.

In the next place let us consider how leagues and oaths, according to the poetry of **Homer**, are violated with the will of the mighty **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>, and of **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> acting in subserviency to the will of her father: for this also **Socrates** reprobates, as referring the principle of evils to the first of the Gods.

And here indeed it is worth while especially to doubt, how he who makes divinity to be the cause of these things, does not make him to be the cause of the greatest and real evils. For **Homer** cannot here be defended by saying, that he represents poverty, disease, and things of this kind, as proceeding from the Gods, but he ascribes to divinity the cause of those things which are acknowledged by all men to be evils. **Timæus**, indeed, in **Plato**, represents the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The Divine Craftsman or creator who brings order to the material world.</note> as entirely prescribing laws to souls prior to their descent into <term>generation</term> <note>The realm of physical life, birth, and death, as opposed to the eternal realm of being.</note>, that he may not be accused as the cause of their consequent evils; but these verses of **Homer** admit that the principle of the greatest evils is imparted to them from divinity, when they have descended, and are conversant with generation. How then shall we reply to these animadversions, so as to harmonize the doctrine of **Homer** with the nature of things, and the narration of **Plato**? We may reply as follows: That fables of this kind are not adapted to the habit of youth, as has been asserted by us before, and we shall now, and in all that follows, repeat the assertion. For it is not possible for youth to distinguish the nature of things, nor to refer the apparent signs of truth to an unapparent theory <note>A hidden or symbolic spiritual interpretation that lies beneath the literal story.</note>, nor to see how every thing in the universe is accomplished according to the will of divinity, through other intervening causes. But we shall show that these things are agreeable to the philosophy of **Plato**.

The **Athenian guest** <note>The primary speaker in Plato’s *Laws*, representing the philosopher's mature views on law and theology.</note> then, in the *Laws*, says, "that God is the beginning, the middle, and end of all things, and that justice follows him, taking vengeance on those that desert the divine law: but these, as he informs us, are such as through youth and folly have their soul inflamed with insolence, and for a certain time appear to themselves to govern, but afterwards suffer the proper punishment of their conduct from justice, and entirely subvert themselves, their city, and their family." These things are asserted by the **Athenian guest** *politically*; but **Homer** <note>original footnote 1: The Greek text previously read "but nevertheless" (ἁ δὲ ὀμως), but is here corrected to "but Homer" (ὁ δὲ 'Ομηρος).</note>, relating them in a *divinely inspired manner* (<term>entheastikōs</term> <note>original: ενθεαστικως; to speak while possessed by or filled with a god.</note>), says that those who have often sinned, and committed the greatest crimes, are punished for their offences according to the single will of **Jupiter** <note>The king of the gods, Zeus.</note>, and are deprived of life together with their wives and children. He further informs us, that **Jupiter** first of all accomplishes this punishment, and in a manner exempt and unapparent to all; but **Minerva** <note>The goddess of wisdom, Athena.</note> in the second place, being subservient to and cooperating with the *paternal providence* of **Jupiter**: for, as **Orpheus** <note>A legendary poet and prophet; the author cites Orphic fragments to support the theological hierarchy.</note> says, "she is the powerful queen of *the intellect of Saturnian Jove* <note>original footnote 2: Δεινη γαρ Κρονιδαο νοου κραντειρα τετυκται (Deinē gar Kronidao noou kranteira tetyktai); literally: "For she is the dread queen who brings to fulfillment the mind of the son of Cronus."</note>." The same poet likewise adds, "*that his brain who violates leagues and oaths flows on the ground like wine.*" 

In consequence, therefore, of this violation, such men subject themselves to justice, and render themselves adapted to punishment. Hence the violation of leagues and oaths is especially perpetrated by those who, prior to this, have deserved the vengeance of the Gods, who justly govern mortal affairs, and thus punish former crimes. But such are said to be moved, and led forth into energy by the Gods themselves: not that the Gods render men who are to be punished impious and unjust, but as calling into energy those that are adapted to the perpetration of such-like actions, that by once energizing according to their inward habit, and producing into light the progeny of depraved actions with which they are pregnant, they may become worthy of punishment. For we should rather say, according to **Plato**, that vengeance, the attendant of justice, is perfected in such, than divine justice itself; since the just and justice are beautiful things. But both he on whom vengeance is inflicted, and he on whom it is not, are miserable. Men therefore, who have committed many and the greatest crimes, and who have a depraved habit which is parturient with greater and

And in this case **Minerva** is not the cause of the election, but the improbity <note>Wickedness or lack of moral integrity.</note> of him by whom the election is made. For neither is the prophet in **Plato** the cause of a tyrannic life, but the intemperance of him that chose it. Hence **Pandarus**, in obeying **Minerva**, is said to suffer this through his stupidity. For indeed (to speak accurately) he did not obey **Minerva**, but the avaricious and stupid habit of his soul. 

Though, is it not wonderful that **Minerva**, in this instance, is not the cause of wisdom, but of folly? But, says **Plotinus**, “Craft is produced from a <term>defluxion</term> <note>A "flowing down" or degradation; Plotinus argues that divine qualities are distorted when they are received by an imperfect or corrupted soul.</note> of intellect; an illumination of temperance becomes intemperance; and audacity is the gift of fortitude.” For such as are the forms of life, such also from necessity must be the participations from more excellent natures. Hence some participate of intelligibles intellectually, others according to opinion, and others phantastically <note>Through the "phantasy" or imagination, rather than through pure reason.</note>. Others again participate of passions impassively, others with mediocrity of passion, and others with perfect passivity. But all things are moved by the **Gods**, according to their respective aptitudes. So that the violation of oaths did not proceed from **Jupiter** and **Minerva**, but from **Pandarus** and the **Trojans**. justice, and as preparing those by whom it was perpetrated for the perfect punishment of their guilt.

Nor is a divine nature the cause of true evils to souls, but the depraved habits of these are the sources to them of their depraved <term>energies</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "energy" (energeia) refers to the active expression or external manifestation of an internal state or potential.</note>. But every energy, though it proceeds with depravity into the universe, is under the direction of presiding Gods, and of a more total or partial <term>providence</term> <note>The idea that the universe is governed by divine foresight that ensures everything eventually serves a good or just end.</note>. For it becomes, says **Plotinus** <note>A major Greek philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism (3rd century AD).</note>, an unjust action to him who does it, so far as pertains to the doing it, but just to him who suffers for it, so far as he suffers <note>original: "το άδικον τω ποιήσαντι... δίκαιον τω παθόντι." Plotinus argues that while a crime is morally wrong for the criminal, the victim's experience of it may be a necessary karmic or cosmic correction.</note>. And so far as an action of this kind is atheistical, it originates from a partial cause, which gives perfection to an action full of passion; but so far as it is good, it obtains from presiding powers its proper end. For it is necessary that the authors of the greatest crimes should some time or other be called to punishment; but this would never take place, unless their depravity received its completion. Many habits therefore, remaining <term>unenergetic</term> <note>Dormant; qualities that exist in the soul but have not yet been acted upon.</note>, render those by whom they are possessed incapable of obtaining their proper cure. Hence, on the Gods consulting concerning bringing the war to an end, and saving the **Trojans**, the Goddess who presides over justice <note>Referencing Themis.</note> prevents any energy of this kind, that the **Trojans** may more swiftly suffer the punishment of their crimes; and **Minerva**, who cooperates with this divinity, excites to the violation of the oath, that, <term>energizing</term> according to the whole of their depravity, they may receive the punishment of the whole of it. For neither was it good for them to remain without a cure, nor that their latent depravity should be healed prior to their second offences. All their unjust life therefore being unfolded, punishment follows, correcting the whole of their impious conduct.

## VI. WHAT THE JUDGMENT OF THE GODS IS IN THE FABLES OF THE POET, AND WHAT DIFFERENCES OF LIVES IT OBSCURELY SIGNIFIES. ##

Again, it is not proper to think that the celebrated <term>judgment of the Gods</term> <note>This refers to the "Judgment of Paris," a famous myth where the Trojan prince Paris was asked to decide which goddess—Juno (Hera), Minerva (Athena), or Venus (Aphrodite)—was the most beautiful.</note>, which fables say was accomplished by Paris, was in reality a strife of the Gods with each other, under the judgment of a <term>barbarian</term> <note>In ancient Greek texts, "barbarian" was a standard term for anyone who did not speak Greek, such as the Trojans, and did not necessarily carry the modern connotation of being uncivilized.</note>; but we ought to consider the elections of lives, which Plato delivers in many places, as subsisting under the Gods who are the inspective guardians of souls. And this indeed Plato clearly teaches us in the *Phædrus*, when he says that a royal life is the gift of Juno, a philosophic life of Jupiter, and an <term>amatory life</term> <note>An "amatory" life refers to one dedicated to Love and the pursuit of Beauty, which in Platonic thought is a path toward spiritual enlightenment.</note> of Venus. Since therefore souls, from among a multitude of lives proposed to them from the universe, embrace some according to their own judgment and reject others, hence fables, transferring to the Gods themselves the peculiarities of lives, assert that not the diversities of living, but the Gods that preside over these diversities, are judged by those that choose them. 

According to this reasoning, Paris also is said to have been appointed a judge of Minerva, Juno and Venus; and that of three lives which were proposed to him, he chose the amatory life: and this not with prudence, but recurring to apparent beauty, and pursuing the image of that beauty which is <term>intelligible</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "intelligible" refers to the higher realm of ideas and truths that can only be grasped by the mind, as opposed to "sensible" things seen with the eyes.</note>. For he who is truly amatory, taking intellect and prudence for his guides, and with these contemplating both true and apparent beauty, is no less the votary of Minerva than of Venus. But he who alone pursues the amatory form of life by itself, and this accompanied with passion, deserts true beauty,

### VII. WHAT THE MUTATIONS OF THE GODS ARE, WHICH ARE INTRODUCED IN FABLES, AND IN HOW MANY WAYS, AND THROUGH WHAT CAUSES, THEY ARE DEVISED. ###

Since a divine nature is not only beneficent, but likewise immutable, without form, simple, and always subsisting according to the same, and after the same manner, Socrates very properly considers the following verses of Homer worthy of animadversion <note>An "animadversion" is a critical observation or a formal expression of disapproval.</note>,

> ->The Gods at times, resembling foreign guests,<-
> ->Wander o'er cities in all-various forms ⁱ.<-

<margin>ⁱ Odyssey, Book 17, verse 485.</margin>

Indeed, that fables of this kind ought not to be heard by those who genuinely receive a political education, is perfectly evident; since it is requisite that the paradigm of a polity <note>A "polity" refers to a form of civil government or a structured society.</note> which is to be stable, should be immutable, and not obnoxious <note>In this older sense, "obnoxious" means vulnerable or subject to something.</note> to all-various mutations. In like manner we should form a judgment of the conceptions of Homer, not from what is said by the suitors <note>The "suitors" are the antagonistic characters in the *Odyssey* who represent moral corruption.</note>, or any other depraved character in his poems, but from what the poet himself, or Nestor, or Ulysses, appears to say.

If any one however is willing to ascribe this dogma concerning the mutation <note>The word "mutation" here refers to the idea of "divine change," or gods shifting their shapes and forms.</note> of the Gods to Homer himself, he will not be destitute of arguments which accord with all sacred concerns, with the greatest sacrifices and mysteries, and with those appearances of the Gods which both in dreams and true visions, the rumour of mankind has supernally <note>Meaning "from a higher or heavenly source."</note> received. For in all these the Gods extend many forms of themselves, and appear passing into many figures. And sometimes an unfigured <note>Formless or without a specific physical shape.</note> light of them presents itself to the view; at other times this light is fashioned in a human form, and at others again assumes a different shape. These things also the discipline of divine origin pertaining to sacred concerns delivers. For thus the Oracles <gloss>¹</gloss> <note>¹ Specifically the Chaldæan Oracles, a set of mystical texts from the 2nd century AD that were highly influential to late-Platonic philosophy. > “A similar fire extending itself by leaps through the waves of the air; or an unfigured fire whence a voice runs before; or a light beheld near, every way splendid, resounding and convolved <note>Coiled or swirling.</note>. But also to behold a horse full of refulgent light; or a boy carried on the swift back of a horse,—a boy fiery, or clothed with gold, or, on the contrary, naked; or shooting an arrow, and standing on the back of the horse.”

And such things as the oracles add after these, not at any time attributing either internal change, or variety, or any mutation to a divine nature, but indicating its various participations <note>In Neoplatonism, "participation" is the way a lower level of reality (like a human soul) receives or "shares in" the influence of a higher, unchanging reality (like a god).</note>. For that which is simple in the Gods appears various to those by whom it is seen, they neither being changed, nor wishing to deceive; but nature herself giving a determination to the characteristics of the Gods, according to the measures of the participants. For that which is participated, being one, is variously participated by intellect, the <term>rational soul</term> <note>The part of the human soul capable of logical reasoning and understanding universal truths.</note>, the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" or imagination acts as a bridge between the senses and the intellect, often presenting ideas in the form of mental images or "figures."</note>, and sense. Hence that which is participated <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "participation" is the relationship where a lower being receives a quality or essence from a higher source.</note> is uniform according to the summit of its subsistence <note>The "summit of its subsistence" refers to the highest, most essential level of a being's existence.</note>, but multiform according to participation. Whether, therefore, some of the Gods have appeared similar to guests, or have been seen in some other form, it is not proper to attribute the apparent mutation <note>A "mutation" is a change or transformation.</note> to them, but we should say that the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" refers to the faculty of imagination or the way an image is formed in the mind of the observer.</note> is varied in the different recipients. And this is one way in which the poetry of Homer delivers multiform mutations of immutable natures.

But there is another way, when a divine nature itself, which is all-powerful and full of all-various forms, extends various spectacles to those that behold it. For then, according to the variety of powers which it possesses, it is said to be changed into many forms, at different times extending different powers; always indeed energizing <note>To "energize" here means to actively exert power or influence.</note> according to all its powers, but perpetually appearing various to the transitive intellections <note>A technical term referring to the way human thoughts move from one subject to another in a sequence, unlike divine thought which understands all at once.</note> of souls, through the multitude which it comprehends. For the last of those genera that are the perpetual attendants of the Gods are manifested by these figures. And here you may see how particulars of this kind are devised according to the order of things. For that which is simple is adapted to a divine nature, that which is universal to an angelic, and the rational nature to both these; and that which is partial and irrational accords with a dæmoniacal nature: for a life of this kind is connected with the dæmoniacal order. And thus much concerning the modes according to which the Homeric fables devise mutations of things immutable, and introduce various forms to uniform natures.

### VIII. CONCERNING THE DREAM SENT TO AGAMEMNON, WHICH APPEARS TO ACCUSE THE GODS OF FALSEHOOD, AND HOW IT MAY BE SHOWN THAT A DIVINE NATURE IS VOID OF FALSEHOOD.

It now remains that we speak concerning the dream sent by Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note> to Agamemnon; for Socrates, at the end of his theological types <term>Theological types: the rules or "canons" for representing the gods established by Plato in the "Republic."</term>, reprobates <note>To reprobate here means to strongly disapprove of or condemn the idea that a god would send a lying dream.</note>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Homeric myths against the criticisms raised by Socrates in the Republic. Having previously discussed how gods appear to mortals, it now addresses the "lying dream" sent by Jupiter to Agamemnon in the Iliad.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO BOOKS II. AND III. OF THE REPUBLIC:</header>

[Socrates] debates this, because the whole of a divine and dæmoniacal <term>dæmoniacal: pertaining to "daimons," which in Greek philosophy were intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</term> nature is without falsehood, as he collects by demonstrative arguments. But Homer says that Agamemnon was deceived through this dream. Though, is it not absurd, if this dream is from Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the Greek gods.</note>, according to the assertion of the poet, that this alone nearly, of all the particulars which are mentioned as deriving their origin from Jupiter, should be attended with fraud?

In answer to this objection, we may say what is usually asserted by most of the interpreters, that the fallacy had its subsistence in the phantasy <term>phantasy: the faculty of imagination or the way the mind interprets internal images.</term> of Agamemnon. For Jupiter in his speech to the dream, and the dream again in its address to Agamemnon, evidently indicate that it would be requisite to call together *all* the army, and to attack the enemy with *all* his forces; for this is the meaning of the word **with the whole army** <note>original: "πανσυδιη" (*pansudiē*), meaning with all speed or with one's entire force.</note>, which is used in both the speeches. But Agamemnon, not understanding the mandate, neglected the greatest part of his army, and, engaging in battle without the aid of Achilles, was frustrated in his expectations through his unskilfulness in judging of divine visions. So that Jupiter is not the cause of the deception, but he who did not properly understand the mandates of Jupiter.

We shall also add the solution given by our preceptor Syrianus <note>A celebrated Neoplatonist philosopher (died c. 437 AD) and the teacher of Proclus.</note>, which both accedes to the meaning of Homer and the truth of things. For, if Jupiter is represented as providing for the honour of the hero Achilles, and consulting how he may destroy the greatest number of the Greeks, is it not necessary that he must previously comprehend in himself the cause of the deception? For, if Achilles had been associated with the army, the Greeks would not have been destroyed, nor would they have been punished for their unjust conduct towards him. It is better therefore to say that the deception was from divinity for the good of the deceived. For good is better than truth. And among the Gods, indeed, they are conjoined with each other: for neither is intellect without divinity, nor divinity without an intellectual essence <note>In this philosophy, the "intellectual essence" is the highest form of reality, where thought and being are one.</note>. But in their participants <note>Individuals (like humans) who receive or "participate" in divine qualities.</note> they are often separated; and good is produced through falsehood, and truth is frustrated of good. Whence also Socrates himself, when he is framing laws for the guardians of his republic, orders falsehood to be employed, through the opinion of the stupid, who are not otherwise able to obtain the good which is adapted to their condition.
