...condition. <note>The text begins mid-word, completing a thought from the previous page regarding Agamemnon's mental state.</note> If, therefore, it is said that the divine benefits some through truth and others through falsehoods <note>In this context, "falsehoods" refers to myths, symbols, or allegories that are not literally true but contain spiritual lessons.</note>, and at the same time leads all of them toward the good, it is not at all surprising. For, among created things, some exist without matter, while others exist with matter, which is naturally prone to error; or rather, matter itself is a kind of "true deception." Thus, in the <term>providence: the divine care or guidance of the universe and souls.</term> of souls, if they are—as we have said—benefited by the divine in different ways, some in a spiritual way through pure truth and others in a material way through symbols, such divine activity is perfectly suited to the nature of the Gods.

But, if necessary, we may also assert that deception and falsehood are actually created within the person receiving the message. This happens according to the divine will, so that someone who has acted wrongly may become more worthy through the experience of being deceived. It is just like how material things are created in these lower regions according to a <term>demiurgic: relating to a "demiurge," a divine craftsman who shapes the physical world.</term> plan, so that birth and death can exist to complete the cycle of the universe. Therefore, God does not deceive; rather, the one who is deceived deceives himself. This occurs by the will of the divine for the ultimate good of the person who experiences the deception. For, while God acts in a purely spiritual way, that which is produced in our world appears in a material form. While He acts <term>impartibly: as a single, undivided whole.</term>, the result of that action is received <term>partibly: in separate, divided pieces.</term> by us. And while He signals through pure intellect, a "shadowy" falsehood only appears in the mind of the person who receives the signal. The divine poet Homer himself shows that truth lives with the Gods, while deception arises from the opinions of those who receive it, when he depicts Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the Greek gods.</note> commanding the dream, saying:

->*All that I order tell with perfect truth.*<-

How then is there falsehood in the divine, according to Homer? And how is the divine the cause of deception? We can only say He is the cause in the sense that even the "shadowy" existence of deception in this lower world is not against His will. However, the minds of young people are not yet capable of distinguishing or understanding how the "Wholes" <note>A philosophical term for universal, perfect realities.</note> remain free of evil, even though evil appears in the individual things that receive them. They cannot see how beings more excellent than us do not deceive, even when we are often deceived—and that when we are deceived, we experience it according to the plan of providence.

## IX. A COMMON APOLOGY BOTH FOR THE HOMERIC AND PLATONIC FABLES, IN WHICH THEY SPEAK OF THE JUDGMENTS IN HADES, OF SOULS, AND THE DIFFERENT ALLOTMENTS WHICH THEY RECEIVE ON DEPARTING FROM THEIR BODIES, ACCORDING TO THE IDIOMS OF THE LIFE IN THE BODY.

Having then discussed these things, let us examine what is written in the third book of the *Republic*, and, prior to other things, what the poet <note>Referring to Homer.</note> either himself asserts, or introduces another asserting, mythologically concerning <term>Hades: the underworld or the state of the soul after death.</term>; and let us consider whether they contain any thing of truth, and accord with the narrations of Plato. What then are we to understand, when the poet represents Achilles as preferring servitude in the present life to the possession of every thing in Hades? <note>In Book 11 of the Odyssey, the ghost of Achilles famously tells Odysseus he would rather be a landless laborer on earth than the king of all the dead.</note> What is the meaning of those dreadful habitations, which are odious to the Gods, of the image and the soul, of shades wandering without intellect, of lives compared to shadows, of the lamentations of souls passing thither, of their being assimilated to bats, of smoke, a crashing noise, and such like particulars, which the poems of Homer contain? What likewise are the rivers in Hades, and those appellations which are the most tragical? For these Socrates <term>reprobates: expresses strong disapproval or condemnation.</term>, but at the same time adds, what is common to all fables, “that they contribute to something else; but we (says he) are afraid for our guardians, lest from these terrible relations, they should think death to be dreadful.”

However, that Socrates himself in many places uses names and <term>enigmas: symbolic or obscure riddles intended to convey deeper truths.</term> of this kind, is obvious to every one. For, that I may omit the rivers mentioned in the *Phædo*, the wanderings of souls, their anxieties, the three roads, the punishments, the being carried in rivers, the lamentations and exclamations there, and the supplications of injurers to the injured, of all which Plato says Hades is full;—though these things should be omitted, yet does not what we find written at the end of the *Republic* accord with the intention of the Homeric poetry, viz. the bellowing mouth, <term>Tartarus: the deepest abyss of the underworld used as a place of punishment.</term>, fiery <term>dæmons: spiritual beings or tutelary spirits, here appearing as agents of punishment.</term>, the tearing off the flesh of the tyrant <note>original: "Aridæus"</note> <term>Aridæus: usually rendered as Ardiaeus; a tyrant in the "Myth of Er" who is cast into Tartarus for his crimes.</term>, and souls full of dust and filth? For, what is there in these which falls short of the tragical in the extreme?

### X. WHAT THE CAUSES ARE THROUGH WHICH THE POETRY OF HOMER ASCRIBES LAMENTATIONS BOTH TO HEROES AND GODS; AND LIKEWISE TO THE BEST OF HEROES AND THE GREATEST OF THE GODS.

It now follows that we should consider how the poetry of **Homer** does not represent one of us weeping and lamenting, when he also ascribes these effects of sorrow to his heroes, but makes the Gods themselves to weep, for the death of mortals whom they loved; though, according to **Plato**, **Socrates** neither wept, nor suffered any <term>perturbation: a state of mental agitation or disturbance</term> of mind, when his <term>familiars: close friends or disciples</term> wept on account of his approaching death; but **Apollodorus**, who wept abundantly, and any other who was similarly affected, were reproved by their master. But the divine poet represents his heroes immoderately lamenting the loss of their familiars. And even if such passions were proper in men who are allotted a mortal nature, yet they ought not to be ascribed to the Gods themselves. <margin>¹ That is, **Jupiter** <note>original: "Jupiter". These things **Socrates** <term>reprobates: strongly disapproves of</term> in **Homer**, and expels from the education of youth, fearful lest some impediment should arise, through such-like assertions, to a right discipline according to virtue. For education is particularly <term>conversant: concerned or familiar</term> with pleasure and pain; which being increased, the legislator must necessarily be <term>frustrated: blocked or defeated</term> of his proper end.

To these objections we reply, that since the poet introduces heroes engaged in practical affairs, and living a life adapted to these, he very properly represents them as affected with particular events, and living conformably to such affections. For to philosophers, and those who <term>energize cathartically: act in a way that purifies the soul from material influence</term>, pleasures and pains, and the mixtures of these, are by no means adapted; since they are separated from these, lay aside all the trifling of mortality, and hasten to be divested of the forms of life with which they are surrounded from the elements, rapidly withdrawing themselves from material passions the offspring of <term>generation: the cycle of physical birth and death</term>. But pleasures, pains, sympathies, and a scene of all-various passions, are coordinated to those engaged in war, and who energize according to the passive part of the soul. And how could the vehement about actions take place, without the impulse of the appetites? **Priam**, therefore, and **Achilles**, neither being philosophers, nor willing to separate themselves from generation, nor living after the manner of the guardians of **Plato’s** republic,—if they lament and commiserate their <term>familiars: close friends or family</term>, it is by no means wonderful. For the loss of friends, the being destitute of children, and the subversions of cities, appear to warriors to impart a great portion of misery. The accomplishment of mighty deeds, therefore, is adapted to these, as being allotted an heroic nature; and in conjunction with this the pathetic, from their being conversant with particulars.

### XI. THE CAUSE OF THE LAUGHTER ATTRIBUTED TO THE GODS IN MYTHS, AND WHY HOMER’S POETRY PORTRAYS THE GODS LAUGHING UNCONTROLLABLY AT VULCAN.

Let us in the next place consider whether myths properly attribute to the Gods a passion contrary to the one we have just discussed—namely, immoderate laughter—which was thought worthy of criticism by **Socrates**.

->When the Gods beheld **Vulcan** <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and craftsmanship.</note> serving as their cupbearer,<-
->Unextinguishable laughter rose among them ¹.<-

What then is the laughter of the Gods? And why do they laugh because **Vulcan** is moving and working? <term>Theologists: ancient scholars of divine matters</term> say that **Vulcan**, as we have observed elsewhere, is the <term>demiurgus: a divine craftsman or architect of the physical universe</term> and the maker of everything that can be seen ². Hence he is said to have constructed dwellings for the Gods:

->Then to their own homes the Gods depart,<-
->Formed by lame **Vulcan** with transcendent art.<-

For that which is moved with a motion about intellect and prudence does not, says **Timæus** <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue of the same name who explains the creation of the universe.</note>, require feet. He is likewise said to preside over the brazier's art <note>The craft of working in brass or metal; blacksmithing.</note>, and he himself energizes working in brass. But since every providential energy about a *sensible nature* <term>sensible nature: the physical world that can be perceived by the five senses</term>, according to which the Gods assist the fabrication of **Vulcan**, is said to be the *sport* of divinity, hence **Timæus** also appears to me to call the mundane Gods *junior* <note>In Plato’s *Timaeus*, the "junior gods" are those appointed by the supreme creator to craft mortal bodies and govern the physical world.</note>, as presiding over things which are perpetually in generation, or becoming to be, and which may be considered as ludicrous. 

The authors of fables are accustomed to call this peculiarity of the providence of the Gods energizing about the world, *laughter*. And when the poet says that the Gods, being delighted with the motion of **Vulcan**, laughed with inextinguishable laughter, nothing else is indicated than that they are cooperating artificers; that they jointly give perfection to the art of **Vulcan**, and supernally <note>From a higher or heavenly realm.</note> impart joy to the universe. For **Vulcan** suspends all their mundane receptacles <note>The physical bodies or celestial spheres that "hold" the divine essence in the material world.</note>, and extends to the providence of the Gods whole physical powers. 

But the Gods, energizing with a facility adapted to their nature, and not departing ¹ from their proper hilarity, confer on these powers also their characteristic gifts, and move wholes by their perfective providence. In short, we must define the *laughter* of the Gods to be their exuberant energy in the universe, and the cause of the gladness of all mundane natures. But, as such a providence is incomprehensible, and the communication of all goods from the Gods is never-failing, we must allow that the poet very properly calls their laughter *unextinguished*. 

And here you may again see how what we have said is conformable to the nature of things. For fables do not assert that the Gods always weep, but that they laugh without ceasing. For *tears* are symbols of their providence in mortal and frail concerns, and which now rise into existence, and then perish; but *laughter* is a sign of their energy in wholes, and those perfect natures in the universe which are perpetually moved with undeviating sameness. On which account I think, when we divide <term>demiurgic: relating to the divine creation or "crafting" of the world</term> productions into Gods and men, we attribute laughter to the generation of the Gods, but tears to the formation of men and animals; whence

All the divine orders, therefore, proceeding from the one principle of wholes, which Plato usually calls *the good* <note>The supreme principle in Platonic philosophy, considered the source of all being and truth</note>, and from those biformed <note>having two forms or aspects</note> causes proximately appearing after this principle, which Socrates in the Philebus <note>one of Plato’s dialogues concerning the nature of pleasure and the highest good</note> denominates *bound* <term>Limit or Peras: the principle that provides order, structure, and definition to the universe</term> and *infinity* <term>The Unlimited or Apeiria: the principle of potential, power, and endless expansion</term>, but other wise men have venerated by other names; these orders likewise being divided and separated from each other, in a manner adapted to the Gods, through those second biformed principles,—the interpreters of the truth concerning the Gods usually oppose in their divisions the male to the female, the even to the odd, and the paternal to the maternal genera. But these divine orders again hastening to union and a connate <note>innate or naturally linked</note> communion, through the first cause, which is the leader of united goods to all beings, hence I think the authors of fables took occasion in their symbolical theory to ascribe marriage to the Gods, connexions, and a progeny from these, and also celebrated the connexions and conjunctions of their progeny, till they had perfectly contemplated the whole extent of a divine nature, diversified by such like progressions and conjunctions supernally <note>from a higher or heavenly source</note>, as far as to mundane <note>pertaining to the physical world</note> natures. 

As therefore, among the Gods prior to the fabrication of the world, they celebrate the connexions of Saturn <note>the Roman name for Cronus</note> and Rhea, of Heaven <note>Uranus</note> and Earth <note>Gaia</note>, and their cogenerations, in the same manner also, among the fabricators of the universe, they inform us that the first conjunction is that of Jupiter <note>the Roman name for Zeus</note> and Juno <note>the Roman name for Hera</note>; Jupiter being allotted a paternal dignity, but Juno being the mother of every thing of which Jupiter is the father. The former likewise produces all things in the rank of a *monad* <term>the number one, representing unity and the source of all things</term>, but the latter in conjunction with him gives subsistence to secondary natures, according to the *prolific duad* <term>the number two, representing multiplicity and the power of generation</term>: and the former is assimilated to *intelligible bound*, but the latter to *intelligible infinity*. For, according to every order of Gods, it is requisite that there should be primary causes subsisting analogously to those two principles. But, to the union of these greatest divinities, it is necessary that there should previously subsist a oneness of transcendency of the monadic and demiurgic God <term>the Creator or "Craftsman" of the universe who shapes the world according to divine patterns</term>, and a perfect conversion <note>the process of a created thing turning back toward its divine source to find its purpose or completion</note> to him of the generative and dyadic cause. Through these causes, as it appears to me, *Juno* <note>Hera; the goddess representing the maternal, generative power of the soul that organizes the material world</note> hastening to a connection with *Jupiter* <note>Zeus; the paternal demiurge or supreme intellect that orders the cosmos</note>, perfects her whole essence, and prepares it with all-various powers—the undefiled, the generative, the intellectual, and the unific; but *Jupiter* excites the divine love in himself, according to which he also fills his proximate participants with good, and extends to them a cause collective of multitude, and an energy convertive of secondary natures to himself. But the union and indissoluble conjunction of both these divinities is effected separate from the universe, and exempt from the mundane receptacles. For *Jupiter* elevates to this communion, *Juno* extending to him that which is subordinate and mundane; the Gods indeed being always united, but fables separating them from each other; and referring a connection separate* from the universe to the will of *Jupiter*, but the common cooperation of these divinities proceeding into the world, to the providence of *Juno*. The reason of this is, that everywhere the paternal cause is the leader of exempt and more uniform good, but the maternal of that good which is proximate to its participants, and is multiplied according to all-various progressions. With great propriety, therefore, are sleep and wakefulness usurped separately in the symbols of fables; wakefulness manifesting the providence of the Gods about the world, but sleep a life separate from all subordinate natures; though the Gods at the same time both providentially energize about the universe, and are established in themselves. But as *Timaeus* <note>Referring to the narrator of Plato's dialogue of the same name, which explores cosmology and the creation of the world</note> represents the <term>demiurge</term> <note>the divine craftsman who shapes the material world</note> of wholes, at one time energizing, and giving subsistence to the earth, the heavens, the planets, the fixed stars, the circles of the soul, and the mundane intellect, but at another time abiding in himself, after his accustomed manner, and exempt from all those powers that energize in the universe; so, long before *Timaeus*, fables represent the father of all mundane natures, at one time awake, and at another asleep, for the purpose of indicating his twofold life and energy. "[He produces] worlds," <note>This quote is likely from the *Chaldean Oracles*, a collection of mystical verses highly regarded by Neoplatonists. It refers to the Demiurge or creator-god bringing the various levels of existence into being.</note> says one of the Gods. According to the former **energy** <note>In this context, 'energy' refers to 'energeia'—the active expression or operation of a divine power.</note>, therefore, he may be said to be awake; for wakefulness with us is an energy of sense; but according to the latter to sleep, as separated from **sensibles** <term>sensibles: objects that can be perceived by the five senses, as opposed to 'intelligibles' which are perceived by the mind</term>, and exhibiting a life defined according to a perfect intellect. It may also be said, that he consults about human affairs when awake; for according to this life he provides for all **mundane** <note>original: "mundanus"; meaning belonging to the physical world or cosmos</note> concerns; but that when asleep, and led together with Juno to a separate union, he is not forgetful of the other energy, but, possessing and energizing according to it, at the same time contains both. For he does not, like nature, produce secondary things without intelligence, nor through intelligence is his providence in subordinate natures diminished, but at the same time he both governs the objects of his providence according to justice, and ascends to his intelligible watch-tower. The fable, therefore, indicates this exempt transcendency, when it says that his connection with Juno was on mount *Ida*; for there Juno arriving gave herself to the embraces of the mighty Jupiter. What else, then, shall we say mount *Ida* obscurely signifies, but the region of *ideas* <note>The author is making a linguistic connection between the name 'Ida' and the Greek word 'ideai' (Ideas or Forms), suggesting the mountain represents the realm of pure, perfect concepts.</note> and an intelligible nature, to which Jupiter ascends, and elevates Juno through love;—not converting himself to the participant, but through excess of goodness imparting this second union with himself, and with that which is intelligible? For such are the loves of more excellent natures,—they are convertive of things subordinate to things first, give completion to the good which they contain, and are perfective of subject natures. The fable, therefore, does not diminish the dignity of the mighty Jupiter, by representing him as having connection on the ground with Juno, and refusing to enter into her bed-chamber; for by this it insinuates that the connection was **supermundane** <note>Beyond or above the physical universe</note>, and not mundane. The chamber, therefore, constructed by Vulcan indicates the orderly composition of the universe, and the sensible region; for Vulcan, as we have said before, is the artificer of the universe.

In producing the contrarieties of the elements, too, he may be said to have generated them according to the **Mars** which he contains in himself; but, in devising friendship, to have energized according to the power of **Venus**. And in binding together the productions of **Venus** with those of **Mars**, he appears to have previously comprehended in himself, <term>paradigmatically</term> <note>As a perfect model or example.</note>, the art of **Vulcan**. He is therefore all things, and energizes in conjunction with all the Gods. The <term>junior artificers</term> <note>Lesser deities who, according to Plato, were tasked by the Creator to fashion the mortal parts of living beings.</note> also, imitating their father, fabricate mortal animals, and again receive them when they are corrupted, generating, in conjunction with **Vulcan**, sublunary bonds, and previously containing in themselves the causes of their solution <note>The "solution" here refers to the dissolving or breaking of the bonds, leading to death.</note>. For every where, he who comprehends in himself a bond, knows also the necessity of its solution.

## XV. WHAT MUST BE SAID TO THE <term>ANIMADVERSIONS</term> <note>Critical remarks or censures; specifically, the objections Socrates raises against Homeric poetry in Plato’s "Republic."</note> OF SOCRATES, RESPECTING THE AVARICE ASCRIBED BY HOMER TO HIS HEROES.

Let us now consider those places in the poems of **Homer**, which, according to **Socrates**, increase the love of riches in our souls. For why does **Phœnix** <note>The tutor and father-figure to Achilles.</note> advise **Achilles** to receive gifts when he lays aside his anger, but otherwise not to lay it aside? Why also does **Achilles** receive gifts from **Agamemnon** for his insolence, and refuse to restore the dead body of **Hector**, unless it was redeemed with money? For he who becomes an auditor of things of this kind is in danger of falling into a dire and insatiable avarice. To these objections we shall briefly say, that **Phœnix** advises **Achilles** to lay aside his anger on receiving the gifts, and **Achilles**, on receiving them, did lay it aside, both of them considering the gifts as an argument of the repentance of the giver; but not that they might satisfy the avaricious disposition of their soul, nor considering an increase of riches as the boundary of <term>felicity</term> <note>Supreme happiness or the ultimate goal of a well-lived life.</note>. For they did not from the first demand these presents, but received them when they were spontaneously offered. But if **Achilles** restored the dead body of **Hector** to **Priam**, on its being redeemed by money, perhaps we may say that it was at that time customary to receive a ransom for the bodies of enemies. This also must be considered, that it belongs to the art of commanding an army, to cut off the riches of the enemy, but to increase the property of those who are compelled to oppose the enemy in a foreign country. But all these and such-like particulars may be defended as the transactions of those heroes who energized according to circumstances, and whose actions are to be estimated according to other manners than those of common men: they are, however, entirely unfit to be heard by those educated under the legislator of **Socrates**, whose geniuses are philosophic, whose erudition regards a philosophic life, and who are entirely deprived of possessions and property <note>In Plato's "Republic," the "Guardians" or ruling class were forbidden from owning private property to ensure their absolute focus on the common good.</note>.

If you are willing, we may also add to what has been said respecting **Achilles**, that he himself accuses **Agamemnon** of avarice, and reprobates this passion as disgraceful.

> <term>Atrides</term> <note>A name for Agamemnon, meaning "Son of Atreus."</note>, who in glory art the first,
> And no less avaricious than renown’d¹!

# XVI. IN WHAT MANNER IT IS REQUISITE TO APOLOGIZE FOR THE NEGLIGENCE OF HEROES RESPECTING A DIVINE NATURE, WHICH APPEARS TO TAKE PLACE IN THE POETRY OF HOMER.

It now follows that we should consider how we are to answer **Socrates**, when he accuses **Achilles** of negligence respecting a divine nature. For how can he be pious and a worshipper of the Gods, who dares to say to **Apollo**,

->Me thou hast injur'd most pernicious God¹?<-

who also opposes the river **Xanthus** though a God, and presents his locks to the dead body of **Patroclus**, though he had promised them to the river **Sperchius**? That **Achilles** therefore, according to **Homer**, was remarkably cautious respecting a divine nature, is evident from his advising the Greeks to reverence **Apollo**, to send a sacrifice to him, and to appease **Chryses** the priest of **Apollo**. This also follows from his readily obeying the commands of **Minerva** <note>original: "Minerva" — The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note>, when she appeared to him, though contrary to the impulse of his wrath. He likewise asserts that a subserviency to the Gods, and a compliance with the will of more excellent natures, is of all things the most useful; and offers a libation and prays to **Jupiter** <note>original: "Jupiter" — The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note>, with science adapted to the Gods. For his first purifying the bowl, and in an especial manner consecrating it to **Jupiter** alone, and standing in the middle of the enclosure, invoking the power that pervades every where from the middle of the universe, afford a sufficiently conspicuous argument of his piety to a divine nature, and of his knowledge of the signs adapted to the objects of worship.

But if he appears to have spoken to **Apollo** more boldly than is fit, it is requisite to know that the Apolloniacal orders <term>Apolloniacal orders: The various levels of divine being associated with Apollo, ranging from the highest gods to lower angels and spirits.</term> pervade from on high, as far as to the last of things; and some of them are divine, others angelic, and others dæmoniacal <note>original: "dæmoniacal" — Here referring to 'daemons,' which in Greek philosophy were intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings.</note>, and these multiformly divided. It must be considered, therefore, that these words were not addressed—

For he who preserves uninjured a principal enemy, becomes more than any one harmful to the person injured, by impeding his avenging the injury. # CONTAINING AN APOLOGY FOR THE FABLES OF HOMER.

Does not therefore the poetry of Homer by these things make us more modest respecting a divine nature, since we learn from it that even the most subordinate powers cannot be offended with impunity? Though I am not ignorant that those who are skilled in <term>mystic sacrifices</term> <note>This refers to theurgy, a Neoplatonic practice of ritual magic intended to communicate with or invoke the gods.</note> dare many things of this kind respecting <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic tradition, "daemons" are not evil spirits, but mediating beings that rank between gods and humans.</note>; but perhaps they are defended by more divine natures from sustaining any such injury from subordinate powers. In the mean time justice follows other men, correcting the <term>improbity</term> <note>Wickedness or lack of integrity.</note> of their speech.

It is also not difficult to reply to what is said in objection to the contest of Achilles with the river Xanthus. For he was not disobedient to the God himself, but he either contended with the apparent water which hindered his impulse against the enemy, or with some one of the <term>indigenous powers</term> <note>The local spirits or deities traditionally associated with specific rivers or regions.</note>, the associate of the Gods in battle: for <term>Minerva</term> <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note> and <term>Neptune</term> <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Poseidon.</note> were present with him, and afforded him assistance. And it appears to me, indeed, that the poetry of Homer devises contests according to all possible diversities; sometimes relating the battles of men with men, and sometimes of the <term>more excellent genera</term> <note>A Neoplatonic term for the hierarchy of beings—gods, angels, daemons, and heroes—that are superior to humanity.</note> with each other, as in what is called *theomachy*, or the battles of the Gods; and sometimes, as in the instance before us, the oppositions of heroes to certain dæmoniacal natures; indicating to those that are able to understand things of this kind, that the first of last natures are after a manner equal to the last of such as are first, and particularly when they are guarded and moved by the Gods. Hence, not only Achilles is said to have contended with Xanthus, but <term>Hercules</term> also with the river <term>Achelous</term>, of whose life Achilles being emulous, he did not avoid similar contests.

Lastly, we may solve the third of the proposed inquiries by saying that the first and principal design of Achilles was, on returning to his country, to offer to the river <term>Sperchius</term> his locks, as he had promised; but when he despaired of his return, in consequence of hearing from his mother,

> ->Soon after Hector shall thy death succeed,<-

was it not then necessary that he should cut off his hair in honour of his friend <note>Achilles cuts his hair as a funeral offering for his companion Patroclus, having realized he would not live to return home.</note>? For Socrates in Plato received the crowns which Alcibiades

## XVII. A DEFENSE FOR THE UNWORTHY TREATMENT OF THE DEAD BODY OF HECTOR, AND FOR THE TWELVE TROJANS SLAIN AND BURNT ON THE FUNERAL PILE OF PATROCLUS, SINCE THESE THINGS EVIDENTLY APPEAR TO BE CRUEL, ABSURD, AND UNBECOMING THE CHARACTER OF HEROES.

It now remains that we consider the conduct of Achilles to Hector, his dragging him round the tomb of Patroclus, and his sacrificing twelve Trojan youths on his pile; for these things, says <term>Socrates</term> <note>In Plato’s Republic, Socrates criticizes Homer for depicting Achilles—a hero of divine descent—committing such violent and vengeful acts.</note>, cannot be truly ascribed to Achilles, who was the son of a Goddess, and of the most <term>temperate</term> <note>Self-controlled and moderate.</note> <term>Peleus</term> <note>The father of Achilles, noted for his virtue.</note> descended from <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The Roman name for the supreme Greek god, Zeus.</note>, and who was educated by the wise <term>Chiron</term> <note>The centaur known for his wisdom and for tutoring the greatest Greek heroes.</note>. In the first place, then, it is said by the ancients that this was the custom of the <term>Thessalians</term> <note>People from Thessaly, the homeland of Achilles.</note>, as the <term>Cyrenæan poet</term> <note>Likely referring to Callimachus, a famous Greek scholar-poet from Cyrene.</note> also testifies, when he informs us, “that it is an ancient Thessalian custom, to drag round the tomb of the slain the body of the slaughterer.”

Achilles therefore thus acted conformably to the custom of his country, that all due honors might be paid to the funeral of Patroclus. But if Hector dragged Patroclus when a dead body, threatened to cut off his head, and cast his corpse to the Trojan dogs, which is also told to Achilles by <term>Iris</term> <note>The messenger goddess of the rainbow.</note>—

> A prey to dogs he dooms the corpse to lie,
> And marks the place to fix his head on high *.
> Rise and prevent (if yet you think of fame)
> Your friend’s disgrace, your own eternal shame!

does not Achilles, therefore, inflict a proper punishment on Hector, in dragging him round the tomb of Patroclus? For thus he both revenges the cruelty of Hector, and openly testifies his benevolence to his friend.

**W**HEN I had said these things I imagined that the debate was at an end; but this it seems was only the introduction: for Glauco <note>Glaucon, Plato's older brother and a primary interlocutor in the dialogue.</note>, as he is on all occasions most courageous, so truly at that time did not approve of Thrasymachus <note>The Sophist who, in Book I, argued that justice is merely "the advantage of the stronger."</note> in giving up the debate; but said, Socrates, do you wish to seem to have persuaded us, or to have persuaded us in reality, that in every respect it is better to be just than unjust? I would choose, said I, to do it in reality, if it depended on me. You do not then, said he, do what you desire. For, tell me, does there appear to you any good of this kind, such as we would choose to have; not regarding the consequences, but embracing it for its own sake? as joy, and such pleasures as are harmless; though nothing else arises afterwards from these pleasures, than that the possession gives us delight. There seems to me, said I, to be something of this kind. But what? is there something too, which we both love for its own sake, and also for what arises from it? as wisdom, sight, and health; for we somehow embrace these things on both accounts. Yes, said I. But do you perceive, said he, a third species of good, among which is bodily labour, to be healed when sick, to practise physic <note>The practice of medicine.</note>, or other lucrative employment? for we say, those things are troublesome, but that they profit us; and we should not choose these things for their own sake, but on account of the rewards and those other advantages which arise from them. There is then, indeed, said I, likewise this third kind. But what now? in which of these, said he, do you place justice? I imagine, said I, in the most handsome <note>original: kalos; meaning the most noble, beautiful, or morally excellent category.</note>; which, both on its own account, and for the sake of what arises from it, is desired by the man who is in pursuit of happiness. ...this discourse proceeded, Socrates, because, O wonderful man! <note>Adeimantus uses a slightly ironic or respectful address common in Socratic dialogues to urge Socrates to take the argument seriously.</note> among all those of you that call yourselves the commenders of justice, beginning from those ancient heroes of whom any accounts are left to the men of the present time, no one has at any time condemned injustice, nor commended justice, otherwise than regarding the reputations, honors and rewards arising from them: but no one has hitherto sufficiently examined, neither in poetry nor in prose discourse, either of them in itself, and subsisting by its own power, in the soul of him who possesses it, and concealed from both gods and men: how that the one is the greatest of all the evils which the soul has within it, and justice the greatest good: for, if it had thus from the beginning been spoken of by you all, and you had so persuaded us from our youth, we should not need to watch over our neighbor lest he should do us injustice, but every man would have been the best guardian over himself, afraid lest in doing injustice he should dwell with the greatest evil. Let us look at this matter in the same way as if someone had ordered people who are not very sharp-sighted to read small letters from a distance, and one should afterwards understand that the same letters are written larger somewhere else, and on a larger field. It would appear preferable, I imagine, first to read these larger letters, and then consider the smaller ones, if they happen to be the same. <note>Socrates is using a famous analogy here: it is easier to see the "big picture" of justice in a society than to see it hidden within a single human heart.</note>

"Perfectly right," said Adimantus. 

"But what of this kind, Socrates, do you perceive in the inquiry concerning justice?" 

"I shall tell you," said I. "Do we not say there is justice in one man, and there is likewise justice in a whole state?" 

"It is certainly so," he replied. 

"Is not a state a greater object than one man?" 

"Greater," said he. 

"It is likely, then, that justice should be larger in what is greater, and be more easy to be understood. We shall first, then, if you are inclined, inquire what justice is in states; and then, after the same manner, we shall consider it in each individual, contemplating the similarity of the greater in the idea of the lesser." 

"You seem to me," said he, "to be right." 

"If then," said I, "we contemplate a state in our discourse as it is being created, shall we not perceive its justice and injustice as they come to exist?" 

"Perhaps," said he. 

"And is there not ground to hope, if this exists, that we shall more easily find what we seek for?" 

"Most certainly." 

"It seems, then, we ought to attempt to succeed, for I imagine this to be a work of no small importance. Consider then." 

"We are considering," said Adimantus, "and you should do the same."

"A city, then," said I, "as I imagine, takes its rise from this: that none of us happens to be **self-sufficient**, <term>self-sufficient: the state of being able to provide for all one's own needs (Greek: *autarkeia*).</term> but instead lacks many things. Or do you imagine there is any other origin for building a city?" 

"None other," said he. 

"Thus, then, one person takes in another for one need, and another for another; as they stand in need of many things, they assemble into one habitation many companions and assistants; and to this joint-habitation we give the name 'city', do we not?" 

"Certainly." 

"And they mutually exchange with one another, each judging that, if he either gives or takes in exchange, it will be for his own advantage." 

"Certainly." 

"Come, then," said I, "let us, in our discourse, make a city from the beginning. And, it seems, our **indigence** <note>original: *chreia* — meaning need or necessity.</note> has made it." 

"Why not?" 

"But the first and the greatest of wants is the preparation of food, in order to subsist and live." 

"By all means." 

"The second is of lodging. The third of clothing; and such like." 

"It is so." 

"But, come," said I, "how shall the city be able to make so great a provision? Shall not one be a husbandman <note>A farmer or agriculturist.</note>, another a mason, and some other a weaver?"

...shall we add to them a shoemaker, or some other person who provides for the physical necessities of the body? 

"Certainly," he replied.

"So then, the most basic city would consist of four or five men?" 

"It seems so." 

"But what now? Must each of these men do his work for all of them in common? For example, shall the <term>farmer<gloss>husbandman</gloss></term>, being one person, prepare food for four, and spend four times as much time and labor in preparing food to share it with the others? Or, neglecting the others, shall he produce only a fourth of this food for himself alone, in a fourth of the time? And, of the remaining three parts of his time, shall he spend one in building a house, another in making clothes, and the other in making shoes, rather than taking the trouble to share with others, and instead just minding his own business by himself?"

Adimantus said, "Socrates, the first way is probably easier than the second." 

"No, certainly," said I; "that would be absurd. For, while you are speaking, I am considering that we are not born perfectly resembling one another; rather, we differ in our <term>natural dispositions<gloss>genius</gloss></term>. One person is fitted for doing one thing, and another for doing something else. Does it not seem so to you?" 

"It does." 

"But what now? Will a man do better if he works in many crafts, or if he sticks to one?" 

"When he sticks to one," he said. 

"But this, I imagine, is also plain: that if one misses the <term>proper moment<gloss>season</gloss></term> for any work, the work is ruined." 

"That is plain." 

"For I imagine the work will not wait for the workman to be at leisure; rather, the workman must attend closely to the work, and not treat it as a <term>side-job<gloss>by-job</gloss></term>." 

"He must." 

"And from this it appears that more will be done—and better, and with greater ease—when every person does only one thing, according to their natural talents, at the proper time, and is freed from other distractions." <note>This is the famous "Principle of Specialization" or "Division of Labor," which Socrates argues is the foundation of a functional and just society.</note>

"Most certainly," he said.

"True." 

"Carpenters, then, and blacksmiths, and other such craftsmen, being admitted into our little city, will make it quite full." <note>original: "throng"</note>

"Certainly." 

"But it would not be a very great matter, either, if we gave them cattle-drivers, shepherds, and other herdsmen, so that the farmers might have oxen for plowing..."

"By no means," said he.

"But are the Gods," said I, "such as, though in themselves they never change, yet make us imagine they appear in various forms, deceiving us and playing the <term>mountebanks</term> <note>A "mountebank" is a deceptive performer or a charlatan who tricks a crowd.</note>?"

"Perhaps," said he.

"But what?" said I, "Can a God cheat, holding forth a phantasm, either in word or deed?"

"I do not know," said he.

"Do you not know," said I, "that what is truly a cheat, if we may be allowed to say so, both all the Gods and men abhor?"

"How do you say?" replied he.

"Thus," said I: "That to offer a cheat to the most principal part of themselves, and that about their most principal interests, is what none willingly incline to do; but, of all things, everyone is most afraid of possessing a cheat there."

"Neither as yet," said he, "do I understand you."

"Because," said I, "you think I am saying something <term>venerable</term> <note>Socrates suggests Adimantus is looking for a deep, mystical meaning, whereas Socrates is making a practical point about the soul.</note>; but I am saying that to cheat the soul concerning realities—to be so cheated, to be ignorant, and there to have obtained and to keep a falsehood—is what everyone would least of all choose. A cheat in the soul is what they most especially hate."

"Most especially," said he.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adimantus from page 225. Having concluded that the Gods do not change their physical forms, they now examine whether the Gods would ever deceive us through lies or illusions. This leads to the establishment of the second "model" or rule for religious poetry: that God is perfectly truthful.</meta>

<page-num>226</page-num>

-># THE REPUBLIC.<-

...a kind of imitation of what the soul feels; and an image arising afterwards, and not an absolute, pure deception. Is it not so?

"Entirely," he said.

"But this real lie <note>Socrates distinguishes between a 'lie in the soul' (being truly ignorant or deceived about reality) and a 'lie in words' (a spoken falsehood). The former is hated by everyone; the latter can sometimes be useful.</note> is not only hated by the Gods, but by men as well."

"So it appears."

"But what now? Regarding the deception in words, when is it useful enough that it does not deserve to be hated? Is it not when it is used against our enemies, or even with those we call our friends, when in a fit of madness or some other ailment, they attempt to do something harmful? In that case, it is useful as a preventive measure, like a drug. And in those fables we were just mentioning, since we do not know the exact truth concerning ancient events, we make a lie resemble the truth as much as possible to make it useful. Is it not so?"

"It is," he said, "perfectly so."

"In which of these cases, then, is a lie useful to God? Would he create a lie resembling the truth because he is ignorant of ancient things?"

"That would be ridiculous," he said.

"Then God is not a lying poet."

"I do not think so."

"But would he create a lie through fear of his enemies?"

"Far from it."

"But perhaps on account of the folly or madness of his family?"

"But," he said, "none of the foolish or mad are friends of God."

"There is then no reason at all for God to tell a lie."

"There is none."

"The divine and godlike nature is then, in all respects, without a lie?"

"Altogether," he said.

"God then is simple and true, both in word and deed; he neither changes himself, nor deceives others—neither by visions, nor by speech, nor by the sending of signs; neither when we are awake, nor when we sleep."

"So it appears to me," he said, "at least while you are speaking."

"You agree then," I said, "that this shall be the second model by which we are to speak and compose poetry concerning the Gods: that they are neither <term>mountebanks</term> <note>A 'mountebank' is a deceiver or a trickster who puts on a show to mislead people; here, it refers to a god who would use tricks to change their appearance.</note> who change themselves, nor do they mislead us with lies in word or deed?"

"I agree."

"While then we praise many other things in **Homer**, we shall not praise this: the dream sent by **Jupiter** <note>original: "Zeus"</note> to **Agamemnon** <note>In the *Iliad*, Zeus sends a deceptive dream to King Agamemnon to trick him into attacking Troy prematurely.</note>. Neither shall we praise **Æschylus** <note>One of the great Athenian tragic playwrights.</note>, when he portrays **Thetis** saying that **Apollo** had sung at her marriage, that:

> A comely offspring she should raise,
> From sickness free, of lengthened days:
> Apollo, singing all my fate,
> And praising high my Godlike state,
> Rejoiced my heart; and 'twas my hope,
> That all was true Apollo spoke.

# THE REPUBLIC.

## BOOK III.

---

**THESE** things, then, I said, and others like them, are what children should hear—and what they should not hear—concerning the gods. This applies to those who are to honor the gods and their parents, and who value friendship with one another. And I imagine, he replied, that these views are correct. But what follows? If they are to be brave, must we not tell them stories that will make them fear death as little as possible? Or do you think anyone can ever be brave while harboring such a fear within them? Not I, truly, he said. And what of this: do you think anyone can be free from the fear of death if they believe that <term>Hades</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Hades is the underworld or the realm of the dead. Socrates argues that if it is depicted as a miserable place, soldiers will fear death and act like cowards to avoid it.</note> exists and is a place of terror? Do you think a soldier would choose death in battle over defeat and slavery if he held such beliefs? By no means, he answered.

It seems, then, that we must also supervise those who take it upon themselves to tell these kinds of stories. We must ask them not to disparage the underworld so generally, but rather to praise it; for their current descriptions are neither true nor helpful to those who are destined to be soldiers. We certainly should, he said. Starting then, I said, with the following verse, we shall delete all passages of this type:

<margin>Homer, Odyssey, Book 11</margin>
> I would rather be a lowly serf on earth,
> Serving a poor man with little to eat,
> Than rule over all the wasted dead below. <note>original: "I'd rather, as a rustic slave, submit..." This is a famous quote from the ghost of Achilles in the *Odyssey*. Socrates wants to remove it because it implies that even the most miserable life on earth is better than the afterlife.</note>

And this:

> The house of the dead appears to mortals and gods alike
> To be dreadful, squalid, and a place the gods abhor. <note>original: Homer, Iliad, Book 20. This description of the home of Pluto (Hades) is rejected by Socrates for making the afterlife seem repulsive.</note>

That is plain.

We say so.

For, if, friend *Adimantus*, our youth should seriously hear such things as these, and not laugh at them as spoken most unsuitably, hardly would any one think it unworthy of himself, of himself being a man, or check himself, if he should happen either to say or to do any thing of the kind; but, without any shame or endurance, would, on small sufferings, sing many lamentations and moans. You say most true, replied he. They must not, therefore, do in this manner, as our reasoning now has evinced to us; which we must believe, till some one persuade us by some better. They must not, indeed. But, surely, neither ought we to be given to excessive laughter; for, where a man gives himself to violent laughter, such a disposition commonly requires a violent change <note>Socrates argues that extreme emotions are unstable; a person who laughs uncontrollably is prone to equally extreme swings into other emotions.</note>. It seems so, said he. Nor, if any one shall represent worthy men as overcome by laughter, must we allow it, much less if he thus represent the Gods. Much less, indeed, said he. Neither, then, shall we receive such things as these from *Homer* concerning the Gods:

> ->*Vulcan* serving as cupbearer when the Gods beheld,<-
> ->Amidst them unextinguished laughter rose¹.<-
<note>original: "Vulcan miniſtrant" refers to Hephaestus (Vulcan) acting as a servant to the other gods, a sight Homer depicts as comical.</note>

This is not to be admitted, according to your reasoning. If you incline, said he, to call it my reasoning; this, indeed, is not to be admitted. But surely the truth is much more to be valued. For, if lately we reasoned right, and if indeed a lie be unprofitable to the Gods, but useful to men, in the way of a drug <note>The Greek term used here is *pharmakon*, meaning both "drug" and "poison." Socrates suggests that a lie can be used "medicinally" by a ruler for the benefit of the state.</note>, it is plain that such a thing is to be entrusted only to the physicians, but not to be touched by private persons. It is plain, said he. It belongs then to the governors of the city, if to any others, to make a lie, with reference either to enemies or citizens, for the good of the city; but none of the rest must venture on such a thing. But for a private person to tell a lie to such governors; we will call it the same, and even a greater offence, than for the patient to tell a lie to the physician; or for the man who learns his exercises <note>A student in a gymnasium or an athlete.</note>, not to tell his master the truth as to the indispositions of his body: or for one not to tell the pilot the real state of things, respecting the ship and sailors, in what condition himself and the other sailors are. We shall not nourish, then, such workmen as make harps and spinets <note>The translator uses "spinet," a 17th-century keyboard instrument, to represent complex multi-stringed Greek instruments like the *trigonos* or *sambuca*.</note>, and all those instruments which consist of many strings, and produce a variety of harmony. We shall not, as it appears. 

But what? Will you admit into your city such workmen as make pipes, or pipers? for, are not the instruments which consist of the greatest number of strings, and those that produce all kinds of harmony, imitations of the pipe? It is plain, replied he. There are left you still, said I, the lyre and the harp, as useful for your city, and there might likewise be some reed for shepherds in the fields. Thus reason, said he, shows us. Socrates uses this myth to side with the "orderly" lyre over the "chaotic" pipe.</note>

<summary>Socrates and Glauco narrow down the permitted musical modes to the Doric and Phrygian, favoring music that inspires courage and self-restraint. They also ban complex, multi-stringed instruments and pipes in favor of the simpler lyre and harp.</summary>

"After what manner?" said he. 

"In procuring to himself," said I, "a lingering death; for, whilst he was constantly attentive to his disease, which was mortal, he was not able, as I imagine, to cure himself; though, neglecting every thing besides, he was still using medicines; and thus he passed his life, still in the greatest uneasiness if he departed in the least from his accustomed diet; and through this wisdom of his, struggling long with death, he arrived at old age." 

"A mighty reward," said he, "he reaped of his art!" 

"Such as became one," said I, "who did not understand that it was not from ignorance or inexperience of this method of cure that Æsculapius did not discover it to his descendants; but because he knew that, in all well regulated states, there was some certain work enjoined every one in the city, which was necessary to be done, and that no one was to be allowed to have the leisure of being sick through the whole of life, and to be attentive only to the taking of medicines. This we may pleasantly observe in the case of labouring people; but we do not observe it in the case of the rich, and such as are counted happy." 

"How?" said he. 

"A smith," replied I, "when he falls sick, thinks it fit to take from the physician some potion, to throw up his disease, or purge it downwards, or, by means of caustic or amputation, to be freed from the trouble: but if any one prescribe for him a long regimen, putting caps on his head <note>Likely referring to the ancient practice of using bandages or specific head coverings as part of a complex recovery process.</note>, and other such things, he quickly tells him that he has not leisure to lie sick, nor does it avail him to live in this manner, attentive to his trouble, and negligent of his proper work; and so, bidding such a physician farewell, he returns to his ordinary diet; and, if he recovers his health, he continues to manage his own affairs; but if his body be not able to support the disease, he dies, and is freed from troubles." 

"It seems proper," said he, "for such an one to use the medicinal art in this way."

And if again any from among these shall be born of a golden or silver kind, they shall pay them honour, and prefer them; those to the guardianship, and these to the auxiliary rank: it being pronounced by the oracle, that the state is then to perish when iron or brass shall have the guardianship of it. For all which reasons, said I, let us affirm, that our guardians are thus to be constituted with reference both to their houses and to other things. And let us settle these things by law. Shall we? By all means, said *Glauco*.

## BOOK IV.

**ADIMANTUS** replied to this by saying, "Socrates, what will you say in your own defense if someone argues that you are not making these men <note>The "men" refers to the Guardians, the ruling class of the ideal city.</note> very happy? For although the city’s existence is owed to them, they enjoy none of its advantages. Unlike others, they do not own land, build beautiful and large houses, or buy fine furniture. They do not offer sacrifices to the gods at their own expense, or host guests, or possess the gold and silver you just mentioned—all the things usually thought to make a person happy. Instead," he continued, "one might say that they seem like nothing more than <term>hired auxiliaries</term> <note original="epikouroi">The warrior class tasked with defending the city and supporting the Rulers.</note> who possess nothing in the city except the duty of standing guard."

"Yes," I said, "and they do it only for their basic maintenance, without receiving any extra pay as others do. Because of this, they aren't even allowed to travel abroad for their own pleasure, or give money to others, or spend it in the ways that people who are considered 'happy' usually do. You have left out these and many other such points from your accusation."

"Well," said he, "let those things be added to the charge as well."

"You ask, then, how we shall defend ourselves?"

"I do."

We believed that in such a city we would most likely find **justice**, just as we would find **injustice** in a poorly managed one. This indeed, said he, is even more of a trifle than the other.

We do not here, my good Adimantus, as one might imagine, impose many great requirements on them. They are all quite simple, provided they take care of one "grand point," as the saying goes—or rather, a point that is sufficient to take the place of all others.

What is that? he asked.

Education, I said, and nurture. That, he said, would be most right.

And surely, said I, if a republic is once set in motion, it proceeds happily, increasing like a circle. While good education and nurture are preserved, they produce men of good character; and these men, benefiting from such an education, produce offspring even better than themselves—both in general character and in regard to procreation—just as we see with other animals.

It is likely, said he.

Well, I said, let us assume that is the case.

It certainly seems so to me, he replied.

How could they? he said.

But when children play proper games from infancy, and when music leads them to embrace lawfulness (unlike those others), this music stays with them in everything they do. It grows with them and repairs whatever parts of the city might have previously fallen into decay.

That is very true, he said.

And these men, I said, will then rediscover those small rules of behavior which their predecessors completely destroyed.

But what now, by the gods, said I, as to those laws relative to matters of exchange, and to their traffic one with another in the <term>forum</term> <note>The marketplace or 'agora', which served as the center of commercial and social life in a Greek city.</note>, and, if you please, their traffic likewise among their handicrafts, their scandals, bodily hurt, and raising of lawsuits; their institution of judges, and likewise such <term>imposts</term> <note>Customs duties or taxes on goods.</note> and payments of taxes as may be necessary either in the forum or at shores; or in general whatever laws are <term>municipal</term> <note>Refers to 'astynomical' laws, or those governing the internal order and infrastructure of the city.</note>, civil, or marine, or what other laws there may be of this kind; shall we dare to establish any of these? 

It is improper, said he, to prescribe these to <term>good and worthy men</term> <note>The Greek term is 'kaloi kagathoi', referring to citizens who have achieved a balance of moral and physical excellence.</note>; for they will easily find out the most of them, such as ought to be established by law. Yes, said I, friend, if at least God grant them the preservation of the laws we formerly explained. And if not, said he, they will spend the whole of their life making and amending many such laws as these, imagining that they shall thus attain to that which is best. 

You say that such as these shall lead a life, said I, like those who are sick, and at the same time unwilling, through intemperance, to quit an unwholesome diet. Entirely so. And these truly must live very pleasantly; for, though they deal with physicians, they gain nothing, but render their diseases greater and more complex; and they still hope, that when any one recommends any medicine to them, they shall, by means of it, be made whole. This is entirely the situation of such diseased persons as these. 

But what, said I, is not this pleasant in them? to count that man the most hateful of all, who tells them the truth; that, till one give over drunkenness and gluttony, and unchaste pleasure, and laziness, neither drugs nor <term>caustics</term> <note>Chemical substances used to burn away or cauterize infected tissue.</note>, nor amputations, nor charms, nor applications, nor any other such things as these, will be of any avail. That, said he, is not quite pleasant; for to be enraged at one who tells us what is right, has nothing pleasant in it. You are no admirer, said I, as it would seem, of this sort of men. No, truly.

Instead, we should say that they have within them both a straight line <note>The axis of the top.</note> and a periphery <note>The outer circumference or edge.</note>; and that, with relation to the straight line, they stood still (for they did not lean to any side); but with relation to the periphery, they moved in a circle. But, when its perpendicularity <note>The upright center-line of the top.</note> declines either to the right or left hand, forwards or backwards, while it is at the same time whirling round; then in no respect does it stand. 

Very right, said he.

[...opposite to] one another; whether they be actions or passions <note>original: "pathēmata." In historical philosophy, "passions" refers to any state where the soul is acted upon or affected by something else, rather than just strong emotions.</note>, for in this there is no difference; to assent, namely, and to dissent, to desire to obtain a thing, and to reject it; to draw something towards oneself, and to push it away? For example, will you not always say that the soul of one who has desire goes out after that which it desires, or draws near to it that which it wishes to have? Or again, insofar as it wants something to be provided, like one who merely sees an object, does the soul not signal to have it brought near, desiring the actual possession of it? I would say so.

But what of being unwilling, *not* to wish, nor to desire? Shall we not deem these to be of the same kind as pushing something away from the soul and driving it off, and everything else which is opposite to the former? Why not? This being the case, shall we say there is a certain species of desires? And that the most obvious are those which we call thirst and hunger? We shall say so, replied he.

Is not the one the desire of drinking, and the other of eating? *Yes.* Is it then, when considered simply as thirst, a desire in the soul for something further than drink? *It is* according to the nature of the thirst. Is there then a thirst for a hot drink, or a cold, of much or of little, or in short of some particular kind of drink? For if there be any heat accompanying the thirst, it readily causes a desire for a cold drink; but *if* cold accompanies it, then there is excited a desire for a warm drink. If the thirst be great, through many circumstances, it causes a desire for much drink, but *if* small, a desire for a little drink. But the desire itself—thirst—never creates the desire for anything else but drink itself, as its nature prompts; and in like manner, the appetite of hunger is related to food <note>The original text uses "meat," which in older English was a general term for any solid food.</note>.

Thus every desire, said he, in itself, is for that alone of which it is the desire; but to be a desire for such or such a particular kind are adventitious <term>adventitious: conditions that are added or external to the basic nature of a thing.</term> circumstances. Let not then anyone, said I, cause us any trouble by suggesting we were careless—claiming that no one desired drink, but *good* drink; or food, but *good* food; for indeed all men desire that which is *good*. If then thirst be a desire, they might say it is for what is *good*, whether it be drink or whatever else it is the desire for. And the same for all desires.

<summary>Socrates argues that basic desires like thirst and hunger are simple impulses for their respective objects (drink and food) rather than for specific "good" versions of those objects. This distinction allows him to separate raw biological appetite from the rational part of the soul that makes value judgments.</summary>

Why not? And in what respects, and after what manner, the individual is brave, in the same respect, and after the same manner, is a city brave. And so in all other respects, both of them are the same as to virtue. Of necessity. And I think, Glauco, we shall say that a man is just in the same way as we said a city was so? This likewise is quite necessary. But have we not somehow forgot this, that the city was just, when every one of the three species in it did each its own work? ...each of us will be just, and do his own work, when he doth his own affairs within himself. We must, said he, carefully remember it. Is it not then proper that the <term>rational part</term> <note>The "logistikon": the part of the soul that seeks truth and is capable of logic and reasoning.</note> should govern, as it is wise, and hath the care of the whole soul? and that the <term>irascible part</term> <note>The "thymos": the spirited part of the soul, responsible for anger, ambition, and the drive for honor.</note> should be obedient, and an auxiliary of the other? Certainly. Shall not then the mixture, as we observed, of <term>music and gymnastic</term> <note>In the Greek tradition, "music" referred to all the arts and intellectual pursuits, while "gymnastic" referred to physical training.</note> make these two harmonious, raising and nourishing the one with beautiful reasonings and disciplines, and unbending the other, soothing and rendering it mild by harmony and rhythm? Most perfectly, said he. And when those two are in this manner nourished, and have been truly taught, and instructed in their own affairs, let them be set over the <term>concupiscible part</term> <note>The "epithymetikon": the appetitive part of the soul that governs physical desires like hunger, thirst, and the acquisition of wealth.</note>, which in every one is the greater part of the soul, and in its nature most insatiably desirous of being gratified: and let them take care of this part, lest, being filled with these bodily pleasures, as they are called, it become great and vigorous, and do not its own work, but attempt to enslave and rule over those it ought not, and overturn the whole life of all in general. Entirely so, said he. And might he not, said I, by this principle, guard likewise in the best manner against enemies from without, by its influence both over the whole soul and body likewise, the one deliberating, and the other fighting in obedience to its leader, and executing with fortitude the things deliberated? It is so. And I think that we call a man brave, when, through all the pains and pleasures of life, the irascible part preserves the opinion dictated by reason concerning what is terrible, and what is not. Right, said he. And we call him wise, from that small part which governs in him, and dictates these things, having in it the knowledge of what is advantageous for each one, and for the whole community of the three themselves. Perfectly so. But what, do we not call him <term>temperate</term> <note>In this context, temperance (sophrosyne) is defined as the harmonious agreement between the three parts of the soul that reason should be the ruler.</note>, moreover, from the friendship and harmony of these very things, when the governing and governed agree in one, that reason ought to govern, and when they do not raise sedition? Temperance, said he, is no other than this, both as to the city and the individual. But, as we have often said, he shall be just, by these things, and in this manner. It is quite necessary. What then, said I, has any thing blunted us, that we should think justice to be any thing else than what it has appeared to be in a city? Nothing appears to me at least, said he, to have done it.

Such as this: if we were obliged to declare concerning such a city, and concerning a man born and educated conformably to it, whether we thought such a one, when intrusted with gold or silver, would embezzle it; do you imagine that any one would think such a one would do it sooner than those who are not of such a kind? No one, said he. Will not such a one then be free of sacrileges, thefts, treacheries, against companions in private, or the city in public? He will be free. Nor will he ever, in any shape, be faithless, either as to his oaths, or other declarations. How can he? Adulteries, and neglect of parents, impiety against the Gods, will belong to every one else, sooner than to such an one. They will belong to every one else, truly, said he. Do you desire justice to be any thing else, but such a power as produces such men and cities? Not I, truly, said he, for my part.

Our <term>dream</term> <note>Socrates refers to an earlier stage of the conversation where they hypothesized that finding justice in a city would help them find it in an individual. It appears so.

To do injustice then, said I, and to be injurious, and likewise to do justly, all these must be very manifest, if, to wit, injustice and justice are so. As how? Because they are no way different from what is salutary <note>Healthy or beneficial.</note> or noxious: as these are in the body, so are the others in the soul. How? said he. Such things as are healthy constitute health, and such as are noxious produce disease. Yes. And must not the doing justly produce justice, and doing unjustly produce injustice? Of necessity. And injustice is to govern and be governed by one another, contrary to nature. Plainly so, said he. ...the acquisition of virtue? and do not dishonorable actions lead to vice?

Of necessity.

What remains for us to consider, it seems, is whether it is profitable to act justly, to pursue what is honorable, and to be just—whether or not a person is known to be so—or to act unjustly and be unjust, even if one is never punished or corrected through discipline?

But, Socrates, he said, this inquiry seems to me to be ridiculous now. For if life is thought not worth living when the nature of the body is ruined—even if one has all kinds of food and drink, all kinds of wealth, and every kind of power—then how can life be worth living when the nature of that very principle by which we live <note>This refers to the soul (psyche), which the Greeks believed was the vital principle that gave life to the body.</note> is disordered and utterly corrupted? Is it worth living even if one can do anything else they desire, except for finding a way to be liberated from vice and injustice and to acquire justice and virtue? Especially since both of these states have been shown to be as we have described them.

It would be truly ridiculous, I said. But, since we have reached a point that allows us to see most clearly that these things are so, we must not grow weary.

By Jupiter <note>original: "Ma Dia" (Greek) or "per Iovem" (Latin). An oath to the king of the gods, here rendered using the Roman name Jupiter.</note>, he said, we must not desist in the least.

Come then, I said, so that you may also see how many forms vice possesses—forms which, as I imagine, are well worth our attention.

I am attending, he said; only tell me.

And truly now, I said, since we have reached this part of our discussion, it appears to me—as if from a high vantage point <note>Socrates uses the metaphor of a "lookout" or "watchtower" to survey the landscape of human morality.</note>—that there is one single form of virtue, but the forms of vice are infinite. Among these, there are four that deserve to be mentioned.

How do you mean? he replied.

There seem to be as many species of the soul as there are forms of <term>republics</term> <note>The word used here is "politeia," which refers to the constitution or political structure of a city-state.</note>.

There are five types of republics, I said, and five types of the soul.

Tell me, he said, what are these?

I say, I replied, that the one we have just gone through is one species of a republic. It may be called by two names: if there is one man among the rulers who surpasses the rest, it may be called a **Monarchy**; if there are several in power, it is called an **Aristocracy** <note>In Plato’s sense, "Aristocracy" means "rule by the best" (the most virtuous), not necessarily the hereditary nobility.</note>.

True, he said.

I call this, then, one species, I said; for whether they be many or only one who governs, they will never change the fundamental laws of the city, provided they follow the upbringing and education we have described.

That is not likely, he said.

**I** call then indeed both such a city and republic, and such a man as we have described, good and upright; and if this republic be an upright one, I deem the others bad and erroneous, both as to the regulations in cities, and the establishing the temper of soul of individuals, and that in four species of <term>depravity<note>In this context, depravity refers to the specific ways a government or a human soul deviates from the ideal "upright" or just state.</note></term>. Not at all, said Adimantus, speaking now aloud. And I replied, What then will not you let pass? You, said he, for it was to you I alluded. Let us see if we can find a way out <note>Original: "out-gate."</note> anywhere; for we did acknowledge that different natures ought to study different things, and that the nature of man and woman is different. Yet now we say that these different natures ought to study the same things—this is the very point you accuse us of. 

"Exactly."

"How generous, Glaucon," I said, "is the power of the art of <term>contradiction<note>The Greek term is *eristikos*, or 'eristic'—the practice of arguing to win or score points rather than to find the truth.</note></term>!"

"Why do you say that?" 

"Because," I replied, "many people seem to fall into it against their will. They imagine they are not merely <term>quibbling<note>Original: "cavilling."</note></term> but reasoning truly, simply because they are unable to analyze a subject by dividing it into its proper parts. Because of this failure, they pursue a mere contradiction of words rather than a real investigation of the matter."

"That is indeed the case with many," he said, "but does it apply to us at this moment?"

"Entirely so," I said. "We seem to have fallen into a contradiction without meaning to."

"How?"

"Because we have very forcefully and keenly insisted that if natures are not the same, they must not have the same employments. However, we haven't stopped to consider what *kind* of 'sameness' or 'difference' in nature we are talking about, nor what goal we had in mind when we assigned different pursuits to different natures and the same pursuits to the same natures."

"We have never considered it," he said.

"It is therefore still within our power," I replied, "to ask ourselves whether the nature of a bald man and the nature of a man with long hair are the same or opposite. And if we agree they are different, then if bald men are shoemakers, should we forbid long-haired men from the trade? Or if long-haired men make shoes, should we forbid the bald ones?"

"That would be ridiculous," he replied.

"And is it ridiculous for any reason," I said, "other than because we never meant 'difference in nature' in a general sense? We were only looking at the specific kind of diversity or sameness that relates to their actual occupations. For example, we say that a man with a <term>medical mind<note>Original: "medical soul," referring to a natural aptitude or disposition toward healing.</note></term> and a physician have the same nature. Don't you think so?"

"I do."

"But a physician and an architect have different natures?"

"Entirely."

"And so," I replied, "regarding the nature of men and women: if it appears they differ in their fitness for a specific art or employment, we shall say that these different tasks must be assigned to each separately. But if their nature appears to differ only in this—that the female brings forth children and the male begets them—we shall say that this does not prove the man is different from the woman in the specific way we are discussing. We shall still believe that..."
