"And the law," said I, "must be the same. If any of those men, who are yet of the age for generating, shall touch women of a proper age, without the concurrence of the magistrate <term>magistrate: an official or governor responsible for enforcing the city's laws</term>, we shall consider him as having raised to the state a bastardly, illegitimate and unhallowed child."

"Most right," said he.

"And I imagine, that when the women and men exceed the age of generating, we shall permit the men to cohabit with any woman they incline, besides their daughter and mother, and those who are the children of their daughters, or those upwards from their mother: and so likewise the women to embrace any but a son and father, and the children of these, either downwards or upwards: all this liberty we will allow them, after we have enjoined them to attend carefully, in the first place, if any thing should be conceived, not to bring it to the light; but if, by any accident, it should be brought forth, to expose it <note>This refers to "infant exposure," a practice in antiquity where unwanted or "unregulated" infants were left outdoors to die of the elements or be picked up by strangers.</note> as a creature for which no provision is made."

"All these things," said he, "are reasonably said. But how shall fathers and daughters, and those other relations you now mentioned, be known of one another?"

"They shall not be known at all," said I. "But from the day on which any one is a bridegroom, whatever children are born in the tenth or in the seventh month <note>The Greeks calculated pregnancy in lunar months; ten months was considered a full-term pregnancy.</note>, after it, all these he shall call, the male his sons, and the female his daughters, and they shall call him father. And in the same way again, he shall call the children of these grandchildren, and they again shall call them grandfathers and grandmothers: and those who were born in that period in which their fathers and mothers were begetting children, they shall call sisters and brothers, so as not to touch each other, as I just now said. But the law shall allow brothers and sisters to live together, if their lot <note>A reference to the rigged lottery system used to pair citizens for mating.</note> so fall out, and..."

...among these <term>powers</term> <note>original: "dynamis." In Greek philosophy, this refers to a faculty, capacity, or potential of the soul—like the "power" of sight or the "power" of reasoning.</note>, if you understand what I mean to call a species.

But as to power, I regard that alone about which it is conversant, and what it effects; and on this account I have called each of these a power. And the power which is conversant about and effects one and the same thing, I call the same power, but that conversant about and effecting a different thing, I call a different power: but what say you? In what manner do you call it? 

Just so, replied he.

In this context, science does not mean modern laboratory research, but rather "certain knowledge" or "true understanding" of things that never change.</note> is itself a certain power, or to what class do you refer it? 

I refer it to this class of power, said he, as it is of all powers the most strong.

By no means to power, said he; for that by which we form opinions is nothing else but <term>opinion</term> <note>original: "doxa." This refers to beliefs or appearances—things we think are true but cannot prove or which concern the physical world that is constantly changing.</note>.

You say right, said I. And it is plain that we have allowed opinion to be a different thing from science. 

We have. 

Each of them then has naturally a different power over a different thing. 

Of necessity.

Impossible, said he, from what we have allowed: since they are naturally powers of different things, and both of them are powers, opinion and science, and each of them different from the other, as we have said; from these things it cannot be, that what is opined is the same with that which is known. 

If then being itself be known, must it not be different from the being which is perceived by opinion? 

Different.

Impossible.

Yes.

Right. And now that which we call opinion, has appeared to be between them. It has appeared. 

It yet remains for us, as it seems, to discover that which participates of both these—of being, and of non-being—and which with propriety can be called neither of them perfectly. If it appears to be that which is the subject of opinion, we may justly call it so, assigning the extremes to the extremes, and the middle to the middle. Shall we not do thus? Thus. These things being determined, let this worthy man, I will say, tell and answer me—he who reckons that beauty, and a certain <term>idea of beauty</term> <note>Plato’s Theory of Forms suggests that there is one perfect "Idea" or "Form" of Beauty that exists eternally, while physical "beautiful things" are just temporary reflections.</note> there is none, always the same, and in the same respects; but this lover of beautiful objects reckons there are many beautiful things, but can never endure to be told that there is one beautiful, and one just, and so of others. 

Of all these many things, excellent man! shall we say to him, is there any which will not appear deformed? And of those just things, which will not appear unjust? Of those holy things, which will not appear profane? No; but of necessity, said he, the beautiful things themselves must in some respects appear even deformed, and others in like manner. But what? Many things which are double, or twofold—do they less really appear to be halves than doubles? No less. And things great and small, light and heavy—shall they be named what we call them, any more than their opposite? No; but each of them, said he, always participates of both. Whether then is each of these many things that which it is said to be, or is it not?

It is like the riddles told at banquets, he said, or the children’s riddle about the <term>eunuch</term> <note>original: "eunuchus." A man who has been castrated.</note> striking the bat—puzzling one another about what he struck it with and how far the hit went. <note>The "Riddle of the Eunuch" is a famous ancient puzzle: A man who is not a man (a eunuch) saw and did not see (due to poor sight) a bird that was not a bird (a bat) sitting on a branch that was not a branch (a reed); he hit it and did not hit it (he missed or used a pumice stone, which is "stone but not stone"). It illustrates things that both "are" and "are not."</note> For all these things have a double meaning; it is impossible to know for certain whether they "are" or "are not," or whether they are both, or neither of the two.

How can you deal with them then? I asked. Do you have a better place for them than this middle ground between <term>being</term> <note>True existence or eternal reality.</note> and <term>non-being</term>? <note>Nothingness or total ignorance.</note> For nothing seems more obscure than "non-being" (in the sense of having no existence at all), nor more clear than "being" (in the sense of real, unchanging existence).

That is very true, he said.

It seems we have discovered, then, that most of the common standards held by the public concerning <term>beauty</term> <note>The Greek "to kalon" refers to both physical beauty and moral goodness.</note> and other such things, are tossed about somewhere between "being" and "non-being."

We have indeed discovered that, he replied.

But we previously agreed that if any such thing should appear, it ought to be called the subject of **opinion**, not the subject of **knowledge**. That which fluctuates between the two states is perceived by the faculty that sits between the two.

We did agree.

Therefore, we will say that those who look at many beautiful things, but never perceive **beauty itself**—and are unable to follow anyone else who might lead them to it—and those who see many just things, but never **justice itself**, and so on with everything else, such people have **opinions** about all things, but they **know** nothing of the things they opine.

Necessarily so, he said.

But what about those who perceive the things themselves, which always exist in the same manner and in the same respect? Shall we not say that they have **knowledge**, rather than just opinion?

This is also a necessity.

And shall we not say that these people embrace and love the things of which they have knowledge, while the others love the things of which they have opinion? Do we not remember saying that the latter group beheld and loved fine sounds, colors, and such things, but they do not accept that "beauty itself" has any real existence?

We remember.

Will we be doing them an injustice if we call them **"lovers of opinion"** <note>original: "philodoxoi." A play on words with "philosopher." It literally means "those who love appearances or reputation."</note> rather than **philosophers**? And yet, they will be very angry with us if we call them that.

Not if they take my advice, he said; for it is not right to be angry with the truth.

But those who admire everything that has a real existence are to be called **philosophers**, and not "lovers of opinion."

By all means.

"Those who are philosophers," I said, "Glaucon, and those who are not, have finally—after a long and winding discussion—revealed with some difficulty who they each are."

For it is not natural for the pilot to entreat the sailors to allow him to govern them, nor for the wise to be hanging around the gates of the rich. 

Whoever wittily said the opposite was mistaken <note>This is a reference to a saying attributed to Aristippus or Simonides, suggesting that wise men are found at the doors of the rich because they know what they need.</note>; for the truly natural method is that whoever is sick—whether rich or poor—must of necessity go to the gates of the physician, and whoever wants to be governed must wait on him who is able to govern. It is not natural that a governor who is truly of any value should have to entreat the governed to subject themselves to his government. 

But you will not go far wrong if you compare our present political governors to those sailors we just mentioned, and those whom they call "insignificant star-gazers" to those who are truly pilots. 

Most right, said he.

<margin>Philosophy's bad reputation</margin>

[Ph]ilosophy <note>The OCR reads "lofophy," likely due to a dropped leading letter in the original printing.</note> is brought into disrepute by those who claim to study it; most of whom, as you say, the critics of philosophy call completely depraved, and even the very best of them are considered to be of no use to the state. I agreed that you were speaking the truth, did I not? 

You did. 

And have we not already fully explained the reason why the best of them are considered useless? <note>Socrates refers back to the "Ship of State" allegory, where the true pilot is ignored by the rowdy crew.</note> 

We have. 

Would you like us, then, to next explain the reason why most of them must necessarily be depraved, and try to demonstrate that philosophy itself is not the cause of this? 

Entirely so. 

Let us listen, then, and begin our reasoning by recalling what we previously noted regarding the natural character that must belong to a good and worthy man. As you may remember, the leading part of his character was **truth**, which he must pursue entirely and by all means; otherwise, he is a mere boaster and can never truly participate in philosophy. 

That was indeed said. 

Is this not one part of his character that is completely contrary to the current public opinion of him? 

It is very much so, he replied. 

Will it not, then, be a strong defense if we can show that the true lover of learning is naturally inclined to strive toward the knowledge of <term>real being</term> <note>In Plato’s thought, "real being" refers to the eternal, unchanging truths (Forms) rather than the shifting objects of our physical senses.</note>? He does not stop at the many individual things which are merely the objects of opinion, but moves forward. His love of truth is not blunted nor does it cease until he makes contact with the nature of every thing as it truly is, using that specific part of the soul whose job it is to grasp such things. 

Now, it is the function of that part of the soul which is allied to real being to do this. When the true lover of learning approaches and unites with reality, he gives birth to intellect and truth. He will then possess true knowledge, truly live, and be nourished; only then is he released from the pains of <term>parturition</term> <note>parturition: the act of giving birth. Socrates often used the metaphor of "midwifery" to describe how he helped others bring forth the truth from their own souls.</note>, and not before. 

This, he said, would be a most reasonable defense. 

Now, would it be the nature of such a person to love falsehood, or, quite the opposite, to hate it? 

To hate it, he said. 

But where truth leads the way, I do not think we can ever say that a "procession of evils" follows in her tracks. 

How could we? 

On the contrary, we can assert that she is followed by a healthy and moderate character, accompanied by **temperance** <note>Temperance refers to self-control and moderation in all things.</note>. 

Right, he said. 

Why, then, do we need to list and arrange the entire set of qualities belonging to the philosophic nature all over again? For you surely remember that this character also requires fortitude, magnanimity, a quickness for learning, and—

And on this account we have gone over again the genius <term>genius</term> <note>In this 18th-century translation style, "genius" refers to one’s innate character, natural disposition, or talent.</note> of true philosophers, and have necessarily defined what it is. 

It is so, said he. 

It is necessary now, said I, that we consider the corruptions of this genius, and in what manner it is destroyed in the most; but one small particular escapes us: who those are that they call not depraved, but useless. And next, what those geniuses are which counterfeit the philosophic nature, and pretend to its pursuit: and what is the nature of those souls who aspire to a pursuit which does not belong to them, and is above their reach: for these, by their manifold errors, have everywhere, and among all men, introduced this opinion of philosophy which you mention. 

What sort of corruptions, said he, do you mean? 

I shall endeavour to rehearse them, said I, if I be able. And this now, I think, everyone will allow us, that such a genius, with all those qualifications we have enjoined one who is to be a perfect philosopher, rarely arises among men, and that there are but few of them: do not you think so? 

Entirely so. 

And of those few, consider how many and how great are the causes of corruption. 

What are they? 

That which is most of all wonderful to hear, that each of those things we commended in the genius of a philosopher, corrupts the soul which possesses them, and withdraws it from philosophy; fortitude <note>Courage or mental strength.</note>, I mean, and temperance <note>Self-control or moderation.</note>, and all those other qualifications which we have discussed. 

That is strange to hear, said he. 

And further still, said I, besides these things, all those which are commonly called good, such as beauty, riches, strength of body, a powerful alliance in the city, and everything akin to these, corrupt and withdraw it from philosophy; for you have now a specimen of what I mean. 

I have, replied he; and would gladly understand more accurately what you say. 

Understand then, said I, the whole of it aright, and it will appear manifest, and what we formerly said will not seem to be absurd.

When do they effect this? he replied. 

When many of them, said I, are sat down, crowded together in a public assembly, in their courts of justice, the theater, or the camp, or any other public meeting of the people. <note>
**The Diomedæan Necessity:** This is a proverbial expression applied to those who act out of sheer necessity. It originates from the following story: Diomedes and Ulysses (Odysseus), having stolen the Palladium (a sacred statue of Athena) from Ilium (Troy), were returning by night to their ships. Ulysses, wanting the glory for himself, tried to kill Diomedes, who was walking ahead with the statue. Diomedes saw the shadow of Ulysses’ sword in the moonlight, grabbed him, bound his hands, and forced him to walk in front while striking him with the flat of his sword until they reached the Greek camp. 

This note is adapted from the *Greek Scholia* (ancient academic commentaries) on Plato, collected from many manuscripts by David Ruhnken and published at Lyons in 1800. As this work has only recently reached me, I could not use it earlier, but I will supply further information from it in the additional notes at the end of this volume. Unfortunately, these ancient comments are mostly focused on grammar.

"By the sight," said he. 

"And is it not," said I, "by hearing that we perceive what is heard; and by the other senses, all the other objects of sense?" 

"Why not?"

"I have not entirely perceived it," replied he. 

"But consider it in this manner. "There is nothing," said he. 

"Imagine then," said I, "that neither do many others (that I may not say none) require any such thing: or can you mention any one that does require it?" 

"Not I," replied he.

"How?"

"What is that you speak of?" said he. 

"What you call light," said I.

When therefore Plato says that *the good reigns over intelligibles*, he means that good which is superior to essence.

But to lead us up to this supreme good, he appears to employ three orders of good as so many steps in this arduous ascent; namely: that which is imparticipable <term>imparticipable: a technical term for a principle so pure and transcendent that it cannot be divided or "shared" by lower things, but remains independent.</term> and superessential, that which is imparticipable and essential, and that which is essential and participable. For the idea of *the good* signifies a participated form <term>participated form: an idea or quality that is present within something else, such as the quality of "goodness" appearing in a person</term>, a separate intelligible <term>separate intelligible: a reality that exists on its own, independent of physical matter, and can only be understood by the mind</term>, and that which has a separate subsistence prior to intelligibles; since the term *idea*, according to Plato, indicates that object of desire which is established prior to all things, viz. prior to all things belonging to a certain series. Thus, for instance, *the good* in our nature is prior to every thing else pertaining to the soul; *the good* which ranks among forms is prior to every thing which is the source of essential perfection; and *the good* which reigns in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of eternal truths and forms that exist beyond the physical world we see with our eyes.</note> is prior to every series, and to all things.

Again, when Socrates says, “Let us at present dismiss this inquiry what *the good* is, for it appears to me a greater thing than we can arrive at according to our present impulse,” it may be inferred, that though he appears to say something concerning *the good* from an image, and to unveil something pertaining to things occult <note>In this context, "occult" simply means hidden or secret truths that are not immediately obvious.</note>, yet he does not unfold the whole truth concerning it; and this perhaps in consequence of Thrasymachus and Clitopho <note>Thrasymachus and Clitopho are characters in the Republic known for their cynical or worldly views; the commentator suggests Socrates withholds the highest truths from those who are not philosophically or spiritually ready.</note> being present, and not thinking it fit to disclose the most mystical truths to sophists. Hence, on his asserting afterwards that *the good* is superessential <term>superessential: existing above and beyond the very nature of "being" or "existence" itself</term>, he appeared to Glauco to speak ridiculously; and in consequence of Glauco in vain attempting the vision of that which is beyond all things, he again says that he willingly omits many things, and alone unfolds the analogy respecting the sun. But if his hearers had been adapted to such discourses, he would have disclosed to us many and truly theological particulars respecting it; and such as he discloses to us in the Parmenides <note>Plato’s "Parmenides" is one of his most challenging dialogues, dealing with the nature of "The One," the ultimate source of all reality.</note> concerning *the one*.

As we have said, therefore, Plato, transferring the investigation from *the good* which is in us, and concerning which those inquire who say that it is prudence or pleasure, to *the good* itself, and beginning the image respecting the sun, in the first place, he exhorts his hearers to take care that he does not give them an adulterate account <note>original: "adulterate" — here used in the sense of a counterfeit or distorted version, like a fake coin.</note> of the offspring of *the good*; calling the sun the offspring, and transferring the term adulterate from the impressions in coin. He also indicates that the mode of teaching by analogy is not safe. For there is danger of introducing sophistry into the demonstration, by considering things beyond what the analogy will admit. Thus, in the present instance, if in consequence of Plato asserting that the sun is analogous to *the good*, so far as the former is the cause of light, as the latter is of truth, some one should consider the sun, no longer as the cause alone of light, but so far as it is moved, and should investigate that which is similar to this motion, in *the good*, he would no longer preserve the proper analogy. For the sun is not analogously assumed, so far as he is a thing caused, but so far as he is a cause alone; since it is impossible to assume any thing which is in all respects similar to *the good*. For every thing posterior to *the good*, by the assumption of something becomes worse than *the good*; one thing by assuming intelligence, as *intellect*; another by assuming motion, as *soul*; and another by the assumption of generation <term>generation: the process of coming into being or physical birth</term>, as *body*. For every thing which is assumed analogously *to the good*, must necessarily possess dissimilitude in conjunction with similitude. Analogies however and ratios are not assumed according to the dissimilar, but on the contrary according to the similar.

Again, when in the beginning of this discourse about *the good*, and wishing to determine that some forms are intelligible and others sensible, he makes mention of the beautiful itself and the *good* itself, and, placing these as the forms of many things beautiful and good, he says that sensible forms are seen indeed, but are not the objects of intellect, but that ideas are the objects of intellect, and not of the sensible eye,—it is evident that he refers us to ideas, and the universal prior to the many. If therefore Plato had added nothing further, we should not have had any authority from the Republic for conceiving any other good than this, which is the first among forms that give perfection to things; but since he touches on the analogy respecting the sun, sight and light, he in a wonderful manner asserts that all intelligible <term>intelligible: things that can only be understood by the mind or intellect, such as mathematical truths or abstract concepts, as opposed to physical things we see</term> ideas, the beautiful itself, *the good* itself, the just itself, and not these only, but those of actions also, are illuminated by *the good*. Here therefore he ascends to the first cause of wholes, which he is unable to call by a better name than *the good*: for *the good* is the most venerable of all things, and is that which all things desire; and that which all things desire is the cause of all. Fearful however lest we should apprehend a first of such a kind as that good which is the cause of perfection alone in ideas, he shows in the first place that *the good* is beyond science and truth, in the same manner as the sun is beyond sight and light; and afterwards he evinces that it is the primary cause of intelligibles, and is superessential <term>superessential: existing above or beyond the level of essence or "being"; a state of existence so high it surpasses our definitions of reality</term>, in the same manner as the sun is above generation <note>original: "generatio" — in this context, the physical world of birth, change, and decay</note>; and thus he shows that the *good* itself is the first cause of the good and the beautiful in forms, and of all intelligible essences.

But that we may not deviate from the doctrine through analogy, he says that the sun is analogous *to the good*, not according to any thing else than his being the cause of light, through which all visible things are seen: I mean, not so far as the sun has a body, and a corporeal place, and is moveable. And again, such a light is analogous to truth, not so far as it possesses interval, or all-various refractions, but so far only as it imparts the power of being seen to things visible, and sight to things that see; in the same manner as truth imparts to intelligibles the power of being intellectually apprehended, and to intelligent natures the power of intellectual perception; and visible objects are analogous to intelligibles, not as subsisting in place and being moved, but as visible alone.

These things being premised, it is shown by Socrates that *the good* is beyond truth, in the same manner as the sun is beyond light: and hence it follows that *the good* does not participate of truth. For that which is above truth neither *is truly*, nor *can truly* be any thing else: so that if *the good is*, but is not *truly*, it will be that which is not *truly* being. But this is impossible. For, according to Plato, that which is not *truly* being subsists after true being. But *the good* is not true being, since it generates truth; and it must be entirely unreceptive of that which it generates. But all true being necessarily participates of truth. Hence it follows that *the good*

Again, when Socrates says: “You know that the eyes, when they are no longer directed towards objects whose colors are shone upon by the light of day, but by the splendor of the night, grow dim, and appear almost blind, as if they had in them no pure sight. But when they turn to objects which the sun illuminates, then I think they see clearly, and in those very eyes there appears now to be sight.” Here, he makes a division in visible things into colors, light, eyes, and the sun. Afterwards he brings forward things analogous to these in the objects of the intellect <term>intellect: in this context, the higher mind capable of grasping abstract truths beyond the physical senses</term>, as follows: “Understand then in the same manner with reference to the soul: when it firmly adheres to that which truth and real being enlighten, then it understands and knows it, and appears to possess intellect; but when it adheres to that which is blended with darkness, which is born <note>original: "generated"</note> and which perishes, it is then dealing with opinion, its vision becomes blunted, it wanders from one opinion to another, and resembles one without intellect.” Socrates, therefore, assumes being to be analogous to color, truth to light, and the *good* to the sun. He also places being after truth, in the same way that color comes after light and the sun. The *good* therefore is beyond being. For he does not say "that which *beings* enlighten," but "that which *being* enlightens." If therefore the *good* is above being, it will also necessarily be above essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing; that which makes a thing what it is</term>.

Having asserted these things through analogy, he adds something even greater: that the *good* is the cause of intelligibles <term>intelligibles: realities that can only be understood by the mind, such as mathematical laws or moral truths, rather than perceived by the senses</term>, not only of their being understood, but also of their very essence. This is just as the sun is the cause of visible things—not only of their being seen, but of their birth, nourishment, and growth; and, just as the sun is not the birth itself, in the same way the *good* is not essence. It is evident, therefore, that the *good*, being the cause of an intelligible essence, will be in the most eminent degree superessential <term>superessential: (Greek: *hyperousios*) existing beyond the category of 'being' or 'essence' itself; the ultimate source that transcends existence</term>; for these, as will appear from the *Parmenides* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the "One" and the many</note>, are superessential essences, or, in other words, beings absorbed in the superessential. It likewise follows from this analogy that truth also is superessential: for Socrates says that this illuminates all things that are known, in the same way that the light of the sun illuminates visible objects. Truth indeed appears to be an illumination from the superessential principle of all things, which both the mind and the objects of the mind participate in, and which unites them to themselves and to each other. Hence it is said to give the power of being understood to the former, and the power of vision to the latter: for these could not be joined without a certain common bond. Just as light illuminates the things seen and the eyes that see, but joins both through their similarity—giving to both a greater light than they contained before—in the same way, the thinking mind and the thing being thought, being united by truth, merge with each other.

From this, it will also follow that the *good* cannot be known either by opinion or by science. That it cannot be known by opinion is easily proved. For Plato, with great propriety, considers the object of opinion as that which is partly being and partly non-being. It is also evident that the *good* is not the object of science. For, if every object of science is known

It can therefore only be known by a divine projection of the summit of the soul, a projection of that which is better than intellect, and which Plato * calls the ray of the soul. According to Plato, the soul inclining this ray should project herself to *the good* through an ablation <term>ablation: the process of "taking away" or stripping away all specific qualities to reach a pure, simple truth</term> of all things posterior to it. For he clearly says that it is necessary to take away the idea of the *good* from all things, and thus to incline towards it the ray of the soul, if we intend to perceive it, *itself by itself*. From these things therefore it is evident, by what kind of knowledge *the good* is known, how it is known, and how it is the last discipline, and what the dialectic method contributes to the vision of it, by leading the intellect of the soul up to it, through a scientific series of ablations.

Again, since Socrates asserts that *the good* is not only beyond essence, but likewise above that which is <note>original Greek: "epekeina tou einai", meaning "beyond being"</note>, it follows that it is not proper to say *the good is*; and hence neither is it proper to say that it is not; for again this assertion *that it is not* is common to other things, to which non-being is adapted. Both therefore must be said, that it is neither being nor non-being; and in consequence of this, it is called by some unknown and ineffable; since every thing is either being or non-being. Nor must we suppose, when Plato calls *the good* known, and the last discipline, and every thing of this kind, that he removes us from an indefinite energy about it, and apprehends it to be known in such a manner as beings: for these are known, and are the objects of scientific knowledge, according to that most accurate mode of science which he defines, and according to which he despises the sciences which originate from hypothesis. For thus he speaks, teaching us his conceptions about these particulars: that other sciences, or which appear to be such, make hypotheses their principles; but dialectic <term>dialectic: the highest form of philosophical reasoning that seeks the ultimate truth without relying on unproven assumptions</term> alone being impelled to the principle, takes away hypotheses, till it discovers that which is truly the principle, not as an hypothesis, but truly unhypothetical. But such a principle is *the one*, in which every subsistence of things known terminates. From these things, therefore, it is evident, that calling dialectic the defensive enclosure of things which appear to be sciences, and defining that which is truly science, he says that dialectic, beginning from an unhypothetic principle, considers the nature of every thing. If therefore beholding also the idiom of *the good*, and in what respect it differs from other things, this science speculates from an unhypothetic principle, this perhaps will be a certain science, and a science of *the good*, what it truly is, or is not. But if this is the principle of all things, and a principle cannot be assumed of a principle, by what contrivance can it be said that there is a certain science of *the good*? —comprehended is properly a scientific object: but *the good* is not grasped from a principle that requires no further proof, because it does not have any prior principle at all. From this it also follows again that *the good* is not "being" <note>In this context, "being" refers to the realm of things that exist and can be defined. Because the Good is the source of existence, it is considered "beyond being."</note>, since Plato most clearly asserts that science is concerned with being; whereas faith pertains to that which appears and is sensible, the dianoëtic <term>dianoëtic: relating to the mathematical or discursive reasoning of the mind, which stands between simple opinion and pure intellectual intuition</term> power to dianoëtic objects, assimilation to things assimilated, opinion to sensibles and things assimilated, and intelligence to intelligibles. And he does not only assert this here, but in the *Timaeus* also he says, "That what essence is to generation <note>Essence refers to eternal things; generation refers to things that are born and die.</note>, that faith is to truth," and he attributes arguments which cannot be refuted to beings, but likely arguments to generated natures, signifying that science is the observation of true beings. If therefore being is the object of scientific knowledge, but *the good* cannot be scientifically known, *the good* is not being.

Hence we must conclude that *the good* is only to be known by an ablation <term>ablation: the process of "taking away" or stripping away all specific qualities to reach a pure, simple truth</term> of all things from its ineffable <note>ineffable: too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note> nature; and this is what Socrates hints at when, in the 7th book, he speaks of separating the idea of *the good* from all others, and—as if in a battle—piercing through all arguments. It is therefore neither science, nor truth, nor being: and if we use these things as principles and consider the consequences, we shall find that if *the good* is not being, it is neither the "same" nor "different," neither moved nor at rest, possesses neither shape nor number, is neither similar nor dissimilar, neither equal nor unequal, nor does it participate in time; all of which Parmenides <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue "Parmenides," which explores the nature of "The One."</note> gathers in the first hypothesis, and, having gathered them, adds that there is neither science nor opinion of *the one*, for it is beyond generation and essence. So that whatever is asserted of *the one*, in the *Parmenides* of Plato, must also necessarily be asserted of *the good*, based on what is delivered here by Plato concerning it; and hence *the good*, according to Plato, is the same as *the one*. We not only have this information from the assertions of Socrates—that *the good* is not the object of scientific knowledge—but we also learn that it may be known in another way through arguments and the process of stripping away qualities.

...seem to me to speak of an arduous undertaking: but you want, however, to determine that the perception of real being, and that which is <term>intelligible</term> <note>Things that can only be understood by the mind, rather than perceived by the five senses.</note>, by the science of reasoning, are more conspicuous than the discoveries made by the arts, as they are called, which have <term>hypotheses</term> <note>Starting assumptions or axioms that are taken for granted without being proven.</note> for their first principles; and that those who behold these are obliged to behold them with their <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>original: "dianoia." Referring to the power of discursive reasoning, particularly the kind of step-by-step logic used in mathematics.</note> power, and not with their senses. But as they are not able to perceive, by ascending to the principle, but from hypotheses, they appear to you not to possess intellect respecting them, though they are intelligible in conjunction with the principle. You also appear to me to call the habit of geometrical and such like concerns, the dianoëtic part, and—

---

the similitude and coherence of secondary natures always proceeding from such as are first, no vacuum by its intervention separating them from each other. For, as *the one* <note>In this philosophy, "The One" is the supreme, unified source of all existence from which everything else flows.</note> produces all things, it is necessary that their procession from him should be continued: for the continued is allied to *the one*. And the cause of this continuity is the similitude of those sections which are in a consequent to those which are in a precedent order: for similitude is oneness. On this account he assumes one line, but this he cuts into two parts, and these not equal but unequal: the parts are however two. For in the *Philebus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning pleasure and the "good life."</note> he exhorts those that speculate things, *after the one*, to consider two things, if they have a subsistence, if not, the number which is allied to the <term>duad</term> <note>The principle of duality or "twoness."</note>. The division therefore of all things into unequal parts, indicates the rank of the divided natures, the inequality according to continuity exhibiting an image of inequality according to <term>hyparxis</term> <note>A technical term in Neoplatonism referring to the "essential existence" or the very foundation of a thing's being.</note>. But each of these unequal sections he cuts analogous to the first division of the line; this analogy again clearly manifesting the subjection through sameness of secondary from primary natures. For analogy is identity of ratio, and the most beautiful of bonds, as we learn in the *Timæus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the physical universe.</note>, and is the judgment of Jupiter, as we are informed in the *Laws* <note>Plato’s last and longest dialogue regarding ethics and government.</note>. As therefore the universe was fabricated according to analogy, all things receiving an indissoluble friendship with each other, so all things proceed bound, and in mutual consent through analogy.

But as there are four sections of one line, two of these, which complete its larger section, Plato establishes as the genus of the intelligible, but the other two, which form the lesser division, as the genus of that which is visible. For it was necessary to assign the larger section to the intelligible, as being more excellent, and comprehending the other, but the lesser to that which is visible; for it is comprehended in the intelligible order according to cause. And that which is comprehended is every where less than that which comprehends, whether the comprehension is considered according to essence, or according to power, or according to energy; as is seen in all continued and divided natures.

I only add that Plato in this representation of the series of things, by the sections of a line, follows the Pythagoreans, Brontinus and Archytas; but his explanation is both more elegant and more extended, as the learned reader may be convinced by consulting that part of the *Greek Anecdotes* <note>original: "Anecdota Græca." A collection of previously unpublished Greek texts compiled by the scholar Jean-Baptiste Gaspard d'Ansse de Villoison.</note> of Villoison, which contains the *Treatise of Jamblichus on the common Mathematical Science*.

**AFTER** these things now, said I, compare our nature—in respect to its <term>erudition</term> <note>Education and the cultivation of the mind.</note> and the lack thereof—to a condition such as this. Imagine people living in a subterranean dwelling like a cave, with an entrance that opens toward the light and extends across the whole width of the cavern. Suppose they have been in this cave since their childhood, with chains on both their legs and their necks, so that they must remain there and can only look forward, unable to turn their heads because of the shackles. Suppose, further, that the light of a fire is burning far above and behind them, and that between the fire and the prisoners there is a path on higher ground. Along this path, imagine a low wall has been built, like the screens used by <term>mountebanks</term> <note>Traveling performers or puppeteers who show their tricks or puppets above a partition to hide themselves.</note> to display their wonders.

I see it, said he.

Behold now, along this wall, men carrying all sorts of <term>utensils</term> <note>Various man-made tools and artifacts.</note> that reach above the wall, including statues of men and other animals made of wood and stone, and furniture of every kind. And, as you might expect, some of those carrying these objects are speaking, while others are silent.

You describe a strange comparison, said he, and strange prisoners.

But they are like us, I replied; for in the first place, do you think such people would see anything of themselves or of one another, except for the <term>shadows</term> <note>The shadows represent the lowest level of reality—mere appearances that people mistake for the truth.</note> cast by the fire on the wall of the cave facing them?

How could they, he asked, if they have been forced to keep their heads still throughout their entire lives?

And what about the objects being carried along the wall? Would they not see the very same shadows of them?

Certainly, he said.

Necessarily so, he said.

After these things, he says "that the man who is to be led from the cave will more easily see what the heavens contain, and the heavens themselves, by looking in the night to the light of the stars, and the moon, than by day looking on the sun, and the light of the sun." By this he signifies the contemplation of <term>intelligibles</term> <note>These are the "Forms" or "Ideas"—abstract, perfect truths that can only be understood by the mind, not by the physical eyes.</note>: for the stars and their light are imitations of intelligibles, so far as all of them partake of the form of the sun, in the same manner as intelligibles are characterized by the nature of *the good*. After the contemplation of these, and after the eye is through these accustomed to the light, as it is requisite in the visible region to see the sun himself in the last place, in like manner, according to Plato, the *idea of the good* must be seen the last in the intelligible region. He likewise adds, in a truly divine manner, that it is scarcely to be seen; for we can only be conjoined with it through the intelligible, in the vestibule of which it is beheld by ascending souls. The intelligible indeed is the first participant of *the good*, and indicates from itself to those that are able to behold it, what that nature is, if it be lawful so to speak, which is the <term>superintelligible</term> <note>Something existing beyond even the reach of the highest human or divine intellect; the ultimate source.</note> cause of the light it contains. For the light in an intelligible essence is more divine than that in intellectual natures, in the same manner as the light in the stars is more divine than that which is in the eyes that behold them. Thus also Socrates, in the *Philebus*, says, that *the good* is apprehended with difficulty, and is scarcely to be seen, and that it is found with three <term>monads</term> <note>From the Greek *monas*, meaning a primary unit or fundamental principle.</note>, and these intelligible, arranged in its vestibule, *truth, beauty, and symmetry*. For these three produce the first being, or being itself, and through these the whole intelligible order is unfolded into light. With great propriety, therefore, does Plato assert, that the idea of *the good* is to be seen the last thing in the intelligible: for the intelligible is the seat of its vision. Hence it is seen in this, as in its first participant, though it is beyond every intelligible. ...the same condition as the eye, if it were unable otherwise, than with the whole body, to turn from darkness to light, must, in like manner, with the whole soul, be turned from <term>generation</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "generation" refers to the physical world of change, birth, and decay, as opposed to the eternal world of "Being."</note>, till it be able to endure the contemplation of being itself, and the most splendid of being; and this we call the *good*. It is likely, replied he. By both necessity and persuasion, he makes them share with one another the advantages with which they are severally able to benefit the community. When the legislator creates such men in the city, he does so not to permit them to go wherever they please, but so that he may employ them to bind the city together.

For when you are accustomed to the darkness, you will perceive things there infinitely better than the others do. ...of you, shall the city be inhabited, and not as a dream, as most cities are at present inhabited by such as both fight with one another about shadows <note>This refers to the Cave Allegory, where prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for reality. "Entirely so," replied he.

"Impossible," said he. "For we prescribe just things to just men. And each of them enters on <term>magistracy</term> <note>A term for holding public office or a position of government authority.</note> from this consideration beyond all others: that they are under a necessity of governing after a manner contrary to all the present governors of all other cities."

For in it alone shall those govern who are **truly rich**, not in gold, but in that in which a happy man ought to be rich: in a good and prudent life. But if, while they are poor and destitute of goods of their own, they come to the public, thinking they ought to pillage good from it, it is not possible to have the city rightly established. For the contest being who shall govern, such a war being domestic and internal, it destroys both themselves and the rest of the city." 

"Most true," said he.

"Let us then establish this as the second branch of study for our youth." 

"Let us do so," he said. 

"And what about the third? Shall we establish astronomy? Or do you think otherwise?" 

"I agree," he said. "Being skilled in the cycles of months and years is useful not only for agriculture and sailing but just as much for the art of war." 

"You are amusing," I said. "You seem to be afraid that the public will think you are recommending useless subjects. But this is not a trivial matter, even though it is hard to convince people that these studies <term>purify and awaken|exsuscitated</term> an organ of the soul <note>Plato refers here to the "eye of the mind" or the intellect, which he believes must be "cleansed" of worldly distractions to see higher truths.</note> that is blinded and buried by other activities. That organ is worth more than ten thousand physical eyes, for truth is seen by it alone. Those who agree with this will think your reasoning is wonderful; but those who have never noticed this will likely think you are talking nonsense, for they see no other practical benefit in these things."

"Now, decide which group you are arguing with—or if you are conducting the argument primarily for your own sake, though you wouldn't begrudge anyone else who might benefit from it."

"I prefer," he replied, "to reason, question, and answer primarily for my own sake." 

"Then let us go back a step," I said, "for we did not correctly choose what follows geometry." 

"How so?" he asked. 

"After studying flat surfaces," I said, "we jumped to solids in motion <note>This refers to astronomy, the study of the moving heavenly bodies.</note> before considering the solids by themselves. The right way would be to take the third study immediately after the second—and that is the study of <term>three-dimensional solids|cubes</term>." 

"That is true," he replied. "But Socrates, those things don't seem to have been discovered yet." 

"There are two reasons for that," I said. "First, because no city values them, they are not properly investigated because they are difficult. Second, those who do investigate them need a leader, and without one, they cannot make discoveries. In the first place, such a leader is hard to find..."

"Why is that?"

"Because," I said, "a free man should not learn any subject like a slave. While physical labor, when endured under compulsion, does no harm to the body, no study that is forced stays in the soul."

"True," he said.

"Therefore, my friend," I said, "do not use compulsion with the children in their education. Instead, let them learn through play. This will also allow you to better see the natural inclination of each child's genius."

"What you say is reasonable," he replied.

"Do you remember," I asked, "that we said the boys should even be taken to war as spectators, on horseback? They are to be brought close to the action—provided it is safe—so that, like young hounds, they may get a taste of blood." <note>This is a metaphor for exposing the future protectors of the city to the realities of their duty at a young age to test their courage and instinct.</note>

"I remember," he said.

"Whoever appears the most capable in all these labors, studies, and dangers must be selected for a specific group."

"At what age?" he asked.

"When they have finished their necessary physical exercises," I replied. "During that period—whether it lasts two or three years—it is impossible to do anything else. Fatigue and sleep are enemies of learning. Furthermore, these physical exercises are themselves a significant test of how each of them performs."

"Certainly," he said.

The subjects they studied separately in their youth should now be brought together into a single, comprehensive view. This allows them to see the connection between the various disciplines and the nature of true reality."

"Indeed," he said, "only this kind of learning remains firm in those who possess it."

Can you guess how such a person would feel toward his flatterers and toward his supposed parents—both when he was unaware of the deception and when he discovered it? Or would you like to hear my prediction?" 

"I would like to," he said. 

"I predict then," I said, "that he will show more honor to his father, mother, and other supposed relatives than to the flatterers. He will be less likely to neglect them when they are in need, less likely to do or say anything wrong to them, and in important matters, less likely to disobey them than the flatterers—at least during the time he does not know the truth." 

"That is likely," he said. 

"But when he realizes the true state of affairs," I continued, "I predict that he will then become less respectful toward them and more attentive to the flatterers. He will be much more influenced by them than before and live according to their ways, associating with them openly. As for his supposed father and relatives, unless he has a naturally good disposition, he will have no regard for them." 

"You have described exactly what would happen," he said. "But how does this comparison relate to those..."

"Are not now then," said I, "our discourses sufficient both concerning such a city as this, and concerning a man similar to it? For it is also now evident what kind of a man we shall say he ought to be." 

"It is evident," replied he; "and your inquiry seems to me to be at an end."

Both our contemplation and judgment, said he, would in this manner at least be agreeable to reason. 

Come then, said I, let us endeavour to relate in what manner a *Timocracy* arises out of an *Aristocracy*. Or is not this plain, that every republic changes, by means of that part which possesses the magistracies <note>the high offices of government or the ruling class.</note>, when in this itself there arises sedition <note>internal strife, factionalism, or civil discord.</note>; but whilst this agrees with itself, though the state be extremely small, it is impossible to be changed?

The period for that which is divinely generated<gloss>2</gloss> is that which the perfect number <note>The "perfect number" here refers to a complex mathematical ratio Plato uses to describe the cosmic cycle of the state's decline; it is often called the "Nuptial Number."</note>...

<gloss>1</gloss> Not all parts of the universe are able to share in the divine providence <note>original: "providentia"; the protective care of God or nature.</note> in the same way; some parts enjoy this eternally, and others only for a time; some in a primary degree and others in a secondary degree. For the universe, being a perfect whole, must have a first, a middle, and a last part. Its first parts, having the most excellent way of existing, must always exist according to nature; its last parts must sometimes exist according to nature, and sometimes contrary to it. Hence the celestial bodies—which are the primary parts of the universe—perpetually exist according to nature, both the entire spheres and the many parts coordinated with them (see the Introduction to the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato’s dialogues that explains the creation of the universe by a divine craftsman.</note>). The only change they experience is a change of shape and the variation of light at different times. However, in the earthly <term>sublunary: the region "under the moon," referring to the Earth where things are subject to change and decay.</term> region, while the elements themselves remain according to nature, the individual parts of those elements sometimes exist naturally and sometimes unnaturally. This is the only way the cycle of generation can reveal all the variety it contains.

The different periods in which these changes happen are called by Plato, quite appropriately, periods of *fertility* and *sterility*. In these periods, a fertility or sterility of men, animals, and plants occurs. Thus, in fertile periods, mankind will be more numerous and generally superior in mental and bodily talents compared to the men of a barren period. The same reasoning applies to animals and plants. The famous "Heroic Age" <note>A period in Greek mythology where semi-divine heroes like Achilles and Hercules lived.</note> was the result of one of these fertile periods, when men who surpassed the rest of humanity in both practical and intellectual virtue were abundant on the earth.

<gloss>2</gloss> An ancient commentator <term>Scholiast: an ancient or medieval commentator who wrote explanatory notes (scholia) in the margins of manuscripts.</term> on this passage rightly observes that Plato, by "that which is divinely generated," does not mean the whole world (though the term applies to it primarily), nor just the heavenly regions, nor just the earthly world, but *everything that moves perpetually in a circle*, whether in the heavens or below the moon. Insofar as a thing is physical, he calls it *generated* (since no body can create itself); but insofar as it moves perpetually, he calls it *divine*, for it imitates the most divine things which possess an ever-watchful life.

<summary>Socrates explains that even the ideal state must eventually decay because all created things are subject to cycles of "fertility and sterility" governed by cosmic orbits. He introduces the idea that even wise rulers will eventually fail to calculate the "perfect number" required for ideal human breeding, leading to the city's decline.</summary>

the perfect number mentioned here by Plato, we must not only direct our attention to a perfect number in vulgar arithmetic, for this is rather numbered than number, tends to perfection, and is never perfect, as being always in generation; but we must survey the cause of this number, which is indeed intellectual, but comprehends the definite boundary of every period of the world.

> <note>original Greek text:</note> By "divinely generated" he does not mean the whole world—though primarily it refers to this—nor only what is in the heavens, nor only what is beneath the moon, but everything that is ever-moving and revolving, whether in the heavens or beneath the moon. As a corporeal thing it is called "generated," for no body is self-subsistent; but as it is ever-moving, it is "divine," for it imitates the most divine of beings <note>reading *theiotata* for *theiotaton*</note> which possess an unwearied life. Regarding the perfect number, one must not only think of it as counting on the fingers; for this is rather a numbered thing than a number, and is always becoming perfect but is never truly perfect, as it is always in a state of generation. Instead, we must understand its cause as being intellectual, encompassing the finite boundary of the entire period of the world.

$^{1}$ The obscurity of these numbers, which is so great as to have become proverbial among the ancients, is not elucidated by any of those invaluable remains of Grecian philosophy which have survived to the present time. And yet it may be fairly concluded that this mysterious passage was most satisfactorily unfolded by the commentaries of such men as Jamblichus, Syrianus and Proclus, on this part of the Republic, though they have unfortunately perished in the wreck of ages. The following attempt, however, may perhaps show that it is not impossible to penetrate this mystery, though deprived of such mighty aid, since it is only to be solved by the assistance of *Mathesis* <note>The personification of learning or mathematics.</note>, who at all times willingly acts ministrant to Inspiration.

In the first place then, let us consider what Plato means by augmentations surpassing and surpassed; things assimilating and dissimilating, increasing and decreasing, correspondent and effable.

Augmentations surpassing, are ratios of greater inequality, viz. when the greater is compared to the lesser, and are multiples \*, superparticulars, superpartients, multiple-superparticulars

---

\* Multiplex ratio is when a greater quantity contains a lesser many times. Superparticular ratio is when the greater contains the lesser quantity once, and some part of it besides; and superpartient ratio, is when the greater contains the lesser quantity once, and certain parts of it likewise. Again, multiple superparticular ratio is when the greater contains the lesser many times and some part of it besides; and multiple superpartient ratio is when the greater contains the lesser many times, and also some of its parts.

particulars and <term>multiple-superpartients</term> <note>A complex ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number multiple times plus several fractional parts.</note>. But augmentations surpassed are, ratios of lesser inequality, viz. when the lesser is compared with the greater quantity, as for instance, sub-multiples, subsuperparticulars, subsuperpartients, and those which are composed from these three. These numbers are called by Plato *assimilating* and *dissimilating*, which are denominated by mathematicians *similar* \* and *dissimilar*: but he calls those *increasing* and *decreasing*, which they denominate *abounding* † and *diminished*, or more than *perfect* and *imperfect*. Things correspondent and <term>effable</term> <note>From the Latin 'effabilis', meaning things that can be expressed or spoken; in mathematics, these are rational numbers that can be stated as integers or simple fractions.</note>, are boundaries which correspond in ratio with each other, and can be expressed in numbers either integral or fractional, such as these four terms or boundaries, 27, 18, 12, 8, which are in <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2, where the first number is 1.5 times the second.</note> and subsesquialter ratios; since these mutually correspond in ratio, and are effable. For effable quantities are those which can be expressed in whole numbers, or fractions; and, in like manner, <term>ineffable</term> <note>Irrational numbers, such as square roots, which cannot be expressed as a simple fraction or finite decimal.</note> quantities are such as cannot be expressed in either of these, and are called by modern mathematicians surds.

In the next place, let us consider what we are to understand by the *sesquitertian progeny when conjoined with the pentad and thrice increased, affording two harmonies*. By the *sesquitertian progeny* <note>The ratio of 4:3.</note> then Plato means the number 95: for this number is composed from the addition of the squares of the numbers 4 and 3, which form the first <term>sesquitertian</term> ratio, (viz. 25) and the number 70, which is composed from 40 and 30, and therefore consists of two numbers in a sesquitertian ratio. Hence, as 95 is composed from 25 and 70, it may with great propriety be called a sesquitertian progeny. This number conjoined with 5 <note>The "pentad."</note> and thrice increased produces ten thousand and a million: for 100 X 100 = 10000, and 10000 X 100 = 1000000. But it must here be observed that these two numbers, as will shortly be seen, appear to be considered by Plato as analogous to two <term>parallelopipedons</term> <note>A solid figure with six faces that are parallelograms; similar to a rectangular box.</note>, the former, viz. ten thousand, being formed from 10 X 10 X 100, and the latter from 1000 X 10 X 100. These two numbers are called by Plato two harmonies, for the following reason: Simplicius, in his Commentary on Aristotle's books *On the Heavens* <note>original: "De Coelo"</note>, informs us that a cube was denominated by the Pythagoreans *harmony*, because it consists of 12 bounding lines, 8 angles, and 6 *sides*; and 12, 8, 6, are in harmonic proportion: for the difference between 12 and 8 is to the difference between 8 and 6, i. e. 4 is to 2 as the first term to the third, i. e. as 12 to 6, which, as is well known, is the law of harmonic proportion. As a parallelopipedon therefore has the same number of sides, angles, and bounding lines as a cube, the reason is obvious why the numbers 10000 and 1000000 are called by Plato harmonies. Hence also it is evident why he says "that the other of these harmonies, viz. a

Again, when he says “that the number 1,000,000 consists of a hundred numbers from <term>effable diameters</term> <note>In ancient mathematics, these are rational whole numbers that closely approximate the square root of a non-square number. For example, if a square has a side of 5, the diagonal (diameter) squared is 50. Since 50 has no perfect square root, 7 is the "effable" diameter because 7 squared is 49—nearly 50.</note> of <term>pentads</term> <note>The number five.</note>, each being deficient by unity, and from two that are ineffable, and from a hundred cubes of the triad,” his meaning is as follows: The number 1,000,000 consists of a hundred numbers, i. e. of a hundred such numbers as 10,000, each of which is composed from effable diameters of pentads, &c. But in order to understand the truth of this assertion, it is necessary to observe that there are certain numbers which are called by arithmeticians effable diameters. These also are twofold; for some are the diameters of even squares, and others of odd squares. And the diameters of effable even squares, when multiplied into themselves, produce square numbers double of the squares of which they are the diameters, with an excess of unity: Thus, for instance, the number 3 multiplied into itself produces 9, which is double of the square number 4, with an excess of unity; and therefore 3 will be the diameter of the even square 4. But the diameters of effable odd squares are in power double of the squares of which they are the diameters, by a deficiency of unity. Thus, the number 7 multiplied into itself produces 49, which is double of the odd square number 25 by a deficiency of unity. This being premised, it follows that the number 10,000 will consist of a certain number of <term>heptads</term> <note>The number seven.</note>; for 7 is the effable diameter of the square number 25: and from what follows it will be found that this number is 1386.

But the number 10,000 not only consists of 1,386 heptads, but Plato also adds, “from two numbers that are ineffable*,” viz. from two numbers the roots of which cannot be exactly obtained, nor expressed either in whole numbers or fractions, such as the roots of the numbers 2 and 3. The numbers 15 and 13 are also of this kind; and, as we shall see, appear to be the numbers signified by Plato. "This indeed," he said, "is the character of that kind of state <note>This refers to Timocracy, a government based on honor and military glory.</note>."

"And will such a person," I asked, "not despise money while he is young? But the older he grows, the more he will always value it, because he shares a greedy nature <note>original: 'covetous genius'</note> and is not sincerely devoted to virtue, because he lacks the best guardian."

"What guardian?" asked Adimantus.

"Reason," I said, "accompanied by the arts. This is the only internal preservative of virtue that stays with the possessor throughout their whole life."

"You speak well," he replied.

"And certainly," I said, "such a **timocratic** youth resembles such a city."

"Certainly."

"And such a person," I said, "is formed in roughly this manner: He happens sometimes to be the young son of a worthy father who lives in a poorly regulated city. This father avoids honors, public offices <term>magistracies: positions within the government or civil administration</term>, lawsuits, and all such public business, and is willing to live unnoticed in obscurity so that he may avoid trouble."

"In what way then," he asked, "is the son formed?"

"When, first of all," I said, "he hears his mother venting her anger because her husband is not in the government. She complains that she is neglected among other women on this account, and she notices that he is not particularly focused on acquiring wealth, nor does he fight and insult others privately or publicly in the courts of justice. Instead, he behaves with indifference on all these occasions. She perceives him as always focusing on his own thoughts, treating her with neither extreme respect nor contempt. On all these accounts, being filled with indignation, she tells her son that his father is unmanly and extremely lazy, and repeats all the other things that wives are accustomed to complain <note>original: 'cant over'</note> about regarding such husbands."

"They are very many indeed," said Adimantus, "and very much in their usual spirit."

"And you know," I said, "that the servants of such families also say the same things privately to the sons, at least those who appear well-meaning. If they see someone who owes the father money whom the father does not sue, or someone else who..."

I think so, said he.

There is no other change, said he, of an ambitious youth to a covetous one so sudden and so powerful.

## THE TRANSITION TO DEMOCRACY

<term>Democracy</term> <note>In Plato’s context, democracy is viewed skeptically as a system that emerges when the poor revolt against the rich, leading to a state of extreme liberty that he fears will eventually devolve into chaos.</note> now, as seems, is next to be considered, in what manner it arises, and what kind of man it produces when arisen; that, understanding the nature of such a man, we may bring him to a trial. We shall in this method, said he, proceed consistently with ourselves. Is not, said I, the change from Oligarchy to Democracy produced in some such way as this, through the insatiable desire of the proposed good, viz. the desire of becoming as rich as possible? How? As those who are its governors govern on account of their possessing great riches, they will be unwilling, I think, to restrain by law such of the youth as are dissolute from having the liberty of squandering and wasting their substance; that so, by purchasing the substance of such persons, and lending them on <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of lending money at high interest rates, which Plato sees as a predatory tool used by the ruling class to further impoverish the citizens.</note>, they may still become both richer, and be held in greater honour. They will be more unwilling than any other. And is not this already manifest in the city, that it is impossible for the citizens to esteem riches, and at the same time sufficiently possess <term>temperance</term> <note>Self-control or moderation; one of the four cardinal virtues in Plato's philosophy.</note>, but either the one or the other must of necessity be neglected? It is abundantly plain, said he. 

But whilst in Oligarchies they neglect education, and suffer the youth to grow licentious, they are sometimes under a necessity of becoming poor, and these such as are of no ungenerous disposition. These things are so. May not such be justly called necessary, which we are not able to remove, and such as when gratified are of advantage to us? For both these kinds our nature is under a necessity to pursue; is it not? 

Very strongly. 

This then we shall justly say makes the necessary part in our desires. 

Justly. But...

What comes next? Such desires as a man may banish, if he studies how to do so from his youth—and those which do no good even while they remain—if we say of these that they are not "necessary," shall we not be speaking the truth?

Right indeed.

Let us select a <term>paradigm</term> <note>A model, pattern, or archetypal example used for comparison.</note> of each of them, so that we may understand what they are by using an example.

It is proper.

Is not the desire for eating—at least so far as it leads to health and a good physical condition—and the desire for basic food and <term>victuals</term> <note>Provisions or food supplies necessary for survival.</note>, of the "necessary" kind?

I think so.

The desire for food, at least, is indeed necessary for two reasons: because the food is beneficial, and because the lack of it would bring life to an end altogether.

It is.

And the desire for specific <term>victuals</term> is likewise necessary if it contributes in any way toward the healthy condition of the body.

Certainly.

But what of the rest? If a desire for these things goes beyond these basic purposes—or if it is a desire for more exotic foods than these, yet is a desire capable of being restrained in youth and removed through discipline—and if it is hurtful both to the body and to the soul’s pursuit of wisdom and <term>temperance</term> <note>The virtue of self-control, moderation, and emotional balance.</note>, may not such a desire be rightly called "unnecessary"?

Most rightly, indeed.

And may we not call these "expensive" desires, and the others "frugal," as the latter are more helpful to the practical actions of life?

Why not?

In the same manner, surely, shall we speak of sexual desires, and the others.

In the same manner.

And did we not, by the person we just now called the <term>drone</term> <note>A metaphor for a person who consumes social or family wealth without producing anything, much like a male bee in a hive that does no work.</note>, mean one who was full of such unnecessary desires and pleasures, and was governed by them? And that he who was governed by "necessary" desires was the <term>parsimonious</term> <note>Extremely frugal or stingy; in this context, the disciplined but narrow-minded character of the Oligarch.</note> and Oligarchic man?

Without doubt.

"Let us again mention," said I, "how the Democratic man arises from the Oligarchic; and to me he appears to arise largely in this way."

How?

"When a young man is raised as we just mentioned—without proper instruction and in a stingy, <term>parsimonious</term> manner—and he comes to taste the 'honey of the drones' and associates with those intense and terrible creatures who are able to provide all sorts of pleasures, in every variety and from every quarter; then, you must imagine, there begins a change within him, shifting from the Oligarchic to the Democratic nature."

There is a great necessity for it, he said.

And just as a city changes its government when one party receives an alliance from outside with a group that is similar to it, does not the youth change in the same manner? Is he not changed when one species of desires from the outside assists a similar and related species of desires within him?

And such a one, I think, after this leads his life, expending his substance, his labour, and his time, no more on the necessary than the unnecessary pleasures: and if he be fortunate, and not excessively debauched, when he is somewhat more advanced in years, and when the great crowd of desires is over, he admits a part of those which were expelled, and does not deliver himself wholly up to such as had intruded, but regulates his pleasures by a sort of equality, and so lives delivering up the government of himself to every incidental desire as it may happen, till it be satisfied, and then to another, undervaluing none of them, but indulging them all alike.

And such a one, said I, does not listen to true reasoning, nor admit it into the **citadel** <note>The highest part of the soul (the rational part), which should ideally be occupied by wisdom and discipline.</note>, if any should tell him that there are some pleasures of the worthy and the good desires, and others of the depraved, and that he ought to pursue and honour those, but to chastise and enslave these. Whoever is thus affected, said he, vehemently acts in this manner. 

And does he not live, said I, from day to day, gratifying after this manner every incidental desire, sometimes indulging himself in intoxication, and in music, sometimes drinking water, and extenuating himself by abstinence; and then again attending to the <term>gymnic exercises</term> <note>Athletic or gymnastic training, a central part of Greek education.</note>? Sometimes too he is quite indolent and careless about every thing; then again he applies as it were to philosophy; many times he acts the part of a politician, and in a desultory manner says and does whatever happens. Doing anything to excess usually causes a massive shift to the opposite extreme: we see this in the seasons, in plants, in our own bodies, and in political states as much as in anything else. It is likely, he said. And excessive liberty seems to change into nothing other than excessive slavery, both for the individual person and for the city. That is very likely. It is probable then, I said, that Tyranny is born from no other form of government than Democracy; from the height of liberty, I believe, comes the greatest and most brutal slavery. It is reasonable, he said, to think so.

Here, "disease" refers to a specific group of people who destabilize the state.</note> enslaves a Democracy, just as a different disease destroys an Oligarchy? You are right, he replied. 

That disease, I said, is the class of idle and wasteful men. One part of them is brave and acts as leaders, while the other is more cowardly and follows. We compared them to **drones**; some with stings, and others without. And rightly so, he said. These two groups, I said, cause a disturbance whenever they appear in a republic, much like phlegm and bile do in a human body. A wise physician and lawmaker of a city—no less than a skilled beekeeper—must be wary of them from a distance to ensure they never enter the hive. But if they have already entered, they must be cut out as quickly as possible, along with the very "cells" <note>The "cells" here refer to the political factions or social structures that house these agitators.</note> they inhabit.

One part is this class of "drones" we mentioned; it grows here through a lack of restraint just as much as it did in the Oligarchy. It does. But it is much more fierce in a Democracy than in an Oligarchy. How? In an Oligarchy, this group is weak because it is excluded from honors and held out of public office. But in a Democracy, this group—with a few exceptions—is the presiding party. It says and does the most outrageous things. When it enters the courts of justice, it creates a constant buzzing <note>Continuing the "drone" metaphor: the agitators drown out opposition through noise and intimidation.</note> and cannot endure anyone else speaking differently. Consequently, almost everything in such a republic is managed by this party. 

Extremely so, he said.
