What about the man himself, and the city in which such a person arises? 

"By all means," he said, "let us consider it."

"In his early days," I said, "during that first season of power, doesn't he smile and greet everyone he meets? He claims he is no tyrant at all, and he promises many things both in private and in public. He cancels debts and distributes land to the common people and to those in his inner circle. He makes every effort to appear mild-mannered and devoted to his country."

"He must do that," he replied.

"But I think that once he has dealt with his foreign enemies—either by reaching an agreement with some or destroying others—and there is finally peace on those borders, he immediately starts up some new wars. He does this so that the people will always feel they need a leader."

"That is very likely."

"And isn't his goal also to keep the citizens poor by demanding heavy taxes? This forces them to focus on their daily survival, making them much less likely to plot against him."

"That is clear."

"Furthermore, if he suspects that any people with a free spirit <note>Socrates refers here to individuals with "eleutheros"—the mindset of a free person who values liberty over subservience.</note> will refuse to submit to his rule, he finds a pretext to destroy them by exposing them to the enemy. For all these reasons, a tyrant is always forced to keep the city at war."

"It is a necessity," he said.

"And while he is doing this, he inevitably becomes more and more hated by his own citizens."

"Why wouldn't he?"

"Then, some of those who helped him gain power—those who hold high positions and possess a more courageous spirit—will begin to speak freely. They will criticize what is happening, both to him and to one another."

"That is likely."

"Therefore, the tyrant must cut all of them off if he wants to keep ruling. He cannot stop until he has eliminated everyone of any value, whether they were his friends or his enemies."

"That is plain to see."

"He must, then, carefully watch to see who is brave, who is high-minded, who is wise, and who is wealthy. He is 'blessed' by a fate that forces him—whether he wants to or not—to be an enemy to all such people. He must continue to lay traps for them until he has <term>purified</term> <note>Socrates uses the word "purify" (katharsis) ironically. Usually, this means removing the "dirt" or the "bad" to leave what is pure. The tyrant does the opposite: he removes the "best" people to leave only the "worst."</note> the city."

"A beautiful kind of purification!" he remarked.

"Yes," I said, "it is the exact opposite of what physicians do for the body. A doctor removes what is bad and leaves what is good; the tyrant removes the good and leaves the bad."

"It seems he is forced to do it," he said, "if he intends to rule."

"He is bound, then, by a truly 'blessed' necessity," I said, "which gives him a choice: either he must live with a mass of worthless people who hate him, or he must not live at all."

"That is exactly the situation he is in," he replied.

"And the more he is hated by his citizens for these actions, the more he will need a greater number of bodyguards—and more faithful ones—won't he?"

"How could he not?"

"Who, then, are these faithful followers, and from where will he bring them?"

"Many," he said, "will come flying of their own accord, if he offers them pay."

"By the dog," <note>A favorite oath of Socrates, likely a respectful reference to the Egyptian god Anubis or a way to avoid taking the names of the Greek gods in vain.</note> I said, "it seems you are talking again about those foreign <term>drones</term> <note>In Plato’s metaphor, "drones" are people who live off the labor of others, often becoming the rowdy or criminal element of a city.</note> of all different kinds."

"You are right," he replied.

"But what about those at home?" I asked. "Would he not want them to serve as his guards too?"

"How so?"

"By taking the slaves away from the citizens, granting them their freedom, and making them his own personal bodyguards."

"Certainly," he said, "for these are the men most loyal to him."

"What a blessed possession a tyrant has!" I said. "If he chooses such men as friends and faithful followers after he has destroyed his former ones."

"But those," he said, "are indeed the ones he employs."

"And such companions," I said, "admire him, and these new citizens spend their time with him, while the good and worthy men both hate him and flee from him."

"Why wouldn't they?"

"It is not without reason," I said, "that tragedy is generally thought to be a wise thing, and that Euripides <note>A famous Athenian playwright known for his psychological depth and complex characters.</note> is thought to excel in it."

"For what reason?"

"Because he uttered this phrase, which shows a very concentrated thought: 'Tyrants are wise through their association with the wise.' <note>original: "σοφῶν ὁμιλίᾳ" (sophōn homilia). Socrates is being ironic here, suggesting that the "wise" people surrounding a tyrant are actually just flatterers.</note> He clearly meant that those the tyrant spends time with are the wise ones."

"He also praises Tyranny as something divine," he said, "and says many other things about it, as do the other poets."

"Therefore," I said, "the composers of tragedy, being wise as they are, will forgive us—and those who establish governments similar to ours—for not admitting them into our republic, since they are singers of praises for Tyranny."

"I think," he said, "that those among them who are more refined will certainly forgive us."

"But as they go around to other cities," I said, "gathering crowds and hiring out their beautiful, grand, and persuasive voices, they will pull republics toward Tyrannies and Democracies."

"Very much so."

"And don't they also receive rewards and honors, especially from Tyrants, as you would expect, and secondly from Democracy? But the further they go toward the higher forms of government, <note>Socrates implies that as the government becomes more orderly and virtuous, the influence of these populist poets fades.</note> their honor fails them, as if it were too out of breath to continue."

"Entirely so."

"We have digressed this far," I said, "but now let us return to how that army of the Tyrant—so beautiful, numerous, varied, and ever-changing—will be maintained."

"It is clear," he said—

...he said, that if at any time there are any sacred treasures <note>These were funds or offerings kept in temples, which were often used as a city's emergency reserve.</note> in the city, the tyrant will spend them. He will do this so that the proceeds from the sale of these items can meet his demands, allowing him to require only lighter taxes from the people for a time. 

"But what will they do when these funds run out?" he asked. 

"It is clear," I said, "that he and his drunken companions, along with his associates—both male and female—will then be maintained out of the paternal inheritance." <note>Plato uses "paternal inheritance" metaphorically here to refer to the wealth and resources of the citizens who originally gave the tyrant his power.</note>

"I understand," he said. "The people who created the Tyrant will be the ones to feed him and his companions." 

"They will be under great necessity to do so," he replied. 

"But what do you say to this?" I asked. "What if the people become enraged and say that it is not just for a son who has reached maturity to be supported by his father? Instead, they might argue the father should be supported by the son. They might say they did not establish him for the purpose of becoming slaves to his own slaves once he grew up, or to maintain him and his rowdy attendants. Rather, they placed him in power so that they might be set free from the wealthy elite—those often called the 'good and worthy'—by having him as their champion. And now, what if they order him and his companions to leave the city, just as a father drives a son out of the house along with his turbulent, drunken friends?"

"Then, by Jupiter," <note>original: "per Iovem" (Latin) / "ma Dia" (Greek). A common oath used to express strong emphasis.</note> he said, "the people shall finally realize what a beast they are themselves, and what kind of beast they have given birth to, embraced, and nurtured. They will realize that while they are the weaker party, they are attempting to drive out the stronger."

"What do you mean?" I asked. "Will the Tyrant actually dare to use violence against his 'father' <note>The "father" here represents the body of citizens (the Demos) who first supported the tyrant's rise.</note>, and if he cannot persuade him, will he strike him?" 

"Yes," he said, "he will even strip him of his armor."

"Then you are calling the Tyrant a <term>parricide</term> <note>A person who kills their father or a close relative. Plato uses this harsh term to show the ultimate betrayal of the citizens by their leader.</note> and a miserable caretaker of the elderly," I said. "And yet, it seems that Tyranny is truly of this nature. According to the proverb, the people, in trying to escape the 'smoke' of slavery under free men, have fallen into the 'fire' of a slavish despotism. <note>original: "fugiens fumum, incidit in ignem". This is the ancient version of the phrase "out of the frying pan and into the fire."</note> Instead of that excessive and poorly timed liberty they once had, they now find themselves embracing the most rigorous and wretched slavery—the kind endured by bond-men."

"That is exactly how it happens," he said. 

"Well then," I said, "would it not be modest of us to say that we have sufficiently shown how Tyranny arises out of Democracy, and what its nature is once it has emerged?"

"Very sufficiently indeed," he replied.

->**THE**<- tyrannical man himself, said I, remains yet to be considered: in what manner he arises out of the **Democratic** man <note>In Plato’s philosophy, the "Democratic man" is someone who treats all his desires as equal, whether they are good or bad.</note>, and, when he does arise, what kind of man he is, and what kind of life he leads, whether miserable or blessed. 

"He indeed yet remains," said he. 

"Do you know," said I, "what I still want?" 

"What is it?" 

"We do not appear to me to have sufficiently distinguished with respect to the **desires**; of what kind they are, and how many; and whilst this is defective, the inquiry we make will be less evident." 

"May it not be done opportunely yet?" said he. 

"Certainly. And consider what it is I wish to know about them; for it is this: Of those pleasures and desires which are not necessary, some appear to me to be repugnant to law <note>original: *paranomoi* — these are "lawless" or "shameful" desires that violate social and moral norms.</note>: these indeed seem to be <term>ingenerated</term> <note>Born within or innate to a person.</note> in every one; but being punished by the laws, and the better desires, in conjunction with reason, they either forsake some men altogether, or are less numerous and feeble; in others they are more powerful, and more numerous." 

"Will you inform me what these are?" said he. 

"Such," said I, "as are excited in sleep; when the other part of the soul, such as is **rational** and mild, and which governs in it, is asleep, and the part which is **savage** and rustic, being filled with food or intoxication, frisks about, and, driving away sleep, seeks to go and accomplish its practices. In such a state, you know it dares to do everything, as being loosed and disengaged from all modesty and prudence: for it scruples not the embraces, as it imagines, of a mother, or of any one else, whether of Gods, of men, or of beasts; nor to kill any one, nor to abstain from any sort of food—and, in one word, is wanting in no folly nor impudence." 

"You say most true," replied he. 

"But I imagine, when a man is in health, and lives temperately, and goes to sleep, having excited the **rational** part, and feasted it with worthy reasonings..."

Socrates argues that we often mistake this neutral "quiet" state for actual joy because of its contrast with intense pain.</note> And when any one ceaseth, said I, to feel joy, this **tranquillity** from pleasure will be painful. It is likely, said he.

And surely at least, when any thing pleasant or any thing painful is in the soul, both sensations are a certain **motion**; are they not? Yes. But did not that which is neither painful nor pleasant appear just now to be **tranquillity**, and in the middle of these two? It appears so, indeed. How is it right, then, to deem it pleasant not to be in pain, or painful not to enjoy pleasure? It is by no means right. 

In these cases, then, **tranquillity** is not really so, said I, but it appears pleasant in respect of the painful, and painful in respect of the pleasant. And there is nothing genuine in these appearances as to the truth of pleasure, but a certain <term>magical delusion</term>. <note>Socrates uses the term *goeteia* (sorcery or enchantment) to describe how the mind is "tricked" by context. Just as a gray object looks white next to something black, the neutral state of rest looks like pleasure when compared to agony.</note> As our reasoning shows, said he. 

Consider then, said I, the pleasures which do not arise from the cessation of pains, that you may not frequently in the present discourse suppose that these two naturally thus subsist, viz. that pleasure is the cessation of pain, and pain the cessation of pleasure. Most necessarily, said he. 

Such then as are unacquainted with wisdom and virtue, and are always occupied in feastings and such like, are carried, as it appears, to the "below," and back again to the "middle," and there they wander for life. "Entirely so," said he.

"Shall not every one then, who possesses intellect, regulate his life by directing all of his powers toward this goal? In the first place, will he not honor those <term>disciplines<gloss>In this context, 'disciplines' refers to 'mathemata' or branches of learning—specifically those like music, gymnastics, and mathematics that Plato believed shaped the character.</gloss></term> which will make his soul like this, while despising all other things?"

"It is plain that he will," he said.

"And next," said I, "with reference to a good physical condition and its nourishment, he will spend his life attending to these—not so that he may indulge in brutal and irrational pleasure, nor even just for the sake of health. He will not make it his primary goal to become strong, healthy, and beautiful unless these things also help him to become <term>temperate<gloss>The quality of self-control and moderation, ensuring the lower desires do not overwhelm reason.</gloss></term>. Instead, he appears to always adjust the harmony of the body for the sake of the **symphony** <note>original: "symphonia." Plato uses musical metaphors to describe a soul where reason, spirit, and desire work together in agreement.</note> that is in the soul."

"By all means," said he, "if indeed he is to be truly **musical**." <term>musical<gloss>To the Greeks, a 'musical' person was someone whose soul was balanced and 'in tune' through the study of the arts, poetry, and philosophy, not just someone who played an instrument.</gloss></term>

"That arrangement, then," said I, "and the harmony arising from the possession of wealth and that vulgar magnificence—he will not allow these to increase to infinity just because he is dazzled by the 'happiness' of the crowd, for that would only bring infinite evils upon himself."

"I do not think he would," he said.

"But looking," said I, "to the <term>polity<gloss>The Greek word is 'politeia,' meaning a constitution or a system of government. Here, Socrates refers to the 'government' of the individual's own mind and soul.</gloss></term> within himself, and taking care that nothing there be moved out of its place—whether through having too much property or too little—he will govern himself in this manner as far as he is able, adding to his substance or spending from it only as it fits that internal balance."

"Entirely so," said he.

"He will look at honors in the same way; some he will willingly partake of and taste, if he judges they will make him a better man. But those honors which he thinks would dissolve the healthy state of soul that exists within him, he will flee from, both in private and in public."

"He will not, then," said he, "be willing to act in **politics**, if he truly cares for this."

"Yes, truly," said I, "in his own city, and greatly so. But probably not in his native land <note>Socrates suggests the philosopher might find it impossible to participate in the corrupt politics of actual cities (like Athens), but will be a leader in the 'city' of his own soul.</note>, unless some divine fortune befalls him."

"I understand," said he. "You mean in the city we have now established, which exists in our reasoning—since it exists nowhere on earth, at least as I imagine."

"But in heaven, probably, there is a **model** of it," said I, "for any one who wishes to contemplate it, and by contemplating it, to regulate himself accordingly. And it is of no consequence to him whether it actually exists anywhere, or shall ever exist here on earth. He performs the duties of this city alone, and of no other."

"That is reasonable," he said.

->THE END OF THE NINTH BOOK.<-

## BOOK X.

**I** OBSERVE, I said, with reference to many other things, that we have established a city in a right manner, beyond what all others have done, and among these establishments, I mean that respecting <term>poetry<gloss>In the Greek 'poiesis,' which implies 'making' or 'creating' in a broad sense, though here specifically referring to mimetic arts like drama and epic verse.</gloss></term>¹ as none of the least.

---

¹ <note>The following commentary on poetry is by <term>Proclus<gloss>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) whose work sought to provide a philosophical defense of Homer and other poets within a Platonic framework.</gloss></term>, taken from his *Commentary on the Republic*. This note explains Proclus's view that there are different levels of poetry corresponding to different levels of the human soul.</note> The following admirable account of <term>poetry</term>, from the *Explanation of the more difficult questions in the Republic* by <term>Proclus</term>, will I doubt not be highly acceptable to the reader, as it both contains a most accurate and scientific division of poetry, and perfectly reconciles the prince of philosophers [Plato] with the first of poets [Homer].

“There are three lives in the <term>soul</term>, of which the best and most perfect is that according to which it is conjoined with the Gods, and lives a life most allied, and through the highest similitude united to them; no longer subsisting from itself but from them, running under its own <term>intellect</term>, exciting the ineffable impression of *the one* <note>original: "to hen." In Neoplatonist thought, "The One" is the ultimate, simple source of all existence.</note> which it contains, and connecting like with like, its own light with that of the Gods, and that which is most uniform in its own essence and life, with *the one* which is above all essence and life. 

That which is second to this in dignity and power, has a middle arrangement in the middle of the soul, according to which indeed it is converted to itself, descending from a divinely inspired life; and placing intellect and science as the principles of its energy, it evolves the multitude of its reasons, surveys the all-various mutations of forms, collects into sameness intellect, and that which is the object of intellect, and expresses in images an intellectual and intelligible essence. 

The third life of the soul is that which accords with its inferior powers, and energizes together with them, employing <term>phantasies<gloss>Mental imagery or the faculty of imagination that processes sensory data.</gloss></term> and irrational senses, and being entirely filled with things of a subordinate nature.

“As there are therefore these three forms of life in souls, the poetic division also supernally proceeds together with the multiform lives of the soul, and is diversified into first, middle, and last genera of energy. For, of poetry also, one kind has the highest subsistence, is full of divine goods, and establishes the soul in the causes themselves of things, according to a certain ineffable union, leading that which is filled, into sameness with its replenishing source; the former immaterially subjecting itself to illumination, but the latter being incited to a communication of light; thus according to the <term>Oracle<gloss>This refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a collection of mystical verses from the 2nd century AD that Neoplatonists treated as sacred scripture.</gloss></term> ‘perfecting works, by mingling the rivers of incorruptible fire.’ It also produces one divine bond and a unifying mixture of that which is participated and the participant, establishing the whole of that which is subordinate in that which is more **excellent**,” <note>The word "excellent" here matches the catchword provided for continuity.</note>

As therefore we say that prophetic fury exists according to truth, and the amatory according to beauty, in like manner we say, that the poetic madness is defined according to divine symmetry.

“The second kind of poetry which is subordinate to this first and divinely inspired species, and which has a middle existence in the soul, is assigned its essence according to a scientific and intellectual habit. Hence it knows the essence of things, and loves to contemplate beautiful works and reasonings, and leads forth every thing into a measured and rhythmical interpretation. For you will find many offspring of good poets to be of this kind, emulous of those that are truly wise, full of admonition, the best counsels, and intellectual symmetry. It likewise extends the communication of prudence and every other virtue to those of a naturally good disposition, and affords a <term>reminiscence<gloss>A reference to the Platonic doctrine of 'anamnesis,' the idea that the soul 'remembers' eternal truths it knew before birth.</gloss></term> of the periods of the soul, of its eternal reasons, and various powers.

“The third species of poetry subsequent to these, is mingled with opinions and <term>phantasies<gloss>Mental images or appearances rather than true realities.</gloss></term>, receives its completion through imitation, and is said to be, and is nothing else than imitative poetry. At one time, it alone uses assimilation, and at another time defends apparent and not real assimilation. It considerably raises very moderate passions, astonishes the hearers; together with appropriate names and words, changes of harmonies and varieties of rhythms, changes the dispositions of souls; and indicates the nature of things not such as they are, but such as they appear to the many; being a certain <term>adumbration<gloss>A faint sketch or shadowy representation.</gloss></term>, and not an accurate knowledge of things. It also establishes as its end the delight of the hearers; and particularly looks to the passive part of the soul, which is naturally adapted to rejoice and be afflicted. But of this species of poetry, as we have said, one division is *assimilative*, which is extended to rectitude of imitation, but the other is *phantastic*, and affords apparent imitation alone.

“Such then in short are the types of poetry. It now remains to show that these are also mentioned by Plato, and to relate such particulars as are conformable to his dogmas respecting each. For, these things being previously determined, it will I think be easy to assign apt reasons respecting the subsequent species. > “In the next place, he describes the habit of the soul possessed by the Muses; and says it ought to be *tender and solitary*. For a soul hard and resisting, and inobedient to divine illumination, is disposed contrary to the energy of divinely inspired possession; since it thus rather subsists from itself than from that which illuminates, and is incapable of being properly impressed with its gifts. But a soul which is possessed by other all-various opinions, and is filled with reasonings foreign from a divine nature, obscures divine inspiration, mingling with the motions thence derived its own lives and energies. > “In the third place, therefore, he adds the common employment of such an aptitude, and of possession and mania from the Muses. But Bacchic fury is a divinely inspired motion, and an unwearied dance, as it were, towards a divine nature, giving perfection to the possessed. ->“...[the poet's] subject may be, just as you do concerning Homer; but, not doing it through any rules of art, each of them is able to succeed through a divine destiny in that species of poetry only to which he is impelled by the Muse.”<-

In all these citations, therefore, Plato clearly establishes that divine poetry originates in a divine cause, which he calls a Muse. In this, he is imitating Homer, who at one time addresses the general crowd of Muses and at another time looks to the unity of the whole group, as when he says, “O Muses, sing,” and “Sing me the man, O Muse.” In the midst of this principle of divine movements and the last <term>echoes<gloss>The original Greek text here was "apochēmatōn" (departures), but the translator notes it should be "apēchēmatōn" (echoes).</gloss></term> of inspiration—which are seen in <term>rhapsodists<gloss>Professional reciters of epic poetry.</gloss></term> through a kind of spiritual sympathy—Plato establishes "poetic mania." This is a state of being moved and moving others, being filled from above, and passing on to others the illumination that starts there. This process connects the very last participants back to the single, original source <note>original: "participated monad," referring to the one divine source from which the chain of inspiration begins.</note>.

With these ideas, we may also harmonize what the "Athenian guest" <note>A character in Plato's *Laws* who represents the philosopher's mature views.</note> says in the third book of the *Laws* concerning poetry, and what Timæus says about poets. For the former says, “That the poetic race is divinely inspired, that it composes sacred hymns, and, with the help of certain Graces and Muses, relates many things that have truly happened.” The latter <note>Timæus, in the dialogue of the same name.</note> encourages us to follow poets inspired by Phœbus <note>Phœbus is another name for Apollo, the god of prophecy and the arts.</note>, as they are “the sons of Gods and know the affairs of their ancestors, even though their claims are not based on probability and lack logical demonstration.” 

From all this, it is easy to understand Plato’s true opinion regarding divine poetry and the poets who embody it. These poets are essentially messengers of divine names and are deeply acquainted with the history of their divine fathers. Therefore, when Plato notices mythical fictions and "corrects" the more serious parts of poetic writings—such as stories about gods being bound, castrated, falling in love, having sexual connections, or weeping and laughing—we must say that he is actually testifying that these things are properly included. They are part of a deeper theory concealed within these symbols, as if under veils. 

For a person who believes that poets are especially worthy of belief regarding the Gods (even when they speak without logical proof) must certainly admire <term>divinely inspired fables<gloss>The translator notes the original Greek "tois en tois mythois" (the things in the fables) should be read as "tous entheous mythous" (divinely inspired fables).</gloss></term> through which the poets deliver the truth about divine natures. And he who calls the poetic race "divine" cannot also believe they hold an impious or <term>gigantic opinion<gloss>Likening the poets to the "Giants" of myth who rebelled against the gods; i.e., an impious or rebellious view.</gloss></term> regarding the divine. Likewise, he who shows that the claims of poets are accompanied by the Graces and Muses must consider any unrefined or unharmonious imagination to be very far from the vision of divine poets. 

Therefore, when in his *Republic* he establishes a law that poetry and the use of fables are not suited for the ears of the young, he is not despising poetry itself. Rather, he is protecting the <term>juvenile habit<gloss>The unformed or immature mind.</gloss></term> of the youth, who is not yet trained to hear such things, from this kind of fiction. For, as he says in the *Second Alcibiades*, “The whole of poetry is naturally <term>enigmatical<gloss>Coded or containing hidden meanings that are not immediately obvious.</gloss></term>, and its meaning is not obvious to everyone.” And hence, in the *Republic*, he clearly says, “That a youth is not...”

<summary>This page argues that Plato viewed poetry as a divine inspiration from the Muses rather than a mere craft. It explains that the shocking myths of the gods are actually "enigmatic" symbols of higher truths that should be kept from the young until they are intellectually mature enough to decode them.</summary>

We say therefore that such a one will conduct himself in the most difficult war, in a manner nearly as much superior to the other, as justice, temperance, and prudence, when conjoined with fortitude, are superior to fortitude alone. For no one can be found faithful and sound in seditions without the whole of virtue.” Here, therefore, he admits Theognis as partaking of political science, and all the virtues.

But in the *Second Alcibiades*, defining the most right and safe mode of prayer, he refers it to a certain wise poet: “To me,” says he, “Alcibiades, it seems probable that some wise man or other, happening to be connected with certain persons void of understanding, and observing them to pursue and pray for things which it were better for them still to be without, but which appeared to them good, composed for their use a common prayer; the words of which are nearly these: King Jupiter <note>original: "Zeus." The translator uses the Roman name for the king of the Gods.</note>, grant us what is good, be it or not the subject of our prayers, and avert from us what is evil, though we should pray for it.” For the scientific man alone knows how to distinguish the separation of good and evil, and a converse with a divine nature adapted to the middle habits of men. And on this account Socrates calls the poet that composed this prayer a wise man, as forming a judgment of the natures of those that prayed, neither through divine inspiration, nor right opinion, but through science alone, as regarding their habits, and preserving that which becomes the beneficent powers of the Gods. > “In the third place, therefore, let us speak concerning imitative poetry, which, we have already said, at one time assimilates things, and at another expresses them according to appearance.—The Athenian guest <note>The protagonist of Plato’s *Laws*.</note> clearly delivers to us the assimilative part of this poetry; but Socrates, in the Republic, describes its phantastic part: and how these differ from each other, I mean the <term>assimilative<gloss>In Greek, 'eikastikē'; the art of making a likeness that matches the exact proportions and colors of the original.</gloss></term> and <term>phantastic<gloss>In Greek, 'phantastikē'; the art of making an 'appearance' that looks correct to the eye but actually distorts true proportions, like a statue with an enlarged head so it doesn't look too small from below.</gloss></term> species of imitation; the Eleatean guest <note>The 'Stranger' from Plato’s dialogue, the *Sophist*.</note> sufficiently informs us: ‘For I appear,’ says he, ‘to perceive two species of imitation, one, the conjectural or assimilative art, which then especially takes place when some one gives birth to imitation by imparting to every particular such things as are fit, in length, breadth, and depth, according to the symmetries of its exemplar, and besides these things colors also.—THEÆTETUS. Do not all imitators endeavor to effect this?—GUEST. Not those who perform or paint any great work. For, if they were to impart to them the true symmetry of things beautiful, you know that the parts above would appear smaller, and those below larger than is fit; through the one being seen by us afar off, and the other near.—THEÆTETUS. Entirely so. Artists therefore, bidding farewell to truth, do not produce in images truly beautiful symmetries, but those which appear to be so.’ Very properly therefore, I think, does the Eleatean guest at the end of the dialogue, wishing to bind the <term>sophist<gloss>A teacher of rhetoric often criticized by Plato for prioritizing persuasion and appearance over truth.</gloss></term> by the definitive method, establish one part of the art effective of images to be assimilative, and the other phantastic; the one fabricating the image such as is the exemplar; the other preparing that which it produces to appear like that which it imitates. However, of assimilative poetry, the Athenian guest speaks separately in the second book of the *Laws*, where he treats of music which does not make pleasure its end, but a true and similar imitation of its exemplar, to which place we refer the reader.

> “But Socrates speaking in this book of phantastic poetry, and having shown that a poet of this kind is the third from truth, and imitative, compares such poetry to a picture, which represents not the works of nature but of artificers, and these not such as they are, but such as they appear. <note>In Plato’s 'Allegory of the Bed,' God creates the Form, the carpenter creates the physical bed, and the painter creates a 'phantastic' image of the bed—thus, the artist is 'third from the truth.'</note> Hence, he clearly evinces that the phantastic species of poetry regards pleasure alone, and the delight of those that hear it. For, of imitative poetry, the phantastic falls short of the assimilative, so far as the latter regards rectitude of imitation, but the former the pleasure produced in the multitude from the energies of the <term>phantasy<gloss>The faculty of imagination or appearance-making.</gloss></term>. Such then are the genera of poetry which are thought worthy of distinction by Plato; one, as better than science <note>Inspired poetry.</note>, another as scientific, a third as conversant with, and a fourth as falling off from, right opinion.

When a poet holds conceptions about the Gods themselves, then he acts according to the first and divinely inspired species of poetry <note>This is "enthusiastic" poetry, the highest form, where the poet is a vehicle for divine truth.</note>. But when he relates the life of the soul, the diversities in its nature, and the political concerns that pertain to it, then he speaks specifically from a scientific perspective. Again, when he presents us with forms of imitation adapted to things and persons themselves, then he employs <term>assimilative imitation</term> <gloss>The art of creating an accurate likeness of reality, matching the true proportions and qualities of the subject.</gloss>. But when he directs his attention only to that which appears to the common crowd, and not to the truth of things—thus seducing the souls of his hearers—then he is a poet according to the <term>phantastic species</term> <gloss>A deceptive form of art that prioritizes how things look from a distance or a certain perspective rather than how they actually are.</gloss>. 

To illustrate what I mean, let me begin with this last type of imitation: the poet sometimes describes the rising and setting of the sun, not as it actually is, nor how the movement is truly effected, nor even imitating its true nature in his verses, but simply as it appears to us from a distance. This, and everything of this kind, may be called the phantastic part of his poetry. 

But when he imitates heroes warring, or consulting, or speaking according to the realities of life—portraying some as prudent, others as brave, and others as ambitious—then I should say that this is the work of <term>assimilative poetry</term>. 

Again, when he reveals and teaches the diversity of the different parts of the soul, or the difference between the physical image and the soul that uses it, or the order of the elements in the universe—namely of earth, water, air, and heaven—then I should confidently assert that this originated from the scientific power of poetry. 

And after all these, when he teaches us concerning the <term>demiurgic monad</term> <gloss>The "Creator" or unified source of the material world.</gloss>, and the triple distribution of the whole universe <note>Refers to the mythological division of the world between Zeus (heaven), Poseidon (sea), and Hades (underworld).</note>, or concerning the bonds of Vulcan <note>The myth where Vulcan (Hephaestus) used invisible chains to trap Mars and Venus.</note>, or the connection of the paternal intellection of Jupiter <note>The divine wisdom or "thought" of the king of the gods.</note> with the prolific divinity of Juno, then I should say that he is clearly enthusiastic, and that such fables are devised by him because he is possessed by the Muses. 

Homer himself also shows this in the character of the bard Demodocus, describing an energy originating from the Gods; Ulysses says of Demodocus's song that he began it impelled by a God, that he was divinely inspired, and that the Muse (or the God who leads the Muses) loved him:

> The Muse, Jove's daughter, or Apollo, taught
> Thee aptly thus the fate of Greece to sing,
> And all the Grecians, hardy deeds and toils *.

It is a well-known opinion that Homer intended to represent himself through Demodocus, introducing him as a pattern of his own misfortunes. And the verses,

> With clouds of darkness quenched his visual ray,
> But gave him skill to raise the lofty lay,

appear to refer directly to the legendary blindness of Homer. He therefore clearly contends that Demodocus says what he does from divine inspiration. It is fortunate that we have mentioned Demodocus and his divinely inspired song, for it appears to me that the musicians mentioned by Homer demonstrate the types of poetry mentioned above. Nor are we singular in this opinion; but, as we have before observed, Plato himself, in many places, calls him a divine poet, the most divine of poets, and in the highest degree worthy of imitation. But the imitative and at the same time phantastic poetry has a most obscure subsistence in Homer; since he never uses it but for the purpose of procuring credibility from the vulgar, and when it is perfectly unavoidable. 

As therefore, if a man entering into a well regulated city, and beholding intoxication there employed for a certain useful purpose, should neither imitate the prudence in the city, nor its whole order, but intoxication itself alone,—as in this case the city is not to be blamed as the cause of his conduct, but the peculiar imbecility of his judgment; in like manner, I think, tragic poets, being emulous of the last species of Homeric poetry, should refer the principle of their error not to Homer, but to their own impotency. Homer therefore may be called the leader of tragedy, so far as tragic poets emulate him in other respects, and distribute the different parts of his poetry; imitating *phantastically* what he asserts *assimilatively* <term>assimilatively</term> <gloss>Creating an accurate likeness based on the true proportions and nature of the subject.</gloss>, and adapting to the ears of the vulgar what he composes scientifically. Homer, however, is not only the teacher of tragedy (for he is this according to the last species of his poetry), but likewise of the whole of that which is imitative in Plato, and of the whole theory of that philosopher.”

***

The reason Plato critiqued the imitative type of poetry was the corruption of the age in which he lived. During that time, philosophy was looked down upon—accused by some of being useless and by others completely condemned. In contrast, poetry was admired excessively. Its power of imitation was a point of competition; it was seen as the only thing sufficient for educational <note>original: "disciplinative"</note> purposes. Because poets imitated everything, they convinced themselves they knew everything, as Socrates points out in this dialogue. Therefore, Plato, frustrated by the spread of such an opinion, demonstrates that the poetic and imitative category wanders far from the truth which philosophy—the savior of souls—provides. 

Out of the same kind desire that led him to accuse the sophists <term>sophists</term> <gloss>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments to win debates rather than seeking truth.</gloss> and popular speakers of being unable to help people become virtuous, he also blames the poets. He specifically targets the writers of tragedy and those imitators who invent things merely to charm their listeners rather than to encourage virtue—those who enchant the crowds without actually teaching them. He believes Homer deserves similar criticism because he is the leader of this type of poetry and provides the "seeds" for tragic imitation. It was necessary to pull the people of his time away from their overwhelming awe of poetry, which caused them to neglect true learning. To instruct the public, correct foolish fantasies, and encourage a life of philosophy, he rejects the tragedians—who were then called "public teachers"—as people who focus on nothing healthy. At the same time, he sets aside his deep respect for Homer and, placing him in the same category as tragic poets, criticizes him as an imitator.

"It is not surprising that the same poet is called by him both 'divine' and 'third from the truth.' For, insofar as he is inspired by the Muses, he is divine; but insofar as he is an imitator, he is third from the truth."

***

<gloss>1</gloss> We should not imagine that Plato, by speaking of the "idea" of a bed or a table, means that there is a perfect Form of these things in the mind of the demiurge <term>demiurge</term> <gloss>The divine "Craftsman" or creator of the physical world in Platonic philosophy.</gloss> of the universe. In short, there are no divine Ideas for man-made objects. Instead, he uses the word "idea" to refer to the "reason" or "productive principle" that exists in the thinking mind <note>original: "dianoëtic power"; refers to the capacity for logical, step-by-step reasoning.</note> of the craftsman. He says this reason is a child of the deity because he believes that this very principle of art itself...

***

The idea that souls receive knowledge from divinity is well observed by Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note> in his commentary on the *Parmenides*. He notes that an argument for this truth is found here—that Plato calls a poet "the third from the truth" (or three steps removed). He places the poet in the same category as a painter, who does not make a bed, but only the image of it. The "Form" of the bed, therefore, exists in the <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>From the Greek "dianoia," referring to the capacity for discursive reason or mathematical thought; the part of the soul that bridges the gap between physical objects and pure spiritual forms.</note> part of the craftsman's mind and ranks as first with respect to truth; the physical bed which he builds is second; and the bed which is painted is the third. But if there were an "Idea" of a bed existing directly in the intellect of the Divine, the painter would be the fourth and not the third from the truth.

Therefore, Glaucon, I said, when you meet with the <term>encomiasts<gloss>those who deliver formal speeches of high praise</gloss></term> of Homer, who tell how this poet instructed Greece, and that he deserves to be taken as a master to teach a man both the management and the knowledge of human affairs, and that a man should regulate the whole of his life according to this poet, we should indeed love and embrace such people, as they are doing the best they are able. We should agree with them that Homer is the most poetical and the first of the tragic writers. But they must also know that hymns to the Gods and the praises of virtuous men are the only forms of poetry to be admitted into our city. If you admit the "pleasurable muse" in the form of songs or epic verses, you will find that pleasure and pain will reign in your city instead of law and that reason which has always appeared best to the community.

Most true, he said.

Let these things now be our apology, I said, when we recollect what we have said regarding poetry: that we were then quite right to dismiss it from our republic, since its nature is as we have described. For reason itself obliged us to do so. And let us further tell the poet, lest she accuse us of a certain roughness or rusticity, that there is an ancient disagreement between philosophy and poetry. ...show this? I should otherwise act unjustly, said I. And I think you yourself can show it, for it is in no respect difficult. How should it not? Its own connate evil then and baseness destroys each particular; or, if this does not destroy it, nothing else can ever destroy it. For that which is good can never destroy any thing, nor yet that which is neither good nor evil. How can they? said he. 

If then we shall be able to find, among beings, any one which has indeed some evil which renders it base, but is not however able to dissolve and destroy it, shall we not then know that a being thus constituted cannot be destroyed at all? So, replied he, it appears. What then? said I. Is there not something which renders the soul evil? Certainly, replied he; all these things which we have now mentioned, injustice, intemperance, cowardice, ignorance. 

But does then any of these dissolve and destroy it? And attend now, that we may not be imposed on, in thinking that an unjust and foolish man, when he is detected acting unjustly, is then destroyed through his injustice, which is the baseness of his soul: but consider it thus. As disease, which is the baseness of animal body, dissolves and destroys body, and reduces it to be no longer that body; so all those things we mentioned, being destroyed by their own proper evil adhering to them and possessing them, are reduced to a non-existence. Is it not so? Yes. Consider now the soul in the same manner. For consider, **Glauco** <note>Glauco (Glaucon) was Plato's older brother and one of the primary conversationalists in the Republic.</note>, said I, that neither by the baseness of victuals, whether it be their mouldiness, or rottenness, or what-ever else, do we imagine our body can be destroyed; but if this baseness in them create in the body a depravity of the body, we will say that, through their means, the body is destroyed by its own evil, which is disease. But we will never allow that by the baseness of food, which is one thing, the body, which is another thing, can ever by this foreign evil, without creating in it its own peculiar evil, be at any time destroyed. You say most right, replied he.

According to the same reasoning, then, said I, unless the baseness of the body create a baseness of the soul, let us never allow that the soul can be destroyed by an evil which is foreign, without its own peculiar evil, one thing by the evil of another. There is reason for it, said he. Let us then either refute these things as not good reasoning; or, so long as they are unrefuted, let us at no time say, that the soul shall be ever in any degree the more destroyed, either by burning fever, or by any other disease, or by slaughter, not even though a man should cut the whole body into the smallest parts possible, till some one show that, through these sufferings of the body, the soul herself becomes more unjust and unholy. But we will never allow it to be said, that when a foreign evil befalls any thing, whilst its own proper evil is not within it, either the soul or any thing else is destroyed.

But this at least, said he, no one can ever show, that the souls of those who die are by death rendered more unjust. He said his soul, at the moment of death, seemed to be released from certain bonds and rose up while the body lay still. Having ascended above the earth, he saw places of every kind, in their shapes and colors, and the flowing of rivers untouched by men; and finally, he arrived at a certain sacred place of <term>Vesta<gloss>The goddess of the hearth, known as Hestia in Greek</gloss></term>, which was attended by divine powers in indescribable female forms. <note>original: "Κλεωνυμος ὁ Αθηναιος... απεριηγητοις."</note>

The second example is from the historian Naumachius, “who flourished (says Proclus) in the time of our ancestors, and is of one Polycritus, who was an illustrious and principal man among the Ætolians. This Polycritus died, and returned to life in the ninth month after his death; came to the general assembly of the Ætolians, and joined with them in their consultations about what measures were best to be adopted. Hiero the Ephesian, and other historians, testify the truth of this, in that account of transactions which they sent to king Antigonus, and their other absent friends.” 

The most illustrious of the Aetolians, who had held the office of Aetoliarch <note>A leader or magistrate of the Aetolian League</note>, both died and returned to life in the ninth month after his death, and came to the common assembly of the Aetolians and gave the best advice concerning the matters they were discussing; and of this there are witnesses: Hiero the Ephesian and other historians, who wrote about these events to King Antigonus and others of their friends who were absent. <note>original: "Τον επιφανεστατον... γραψαντα."</note>

The third is as follows: “In Nicopolis also (says Proclus), not long since, the same thing happened to one Eurynous. This man, who was buried before the city, revived fifteen days after, and said that he saw and heard many wonderful things under the earth, which he was ordered not to relate. He lived some time after this, and his conduct was more just after his revival than before.” 

And not only this, but also in Nicopolis, among those things which occurred not long ago, a man named Eurynous suffered this same thing, and having been buried before the city by his relatives, he returned to life on the fifteenth day after his burial, and said that he saw and heard many wonderful things under the earth; but he was ordered [to...] <note>original: "Και ου τουτο μονον... κελευσθαι δε"</note>

The fourth account is of Rufus, a priest of the Thessalonians, who lived near the time of the historian Naumachius. This man was restored to life the third day after his death, for the purpose of performing certain sacred ceremonies, which he had promised to perform, and, having fulfilled his promise, again died. As the author says, "Rufus, a man from Philippi in Macedonia who had been honored with the high-priesthood in Thessaloniki, died and returned to life on the third day. Upon reviving, he declared that he had been sent back by the gods of the underworld to perform the public spectacles he had promised the people; having lived until their completion, he died once more." <note>original Greek: Χθὲς, ὥς φησι... αὖθις αποθανεῖν.</note>

The fifth and last is of one Philonnæa, who lived under the reign of Philip. “She was the daughter (says Proclus) of Demostratus and Charite, who lived in Amphipolis, and died soon after her marriage to one Craterus. She revived, however, in the sixth month after her death, and, through her love of a youth named Machates, who came to Demostratus from his own country Pella, had connection with him privately for many nights successively. This amour, however, being at length detected, she again died; previous to which she declared, that she acted in this manner according to the will of terrestrial <term>dæmons<gloss>In the ancient world, "daimones" were not necessarily evil; they were spiritual beings or "genii" that mediated between gods and mortals.</gloss></term>. Her dead body was seen by every one, lying in her father’s house; and on digging the place, which prior to this had contained her body, it was seen to be empty, by those of her kindred who came thither, through unbelief of what had happened to her. The truth of this relation is testified both by the epistles of Hipparchus and those of Arridæus, to Philip, in which they give an account of the affairs of Amphipolis:” The crowning example of this is Philonnæa, who lived during the reign of King Philip. She was the daughter of Demostratus and Charite of Amphipolis and had died shortly after her marriage to Craterus. Six months after her death, she returned to life and, out of love for a youth named Machates—who had come from his home in Pella to visit Demostratus—she secretly visited him for many consecutive nights. When she was eventually discovered, she died again, but not before stating that she had acted according to the will of the spirits of the earth. Her corpse was seen by everyone in her father’s house, and when her original grave was opened by skeptical relatives, it was found to be empty. These events are documented in letters sent to King Philip by Hipparchus and Arridæus, the governors of Amphipolis. <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὸν κολοφῶνα... πρὸς Φίλιππον.</note>

Proclus then with his usual sagacity observes, concerning the cause of this phænomenon, as follows: “Many other of the antients have collected a history of those that have apparently died, and afterwards revived; and among these are, the natural philosopher Democritus, in his writings concerning Hades, and that wonderful Conotes, the familiar of Plato. * * * For the death was not, as it seemed, an entire desertion of the whole life of the body, but a cessation, caused by some blow, or perhaps a wound. But the bonds of the soul yet remained rooted about the marrow, and the heart contained in its profundity the <term>empyreuma<gloss>From the Greek 'empyros' (in fire); the vital spark or internal heat believed by ancients to be the seat of life.</gloss></term> of life; and this remaining, it again acquired the life which had been extinguished, becoming adapted to animation.” Many other ancient writers have gathered accounts of those who appeared to die and then returned to life. Among these are the scientist Democritus in his works on the underworld, and that remarkable man Conotes, the associate of Plato... <note>original Greek: Τὴν μὲν περὶ τῶν αποθανεῖν... τὸν Πλάτωνος.</note>

one monad <note>original: "monas"; a single, unified source</note> prior to the three, which Socrates calls **necessity**, not as governing wholes by violence, nor as obliterating the self-motive nature of our life, nor as deprived of intellect and the most excellent knowledge, but as comprehending all things intellectually, and introducing bound to things indefinite, and order to things disordered. It is likewise so called by Socrates, as causing all things to be obedient to its government, and extending them to the good, as subjecting them to <term>demiurgic laws</term> <note>Laws relating to the "Demiurge," the divine craftsman who shapes the material world according to eternal forms.</note>, and guarding all things within the world, and as circularly comprehending every thing in the universe, and leaving nothing void of the justice which pertains to it, nor suffering it to escape the divine law.

“With respect to the order in which the Fates are arranged, it appears from Plato in the *Laws*, that the first is Lachesis, the second Clotho, and the third Atropos. And here it must be diligently observed, that Socrates uses the parts of time as symbols of comprehension according to cause. For that which *was*, was once future and the present, and that which now *is*, was once future; but the future is not yet the past, but has the whole of its essence in becoming the future. These three causes, therefore, or the three Fates, are analogous to these three portions of time: and of these, the most perfect, and which comprehends the others, is that which sings the past; for the past, having once been both the present and the future, may be considered as comprehending these. The next to this in perfection is the *present*, which partly comprehends, and is partly comprehended; for it comprehends the future, and is comprehended in the past. But the third is the future, which is comprehended both in the past and the present; the latter unfolding, and the former bounding, its progression. Hence Lachesis is the primary cause, comprehending in herself the others; and Clotho is allotted a superior, but Atropos an inferior order. And on this account Lachesis moves with both her hands, as in a greater and more total degree, giving completion to the more partial energies of the other two. But Clotho turns the spindle with her right hand, and Atropos with her left, so far as the former precedes with respect to energy, but the latter follows, and, in conjunction with the former, governs all things. For in mortal animals the right hand is the principle of motion; and in the wholes of the universe the motion to the right hand comprehends that to the left.

“Observe too, that as it was before said that the whole spindle is turned on the knees of Necessity, so the fable suspends the providence about partial souls from the knees of Lachesis, who, with her hands, as with her more elevated powers, perpetually moves the universe, but possesses with subjection in her knees the causes of the periods of souls.

“In the next place, let us consider the symbols with which the fable celebrates their dominion. Their walking then in the celestial circles signifies their exempt and separate government. But their being seated on thrones, and not in the circles themselves, like the Sirens, indicates that the receptacles which are first illuminated by them are established above the celestial orbs. For a throne is the vehicle and receptacle of those that are seated on it: and this perspicuously signifies that these divinities are proximately placed above the mundane Gods. Their being seated at equal distances manifests their orderly separation, their subjection proceeding according to

When he had said these things, he threw the lots to all of them, and each took up the one which fell beside him, and was allowed to take no other. When he had taken it, he knew what number he had drawn. After this, he placed on the ground before them the models of lives, many more than those we see at present. These were of every kind: there were lives of all sorts of animals, and human lives of every variety. Among these there were also tyrannies—some of them lasting a lifetime, and others destroyed in the midst of their great—

---

analogy, and their distribution derived from above from their mother: for that which is orderly in progression, and follows dignity in action, is imparted to the Fates from that source. The crowns on their heads indicate the purity * of their intellectual summits. Their white garments signify that the beings who participate in these divinities are intellectual, filled with light <note>original: "luciform"</note>, and full of divine splendor. And as it is said that one of these sings of the past, the second of the present, and the third of the future, this indicates that all their outward actions are elegant, intellectual, and full of harmony.

"Lastly, the Sirens signify the divine souls of the celestial spheres, who lean all things through harmonic motion toward their ruling Gods. The song of these Sirens, and the well-measured motion of the heavens, are perfected by the Fates, who call forth the <term>fabricative energy</term> <note>The creative or "demiurgic" power that shapes and maintains the physical world.</note> of Necessity into the universe through intellectual hymns, and convert all things to themselves through the harmonious and elegant motion of the whole."

* For crowns are made of gold; and gold, because it cannot be corrupted and never rusts, is an image of intellectual and divine purity.

There then, as appears, friend Glauco <note>Glauco was Plato's older brother and one of the primary people participating in this philosophical dialogue.</note>, is the whole danger of man. And hence this of all things is most to be studied, in what manner every one of us, omitting other disciplines, shall become an inquirer and learner in this study, if, by any means, he be able to learn and find out who will make him expert and intelligent to discern a good life, and a bad; and to choose every where, and at all times, the best of what is possible, considering all the things now mentioned, both compounded and separated from one another, what they are with respect to the virtue of life. And to understand what good or evil beauty operates when mixed with poverty, or riches, and with this or the other habit of soul; and what is effected by noble and ignoble descent, by privacy, and by public station, by strength and weakness, docility and indocility, and every thing else of the kind which naturally pertains to the soul, and likewise of what is acquired, when blended one with another; so as to be able from all these things to compute, and, having an eye to the nature of the soul, to comprehend both the worse and the better life, pronouncing that to be the worse which shall lead the soul to become more unjust, and that to be the better life which shall lead it to become more just, and to dismiss every other consideration. For we have seen, that in life, and in death, this is the best choice. But it is necessary that a man should have this opinion firm as an adamant <note>A legendary stone or metal—like a diamond—representing something unbreakable and everlasting.</note> in him, when he departs to Hades <note>The Greek term for the underworld or the realm of the dead.</note>, that there also he may be unmoved by riches, or any such evils, and may not, falling into tyrannies, and other such practices, do many and incurable mischiefs, and himself suffer still greater: but may know how to choose always the middle life <note>Often called the "Golden Mean," this is the philosophical ideal of avoiding extremes (like extreme wealth or extreme poverty) to maintain moral balance.</note>, as to these things, and to shun the extremes on either hand, both in this life as far as is possible, and in the whole of hereafter. This spectacle, he said, was worthy to behold, in what manner the several souls made choice of their lives. He said that the plain is void of trees and everything that the earth produces. When night came on, they encamped beside the river <term>Ameleté: "Unmindfulness" or "Indifference"; the name suggests a lack of care for spiritual truths</term>, whose water no vessel contains. Of this water, all of them must necessarily drink a certain measure, and such of them as are not preserved by prudence drink more than the measure, and he who drinks always forgets everything. 

But after they were laid asleep, and it became midnight, there was thunder and an earthquake, and they were then on a sudden carried upwards, some one way and some another, approaching to <term>generation: the process of being born into a physical body</term> like falling stars. He himself, however, was forbidden to drink of the water. Where and in what manner he came back into his body, he was entirely ignorant; but suddenly looking up in the morning, he saw himself already laid on the funeral pile <note>In the myth, Er was a soldier who died in battle; his body remained undecayed for twelve days, after which he "awoke" on his funeral pyre to tell the living what he had seen in the afterlife.</note>. 

And this fable, Glauco, hath been preserved, and is not lost, and it may preserve us if we are persuaded by it; for thus we shall happily pass over the river <term>Lethe: the river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld</term>, and shall not contaminate the soul.

But if the company will be persuaded by me; considering the soul to be immortal, and able to bear all evil and all good, we shall always persevere in the road which leads above; and shall by all means pursue justice in conjunction with prudence, in order that we may be friends both to ourselves and to the Gods, both whilst we remain here, and when we receive its rewards, like victors assembled together; and we shall, both here, and in that journey of a thousand years which we have described, enjoy a happy life.

<note>The following paragraph is a commentary providing a Neoplatonic philosophical interpretation of the myth's symbols.</note>

When eternal concerns are neglected, things eternal are ignored; hence he says that souls descending into the plain of Lethe encamp beside the river Amelete—that is, through a connection with the body, they pass into extreme negligence. There they fall asleep, signifying their being merged in a corporeal nature, no longer possessing vigilant energies, and being alone occupied with things similar to the delusions of dreams. 

But when he says that no vessel contains the water of Amelete, this signifies that nothing can restrain the ever-flowing nature of the body. This, however, it must be observed, is the condition of the soul while connected with a gross <term>aërial body: a "subtle" or "spirit" body that Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabited between its divine state and its physical birth</term>, and before its perfect descent to the earth: for the descent from celestial bodies to such as are <term>terrene: earthly or physical</term> is effected through an aërial body. Souls, therefore, being laid asleep in this body, at midnight fall to the earth; that is, when they enter into a physical body, they become involved in profound night.

->THE FOLLOWING ADDITIONAL NOTES ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES ARE EXTRACTED FROM THE MANUSCRIPT COMMENTARY OF PROCLUS ON THAT DIALOGUE.<-

**Page 16.** *Son of Clinias! you wonder, I suppose, etc.*

**T**HE prefaces <note>original Greek: "ta prooimia"</note> of Plato’s dialogues accord with the whole scope of them; and are neither devised by Plato for the sake of dramatic allurement, since this mode of writing is very remote from the magnitude of the philosopher’s conceptions, nor are they merely historical; but each is suspended from the design of the dialogue to which it belongs.

Every thing in the dialogues of Plato, in the same manner as in the <term>mysteries <note>Sacred rituals and ceremonies of ancient Greece, such as those at Eleusis, which were meant to convey secret spiritual truths to initiates.</note></term>, is referred to the whole perfection of the particulars which are investigated. Agreeably to this, Plato in the very beginning of this dialogue appears to me to indicate in a beautiful manner the scope of the whole composition. For his design, as we have said, was to unfold our nature, and the whole essence according to which each of us is defined; and to unveil the Delphic mandate <term>KNOW THYSELF <note>original: "Gnothi Seauton." This famous inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi is the core theme of the First Alcibiades, where Socrates argues that one cannot care for their affairs without first knowing their own soul.</note></term> through demonstrative methods. But the preface itself converts the young man to himself, and represents him as exploring his own pre-subsisting conceptions; and, at the same time that it converts him to himself, leads him to a survey, as from a watch-tower, of Socratic science. For an investigation of the cause through which Socrates alone, of all his lovers, does not change his love, but began to love him prior to others, and is not altered when the rest no longer love, evinces him to be a spectator of the whole life of Socrates. The forms of <term>conversion <note>In the philosophy of Proclus, "conversion" (epistrophē) is the process by which a soul turns its attention away from external, material things and back toward its own divine source.</note></term> therefore are triple. For every thing which is converted, is either converted to that which is worse than itself, through apostatizing from its proper perfection, or is led back to

A conversion indeed to that which is worse, is a passion of the soul whose wings suffer a shedding <note>original: "defluxion"; a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul loses its wings and falls into a body</note>, and that is now placed in oblivion both of herself, and of natures prior to herself. But a conversion both to itself and to a more excellent nature, takes place not in souls only, but in divine natures themselves, as **Parmenides** teaches us, when he establishes two species of conversion, and shows how a divine nature is converted to itself, and is in itself, and how it is converted to that which is prior to itself, so far as it is comprehended in another, and is united with a better nature. On this account **Socrates** at the end of this dialogue says, that he who is converted to and becomes a spectator of himself, will by this mean behold the whole of a divine nature, and through a conversion to himself will be led to an elevated survey of divinity, and to a conversion to that which is better than himself. These things, therefore, the preface indicates. For it leads **Alcibiades** from a life tending to externals to a survey of himself, and recalls him through a knowledge of himself to a love of Socratic science; since a desire to learn the cause of the conduct of **Socrates** is to become a lover of the pre-subsisting science which he contains.

Again, **Plato** signifies in the preface, besides other things, that a worthy man will always employ his knowledge on objects properly co-ordinated to that knowledge; and that he will never attempt to possess a stable, definite and immutable knowledge of things contingent and mutable, nor a dubious, indefinite, and disordered apprehension of things necessary, and which always possesses a sameness of subsistence. But, according to the distinction adopted by **Socrates** in the *Republic*, he will conjointly contemplate all <term>intelligibles <note>Pure, eternal truths or 'Forms' that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note></term> with simple, uniform, and intellectual knowledge; but will survey the middle reasons of things with a scientific and <term>dianoëtic <note>From 'dianoia'; referring to discursive, step-by-step logical reasoning rather than direct intellectual intuition.</note></term> evolution and composition. Again, with the sensitive power which is the third from truth, he will touch upon proper objects of knowledge, through instruments of sense, distinguishing in a becoming manner every object of sense. And lastly, by an assimilative power he will apprehend the images of <term>sensibles <note>Physical objects perceived through the five senses.</note></term>. And indeed **Timæus**, distinguishing cognitions analogously to the objects of knowledge, exhorts us to judge of true beings by intelligence in conjunction with reason; but

which are not beings, but are perpetually shifting between <term>generation and corruption <note>The cycle of birth and decay inherent to the physical world.</note></term>, by opinion and sense. He also adds, that the reasons pertaining to true beings cannot be confuted, and are indubitable; but those which belong to things borne along in the rapid flux of generation, are conjectural and contingent. For everywhere reasons imitate the things of which they are the interpreters.

In the third place, Socrates in the *Cratylus* says that the names of things eternal have a certain alliance with the things themselves; but that the names of things generated and corrupted are multiformly changed, and partake much of position, through the unstable <term>lation <note>From the Latin 'latio,' meaning a bearing or movement; here it refers to the shifting, unstable motion of physical objects.</note></term> of their subjects. If therefore the knowledge of things which subsist perpetually the same, differs from that of things contingent, and reasons are allotted an all-various mutation, and different names accord with different things, is it wonderful that Socrates, who is here discoursing concerning an unstable nature, should use the word **I suppose** <note>original: "οἶμαι" (oimai)</note>? which signifies that the nature of the thing known is mutable, but does not accuse the knowledge of Socrates as indefinite, mingled with ignorance, and dubious.

->P. 25. *You have looked down on your admirers.*<-

Alcibiades, by despising those that were unworthy of his love, and admiring those that were worthy of it, testifies his great alliance to the beautiful, and that he was abundantly prepared for the reception of virtue. But perhaps some one may be desirous to learn why elevated and grand conceptions move divine lovers, and appear to deserve diligent attention. We reply, that such manners seem to possess an alliance with divine beauty. For to despise things present as shadowy representations, and of no worth, and to investigate something prior to these, which is great and wonderful and transcends the conceptions of the multitude, is an evident argument of the <term>parturiency <note>The state of being in labor or about to give birth; here it refers to the soul's productive struggle to "bring forth" its innate understanding of beauty.</note></term> of the soul about the beautiful. Hence Socrates in the *Republic* represents souls which are about to descend from the heavens, as choosing a commanding and magnificent life. For they still retain the echo, as it were, of the life which is there, and, in consequence of this, convert themselves to power and dominion, and despise everything else as trifling and of no worth. But this affection is the principle of safety to souls. For to consider human concerns as small, and vile, and not worthy of serious attention, and to investigate that form of life

The design of all that has been recently said is to purify our <term>dianoëtic <note>From the Greek 'dianoia,' referring to the soul's capacity for discursive reasoning or logical thought.</note></term> part from <term>two-fold ignorance <note>A state of profound confusion where one does not know a truth, but is also unaware of their own ignorance, believing they actually possess knowledge.</note></term>, and to remove all that blocks our resumption of true knowledge <note>The text uses "science" in the classical sense of 'episteme,' meaning certain, demonstrated knowledge rather than modern empirical science.</note>. For it is impossible for imperfect things to obtain their proper perfection in any other way than by a purification of impediments; for that which purifies everywhere possesses this power. 

But the true purification of the soul is triple; one kind proceeding through the <term>telestic art <note>The ritual or priestly art associated with the sacred mysteries and religious initiations.</note></term> \*, concerning which Socrates speaks in the *Phaedrus*; another through philosophy, concerning which much is said in the *Phaedo*; for there prudence and each of the other virtues is called a certain purification; but the purification through this <term>dialectic science <note>The philosophical method of cross-examination (elenchus) and logical analysis used to arrive at truth.</note></term> leads to contradiction, refutes the inequality of beliefs <note>original: "dogmas"</note>, and liberates us from two-fold ignorance. 

Purification therefore being triple, Socrates here employs the third of these on Alcibiades: for those that labor under <term>two-fold ignorance</term> are benefited by this purification. Hence Socrates does not assert anything of truth, until he has removed those opinions which block the soul in her understanding of truth. Simple ignorance indeed exists between knowledge and two-fold ignorance; and the first transition is from knowledge to simple ignorance, and the next ascent is from simple ignorance to knowledge. 

At the same time likewise, this ascent separates us from opinion tending toward external things, and turns the soul back to herself; it makes her explore her own proper beliefs, remove that which blocks her knowledge, and fill up what is lacking. For, as the body, when disturbed by foreign fluids <note>original: "humours"—referring to the ancient medical theory of the four bodily fluids.</note> often spoils its nourishment and changes the benefit arising from it into a harmful quality, so the soul, being disturbed through false opinion and receiving the assistance granted from knowledge in a manner adapted to her own habit, produces a principle of greater false opinion and deception. The purification therefore which precedes all the arguments of Socrates is summarized in these words; and it may be said to resemble the telestic purifications which take place previous to the operations of the—

From hence we may rightly understand who it is that instructs, and who is instructed. For it is fit that he who instructs should accurately know the aptitudes of those that are instructed, and conformably to these should direct his attention; since every one is not to be disciplined in a similar manner. But he who is naturally a philosopher is to be led back to an <term>incorporeal essence <note>A non-physical, spiritual reality or being.</note></term> in one way, he who is a lover in another, and the musician in a still different way. <note>This refers to the Platonic triad of souls—the philosopher, the lover, and the musician—who each pursue beauty and truth through different worldly paths.</note> And again, he who through the imagination of that facility of energy which belongs to a divine nature is astonished about pleasure, is to be led back in one way; he who through the desire of being sufficient to himself desires the possession of riches, in another way; and in a still different way, he who through the conception of divine power is busily employed about apparent power. For, images everywhere assuming the appearance of their principles draw aside unintelligent souls; but it is requisite, departing from these, to pass on to those true and real beings. And this was the mode of the Socratic doctrine, to lead up every one to the proper object of his desire. Hence, to the lover of pleasure he pointed out that which is pleasurable with purity, and unmingled with pain; for it is evident that this will be more eligible to him who pursues pleasure, than that which is mingled with its contrary. To the lover of riches he indicated where that which is truly sufficient to itself abides, and which is in no respect filled with indigence; for this must be more ardently pursued by him who aspires after self-perfection, and avoids indigence.
