He showed where that which is powerful and governs is to be found, and what the nature is of the ruling form of life which is free from all subjection; for this will be considered more honorable to the ambitious man than that which is mingled with things to be avoided. Power, therefore, self-sufficiency, and pleasure are not to be found in material things. For matter is <term>imbecility <note>In this historical context, "imbecility" refers to inherent weakness, frailty, or a lack of power, rather than an intellectual disability.</note></term> and poverty, and is the cause of corruption and pain. But it is evident that these, if they are anywhere to be found, are in immaterial and separate natures. 

These natures, therefore, are the proper objects of love, and to these an ascent must be made. In this manner, the one who instructs ought to introduce discipline based on the natural aptitudes of each student, ensuring their safety; meanwhile, the student should submit to the instructor and be led gradually toward the truth. This process involves moving away from mere images and a <term>subterranean cavern <note>An allusion to the famous Allegory of the Cave in Book VII of Plato's Republic, where prisoners mistake shadows for reality.</note></term> toward the light and true essence. On every side, the student should extend himself toward that which is unmixed with its contrary, dismissing that which is divisible and shadowy, and instead aspiring after that which is universal and indivisible. 

For the "Total Good," as Socrates says in the <term>Philebus <note>A late Socratic dialogue by Plato focusing on the relationship between pleasure and wisdom.</note></term>, is not merely desirable, nor just perfect, sufficient, and able to fulfill other things; rather, it encompasses all these at once: the perfect, the sufficient, and the desirable. It draws all things toward itself and grants well-being to all, though it is viewed by the masses only in part. Hence, some people, looking only at the "desirable" aspect it contains, pursue pleasure, which is merely its image. Others, looking only at the "perfect," are busily occupied with gathering riches, for in wealth they see a likeness of perfection. Still others, tending toward the "sufficient," are awestruck by power, for power carries with it a <term>phantasm <note>An illusion or deceptive appearance.</note></term> of self-sufficiency. To dismiss these partial understandings of the Good, to look toward its whole nature, and to be led back to its all-perfect fullness, properly separates the student from a life tied to mere images.

And in consequence of possessing the reasons of things <note>In Neoplatonism, "reasons" (logoi) are the innate blueprints or essential principles of reality that the soul contains naturally.</note>, they have as it were agitated conceptions concerning them; but being vanquished by the potion of oblivion <note>A reference to the River Lethe, symbolizing the loss of memory the soul suffers when entering a physical body.</note>, they are incapable of expressing their conceptions, and referring them to science. Hence they contain them indigested and scarcely respiring, and on this account they are vanquished by **two-fold ignorance**. For they think that they know through these innate conceptions, but they are ignorant through oblivion; and hence arise deception, and an appearance of knowledge without the reality (<term>seeming <note>original: "δοκησις" (dokesis). This refers to an unfounded opinion or the mere illusion of knowing.</note></term>). He therefore who is involved in two-fold ignorance is remote from an investigation of things, in the same manner as he is who possesses scientific knowledge. For neither is it the province of a wise man to philosophise, nor of him who labours under the disease of two-fold ignorance; but this evidently belongs to him who is established according to **simple ignorance**. 

For he who is ignorant in a two-fold respect, is according to this similar to the wise man; just as matter, as some one rightly observes, possesses a dissimilar similitude to divinity. For, as matter is without form, so also is divinity. Each likewise is infinite and unknown; though this is true of the one according to that which is better <note>Divinity is unknown because it is "above" our understanding.</note>, and of the other according to that which is worse than all things <note>Matter is unknown because it is "below" or lacks any defining form or quality.</note>. Thus therefore the man of science, and the ignorant in a two-fold respect, do not investigate any thing; the one in consequence of being wise, and as it were full of knowledge; and the other in consequence of not even assuming the principles of investigation, through the falsehood with which he is surrounded. 

But he who possesses **simple ignorance** subsists in a certain respect between the man of science and him who doubles his deception. For he in short who knows himself, and is converted to himself <note>To be "converted to oneself" means to turn the attention inward away from the external world to examine one's own soul.</note>, is superior to him who is perfectly ignorant of himself; but he who on beholding himself does not perceive knowledge but ignorance, is inferior to the man of science. In well instituted polities, therefore, youth are instructed by the guardians in these disciplines: and among the Athenians certain images of these were preserved; grammar having a reference to dialectic discipline; playing on the harp pertaining to music, and wrestling to gymnastic; in which those youths that were well-born were instructed. And hence Socrates says that Alcibiades had learnt these, as having had an education adapted to a well-born youth.

by <term>Venus</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, each stage of human life is governed by a different planet, reflecting the soul's journey through physical generation and back toward the divine.</note>; because then we begin to produce seed, and the generative powers of nature are put in motion. The fourth age is <term>solar</term>; for then our youth is in its vigour and full perfection, subsisting as a medium between generation and decay; for such is the order which vigour is allotted. The fifth age is governed by <term>Mars</term>; in which we principally aspire after power and superiority over others. The sixth age is governed by <term>Jupiter</term>; for in this we give ourselves up to prudence, and pursue an active and political life. And the seventh age is <term>Saturnian</term>, in which it is natural to separate ourselves from generation, and transfer ourselves to an incorporeal life. And thus much we have discussed, in order to procure belief that letters and the whole of education are suspended from the <term>Mercurial</term> series <note>The "Mercurial series" refers to things under the protection of Mercury (Hermes), the god of language, learning, and interpretation.</note>.

But it is worth while to consider on what account <term>Alcibiades</term> <note>An influential and controversial Athenian statesman and student of Socrates.</note> refused to learn to play on wind-instruments, though this art pertains to music. It has then been said by some, that being vain of his person from his youth, he avoided that deformity of the face which is occasioned by blowing the pipe or flute. But it is better to say, that well-instituted polities are averse to the art of playing on wind-instruments; and therefore neither does <term>Plato</term> admit it. The cause of this is the variety of this instrument, the pipe <note>original: *tibia* or *aulos*. In antiquity, the "pipe" or *aulos* was a double-reed instrument, more like an oboe than a modern flute.</note>, which shows that the art which uses it should be avoided. For instruments called <term>Panharmonia</term> <note>From the Greek *pan-harmonia*, meaning "all-harmony." These were complex instruments capable of playing many different scales or "modes" simultaneously, which philosophers like Plato found morally destabilizing.</note>, and those consisting of many strings, are imitations of pipes. For every hole of the pipe emits, as they say, three sounds at least; but if the cavity above the holes be opened, then each hole will emit more than three sounds. It is however requisite not to admit all music in education, but that part of it only which is simple. Further still: of these musical instruments, some are repressive, and others motive; some are adapted to rest, and others to motion. The repressive therefore are most useful for education, leading our manners into order, repressing the turbulency of youth, and bringing its agitated nature to quietness and temperance. But the motive instruments are adapted to enthusiastic energy: and hence, in the mysteries and mystic sacrifices, the pipe is useful; for the motive power of it is employed for the purpose of exciting the <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>Referring to the soul's power of discursive reasoning or intellectual thought (*dianoia*).</note> power to a divine nature. For here it is requisite that the irrational part should be laid asleep, and the rational excited. Hence, those that instruct youth use repressive instruments, but initiators such as are motive: for that which is disciplined is the irrational part; but it is reason which is initiated, and which energizes enthusiastically.

## ADDITIONAL NOTES

->Page 36. *How is this, friend Alcibiades, etc.*<-

The descent of the soul into the body separates it from divine souls—from whom it is filled with intelligence, power, and purity—and joins it with the world of change, nature, and material things. From these material things, the soul is filled with forgetfulness, wandering, and ignorance. For, in its descent, many-sided lives and various "garments" <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "vestments" or garments refer to the layers of energetic or material influence the soul picks up as it descends through the planetary spheres toward Earth.</note> grow upon it, which draw it down into a mortal composition and darken its vision of true reality. 

It is necessary, therefore, that the soul which is to be led correctly back to that ever-watchful divine nature should cut away those secondary and tertiary powers that have become attached to its essence. These are like the weeds, stones, and shells that encrust the body of the **marine Glaucus** <note>In Greek mythology, Glaucus was a fisherman who became a sea-god; his original form was hidden by layers of seaweed and shells. Plato and later philosophers used him as a metaphor for the soul obscured by the "crust" of physical desires and material life.</note>; the soul must restrain its outward-facing impulses and remember the true beings and the divine essence from which it descended, and toward which our whole life should strive. 

The parts or powers in us that require perfection are: the **irrational life**, which is naturally suited to be shaped and disciplined through good habits; the <term>proæretic</term> <note>original: προαίρεσις (proairesis). This refers to our faculty of "deliberate choice" or the moral will that chooses between different courses of action.</note> part, which must be pulled away from irrational cravings and its connection to them; and besides these, our <term>gnostic power</term> <note>From the Greek 'gnosis,' meaning the faculty of the soul capable of higher spiritual knowledge and intuition.</note>, which requires a **reminiscence** <note>The Platonic theory of 'reminiscence' (anamnesis) suggests that learning is actually the soul remembering the divine truths it knew before it was born into a physical body.</note> of true beings. 

The part of the soul that remembers is different from the part that is organized through manners; and different from both of these is the part that becomes more balanced through warnings and instructions. It is necessary, therefore, that education should harmonize with these three parts:
1. First, it should perfect us through the correctness of our **manners** (habits).
2. Second, through **warnings and precepts**.
3. Third, it should awaken our **innate reasons** and purify the knowledge that essentially exists within our souls through **reminiscence**. 

Such is the nature and the order of the perfection suited to souls that fall into bodies.

Since these things are established, the third of these parts—the rational nature—reaches perfection through study and discovery. For the soul is essentially <term>self-motive</term> <note>The soul is 'self-moving' because it is the source of its own life and activity, unlike physical matter which only moves when acted upon by something else.</note>. However, as a result of connecting with the body, it participates in a certain way in <term>alter-motion</term> <note>Movement caused by an external force; 'other-motion'.</note>. Just as the soul gives the body a final reflection of self-motion (life), so it receives a representation of being moved by external things through its close relationship with the body. Through the power of self-motion, therefore, the soul acquires knowledge, and...

More perfect souls, however, are more inventive; but the more imperfect are indigent of external assistance. For, some are more self-motive, and are less replete with a subordinate nature; but others are less self-motive, and are more passive from a corporeal nature. 

As they advance however in perfection, are excited from body, and collect their powers from matter, they become more prolific, and more inventive of the things about which they were before unprolific and dubious, through the sluggishness and privation of life proceeding from matter, and the **sleep of generation** <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the state of the soul when it is born into the physical world, suggesting that our earthly life is a kind of spiritual sleep or forgetfulness.</note>. We therefore, thus preserving the medium of a **rational essence** <note>The "middle ground" of human existence; the soul is positioned between the purely divine intellects and the purely physical animals.</note>, can assign the causes of the more imperfect and perfect habits in the soul; and we say, that such are the paths of the perfection of souls. 

But those who do not preserve this medium, but either rise to that which is better, or decline to that which is worse, fall off from the truth respecting these particulars. For we do not admit their arguments who say, that the soul coming into a moist body, and being thence darkened, is stupid from the beginning <margin>* This appears to have been the opinion of Heraclitus. <note>Heraclitus famously stated that "a dry soul is wisest and best," implying that the "moisture" of physical desires and material embodiment clouds human intelligence.</note></margin>; but that, this moisture becoming exhaled, through the innate heat, and possessing greater symmetry, the power of **intellectual prudence** in the soul is rejuvenated. For this mode of perfection is corporeal and material, and supposes that the perfection of the soul is consequent to the temperament of the body; though prior to the elements, and prior to the whole of generation, the soul had a subsistence, and was a life unmingled with body and nature. 

Nor, again, do we assent to those who say that the soul is a portion of the **divine essence** <margin>† This was the opinion of the Stoics. <note>The Stoics believed the human soul was a literal fragment of the divine fire that governs the universe.</note></margin>; that this portion is similar to the whole, and is always perfect; and that tumult and passions subsist about the animal. For those who assert these things make the soul ever-perfect, and ever-scientific, at no time requiring **reminiscence** <term>reminiscence</term> <note>Plato’s theory that "learning" is actually the process of the soul remembering the divine truths it knew before it was born into a body.</note>, and always impassive, and free from the defilement of evil. 

**Timaeus**, however, says, that our essence does not subsist entirely from the first genera, in the same manner as the souls superior to ours, but from such as are second and third <note>In Plato’s *Timaeus*, the Creator (Demiurge) creates human souls using the "leftovers" or less pure versions of the ingredients used to make the World Soul.</note>. And **Socrates**, in the **Phaedrus**, says that our powers are mingled with that which is contrary to good, and are filled with opposition to each other; and that, through this, sometimes the better and sometimes the worse parts are victorious. But what occasion is there to say more on this subject, since Socrates...

<meta>This page continues a deep-dive into the Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato’s "First Alcibiades." It addresses the soul's capacity for learning and how it moves from a state of forgetfulness or ignorance to a state of wisdom through the help of a teacher and the passage of time.</meta>

## ADDITIONAL NOTES

[Plato] himself says, in that dialogue <note>Referring to the *Phaedrus*, where Plato uses the famous allegory of the soul as a chariot pulled by two horses.</note>, that the charioteer <note>This refers to the "dianoëtic" power of the soul—the capacity for scientific and logical reasoning.</note> becomes depraved, and that through his depravity many souls become lame, and many lose their wings, though the **charioteering power** (<term>the power of the charioteer</term> <note>original Greek: ηνιοχωτικη δυναμις [hēniokhōtikē dynamis]</note>) is one of the more venerable powers of the soul? For it is this which has a reminiscence of divine natures, and which uses second and third powers as ministrant <note>serving as assistants or subordinates</note> to reminiscence <note>The Platonic theory that learning is actually a process of "remembering" knowledge the soul possessed before birth.</note>. These things, therefore, are clearly asserted in the *Phædrus*.

As we have said, then, the measures of the soul are to be preserved; and the reasons concerning its perfection are neither to be referred to it from corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> natures, nor from such as are divine; that thus we may be fit interpreters of Plato, and not distort the words of the philosopher by forcing them to a coincidence with our own opinion. Since, therefore, the soul is at one time imperfect, and is again perfected, and becomes oblivious of divine natures, and again remembers them, it is evident that time contributes to its perfection. For how could it change from folly to wisdom, and in short to virtue from vice, unless it made these mutations in time? For all mutation <note>change</note> subsists in time. And thus much concerning the perfection of the soul in general.

From what has been said, then, we may collect that he who knows what is **just** passes from ignorance to a knowledge of it; and that he neither has the reason of the **just** always at hand, in the same manner as the natures superior to man (for we are born at first imperfect), nor again that the knowledge of it arrives to us through the mutation of the body. For our essence is not corporeal, nor composed from material genera. It remains, therefore, that either **discipline** or **invention** <note>In this context, "invention" refers to the soul discovering truths within itself, while "discipline" refers to being taught by another.</note> must precede knowledge; and Alcibiades is very properly requested to tell who was the cause of his acquiring discipline, and whence he knows what *the just* is, if he does know. For it is necessary, as we have often said, that *discipline* should be the leader of knowledge imparted by another; and a *teacher*, of discipline. For discipline is a motion; but all motion requires a moving cause. It requires therefore a teacher, for he is the cause of discipline.

# ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.

<margin>The eye of the soul</margin>
The preceding argument excites the eye of the soul <note>A common Platonic metaphor for the intellect or the capacity for spiritual insight.</note>, and exercises it for the perception of truth, further observing as follows: “Again, the discourse proceeds from invention <note>In this context, "invention" refers to "discovery"—finding knowledge within oneself rather than being taught it by another.</note> to simple ignorance; for no one would attempt to investigate that which he thinks he knows. It is necessary, therefore, that simple ignorance should be the beginning of investigation. For investigation is a desire for knowledge in things of which we suspect that we are ignorant. This being the case, it is necessary that the time should be known in which we suspected that we did not know: and hence Socrates desires Alcibiades to tell him the time in which he suspected his want of knowledge. For, as we have before observed, it is necessary that all such mutations <note>Changes or transitions in the state of the soul.</note> should be measured by time. 

Hence the **divine Aristotle** <note>original: "dæmoniacal" from the Greek *daimonios*, an honorific meaning "inspired" or "supernatural" in intellect.</note>, also, here admits motion in the soul, and a mutation according to time. But that an association with the body, and a transition from vice to virtue, require time, is manifest to every one. As some however have said, that the soul when subsisting by itself does not require time for its energies, but that on the contrary it generates time; this assertion I think requires some consideration. For time is two-fold; one kind being that which is bound together with the natural life and corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> motion of the universe, and another kind that which pervades through the life of an incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> nature. This latter time, therefore, measures the periods of divine souls, and perfects the separate energies of ours. But the former, which is extended with a life according to nature, measures that life of our souls which exists with the body, but by no means that life of the soul which lives itself by itself.”

Discipline <note>In this context, "discipline" refers to the process of being taught or instructed by another.</note> being two-fold, and at one time proceeding from more excellent causes to such as are subordinate, according to which the demiurgus <note>The "Divine Architect" or "Creator" in Platonic philosophy.</note> in the *Timæus* <note>One of Plato’s most famous dialogues, concerning the creation of the universe.</note> says to the junior Gods, “Learn what I now say to you indicating my desire;” but at another time proceeding from a cause externally moving, according to which we are accustomed to inscribe <note>To categorize or recognize.</note> certain persons as teachers; and invention <note>Discovery—the act of finding knowledge within oneself.</note> ranking between these;—for it is subordinate to the knowledge imparted to the soul from the Gods, but is more perfect than reminiscence <note>Recollection; Plato’s theory that all learning is actually the soul "remembering" what it knew before birth.</note> externally derived;—this being the case, Alcibiades had not any conception of discipline from a more excellent cause, except so far as looking to the science essentially inherent in us, in a dormant state, which is imparted from the Gods, and by which he was led to conjecture <note>To guess or suppose based on incomplete information.</note> that he accurately knew the nature of the just.

...being ambitious, suspended his opinion from the multitude, and about this was filled with astonishment. Socrates therefore shows him, first, that the opinion of the multitude possesses no authority in the judgment and knowledge of things; and that it is not proper for him to adhere to it, whose view is directed to the beautiful: and, in the second place, that the multitude is the cause of false opinion, producing in us from our youth depraved imaginations and various passions. Scientific reasoning <note>In Platonic philosophy, "science" or "scientific reasoning" refers to *episteme*—a certain, unchanging knowledge of reality, rather than modern experimental science.</note> therefore is necessary, in order to give a right direction to that part of us which is perverted by an association with the multitude; to apply a remedy to our passive part, and to purify that which is filled with impurity; for thus we shall become adapted to a reminiscence <note>The original Greek text uses the word *anaktēsin* (recovery), but the translator suggests it should be *anamnēsis* (reminiscence), which refers to the Platonic theory that the soul "remembers" truths it knew before being born into a body.</note> of science. In the third place, Socrates shows, that in each of us, as he says, there is a many-headed wild beast <note>A famous metaphor from Plato’s *Republic* representing the irrational, desiring part of the human soul which is difficult to tame.</note>, which is analogous to the multitude; for this is what the people is in a city, *viz.* <note>An abbreviation for the Latin "videlicet," meaning "namely" or "that is to say."</note> the various and material form of the soul, which is our lowest part. The present reasoning therefore exhorts us to depart from boundless desire, and to lay aside the multitude of life, and our inward people, as not being a judge worthy of belief respecting the nature of things, nor a recipient of any whole science; for nothing irrational is naturally adapted to partake of science. In the fourth place, therefore, we say, that the present reasoning does not think fit to admit into science and an intellectual life an apostacy <note>Here meaning a turning away or falling away from a higher state.</note> and flight from *the one*, together with diversity, and all-various division; but indicates that all these should be rejected as foreign from intellect and divine union. For it is requisite not only to fly from external, but also from the multitude in the soul; nor this alone, but also to abandon multitude of every kind.

In the first place, therefore, we must fly from “the multitude of men going along in a herd,” as the oracle <note>Referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a collection of mystical texts from the 2nd century AD often quoted by later Platonic philosophers.</note> says, and must neither communicate with their lives, nor with their opinions. In the next place we must fly from multiform appetites, which divide us about body, and make us to be at different times impelled to different externals; at one time to irrational pleasures, and at another to actions indefinite, and which war on each other: for these fill us with penitence and evils. We must also fly from the senses which are nourished with us, and which deceive...

our <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>This term refers to the soul’s capacity for discursive reasoning—the step-by-step logic we use to think through problems.</note> part : for they are multiform, at different times are conversant with different sensibles <note>Objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, and assert nothing sane, nothing accurate, as Socrates himself says*. For science is not the summit of knowledge, but prior to this is intellect ; I do not only mean that intellect which is exempt from soul, but an illumination § from thence, which is infused into the soul, and concerning which Aristotle says, “ that it is intellect by which we know terms ||,” and Timæus, “ that it is ingenerated in nothing else than soul.” Ascending therefore to this intellect, we must contemplate together with it an intelligible essence ; with simple and indivisible projections surveying the simple, accurate, and indivisible genera of beings. excite the supreme <term>hyparxis</term> <note>From the Greek *hyparxis*, meaning "existence" or "essential reality." In this context, it refers to the very peak or "flower" of the soul where it is most unified.</note> or summit of the soul, according to which we are one, and under which the multitude we contain is united. For as by our intellect we pass into contact with a divine intellect, so by our unity, and as it were the flower of our essence, it is lawful to touch the *first one*, the source of union to all things. For the similar is every where to be comprehended by the similar; objects of science by science; intelligibles by intellect; and the most united measures of beings, by *the one* of the soul. And this is the very summit of our energies. According to this we become divine, flying from all multitude, verging to our own union, becoming one, and energizing uniformly. And thus proceeding through the gradations of knowledge, you may see the rectitude of the Socratic exhortation <note>This refers to the famous command "Know Thyself," which Socrates uses in the *Alcibiades* to lead the student toward an understanding of the soul's true nature.</note>.

But if you are willing also to consider the admonition according to the objects of knowledge, fly from all sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived through the five senses.</note>; for they are divulged <note>In this older sense, "divulged" means scattered, spread apart, or separated.</note> from each other, are divisible, and perfectly mutable, and therefore cannot be apprehended by genuine knowledge. From these, therefore, transfer yourself to an incorporeal essence: for every thing sensible has an adventitious <note>Coming from the outside; not inherent to its own nature.</note> union, and is of itself dissipated, and full of infinity. Hence also its good is divisible and adventitious, is distant from itself and discordant, and possesses its <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A technical term for the "underlying reality" or "substance" of a thing.</note> in a foreign seat. Having therefore ascended thither, and being established among incorporeals, you will behold the order pertaining to soul above bodies, self-motive and self-energetic, and subsisting in and from itself, but at the same time multiplied, and anticipating in itself a certain representation of an essence divisible about bodies. There likewise you will see an all-various multitude of habitudes of reasons, analogies, bonds, wholes, and parts, circles characterized by the nature of soul, a variety of powers, and a perfection neither eternal nor at once wholly stable, but evolved according to time, and subsisting in discursive energies <note>Step-by-step logical reasoning, as opposed to the instant, all-at-once "intellection" of the higher mind.</note>: for such is the nature of soul. After the multitude in souls, extend yourself to intellect, and the intellectual kingdoms, that you may apprehend the union of things, and become a spectator of the nature of intellect. There behold an essence abiding in eternity, a fervid life and sleepless <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of pure, intuitive thought or understanding.</note>, to which nothing of life is wanting, and which does not desire the chariot of time to the perfection of its nature. When you have surveyed these, and have also seen by how great an interval they are superior to souls, inquire whether there is any multitude there, and if intellect, since it is one, is likewise all-perfect,

You see then that the present reasoning affords us no small assistance, in exhorting us to fly from the multitude <note>In this context, "multitude" refers to the fragmented, distracting, and changing nature of the material world.</note>; and how it contributes to the entire **salvation**† of the soul, if we direct our attention to the multitude which pervades through all things. <margin>‡ *Generation* <note>In Platonic thought, "generation" refers to the physical world of birth, death, and constant change, as opposed to the eternal world of "being."</note> signifies, according to Plato and his best disciples, the whole of a sensible nature.</margin>

From this it is also evident that souls do not collect their knowledge from sensible things <note>Objects perceived through the five senses.</note>, nor do they discover *the whole and the one* by looking at things that are partial and divisible. Instead, they call forth discipline from within themselves and correct the imperfection of the phenomena <note>Outward appearances or physical events.</note>. For it is not right to think that things which have no real, stable existence should be the leading causes of knowledge in the soul. Nor should we think that things which oppose each other, which require the soul’s reasoning to make sense of them, and which are ambiguous, should precede science <note>In the classical sense, "science" (*episteme*) means certain, unchanging knowledge of eternal truths.</note>, which possesses a consistency of existence. It is not possible for things that are constantly changing to generate the reasons established in unity, nor for indefinite things to be the causes of definite intelligence. 

It is not proper, therefore, that the truth of eternal things should be received from *the many*, nor the discrimination of universals from sensible objects, nor a judgment respecting what is good from irrational natures. Rather, it is necessary that the soul, entering within herself, should investigate in herself *the true and the good*, and the eternal reasons of things. For the essence of the soul is full of these, but they are concealed in the oblivion produced by **generation** ‡ <note>This refers to the Platonic doctrine of "recollection": the soul is born with all knowledge but "forgets" it upon entering a physical body.</note>. Hence the soul, in investigating truth, looks to external things even though she essentially contains truth within herself; deserting her own essence, she explores *the good* in things foreign to her nature. From this realization, then, the beginning of the knowledge of ourselves is derived. For if we look only to the multitude of men, we shall—

### P. 39. *And must not all those who have the knowledge of any thing agree together on that subject, &c.*

**Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was the head of the Platonic Academy in Athens and a master of late antique philosophy.</note> on this part having observed that it is requisite to consider dissension as an argument of ignorance, and concord as an argument of knowledge, for all those that know the truth do not disagree with each other, after this adds as follows:

“ But this to some may appear to be false; since those that accord with each other do not all of them possess a <term>scientific</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "scientific" knowledge (episteme) refers to certain, unchanging knowledge of eternal truths, as opposed to mere opinion or observation.</note> knowledge of that respecting which they agree. For, in the present time, the multitude <gloss>* Viz. the Christians.</gloss> <note>Proclus, a devoted pagan, often used the term "the multitude" or "atheists" to refer to the growing Christian population of his time, whom he viewed as lacking philosophical science.</note> through the want of science accord with each other in denying the existence of the Gods. In answer to this doubt, we reply in the first place, that the depraved man cannot accord with himself; for it is necessary, being vicious, that he should be in **sedition** <note>Meaning internal rebellion or conflict.</note> with his own life; perceiving indeed the truth through his rational nature, but through passions and material phantasies <note>Mental images or sensory impressions that distract the mind.</note> being led to ignorance and contention with himself. The atheist therefore and intemperate man, according to their <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>Dianoëtic refers to the "dianoia," the soul's faculty of discursive reasoning or logical thinking.</note> part, which is adapted to a divine nature, and which is of a beneficent destiny, assert things temperate and divine; but, according to their desires and phantasies, they are atheistically and intemperately affected <gloss>† Hence the unscientific do not *truly* accord with each other: for the rational part in them secretly dissents to what the irrational part admits.</gloss>. And, in short, according to the irrational soul, they introduce war in themselves, and all-various perturbation. Every vicious man therefore is discordant with himself; and this being the case, he is much more so with others. For, how can he consent with those external to himself, who is seditiously affected towards himself? All atheistical, intemperate, and unjust men, therefore, dissent with each other, and we can never be harmoniously disposed while we are unscientific.

“ This however is attended with much doubt: for, if dissension is an argument of the want of science, we must say that philosophers are unscientific, since they also disagree with each other, subvert the hypotheses of each other, and patronize different systems.

## ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.

This doubt may be dissolved by saying that dissension is two-fold: one kind being the dissonance of the ignorant, both with themselves and with each other, and the other of the ignorant with the <term>scientific</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "scientific" (epistemonikos) does not mean modern experimental science, but rather "certain knowledge" derived from first principles and logical demonstration.</note>; for both these belong to the ignorant, but by no means to the scientific, since they accord with themselves *. Nor do the scientific disagree with the unscientific; for, on the contrary, they perfect and adorn them, and call them upwards to their own order; but it is the unscientific who separate themselves from the scientific. For through the dissonance in themselves they dissent from those that are better than themselves. Those that are endued with knowledge, therefore, and those that are deprived of it, do not disagree with each other; nor, in short, must it be said that the scientific differ. Hence the doubt is very far from affecting true philosophers: for these through similitude and sameness are united to each other; and being allotted a knowledge entirely exempt from the unscientific, neither are they discordant with them.

> "But the cause of the concord of the scientific is, first, the definite nature of things, and the criteria of knowledge, being the same with all men; and secondly, because, in the first principles of things, intellect is united to itself, and hence every thing which participates of intellect participates of unity. Science therefore is an illumination of intellect, but concord of <term>the one</term> <note>The "One" is the supreme principle in Neoplatonism, the source of all unity and existence. True harmony is seen as a reflection of this ultimate oneness.</note>: for it is a union of things different. And hence it is necessary that those which participate of the same science should accord with each other; for dissension and discord fall off from *the one*."

**P. 42. *Are you sensible that what you said last was not fairly said, Alcibiades? &c.***

If the principal end of this dialogue is to lead us to the knowledge of ourselves, and to show that our essence consists in forms and reasons <note>Original: "formis et rationibus." In this context, "forms" are the eternal blueprints of reality, and "reasons" (logoi) are the principles that give structure to the soul.</note>, that it produces all sciences from itself, and knows in itself every thing divine, and the forms of nature; the present passage, which evinces that the cause of all the preceding answers and conclusions is in Alcibiades, must greatly contribute to this end. For the soul does not possess an adventitious knowledge of things, nor, like an unwritten tablet <note>A reference to the "tabula rasa." Proclus rejects the idea that the human mind is born empty; instead, he believes the soul already contains all truth and must simply be prompted to remember it.</note>, does it externally receive the images of divine ideas. Now, therefore, Alcibiades begins to know himself, and also to know that he is converted to himself; and knowing his—

...own <term>energy</term> <note>In this context, "energy" (energeia) refers to the active exercise of the mind or the "acting out" of one's nature, rather than physical force.</note> and knowledge, he becomes one with the thing known. This mode of conversion, therefore, leads the soul to the contemplation of its <term>essence</term> <note>Essence (ousia) refers to the fundamental nature or true "being" of the soul, stripped of external distractions.</note>. Hence it is necessary, that the soul should first receive a knowledge of herself; in the second place, that she should consider the powers which she is allotted; and, in the third place, how she is impelled to ascend from things more imperfect as far as to first causes. Alcibiades, therefore, is now converted through energy to energy, and, through this, to that which energizes. For, at the same time, the subject becomes apparent, which is generative of its proper energies. But, again, through energy he is converted to power, and through this again to essence: for powers are nearer to essence, and finally connect energy with essence. Hence, all these become one and concur with each other, essence being in energy, and energy becoming essential; for essence becomes intellectual in energy, and energy becomes connate to essence according to its perfection.

Again: since ignorance is involuntary to all men, and especially an ignorance of themselves and of things the most honourable; hence, to ancient and wise men, the method through arguments, which places false opinions parallel to such as are true \*, appeared to be most useful for the purpose of liberating the soul from this ignorance; since it unfolds the discord of false, and the concord of true opinions with each other. For, when the passions are shown to be in opposition with opinions, and, again, the passions with each other, and after the same manner opinions, then the depravity of ignorance becomes most conspicuous; and he who is ignorant perceives his own calamity, and rejoices to be liberated from so great an evil. When therefore any one is not only convinced by arguments that he is ignorant in things of the greatest consequence, but is also confuted by himself, then he in a still greater degree rejoices in and embraces the <term>confutation</term> <note>The process of "elenchus" or cross-examination, where a person is shown that their own beliefs are contradictory.</note>, and multiplies the remedy produced by it. If, therefore, Socrates in his dialectic conversations evinces that it is the same person who answers and is interrogated, and that the answers do not proceed from the interrogator who appears to confute; it is perfectly evident that he who is thus confuted is confuted by himself, and does not suffer this externally; so that this mode of cure is most appropriate. In the third place, we repeat that while irrational animals are governed by external impulses—lacking the power to rule or preserve themselves—the human soul is naturally designed to act upon itself, to move itself, and to grant itself what is good, thanks to its <term>self-moving</term> <note>The soul’s ability to initiate its own thoughts and actions, independent of physical triggers.</note> and <term>self-acting</term> <note>The capacity of the soul to generate its own internal activities or "energies."</note> nature. Therefore, a <term>refutation</term> <note>original: "confutatio"; the Socratic method of cross-examination (elenchus) that leads a student to realize their own ignorance.</note> that begins from within ourselves is perfectly suited to the soul's essence. The reasoning that shows the person answering the questions is actually the same as the person speaking clearly aligns with our true nature and activities. Our purification is not something forced on us from the outside; it begins within the soul itself. All evil is external and foreign to the soul, but good is internal, as the soul is naturally <term>good-formed</term> <note>original: "boniform"; having a natural shape or disposition toward "The Good."</note>. The more perfect the soul becomes, the more she enjoys a life moved by her own will. She is only moved by external things when her nature is tied to a physical body and she feels "corporeal sympathy" for it. Consequently, whatever she receives from the outside remains outside of her, like a <term>phantom</term> <note>A mental image or sensory impression that lacks true reality.</note> or a mere object of the senses. Only those things that operate from within her, and are produced by her, truly reside within her. She is therefore purified by herself, just as reason begins and ends within itself. If a person answering a question is refuted, they are being purified; and since the soul's nature is to be self-moving, that person is effectively purifying themselves and being freed from ignorance. By applying this refutation to themselves, they act in harmony with their own self-moving nature.

Furthermore, this line of reasoning confirms the doctrine that learning is actually <term>recollection</term> <note>The Platonic theory (anamnesis) that the soul does not "learn" new things, but remembers eternal truths it forgot upon entering a body.</note>. A major argument for this is that those who provide answers in a dialogue draw everything from within themselves. This proves that souls pull reasons out of their own depths and only require a spark to ignite them. Souls are not <term>blank slates</term> <note>original: "unwritten tablets"; the idea that the mind is empty at birth (tabula rasa), which the author here rejects.</note> that receive impressions from the outside; they are always "written upon," with the Writer living in the very recesses of the soul. However, not everyone can read what is written there, as their internal eye is buried in the <term>forgetfulness of birth</term> <note>original: "oblivion of generation"; the loss of divine memory caused by the soul descending into a physical, material existence.</note>, which also causes them to be stained by passions. Therefore, all that is required is a <term>stripping away</term> <note>original: "ablation"; the removal of layers of ignorance or sensory distraction.</note> of what darkens the mind; there is no need for external or imported knowledge. The soul contains the gates of truth within herself, but they are barred by earthly...

If, therefore, anyone can accurately demonstrate that souls are indeed moved by external things, but that they draw out from within themselves <term>scientific answers</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "scientific" (epistemonikos) refers to knowledge that is certain, logical, and derived from the soul's own innate reasons, rather than just observing the physical world.</note>, he will prove the truth of the Platonic assertion: that the soul already knows all things, and only requires an external spark to answer with true knowledge.

In another way, this principle also applies to Socrates. To purify someone who needs help—assisting them so they can eventually help themselves—is the work of a <term>dæmoniacal power</term> <note>From the Greek "daimon." These spirits do not act upon us from the outside; rather, they govern us from within, like a pilot at the rudder of a ship. They do not treat us as mere physical bodies, which are moved only by outside forces, but they care for us as <term>self-motive</term> <note>The "self-moving" nature of the soul; the idea that our true selves initiate our own thoughts and choices.</note> beings. In this way, they share goodness with us and help us purge our passions. Therefore, Socrates—who serves as a "good spirit" to his student Alcibiades—shows him that he is not being defeated by anyone other than himself.

### P. 43. *In those assertions, was it not said that Alcibiades, &c.*

The **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized ethics, logic, and staying calm in the face of external events.</note> rightly say that a man who lacks education blames others, rather than himself, for his own <term>infelicity</term> <note>Unhappiness or misfortune.</note>. However, the man who has begun to make progress in knowledge attributes the cause of his bad words or actions to himself. Finally, the man who is properly disciplined blames neither himself nor others; he does not neglect anything necessary, but has become the master of his own discovery. 

These stages are clearly shown to us in the character of Alcibiades. While suffering from **two-fold ignorance** <note>A state where one does not know the truth, but is also unaware of their own ignorance, falsely believing they are knowledgeable.</note>, he does not blame himself, but Socrates. Later, when he moves to **simple ignorance** <note>The state of realizing that one does not know; the first step toward true learning.</note>, he blames himself for his inner conflict, not his teacher. If he ever reached the state of true knowledge, he would blame neither himself nor another. At that point, nothing in him would be out of tune or clashing; all the motions of his soul would be clear, <term>effable</term> <note>Expressible in words; logical and clear.</note>, and purely intellectual. 

Conflict within the masses occurs because people receive conflicting messages: some from their physical senses, some from the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The "imagination" or the faculty that produces mental images.</note>, and others from mere opinion; some from anger, and others from desire. Such passions in men are not just triggered by their **dogmas** <note>Beliefs or doctrines.</note>, as the Stoics claim; on the contrary, it is because of these passions and appetites that people change their opinions, accepting corrupt ideas in place of worthy ones.

<header>ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.</header>

## ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.

Therefore, souls that derive from many principles and powers of a lower condition, receiving within themselves diverse motions, possess a soul that is discordant and unharmonized. But those who are **scientific** <note>In this context, "scientific" refers to someone possessing certain, demonstrated knowledge (episteme) rather than mere opinion.</note> receive the whole of their knowledge from a single principle prior to themselves: for intellect provides them with principles; and true doctrines are the offspring of intellect, existing in union with simplicity. From such a unified principle, therefore, all things harmonize with each other.

Indeed, what is now said by Socrates follows very appropriately from what has been demonstrated, and is referred to Alcibiades himself, representing him as accusing himself. For, in order to produce the most striking **confutations** <note>A "confutation" is the act of proving an argument or person to be wrong; a refutation.</note>, the ancients attributed the most severe assertions to other persons; and this method they adopted commonly. Thus Homer refers the reproving of Achilles to Peleus <note>Peleus was the father of Achilles. By quoting the father’s advice, the rebuke is softened.</note>, and Demosthenes refers the rebuking of the Athenians to the Greeks in general: and in like manner Plato refers to laws and philosophy the reproving of his hearers. For rebukes are softened when they are transferred to others who are absent from us. But when he who refutes is not another, but a man refutes himself, then the refutation appears, to the one refuted, to be much less painful. This, therefore, Socrates effects. For he represents Alcibiades as being refuted by Alcibiades; softening by this method the intensity of the reproof, and revealing the close connection of the teacher to the student.

Proclus concludes his commentary on this passage as follows: “That ignorance is a **mania** <note>From the Greek "mania," implying a state of being out of one's mind or delusional.</note> of long duration, and especially **double ignorance** <note>Double ignorance is the state of not knowing, and not knowing that one does not know—the most difficult state to remedy.</note>, is a paradox, but is at the same time most true. ->P. 44. *For I suppose that justice and interest are not the same thing, &c.*<-

The dogma, that the **just** is the same with the **profitable** <note>In Greek philosophy, the "profitable" or "expedient" refers to what is truly beneficial for a person's well-being and happiness.</note>, contains the whole of moral philosophy. For those who suppose these to be different, must necessarily admit, that **felicity** <note>True happiness or flourishing, often translating the Greek word *eudaimonia*.</note> receives its completion from externals; since, in these, the profitable appears very often to be separated from the just. But those who consider both to be the same, and acknowledge that the true good of man is in the soul, must necessarily refer each of us to soul. Hence Socrates thinks, that this is the beginning of the whole of the philosophy concerning the end of man, and of the knowledge of ourselves. But the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed pleasure was the highest good.</note> and **Stoics** <note>Philosophers who taught that virtue is the only good and that we should live in accordance with nature.</note>, who place the end of man in a life according to nature, and those who give completion to our good from things necessary, as the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school, known for walking while they discussed philosophy.</note>, cannot genuinely preserve the sameness of the just and the profitable. And, in like manner, this cannot be effected by those who make man to be an animated body, or a composite from body and soul. For some fly from wounds and death unjustly, that the animal may be saved; since the good of every animal consists in a subsistence according to nature; so that, in this case, the profitable differs from the just. But those who place the end of man in soul **unindigent** <note>Meaning "not lacking" or "not needing."</note> of corporeal possessions, and who assert that man is a soul using the body as an instrument, these admit that the just is the same with the profitable: for they place both in the soul, and separate the passions of the instruments from those by whom they are employed.

->P. 45. *Why, my good friend, suppose me to be the assembly and the people, &c.*<-

Proclus here observes that it is the province of the same science to persuade one person and many; an assertion which is, as it were, a certain hymn and praise of science. For the great excellence of science is evident in this: that, following the imitation of the divine intellect, the same science fills an individual and, at the same time, all those who receive it. It is indivisible, and being established within itself, it perfects all its participants; and like the intellect, it communicates itself to all while remaining separate from each. These things prove that our essence is separate from the body and remains within itself, since science—which is our perfection—is allotted such a power. For physical powers diminish themselves when they are shared; but science, remaining one and the same, sufficient to itself and undiminished, imparts itself in a similar manner to one and to many. Thus, too, the soul is present to the whole body and all its parts, though one part participates in it in a different manner from another.

P. 47. *Tell me then, do you say, that some just actions are advantageous, &c.*

The proposed inquiry concerning things just and profitable <note>In Greek ethics, "profitable" (sympheron) refers to what is truly advantageous or beneficial for one's well-being.</note>, whether they are the same, or are divided from each other according to the diversity of subjects, contributes to the whole of philosophy, and adheres to the whole truth of things. For all ethical discussion and the invention of the end of man <note>The "end" (telos) refers to the ultimate purpose or highest good of human life.</note> depend on this dogma, and the speculation of our essence becomes through this especially apparent. For, if the just is, in reality, the same with the profitable, and these are not separated from each other, our good will consist in virtue alone; and neither will the particulars which are beheld about the body contribute any thing as goods to the felicity <note>Happiness or flourishing (eudaimonia).</note> of human life; nor, by a much greater reason, will things external to the body procure the full perfection of good; but one only good is established in souls themselves, unmingled, pure, immaterial, and is neither filled with corporeal nor with external goods or evils. But if there is something just, as according to <term>Alcibiades</term> there is, but unprofitable, and again something profitable but unjust, then apparent goods, such as health and riches, must necessarily give completion to a happy life. For mankind perform many things for the sake of these, and, surveying the good which they contain, abandon the love of justice. And to these, indeed, those who for the sake of what is just despise the flourishing condition of the body, and the acquisition of wealth, appear to act justly, and in a manner laudable, to the multitude, but by no means profitably, because they do not perceive that the profitable is stably seated in the soul herself, but consider it as situated in things scattered, and which have an external subsistence, and are necessary rather than good. But these men give phantasy <note>The faculty of imagination or sensory-representation, which Neoplatonists believed could mislead the soul if not governed by reason.</note> and sense the precedency to intellect and science.

Hence, as Aristotle* says, intellect is lovely and desirable; for all things that participate of intellect are beautiful; and matter, which of itself is void of beauty, because it is formless, at the same time that it is invested with figures and forms, receives also the representations of the power of beauty. Lastly, *the good* characterizes the whole of a divine essence. For every thing divine according to a divine <term>hyparxis</term> <note>The most fundamental "peak" or "seed" of a being's existence; its pure subsistence prior to its activity.</note> is good; since the Gods are the causes of being; and if they cause all things to subsist about themselves, they are essentially good, and illuminate all things with good. *The good* therefore is bound in souls according to *the just*, through *the beautiful*; and every order of souls is united to the Gods through *intellectual essences* as media; so that an incorporeal nature is one and uniform, and the whole of it verges to the good; but division is in the images of this nature, which are not able to express primary causes according to their indivisible essence. From these things therefore it is evident that the present demonstration contributes in no small degree to theology, and, as I may say, to the whole of philosophy.

But the whole <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> which collects that the just is profitable is as follows: Every thing just is beautiful: Every thing beautiful is good: Every thing just, therefore, is good. But the good is the same with the profitable: Every thing just, therefore, is profitable. This syllogism is primarily in the first figure <note>A technical term in Aristotelian logic referring to the most direct form of logical deduction.</note>, comprehending the minor in the major terms, and evincing the major terms reciprocating with the minor. For, again, beginning from *the good*, we shall be able to form the same conclusion. Every thing good is beautiful: Every thing beautiful is just: Every thing good, therefore, is just. But the profitable is the same with the good: The just, therefore, is the same with the profitable.

In the first principles of things, indeed, *the good* is exempt from *the beautiful*, and *the beautiful* is placed above *justice*. For the first of these is prior to intelligibles, established in inaccessible retreats: the second subsists occultly in the first of intelligibles† <note>In the realm of "Being," which Neoplatonists considered the highest level of reality that the mind can grasp.</note>, and more clearly in the extremity of that order‡ <note>Specifically in the "intelligible intellect," the stage where thought begins to differentiate itself.</note>: and the third of these subsists uniformly in the first order of intellectuals§ <note>The "intelligible-intellectual" order, a bridge between pure being and active divine thought.</note>, and secondarily at the extremity of the intellectual progression of Gods. the beautiful in *intellects* <note>In this context, "intellects" refers to the divine or cosmic minds (the *Noes*) that exist above the human level.</note>, and the *just* in *souls*. Whence the *just* is indeed *beautiful*, but not *every thing beautiful is just*. And *every thing beautiful is good*, but the fountain of all good is expanded above all *beauty*. And the *just* indeed is *good*, being conjoined with the *good* through *beauty* as the medium; but the *good* is beyond both. Thus also you will find, by looking to the last of things, that the material cause <note>The "material cause" refers to matter itself, the raw "stuff" of the universe which, in this philosophy, is the furthest removed from the divine source.</note>, although it is good <note>Good only in the sense that it exists as part of the created order.</note>, is base, and void of beauty: for it participates indeed of *the one* <note>The One: the ultimate, single source of all reality.</note>, but is destitute of form. And a sensible nature <note>The physical world we perceive through our senses.</note> possesses indeed a representation of beauty, but not of justice. For, as Socrates says in the *Phædrus*,

> "there is no splendour of justice and temperance in these sensible similitudes <note>Physical objects or "likenesses" in our world.</note>; but beauty has alone this privilege, that it is the most apparent, and the most lovely of all things."

Hence where the *just* is, there also is the *beautiful*; and where the *beautiful*, there also is the *good*, whether you are willing to look to the first principles, or to the illuminations of them as far as to the last of things. For all things participate of *the good*; for it is the principle of all: but *the beautiful* is alone received by the participants of form; and *the just* by those natures alone that participate of soul. But in the middle centre of all things, such as the soul is, all these are connected with each other, *the good, the beautiful, the just*. And the *good* of it is *beautiful*, and the *just* is at the same time *beautiful* and *good*.

Nor is the assertion true in this triad <note>A group of three related principles.</note> only, but also in many other particulars. Thus, for instance, in the principles of things *being* is beyond life, and life is beyond *intellect* \*. And again, in the effects of these, not every thing which participates of being participates also of life, nor every thing which participates of life participates also of intellect; but, on the contrary, all intellectual natures *live*, and *are*, and *vital* natures partake of *being*. All these however are united with each other in the soul. Hence, *being* in it is *life* and *intellect*; *life* is *intellect* and *essence*; and *intellect* is *essence* and *life*. For

---

\* *Being, life, and intellect*, considered according to their highest subsistence, form the intelligible triad, or the first all-perfect procession from the ineffable cause of all, as is beautifully shown by Proclus in his third book *On the Theology of Plato*. But that *being* is beyond life, and *life* beyond *intellect*, is evident from this consideration, that the progressions of superior are more extended than those of inferior causes. Hence, though whatever lives has a *being*, and whatever possesses *intellect* lives, yet some things have being without life or *intellect* <note>Such as a rock, which has "being" but no "life."</note>, and others have being and life without *intellect* <note>Such as a plant, which has "being" and "life" but no "reason" or "intellect."</note>. And hence, as the progressions of *being* are more extended than those of *life*, and of life than those of *intellect*, we conclude that *being* is superior to *life*, and *life* to *intellect*.

There is one simplicity in it, and one subsistence <note>Subsistence: In this philosophical context, this refers to a thing's underlying reality or its "actual existence" as a distinct entity.</note>; nor are life and intelligence there adventitious <note>Adventitious: Coming from outside or added on; the author is saying life and mind are built-in, not extra features.</note>; but its *intellect* is *vital* and *essential*, its *life* is *essentially intellectual*, and its *essence* is *vital* and *intellectual*. According to the same reasoning, therefore, its *good* is replete with *beauty* and *justice*; its *beauty* is *perfect* and *good*, and entirely *just*; and the *just* in it is mingled with *beauty* and *good*. The subject indeed is one, but the reasons <gloss>original: *logoi*, here meaning productive principles</gloss> are different. And again, neither must we consider the identity of those three according to reasons, nor their difference according to the subject; but we must preserve the reasons of them different from each other, and the subject one, because everywhere these three are con-subsistent <note>Con-subsistent: Existing together as part of the same fundamental nature.</note> with each other, according to the energies of the soul. For, as the reasons of the virtues are different, but it is one thing which partakes of them all, and it is not possible to participate of justice and be destitute of temperance, or to participate of these without the other virtues; in like manner this triad <note>The Triad: The grouping of the Good, the Beautiful, and the Just.</note> is united with itself, and everything *good* is at the same time full of the *beautiful*, and the *just*, and each of the latter is introduced in conjunction with the former. Hence Socrates conjoins the *just* with the *good*, through the *beautiful*: for this is their medium and bond. But the most beautiful bond, says Timaeus <note>Timaeus: A character in Plato’s dialogues who explains the mathematical and physical creation of the world.</note>, is that which makes itself and the things bound eminently one. *The beautiful*, therefore, much more than any other bond collects and unites those two, *the just* and the *good*. And thus much concerning the whole demonstration.

If, however, other demonstrations are requisite of this proposition, which says, "Every thing just is beautiful," let us make it more evident through many arguments. Since therefore the soul is a multitude, and one part of it is first, another middle, and another last, when do we say that justice is produced in the soul? Is it when the middle, or the last part, endeavors to rule over the better part, or when the first governs the middle, and the middle the last? But, if when the worse rule over the more excellent, the worse will not be naturally such: for that to which dominion belongs is naturally more excellent, and more honourable. If, therefore, it is impossible that the same thing can be naturally better and worse, it is necessary that the just should then be beheld in souls themselves, when that which is best in them governs the whole life, and the middle being in subjection to

For then each of the parts ranks according to its desert, the one governing with royal authority, another acting as a satellite <note>Satellite: In this historical context, a "satellite" refers to an attendant or a loyal follower who revolves around a superior power.</note>, and another ministering to the powers of the more excellent. The just therefore is naturally distributive of that which is adapted to each of the parts of the soul. It is also the cause to each of performing its proper duty, and of possessing its proper rank, and thus preserves good order about the whole soul. But order and symmetry are naturally beautiful. Justice, therefore, is the source of beauty to the soul, and is itself beautiful.

The just however is two-fold; one consisting in contracts, and which regards arithmetical equality <note>Arithmetical equality: A simple form of fairness where everyone receives exactly the same amount, regardless of status or merit.</note>, and the other in distributions, and which entirely requires geometric equality <note>Geometric equality: A proportional form of fairness where rewards or duties are distributed based on a person’s worth, ability, or status.</note>. In contracts, therefore, it observes arithmetical equality, that we may not act unjustly by our associate, receiving from him more than is proper; but by fitly distributing unequal things to such as are unequal, it observes geometric equality, so that such as is the difference of persons with respect to each other, such also may be the difference as to worth of the things distributed, to each other. Every thing just, therefore, is, as we have said, equal; but every thing equal is beautiful. For the unequal is base <gloss>base: lacking in quality, ugly, or morally low</gloss>, and void of symmetry, since it is also incongruous. Every thing just, therefore, is beautiful.

In the third place, beauty no otherwise subsists in bodies, than when form <note>Form: The shaping principle or "idea" that gives matter its structure and identity.</note> rules over matter; for matter is void of beauty and base; and when form is vanquished by matter, it is filled with baseness, and a privation of form in consequence of becoming similar to the subject nature. The proposition consequent to this, that every thing beautiful is good, Socrates extends, but Alcibiades does not admit. This was owing to his considering the beautiful to be beautiful by position <note>By position: This refers to things that are considered "beautiful" only because of social convention or human opinion, rather than having an objective, natural quality of beauty.</note>, and not by nature. Hence he also grants that **the just** is beautiful; for it is thus considered by the multitude, and separates *the beautiful from the good*. For to the former of these he gives a subsistence merely from opinion, asserting that *the beautiful* is the becoming, and what is generally admitted: but to the latter he gives a subsistence according to truth; for he does not say that *the good* is from position. This proposition, therefore, that every thing beautiful is good, we shall show to be in every respect true. <meta>This page continues the logical demonstration that the "Just" and the "Beautiful" are ultimately linked to the "Good." The previous page established that justice provides measure and perfection to the soul; this page moves into a formal syllogism to prove that everything beautiful is also inherently good.</meta>

# ON THE FIRST ALCIBIADES.

...it charms those who are capable of perceiving it. For this reason, love is said to lead the lover toward beauty. Now, anything lovely is also desirable, because love is essentially a strong and intense desire for something. Furthermore, whatever experiences love is <term>indigent</term> <note>Indigent: In Platonic philosophy, this refers to a state of "need" or "lack." Love is viewed as the child of Poverty and Resource, always seeking to fill a void by attaining the beautiful or the good.</note> of the thing it desires. 

Everything that is truly desirable is "good," whether it is truly good or only appears to be so. It is clearly demonstrated by Socrates in the *Meno* <note>The *Meno* is a dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of virtue and whether it can be taught.</note> that no one who truly recognizes evil for what it is can actually desire it. Therefore, everything desirable is good. If something is primarily desirable, it is also primarily good; if it is only apparently desirable, its "goodness" is likewise only apparent. 

Briefly, for each of these terms, we must distinguish between what is "apparent" and what is "true." If a thing is apparently beautiful, it is also apparently lovely and desirable, and its "good" is tied to that specific kind of beauty. But if a thing is naturally (truly) beautiful, it is also naturally lovely and desirable. 

What, then, should we call the "desirable" in this context? Could it be evil? No, for it is impossible for any being to desire evil if they recognize it as such; all beings naturally desire the good. There is no such thing as a desire for evil, nor for things that are neither good nor evil—for such neutral things are only pursued for the sake of something else and are never the final goal. Since every desirable thing is an "end" or goal, if something evil is desired, it is only because it mistakenly appears to be good.

In the same way, if something that is not truly beautiful is loved, it is loved because it seems to be beautiful. Therefore, if everything beautiful is lovely, and everything lovely is desirable, and everything desirable is good, it follows that everything beautiful is good. 

The reverse is also true: everything good is desirable. This is immediately obvious. Everything desirable is also lovely, for love and desire are directed toward the same objects. They only differ in their intensity—whether the desire is "relaxed" or "vehement." Socrates also explains this in the *Banquet* <note>The *Banquet* refers to Plato’s *Symposium*, a dialogue centered on the nature of Love (Eros).</note>, where he guides love toward *the good* by way of *the beautiful*. He states that *the good* is just as lovely as *the beautiful*. 

If, therefore, every "good" is desirable, and everything desirable is lovely, and everything lovely is beautiful (since love is always close to beauty), then it follows that every "good" is also beautiful. Let no one argue that *the good* exists far above beauty, nor that there are two separate kinds of "loveliness." We are not currently debating the ultimate first principles of the universe, but rather the nature of *the beautiful* and *the good* as they exist within us. Consequently, the "good" that exists within human nature is at once both desirable and lovely.

<meta>Hence</meta>

Hence we obtain *the good* through love, and a vehement pursuit of it. Hence Diotima, in the Banquet <note>The "Banquet" refers to Plato’s *Symposium*, a dialogue about the nature of Love. ->P. 47. *But what as to actions which are beautiful, &c.*<-

The multitude falsely think that wounds and death are evils. For what among these can be an evil to us whose essence consists in soul? since neither do the <term>passions</term> <note>Passions: From the Latin *passio* (to undergo or suffer). Here, it refers to things that happen to an object—like a tool being dropped or broken—rather than the emotions of a person.</note> of instruments change the virtues of those that use them. Neither, therefore, does the carpenter, if his saw happens to be blunted, lose his art; nor, if our felicity <note>Felicity: Intense happiness or the state of being "blessed."</note> consisted in the carpenter's art, should we call any one unhappy who was deprived of his saw; since, as the soul has an instrument <note>In Platonic thought, the body is viewed merely as the "instrument" or tool of the soul.</note>, so also we may perceive other instruments of the body, through which the body moves things external to it, the defects of which do not injure the good habit of the body. After the same manner, therefore, the passions of the body do not pervade to the soul; so that death, though it is an evil of the body, yet is not an evil of the soul. Hence, if the beauty of action is in the soul, and the evil of it in something else, it has not yet been shown that the same thing is beautiful and evil.

Again, we may also logically prove that the <term>essential</term> <note>Essential: The qualities that make a thing what it truly is. For example, the "essence" of a brave act is the courage behind it.</note> is one thing, and the <term>accidental</term> <note>Accidental: In logic, an "accident" is a property that a thing happens to have, but which isn't necessary to its nature. Dying in battle is an "accident" of a brave act, not its essence.</note> another; and Socrates chooses this mode of solution as more known to the young man. For a brave action is essentially beautiful, but evil, if it is so, accidentally, because it happens to him who acts bravely to die. For let death, if you will, be among the number of evils; yet a brave action, so far as it is brave and therefore beautiful, is not evil, but it is evil only accidentally. The beautiful, therefore, is one thing, and evil another; nor is a thing so far as beautiful shown to be evil, but only accidentally on account of death.
