### BOOK I.

**P. 104. *Are they to have torches, and give them to one another?***

**I**N the Panathenæan, Hephæstian, and Promethean festivals <note>These were major religious celebrations in ancient Athens. The Panathenæa honored Athena; the Hephæstia honored Hephaestus, the god of fire and craftsmanship; and the Promethea honored the Titan Prometheus, who famously stole fire from the gods to give to humanity.</note>, it was customary for young men to run with torches or lamps: and in this contest he alone was victorious, whose lamp remained unextinguished in the race. As a lamp or torch, therefore, from the naturally ascending nature of fire, may be considered as a proper image of our rational part <note>A reference to the human intellect or soul, which ancient philosophers believed tended upward toward divine truths, just as fire reaches toward the sky.</note>, this custom perhaps was intended to signify that he is the true conqueror in the race of life, whose rational part is not extinguished, or, in other words, does not become dormant in the career.

**P. 105. Note. *This nocturnal solemnity was the lesser Panathenæa.***

As in the greater Panathenæa the veil of Minerva <note>Minerva is the Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena. The "veil" refers to the *peplos*, a sacred robe woven by Athenian maidens and presented to the goddess.</note> was carried about in which the Giants were represented vanquished by the Olympian Gods, so in the lesser Panathenæa another veil was exhibited, in which the Athenians, who were the pupils of Minerva, were represented victorious in the battle against the inhabitants of the Atlantic island <note>A reference to the legendary conflict between Athens and Atlantis.</note>. These festivals signified the beautiful order which proceeds into the world from intellect, and the unconfused distinction of mundane contrarieties. The veil of Minerva is an emblem of that one life or nature of the universe, which the Goddess weaves by those intellectual vital powers which she contains. The battle of the Giants against the Olympian Gods signifies the opposition between the last <term>demiurgic</term> <note>Demiurgic: Pertaining to the "Demiurge," a philosophical term for a craftsman-like creator god who shapes the physical world out of pre-existing matter.</note> powers of the universe (or those powers which partially fabricate and proximately preside over mundane natures) and such as are first. Minerva is said to have vanquished the Giants, because she rules over these ultimate artificers.

## B O O K  II.

->P. 222. *Is not God essentially good?*<-

It is well observed by Proclus (in Plato’s *Politics* <note>The "Republic" was often referred to by its Greek title "Politeia" or the Latin "Res Publica," here translated as "Politics."</note> p. 355.), that when Plato says in this place, God is essentially good, he means every God; for the addition of the article either alone signifies transcendency, as when we say **the poet** (original: *ho poiētēs*), assigning this prerogative to the chief of poets <note>Usually referring to Homer.</note>, or the whole multitude, as when we say **the rational man**, adding the article as a substitute for **every**. Since Plato therefore says **the God [is] good** (original: *ho theos agathos*), he either means the first, or every God. But that he does not mean the first only, is evident from his concluding after this, that **every God** is as much as possible most beautiful and excellent. ## BOOK III.

P. 241. *And we should send him to some other city, pouring oil on his head, and crowning him with wool.* <note>In Book III of the *Republic*, Socrates discusses the role of poetry. The Greek Scholium <note>A "scholium" is an ancient explanatory note or comment found in the margins of classical manuscripts.</note> on this part is as follows: <note>original: "παροιμια επι των απο της χρειας αφιεμενων· και γαρ επι των ἑορτων εοικασιν οἱ ανθρωποι μυρῳ κατα της κεφαλης καταχεισθαι, ὡς αν σχολαζοντες απο των εργων, και μονον σχολαζοντες θυμηδιᾳ· και παλιν, τοις απο δουλειας μεταγομενοις επ’ ελευθεριαν, εριου καταγμα κατα της κεφαλης, ενδεσμουμενον το επισημον. Αλλως· μυρου καταχεειν των εν τοις ἁγιωτατοις ἱεροις αγαλματων θεμις ην, εριῳ τε στεφειν αυτα, και τουτο κατα τινα ἱερατικον νομον, ὡς ὁ μεγας Προκλος φησιν."</note> that is to say: “This is a proverb applied to those who are dismissed from business. For in festivals men poured oil on their head, as then resting from their usual avocations <note>An "avocation" here refers to one's regular work or daily labor.</note>, and being alone at leisure for delight. Slaves also, when manumitted <note>To be "manumitted" is to be formally released from slavery.</note>, wore wool rolled round their head, as a sign of their manumission. Or thus: It was lawful to pour oil on the statues in the most holy temples, and to crown them with wool, and this according to a certain sacred law, as the great Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was the last great head of the Platonic Academy in Athens and a central figure in Neoplatonism.</note> says.”

P. 258. *But the God when he formed you, mixed gold in the formation of such of you as are able to govern, &c.* <note>This refers to Plato's "Noble Lie" or the "Myth of the Metals," where citizens are told their souls contain different metals to justify their social roles.</note>

Plato here alludes to the different ages of mankind, which are celebrated by Hesiod <note>Hesiod was an 8th-century BC Greek poet whose poem "Works and Days" describes the historical decline of man through the Ages of Gold, Silver, Bronze, Heroes, and Iron.</note>, in his *Works and Days*, and which signify the different lives passed through by the individuals of the human species. Among these, the golden age indicates an intellectual life. For such a life is pure, impassive, and free from sorrow; and of this impassivity and purity gold is an image, from never being subject to rust or putrefaction. Such a life, too, is very properly said to be under Saturn <note>Saturn is the Roman name for the Greek god Cronus. In Neoplatonism, Cronus/Saturn represents "pure intellect" (Nous).</note>, because Saturn, as will be shown in the notes to the *Cratylus* <note>The *Cratylus* is a Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of names and language.</note>, is an intellectual God. By the *silver age* a rustic and natural life is implied, in which the attention of the rational soul is entirely directed to the care of the body, but without proceeding to the extremity of vice. And by the *brazen age* <note>The "brazen age" refers to the Age of Bronze, characterized in Greek myth by violence and warfare.</note>, a dire, tyrannic, and cruel life, is implied, which is entirely passive, and proceeds to the very extremity of vice.

### BOOK IV.

The following extract from the exposition of the more difficult questions in the Republic, by Proclus <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was a hugely influential Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who headed the Platonic Academy in Athens. His commentaries are often used to interpret Plato’s deeper metaphysical meanings.</note>, (p. 407) will, I doubt not, from its great excellence be very acceptable to the reader. It is concerning the demonstrations in the fourth book of the Republic, that there are three parts of the human soul, and four virtues in it. The scientific accuracy of division, solidity of judgment, and profundity of conception which Proclus has displayed in this discussion can never be sufficiently admired; and it was not without reason, though doubtless without much acquaintance with the works of this wonderful man, that a certain scurrilous writer\*, who appears to be a man of no science, moderately learned, and an indifferent poet, calls him the animated rival of Plato.

> “I here consider virtue not ambiguously, and in the same manner as when we ascribe virtues to things inanimate, but that which is properly so denominated. This therefore we say is vital, is the perfection of life, and is the cause of well-being, and not of being to those by whom it is possessed. But since life is twofold, one kind being <term>gnostic</term> <note>relating to knowledge, intellect, or the cognitive faculties of the soul</note>, and the other <term>orectic</term> <note>relating to desire, appetite, or the emotional drive</note>, or appetitive, virtue will be a certain perfection both of the orectic and of the gnostic form of life. Hence it is requisite that there should not be one virtue only, nor yet more than one of the same species, the one not being so divided as similar parts are divided from each other, differing only in quantity; but it is necessary that there should be many and dissimilar virtues. For such as is the condition of subjects, such also must be their perfections. Hence the virtues of things differing in species must also be specifically different; but of things possessing the same species, there is one specific virtue: for there is one perfection of one essence, whether the cause of being is the same with that of well-being to things, since such as is the being which it imparts, such also is the well-being, or whether it is different. Hence Socrates in his Republic makes a distribution into three <term>genera</term> <note>classes or categories</note>, viz. into guardians, auxiliaries, and mercenaries, before he indicates what the different kinds of virtue are in the best <term>polity</term> <note>the form of government or the ideal state structure</note>; and before he distributes the virtues analogously in one soul, he shows that there are three parts of the soul essen-

“To these things also it is requisite to add, for the purpose of facilitating the objects of discussion, that there is one perfection and energy of a thing considered by itself, and another according to its habitude <note>A "habitude" refers to a state, disposition, or the specific relationship one thing has toward another.</note> to something else; so that the <term>hyparxis</term> <note>original: ὕπαρξις; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the "summit of essence" or the primary foundation of a thing's existence.</note> of a thing (or the summit of its essence) is different from the proximity or alliance which it has with another. For there is not the same perfection of man, and of a man who is a despot <note>Here used in the classical sense of a "master" or "ruler" of a household or state.</note>, as neither is man the same with a despot; nor is it the same thing to behold the soul simply, and the soul as governing the body. Hence it is not the same thing to consider the essential and the relative perfection of a thing. Neither, therefore, must we consider the energy of a thing essentially originating from itself, and solely directed to itself in the same manner as the energy of that which governs or is governed; for government, and the being governed, are certain habitudes. Nothing indeed hinders but that the same thing may perform a certain action, not as governing or as governed, but as possessing a certain essence by itself, and an energy which it is allotted consequent to its essence. Thus for instance, the rational power in us when it lives <term>cathartically</term> <note>original: καθαρτικῶς; meaning "purifyingly." This refers to a state where the soul cleanses itself from material distractions to focus on pure thought.</note> \*, performs its proper work theoretically <note>In the sense of "contemplatively" or through "vision" (theoria).</note>, being naturally adapted thus to live according to its essence; but in this case it does not perform the office of a governor, as the irrational parts contribute nothing to that energy which is directed to itself. Rightly, therefore, does Socrates show that every governing art imparts good to the governed; so that when the rational part extends good to itself alone, purifying and investigating itself, it does not then possess the life of a governor. Thus also when anger acts conformably to its nature, being alone moved as an appetite avenging incidental molestations, it does not then preserve the habitude of that which is governed, with respect to reason, but alone acts as anger: for the desire of vengeance is the work of anger, and not to energize in obedience to reason. In like manner the desiderative part <note>The part of the soul associated with physical desires and appetites.</note> of the soul, when it immoderately aspires after pleasure, then lives according to its own nature: for this is the work of desire, to love pleasure, not some particular, but every pleasure, and this not as governed by reason, whose province it is to measure its appetite. "Since however all the parts are conjoined with each other, and give completion to one life, it is necessary to consider them according to their relative energy <note>In this context, "energy" refers to the active expression or function of a thing's nature.</note>, and thus to perceive the virtue and the vice of each. Hence we must define political virtue to be a habit perfective of the relative life of the parts of the soul; and its contrary, political vice, to be a habit corruptive of the vital habitude <note>A "habitude" is the specific state or relationship one part has toward another within a system.</note> of the parts to each other. Beginning from hence also, it is requisite to see that, in the different kinds of polities, the life of every individual is two-fold, one pertaining to himself, and the other relative; and again, that in these virtue and vice have a similar subsistence. 

For let the guardian <note>The "Guardians" are the philosopher-rulers in Plato’s ideal city, representing the rational part of the soul.</note> be one who contemplates real beings <note>This refers to the "Forms" or "Ideas"—the eternal, unchanging truths that Plato believed were the only true reality.</note>, and ascends by intellectual energy as far as to the *good itself*. He therefore so far as man performs an energy adapted to himself, but abandons a governing life. Hence Socrates does not permit him to abide in such an energy, but brings him down again to a providential care of the city, that he may be a true guardian, leaving a life according to intellect as his last energy. 

Again, let the auxiliary <note>The "Auxiliaries" are the warrior class, representing the "spirited" or emotional part of the soul that provides courage.</note>, because he is the lord of all in the city, pay no attention to the governors, but act in every thing according to casual impulse, and use his power immoderately. This man indeed, as a soldier, will accomplish the energy which is adapted to him; for this consists in fighting; but he will no longer act as one governed. For it is requisite that the governed should look to the conceptions of the governor. Hence the soldier when obedient to the governor, preserves the virtue proper to one governed, but when he opposes the governor, he corrupts his own relative virtue. 

Lastly, let the mercenary <note>Though usually meaning a hired soldier, here the "mercenary" refers to the third class of the city: the producers, merchants, and craftsmen who are motivated by desire and the acquisition of wealth.</note> be one who only lives for himself, and who is alone busily employed in the acquisition of wealth. This man therefore performs his proper work, so far as he is what he is said to be, a mercenary, but he has not yet the vice or the virtue of one governed. But if he becomes a member of political society, and ranks as one who is governed, he will now live with habitude to this: and when he is obedient to the governors according to this habitude, and accumulates wealth conformably to their will, and after the manner which they define, he will possess virtue adapted to a governed mercenary; but when he deviates from the will of the governors, and does not observe their mandates, he is, so far as one governed, a depraved mercenary. For, the guardian <note>The "Guardians" are the philosopher-kings of Plato's ideal city.</note> governing the auxiliaries <note>The "Auxiliaries" are the warrior class who support the Guardians and protect the state.</note>, energizes externally, imitating inward reason governing anger. And, in a similar manner, the auxiliary governs the mercenary tribe <note>The "mercenary tribe" refers to the common citizens or the producing class, driven by economic desires.</note>, imitating in his external energy, the inward dominion of anger over desire. All dominions therefore are habitudes <note>A "habitude" is a state of being or a relationship between different parts.</note>, both those belonging to the soul, and those that are political; but the external are imitations of the internal; and the former are secondary energies of the latter, which are primary. The true political science, therefore, subsists about the habitudes of the soul, this being that which adorns both the governors and the governed; or rather it is one habit possessing two-fold energies, the inward governing and being governed, and the external adorning political affairs.

For this always adheres to the body, and never abandons its life; but anger <note>In Platonic philosophy, "anger" (or *thumos*) refers to the "spirited" part of the soul—the seat of courage, emotion, and the drive for honor, rather than just the emotion of rage.</note> often despises the body and a life in conjunction with it, aspiring after another object of desire, which does not pertain to the body. 

These then, being three, one of which, reason, ought to govern only, but another, as body, to be governed only, and another to govern, and at the same time to be governed, according to an order in the middle of the extremes,—hence, the governors are two, the one primary, and the other secondary, and the things governed according to the same reasoning are also two. It is requisite, therefore, that the part which alone and primarily governs should possess one virtue perfective of governing habitude <note>A "habitude" is a stable disposition or state of being.</note>; but that the part which governs secondarily, and is governed primarily, should possess two-fold virtues perfective of two habitudes. For, as the perfections of different <term>hyparxes</term> <note>original: "hyparxes." This Greek term refers to the essential existence or the foundational "being" of a thing.</note> are different, so also the perfections of different habitudes. 

But it is necessary that the part which is alone governed should possess one perfective virtue. Reason, therefore, which, as we have shown, ought only to govern, has for its ruling virtue prudence, according to which it bounds both for itself and others the measures of actions. Desire <note>The "desiderative" or appetitive part of the soul, responsible for physical needs and cravings.</note>, which ought only to be governed, has for its virtue temperance, according to which it measures its appetites, converting itself to reason, from which it receives a rational impulse, through custom and discipline. But anger, which naturally governs and is governed, possesses, so far as it governs, fortitude, through which it humiliates the desiderative part, and preserves itself invulnerable from its attacks; but, so far as it is governed, it possesses temperance, through which it also desires to be disciplined by the measures of reason. 

If reason, however, as governing both, and as the cause of conversion to itself, and of their submitting to measure, comprehends the principle which it imparts to them, this principle will be temperance, beginning indeed from reason, but ending in desire through anger as a medium; and thus the harmony <term>diapason</term> * will be produced from the three, viz. from reason, anger, and desire. ## ADDITIONAL NOTES

in one part produces the symphony called <term>diatessaron</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"; a Greek term meaning "through four," referring to the musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note> \*, and in another that which is denominated <term>diapente</term> <note>original: "diapente"; meaning "through five," referring to the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> †; the symphony of reason to anger forming the <term>diapente</term>, and that of anger to desire the <term>diatessaron</term>. This latter the <term>Pythagoræans</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe and the soul were structured according to mathematical and musical ratios.</note> denominate a syllable, as not being a perfect symphony; but they assert that the <term>diapente</term> ought rather to be called a symphony than this; just as we must assert that anger has a greater symphony with reason, than desire has with anger, though the interval between the latter is less than that which subsists between the former: for both these are appetites, but the other two are reason and appetite. There is more symphony, therefore, between anger and reason, though the interval is greater, than between desire and anger, though the interval is lesser. For, as we have before observed, anger naturally co-arranges itself with reason, and is more disposed to league with it in battle than with desire, when reason and desire war on each other. And hence, a greater symphony must be assigned to anger and reason, than to desire and anger. But from all these it must be said that a <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "diapason"; meaning "through all," referring to the musical interval of an octave, which encompasses all the notes of the scale.</note> is produced, which the <term>Pythagoræans</term> denominate by far the sweetest and the purest of all symphonies. For this, indeed, is truly a symphony, since among all others it alone possesses the peculiarity of which <term>Timæus</term> <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue of the same name who explains the creation of the world through mathematics and music.</note> speaks, viz. that the motions of the sharper sounds ceasing, embrace those that are more flat, and embracing them conjoin the beginning with the end, and produce one motion gradually terminating from the sharp in the flat. Since, therefore, of all symphonies the <term>diapason</term> is alone allotted this perogative, it will be adapted to the harmony of the soul, pervading through all the parts, conjoining the superior with the inferior motions, connascently <note>Meaning "born together" or existing from birth; naturally linked.</note> harmonizing the <term>intensions</term> <note>The tightening or increasing of pitch/tension.</note> of the one with the <term>remissions</term> <note>The loosening or lowering of pitch/tension.</note> of the other, and truly producing one life from many. And thus in the way of digression we have shown how <term>Socrates</term> denominates temperance the harmony <term>diapason</term>.

<meta>This page continues the "Additional Notes" commentary on Plato's Republic. It develops the discussion of the tripartite soul—consisting of reason, anger (the spirited part), and desire—focusing on how these parts interact, their respective virtues, and their origins as described in the Timaeus.</meta>

### ON THE REPUBLIC.

...is governed, and to another as that which both governs and is governed; so that through this each part energizes according to its proper order, the one as governing, the other as governed, and a third as both. And here it may be inquired how **anger**, since it both governs and is governed, has the virtue of **temperance** <note>original: "temperantia"; the virtue of moderation or self-control.</note> in common with **desire** so far as it is governed, but has not any virtue in common with **reason** so far as it governs, but possesses **fortitude** <note>original: "fortitudo"; the virtue of courage or spiritedness.</note> as its proper virtue. 

To this it may be replied, that there is, as we have said, a greater interval between anger and reason, according to essence, than between desire and anger, though when reason and desire oppose each other, anger is by no means the ally of the latter, but takes the part of the former. But it does this through the <term>pertinacity</term> <note>Stubborn persistence or obstinacy.</note> of desire, through which it often <term>contumaciously</term> <note>In a rebellious or stubbornly disobedient manner.</note> excites reason against desire, and not through any alliance with reason. So that on this account it has a common virtue with desire, so far as it is governed, but a different virtue from reason, so far as governing. 

For the governing power of anger is perfectly different from that of reason, which begins its government from itself. For reason first governs itself, and adorns itself, prior to other things, and does not suffer its proper appetite to remain dubious, and to tend to that which is worse. After this, it measures the appetites of the irrational parts, and recalls them to its own judgment and appetite. 

But anger is not governed by itself, but <term>supernally</term> <note>From a higher or heavenly position; here, coming from the higher faculty of reason.</note> issues its mandates to the worst part alone. For, that which is irrational is never at any time able to govern itself, nor to bound and be converted to itself. That anger, however, is more allied to desire than to reason, according to **Plato**, is evident: for both these are from the same fathers *, but reason is the offspring of a different father; both are mortal, and rise and perish in conjunction, but reason is immortal; both are destitute of knowledge, but reason is naturally <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: "gnosticus"; from the Greek "gnostikos," meaning having the capacity for knowledge or rational understanding.</note>. 

As therefore to be governed is common both to anger and desire, for so far as both are irrational, and require to be adorned by another, they are governed, hence they possess a common virtue which converts them to a desire of that which governs. But as the government of reason is different from that of desire...

In the manner above mentioned, as governors they possess a different ruling virtue; the one <term>gnostic</term> <note>From the Greek 'gnostikos,' meaning relating to knowledge or the intellectual ability to perceive truth.</note>, for it is reason; the other <term>vital</term> <note>Relating to the life-force or the soul's energetic impulses rather than abstract thought.</note>, for it is appetite. When, therefore, appetite governs appetite, there is need of **fortitude** in order to preserve appetite uninjured; but when reason rules over appetite, there is need of **prudence**, preparing reason to judge rightly. And on this account prudence is the ruling virtue of reason, whose province it is to know and to judge rightly, and to govern natures which possess the power of judging. **Fortitude** is the ruling virtue of <term>anger</term> <note>In this context, 'anger' (thymos) refers to the 'spirited' part of the soul, which drives humans toward honor, courage, and indignation against injustice.</note>, which is alone vital, and is destitute of judgment, but is an appetite wishing to have dominion over a worse appetite, the opposition of which it cannot endure. 

But if, as we have before observed, there is a greater interval between the higher than between the lower of these, and a greater harmony arises from the former than the latter, it is by no means wonderful: for the brevity of life obscures the harmony; since in natures whose life is more extended it is greater, and in those whose life is less extended it is evidently less. We have therefore shown that the virtues are only four, and what is the work of each. It will now, therefore, be manifest how they are to be arranged in <term>republics</term> <note>The 'Polis' or organized city-state as described in Plato's philosophy.</note>. 

For it is evident that **prudence** must be especially placed in the governor who consults for the good of the city. For, of what can he who consults be in greater need than of prudence, the province of which is to perceive the good and ill in every action? But in the warring and guardian <term>genus</term> <note>Class or category of citizens.</note> **fortitude** is requisite. For fame calls those men brave who intrepidly endure dangers, resist adversaries, and despise death. That they may subdue, therefore, all those that endeavour to subvert the republic, it is fit that they should be brave; but they ought to receive the measures of their energies from those that are the true governors, and in this be **temperate**, looking to their will. 

And in him who ranks in the last place, and provides all that is necessary, **temperance** is requisite, lest, being inflated by affluence, he should arrogate to himself dominion, thinking that he is sufficient to himself with respect to <term>felicity</term> <note>Happiness or the ultimate good.</note>, and should thus despise the governors, in consequence of an abundance in things necessary imparting a representation of good. **Temperance**, therefore, is requisite to this character, that he may be obedient to the governors, and may submit to them; as in the universe, according to **_Timæus_**, <term>necessity</term> <note>The material or 'errant' cause in the universe which must be persuaded by reason.</note> follows <term>intellect</term> <note>The divine ordering mind.</note>. In the political genera, therefore, Socrates wishing to behold all the virtues, in the first place orderly arranges the political genera,—I say orderly, because he first considers men solely employed about necessaries, without war, unskilled in <term>discipline</term> <note>Here meaning formal education and training in virtue.</note>, living according to nature, satisfied with as little as possible, and conducting themselves temperately: and, in the second place, he shows that when their possessions are increased, they are necessarily led through their external enemies to direct their attention to military affairs. In consequence of this, he shows that discipline then becomes necessary, men passing from a physical to a defensive life, as they could not otherwise defend themselves when unjustly injured by their neighbours. It is requisite, therefore, that there should be those who may fight in defence of the husbandmen; for the same person cannot accomplish both these, since an aptitude for agriculture is different from an aptitude for war. But as aptitudes differ, so also perfections, and it is requisite that every one should be perfected according to his own nature, if he is not to possess an adulterated and unnatural life. The person were a soldier and a husbandman, he could not attend to the seasons of his proper works, being compelled to take up arms when he ought to cultivate the land, to plough or plant when he should engage in war, to carry rural instead of warlike implements, the spade for the shield, and to be in want of necessaries by neglecting the concerns of agriculture. But each of these requires a different discipline, for the manners of each are different. Socrates, therefore, instructs us in a two-fold kind of discipline, one pertaining to the soul, and the other to the body. For soldiers require a robust body, in order to endure the necessary labours of war. 

And as there are two kinds of discipline, one according to **music** <note>In the Platonic sense, "music" (mousikē) refers to all the arts over which the Muses preside, including poetry, literature, and ethics, not just melody.</note> and the other according to **gymnastic** <note>Physical training and athletics meant to strengthen and discipline the body.</note>, it appears to me that Socrates considers those to be most adapted to universal government, whose nature is more adapted to music, and who are better skilled in it than others. So that we shall not err in asserting, that those who are naturally adapted, and are more propense to music than others, are chosen as guardians by Socrates, though he alone says that the most excellent characters are to be chosen as governors, but does not add in what it is that they are most excellent.

Socrates, therefore, having established these three genera, in order to give completion to the city, indicates whence we may call the city wise, whence brave, temperate, and just. Hence, he says, poets also are to be compelled to compose such verses as have a tendency to these types. And if it also learns the **mathematical disciplines** and **dialectic** <note>The highest branch of philosophy, dealing with the investigation of truth through logical argument and the first principles of reality.</note>, it will be in a still greater degree wise and scientific. ### ON THE REPUBLIC.

The <term>mercenary</term> <note>In this classical context, the 'mercenary' class (or producer class) refers to the farmers, artisans, and merchants who provide for the city’s physical needs and wealth, rather than hired soldiers.</note> genus requires **temperance**: for an affluence of things necessary is especially in want of this virtue, since an abundance of these leads to an intemperate life. These three genera therefore mutually according with each other, and preserving their own energy with respect to governing and being governed, **justice** is the result of such a subsistence. For all men, as well those that praise as those that revile justice, say that just conduct consists in not desiring the possessions of others. Hence its enemies reprobate it, because it is content with its own property, when at the same time it ought to possess all things. And thus far, indeed, **Socrates**, considering justice as the founder of cities, does not reprobate its accusers: for they say that justice is that which is beautiful by law <note>The argument here refers to 'Nomos' (law/convention). Socrates' critics often argued that justice was merely a social contract created by the weak to restrain the strong, rather than something naturally good.</note>; and they honour it as a thing necessary; since no one is willing to be injured contrary to the laws, because this is the extremity of evils. But, according to these men, to act unjustly is the greatest good; and justice, having a middle subsistence, is neither good nor evil, but necessary. As we have said, therefore, though **Socrates** considers justice as a plenitude of good, yet he does not reprobate its accusers: for it is admitted to be that which is beautiful by law. Now, therefore, inculcating that it is truly good, and that it is beautiful by nature, he adds, that it also imparts strength to the other virtues: for each through this performs its own proper work, and none of the rest preserves a city so much as this. It is shown therefore by **Socrates**, that a permutation of the pursuits of the guardian, the auxiliary, and the <term>mercenary</term>, is the most perfect destruction of a <term>polity</term> <note>The 'polity' (politeia) refers to the constitution, structure, and essential health of the city-state.</note>.

If, therefore, justice is a standard to each of the other virtues, which the accusers of justice acknowledge to be naturally beautiful, as, for instance, to **prudence** <note>Often called 'phronesis,' this is the practical wisdom required to act rightly and govern effectively.</note>, for all men naturally desire its possession, and those that blame prudence either blame it prudently, and in this case prudence is not to be blamed, rightly blaming itself, or they blame it imprudently, and in this case prudence is not blameable, not being rightly blamed,—this being admitted, it necessarily follows that justice is naturally good in the same manner as prudence, and that it is not beautiful only by law. **Socrates**, having indicated these particulars respecting the virtues in the political genera, passes on to the virtues of the parts of the <term>soul</term> <note>Plato’s theory of the 'tripartite soul' mirrors his city: it consists of the rational part (the rulers), the spirited part (the soldiers), and the appetitive part (the producers).</note>, which we have said are prior to these, and discourses in a three-fold respect concerning them. For, in the first place, he shows that the diversities of men arise from no other cause than the difference...

This therefore he demonstrates in the second place, previously assuming as a thing universally acknowledged, that it is impossible for the same thing, according to the same, and with reference to the same, to do or suffer contraries; but that this may be accomplished by the same thing in a different respect. Thus, the same thing may be heated and refrigerated, be at rest and be moved, impart heat and cold, according to different parts. And the same thing, not with reference to the same but to different things, may be able to do and suffer contraries. Thus, the same thing may be capable of being illuminated and darkened with reference to other things, being illuminated by one thing and darkened by another. Thus, too, the same thing may be the cause of increase and diminution, according to the same, *i. e.* so far as it is the same, with reference to different things; as <term>nutriment</term><note>Food or sustenance.</note>, which, at the same time that it flourishes the members of the body, is itself diminished.

In short, reason and anger may at the same time suffer contraries with respect to the same thing, when, in consequence of an injury being sustained, the latter persuades to vengeance, and the former to endurance. Reason therefore and anger are not the same: for it is impossible that the same thing can do or suffer contraries <note>The "Principle of Non-Contradiction": a single entity cannot act in two opposing ways at the exact same time and in the same respect.</note>, according to the same with relation to the same. Again, reason and desire exclaim contraries, as in the instance above mentioned, with respect to drinking in a fever; but it is impossible for the same thing to do or suffer contraries according to the same with reference to the same. Reason therefore and desire are not the same. Again, anger and desire, with respect to the same thing, speak oppositely in those engaged in battle, and oppressed with hunger; but as the same thing cannot be contrarily affected with respect to the same, anger and desire are not the same. Hence these three differ from each other essentially.

So that, if it should be said, one of these acts, and the other suffers, and that action and passion oppose each other, it is evident that the motions themselves must much more differ from each other: for a contrary effect is the cause of a contrary passion. So that, if any passion has an effect contrary to that of any other, the passion of the one will be contrary to that of the other. oppose each other, and suffer <term>contraries</term><note>In logic and philosophy, "contraries" are opposing forces or qualities that cannot exist in the same thing at the same time, such as hot and cold.</note>, do not essentially differ, neither will the others necessarily differ, because they are passive to contraries.

In thus doubting, however, we forget that desire is called by Socrates a **many-headed beast** <note>This famous metaphor from Book IX of Plato’s Republic illustrates how human desires are diverse, wild, and often in conflict with one another.</note>, because the irrational life is both one and many, as being proximate to the body, which is entirely manifold and divisible; just as that which is allied to the rational intellect is more <term>impartible</term><note>Existing as a single, unified whole that cannot be divided into smaller pieces.</note> than any other of the parts belonging to the soul. The **desiderative part** <note>The appetitive part of the soul (*epithumia* in Greek), which seeks food, sex, and money.</note>, therefore, is essentially one and many, and on this account possesses warring powers proceeding from different essences, that through this it may be <term>connascent</term><note>Grown together or sharing the same biological origin; linked from birth.</note> with body: for this also consists from contraries. Hence this part is one, so far as it possesses one appetite, the love of body, according to which it also differs from the rational parts. 

For the **irascible part** <note>The "spirited" part of the soul (*thumos*), which governs anger, courage, and the desire for honor.</note> is adverse to body, in consequence of aspiring after victory and honour, and through these often casting aside the body, and despising a life in conjunction with it. Nor is the rational part a lover of body, because the object of its appetite is true good. It remains therefore that the desiderative part alone is attached to body, whether it aspires after pleasures or riches: for both these are corporeal. For we are compelled, as Socrates says in the *Phædo* <note>In Plato's *Phaedo*, Socrates argues that the body's needs are the primary cause of war and greed, distracting the soul from truth.</note>, to acquire riches, in consequence of being subservient to the body and the desires of the body; and the lover of riches never despises the body, though it may sometimes happen that he may die through his attention to wealth. 

So that the desiderative part, so far as it is simply a lover of body, is one; but, so far as it is a lover of riches and pleasure, is not one. Hence Plato does not say that it is many animals, but calls it one animal having many heads, and living at different times according to its different heads, but being always a lover of body. The desiderative part therefore is, as we have said, the third, as the rational part which aspires after intellect is the first, and the irascible which desires power ranks as a medium. For power subsists between intellect and the summit of essence; and a representation of this summit proceeds into the third part of the soul; whence he who alone participates of this is a lover of body. A representation of power is seen in the part prior to this; and hence this part desires power: but the image of intellect is apparent in the first part; and hence reason aspires after <term>intellection</term><note>The act of the mind grasping eternal truths or using the pure intellect.</note>. The last part of the soul therefore is a lover of body, and is solely intent to the preservation of the body.

***

\* Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) whose commentaries on Plato were highly influential.</note> here means the **dianoëtic power** <note>The faculty of discursive reason, or logical thinking, which operates between pure intuition and sensory perception.</note> of the soul, of which intellect is the summit.

Since, however, body is two-fold, one being that in which the soul **subsists** <note>original: "fubfifts"; meaning to exist or have its being within something.</note>, and the other that by which it is preserved, as the soul is incapable in its present state of being preserved by itself, hence it has two-fold appetites, one of leading into a natural condition the body in which it resides, and according to this appetite it becomes a **lover of pleasure**, all pleasure being an introduction to nature; but the other of these appetites leads it to procure that of which its containing body is **indigent** <term>indigent</term><note>Lacking the basic necessities; in this context, the physical needs of the body.</note>; and according to this appetite it becomes a **lover of riches**, the acquisition of wealth being desired for the sake of paying attention to the body. It is necessary, therefore, that these powers should always accord with each other,—I mean that the one should desire the preservation of the body in which it resides, and that the other should desire things necessary to its safety. 

But since one of these appetites aspires after that path which is natural to the body, instead of preserving it, hence through a love of pleasure it destroys it, and defiles it with ten thousand stains; but the other desires riches, not for the purpose of satisfying the necessary wants of the body, but as a principal good. This being the case, these appetites pursue different ends, which oppose each other because they are material. Hence the one by its own destruction contributes to the increase of the other. For the infinite appetite of pleasure is attended with a consumption of wealth, and an increase of wealth requires a diminution of things which contribute to the pleasures of the body. Here, therefore, in a contention concerning ends as principal goods, these appetites differ from each other. For the appetite of desire is not directed to one thing, viz. that the body may subsist according to nature, but to two things, the affluence of one of which is accomplished through the indigence of the other. Since then the end of these appetites is one according to nature, hence Socrates establishes one part of the soul in desire, though it is **many-headed** <note>A recurring Platonic metaphor for the appetitive part of the soul, representing its diverse and often unruly physical cravings.</note>, which is not the case, as we have shown, with reason and anger.

Having therefore given an essential division to the parts of the soul, let us, in the third place, consider how Socrates here disposes the **four virtues** <note>The "cardinal virtues" of Greek philosophy: Prudence (wisdom), Fortitude (courage), Temperance (self-control), and Justice.</note>. If then he had been willing to speak in a manner more known to the multitude, he would have said, that **prudence** is the virtue of reason, **fortitude** of anger, **justice** of the desire of riches, and **temperance** of the love of pleasure. But now, as he thought proper to distribute them in a manner inaccessible to the multitude, and to show the analogy in the

By relating political types <note>original: "genera"</note> to the virtues, he demonstrates that **prudence** is a state <note>original: "habit"; in this context, a "habit" refers to a stable disposition or quality of the soul.</note> that perfects that which alone ought to govern the other parts of the soul; and that **fortitude** is a state that perfects that which should govern secondarily within it. And having established these two principal virtues, he says that the other virtues belong to the two ruling parts. Hence, he asserts that **temperance** is a state which leads the governed into concord with the governors, with respect to who should rule; so that the lowest part may agree with the other two, and the middle part with the one part above it. But he says that **justice** is a state which prescribes to each of the parts, both the governing and governed, its proper work. For it is necessary that they should accord with each other, some in governing, and others in being governed; and that the actions of some should be adapted to governors, and of others to the governed. For to govern and to be governed are observed in a certain form of life which justice imparts, distributing to the governor that which is alone adapted to him—to deliberate for the governed—and to the governed to be obedient to the governor. After this manner Socrates discourses concerning the virtues, and it is evident that they must necessarily be such and so many.

One thing therefore only remains to be considered: namely, from where it becomes clear that there are only three parts of the soul which are the recipients of these virtues. For Socrates has shown that these essentially differ from each other; but whether there are these parts only, and neither more nor less, requires some consideration; since, if there are more than three, we shall also be in need of other virtues. It is admitted then, that if there are two things which possess contrary properties, there will be three **means** <term>media</term><note>Intervening steps or connecting links between two extremes.</note>, as is proved to be the case in the elements <note>This refers to the classical elements: fire, air, water, and earth. This is shown in the *Timaeus*, where it is proved that the three elements—fire, air, and water—are the connecting media of the two contrary extremes, heaven and earth.</note>, two of these being received from that which has a more immediate situation, and one from the remaining element which is more remote. This being assumed, let us see what the characteristics of **reason** and **body** are. Reason therefore is **indivisible** <note>original: "impartible"; unable to be separated into parts.</note>, but body is **divisible** <note>original: "partible"; capable of being divided.</note>: reason is capable of intellect, but body is destitute of intelligence. And these things are assumed, one from the essence of reason, another from life, and another from knowledge. It may however appear that Socrates does not leave us with these parts only, when he says, “*Each of us is in a good state when each of these three parts performs its proper office, and they are brought into harmony with each other through temperance, and when this is the case with any other parts which may exist between these.*” For by this he may seem, as I have said, not to leave us with only these three parts, but to admit that there is something in us which neither aspires after honor nor riches, but exists between these. However, Socrates, when he indicates this, does not mean to assert that the lives of the soul are unmixed; as, for instance, that a life according to reason is unmixed with the other parts; that a life according to anger has no connection with the extremes; and that a life according to desire alone is not mixed with those above it; but rather that there are certain lives *between* these. 

Thus, some lead a life according to both reason and anger, being lovers of learning and at the same time ambitious. Others live according to anger and desire, being lovers of both honors and riches; and they either pursue honors so that they may become rich, or scatter their riches so that they may be honored by those who admire wealth. This is just as those mentioned before either pursue <term>disciplines</term> <note>Specific branches of study or knowledge, such as mathematics or philosophy.</note> so that they may be honored for their learning—or they pursue honor so that, being honored by those who possess knowledge, they also may share in it. These, then, are the forms of life between reason and anger, and between anger and desire; they are not "other" parts of the soul, but become various instead of simple because of the mixture of these primary parts. <meta>catchword: sensitive</meta>

Each of those three parts is, in itself, simple: one part alone is a lover of **discipline** <note>In this context, discipline refers to the pursuit of philosophy and structured learning.</note>, despising all honor and every physical thing, as it is dedicated to one goal: the knowledge of truth. Another part is ambitious and fierce; it despises the body as if it were a mere shadow and is insatiable for one thing alone: **honor**. The third part, **desire**, is focused solely on the body and physical needs, considering honors and learning to be nothing more than trifles. 

Because these parts are simple and unmixed, Socrates says that the various ways of living—which are mixtures of these parts—exist in the space between them. All of these, along with the unmixed parts, ought to be brought into accord through the "best harmony." This harmony acts as a measure for our appetite for learning, our pursuit of honor, and our care for the body, ensuring that the desires of the other parts become consistent and do not disagree with **reason**. We should not think, therefore, that Socrates is merely pointing out other parts that make a person virtuous, but rather how these parts mix to generate the various types of characters found in a society.

From what has been demonstrated, it is evident that the soul is neither a single unit nor divided into more than the parts mentioned above—with the exception that the **sensitive nature** <note>The faculty of sense perception.</note> is different from all of them. It differs from reason because it is irrational and is found in irrational animals. It also differs from the two irrational parts (anger and desire) because those are <term>orective</term> <note>From the Greek 'orexis,' referring to the soul's "reaching out" or appetitive drive toward an object.</note>, whereas the sensitive nature is <term>gnostic</term> <note>From the Greek 'gnosis,' meaning "knowledge." Here it refers to a faculty that perceives or knows information rather than just desiring it.</note>. 

Indeed, the power of sense is present in beings that do not experience appetite, such as **celestial natures** <note>The stars and planets, which ancient philosophers believed were living, divine beings that could perceive but did not have base physical hungers.</note>. However, the orective (desiring) part necessarily requires sense, for appetites are triggered by what we perceive. Thus, an animal is defined by its ability to sense, not just its ability to desire, for sense is present in all animals. This is why **Timaeus** <note>A character in Plato’s dialogues who explains the creation of the universe and the nature of living things.</note> says that even plants have a sensation of what is pleasant and painful, and he therefore considers them to be animals—for everything that partakes in life is an animal. Sense, therefore, being different from the three primary parts of the soul, is situated beneath all of them *.

<term>sensitive power<note>Also known as the faculty of sense perception, this is the soul's ability to interact with the physical world through the body.</note></term>. So far, therefore, as this power is directed in its energies to externals, it is sensitive; but so far as it possesses in itself what it has seen or heard, or the types which it has received from any other sense, it exerts the power of memory. Such then is imagination. Socrates also in the *Philebus*, when he says that the painter in us is different from the scribe, who through the senses writes in the soul imitations of the passions which the senses announce, no longer energizing after the same manner with sense, but itself by itself exciting the types received from them, — when he asserts this, he indicates, by arranging the painter according to the <term>phantastic power<note>The faculty of imagination (from the Greek 'phantasia'), which creates or recalls mental images.</note></term>, but the scribe according to the <term>common sense<note>In classical philosophy, the "common sense" (sensus communis) is the internal faculty that synthesizes the data from the five individual senses into a single, unified experience.</note></term>, that these are essentially different from each other. In the *Theætetus*, also, he clearly separates that which judges concerning sensible impressions, from sense in which the seals of sensibles are expressed. But whether these essentially differ from each other or not, this is evident, that memory and sense are different, though the essence of these is divided about one subject which possesses an essential multitude; and that **memory is nearer to reason than sense**, because it receives types from the former as well as from the latter; sense receiving no impressions from reason. And thus much concerning things useful to political virtue, and to those that are instructed in it.

As I know, however, that Porphyry in his <term>Mixed Problems<note>Original: *Symmikta Zetemata*. This was a scholarly work by the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry addressing various philosophical dilemmas.</note></term> relates a certain conversation between Medius the Stoic and Longinus respecting the parts of the soul, I do not think it proper to let it pass unnoticed. Medius therefore having made the soul to consist of eight parts, and having divided it into that which governs, into the five senses, into that which is <term>spermatic<note>The procreative or generative power of the soul.</note></term>, and lastly into that which is vocal, Longinus asked him, why he divided the soul, being one, into eight parts? And Medius, in reply, asked Longinus, why, according to Plato, he made the soul, which is one, to be triple? This then deserves to be considered. For it is evident that the inquiry is not the same with the Stoics, who make the soul to consist of eight, as with Plato, who distributes it into three parts. For the Stoics make corporeal differences of parts; and hence it may be reasonably objected to them, how the soul is one, since it is divided into eight parts, without any connecting bond? But Plato, since he asserts that the soul is <term>incorporeal<note>Existing without a physical body or substance; purely spiritual or mental.</note></term>, and incorporeal natures are united to each other without confusion, is not involved in the same difficulty.

Plato may also be defended after another manner by saying that, according to him, reason is of a more divine essence, but the irrational part of a much inferior nature; and that the former connects and adorns, but that the latter is connected and adorned; just as form when conjoined with matter introduces unity, and we do not require any thing else which may unite these to each other. <margin>† That part of the soul which energizes <term>dianoëtically<note>Through logical, step-by-step discursive reasoning.</note></term> and scientifically is called by Plato, in the *Timaeus*, *the circle of sameness*; and that which energizes according to opinion, *the circle of difference*.</margin>
In the last place, appetite and knowledge are contained in the rational soul. And its appetite is either directed to being <note>True, eternal reality.</note>, or to generation <note>The world of change, birth, and decay.</note>, through which it ascends to real being, and falls again into the regions of sense. The former appetite, therefore, is philosophic, and the latter is enamoured with generation. In like manner, with respect to its knowledge, that which pertains to the <term>circle of sameness<note>A metaphor for the soul's ability to contemplate eternal, unchanging truths.</note></term> † is the knowledge of intelligibles <note>Things understood by the intellect alone, such as mathematical truths or Forms.</note>, but that which pertains to the <term>circle of difference<note>A metaphor for the soul's ability to perceive the shifting, diverse objects of the physical world.</note></term> is the knowledge of sensibles. Hence, through these the soul elevates herself to the vision of the former, and investigates the nature of the latter. 

The irrational powers, therefore, are images of these: the <term>orective<note>From the Greek 'orektikos,' relating to desire or appetite.</note></term> of the rational appetites, and the <term>gnostic<note>From the Greek 'gnostikos,' relating to the capacity for knowing.</note></term> of rational knowledges. The <term>phantastic<note>The faculty of imagination.</note></term> is indeed the image of intelligible knowledge, and the sensitive is the image of <term>doxastic<note>From 'doxa' (opinion); knowledge that deals with appearances rather than certainties.</note></term> knowledge. Thus, too, the appetite of the <term>irascible part<note>The 'spirited' part of the soul associated with courage, anger, and the pursuit of honor.</note></term> is an image of the re-elevating appetite; and the <term>desiderative part<note>The part of the soul associated with basic physical urges and cravings.</note></term> is an image of that appetite which produces generation: for this clings to the body, in the same manner as the former embraces generation. And anger despises the body, but looks to honour—the good of incorporeal natures. The <term>phantasy<note>Imagination.</note></term> being a figured reflection of intelligibles, wills to be the knowledge of certain things; but sense is conversant with the same object as opinion, namely, a generated nature.

# BOOK TWO.
## ON THE NATURE OF THE GODS. <note>original: "DE NATVRA DEORVM"</note>

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>

While many subjects in philosophy have by no means been sufficiently explained as of yet, the question concerning the nature of the gods is particularly difficult and obscure, Brutus—as you well know. This study is both most beautiful for the enlightenment of the mind and necessary for the regulation of religious practice. Regarding this matter, the opinions of the most learned men are so varied and so conflicting that it ought to serve as a strong argument that the starting point of philosophy is <term>certain knowledge</term> <note>original: "scientiam" — here referring to a grounded or certain understanding as opposed to mere opinion.</note>, and that the <term>Academics</term> <note>The Academics were followers of the school of philosophy founded by Plato; in Cicero's time, they were known for their skepticism and the practice of arguing against any settled "dogma" to find the truth.</note> acted wisely in withholding their assent from uncertain matters. For what is more shameful than rashness? Or what is so rash and so unworthy of the gravity and consistency of a wise man, as either to hold a false opinion or to defend, without any doubt, that which has not been sufficiently examined, perceived, and understood?

<margin>The opinions of the philosophers.</margin>

For instance, on this question, most have said that gods exist—which is the most probable view and the conclusion to which we are all led by the guidance of nature. Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC) was a celebrated early Roman poet; Cicero often quotes him as an authority on traditional Roman thought.</note> holds that gods exist, but that they do not concern themselves with human affairs. <insert>Others</insert> <note>original: "alii" — likely referring to the Epicureans, who believed the gods lived in a state of perfect peace, detached from the world.</note> on the contrary, such as the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that believed the universe was a rational, organized system governed by a divine, providential intelligence.</note>, believe both that gods exist and that the world is governed by their wisdom and providence.

### INTRODUCTION.

**PLATO**, in composing the following books of Laws after his Republic, appears to have acted in perfect conformity to the genius of his philosophy, which every where ascends to things more universal and thence descends to things more particular, and contends that the latter can only be accurately known by contemplating the former. <note>Plato’s method involves looking at the big picture—the ideal state—before applying those principles to the specific details of human life.</note> As, therefore, in his Republic, or, the <term>great polity</term> <note>The "Republic" (Politeia), where Plato describes a perfect, communal society.</note>, he assigned all things in common, so here he distributes land and a habitation, a wife and children, to every individual.

<margin>* For those proceeding directly to the sacred cave of Jupiter, which was the most holy of all, where the most venerable and unutterable of the mysteries were celebrated. — Greek Scholiast on Plato, page 214. <note>original: "προσεχως δ' ωρμημενοις επι το του Διος αντρον ιερον, τουτο γενομενον αγιωτατον, εν ω τα σεπτοτατα και αρρητοτατα των μυστηριων επιτελειτο."</note></margin>

The Athenian guest, the chief speaker in this Dialogue, is Plato himself, as is well observed by the <term>Greek Scholiast</term> <note>An ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes (scholia) on classical texts.</note>, whom we have frequently cited in the Notes to the Republic. For this guest observes, in the course of the Laws, that he had already completed two polities; so that either these must be the polities of Plato, or, if this is not admitted, Plato will be the same with the Athenian guest. Plato, therefore, travelling to Crete, met near Cnossus with Megillus the Lacedæmonian, and Clinias the Cretan, whom, together with nine others, the Cnossians had invited to their country that they might there establish a colony, build a city, and give it laws. Megillus then and Clinias, says the Scholiast, betook themselves to the sacred cavern of Jupiter, which was the most holy of all others, and in which the most venerable and arcane of the mysteries were performed*. The Athenian guest meeting with these two, and having asked them in what design they were engaged, they replied, In the establishment of laws. However, as they had been asked many things concerning laws by the guest, and had by no means satisfactorily answered his questions, and as he appeared to them to be well skilled in the subject, they request him to assist them in framing laws for the city.

The genius of Plato in composing these laws is truly admirable; for, prompted by a <term>philanthropy</term> <note>In this context, it refers to a divine-like benevolence or love for humanity's well-being.</note> of which a resemblance has from time imme-

### INTRODUCTION.

<margin>¹ Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*, 94.</margin>
...immemorial been rarely seen, he has devised certain exhortatory introductions, which he calls prefaces, to the several laws, that the citizens may be led by persuasion, and not by terror, to act legally, and that they may spontaneously obey the laws as paternal injunctions, and not unwillingly submit to them as the mandates of a tyrant. <note>Plato believed that for a law to be effective, citizens should understand the reasoning behind it rather than just fearing punishment.</note> The observation, therefore, of **Seneca¹**, that ‘nothing can be more trifling, nothing more frigid, than a law with a prologue,’ is frigid and trifling in the extreme, when applied, as Seneca does apply it, to Plato’s prefaces to his Laws. <note>Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher who favored a more direct, commanding style of law.</note> But Seneca was ignorant of the benevolent intention of the **divine philosopher**, in this instance, and perfectly unskilled in his doctrines. Can the objections, therefore, of such a *Roman* be of any weight against such a *Greek*?

In short, Plato, in this work, appears to have most happily blended the **Socratic philanthropy** <note>Socrates' focus on human ethics and the love of mankind.</note> with the **Pythagoric intellectual elevation**. <note>The mystical and mathematical transcendence associated with Pythagoras.</note> Hence, besides an easy accommodation to familiar discourse, and the ethical peculiarity, in the tenth book, in perfect conformity to the dogmas of the **Pythagoreans**, he demonstrates the existence of the Gods and Providence, and shows that the divinities possess immutable perfection. This book, indeed, may be considered as forming one of the most important parts of the writings of Plato, as it indisputably proves that he was a firm believer in the religion of his country, and that, when properly understood, the theology of the Pagans is the <term>ultimate peak</term> <note>original: "ne plus ultra"</note> of sublimity. An introduction, therefore, of considerable extent will be prefixed to that book, which I earnestly recommend to the diligent perusal of the liberal reader.

# THE LAWS.

## BOOK I.

### *PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.*

->An ATHENIAN GUEST,<-
->CLINIAS the Cretan, and<-
->MEGILLUS the Lacedæmonian.<- <note>A Lacedæmonian is a person from Sparta.</note>

**GUEST.** Do you think, O guests, that a God, or some man, was the cause of the establishment of laws?

**CLIN.** A God, O guest, a God, as it is most just to assert: with us, indeed, Jupiter <note>The Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus.</note>; but, with the Lacedæmonians (whence originated this our guest), I think, Apollo dictated the laws. Is it not so?

**MEGIL.** It is.

**GUEST.** Whether, therefore, do you speak according to Homer <note>The legendary Greek poet.</note>, namely that Minos <note>Minos was an intellectual hero, or, in other words, a hero who acted according to intellectual virtue; and, as he was illuminated by Jupiter, from whom he proceeded, he is on this account said to have conversed with his father. For an ample account of heroes, see the Notes to the Cratylus (another of Plato's dialogues).</note> every year, for the space of nine years, went to converse with his father, and established laws for your cities, according to his conceptions?

**CLIN.** It is so said by us: and, likewise, that his brother Rhadamanthus (you have heard the name) was most just. We Cretans, therefore, say that he obtained this praise, from his distributing, at that time, things pertaining to justice in a proper manner.

# THE LAWS.

**GUEST.** His renown is indeed beautiful, and highly becoming the son of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>. But since both you and this other have been educated in legal institutions of this kind, I persuade myself, it will not be unpleasant to us to speak and hear about the establishment of cities and laws, at the same time that we are proceeding on our journey. But the way from Cnossus <note>Knossos, the grand capital of Minoan Crete.</note> to the cavern <gloss>According to the Greek Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or teacher who wrote explanatory notes in the margins of manuscripts.</note>, not only the greatest mysteries of Jupiter but also those of the Curetes <note>Minor gods or legendary guardians who protected the infant Zeus by clashing their shields to drown out his cries.</note> were performed in this cavern.</gloss> and temple of Jupiter is, as we have heard, sufficiently long; and the resting-places along the road are, as it is proper they should be during the present hot weather, shady, from their position under lofty trees. It will likewise be suitable to our age, to rest in them frequently; and thus, by the allurements of discourse, render the whole of our journey easy.

**CLIN.** Indeed, O guest, in the course of our journey, we shall meet in the groves with cypress trees of an admirable height and beauty, and meadows in which while we rest we may discourse.

**GUEST.** You speak rightly.

**CLIN.** Entirely so. We shall however speak with more confidence when we become spectators of these. But let us now proceed on our journey with good fortune.

**GUEST.** Let it be so. But inform me, why the law instituted for you public feasts, <term>gymnastic exercises</term> <note>In ancient Greece, this referred to a comprehensive system of physical and mental training performed in a gymnasium.</note>, and the custom of using arms.

**CLIN.** I think, O guest, that these particulars respecting us may be apprehended with perfect ease. For you see that the nature of the whole region of Crete is not plain, like that of Thessaly <note>A region in northern Greece famous for its flat plains and excellent horses.</note>. On this account, with them, horses are more used, and, with us, courses on foot. For this, irregularity of the ground is more adapted to the exercise of pedestrial races. Hence, for this purpose, it is necessary that the arms should be lighter, that they may not hinder the race by their weight. But lightness of bows and arrows seems to be adapted to this purpose. All these particulars, therefore, are subservient to our use in war; and the <term>legislator</term> <note>The "law-giver," in this case the legendary King Minos.</note>, as it appears to me, looking to this, established every thing. For he seems to have instituted public banquets, in consequence of perceiving that all men, when they engaged in war, were compelled by the thing itself, for the sake of their own defence, to feast at that time together.

# THE LAWS.

But he <note>Referring to the legendary Cretan lawmaker, Minos.</note> appears to me to be accused of foolishness by the common people, because they have not learned that cities are perpetually at war with one another. But if during a time of war it is necessary to feast together for the sake of defense, and for certain rulers and subjects to act as armed defenders, this should also be done in times of peace. For what most people call "peace" is only a name; in reality, a state of war is perpetually proclaimed by nature among all cities against all others. If you look at it this way, you will find that the Cretan legislator established all our laws, both public and private, as if he were always looking toward war. He ordered us to protect these laws as if no other possessions or studies were useful unless a person was victorious in war; he believed that all the goods of the defeated become the property of the victors.

**GUEST.** You appear to me, my friend, to be well-practiced in explaining the Cretan laws. But explain this even more clearly to me. You seem to say that a city is well-established only when it is organized to defeat other cities in war. Is that not so?

**CLIN.** It is perfectly so; and I think that our other guest here will be of the same opinion.

**MEGIL.** How could a Lacedæmonian <note>A person from Sparta, a Greek city-state famous for its strict military lifestyle and laws.</note>, O divine man, answer any other way?

**GUEST.** Does this principle apply only between cities, or does it also apply between one village and another?

**CLIN.** It applies to villages as well.

**GUEST.** Is it exactly the same?

**CLIN.** It is.

**GUEST.** But what then? Is it also the same between one house and another in the same village, and between one man and another?

**CLIN.** The same.

**GUEST.** But what shall we say of a man’s relationship to himself? Shall we consider him an enemy to himself? Or how shall we describe it?

**CLIN.** O Athenian guest! I am unwilling to call you merely "Attic" <note>Attica was the region surrounding Athens. Clinias is suggesting the Guest is too wise for a simple regional label.</note>, because you seem to deserve being called by the name of the Goddess Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare. original: "Minerva"</note>. For you have correctly traced the conversation back to its first principles...

you render it more clear; and, by this mean, are able to find with facility that which has now been rightly asserted,—I mean, that all men are enemies to all, both publicly and privately, and likewise, that each individual is an enemy to himself.

**GUEST.** How do you say, O wonderful man? <note>A respectful and common Greek form of address used to express surprise or admiration during a debate.</note>

**CLIN.** This, O guest; that for a man to vanquish himself is the first and best of all victories, but to be vanquished by himself is a thing the most shameful and vile. For these things signify that there is war in each of us against ourselves.

**GUEST.** Again, therefore, let us resume the discourse. For, since each of us is either better or worse than himself, whether shall we say that a house, a village, and a city, have this same thing in them, or not?

**CLIN.** Do you mean that one is better, and the other worse than itself?

**GUEST.** I do.

**CLIN.** Concerning this also you have rightly inquired. For this does not less happen to cities, but in the highest degree. For, in those in which the better vanquish the multitude and the worse, such a city is with propriety <note>In a way that is correct or appropriate.</note> said to be better than itself, and may with the greatest justice be praised for such a victory. But the contrary must be the case with a contrary city.

**GUEST.** Whether, therefore, here, the worse is at any time more excellent than the better, must be left uninvestigated; (for it would require a prolix <note>Meaning long-winded or tediously wordy.</note> discussion;) but I understand what is at present asserted by you, thus: That sometimes citizens who are allied to each other, and of the same city, being unjust and numerous, will forcibly attack the just, being fewer in number, that they may subject them to slavery; and that, when they conquer, the city may be justly said to be inferior to itself, and at the same time depraved <note>Corrupt or morally debased.</note>, but, when they are conquered, better than itself, and good.

**CLIN.** What is now said, O guest, is wonderful in the extreme; but, at the same time, thus to confess is most necessary.

**GUEST.** Come then, let us again consider this. Many brothers may be born from one father, and from one mother. Nor is it at all wonderful that the greater part of them should be unjust, and the lesser just.

**CLIN.** It is not wonderful.

**GUEST.** Nor will it be proper for me and you to investigate this, that

...when the <term>base<gloss>the morally inferior or those of lower character</gloss></term> vanquish the better, both the house and every kind of alliance may be called "inferior to themselves." **GUEST.** Let us besides consider this: Can any one become a judge of such brothers as we have just spoken of?

**CLIN.** Doubtless.

**GUEST.** Which, therefore, will be the better judge? He who cuts off <note>Meaning to execute or exile.</note> those that are unworthy and orders the worthy to govern themselves? Or he who causes the worthy to govern, but suffers the unworthy to live, provided they are willing to be governed? But we will say that a third type of judge is best with respect to virtue, if such a one can be found: one who, receiving a discordant alliance, will not destroy any one, but, reconciling the disagreeing parties, will establish for them laws by which they may be enabled to preserve friendship toward each other.

**CLIN.** Such a judge and legislator would be by far the best.

**GUEST.** And he will frame laws for them by acting in a manner contrary to looking only at war.

**CLIN.** This indeed is true.

**GUEST.** But what about this—Does he who aptly constitutes a city look to external war, and by this mean principally adorn the lives of the citizens? Or does he look to the war produced within the city, which is called <term>sedition<gloss>civil unrest, strife, or internal rebellion</gloss></term>, which every person would particularly wish not to arise in his city, and that, when it does arise, the city may be liberated from it with the utmost celerity <note>Quickness or speed.</note>?

**CLIN.** It is evident that he would look to the latter.

**GUEST.** Whether would any one choose that peace should be the result of sedition in consequence of one part of the citizens being destroyed and the other part being victorious, or rather that peace and friendship should be the consequence of reconciliation, and thus the mind of the citizens be necessarily directed to external wars?

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that the best judge or legislator is not one who destroys the "bad" elements of society, but a reconciler who creates laws to foster internal friendship. He concludes that a lawmaker should prioritize ending internal civil strife (sedition) over preparing for external war.</summary>

But there are two kinds of goods, one human, and the other divine; and the former is suspended from the latter.
