# THE LAWS.

->THE LAWS.<-

...after <term>intellect</term><note>Original: "nous." In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the highest capacity of the human mind to perceive divine truth and order.</note> is a temperate habit of the soul. From these mingled with fortitude, the third in order will be justice. And the fourth will be fortitude. All which are to be placed, according to nature, before those human goods. A legislator, therefore, ought to follow this order, and should command the citizens to look to these divine goods in all their actions. But, of these, human goods should be referred to divine goods, and all divine goods to their leader, intellect. 

After these things, he ought to pay attention to the marriages of the citizens, and to the procreation and education of children, both male and female, and likewise to the young, and those who are advancing to old age. Such too, among these, as behave well, he should honour as they deserve, but should reprobate <note>To strongly condemn or disapprove of.</note> in all the conversations of these, their pains, pleasures, and desires. He should likewise consider, and act as a guardian over, the studies of all lovers; and, through the laws, praise such as are worthy, and blame the contraries to these. With respect to anger and fear, too, he will show what in each of these is laudable, and what to be avoided; likewise what <term>perturbations</term><note>Disturbances or agitations of the mind that cloud rational judgment.</note> are produced in the soul through misfortune, and what the means by which these are avoided in prosperity. Lastly, he will show what passions men are subject to, through disease, war, poverty, or the contraries to these; and in all such things he will teach and define what is beautiful, or otherwise, in the disposition of each. 

After this, it is necessary that the legislator should pay attention to the possessions and expenses of the citizens, so as to know how they are conducted, together with societies, and their dissolutions, whether voluntarily or involuntarily instituted; where justice is found among these, and where it is wanting; that by these means he may distribute honours to those that obey the laws, and punish those who cannot be persuaded to obey them. In the last place, having instituted every thing as far as to the end of every <term>polity</term><note>A form of government or a specific constitution of a city-state.</note>, it is necessary he should establish the manner in which the monuments of the dead should be raised, and what honours are to be paid to them. 

The legislator, having established all these particulars, should place over them guardians, some of whom conduct public affairs according to <term>prudence</term><note>Practical wisdom (phronesis), or the ability to govern oneself and others by use of reason.</note>, but others according to <term>true opinion</term><note>In Plato’s thought, "true opinion" is a correct belief that has not yet been fully grounded in philosophical reasoning, whereas "intellect" represents certain knowledge.</note>; so that intellect, binding all these together, may evince that the city follows temperance and justice, and not riches or ambition. After this manner, O guests, I have wished, and am now desirous, you would explain how all these particulars are to be found in those laws which are called <margin>called</margin> <note>This margin note serves as a "catchword," repeating the first word of the following page to ensure the pages were bound in the correct order.</note>

**GUEST.** The next question, therefore, will be, whether or not the Laconian <note>Laconian: Referring to the Spartans, who lived in the region of Laconia.</note> and Cretan polity <note>Polity: A specific form of government or the organized structure of a society.</note> is reprehensible. Perhaps, indeed, I can better relate what is said by the multitude on this occasion, than either of you. As to your laws, though they should be but of a moderate degree of excellence, yet you certainly have one most beautiful law, which forbids any youth from inquiring whether the laws are well or ill established, but orders them all to accord, with one voice, and with one mouth, that they are all beautifully constituted, as if they had been established by the Gods; and that, if any young man asserts the contrary, no one shall by any means listen to his discourse: but that an old man, if he has any thing to urge against them, shall relate his objections to the rulers, and his equals in age, yet not in the presence of any young man.

**CLIN.** You speak most properly, O guest: and though at the time this law was established you were absent from the thought of the founder, yet you appear to me to conjecture his intention sufficiently, as if you were a prophet <note>In this context, "prophet" refers to someone who can intuitively grasp deep or divine intentions.</note>, and to speak the truth in the most eminent degree.

**GUEST.** At present, therefore, let us be free from young men; but we, on account of our old age, are permitted by the legislator to speak about the laws among ourselves, without committing any offence.

**CLIN.** We are so. Do not spare, therefore, but freely reprove our laws. For it is not dishonourable to know if any thing is not beautifully established; but, by this mean, a remedy is applied, when what is asserted is received with a benevolent, and not an envious mind.

**GUEST.** You speak well. I shall not, however, reprehend the laws till I have diligently considered them to the utmost of my ability; or rather, I shall proceed in this affair by doubting. For you alone, of all the Greeks and Barbarians <note>Barbarians: To the ancient Greeks, this term referred to anyone who did not speak Greek, rather than implying a lack of civilization.</note> with whom we are acquainted, the legislator has ordered to abstain from the greatest pleasures and sports, and not to taste them. But with respect to pains and fears, which we have lately discussed, he was of opinion, that if any one avoided them from his infancy, when he came to endure necessary pains, fears, and labours, he would avoid those who are exercised in them, and would become their slave. This legislator ought, in my opinion, to have thought the same respecting pleasures, and to have said to himself: If the citizens should from childhood be unexperienced in the greatest pleasures, and never be taught how to sustain the attacks of pleasure, or informed that they should never be compelled to do any thing base <note>Base: Morally low, dishonourable, or shameful.</note> for the sake of the sweetness with which pleasure is attended, they would be induced to act in the same manner as those who are vanquished by fear, and would become servile in a different and yet baser manner than those who are able to endure the assaults of pleasure, but yet procure pleasures for themselves, and are sometimes the worst of men. The soul of such, likewise, is partly a slave, and partly free; and they do not deserve to be called simply brave, and free. Consider, therefore, whether any thing that has been now said appears to you to be proper.

**CLIN.** It does. But immediately and readily to assent to things of such great importance would be the province of young men, or rather of stupid men.

->THE LAWS.<-

The discourse we have proposed must continue until it reaches the subject of divinity <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "divine" often represents the ultimate source of order and reason which laws should reflect.</note>.

**CLINIAS.** We should certainly proceed in that manner, if you agree.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** While I explain what I believe the nature of education <term>discipline</term> <note>original: "disciplina"; Greek: "paideia". This refers to the total upbringing and moral development of a citizen, rather than just academic schooling.</note> to be, please consider whether my definition matches your own opinion.

**CLINIAS.** You may begin whenever you like.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** I assert, then, that those who are destined to become great men must, from their very childhood, practice their future pursuits—both in play and in serious work—in ways suited to those goals. For example, if someone is to become a good farmer <term>husbandman</term> or architect, he ought to spend his childhood play either tilling the ground or building toy <note>original: "puerile"</note> houses. Whoever is in charge of their education should provide each of them with small tools that are imitations of the real ones. Furthermore, they should learn the basic skills necessary for their future trades. For instance, a builder should learn how to use a ruler and how to measure. One destined to be a warrior should practice riding a horse in his games, or do something similar. The teacher should try, through these games, to direct the children's pleasures and desires toward the goal they must reach when they are grown. We say that the very peak of education is a proper upbringing, which leads the soul of a child at play to a love for the work he will eventually do as a man, once he has achieved excellence <note>original: "virtue of his art"</note> in his profession. Consider now whether this assertion pleases you.

**CLINIAS.** How could it not?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Then we must not leave our definition of education <term>discipline</term> vague. At present, when we praise or criticize a person’s upbringing, we say one man is educated and another is uneducated <note>original: "undisciplined"</note>, even though the latter might be highly skilled in cooking, navigation, or similar trades. It seems we do not consider these technical skills to be "education" in the true sense. Rather, we mean the training that leads a child to desire and love virtue, and through which he gains the perfection needed to know how to rule others and be ruled himself with justice. This is what our argument defines as education; from this it appears—

# THE LAWS.

<page-num>28</page-num>

->THE LAWS.<-

...that this alone ought to be called education <note>original: "discipline"; Greek: *paideia*. As established on the previous page, this refers to the total moral and civic upbringing of a person.</note>, according to our sentiments; but that the training which tends only to the acquisition of wealth, or bodily strength, or any other specific skill without intellect and justice, is merely mechanical and unfit for a free citizen <term>illiberal</term> <note>In the ancient world, "illiberal" referred to skills or trades practiced by slaves or lower classes, which were thought to provide no moral benefit to the soul.</note>, and does not in any respect deserve to be called education. We shall not, however, argue over a word. But let the point we just agreed upon remain: that those who are properly educated become, for the most part, good men. Therefore, it is by no means right to despise education, because it is the first of all beautiful things available to the most excellent men. And if at any time someone who has been properly educated should stray from the right path, he is capable of being corrected; and this improvement he may always strive for, according to his ability, throughout his whole life.

**CLINIAS.** You are right, and we agree with what you say.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** But we previously granted that those who are capable of governing themselves are good, while those who do not possess this ability are bad.

**CLINIAS.** You speak most rightly.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Let us therefore revisit this assertion so that our meaning may become clearer. Allow me to use an image <note>The Guest often uses "images" or metaphors to explain complex philosophical concepts.</note>, if I might be able to demonstrate this to you more clearly.

**CLINIAS.** Please, speak.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Do we not consider each of us to be a single individual?

**CLINIAS.** We do.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** But do we not also contain within ourselves two foolish and opposing counselors, which we call **pleasure** and **pain**?

**CLINIAS.** This also we admit.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Connected with these are our opinions about the future, the common name for which is **hope**. Specifically, the hope felt before pain is called **fear**, while the hope felt before its opposite <note>pleasure</note> is called **confidence**. Alongside all of these is a reasoning process, determining which of them is better or worse; and this reasoning, when it becomes the common decree <term>dogma</term> <note>original: "dogma". In this context, it refers to a formal decision or principle reached by the community.</note> of the city, is called **law**.

**CLINIAS.** I can scarcely follow you. However, proceed with what remains as if I were able to keep up.

**MEGILLUS.** I am also affected in the same way.

# THE LAWS.

<page-num>29</page-num>

->THE LAWS.<-

**GUEST.** But we should think about these things in the following way. Let us consider that each of us is a puppet <note>The original English text uses "prodigy," translating the Greek *thauma*, which refers to a marvelous puppet or marionette.</note> fashioned by divine animals <note>Plato uses "divine animals" to refer to the "mundane" or "junior gods" who, in his work *Timaeus*, are responsible for creating the mortal parts of the soul.</note>, whether we were created as their plaything or for some serious purpose; for of this we are uncertain. We do know, however, that these passions are within us like sinews or ropes <note>original: "nerves"; from the Greek *neura*, meaning both nerves/sinews and the strings of a puppet.</note> that pull us in opposite directions, and because they are contrary to one another, they pull us toward opposite actions, where virtue and vice sit on either side.

Reason tells us that we must always follow one of these strings and never let go of it, even as we resist the pull of the other "nerves." This is the **golden and sacred guidance of the reasoning power**, which we call the common law of the city. While the other strings are hard and made of iron, this one is soft because it is made of gold. Furthermore, this golden string is uniform, while the others take all sorts of different shapes.

It is necessary, therefore, that we always follow the most beautiful guidance of the law. For since the power of reasoning is beautiful and gentle rather than violent, it requires assistants to help it guide us, so that the **golden race** <note>This refers to the "intellectual form of life," or a life lived according to the highest intellect. This mirrors the "Golden Age" or "Golden Class" mentioned in Plato's *Republic*.</note> within us may overcome the lower parts of our nature. In this way, this "fable" of us being wonderful puppets will help preserve virtue. We will also understand more clearly what it means for a person to be "superior" or "inferior" to themselves. Both cities and individuals, by grasping the true nature of these internal "strings," ought to live according to them. 

We will also see that a city—whether it receives this wisdom from the Gods or from a wise person who understands these matters—will establish this reason as law, using it to govern its own affairs and its relationships with other cities. Thus, vice and virtue will be more clearly distinguished. As this distinction becomes more obvious, our methods of education and other studies will perhaps become clearer as well. This will also be the case regarding the custom of drinking parties <note>Greek: *symposia*.</note>, which might otherwise seem like a trivial subject to discuss at such length.

**CLINIAS.** Perhaps it will be shown that such a topic is indeed worthy of a long discussion.

This internal struggle defines virtue and provides the philosophical basis for a city's legal system.</summary>

**Guest.** You speak well. We will therefore endeavor to explain what appears to be praiseworthy in a custom of this kind.

**Clin.** Speak then.

**Guest.** If to this **wonderful puppet** <note>The original text uses "prodigy" or "wonderful thing," translating the Greek *thauma*, which refers to a marvelous marionette or puppet controlled by strings.</note> we should add intoxication, what sort of being would we create?

**Clin.** What is your aim in asking this question?

**Guest.** I have no specific aim other than to ask: what would happen if this "marvelous thing" became drunk? Let me try to explain more clearly what I mean. My question is this: Does the drinking of wine make feelings of <term>pleasure, pain, anger, and love</term> more intense?

**Clin.** It certainly does.

**Guest.** Does it likewise make the senses, memory, opinions, and <term>prudence</term> <note>Original: *phronesis*; a type of practical wisdom or intelligence.</note> more intense? Or does it entirely extinguish these when someone has drunk to the point of intoxication?

**Clin.** It entirely extinguishes them.

**Guest.** Such a person, therefore, returns to the same state of soul they possessed when they were a boy.

**Clin.** Exactly so.

**Guest.** Consequently, at that time, such a person has the least possible command over themselves.

**Clin.** The very least.

**Guest.** Shall we, therefore, call such a person most <term>depraved</term> <note>In this context, "depraved" suggests a loss of moral order and rational control rather than just "evil."</note>?

**Clin.** Very much so.

**Guest.** It appears then that not only does an old man "become a child a second time," but the same is also true of a man when he is intoxicated.

**Clin.** You speak most excellently, Guest.

**Guest.** Is there any reason that could persuade us that we ought to taste this liquor, rather than avoiding it with all our power?

**Clin.** It seems there is; and you just now said you were prepared to show it.

**Guest.** You have correctly reminded me; and I am ready now, especially since you have both said you are willing to listen with <term>alacrity</term> <note>Eagerness or cheerful readiness.</note>.

**Clin.** How could we not listen? If for no other reason, we would listen for the sake of the "wonderful and absurd" arguments this topic contains.

...not only does a person return to a child-like state, but is it necessary that a man should at any time voluntarily hurl himself into every kind of **depravity**? <note>This continues the thought from the previous page: "not only does [a person return to a child-like state, but is it necessary...]" In this context, "depravity" refers to the loss of rational control.</note>

**CLIN.** Certainly.

The Athenian Guest argues that wine serves as a safe, controlled environment to test a person's character and self-control before they are faced with real-world temptations or dangers.</meta>

# THE LAWS.

<page-num>35</page-num>

->THE LAWS.<-

**GUEST.** You remember quite correctly. But since we must consider how to practice **fortitude** and fearlessness, we should also ask whether we ought to practice the opposite qualities when dealing with the opposite of fear.

**CLIN.** That seems likely.

**GUEST.** In those situations where we are naturally prone to being remarkably confident and **audacious**, <note>Audacious here implies a reckless or over-bold spirit.</note> it seems we should practice how to be as little **impudent** and reckless as possible. Instead, we should become "timid" when it comes to the daring to speak, suffer, or do anything base <note>In this context, "base" means morally low or shameful.</note>.

**CLIN.** It certainly appears so.

**GUEST.** Are these not the very things that affect us in this way—anger, love, insolence, ignorance, greed, and cowardice? And in addition to these, do not wealth, beauty, strength, and everything that intoxicates men with pleasure and makes them lose their senses act the same way? To make an easy and harmless test of all these traits, and then to practice moderation, what better method is there than the use of **wine**? <note>The Guest is arguing that social drinking acts as a "stress test" for the soul.</note> This allows us to explore a person’s character through the playfulness of wine, provided it is done with careful supervision. Consider this: which is better? To test a harsh and unrefined soul—the kind from which a thousand injustices grow—by entering into business contracts with him, or by observing him at the festivals of **Bacchus**? <note>original: "Bacchus." The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and theater.</note> Is it better to test a man's susceptibility to lust by putting his sons, daughters, and wife at risk, or by seeing how he behaves when his soul is softened by wine? In short, among ten thousand ways to judge a person’s character, you will not find a method more convenient, safe, or easy than this "test by wine," so long as it is done in jest. We should therefore believe that neither the Cretans nor any other nation would doubt that this is a useful and safe way to test one another.

**CLIN.** What you say is true.

**GUEST.** This, then, is one of the most useful things: to know the natures and habits of souls through that art whose job it is to treat them. And this, I believe, is the province of the **politic art**. <term>politic art</term> <note>From the Greek *politikē technē*, meaning the "art of statesmanship" or the science of governing a city-state.</note> Or is it not?

**CLIN.** It is entirely so.

When such things as pertain to the divinities are properly accomplished, the tables follow, at which hymns are sung in praise of the God who is honoured in the festival. Social drinking succeeds, with songs which are partly serious and partly jocose, according to the different dispositions of the company. Accusations are silent, and the judge does not pass sentence; but such things as produce pleasure alone flourish. The slave is not afraid of blows from his master, and pedagogues <term>pedagogue: a tutor or attendant, usually a slave, who supervised a child's conduct and accompanied them to school</term> are mild to youth.

> "In the evening they sup splendidly, at which time there are so many torches that the city is full of light. Then to drink even to intoxication is not perfectly disgraceful; for the occasion in a certain respect appears to take away the opprobrium <term>opprobrium: public disgrace or shame arising from conduct considered shameful</term>. On the following day the divinity is not neglected; but many of those that worshipped on the preceding day do not again come to the shows. Those that contend in the composition of verses attend on this, but those with whom the contest is in the scenes, on the preceding day. The third day also is not far short of these; and pleasure and hilarity are extended with the time of the festival. When the solemnity ends, prayers are offered for futurity, that they, their children and families may again be spectators of it; after which the strangers depart, and the citizens accompany them."

**CLIN.** That it does.

Or he, who, though he is not altogether able to act or think rightly, with respect to his voice and body, yet acts rightly with respect to pleasure and pain; embracing such things as are beautiful, and hating such as are base?
**CLIN.** You speak, O guest, of a mighty difference of discipline.
**GUEST.** If, therefore, we three possess a knowledge of the beautiful in singing and dancing, we also know when any one is properly or improperly disciplined: but, if we are ignorant of this, we shall not be able to know what is the defence of discipline, and where it is to be found. **CLIN.** It is far from being the case.

**GUEST.** What then shall we say is the cause of our error? Is it because not the same things are beautiful to all? Or shall we say that they are the same things, but do not appear to be the same? For no one will say that a vicious is better than a virtuous choir; or that he is delighted with depraved figures, but others with a muse contrary to this. Though, indeed, most men assert, that the rectitude of music consists in a power which imparts pleasure to the soul. This, however, is neither to be endured, nor is it holy by any means to make such an assertion. But this is more probably the cause of our error.

But those to whom they appear contrary to nature, or manners, or custom, can neither rejoice in nor praise them, but must necessarily denominate them base <note>In this context, "base" (*aischron*) means more than just "lowly"; it refers to something that is morally ugly or shameful.</note>. And those, again, to whom these particulars happen right by nature, but the contrary from custom; or right from custom, but the contrary from nature;—these will denominate things contrary to pleasures, laudable. For they will assert that each of these is pleasant, but at the same time base. Hence, before others, whom they consider as intelligent persons, they will be ashamed that their body should be moved after that manner, and will blush to sing, and to call such things beautiful, or deserving serious attention; but, by themselves, they will be delighted with them.

**CLIN.** You speak with the utmost rectitude.

**GUEST.** Does he then suffer any injury who is delighted with base figures <note>Refers to the physical postures or gestures in a dance.</note> or melodies; or do they receive any advantage who are pleased with the contraries to these?

**CLIN.** It is probable.

**GUEST.** Is it only probable, or also necessary, that the same thing should happen as takes place when any one, being conversant with the depraved habits of depraved men, does not hate, but rejoices in and admits them; and yet blames them in jest, having a dreaming perception of his own depravity? For, in this case, it is necessary that he should be assimilated <note>To be "assimilated" means to become like the thing one admires; Plato argues that we eventually embody the character of the music and art we enjoy.</note> to the things in which he rejoices, although he should be ashamed to praise them. But what greater good, or evil, shall we say, can possibly happen to us than a thing of this kind?

**CLIN.** I think, none.

**GUEST.** But where laws are beautifully established, or will be in some future period of time, can we think it will be lawful for poets, in discipline and sport respecting the Muses <note>The "Muses" here represent the entirety of the arts, including music, poetry, and dance.</note>, to teach in their poetical compositions whatever delights them, by rhythm, or melody, or verse, and to form in choirs <note>The "choir" (*choros*) was a fundamental educational unit in a Greek city, where young people learned citizenship through song and dance.</note> the boys and young men of well instituted polities <note>A "polity" (*politeia*) is a form of government or a civil society.</note>, either to virtue or vice?

**CLIN.** It is contrary to reason to suppose this would be allowed.

**CLINIAS.** And what exactly is the law regarding such things in Egypt?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** It is truly remarkable to hear. It seems that long ago, they recognized the principle we are now discussing: that the youth in a city must be habituated to beautiful forms and beautiful melodies. They established a system of exhibiting these ideal standards in their temples to define their qualities. Beyond these established models, it is illegal for painters or any other visual artists to introduce any innovations, or even to conceive of styles other than those of their own country. This prohibition remains in effect today, both for the visual arts and for the whole of music. If you look closely, you will find that paintings and sculptures produced ten thousand years ago—and I mean that literally, not just as a figure of speech—are neither more beautiful nor less skillfully made than the works of today. They are crafted using the exact same artistic principles.

**CLINIAS.** You describe a truly extraordinary situation.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** It is, however, a masterpiece of law and political strategy. It proves that a legislator can firmly establish laws for these matters and confidently introduce melodies that possess a "natural rectitude" <note>This "rectitude" or "correctness" refers to art that accurately reflects moral truth and the harmony of the universe, rather than art that simply seeks to please the audience.</note>. The constant human search for new pleasures and pains—which drives the demand for new music—does not have the power to corrupt a choir that has been consecrated by its antiquity. At least, it appears the Egyptian traditions were entirely resistant to such corruption.

**CLIN.** I do not know, O guest of ours, for what reason you again <term>degrade</term> <note>Clinias is likely referring to the Guest’s earlier suggestion that existing laws or musical traditions aren't as "correct" or "noble" as they should be.</note> our legislators.

Thus, for example, a grace follows food and drink, and every kind of nourishment, and this grace we call pleasure: but if it contributes to health, we denominate it rectitude and utility.

**CLIN.** Entirely so.

**GUEST.** Thus, too, a grace follows <term>discipline</term> <note>Here referring to the process of learning or education (*paideia*).</note>, which is also called pleasure; and the truth resulting from discipline is denominated rectitude and advantage, the beneficial and the becoming.

**CLIN.** It is so.

**CLIN.** Certainly.

**GUEST.** But, in short, the equality of such things <note>The Guest means how accurately the imitation matches the original thing it is representing.</note>, rather than pleasure, renders them such and so great.

**CLIN.** It is well said.

**GUEST.** Hence that alone can be rightly judged by pleasure, which neither affords a certain advantage, nor truth, nor similitude; nor yet again is the cause of any injury, but which alone exists for the sake of that grace which follows other things, and which may be most beautifully denominated pleasure, when none of these attend it.

**CLIN.** Do you alone speak of <term>innoxious pleasure</term>? <note>Harmless pleasure that doesn't lead to any significant positive or negative result.</note>

**CLINIAS.** You speak most truly.

**GUEST.** Shall we not then assert, based on what has just been said, that all imitations—and even the concept of <term>equality</term>—should be judged least of all by the pleasure they provide or by personal opinions? For it does not follow that because a thing *appears* to someone to be equal, or because someone is *delighted* by it, that the thing is therefore equal or possesses <term>symmetry</term> <note>In this context, symmetry refers to the mathematical proportion and harmony of the parts in relation to the whole.</note>. Rather, these qualities are determined by truth, more than by anything else.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**GUEST.** Do we not also say that all music is <term>assimilative</term> <note>The quality of making itself similar to, or taking the form of, something else; essentially, the act of representation.</note> and imitative?

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**GUEST.** Therefore, we should never admit the claim that music is to be judged by the pleasure it gives. We should not seek out such pleasure-centered music as if it were a serious matter. Instead, we must seek only that music which possesses <term>similitude</term> <note>An accurate likeness or resemblance to the subject being imitated.</note> through its imitation of the beautiful.

**CLINIAS.** Most true.

**GUEST.** Those, therefore, who seek out the most beautiful singing and the most beautiful <term>muse</term> <note>The "muse" here refers to the specific style of artistic and intellectual inspiration governing music and poetry.</note> should not, it seems, look for what is pleasant in them, but for what is right. For the <term>rectitude</term> <note>From the Latin *rectitudo*; here meaning the "correctness" or "accuracy" of the representation.</note> of an imitation, as we have said, consists in expressing the true size and quality of the thing it represents, exactly as they are.

**CLINIAS.** How could it be otherwise?

**GUEST.** Now, everyone will acknowledge that all poems are a form of assimilation and imitation. Do you not think that all poets, listeners, and performers would agree to this?

**CLINIAS.** Very much so.

**GUEST.** But it is necessary, it seems, to understand the nature of a poem if one wishes to avoid making an error in judgment. For he who does not know the <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note> of a poem—what it means or what it is meant to be an image of—will never understand whether the poet’s intention was correct or erroneous.

**CLINIAS.** It is impossible that he should.

**GUEST.** And can someone who does not know if a performance is correct ever be able to judge whether it is performed well or poorly? I do not indeed—

<meta>This page concludes Book II of Plato’s "Laws." The Athenian Guest finishes his lengthy argument on the "choir of Dionysus"—the idea that structured drinking parties (symposia) can be used as a tool for moral education and testing a citizen's self-control.</meta>

->64<-

**THE GUEST.** One part of this, as we said, we have already discussed; we should now endeavor to discuss the remaining part.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**THE GUEST.** We will, therefore, first of all bring to a conclusion the <term>choir of intoxication</term> <note>The Guest refers here to the "Choir of Dionysus," a conceptual group of older citizens who use wine to regain the spirit of youth and participate in the musical education of the city.</note>, if that is agreeable to you.

**CLINIAS.** Of what are you speaking?

**THE GUEST.** If a city treats <term>drinking associations</term> <note>original: "symposia." These were highly structured social gatherings for drinking, poetry, and conversation.</note> as a serious concern, governed by law and order as an exercise for acquiring <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "sophrosyne," meaning self-control, moderation, and sound-mindedness.</note>, and does not avoid other pleasures but engages in them to master them—then it may be allowed to use all of these. But if a city treats these drinking associations as mere sport, allowing anyone to drink when and with whom they please without restraint, I would not suggest that such a city, or any individual in it, should ever make use of intoxication. Instead, I would much prefer the law of the <term>Carthaginians</term> <note>The North African power of Carthage was known to have strict laws regarding military discipline and sobriety.</note> to the customs of the Cretans and <term>Lacedæmonians</term> <note>The Spartans.</note>. For Carthaginian law forbids anyone in the military camp from tasting wine, ordering that only water be drunk during that entire period. Likewise, I would not permit it to be drunk in the city by male or female slaves; nor by magistrates during their year of office; nor by <term>pilots</term> <note>In this context, specifically the helmsmen of ships, whose sobriety was vital for safety.</note> or judges while engaged in their duties; nor, in short, by anyone deliberating on important matters. Furthermore, I would not permit it to be drunk by anyone during the day, unless for the sake of physical exercise or illness; nor by a man and woman at night when they intend to conceive children. Many other instances could be cited where those of sound mind and good laws will abstain from wine. Consequently, by this reasoning, no city has any need for a great number of vineyards. All other agricultural concerns and matters of diet should be orderly arranged, and wine should be used perhaps most moderately of all things. This, if it is agreeable to you, my guests, shall be the conclusion of my discourse regarding wine.

**CLINIAS.** Beautifully said; we agree it should be so.

**MEGIL.** Speak yet more clearly.

**GUEST.** This then will be most clear.

**MEGIL.** What?

**GUEST.** If any one gives a greater power to lesser things, so as to neglect <term>mediocrity</term> <note>In this context, "mediocrity" does not mean "ordinariness," but rather "the mean" or "the middle way"—the Greek ideal of moderation (sophrosyne) where nothing is done in excess.</note>,—as, for instance, sails to ships, food to bodies, and dominion to souls—he would subvert all things. For, becoming insolent, some of these would rush to diseases, and others to injustice, the offspring of insolence. What then do we mean to say? It is this, my friends, that the nature of a mortal soul is such, that no one of these can, when young and unrestrained, bear the greatest dominion without having its <term>dianoëtic power</term> <note>dianoëtic: relating to "dianoia," the faculty of discursive reasoning or intellectual thought. It is the part of the soul that processes logic and mathematical concepts.</note> filled with folly, which is the greatest disease; and that, besides this, it will hate its nearest friends; which circumstance, when happening, will swiftly destroy it, and obscure the whole of its power. **MEGILLUS.** What laws do you speak of?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Those which were then established about music, that we may show from the beginning how liberty came to be bestowed in an extreme degree. For then music was divided by us into certain species and figures; and one species of the ode consisted in prayers to the Gods, which are called by the name of hymns. But another species of the ode, contrary to this, may be said especially to consist in lamentations. Again, another species consists in <term>paeans</term> <note>original: "pæons" — songs of praise or thanksgiving, usually dedicated to Apollo</note>: another celebrates the generation of Bacchus <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and theater</note>, and is, I think, called <term>dithyrambos</term> <note>A passionate, choral hymn sung and danced in honor of Dionysus</note>: and another species is denominated laws <note>The Greek word "nomoi" means both "laws" and "musical modes" or "melodies." This double meaning is central to the Guest's argument</note> pertaining to the harp. These, and some others, being established, it was not lawful to use one species of melody instead of another. 

But the authority of knowing these, and, at the same time, judging respecting them, and condemning them when improper, was not invested in the pipe <note>The "aulos," a Greek reed instrument often associated with emotional or chaotic music</note>, nor in the ignorant clamors of the multitude, as at present, nor yet in those who express their applause by clapping their hands—but in men illustrious for their erudition, and who were permitted to hear to the end in silence. But boys, <term>pedagogues</term> <note>original: "pædagogues" — tutors or household slaves who supervised children</note>, and the numerous vulgar, were admonished to behave orderly by a rod <note>This refers to the "rhabdouchoi" or staff-bearers who maintained order and enforced silence in the ancient theaters</note>. 

These things being established in so orderly a manner, the multitude of citizens willingly submitted to be governed, and did not dare to judge in a tumultuous manner. But after this, in the course of time, the poets themselves became the leaders of this unlawful privation of the muse. These, indeed, naturally possessed the poetic genius, but were unskilled to a degree of folly in what is just and lawful respecting music. They likewise celebrated the <term>orgies</term> <note>In this context, the word refers to the sacred rites or mysteries of a god, not necessarily the modern sense of the word</note> of Bacchus, and pursued pleasure more than was becoming. 

Besides this, they mingled lamentations with hymns, and paeans with dithyrambic compositions. They imitated with harps the sound of the pipe, and mingled all things with all, involuntarily deceiving through their ignorance of music. For they asserted that it did not possess any rectitude whatever; but that any one, whether he was a worthy or a worthless man, might judge with the greatest rectitude from the pleasure which it produced in the hearer. Composing, therefore, poems of this kind, and thus speaking publicly, they caused the multitude to act in an unlawful and daring manner with respect to music, by persuading them that they were sufficient judges of harmony. Hence theatres, from being silent, came to be noisy, as if capable of hearing what in the muses was beautiful, or the contrary:

But if by all this we have accomplished any thing of consequence, what can be said against us, O Megillus and Clinias?

**CLINIAS.** I seem to myself, O guest, to perceive something. For it appears that we have fortunately discussed all these particulars. For I nearly am at present in want of them; and both you and Megillus here have very opportunely met with me. For I will not conceal from you that which has now happened to me, but I will make it serve as an omen. The greatest part of Crete, then, endeavours at present to establish a certain colony, and commits the management of it to the <term>Cnoffians</term> <note>Also spelled "Cnossians," these were the people of Knossos, the legendary center of Minoan civilization on Crete.</note>. But the city of the Cnoffians appoints me and nine others to manage this affair; and at the same time orders us to establish those laws which please us Cretans, and which may be collected from other nations. And if those of other nations shall appear to be better than our own, it enjoins us not to reject them because they are foreign. We shall now, therefore, bestow this favour both upon ourselves and you. For, making a selection out of what has been said, we shall establish a city in our discourse, and consider it from the first time of its being inhabited. For thus a consideration of the object of our inquiry will take place, and which at the same time may be useful to me in the establishment of my future city.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** You do not announce war, O guest. Unless, therefore, it should not be agreeable to Megillus, be persuaded that I shall give you every assistance in my power.

**CLINIAS.** You speak well.

**MEGILLUS.** You may likewise depend on my assistance.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** You both speak in the most becoming manner. Let us therefore endeavour, in the first place, to build a city in discourse.

**C**OME then, what kind of a city is it proper to think this should be? I do not now ask about its present or future name (for this, perhaps, may be owing to its colonization, or some particular place; or, perhaps, the surname of some river or fountain, or of the Gods there resident, may have given a denomination to the new city by its celebrity); but this is rather what I wish to ask concerning it, whether it is situated near the sea, or on the main land?

**CLINIAS.** The city, of which we are now speaking, O guest, is distant from the sea about eighty <term>stadia</term> <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of length. Eighty stadia is roughly 9 miles (14.5 kilometers).</note>.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Are there any ports near it, or is it entirely without a port?

**CLINIAS.** It is furnished with ports, O guest, in the greatest possible degree.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Strange! What do you say? But is this region likewise <term>all-prolific</term> <note>Meaning the land is fertile enough to produce all necessary resources, allowing the city to be self-sufficient.</note>, or is it <term>indigent</term> <note>Lacking or in need of resources.</note> of some things?

**CLINIAS.** It is nearly indigent of nothing.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Is any city situated near it?

**CLINIAS.** Not very much so; on which account it became colonized. For, an ancient expulsion of the inhabitants having taken place in this city, the country was rendered desolate for an immense space of time.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** But how is it circumstanced with respect to plains, mountains, and woods?

**CLINIAS.** It is similar to the whole of the rest of Crete.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Do you mean to say that it is more rough than plain?

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** It is not therefore incurably unfit for the acquisition of virtue. For, if it was situated near the sea, and abounded with ports, but was not all-prolific,

For it is with me a fundamental position, that he only establishes laws in a proper manner, who, like an archer, always directs his attention thither where alone something of the <term>beautiful in conduct</term> <note>The Greek concept of *to kalon*, often translated as "the beautiful" or "the noble," refers to moral excellence and honor.</note> will always follow, but who leaves all other things, whether riches or anything else of this kind, when they subsist without beautiful manners.

For, instead of fighting on land, and in a legal manner, in consequence of becoming sailors they were accustomed to leap running in close array into the ships, and again rapidly to abandon them; and appeared to themselves to act in no respect base, in not daring to die, and wait for the attacks of the enemy. But they had a plausible pretext at hand, asserting that, by throwing away their arms, they could not be accused of shameful flight. They say, that language of this kind came to be adopted in consequence of naval engagements; language by no means worthy of infinite praise, but the contrary. For it is never proper to be accustomed to base manners, and especially for the best part of the citizens. **ATHENIAN GUEST.** ...who the people are that are to inhabit your <term>colony</term> <note>In the ancient Greek world, a colony (*apoikia*) was a new, independent city-state established by a mother city, often to relieve overpopulation or provide new farmland.</note>; whether such as are willing from every part of <note>Crete: A large Mediterranean island renowned in antiquity for its ancient traditions and legal systems.</note> Crete, so as that a great multitude will be collected from its several cities; or whether they are such as are chosen for the purpose of cultivating the land? The Guest is pointing out that the current population of the region already includes migrants from these diverse areas.</note> Argos, and Aegina, and other parts of Greece, inhabit this region. **GUEST.** This establishment of a colony, therefore, is not similarly easy to cities, since it does not take place after the manner of a swarming of bees, one race of friends proceeding from one region, and from friends, in order to form a settlement, being as it were besieged by a certain narrowness of land, or forced by other inconveniences of a similar nature. But it sometimes happens that a part of a city, being violently urged by <term>seditions</term> <note>Political unrest or civil strife within a city-state.</note>, is compelled to settle in some other place. And sometimes a whole city is forced to fly, in consequence of being vanquished in war. It is, therefore, partly easy for these to be colonized, and governed by laws, and partly difficult. For, when a colony is of one race, speaking the same language, and obeying the same laws, it is united by a certain friendship, and has a communion of priests, and every thing else of a similar kind; but it will not easily endure different laws, and a <term>polity</term> <note>The Greek *politeia*, referring to the constitution or political structure of a city.</note> foreign to its own. But such a colony, having been forced to sedition through the badness of its laws, and still desiring through custom those pristine manners by which it was corrupted, becomes, in consequence of this, refractory and disobedient to its colonizer and legislator. But when a colony is composed of all-various tribes, it will perhaps be more willingly obedient to certain new laws; but to conspire together, and, like horses under one yoke, to blow as it is said the same blast, requires a long time, and is extremely difficult. But legislation and the establishment of cities are the most perfect of all things with respect to the <term>virtue</term> <note>The Greek *arete*, meaning excellence of character and the fulfillment of one's purpose as a citizen.</note> of men.

**CLINIAS.** That seems likely; but please explain a bit more clearly why you said that.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** My good friend, I feel as though I have said something rather cynical while I was praising and reflecting on legislators. But if we have spoken at the right moment, there should be no problem. And yet, why should I be troubled? For nearly all human affairs seem to work in this way.

**CLINIAS.** What are you referring to?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** I was about to say that no human being ever actually establishes laws. Instead, <term>fortune</term> <note>original: "tyche". In Greek thought, this refers to random chance or luck, often seen as a force that disrupts human plans.</note> and all sorts of accidents, happening in all sorts of ways, are what give us our laws. It might be the violence of war that overturns a government and changes its laws, or the crushing weight of poverty. Disease, too, often forces people to innovate—especially during <term>pestilences</term> <note>Large-scale outbreaks of disease, like the Plague of Athens, which often led to a breakdown of traditional social order.</note> or when bad weather and failed harvests last for many years. Anyone who looks at these things would feel compelled to say, as I just did, that no mortal ever makes a law, but that nearly all human affairs are governed by luck. This might also be said about steering a ship, practicing medicine, or commanding an army. In all these cases, it seems true.

**CLINIAS.** What is true?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** That God—and along with God, <term>fortune and opportunity</term> <note>original: "tyche kai kairos". "Kairos" refers to the "right moment" or a critical turning point where action must be taken.</note>—govern every human affair. However, we must allow for a third, gentler factor: <term>art</term> <note>original: "techne". This refers to human skill, craft, or technical expertise. Plato is arguing that while we can't control luck, we can use our skill to navigate it.</note>. I believe it makes a massive difference whether you have the skill of a pilot or not during a storm. Wouldn't you agree?

**CLINIAS.** I certainly would.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Does the same not follow in other matters? Indeed, we must apply this same logic to lawmaking. Even when all the other conditions for a happy life in a country are met, a city still needs a legislator who possesses the true skill of his craft.

**CLINIAS.** You speak the truth.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Therefore, shouldn't a person who possesses the skill in any of these areas pray that fortune provides the right conditions, so that they don't have to rely entirely on luck?

**CLINIAS.** Most certainly.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** And wouldn’t everyone else we just mentioned speak in this same way, if someone asked them to reveal what they were praying for?

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** And I believe a <term>legislator</term> <note>A lawmaker or "nomothete," whose task is to draft the foundational legal code of a new city.</note> would do exactly the same.

**CLINIAS.** I think so too.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Come then, lawmaker (for we are addressing him now), tell us: what kind of city should we give you, and in what condition, so that you can take what is left there and govern it effectively? What would be the right thing for him to say next? Shouldn't we expect the lawmaker to speak like this?

**CLINIAS.** Like what?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** He will say: "Give me a city ruled by a <term>tyrant</term> <note>In ancient Greek thought, a 'tyrant' was an absolute ruler with total power. Here, the Guest is not looking for a cruel dictator, but a single individual who has the power to change the laws instantly without being blocked by committees or tradition.</note>." But let this tyrant be a young man with a good memory, a quick learner, brave, and naturally noble. And let that quality which we previously said must accompany every part of virtue be present in the tyrant's soul, so that his other qualities can actually be useful.

**CLINIAS.** Our guest, Megillus, seems to be saying that <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "sophrosyne". This refers to self-control, moderation, and a balanced mind.</note> is the quality that must follow the other virtues. Is that right?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** I am speaking, Clinias, of **popular temperance**,¹ and not the kind that someone might praise by calling it "wisdom." I mean that natural self-control that blooms instinctively in children and even in wild animals, where some are naturally unable to resist pleasures while others are naturally disciplined. This kind of temperance, when it exists on its own—separate from the many other things we call "good"—is not even worth mentioning, in my opinion. Do you follow me?

**CLINIAS.** Perfectly.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Our tyrant, then, must possess this natural self-control in addition to the other traits we mentioned, if the city is to adopt a <term>polity</term> <note>A system of government or a constitution.</note> through which it can live most happily in the fastest and best way possible. For no other political arrangement could ever be faster or more effective than this one.

***

¹ <note>Plato is referring here to "physical virtues"—those natural traits we are born with. In the philosophical tradition this text represents, these are seen as the foundation for higher stages of character: moral, political, "cathartic" (purifying), and "theoretic" (contemplative) virtues. For a deeper explanation of this hierarchy, one would look to the notes on the *Phaedo* (Plato's dialogue regarding the soul).</note>

**CLINIAS.** But how, my guest, and by what arguments can anyone who claims this convince himself that he is speaking correctly?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** It is easy to understand, Clinias, that this is simply the natural way of things.

**CLINIAS.** What do you mean? Do you not mean to claim this is true if the tyrant is a young man—self-controlled, quick to learn, possessing a good memory, brave, generous, and lucky?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Add nothing else, except that he proves to be a <term>legislator</term> <note>A "nomothete" or law-giver; a wise person tasked with drafting the foundational laws of a society.</note> worthy of praise, and that a certain luck leads him to this task. For if this happens, almost everything will be accomplished by a divine nature—the same nature that brings success to any city when it wishes for it to be truly prosperous. However, this success happens to a lesser degree <note>literally "in the second degree"</note> when two such characters are the rulers; even less so in the third degree, when there are three. The difficulty of achieving a prosperous government increases in proportion to the number of such rulers. Conversely, the ease of the task increases the fewer such rulers there are.

**CLINIAS.** You seem to be saying that the best city is created from a <term>tyranny</term> <note>In this context, an absolute rule by one person. Plato argues that if an absolute ruler is virtuous, they can change the laws for the better more quickly than a committee can.</note>, when a most excellent <term>legislator</term> works alongside a modest <term>tyrant</term>; and that the city is easily and rapidly transformed into its best version. You also seem to say that the second-best city is produced from an <term>oligarchy</term>, and the third from a <term>democracy</term>. Or is that not what you mean?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Not at all. Rather, the first and best city is produced from a <term>tyranny</term>; the second, from a <term>royal polity</term>¹; the third, from a certain kind of <term>democracy</term>; and in the fourth place, an <term>oligarchy</term>² will only be able to accept a transformation of this kind with the greatest difficulty. This is because, in an oligarchy, power is shared among many people. But we say these transformations will only take place when a true <term>legislator</term>—one who is naturally gifted for the role—is found, and when he shares a certain strength of purpose with those in the city who are capable of achieving great things. Where the rulers are fewest in number but most powerful, as in a <term>tyranny</term>, this transformation is accustomed to taking place in a rapid and easy manner.

***

¹ According to Plato, a <term>royal polity</term> <note>original: "basileia"</note> is created when everything is managed according to reason, and the supreme ruler is the best of men.
² An <term>oligarchy</term> <note>Rule by the few.</note> occurs when only a few people—and specifically the worst among them—rule the city. See the *Republic* <note>Plato's other major work on the ideal state.</note>.

<meta>Catchword: CLIN.</meta>

He must demonstrate everything through his own actions; he should praise and honor certain behaviors while blaming others, and he should shame those who do not follow his commands in their daily lives.

**CLINIAS.** How could we believe anything else, except that the other citizens will quickly follow a leader who possesses such powers of persuasion and force?

Such a thing does not happen today through any other way, nor will it ever. Indeed, this is not difficult for us to imagine, nor is it impossible to achieve. <page-num>110</page-num>

# THE LAWS.

...according to an ancient saying, God <note>original: "divinity"</note>—who contains within himself the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things—completes his straight course by revolving in a circular motion <note>This "circular progression" refers to the eternal and unchanging nature of divine action, which always remains consistent with itself while governing the world.</note> according to nature. Justice always follows him, acting as the punisher of those who abandon the divine law. The man who intends to be happy in the future will follow Justice in a humble and composed manner. 

But the man who is elevated by arrogance—whether because he excels in wealth, honors, or physical beauty—and whose soul is inflamed with insolence due to his youth and lack of intellect, thinks he does not need a ruler or a leader. Instead, he believes he is fully capable of leading others. Such a man is left abandoned by God. Being thus abandoned, he finds others like himself and acts with bravado, throwing everything into confusion. To many people, he may appear to be a person of great importance; but shortly afterward, he suffers the inescapable punishment of Justice, and he completely destroys himself, his household, and his country. Since these things are so, what should a prudent man do or think, and what should he avoid in both his actions and his thoughts?

**CLINIAS.** It is evident that every man ought to consider how he may be counted among those who follow God.

**GUEST.** What action, then, is friendly to and follows God? There is one principle, which possesses an ancient logic: that like is friendly to like when it is moderate; but those things that are immoderate <note>Meaning lacking in balance, restraint, or "measure."</note> are neither friendly to each other nor to that which is moderate. Now, God is the supreme measure of all things for us—much more so than any man could ever be, despite what some say. Therefore, he who wishes to become a friend to a being of this nature must, to the best of his ability, become like him. According to this reasoning, every temperate man <note>A "temperate" man (sophron) is one who possesses self-control and moral balance.</note> is a friend to God, for he is similar to him. But the intemperate man is dissimilar, different, and unjust; and other things follow from the same—

...reasoning will proceed in a similar manner. But we should understand that which follows these things, and which in my opinion is *the most beautiful*, and THE MOST TRUE<gloss>1</gloss> of all assertions: that for a good man to sacrifice to and interact with the GODS is, of all things, the most beautiful, the best, and the most useful way to achieve a happy life; and that, besides this, it is *fitting in the highest degree*. To receive gifts from one who is defiled is never appropriate for either a good man or a God. In vain, therefore, do the unholy spend much labor on the Gods; but such labor is most timely for all holy men. 

Such then is the goal which we ought to respect. But to the Gods superior to these, he will attribute things according to the odd number, and those opposite to the particulars we have just mentioned. 

After these Gods, a wise man will celebrate the <term>orgies: here meaning sacred rites or secret religious ceremonies, rather than the modern sense of revelry</term> of <term>dæmons: intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and mortals</term>, and after these, the honors of heroes. In the next place, statues of the household Gods must follow, which must be sacrificed to individually according to the law. After these things, such honors as are lawful must be paid to living parents. For to these, the first, greatest, and most ancient of all debts are to be paid. For everyone ought to believe that the whole of his possessions belongs to those by whom he was begotten and educated, and that he ought to supply their wants from these to the utmost of his power; beginning in the first place from his external possessions; in the second place, supplying them from those of his body; and, in the third place, from those of his soul: sharing all these in order to discharge the debt which he owes his parents for the care they have be-

But, on the death of parents, the most decent and beautiful monuments are to be raised to them; not exceeding the usual magnitude, nor yet less than those which our ancestors erected for their parents. Every year, too, attention ought to be paid to the decoration of their tombs. They ought likewise to be continually remembered and reverenced—and this with a moderate expense, adapted to the condition of our fortune. By always acting, therefore, and living in this manner, we shall each of us be rewarded according to our deserts, both by the Gods and those natures superior to our own, and shall pass the greatest part of our life in good hope. 

But the course of the laws themselves will show in what manner we ought to behave towards our offspring, relations, friends, fellow-citizens, and strangers, so as to conduct ourselves piously towards all these, and render our life pleasant, and adorned according to law; and this it will accomplish, partly by persuading, and partly by punishing through violence and justice, such manners as will not submit to persuasion; and thus, through the favoring will of the Gods, will render our city blessed and happy. But what a legislator whose conceptions are the same as mine ought necessarily to say of these things, but which cannot be adapted to the form of law, it appears to me an example should be presented, both to the legislator and those to whom he gives laws; and that, having discussed what remains to the utmost of our ability, we should after this commence the thesis of laws <term>thesis of laws: the formal proposal or laying down of the actual legal code, as opposed to the philosophical preamble currently being discussed</term>. Such things, indeed, cannot be easily comprehended in one description, so as to explain the manner in which they subsist; but we may thus be able to assert something stable respecting them.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Marriage laws, therefore, being established first of all, will appear to be well-founded with respect to the moral integrity of every city.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** We will, therefore, first of all speak of the simple law, which, perhaps, would exist in the following manner: "Every man should marry between thirty and thirty-five years of age; but he who does not shall be punished with both a fine and public disgrace." The fine would be a certain amount of money, and the disgrace would be of this or that particular kind. Let this then be the "simple" version of the law regarding marriage. But let the following be the "twofold" law. Every man should marry between the ages of thirty and thirty-five, considering, at the same time, that the human race shares in a certain nature of **immortality** <note>Plato argues that while individual humans die, the "race" remains immortal through the chain of children and grandchildren, effectively allowing a person to stay "connected" to time forever.</note>, which every person naturally desires to the highest degree. For the effort of mankind not to remain without a name after death is a desire of this kind. The human race, therefore, is something **connate** <term>connate</term> <note>Meaning "born with" or "inherently linked." Plato is saying humanity's existence is woven into the fabric of time itself.</note> with the whole of time, following and being joined with it to the end, becoming immortal by leaving children's children, and participating in immortality by being one and the same through the process of generation. For a man to willingly deprive himself of this is by no means a holy act; and he intentionally deprives himself who neglects having a wife and children. He, therefore, who is persuaded by this explanation shall be free from the punishment of a fine. But he who is not obedient to it, and who is not married by the time he is thirty-five years old, shall be fined every year a certain sum of money, so that his solitary life may not seem profitable or pleasant to him; and he shall not share in those honors which the younger people in a city pay to their elders. When these two versions are compared, it is possible to judge whether a law ought to be "double"—combining persuasion with threats—or whether it should be "simple" and short, employing only threats.

**MEGILLUS.** According to the **Laconic mode** <term>Laconic mode</term> <note>The "Laconic" style refers to the people of Laconia (Spartans), who were famous for being "men of few words" and preferring short, blunt speech.</note>, O Guest, the shorter version ought always to be preferred. Using this as a **paradigm** <note>A model or pattern to be followed.</note>, if these two types of laws were proposed for every subject, I would choose the longer version every time. It is, however, proper that the laws we have now established should be approved by—

# THE LAWS,

## BOOK V.

---

**L**ET every one then hear who has already heard what we have said respecting the Gods, and our dear progenitors <note>original: "progenitors" — meaning one’s ancestors and parents, whom Plato views as sacred figures within the family hierarchy.</note>. For, after the Gods, a man’s soul is the most divine of all his possessions, as being his most intimate property. But a man’s possessions are in every respect twofold. And the more excellent, and the better, possess **dominion** <term>dominion</term> <note>The power to rule or govern. In Plato’s view, the "better" part of a human (the soul) should naturally rule over the "worse" part (the body).</note>, but the inferior, and worse, are subject to command. The former, therefore, are always to be honoured before the latter. Hence, I properly exhort every man, when I say that he ought to honour his own soul in the second place, after our lords, the Gods, and their attendants <note>Plato refers here to "daemons" or lesser divine spirits that were thought to act as intermediaries between gods and humans.</note>. But, in short, no one honours his soul properly, though he appears to do so. For honour is, in a certain respect, a divine good: but nothing evil is honourable. He, therefore, who thinks that he enlarges his soul by certain discourses or gifts, when, at the same time, he does not render it better than it was before, appears indeed to honour it, but by no means does so. For every man, from his very childhood, thinks himself sufficient to know all things, and that he honours his soul by praising it, and by freely permitting it to do whatever it pleases. But we now say that he who acts in this manner injures, and does not honour, his soul. And yet it is necessary, as we have said, that it should be honoured in the second place after the Gods. Nor does he honour it who does not consider himself as the cause of his own errors, and of his numerous and mighty vices, but lays the blame upon others, and is always careful to exonerate himself <note>Plato emphasizes personal moral responsibility; blaming others for one's own failings is seen here as a failure to respect one's own soul.</note>. Such a one appears, indeed, to honour it, though this is far from being the case: for he injures it. Nor does he in any respect honour his soul who gratifies himself with pleasures contrary to reason, and the praise of the **legislator** <note>The law-giver or the moral authority of the state who defines what is virtuous.</note>: for he dishonours it, by filling it with vice and repentance. Nor yet does a man

...honor his soul, when he does not strenuously endure labors that are praised, or fear and pain, but sinks under them; for by doing all these things he dishonors his soul. Nor, again, does he honor his soul who thinks that merely to live is a thing in every respect good; for by such a conception he dishonors it. For he agrees with those who think that everything in the afterlife <note>original: "Hades" — the Greek underworld, the destination of all souls after death.</note> pertaining to the soul is bad; he neither opposes this view nor teaches that he is ignorant whether, on the contrary, the things concerning the Gods who dwell there are not the greatest of all goods. 

Nor yet, when anyone honors a certain physical beauty above virtue, is it at all different from truly and entirely dishonouring the soul. For such a person falsely asserts that the body is more honorable than the soul. For nothing born of the earth <note>referring to mortal, physical, or material things.</note> is more honorable than things that are heavenly <note>original: "Olympian" — referring to the dwelling of the Gods, representing spiritual and eternal perfection.</note>. But he who holds an opinion different from this regarding the soul is ignorant that he neglects this most admirable possession. 

Nor, again, does he adorn his soul with gifts who desires to possess riches in an unbecoming manner, or who is not grieved when he possesses them unjustly; indeed, such a person entirely fails to honor his soul. For he gives up that which is honorable, and at the same time beautiful, in his soul for the sake of a little gold; when, in fact, all the gold both upon and under the earth is of no equal value to virtue. 

In short, he who is not willing, by all possible means, to abstain from such things as the **legislator** <term>legislator</term> <note>The law-giver, in this context specifically referring to the one who crafts the fundamental moral and legal framework of the city.</note> ranks among the base and vicious, and to pursue to the utmost of his power such things as he places among the good and beautiful, does not perceive that, in all these things, he renders his soul—which is a most divine possession—in the highest degree dishonorable and base. 

For, in short, no one considers what is the greatest punishment for evil conduct: which is **becoming similar to vicious men**. But he who becomes similar to them avoids good men and good arguments, separates himself from the good, and becomes joined <note>original: "agglutinated" — stuck or glued together; a strong term for becoming inseparable from vice.</note> to the vicious, earnestly desiring their company. But, as a consequence of intimately associating with these, he must necessarily do and suffer such things as they naturally do and say to each other. 

Such a state, therefore, is not justice (for the just and justice are beautiful), but **punishment**; this being a state following after injustice, of which both he who partakes, and he who does not partake, are miserable: the one because he is not cured of his vice, and the other because, while many others are saved, he perishes. But, that I may sum up...

->THE LAWS.<-

To sum up everything, our honor consists in following things of a more excellent nature, and in making those things that are worse—but yet capable of being improved—as good as possible. No possession belonging to a man is more naturally suited to flee from evil, and to investigate and choose the best of all things, than the soul; nor, once it has chosen, is anything better suited to live in partnership with that good for the rest of life. On this account, the soul must be honored in the second degree <note>The Athenian Guest previously established that the Gods receive the first and highest honor; the soul follows immediately after.</note>. 

But every person will understand that the third honor, according to nature, is that of the body. It is, however, necessary to contemplate these honors and consider which of them are true and which are false <note>original: "adulterated" — meaning a corrupted or counterfeit version of honor.</note>. This is the business of a legislator. But he appears to me to announce what these honors are and what kind they should be; for instance, that the body is honorable not when it is beautiful, or strong, or swift, nor yet when it is large or healthy (though under these circumstances it <note>OCR originally read "i", likely a printing error for "it"</note> appears to be so to many), nor even when it possesses the opposites of these traits. 

Instead, those physical qualities that fall in the middle—touching upon the balance of this entire condition—are by far more moderate and safe. For the former extremes of beauty and strength render the soul arrogant and over-confident, while the latter extremes of weakness or illness make it humble and servile. 

The same logic applies to the possession of riches and property of every kind. For the possession of these things in an excessive degree produces hatred and civil unrest <note>original: "sedition" — internal conflict or rebellion within a city-state.</note>, both among cities and individuals. Conversely, a life of slavery is for the most part the consequence of a deficiency of these things. No one, therefore, should dedicate themselves to the acquisition of wealth for the sake of their children, merely to leave them extremely rich: for this will be better neither for the children nor for the city. 

The property of young men which is neither so great as to invite flattery <note>original: "adulation" — excessive praise or fawning used to manipulate the wealthy.</note>, nor so small as to lack the things necessary for life, is the most harmonious and the best of all. For when our wealth is in "symphony" and harmony with us in all things, it renders our life free from pain. It is proper, therefore, to leave children an abundance not of gold, but of modesty <note>original: "aidos" — a Greek concept involving a sense of shame, reverence, and respect for others.</note>. 

But we think that we shall accomplish this simply by scolding impudent young men. This, however, is not to be achieved by exhorting young men in the manner used today—I mean, by telling them that they ought to be modest in everything. A prudent legislator will instead advise old men to behave modestly before the youth, and above all things to take care that no young man ever sees or hears an elder doing or saying anything shameful <note>original: "base" — morally low or dishonorable.</note>. For where old men are void of shame, there young men will also be shamelessly bold.

For it is proper that he who is destined to be a great man should neither love himself, nor the things pertaining to himself, but that he should love just actions, whether they are accomplished by himself or by another. 

In consequence of this error, every man’s ignorance appears to himself to be wisdom. Hence, in short, though we do not know any thing, we are of opinion that we know all things. But, not permitting others to do that of which we ourselves are ignorant, we are compelled to err from their conduct. On this account every man ought to avoid the vehement love of himself, and to follow one better than himself, without paying any attention to shame.
