<meta>This page continues the Athenian’s discussion from page 126. Having established that human life is a constant "influx" of experience and that we must rely on recollection and divine hope, he now turns to the practical psychological calculus of the "four lives." He argues that our choices are fundamentally driven by the balance of pleasure and pain.</meta>

<page-num>127</page-num>

-># THE LAWS.<-

...that we are unwilling to possess each of these in an equal manner. All these <note>Referring to the categories of pleasures and pains mentioned previously.</note> both differ and at the same time do not differ in their quantity and magnitude, in their intensity, equality, and in those things that are the opposite of these, specifically regarding how we choose them. 

Because these factors are structured this way, we naturally desire a life in which many of both pleasure and pain exist in a great and vehement degree, but in which the pleasures outweigh the pains. However, we do not desire a life in which the opposites of these—the pains—are the dominant force. Furthermore, we do not wish for a life where there are only a few experiences of a small and isolated nature if the painful circumstances outweigh the pleasant ones. Instead, we desire a life in which the opposite is true. 

As we have stated before, we should consider a life to be in "equilibrium" when these two forces possess equal power. We desire the life that surpasses in the things that please us, and we are unwilling to accept the one that exceeds in the things that hurt us. It is necessary to understand that all our lives are naturally bound to these conditions; beyond this, we must recognize what things we naturally desire. If we were to say we wanted anything other than these, we would only be speaking out of ignorance and a lack of skill in understanding how to live. 

What, then, are these types of lives? What kind of lives must a person—one who perceives what is truly desirable and voluntary—choose for himself to set a personal law? By choosing what is friendly, pleasant, the best, and the most beautiful, how can one lead the most blessed life possible for a human being? 

We identify one life as **temperate**, another as **prudent**, another as **brave**, and we place a **healthy life** in the fourth position. We likewise establish four other lives that are the opposites of these: the **imprudent**, the **timid**, the **intemperate**, and the **diseased**. 

Therefore, anyone who knows what a <term>temperate life</term><note>Original Greek: *sophron*. A life characterized by self-control, moderation, and balance.</note> is will argue that it is mild in all things. It brings quiet pains, quiet pleasures, calm desires, and loves that are not "insane." On the other hand, an <term>intemperate life</term><note>A life lacking in self-restraint or moderation.</note> is reckless in everything, imparting intense pains, intense pleasures, violent and wild desires, and the most insane loves. 

In a temperate life, the pleasures outweigh the pains in magnitude, quantity, and frequency; however, in an intemperate life, the pains outweigh the pleasures. Consequently, one of these lives is necessarily more pleasant to us according to our nature, while the other is more painful. Nature itself does not permit a person who wishes to live pleasantly to choose an intemperate way of life on purpose. But it is evident,

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger’s psychological analysis of the "four lives" (the temperate, the brave, the wise, and the healthy). Having argued that we naturally choose the life where pleasure outweighs pain, he concludes that the virtuous life is the only one that truly satisfies this human desire. He then transitions from this philosophical "preface" to the practical work of drafting laws for a new city-state.</meta>

<page-num>128</page-num>

-># THE LAWS.<-

It is clear, if what we have now asserted is right, that every <term>intemperate</term> <note>original: "intemperate" (lacking self-control or restraint)</note> man is necessarily so against his own will. For the common people everywhere live without <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "temperance" (sophrosyne), the virtue of moderation and self-mastery</note>, either because they lack proper education, or because they lack self-control, or through a combination of both. The same logic should be applied when considering a diseased life versus a healthy life: both involve pleasures and pains, but in a healthy life, the pleasures outweigh the pains, while in a life of disease, the pains outweigh the pleasures. Our will, however, when choosing how to live, never consents to a life where pain exceeds pleasure; rather, we judge the life in which pleasure is dominant to be the more desirable one. 

We can also say that the temperate man experiences things that are fewer, smaller, and more refined than the intemperate man; the same is true for the prudent man compared to the foolish, and the brave man compared to the coward. The virtuous man’s life surpasses the others in pleasure, while the others surpass his in pain. Thus, the brave man has more pleasure than the coward, and the prudent man more than the foolish. In short, the life that embraces virtue—whether of the body or the soul—is more pleasant than a life of depravity. Beyond this, it excels other ways of living in beauty, correctness, virtue, and reputation. The result is that the person who lives virtuously lives more happily in every single respect and in total. Here, then, let the **preface to the laws** end.

But, following the preface, it is necessary for the law itself to follow; or more accurately, we must now write the laws of a <term>polity</term> <note>A system of government or an organized civil society.</note>. Just as a fabric is not woven from identical threads—since there is a difference in quality, with some threads being firm and strong while others are softer and more flexible—so too must we distinguish between those who will hold great power in the city and those who have received only a basic education. 

There are, however, two parts to establishing a polity: first, the appointment of governors, and second, the laws given to those governors themselves. But before any of this can happen, we must consider the following: when a shepherd, a cattle-herder, or a horse-breeder begins their work, they never attempt to care for their animals until they have first performed a <term>purification</term> <note>In the context of statecraft, "purification" refers to the act of "weeding out" or purging undesirable elements from a population before founding a new society.</note> suited to each of them. This involves separating the healthy from the sick, and the well-bred from the poorly-bred. They send the latter to other herds, keeping only the former; they know that otherwise, their labor would be wasted on bodies and souls that a flawed nature...

...will, indeed, be most proper to speak of the best <term>polity</term> <note>A system of government or a constitutionally organized state.</note>, and likewise of a second and third, and then leave it to every one’s option to choose that which pleases him the most. We therefore shall act in this manner; and, after we have spoken of a polity which is first, of one which is second, and of another which is the third in virtue, we shall leave it to the option of Clinias, and any other who may be present at the selection of these, to attribute to his country whichever of them he pleases. 

The first city and polity, therefore, and the best laws, subsist there where through the whole city that ancient proverb takes place in the most eminent degree, that "all things are common among friends." This then must be asserted, whether it now is or ever was adopted, that women, children, and all possessions should be common; and that private property should by all possible means be exterminated from life. Things too which are private by nature should everywhere, as much as possible, become common; such as the eyes, the ears, and the hands. For seeing, hearing, and acting, should be employed for common advantage. 

In like manner, all men should praise and blame the same things, rejoice in and be afflicted with the same circumstances, and as much as possible adopt such laws as will unite the city in the most eminent degree. No one can establish any bound of virtue more transcendently proper than this. The inhabitants of such a city, whether they are Gods <note>Namely, Gods according to similitude. On this account it is not proper to consider any other <term>paradigm</term> <note>An ideal model or pattern to be followed.</note> of a polity, but, inspecting this, we ought to explore such a one to the utmost of our power. But we say that the intention of a <term>politician</term> <note>In Plato’s context, a "statesman" or one who understands the art of governing for the sake of the soul.</note> who is gifted with intellect is not what the multitude says is the intention of a good legislator—by which I mean the idea that the city should be greater and richer than others, and that it should for the most part have dominion over the land and sea. To which they add that he who establishes laws properly ought to wish that the city may be the best and the most happy. But of these goals, some are capable of happening, while others are not. The legislator, therefore, will wish for what is possible, but he will not wish for the impossible to take place. For in the latter case, his wish would be in vain; therefore, he would not even attempt it.

For it is almost a necessity that people must be happy and, at the same time, worthy <note>Meaning virtuous or of good character.</note>. This then will be the object of his wish. ...one, however, may perhaps say, "Why not?" Because we say that the possession which is obtained from both just and unjust conduct is more than double that which is obtained by just means alone; and that the expenses which are neither becoming nor base are doubly less than those which are becoming and performed in a becoming manner. He, therefore, who acts in a contrary manner will never be richer than him who acquires more than double and spends less than half. 

But of these, the one is worthy, but the other not worthy, because he is parsimonious <note>Excessively frugal or stingy.</note>. Sometimes, indeed, this latter character is perfectly vicious; but, as we have just now said, he is never good. For he who receives both justly and unjustly, and spends neither justly nor unjustly, is indeed rich because he is parsimonious; but he who is perfectly vicious, as being for the most part prodigal <note>Spending money in a wasteful or reckless way.</note>, is extremely poor. And he who spends in a becoming manner, and alone acquires justly, will never at any time become remarkably rich, nor yet excessively poor; so that our assertion is right: that the very rich are not good men. But, if they are not good, they are not happy. 

With us, however, the establishment of laws looks to this: that the citizens may become most happy, and in the highest degree friends to each other. But the citizens will never be friends where there is much judicial controversy and unjust transactions with each other, but rather where the least of these is found. We have said, too, that there ought to be neither gold nor silver in the city, nor yet an anxious pursuit of gain through <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>Manual trades or crafts which were often looked down upon by ancient philosophers as distracting from civic duty and virtue.</note> and <term>usury</term> <note>Lending money at interest.</note>, or base cattle, but that wealth should be acquired from such things as agriculture imparts and affords. Yet this must be done in such a manner that it may not compel the citizens to neglect those things for the sake of which riches are desired—these are the soul and body, which without <term>gymnastic</term> <note>Physical education and athletic training.</note> and the other disciplines will never be of any worth. 

On this account, we have said more than once that an attention to money ought to be honored in the last place. For, since all the concerns in which every man is seriously engaged are three, an attention to riches properly ranks in the last and third place; the concerns of the body possess the middle; and those of the soul the first place. And, indeed, the <term>polity</term> <note>The form of government or constitution.</note> which we are now considering will be governed by proper laws if it distributes honors in this manner. But if any of the laws established in it shall appear to prefer the health of the body to temperance, or riches to both health and temperance, it will appear to be improperly established. A legislator, therefore,

This will be carried out in a fitting manner when every person who becomes an inhabitant of the colony possesses everything else equally. However, since this is not possible—as one person coming to settle there will possess more money and another less—it is necessary, for the sake of many advantages and for equality within the city, that property should be held unequally. This ensures that when citizens receive magistracies <term>Public offices or positions of government authority.</term>, taxes, and distributions, they do so according to the honor attached to each rank. This is not based solely on their own virtue or that of their ancestors, nor on the strength or beauty of their bodies, but rather on a system where these honors are equalized as much as possible—that is, distributed unequally but proportionally—so that the citizens do not disagree with one another. For this reason, it is necessary to have four divisions based on the size of possessions. These should be called the first, second, third, and fourth divisions (or some other names), so that whether citizens keep the same property, or become rich after being poor, or poor after being rich, each person may move to the property rank that fits their current status. For this purpose, I shall propose the following legal scheme:

We say that in a city which is to remain free from that greatest of diseases—which is more accurately called discord or sedition <term>Conduct or speech inciting people to rebel against the authority of a state; here referring to class warfare between the rich and poor.</term>—none of the citizens should be either extremely poor or extremely rich, for both conditions produce unrest. Therefore, it is now necessary for a legislator to define the limits for each. Let the limit of poverty be the value of the basic allotted distribution, which must remain stable; no magistrate, nor anyone who loves honor for the sake of virtue, should ever allow this minimum to be reduced for anyone. Once the legislator has established the measure of these distributions, he will permit a citizen to possess double, triple, or even quadruple this amount. But if anyone acquires more than this—whether it is found, received as a gift, earned through mechanical arts <term>Manual trades or crafts, which were often considered "base" compared to agriculture or politics in ancient Greece.</term>, or gained by any other such stroke of luck—he must give the remainder to the city and to the Gods, the guardians of the...

# THE LAWS,

## BOOK VI.

**AFTER** all that has now been said, the next thing that remains for you to do will be the establishment of <term>magistrates</term> <note>Public officials or civil officers who hold executive or judicial power within the city-state.</note> in the city.

**CLINIAS.** It will be so.

**GUEST.** Two distinct categories are found to exist regarding the organization of a <term>polity</term> <note>A system of organized government or a specific civil society.</note>. In the first place, the establishment of magistrates: how many there ought to be, and in what manner they ought to be appointed. In the next place, we must consider the laws which are to be assigned to the various magistrates—specifically, what laws, how many, and what kind will be suited to each office. But, before we choose the magistrates, let us mention some specific details regarding their election.

**CLINIAS.** What details are these?

**GUEST.** These: It must be perfectly evident that, since legislation is a monumental task, a person who fails to appoint proper magistrates in a well-regulated city will find no benefit from even the best-established laws. Instead, such an oversight will result in a great deal of mockery, and that person will become the cause of the city being burdened with the heaviest injuries and disasters.

**CLINIAS.** Undoubtedly.

**GUEST.** We will, therefore, consider this as it applies to you now, my friend, regarding this government and city. For you see it is necessary that those who properly undertake the office of magistrate should have been sufficiently tested from their youth, as should their family lineage, up until the time of their election. Furthermore, it is necessary that those who are to choose the magistrates should be educated in lawful customs, so that they may be able to judge correctly who should be accepted for office and who should be rejected.

<summary>Book VI begins with the Athenian Stranger explaining that the success of a city depends not just on good laws, but on the careful selection and education of the officials who enforce them. He emphasizes that poorly chosen leaders will lead to the city's ruin and public ridicule.</summary>

On the third day <note>This continues the multi-day election process for the Council, a representative body governing the city's daily affairs.</note>, nominees shall be selected from the property of the third order <note>The citizens are divided into four classes or "orders" based on their wealth. The third order represents the middle-to-lower income group.</note>. Participation for these first three orders is mandatory; however, those in the fourth and smallest property order are exempt from any fine if they choose not to act as a counsellor. On the fourth day, nominees shall be selected from the fourth and smallest property order. On this day, those from the third and fourth orders are exempt from fines for not participating. However, any citizen from the first or second orders who refuses to participate shall be fined: a member of the second rank will pay a fine three times the standard amount, and a member of the first rank will pay four times the standard amount <note>The law imposes higher penalties on the wealthy to ensure they fulfill their civic duties, while being more lenient toward the poor who may need to work.</note>. 

On the fifth day, the magistrates shall display the names of all the selected nominees for all citizens to see. Every man chosen must serve as a counsellor; if he refuses, he will be charged the initial fine. From this large pool of nominees, half—that is, one hundred and eighty people—shall be chosen by lot to serve as the Council for the year.

This method of election establishes a middle ground between a monarchy and a democracy, a balance that every government should strive to maintain. For true friendship cannot exist between slaves and masters, nor between the wicked and the virtuous, if they are treated as though they are exactly the same. When equal honors are given to unequal people, the result is actually inequality, unless a sense of proportion is applied; it is this lack of proportion that causes cities to be filled with <term>seditions</term> <note>original: "stasis"—civil unrest, internal conflict, or factional fighting within a city.</note>. There is an ancient and true saying that "equality produces friendship," which is a very elegant and correct idea. However, we are often confused because it is not always clear what kind of "equality" is being discussed.

In reality, there are two distinct types of equality. They share the same name, but they are almost opposite in practice. Any city or lawmaker can easily apply the first type: the equality of measure, weight, and number <note>This is "arithmetical equality," where everyone gets the exact same amount regardless of effort or merit.</note>. But the second type—the truest and best equality—is much harder to perceive. This is the **judgment of Jupiter** <note>original: "Dios krisis"—This refers to the "Judgment of Zeus," meaning a divine or perfect distribution of justice based on merit.</note>. Though humans only use a small portion of it, whenever it is applied by cities or individuals, it produces everything good. This higher equality distributes more to the greater and less to the lesser, giving to each person what is appropriate to their nature.

But let the attention which is to be paid to things of this kind be as follows:—Sixty men should each of them defend their own place, not only on account of enemies, but for the sake of those who call themselves friends. And if any one, whether he is a servant or free, injures his neighbour, or any other citizen, if the offence is small, he shall be judged by those five governors, but if great, by seventeen men, together with the twelve, and shall be fined as far as to three <term>minæ</term> <note>A mina was a Greek unit of currency and weight; three minae would be a significant fine for a common citizen.</note>.

But no judge or magistrate ought to be exempt from giving an account of his conduct when called upon, except such as like kings bring things to a conclusion. Besides this, the <term>præfects of the land</term> <note>The agronomoi, or rural inspectors.</note>, if they behave insolently towards the subjects of their care, by enjoining them unequal tasks, or taking any thing by force from the husbandmen, or if they receive any thing which is given through flattery, or distribute justice unjustly, in consequence of yielding to <term>adulation</term> <note>Excessive flattery or sycophancy used to influence a decision.</note>;—in any of these cases, they shall be disgraced by the whole city. But for other injuries which they may commit in their office, they shall voluntarily be fined by the inhabitants of the same village, and by their neighbours, as far as to one <term>mina</term>. If, however, they are unwilling, either for greater or smaller injuries, to pay the proper fine, in consequence of believing that, during their transitions from place to place every month, they shall escape punishment,—in this case, they shall be sentenced by a common judgment to pay the injured person the double of his loss. So that he who has acted in a becoming manner as a servant, ought to glory in his conduct more than he who has properly exercised the authority of a master:—in the first place, as having been properly subservient to the laws, which is the same as being a servant to the Gods; and in the next place, to old men who have conducted themselves in an honourable manner towards youth.

If any public magistrate dies before they have served for at least thirty days, a replacement shall be chosen by the same group responsible for that office. Likewise, when any guardian of <term>orphans</term> <note>in this context, children who have lost their parents and require legal protection for their inheritance and upbringing</note> dies, the relatives on both the father's and mother's side—as far as first cousins—who are present at the time, must appoint a replacement within ten days. If they fail to do so, each relative will be fined one <term>drachma</term> <note>original: "drachma." A silver coin that represented a standard unit of currency in ancient Greece</note> per day until a new guardian is appointed.

A city ceases to be a functional city if its courts of justice are not properly established. A "mute" judge—one who, during their questioning, does not speak more than the <term>litigants</term> <note>the parties involved in a legal dispute</note>—will never be able to decide a case justly. For this reason, judges cannot rule well if there are too many of them, nor if there are only a few who are of poor character. It is essential that the matter under inquiry be clearly stated by both sides. Time, patience, and frequent questioning are necessary to resolve legal doubts.

Because of this, those involved in a dispute should first go to their neighbors and friends to discuss their complaints. If they cannot resolve the case with their help, they should proceed to a second court. If these first two efforts fail to reconcile them, a third court shall bring the matter to a final conclusion. 

In some respects, the establishment of courts is a form of electing magistrates, as every magistrate must act as a judge in certain matters. While not every judge is a full magistrate, a judge is, in a sense, a significant magistrate on the day they are presiding over a trial. Therefore, considering judges as magistrates, let us define which ones are suited for our purposes, what cases they will oversee, and how many are required for each task. -># THE LAWS.<-

...ornamented by the governors of choirs <note>In ancient Greek cities, "choirs" or choruses were central to religious and civic life, involving music, dance, and poetry performed at public festivals.</note>, and likewise by the legislators, in conjunction with the guardians of the laws <note>The *nomophylakes*, or high-ranking officials responsible for ensuring that the laws were respected and properly implemented.</note>, that they may supply what we have left deficient. But it is necessary, as we have said, respecting all such things as are small and numerous, that some particulars should be omitted by the legislator, in which the magistrates becoming every year skilful, and being admonished by experience, they may be able every year to supply what is deficient; till it shall appear that these discussions and legal institutes have obtained a sufficient bound. The space of ten years, therefore, will be a length of time both moderate and sufficient for obtaining an experience in sacrifices and choirs, and every other particular. 

But in order to accomplish this, he who supplies these deficiencies should live in common with the legislator: and on his death, the several magistrates having informed the guardians of the laws of his decease, must supply his place in correcting what is amiss, till every thing shall appear to have attained the consummation of excellence. When this period arrives, having given stability to these institutes, they are to be used in conjunction with other laws which the legislator has ordained from the beginning; respecting which, nothing should ever be voluntarily changed. But if any necessity shall, at any time, appear to urge a <term>mutation</term> <note>A change or alteration in the legal code.</note>, all the magistrates ought to consult together on this occasion, all the people should be assembled, and all the oracles of the Gods explored. If all these accord, then a change in the laws may be made, but by no means unless this is the case; but that which impedes, shall always obtain dominion according to law. 

Whenever, therefore, any one who has arrived at five-and-twenty years of age, beholding and being beheld by others, believes that he has found one of his own disposition, and adapted for the <term>communion</term> <note>In this context, the shared life and partnership of marriage.</note> and procreation of children, he shall marry within thirty-five years of age. But, in the first place, let him hear how the becoming and adapted are to be investigated. For it is requisite, as **Clinias** says, prior to the laws, to give a preface accommodated to each.

**CLINIAS.** You very properly remind us, O guest; and your discourse appears to me to be both seasonable and highly fitting.

**GUEST.** You speak well. Let us, therefore, speak as follows: O young man, born of good parents, it is proper to contract those marriages which appear honourable to prudent men. But these exhort neither to avoid marriage with the poor, nor to pursue with avidity marriage with the rich, but, all other things being equal <note>original: "cæteris paribus"</note>, always honouring the inferior, to enter into communion with it.

He, therefore, who in all his actions is more rash and hasty than is becoming, should desire that the daughter of parents of more composed manners may be united to him in marriage; but he who is naturally of a contrary disposition should enter into alliance with a contrary character. 

And in every marriage this one thing should be observed: that every one should enter into such a matrimonial connection as is advantageous to the city, and not such a one as is most pleasant to himself. For every one always naturally tends to that which is most similar to himself; whence the whole city becomes anomalous <note>Inconsistent or unequal in its social makeup.</note> both in wealth and manners, when it partakes in the highest degree of those things which we are unwilling should happen to ourselves. 

If, then, in our discourse we should order by law that the rich should not marry with the rich, nor the powerful with the powerful, but should compel those whose manners are more hasty to marry those whose manners are more slow, and the more slow to marry with the more hasty, we should not only appear ridiculous to, but excite the anger of, the multitude. For it is not easy to understand that a city ought to be like a cup, in which the mad wine, when first poured forth, effervesces; but, being corrected by another deity <note>original: "Viz. water." In Greek tradition, mixing wine with water was seen as an act of "sobering" the drink, often attributed to a god like Dionysus or Hera in a different aspect.</note>, who is a sober God, and thus obtaining a beautiful conjunction, it becomes a good and moderate drink. 

But no one, as I may say, is able to see this taking place in the formation of children by the mingling of the sexes. On this account, therefore, we should not compel the citizens to things of this kind by law, but endeavour to charm them into the persuasion that they ought to prefer equability <note>A state of balance or evenness of temperament.</note> in the natural disposition of their children to the equality of the most opulent alliance; and that we ought to deter, by disgrace, him who makes riches the object of his pursuit in marriage, and not compel him to a contrary mode of conduct by a written law. 

Let these, then, be the exhortations respecting marriages, together with what we have previously asserted—I mean, that we ought to aspire after perpetuity of nature, by always leaving behind us children of children, as servants of divinity, instead of ourselves. ->### THE LAWS.<-

authority in this affair must always be vested in the nearest kindred, in conjunction with the guardians. If any thing preparatory to initiation, or other sacred operation, shall be found necessary for things future, present, or past, pertaining to marriage, it will be proper to interrogate the interpreters <note>original: *exegetai*; these were official religious interpreters in Athens who provided guidance on sacred law and traditional rituals.</note> of sacred concerns; and each person, being persuaded by these, should think that he has accomplished every thing sufficiently. To drink, however, to intoxication, is never at any time becoming, nor safe, except in the festivals of that **God who is the giver of wine** <note>Dionysus (Bacchus), the god of wine and ecstasy.</note>. Neither, therefore, is it proper that this should take place at the nuptial feast, when the bride and bridegroom ought particularly to be in a sound state of mind, as having changed the former condition of their life in no small degree; and in order, at the same time, that offspring may always be produced as much as possible from prudent parents. For it is nearly immanifest what night or day may generate offspring in conjunction with divinity. Children, therefore, ought not to be begotten when the body is in a relaxed and disfluent state through ebriety <note>intoxication or drunkenness</note>, but when it is compact, stable, and quiet. 

But he who is filled with wine hurries and is hurried away every where, being agitated with insane fury both in body and soul. Hence, he who is intoxicated, as being delirious, must disseminate in a vicious manner. So that it is probable such a one will beget offspring anomalous, unfaithful, and void of rectitude, both in their manners and corporeal frame. Hence, it is requisite to guard against intoxication, both through the whole year, and through the whole of life, but especially at the time of procreation, and neither to do such things as spontaneously introduce disease, nor such as participate of insolence or injustice. For, these being necessarily impressed in the souls and bodies of the offspring in a foetal state, the impressions become worse than their originals. But especially on the wedding day and night <meta>catchword: night</meta>

For it incites them to fly within these for shelter, and not repel the enemy; and leads them to think that the safety of the city does not consist in guarding it perpetually both night and day, but that, sleeping under the protection of walls and gates, they shall be truly safe; as if they were born for sloth, and not to labour. They are, indeed, ignorant that ease is truly produced from labour; and, as it appears to me, labour is again the natural result of base ease.

But, if there is any occasion of walls for men, the houses of individuals should be so raised from the first, that the whole city, by its equality and similitude, may be one wall, and that all the houses may have a sufficiently secure passage to the different roads of the city. And in this case, indeed, the city, having the form of one house, will be no unpleasant spectacle, and will be in every respect adapted to the ease of its guards and the safety of the whole. But when children are begotten according to law, if any one has connection with another man's wife, or a woman with any man but her husband, while children are begotten by them, let them be punished in the manner mentioned above when they did not beget children. 

In the next place, let the married men and women that live temperately with respect to all such things as these, be honoured, but those that live in a contrary manner be disgraced. And if the greater part of the citizens conduct themselves with moderation in things of this kind, let these particulars be passed over in silence, without being established by law. But if the conduct of the greater part is disordered in things of this kind, let them be legally established, and a judgment made of such conduct according to the established laws. 

The first year is the beginning of the whole of life to every one. This ought to be written in paternal temples, as the beginning of life, both to boys and girls. **C**hildren, therefore, both male and female, having been born, we shall act with the greatest propriety by speaking next about their education <term>education: The Greek concept of *paideia*, which encompasses not just schooling, but the total physical, mental, and moral upbringing of a citizen.</term> and discipline; for to pass this over in silence is completely impossible. However, when it is discussed, it will appear to us to be more like a kind of teaching and advice than formal laws. For the many small and hidden circumstances that happen privately in every home—since they arise easily through the pain, pleasure, and desires of individuals and often go against the intentions of the legislator—make the characters of the citizens diverse and inconsistent. This is harmful to cities. Because these instances are so small and frequent, it would be inappropriate and unseemly to punish them with legal fines. It would also lead to the destruction of written laws, as men would become accustomed to breaking the law in many small matters. Thus, it is difficult to establish laws for these things, yet impossible to leave them in silence. I will try to make my meaning clear by bringing an example to light, as what has been said so far seems a bit obscure.

**C**LINIAS. You speak most truly.

**G**UEST <note>The "Guest" is the Athenian Stranger, the main speaker in this dialogue, who is guiding the Cretan Clinas and the Spartan Megillus in designing a perfect city.</note>. **G**UEST. And I think that the most beautiful bodies are simply those which, right from earliest infancy, grow in the most proper manner.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**CLINIAS.** That is true.

**GUEST.** What then? When there is a massive influx of growth without a great deal of moderate exercise, do we not know that it produces ten thousand ailments in the body?

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**GUEST.** Therefore, a great deal of exercise is necessary during the time when abundant nourishment is being added to the body.

**CLINIAS.** What are you saying, Guest? Shall we order newborns and the very young to undergo the most strenuous labor?

**GUEST.** By no means. I am speaking of an even earlier stage: those who are still being nourished in their mother's womb.

**CLINIAS.** What do you mean, my good man? Are you actually speaking of those who are still carried in the womb?

**GUEST.** I am. However, it is not surprising that you might be unfamiliar with the "exercise" of such as these. Even though it may seem absurd, I am willing to explain it to you.

**CLINIAS.** By all means, please do.

**GUEST.** In our city <note>The Guest is from Athens, where certain sports were more common than in the Cretan or Spartan societies of the other speakers.</note>, this sort of thing is more easily understood because children there engage in certain sports more than is perhaps proper. In addition to the training, they take each bird by the wing and walk many stadia <term>stadia: An ancient Greek unit of distance; one stadium was approximately 600 feet or 185 meters.</term> with the smaller birds in their hands and the larger ones under their arms. By this practice, they demonstrate to anyone capable of understanding that all bodies benefit from motion and shaking—provided it does not reach the point of exhaustion. This applies whether the motion comes from the body itself, or from being carried in a carriage, on a ship, on a horse, or by any other means. Because of...

**GUEST.** Let us accept this, then, as a basic principle for both the body and the soul of very young children: that nourishment and constant movement, applied both day and night, are beneficial for all young bodies and souls—but especially for the very youngest. Ideally, they should live in a state as close as possible to someone constantly sailing at sea. Since that is impossible, we should try to approach that condition as nearly as we can when we care for infants. We can infer that this is the right course because both the nurses of infants and those who perform the healing rituals of the **Corybantes** <term>Corybantes: Priests of the goddess Cybele known for performing wild, rhythmic music and ecstatic dances used as a form of "musical therapy" to heal emotional or mental distress.</term> have found it useful through experience. For when mothers want to help children who have trouble sleeping, they do not try to achieve it through silence; instead, they do the opposite, moving them gently in their arms. They don't use silence, either, but sing to them. In short, they "enchant" their children with melody, much like a flute player. This is the same method used in the remedies for the "mad" **Bacchanalians** <term>Bacchanalians: Followers of the god Bacchus (Dionysus) who engaged in frenzied, rhythmic rituals to achieve religious ecstasy.</term>, employing both the dance and the "Muse of motion."

**CLINIAS.** What, then, Guest, is the specific reason for this?

**GUEST.** It is not very difficult to understand.

**CLINIAS.** How so?

**GUEST.** Both of these conditions—the child's distress and the worshippers' frenzy—are rooted in fear. They are types of terror that arise from a poor state of the soul. Therefore, when someone applies an external agitation to these kinds of feelings, this external motion overpowers the internal, chaotic, and "insane" movement. Once that internal motion is defeated, it brings a peaceful quiet to the soul and settles the pounding of the heart, which was otherwise unbearable. In some cases, this leads to the benefit of sleep; in others, for those who are awake, it restores them from a state of madness to a state of sound mind through dancing and the music of the flute, in connection with the gods to whom they offer sacrifices. These explanations carry a good deal of logic.

**CLINIAS.** They certainly do.

**GUEST.** But if these practices have such power, we should understand one thing: any soul that has been familiar with fear since infancy will be more accustomed to being afraid. Everyone will admit that this is a training in cowardice, rather than in courage.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**CLINIAS.** Undoubtedly.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** This, then, is a core principle for us: that luxury makes the temperament of youth irritable, quick to anger, and violently agitated by trivial things. Conversely, excessive and harsh servitude <note>The Guest refers here to an upbringing that is too strict or oppressive.</note> causes them to be dejected, ungenerous, haters of mankind, and unfit for living in a society.

**CLINIAS.** But how will the entire city be able to educate infants, who are incapable of understanding what is said to them, and who cannot yet experience any formal discipline?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** In this way: Every animal, as soon as it is born, is accustomed to making certain sounds with a loud voice; and this is particularly true of the human species, which adds weeping to this crying out.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Nurses, therefore, wishing to know what infants need, guess based on the things they offer them. If something makes the child silent, they consider it to have been offered in a proper manner; but if the child cries and makes a noise, they consider it improperly offered. For in children, crying out and tears are signs—by no means happy ones—of the things they love and hate. This period of life lasts no less than three years, which is a significant portion of time to pass through either well or poorly.

**GUEST.** That all these particulars which we are now discussing are called by many "unwritten laws" <note>Ancient Greeks distinguished between written statutes and *agraphoi nomoi*—unwritten customs and traditions that hold a society together.</note>, and those which are named the laws of a country are actually nothing more than a collection of these. Furthermore, what we just said—that these matters should neither be called formal laws, nor be left in silence—was a point well made. For these customs are the bonds of every <term>polity: the organized society or the form of government of a city-state</term>. They exist between all the laws that are already written or will be written in the future. They are the ancestral customs of a country, and they are ancient in every sense. These traditions, when established properly and made familiar through habit, will provide a safeguard for the written laws. But when they are established poorly, confusion will follow. It is just like in buildings: when the pillars that support them are taken away, the whole structure falls to the ground. Some parts collapse onto others, and those beautiful parts of the building that were raised high on the pillars become a heap of ruins because their supports have failed. 

Considering this, Clinias, it is necessary that you should strengthen your city on all sides, since it is a new city. To the best of your power, you should not omit anything, whether great or small, that might be called laws, manners, or habits of study. For a city is bound together by all of these; no single one of them can remain stable without the others. So, we should not be surprised if the body of law grows quite long, because so many small things appear to be legal matters, or because many customs are flowing together at once.

**CLIN.** You speak correctly; we shall keep this in mind.

Play, however, is a natural and spontaneous activity for children; when they engage in it, they nearly invent the games themselves. One woman from each of the twelve tribes should be placed in charge of the nurses and the entire group <note>The Greek term *agelē*, translated here as "herd," refers to the organized groups of children in ancient Dorian educational systems</note> for the duration of a year. Her duty is to ensure that everything prescribed by the guardians of the law is carried out in an orderly fashion. These women should be chosen by those who preside over marriages, picking one from each tribe who is of a similar age to themselves.

She is authorized to punish any person acting unjustly—including male and female slaves or foreign residents of either sex—by using the city servants. However, if a citizen is involved and she is uncertain about the proper punishment, she must bring them before the <term>ædiles: Roman-style city magistrates; here, the translator uses the Latin term for the Greek *astynomoi*, or city-wardens, who oversaw public order</term> to receive a sentence. It is also necessary that their attention be turned toward formal training <note>original: "disciplines"</note>. Boys should be sent to instructors for equestrian exercises, archery, javelins, and slinging. Girls should also receive this training if it is permitted for them, especially so they may become familiar with the use of weapons. At present, however, almost all men are ignorant of how these matters are actually circumstances.

**CLIN.** What do you mean?

**GUEST.** That there is a natural difference between the right and left hands regarding various actions of the hands. For the feet and the lower parts of the body, there appears to be no difference in their capacity for labor. But in our hands, we each of us become, as it were, "lame" through the ignorance of our nurses and mothers. By nature, each limb possesses nearly equal power; but because we do not use them properly, through habit we create a difference between them. Indeed, in certain tasks, there is no great difference in the use of the hands.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the upbringing of children in the ideal state. # THE LAWS.

->[Page 188]<-

Thus, using the lyre with the left hand and the pick <note>original: "plectrum"</note> with the right is a matter of no great consequence; and the same is true for other tasks of a similar nature. However, failing to apply this principle in other areas is nearly a form of folly. The customs of the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of the Eurasian Steppe, renowned in antiquity for their skill as mounted archers.</note> prove the truth of these observations. They do not merely hold the bow in their left hand and the arrow in their right, but use both hands for both tasks interchangeably. There are many other examples of this among chariot drivers and others. From all of this, we can learn that those who make the left hand weaker <note>original: "imbecil"</note> than the right are acting against nature. 

As I have said, this is of little consequence when dealing with picks made of horn <note>original: "horned plectra"</note> and similar instruments; but in battle, where it is necessary to use iron weapons, bows, and spears, it is of great consequence. It is of the highest importance when one must use arms against arms. There is, indeed, a great difference between one who has learned and one who has not, and between one who has exercised and one who has not. For instance, a man perfectly trained in the <term>pancration: an ancient Greek combat sport that combined elements of boxing and wrestling, allowing almost any tactic except biting or eye-gouging</term>, or in boxing or wrestling, is not unable to fight from his left side. However, he becomes clumsy and confused in his movements if his opponent forces him to change position and fight from his right side. 

The same principle, in my opinion, should be considered proper for the use of arms and everything else. For a person who possesses a twofold power—that is, the ability to defend themselves and to defeat others—should not, as far as they are able, allow either of these powers to remain idle or unskilled. If anyone possessed the nature of Geryon or Briareus <note>Geryon was a giant often depicted with three bodies, and Briareus was one of the "Hundred-Handers" (Hecatoncheires) of Greek mythology.</note>, since they would be capable of using a hundred hands, they ought to be able to hurl a hundred spears with all those hands. 

All these matters should be under the direction of the male and female governors. The female governors should inspect the play and the nourishment of the children, while the male governors oversee their training <note>original: "disciplines"</note>. This ensures that all boys and girls, having the full use of both their feet and both their hands, may as much as possible avoid damaging their natural abilities through habit. 

It follows that two types of education must be used: gymnastics for the needs of the body, and music for the well-being of the soul. Furthermore, gymnastics is divided into two parts: dancing and wrestling. Of dancing, one kind mimics the style of the Muse, preserving a sense of grandeur combined with a spirit of freedom <note>original: "liberal"</note>; another kind is practiced for the sake of physical fitness, agility, and the beauty of the various parts and members of the body,

...body, aptly bends and stretches each part, imparting to them a rhythmical motion, while at the same time following the entire order of the dance. 

Regarding wrestling, we must consider the styles adopted by Antæus <note>A giant of Libya who wrestled travelers to the death; he was famously defeated by Heracles.</note> or Cercyon <note>A King of Eleusis who challenged passers-by to a wrestling match to the death; he was killed by Theseus.</note> as part of their arts. But the specifics of proper wrestling—clinging around the neck, or with the hands, or around the sides—when the desire for victory and a healthy body are applied for the sake of strength and health, these are useful for every purpose and are not to be omitted. Instead, both teachers and students are to be instructed that, when we establish the laws regarding these exercises, such details should be kindly shared by the teacher and gratefully received by the student. 

Nor must we omit those imitations in choirs that are worthy of being copied: in this case, the armed sports of the Curetes <note>Mythological armed youths who performed clashing dances to protect the infant Zeus.</note> and, in Lacedæmon <note>The region of Greece where Sparta was located.</note>, those of the Dioscuri <note>The "sons of Zeus," the twins Castor and Pollux.</note>. Even our virgin mistress Minerva <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena; she was the patron of wisdom and strategic war, often depicted in full armor.</note>, taking delight in the sport of the choir, does not think it right to play with empty hands; rather, being perfectly adorned in full armor, she completes the dance in this manner. It is proper that all boys and girls should imitate the goddess in this regard, honoring her kindness both for the necessity of war and for the sake of festivals. 

It is likewise proper that boys, immediately before they go to battle, should offer prayers and lead sacred processions in honor of all the Gods. They should be adorned with arms and horses, performing their prayers to the Gods and the sons of the Gods, sometimes moving swifter and sometimes slower in their dancing and as they proceed toward battle. Contests and the practice rounds for contests should be used for no other purpose than these. For these exercises, in both peace and war, are useful to a city and to private families. 

However, other types of labor, sports, and physical exercises are not, O Megillus and Clinias, suited for free citizens <note>original: "liberal," meaning fitting for a free person (liber) rather than a slave.</note>. And thus, the subject of gymnastics, which I said in our earlier discussion needed to be addressed, is now nearly finished. But, if you have any better ideas than these, speak and do not hold them back.

# THE LAWS.

**CLEINIAS.** It is not easy, stranger, to find anything better to say about physical training and competition if we were to set these points aside.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** It follows, therefore, that we should speak about the gifts of the Muses and Apollo <note>In Greek education, "music" (presided over by the Muses) and the arts of Apollo included poetry, song, and dance, which were used to mold a citizen's character.</note>, which we previously thought we had discussed thoroughly enough that only the details of physical training remained. But it is now clear that there is something regarding these arts that must be mentioned before anything else. We shall, therefore, speak of this next.

**CLEINIAS.** By all means.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Listen to me, then; for you have already followed what has been discussed so far. At the same time, it is necessary that both the speaker and the listener be cautious when mentioning something that is strikingly strange and unusual. This is the case right now. For I am about to assert something that cannot be spoken of without a certain fear; yet, taking courage, I will not hold back.

**CLEINIAS.** What is this thing, stranger?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** I say that all cities are unaware that the stability or the changing of <term>sports: the original Greek term is *paidia*, referring to children’s play, games, and pastimes</term> is the most vital factor in the establishment of laws. For when it is arranged so that the same children always play the same games, and take delight in them in the same way and under the same rules, then the legal institutions are allowed to remain established in peace. 

But when these games are changed and innovations are made in them—so that young people are constantly engaged in new sorts of play, changing the movements of their bodies and their equipment, and always forming new opinions on what is "proper" or "improper" in these matters—they begin to give the highest honor to those who invent new forms, colors, and such things. When this happens, we say (and we say it with absolute truth) that no greater mischief can befall a city. For it secretly alters the character of the youth and causes them to despise what is ancient and honor only what is new. I say again, there is nothing more damaging to a city than this belief and way of thinking. Hear, then, what a great evil I claim this to be.

**CLEINIAS.** Do you mean that it is a mistake to criticize the ancient institutions of a city?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Precisely so.

**CLEINIAS.** You will not find us to be resentful listeners of this argument, but rather as well-disposed as possible.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** Come then, let us listen to this with even greater attention and discuss it among ourselves. We find that <term>change: the Athenian uses the concept of *metabole*, meaning a shift or revolution</term> in all things—except for those things that are already evil—is extremely <note>The original text uses "pernicious," meaning highly destructive or harmful</note> at all times. This is true for the physical health of our bodies, the habits of our souls, and, in short, for everything except, as I just mentioned, things that are already bad. 

If someone looks at the body, for instance, and considers how it becomes accustomed to certain types of food, drink, and exercise, he will find that the body is at first unsettled by them. However, over time, the body becomes comfortable with this <term>diet: in this context, the Greek *diaita* refers to a person's entire way of life or daily regimen</term>. The body becomes healthy, familiar, and friendly with this routine, finding both health and pleasure in it. He will also find that if the body is ever forced to change any part of this established routine, it is initially stricken by illness and does not recover its health until it becomes accustomed to the new habits. 

The same principle must be considered when looking at the thoughts of men and the nature of their souls. For every soul feels a deep respect and a certain fear toward changing the laws in which it was raised, especially when—through some divine good fortune—those laws have remained unchanged for a long time. In such cases, no one remembers or has ever heard of a time when things were different than they are now. 

The legislator, therefore, must find a way to ensure this stability in the city. I have discovered the following method: As I said before, most people believe that when the <term>games of youth: the original term is *paidia*, referring to children’s play and pastimes</term> are changed, it is merely a matter of play and not something of great consequence. Because of this, they do not resist these changes, but simply go along with them. 

They do not realize that children who take part in these new games necessarily become different men than they would have been if their old games had remained. Because they become different men, they will seek out a different kind of life, which leads them to different interests and different laws. No one seems to fear that this leads to the greatest of all evils for a city. While changes in the outward forms of games may seem less harmful, I believe that frequent <term>innovations: the introduction of new ideas or methods that disrupt tradition</term> in what we praise and what we criticize are the most dangerous of all evils and must be feared above all.

**CLEINIAS.** Undoubtedly.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** What then? Shall we trust our earlier discussion, in which...

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** ...did we not say that the specific details regarding rhythm and every kind of music are imitations of the characters of better and worse men? Or how should we put it?

**CLEINIAS.** What kind of art are you speaking of?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** The rule that every kind of dancing and melody should be consecrated. This is done by first establishing festivals at certain times of the year in honor of the various Gods, the sons of Gods, and <term>daemons: in Greek thought, these are divine intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</term>. After this, the sacrifices to the different divinities are organized, along with the odes and <term>choirs: specifically "choros," referring to a group that both sings and performs ritual dances</term> with which the sacrifices are to be honored. Once these things are established, all the citizens in common should sacrifice to the <note>The Fates, or Moirai, were the three goddesses who spun, measured, and cut the thread of human life</note> Fates and to all the other Gods, dedicating specific odes to each of the Gods and their attendants. 

However, if anyone introduces other hymns and choirs in honor of the Gods than those established by law, the priests and priestesses—together with the guardians of the laws—shall, in a holy and legal manner, restrain him in his attempt. And if the person who is restrained does not submit willingly, he shall suffer the punishment for his <term>impiety: "asebeia," or the crime of disrespecting the gods and state religion</term> throughout the rest of his life, brought against him by anyone who wishes to do so.

**CLEINIAS.** That is right.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** But since we have reached this point in our discussion, we should behave in a fitting manner.

**CLEINIAS.** What are you referring to?

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** All men—not only the young but the old as well—when they see or hear something unusual, do not immediately agree with what is uncertain about it, nor do they rush to embrace it. They inquire and do not proceed any further until they have a firm assurance regarding the road they should take. We should act in a similar way...

If a person has been raised with a prudent and orderly Muse, they will hate a vulgar or "sweet" Muse when they hear it, calling it illiberal <term>illiberal: lacking the refinement or dignity expected of a free citizen; vulgar</term>. But someone raised with a common and popular Muse will find the opposite style to be cold and unpleasant. Therefore, as I just said, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant style has a special claim to being "better." The real difference lies in whether the music is beneficial or harmful: one style makes those who are educated in it better people, and the other makes them worse.

For it ought to be considered as base, and not fitting for a free citizen, to pass the whole night in sleep, and not to be always the first that is roused and seen by all his domestics; whether it is proper to call a thing of this kind a law or a social custom. 

Besides this, it ought to be reckoned as shameful by female slaves if the mistress is roused by them, instead of being herself the first to wake the rest—namely, both male and female slaves, her children, and in short, if possible, the whole house. All free persons, therefore, rising by night, should perform the many necessary political and <term>economic: originally referring to 'oikonomikos' or household management duties</term> duties of their stations; the governors performing those pertaining to the city, and masters and mistresses performing those pertaining to their families. 

For much sleep is neither naturally adapted to our bodies nor to our souls, nor to the actions we must perform. For he who is asleep is of no more worth than that which is destitute of life; but whoever among us is careful in the highest degree that he may live and be wise will be vigilant for the greatest part of his time, sleeping no longer than is necessary to the preservation of health. But much sleep will not be required for someone who is accustomed to good habits. 

Magistrates, indeed, who are vigilant by night in cities, are a terror to evil men—whether they are enemies or criminal citizens—but are admired and honored by the just and the wise; they are both useful to themselves and to the whole city. So that I think I cannot propose a better paradigm to the guardian of the laws, and to the preceptor of youth, than this: that they should exhort the masters to teach boys these things, together with such particulars as are consequent and similar to these, whether they are written in prose or verse, or are simply asserted without being written, but are conformable to these laws, and are, therefore, by no means to be neglected, but committed to writing. And, in the first place, the teachers themselves should be compelled to learn and praise these assertions; but those teachers must not act in the capacity of teachers by whom they are not approved. And, finally, boys must be committed to the care of those preceptors by whom these assertions are approved and praised. And he who is more modest, and more exercised in fortitude, is moved in a less degree. But he who is timid, and unexercised in temperance, sustains greater and more vehement mutations of motion. And, in short, every one that emits a sound, whether in singing or in speaking, is not entirely able to accomplish this with a quiet body. 

On this account the imitations of words by figures of the body produced the whole of the art of dancing. Some of us, therefore, in all these move elegantly, but others inelegantly. For the whole of our <term>polity</term> <note>The word "polity" refers to the constitutional order and the way of life within the city-state.</note> is an imitation of the most beautiful and most excellent life, which we say is, in reality, the most true tragedy <gloss>¹</gloss>. Now, therefore, O boys, offspring of soft Muses, we shall, in the first place, show your odes, together with ours, to the governors; and if the things said by you shall appear to be the same, or better than those which are said by us, we will give the <term>choir</term> <note>The "choir" refers to the *choregia*, the public funding and state-sanctioned chorus required to stage a play in ancient Greece.</note> to you: but if this should not be the case, we shall never, O friends, be able to give you the choir." GUEST. Three disciplines, however, still remain for the freeborn. One of these is computation, and the particulars respecting numbers <note>The Athenian refers here to basic arithmetic and the theory of numbers, which Plato considered foundational for logical thinking.</note>. He, therefore, who is of opinion that all these are disciplines not necessary for one who is about to know the most beautiful disciplines, will think in a very stupid manner. First, the Egyptians have devised a method of reckoning for children that is so natural it is learned through sport and pleasure. For example, they distribute apples and garlands to groups of many children or few, using the same numbers to teach addition and subtraction. They also use numbers to organize the pairings of boxers and wrestlers, determining the order of their matches. Likewise, when they play, they mix together vessels made of gold, brass, and silver, or distribute them separately. As I said before, they adapt the use of necessary numbers to these games. **CLINIAS:** About what? Inform us, O Stranger, what it is you mean.

**STRANGER:** I will tell you. Or, rather, I will point it out to you by questioning. And do you answer me a trifling question. Do you know what length is?

**CLINIAS:** Undoubtedly.

**STRANGER:** And what breadth is?

**CLINIAS:** Entirely so.

**STRANGER:** And do you know that these are two things, and that the third of these is depth?

**CLINIAS:** How is it possible that I should not?

**STRANGER:** Does it not, therefore, appear to you that all these may be measured by each other?

**CLINIAS:** It does.

**STRANGER:** I mean length by length, and breadth by breadth; and that, in a similar manner, depth is naturally capable of being measured by depth.

**CLINIAS:** Very much so.

**STRANGER:** But, if some among these can neither do this vehemently, nor remissly, but some are able, and others not <note>original: "some are able, and others not" — this refers to the mathematical concept of being <term>incommensurable</term>, meaning two quantities cannot be measured by the same shared unit, such as the ratio of a square's side to its diagonal.</note>, and yet you think it can be effected by all, in what manner are you circumstanced with respect to these?

**CLINIAS:** Badly, it is evident.

**STRANGER:** But again, do not all the Greeks, after a manner, think that length, breadth, and depth, can be mutually measured by each other?

**CLINIAS:** Entirely so.

<summary>The Athenian Stranger describes the general ignorance regarding the dimensions of length, breadth, and depth as "swinish" and shameful. **CLINIAS:** Perhaps so. It appears, therefore, that the game of chess and these subjects of study are very different from each other.

**GUEST:** These things, then, I say, O Clinias, ought to be learned by the youth. For they are neither harmful nor difficult; and when they are learned alongside sport, they will be advantageous and never detrimental to the city. But, if any one says otherwise, let us hear him.

**CLINIAS:** Undoubtedly.

**GUEST:** If, then, it should appear that these things are as we say, it is evident that we should embrace them; but if it should appear that they are not so, we should reject them.

**CLINIAS:** Evidently so. Ought not these, therefore, O Guest, to be now established by us as necessary subjects of study, so that the details of our laws may not be discussed in vain?

**GUEST:** Let them be established, then—but only as "pledges" from another <term>polity</term> <note>Polity: A form of government or a specific constitution. Here, the Stranger suggests these laws are borrowed on trial from his theoretical ideal state.</note>, which may be dissolved if they should in no way please us who establish them, or you for whom they are established.

**CLINIAS:** The condition you propose is fair. But consider after this the study of the stars, whether choosing this for our youth pleases us, or the contrary.

...thus far learned. Do you, therefore, endeavor to show that these things are so, and we will follow you as your disciples.

**GUEST:** It is not easy to learn what I am saying, nor is it, on the other hand, entirely difficult; nor does it require a great length of time. As proof of this, I myself have heard these things neither recently nor very long ago, and yet I am able to make them clear in a short time. If they were truly difficult, I, who am elderly, would not be able to explain them to you, who are likewise elderly.

**CLINIAS:** True. But what is this branch of study <note>original: "discipline"</note> which you call admirable, which you say is fit for youth to learn, but of which we are ignorant? Endeavor to speak about it with the utmost clarity.

**GUEST:** I will endeavor to do so. The belief <note>original: "dogma"</note> then, O best of men, regarding the sun, the moon, and the other stars—the idea that they "wander" at any time—is not right; the very contrary of this is true. For each of them perpetually travels in a circle along one and the same path, and not many paths, even though they appear to move through many. Furthermore, we are wrong to think that the swiftest of them is the slowest, or that the slowest is the swiftest. These things naturally exist in a specific way, but we have been under the impression that they exist otherwise. 

Suppose we were watching the horse races or the long-distance runners at the **Olympic games**. If we were to call the swiftest runner the slowest, and the slowest the swiftest, and then sang our praises <note>original: "encomiums"</note> celebrating the loser as the victor, I do not think our praises would be proper, nor would they be pleasing to the racers. But now, when we make this same error regarding the Gods, do we not think that—just as such conduct in the games is ridiculous and wrong—this is also true in the present case?

**CLINIAS:** It is indeed ridiculous.

**GUEST:** Therefore, we do not please the divinity when, in singing hymns to the Gods, we celebrate them falsely.

**CLINIAS:** That is most true, if things are indeed as you say.

**GUEST:** If, therefore, we can demonstrate that they move in this orderly way, all these details should be learned up to that point; but, if we cannot show it, they must be dismissed. Let us let this be our determination.

**CLINIAS:** By all means.

<summary>The Guest explains that the planets are not "wanderers" but move in consistent circular paths, arguing that misidentifying their speeds and movements is a form of disrespect to the divine order.</summary>

GUEST. It is proper, therefore, now to say, that the legal institutions respecting the subjects of study <note>original: "disciplines of erudition"; referring to the curriculum of music, gymnastics, and mathematics discussed previously</note> have reached their completion. But it is necessary to think in a similar way regarding hunting, and everything else of this kind. For it appears that the office of a legislator is something more than merely establishing laws; he ought to make use of that middle ground which naturally exists between advice <note>original: "admonition"</note> and the laws. This is a point that has often occurred to us during our discussion, and especially when we spoke concerning the education of children. For we said there were many things pertaining to education which could not be established by formal law, and that it was foolish to even attempt it. 

But when laws are written this way, and the whole system of government <note>original: "polity"</note> is established, the highest praise for a virtuous citizen is not simply that he obeys the laws perfectly. Rather, the more perfect praise is for the citizen who leads a pure life because he is obedient to the *spirit* of the legislator’s writings—those in which he establishes, praises, and blames certain behaviors. For this is the most proper praise of a citizen. In reality, the legislator ought not only to write laws, but should add to them his own views on what is beautiful and what is not. The citizen who has reached the peak of virtue should observe these moral guidelines no less than those specific rules that carry legal punishments. 

But we will call upon the subject of our present discussion as a witness to this, for it will make our intention clearer. Hunting is a subject of great variety, which we now group under a single name. There is the hunting of water animals, much hunting of birds <note>original: "aërial animals"</note>, and even more of land animals. This includes not only wild beasts but even the hunting of men <note>In Greek philosophy, "hunting" was a broad metaphor for any pursuit; "hunting of men" referred to warfare, kidnapping, or even the pursuit of followers or friends through persuasion</note>. Of this last kind, one part relates to war and another to friendship; one is praiseworthy, while the other is to be blamed. Even the thefts of robbers and the raids of armies are forms of hunting. 

The legislator, therefore, who establishes laws about hunting, cannot leave these categories unnoticed, nor can he simply impose fines and threats on every single act in a specific order. What, then, is to be done about such things? The legislator ought to praise and blame what is commendable or shameful in hunting, with an eye toward the training and studies of the youth. And young men, when they hear these things, should be obedient to him. They should not allow either the pursuit of pleasure or the fear of hard work to prevent them from following the legislator’s directions. Rather, they should honor what is said and...

...enjoined with praise, than what is established with threatenings and fines. These things being premised, the praise and blame of hunting will follow in a becoming manner. For that hunting is to be praised which improves the souls of young men, but that which has a contrary tendency is to be blamed. Let us therefore discuss what follows, calling upon young men through prayer:

> "O friends, may never any desire or love of marine fishing, or of fishing with a hook, seize you; nor, in short, of laboring to catch any aquatic animals with a bow net <note>A 'bow net' is a type of basket-like trap used for catching fish or crustaceans.</note>, either by day or by night! May you likewise be void of all inclination to piracy, by which you would become unjust and atrocious hunters of men on the sea! And may you never in the least desire to commit theft in the region and city to which you belong, or to hunt birds, which, though a fascinating, is not a very liberal <note>In this context, 'liberal' refers to a pursuit worthy of a free-born citizen (from the Latin *liberalis*), as opposed to a menial or trivial one.</note> pursuit!"

The hunting, therefore, of pedestrial <note>land-dwelling</note> animals alone remains for our athletæ <note>term: athletæ; here referring not just to sports players, but to those training their bodies and minds for the service of the state.</note>. But, of this, that kind which is performed by sleeping in turns, and is called nocturnal <note>night hunting</note>, as it belongs to sluggish men, is not worthy of praise. Nor yet that which during a remission of labors vanquishes the fierce strength of wild beasts by nets and snares, and not by patient endurance. That hunting, therefore, of wild beasts alone remains as the best of all, which is accomplished by horses, dogs, and corporeal strength and skill. For those that are anxious to obtain divine fortitude will vanquish savage animals by hunting them in the course, and with wounds, darts, and their own hands. And thus much may suffice respecting the praise and blame of all these particulars. 

However, let the law be this: No one shall impede these truly sacred hunters from hunting wherever they please. But no one shall suffer <note>allow</note> any person to engage in nocturnal hunting with nets and dogs. Fowling <note>bird hunting</note> shall be permitted in uncultivated places and in mountains; but any one who may happen to be present shall forbid it in cultivated and sacred places. A fisherman shall not be suffered to hunt, either in ports or sacred rivers, marshes, or pools; but in other places he may be permitted to hunt so long as he does not use a mixture of juices <note>original: "succis"; likely referring to the practice of using herbal or chemical poisons to stun fish.</note>. Now, therefore, it is proper to say, that the legal institutions respecting discipline have obtained their completion.

**CLINIAS.** You speak well.

To those who live happily, one thing must be present above all others: they must neither harm others nor be harmed by others. Of these two, the former is not very difficult; but the latter is extremely difficult, and it cannot be perfectly achieved except by becoming perfectly good <gloss>1</gloss>. 

The same principle applies to a city. When it is good, its life is <term>pacific</term> <note>peaceful</note>; but when it is corrupt, it is plagued by both external and internal war. Since this is almost always the case, cities should not practice for war only during wartime, but rather during the time of peace. It is necessary, therefore, that a city guided by intellect should practice military exercises every month for at least one full day—or more frequently if the <term>magistrates</term> <note>public officials with executive and judicial authority</note> see fit—without fearing either heat or cold. The magistrates, along with the women and boys, should participate in these exercises so that every inhabitant of the city is prepared whenever the governors decide to lead out the whole population. 

For this purpose, impressive games must be designed alongside religious sacrifices, so that "festive battles" may take place, clearly and accurately mimicking the actual struggles of war. It is also necessary that rewards for bravery should be distributed to the participants; the winners should be praised and the losers criticized, based on how they have conducted themselves in these contests and throughout their entire lives.
