Will he not likewise order, that both greater and lesser gymnastic exercises should be performed every month at least, that each may contend in taking possession of places, or acting on the defensive in every part of the city; truly imitating every thing pertaining to war, and fighting with balls and with darts, which approach as near as possible to true and dangerous darts? And this, that the sportive contests of the citizens with each other may not be entirely destitute of fear, but may excite terror, and thus, after a manner, evince who is <term>magnanimous</term> <note>original: "megalopsychos"; literally 'great-souled'. This refers to a person possessing high-minded courage and a noble spirit</note>, and who is not? For, thus he may be able in a proper manner to honour some, and disgrace others, and render the whole city through the whole of life useful for true contention. But, if any one should happen to die in these contests through involuntary slaughter, let it be established that the <term>homicide</term> <note>original: "phonous"; one who has killed another, whether intentionally or not</note>, when he has made an <term>expiation</term> <note>original: "katharsis"; a ritual purification or cleansing required by law and religion to remove the 'stain' of killing before a person could return to society</note> according to law, shall be considered in future as pure. For the legislator ought to think that, in the place of a few who may happen to die, others again will succeed not worse than the slain: but that fear becoming, as it were, extinct in all these, he will no longer be able to distinguish the better from the worse; which is, in no small degree, a greater evil to the city than the involuntary destruction of a few individuals.

**CLIN.** We agree with you, O guest <note>The 'Guest' is the Athenian Stranger, the primary voice of wisdom in this dialogue</note>, that these things ought to be legally established, and attended to by all the city.

**GUEST.** Do we, therefore, all of us know the reason, why in cities at present there is scarcely any such choir and contest, or, at least, in a very small degree? Shall we say that this happens through the ignorance of the multitude and of the legislators?

**CLIN.** Perhaps so.

**GUEST.** By no means, O blessed Clinias! But it is proper to say that there are two causes of this, and those very sufficient.

Furthermore, such a person would not agree with the principle we said a legislator must always observe: he must consider whether a legal institution contributes to **virtue** or not. For instance, he should consider whether the practice we just mentioned would be honorable (or at least not shameful) if established by law, and how much it would help one acquire virtue. Would it produce a habit of **courage** <term>fortitude</term> in the soul of the one who yields, or a kind of **moderation** <term>temperance</term> in the soul of the one who pursues? Or shall we say that no one will be convinced of this, but rather of the exact opposite? For everyone will criticize the **weakness** <term>effeminacy</term> <note>original: "effeminacy"; in this context, it refers to the Greek concept of *malakia*, a lack of self-control or "softness" that was considered a moral failing in men</note> of the one who gives in to pleasure and lacks endurance. And will not everyone condemn the attempt to imitate the female sex? What man, then, would establish such a thing by law? Almost no one who has the true spirit of law in his mind. How, then, can we truly understand the nature of friendship, desire, and love, as we have discussed them? For,

**GUEST.** <note>The "Guest" is the Athenian Stranger, the primary speaker in Plato's *Laws*, who acts as a wise legislator.</note> Since there are two types of friendship, and a third kind arising from a combination of both—all referred to by a single name—it creates a great deal of confusion and obscurity.

**CLINIAS.** In what way?

**GUEST.** We call someone a "friend" when they are similar to another in virtue, or equal to them. However, we also use the word "friend" for a poor man who is dependent on a rich man, even though they are of completely different backgrounds. When either of these types of friendship becomes intense, we call it "love."

**CLINIAS.** That is correct.

**GUEST.** The friendship that arises between opposites is often harsh and unrefined, and the feeling is rarely mutual. But friendship between those who are similar is gentle and remains mutual throughout their lives. The "mixed" kind, however, is difficult to understand. It is hard to discern what a person driven by this third type of love actually wants. Being pulled in two opposite directions, he is conflicted about how to act: one impulse urges him to enjoy the <note>original: "flower of his age"</note> youthful beauty of the beloved, while the other warns him against it. For the lover of the body, who hungers for physical beauty like a piece of ripe fruit, tries only to satisfy his own appetite and places no value on the character of the beloved’s soul. 

But a person who places little importance on physical desire—viewing the body with his soul rather than lusting after it—is a true lover of the soul. He considers physical indulgence to be a disgrace. Instead, he honors and practices <term>temperance</term> <note>Sophrosyne: self-control and moderation.</note>, <term>fortitude</term> <note>Andreia: courage or moral strength.</note>, <term>magnificence</term> <note>Megalopsychia: nobility of spirit or generosity.</note>, and <term>prudence</term>. His only wish is to live purely with a partner who is equally pure. The "mixed" love is the one we just mentioned as the third kind. Since there are these three variations, should the law forbid all of them? Or is it obvious that we should want the love based on virtue—which encourages a young person to reach their highest potential—to exist in our city, while expelling the other two if possible? What do you say, my friend Megillus?

**MEGILLUS.** You have explained these matters, Guest, in a way that is perfectly beautiful.

**GUEST.** I suspected, my friend, that you would agree with me. However, it is not necessary for me to ask what your <note>The text cuts off here as the Guest begins to ask about the specific laws of Megillus’s home, Sparta.</note>

# THE LAWS,

## BOOK IX.

---

**A**s judicial affairs follow all the preceding details, discussing them now will follow the natural order of lawmaking. We have already partially shown what specific areas require judgments—namely, agriculture and similar matters—though we have not yet clearly spoken of the most significant legal judgments, nor shown what punishments should be inflicted, or who the judges should be. It follows, then, that we should speak of these matters now.

**CLIN.** <note>Clinias, a Cretan and one of the three participants in the dialogue.</note> Right.

**GUEST.** <note>The "Athenian Guest," the primary speaker who represents Plato’s own philosophical views on legislation.</note> In a way, it is a shameful thing that the city we say will be properly inhabited—and furnished with everything needed for the study of virtue—should even need to observe the kinds of laws we are about to establish. To assume that in such a city a man capable of the greatest wickedness will be born, making it necessary to create laws in anticipation and issue threats if such a character should arise, is, as I have said, somewhat shameful. This is done to prevent the greatest atrocities, and to ensure that when they are committed, they may be legally punished. 

However, we are not like the ancient <term>legislators</term> <note>The Athenian refers to mythical lawgivers like Minos or Lycurgus, who were said to have received laws directly from the gods.</note> who gave laws to heroes and the sons of gods—legislators who were themselves descended from gods. We are men, and we are currently giving laws to those born from the seed of men. Since this is the case, we may justly fear that one of our citizens might be so naturally stubborn and untamed as to be impossible to soften—much like beans or peas that have been blasted by thunder and cannot be cooked by fire. Therefore, the first law we shall establish (though it is not pleasant for us to do so) concerns <term>sacrilege</term> <note>original: "sacrilegium"—specifically the crime of robbing a temple or stealing property dedicated to the gods.</note>, if any—

...one shall dare to commit it. Indeed, we neither wish, nor do we very much fear, that a citizen, when properly educated, will ever suffer from this disease <note>Plato frequently compares vice and criminal intent to a "disease" of the soul that needs to be treated by the legislator.</note>. However, the servants of these citizens, as well as foreigners and the slaves of foreigners, will attempt many such acts. It is primarily for their sake—and because I fear the inherent frailty <note>original: "imbecility." In this context, it refers to the moral and physical weakness of human nature.</note> of all humanity—that I shall speak about the law of **sacrilege** <term>sacrilege</term> <note>In the ancient world, sacrilege usually referred to the theft of property from a temple (temple-robbery) or the desecration of a holy site.</note>, and all other such crimes that are either difficult to cure or entirely incurable. 

According to what we have previously agreed upon, the preface to these laws should be as brief as possible. One might address a person who is driven by a corrupt desire, day and night, to plunder temples, by mingling warnings with the following speech:

> O wonderful man, it is neither a human nor a divine impulse that drives you to commit sacrilege. Rather, it is a certain detestable madness arising from ancient and unpurified crimes <note>Plato suggests that the urge to commit a great crime is often the result of an ancestral "curse" or past unatoned-for wrongs that have corrupted the character.</note>, which you must dread with all your might. Listen, then, to how you must handle this fear. When such a thought attacks you, seek out rituals of **expiation** <term>expiation</term> <note>Religious ceremonies performed to "wash away" the spiritual stain of guilt or sinful thoughts.</note>; go as a suppliant to the temples of those Gods who ward off evil, and seek the company of good men. Listen to them and try to say yourself that every man ought to honor what is beautiful and just. Flee from the company of the wicked without ever looking back. If your disease subsides because of these actions, you have done well; but if not, consider that it is better to die, and liberate yourself from life.

Since we have "sung" these **exordia** <term>exordia</term> <note>Literally "introductions" or "preambles." Plato believes laws should have a persuasive musical or rhetorical opening to appeal to the citizen's reason before the punishment appeals to their fear.</note> to those whose thoughts lead them to impious deeds destructive to the city, the law should remain silent toward the man who obeys. But for the man who will not be persuaded, we must follow the preface with a "higher strain" <note>This refers to the formal, more severe language of the actual legal penalty.</note> of music. 

Anyone caught in the act of sacrilege, if he is a slave or a foreigner, shall have his misfortune "written" on his face and hands <note>This refers to the practice of branding criminals with hot irons as a permanent mark of their crime.</note>. After he has received as many lashes with a whip as the judges deem appropriate, he shall be driven naked beyond the borders of the territory. Perhaps, by being brought to his senses through this punishment, he will become a better man. Indeed, no punishment established by law is intended to cause harm; rather, it usually accomplishes one of two things: it makes the one who suffers it either better or at least less wicked. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal treatment of "incurable" criminals—those whose crimes are so severe that the state determines they cannot be rehabilitated. # THE LAWS.

...<note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the "madness" of the criminal.</note> unspeakable crime <note>original: "arcane." In this context, it refers to crimes that are so heinous they are considered a "pollution" or an offense against the sacred order.</note> toward the Gods, or his parents, or his country, the judge shall pronounce such a person to be incurable. This judgment is based on the consideration that although he has been well-nourished and disciplined from his childhood, he has still not abstained from the greatest vices. For such a man, death is the least of evils. Therefore, so that others may benefit from his example, he shall be marked with infamy, expelled beyond the boundaries of the region, and there be put to death.

However, let his children and his race be honored and praised if they avoid his ways, like those who bravely fly from evil toward good. It will not be proper for the riches of any such person to become public property in a <term>polity</term> <note>A "polity" here refers to Plato's ideal state, Magnesia, where the social structure depends on a fixed number of citizens.</note> where the same and equal <term>allotments</term> <note>In Magnesia, the land is divided into 5,040 equal plots (allotments), which must never be subdivided or concentrated in the hands of a few.</note> must be perpetually preserved. 

When anyone commits a crime that is to be punished with a fine, he shall be fined only as much as he possesses above his allotted portion; the lot itself shall remain entire. The **guardians of the laws**, considering this affair accurately from written records, should always provide a clear statement to the judges so that no one is ever deprived of his land allotment through a lack of money. 

If anyone appears to deserve a greater fine, and none of his friends are willing to stand as a bond for him to secure his liberty, he shall be punished with lasting and visible bonds <note>Likely referring to public imprisonment or being kept in chains.</note> and with specific public shames. But let no offense ever go unpunished, nor any fugitive escape; let the criminal be punished with death, or bonds, or stripes, or certain "squalid seats" <note>A form of public humiliation where the offender was forced to sit in a lowly or uncomfortable position in a public place.</note>, or by standing, or by being exhibited in temples at the edge of the territory, or by the fines we mentioned before.

He should look to these two things: injustice and detriment. He should also, as much as possible, legally compensate the person who has suffered a damage, restore what has been lost, raise what has fallen, and repair the ravages of death and wounds. **GUEST.** Besides this, too, we do not call pleasure the same as anger, but we say that it possesses dominion from a contrary power, and that it persuades us, with a violent deception, to do whatever it pleases.

**CLINIAS.** And very much so.

**GUEST.** He, likewise, who says that **ignorance** is the third cause of crimes will not be deceived. But he will be a better legislator who gives this a twofold division. He should consider one kind as **simple ignorance**, which is the cause of light offenses. But the other is **double ignorance**, which occurs when someone is lacking discipline—not only because they are held back by ignorance, but because they have an "opinion of wisdom." They think they have a perfect knowledge of things about which they are entirely ignorant. When these types of errors are backed by power and strength, they are the causes of mighty and brutal crimes. But when they are accompanied by weakness <note>original: "imbecility." In this context, it refers to the physical or social lack of power found in the young or the very old.</note>—as in the case of crimes committed by children or the elderly—they are still considered crimes, and laws are to be established for those that commit them. However, at the same time, they should be reckoned the mildest of all crimes and as deserving the most abundant indulgence.

**CLINIAS.** You speak reasonably.

# THE LAWS.

->257<-

**GUEST.** Nearly all of us, therefore, speak of pleasure and anger as forces that some of us master while others are defeated by them; and this is indeed the case.
**CLINIAS.** Absolutely.
**GUEST.** But we have never heard it said that one of us is "superior" to ignorance, or that another is "vanquished" by it.
**CLINIAS.** That is very true.
**GUEST.** Yet we say that all these things—pleasure, anger, and ignorance—lure us toward their own will and often pull us in opposite directions at the same time.
**CLINIAS.** Very often, indeed.
**GUEST.** Now, I will explain to you clearly, without complicated distinctions, what I mean by the **just** and the **unjust**. I define **injustice** <note>The Guest provides a psychological definition: injustice is the state where the passions (the "tyrants") overthrow the soul's internal order.</note> as the tyranny of anger, fear, pleasure, pain, envy, and desire within the soul, regardless of whether this internal tyrant actually causes harm to anyone else or not. Conversely, when the opinion of what is "best" governs the soul—whether that opinion is held by a city or a private individual—and it brings order to the whole person, I call this **justice**. This remains true even if that opinion leads a person into error in some specific way; everything done according to this guiding principle I call "just." <note>Plato suggests that acting on one's best rational judgment is "just" because it maintains the soul's proper hierarchy, even if the judgment itself is factually mistaken.</note> I would further add that the life of someone obedient to such a principle is of the highest quality. However, the general public often mistakes a mistake made under this principle for "involuntary injustice." But our goal right now is not to argue over names. Since we have demonstrated that there are three types of crimes, let us fix them more firmly in our memory. First, there is the category of pain, which we call anger and fear.
**CLINIAS.** Exactly.
**GUEST.** Second, there is the category of pleasure and desires. Third, there is the category of hopes and the desire for a true opinion about what is best. When this third category is divided into two parts, we end up with five types of actions for which laws must be made, falling into two main <term>genera</term> <note>In legal and philosophical logic, "genera" refers to broad classes or categories that contain several "species" or sub-types.</note>.
**CLINIAS.** And what are these?
**GUEST.** The first includes every action performed through open violence and force. The second includes those done in darkness and through secret deception. Sometimes actions involve both; such crimes, if they are to be handled properly, should be restrained by the strictest possible laws.

Murder, therefore, as it appears, must receive a twofold distribution; and both of them nearly are produced by anger. In reality, indeed, they are but **images** <note>Plato often uses the term "images" to describe things that resemble a pure category (like "voluntary") but are complicated by human emotion or circumstance.</note> of the voluntary and involuntary. For, he who retains his anger, and does not immediately and suddenly, but with stratagem, at some distance of time, avenge himself, is **similar** to one who murders voluntarily. But he who does not conceal his anger, but immediately follows its impulse without premeditation, is **similar** to one who murders involuntarily. However, he is not altogether involuntary, but an image of one that acts involuntarily. On this account, it is difficult to determine respecting murders committed through anger, whether they should be established by law as voluntary or involuntary actions. 

The best and the truest method, therefore, that can be adopted is, to consider both these kinds of murder as images, and to divide them apart from each other, so as to class the one under **premeditated**, and the other under **unpremeditated** actions. Severer punishments, therefore, are to be ordained for those that commit murder through anger, with premeditation; but milder punishments for those that murder without deliberation, and suddenly. # THE LAWS.

->264<-

<meta>catchword: discipline,</meta>

discipline, generates ten thousand loves of infinite riches. But we say that the want of discipline is the cause why both among the Greeks and **Barbarians** <note>A term used by the Greeks to describe any non-Greek person or culture.</note> riches are praised in a vicious manner. For they place these in the first, though they belong to the third, rank of things good; and, through this opinion, destroy both themselves and posterity. For, to speak the truth to all cities respecting riches, is the most beautiful and the best of all things. But the truth is, that riches subsist for the sake of the body, and the body subsists for the sake of the soul. Since, therefore, those things are good for the sake of which riches naturally subsist, they will rank in the third place after the virtue of the body and soul. This reason, therefore, will inform us as a teacher, that he who desires to be happy ought not to seek after wealth indiscriminately, but in a just and temperate manner. For thus murders would not be committed in cities, which require to be purified by murders. 

But now, as I said in the beginning of this discussion, this is one and the greatest cause of the greatest punishments of voluntary murder. The second is the habit of an ambitious soul, which generates envy; and this is bitter to those that dwell together, and especially to him by whom it is possessed, and afterwards to the best persons in the city. But cowardly and unjust fears rank in the third place, which produce many murders, when such things have been transacted by any one, or are at present transacted, as no one wishes to be conscious have taken place, or do take place. On this account they take away by death those that might give information of such transactions, when they cannot prevent them from making a discovery by any other means. And thus much for a preface to all these particulars. 

To which may be added, what many who are studious respecting the mysteries have heard about things of this kind, of the truth of which they are vehemently persuaded,—I mean, that such actions are punished in **Hades** <note>The Greek underworld and the realm of the dead.</note>, and that the perpetrators of them, again returning hither, necessarily suffer punishment according to nature, and end their days by suffering the very same kind of death which they caused another to suffer. For him, therefore, who from this preface is persuaded, and is in every respect afraid of such a punishment, there is no occasion to establish a law respecting voluntary murder: but for him who will not be persuaded by it let the following law be ordained. And thus far we have given laws concerning that education and discipline of the living soul, which if it is fortunately endued with, it may be suffered to live, but of which if it is unfortunately deprived, it must be put to death: and we have likewise ordained such punishments as murders deserve. It now remains that we should define, to the utmost of our power, what violent, voluntary, and involuntary actions are, and how many they are in number, and what are the punishments accommodated to each. For these, as it appears, will be properly discussed after those. But even the vilest **legislator** <term>legislator: the person responsible for drafting the laws and constitution of the state.</term> will place the consideration of wounds, and **mutilations** <note>Referring here to permanent physical injury or the loss of a limb.</note> from wounds, after murder. Wounds, therefore, are to be divided in the same manner as murders. For some of them are inflicted involuntarily; others through anger; some through fear; and some voluntarily and from design. Respecting all these, the following observations must be premised. 

It is necessary that laws should be established for men, and that they should live according to law, or they would in no respect differ from the most savage animals. But this is owing to the nature of men, which is never found to be sufficient of itself to know what is advantageous to a human **polity** <term>polity: the organized society, government, or political structure of a city-state.</term>; and, when it does know this, is never always able to do and wish that which is best. For it is, in the first place, difficult to know that not private but public advantage must necessarily be attended to by the political and true art; (for that which is common binds, but that which is private **dilacerates** <note>original: "dilacerates"; to tear apart or violently rend into pieces.</note>, cities,) and that it is more advantageous, both to the public and individuals, that common concerns should be well established, than such as are private. 

In the second place, though some one should know sufficiently from art, that these things naturally subsist in this manner, yet, after this, if he should govern the city with an unrestrained authority, he would be incapable of persevering in this **dogma** <term>dogma: a firmly held principle or belief, in this context referring to the philosophical truth of the common good.</term>, and of living in the opinion that common advantage should be nourished in a city, and private follow the general good. But the mortal nature will always impel him to **prerogative** <term>prerogative: the pursuit of special rights or personal advantages over others.</term> and private advantage: for this nature avoids pain, and pursues pleasure, in an irrational manner; prefers both these to that which is more just and excellent; and, producing darkness in itself, fills at length both itself and the whole city with evils of every kind. 

Indeed, if any man, through a divine destiny, should be naturally sufficient to comprehend what is the public good, he would require no laws for the government of himself; for neither any law, nor any order, is better than **science** <term>science: used here in the classical sense of 'episteme'—certain, absolute knowledge or wisdom.</term>; nor is it lawful that **intellect** <note>Plato argues that if a person had perfect reason or 'Nous,' they would be a "living law" and would not need written rules.</note> should be subservient and a slave to any thing, but that it should be the ruler of all things, if it is thus true, and really free by nature. And thus much we have said for the sake of these things. Now, let us ordain what he who wounds or injures another ought to suffer or pay. For it is easy for every one to comprehend properly whether any one is wounded or not, who it is that is wounded, in what part, and after what manner. It is, therefore, equally impossible to refer all of these—or none of them—to courts of justice. For this one thing, in all these cases, must necessarily be referred to the decision of justice: I mean, whether each of these acts was done or not. On the other hand, it is nearly impossible for a law to determine nothing regarding the fine for such injuries, just as it is impossible for the law to determine every detail, both small and great, by itself.

**CLIN.** What then shall we say after this?

**GUEST.** That some things should be referred to courts of justice, but that others should be determined by the **legislator** <term>legislator: the primary law-giver who establishes the framework of the state's legal code.</term> himself.

**CLIN.** What are the particulars then which the legislator must decide, and what are those which must be decided by courts of justice?

**GUEST.** With the greatest propriety, after these things, the following assertions may be made: That, in a city in which the courts of justice are depraved and dumb, where the opinions of the judges are concealed and sentence is privately passed; and in which something still more dire than this takes place—when each of the judges decides, not in silence, but in the midst of tumult, as in a theatre, with **rhetoricians** <term>rhetoricians: professional orators who used persuasive, often emotional speech to sway public opinion or legal outcomes.</term> praising and blaming with loud exclamations—then a heavy calamity befalls the whole city. If, therefore, by some necessity, one were compelled to give laws to such courts of justice, it would not be a fortunate circumstance; but, at the same time, he who is forced to give them should commit only the smallest fines to the judges' discretion, but should clearly ordain the greatest part of them himself. But in a city in which courts of justice are established with as much propriety as possible, and the judges are well educated and examined with the greatest accuracy; in such a city, it will be proper and becoming to refer many things to the decision of such judges regarding the punishment of those who are condemned. When children inflict any such wounds on their parents, the judges shall be those that have passed beyond their **sixtieth year**, and whose children are truly their own, and not such as are adopted. He that in this case is condemned shall be put to death, or suffer some greater punishment, or one that is not much less; but no one of his kindred shall be permitted to judge him, though he should be of the age prescribed by law. 

But if a slave wounds any free-born person in anger, his master shall deliver him to the wounded person, that he may punish him in whatever manner he pleases: but if his master does not deliver him, he himself shall make a compensation for the injury. In a similar manner, let no violence be offered to a stranger, whether he has resided for some time in the city, or has but recently taken up his abode in it. But if it shall appear that the stranger has not acted unjustly, after threatening and disgracing the person that brought him before the prefects of the city, let both be dismissed.

# INTRODUCTION
### TO
## THE TENTH BOOK OF THE LAWS.

---

**T**HE following book may be rightly seen as one of the most vital parts of Plato’s writings. In it, he proves the existence of divine beings—the direct offspring of the ultimate, indescribable source of all things <note>The "ineffable principle" refers to "The One" or "The Good," the highest concept in Plato's philosophy from which all reality flows.</note>. He shows that these divine beings provide for everything and rule the universe with perfect justice. This book is also significant because it provides undeniable proof that Plato stayed true to the religion of his own people. This has often been questioned by those who do not understand the true nature of that ancient faith or its incredible depth. 

Because Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a later Greek philosopher who specialized in explaining Plato's complex ideas.</note> explored Plato’s teachings on these three subjects with such great insight in his first book *On the Theology of Plato*, the following translation from that work is included here for the reader's benefit:

I. In the *Laws*, Plato makes three main claims: That there are Gods, that they look after all things with care <note>This is the concept of "Divine Providence."</note>, and that they direct everything according to justice. He also argues that they cannot be influenced or corrupted by lower beings. It is clear to everyone that these are the most important principles of all religious thought. For what is more fundamental than the <term>essential existence</term> <note>original: "hyparxis" — a technical term meaning the core reality or "being" of a thing</note> of the Gods, their kindly care, or their unchanging and perfect power? Through this power, the Gods create lower forms of life in an orderly way, preserving them and drawing them back to themselves in total purity. While they govern others, they are never affected by those beneath them, nor are they changed by the shifting variety of the things they care for. We will learn how these concepts are naturally categorized if we first try to understand through logic the—

Of all beings, then, it is necessary that some should move only, that others should be moved only, and that the natures which subsist between these should both be moved and move; and this in such a manner, that either they must necessarily be moved by others, and move others, or be <term>self-motive</term> <note>The power of a being, like a soul, to initiate its own movement or change.</note>. These four <term>hypostases</term>¹ succeed each other in an orderly progression. For, prior to that which is moved only, and is passive to other primary causes, is that which moves others, and is moved by others; and beyond this is the <term>self-motive</term> nature, originating from itself, and, in consequence of moving itself, imparting to others also the representation of being moved. And after all those which participate of efficient or passive motion the immovable nature succeeds. For every thing <term>self-motive</term>, as possessing its perfection in a life attended with mutation and interval, is suspended from another more ancient cause, which always subsists according to the same things, and after the same manner, and whose life is not according to time, but in <term>eternity</term>: for time is the image of eternity. If, therefore, all things which are moved by themselves are moved according to time, but the eternal form of motion is beyond that which is borne along according to time, the <term>self-motive</term> nature will be the second in order, and not the first among beings. And again, that which moves others, and is moved by others, must necessarily be suspended from a <term>self-motive</term> nature: and not this only, but likewise every <term>alter-motive</term> <note>Something that only moves because it is acted upon by an external force.</note> composition or constitution of things, as the <term>Athenian guest</term> <note>The lead character in the *Laws*, often thought to represent Plato’s own voice.</note> demonstrates. For, says he, if every thing which is moved should stop², there will not be that which is first moved, unless the <term>self-motive</term> natures have a subsistence in beings. For the immovable is by no means naturally adapted to be moved, nor would it then be that which is first moved. And the <term>alter-motive</term> nature will require another moving power. If, therefore, the self-motive is more ancient than the alter-motive essence, but soul is primarily self-motive—from which the image of self-motion spreads to bodies—soul will be beyond bodies, and the motion of every body will be the offspring of the soul and of its internal motion. Hence, it is necessary that the whole of heaven, and all the bodies it contains, possessing such a variety of motion, and these moved according to nature (for to every body of this kind a circular motion is natural <gloss>This refers to the classical belief that celestial bodies move in perfect circles as their natural state.</gloss>), should have ruling souls, essentially more ancient than bodies, moving in themselves, and from above illuminating bodies with the power of being moved. With respect to these souls, therefore, which orderly distribute the whole world and its parts, and move and give life to everything corporeal—and which, of itself, is destitute of life, breathing in the cause of motion—with respect to these, it is necessary that they should either move all things rationally, or according to a contrary mode, which it is not lawful to assert. 

But if this world, and everything which has an orderly existence in it, and which is steadily moved and perpetually carried along according to nature, are referred to an irrational soul, which both moves itself and other things, neither the order of the periods, nor motion essentially bounded according to one reason, nor the position of bodies, nor anything else which is generated according to nature, will have a stable cause, and which is able to arrange everything according to the same things, and after the same manner. For everything irrational is naturally adapted to be adorned by another, since, of itself, it is indefinite and disordered. But to commit all heaven to a thing of this kind, and a circulation which revolves according to the same reason, and after the same manner, by no means accords with the nature of things, nor with our untrained conceptions. If, on the contrary, an intellectual and rational soul governs all things, and if everything which eternally revolves is under the dominion of such a soul, and there is nothing of the <term>wholes</term> <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "wholes" refers to the totalities of the universe, such as the entire sphere of the stars or the whole of an element, rather than individual parts.</note> destitute of soul

But if it is intellectual according to participation, there will be another intellect in energy more ancient than soul, which will possess intellection essentially, and which comprehends in itself, by its very essence, an uniform knowledge of wholes; since it is also necessary that the soul which is essentialized according to reason, should possess a subsistence according to intellect through participation, and that an intellectual nature should be twofold,—one primarily in a divine intellect itself, and another secondarily in soul, and proceeding from this divine intellect.

You may also add, if you are willing, the presence of intellectual illumination in body. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section concerning the Tenth Book of the Laws. ## INTRODUCTION TO THE

As mentioned previously, some beings enjoy a divine nature more closely, while others are more distant. Divinity itself exists prior to the essence of Intellect, using it as a vehicle; however, Intellect is considered most divine because it is the first thing to be deified <note>The process of being filled with or transformed by divine presence.</note>. The Soul is divine as long as it uses Intellect as a bridge. Even the physical body that shares in such a soul is divine in its own way (since the illumination of divine light shines down from above even to the lowest levels of existence), but the body on its own is not divine. The Soul, however, by focusing on Intellect and living through its own power, is the first level of the truly divine.

The same logic must also be applied to each of the celestial spheres and the bodies they contain. All of these imitate the whole of the heavens, since they have a permanent place in the cosmic order. The <term>sublunary</term> <note>The region "below the moon," referring to the Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to change and decay.</note> elements are not completely subject to change in their core essence; instead, they remain stable as part of the universal <term>wholenesses</term>¹ in the universe and contain within themselves individual <term>animals</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, the term "animal" (*zoon*) refers to any living being possessed of a soul, including the stars, the planets, and the Earth itself.</note>. Every "wholeness" has, alongside itself, more specific <term>hypostases</term> <note>The underlying realities or distinct levels of existence.</note>. Therefore, just as the number of stars moves in harmony with the celestial spheres, and just as a multitude of earthly creatures exists here on Earth alongside the planet’s own "wholeness," it is necessary that every element between heaven and earth should be filled with its own appropriate numbers. After all, how could the highest and lowest parts of the universe be organized with their parts unless the same logic applied to everything in the middle?

If each of the spheres is a living "animal," is permanently established in the same way, and completes the universe—participating in life through its soul, preserving its order through intellect, and acting as a leader of its parts through divine union—then it follows that not only the universe as a whole, but each of its eternal parts, is alive, gifted with intellect, and as similar to the whole as possible. Each of these parts is a "universe" in its own right relative to the things that belong to it. In short, there is one "wholeness" for the entire physical form of the universe, but there are many others beneath it that depend upon that one.

In the same way, "the same" is more linked to its cause than "the different," and "the bound" <note>Referring to *Peras* or Limit, the principle of order.</note> more than "the infinite" <note>Referring to *Apeiron*, the principle of unlimited possibility or chaos.</note>. II. Let us now turn our attention to the second point demonstrated in the following book: namely, that the Gods providently attend to both the "wholes" <note>The large-scale structures of the universe, like galaxies or elements.</note> and the individual parts. That which is <term>self-motive</term> <note>Specifically, the soul, which has the power to move itself without an external push.</note>, then, is the principle of motion and existence for all things in the world; life proceeds from the soul, along with physical movement and other types of change. A progression into being also comes from this soul—and even more so from an intellectual essence. This essence holds within itself the life of <term>self-motive</term> things and exists prior to any activity that happens in time. But this progression into being comes in even greater degree from an <term>hyparxis</term> <note>The foundational "oneness" or supreme essence of a being's existence.</note> characterized by unity. This unity contains both intellect and soul, fills them with total goodness, and reaches down to the very last and lowest of things. 

For while all parts of the world are not able to share in life, or in intellect and <term>gnostic power</term> <note>The capacity for knowledge or perception.</note>, all things share in *the One*, even down to matter itself. Everything—wholes and parts, things that follow nature and things that go against it—participates in this. Nothing is without a cause of this kind, nor can anything that exists be deprived of *the One*. If, therefore, the Gods (who are defined by this unity) produce all things and hold all things within their mysterious, all-encompassing powers, how could they not also possess a providence that flows from above down to the most specific, individual things? For it is right in every case that offspring should enjoy the care of their causes. All <term>alter-motive</term> <note>Things that cannot move themselves and must be moved by an external force, such as inanimate matter.</note> beings are the offspring of <term>self-motive</term> natures; and things that exist in time (whether for the whole of time or just a part) are the effects of things that are eternal; because per-

...perpetual being is the cause of existence for things that only have a temporary life. It is necessary, therefore, that all these things should share in the providence <note>divine care and foresight</note> of the causes that came before them. They are given life by the Gods who are connected with souls, and they move in circles according to the cycles of time; but they receive the stable foundation of their forms from the **intellectual Gods**¹; and they receive within themselves the presence of unity, measure, and the distribution of goodness from the **first Gods**². 

Hence, it must be that either the Gods know what they have produced—because caring for their own offspring is natural to them—and they not only give existence to lower natures and provide them with life, essence, and unity, but also understand the primary cause of the good within them; or, we must say that the Gods are ignorant of what belongs to them, which is a forbidden thing to claim. For how can there be ignorance of beautiful things among those who are the causes of beauty? Or how can there be ignorance of good things among those who are granted an **existence** <term>hyparxis: the very foundation or "super-being" of a divine entity</term> defined by the nature of the Good?

Indeed, if the Gods are ignorant of their own children, then souls do not govern the universe according to a divine Intellect, nor are intellects carried within souls, nor do the "unities" <note>the Henads, or the highest aspects of the Gods</note> of the Gods hold all knowledge within themselves—all of which we have already proven in earlier sections. But if the Gods do know their progeny—being the fathers, leaders, and rulers of everything in the world—then the care of these governed things naturally belongs to them as the ones who generated them. Should we then say that the Gods, knowing the laws of nature, are capable of fulfilling them? Or should we say that through some **weakness** <note>original: "imbecility"</note> of their providence they are deprived of their own possessions or offspring? For if they abandon the care of all things through weakness, what could possibly cause such weakness? They do not move things as an external force, nor are other things the cause of their essence while they merely take over the government of what others produced; rather, as if from the stern of a ship, they direct all...

It remains, therefore, that the Gods must know what is adapted to every thing, and possess a power perfective of, and a dominion which rules over, all things. But if they know what is according to nature, and this—to those that generate all things—is to take care of all things, an abundance of power is not deprived of this providential attention.

It may also be inquired, whether the will of providence is in the Gods? Or whether this alone is wanting to their knowledge and power, and that, on this account, things are deprived of their care? For if, knowing what is adapted to themselves, and being able to fill the objects of their knowledge, they are not willing to provide for their own progeny, they will be indigent of goodness, will be no longer unenvying, and, by such an hypothesis, we shall subvert the **existence** <term>hyparxis: the primary foundation or "super-being" of a divine entity</term> according to which they are given their nature <note>original: "essentialized"</note>. Thus providing, therefore, for all things, they appear to be in no way lacking in the supply of goods. Let no one, however, imagine a providence of such a kind as to stretch the Gods out toward secondary natures and rob them of their lofty independence <note>original: "exempt transcendency"</note>, or attribute to them—who are established far away from all mortal troubles—a busy activity and a life of labor. For their blessedness is not willing to be stained with the difficulty of management; since even the life of worthy men is accompanied by an ease of action and is free from trouble and pain. But all labors, which are the result of agitation, arise from the resistance of matter. If, however, it is necessary to define the way in which the providence of the Gods acts, we must establish it to be effortless, pure, non-physical, and beyond description <note>original: "ineffable"</note>. For they do not govern all things in the same way as men do when they attend to their own affairs—namely, by asking what is appropriate, investigating the good of any specific thing through hesitant reasoning, looking toward outside things, and following after results; but, by previously holding within themselves the blueprints of the whole universe, producing from within themselves the <term>essences</term> <note>The fundamental natures or "whatness" of things.</note> of all things, and looking toward themselves, they lead, perfect, and fill all things with good through a silent path. They produce neither like nature, which acts only by its very essence without choice, nor like individual souls, who act with will but lack the power to create essence; instead, they hold both of these together in a deep union. And they indeed will what they are able to accomplish by their very essence; but, being able to accomplish and produce all things by their very essence, they contain, in a will free from envy, the cause of all production. ### III.

In the third place, let us consider how we are to understand the immutability of a divine nature, which conducts all things according to justice, without departing from undeviating rectitude, both in the providence of all other things and of human affairs. This, then, I think, must be apparent to every one, that every where that which governs according to nature, and pays every attention to the <term>felicity</term> <note>Meaning "happiness" or "well-being" in a deep, flourishing sense.</note> of the governed, must lead and direct them to that which is best. For neither will the pilot, in governing sailors and a ship, have any other principal end than the safety of those that sail in the vessel, and of the vessel itself; nor will the physician, being the curator of the sick, either cut the body, or administer medicines for the sake of any thing else than the health of the subjects of his care; nor can it be said that the general or guardian looks to any other end, than the latter the liberty of those whom he preserves, and the former that of his soldiers. Nor does any other, to whom the government and care of any thing are committed, endeavour to subvert the good of his charge, over which he presides, and, aiming at which, he disposes every thing pertaining to the objects of his government in a becoming manner. If, therefore, we grant that the Gods are the governors of all things, and acknowledge that their providence is extended to all things, goodness being the characteristic of their nature, and that they possess every virtue, how is it possible for them to neglect the felicity of the subjects of their <term>providential energy</term>? <note>This refers to the active, outflowing power by which the divine cares for the universe.</note> Or how can they be inferior to other leaders in the providence of things subordinate? since the Gods always look to that which is better, and establish this as the end of all their government; but other leaders overlook the good of men, and embrace vice rather than virtue, being perverted by the gifts of the depraved. In short, whether you are willing to call them leaders, or governors, or guardians, or fathers, a divine nature will not appear to be indigent of any one of such-like appellations. For all things venerable and honourable subsist in them primarily: and, on this account, here also some things are naturally more venerable

# THE LAWS,

## BOOK X.

**AFTER** the laws concerning physical wounds, let the following general law be established regarding violence of every kind: no person shall carry away or take anything that belongs to another, nor shall they use their neighbor’s property without the owner’s consent. For all the evils mentioned previously have depended, depend now, and will continue to depend on this single principle. 

Among the remaining evils, the greatest are the lack of self-control and the <term>insolence</term> <note>original: "hybris" (ὕβρις); a central Greek concept referring to excessive pride or defiance toward the gods and the social order, often leading to a downfall.</note> of young men. The first of these manifests as insulting and harmful behavior toward sacred matters. Such lack of restraint and arrogance in the young are especially dangerous when they occur in public and holy places, within the tribes, or in other similar community groups. 

The second class of these crimes, which ranks just below the first, are those committed against private religious shrines and <term>sepulchres</term> <note>Tombs or burial vaults.</note>. The third rank of offenses, separate from those mentioned above, consists of insolent behavior toward one's parents. The fourth kind of insolence occurs when a person, out of contempt for the <term>magistrates</term> <note>Public officials or administrators of the law.</note>, takes or uses their property against their will. The fifth involves unjustly attacking or questioning the political conduct and integrity of a citizen. 

A common law must be established for each of these. Regarding <term>sacrilege</term> <note>The theft or violation of something sacred; in the Greek context, specifically "hierosylia," or robbing a temple.</note>, we have already summarized how it should be punished when committed through violence or in secret. Now, let us discuss the punishment for those who speak or act insolently toward the Gods. Before we begin, however, we offer the following as a means of <term>atonement</term> <note>A preliminary statement or "prelude" intended to persuade the citizen toward piety rather than just threatening punishment.</note>: any person who truly believes in the Gods, in accordance with the laws, will never voluntarily commit an impious act or speak against the law.

<summary>Plato introduces the legal framework for Book X, categorizing five types of social and religious "insolence" (hybris) and asserting that true belief in the Gods is the primary defense against impiety and lawlessness.</summary>

To which we may add, that all men, both Greeks and <term>Barbarians</term> <note>In the Greek context, this refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples, not necessarily "uncivilized" people.</note>, believe that there are Gods.

**CLIN.** O guest, what a terrible thing you have described, and what a plague to young men, both publicly to cities and to private families!

**GUEST.** You speak truly, Clinias. What then ought a legislator to do in this case? If, therefore, any refuse to obey his laws, ought he to punish some with death, others with whipping and imprisonment, others with loss of status, and others with poverty and exile? Or ought he to pay attention to persuasion and gentle methods at the same time that he is establishing laws?

**GUEST.** O most prompt Clinias, is it not difficult to follow by a reasoning process things asserted by the **multitude** <note>The common people or the masses, who may hold unexamined or materialistic beliefs.</note>, and which are of a very extended nature?

**CLIN.** But what, O guest? Shall we patiently endure to discourse in so **prolix** <term>prolix</term> <note>Tediously wordy or long-winded.</note> a manner about intoxication and music <note>Referring to the extensive discussions on drinking parties and musical education found in the opening books of *The Laws*.</note>, and shall we not be equally ready to speak about the Gods and similar matters? Besides, such an undertaking will be of the greatest assistance to legislation when it is conducted prudently. This is because those written mandates pertaining to the laws—which have always been subject to criticism—will thus remain entirely undisturbed. Therefore, we ought not to be terrified if these things are difficult to hear at first; when they are often repeated, they may be understood even by someone who is usually difficult to instruct due to a lack of aptitude. Though these arguments may be long, if they are useful, they should not be considered as having no consequence. Nor does it appear to me to be **holy** <note>In the sense of a religious or moral duty to the truth.</note> not to assist these assertions to the utmost of our power.

**MEGIL.** O guest Clinias, you appear to me to speak most excellently.

**GUEST.** He does very much so indeed.

**MEGIL.** Let us, therefore, do as he says. For, if assertions of this kind were not, as I may say, scattered among all men, there would be no occasion for arguments to prove that there are Gods; but now this is necessary. Since, therefore, the greatest laws are corrupted by **vicious** <note>In the classical sense, "vicious" means full of vice or morally corrupt.</note> men, to whom does it pertain to give assistance to them more than to the legislator?

**CLIN.** To no one.

**GUEST.** But inform me again, O Clinias, (for it is proper that you should partake of this discourse,) does it not appear that he who asserts the above-mentioned particulars considers fire and water, earth and air, as the first of **all**... <margin>The Guest begins to examine the materialist view that the four elements are the primary causes of the universe.</margin>

Consider this: if it were necessary for the three of us to cross a very rapid river, and I, being the youngest of the three and having experience with many rivers, should say that I ought to first try to cross it by myself. I would leave you in safety while I see if it can be crossed by you, who are older than me. Afterward, if I find it safe, I would call you to cross the river with me; or, if it were too deep for you, I would face the danger alone. Would I not seem to be speaking reasonably in that case? 

In the same way, the discourse we are now entering is quite intense—perhaps even beyond your current strength. I worry it might cause you a "dark giddiness" <note>A metaphor for the confusion one feels when confronted with abstract, high-level metaphysical arguments.</note> by leading you into questions you aren't used to, eventually overwhelming you with shame and sorrow. Therefore, it seems to me that in this case, I should first interrogate myself while you listen in safety, and then answer my own questions, proceeding this way until the whole of this discourse is finished.

**CLIN.** You appear to us, O guest, to speak most excellently: do, therefore, as you say.

On this account it becomes the fountain of all wonderful things, proceeding homologously <term>homologously: agreeing in proportion or following the same law of motion</term> according to slowness and swiftness, in large and small circles, and thus accomplishing what to some one it might appear impossible to accomplish.

which moves both itself and others, which is adapted to all actions and passions <note>In classical philosophy, "passions" refers to being acted upon or receiving an influence from an external source, the counterpart to "actions."</note>, and which is truly denominated the mutation and motion of all things?

But how is it possible that a thing which is moved by another can ever be the first of things changed? It is certainly impossible. But when a thing moving itself causes mutation in something else, and this latter in some other, and ten thousand things are thus moved in succession,—whether or no in this case will there be any other principle <term>principle: from the Greek *archē*, meaning the starting point, origin, or first cause of something</term> of all the motion than the mutation of that which moves itself?

**CLIN.** You speak most excellently. These things, therefore, must be granted.

**GUEST.** Further still, let us thus interrogate and answer ourselves. If all generated natures should, after a manner, stand still, as many of those we are now addressing dare to say they do, which among the above-mentioned motions would necessarily first take place?

**CLIN.** Doubtless that which moves itself. For the motion depending on another could not by any means take place till it had previously undergone some mutation.

**GUEST.** We must say, therefore, ‘that the principle of all motions, and which first subsists in things abiding and in motion, is that which moves itself; and that this is necessarily the most ancient and the most powerful <term>mutation</term> <note>original: "mutatio"; in this context, it refers to any kind of change or movement.</note> of all things: but that the second is that which is changed by another, and at the same time moves others.

**GUEST.** A twofold distinction is found in other things, and in number. Thus, for instance, in number, the name indeed is the "even," but the definition is "one number divided into two equal parts."

**CLIN.** How is it possible they should not acknowledge this? <note>Clinias agrees that the Gods must be recognized as virtuous and active.</note>

**GUEST.** But the Gods cannot be negligent through indolence and sluggishness; for timidity is not present with them.

**GUEST.** It remains, therefore, that if they neglect a few things, and such as are small in the universe, they must either do so because they know that things of this nature ought by no means to be taken care of, or because they are ignorant that they ought to be taken care of; for, can there be any other alternative?

**CLIN.** None.

**GUEST.** Whether, therefore, O most excellent and best of men, shall we consider you as saying that the Gods neglect these in consequence of being ignorant that they ought to be taken care of; or that, like the most depraved of men, they know that this is proper, but are prevented from acting agreeably to their knowledge, through being vanquished by certain pleasures or pains?

**CLIN.** What?

**GUEST.** Every thing, therefore, that participates of soul is changed, and possesses in itself the cause of this mutation; but, when changed, it is borne along according to the order and law of fate. And those souls whose manners are less changed, have a less extended progression; for they proceed no further than the superficies <term>superficies: the outer surface or boundary</term> of the region. But those whose manners are more changed, and are more unjust, fall into depth, and into the places beneath, which are denominated Hades <note>original: "Ἅιδης" (Hades). The Greek underworld or the state of the soul after death.</note>, and the like, where they are vehemently terrified, and conversant with dreams, both living and when freed from body. A greater soul, however, when it participates either of virtue or vice, becoming in this case strong, through its own will, and converse with other natures, if, mingling with divine virtue, it becomes eminently divine, then it is translated into another better place, which is entirely holy: but if it mingles itself with the contrary to divine virtue, then its life is transferred into a contrary place. This then, O boy and young man, who think that you are neglected by the Gods, is the judgment of the Olympian divinities <note>The primary gods of the Greek pantheon who dwell on Mount Olympus.</note>;—that he who is more depraved shall depart to more depraved souls, but he

**CLIN.** Speak of better things! For how could it be possible for the Gods to resemble any of these failures?

**GUEST.** Are not all the Gods the greatest of all guardians, and the guardians of our most important affairs?

**CLIN.** Very much so.

**GUEST.** Shall we say, then, that those who guard the most beautiful things, and who are themselves supreme in virtue, are worse than dogs or men of ordinary character? For even average men never betray justice by accepting unholy gifts from the wicked.

**CLIN.** By no means; such a claim is intolerable. Anyone who holds such an opinion may rightly be considered the worst and most impious <term>impious: showing a profound lack of respect for God or sacred things</term> of men.

**GUEST.** We may say, then, that we have sufficiently proven the three points we proposed: first, that the Gods exist; second, that they care for all things; and third, that they are not to be swayed by gifts in a way that contradicts justice.

**CLIN.** Undoubtedly; we agree with these arguments.

**GUEST.** I must admit, I have spoken somewhat forcefully because of the stubbornness of wicked men. My friend Clinias, I have used a contentious <note>original: "philoneikia"; meaning an argumentative or competitive style of speaking</note> tone out of fear that our adversaries might think they have won. I did not want them to imagine they have the freedom to do whatever they please based on their false ideas about the Gods. It was this earnest desire to prevent such behavior that led me to speak in this more unusual way. But if our short discussion has managed to persuade these men to turn away from their current views and embrace a different way of life, then our introduction to the laws regarding impiety will have been beautifully delivered.

**GUEST.** After the preface, therefore, the discourse which is the interpreter of the laws will properly follow, proclaiming to all impious persons, that they must depart from their depraved manners, and betake themselves to such as are pious. Let bonds, then, be the punishment of all impious conduct. With respect to impiety, there are three causes of it, as we have already mentioned; and since two things take place from each of such-like causes, there will be six genera of crimes against the Gods, which require neither an equal nor a similar punishment. For some, who though they do not in any respect believe there are Gods, yet, from naturally possessing a just disposition, hate the vicious, and, through being indignant with injustice, neither commit unjust actions themselves, nor associate with, but avoid, unjust men, and love the just. # THE LAWS,

## BOOK XI.

---

**IT** now remains that we should speak of mutual compacts <term>compacts: formal agreements or contracts between citizens</term>, and the order which they ought to receive. But a thing of this kind is, in a certain respect, simple. I mean, that no one shall touch my property, nor move the least thing belonging to me, without my consent. And I, if I am endued with a sound mind, shall act in the same manner with respect to the property of others. In the first place, then, we shall speak about such treasures, as some one may deposit both for himself and those belonging to him, who is not descended from my parents <note>In the legal framework of Plato's city, inheritance and property were strictly tied to family lineage. A "treasure" found in the earth was not "finders keepers" if it did not belong to one's own ancestors.</note>, and which I should never pray that I might find, nor, if I did find, should move, nor be induced to partake of, by those who are called *diviners* <note>original: "μάντεσιν" (mantesin). Professional soothsayers in the ancient world were sometimes hired to use supernatural means to locate buried gold or hidden caches.</note>. For I should never be so much benefited by the possession of riches, when obtained after this manner, as I should excel in the virtue of the soul, and in justice, by not receiving them. For thus I should acquire one possession instead of another, a better in that which is better; preferring the prior possession of justice in the soul, to wealth. For it is well said of many particulars, that *things immovable should not be moved* <note>This was a common Greek proverb (likely referring to the "Camarina" myth) used as a warning against disturbing ancestral or sacred things that are better left untouched.</note>; and it may be said of this, as being one of them. It is likewise proper to be persuaded by what is commonly asserted about these things, that such particulars do not contribute to the procreation of children <note>Plato suggests that ill-gotten gains do not provide a foundation for a healthy or virtuous family legacy.</note>. But he who takes no care of children, and neglects the legislator, and, therefore, takes away that which neither he nor his grandfather deposited, such a one corrupts the most beautiful and simple law, which was established by a man by no means ignoble <note>Plato is likely referring to Solon, the legendary Athenian lawgiver, who famously decreed: "Take not up what you laid not down."</note>, and which says, *You shall not take away that which you have not deposited.* What then ought he to suffer, who despises these two legislators, and who takes away that which he did not himself deposit, and which is not a small...

<meta>Catchword: affair,</meta>

<summary>Book XI begins with a discussion on civil law and property, establishing the moral principle that citizens should not touch property that is not theirs. Plato specifically addresses "treasure troves," arguing that discovering hidden wealth does not grant ownership and that choosing justice over found riches is a greater gain for the soul.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Book XI, civil law, property rights, contracts, justice, treasure trove, Solon, ethics of wealth, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# THE LAWS.

...affair, but a mighty treasure? Divinity <note>original: "Θεός" (Theos). Plato uses this to refer to the divine order or the collective power of the gods.</note>, indeed, knows what punishment he ought to suffer from the Gods. But let us declare what he ought to suffer from men. Let him who first perceives him, give information of the affair:—if it happens in the city, to the **ædiles** <term>ædiles: urban magistrates responsible for public order and buildings</term>; if in the forum, to the **præfects of the markets** <term>præfects of the markets: officials who regulated commercial activity and fair trade</term>; and, if in any other part of the region, to those that take care of the land, and the governors of these. 

When the affair becomes apparent, let the city send to Delphi <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Delphi was the highest religious authority in the Greek world; the city would consult the oracle to determine the proper religious atonement for disturbing hidden property.</note>, and let what the God determines, both respecting the money and him that has moved it, be performed by the city conformable to the oracle. And if he who gives the information is free-born, let him be considered as a virtuous character; but, if he does not give information, as a vicious character. If he who reveals the affair is a slave, it will be proper that he should be made free by the city, and that the city should pay his master the price of his manumission <term>manumission: the legal act of freeing a slave</term>; but, if he does not reveal it, let him be punished with death. 

Let a similar law follow this, respecting things small and great. If a man leaves any property, whether willingly or unwillingly, let him who may happen to meet with it suffer it to remain; considering that the **dæmon** <term>dæmon: a guardian spirit or minor deity, in this case, a protector of travelers and the integrity of the road</term> who presides over roads defends things of this kind, which are dedicated to Divinity by law. When any one, being unpersuaded by this law, takes away such property to his own house, if he is but of little worth, being a slave, let him receive many lashes with a whip, from any one not less than thirty years of age who may happen to meet him. 

But, if he is free-born, besides being considered as illiberal <note>In this context, "illiberal" means behaving in a manner beneath the dignity and moral standing expected of a free citizen.</note>, and void of law, let him pay as a fine ten times the worth of what he took away to its proper owner.

When any one accuses another of holding his property, whether it be much or little, and the person who detains it acknowledges that it is in his possession, but denies that it is his who demands it,—if a written account of the affair is given to the magistrates according to law, he who detains it shall be called before a magistrate, and if it shall appear to be the property of the accuser, it shall be restored to him. But if it shall be found to belong to neither, but to some absent person, if its possessor will not engage to restore it to the absent person, let him be compelled to deposit it. 

If a written account of the affair is not given to the magistrates, let the property be deposited with the three oldest magistrates till sentence is passed. And, if the subject of dispute is an animal, let him who upon trial is cast <note>To be "cast" in a legal sense means to lose the case or be judged against.</note>, pay the magistrates the expense of its keeping; but let the affair be decided by the magistrates.

However, it is requisite to lay down a preface, in the same manner as in other laws. Every man, indeed, ought to consider **adulteration** <note>In this context, "adulteration" refers to the act of debasing or falsifying goods—for example, mixing inferior materials into a product to deceive the buyer.</note>, lying, and deception, as forming one genus, about which it is usual for the multitude to say, though very erroneously, that when each of these is opportunely adopted, the result is frequently proper. But as they leave the occasion, the where, and the when, disorderly and indefinitely, they often by this assertion both injure themselves and others. The legislator, however, should not suffer this indefinite to be unnoticed, but greater or lesser boundaries ought always to be clearly determined. Let them, therefore, now be determined. Let no one tell a lie, or deceive, or adulterate any thing, calling at the same time on the Gods, unless he is desirous of becoming odious to **Divinity** <note>Plato views the marketplace not just as a center of trade, but as a space where one's piety is tested; deceiving a fellow citizen while invoking the Gods is considered a profound religious offense.</note>. This, however, will be the case with him, in the first place, who, swearing falsely, despises the Gods; and, in the second place, with him who speaks falsely before those that are better than himself. But the good are more excellent than the bad, and, in short, the elder than the younger. On this account, parents are better than their offspring, men than women and children, and governors than the governed. All these ought to be reverenced in every government, and especially in political governments, for the sake of which we have engaged in the present discussion. For he who adulterates any thing in the **forum** <term>forum: the Latin translation of the Greek "agora," the central marketplace and public meeting space of the city</term>, lies and deceives, and, calling on the Gods, swears falsely before the **guardians of the forum** <term>guardians of the forum: known in Greek as the "agoranomoi," these were elected officials responsible for maintaining order and fair weights and measures in the marketplace</term>, and violates their laws, neither fearing men, nor reverencing the Gods. To be careful, indeed, not to contaminate the names of the Gods, is in every respect beautiful; for they ought not to be used in common like other names, but every thing pertaining to the Gods should be preserved in a pure and holy manner. Let the following law, therefore, be established for those who will not be persuaded to act in this manner:—He who sells any thing in the forum shall not be suffered to fix two prices to any article; but when he has fixed a simple price, if he does not sell it, he shall take it away, and be allowed to bring it back again on the same day, without valuing it at a higher price than before. Let praise, and taking an oath, never be employed in selling. And if any one is disobedient to this law, any citizen, not less than thirty years of age, who detects him in swearing, shall strike him with impunity; and if he neglects to do this, let him be considered as a betrayer of the laws. We have now said, expose the fraud of such a person, if he is able, before a magistrate; and let a slave, or an inhabitant <note>A resident alien, or "metic," who lived in the city but did not have full citizenship.</note>, bring with him the adulterated article. Let a citizen, who neglects to accuse such a one, be pronounced a bad man, as one who defrauds the Gods: but, if he accuses him, let him dedicate the adulterated article to the Gods who preside over the marketplace <note>original: "forum"; in a Greek context, this refers to the *agora*.</note>. Let him who openly sells things of this kind, besides being deprived of the adulterated article, receive publicly as many lashes with a whip as there are <term>drachmas</term> <note>A drachma was a standard Greek silver coin; the punishment was scaled to the value of the fraud.</note> in the sum for which he sold the article; a crier at the same time proclaiming in the marketplace the cause of his being whipped. Let the prefects of the markets, and the guardians of the laws, endeavour to detect all the adulterations and evil practices of the sellers, by making inquiry of men skilled in vendible articles, and cause to be written on a pillar before the marketplace what a seller ought to do, and what not, so that men of this kind may clearly know how to act according to law in disposing of their respective articles. As to the particulars relating to the <term>market officials</term> <note>original: "ædiles"; these were the *agoranomoi* who oversaw trade and public order.</note>, we have spoken of these sufficiently above. But if it should appear that any thing is wanting to these, let them supply the deficiency by communicating with the guardians of the laws, and afterwards let them write their first and second legal institutions on a pillar <note>Laws were often carved into stone pillars (stelae) and placed in public view to ensure no citizen could claim ignorance.</note>.

After adulteration it follows that we should speak of <term>retail trade</term> <note>original: "cauponation," referring to the keeping of an inn, a tavern, or any shop for retail exchange.</note>. But about the whole of this we shall first of all give our advice, and the reasons for such advice, and afterwards establish a law respecting it. For all retail trade in a city does not exist for the sake of injuring the city, but naturally for the sake of the contrary. For how is it possible that he should not benefit the city who causes money, from being possessed in an unequal and irregular manner, to be possessed equably, and with due proportion? It is requisite to say, that the power of money, the merchant, the mercenary character <note>A person who works for hire or wages.</note>, and the inn-keeper, will accomplish this for us. For these, and others of this kind, whether they act in a more becoming or a more base manner, endeavour to supply the needs of others, and render possessions equal. But let us consider the reason why this appears neither beautiful nor becoming, and why it is slandered; so that though we may not procure a remedy for the whole by law, yet we may for a part.
