-># THE LAWS.<-

**CLINIAS.** This matter, as it appears, is no small thing and requires a high degree of virtue.

**ATHENIAN GUEST.** What are you saying, my friend Clinias? Only a small portion of humanity is naturally inclined, or has been so well educated, that they can act with moderation when they are in need or driven by desire. Rare are those who, when they have the power to acquire great wealth, behave soberly and prefer balance over excess. But the common crowd behaves in the exact opposite way. They desire without limit; when they could be moderately wealthy, they choose instead to seek immense riches. This is why everyone involved in <term>retail trade</term> <note>original: "cauponation"; referring specifically to the business of buying and selling goods for profit or running an inn, which was often viewed with suspicion in the ancient world.</note> and commerce is slandered and falls into shameful disgrace. 

For if someone were to compel—though it is ridiculous even to mention it, as it has never happened and never will—the best of men to keep an inn for a certain time, or a <term>tavern</term> <note>original: "victualling-house"; a place providing food and drink to travelers.</note>, or to do any such thing; or if the most virtuous women were forced by fate into such jobs, we would soon realize that these are honest and honorable occupations. If they were managed according to sound reason, these people would be honored as if they were performing the roles of mothers and nurses. 

But as it stands, inns and taverns are built in lonely places far from cities. They offer shelter to those caught in storms and a cool rest for those suffering from heat. However, they do not treat those who seek refuge as friends with hospitality; instead, they treat them like enemies and captives, forcing them to pay a "ransom" and plundering them of their money. These base actions, and others like them, bring a bad reputation to the very jobs meant to help those in need. 

A legislator must always find a remedy for these issues. It is an old and true proverb that it is hard to fight against two things at once—as we see in diseases and many other cases. In this situation, the fight is against two opposites: poverty and wealth. Wealth corrupts the human soul through luxury, while poverty drives people to shamelessness through suffering. What remedy can be found for this sickness in a government governed by intellect? In the first place, we must try our best to ensure that the state relies on <term>retail trade</term> <note>original: "cauponation".</note> as little as possible. And in the next place, we <meta>The catchword "muft" in the OCR is a transcription of "must," which would begin the first sentence of the following page.</meta>

It is proper, likewise, that the guardians of the law should consider that they are not only guardians of those who are easily prevented from acting in an illegal and vicious manner, viz. those who are well-born and educated; but that they are much more guardians of those who are different from these, and who engage in employments by which they are strongly impelled to <term>wickedness</term> <note>original: "improbity"; a lack of moral integrity or honesty.</note>.

Reverencing, therefore, the Gods that are the authors of these arts, it will not be proper to deceive them, by lying about things of this kind. Let the same law too consult for the craftsman as for the seller of vendible articles. Let care be taken, therefore, that he does not ask more than the worth of his work, but let his demand be most simple, and accommodated to its worth. For an artist knows the worth of his work. In cities, therefore, consisting of free men, it is not proper that an artist should endeavour to deceive the simple <note>referring to those who do not possess the specialized knowledge of the craft.</note> by art, which is naturally clear and void of falsehood. Hence, when this is the case, the injurer shall make a proper recompense to the injured person.

As we have, however, made mention of <term>artificers</term> <note>original: "artificers"; here referring to skilled craftsmen or professionals in any trade.</note>, and as commanders of armies and military arts are artificers of safety to a city, it is but just that we should also speak of these. Let the following law, therefore, be established for these, mingled with praise, and which does not compel, but consults the multitude of the citizens: that such good men shall be honoured in the second place, as have been saviours of the whole city, whether by their valour, or by warlike devices; for the first honour must be given to those who have been remarkably obedient to the written laws of good legislators. 

We have, therefore, now nearly spoken sufficiently of the greatest <term>compacts</term> <note>meaning legal contracts or social agreements.</note> among men, except those pertaining to orphans, and the guardians of orphans. The beginning of all these is the desire of the <term>testator</term> <note>A person who has made a will or given instructions for the distribution of their property after death.</note>, and the fortune of those that make no will. I have said it is necessary to speak of these, O <term>Clinias</term> <note>A Cretan character in the dialogue who is helping to establish the laws for a new colony.</note>, in consequence of looking to the difficulty respecting them: for it is not possible to leave them in a disordered manner. For testators would desire many things differing from each other, and contrary to the laws, to the manners of the living, and to their ancestors, if any one should simply give them permission to make their wills in whatever manner they pleased, and should ordain, that every will made near the end of life shall be properly executed. For most men, when they consider themselves as about to die, are affected with <term>stupidity and remissness</term> <note>original: "stupidity and remissness"; referring to the mental fog, weakness, or lack of judgment that often accompanies terminal illness.</note>.

CLIN. How so?

GUEST. Desiring to be the lord of all things, it is usual for him to speak with anger.

CLIN. What does he say at this time?

...with public disgrace <note>original: "infamy." In ancient Greek law, this likely refers to *atimia*, a loss of civil rights and social standing.</note>—this being a punishment for a person of reason that is far heavier than a very large fine. For after the education and discipline of the first generation which we have already discussed, we must now find a way to ensure that orphans suffer as little as possible from their misfortune. 

First, we propose that the Guardians of the Laws <term>Guardians of the Laws: Known as the *Nomophylakes*, these were high-ranking officials in Plato’s proposed city responsible for overseeing the administration of the law.</term> should be appointed as their guardians in place of their parents, and they must be no worse than the parents they replace. Let this serve as our introduction regarding the education of orphans and the appointment of their tutors. It was appropriate for us to mention earlier that the souls of the deceased possess a certain power that allows them to watch over human affairs with a providential care. This is indeed true, though proving it would require a very long explanation. It is also right to believe in the many ancient traditions concerning such things. Any legislator, unless they are completely out of their mind, should believe in the truth of these traditions. 

Because these matters are naturally so, those who look after the desolate condition of orphans should, first and foremost, fear the Gods above. Next, they should fear the souls of the deceased, who naturally take a special interest in their own offspring; these spirits are kind to those who honor them but hostile toward those who neglect them. 

Furthermore, the souls of the living who have reached old age—who live in a happy city governed by good laws and receive the highest honors, and whose children and grandchildren live pleasant lives because they are well-cared for—these elders also keenly hear and perceive such matters. They are benevolent toward those who act justly toward orphans, but they are deeply indignant with those who harm them. For they consider the care of an orphan to be the greatest and most sacred of all trusts <note>original: "deposit," referring to the Greek *parakatatheke*, a legal and moral obligation to return or protect something entrusted to one's care.</note>. 

It is necessary, therefore, that any tutor or magistrate with even a small degree of intelligence should pay attention to these details. They must devote as much care to the discipline and education of orphans as they would to their own children. He who is persuaded by this introduction to the law, and who acts justly toward orphans, will clearly be exempt from the legislator's anger in these matters. The laws which follow relate to the tutors <term>tutor: In this context, a "tutor" is a legal guardian responsible for the person and property of a minor, rather than just a teacher.</term> of orphans, and the attention which magistrates should pay to these tutors. If, therefore, they possessed a model <note>original: "paradigm." This refers to a perfect example or standard to be followed.</note> of the education of free children—with the tutors taking care of both these orphans and their own concerns—and if they had laws respecting these children that were sufficiently distinct, we would not need to establish specific laws for tutors as if they differed from others. We would not need to distinguish the life of orphans from those who are not orphans by various special pursuits. 

But now, in every matter of this kind, the loss of parents does not seem to differ much from the state of being under a father’s government; however, society is often unwilling to equalize the honor, dishonor, and protective care given to orphans. Hence the law, through its attention to orphans, both consoles and threatens. And further still, it will be very appropriate for the law to issue the following warning: 

"He who takes care of either a female or a male orphan, and who is appointed from among the guardians of the law <term>guardians of the law: Known as the *Nomophylakes*, these were the highest-ranking officials in Plato’s ideal city, responsible for overseeing the administration of the law.</term> to oversee their tutor, shall possess the same affection for the orphans entrusted to his care as if they were his own offspring. He shall bestow no less attention to their affairs, but even more, than he does to his own." 

Let every person, therefore, take care of orphans according to this law. But, if any one acts contrary to this law in affairs of this kind, let such a tutor be condemned by a magistrate. And if it shall appear to the kindred of the orphans, or to any other citizen, that the tutor has acted negligently or wickedly, let him be brought before a court of judgment and made to pay a four-fold restitution <note>A significant penalty of four times the original value, meant to act as a powerful deterrent against the exploitation of the vulnerable.</note> of the loss sustained; let one half of this be given to the boy, and the other half to the accuser. 

When an orphan reaches puberty <note>In the context of Plato's *Laws*, this refers to the age of legal majority, usually around eighteen to twenty years old.</note>, if he believes that he has been neglected by his tutor, let him be permitted to call his tutor to an account for five years from the time that the guardianship is finished. And if any tutor is condemned, let a court of justice determine what he ought to suffer, or what fine he ought to pay. If any magistrate shall appear to have injured an orphan through negligence, let a court of justice determine the restitution which he ought to make. But, if he shall appear to have injured the orphan through purposeful injustice, besides making restitution, let him be deprived of the office of a guardian of the law; and let another common guardian of the city be appointed in his place by the region and the city.

...city. Greater discord occurs between fathers and sons, and sons and fathers, than is fitting. In such cases, fathers believe the legislator should allow them to renounce their sons by a public crier <note>original: "apokeryxis." This was a formal, public legal act in which a father disinherited a son and severed all legal ties.</note>, so that they are no longer their sons according to the law. On the other hand, sons believe they should be allowed to accuse their fathers of madness when they are disgracefully circumstanced through disease or old age. These things usually take place when the manners of men are perfectly corrupt. For, if only half of these evils existed—if the parents alone, or the children alone, were vicious—the calamities born of such great hatred would not exist.

Indeed, in any other type of government, a son abandoned by his father would not necessarily be forced to leave the city. But, in a city governed by these laws, he who is given up by his father must necessarily take up his residence in some other place. For no one is allowed to join himself with any family beyond the **<term>five thousand and forty houses</term>** <note>Plato’s plan for the city of Magnesia fixed the population at exactly 5,040 households to ensure each family had a plot of land and that the city remained manageable.</note>. On this account, it is necessary that the son who is abandoned by his father should not only be driven from his father’s house, but from his whole race. 

It is proper, therefore, in matters of this kind, to act according to the following law:

When any man, through an unfortunate anger—whether he is justly enraged or not—desires to be liberated from an alliance with the one he has fathered and educated, let him not be permitted to accomplish his desire in an improper manner or immediately. But, in the first place, let him assemble his own relations, as far as his cousins, and, in a similar manner, those of his son on the mother’s side. When they are assembled, let him accuse his son to them, and show them that he deserves to be expelled from all his kindred. Let the son also be permitted to defend himself, and endeavour to prove that he does not deserve to suffer anything of this kind. 

And if the father persuades them that his accusation is just, and all the relations, both male and female—excepting the father, mother, and the son himself—vote for his being abandoned; when this is the case, let a father be permitted to renounce his son, but by no means when this is not the case. 

If any citizen wishes to adopt a son whom his father abandons, let him not be restrained from adopting him by any law. For the character of youth naturally undergoes many changes throughout life. But, if no one in the space of ten years wishes to adopt such a son, let those whose duty it is to send offspring into a **<term>colony</term>** <note>A "colony" in this context refers to a new settlement established by the city to manage surplus population or individuals who no longer have a place in the original 5,040 households.</note> take care that this rejected son is made an inhabitant of such a colony.

It appears, indeed, that the characters of such people are far from being mild; for this reason, we should endeavor to match them with partners of more profound and gentle temperaments. If a female slave has a sexual relationship with a male slave, or with a free-born man, or with a **<term>freedman</term>** <note>A former slave who has been legally released from bondage but often still held certain social or legal obligations to their former master.</note>, the offspring shall be the property of the female slave’s master. In the case of a master fathering a child with a slave, the **<term>guardians of the law</term>** <note>The high-ranking officials responsible for maintaining the legal and moral order of the city.</note> shall banish the child and its mother.

Nevertheless, neither God nor any man of sound mind would ever advise anyone to neglect their parents. In fact, an explanation of how one should properly worship the Gods serves as an excellent introduction to the topic of honoring or dishonoring one's parents. Ancient laws concerning the Gods are established among all men in two ways: some of the **Gods** <note>Plato is referring here to the "visible" gods: the stars, planets, and other celestial bodies, which he viewed as divine, living beings.</note> we perceive clearly and honor directly, while for others, we create **<term>images</term>** <note>Original Greek: *agalmata*. These are statues or physical representations of deities that people use as a focus for worship.</note>. Although these statues are inanimate, we believe that the living Gods themselves will be well-disposed and favorable toward us because of the honor we show to their likenesses.

Therefore, if someone has a father or mother—or their grandparents—living in their home who are worn out by old age, they should treat them like precious treasures. Such a person should realize that no other statue or image in the house is more powerful or effective in gaining the favor of the Gods than these living elders, provided they are treated with the proper reverence.

No one should think that the Gods only listen to a father’s or mother’s natural prayers when they are being mistreated; the Gods also hear them when they are honored and deeply loved. For this reason, when parents in their prayers earnestly call upon the Gods to bless their children, should we not believe that they are heard just as clearly, and that the Gods grant them good things? Otherwise, the Gods would not be fair distributors of blessings—a trait that is utterly beneath them.

CLINIAS: Certainly.

THE GUEST: Therefore, as we noted a little while ago, we should believe that we can possess no "image" or statue that is more honored by the Gods than our fathers, grandfathers, mothers, and grandmothers when they are worn out by old age. When someone honors these elderly relatives, the Divine rejoices; if it were otherwise, the Gods would not listen to their prayers. Indeed, we should consider the "living image" of our **<term>progenitors</term>** <note>A direct ancestor, such as a parent or grandparent.</note> to be far more wonderful than lifeless statues. These living images, when we treat them with reverence, pray for our success, but they do the opposite when we despise them. Lifeless statues do neither. Thus, a person who behaves rightly toward their father, grandfather, and all such elders possesses the most powerful of all "images" for winning divine favor.

CLINIAS: You speak most beautifully.

THE GUEST: Every person endowed with intellect will fear and honor the prayers of their parents, knowing that they have often brought either great benefit or great harm to many. These things are established by the laws of nature. To good men, their aged ancestors—when they live to the very end of their lives—will be seen as a treasure; and if they die before that time, they will be deeply missed. To the wicked, however, they are terrifying in the extreme. Therefore, let everyone, convinced by these arguments, honor their parents according to the law. But if any one is accused of witchcraft, without being a diviner, let his punishment in a similar manner be determined by a court of justice. Let him who injures another by fraud or force, pay a great fine, if the injury is great, but a smaller fine, if the injury is small; and let restitution in all cases be equivalent to the loss sustained. And, in all injuries, let the injurer be fined till he is amended. 

If it shall appear that any one was impelled to injure another, by a folly foreign to his nature, through the imprudence of youth, let him be sentenced to pay a lighter fine; but if by his own proper folly, or through the **<term>incontinence</term>** <note>In this context, incontinence (*akrasia*) refers to a lack of self-mastery or the inability to restrain one's impulses and desires.</note> of pleasures and pains, or through fear, envy, certain desires, or anger difficult to cure, a heavier fine. ### THE LAWS.

For the sake of all these particulars, and looking to all these, the laws—like good archers—should consider this as a mark: namely, the magnitude of punishment and the proper desert in each offense. <note>Plato often uses the metaphor of an archer (toxotēs) to describe the legislator's need to "aim" at virtue and the common good.</note> A judge, therefore, ought to act in this manner as the minister of the legislature, since it is permitted him by law to establish what punishment offenders ought to suffer; and, like a painter, he should diligently copy his original. 

This, indeed, O **Megillus** and **Clinias** <note>These are the two interlocutors listening to the "Athenian Stranger": Megillus is a Spartan and Clinias is a Cretan.</note>, should be done by us at present, in the most beautiful and best manner; and we should establish what punishments ought to be inflicted, both on base actions committed by fraud, and those committed by violence; and this in such a manner as the Gods, and the sons of the Gods, will permit us to establish. 

Let no one then who is insane be openly seen in the city, but let the relations of the insane person keep him secure at home, in the best manner they are able. If they do not, let them be fined. And let him who possesses the largest estate be fined a hundred **<term>drachms</term>** <note>A drachm was a standard unit of silver currency; for context, a skilled laborer in the 4th century BCE might earn one drachm per day.</note>, if he is negligent in securing an insane person, whether he be a slave, or free. But let him who possesses the next estate to this be fined four out of five parts of a **<term>mina</term>** <note>A mina was equal to 100 drachms. Plato’s fines are graduated according to the four property classes of his ideal city.</note>; he who possesses a third estate, three parts of a mina; and, he who possesses a fourth estate, four parts. <note>The text suggests a progressive fine where the wealthiest pay the most, though the fractions here specifically align with the four property classes Plato established earlier in the work.</note> 

Many, indeed, are rendered insane by various means. Some, as those of whom we have just spoken, through disease. Others through anger, and the vicious education of a depraved nature; who, being incited by a trifling enmity, talk loudly, and blaspheme each other. But nothing of this kind ought to take place in a city governed by good laws. 

With respect to every kind of slander, therefore, let the following law be established: Let no one slander another. But when one person in discourse with another is doubtful of any particular, let him with whom he discourses instruct both him and those that are present in the truth of the case, and entirely abstain from slander. For men, when they slander each other with base words, are to be considered as effeminate. And, in the first place, from words, which are a light thing, hatred and grievous enmities are often produced in reality. For he who is gratified with anger—which is a thing of an unpleasant nature, and is filled with it as with noxious aliment <note>original: "alimentum"—meaning food or nourishment. Plato views anger as a poisonous "food" that corrupts the soul.</note>—such a one, being rendered as rustic and savage in this part of his soul as he was once gentle and mild through discipline, leads a morose life, and receives from anger this bitter grace. Let a male and female slave, and a boy, be alone permitted to bear witness and defend a cause in cases of murder, if they can give sufficient security <note>This refers to a legal bond or bail to ensure they remain available for the duration of the proceedings.</note> for their appearance at the trial, if they should happen to be accused of bearing false witness.

But if he shall be found to have given false witness thrice, let him not be permitted ever to bear witness again. Afterwards, let the magistrate deliver him to a court of justice, and, if he is convicted, let him be put to death. 

When in any lawsuit false witnesses are detected, and are found to be the means of an opponent gaining his cause, if more than half of the witnesses are condemned, let no judgment be passed from their evidence. But it is proper in this case diligently to inquire, whether or not any sentence should be passed; that, in whatever manner the cause may be determined, by this means justice may be done. 

Since, however, there are many beautiful things in the life of man, in most of them dire calamities are, as it were, naturally inherent, through which they are stained and defiled. ...these arguments we pass over in silence: but let the following law be announced for those that are unpersuaded by them:—If it shall appear that any one endeavours to give a contrary direction to the power of justice in the souls of the judges <note>This refers to the attempt to corrupt the moral judgment of the court or to sway the judges away from the truth of the law.</note>, and either excites or patronizes <note>original: "patronize" - here meaning to act as a legal advocate, supporter, or professional speaker for another's cause.</note> many unseasonable <term>lawsuits</term> <note>Cases brought without merit, at inappropriate times, or specifically to harass others.</note>, let any one who is willing charge him with acting basely in judicial matters, or with patronizing a bad cause. 

And let the cause be tried in a select court of justice. If, too, he is condemned, let the court of justice determine whether he acted in this manner through <term>avarice</term> <note>An extreme greed for wealth or material gain.</note> or love of contention <note>A psychological drive to argue or fight for the sake of the conflict itself rather than for justice.</note>. And if through a love of contention, let the judges appoint him a certain time, beyond which he shall neither plead any cause himself, nor patronize that of another. But if through avarice, if he is a stranger, let him depart from the city without ever returning to it again, or if he neglects to do this, let him be put to death. If he is a citizen, in consequence of thus improperly honouring money <note>Plato views the pursuit of wealth over justice as a fundamental betrayal of a citizen's duty to the state.</note>, let him be immediately put to death. Likewise, let him be put to death who has been found by a court of justice to have acted twice in this manner.

**I**F an ambassador or a herald <note>original: "crier" — a public officer who makes official proclamations.</note> deceives the city in any thing committed to his charge, or does not announce what he is sent to proclaim; or again, when returning from friends or enemies, does not truly relate the message he received from them, let a written information be drawn up against such a one, as irreligiously despising, contrary to law, the denunciations and mandates of <term>Hermes</term> <note>The messenger of the gods; in Greek mythology, he presided over communication, travel, and diplomacy.</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The Roman name for Zeus, here invoked as the protector of oaths and international relations.</note>. And if he is condemned, let the judges determine what he ought to suffer, or what fine he ought to pay. 

The theft of money is, indeed, illiberal, but rapine <note>The violent seizure of property; robbery.</note> is base. But no one of the sons of <term>Jupiter</term> will ever do any thing of this kind, in consequence of being delighted either with fraud or force. Let no one, therefore, acting in a disorderly manner through poets, or certain mythologists, be falsely persuaded that if he thieves either by fraud or force, he does not act basely, but does that which the Gods themselves have done. <note>Plato is here critiquing traditional myths—such as those of Hermes stealing Apollo’s cattle—which he believes set a poor moral example for citizens.</note> For this is neither true nor becoming: but he who illegally acts in this manner, is neither a God, nor a son of the Gods. But it is proper that these things should be known by the <term>legislator</term> <note>The lawgiver or founder of the state's legal code.</note> rather than by all poets. 

He, therefore, who is persuaded by this our discourse, is happy, and will be happy through the whole of time; but he who is unpersuaded by it, must be restrained by the following law:—If any one commits any public theft, whether it is great or small, he ought to suffer the same punishment. For he who takes away a thing of small consequence, thieves with the same desire, though with less force. But he who moves any thing of greater consequence, and does not restore it to its proper place, is wholly unjust. The law, however, thinks it proper that the one should be less punished than the other, not on account of the smallness of the theft,

If a slave, or a stranger <note>A non-citizen living in the city-state.</note>, is accused and condemned of any public theft <note>Theft of state property or communal funds.</note>, let sentence be passed on him what he ought to suffer, or what fine he ought to pay, as if it were probable that he might be cured. For the sake of war, indeed, many consultations and many laws are very properly instituted. The greatest of all things, however, consists in this, that neither any male or female be at any time without a governor <note>In this context, a leader, commander, or official supervisor.</note>, nor the soul of any citizen be ever accustomed, either seriously or in sport, to do any thing from itself alone; but that in all war, and in all peace, it perpetually looks to a governor, and lives following his mandates, so as to comply with them in the smallest particular; to stand when he commands, walk, engage in <term>gymnastic exercises</term> <note>Physical training, which for the Greeks was essential for both health and military readiness.</note>, wash, eat, rise by night for the purpose of keeping guard and giving signals; and in dangers themselves, neither to pursue nor give way to any one, without the mandate of the governors. 

And, in one word, that it should never be taught to do or know any thing separate from others; but that the life of all men should, in the highest degree, in all things be collected into one, subsist together, and be common. For nothing will ever be more excellent, better, or more artificial <note>In the sense of being "well-crafted" or "skilfully designed."</note> than this, for the purpose of procuring safety and victory in war. In peace, too, men should be accustomed from their childhood to govern others, and to be governed by others. But <term>anarchy</term> <note>From the Greek word meaning "without a leader"; here, it refers to a lack of order or obedience.</note> should be expelled from all life, both from that of men, and of beasts that are in subjection to men. 

All choirs <note>Groups of singers and dancers; in ancient Greece, choral training was a form of civic and physical education.</note>, too, should be celebrated, with a view to the best mode of conducting war; and all facility, dexterity, and promptitude, should be studied for the sake of this. On this account, too, we ought to accustom ourselves to endurance of hunger and thirst, cold and heat, and a hard bed. And, what is greatest of all, for the sake of this we should be careful not to corrupt the power of the head and feet by the tegument <note>A covering or layer, such as a hat or a shoe.</note> of foreign clothing, which destroys the generation and nature of our proper hairs and shoes <note>The author suggests that the natural toughness of the skin and hair acts as a better "shoe" or "hat" than artificial ones.</note>. For these extremities, when preserved, possess the greatest power of the whole body, but the contrary when they are not preserved. And one of these <note>The feet.</note> is in the highest degree subservient to the whole body; but the other <note>The head.</note> is endued with a principal authority, naturally...

But, if any one engages in battle, and leaves the army before he is dismissed by his commanding officers, let him be tried by the same judges as the deserter was tried by, whom we mentioned above, and, if condemned, let him be similarly punished. But we ought to endeavour, to the utmost of our power, to separate the greater and the most grievous evil from the contrary. In slandering, therefore, the very words employed for the purpose, possess a certain division. For, as the throwing away arms <term>rhipsaspia</term> <note>A specific legal and social crime in ancient Greece; literally "shield-throwing."</note> cannot be justly asserted in all cases, but the losing them may; in like manner, he is not to be similarly called a thrower away of his shield who loses it by force, as he who voluntarily throws it away. Let the following law, therefore, be established:—If any one, being assaulted by enemies, and having arms, does not defend himself against them, but voluntarily drops them, or throws them away, preferring a base life, in conjunction with infamy, to a beautiful and happy death, accompanied with fortitude, let sentence be passed on such a one, as a thrower away of arms, but let the judge neglect to consider the losing of arms mentioned above. For it is requisite always to punish the vicious, that they may become better, but not the unfortunate. For no advantage would be derived from an action of this kind.

->**The Justice of Rhadamanthus**<-

<term>Rhadamanthus</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus was a son of Zeus and a judge of the dead, known for his absolute and swift justice.</note>, indeed, deserves to be admired with respect to his decision of judicial affairs. For he perceived that the men of that time evidently believed that there were Gods, and this very properly, because at that time many of them were the progeny of the Gods; and he is said to have been one of these. He appears, therefore, to have conceived that causes ought not to be referred to any human judge, but to the Gods; and, on this account, causes were decided by him in a simple and rapid manner. For, causing the litigants in every case to take an oath, he determined causes rapidly and with safety. 

But now, as we have said, a certain part of mankind denies that there are Gods; others conceive that they take no care of us; and the opinion of the greatest and worst part is, that they may be appeased by trifling sacrifices and abundance of flattery, and that those who thus appease them, may with impunity defraud others of great sums of money. Hence, the art of Rhadamanthus in judicial affairs will not be adapted to men of the present time. The opinions of men, therefore, respecting the Gods being changed, it is necessary that laws also should be changed. ...attendant <note>The OCR text fragment "dant" likely completes the word "attendant" from the previous page.</note>, may be committed to writing without an oath. For if every person in the city were freely permitted to take an oath—given that many cases are brought before judges every day—almost everyone would become a <term>perjurer</term> <note>Someone who intentionally tells a lie while under a lawful oath.</note> through the social bonds formed at shared feasts, other associations, and private meetings. 

Let it, therefore, be established by law that the person who is about to be judged shall swear an oath to the judge, and that those who appoint public <term>magistrates</term> <note>Civil officers or judges who administer the law.</note> shall do so either through oaths or by <term>suffrages</term> <note>A vote given in deciding a controverted question or electing a person to office.</note>. Likewise, an oath shall be taken by the judge of the choirs and all music, as well as the presidents and those who confer rewards for <term>gymnastic</term> <note>Athletic training and physical education, central to Greek life.</note> and equestrian exercises. In short, oaths should be used in all cases where, in the common opinion of men, perjury does not lead to personal gain. 

However, in cases where a person might derive a great advantage from lying under oath, the matter should be judged without an oath. Likewise, in judicial proceedings, the litigants must not be permitted to swear oaths for the sake of persuasion, nor to call down curses upon themselves and their families, nor to employ "base supplications" or "feminine excitations to pity" <note>This refers to the common practice in ancient courts where defendants would bring their weeping families or use emotional outbursts to sway the jury’s emotions rather than arguing the facts.</note>. Instead, they should always teach and learn what is just in an honorable manner. If they fail to act this way, the magistrates should bring them back to the specific matter at hand, treating them as people who are speaking beside the point. 

When strangers <note>Non-citizens or visiting foreigners.</note>, like us, have a dispute among themselves, they may be permitted to take an oath if they wish. Since they are not allowed to settle permanently in the city, there is no fear that they will corrupt others. 

In the same manner, justice should be carried out among free men if someone is not persuaded by the city’s rules in matters that do not involve physical blows, imprisonment, or death. If someone fails to attend the celebration of a choir, a solemn procession, or any other public adornments of this kind, or misses a public office—such as those involving peaceful sacrifices or wartime taxes—the damage must be repaired as soon as possible. Alternatively, a <term>pledge</term> <note>A piece of property seized by the state to guarantee payment of a fine.</note> should be taken by the official designated by the city and the law. When the time limit has expired, the pledge shall be sold and the money put toward public use. 

But, if a larger fine is required, the magistrates must bring those who refuse to pay before a court of justice and compel them to pay the fine enacted by the laws. ...ports commodities, nor admits foreigners <note>The text likely refers to a city that neither exports its own goods nor accepts foreign imports, a strategy used to maintain economic and moral independence.</note>. The <term>legislator</term> <note>The lawgiver or founding statesman, such as the Athenian Stranger in this dialogue.</note>, therefore, ought to consult about these particulars, employing, in the first place, persuasion to the utmost of his power. The mixture, indeed, of different nations naturally causes a mixture of all-various manners; and the association of strangers with strangers produces innovations <note>In the context of Platonic philosophy, "innovation" is often viewed with suspicion as it can destabilize the established laws and traditional customs of a city.</note> which injure in the highest degree cities that are well governed through good laws. 

But, to the greater part of cities, as being by no means well governed, it is of no consequence if as well the old as the young travel into other countries whenever they please, and receive foreigners in their own country. But, on the contrary, in these <note>Referring to the ideal, well-governed cities.</note> never to receive strangers, and never to visit foreign countries, would appear rustic and savage to other men, who would call the city by opprobrious names, such as, that it is the enemy of strangers, and that its manners are arrogant and morose. The appearing, however, to be good, or not good, to others, ought never to be considered as a thing of small importance. For the multitude, though deprived of virtue themselves, are capable of distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy: and in certain vicious characters there is something divine, and a power of conjecturing well. So that many, and even some that are vicious in the extreme, are able to distinguish, both in words and opinions, the better from the worse sort of men. 

On this account, the multitude of cities are very properly exhorted not to despise the good opinion of the multitude. For it is a thing of the greatest rectitude and magnitude, when a man is truly good himself, that he should aspire after a renowned life; since, without this, a man will by no means become perfect. On this account, it will be proper that the city which is to be inhabited about Crete <note>The dialogue takes place on Crete and concerns the laws for a hypothetical new colony named Magnesia.</note> should endeavour to obtain the most beautiful and excellent reputation for virtue among other men. But there is every reason to hope, that this city in a short time will be beheld both by the Sun and other Gods, in well-governed cities and regions, living according to reason. 

Let the following law, therefore, be established respecting travelling into other regions and places, and the reception of guests:—In the first place, let it not be lawful for him who is less than forty years of age by any means to travel; and further still, let no person be permitted to travel privately; but let <term>cryers</term> <note>Heralds who represent the state in official proclamations.</note>, <term>ambassadors</term> <note>Envoys sent to other cities for diplomatic purposes.</note>, or certain <term>speculators</term> <note>From the Greek *theoroi*, meaning official observers or inspectors sent to witness foreign festivals or study foreign laws to bring back improvements for their own city.</note>, be allowed to travel publicly. Out of reverence for **Jupiter**, the protector of guests <note>original: "hospitable Jupiter" or Zeus Xenios; the god who oversaw the sacred laws of hospitality (Xenia).</note>, we should welcome men into our city. For foreigners should not be expelled with food and sacrificial victims, as the inhabitants of the **Nile** <note>The Greeks often perceived the Egyptians as being uniquely hostile to outsiders, unlike the Greek ideal of welcoming travelers.</note> do at present, nor should they be driven away by savage edicts <note>This likely refers to "xenelasia," the Spartan practice of periodically expelling foreigners to prevent their customs from influencing the local population.</note>. 

Let every **surety** <term>surety</term> <note>A person who takes legal responsibility for another person’s debt or appearance in court.</note> be held responsible for another in a public and clear manner. Let the entire transaction be recorded in writing before at least three witnesses if the security is valued within a hundred **drachms** <term>drachms</term> <note>The drachm was a standard silver coin in ancient Greece; for context, one drachm was roughly a daily wage for a skilled laborer.</note>. However, if the value exceeds a thousand, there must be at least five witnesses. If the surety is a shopkeeper, he must be someone who conducts his business honestly; otherwise, he should not be considered worthy of trust.

If someone wishes to search another person's house for something belonging to him, let him first swear by the legal Gods that he truly expects to find what he is looking for there. Next, let him enter the house naked, or wearing only a tunic and without a belt <note>This ritual requirement ensured that the person searching could not hide a stolen object on his person to "plant" it in the house and frame the occupant.</note>. Then, let him be allowed to search the house and examine everything, whether it is sealed or unsealed. 

But if the occupant refuses entry to the person wishing to search, the person who was denied access may bring a legal action against him for the value of the lost item. If the occupant is found guilty, he must pay twice the value of the loss. If the master of the house happens to be away during such an occasion, those present should allow only unsealed items to be examined. The searcher should then seal the items that were already sealed with his own **signet** <term>signet</term> <note>A seal, often on a ring, used to mark property or secure containers against tampering.</note>, and he may leave a guard of his choosing at the house for five days. 

If the master is away for longer than five days, the searcher should bring the **ædiles** <term>ædiles</term> <note>original: "astynomoi"; city officials responsible for public order, streets, and buildings.</note> with him to break open the seals. After examining the items alongside the servants and the <term>ædiles</term>, he must seal them again. 

Regarding disputes over property, the time limit for resolving them must not be left vague; this prevents constant arguments over houses and land. If someone is in possession of an item and has used it openly for one year in the city, in the **forum** <term>forum</term> <note>original: "agora"; the central marketplace and public meeting space of the city.</note>, or in the temples, and no one has claimed it during that time, then no one shall be permitted to claim it as their own later. If the person used the item openly in the fields rather than the city or forum, and the rightful owner does not come forward within five years, then no one shall be allowed to demand its return after that period.

But if the **plaintiff** <note>The person who brings a case against another in a court of law.</note>, being repulsed by the first judgment, is not satisfied, but appeals to a second—if he vanquishes let him receive a fifth part, but if he is vanquished let him lose the same part. And if he goes to a third court of justice, not being satisfied with the former judgments, let the defendant, if vanquished, pay (as we have said) the sum that is owing, and the half of it besides; but let the plaintiff pay the half only. 

With respect to the allotments of courts of justice, the perfection and establishment of things ministrant to the **magistrates**, the times in which each of these ought to take place, the particulars respecting votes, the delays, terms, citations and repulses which take place in judicial affairs, and whatever else necessarily pertains to these—all this we have already discussed. However, according to the proverb, *what is beautiful and right may be spoken twice and thrice.* <note>original: "δὶς καὶ τρὶς τὸ καλόν" (dis kai tris to kalon). A common Greek expression used by Plato to suggest that good advice or important truths are worth repeating for clarity.</note> All such legal particulars, therefore, as are small and easy to be discovered, when omitted by an aged **legislator**, ought to be filled up by a junior legislator. <note>Plato suggests that while the founding laws are set by an elder, younger officials must handle the evolving minor details and practical applications.</note> 

And thus much may suffice concerning private courts of justice. But such as are public and common, and which are employed by magistrates to proper purposes, are found in many cities established in no unbecoming manner by **equitable** <note>Fair, impartial, and guided by the spirit of the law rather than just the letter.</note> men. Whence it is requisite that the guardians of the laws should procure such things as are adapted to this new **polity** <note>original: "politeia"; the specific form of government or social order of the city.</note>, by reasoning, correcting, and exploring them, till they appear to them to be sufficiently established; and then bringing them to a conclusion, that they should seal them as things immovable, and use them through the whole of life. 

With respect to the silence of judges, the praises which are given them, or the contrary, and likewise concerning things just, good, and becoming, which differ in other cities, we have already spoken, and shall again speak in the end. But it is requisite that he who in future will be an **equitable judge** should look to all these particulars, and being in possession of them, when committed to writing, should make them the object of his study. For **written laws** are more calculated to make him who learns them better, than all other disciplines,

It is likewise proper to believe the legislator in other things; and when he asserts that the soul is in every respect different from the body; and that, in the present life, it causes each of us to be that which each of us is; but, that body follows each of us like an image; and, that bodies may be beautifully said to be the images of the perfectly dead. That, besides this, each of us may be truly denominated an **immortal soul** <note>A central Platonic doctrine: the physical body is a mere shell or shadow, while the soul is the true self that survives death.</note>, which will depart to other Gods to give an account of its conduct, as the law of our country asserts. This, however, is a circumstance which produces confidence in the good, but is terrible in the extreme to the evil; for no great assistance can be rendered them after death. Hence, it is necessary to give them all proper assistance while living, that they may live in the most just and holy manner, and that after the present life they may escape the punishments which await the commission of crimes.

Since this, then, is the case, we ought by no means to ruin our families, in consequence of thinking that this **mass of flesh** <note>A dismissive reference to the physical body, emphasizing its lack of importance compared to the soul.</note> which is buried is truly our relative; but we should be persuaded that the son or brother, or any person for whom we have an affection, and whom we consider as buried, has departed hence in consequence of having finished and filled up his **fate** <note>original: "moira" — the allotted portion of life or destiny.</note>. Let these, then, be the established laws regarding these details. 

He who obeys these laws shall be free from punishment; but he who disobeys one of the guardians of the laws shall be punished by all of them in a manner that they all agree is appropriate. Regarding other details—such as the specifics of tombs, or the treatment of those who are denied burial due to <term>patricide<note>The murder of one's own father.</note></term> or <term>sacrilege<note>The violation or theft of anything sacred, particularly from a temple.</note></term>—we have already spoken of these and established them legally. 

Thus, the work of legislation has now nearly reached its completion. However, we must remember that the end of all things is not achieved simply by them being performed, or possessed, or lived in, but by them being properly finalized and firmly established. For in this kind of preservation, it is right to think that what needed to be done is truly finished, but before this state is reached, the whole project remains imperfect.

**CLIN.** In what particular things do you mean?

**GUEST.** As we have said that there are four species of virtue, it is evident that each of them must necessarily be one, since they are four in total.

**GUEST.** Ought not, therefore, interpreters, teachers, legislators, and guardians of others, to teach those who desire to know and to perceive things of this kind, or who require punishment and reproof, what power virtue and vice possess; and must they not, through information of this kind, in every respect excel others? Or will any poet coming into the city, or any instructor of youth, be considered as better than him who excels in all virtue? **CLIN.** It will not appear wonderful.

**GUEST.** What then? Shall we do what we just now spoke of? Or shall we consider how we may enable the guardians to excel others in virtue, both in words and in reality? **CLIN.** How, therefore, O guest, and after what manner, shall we speak, assimilating it to a thing of this kind?

**GUEST.** It is evident that the city itself will resemble the cavity of the head; and that the junior guardians, who are ingenuous and sagacious, will be placed, as it were, on the highest summit, whence they can survey, in a circle, the whole city, and, while they defend it, deliver the senses to the memory, and announce to the elders every thing that takes place in the city. But these being assimilated to <term>intellect</term> <note>In this analogy, the younger guardians act as the "eyes and ears" (senses), while the elders act as the "brain" (intellect) that processes information and makes decisions.</note>, through understanding in the highest perfection a multitude of things which are worthy of regard, they will consult for the city, and employ the junior guardians as agents in their consultations. For thus both will truly preserve the city in common. Whether, therefore, shall we say they are to be established in this manner, or not? Or shall we say that they are all to be considered as equal, and not accurately determine the difference between them, in education and discipline?

**CLIN.** But this, O wonderful man, is impossible.

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

## THE EPINOMIS.

---

**THE** <term>Epinomis</term> <note>The title literally translates to "After the Laws" or "Supplement to the Laws."</note>, or Nocturnal Convention <note>The "Nocturnal Council" or "Convention" was a high-level assembly described in Plato's *Laws* that met before dawn to study the philosophical foundations of legislation.</note>, was not written by Plato, but, as we are informed by <note>Diogenes Laertius: A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers whose work is a primary source for the lives of ancient thinkers.</note> Diogenes Laertius, by Philip Opuntius <note>Also known as Philip of Opus, an astronomer and mathematician who was a member of Plato's Academy and is said to have edited Plato's *Laws*.</note>, one of Plato’s disciples. This dialogue, which, as its name implies, is a supplement to the Laws, is highly valuable, both for its great antiquity, its author being contemporary with Plato, and the <term>recondite</term> <note>Information that is deep, complex, or hidden from the average person; specialized knowledge.</note> wisdom which it contains. However, notwithstanding its great intrinsic excellence, it appears to me that any one much conversant with the writings of Plato might easily discover that it was not written by that philosopher, though antiquity had been totally silent in this particular ; for, where shall we find in it either his heroical strength and magnificence of diction, or his profundity, accuracy, and sublimity of conception ?

This dialogue is also very properly inscribed *The Philosopher*, since the design of it, as the author informs us in the very beginning, is to show what wisdom is, and how it may be obtained. Before, however, he teaches us what wisdom is, he inquires what it is not ; and having premised certain things necessary to its definition, he shows that the august name of wisdom can by no means accord with those arts which are subservient to the necessaries and conveniences of life, such as politics, agriculture, architecture, rhetoric, and the like. After this, he enumerates the speculative disciplines, and, in the first place, not only praises but admires arithmetic, which, according to Plato, most of all things sharpens the wit, strengthens the memory, and renders the mind prompt and adapted to every speculation and action. The arithmetic, however, which is here so deservedly praised, is not that which is commonly taught, and which is subservient to merchandize and traffic ;

<meta>catchword: but</meta>

<summary>This introduction identifies Philip of Opus as the likely author of the Epinomis and positions the work as a philosophical sequel to Plato's Laws. It explores the definition of true wisdom, distinguishing it from practical crafts and highlighting the importance of theoretical arithmetic.</summary>
<keywords>Epinomis, Plato, Philip of Opus, Diogenes Laertius, wisdom, arithmetic, Laws, speculative disciplines</keywords>

--- Page 1075 ---
<meta>This page continues the Introduction to the "Epinomis," concluding a sentence from page 387 regarding the nature of mathematical science as discussed in the dialogue. It focuses on the transition from practical mathematics to the spiritual contemplation of the divine.</meta>

->INTRODUCTION TO THE EPINOMIS.<-

...but it is entirely speculative <note>In this context, "speculative" refers to the pursuit of theoretical knowledge or contemplation for its own sake, rather than for practical application.</note>, and considers the properties of pure numbers unconnected with anything sensible <note>Meaning anything that can be perceived by the physical senses; here, it refers to abstract numbers rather than physical objects.</note>. Of this arithmetic, Euclid <note>The famous Greek mathematician (c. 300 BC) known for his "Elements," which covered geometry and number theory.</note> and Nicomachus <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa (c. 60–120 AD), a mathematician whose "Introduction to Arithmetic" was a standard textbook in antiquity.</note> have transmitted to us the elements; but the study of it is at present neglected, because it is not calculated to promote gain, facilitate calculation, or expedite business. The author also adds, that number was delivered by divinity to men, as a necessary instrument of reason and discursive energy <note>A technical term in Platonic philosophy referring to the process of the mind moving logically from one premise to another, step-by-step.</note>; and that, this being taken away, the soul would appear to be destitute of intellect, and arts and sciences entirely vanish. He also praises geometry, astronomy, music, and physics; and places dialectic <note>In Platonism, the highest form of philosophy and reasoning that deals with first principles and the true nature of reality.</note>, i. e. metaphysics, or *wisdom*, before all the other sciences, because it employs these as steps in the discovery and adoration of Divinity. He likewise shows that there are three employments of this queen of the sciences about other disciplines. The first consists in beholding the multitude of all these; the second, in surveying the communion and connection in all of them; and the third considers in what manner this multitude and its union contribute to *the one itself* <note>The ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic thought, representing absolute unity and the "Good."</note> and divine good. Lastly, the reader may learn from this dialogue, that as religion consists in the worship, so wisdom in the contemplation of Divinity; and that human felicity <note>Happiness, well-being, or the ultimate fulfillment of human life.</note> and the end of laws are only to be obtained in the union of both.

**A**CCORDING to our agreement, O guest, we are all of us rightly assembled, being three, I, and you, and Megillus here, for the purpose of considering after what manner we should investigate **prudence** <note>original: *prudentia*; translating the Greek *phronēsis*. In this context, it refers to practical wisdom or the mental capacity to live well and make right decisions.</note>; which when understood, we say that it causes the human habit to subsist in the most beautiful manner possible to man, with respect to itself. For we have discussed every thing else respecting the establishment of laws. We should now endeavour not to leave this uninvestigated: for, if we do, we shall nearly leave that imperfect, for the sake of rendering which apparent from the beginning to the end we have all of us proceeded thus far.

# THE <term>EPINOMIS</term>; <note>This title likely means "The After-Law" or "Supplement to the Laws," as the dialogue serves as an appendix to Plato's "Laws."</note> OR,

...appears to you as well as to me, that by speaking as follows about this affair we shall speak well. For I say it is not possible for men in this life, except a few, to become blessed and happy. But the hope is beautiful that after death we shall obtain every thing, for the sake of which we cheerfully live and die in the best manner we are able. Nor is my assertion novel, but that which we all after a certain manner know, as well **Barbarians** <note>In ancient Greek thought, a "Barbarian" was simply anyone who did not speak the Greek language.</note> as Greeks. For the production of every animal is in the beginning difficult. In the first place, the participation of the <term>fœtal habit</term> <note>The physical state of being in the womb or the initial condition of an embryo.</note> is difficult; and, in the next place, to be nourished and educated. And, as we all say, these things are accomplished through ten thousand labours. The time, too, is short, not only with respect to the endurance of calamities, but every thing else which causes human life to take breath, as it were, about a medium. For old age swiftly arriving makes every one who is not full of **puerile opinion** <note>Childish or immature beliefs that have not been tested by philosophy or experience.</note> unwilling to return to life again, when he considers the life he has lived.

And is not the subject of our present investigation an argument of the truth of these assertions? For we investigate how we may become wise, taking it for granted that there is in each of us a power by which this may be accomplished. But wisdom then flies from us, when we apply ourselves to any of those things which are called by the name of **art** or **prudence**, or to any other such particulars as we rank among the sciences; because no one of these, as being conversant with human affairs, deserves to be called by the appellation of wisdom. The soul, however, vehemently confides and prophesies, that she naturally possesses this power: but what it is, and when, and how it subsists, she is not altogether able to discover. But do not our doubting and investigation respecting wisdom refer to this exceedingly, viz. <note>An abbreviation for "videlicet," meaning "namely" or "that is to say."</note> that there is abundance of hope for such as are able to examine both themselves and others prudently, and in an according manner, through every kind of reasoning and disputation? Shall we say that these things are so, or not?

CLIN. We admit that they are, O guest, hoping that we shall in time, together with you, entertain the most true opinions respecting them.

GUEST. In the first place, then, let us discuss those other pursuits which are, indeed, called sciences, but do not render him wise who receives and possesses them; that, removing these out of the way, we may endeavour to assign the particulars of which we are in want, and, when assigned, to learn **them.**

Let the first art then be that which orders us to abstain from the eating of human flesh; this, according to the fable, being the practice of mankind formerly, after the manner of savage animals, and which recalls us to **legal nutriment.** <note>Lawful food that is socially and morally acceptable, as opposed to the "savage" act of cannibalism.</note> The ancients, indeed, were and are benevolent to us. Let us, however, bid farewell to those whom we call the first men. Nor yet will the whole of agriculture be able to accomplish this. For we all of us appear to undertake the cultivation of the earth, not from art but nature, through the favour of Divinity. 

But neither can the construction of houses, the whole of **architecture**, the making of every kind of furniture, the art of the **coppersmith**, and the apparatus of **tectonic**, **plastic**, **plectic**, <note>The author lists specialized crafts: "tectonic" refers to carpentry and woodworking, "plastic" refers to molding materials like clay or wax, and "plectic" refers to weaving or braiding.</note> and, in short, of all instruments which are accommodated to the vulgar, but are not subservient to virtue, accomplish this. Nor, again, can the whole of hunting, though it is various and artificial, confer magnificence on the wise man. Nor yet **divination**, or the interpreting art; for these alone know that which is asserted, but they do not understand whether it is true or not. 

Since then we see that none of those arts by which necessaries are procured can make any one wise, after this that discipline remains which is for the most part imitative, but by no means serious. For imitation is here effected by means of many instruments, and through many gestures of bodies not altogether graceful. In discourse, too, there is imitation in every **Muse**; <note>In this context, "Muse" refers to the various arts of poetry, song, and storytelling over which the nine Muses presided.</note> and in things of which the **graphic art** <note>The art of drawing or painting.</note> is the mother, where things, many and all-various, are expressed in moist and dry bodies; none of which, though fabricated with the greatest diligence, can in any respect render a man wise. For the soul of this animal <note>Referring to the human being as a living creature.</note> would scarcely any longer be able to receive every virtue, if deprived of reason. But the animal which does not know two and three, the even and the odd, and is entirely ignorant of <term>number</term>, will never be able to give a reason respecting those things of which it alone possesses sensation and memory; but nothing hinders it from possessing the other virtues, I mean fortitude and temperance, without this knowledge. However, he who is void of true reason can never become wise. And he to whom <term>wisdom</term> is not present, which is the greatest part of the whole of virtue, as in this case he will not be perfectly good, so he will never be happy. This must be understood by anyone who intends to be truly happy. To this we may add that anyone who is ignorant of what is just, good, and beautiful, and who has not formed a true opinion about these things, cannot use the power of number to convince either himself or others.

But let us now consider how we first learned to count. Where did we get the ability to perceive "one" and "two," so that we might understand the knowledge the universe has given us? Nature has not given most animals the ability to count through their parents. Instead, <term>Divinity</term> <note>God or the divine intelligence governing the cosmos.</note> first planted in us the capacity to understand number by pointing it out to us. Later, he made it even more obvious to us. In this unfolding of the world, nothing can be seen more beautiful—if one thing is compared to another—than the <term>nature of the day</term> <note>original: "genus of day."</note>. Next, look at the night, which possesses the greatest variety. By observing these things revolving continually, you will see many days and many nights, in which the heavens never stop teaching men "one" and "two," so that even the most <term>unintelligent</term> <note>original: "indocile," meaning someone who is difficult to teach or slow to learn.</note> person may learn to count. For in this way, each of us, by observing these cycles, can understand "three," "four," and the concept of "many." From these elements, the Divine Architect made the moon; at one time it appears larger, and at another smaller, changing continually over the course of fifteen days and nights. This constitutes a full period, if one is willing to view the whole cycle as a single unit. Thus, as I might say, even the most difficult animal to teach may learn to count, if they are a creature to whom Divinity has given the capacity to learn. Up to this point, every animal has the ability to become skilled in arithmetic by considering a single thing by itself. As we have said, the moon—by increasing and decreasing—established the months for the purpose of organizing the year. It caused us to compare every number with another number through prosperous fortune. Because of this, the earth bears fruit for us and becomes fertile, acting as the nurse of all animals; and winds and rains are produced that are neither excessive nor overwhelming. But if anything evil happens in these matters, it is proper to blame not a divine nature, but human nature, for unjustly managing its own life.

To us, therefore, as we investigate laws, it has appeared that other things which are best for men are easy to recognize. We have seen that anyone can sufficiently understand and perform what we have asserted regarding these things, provided they understand what is advantageous and what is not. Indeed, it has been shown by us, and it remains clear, that all other pursuits are not extremely difficult; but to determine the manner in which men may be rendered good is perfectly difficult.

Furthermore, to possess other goods in a proper manner is, as has been said, possible and not difficult—I mean riches and the health of the body. In the first place, therefore, as we have said, we must consider that there are these two genera of animals. And we again say that both of them are visible; the one, as it appears, consisting wholly of fire, and the other of earth. We must likewise assert, that the earthly genus is moved in a disorderly manner, but that which consists of fire, in perfect order. It is proper, therefore, to consider that which is moved without order as stupid. But it is requisite to establish this as a great argument, that the natures which revolve in the heavens are endued with <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus" / "nous" (Greek). In Platonic thought, this is the highest form of reason or "divine mind."</note>—I mean, that they always proceed according to the same and in a similar manner, and both do and suffer the same. 

But the necessity of a soul possessing intellect is by far the greatest of all necessities ¹. For it promulgates laws governing and not governed. But when soul, which is a thing of the most excellent nature, deliberates according to the most excellent intellect, then that which is perfect according to intellect takes place in reality, nor can an <term>adamant</term> <note>An ancient term for the hardest possible substance, often used metaphorically for something unchangeable or unbreakable.</note> be more firm and inconvertible than such a soul. Indeed, the <term>three fates</term> <note>The Moirae of Greek mythology: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life/destiny.</note> preserve perfect that which is deliberated by each of the Gods with the best counsel. It is requisite, therefore, men should be convinced that the stars, and the whole of this progression, are endued with intellect, from this circumstance, that they always perform the same things. For in the past time they have deliberated for a wonderfully extended period respecting their actions. But they are not, in deliberating, agitated upwards and downwards, nor do they wander and revolve in a disorderly manner, acting differently at different times. The contrary of this, however, appears to many of us—I mean, that because they perform the same things, and in a similar manner, they are without a soul. But it is only fitting for a person who attributes to the Gods things that are more beautiful, more excellent, and more suited to their nature, to believe it is necessary to view them as possessing <term>intellect</term> <note>In this context, intellect refers to *Nous*, the highest form of divine reason that maintains order in the universe.</note>, because they always accomplish the same tasks according to the same patterns and in a similar way. That we are right to consider them as animated (possessing souls) can be proven, first of all, by their sheer size. In reality, they are not as small as they appear to be; instead, it should be believed that each of them is of an immense magnitude, as can be shown through sufficient logical demonstrations. We may rightly conclude that the sun as a whole is larger than the entire earth, and that all the stars possess a wonderful size. We should consider, therefore, how such a great bulk can be made to revolve by a specific nature, perpetually and in the same amount of time. I assert, therefore, that the Divine is the cause of this, and that it cannot be accomplished in any other way. For a body can only become animated through a God, as we have already shown. 

Since the Divine is the cause of its life, and all things are easy for a God, he first generated every body and every mass in the heavens as a living animal; and next, he caused it to move in that manner which he conceived, through <term>dianoëtic energy</term> <note>This refers to the activity of discursive reason, or the step-by-step rational thought process of the divine mind.</note>, to be the best. And now, regarding all these specifics, we shall make one true assertion: it is impossible that the earth, the heavens, all the stars, and all the masses composed from these could exist unless a soul is either present with each or resident within each. This soul enables them to revolve with such accuracy according to years, and months, and days, thus securing every good thing for all of us. But it is necessary that, as much as man is more lowly than these celestial animals, he should speak with less triviality and only assert what is clearly evident about them. [The con]ceptions <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a thought about how human ideas regarding the divine have evolved.</note> of men, respecting the nature and actions of the Gods, were neither such as wise men would frame, nor those that succeeded them. For they asserted that fire and water, and the other bodies, were the most ancient of all things; but that the particulars belonging to that wonderful thing, the soul, were of later origin. <note>The author is criticizing "materialist" philosophers who believed physical elements came before consciousness or the soul.</note> Hence, they considered the <term>lation</term> <note>From the Latin *latio*, meaning "local motion" or the act of being moved from one place to another.</note> of body as better and more honorable, and as moving itself through heat and cold, and everything else of this kind: but they asserted that the soul moved neither the body nor itself. 

But now, since we say that if the soul exists in the body, it is not at all wonderful that it should move and carry about both the body and itself, there can be no reason to disbelieve its ability to carry about a certain weight. Hence, as we now think it proper to assert that the soul is the cause of the universe; and as among things, some are good and others evil, it is not at all wonderful that the soul should be the cause of every <term>lation</term> and motion. However, a motion which tends toward the good should proceed from the best soul, while a motion to the contrary proceeds from a contrary soul. But it is necessary that things which are good should have vanquished—and should continue to vanquish—things which are not so. All these particulars have been asserted by us according to Justice, the avenger of the impious. <note>Justice is personified here as a divine force that punishes those who lack reverence for the natural and divine order.</note> With respect, however, to that which we have just now examined, we ought not to hesitate in asserting that a good man is a wise man.

Let us however see whether this wisdom, which we were searching for some time ago, can be acquired by discipline or art. For, if we are destitute of the knowledge of this, we shall be ignorant of things that are just. This is how it appears to me, and therefore I assert this to be the case. For, having explored high and low, I will endeavor to show you that which has become apparent to me. For when the greatest part of virtue is neglected, it becomes the cause of ignorance, as what we have just now said appears to me most clearly to signify. But no one shall persuade us that there is any part of virtue belonging to the mortal race greater than piety. <note>Piety here refers to a proper religious and scientific respect for the heavens and the divine order.</note> We must likewise assert that this is not produced in the most excellent natures through the greatest ignorance. But those are the most excellent natures which are most rarely found, and which, when found, benefit others in the highest degree. <meta>Catchword: within</meta>

We have observed that the moon completes its cycle most rapidly, and thus, before all other bodies, it establishes the month and the full moon. Secondly, we must consider the sun, which defines the solstices throughout its entire cycle, along with the other celestial bodies that revolve in its company. But rather than repeating the same points, we must contemplate the revolutions of all these natures we have previously mentioned. These are not easily understood; therefore, we must prepare human nature for this task through the <term>mathematical disciplines</term> <note>These were the "liberal arts" of the ancient world, intended to lead the mind from physical things to abstract truths.</note>, specifically through long exercise and labor beginning in youth.

For this reason, the study of mathematics is necessary. The first and greatest of these is the study of **numbers**—not those associated with physical objects, but the study of the very nature and power of the **even** and the **odd**, and how they contribute to our understanding of the reality of things. 

Following this in orderly succession is that which is quite ridiculously called **geometry** <note>original: "γεωμετρία" (geometria). The author notes that the name literally means "earth-measuring," which he considers a lowly, mechanical task compared to the high science of shapes.</note>. In this study, the way numbers—which are naturally unlike one another—can be compared to flat surfaces becomes clear. To anyone capable of understanding it, this will appear not as a human discovery, but as a divine miracle. 

After this, one must consider those numbers that receive a **triple increase** <note>This refers to the "third power" or cubing of a number, moving from a flat plane into three-dimensional space.</note> and are similar to the nature of a **solid**. Likewise, one must study those numbers that are dissimilar to this nature, which is also called "geometry" by those who practice it. To those capable of understanding it, it is a divine and wonderful thing to see how the power of things always revolves around the **double** <note>The ratio of 1 to 2, or "duple proportion."</note>, and its opposite, according to each proportion, as every nature is shaped according to its kind and species. The first power of the **double**, therefore, proceeds according to number in the ratio of one to two, being a double <note>In ancient mathematics, numbers were categorized as linear (like 2), superficial or square (like 4, which is 2 times 2), and cubic or solid (like 8, which is 2 times 2 times 2). The "double proportion" was considered perfect because it is the first ratio created between 1 and 2, and was thought to contain all other proportions within it.</note> according to its power.
