But further, the **Platonists** admit, with **Democritus** and **Empedocles**, that certain material images of things flow through the pores of bodies, and preserve, to a certain distance, not only the qualities but likewise the shape of the bodies from which they flow. <note>Democritus and Empedocles proposed an "effluence" theory, suggesting that objects constantly shed thin, film-like layers of themselves—called *eidola*—which travel through the air to reach our senses.</note> And these radial images are intimated by **Plato** in this dialogue, in the *Sophist*, and in the seventh book of his *Republic*; in commenting on the last of which, **Proclus** observes as follows:

<margin>† See Proclus on Plato's *Republic* (Politics), page 430.</margin>

“According to **Plato**, (says he) representations of things are <term>hypostases</term> <note>hypostases: Substantial realities or underlying existences, rather than mere illusions.</note> of certain images fabricated by a **daemonic art**, <note>daemonic art: In the Neoplatonic sense, "daemonic" refers to intermediary spiritual forces or natural mechanics that operate between the divine and the physical, not necessarily "evil" spirits.</note> as he teaches us in the *Sophist*; for shadows, of which they say images are the companions, possess a nature of this kind. For these are the effigies of bodies and figures, and have an abundant sympathy with the things from which they fall; as is evident from what the arts of magicians are able to effect, and from what they tell us concerning images and shadows. But why should I speak of the powers of magicians, when irrational animals are able to operate through images and shadows, prior to all reason? In the next place, with respect to matter, and the various epithets by which **Plato** calls it in this dialogue, it is necessary to observe, that as in an ascending series of subjects we must arrive at length at something which is better than all things, so in a descending series our progression must be stopped by something which is worse than all things, and which is the general receptacle of the last procession of forms. And this is what the ancients called matter, and which they considered as nothing more than a certain indefiniteness of an incorporeal, indivisible, and intellectual nature, and as something which is not formally impressed and bounded by three dimensions, but is entirely remitted and resolved, and is on all sides rapidly flowing from being into non-entity. <note>non-entity: Non-being or the state of having no existence.</note> But this opinion concerning matter, says **Simplicius**¹, seems to have been adopted by the first **Pythagoreans** among the **Greeks**; and after these by **Plato**, according to the relation of **Moderatus**. <note>Moderatus of Gades: A 1st-century philosopher who linked Pythagorean numerology with Platonic philosophy.</note> For he shows us—"that, according to the **Pythagoreans**, there is a *first one* subsisting prior to the essence of things and every substance; that after this, true being and intelligible or forms subsist: *and, in the third place, that which pertains to soul, and which participates of the one and of intellectual forms.* But after this (says he) the last nature, which is that of <unclear>sensibles</unclear>, <note>sensibles: Physical objects that can be perceived by the senses.</note> subsists; which does not participate of the preceding natures, but is thus affected and formed according to the representation of these; since the matter of sensible natures is the shadow of that non-being which primarily subsists in quantity, or rather may be said to depend upon, and be produced by, this." Hence **Porphyry**, in his second book on Matter, says **Simplicius**, observes that **Plato** calls matter, quantity, which is formless, indivisible, and without figure; but capacious, and the receptacle of form, figure, division, quality, and other things of a similar kind. to the privation <note>Privation: In philosophy, the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present. Here, matter is defined by what it lacks—namely, order and form.</note> of a uniform reason, which comprehends all the reasons of beings in itself, is the paradigm of the matter of bodies; which, says Porphyry, both Plato and the Pythagoreans call a <term>quantum <gloss>quantity or magnitude</gloss></term>, not after the same manner as form is a *quantum*, but according to privation and analysis, extension and <term>divulsion <gloss>a violent pulling apart or separation</gloss></term>, and its mutation from being. Matter, therefore, according to this doctrine, as Simplicius well observes, is nothing else than the permutation and vicissitude of sensible forms, with respect to intelligibles; since from thence they verge downwards, and extend to perfect non-entity, or the last of things—that is, to matter itself. Hence, says he, because dregs and matter are always the last of things, the Egyptians assert that matter, which they enigmatically denominate water, is the dregs of the first life; subsisting as a certain mire or mud, the receptacle of generable and sensible natures; and which is not any definite form, but a certain constitution of subsistence, in the same manner as that which is indivisible, immaterial and true being, is a constitution of an intelligible nature. And though all forms subsist both in intelligibles and in matter, yet in the former they subsist without matter, indivisibly and truly; but in the latter divisibly, and after the manner of shadows. And on this account every sensible form is dissipated through its union with material interval, and falls from the stability and reality of being.

But the following profound and admirable description of matter by Plotinus (*Ennead.* 3, lib. 6) will, I doubt not, be gratefully received by the Platonic reader.—

> “Since matter (says he) is neither soul, nor intellect, nor life, nor form, nor reason, nor bound, but a certain indefiniteness; nor yet capacity, for what can it produce? since it is foreign from all these, it cannot merit the appellation of being; but is deservedly called non-entity. Nor yet is it non-entity in the same manner as motion and permanency are non-beings, considered as different from being: but it is true non-entity; the mere shadow and imagination of bulk, and the desire of subsistence; remaining fixed without abiding, of itself invisible, and avoiding the desire of him who is anxious to perceive its nature. Hence, when no one perceives it, it is then in a manner present; but cannot be viewed by him who strives intently to behold it. Again, in itself contraries always appear; the small and the great, the less and the more, deficience and excess. So that it is a phantom, neither abiding nor yet able to fly away; capable of no one denomination, and

Hence, too, in each of its vanishing appellations, it eludes our search: for, if we think of it as something great, it is in the mean time small; if as something more, it becomes less; and the apparent being which we meet with in its image is <term>non-being <gloss>Greek: me on; that which lacks the stability of true reality</gloss></term>, and, as it were, a flying mockery. They seem, indeed, to effect something in the subject matter, but in reality produce nothing; from their debile and flowing nature being endued with no solidity and no rebounding power. And since matter likewise has no solidity, they penetrate it without division, like images in water, or as if any one should fill a vacuum with forms.”

Such, then, being the true condition of matter and her inherent shadowy forms, we may safely conclude that whatever becomes <term>corporeal <gloss>physical or bodily</gloss></term> in an eminent degree has but little power of recalling itself into one; and that a nature of this kind is ready by every trifling impulse to remain as it is impelled; to rush from the embraces of bound, and hasten into multitude and <term>non-entity <gloss>the state of not being a real, unified thing</gloss></term>. Lastly, when Plato composes the elements from mathematical planes, it is necessary to observe that, as these are physical planes, they must not only have length and breadth, but likewise depth, that they may be able to subsist as principles in natural effects.—“For the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that numbers and geometry were the fundamental building blocks of reality.</note> (says Simplicius *) considered every physical body as a figured quantity, and as in itself matter, but fashioned with different figures. That, besides this, it differs from a mathematical body in being material and tangible, receiving its tangibility from its bulk, and not either from heat or cold. Hence, from the subject matter being impressed with different figures, they assert that the four elements of the elements subsist. For these elements rank more in the nature of principles, as for instance, the cubic of earth; not that earth has wholly a cubic figure, but that each of the parts of earth is composed from many cubes, which through their smallness are invisible to our sight; and in the same manner the other elements from other primary figures. They add too, that from this difference of figures all the other properties of the elements ensue, and their mutations into each other. For, if it is inquired why much air is produced from a little water, they can very readily assign the cause by saying, that the elements of water are many, and that, the <term>icosahedrons <gloss>A 20-sided solid; in Platonic geometry, this represents Water.</gloss></term> of water being divided, many <term>octahedrons <gloss>An 8-sided solid; in Platonic geometry, this represents Air.</gloss></term>, and consequently a great quantity of air, will be produced.”

Simplicius <note>A 6th-century philosopher known for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle and efforts to harmonize Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note> likewise informs us, that the more ancient of Plato’s interpreters, among which the divine Iamblichus ranks, considered Plato as speaking symbolically in this part concerning the figures of the elements; but the latter Platonic philosophers, among whom Proclus <note>One of the last major Greek philosophers (5th century), who provided highly systematic and detailed explanations of Platonic doctrines.</note>, in my opinion, ranks as the most eminent, explained this part according to its literal meaning. And Simplicius, in the same book, has fortunately preserved the arguments of Proclus in defence of Plato’s doctrine respecting these planes, against the objections of Aristotle.

I trust, therefore, that the candid and liberal reader will gratefully accept these fruits of my application to the Platonic philosophy; and as this introduction and the following translation were the result of no moderate labor and perseverance, I earnestly hope they may be the means of awakening some few at least from the sleep of oblivion, of recalling their attention from fluctuating and delusive objects to permanent and real being; and thus may at length lead them back to their paternal port <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the soul returning to its divine origin or true home.</note>, as the only retreat which can confer perfect security and rest.

[...run over] them again briefly from the beginning, that they may be more firmly established in our minds; namely, what kind of republic appeared to me to be the best, and from what sort of men such a republic ought to be composed.

**Timaeus.** And by us, indeed, Socrates, all that you said was approved in the highest degree.

**Socrates.** Did we not, in the first place, separate husbandmen <term>husbandmen: farmers or those who manage the land</term> and other artificers <term>artificers: skilled craftsmen and manual laborers</term> from those whom we considered as the defenders of the city?

**Timaeus.** Certainly.

**Socrates.** And when we had assigned to every one that which was accommodated to his nature, and had prescribed only one particular employment to every particular art, we likewise assigned to the military tribe one province only, I mean that of protecting the city; and this as well from the hostile incursions of internal as of external enemies; but yet in such a manner as to administer justice mildly to the subjects of their government, as being naturally friends, and to behave with warlike fierceness against their enemies in battle.

**Timaeus.** Entirely so.

**Socrates.** For we asserted, I think, that the souls of the guardians should be of such a nature, as at the same time to be both irascible <term>irascible: prone to "thumos" or spiritedness; the capacity for righteous anger and bravery</term> and philosophic in a remarkable degree; so that they might be gentle to their friends, and bold and ferocious to their enemies.

**Timaeus.** You did so.

**Socrates.** But what did we assert concerning their education? Was it not that they should be instructed in gymnastic exercises, in music, and other becoming disciplines?

**Timaeus.** Entirely so.

**Socrates.** We likewise established, that those who were so educated should neither consider gold, or silver, or any goods of a similar kind, as their own private property; but that rather, after the manner of adjutants <term>adjutants: assistants or helpers; here meaning they serve the state rather than rule for profit</term>, they should receive the wages of guardianship from those whom they defend and preserve; and that their recompense should be no more than is sufficient to a moderate subsistence. That, besides this, they should use their public stipend in common, and for the purpose of procuring a common subsistence with each other; so that, neglecting every other concern, they may employ their attention solely on virtue, and the discharge of their peculiar employment.

**Timaeus.** These things also were related by you.

**Socrates.** Of women too we asserted, that they should be educated in such a manner, as to be aptly conformed <note>original: "conformed similar to the natures of men"</note> to the natures of men; with whom they should perform in common both the duties of war, and whatever else belongs to the business of life.

For we ordered that the marriages and children should be common <term>common: shared by the whole community rather than belonging to private families</term>; as we were particularly careful that no one might be able to distinguish his own children, but that all might consider all as their kindred; that hence those of an equal age might regard themselves as brothers and sisters; but that the younger might reverence the elder as their parents and grandfathers, and the elder might esteem the younger as their children and grandsons.

**Timaeus.** These things, indeed, as you say, are easily remembered.

**Socrates.** But that they might from their birth acquire a disposition as far as possible the best, we decreed that the rulers whom we placed over the marriage rites should, through the means of certain lots <term>lots: a system of drawing names, which Socrates suggests should be secretly manipulated by the rulers to ensure the best citizens pair together</term>, take care that in the nuptial league the worthy were mingled with the worthy; that no discord may arise in this connection when it does not prove prosperous in the end; but that all the blame may be referred to fortune <note>In the "Republic," Socrates explains that rulers should rig the lottery so that the best people breed together, while making the citizens believe it is just a matter of random "fortune."</note>, and not to the guardians of such a conjunction.

**Timaeus.** We remember this likewise.

**Socrates.** We also ordered that the children of the good should be properly educated, but that those of the bad should be secretly sent to some other city; yet so that such of the adult among these as should be found to be of a good disposition should be recalled from exile; while, on the contrary, those who were retained from the first in the city as good, but proved afterwards bad, should be similarly banished.

**Timaeus.** Just so.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates has just finished summarizing his vision of the ideal republic. He now challenges his companions—Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates—to show how this theoretical city would function in practice, specifically in times of war and diplomacy.</meta>

# THE TIMÆUS.

If someone, on beholding beautiful animals—whether represented in a picture or really alive, but in a state of perfect rest—should desire to behold them in motion, and struggling, as it were, to imitate those gestures which seem particularly adapted to the nature of bodies; in such a manner am I affected towards the form of that republic which we have described. For I should gladly hear anyone relating the contests of our city with other nations: when it engages in a becoming manner in war, and acts during such an engagement in a manner worthy of its institution <term>institution: referring here to the city's foundational laws and educational system</term>, both with respect to practical achievements and verbal negotiations. 

For indeed, O Critias and Hermocrates, I am conscious of my own inability to praise such men and such a city according to their desert. Indeed, that I should be incapable of such an undertaking is not wonderful, since the same imbecility <note>In this context, "imbecility" refers to a lack of strength or capability rather than a mental deficiency.</note> seems to have attended poets both of the past and present age. Not that I despise the poetic tribe; but it appears from hence evident, that, as these kind of men are studious of imitation, they easily and in the best manner express things in which they have been educated; while, on the contrary, whatever is foreign from their education they imitate with difficulty in actions, and with still more difficulty in words. 

But with respect to the tribe of Sophists <term>Sophists: traveling teachers in ancient Greece who were paid to teach rhetoric and philosophy, often viewed with suspicion by Socrates for prioritizing persuasion over truth</term>, though I consider them as skilled both in the art of speaking and in many other illustrious arts; yet, as they have no settled abode, but wander daily through a multitude of cities, I am afraid lest, with respect to the institutions of philosophers and politicians, they should not be able to conjecture the quality and magnitude of those concerns which wise and politic men are engaged in with individuals, in warlike undertakings, both in actions and discourse. 

It remains, therefore, that I should apply to you, who excel in the study of wisdom and civil administration, as well naturally as through the assistance of proper discipline and institution. ¹ The *Apaturia*, according to Proclus <note>Proclus was a 5th-century philosopher who wrote detailed commentaries on Plato’s works</note> and Suidas <note>The Suda (or Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world</note>, were festivals in honor of Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>, which were publicly celebrated for the space of three days. When, therefore, an artificer <note>The "artificer" (often called the Demiurge) is the divine craftsman who shapes the physical world.</note>, in the fabrication of any work, looks to that which always subsists according to *same*, and, employing a paradigm <note>original: 'paradigm' (paradeigma); an eternal model or blueprint.</note> of this kind, expresses the idea and power in his work, it is then necessary that the whole of his production should be beautiful. But we have before asserted, that whatever is generated is necessarily generated from some cause. To discover, therefore, the artificer <note>The "artificer" refers to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman of the Platonic universe.</note> and father of the universe is indeed difficult; and when found it is impossible to reveal him through the ministry of discourse to all men.

Again: this is to be considered concerning him, I mean, according to what **paradigm** <term>paradigm (paradeigma): an eternal, perfect model or "blueprint" that exists in the divine mind.</term> extending himself, he fabricated the world—whether towards an **exemplar** <note>Exemplar: the original pattern or "ideal" version of a thing.</note>, subsisting according to that which is always the same, and similarly affected, or towards that which is generated. But, indeed, if this world is beautiful, and its artificer good, it is evident that he looked towards an eternal exemplar in its fabrication. But if the world be far from beautiful, which it is not lawful to assert, he necessarily beheld a generated instead of an eternal exemplar. But it is perfectly evident that he regarded an

---

sensible world, time in things moved, and the **transitive intellection** <note>Transitive intellection: a form of thinking that moves step-by-step from one idea to another, unlike the static, eternal knowledge of the divine.</note> of souls. But that every motion subsists according to a part, and that the whole of it is not present at once, is evident. And if the essence of the world possesses generation, and the perpetuity of it is according to a temporal infinity, it may be inferred, that between things eternally perpetual, and such as are generated in a part of time, it is necessary that nature should subsist which is generated infinitely. It is also requisite that a nature of this kind should be generated infinitely in a twofold respect, viz. either that the whole of it should be perpetual through the whole of time, but that the parts should subsist in the parts of time, as is the case with the **sublunary elements** <note>Sublunary elements: the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) found below the orbit of the moon, which are subject to constant change and decay.</note>, or that both the whole and the parts of it should be co-extended with the perpetuity of all time, as is the case with the heavenly bodies. For the perpetuity according to eternity is not the same with the perpetuity of the whole of time, as neither is the infinity of eternity and time the same; because eternity is not the same with time, the former being infinite life at once total and full, or, the whole of which is ever present to itself, and the latter being a flowing image of such a life.

Further still, says **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher whose extensive commentaries on Plato preserved much of ancient cosmological thought.</note>, the term *generated* has a multifarious meaning. For it signifies that which has a temporal beginning, every thing which proceeds from a cause, that which is essentially a composite, and that which is naturally capable of being generated, though it should not be generated. The term *generated*, therefore, being multifariously predicated, that which is generated according to time possesses all the modes of generation. For it proceeds from a cause, is a composite, and is naturally capable of being generated. Hence, as that which is generated in a part of time begins at one time, and arrives at perfection in another, so the world, which is generated according to the whole of time, is always beginning, and always perfect. And it has indeed a certain beginning of generation, so far as it is perfected by its cause, but has not a certain beginning so far as it has not a beginning of a certain partial time.

¹ Plato, says **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note>, had prior to this made two things the leaders: the **intelligible** <note>That which can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note> and that which is generated (or **paradigm** and image). Plato, therefore, clearly divides reasonings and knowledges with the things known. **Parmenides** <note>An earlier Greek philosopher known for his poem on the nature of "Being."</note> also, though obscure through his poetry, says that there are twofold knowledges, truth and faith, of twofold things: viz. of beings and non-beings. The "faith," however, which Plato now assumes appears to be different from that of which he speaks in the sixth book of his *Republic*, in the section of a line; for that is irrational knowledge, which is divided from conjecture but arranged according to sense. But the present faith is rational, though it is mingled with irrational knowledges, employing sense and conjecture; and hence it is filled with much of the unstable. For, receiving *that* a thing is from sense or conjecture, it thus assigns the causes: but these knowledges possess much of the confused and unstable. 

Hence Socrates in the *Phædo* very much blames the senses, because we neither see nor hear any thing accurately. How then can knowledge, originating from sense, possess the accurate and irreprehensible? For those powers that employ science alone collect with accuracy every thing which is the object of their knowledge; but those powers that energize with sense err and fall off from the accurate, through sense, and through the unstable nature of the thing known. 

For what can any one assert of that which is material, since it is always changing and flowing, and is not naturally adapted to abide for a moment? And with respect to a celestial nature, in consequence of being very remote from us, it is not easily known, nor scientifically apprehended; but we must be satisfied with an approximation to the truth, and with probability in the speculation of it. For every thing which is in place requires a residence there, in order to a perfect knowledge of its nature. # THE TIMÆUS.

->THE TIMÆUS.<-

He reduced the universe from this state of wild disorder into a state of order, considering that such a condition was by far the best. For it never was lawful, nor is it now, for the most perfect cause to produce anything other than the most beautiful of effects. In consequence of a reasoning <gloss>1</gloss> process, therefore, he found that among things that are naturally visible <gloss>2</gloss> there was nothing—when viewed as a whole—that was void of intelligence which could ever be more beautiful than a whole which possesses intellect. At the same time, he discovered that it was impossible for intellect to be present in any being without the presence of a soul. Hence, as the result of this reasoning, placing intellect in the soul and the soul in the body, he fabricated the universe; so that it might be a work that is naturally the most beautiful and the best. In this manner, therefore, according to

<note>The text here transitions into a commentary on the nature of creation, likely by the translator Thomas Taylor, referencing the philosopher Proclus.</note>

the opposite. To which we may add, that the work of the **Demiurge** <term>Demiurge: From the Greek *demiourgos*, meaning a craftsman or artisan. In this context, it refers to the divine figure who shapes the material world.</term> is twofold: one part is the creation of the body of the world, and the other is the decoration or ordering of it. Plato, beginning with the decoration, rightly represents everything corporeal as moving in a confused and disordered manner; this is because such is the natural motion of matter when it is not yet guided by an intellectual soul.

It also deserves to be noticed that Plato, in describing this state of confusion and disorder prior to the world's formal creation, imitates the ancient **theologians** <note>original: *theologists*. Referring here to ancient Greek poets like Hesiod who wrote about the origins of the gods.</note>. For, just as they describe the battles and rebellions of the **Titans** <note>The Titans represented the raw, chaotic forces of nature which had to be subdued by the Olympian Gods to establish a stable universe.</note> against the Olympian Gods, so Plato presupposes these two states: the unadorned chaos and the Creator of the world, so that the former may be beautified and share in a divine order. The ancient poets introduced these themes through mythology, for they set the powers that preside over material bodies against the Olympian deities; but Plato approaches this philosophically, showing how order is transferred from the Gods to the subjects they govern.

<gloss>1</gloss> The Creator of the universe, through the fullness of his power, makes different things using different powers. Because he contains within himself the cause of all things made, he gives existence to the whole world in one way, and to its individual parts in another. Thus, through one act of intelligence, he adorns the whole world and generates it all at once—which is why the world is considered a single living animal. However, through "reasoning," he produces its parts. He produces these as "wholes" because he is the creator of "total" natures: namely, total intellect, total soul, and the entire bulk of matter. Because of this, when he is composing parts, he is said to create by "reasoning." In this context, "reasoning" signifies a cause that distributes things into their proper places; it does not mean the reasoning of someone who is doubting. Neither art nor science doubts; rather, it is the artist or the scientist who doubts when they lack their necessary skills. If these human experts do not doubt when they are perfect in their craft, can we suppose that the supreme Intellect, the creator and father of the universe, experiences doubt?

<gloss>2</gloss> This refers to "intelligibles"—the eternal, perfect patterns of things. That these are "visible" is clear from Plato’s words later on, where he says, "Whatever ideas intellect perceived in the animal itself," etc. As the philosopher **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonic philosopher whose commentaries on Plato heavily influenced this translation.</note> beautifully observes, some things are visible to us, while others are visible "according to nature." The things visible to us are, in their own nature, dark and obscure; but things naturally visible are truly known and shine with divine light. Such are the "intelligibles" or eternal forms.

# THE TIMÆUS.

->THE TIMÆUS.<-

to an assimilative reason <note>Reasoning that aims to make a copy resemble its original model.</note>, it is necessary to call the world a living being, endowed with intellect, and generated through the providence of the Divine.

This being determined, let us consider what follows; and, in the next place, after the likeness of what animals the composing craftsman <term>craftsman: Here referring to the Demiurge, the divine figure who shapes the material world.</term> constituted the world. Indeed, we must by no means think that he fashioned it similar to such animals as exist only as a part, or have a partial existence: for, if it had been made like an imperfect animal, it certainly would not have been beautiful. But we should rather establish it as the most similar of all things to that Animal <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Intelligible Animal" is the divine blueprint or "Form" that contains the ideas of all living creatures.</note>, of which other animals—both considered separately and according to their kinds—are nothing more than parts. For this original, indeed, contains all intelligible <term>intelligible: Existing in the realm of pure thought or intellect, rather than the physical world.</term> animals within itself; just as this physical world contains us and the other animals which we can see. For, as the Divine was willing to make this universe resemble, in the highest degree, that which is the most beautiful and perfectly complete of all thought-based objects, he composed it as one visible living being, containing within itself all such animals as are related to its nature. 

Do we therefore rightly conclude that there is but one universe; or is it more correct to assert that there are many and infinite? In truth, there can be but one, if it is admitted that it was built according to a model <note>original: *exemplar*</note>. For that which encompasses all possible living beings can never be secondary to any other. If there were two such worlds, another "animal" would be required to surround them both, of which they would be mere parts; in that case, it would be more proper to say the universe was modeled after that third encompassing one, rather than the other two. Therefore, so that the world might be similar to the all-perfect Living Being in its uniqueness—on this account the craftsman produced neither two nor infinite worlds; but heaven, or the universe, was generated and will remain one and only-begotten <note>original: *monogenēs*. In this context, it means unique or the only one of its kind.</note>.

But since it is necessary that a physical nature should be visible and tangible, and since nothing can be visible without fire, and nothing tangible without something solid, and nothing solid without earth—hence the Divine, beginning the work of fabrication, composed the body of the universe from fire and earth. But it is impossible for two things alone to hold together without the intervention of a third; for a certain collective bond <note>Plato is introducing the idea that mathematical proportion acts as the "glue" for the physical elements.</note> is necessary in the middle of the two. And that is the most beautiful of bonds which renders both itself and the things it binds remarkably one. But the...

...the most beautiful analogy <note>In Platonic philosophy, "analogy" refers to a geometric proportion (e.g., A is to B as B is to C) that creates a perfect bond between different parts.</note> naturally produces this effect. For when either in three numbers, or masses, or powers, as is the middle to the last, so is the first to the middle; and again, as is the last to the middle, so is the middle to the first: then the middle becoming both first and last, and the last and the first passing each of them into a middle position, they become all of them necessarily the same, as to relation to each other. But, being made the same with each other, all are one. If, then, it were necessary that the universe should be a superficies <term>superficies: A flat, two-dimensional surface or plane.</term> only, and have no depth, one medium <term>medium: A middle term in a mathematical sequence that links two extremes.</term> would indeed be sufficient, both for the purpose of binding itself and the natures which it contains. 

But now it is requisite that the world should be a solid; and solids are never harmonized together by one, but always with two mediums. Hence, the Divinity placed water and air in the middle of fire and earth, and fabricated them as much as possible in the same ratio to each other; so that fire might be to air as air to water; and that as air is to water so water might be to earth. And from this conjunction and composition he rendered the world visible and tangible. Hence, from things of this kind, which are four in number, it must be confessed that the body of the universe was generated through analogy, conspiring into friendship with itself from their conjunction, and so aptly cohering in all its parts, as to be indissoluble <note>The world is so perfectly put together that only the one who built it—the Creator—has the power to take it apart.</note> except by its artificer <term>artificer: The Demiurge, or divine craftsman, who shapes the material world.</term>, who bound it in this union and consent.

The composition of the world, therefore, received one *whole* of each of these four natures. For its composing artificer constituted it from *all* fire, water, air, and earth; leaving no part of any one of these, nor any power external to the world. For by a reasoning process he concluded that it would thus be a whole animal <note>Plato views the entire universe as a "living animal" or organism that encompasses all other living things.</note>, in the highest degree perfect from perfect parts: that, besides this, it would be one, as nothing would be left from which any other such nature might be produced; and lastly, that it would be neither obnoxious <note>In this older sense, "obnoxious" means vulnerable or subject to harm.</note> to old age nor disease. For he perceived that the heat and cold from which bodies are composed, and all such things as possess vigorous powers, when surrounding bodies externally, and acceding to them unseasonably, dissolve their union, and, introducing diseases and old age, cause them to perish by decay. Hence, through this cause and this reasoning process, he fabricated the universe one whole, composed from all wholes, perfect, undecaying, and without disease. He likewise gave to it a figure becoming and allied to its nature. For to the animal which was destined to

For he considered that the similar was infinitely more beautiful than the dissimilar.

Besides this, he accurately polished the external circumference of the spherical world, and rendered it perfectly smooth <note>The "smoothness" mentioned here refers to the universe's ability to perfectly reflect and receive divine light, much like a mirror.</note>. Nor was the addition of eyes <note>The universe does not need eyes because there is nothing outside of it to see; it is an all-encompassing whole.</note> requisite to the universe; for nothing visible remained external to itself.

According to him <note>Referring to the philosopher Proclus (412–485 AD), whose commentary clarifies Plato’s text.</note>, the world is an animal, and an animal is characterized by sense. In order, therefore, to understand what the nature of that sense is which the world possesses, it will be necessary to make the following division.

Of sense, therefore, the first and most principal is that which imitates intellect. For everywhere, things which rank as first possess an imitation of things prior to them. Hence, that which is conjoined with first natures is that which has a sensible perception of itself, comprehended in itself, not passing from one thing to another—for this would be divided sense—nor proceeding to externals—for this is imperfect—but possessing the whole of that which is sensible in itself, and which may be rather called consciousness than sense.

The next to this is that which proceeds indeed, and does not abide like the former, but yet proceeds according to a perfect energy, and always, on all sides, similarly apprehends that which is known; which is likewise purified from all passion <term>passion: here meaning "suffering" or being acted upon by an outside force.</term>, and from all that weakness which is peculiar to divisible and material organs.

The third is that which is passive to things external, and is mingled from passion and knowledge; originating, indeed, from passion, but ending in knowledge.

The last sense is that with which a most obscure knowledge is present, which is full of passion, and is proximate to physical sympathy, as not knowing the forms of sensible things; as, for instance, that what operates is hot or cold, but that what falls upon it is alone pleasant or painful; for such is the sense of plants, as Timaeus informs us in the course of this dialogue, being the apprehension of that which is alone pleasant and painful from things sensible.

Sense, therefore, thus proceeding from the highest level downward, the world is sensitive according to the first sense. For it is visible, and an eye, according to the whole of itself, since the sun also is called an eye, and each of the stars. The world, therefore, is wholly sight and the thing seen, and is *truly* to be comprehended by sense and opinion. Hence, it contains all-perfect knowledge, indivisible sense, and is itself sensible, the instrument of sense, and sense; just as also its artificer is intellect, intelligence, and the intelligible. And as it comprehends partial bodies in its whole body, so likewise it contains many senses in its total sense.

From an essence impartible <note>Indivisible or unable to be broken into parts.</note>, and always subsisting according to sameness—

<sup>1</sup> The happiness of any being is the proper perfection of that being; and hence, as the perfections of beings differ, so also do their felicities. A felicity, therefore, in the present case must be assumed, adapted to the universe. For, since the world is suspended from a paternal intellect and a total fabricative energy, and lives according to those causes, it is happy in a degree consequent to these. The world, therefore, living according to the will of the father, and preserving immutably the intellectual good which is thence imparted, is very justly said to be happy. But the first form of felicity, says Proclus, and which is all-perfect, is that of the world. The second is that of the mundane Gods, whom Plato in the *Phædrus* calls happy divinities, following the mighty Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, representing the highest ordering principle.</note>. The third is that which subsists in the genera superior to our nature, namely <note>original: *viz.*</note> angels, dæmons <note>In Greek thought, *daimones* were guardian spirits or intermediaries between gods and men, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, and heroes; for the felicity of each of these is different. The fourth is that which subsists in undefiled souls, who make blameless descents into mortality, and exhibit an inflexible and untamed life; such as were the souls of Hercules, Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, etc. The fifth is the felicity of partial souls; and this is multiform: for a soul the attendant of the moon is not happy after the same manner as the soul that is suspended from the solar order; but as the form of life is different, so also the perfection is limited by different measures. And the last form of felicity is that which is seen in irrational animals.

<sup>2</sup> The Orphic writers, says Proclus, (in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, page 184 <note>original: *in Tim. p. 184.*</note>) do not predicate the impartible of every intelligible or intellectual order, but, according to them, there is something better than this appellation; just as, with respect to other names, they do not adapt king and father to all orders. Where, then, shall we first perceive the indivisible according to Orpheus, that we may thus understand the divinely intellectual conception of Plato? Orpheus, therefore, establishing one demiurgus <note>Craftsman/creator.</note> of all divided fabrication, who is analogous to the one father that generates total fabrication, produces from him the whole mundane intellectual multitude, the number of souls, and corporeal compositions. This demiurgus (namely <note>original: *viz.*</note> Bacchus <note>Dionysus in Greek mythology.</note>), therefore, generates all these unitedly; but the Gods who are placed about him divide and separate his fabrications. For, as he gave subsistence to intellects, souls and bodies, and souls and bodies receive in themselves much division and separation into parts, but intellect remains united and undivided, being all things in one, and comprehending...

But he began to divide as follows:—In the first place, he received one part from the whole. Proclus further observes, “that the theologians also establish about subterranean <note>underground or "hellish" realms</note> places the powers of the highest Gods; and that Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, used here as the supreme craftsman or Demiurge</note> himself is represented by them as adorning those places in order to adapt them to the participation of such mighty Gods. That, if this be the case, we ought much more to think, concerning the soul of the universe, that it adorns every thing which appears to have a disordered subsistence, possesses the cause of its existence, and arranges it in a becoming manner according to this cause. For, how can it govern the universe, or conduct all things according to intellect, unless it orderly disposes that which is disordered, and co-harmonizes things last <note>the most material or "lowest" things</note> with the one life of the world? If also the causes of these pre-exist in the demiurgus <term>demiurgus: the divine Craftsman or creator of the physical world</term>, as Orpheus <note>The legendary poet associated with the Orphic mystery religion</note> says, what wonder is it that the whole soul which possesses all such things in a manner adapted to itself, as a divine intellect possesses demiurgically, should also comprehend the cause of things last in the world, and of that which is as it were the sediment of wholes? For soul prior to the apparent and sensible comprehends an unapparent world.”

Proclus concludes with observing, that the whole number of the essential monads <term>monads: fundamental, indivisible units of being</term> in the soul is 105,947*; the soul thus proceeding according to all the orders of numbers. For it proceeds decadically <note>based on the number 10</note> indeed, that it may become the mundane <note>world-dwelling</note> soul; since the decad is the number of the world: but pentadically <note>based on the number 5</note>, that it may be converted to itself; for the pentad is self-convertive. It also proceeds enneadically <note>based on the number 9</note> (or according to the number 9), that it may not only connect the universe monadically, but may proceed to the last of things after departing from the monad: tetradically <note>based on the number 4</note>, as collecting the four-part division of things into one, and hebdomadically <note>based on the number 7</note> (or according to the number 7), as converting all things to the monad, to which the number seven is alone referred, this number being motherless and masculine <note>In Pythagorean numerology, 7 was considered "virgin" because it is not a product of other numbers in the first decade</note>. And the whole of this number is indeed in the soul of the world totally, viz. has a total subsistence; but in divine souls, as energizing towards the mundane soul, it is contained totally and partially. In dæmoniacal <note>referring to 'daemons,' intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note> souls, as energizing yet more partially, it subsists on the contrary partially and totally; and in human souls partially and gnostically <note>related to knowledge or cognition</note> alone.

<margin>The creation of the periods of time.</margin>

¹ What day and night, month and year, are, says <term>Proclus</term> <note>A famous Greek philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) who wrote this extensive commentary on Plato's work.</note>, and how these are said to be parts of time—whereas *was* and *will be* are species <note>Types or categories of time, rather than physical segments.</note>, and not parts—requires much discussion and profound consideration. If then we should say that day is air illuminated by the sun, in the first place, we should speak of something which takes place in day, and not that which day is; for, when we say that the day is long or short, we certainly do not predicate an increase or decrease of the air; and, in the next place, it is difficult to devise how this will be a part of time. 

But if we say that day is the temporal interval according to which the sun proceeds from the east to the west, we shall perhaps avoid the former objections, but we shall fall into more impervious difficulties. For whether, surveying this interval itself without relation to the sun, we say that it is day, how does it happen, since the same interval is every where according to the same, that day is not every where? And if we consider this interval in connection with the solar motion, if it is simply so considered, day will always be in the heavens, and there will be no night; and how is it possible that a part of time should not be every where? For night, day, and month, are here clearly said to be parts of time. 

But if we connect this interval with the circulation of the sun, not simply, but assert that day is the portion of the sun's course from east to west, but night that portion which is produced by his course from west to east, the heavens will not possess those nights and days which are said to be parts of time; and it is also evident that neither will they possess months and years. 

But we assert of time, both considered according to the whole of itself, and every part of its progression, that it is present to the whole world: for one and the same *now* is every where the same. It is necessary, therefore, that day and the other parts of time should be every where the same, though they are participated partibly <note>Experienced in fragments or divided sections by us on Earth.</note>, and with <term>divulsion</term> <note>A separation or tearing apart; here, the way the unified concept of time is broken into pieces by physical objects.</note> by sensible fabrications. Hence he says in the plural number *nights* and *days*, as also *months* and *years*. But these are obvious to all men: for the unapparent causes of these have a uniform subsistence prior to things multiplied, and which circulate infinitely. Things immovable also subsist prior to such as are moved, and intellectual natures are prior to sensibles. Such, therefore, must be our conceptions of night and day according to their first subsistence.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s "Timaeus," specifically focusing on the distinction between the "parts" of time (days, years) and the "species" of time (past and future). It builds on the previous page's discussion of how time was created alongside the universe to act as a moving image of eternity.</meta>

-># THE TIMÆUS.<-

...had no subsistence prior to the universe, but which together with it rose into existence. And all these, indeed, are the proper parts of time. But the terms *it was* and *it will be*, which express the species <note>In this context, "species" refers to the different forms or categories that time takes, rather than physical segments.</note> of generated time, are transferred by us to an eternal essence <note>The realm of the divine or the "Forms," which exists outside of time and change.</note>, through oblivion of the truth. For we assert of such an essence that it was, *is*, and *will be*; while according to truth the term *it is* is alone accommodated to its nature. But we should affirm, that *to have been* and *to be hereafter* are expressions alone accommodated to generation <note>The physical world of "becoming," where things are born, change, and die.</note>, proceeding according to the flux of time: for these 

greatest strength, and measuring all things in conjunction with time. For neither day nor night, nor month, is without the sun, nor much more year, nor any other mundane nature. I do not here speak according to the apparent fabrication of things alone, for the apparent sun is the cause of these measures, but also according to that fabrication which is unapparent. For, ascending higher, we shall find that the more true sun <note>original: "sun considered according to its subsistence in the supermundane order of Gods." This refers to a spiritual or intellectual "Sun" that exists in the higher realms of reality, beyond the physical star we see.</note> measures all things in conjunction with time, being itself in reality time of time, according to the oracle <note>original: "one of the Chaldæan Oracles." These were a collection of mystical, philosophical poems from the 2nd century AD that Neoplatonists like Proclus held in high regard.</note> of the Gods concerning it. For that Plato not only knew these apparent parts of time, but also those divine parts to which these are homonymous <note>Things that share the same name but have different natures; here, the physical day versus the divine "day."</note>, is evident from the tenth book of his *Laws*. For he there asserts that we call hours and months divine, as having the same divine lives, and divine intellects presiding over them, as the universe. But, if he now speaks about the apparent parts of time, it is by no means wonderful; because now his design is to <term>physiologize</term> <note>To "physiologize" is to speak or write about the nature of the physical world and its governing laws.</note>. Let these, therefore, be the parts of time, of which some are accommodated to the <term>inerratic Gods</term> <note>The "fixed" stars, which do not appear to wander like the planets.</note>, others to the Gods that revolve about the poles of the oblique circle <note>The ecliptic or the zodiacal path of the planets.</note>, and others to other Gods, or attendants of the Gods, or to mortal animals, or the more sublime or more abject parts of the universe.

But Plato says that *was* and *will be* are species and not parts of time, in the same manner as days and nights, and months and years: for by these he represents to us those divine orders which give completion to the whole series of time; and on this account he calls them parts of time. But *was* and *will be* are entirely beheld according to each of these; and hence they are certain species, not having as it were a peculiar matter; I mean a diurnal or nocturnal matter, or any other of this kind. If then these are the species of time which was generated together with the world, there was no generation prior to the world. Neither, therefore, was there any motion: for in every motion there are these species of time, because there are prior and posterior. But, if there was not motion, neither was there inordinate motion. In vain, therefore, do the followers of <term>Atticus</term> <note>A philosopher from the 2nd century AD who argued that the world had a beginning in time and that chaotic matter existed before creation.</note> say, that there was time prior to the generation of the world, but not subsisting in order: for where time is there also there is past and future; and where these are, *was* and *will be* must likewise be found. But *was* and *will be* are species of time generated by the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator of the physical universe.</note>: and hence time was not prior to the fabrication of the world. Proclus after this observes, that *was* indicates the perfective order of time, but *will be* the unfolding, in the same manner as *is*, the connective order of time. For time unfolds things which yet are not, connects things present, and perfects things past, and introduces a boundary to them adapted to their periods.

Proclus argues against thinkers like Atticus, asserting that time and the physical world were created simultaneously by the Demiurge, meaning no "chaotic time" existed beforehand.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 492, where the distinction between the "parts" of time (days, months, years) and the "species" of time (past, present, future) was introduced. It explores the relationship between the eternal "Is" and the temporal "was" and "will be."</meta>

-># THE TIMÆUS.<-

The parts of time are specific motions. But that which exists forever as the same and immovable neither becomes older nor younger at any time; it has never been created in the past, nor will it be in some future cycle of time. It does not accept any condition of existence that "generation" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "generation" refers to the world of physical things that are born, change, and die, as opposed to the eternal world of "Being."</note> applies to things caught up in its powerful, swirling motion. For all these are nothing more than forms of time that imitate eternity, rolling in a circle according to number. Besides this, we also frequently claim that a thing which was *generated* (created), is *generated*: that what exists in the state of **BECOMING TO BE**, is *in generation*; that what **WILL BE**, **IS TO BE**; and that **NON-BEING IS NOT**: none of these claims is strictly true. But perhaps a thorough discussion of these matters is not suited to the present debate.

But time¹ was generated together with the universe, so that by being produced together they might be dissolved together, if any such dissolution should ever happen.

<note>
¹ Proclus, a later philosopher and commentator on Plato, explains that Plato claims time was created alongside the universe—which is endowed with a soul and intelligence—because the world first experiences time through its soul and its physical body. But when Plato says "that, being produced together, they may together be dissolved, if any dissolution should ever happen to these," he is actually showing that the universe is uncreated and indestructible. 

Logic dictates that if the universe was created, it must have been created *in* time. However, if it was created *simultaneously* with time, then it was not created "in" time—because time itself cannot be created in time (otherwise there would be a time before time began). Therefore, the universe was not "created" <note>That is, it was not created in the common sense of having a beginning in time.</note> in the usual sense. 

Furthermore, if everything that is destroyed is destroyed at a certain time, but time itself cannot be destroyed within a part of itself, then time can never be destroyed. Consequently, the universe will never be destroyed as long as time exists. Time is also indestructible because of its simple nature, unless one considers the movement away from and back toward the <term>Demiurge (the divine craftsman or creator of the world)</term> as a form of "creation" and "destruction." In this sense, the universe only has a beginning and end in terms of its ultimate cause. 

Just as someone might say that the <note>original: "heptad"</note> <term>number seven (often associated with the seven planets known in antiquity)</term> is linked to the <note>original: "circulations of the other nature," meaning the paths of the planets through the zodiac.</note> orbits of the planets to show they can never be even in number, so too must we understand the absolute indestructibility of the world and of time. The reason time was created with the universe is to ensure the universe remains indestructible.
</note>

<note>
$^1$ Plato, says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Greek philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note>, here provides the primary and leading cause of visible time. But if it has a more accurate cycle, it is rightly said to be the measure of measures, and to know from itself the periodic measures of the other planets, the proportions they contain, and the speed of some compared with others. It also copies, to a greater degree than the other planets, the permanence of eternity by constantly revolving in the same unchanging way. This, then, is its difference compared to the planets.

But the sun is, in another way, a more visible measure than the sphere of fixed stars <note>original: "inerratic sphere." This refers to the outermost shell of the universe where the stars do not move relative to each other.</note>; for while that sphere also has its own proper measure and unchanging number for its motion, the solar light makes this measure and the whole unfolding of visible time clear and known. Hence Plato says "that these circles might possess a certain conspicuous measure:" for though there is a measure in the other stars, it is not *conspicuous* <note>meaning "easily seen" or "obvious."</note>. But the sun reveals both other intellectual truths and time itself into the light. You must not, however, say that the solar light was created just for the sake of measuring; for how is it possible that whole systems exist for the sake of their parts, or governing powers for the sake of those they govern, or eternal things for the sake of those that decay? We should rather say that light reveals the whole of time, possessing a power to unfold it, and calls forth its celestial unity <note>original: "supermundane monad," a term for a primary, singular source existing above the physical world.</note> and its one measure to the task of measuring the cycles of bodies. It is the light of the sun, therefore, which makes every moving thing have a visible measure. And this is its primary purpose. But after serving the whole universe, it also benefits the individual parts as a secondary effect; for it provides the creation of number and a measure to those things that are capable of receiving them.

On this account, Plato appears to me to describe two different ways the sun was brought into being: one along with the seven governors of the world <note>The seven classical planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon.</note>, when he shapes their bodies and places them in their revolving spheres; but the other is the *enkindling* of its light, through which it receives power from beyond this world. For it is one thing for the bulk of the sun to generate itself, and another to be generated with a governing quality <note>original: "idiom." A specific, defining characteristic.</note> through which it is called the king of everything visible and is established as an analogy to the primary fountain of all good. 

For, just as the *Good itself* <note>The supreme principle in Plato’s philosophy, which sits above even the realm of pure intellect.</note>, being superior to the *intelligible* <note>The realm of forms or ideas that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>, illuminates both the intellect and the objects of thought, so the sun—being superior to the visible world—illuminates light and everything else that can be seen. But if the sun is above the visible world, it must have a nature that is beyond the physical <note>original: "supermundane."</note>; for the world is visible and tangible and possesses a body. We must, therefore, look at the sun in two ways: as one of the seven physical governors of the world, and as the leader of all things, acting both within the world and beyond it, by which he illuminates all with divine light. 

Just as the *Good* generates truth, which makes both the intelligible and intellectual orders divine; and as Phanes <note>A primeval deity in Orphic mythology, often associated with light and the creation of the universe.</note>, according to Orpheus, emits intelligible light which fills all the intellectual Gods with wisdom; and as Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, here acting as the kingly, world-shaping intellect.</note> enkindles an intellectual and creative light in all natures beyond our world, so the sun illuminates everything visible through this pure light. But that which illuminates is always in a higher rank than the things which are illuminated. For the *Good* is not merely an object of thought, nor is Phanes merely intellectual, nor is Jupiter merely of this world. From this reasoning, the sun, being beyond the physical world, emits the fountains of light. And the most secret and mystical teachings place the "wholeness" of the sun in that higher order; for there a "solar world" and total light exist, as the oracles of the Chaldæans <note>The "Chaldæan Oracles" were a collection of mystical poems from the 2nd century AD, highly revered by later Platonists.</note> say, and as I am convinced. Why, then, some one may say, was not the light of the sun enkindled in the first of the periods from the earth? Because, I reply, the effulgence of the sun is of itself incommensurate with generation; but the moon, existing as a medium, and first receiving his light, renders it more commensurate with generation. For, as Aristotle says, the moon is, as it were, a lesser sun. And it is requisite that what is proximately above generation should not be the most splendid and luminous. For it is not lawful that a thing of this kind should approach to that which is dark; but what is proximate to the darkness of generation must necessarily be luminous in a secondary degree, always possessing, indeed, its proper light, but evincing a mutation in its participation of a more excellent light. It is likewise requisite that it should exhibit this mutation in an orderly manner, that through this mutation it may be the paradigm of that very mutable nature which matter introduces to generated things.

But that the stars, and all heaven, receive light from the sun, may be easily perceived. For that which is common in many things derives its subsistence from one cause, which is either <term>exempt</term> <note>A cause that exists on a higher level of reality than its effects.</note> or <term>coordinate</term> <note>A cause that exists on the same level as its effects.</note>; and the coordinate cause is that which first participates of that form. But that first participates in which this form especially subsists the first. If, therefore, light especially subsists in the sun, the sun will be the first light, and from this the light in other things will be derived.

<meta>This page continues from page 497/498, where the discussion of time, the movement of the planets (the "wanderings"), and the "Great Year" concluded. We now transition from the creation of time to the creation of the various forms of life intended to populate the universe.</meta>

->### THE TIMÆUS.<-

And indeed the Artificer <note>The Demiurge, or the divine craftsman who shapes the material world in Plato's philosophy.</note> fabricated other forms, as far as to the generation of time, according to the similarity of the world's <term>exemplar</term> <note>exemplar: the eternal, intelligible model or blueprint upon which the physical world is based.</note>.

But as the universe did not yet contain all animals in its capacious receptacle, in this respect it was dissimilar to its <term>exemplar</term>. Its Artificer, therefore, supplied this defect by impressing it with forms, according to the nature of its <term>paradigm</term> <note>paradigm: another term for the original archetype or pattern.</note>. Whatever ideas, therefore, intellect perceived by the <term>dianoëtic energy</term> <note>dianoëtic energy: the power of discursive reasoning or logical thought that moves from one premise to another.</note> in "animal itself" <note>This refers to the "Intelligible Animal," the perfect Form containing all life forms.</note>, such and so many he conceived it necessary for the universe to contain. But these ideas are four: One, the celestial genus of Gods; another, winged and air-wandering; a third, the aquatic form; and a fourth, that which is pedestrian and terrestrial. 

The idea, therefore, of that which is divine, or the <term>inerratic sphere</term> <note>inerratic sphere: the sphere of the "fixed stars" which do not "wander" like planets.</note>, he for the most part fabricated from fire, that it might be most splendid and beautiful to behold. And as he meant to assimilate it to the universe, he rendered it circular; placed it in the wisdom of the best nature; ordered it to become the attendant of that which is best; and gave it a circular distribution about the heavens, that it might be a *true world*, adorned with a fair variety in its every part. 

But he adapted to each of the divine bodies two motions; one by which they might revolve in *<term>same</term>* <note>same: refers to the "Circle of the Same," representing identity, stability, and the celestial equator.</note> according to *<term>same</term>*, by always thinking the same things in themselves about *<term>same</term>*; the other through which they might be led with an advancing motion from the dominion of the *<term>same</term>* and similar circulation. He likewise rendered them immovable and stable as to the other five motions <note>In Platonic physics, there are six motions: up, down, left, right, forward, and backward. The stars only use the seventh: rotation.</note>, that each of them might become in an eminent degree the best. And on this account such of the stars as are inerratic were generated, which are divine animals; and, in consequence of this, always abide revolving in that which is *<term>same</term>*.

Thus, for instance, the celestial produce sublunary <note>Referring to the region below the moon—the earthly realm of change and decay.</note> Gods, and these generate mortal animals; the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the universe.</note> at the same time fabricating these in conjunction with the celestial and sublunary Divinities. For in speaking he understands all things, and by understanding all things he also makes the mortal genera of animals; these requiring another proximate generating cause, so far as they are mortal, and through this receiving a progression into being. But the character of the words is enthusiastic <note>original: "enthusiastic" – here meaning "divinely inspired" or "possessed by a god."</note>, shining with intellectual intuitions, pure and venerable as being perfected by the father of the Gods, differing from and transcending human conceptions, delicate, and at the same time terrific, full of grace and beauty—at once concise and perfectly accurate. Plato, therefore, particularly studies these things in the imitations of divine speeches; as he also evinces in the *Republic*, when he represents the Muses speaking sublimely, and the prophet ascending to a lofty seat. He also adorns both these speeches with conciseness and venerableness, employing the accurate powers of <term>colons</term> <note>In ancient rhetoric, "colons" are the rhythmic clauses or members that make up a sentence.</note>, directly shadowing forth divine intellections through such a form of words. But in the words before us he omits no transcendency either of the grand and robust in the sentences and the names adapted to these devices, or of magnitude in the conceptions and the figures which give completion to this idea. Besides this, also, much distinction and purity, the unfolding of truth, and the illustrious prerogatives of beauty, are mingled with the idea of magnitude, this being especially adapted to the subject things, to the speaker, and to the hearers. For the objects of this speech are, the perfection of the universe, an assimilation to all-perfect animal, and the generation of all mortal animals; the maker of all things at the same time subsisting and adorning all things, through exempt transcendency, but the secondary fabricators adding what was wanting to the formation of the universe. All, therefore, being great and divine, as well the persons as the things, and shining with beauty and a distinction from each other, Plato has employed words adapted to the form of the speech.

Homer also, when energizing enthusiastically, represents Jupiter speaking, converting to himself the twofold coordinations of Gods, becoming himself, as it were, the centre of all the divine genera in the world, and making all things obedient to his intellection. But at one time he conjoins the multitude of Gods with himself without a medium, and at another through Themis <note>The goddess of divine law and order.</note> as the medium.

For their unmingled nature is not without providential energy, nor is their providence mingled with matter. Since, therefore, the Gods that govern the world, and the <term>dæmons</term> <note>In this context, dæmons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that serve as attendants to the higher gods.</note> the attendants of these, receive after this manner unmingled purity and providential administration from their father; at one time he converts them to himself without a medium, and illuminates them with a separate, unmingled, and pure form of life. Whence also I think he orders them to be separated from all things, to remain exempt in Olympus <note>Olympus here represents the highest intellectual or spiritual realm, rather than the physical mountain.</note>, and neither convert themselves to Greeks nor Barbarians <note>A traditional way of saying "the whole of humanity"; Proclus uses this to mean the gods transcend all earthly divisions.</note>; which is just the same as to say, that they must transcend the twofold orders of mundane <note>Relating to the physical world or cosmos.</note> natures, and abide immutably in undefiled <term>intellection</term> <note>Pure, intuitive thought or divine understanding.</note>. But at another time he converts them to a providential attention to secondary natures, through **Themis**, and calls upon them to direct the mundane battle, and excites different Gods to different works. These Divinities, therefore, especially require the assistance of **Themis**, who contains in herself the divine laws according to which providence is intimately connected with wholes. **Homer**, therefore, divinely delivers twofold speeches, accompanying the twofold energies of **Jupiter**; but **Plato** through this one speech comprehends those twofold modes of discourse. For the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The divine craftsman or architect of the universe.</note> renders the Gods unmingled with secondary natures, and causes them to provide for, and give existence to, mortals. But he orders them to fabricate in imitation of himself: and in an injunction of this kind both these are comprehended, viz. the unmingled through the imitation of the father, for he is separate, being exempt from mundane wholes; but providential energy, through the command to fabricate, nourish and increase mortal natures. Or rather, we may survey both in each; for in imitating the demiurgus they provide for secondary natures, as he does for the immortals; and in fabricating they are separate from the things fabricated. For every demiurgic cause is exempt from the things generated by it; but that which is mingled with and filled from them is imbecil <note>Weak or lacking in power.</note> and inefficacious, and is unable to adorn and fabricate them. And thus much in common respecting the whole of the speech.

Let us then, in the first place, consider what we are to understand by "**Gods of Gods**," and what power it possesses: for that this invocation is collective and convertive of multitude to its <term>monad</term> <note>The "monad" refers to the primary, singular source from which a group or "multitude" originates.</note>, that it calls upwards the natures which have proceeded to the one fabricator of them, and inserts a boundary and divine measure in them, is clear to those who are not entirely unacquainted with such-like discourses. But how those that are allotted the world by their father are called **Gods of Gods**, and according to what conception, cannot easily be indicated to the many; for there is an unfolding of one divine intelligence in these names. **Proclus** then proceeds to relate the explanations given by others of these words; which having rejected as erroneous, he very properly, in my opinion, adopts the following, which is that of his preceptor, the great **Syrianus**. All the mundane Gods are not simply Gods, but they are wholly Gods which participate: for there is in them that which is separate, unapparent, and supermundane, and also that which is the apparent image of them, and has an orderly establishment in the world. And that, indeed, which is unapparent in them is primarily a God, this being undistributed and one; but this vehicle which is suspended from their unapparent essence is secondarily a God. For if, with respect to us, man is twofold, one inward, according to the soul, the other apparent, which we see, much more must both these be asserted of the Gods; since Divinity also is twofold, one
