gives subsistence to the summit of the irrational life, but does not produce this life; since, giving subsistence to <term>dæmons</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, "daemons" are not evil spirits, but intermediate beings between gods and humans.</note>, he certainly also produces the irrational life which they contain, but not this life which the junior Gods <note>The lesser deities tasked by the Demiurge with creating the mortal parts of the human soul and body.</note> weave together in us; for this is alone adapted to souls falling into generation <note>The process of being born into a physical, material body.</note>. The mundane Gods, therefore, illuminate their depending vehicles with rational lives; for they possess intellectual souls. But those dæmons who are properly defined according to reason use irrational powers, which they keep in subjection; but our souls much more possess a life in the vehicle, which is irrational with relation to them. It superabounds however by receiving another irrational life, which is an apostacy from that life in the vehicle which was woven by the junior Gods. All *that* is immortal, therefore, which souls possess according to an imitation of wholes, but the addition of the secondary life is mortal. If, therefore, in the summit of the irrational life, there is one impassive sense, this in the <term>pneumatic vehicle</term> <note>The "subtle" or "spirit-like" body that was believed to carry the soul between the physical world and the stars.</note> will generate one passive sense; and this latter will produce in the <term>shelly body</term> <note>The physical human body, viewed as a heavy, temporary shell for the soul.</note> many and passive senses. The <term>orectic</term> <note>Relating to desire or the appetite.</note> or appetitive power, also, in this summit, will produce many orectic powers in the spirit, possessing something separate from the shelly body, and capable of being disciplined; and these will produce in the body ultimate and material appetitive powers.

$^1$ Namely the vivific Goddess Juno <note>The commentator identifies the "mixing bowl" of the creator with the Goddess Juno (Hera), seen here as a source of life-giving energy.</note>.

$^2$ It is well observed here by <term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note>, that souls possess essential differences, and not differences according to energies only. For, says he, some souls look to total and others to partial intellects; and some employ undefiled intellections, but others at times depart from the contemplation of true beings. Some perpetually fabricate and adorn wholes, but others only sometimes revolve with the Gods. And some always move and govern fate, but others sometimes subsist under the dominion of fate, and are subject to its laws. Some are the leaders to intelligible essence, and others are sometimes allotted the order of those that follow. Some are divine only, and others are transferred into a different order, dæmoniacal, heroical, human. Some employ horses that are good, but others such as are mingled from good and evil <note>An allusion to Plato's Phaedrus, where the soul is compared to a chariot pulled by two horses.</note>. And some possess that life alone which they received from the one fabrication of things, but others the mortal form of life, which was woven to their nature by the junior Gods. Some energize according to all their powers, but others at different times draw forth different lives. By no means, therefore, do our souls possess the same essence with divinity: for the rational nature is different in the two, being in the Gods intellectual, but in our souls mingled with the irrational; and in the middle genera it is defined according to their middle subsistence. In like manner, with respect to every thing else, such as reasons, the form of life, intelligence and time, these subsist divinely in divine souls, but in a human manner in ours.

Proclus also further observes, that the common definition of all souls is as follows: Soul is an essence subsisting between true essence and generation, being mingled from middle genera, divided

...same manner$^1$, yet not similarly incorruptible in the same way, but diminished from the first level of purity to a second and third degree. And having thus composed the whole into an essential number, bound together with all the mathematical means, diatonically harmonized <note>Harmonized according to the intervals of a musical scale, representing the mathematical order of the soul.</note>, living both a single and a twofold life, and possessing the power of knowledge in both a single and a twofold manner.

---

$^1$ <margin>Commentary by Proclus</margin> Timæus, says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato's works.</note>, indicates by these words the similarity, the lower status, and the different stages of progression of individual souls compared to the total World Soul. For he does not only describe their differences alongside their connection based on the primary and secondary creative energies of the <term>demiurge</term> <note>The divine craftsman or creator.</note>, nor only by their union with and separation from the "crater of life" <note>The metaphorical vessel where the substance of souls is mixed.</note>, nor even just by the surplus or lack of essential qualities. He also describes them by the method of their mixture, which is the same and yet not the same. 

For the temperament of these soul-qualities is not similar, nor is the "unmingling of difference" <note>The principle of "Difference" was one of the ingredients used by the Demiurge; in individual souls, this "Difference" is more pronounced, leading to more varied and potentially conflicting natures.</note> the same; for difference is much more abundant in individual souls. Hence, of the "horses" within these souls, one is good but the other is the opposite, being composed of contrary qualities—as is described in the *Phædrus* <note>A reference to Plato’s dialogue, the *Phaedrus*, which uses the allegory of a chariot pulled by two winged horses to describe the human soul: one horse represents noble impulse, the other represents base desire.</note>—as a result of "Difference" having control. For the entire mixture is no longer indestructible in the same way or after the same manner, but only to a second and third degree, since these souls exist in a state of lower ranking and order. 

By the word **incorruptible**, we must understand that which is immutable, undeviating, inflexible, and the spotless form of essence—that which does not turn toward secondary, lesser natures, and does not undergo change or a lower quality of life. It refers to that which is established far beyond the reach of mortality and is exempt from the laws of fate. These qualities are common to every type of soul that perpetually remains above the world of change and "generation" <note>The cycle of birth, death, and material existence.</note>. 

However, the opposites of these qualities are found in those powers that descend into the world of birth: namely, a change of life from pure thought to physical action, sometimes becoming subject to fate, and being mixed with mortal affairs. In these souls, the "immovable" quality is not present in the same way, since they sometimes enter the cycle of birth. Even when it is present, it is not there in the same manner; for a soul that is always engaged in pure understanding is better than one that sometimes wanders away from its own proper <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of pure, intellectual thought or spiritual intuition.</note>. 

Since there is an order even among these souls, some remain undefiled, rarely connecting with the world of birth and never abandoning their own high status. Others, however, are tossed about among all kinds of earthly distractions and wander for thousands of cycles. Timæus indicates the difference between these when he says "in a second and third degree." For souls that descend and become stained with evil are very far removed from those that stay forever on high, free from evil. Souls of a middle rank are those that do descend, but are not defiled. Conversely, it is impossible to be defiled and yet remain in the high heavens, since evil does not exist among the Gods, but only in the mortal realm and in material things.

Again, therefore, it appears from these points that the first class of souls is divine. Everywhere, that which receives divinity holds the leading rank—whether in essences, in intellects, in souls, or in bodies. The second class consists of those souls perpetually joined with the Gods, so that through them, souls that sometimes wander away may be called back to the Gods. The third class is that which falls into the world of birth but descends with purity; it trades a higher life for a lower one but remains free from vice and passions. This class is continuous with the souls that stay forever on high and are always undefiled. 

But the fourth and last class is that which wanders extensively, descending as far as <term>Tartarus</term> <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment and suffering.</note>. These souls are eventually stirred up from those dark depths, developing all kinds of lives, adopting various behaviors, and experiencing different passions at different times. Such a soul also takes on various forms of animals—whether <term>dæmoniacal</term> <note>Intermediate spirits, neither fully god nor fully human.</note>, human, or irrational...

[Having com]posed the universe, he distributed souls equal in number to the stars, inserting each in each: and causing them to ascend as into a **vehicle**¹ <note>The "vehicle" (Greek: *ochēma*) refers to the subtle, celestial body that carries the soul down from the heavens into the physical body.</note>, he pointed out [to them the nature of the universe].

<margin>Commentary by Proclus</margin>
...but is at the same time corrected by **Justice**, returns from earth to heaven, and is circularly led from matter to **intellect** <note>In Neoplatonism, "Intellect" or *Nous* represents the highest level of reality the soul can reach, above mere rational thought.</note>, according to certain orderly periods of wholes. By the words, therefore, "in a certain respect indeed after the same manner, yet not similarly incorruptible according to the same," he signifies that partial <note>Individual or human souls.</note> souls are in a certain respect incorruptible—as for instance, according to their **essence** alone—but that in a certain respect they are not incorruptible, namely, being mingled in their energies with all-various destinies, and conversant with mortal things, and not possessing these energies with invariable sameness and entirety, but sometimes more, and at others less; an all-various inequality subsisting in souls, according to their relationship to mortal natures, from which they derive the privation of incorruptibility according to life.

---

¹ **Vulcan** <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the divine blacksmith. In this philosophical context, he represents the power that crafts the physical form.</note>, who is the artificer of the whole of a corporeal essence, gives subsistence to the **vehicles** of the soul; for he receives souls sent into the world from the **intelligible region** <note>The realm of pure ideas and divine truth.</note>, and gives different habitations to different souls. The **demiurge** <note>The divine craftsman or creator of the world.</note> of all things also gives subsistence to these vehicles; for he is the fabricator of animals, and the completions of the universe, so that he not only produces souls, but also produces them with their proper vehicles. As **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major philosopher whose commentaries on Plato are a primary source for this text.</note> likewise well observes, the conception of **Plato** here is truly wonderful: for he does not represent the demiurge as fashioning these vehicles from the *wholenesses* which are now produced, but he says that he makes these, the **junior Gods** <note>The lesser deities tasked by the Demiurge with creating the mortal parts of living beings.</note> lending parts, and from them composing bodies. But this is an evident argument, that each of these vehicles is in a certain respect self-composed, and not fabricated by an ablation <note>A taking away or cutting off.</note> from other things, lest it should require to be again poured back into something else. For every thing which subsists by being cut off from other things, being cut off with a diminution of the whole to which it belonged, must necessarily be returned to the whole from which it was cut off. For it is necessary that every whole in the universe should perpetually remain a whole: and hence every such vehicle is perpetual, and the same vehicle is always suspended from the soul. 

Besides, how can the soul be any longer said to be mundane <note>Belonging to the world.</note>, if its vehicle is corrupted? For that of which there is nothing in the universe cannot be mundane. For, if partial souls are superior to a life in conjunction with vehicles, they will also be superior to divine souls: but if they are inferior to such a life, how does the demiurge immediately after their generation introduce them into these vehicles? And how can they use them in **Hades** <note>The invisible realm of the dead; the afterlife.</note>, and in the Heavens, unless they had them perpetually suspended from their essence? For, that they use them in Hades, is evident from what **Socrates** says in the *Phædo*, namely, that souls ascending into their vehicles proceed to **Acheron** <note>A river or region in the underworld.</note>: and that they also use them in the Heavens, is evident from the *Phædrus*, in which Socrates says that the vehicles of the Gods proceed equally balanced, but those of the attendants of the Gods, with great difficulty.

From this, also, we may perceive the difference between partial and divine souls: for with respect to the latter, the demiurge is said to place their bodies in their souls, as being every way comprehended by them, these souls not being converted to the objects of their government, but employing one immutable **intellection** <note>The act of pure intellectual understanding.</note>: but, with respect to partial souls, he is said to cause these to ascend into their vehicles; for these are naturally adapted to be frequently in subjection to bodies, and to convert themselves to the subjects of their government; when they also become...

But when he had disseminated them through the several instruments of time <note>The "instruments of time" refer to the planets and heavenly bodies which measure time through their cycles.</note> adapted to each, he declared to them it was necessary that an animal the most religious of all others should make its appearance. parts of the universe as well as their vehicles, act in subserviency to the laws of fate, and no longer live with purity under the divine light of Providence. It must likewise be observed, that the demiurgus <note>The Demiurge is the creator-god in Plato’s philosophy who fashions the material world after the model of the eternal Forms.</note> among other causes contains that of Nature in himself, to which also he converts souls. For, by showing Nature to souls, he also beholds it himself. But he alone beholds things prior to and in himself. Now, therefore, he beholds Nature in himself, which he comprehends supernaturally, or according to cause.

---

<gloss>1</gloss> The demiurgus, says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonic philosopher whose commentaries on Plato are essential for understanding how these texts were interpreted in late antiquity.</note>, comprehends the whole of a material and mortal life in three boundaries, and establishes the causes of it in souls, that they may obtain dominion over it: for dominion is not derived from any thing else than essential precedency. The irrational life, therefore, subsists *intellectually* in the demiurgus, but *rationally* in souls. Nor is this wonderful, since body also subsists incorporeally in the intelligible causes of all things. But this connate sense produced by violent passions, of which Plato now speaks, is that corporeal life which is gnostic <note>From the Greek *gnostikos*, meaning "capable of knowing" or "discerning."</note> of things falling upon it externally, which produces this knowledge through instruments, does not subsist from itself, but from the natures by which it is used, is mingled with material masses, and knows what it knows with passion. For it is necessary to sensation, that a certain agitation should be produced about the instruments of sense; since neither do the motions in the soul pervade every where, and as far as to the body, but there is a motion of the soul belonging to itself by itself, such as is that which is intellectual; nor does every thing about the body extend as far as to the soul, but there is also a certain corporeal passion, which through its obscurity is not able to move the soul. Sense, therefore, is produced not from all passions, but from such as are violent, and which are attended with much agitation. And this is corporeal sense, which is divisible and material, and forms its judgment mingled with passions. But there is another sense prior to this, in the vehicle <note>In Neoplatonism, the "vehicle" (*ochema*) is the subtle, luminous body that carries the soul between the celestial and material realms.</note> of the soul, which with respect to this is immaterial, and is a pure impassive knowledge, itself subsisting by itself, but which is not liberated from form, because it also is corporeal, as being allotted its subsistence in body. And this sense, indeed, has the same nature with the phantasy <note>The "phantasy" or imagination acts as the bridge between raw sensory data and the higher rational mind.</note>; for the being of both is common; but externally proceeding it is called sense, and abiding internally, and surveying **in the spirit** (<term>in the spirit</term>) <note>original: εν τω πνευματι (en tō pneumati). Here "spirit" refers to the subtle breath or "pneuma" that animates the soul's celestial vehicle.</note> forms and figures, it is called phantasy. So far also as it is divided about the spirit, it is sense. For, again, the basis of the rational life is opinion; but the phantasy is the summit of the second, or the irrational life.

violent passions was necessary to all; and, in the second place, love mingled with pleasure and grief. That after these, fear and anger were necessary, with whatever else is either consequent to these, or naturally discordant from a contrary nature. That such souls as subdue these would live <note>The text describes the "Passions of the Soul" which arise immediately upon incarnation, as the pure soul is suddenly impacted by the physical world.</note>

Opinion also and <term>phantasy</term> <note>original: "phantasia." In Platonic thought, this is the faculty of imagination that bridges the gap between raw sensory input and rational thought.</note> are conjoined with each other, and the second is filled from the more excellent with powers. But the middle of the **irrational life** does not receive the impression of the natures superior to it, but is alone the recipient of things external. It is common, however, to this also to know that which is sensible with passivity: but external sense alone pertains to things externally falling upon and moving it, not being able to possess spectacles in itself, since it is <term>partible</term> <note>Meaning it is divisible or spread out across the physical organs, unlike the mind which is "one."</note> and not one; for it is distributed about the organs of sense. There is one sense, therefore, which is impassive and common, another which is common and passive, and a third which is distributed and passive. The first of these belongs to the first **vehicle of the soul**, <note>The "vehicle" (ochēma) is a subtle, quasi-material body that carries the soul between its divine home and the physical world.</note> the second, to the irrational life, and the third, to the animated body.

After sense, Plato arranges **desire**. And this indeed is life, and is also corporeal; but it is a life which perpetually *unweaves the body*, <note>A poetic way of saying that the biological process of life involves the constant breaking down and rebuilding of physical matter.</note> and affords a solace to its wants, and about which pleasure and pain are beheld. For these passions are also present to other parts of the soul; since you may perceive pleasures and pains, both in reason and anger. But corporeal pleasure and pain are produced according to desire. For, with respect to the body, a way contrary to nature, and a privation of life, produce pain in it; but a regression according to nature, and an adaptation to life, are the sources of its pleasure. And that which is afflicted or delighted in these is the desiderative part of the soul. But since these two passions are primary, and the fountains of the other passions, as Plato says in the <term>Philebus</term> and the <term>Laws</term>, <note>Two of Plato's later dialogues; the Philebus focuses on the nature of pleasure, and the Laws on the practical application of ethics in a state.</note> through the mixture of these giving a generation to the other passions, he also denominates love a mixture of pleasure and pain. For, so far as it is conversant with the lovely, it is present with pleasure, but, so far as it is not yet present with it in energy, it is mingled with pain. But he characterizes all the life of desire through love, because this passion is most vehement about it.

In the third place, therefore, he enumerates **anger**. Anger then is also life, but a life which removes every thing painful, and which disturbs the body. Excess and defect also are surveyed about it, such as rashness and timidity, and the things consequent to these, ambition and contention, and all such particulars as take place about mortal concerns. And such is the order of these three generated powers. For as soon as the body is formed it participates of sense: since it would not be an animal, nor would possess appetite, if it were not sensitive. For appetites subsist in conjunction with sense, but the senses are not entirely in conjunction with appetites; and hence the animal is more characterized by the sensitive than by the appetitive nature. But after the possession of sense the animal appears to be pleased and pained, afflicted by the cold, but cherished by the bandages, and led to a condition according to nature. After desire, as age advances, the animal is angered: for anger is the power of a more robust nature. Hence also, among irrational animals, such as are more material alone live according to desire, and partake of pleasure and pain; but such as are more perfect are allotted a more <term>irascible</term> <note>Related to the "spirited" part of the soul, which involves drive, anger, and the defense of one's dignity.</note> life. But prior to these appetites, as we also said of sense, there is a certain summit of them in the spirit of the soul, which summit is a power impulsive and motive of the spirit, guarding and connecting its essence, at one time extending and distributing itself, and at another being led to bound and order, and measured by reason.

And of her horses, one is good, and the other the contrary <note>A reference to Plato's famous chariot allegory in the *Phaedrus*, where the soul is a charioteer driving two winged horses—one noble and one unruly.</note>: and one of these leads her to generation <note>The process of being born into the physical world.</note>, but the other from generation to true being; the one also leads her round the circle of sense, but the other round an *intellectual* essence. Dismissing, therefore, her first habit, which subsists according to an alliance to the whole of generation, and laying aside the irrational nature which connects her with generation, likewise governing her irrational part by *reason*, and extending *intellect* to *opinion*, she will be circularly led to a happy life, from the wandering about the regions of *sense*; which life those that are initiated by Orpheus in the mysteries of Bacchus and Proserpine <note>Orphic and Dionysian mystery religions, which promised their initiates a way to escape the cycle of rebirth and return to a divine state.</note> pray that they may obtain, together with the allotments of the sphere, and a cessation of evil. It is, however, possible for our soul to live according to the circle of sameness, when purified, as Plato says. Cathartic virtue <note>The "purifying" virtues that help the soul detach from physical desires and return to its rational, divine nature.</note>, therefore, alone must be called the salvation of souls; since this cuts off and vehemently obliterates material natures, and the passions which adhere to us from generation, separates the soul, and leads it to *intellect*, and causes it to leave on earth the vehicles with which it is invested. For souls descending receive from the elements different vehicles, aërial, aquatic, and terrestrial; and thus at last enter into this gross bulk. For how, without a medium, could they proceed into this body from immaterial spirits? Hence, before they come into this body, they possess the irrational life, and its vehicle, which is prepared from the simple elements, and from these they enter into the tumultuous, which is so called as being foreign to the connate vehicle of souls, composed from all-various vestments, and causing souls to become heavy. In short, the connate vehicle makes the soul mundane, the second vehicle, a citizen of generation, and the **shelly body**, <note>original: "το οστρεωδες"</note> terrestrial.

But in consequence of his abiding, as soon as his children understood the order of their father, they immediately became obedient to this order; and receiving the immortal principle of mortal animal, in imitation of their artificer, they borrowed from the world the parts of fire and earth, water and air, as things which they should restore back again; and conglutinated the received parts together, not with the same indissoluble bonds which they themselves participated, but gave them a tenacious adherence from thick set nails, invisible through their smallness <note>The "nails" represent the infinitesimal or atomic forces that hold the four elements together to form solid matter.</note>; fabricating the body of each, one from the composition of all; and binding the circulations of the immortal soul in the influxive and effluxive nature of body.

But these circulations ¹, being merged in a profound river <note>The "profound river" is a metaphor for the "stream" of sensory perceptions and the constant physical changes (growth, decay, nutrition) that flood the soul when it enters a body.</note>, neither govern nor are governed, but hurry and are hurried along with violence : in consequence

It is requisite, however, to inquire why souls fall into bodies. Should it be again asked, Why, therefore, are partial souls descending into **generation** <note>The "realm of generation" refers to the physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note> filled with such material perturbation, and such numerous evils? we reply, that this takes place through the inclination arising from their free will; through their vehement familiarity with body; through their sympathy with the image of soul, or that divisible life which is distributed about body; through their abundant mutation from an **intelligible** <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal truths.</note> to a **sensible** <note>The realm of the five senses and physical matter.</note> nature, and from a quiet energy to one entirely conversant with motion; and through a disordered condition of being, naturally arising from the composition of dissimilar natures, viz. of the immortal and mortal, of the intellectual and that which is deprived of intellect, of the indivisible and that which is endued with interval. For all these become the cause to the soul of this mighty tumult and labour in the realms of generation; since we pursue a flying mockery which is ever in motion. And the soul, indeed, by verging to a material life, kindles a light in her dark tenement the body, but she herself becomes situated in obscurity; and by giving life to the body, she destroys herself and her own intellect, in as great a degree as these are capable of receiving destruction. For thus the mortal nature participates of intellect, but the intellectual part of death, and the whole becomes a prodigy, as Plato beautifully observes in his *Laws*, composed of the mortal and immortal, of the intellectual, and that which is deprived of intellect. For this physical law, which binds the soul to the body, is the death of the immortal life, but is the cause of vivification to the mortal body.

For from all these, through the medium of the body, various motions are hurried along, and fall with molestation on the soul. But on this account all these were afterwards, and are even now, denominated **senses**. And these, indeed, both at first and at present¹, are the sources of an abundant and mighty motion, in conjunction through their being unusual, become the causes of astonishment. For, what a great fire is to the former, that the flame of a lamp is to the latter; and what the magnitude of the highest mountains is to men, that the smallest stone in the fields is to infants. And what whirlwinds and cataracts of rain are to others, that a weak motion of the air, or the falling of a little moisture, is to those that are recently born. For sense, being agitated by all these particulars, astonishes the soul of infants, and leads them to desperation and tumult.

These, then, in short, are the causes of the disturbance of souls, viz. the motions of the nutritive part, and the impulses of sense. We must not, however, suppose that the soul suffers any thing through these particulars. For, as if some one standing on the margin of a river should behold the image and form of himself in the floating stream, he indeed will preserve his face unchanged, but the stream being all-variously moved will change the image, so that at different times it will appear to him different, oblique and upright, and perhaps divulced and continuous. Let us suppose, too, that such a one, through being unaccustomed to the spectacle, should think that it was himself that suffered this distortion, in consequence of surveying his shadow in the water, and, thus thinking, should be afflicted and disturbed, astonished and impeded. After the same manner the soul, beholding the image of herself in body, borne along in the **river of generation** <note>The "river of generation" is a Platonic metaphor for the physical world, which is in a constant state of flux, always "becoming" but never truly "being."</note>, and variously disposed at different times, through inward passions and external impulses, is indeed herself **impassive** <note>Meaning "not subject to suffering" or "unchangeable." The soul's true nature remains perfect even if the body is in chaos.</note>, but thinks that she suffers, and, being ignorant of, and mistaking her image for, herself, is disturbed, astonished, and perplexed. 

This passion particularly takes place in infants: but it is also seen in the dreams of those that have arrived at maturity; as when some one, in consequence of nature being wearied in the concoction of food, thinks in a dream that he is wearied through long journeys, or carrying heavy burdens, or suffers something else of this kind. But to return to the words of Plato, the *waves* do not signify, says Proclus, the externally blowing wind, as some say, but the collected agitation, and abundant influx and efflux which take place in youth. But the *inundation* first strikes upon and makes the **pneumatic vehicle** <term>pneumatic vehicle</term> <note>The *pneuma* or "spirit-body" that acts as a middle ground between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note> heavier, for it is this which expresses stains and vapours; and in the second place it strikes upon the soul, for she also is disturbed by the collected and the sudden.

If it should be said that the dianoëtic part may be ignorant in a twofold respect, and that a thing which suffers this is distorted; we reply, that twofold ignorance does not simply belong to the dianoëtic part, but, originating indeed from thence, is implanted in the doxastic part. For, so far as it is ignorance, and a privation of science, so far, being an immobility of the scientific power, it originates from the dianoëtic part. For science and ignorance subsist about the same thing. But, so far as it also adds a false opinion of knowledge, it subsists in the doxastic part. And ignorance is the insanity of the dianoëtic part, possessing, indeed, but concealing, the productive principles of knowledge; but false conception is the insanity of opinion, of which it is also the distortion. For, being false, it also depraves its possessor; since what vice is in action, that falsehood is in knowledge. The period of sameness, therefore, is alone fettered, and is similar to those that are bound, and on this account are impeded in their energies; but the period of difference is agitated, being filled with false opinions. For its proximity to the irrational nature causes it to receive a certain passion from externals.

This page begins mid-sentence, describing why the body was given limbs to navigate the uneven terrain of the physical world.</note> be unable to pass over its inequalities and rough places, the Gods subjected this upright figure of the body to the head, treating the body as a pliable vehicle. Plato believed vision was a physical interaction between light inside the eye and light in the atmosphere.</note>. They condensed this fire throughout the eye, but especially in the middle of those lucid orbs, so that the more dense fire might remain hidden within the recesses of the eyes, while the pure fire could find a passage and fly outward.

Therefore, when the light of day stays near this outward-flowing "river of sight," then "like" meets "like" and they mingle together. A single, unified <term>domestic body</term> <note>A term for the bridge of light created when the eye's internal fire meets external light.</note> is formed along the direct path of the eyes, specifically in the place where the light emitted from within meets the light coming from the outside. Because the whole stream of light now shares the same properties, whenever it touches an object (or is touched by one), the motion produced by that contact spreads through the entire body of the eye until it reaches the soul. This causes the sensation we call **sight**.

But when this related fire <note>The daylight.</note> departs into night, the connection is broken and sight loses its power. For in the dark, the fire from the eye enters an environment that is not like itself; it is changed and becomes extinguished, because it is no longer related to the surrounding air, which is naturally <note>The page ends here, following the catchword "destitute" from the original manuscript.</note> destitute...

But when much rest takes place, sleep attended with few dreams is produced. But with respect to the images produced in mirrors, and all such things as are visible in that which is apparent and smooth, there is nothing in these difficult of solution. For, from the communication of the external and internal fire with each other, and from that fire which subsists about the smooth body, and becomes abundantly multiplied, all such appearances are necessarily produced as take place when the fire of the eyes mingles itself with the fire diffused about the smooth and splendid object of vision. When the smoothness of the mirrors receives this here and there in an elevated manner, it repels the right hand part of the sight to the left of the mirror, and the left to the right. But if the mirror is turned according to the length of the countenance, it causes the whole face to appear resupine <note>Meaning flipped upside down or appearing to lie on its back.</note>, by repelling the downward part of the splendour towards the upward part, and again the upper towards the downward part. But fire and water, air and earth, are all of them visible bodies. *It is, however, necessary that the lover of intellect and science should explore the first causes of prudent nature; and that he should consider such things as are moved by others, and at the same time necessarily give motion to other things, as nothing more than secondary causes.* <note>Plato distinguishes between "primary causes" (the intentions of a divine mind) and "secondary causes" (the physical laws of matter and motion).</note> Hence it is proper that we should speak concerning both kinds of causes; separately of such as fabricate things beautiful and good in conjunction with intellect, and of such as, being left destitute of wisdom, produce each particular in a casual and disorderly manner. Concerning the second causes of the eyes, therefore, which contribute to the possession of the power they are now allotted, what has been already said is sufficient.

But the greatest employment of the eyes, with respect to the use for which they were bestowed on us by the Divinity, we shall now endeavour to explain. For, in my opinion, the sight is the cause of the greatest emolument <note>meaning benefit or advantage</note> to us on the present occasion; since what we are now discoursing concerning the universe could never have been discovered without surveying the stars, the sun, and the heavens. But now, from beholding day and night, we are able to determine by arithmetical calculation the periods of months and years; to acquire a conception of time, and to scrutinize the nature of the universe. But from all this we obtain the possession of philosophy; a greater good than which never was nor ever will be bestowed by the Gods on the mortal race. And this is what I call the greatest benefit of the eyes. But why should I celebrate other particulars of less consequence, which he who is not a philosopher, since destitute of sight, may attempt to explore, but will explore in vain? By us, indeed, it is asserted that Divinity bestowed sight on us for this purpose, that on surveying the circulations of intellect in the heavens we may properly employ the revolutions of our <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>original: "dianoētikos"; referring to the soul's capacity for discursive reasoning or logical thought</note> part, which are allied to their circulations; and may recall the tumultuous motions of our <term>discursive energies</term> <note>the way our minds jump from one thought to another in a disorganized way</note> to the orderly processions of their intellectual periods. That besides this, by learning these and participating right reason according to nature, and imitating the revolutions of Divinity which are entirely <term>inerratic</term> <note>fixed or not wandering, unlike the "wandering" thoughts of humans</note>, we may give stability to the wanderings of our <term>dianoëtic</term> energy.

But concerning voice and hearing, we again assert that they were bestowed on us by the Gods on the same account. For the acquisition of speech pertains to these, and is of the greatest advantage to their possession.

But since these never appear to be the same, who without being covered with confusion can confidently assert that any one of these is *this* rather than *that*? Certainly, no one. Hence it will be far the most safe method of proceeding to speak about them as follows: That the nature which we always perceive becoming something different at different times, such, for instance, as fire, is not fire absolutely, but something *fiery*. And again, that the nature which we denominate water is not absolutely so, but such-like, or *watery*; and that it is not at any time any thing else, as if it possessed any <term>stability of essence</term> <note>A permanent, unchanging reality</note>. And lastly, that they cannot be distinguished by any word, such as we are accustomed to employ when endeavouring to show that any particular is either *this* thing or *that*. For they fly away, incapable of sustaining the affirmation which asserts them to be ***this thing***, of ***such a nature***, belonging to ***this***; and all such appellations as would evince them to be something permanent and real. 

Hence, we ought not to denominate any one of these either this, or that; but something such-like, and a perpetually-revolving similitude. Thus, we should assert that fire is every where ***such-like***, and should speak in the same manner of every thing endued with <term>generation</term> <note>The process of coming into being and passing away</note>. But we should alone distinguish by the appellations of *this*, or *that*, the subject in which each of these appears to be generated, and again to suffer a <term>dissolution</term> <note>Decay or breaking apart</note>. But this subject is by no means to be denominated ***such-like***, as for instance hot or white, or any quality belonging to contraries, or any thing which contraries compose. 

However, let us endeavour to explain more clearly what we mean to express. For if any one, fashioning all possible figures from gold, should without ceasing transform each figure into all; and if, during this operation, some one who is present should, pointing to one of these figures, inquire what it is; it might most safely, with respect to truth, be replied, that it was **gold**: but he who should assert that it is a **triangle**, or any other of the figures which are continually generated, and which ought by no means to be denominated beings, would fall from the truth in the midst of his assertion. But we ought to be content with that answer as most safe, which denominates it ***such-like***, or of such a determinate nature.

It is likewise necessary to understand that the figured nature can never become distinguished with an all-possible variety of forms, unless its receptacle is well prepared for the purpose, and is destitute of all those forms which it is about to receive. For, if it were similar to any one of the supernally intromitted forms, when it received a nature contrary to that to which it is similar, or any form whatever, it would very imperfectly express its similitude, while at the same time it exhibited the very same appearance with the supernally acceding form. And hence it is necessary, that the receptacle which is destined to receive all possible forms should itself be destitute of every form. 

Just as those who are about to prepare sweet-smelling <term>unguents</term> <note>Perfumes or scented ointments</note>, so dispose a certain humid matter as the subject of the ensuing odour, that it may possess no peculiar smell of its own; and as those who wish to impress certain figures in a soft and yielding matter, are careful that it may not appear impressed with any previous figure, but render it as much as possible exquisitely smooth. In the same manner, it is necessary that the subject which is so often destined to receive in a beautiful manner, through the whole of itself, resemblances of eternal beings, should be naturally destitute of all that it receives. 

Hence, we should not denominate this mother and receptacle of that which is generated, visible and every way sensible, either earth, or air, or fire, or water; nor, again, any one of the composites from these, or any thing from which these are generated: but we should call it a certain <term>invisible species</term> <note>A type of existence that cannot be seen with the eyes</note>, and a formless universal recipient, which in the most dubious and scarcely explicable manner participates <note>original: *metechei*; refers to the mysterious way physical matter shares in the reality of the eternal Forms</note>

But when the **artificer** <note>The Demiurge, or Divine Craftsman, who shapes the physical world according to an eternal model.</note> began to adorn the universe, he first of all figured with forms and numbers fire and earth, water and air, which possessed indeed certain traces of the true elements, but were in every respect so constituted, as it becomes any thing to be from which Deity is absent. But every species of body possesses **profundity** <note>Depth; three-dimensionality.</note>; and it is necessary that every depth should comprehend the nature of a plane. Again, the rectitude of the base of a plane is composed from **triangles**. But all triangles originate from two species; one of which possesses one right angle, and the other two acute angles. For, if we are able to accomplish this, we shall obtain the truth concerning the generation of earth and fire, and of those elements which are situated according to **analogy** <note>Meaning a mathematical proportion or relationship.</note> between these. And then we shall not assent to any one who should assert that there are visible bodies more beautiful than these, each of which **subsists** <note>Exists or has its being.</note> according to one kind. We must endeavor, therefore, to harmonize the four sorts of bodies excelling in beauty; and to **evince** <note>To prove or demonstrate clearly.</note> by this means that we sufficiently comprehend the nature of these. 

Of the two triangles indeed the **isosceles** <note>A triangle with two equal sides.</note> is allotted one nature, but the **oblong or scalene** <note>A triangle where all three sides are of different lengths.</note> is characterized by infinity. We ought therefore to choose the most beautiful among infinites, if we wish to commence our investigation in a becoming manner. And if any one shall assert that he has chosen something more beautiful for the composition of these, we shall suffer his opinion to prevail; considering him not as an enemy, but as a friend. Of many triangles, therefore, we shall establish one as most beautiful (neglecting the rest); I mean the **equilateral** <note>A triangle with three equal sides.</note>, which is composed from three parts of a scalene triangle. To assign the reason of this would indeed require a **prolix dissertation** <note>A very long and wordy explanation.</note>; but a pleasant reward will remain for him who by a diligent investigation finds this to be the case. We have, therefore, selected two triangles out of many, from which the body of fire and of the other elements is fabricated; one of which is isosceles, but the other is that which always has its longer side <term>triply greater in power</term> <note>In ancient Greek mathematics, "power" refers to the area of a square formed by a side. This describes a specific right-angled triangle (the 30-60-90 triangle) where the square of the longer leg is three times the square of the shorter leg.</note> than the shorter.

But that which we formerly asserted without sufficient security, it is now necessary more accurately to define. For it appeared to us, though improperly, that all these four natures were mutually generated from each other: but they are in reality generated from the triangles which we have just described:—three of them, indeed, from one triangle containing unequal sides; but the fourth alone is aptly composed from the isosceles triangle. All of them, therefore, are not able, by a **dissolution** <note>The process of breaking down a complex form back into its basic geometric components.</note> into each other, to produce from many small things a mighty few, or the contrary. This indeed can be effected by three of them. For, as all the three are naturally generated from one triangle, when the greater parts are dissolved, many small parts are composed from them, receiving figures accommodated to their natures. And again, when the many small parts being scattered according to triangles produce a number of one bulk, they complete one mighty **species** <note>In this context, a specific "kind" or type of elemental body, such as a particle of air or fire.</note>.

<summary>Timaeus explains that the four elements are constructed from two basic types of triangles: the isosceles and a specific scalene triangle. He clarifies that while three of the elements can transform into one another because they share the same triangular base, the fourth (earth) is unique because it is built from a different triangle.</summary>

of a different kind. And thus much may suffice concerning their mutual generation.

It now remains that we should speak concerning the quality of each of their kinds, and relate from what concurring numbers they were collected together. The **first species** <note>The tetrahedron, which Plato associates with fire.</note> indeed is that which was composed from the fewest triangles. Its basic unit is the triangle whose longer side is twice the length of the shorter side <note>A 30-60-90 degree right triangle.</note>. When two of these are placed together with their diagonals touching, and this is repeated three times so that the diagonals and the shorter sides meet at a single center, one **equilateral triangle** <note>A triangle with three equal sides.</note> is produced from six of these smaller triangles. When four equilateral triangles are joined together, three of their plane angles meet to form one **solid angle** <note>The point or vertex of a 3-dimensional shape.</note>; this is the most obtuse of the plane angles from which it is composed. Thus, from four such triangles, the first solid species was formed, which divides the entire sphere into equal and similar parts.

The **second species** <note>The octahedron, representing air.</note> was formed from the same type of triangles, but it is composed of eight equilateral triangles. These produce a single solid angle from four planes; thus, the second body was completed by the assembly of six such triangles <note>This likely refers to the arrangement of the angles or a specific grouping in the construction.</note>. 

The **third species** <note>The icosahedron, representing water.</note> arose from the joining of **twice sixty elements** <note>120 of the basic scalene triangles.</note> and twelve solid angles. Each of these angles is formed by five equilateral triangles, meaning the shape has twenty equilateral bases in total. In this manner, these elements were generated. 

However, the **isosceles triangle** <note>A triangle with two equal sides, used here to build the fourth element, earth.</note>, when arranged in groups of four with their right angles meeting at the center, forms a single equilateral quadrangle <note>A square.</note>. This generated the nature of the **fourth element** <note>The cube, representing earth.</note>. Six of these squares joined together produced eight solid angles, each made of three plane right angles. Consequently, the figure of the resulting body is **cubical**, having six quadrangular equilateral bases. 

There is also a certain **fifth composition** <note>The dodecahedron, a twelve-sided shape made of pentagons, representing the shape of the entire universe.</note>, which **Divinity** <note>The "Artificer" or Creator of the world.</note> employed in the fabrication of the universe. When he sketched out those forms, the study of them might lead someone to wonder whether it is right to say the number of worlds is infinite or finite. To claim that there are infinite worlds is the **dogma** <note>A fixed belief or principle.</note> of someone who is ignorant about things that one really ought to understand. Let us now, therefore, distribute the four sorts of things which we have generated, into fire, earth, water, and air. And to earth indeed let us assign a **cubical form**: for earth is the most immovable of all these four kinds, and the most plastic, or adapted to formation, of all corporeal natures. But it is in the most eminent degree necessary that this should be the case with that which possesses the most secure and stable bases. Among the triangles, indeed, established at the beginning, such as are equilateral possess firmer bases than such as contain unequal sides. And hence, among the plane figures composed from each, it will be found that the isosceles is necessarily more stable than the equilateral, and the square than the triangle, both when considered according to parts and to the whole. On this account, by distributing this figure to the earth, we shall preserve an assimilative reason. This will be the case too by assigning to water that figure which is more difficultly movable than the other three; to fire, the most easily movable form; and to air, that figure which possesses a middle nature. 

Besides this, we should assign the smallest body to fire, the greatest to water, and one of a middle kind to air. And again, the most acute body to fire, the second from this to air, and the third to water. But, among all these, it is necessary that the body which possesses the fewest bases, should be the most easily movable: for, being every way the most acute, it becomes the most penetrating and incisive of all. It is likewise the most light, because composed from the fewest parts. But that which is second to this, possesses these properties in a secondary respect; and that which ranks as the third, in a third gradation. 

Hence, according to right and assimilative reason, the solid form of the **pyramid** <note>The tetrahedron, which has four triangular faces and is the simplest of the regular solids.</note> is the element and seed of fire. And first with respect to earth: when it meets with fire, becoming dissolved by its acuteness <note>The "sharpness" or narrow angles of the fire-pyramids.</note>, it is borne along; and remains in this dissolved state either in fire, or in the bulk of air, or in that of water—till its parts, associating themselves together, and again becoming mutually harmonized, produce again a body of earth; for it can never pass into another form. And, in the first place, motion is by no means willing to reside in smoothness: for it is difficult, or rather impossible, that a thing in motion should subsist without a mover, or a mover without that which is in motion. But the grouping together caused by compression forces the smaller particles into the empty spaces between the larger ones; for this reason, when the small parts are placed alongside the large, and the former separate the latter while the larger are mixed with the smaller, all of them are carried upward and downward toward their own natural regions. For as each particle changes its size, it also changes its location. Consequently, because these causes ensure that a state of <term>irregularity<note>original: "nature contrary to smoothness." Plato uses "smoothness" to represent uniformity/rest and "irregularity" or "roughness" to represent the inequality required for motion.</note></term> is always preserved, it provides a perpetual motion for these elements, both in the present and for all time to come.

Next, it is necessary to understand that there are many different kinds of fire. For example, there is flame; there is that which emanates from flame, which burns but provides no light to the eyes; and there is that which remains in a burning substance after the flame has been extinguished. In the same way, regarding air, one kind is the most pure, which is called <term>ether</term>; another is the most turbulent, being both murky and dark; and then there is another nameless kind produced by the inequality of the <term>triangles<note>Plato’s physics posits that all matter is composed of two types of basic right-angled triangles which combine to form the geometric solids of the elements.</note></term>.

Regarding water, it is divided into two primary types: the first is <term>liquid<note>original: "humid."</note></term>, and the second is <term>fusible<note>original: "fusile." In Platonic physics, "fusible water" refers to substances like metals (gold, copper) which are solid but can be melted into a liquid state.</note></term>. The liquid kind, because it is composed of small and unequal parts, is easily moved both by itself and by other things due to its lack of uniformity and the shape of its structure. However, the kind composed of large and uniform parts is more stable than the liquid kind; it gathers into a heavy body because of the smoothness and equality of its parts. But when fire enters and dissolves its structure, the substance loses its uniformity and smoothness, and thus shares more in the nature of motion. Once it becomes easily movable, pushed by the surrounding air and spread out over the earth, it "liquefies" (which is described as a breaking down of its bulk) and "flows" upon the earth. 

Furthermore, as the fire escapes upward from the substance—since it cannot depart into a vacuum—the surrounding air is stirred and pushes the moist, still-movable mass into the spaces vacated by the fire, mixing with it. When the mass is forced together again and regains its uniformity and smoothness, the fire—the agent of inequality—having departed, the entire mass returns to a state of internal consistency. Through the departure of these elements, the water is forced into itself; and being thus compressed, if this change happens above the earth, it becomes hail; but if it happens upon the earth, it becomes ice, which occurs as a result of extreme freezing.

Furthermore, bodies composed of both water and earth—where the compressed water blocks the empty spaces of the earth—cannot be penetrated by external water. Some of these mixtures contain less water than earth, such as the entire category of glass and stones called <term>fusile<note>Meltable; specifically stones that can be liquefied by heat.</note></term>. In this way, we have nearly finished describing the various types of matter formed by shapes, combinations, and the way they change into one another. Now, we must try to explain the causes behind how these things are experienced by our bodies.

First, the evidence of our <term>senses<note>Plato argues that physical theories must align with what we actually perceive through our sensory experiences.</note></term> must always be considered in these discussions. However, we have not yet explained the creation of flesh (and things related to flesh), nor that part of the soul which is <term>mortal<note>Plato divides the soul into the "immortal" (rational) part and the "mortal" part, which is responsible for emotions and physical desires and perishes with the body.</note></term>. We should, therefore, establish our other principles first, and then consider what follows from them. bodies: for it is nearly evident to everyone that this <term>sensation<note>original: "passion." In this context, it refers to a physical effect or sensation felt by the body (from the Greek *pathos*).</note></term> is a type of sharpness. We ought to consider the thinness of its angles, the sharpness of its sides, the smallness of its parts, and the speed of its motion; through all these qualities, fire becomes intense and penetrating, swiftly dividing whatever it meets. To understand this, we must recall the <term>shape of its figure<note>Plato's physics posits that fire is composed of tetrahedrons—pyramids with sharp points and edges that "cut" through other substances.</note></term>. Indeed, fire—and no other substance—separates our tissues and distributes them into small parts, producing in us that *sensation* which is very properly called heat. 

But the *sensation* contrary to this, though obvious enough, should not pass without an explanation. When the moist parts of external bodies are larger than the fluid parts within us, they enter our bodies and displace the smaller parts. However, because they are unable to fit into the smaller <term>receptacles<note>The microscopic pores or spaces between the particles of the body.</note></term>, they compress our internal moisture, causing it to change from a restless and uneven state into one that is unmoving and condensed. Anything that is forced together contrary to its nature will naturally resist, trying to push back into its original state. In this struggle and agitation, a trembling and numbness occurs; and this entire *sensation*, along with the force that produces it, is called cold. 

Furthermore, we call an object "hard" if our flesh gives way to it, and "soft" if it yields to the pressure of our flesh. We define them this way in relation to each other. Anything that rests on a small base yields easily to pressure. But that which rests on <term>triangular bases<note>This refers to the "earth" element, which Plato describes as being composed of cubes. These cubes are built from stable triangular components, making earth the most solid and resistant element.</note></term>, being exceptionally firm, is of a most resisting nature; because it is extremely dense, it strongly repels all opposing pressure.

Again, the nature of "heavy" and "light" will become very clear when investigated along with the concepts of "upwards" and "downwards." It is certainly not right to assert that there are naturally two fixed places distant from each other: one called "downwards," toward which all heavy bodies tend, and another called "upwards," toward which everything is pushed against its will. Since the whole universe is <term>spherical<note>Plato argues that in a perfectly round universe, there is no absolute "top" or "bottom," as every point on the surface is an equal distance from the center.</note></term>, all the points on the outer edge are equally distant from the middle. Therefore, the middle point should be considered exactly opposite to all points on the outer edge. In such a world, anyone who describes any part as being "up" or "down" will justly appear...

<sig>VOL. II. 3 Z</sig>

...by such <term>appellations<note>Names or titles.</note></term> to wander from the truth. For the middle place in the universe cannot be properly called either naturally "downwards" or "upwards," but can only be named that which is the middle. But that which <term>environs<note>Surrounds or encompasses; the outer boundary of the universe.</note></term> is neither the middle, nor does it contain any parts within itself that differ from each other in relation to the middle, nor does it possess anything corresponding to an opposite direction. But to that which is every way naturally similar, how can anyone with propriety attribute contrary names? 

For, if there be anything solid, and endowed with equal powers, in the middle of the universe, it will never tend toward any part of the extremities, because of the perfect <term>similitude<note>Symmetry or likeness. In a perfect sphere, every point on the surface is the same distance and relationship to the center, so there is no "natural" pull in one direction over another.</note></term> which they everywhere possess. But if someone moves about this solid in a circle, he will often stand with his feet in opposite directions, and will name the same part of himself both "upwards" and "downwards." Since the universe, therefore, as we have just observed, is of a spherical figure, it is not the part of a prudent man to assert that it has any place which is either "upwards" or "downwards." 

But from where these names originate, and in what things they exist—such that we transfer them from there to the universe—it is our business at present to investigate. If anyone, then, should be seated in that region of the world which for the most part belongs to the nature of fire, and toward which it on all sides tends; and if such a person should acquire the power of taking away parts of fire and causing them to balance; or, placing the parts in a scale, should violently seize the beam and, drawing out the fire, hurl it downwards into the <term>dissimilar air<note>Air is considered "dissimilar" to fire; Plato is describing the effort required to force an element out of its natural home and into the region of a different element.</note></term>—it is evident that in this case a smaller portion of fire would be more easily compelled than a greater. For, when two things are at the same time suspended from one power, it is necessary that the smaller quantity should more easily, and the greater with less readiness, yield to the oppressive force. Hence, the one is called **heavy** and tending **downwards**, while the other is called **light** and tending **upwards**. 

The same thing happens to us who inhabit this terrestrial region. For, walking on the earth and separating the <term>terrene genera<note>Earthly types; substances composed primarily of the element of earth.</note></term> from each other, we sometimes violently hurl a fragment of earth into its dissimilar, the air, and this with a motion contrary to its nature; each region at the same time retaining that to which it is allied. But the smaller portion, being more easily impelled into a dissimilar place than the larger, first of all yields to the violence: and this we denominate **light**, and call the place into which it is violently hurled **upwards**. But again, any one who beholds the cause of the *passion* of smoothness and roughness may be able to disclose it to others. Thus, with respect to that which is naturally easily movable, when any slender <term>passion<note>A slight sensation or physical impact.</note></term> falls upon it, the several parts give themselves up to each other in a <term>circular progression<note>A chain reaction where motion is passed along from one particle to the next, like ripples in a pond.</note></term>, producing the same effect; till, having arrived at the <term>seat of prudence<note>The intellect or the brain, where the soul processes information.</note></term>, they announce the power of that by which the passion was induced. But that which is affected in a contrary manner, being stable and without a circular progression, alone suffers; but does not move any of the parts to which it is proximate. Hence, the parts not mutually giving themselves up to each other, and the first passion in them becoming immovable with respect to the whole animal, that which suffers is rendered void of sensation. This last case indeed happens about the bones and hairs, and such other parts of our composition as are mostly <term>terrene<note>Earthy; made primarily of the element of earth, which is solid and resistant to movement.</note></term>. ...of pleasure and pain as follows:—When a *<term>passion<note>In this context, a "passion" (from the Greek *pathos*) refers to an "affection" or a physical state experienced by the body when acted upon by an external force, rather than an emotion.</note></term>* is produced in us contrary to nature, and with violence and abundance, then it becomes the occasion of pain. And again, when a *<term>passion</term>* conformable to our nature is excited, and this with abundance, it causes pleasure and delight. But that which is contrary to these produces contrary effects. But a *<term>passion</term>*, the whole of which is induced with great facility, is eminently indeed the object of <term>sensation</term>, but does not participate of pleasure and pain. And of this kind are the *<term>passions</term>* subsisting about the sight; to which, as we have above asserted, our body is allied. For such objects as exhibit sections and burnings, and other *<term>passions</term>* of a similar kind, do not cause pain to the sight; nor, again, does the sight receive pleasure when it is restored to the same form as before. But the most vehement and clear <term>sensations</term> influence it with pain, so far as it suffers any thing, strikes against, or comes into contact with, any object. For no violence <term>subsists<note>Remains or exists.</note></term> in the <term>separation<note>The breaking apart or thinning of particles.</note></term> or <term>concretion<note>The gathering or thickening of particles.</note></term> of the sight. 

But such bodies as are composed from larger parts, and which scarcely yield to <term>impulsion<note>The act of being pushed or driven.</note></term>, when they transfer the induced motions to the whole body, contain in themselves pleasures and pains; when varied, indeed, pains, but, when restored to their <term>pristine<note>Original or natural.</note></term> situation, pleasures. Again, whatever bodies in a small degree receive departures and <term>evacuations<note>The process of emptying or losing material.</note></term> of themselves, accompanied at the same time with abundant <term>repletions<note>The process of being filled up.</note></term>,—since such bodies have no sense of evacuation, but are sensible of repletion, they do not affect the mortal part of the soul with any pain, but, on the contrary, influence it with the greatest delight. And the truth of this is manifest from the <term>sensation</term> of sweet odours. But such bodies as suffer an abundant variation, and are scarce able to be restored in a small degree to their pristine situation, are totally affected in a manner contrary to those we have just described. And the truth of this is manifest in the burnings and sections of the body. And thus have we nearly discussed the common <term>passions</term> of the whole body, and the appellations assigned to the causes by which they are produced.

There are, however, no species about the power of the nostrils: for all odours are but <term>half begotten<note>Plato argues that smells are not primary elements themselves, but rather intermediate states or transitions between elements, making them "incomplete" or "half-formed" compared to Earth or Air.</note></term>. On this account, the varieties of these subsist without a name; as they are neither composed from many nor from simple species. But two of these alone receive an appellation, the **pleasant** and the **disagreeable**: the latter of which disturbs and violently assaults all that cavity which lies between the top of the head and the navel; but the former allures this part of the body, and by its amicable ingress preserves it in a condition accommodated to its nature. 

But we ought to consider the third sensitive part of our composition, **hearing**, in such a manner that we may explain through what causes the passions with which it is conversant subsist. <margin>The Fourth Sense: Color</margin>
The fourth sensitive genus now remains for our discussion; which contains in itself an abundant variety, all which are denominated **colours**. But colour is a flame flowing from bodies, and possessing parts <term>commensurate<note>Proportioned or sized exactly to match.</note></term> to the sight with respect to perception. But we have already considered the causes from which sight is produced. It appears then that we may now speak of colours according to <term>assimilative reasons<note>Likely or probable accounts. Plato often uses this phrase (*eikos logos*) to remind readers that physical science is a "likely story" rather than absolute divine truth.</note></term> as follows:

Of things which, proceeding from other parts, fall on the sight, some are greater, others less, and others equal to the parts of the sight. Such as are equal, therefore, cannot be perceived; and these we denominate **diaphanous** <note>Transparent; allowing light to pass through without being altered.</note>. But, among such as are larger or smaller, some of these <term>separate<note>Dilate or expand the visual ray.</note></term>, but others <term>mingle<note>Contract or compress the visual ray.</note></term> the sight, similar to the operations of heat and cold about the flesh, or to things sour, acute and hot about the tongue. But things which affect the sight in this manner are called **black** and **white**; which are indeed the <term>passions<note>In this context, "passions" refers to the physical effects or impressions made upon the senses, rather than emotions.</note></term> of those particulars we have just related, being their sisters, as it were, and the same with them in a different genus; but which, nevertheless, through these causes appear to be different. We should, therefore, speak of them as follows:—That the colour which is <term>segregative<note>Separating or expanding.</note></term> of the sight is **white**; but that which produces an effect contrary to this, **black**. 

But when a more acute motion, and of a different kind of fire, falls upon and separates the sight, as far as to the eyes, at the same time violently propelling and liquefying the transitions of the eyes, then a collected substance of fire and water flows from thence, which we denominate a **tear**; but the motion itself is a fire meeting with the sight in an opposite direction. And, indeed, when a fire, leaping as it were from a certain <term>coruscation<note>A flash or sparkle of light.</note></term>, becomes mingled with another fire, penetrating and extinguished by moisture, from this mixture colours of all-various kinds are produced. In this case we call the passion a **vibrating splendour**, and that which produces it <term>fulgid<note>Brightly shining or glittering.</note></term> and <term>rutilating<note>Glowingly red or golden-red.</note></term>. But a kind of fire which subsists in the middle of these, arriving at the moisture of the eyes, and becoming mingled with it, is by no means splendid: but in consequence of the rays of fire being mingled through moisture, and producing a bloody colour, we denominate the mixture **red**. And when splendour is mingled with red and white, it generates a **yellow** colour. But to relate in what measure each of these is mingled with each, is not the business of one endued with intellect, even though he were well informed in this affair; since he would not be able to produce concerning these either a **necessary**

...necessary or a <term>likely account<note>Original: "assimilative reason." This refers to the *eikos logos*, the idea that because the physical world is a copy of a divine ideal, we can only provide "likely stories" or "probable accounts" of how it works, rather than absolute truths.</note></term>. But **red**, when mingled with **black** and **white**, produces a **purple** colour. And when to these, mingled and burnt together, more of black is added, a more obscure colour is produced. A **ruddy** colour is generated from the mixture of **yellow** and **brown**; but brown from the mixture of black and white. A **pallid** colour arises from the mingling of white and yellow. But that which is **splendid** <note>In the context of Greek color theory, this likely refers to a brilliant, lustrous, or "shining" white or light.</note> conjoined with white, and falling upon abundance of black, gives completion to an **azure** colour. And azure mingled with white generates a **gray** colour. But from the <term>temperament<note>A balanced mixture or proportion.</note></term> of a ruddy colour with black, **green** is produced. All the rest will be nearly evident from these, to any one who, imitating the former mixtures, preserves <term>likely accounts<note>Original: "assimilative reasons."</note></term> in his discourse. 

But if any one undertakes the investigation of these for the sake of the things themselves <note>Meaning, trying to prove these color mixtures through physical experimentation alone rather than philosophical reasoning.</note>, such a one must be ignorant of the difference between a divine and human nature: since a **God** is indeed sufficient for the purpose of mingling many things into one, and of again dissolving the one into many, as being at the same time both knowing and able: but there is no man at present who is able to accomplish either of these undertakings, nor will there ever be one in any future <term>circulation of time<note>The cyclical nature of time and cosmic ages.</note></term>. 

But all these which thus naturally subsist from **necessity**, were assumed in the things which are generated by the **Artificer** <note>The Demiurge, the divine craftsman who shapes the material world.</note> of that which is most beautiful and best, when he produced a self-sufficient and most perfect God <note>In Plato's philosophy, the universe itself is a "living god," a complete and perfect being.</note>; employing, indeed, causes which are subservient to these, but operating himself in the best manner in all generated natures. On this account it is requisite to distinguish two species of causes; the one **necessary**, but the other **divine**. And we should inquire after the divine cause in all things, for the sake of obtaining a blessed life in as great a degree as our nature is capable of receiving it; but we should investigate the necessary cause for the sake of that which is divine. For we should consider, that without these two species of causes, the objects of our pursuit can neither be understood nor apprehended, nor in any other way become participated. 

But since to us at present, as to artificers, matter lies in subjection, the genera of causes serving as prepared materials from which the remaining discourse is to be woven, let us again return with brevity to our first discussions, and swiftly pass from thence to the place at which we are now arrived; by this means endeavouring to establish an end and summit to our disputation, which may harmonize with its beginning.
