It is however evident that <term>Timæus (the main speaker in Plato’s dialogue on the cosmos)</term>, in giving a certain <term>generation (the process of coming into existence or having a source)</term> to the world, establishes it at the same time remote from temporal generation <note>That is, the world has a divine cause, but did not necessarily have a starting "moment" in a human sense of time</note>. For if the world has a *certain*, and not *every* principle of generation, but that which is generated from time has the principle of *all* generation, the world is not generated from time. 

Further still, let us attend to the wonderful hypotheses of <term>Atticus (a 2nd-century philosopher who argued the world had a literal beginning in time)</term>, who says, that what according to <term>Plato</term> was moved in a confused and disordered manner is <term>unbegotten (eternal, having no beginning)</term>; but that the world was generated from time. Since then <term>Plato</term> admits that there is a cause of generation, let us see what he asserts it to be. For the world is <term>sensible (perceivable by the senses)</term> and <term>tangible (able to be touched)</term>. Whether therefore was every thing sensible generated from time, or not every thing? 

For if *every thing*, that which was moved in a confused and disordered manner was also generated from time: for he says, that this likewise was visible. But if not every thing, the reasoning is unsyllogistic <note>meaning the logic does not follow a valid structural form</note>, according to <term>Atticus</term>, and concludes nothing. Unless indeed <term>Atticus</term> should say that the world is visible and tangible, but that what was moved in a confused and disordered manner is not *now* visible, but was so prior to the fabrication of the world, since <term>Plato</term> thus speaks, “Every thing which was visible, being moved in a confused and disordered manner;” but here he says, “The world is visible and tangible, and has a body.” 

<term>Plato</term> therefore shows that every thing which is visible and tangible is generated, but not every thing which *was* so. Should <term>Atticus</term> then thus speak, (for the man is skilful in taking up one word in the place of another,) we must say, that in the definition of what is generated, there is nothing of this kind, but it is simply said, that every thing generated is the object of opinion, in conjunction with <term>irrational sense (perception without the use of higher reasoning)</term>; so that if any thing is perfectly sensible, it will also be generated. But *every* thing visible is sensible, so that what was moved with confusion and disorder was generated. 

Nor is it proper to say that it was unbegotten according to time, but that the universe was generated in time; since either both were generated, or both are unbegotten. For both are similarly called visible and generated by <term>Plato</term>. <note>original: "generaed" — likely a printing error for "generated".</note> But if both were generated, prior to this the world was changed into disorder: for generation to a contrary is entirely from a contrary. And if the maker of the world is good, how is it possible that he should not harmonize it beautifully; or that having beautifully harmonized it, he should destroy it?

But if he <note>Referring to the Demiurge or Divine Creator</note> was not good, how, not being good, did he make it to be orderly and elegantly arranged? For to effect this is the work of a beneficent <term>artificer (a craftsman or creator)</term>. But if being visible and generated, it is not generated according to time, it is not necessary immediately to assign to the universe a temporal generation, because it is said to be visible and generated. And thus much in reply to <term>Atticus (a philosopher who argued for a literal beginning of the world)</term>.

Let us however return to our principles, and inquire whether the world always was, as being eternal, or is not eternal, but <term>consubsistent (existing together)</term> with time, and whether it is self-subsistent, or produced by another. Such then is the inquiry. The answer to which is, that it was produced by another, and is consubsistent with time. But a thing of this kind is <term>generated (having a source of existence outside itself)</term>. For if it has a composite form, it has generation in consequence of its composition. And if it alone subsists from another cause, it is generated, as not producing itself. And if it is eternal, it has its whole subsistence coextended with time. For it was fabricated with reference to something else, and it was generated as a flowing image of <term>real being (the unchanging, spiritual reality)</term>. As therefore that which is composite is to that which is simple, and as time is to eternity, so is <term>generation (the world of change)</term> to <term>essence (the world of true being)</term>. 

If then a simple and uniform essence is eternal, an essence composite, multiform, and conjoined with time, is generation. Hence Plato divinely inquires, whether the world originated from a *certain* principle. For that which was *once* generated, originated from a temporal, fabricative, final, material, and formal principle. For principle being predicated multifariously, that which is produced in time originates according to all these modes. 

But the world originated from a *certain*, and not from *every* principle. What then was this principle? It was not temporal: for that which originates from this, is also allotted the principle of its generation from all the others. It originated indeed from that most leading and proper principle, the <term>final (the purpose or "end" for which something exists)</term>, as Plato himself teaches us in the course of this Dialogue. For it was generated through *the good*, and this is the principle of generation from which it originated. 

In the first place, therefore, he shows that the world is generated, from its composition: for it is tangible and visible. These then are the extremities of the universe: for heaven is visible, but earth is tangible; and the visible is in earth, so far as it participates of light, and the tangible in heaven, so far as a <term>terrene (earthly or physical)</term> nature is comprehended in it according to cause. In short he says that the world has a body, that we may also take into account the middle perfections of the universe. And in this Plato speaks agreeably to the <term>oracle (likely the Chaldean Oracles, a sacred Neoplatonic text)</term>, which says, “The world is an imitation of intellect, but that which is

How, then, should we say the world is "generated"? We reply that it is something that is always in the process of being generated, and will always continue to be generated. For a specific, partial body not only *is* to be generated, but there was a specific point in time when it *was* generated. However, the entirety of heaven, or the universe, exists only in the state of being generated—in a constant "becoming"—and is never a finished product of the past. For just as the light of the sun flows continuously from its source, so too the world is always being generated and always being produced; it is, in a sense, always *advancing* into existence.

### P. 474. *To discover therefore the Artificer and Father of this Universe, &c.*

The terms "Father" and "Artificer" <note>The "Artificer" refers to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman in Plato's philosophy who shapes the material world.</note> differ from one another in their roles: the *former* is the cause of existence and the source of unity, while the latter is the source of powers and the complex essence of things. The Father stably holds all things within himself, whereas the Artificer is the cause of movement, progression, and generation. The Father represents an ineffable and divine Providence, while the Artificer represents the generous sharing of "reasons" <note>original: "logoi," the productive principles or rational blueprints of the natural world.</note> or creative designs. 

Furthermore, the word *universe* in this context refers to physical matter, the celestial spheres, and the elements that complete them. It also includes the vital and intellectual powers that reside within these physical forms. It encompasses all the causes within our world and the collective divinity of the cosmos, around which the various <term>mundane gods</term> <note>Gods associated specifically with the physical cosmos and its cycles.</note> operate. We must also understand "the world" to include the singular Intellect, the divine Soul, the entire mass of the universe, and its connected hierarchy of divine, intellectual, <term>psychical</term> <note>relating to the Soul (from the Greek 'psyche').</note>, and physical numbers—since every <term>monad</term> <note>A primary, indivisible unit or "the One" at the head of a specific category of being.</note> has a multitude that corresponds to it. For the "universe" signifies all of these together. 

Perhaps, too, the addition of the word *this* is meant to show that the world is, in a sense, perceptible to the senses and partial. An entirely intellectual or "intelligible" nature cannot be called *this*, because it contains all intellectual forms within it. But for the visible universe, the particle <term>this</term> <note>original: "τόδε" (tode), a Greek word used to point specifically to a physical object "here and now."</note> is appropriate, because it is assigned a sensible and material nature. It is difficult, therefore, as Plato says, to find the maker of this universe. In the process of discovery, one method starts from primary principles according to science, while another starts from secondary things through <term>reminiscence</term> <note>The Platonic idea that "learning" is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before birth.</note>. And we are able indeed to speak of them *scientifically*, but not *intellectually*: for this, as we have said before, is to discover them. But if the discovery is a silent energy of the soul, how can speech flowing through the mouth be sufficient to lead into light that which is discovered, such as it truly is?

# ON THE TIMÆUS.

After this, Proclus, following—as he says—the light of science, investigates who the <term>demiurgus (the divine craftsman of the universe)</term> is, and in what order of things he ranks. For Numenius the Pythagorean <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who sought to trace Platonic thought back to Pythagoras and even older Eastern wisdom.</note>, as Proclus says, honoring three gods, calls the first *father*, the second *maker*, and the third *work* or *effect* <note>original: "ποιημα"</note>; for the world, according to Numenius, is the third god. This means that for Numenius there is a two-fold creator—namely, the first and second god—while that which is created is the third divinity. 

Proclus, however, argues that Numenius is not acting rightly in this classification. First, Numenius is wrong to group "**the good**" <note>The "Good" in Platonic philosophy refers to the ultimate, supreme principle of the universe, standing above all other gods or beings.</note> with these other causes. For "the good," the supreme principle of all things, is not naturally suited to be joined with specific things, nor to hold a rank secondary to anything else. But in Plato's works, the *father* is ranked after the *artificer*. Furthermore, Numenius groups that which is exempt from all <term>habitude (any relationship, connection, or shared quality)</term>—that is, the ineffable cause of all things—with natures that are below and after him. But these types of relationships should only be attributed to lower-ranking beings; all such connections should be removed from that which is first. Therefore, the role of "paternal" or "fatherly" in the universe cannot be applied to the absolute first principle of things. And, in the third place, it is not right to separate "father" and "artificer," since Plato honors one and the same divinity by both these names. Indeed, one divine act of creation, and one creator and father, are delivered everywhere by Plato.

With respect to Harpocration <note>A student of Atticus and a commentator on Plato’s works.</note>, it would be wonderful if he were consistent with himself in what he says concerning the craftsman. This man makes the craftsman two-fold: he calls the first god "Heaven" and "Saturn," the second "Jupiter" and "Life" <note>original: "Zena"—a Greek form of the name Jupiter/Zeus, which sounds like the Greek word for "to live."</note>, and the third "Heaven" and the "World." Again, however, transferring the first god into another rank, he calls him "Jupiter" and the "king of the intelligible world"; but he calls the second the "Ruler." According to him, the same divinity is simultaneously Jupiter, Saturn, and Heaven. This would mean the first god is all these things, even though Plato, in the dialogue *Parmenides*, takes away from "**the one**" (the first god) every name, every description, and every relationship. We, in fact, do not think it is proper to call the first principle even "father"; but for Harpocration, the first is father, son, and grandson all at once.

Again, Atticus <note>A teacher of Harpocration who insisted on a literal reading of Plato’s creation story.</note>, the teacher of Harpocration, directly identifies the divine craftsman as being the same as "**the good**." However, the craftsman is called *good* <note>original: "αγαθος" (agathos)</note> by Plato, but not *the Good itself* <note>original: "ταγαθον" (tagathon)</note>. The craftsman is also called "**intellect**" by Plato; but "the good" is the cause of all essence and is "beyond being," as we learn from the 6th book of the *Republic*. But what will Atticus say regarding the **paradigm** <note>The eternal "blueprint" or "model" of the world.</note>, which the craftsman looks at while fa-

...fabricating the world? For it is either prior to the <term>demiurge (the divine craftsman)</term>, and so according to Atticus there will be something more ancient than *the good*; or it will be in the demiurge, and so that which is first will be *many*, and not *the one*; or it will be after the demiurge, and so *the good*—which it is not lawful to assert—will be converted to things lower than itself, and will intellectually perceive them. <note>Proclus is arguing that the "pattern" the creator uses cannot exist before, during, or after the creator without causing logical problems for the supreme principle of "the Good."</note>

After these men, Plotinus the philosopher places a two-fold demiurge: one in the <term>intelligible world (the realm of pure thought and reality)</term>, and the other the governor of the universe. And he says rightly: for in a certain respect the mundane intellect is the demiurge of the universe. But the father and artificer, whom he places in the intelligible realm, is transcendently the demiurge; Plotinus calling every thing between *the one* and the world "intelligible": for there, according to him, the true heaven, the kingdom of Saturn, and the intellect of Jupiter, subsist. <note>In this context, Saturn (Cronus) represents pure Intellect, and Jupiter (Zeus) represents the soul or mind that governs the physical world.</note> Just as if any one should say that the sphere of Saturn, that of Jupiter, and that of Mars, are contained in the heavens: for the whole of an intelligible essence is "one many," and is one intellect comprehending many intelligible things. And such is the doctrine of Plotinus.

In the next place, Amelius <note>A 3rd-century student of Plotinus who developed a more complex, three-part division of the Divine Mind.</note> makes a triple demiurge, three intellects, and three kings: one that *is*, the second that *possesses*, and the third that *sees*. But these differ, because the first intellect is truly that which is; but the second is indeed the intelligible which it contains, yet has that which is prior to itself, participates entirely in it, and on this account is the second. And the third is indeed likewise the intelligible which it contains; for every intellect is the same with its conjoined intelligible; but it contains that which is in the second, and sees the first: for that which it possesses is obscure in proportion to its distance from the first. According to Amelius, therefore, these three intellects and artificers are the same as the three kings in Plato, and as Phanes, Heaven, and Saturn, in the works of Orpheus; and that which is especially the demiurge according to him is Phanes. <note>Phanes is a mystical, primeval deity in Orphic tradition, often depicted as emerging from a cosmic egg to create the universe.</note> To Amelius, however, it is proper to say, that Plato is every where accustomed to recur from multitude to the unities from which the order in the many proceeds; or rather prior to Plato, from the very order of things themselves, *the one* is always prior to *multitude*, and every divine order begins from a <term>monad (a single, unified source)</term>. For it is indeed requisite that a divine number should proceed from a <term>triad (a group of three)</term> \*, but prior to the

# ON THE TIMÆUS.
<sig>4 I 2</sig>

the <term>triad</term> <note>A grouping of three; in Neoplatonism, divine realities often proceed in groups of three.</note> is the <term>monad</term> <note>The "One" or a single unit that serves as the source for others.</note>. Where therefore is the **demiurgic monad** <note>The single, primary Divine Craftsman.</note>, that there may be a triad from it? And how is the world one, if it is not fabricated by a single cause? For it is necessary, by a much higher priority, that the cause of the world should be united and be a single unit, so that the world may become "only-begotten" <note>Unique or one-of-a-kind.</note>. Let there then be three artificers; but who is the one prior to the three, looking indeed to one **paradigm** <note>The eternal blueprint or "model" the creator follows.</note>, but making the world <note>Likely a printer's error for 'world'.</note> only-begotten? It is not proper, therefore, that the number of craftsmen should begin from a group of three, but from a single unit.

After Amelius, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century scholar and student of Plotinus who edited his teacher's works.</note>, thinking to agree with Plato, calls the **supermundane soul** <note>A soul that exists above and beyond the physical universe.</note> the **demiurgus** (the craftsman), and the **intellect** of this soul to which he is turned, **animal itself** <note>The "living-being-in-itself," the divine model containing the blueprints for all life.</note>, as being, according to him, the model for the craftsman. It is necessary, therefore, to ask Porphyry: in which of his writings does Plotinus claim the soul is the craftsman? And how does this agree with Plato, who continually calls the craftsman a "god" and "intellect," but never calls him a "soul"? How, likewise, does Plato call the world a god? And how does the craftsman reach through all things in the world? For all things do not possess a soul; but all things do share in the craftsman's providence. Furthermore, divine creation is able to generate intellect and gods; but a soul is not naturally suited to produce anything higher than the level of a soul. I should also mention that it is by no means certain that Plato knew of any **imparticipable soul** <note>A "pure" soul that does not connect to or "participate" in a body.</note>.

To Porphyry succeeds the divine Iamblichus <note>An influential philosopher who shifted Neoplatonism toward ritual and a more complex hierarchy of gods.</note>, who, having written extensively against Porphyry's opinion and overthrew it as being merely the view of Plotinus, gives us his own theology. He calls the entire <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal Forms.</note> the craftsman. If, therefore, he means that all things exist "craftsman-like" within the craftsman—both "being" itself and the intelligible world—he agrees with himself and also with Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet.</note>, who says:

->All that exists in confluent order lies<-
->Within the belly of the mighty Jove.<-
<note>original: "Jove" (Jupiter/Zeus). In this tradition, Zeus swallows the universe to contain all possibilities within himself before beginning creation.</note>

According to Proclus <note>The head of the Academy in Athens in the 5th century and author of this commentary.</note> in his *Elements of Theology*, this must also be true of the immediate and first emergence from the highest god. The first offspring, therefore, from the unspeakable principle of things will be an all-perfect **triad**, the leader of a divine number; and in like manner every divine number will come from a triad, and this from a **monad**: for there is no number prior to three, since unity is the principle of number, and the **duad** <note>The number two.</note> partakes of the nature of both unity and number. This will be clear by considering that it is the property of a number to grow more through multiplication than addition (specifically when multiplied by itself); but unity (1) grows by being added to (1+1=2), but not by being multiplied by itself (1x1=1). Two, because of its middle nature, produces the same result when added to itself as when multiplied by itself (2+2=4 and 2x2=4). See the *Introduction to The Parmenides*.

## ADDITIONAL NOTES

It is not at all surprising that each of the gods should be the universe, but at the same time, each in a different way from the rest; one acts as a creator (demiurgically), another according to **connecting comprehension** (συνοχικως) <note>original: *synochikōs*; this refers to the divine power that holds the universe together and prevents it from dissolving.</note>, another immutably, and another in yet a different manner according to a divine characteristic. 

But if Iamblichus means that the entire span between the world and **the One** <note>The supreme, unified source of all reality in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> is the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The 'Craftsman' or creator-god who fashions the physical world according to eternal models.</note>, this is indeed doubtful, and we may respond to that claim using what he himself has taught us. For where are the kings who existed prior to Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, here representing the ruling creator-god.</note>, who are the fathers of Jupiter? Where are the kings mentioned by Plato, whom Iamblichus places above the world and around **the One**? And how can we say that "eternal being itself" is the first being, but that the Demiurge is the entire intelligible order—who is himself also eternal being as well as the <term>Animal Itself</term> <note>The 'Living Being' or the divine blueprint containing the forms of all living creatures.</note>? For would we not then be forced to say that the Demiurge is not "eternal being," unless he is merely included alongside other eternal beings? 

However, Iamblichus himself—though very prolific on these subjects—has in some of his other writings more accurately praised the demiurgic order. This can be inferred from the fact that, in speaking about the creation by Jupiter in the *Timaeus*, he places the Demiurge in the third rank of these successions, following the **intelligible triads** and the three triads of gods in the **intellectual hebdomad** <note>A group of seven divine intellects or powers.</note>. For he says that these three gods are also celebrated by the Pythagoreans, who call the first of these intellects the highest; it contains within itself total <term>monads</term> <note>Unified, single units of being.</note> that are simple, indivisible, and "good-like" (boniform), remaining within and united with themselves. 

But they say that the most beautiful signs of the **middle intellect**—which gathers together the completion of such natures—are its fertility among the gods, its ability to unite the three intellects, its fulfillment of energy, its generation of divine life, and its role as the source of progression and goodness for everything. And they inform us that the most famous tokens of the **third intellect**, which builds the whole world, are its prolific expansions, its acts of creation, its role in holding together all causes, and its ability to produce all manufactured things. It is proper, therefore, to judge Iamblichus’s theology regarding the creator of the universe from these statements.

After him, **Theodorus** <margin>Theodorus, as well as Iamblichus, was the disciple of Porphyry.</margin>, following Amelius, says that there are three craftsmen; but he does not place them immediately after **the One**, but at the very end of the intelligible <note>The realm of pure Being and Ideas.</note> and intellectual gods. He likewise calls one of these "essential intellect," another "intellec-"

intellectual essence, and another the fountain of souls; and says that the first is indivisible, the second is distributed into wholes, and that the third has made a distribution into particulars. Again, therefore, we may say the same things to him as we said to the noble **Amelius**, that we acknowledge these to be three gods, or analogous to these, but not also three artificers <note>The Greek term *technitai* refers to creators or craftsmen; Proclus argues they are aspects of one creator rather than three distinct creators.</note>; but we say that one of these is the intelligible aspect of the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The 'Demiurge' is the divine craftsman who fashions the material world.</note>, the second his generative power, and the third that which is truly demiurgic intellect. But it is requisite to consider whether the fountain of souls is to be arranged as the third: for power belongs to the middle, as he also says, and hence the fountain of souls should be partially, and not universally, denominated the fountain of life. For the fountain of souls is only one of the fountains in this middle; since life is not in souls only, nor in animated natures alone, but there is also divine and intellectual life prior to that of the soul, which they say, proceeding from this middle, emits a diversity of life from distributed channels. Such then, in short, are the dogmas of ancient interpreters respecting the <term>demiurgus</term>.

Let us now, therefore, briefly relate the conceptions of our preceptor <note>This refers to Syrianus, the teacher of Proclus, whom Proclus highly revered.</note> on this subject, and which we think accord in a very eminent degree with those of **Plato**. The <term>demiurgus</term>, therefore, according to him, possesses the extremity* of the intellectual divine monads <note>Units or singular divine principles.</note>, and the fountains of life, emitting from himself total fabrication, and imparting dominion to the more partial fathers of wholes. He is likewise immovable, being eternally established on the summit of **Olympus**, and ruling over two-fold worlds, the supercelestial and celestial, and comprehending the beginning, middle, and end of all things. For of every demiurgic distribution, one kind is of wholes with a total subsistence, another of wholes with a partial subsistence, another of parts with a total†, and another of parts with a partial subsistence. But fabrication being fourfold, the demiurgic monad binds in itself the total providence of wholes, but a demiurgic triad is suspended from it which governs parts totally, and distributes the power of the

### ADDITIONAL NOTES

...monad <note>The original Greek text erroneously printed "Triad" [original: Τριαδος] instead of "monad" [original: μοναδος].</note>; just as in the other, or partial fabrication, a monad is the leader of a triad which orderly distributes wholes partially, and parts partially. But all the multitude of the triad revolves round the monad, is distributed about it, divides its fabrications, and is filled from it. If these things then are rightly asserted, the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The 'Demiurge' is the divine craftsman or creator of the material world.</note> of wholes is the boundary of the intellectual gods, being established indeed in the intelligible, but full of power, according to which he produces wholes, and converts all things to himself. Hence *Timaeus* calls him *intellect*, and *the best of causes*, and *says that he looks to an intelligible paradigm* <note>The "intelligible paradigm" refers to the eternal world of Forms or Ideas which the creator uses as a blueprint.</note>, that by this he may separate him from the first intelligible gods; but by calling him *intellect*, he places him in an order different from that of the gods, who are both intelligible and intellectual: and by the appellation of the *best of causes*, he establishes him above all other supermundane fabricators. 

He is, therefore, an intellectual god exempt from all other fabricators. But if he was the first† <note>Namely, Saturn (Cronus).</note> deity in the intellectual order, he would possess a permanent characteristic, abiding after his accustomed mode: for this is the illustrious prerogative of the first intellectual god. If he was the second‡ <note>Namely, Rhea.</note> deity of this order he would be particularly the cause of life; but now in generating soul, he energizes indeed together with the crater <note>The 'crater' or mixing bowl is a symbolic vessel used by the Demiurge to mix the ingredients of the soul.</note>, but is essentially intellect. He is therefore no other than the third|| <note>Namely, Jupiter (Zeus).</note> of the intellectual fathers: for his peculiar work is the production of intellect, and not the fabrication of body. For he makes body, yet not alone, but in conjunction with necessity; but he makes intellect through himself. Nor is it his peculiar work to produce soul: for he generates soul together with the crater; but he alone both gives subsistence to and causes intellect to preside over the universe. As he is therefore the maker of intellect, he very properly has also an intellectual order. Hence he is called by Plato, *fabricator and father*; and is neither father alone, nor fabricator alone, nor again, father and fabricator. For the extremes are father§ and fabricator; the former possessing the summit of intelligibles, and subsisting prior to the royal series, and the latter subsisting at the extremity of the order; and the

---

<note>Being itself, or the summit of the intelligible order, is called **father** alone; Phanes, or the extremity of the intelligible order, is called **father and artificer**; Jupiter, or the extremity of the intellectual order, is called **artificer and father**; and Vulcan, who is the fabricator of a corporeal nature, is called **artificer alone**.</note>

It uses Orphic theology and Platonic philosophy to explain how Jupiter (Zeus) functions as the universal creator.</meta>

# ON THE TIMAEUS

...one being the monad of paternal deity, and the other being allotted a fabricative power in the universe. But between both these are a **father and at the same time artificer**, and an **artificer and at the same time father**. For each of these is not the same; in the first, the paternal nature has dominion, and in the second, the fabricative nature has dominion; and the paternal is always superior to the fabricative.

Hence the first of these two intermediate stages is more characterized by the quality of *father*; for, according to the Oracle <note>A reference to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a sacred text for Neoplatonists.</note>, "he is the boundary of the paternal profundity, and the fountain of intellectual natures." But the second of the intermediate stages is more characterized by the quality of *artificer*: for he is the monad of total fabrication <note>The singular source of all creation.</note>. This is why I think the former is called *Metis* <note>original: "$\mu\eta\tau\iota\varsigma$"; meaning 'Wisdom' or 'Counsel'.</note> but the latter is called *Metietes* <note>original: "$\mu\eta\tau\iota\epsilon\tau\eta\varsigma$"; meaning 'The Counselor' or 'The Wise One'.</note>; the former is seen, but the latter is the one who sees. The former is "swallowed up," but the latter is satisfied with the power of the former; and what the former is in the realm of the intelligible, the latter is in the realm of the intellectual; for one is the boundary of the intelligible gods, and the other is the boundary of the intellectual gods.

Likewise, concerning the former, Orpheus <note>A legendary poet and prophet; Proclus treats Orphic poems as foundational theological texts.</note> says: 

> "The father made these things in a dark cavern;" 

But concerning the latter, Plato says: 

> "Of whom I am the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The 'Demiurge' is the divine craftsman or creator of the material world.</note> and father." 

And in his *Politicus* <note>Plato's dialogue 'The Statesman'.</note> he reminds us of the doctrine of the demiurge and father, because the first of these divinities is characterized more by his paternal nature, and the second by his creative peculiarity. But every god is named for his specific trait, even though he contains all things within himself. 

The divinity who is solely *the maker* or *artificer* is the cause of mundane <note>Belonging to the physical world.</note> natures; but he who is both *artificer* and *father* is the cause of both supermundane <note>Beyond the physical world.</note> and mundane natures. He who is *father* and *artificer* is the cause of intellectual, supermundane, and mundane natures; and he who is *father* alone is the cause of everything: intelligible, intellectual, supermundane, and mundane. 

Plato, therefore, representing the demiurge in this way, leaves him ineffable and without a name, as he exists prior to the whole of things in the rank of *the good*. For in every order of gods there is a part that corresponds to *the one*; and this is the monad in every world. But Orpheus also gives him a name, being moved by that divine source; and Plato follows him in this in other parts of his writings: for the Jupiter <note>Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note> he describes, who exists prior to the three fountains <note>original: "fons"; This likely refers to the three "fontal" or source-gods (Zeus, Poseidon, and Pluto) who divide the universe.</note> of Saturn, is the demiurge of the universe.

After the absorption of Phanes <note>An Orphic deity representing the first-born creator; in the myth, Zeus swallows Phanes to contain all of creation within himself.</note>, therefore, the ideas of all things appeared in Jupiter, as the theologist (Orpheus) says:

->Hence with the universe great Jove contains<-
->Heaven's splendid height, and ether's ample plains;<-

## ON THE TIMÆUS.

-> — the golden chain suspended from the upper air <note>original: "æther"; the highest, purest part of the atmosphere, where the gods were thought to reside.</note>. <-

The divine orders above the world <margin>Instead of <note>original: "των θειων πραξεων υπο των εγκοσμιων"</note> "the divine actions under the mundane [worldly] things," as in the original, it is necessary to read as in our translation <note>original: "των θειων ταξεων υπερ των εγκοσμιων"</note> "the divine orders above the mundane [worldly] things."</margin> being denominated Homerically a golden chain <note>A famous metaphor from the Iliad, which Neoplatonists interpreted as the continuous chain of cause and effect linking the highest divinity to the lowest matter.</note>. And Plato, emulating Homer, says in this dialogue, “that the <term>demiurgus [the divine craftsman]</term> *binding intellect in soul, and soul in body*, fabricated the universe, and that he gave subsistence <note>The act of bringing into existence or providing a foundation for being.</note> to the junior gods, through whom also he adorns the parts of the world.” If therefore it is Jupiter who possesses one power, who swallows Phanes <note>In Orphic myth, Phanes is the primordial god of light; by swallowing him, Jupiter contains the blueprints of all things within himself.</note> in whom the intelligible causes of wholes primarily subsist, who produces all things according to the admonitions of Night, and who confers dominion both on other gods and the three sons of Saturn <note>The three sons are Jupiter himself, Neptune, and Pluto, who divided the world among them.</note>, he it is who is the one and whole demiurge of the universe, possessing the fifth order among those gods that rank as kings, as is divinely shown by our preceptor in his Orphic conferences, and on this account he is artificer and father, and each of these totally.

But that Plato also has these conceptions concerning the mighty Jupiter is evident from the appellations which he gives him in the *Cratylus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning the origin of names and language.</note>, evincing that he is the cause and the supplier of life to all things: for, says he, that through which life is imparted to all things is denominated by us <term>through [dia]</term> and <term>to live [zena]</term> <note>Plato plays on the Greek names for Zeus: "Dia" sounds like the word for "through," and "Zena" sounds like the word for "to live," suggesting Jupiter is the one *through* whom we *live*.</note>. But in the *Gorgias*, he coordinates him with the sons of Saturn, and at the same time gives him a subsistence exempt from them, that he may be prior to the three, and may be participated by them, and establishes Law together with him, in the same manner as Orpheus. For, from the admonitions of Night, according to Orpheus, Law is made the assessor <note>One who sits beside another, often as a counselor or assistant.</note> of Jupiter, and is established together with him. Further still, Plato in his *Laws*, conformably to the theologist <note>Refers to Orpheus.</note>, represents total Justice as the associate of Jupiter: and in the *Philebus* he evinces that a royal soul and a royal intellect presubsist in Jupiter according to the reason of cause; agreeably to which he now also describes him as giving subsistence to intellect and soul, as unfolding the laws of fate, and producing all the orders of mundane gods and animals, as far as to the last of things; generating some of these by himself alone, and others through the celestial gods as media <note>Intermediaries.</note>. Nor let any one who admits that it is better than body suppose that it ought to be divided after the same manner as the extremes and intervals <note>In this context, 'interval' refers to physical space or distance between two points.</note> by which body is measured. For things which possess interval, are not totally through the whole of themselves present to themselves, and when divided are not able to preserve an unconfused union. But soul, participating of an impartible <note>Indivisible; that which cannot be split into physical parts.</note> destiny, is united to itself, and exhibits all the same elements subsisting in all the same. Nor again, let any one suppose that this is a section of number. For soul is indeed number, but not that which subsists according to quantity, but that which is essential, self-begotten, uniform, and converted to itself. 

Nor let any one compare the presence of these ratios in all things to <term>spermatic reasons</term> <note>Original: *logoi spermatikoi*. In Neoplatonism, these are "seed-like principles" or formative powers that govern the growth of physical things; the author argues the soul is far superior to these material-leaning forces.</note>: for those are imperfect, corporeal and material, and are in every respect surpassed by the immaterial and pure essence of the reasons of the soul. Nor yet let any one assimilate the above-mentioned parts to the theorems of science, in consequence of each possessing the whole: for we do not now consider the knowledge, but the essence of the soul. Nor is it proper to think that diversities of essences are similar to the distinctions of habits: for the latter are all-variously diversified in those that possess them, but the former are established with a sameness of subsistence in demiurgic boundaries. 

It is requisite, therefore, to suspend the primary principle of the <term>psychogonic division</term> <note>The mathematical "birth" or generation of the soul’s structure as described in Plato's Timaeus.</note> from a demiurgic cause, and from those perfect measures which eternally presubsist in beings, and to which the <term>demiurgus [the divine craftsman]</term> also looking divides the soul. For as he divides this universe by <term>intelligible paradigms</term> <note>The perfect, non-physical models or "blueprints" used by the creator to build the world.</note>, so also he separates the essence of the soul by the most beautiful boundaries, assimilating it to more antient and principal causes. 

The mode, therefore, of division is immaterial, intellectual, undefiled, perfective of the essence of the soul, generative of the multitude it contains, collective through harmony into one order, and connective of things divided; at the same time being the cause of the unmingled purity in the soul, and producing a confluent communion of reasons. # ADDITIONAL NOTES

The soul equally participates of both <note>The soul exists as a bridge between the indivisible realm of pure spirit and the divided realm of physical matter.</note>. Hence it is well observed by the inspired <note>Original: "dæmoniacal." In the Platonic tradition, this refers to a person possessing "daemonic" or supernatural wisdom, not something evil.</note> Aristotle, that there is something indivisible in things that are divisible, by which they are connected*; so that it is much more necessary that something indivisible should remain in things whose nature is not only divisible, but also indivisible. For if it should not remain, that which is made of both will be divisible alone. 

<note>Footnote *: That which ultimately connects physical bodies must necessarily be indivisible; for if the connector also consisted of parts, those parts would require something else to hold them together. This would lead to an infinite loop (original: *ad infinitum*). Therefore, a physical body stays together because of something non-physical (incorporeal).</note>

But it is necessary that the "whole" should remain during the creation of the "parts"; this is evident because the Divine Craftsman <note>Term: <term>Demiurgus</term>. The creator figure in Plato’s philosophy who shapes the material world according to divine patterns.</note> is an eternal creator. He formed the soul as one whole before its division: for he does not produce at one time and destroy at another; but he always produces everything, and does so eternally; and he makes that which is produced remain exactly as it is. The "wholeness," therefore, is not destroyed when it gives life to the parts, but remains and exists before† the parts. For he did not produce the parts before the whole, and then build the whole from them; but, on the contrary, he produced the whole first, and from this gave existence to the parts. Hence the essence of the soul is at the same time a whole and possesses parts, and is both "the one" and "the many." And such is the division which Timaeus <note>The main speaker in Plato’s dialogue of the same name.</note> describes in the soul.

<note>Footnote †: As the philosopher Proclus explains, "Wholeness" exists in three ways: before the parts (as a cause), within the parts (as an organizing principle), and after the parts (as a resulting sum). Here, Proclus is speaking of the first type. A good example is the center of a circle: it exists as the source from which all lines (radii) come out. The lines are secondary to the center.</note>

But let the way we explain this match the nature of the soul. We should stay away from "apparent harmony" (physical sound) and return to "essential and immaterial harmony," moving from the images to the original patterns <note>Term: <term>paradigms</term>. The eternal, perfect templates of which everything in our world is a mere shadow or copy.</note>. For the symphony which flows into the ears, consisting of sounds and physical vibrations, is entirely different from the symphony which is life-giving and intellectual. Let no one, therefore, stop at the mathematical math-problems of this passage, but let him instead awaken in himself a theory suited to the actual essence of the soul. Nor should he think that we should only look to musical intervals or the differences of motions; for these things are very distant from the truth, and are not suited to what we are actually investigating; but let him—

...consider the assertions essentially, and examine how they indicate the medium pertaining to the soul, and how they exhibit <term>demiurgic providence</term> <note>The care and planning exercised by the Divine Craftsman (the Demiurge) in creating the universe.</note>. In the first place, therefore, since wholeness is triple—one being prior to parts, another subsisting from parts, and another in each of the parts—that wholeness of the soul which is now delivered is that which subsists prior to parts; for the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The Divine Craftsman or Creator figure in Platonic philosophy.</note> made it one whole prior to all division, which, as we have said, remains such as it is, without being consumed in the production of the parts: for to be willing to dissolve that which is well harmonized is the province of an evil artificer. He would however dissolve it, if he consumed the whole in the parts. 

But Plato insinuates that wholeness which consists from parts, when he represents the demiurgus consuming the whole mixture in the section of the essence of the soul, and renovating the whole of it through the harmony of its parts; this whole receiving its completion from all according parts. And a little further on he will teach us that wholeness which subsists in each of its parts, when he divides the whole soul into certain circles, and attributes all the above-mentioned ratios to them, which he has already rendered apparent; for he says that the three are in each of the parts, in the same manner as in the whole. Every part, therefore, is in a certain respect a **triadic whole**, after the same manner as the whole. 

Hence it is necessary that the soul should have three wholenesses, because it animates the universe, which is a whole of wholes, each of which is a whole as in a part. As it therefore animates in a two-fold respect—namely, both that which is a whole, and those wholes which are as parts—it requires two wholenesses; and it transcends the natures which are animated, possessing something external to them, so as, in the language of <term>Timæus</term> <note>The main speaker in Plato’s dialogue, for whom the book is named.</note>, to surround the universe as with a veil. Hence by the wholeness prior to parts it entirely runs above the universe, and by the other two connects it, and the natures which it contains; these also subsisting as wholes.

In the next place, we must observe that Plato, proceeding from the beginning to the end, preserves that which is **monadic** <note>Related to the 'Monad' or unity; the principle of oneness.</note> and also that which is **dyadic** <note>Related to the 'Dyad' or duality; the principle of division and difference.</note> in the soul: for he reduces its <term>hyparxis</term> <note>A technical term for the very core of a thing's existence or its "essential reality."</note> into **essence, sameness, and difference**, and bisects number, beginning from one part, into the double and triple; and contemplating the media, he comprehends two in one, and according to each of these unfolds two-fold ratios, the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2, commonly known in music as a "fifth."</note> and <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3, known in music as a "fourth."</note>, and again cuts these into <term>sesquioctaves</term> <note>A ratio of 9:8, representing a whole tone in a musical scale.</note> and **remainders** (<gloss>leimmata</gloss> <note>original: "$\lambda\epsilon\iota\mu\mu\alpha\tau\alpha$". In Greek music theory, these are the small mathematical intervals or "remnants" left over after calculating major steps in a scale.</note>). In what follows also, he divides one length into two, and one figure of the soul into two periods; and, in short, he very properly never separates the dyadic from the monadic;

for to intellect the <term>monadic</term> <note>Relating to the "monad," the principle of absolute unity and oneness.</note> alone is adapted, on which account it is also impartible <note>Indivisible; cannot be broken into parts.</note>, but to body the <term>dyadic</term> <note>Relating to the "duad" or "dyad," the principle of duality, difference, and division.</note>; and hence, in the generation of a corporeal nature, he begins from the duad of fire and earth, and arranges two other genera of elements between these. But soul subsisting between body and intellect is at the same time a monad and a duad; and this because in a certain respect it equally participates of bound and infinity; just as intellect is allied to bound, but body more accords with infinity, through its subject matter, and its division *ad infinitum* <note>Latin for "to infinity."</note>. And if after this manner some have referred the impartible and partible to the monad and indefinite duad, they have spoken agreeably to things themselves; but if they have considered the soul to be number in no respect differing from monadic numbers <note>Simple counting numbers or units.</note>, their assertions have been utterly discordant with the essence of the soul. It is therefore at the same time both a monad and duad, resembling by the monadic, intellectual bound, and by the dyadic, infinity; or by the former being the image of the impartible, and by the latter the paradigm <note>The ideal model or pattern.</note> of partible natures. 

This also should be considered, that Timæus <note>A character in Plato's dialogue of the same name who describes the creation of the universe.</note> here speaks of a two-fold work of the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Divine Craftsman" or creator of the material world.</note>: for he divides the soul into parts, and harmonizes the divided portions, and renders them accordant with each other. But in so doing he at the same time energizes both <term>Dionysiacally</term> <note>Acting like Dionysus (Bacchus), who in myth was torn apart; here representing the process of dividing a single essence into many parts.</note> and <term>Apolloniacally</term> <note>Acting like Apollo, the god of light and music, who brings harmony and order to multiplicity.</note>. For to divide and produce wholes into parts, and to preside over the distribution of species, is Dionysiacal; but to perfect all things harmoniously is Apolloniacal. As the demiurgus, therefore, comprehends in himself the cause of both these gods, he divides and harmonizes the soul: for the <term>hebdomad</term> <note>The number seven.</note> is a number common to both these divinities; since theologists say that Bacchus was divided into seven parts, and they ascribe the <term>heptad</term> <note>Another term for the number seven.</note> to Apollo, as the power that connects all symphonies; for in the monad, duad, and tetrad <note>The numbers 1, 2, and 4.</note>, from which the hebdomad is composed, the <term>disdiapason</term> <note>A musical term for a double octave, which encompasses the primary harmonic ratios.</note> first consists. Hence they call the god, the leader of the hebdomad, and assert that the seventh day is sacred to him: for they say that on that day Apollo was born from Latona, in the same manner as Diana on the sixth day. This number, therefore, in the same manner as the triad <note>The number three.</note>, accedes to the soul from superior causes; the triad indeed from intelligible, but the hebdomad from intellectual* causes. # ON THE TIMÆUS.

The <term>hebdomad</term> <note>A group or series of seven; from the Greek 'hebdomas'.</note> is derived from these gods, so that the division into seven parts may be a sign of the <term>Dionysian series</term> <note>The lineage or sequence of powers associated with the god Dionysus.</note>, and of that <term>dilaceration</term> <note>The ritual tearing apart of the god Dionysus by the Titans in Greek mythology, symbolizing the fragmentation of divine unity into the material world.</note> which is celebrated in fables. For it is necessary that the soul, participating in a Dionysian intellect, and, as Orpheus says, carrying the god on her head, should be divided in the same manner as he is divided; and that the harmony which she possesses in these parts should be a symbol of the <term>Apollonian order</term> <note>The principle of order, harmony, and unification associated with the god Apollo.</note>. For in the fables <note>See the translator’s "Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries."</note> respecting this god, it is Apollo who collects and unites the torn members of <term>Bacchus</term> <note>Another name for Dionysus.</note>, according to the will of his father.

In the next place, three <term>middles</term> <note>In ancient mathematics, "middles" are types of averages or proportions (geometric, harmonic, and arithmetical) that link two numbers.</note> are assumed, which not only in the soul, but also everywhere shadow forth the daughters of <term>Themis</term> <note>The goddess of divine law and order.</note>, who are three, as well as these middles: for the **geometric middle** is the image of <term>Eunomia</term> <note>The goddess of "Good Order" or "Legality."</note>; and hence in the *Laws* Plato says, that she governs political states, and is the judgment of Jupiter, adorning the universe, and containing in herself the truly political science. But the **harmonic middle** is the image of **Justice**, which distributes a greater ratio <note>For example, in the numbers 6, 4, and 3 (which are in harmonic proportion), the ratio of 6 to 4 (1.5) is greater than the ratio of 4 to 3 (1.33).</note> to greater terms, and a lesser to lesser terms, this being the employment of Justice. And the **arithmetical middle** is the image of **Peace**: for it is she, as Plato also says in the *Laws*, who attributes to all things equality according to quantity, and makes people preserve peace with people. For the <term>solid proportion</term> <note>A proportion involving three dimensions or a more complex mathematical unity.</note> prior to these is sacred to their mother Themis, who contains all the powers of these. And thus much generally respecting these three middles.

That we may, however, speak of them more particularly, it is necessary to observe that they unify and connect the essence of the soul; that is, they are unions, analogies, and bonds. Hence <term>Timæus</term> <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue of the same name.</note> also calls them bonds. For above, he says, that the geometric middle is the most beautiful of bonds, and that the others are contained in this; but every bond is a certain union. If, therefore, these middles are bonds, and bonds are unions of the things bound, the consequence is evident. These therefore pervade the whole essence of the soul, and cause it to be one out of many wholes, as they are assigned a power which can bind various forms. But these being three, the geometric binds everything which is essential in souls: for essence is one <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos"; here signifying a productive and connective principle of things, to which mathematical ratio is an analogy.</note> which pervades through all things, and connects things first, middle, and last, in the same manner.

as in the <term>geometric middle</term> <note>A proportion where the ratio between the first and second terms is the same as between the second and third (for example: 2, 4, 8, where the ratio is always 2).</note> there is one and the same ratio which perfectly pervades through three terms. The <term>harmonic middle</term> <note>A mathematical proportion often used in music theory (for example: 6, 4, 3). In Neoplatonic thought, it represents the principle of "sameness" or identity.</note> connects all the divided <term>sameness</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Sameness" and "Difference" are fundamental categories used to describe the nature of reality and the soul.</note> of souls, imparting a communion of reasons to the extremes, and a kindred conjunction; this sameness which it connects being more apparent in more total <note>Refers to "world souls" or higher, more universal souls.</note>, but less apparent in more partial <note>Refers to individual or human souls.</note> souls. And the <term>arithmetic middle</term> <note>A simple average where the difference between terms is equal (for example: 2, 4, 6). It represents "Difference."</note> binds the all-various <term>difference</term> of the progression of the soul, and is less inherent in things greater according to order, but more in such as are lesser. For difference has dominion in more partial natures, just as sameness has in such as are more total and more excellent. Those middles also may be compared with each other, in the same manner as sameness and difference: and as <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental substance or "being" of the soul.</note> is the <term>monad</term> <note>The primary unit or single source from which a series or principle originates.</note> of these, so the <term>geometric middle</term> of those. The <term>geometric middle</term> therefore is the union of all the essences which are comprehended in the <term>thirty-four terms</term> <note>A specific set of numbers used by Plato in his dialogue 'Timaeus' to map out the mathematical intervals of the World Soul.</note>. The harmonic is the union of equally numerous identities, and the arithmetic of differences; all these middles at the same time being extended through all the terms. For how could a certain whole be produced from them, unless they were as much as possible united with each other, essentially indeed by one of these, but variously by the other two? Hence these two become the supplement of the <term>geometric middle</term>, just as sameness and difference contribute to the consummation of essence; for in consequence of their possessing contrariety to each other, the <term>geometric middle</term> conciliates their dissension, and unites their interval. For the <term>harmonic middle</term>, as we have said, distributes greater ratios to greater, and lesser to lesser terms: since it evinces that things greater and more total according to essence are more comprehensive, and transcend in power subject natures. But the <term>arithmetic middle</term>, on the contrary, distributes lesser ratios to greater terms, and greater ratios to lesser terms*. For difference prevails more in subordinate natures, as, on the contrary, the dominion of sameness is more apparent in superior than in inferior natures. And the <term>geometric middle</term> extends the same ratio to all the terms, illuminating union to things first, middle, and last, through the presence of essence to all things. The <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Divine Creator of the universe in Plato's philosophy.</note>, therefore, imparts to the soul three connective unions, which <term>Plato</term> calls middles, because they appear to bind the middle order of the universe. For the geometric collects the multitude of essences, and unites essential progressions; since one

The **duad** <term>duad</term> <note>The number two, representing the first step away from unity and into diversity or "multiplicity."</note> indicates and unfolds all the progressions of essence. Hence, it is also said to be the double of the first part, as it imitates the "indefinite duad" and intelligible infinity. 

But the **third part** <note>The number three.</note> converts the whole soul back to its starting principle. It is this third part which circles back toward the source; it is measured by the first part (being filled with unity from it), but is more specifically connected to the second part. Because of this, it is said to be triple the first part, but **sesquialter** <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2, or one and a half. This is a "fifth" in musical harmony.</note> of the second; for it is contained halfway by the second part, as it does not possess equal power, but is perfectly contained by the first. 

Again, the **fourth** and **fifth** parts peculiarly show how the soul presides over secondary levels of nature. These parts are the intellectual causes of those "incorporeal" things that are divided among physical bodies, since they are **superficies** <term>superficies</term> <note>Geometric surfaces or two-dimensional planes.</note> and **tetragonic** <note>Square numbers: the fourth part is 4 (2x2) and the fifth part is 9 (3x3).</note>. This fourth part is derived from the second, while the fifth is from the third. 

*   The **fourth part** <margin>The number 4.</margin> is the source of "progression" (moving out) and generation.
*   The **fifth part** <margin>The number 9.</margin> is the source of "conversion" (turning back) and perfection.

Both are surfaces; however, one exists as the second part doubled (2x2), and the other proceeds as the third part tripled (3x3). It appears that the one <margin>Namely, 4.</margin>, imitating the process of moving toward a physical body, produces generative powers. The other <margin>Namely, 9.</margin> produces intellectual regressions <note>The "return" or "turning back" of the mind toward its source.</note>. For all knowledge "converts" the one who knows back to the thing being known, just as every nature wishes to generate and make a progression downwards.

The **sixth** and **seventh** parts insert into the soul the primary causes of physical bodies and solid shapes. These numbers are **solids** <note>Cubic numbers: 8 (2x2x2) and 27 (3x3x3).</note>; one <margin>8 is derived from 2.</margin> is derived from the second part, and the other <margin>27 is derived from 3.</margin> from the third. 

But Timaeus, in what he says here, turns the last things back to the first, and the edges of the soul back to its summit. He establishes that one part is eight times the first, and the other is twenty-seven times the first. Thus, the essence of the soul consists of seven parts, existing as it stays in place, moves forward, and returns—serving as the cause for the movement and return of both the souls within bodies and the bodies themselves.

If you like, you may also say that because the soul is granted a **hypostasis** <term>hypostasis</term> <note>An underlying reality or substance; how a thing exists in the hierarchy of being.</note> between indivisible and divisible essences, it imitates the indivisible through the **triad** <note>The number three.</note> and assumes the divisible through the **tetrad** <note>The number four.</note>. But every soul is made from all these terms, because every rational soul is the center of the whole universe. The **harmonic** and **arithmetic middles** <note>Mathematical averages used to find the "notes" between the primary numbers.</note>, therefore, fill these intervals; these have an essential existence and are considered...

We may likewise, approaching nearer to things themselves, say, that the soul, according to one part—namely, its **summit** <note>The highest, most divine point of the soul that remains in contact with pure Intellect.</note>—is united to natures prior to itself; but that, according to the **double and triple parts** <note>The numbers 2 and 3.</note>, it proceeds from intellect and returns to it; and that, according to the **double of the double**, and the **triple of the triple** <note>The numbers 4 (2x2) and 9 (3x3).</note>, it proceeds from itself, and is again converted <note>In this context, "converted" means "turned back" or "returned" to a higher state.</note> to itself; and through its own middle to the principles of its essence; for abiding according to them, it is filled from them with every thing of a secondary nature. What else then does he wish to indicate by these things, than the more partial differences of the ratios of the soul? For the **sesquialter** <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialter." A ratio of 4:3, known as a "perfect fourth."</note> of communion according to the parts in the middle; and the **sesquioctave** <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "sesquioctave." Hence the middles are conjoined with each other according to the **sesquioctave** ratio. For when they are beheld according to opposite genera, they possess the least communion: but each is appropriately conjoined with the extremes. Timæus also adds, that all the **sesquitertian** ratios are filled with the interval of the **sesquioctave** together with the **leimma**, or remainder <term>leimma</term> <note>original: "leimma." <page-num>631</page-num>
<header>ON THE TIMÆUS</header>

These points also agree with what we asserted before: that the world's total harmony is composed of four <term>octaves</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note>, along with a <term>perfect fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note> and a whole tone. For harmony exists within the physical world, within the divine intellect, and within the soul; this is why <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The main character in Plato's dialogue of the same name, representing a Pythagorean philosopher.</note> says that the soul both participates in and *is* harmony. 

However, the world participates in harmony <term>in groups of ten</term> <note>original: "decadically"</note>, the soul <term>in groups of four</term> <note>original: "tetradically"</note>, and the intellect <term>as a single unit</term> <note>original: "monadically"</note>. Just as the <term>Monad</term> <note>The number 1, representing unity.</note> is the cause of the <term>Tetrad</term> <note>The number 4.</note>, and the Tetrad is the cause of the <term>Decad</term> <note>The number 10.</note>, so too is intellectual harmony the provider of the harmony found in the soul, and the soul’s harmony is the source of the harmony we can perceive with our senses. The soul serves as the immediate model for the harmony found in the physical world. 

Since there are five geometric shapes <note>These are the five "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron (pyramid), cube, octahedron, icosahedron, and dodecahedron. Proclus notes that if you add up the sides and angles of all five, they both equal 50, a number related to the "Pentad" or 5.</note> and centers <note>These centers refer to the North, South, East, West, and the middle point between them.</note> in the universe which complete the whole, the harmony of the <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note> is the source of the musical agreement between the world’s various parts. Furthermore, because the universe is divided into nine parts <note>The five centers plus the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) found everywhere.</note>, the <term>9:8 ratio</term> <note>original: "sesquioctave ratio," the mathematical interval of a whole tone.</note> makes its connection proportionate to the soul. 

Here you may see that the soul contains the world through cause and makes it a complete whole. It harmonizes the world as a single unit, as something made of four parts, as five parts, and as a division of nine parts. For the numbers one, four, five, and nine encompass the entire numerical system by which all parts of the world are divided. This is why the ancients viewed the **Muses**, and **Apollo** as the leader of the Muses, as the rulers of the universe. Apollo provides the single, unified harmony for the whole, while the Muses connect its various divided parts. The eight **Sirens** mentioned in Plato's *Republic* also appear to complete these same numerical arrangements. 

Thus, between the one and the nine, the world is organized by the numbers four and five. It is organized by four according to the four types of living beings found in its divine model, but it is organized by five according to the five geometric shapes through which the <term>Creator</term> <note>original: "demiurgus"</note> adorned all things. As Timaeus says, the Creator introduced a "fifth idea" and arranged it harmonically throughout the universe.

## ADDITIONAL NOTES

Let us begin again, then, by stating that the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "divine craftsman" or creator-god who shapes the material world based on eternal patterns.</note> possesses a two-fold power: one that produces **sameness** and another that produces **difference**. As we learn in Plato’s *Parmenides*, he both divides and binds the soul. He is the ultimate cause of these actions so that the soul may become the "middle" of all things—being both unified and divided at the same time. This is because two things exist above the soul: the gods (who are pure unities) and "beings" (natures that are unified). Conversely, two things exist below it: those natures divided among other things <margin>Viz. corporeal forms and qualities.</margin> and those which are entirely divisible <margin>Viz. bodies.</margin>. 

You might also say that **Unity** stands above the gods and beings, while **Matter** stands below bodies. The qualities of **sameness** and **difference**, which characterize the Demiurge’s work, are what make this structure effective. The "sections" and "bonds" created by the Father <note>A title for the Demiurge.</note> serve as the original patterns for all reality. He is the first among the gods to "cut" and "bind" with unbreakable bonds. Ancient theologians hinted at these mysteries when they spoke of <term>Saturnian exsections</term> <note>original: "Saturnian exsections." This refers to the myth of Saturn (Cronus) castrating his father Uranus, which Neoplatonists interpreted as a metaphor for the way divine power divides into different levels of existence.</note> and those bonds which the creator is said to wrap around himself—a story Socrates mentions in the *Cratylus*.

We can also look at numbers as having a "formal" power regarding these divisions, for the parts of the soul are separated according to these mathematical laws. The "middles" and the "ratios" that complete these sections act like bonds. It is impossible to find "material causes" in the soul, as the soul is an <term>incorporeal essence</term> <note>A substance that has no physical body or weight.</note>. 

With these principles established, it becomes clear how the Demiurge—who oversees all division through his powers of separating and binding—divides the three-fold nature and triple mixture of the soul from its primary causes, while the soul itself remains whole and undiminished. Because he designed the soul to be a bridge between an <term>impartible essence</term> <note>Something that cannot be divided into parts, like a pure thought or a mathematical point.</note> and the nature that is divided among physical bodies, and because that indivisible essence is itself triple—**abiding**, **proceeding**, and **returning**—he created a likeness of this in the soul's three parts. 

The first part of the soul represents its **permanency** (staying still); the second part represents its **progression** (moving outward); and the third part represents its **conversion** <note>original: "conversion." In this context, it means "returning" or turning back toward the divine source.</note>. This is perhaps why the second part is said to be double the first: for anything that "proceeds" or moves out must first have a foundation that "abides." Likewise, the third part is said to be triple the first: for anything that "returns" has already proceeded and remained. Because the soul also produces the lower essences that come after it, it contains the entirety of those essences within itself. Thus, it contains every type of non-physical essence, but in a way that is...

---

->* Namely, the forms and qualities found in physical objects. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; † Namely, physical bodies.<-

And as analogy or proportion is more comprehensive than ratio, so the above-mentioned middles afford a greater cause to the soul of connecting the multitude which it contains, this cause pervading intellectually through the whole of it. The **<term>sesquialter</term>** <note>The ratio of 3:2, which creates the musical interval of a "fifth."</note>, **<term>sesquitertian</term>** <note>The ratio of 4:3, which creates the musical interval of a "fourth."</note>, and **<term>sesquioctave</term>** <note>The ratio of 9:8, representing a whole musical tone.</note> ratios are, therefore, certain bonds of a more partial nature, and are comprehended in the middles, not according to different habitudes of them with respect to the extremes, for this is mathematical, but according to causal comprehension and a more total **<term>hypostasis</term>** <note>The underlying reality or essential substance of the soul.</note>.

Again, these bonds contain the second and third progressions of the ratios; the **<term>sesquialter</term>** compressing through five centers the harmony of the ratios; the **<term>sesquitertian</term>**, through the four elements which subsist every where, evincing their power, and rendering all things known and allied to each other; and the **<term>sesquioctave</term>** harmonizing the division into nine and eight. ...is entirely evident. For if the eternal is said to be and is eternal because it participates <note>In Platonic philosophy, a thing "participates" in a higher Form to gain its qualities—for example, a beautiful thing participates in Beauty.</note> in something else, but eternity itself is never said to participate in the **<term>animal itself</term>** <note>The "Animal Itself" (*Autozoon*) is the Platonic Form of the Living Being, the divine blueprint that contains all life within it.</note>, nor does it take its name from it, then it is clear that the "eternal" thing is secondary, while eternity itself is more simple and primary. 

For eternity does not participate in the **animal itself**, because eternity is not an animal; nor is time a visible animal, or any other kind of living creature. For it has been demonstrated that the **animal itself** is "only-begotten" and eternal; therefore, eternity is more excellent than the **animal itself**. This is because an "eternal" thing is not the same as eternity itself, nor can it be better than eternity. Just as we all agree that anything possessing an intellect or a soul must come after Intellect and Soul themselves, in the same way, the "eternal" is secondary to **eternity**. 

But here someone might ask: "What can be more venerable than the **animal itself**, since Plato says it is the most beautiful of **<term>intelligibles</term>** <note>Intelligibles are realities that exist only in the realm of the mind or intellect, beyond the physical world.</note> and is perfect in every way?" 

We reply that it is the "most beautiful" because it receives the very highest peak of beauty through its intense participation in it, not because it transcends the *good*. For Plato does not say it is the *best* of intelligibles. To this we may add that it is not simply the most beautiful of all intelligibles, but specifically of all intelligible animals. Eternity, therefore, is not an animal, but is "infinite life." Furthermore, it is not necessary that something which is "perfect in every way" must be the first principle of all. For that which is "perfect" already contains all things; it contains first, middle, and last parts. But the principle that exists above such divisions must be **<term>super-perfect</term>** <note>A Neoplatonic term for a principle so unified that it exceeds the definition of "perfect," which implies a completed whole made of parts.</note>. Therefore, nothing prevents eternity from being superior to the most beautiful and perfect animal—provided that it is the "best" and "super-perfect"—since there are many different kinds of intelligible animals.

If these points are correctly argued, eternity will not be just one specific **<term>genus of being</term>** <note>Plato identifies five "Great Kinds" or genera in his dialogue *The Sophist*: Being (Essence), Rest (Permanency), Motion, Sameness, and Difference.</note>, as some have believed—such as essence, or permanency, or sameness. All of those are merely parts of the **animal itself**, and each of them has a corresponding opposite:
* **Essence** is opposed to non-being; 
* **Permanency** is opposed to motion; 
* **Sameness** is opposed to difference. 

But nothing is opposed to eternity. All of these—sameness, difference, permanency, and motion—are equally "eternal." This would not be possible if eternity were simply one of them. Eternity, therefore, is not opposed to any of these, nor to anything that comes after it. Even **Time**, which might seem to exist in a way unlike eternity, does not actually oppose it. First, Time does not occupy the same realm as eternity; it deals with things that do not derive their continuous existence directly from eternity. Second, Time is an image of eternity, not its opposite, as Plato states and as we...
