I shall shortly demonstrate this. Eternity, therefore, will not be any one **genus** <note>In this context, a "genus" refers to a primary category of being, such as Being, Rest, or Motion.</note>, nor the whole collection of the **genera of being**; for again, there would be a multitude within it, and it would require a further union of those parts into one. But Eternity is itself that which abides in unity; so if it were a collection, it would abide and yet not abide in one at the same time. It would abide as eternity and as the cause of union for all beings, but it would not abide if it were merely composed of many parts. To all this, we may add that it is **Intellect** <note>The divine mind or "Nous."</note> which encompasses the various categories of being, and the concept of intellect is different from that of eternity, in the same manner as the concept of the soul is different from that of time. For the activity of intellect is **intransitive intelligence** <note>Thought that happens all at once without moving from one idea to the next.</note>, but the activity of eternity is **impartible perpetuity** <note>An unending existence that cannot be divided into past, present, or future.</note>.

What then will eternity be, if it is neither any one of the categories of being, nor a combination of the five <note>The "Five Greatest Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Being, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion.</note>, since all these are eternal and eternity exists prior to them? What else could it be than the **monad** <note>The "Monad" is the single, primary source from which a series of things (like numbers or ideas) originates.</note> of the **intelligible unities**? By "unities," I mean the ideas of the "intelligible animals" <note>The archetypal forms of all living things that exist in the realm of pure thought.</note> and the categories of all these intellectual ideas. Eternity is, therefore, the single container of the very peak of this multitude; it is the cause of the unchanging permanence of all things. It does not exist *within* the multitude of things we can understand, nor is it just a collection of them; rather, it exists in an **exempt manner** <note>Existing independently and superior to the things it governs.</note>, being present to them and by itself organizing and forming them, making them into complete wholes. For a "perfect multitude" is not revealed all at once, nor is the diverse idea of understandable things produced immediately after the **Good** <note>The ultimate source of everything in Platonic thought.</note>; rather, there are certain natures in between. These intermediate natures are more unified than the "all-perfect multitude," but they show a **parturiency** <note>A state of being "ready to give birth" or manifest.</note> and a representation of how wholes are generated and held together within themselves. How many and of what kind these are, the gods know in a divine way, but the mystic doctrine of the *Parmenides* <note>One of Plato's most difficult and spiritual dialogues, dealing with the nature of "The One."</note> will inform us in a human and philosophical manner; we shall refer the reader to that dialogue for accurate instruction in these details. For now, we shall show that eternity is above the **all-perfect animal**, and that it sits directly above it, based on the very words of the philosopher.

Because the **animal itself** <note>The "Animal Itself" (*Autozoon*) is the divine blueprint of all life.</note> is said to be "eternal," it must be secondary to Eternity; and because there is nothing else called "eternal" that comes before it, the "animal itself" must be the very first thing that follows Eternity. How is this evident? Because, I say, there is nothing temporal that comes before the physical world—the world being the image of the "animal itself"—but the world is the first thing to participate in **time**, just as the "animal itself" is the first thing to participate in **eternity**. For if, as eternity is to time, so the **animal itself** is to...

Again, investigating on all sides the intellectual conception of the philosopher about eternity, let us consider what is the meaning of its abiding in *one*. For we inquire, in what *one*? Shall we say, in *the good*, as it has appeared to the most theological of the interpreters? But neither does *the good* abide in itself, through its simplicity, as we learn in the first hypothesis of the Parmenides <note>A dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of the "One."</note>, and therefore much less does any thing else abide in it. For, in short, nothing is in it, nor with it, in consequence of its being exempt from coordination with any thing. Hence it is not usually called good, or one, but *the good and the one*, that we may understand its monadic transcendency, and which is beyond every nature that is known. But now eternity is not said to abide in *the one*, but in one; so that neither does it abide in *the good*. Shall we say then, that by eternity abiding in one, its united nature as it were, its permanency in its own one, and its subsisting as one multitude, are implied? Or, in short, the number of that which does not proceed, that it may be the cause of union to the multitude of intelligibles? Shall we say that this also is true, that it may impart to itself the stable and the whole prior to things eternal? For to abide in one, is to have the whole and the same <term>hyparxis</term> <note>hyparxis: a technical term for a thing's fundamental subsistence or essential existence.</note> invariably present at once. Every divine nature, therefore, begins its energy from itself, so that eternity also establishes itself in one prior to things eternal; and in a similar manner connects itself. Hence being is not the cause of permanency, as Strato* the natural philosopher says it is, but eternity†; and it is the cause of a permanency, not such as is always in generation, or becoming to be, but which, as Timæus says, invariably subsists in one. But if eternity unfolds a duad, though we are often studious to conceal it; for the ever is conjoined with being, according to the same, and eternity is *that which always is* <note>original: "ἐστιν αἰών, ὁ ἀεὶ ὤν" (estin aiōn, ho aei ōn)</note>; if this be the case, it appears to have the monad of being prior to it, and the one being, viz. the highest being, and to abide in this one,

\* Strato was a philosopher of Lampsacus. He was the disciple and successor of Theophrastus; and flourished 289 years before Christ.

† For eternity is stability of being; and in like manner immortality is stability of life, and memory of knowledge.

...united, <note>Continuity from previous page: "...the multitude of intelligibles is united."</note> agreeably to the doctrine of our preceptor <note>Likely referring to Syrianus, the teacher of Proclus.</note>, that the first being may be one prior to the **duad** <note>The "duad" or dyad represents the principle of "twoness" or the first step toward multiplicity.</note>, as not departing from *the one*. And the **duad** indeed in eternity, which causally unfolds multitude, is united to the first being in which eternity abides; but the multitude of intelligibles is united to eternity itself, which in a transcendent and united manner comprehends and connects all their summits. For that the conception of the first being is different from that of eternity is evident; since to be for ever is perfectly different from simply to be. If therefore any thing is *eternal*, this also *is*; but the contrary does not follow, that if any thing *is*, this also is *eternal*. Hence, to be is more total and generative than *to be for ever*, and on this account is nearer to the cause of all beings, of the unities in beings, of generation itself, of matter, and, in short, of all things. These three, therefore, orderly succeed each other; *the one being* <note>original: "το εν ον" (to hen on); this refers to being that is characterized by and wholly absorbed in the absolute unity of "the One."</note>, as the monad of beings; *eternity* as the **duad**, together with being possessing *the ever*; and *the eternal*, which participates both of being and the ever, and is not primarily eternal being, like eternity. And *the one being* is alone the cause of being to all things, whether they are truly or not truly beings; but eternity is the cause of permanency in being. And this is what Strato <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a physicist and head of the Peripatetic school, who had a more materialistic view of being.</note> ought rather to have said, and not to have defined being to be the permanency of things, as he writes in his book *Concerning Being*, transferring the idiom of eternity to being.

->Let us now attend to the following admirable account of time, by Proclus.<-

How then is time said by Plato to be an image of eternity? Is it because eternity abides in *one*, but time proceeds according to *number*? These things however rather indicate their dissimilitude than similitude to each other. For Plato nearly opposes all things to all, *proceeding*, to *abiding*, *according to number*, to *one*, *the image* to *the thing itself*. It is better, therefore, to say, that divinity produced these two as the measures of things, I mean eternity and time, the one of intelligible <note>In this context, "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms, beyond the physical world.</note> and the other of mundane <note>Relating to the physical world or the cosmos.</note> beings. As the world, therefore, is said to be the image of the intelligible, so also the mundane measure is denominated the image of the intelligible measure. Eternity, however, is a measure as the one, but time as number: for each measures the former things <note>As the intelligible triad, or the first procession from the ineffable cause of all, consists—as will be shown in the Introduction to the Parmenides—of *being, life, and intellect*, eternity forms the middle of this triad, *being*, as Plotinus divinely says, infinite life, at once total and full, and abides in the summit of this triad, i.e., in being itself or the first and intelligible being.</note>.

But how is time said to be a moveable image of eternity? Shall we say it is because the whole of it is in motion? Or is this indeed impossible? For nothing is moved according to the whole of itself, not even such things as are essentially changed: for the underlying subject of these remains. Much more, therefore, must that which is moved according to other motions remain stable according to its essence, even if it be increased, changed, or moved from place to place. For if it did not remain stable according to something, it would simultaneously cause the motion to vanish, since all motion must occur in something. Nothing, therefore, as we have said, is moved according to the whole of itself—especially not those perpetual natures which ought to be established in their proper principles and abide in themselves if they are to be continually preserved. But in a particular manner, the image of eternity ought to possess a certain perpetuity according to sameness and stability; so it is impossible that time should be moved according to the whole of itself, since this is not possible for anything else either. Something of it, therefore, must necessarily remain, since everything which is moved is moved because it possesses something belonging to it which <gloss>stays still</gloss> <insert>abides</insert>. Time remains within its own undivided and internal power, yet it is shared by the external powers and by those natures that are measured. It moves forward according to "number"—that is, it moves in accordance with a specific intellectual number. More precisely, it follows the "first number," which, as **Parmenides** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One." Neoplatonists like Proclus interpreted his work as a map of the divine hierarchy.</note> would say, is analogous to *the one being* <note>original: "to hen on"; the first level of reality that possesses both unity and existence.</note> (the first of all beings). This number presides over the realm of the mind in the same way that the first being presides over the realm of pure existence. Time, therefore, moves according to that number, and because of this, it provides a perfectly suited measure to every form in our physical world.

You might also say more accurately that true Time moves according to number by counting those things that participate in it. Time itself is that intellectual number. **Socrates** hints at this in the *Republic* <note>Plato’s *Republic*, Book VII, where Socrates discusses how true mathematical concepts are "seen" by the mind rather than the eyes.</note> when he says that "swiftness itself" and "slowness itself" exist in "true number." These are the standards by which we determine if things measured by time move faster or slower. Because Socrates had already explained this "true number" so perfectly in the *Republic*, the character ***Timæus*** does not speak at length about it here; instead, he focuses on what comes *from* that number. While true Time follows a divine, intellectual number, the Time that ***Timæus*** describes here acts as something that can be counted—a "numerable" image of that higher, essential Time. Through this image, Time assigns different "numbers" or periods to the lives of all things: an ox lives for one specific span, a human for another, and the sun, moon, and stars complete their orbits according to their own distinct measures.

Time, then, is the "measure of motion." It is not just a tool we use to measure things, but the actual force that produces and defines the existence of life and every movement within the world. It measures these things by shaping them to look like their <term>paradigms</term> <note>The eternal "blueprints" or "forms" of things that exist in the divine mind.</note>. Just as Time models itself after Eternity (which contains all these blueprints), it guides the things perfected by it—which move in circles—back toward a noble imitation of those eternal principles. Because of this, <term>theurgists</term> <note>Practitioners of "divine work" or ritual magic intended to unite the soul with the gods.</note> say that Time is a god. They even provide methods for us to call upon this deity so he may reveal himself. They praise him as being both "older and younger" and as a "circulating and eternal God." He is not just a shadow of eternity; he holds eternity within himself even before it reaches our physical senses. They add that he intellectually understands the total "number" of every nature moving in the world, and by this knowledge, he guides their cycles and restores

After all, what benefit would there be for all things in the world to be well-ordered if they did not also have a lasting existence? This is why the philosopher places the cause of time's progression in the Creator, not just in the soul.

Next, looking at the facts themselves, one could say that if the soul created time, the soul would not be "perfected" by time. Yet it is obvious that the soul *is* perfected and measured by time in its activities. This is because anything that does not possess its full power all at once requires time to reach its completion and restoration. Through time, the soul gathers its own "good," which it was unable to grab all at once without the cycles of time. Time, therefore, while it abides, moves in measure; and through its abiding, its measured motions are infinite, and are restored to their pristine state. For moving in measure, the first of intellects about the whole fabrication of things, so far as it perpetually subsists after the same manner, and is intellect according to essence, it is said to be eternal; but so far as it moves in measure, it circularly leads souls, and natures, and bodies, and, in short, periodically restores them to their pristine condition. For the world is moved indeed, as participating of soul; but it is moved in an orderly manner, because it participates of intellect; and it is moved periodically with a motion from the same to the same, imitating the permanency of the intellect which it contains, through the resemblance of time to eternity. And this it is to make the world more similar to its paradigm; viz. by restoring it to one and the same condition, to assimilate it to that which abides in one, through the circulation according to time. ## ADDITIONAL NOTES

[Lead]-ing the same <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "circularly leading the soul..."</note> separate from all inequality, being energetic and restorative of all natural motions, of which it is also the measure. It also exists unmingled with the natures that it measures, according to its own intellectual energy, but it proceeds transitively—moving across things—and according to its unique quality of self-motion. In this respect, it aligns with the order of the **soul**, but it is inherently present in those things that are bounded and perfected by it as a primary cause of nature. It is not, however, exactly similar in all respects to any one thing. For it is necessary that the measure of the whole should be similar to all things and allied to all things, yet not be identical to any single thing being measured.

The motion of time, therefore, progresses by unfolding and dividing a power that is <term>impartible</term> <note>Meaning "indivisible" or "without parts"—a unified spiritual power.</note> and eternal, causing it to appear as if it has parts. It acts as a certain kind of number, receiving all the forms of the <term>monad</term> <note>The "Monad" is the ultimate principle of unity from which all plurality or "number" emerges.</note> in a divisible way, and then circling back to itself. For in this way, the motion of time—proceeding according to the measures within the "temporal monad"—links the end with the beginning infinitely. It possesses a divine order; as the philosopher <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A prominent Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who specialized in the mystical and mathematical interpretation of Plato.</note> says, it is not an order that is merely arranged by something else, but that which does the arranging; it is not an order that follows after previous things, but is the primary leader of all effects. 

This motion is also, at the same time, "measured." This measurement does not come from anything physical or anything that has <term>interval</term> <note>Meaning spatial extension or physical distance.</note>, for it would be ridiculous to suggest that things of a more ancient nature and higher dignity are measured by things that are lower than them. Instead, it is measured by the "temporal monad" alone (which its own progression unfolds) and, with much greater priority, by the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The divine "Craftsman" or Creator-God who brings order to the universe.</note> and by eternity itself. 

In relation to eternity—which is perfectly immovable—time is described as "movable." This is just as one might say that the **soul** is "divisible" among bodies when compared to the **intellect**. It does not mean the soul is *only* divisible, but that when compared to the pure intellect, it may appear so, even though it is indivisible when compared to a physical body. Time, therefore, is not "movable" in itself, but appears so through the way motions participate in it, and by which they are measured and bounded. It is like saying the soul is "divided" among bodies simply because there is a certain divided participation of it within them, even though the soul contains the cause of those bodies. For in this way also, time is "movable" because it possesses the cause of the energy that proceeds externally from it, which appears divided within motions and is separated along with them. Just as motions become "temporal" through their participation in time, so time is called "movable" because it is shared by those motions.

<summary>This page explains that Time acts as a divine, arranging principle that translates eternal, indivisible power into the divisible, circular motions of the physical world. It clarifies that while Time is "movable" compared to the stillness of Eternity, it remains a superior, governing cause that is not measured by the physical things it regulates.</summary>

The demiurgic wholeness <note>The complete, creative power of the Demiurge (the divine Creator).</note>, says Proclus (p. 266), weaves parts in conjunction with wholes, numbers with monads <note>A 'monad' is a primary unit or a principle of unity from which a series of numbers or beings arises.</note>, and makes every part of the universe to be a world, and causes a whole and a universe to subsist in a part. For the world is allotted this from its similitude to **animal itself** <note>In Platonic philosophy, 'Animal itself' (Autozoon) is the eternal, intelligible Archetype or 'Form' of all living creatures.</note>, because animal itself is an entire monad and number, an all-perfect intelligible intellect, and a plenitude of intelligible causes, which it generated so as to abide eternally in itself. For there is one multitude which abides in causes, and another which proceeds and is distributed; since the demiurgus <note>The divine Craftsman of the world.</note> himself also gives subsistence to some genera of gods in himself, and produces others from himself, into secondary and third orders. 

His father Saturn <note>The Greek god Cronus, representing a higher intellectual order in Neoplatonism.</note> likewise generates some divinities as paradigmatic causes <note>The original patterns or blueprints for creation.</note> of fabrication abiding in himself, and others as demiurgic causes coordinated with wholes. And the grandfather of Jupiter <note>The Greek god Zeus.</note>, Heaven <note>The Greek god Uranus.</note>, contains some divinities in, and separates others from himself. Theologists also manifest these things by mystic names, such as *concealment, absorption, and the being educated by Fate.* 

But by a great priority to these, intelligible intellect, the father of wholes, generates some causes, and unfolds them into light, in himself, but produces others from himself; containing within his own comprehensions, such as are uniform, whole, and all-perfect, but producing through difference into other orders such as are multiplied and divided. Since therefore every paternal order gives subsistence to things after this manner, this world, which is an imitation of the intelligible orders, and is elevated to them, very properly contains one *allness* <note>The state of being a complete whole (Greek: 'holotes').</note> prior to partial animals, and another, that which receives its completion from them, and together with the former receives the latter, that it may be most similar both to the demiurgic and paradigmatic cause.

In short, if **animal itself** were the second, eternity would be being; but this is impossible: for being itself is one thing, and eternal being another; the former being the monad <note>A 'monad' is a single, indivisible unit that acts as the source for a series.</note> of being, and the latter the duad <note>A 'duad' represents the principle of duality or the first step away from absolute unity.</note>, having the "ever" connected with being. For **animal itself** must necessarily in a certain respect be intellect, since the image of it entirely subsists with sense, but sense is the image of intellect; so that in that which is primarily animal, intellect will be primarily inherent. If therefore it is secondary to life, it must necessarily subsist according to intelligible intellect: for being intelligible, and an animal, as Plato says, the most beautiful of intelligibles, and only begotten, it will possess this order. God, being himself intellectual, in consequence of containing the whole of an intelligible essence, formal divisions, and the intelligible number, which Plato indicating denominates the ideas of the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine craftsman described in Plato's Timaeus who shapes the material world based on eternal patterns.</note>, *such and so many*, by the former of these appellations manifesting the <term>idioms</term> <note>original: "idioms"; here meaning the unique properties or specific characteristics that distinguish one divine cause from another.</note> of causes, and by the latter, *separation according to number*.

If these things then subsist after this manner, it is not proper to place an infinity of forms in intelligibles: for that which is definite is more allied to principles than the indefinite; and first natures are always more contracted in quantity, but transcend in power natures posterior to and proceeding from them. Nor must we say with some, that <term>animal itself</term> <note>The "animal itself" (Greek: *autozoon*) refers to the "Living Being in itself"—the eternal archetype or blueprint of all life in the universe.</note> is separate from the demiurgus, thus making the intelligible to be external to intellect: for we do not make that which is seen subordinate to that which sees, that it may be external, but we assert that it is prior to it: and more divine intelligibles are understood by such as are more various, as being contained in them; since our soul also entering into itself, is said to discover all things, divinity and wisdom, as Socrates asserts. Animal itself therefore is prior and not external to the demiurgus. And there indeed all things subsist totally and intelligibly, but in the demiurgus intellectually and separately: for in him the definite causes of the sun and moon presubsist, and not one idea alone of the celestial gods, which gives subsistence to all the celestial <term>genera</term> <note>Latin for "kinds" or "classes."</note>. Hence the <term>Chaldæan Oracles</term> <note>A collection of mystical philosophical texts from the 2nd century AD, highly revered by later Platonists as divine revelations.</note> assert *, that his demiurgic energies burst about the bodies of the world like swarms of bees <note>This famous image describes how divine creative power multiplies and spreads into every corner of the material universe without losing its essential unity.</note>: for a divine intellect evolves into every demiurgic multitude the *total* separation of these energies in intellect.

...these at once. Agreeably to this, the discourse of Plato first divinely unfolds the whole number of <term>intelligible ideas</term> <note>Ideas that exist in the realm of pure thought or intellect, serving as the eternal blueprints for everything in the physical world.</note>, and afterwards distributes into parts the progressions which this number contains: for there intelligible multitude is apparent, where the first monads of ideas subsist. And that this is usual with Plato we have before abundantly shown. 

Descending therefore from words to things, let us in the first place see what this <term>tetrad</term> <note>The "tetrad" refers to the number four, which Neoplatonic philosophers viewed as a symbol of completion and the foundation of the physical world's structure.</note> itself of ideas is, and whence this number originates, and in the next place what the four ideas are, and how they subsist in <term>animal itself</term> <note>The "Living Being in itself" (Greek: *autozoon*), which is the single, eternal model containing the blueprints for every kind of living creature.</note>, whether so as that its all-perfect nature receives its completion from these, or after some other manner; for by thus proceeding we shall discover the divinely intellectual conception of Plato. 

It is necessary, however, again to recur to the above-mentioned demonstrations, in which we said that the first, united, and most simple intelligible essence of the gods, proceeding supernally from the unity of unities, but according to a certain mode which is ineffable and incomprehensible by all things, one part of this essence ranks as the first, is occult and paternal; but another part ranks as the second, and is the one power, and incomprehensible measure of wholes; and the third part is that which has proceeded into energy and all various powers, and is at the same time both paternal and fabricative. 

The first of these also is a <term>monad</term> <note>The "Monad" is the principle of absolute unity or "the one."</note>, because it is the summit of the whole intelligible extent, and the fountain and cause of divine numbers; but the second is a <term>duad</term> <note>The "Duad" represents the principle of "two" or duality, marking the first step toward multiplicity and creative power.</note>, for it both abides and proceeds as in intelligible genera, and has the *ever* connected with being; and the third is the tetrad which is now investigated, which receives all the occult cause of the monad, and unfolds in itself its unproceeding power. For such things as subsist in the monad primarily, and with unproceeding union, the tetrad exhibits in a divided manner, now separated according to number, and a production into secondary natures. 

But since the third possesses an order adapted to it, yet also entirely participates of the causes prior to itself, it is not only the tetrad, but besides this which is still greater, as a monad it is allotted a paternal, and as a duad a fabricative and prolific transcendency. So far therefore as it is called animal itself, it is the monad of the nature of all animals, intellectual, vital, and corporeal; but so far as it comprehends at the same time the male and female nature, it is a duad; for these subsist in an appropriate manner in all the orders of animals, in one way in the gods, in another in <term>dæmons</term> <note>In this context, "dæmons" are not evil beings, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the divine gods and mortal humans.</note>, and in another in mortals; but so far as from this duad, it gives subsistence to the four ideas of animals in itself, it is a tetrad; for the fourfold fabrication of things proceeds according to these ideas, and the first productive...

<summary>This page explains the metaphysical progression from divine unity (the Monad) to multiplicity (the Tetrad), illustrating how the "animal itself" serves as the eternal blueprint for all life. It describes how the single source of creation divides into the various categories of gods, spirits, and mortal beings.</summary>

It explains how the universe transitions from a single, unified source (the Monad) through a duality (the Duad) and settles into a foundational four-fold structure (the Tetrad). This tetrad serves as the blueprint for all living things within the world, leading eventually to the "decad" or the perfected ten-fold order of the physical cosmos.</meta>

->654<-

## ADDITIONAL NOTES

<sig>In</sig>

The cause of all wholes is the <term>tetrad</term> <note>The number four. In Pythagorean philosophy, the tetrad was seen as the root of all things and the most perfect number because it builds the first solid figure (a pyramid).</note>. Plato, therefore, teaching this four-fold power of the archetype and the most unified ideas of worldly natures, says that they are four, contained within the **living being in itself** <note>The *autozoon*, or the eternal, spiritual "Animal" that contains the blueprints for every creature that will ever exist.</note>. For there is one idea there, the Living Being itself; and there is also a <term>duad</term> <note>The number two, representing the first movement away from unity toward multiplicity.</note>, namely, the female and the male, or, according to Plato, containing general categories and specific types: for he calls two of the ideas **genera**, namely, those that are intellectual and those that wander through the air, but the other two **species**, as they are subordinate to these. 

There is also a tetrad; and up to this point, the <term>intelligible forms</term> <note>The eternal, perfect templates of things that exist in the divine mind.</note> proceed into other productive principles according to a different number. For according to every level of reality there is an appropriate number: a smaller number encompasses more universal ideas, while a larger, more multiplied number encompasses more specific ones. This is because more divine natures, being concentrated in quantity, possess a greater power; the forms of secondary natures are more numerous than those that came before them. Thus, intellectual forms are more numerous than the "intelligibles" that precede them, those above the world are more numerous than the intellectual ones, and the forms within the physical world are more numerous than those above it. These, then, are the forms which reach the final stage of distribution, just as the intelligibles receive the highest union: for all progression away from the source diminishes power and increases the number of things. 

If, therefore, Timaeus had been speaking about a specific intellectual order, he would have mentioned another number, such as the <term>hebdomad</term> <note>The number seven, often associated with the soul and the moving planets.</note> or the <term>decad</term> <note>The number ten.</note>; but since he speaks about the **intelligible cause** of ideas—which contains all living things that can be thought—he says that the first ideas are four. For there the tetrad exists, proceeding from the <term>intelligible monad</term> <note>The "Monad" is the number one, representing the ultimate, single source of all existence.</note>, and filling the **creative ten** <note>The "demiurgic decad," the full set of ten principles used by the divine creator to build the universe.</note>.

For "the divine number, according to the Pythagorean hymn upon it, proceeds from the hidden places of the undecaying monad, until it arrives at the divine tetrad, which produces the mother of all things, the universal receiver, who is worthy of honor, setting a boundary around all things, steady and tireless, whom both the immortal gods and earth-born men call the sacred **decad**." 

Here the unified and hidden cause of **being** <note>The summit of the intelligible triad, or reality that exists beyond even essence itself.</note> is called the "undecaying monad" and the "hidden places of the monad." However, the manifestation of the vast number of thoughts, which the duad (existing between the one and the four) unfolds, is called the "divine tetrad." Finally, the world itself—which receives the images of all these divine numbers sent down to it from above—is the **decad** (ten): for we may understand these verses as looking toward the creation of the physical world. And this is enough concerning this tetrad.

<note>The last line of these verses, namely, "immortal gods and earth-born men," <note>original: "αθανατοι τε θεοι, και γηγενεεις ανθρωποι"</note> is not found in Proclus, but is added from the Commentaries of Syrianus on Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, where alone it is to be found.</note>
<note>Namely: The summit of the intelligible triad, or super-essential being.</note>

->655<-

### ON THE TIMÆUS

In the next place, let us consider what the four <term>ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal, perfect blueprints in the divine mind that serve as the models for everything in the physical world.</note> are, and what are the things to which they give subsistence: for there are different opinions concerning this. Some especially regarding the words of Plato, asserting that the progression is into gods and the mortal genera <note>The different "kinds" or categories of life.</note>, but others looking to things, that it is into gods and the <term>genera superior to man</term> <note>Referring to higher spiritual beings like angels or daemons that sit between gods and humans in the cosmic hierarchy.</note>, because these exist prior to mortals, and it is necessary that the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Divine Architect" or "Craftsman" who shapes the physical universe using the eternal Ideas as his guide.</note> should not immediately produce mortals from divine natures. 

Others again combine both these views, and follow what is written in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato or his student Philip of Opus, serving as an appendix to the *Laws*.</note>, that gods exist in the heavens, <term>dæmons</term> <note>From the Greek 'daimon'; these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guardian beings that bridge the gap between gods and men.</note> in the air, demigods in water, and men and other mortal animals in the earth. Such then being the diversity of opinion among the interpreters, we admire indeed the "lovers of things" <note>Those who focus on the nature of reality itself rather than just the literal text.</note>, but we shall endeavour to follow our leader <note>original: "Syrianus," the teacher of Proclus and a major figure in Neoplatonism.</note>. 

Hence we say that the **celestial genus of gods** comprehends all the celestial genera, whether they are divine, angelic, or dæmoniacal; but the **air-wandering**, all such as are arranged in the air, whether gods, or their attendant dæmons, or mortal animals that live in the air. Again, that the **aquatic** comprehends all the genera that are allotted water, and those natures that are nourished in water; and the **pedestrian**, the animals that are distributed about the earth, and that subsist and grow in the earth. For the demiurgus is at once the cause of all mundane <note>Worldly or cosmic.</note> natures, and the common father of all things, generating the divine and dæmoniacal genera by and through himself alone, but delivering mortals to the **junior gods** <note>Subordinate divine powers who handle the creation of physical, perishable bodies.</note>, as they are able proximately to generate them. The <term>paradigm</term> <note>The eternal "Model" or "Pattern" of the universe.</note> also is not the cause of some, but by no means of other animals, but it possesses the most total causes of all things.

It is also requisite to consider the proposed words in an appropriate manner, according to every order; as, for instance, the genus of gods arranged in the heavens, in one way, in those that are properly called gods, and in another, in the genera more excellent than man. For we say that there are celestial angels, dæmons, and heroes, and that all these are called gods, because the <term>divine idiom</term> <note>The essential "character" or "property" of divinity.</note> has dominion over their essential peculiarity. Again, we must consider the **winged** and **air-wandering** in one way in the aërial gods, in another in dæmons, and in another in mortals. For that which is **intellectual** in the gods is denominated **winged**; that which is **providential** <note>Relating to the divine care and direction of the world.</note>, **air-wandering**, as pervading through all the sphere of the air, and connectedly containing the whole of it. But in dæmons, the **winged** signifies rapidity of energy; and the **air-wandering** indicates their being everywhere present, and proceeding through all things without impediment.

<note>This refers to Syrianus, the preceptor of Proclus.</note>

<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

## ADDITIONAL NOTES

In the realm of mortals, the **winged** nature manifests as the motion of a single organ; however, in those higher natures that use only circular motion, it represents the power of that movement. Meanwhile, the **air-wandering** nature signifies the various ways beings move through physical bodies, for nothing prevents <term>partial souls</term> <note>Individual souls, such as those of humans or animals, as opposed to the "Universal Soul" that animates the entire cosmos.</note> that inhabit the air from traveling through it. Furthermore, the **aquatic** nature in divine beings indicates a form of leadership that is inseparable from the element of water; this is why the <term>oracle</term> <note>Likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, a sacred text used by Neoplatonists to provide divine authority for their philosophical systems.</note> calls these gods *water-walkers*. Among the spirits who serve the gods, this term signifies a power that holds moisture together. Finally, the **pedestrian** (or walking) nature can mean two things: in one context, it describes the power that governs the lowest levels of existence; in another, it refers to the governance of different parts of the earth at different times through specific movements. This concludes our discussion on these names.

From these points, we can conclude that the <term>intelligible animal itself</term> <note>The "Intelligible Animal" or "Animal-itself" is the ultimate, abstract blueprint of life that exists in the highest realm of reality.</note> is entirely different from the "animal" as it exists within the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The Divine Architect or Creator. While the "Animal-itself" is the pure Idea, the Demiurge is the mind that uses that Idea to build the universe.</note>. The former does not contain the specific, limited ideas of mortal animals. Because the Demiurge wanted to make the physical world a reflection of himself, he created mortal animals to make the world "all-perfect." He holds the specific blueprints for these mortals, deriving them from the immortal categories. He knows mortal animals and understands them *formally* <note>Meaning he understands their essential "Form" or design, rather than just knowing them as physical things.</note>. He intends for the <term>junior gods</term> <note>Lower-ranking deities who, in Platonic thought, are tasked with the "hands-on" work of crafting physical bodies for mortal creatures.</note> to look to him as their model—rather than looking directly at the "Animal-itself"—when they craft these creatures. This is because the Demiurge keeps the ideas of mortals and immortals distinct within himself. In the "Animal-itself," there was only one unified idea for each category (aerial, aquatic, or terrestrial). But in the Demiurge, these are divided: some ideas are for immortal aerial beings, and others are for mortal aerial beings, and the same applies to the water and land categories. Therefore, the "formal multitude" (the variety of designs) in the original Idea is not the same as the variety found in the Demiurge.

We can also see that Plato divides these categories into a **monad** (a single unit) and a **triad** (a group of three), while also using two **duads** (pairings). He does this by setting the highest "celestial" category apart from the other general groups. He calls the celestial and the winged types "genera" (broad families), but describes the aquatic and pedestrian types as "species." The...

the latter possessing an order subordinate to the former, in the same manner as species relates to genus. It is likewise requisite to observe that <term>Plato</term> omits the region of fire in these categories, because the divine genus comprehends the summit of fire. For among **sublunary** <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to everything below the orbit of the Moon—the Earthly world where things are subject to change, birth, and death.</note> bodies, fire does not have any proper region of its own, but exists only through **mutation** <note>In this context, "mutation" refers to the constant process of elements transforming into one another.</note> alone, always requiring the nourishment of air and water. For its proper place, as fire, is on high; but it is not found there in its pure form, since it would be seen (being naturally visible), nor can it arrive there, as it is extinguished by the surrounding air, which is dissimilar to it. 

If, therefore, it is necessary that there should be a "wholeness" of fire, and that possessing a specific form it should exist somewhere—rather than just existing in a state of being generated—and if there is no such fire under the moon, then fire must exist solely in the heavens, remaining as it is and always possessing its proper place. For an upward motion is not a property of fire when it exists according to its own nature, but is only a characteristic of fire when it is existing "contrary to nature" <note>Ancient philosophers believed that an element only moves when it is out of its natural place; once it reaches its "home," it remains still or moves in a perfect circle.</note>. 

Thus also the <term>Sacred Discourse of the Chaldæans</term> <note>This refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a mystical text that Neoplatonists considered to be divine revelation, often used to supplement Plato's philosophy.</note> connects aerial things with the lunar "rattlings," attributing the celestial region to fire, according to the division of the elements in the world. For the fire found in **generation** <note>The realm of "generation" is the physical, changing world we inhabit.</note> is a certain downward flow of the celestial fire, and it dwells in the cavities of the other elements. There is not, however, a separate sphere of fire by itself; rather, the summit of the air imitates the purity of the fire above. We call this sublunary fire, and we call the region under the heavens the <term>place of fire</term>: for this is most similar to the celestial depths, just as the edge of the air is similar to water, which is thick and dark. 

But you should not wonder if the most refined and pure fire is found at the summits of the air, while the most thick and turbid fire is in the heart of the earth. We do not consider this pure fire to be a "wholeness" distinct from the air itself, but rather consider it to be so refined that it is carried within the narrowest pores of the air. It is not seen for two reasons: because it is not distinct from the air, and because it consists of the smallest possible parts. Thus, it does not resist our sight in the same way the light of visible objects does. True fire, therefore, exists in the heavens; but of the fire below the moon, that which is most pure is in the air closest to the celestial regions—which <term>Plato</term> in the course of this Dialogue calls <term>æther</term> <note>The "ether" was often described as the fifth element or the most refined form of fire/air.</note>—and that which is most thick and heavy is contained in the depths of the earth.

* Agreeably to this, <term>Plotinus</term> <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founding philosopher of Neoplatonism.</note> observes, that every body, when in its proper place, is either at rest, or moves circularly.

-># INTRODUCTION<-

->### TO<-

->## THE PARMENIDES.<-

---

**IT** was the custom of Pythagoras and his followers, amongst whom **Plato** holds the most distinguished rank, to conceal divine mysteries under the veil of symbols and figures; to dissemble their wisdom against the arrogant boastings of the Sophists <note>The Sophists were itinerant teachers in ancient Greece often criticized by Plato for prioritizing rhetorical persuasion and profit over the pursuit of objective truth.</note>; to jest seriously, and sport in earnest. Hence, in the following most important dialogue, under the appearance of a certain dialectic <term>dialectic: a method of philosophical inquiry through dialogue, which Taylor identifies here as a spiritual tool rather than just a logical exercise</term> sport, and, as it were, logical discussion, Plato has delivered a complete system of the profound and beautiful theology of the Greeks. For it is not to be supposed that he, who in all his other dialogues introduces discussions adapted to the character of the principal speaker, should in this dialogue deviate from his general plan, and exhibit Parmenides, a venerable and aged philosopher, engaged in the puerile <note>Meaning "childish" or "trivial."</note> exercise of a merely logical disputation. Besides, it was usual with the Pythagoreans and Plato to form an harmonious conjunction of many materials in one subject, partly in imitation of nature, and partly for the sake of elegance and grace. Thus, in the *Phædrus*, Plato mingles oratory with theology; in the *Timæus*, mathematics with physics; and in the present dialogue, dialectic with divine speculations.

<margin>¹ In manuscript: Commentary on the Parmenides, Book 1 <note>original: "Comment. in Parmenidem, lib. i."</note></margin>

But the reader must not suppose that the dialectic of Plato is the same with vulgar dialectic, which is conversant with opinion, and is accurately investigated in Aristotle’s *Topics*: for the business of this first of sciences, which at present is utterly unknown, is to employ definitions, divisions, analyzations, and demonstrations, as primary sciences in the investigation of causes; imitating the progressions of beings from the first principle of things, and their continual conversion to it, as the ultimate object of desire. “But there are three energies,” says Proclus ¹ <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentaries on Plato deeply influenced Taylor's interpretations.</note>, “of this most scientific method:

the first of which is adapted to youth, and is useful for the purpose of rousing their intellect, which is, as it were, in a dormant state; for it is a true exercise of the eye of the soul in the speculation of things, leading forth through opposite positions the essential impression of reasons <term>reasons: here referring to the *logoi*, the inner rational principles or blueprints of reality contained within the soul</term> which it contains, and considering not only the divine path, as it were, which conducts to truth, but exploring whether the deviations from it contain any thing worthy of belief; and, lastly, stimulating the all-various conceptions of the soul. But the second energy takes place when intellect rests from its former investigations, as becoming most familiar with the speculation of beings, and beholds truth itself firmly established upon a pure and holy foundation. And this energy, according to Socrates, by a progression through ideas, evolves the whole of an intelligible nature <term>intelligible nature: the realm of pure reality that can only be grasped by the mind, beyond the physical senses</term>, till it arrives at that which is first; and this by analysing, defining, demonstrating, and dividing, proceeding upwards and downwards, till, having entirely investigated the nature of intelligibles, it raises itself to a nature superior to beings <note>This refers to the "One" or the ultimate Source, which Neoplatonists believed was beyond even the concept of 'Being.'</note>. But the soul being perfectly established in this nature, as in her paternal port <note>A poetic Neoplatonic metaphor for the soul's return to its divine origin.</note>, no longer tends to a more excellent object of desire, as she has now arrived at the end of her search: and you may say that what is delivered in the *Phaedrus* and *Sophist* <note>original Latin: "Phædrus and Sophista"</note> is the employment of this energy, giving a twofold division to some, and a fourfold to other operations of the dialectic art; and on this account it is assigned to such as philosophize purely, and no longer require preparatory exercise, but nourish the intellect of their soul in pure intellection <term>intellection: the act of direct intellectual perception or spiritual understanding</term>. But the third energy, which is exhibitive according to truth, purifies from twofold ignorance <note>A state where one is ignorant, but believes they possess knowledge.</note> when its reasons are employed upon men full of opinion; and this is spoken of in the *Sophist*.” So that the dialectic energy is triple, either subsisting through opposite arguments, or alone unfolding truth, or alone confuting falsehood.

Parmenides by means of this dialectic perfects the conceptions of Socrates about ideas. For, as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentaries on Plato deeply influenced Taylor.</note> well observes, the mode of discourse is every where obstetric <term>obstetric: from the Greek *maieutikos*, referring to the "midwifery" method where the philosopher helps others bring forth their own latent wisdom</term>, but does not confute; and is explorative, but not defensive. But it differs, considered as sometimes proceeding from on high to such things as are last, and sometimes ascending from sensible particulars to such reasons as are accommodated to divine causes; but, according to each of these, it elevates Socrates, calls forth his native conceptions concerning ideas, and causes them to possess an expanded distinction. ->### THE PARMENIDES.<-

In this respect, says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato's works.</note>, Parmenides truly imitates the fatherly cause of the universality of things, who, from the supreme foundation <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or essential substance of all beings</term> of all beings, preserves and perfects all things, and draws them upwards by his unknown and ineffable powers.

With respect to the dramatic apparatus <note>The "dramatic apparatus" refers to the setting, characters, and framing story of the dialogue.</note> of this dialogue, it is necessary to observe that the Athenians had two festivals in honor of Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, the patron goddess of Athens.</note>; the former of which, on account of the greater preparation required in its celebration, was called *the greater Panathenaia*; and the latter, on account of its requiring a less apparatus, was denominated *the lesser Panathenaia* <term>Panathenaia: the city's most important religious festival, involving a procession, athletic games, and poetic recitations</term>. The celebration of them, likewise, was distinguished by longer and shorter periods of time. In consequence, therefore, of the greater festival taking place, sacred to Minerva, Parmenides and Zeno came to Athens, Parmenides being the master, and Zeno his disciple; but both of them Eleatics <note>Followers of the Eleatic school of philosophy, which originated in Elea (Southern Italy) and famously argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One."</note>—and not only this, says Proclus, but partakers of the Pythagorean doctrine, according to the relation of Callimachus the historian.

Parmenides and Zeno, therefore, in a place called the Ceramicus <note>The "Potters' Quarter" of Athens, located just outside the city walls and famous for its public cemetery and monuments.</note>, beyond the walls of the city, and which was sacred to the statues of the Gods, met with one Pythodorus, together with Socrates and many other Athenians, who came thither for the purpose of hearing the writings of Zeno. The ensuing dialogue, which was the consequence of Zeno's discourse, was afterwards related by Pythodorus to one Antiphon, the brother on the mother's side of Adimantus and Glaucus, who were the brothers of Plato, both from the same father and mother; and the dialogue is supposed to be again related by Antiphon to Cephalus and his companions, in consequence of their soliciting Adimantus and Glaucus to request Antiphon for the narration.

Zeno, therefore, having read to the audience a book, in which he endeavoured to exhibit the difficulties attending the doctrine which asserts the existence of *the many* <note>The philosophical view that the world is made of many distinct, separate things, which Zeno argued led to logical absurdities.</note>, and this in order to defend the favourite dogma of Parmenides, who called *being, the One*; Socrates by no means opposes his arguments, but readily admits the errors which must ensue from supposing multitude to exist, without participating in *the One*. However, Socrates does not rest here, but urges Zeno to a speculation of *the One* and the unities which subsist in intelligible natures <term>intelligible natures: the realm of pure reality and Forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</term>, not enduring to dwell on the contemplation of *the One* which sensible things contain: and this leads him to the investigation of ideas in which the unities of things reside. After this Parmenides,

# INTRODUCTION TO

not in the least contradicting Socrates, but completing the contemplation which he had begun, unfolds the entire doctrine of ideas, introducing for this purpose four questions concerning them: whether they have a subsistence <term>subsistence: a term used in Platonism to describe the real, independent existence of a thing</term>; of what things there are ideas, and of what not; what kind of beings they are, and what power they possess: and how they are participated by subordinate natures <note>This refers to the way physical things in the world "share in" or reflect the perfect, eternal Ideas.</note>. And this being discussed, Parmenides ascends from *hence to the one* which subsists above intelligibles <term>intelligibles: realities that can only be perceived by the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses</term> and ideas, and adduces nine hypotheses concerning it; five, supposing *the one* to have a subsistence, and four, supposing it not to subsist; accurately investigating, at the same time, the consequences resulting from these hypotheses. But of this more hereafter.

With respect to ideas, though many invincible arguments may be adduced for their existence, the following appear to me remarkable for their perspicuity and strength. Diversity of powers always indicates diversity of objects. But it is obvious to every one, that the power of intellect is different from the power of sense; that which is sensible, therefore, is one thing, and that which is intelligible another. And as intellect is superior to sense, so is intelligible more excellent than that which is sensible. But that which is sensible has an existence; and by a much greater reason, therefore, that which is intelligible must have a real subsistence. But intelligible is a certain universal species <note>A "universal species" is a general form or concept—for example, the idea of "Humanity" rather than a specific individual human.</note>; for universal reason is always the object of intelligence. And hence there are such things as intelligible and common species of things which we call ideas.

Again, all corporeal <term>corporeal: having a physical body; material</term> natures subsist in time; but whatever subsists in time is measured by time; and whatever is thus conditioned depends on time for the perfection of its being. But time is composed of the past, present, and future. And if we conceive that any one of these periods is taken away from the nature with which it is connected, that nature must immediately perish. Time, therefore, is so essentially and intimately united with the natures which it measures, that their being, such as it is, depends on the existence of time. But time, as is evident, is perpetually flowing, and this in the most rapid manner imagination can conceive. It is evident, therefore, that the natures to which it is so essential must subsist in a manner equally transitory and flowing. As we cannot, therefore, affirm with propriety, of any part of time that it *is*, since even before we can form the assertion

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's Parmenides. # THE PARMENIDES.

the present time is no more, so with respect to all <term>corporeal natures: physical or bodily things</term> (from their <term>subsistence: existence as an independent, underlying reality</term> in time), before we can say that they exist, they lose all identity of being. And hence no one of them is truly that which it is said to be. On the contrary, truth is eternal and immutable: for, if any one should assert that truth is not, he asserts this either truly or falsely; but if falsely, there is such a thing as truth; and if truly, then it is true that there is no such thing as truth. But if it is truly asserted, it can only be true through truth; and, consequently, there is such a thing as truth, which must also be eternal and immutable. Hence, truth cannot subsist in any thing mutable; for that which is situated in a mutable nature is also changed in conjunction with it. But all corporeal natures are continually changed, and hence they are neither true, nor have a true existence. If, therefore, the forms of bodies are imperfect, they are not the first forms; for whatever ranks as first is perfect and entire, since the <term>whole reason: the complete rational principle or definition</term> of every nature is established in that which is first. There are, therefore, certain forms above these, perfect, primary, and entire, and which are not <note>indigent of: needing or dependent upon</note> a subject.

But if the forms of bodies are not true, where do the true forms subsist? Shall we say nowhere? But in this case falsehood would be more powerful than truth, if the former possessed, and the latter had no, subsistence. But this is impossible. For that which is more powerful derives its power from truth; since, unless it was truly more powerful, it would not be that which it is said to be. But, indeed, without the presence of truth, the forms which are said to be false could not subsist; for they would no longer be what they are, unless it was true that they are false. True <term>species: here used as a synonym for the "Forms" or "Ideas"</term>, therefore, have a subsistence somewhere. But does not our soul possess truer species than those which are the objects of <note>sensible inspection: observation through the physical senses</note>, by which it judges, condemns, and corrects them, and understands how far they depart from, and in what respect they agree with, such forms as are true? For he who does not behold true forms, can by no means make a comparison between them and others, and <note>rectify the inaccuracy: correct the flaws</note> of the one by the accurate truth of the other. For the soul, indeed, corrects the visible circle, when it does not touch a plane in one point only; approves or condemns every artificial structure and musical modulation; and judges concerning the goodness or depravity, utility or detriment, beauty or deformity, of every object in na- <margin>nature</margin>

# INTRODUCTION TO

nature. The soul, therefore, possesses truer forms, by which she judges of <term>corporeal natures: physical or bodily things</term>. But neither are these forms in the soul first forms, for they are movable; and though not subsisting in place, yet they have a <term>discursive procession: a step-by-step movement of reasoning rather than immediate, total understanding</term> through the intervals of time. Nor do they always exist <term>in energy: in a state of active, constant operation</term>; for the soul does not always energize through them. Nor do they subsist in a total but in a partial intellect. For as the soul is not total intellect, on account of its <term>self-motive nature: the ability to initiate its own motion or thought</term>, so the intellect which is in soul is not a total and first intellect, but suffers a <note>The author means a "weakening" or "loosening."</note> remission of intellectual union, from its connection with the discursive energies of soul. There is, therefore, above soul, and that intellect which is a part of soul, a certain first intellect, in itself entire and perfectly complete, in which the first and most true species of all things are contained, and which have a subsistence independent of time, place, and motion. And this first intellect is no other than that vital nature <term>the living being itself</term> <note>original Greek: *autozoon*</note>, or *animal itself*, in which Plato in the *Timæus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world.</note> represents the <term>artificer of the universe: the Demiurge or Creator</term> contemplating the ideas of things, and fabricating the machine of the world according to this all-beautiful exemplar.

Again, the artificer of the universe must be a God. Every God operates essentially, or produces from his essence that which he produces, because this is the most perfect mode of production. Every thing which operates essentially produces an image of itself. He, therefore, who fabricated the universe, fabricated it an image of itself. But if this be the case, he contains in himself <term>paradigmatically: as a perfect model or original pattern</term> the causes of the universe: and these causes are ideas. To which we may add, that the perfect must necessarily <note>come before</note> antecede the imperfect; unity, multitude; the indivisible, the divisible; and that which abides perpetually the same, that which subsists in unceasing mutation. From all which it follows, that things do not originate from baser natures, but that they end in these; and that they commence from natures the most perfect, the most beautiful, and the best. For it is not possible that our intellect should be able to apprehend things properly equal, similar, and the like, and that the intellect of the artificer of the universe should not contain in itself the essentially equal, just, beautiful, and good, and, in short, every thing which has a universal and perfect subsistence, and which, from its residence in deity, forms a link of that luminous chain of substances to which we very properly give the appellation of ideas.

It relies heavily on the Neoplatonist philosopher Proclus.</meta>

->### THE PARMENIDES.<-
->VOL. III. C<-

The following additional arguments in defence of the Platonic doctrine of ideas are given for the sake of the liberal and Platonic reader. <note>In this context, "liberal" refers to a reader with a free and open mind, or one educated in the "liberal arts"—studies suitable for a free person seeking wisdom.</note> The whole is nearly extracted from the manuscript Commentary of Proclus on the *Parmenides*. <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was the last great head of the Platonic Academy in Athens; his commentaries are essential for understanding how the ancients interpreted Plato.</note>

This visible world is either <term>self-subsistent: existing independently by its own power</term>, or it derives its subsistence from a superior cause. But if it is admitted to be self-subsistent, many absurd consequences will ensue: for it is necessary that every thing self-subsistent should be <term>impartible: indivisible, or having no parts</term>; because every thing which makes and every thing which generates is entirely incorporeal. For bodies make through incorporeal powers; fire by heat, and snow by coldness. <note>The argument here is that the physical "stuff" of fire isn't the active agent, but rather the abstract quality of "Heat" is the power that acts.</note> But if it is necessary that the maker should be incorporeal, and in things self-subsistent the same thing is the maker and the thing made, the generator and the thing generated, that which is self-subsistent will be perfectly impartible. But the world is not a thing of this kind: for every body is every way divisible, and consequently is not self-subsistent. 

Again: every thing self-subsistent is also <term>self-energetic: capable of acting or operating by its own internal power</term>. For, as it generates itself, it is by a much greater priority naturally adapted to energize in itself, since to make and to generate are no other than to energize. But the world is not <term>self-motive: able to move itself</term>, because it is corporeal. No body, therefore, is naturally adapted to be moved, and at the same time to move according to the whole of itself. For neither can the whole at the same time heat itself, and be heated by itself: for, because it is heated, it will not yet be hot, in consequence of the heat being gradually propagated through all its parts; but, because it heats, it will possess heat, and thus the same thing will be, and yet not be, hot. <note>This is a classic logical paradox: a physical object cannot give a quality it does not yet have, nor can it receive a quality it already possesses at the same moment.</note> As, therefore, it is impossible that any body can move itself according to internal change, neither can this be effected by any other motion. And, in short, every corporeal motion is more similar to <term>passion: the state of being acted upon or receiving an effect</term> than to energy; but a self-motive energy is immaterial and impartible: so that, if the world is corporeal, it will not be self-motive. But, if not self-motive, neither will it be self-subsistent. And if it is not self-subsistent, it is evident that it is produced by another cause.

For, again, that which is not self-subsistent is twofold, viz. it is either better than, or inferior to, cause. And that which is more excellent than cause¹, as is the ineffable principle of things, has something posterior to

# INTRODUCTION TO

...itself, such as is a **self-subsistent** nature <note>A "self-subsistent" nature is something that exists by its own power and does not rely on anything else for its being.</note>. But that which is subordinate to a cause is entirely suspended from a self-subsistent cause. It is necessary, therefore, that the world should subsist from another, more excellent cause. 

But, regarding this cause, does it create according to **free will** and the reasoning energy, or does it produce the universe by its **very essence**? <note>This is a major philosophical distinction: does God "choose" to create the world through a process of thinking (Free Will), or does the world flow out of God naturally because of what He is (Essence), much like light flows from the sun?</note> If it were according to free will, its energy in making would be unstable and ambiguous, and it would exist differently at different times. The world, therefore, would be **corruptible** <note>In this context, "corruptible" means "capable of being destroyed" or "subject to decay."</note>: for anything generated from a cause that moves differently at different times is itself mutable and corruptible. 

Furthermore, if the cause of the universe operated from reasoning and inquiry in producing the world, his energy could not be spontaneous and truly his own. Instead, his essence would be similar to that of the **artificer** <note>The "artificer" refers to the *Demiurge*, the divine craftsman described by Plato.</note>, who does not derive his productions from himself, but procures them as something **adventitious** <note>Something "adventitious" is external or added from the outside, rather than being innate.</note> through learning and inquiry. 

Hence we infer that the world is **eternal**, and that its maker produced it by his very essence; for, in short, everything which acts according to free will also possesses an essential energy. Thus, our **soul**, which acts in many things according to free will, simultaneously imparts life to the body by its very essence. This life does not depend on our free will; otherwise, the animal would be dissolved by every adverse circumstance, as the soul on such occasions would simply condemn its association with the body. 

However, not everything that operates from its very essence also has another energy according to free will. For example, fire heats by its very essence alone, but produces nothing from the energy of will; nor is this done by snow, nor, in short, by any body, insofar as it is a body. 

If, therefore, the **essential energy** is more extended and universal than that of free will, it is evident that it proceeds from a more venerable and elevated cause. This is very fitting, for the creative energy of natures that operate from their very essence is unattended by anxiety. It is especially necessary to conceive of an energy of this kind in divine natures; since we also live more free from anxiety and with greater ease when our life is divine, or lived according to **virtue**. 

If, therefore, there is a cause of the universe operating from his very essence, he is that primarily which his production is secondarily; and that which he is primarily, he imparts in a secondary degree to his production. Thus, fire both imparts heat to something else and is itself hot; and the soul both imparts life and possesses life. This reasoning will be found to...

He will therefore either be ignorant of what he is essentially, or, knowing this, he will also know that he is the object of desire; and, together with this, he will know that all things desire him, and what the natures are by which he is desired: for, of two relatives, to know one definitely, and the other indefinitely, is not the characteristic of science, and much less of intellectual perception. But, knowing definitely the things by which he is desired, he knows the causes of them, in consequence of beholding himself, and not things of a **posterior nature** <note>Things that come after or are dependent upon the primary cause; in this context, the physical world.</note>. If, therefore, he does not in vain possess the causes of all things, he must necessarily, according to them, bound the order of all things, and thus be of all things the immovable cause, as bounding their order by his very essence.

But if, in consequence of designing to make all things, he knows all things, he will possess inward energy, and a conversion to himself subordinate to that which proceeds outwardly, and his knowledge of beings will subsist for the sake of things different from himself. But if this is absurd, by knowing himself he will be the maker of all things. And, if this be the case, he will make things external similar to those which he contains in himself; for such is the natural order of things, that externally proceeding should be suspended from inward energy, the whole world from the **all-perfect monad of ideas** <note>The singular, unified source containing the perfect blueprints (Forms) for everything in the universe.</note>, and the parts of the visible universe from monads which are separated from each other.

# INTRODUCTION TO

Let it then be admitted that man comes from seed; but seed possesses **productive powers** <term>productive powers: the formative principles or "blueprints" (often called *logoi*) that guide the development of a living thing</term> in **capacity** <note>original: "in capacity," meaning potentially rather than actually</note>, and not in **energy** <note>original: "in energy," meaning in a state of full, active reality or actuality</note>. For, since seed is a physical body, it is not naturally suited to possess productive powers in a unified and active way. In every case, a state of "actuality" must come before a state of "potentiality." Because the seed is imperfect, it requires the assistance of something else endowed with a **perfective power** <note>A power capable of bringing a developing thing to its finished, ideal state.</note>. 

You might say this "something else" is the nature of the mother, for she perfects and fashions the offspring through her productive powers. It is not the outward physical form of the mother that creates the infant, but **Nature** <note>Capitalized here to denote Nature as an active, metaphysical force rather than just the physical environment.</note>, which is an **incorporeal power** <note>A non-physical or spiritual force.</note> and the **principle of motion** <note>The internal source or starting point of growth and change.</note>. 

If, therefore, Nature transforms the productive powers of the seed from a state of potentiality to a state of actual existence, Nature herself must possess these productive powers in actuality. Thus, even though Nature is irrational and lacks imagination, she is at the same time the cause of **physical reasons** <term>physical reasons: the rational, formative laws (*logoi*) that dictate how matter is organized into specific shapes and types</term>. 

Just as the nature of a human contains human productive powers, does not the nature of a lion also contain those of a lion? Does it not contain, for instance, the "reasons" or productive powers of the head, the hair, the feet, and the other parts of the lion? If not, how is it that when a tooth is shed, another grows in its place, unless there is an inherent power able to create teeth? How, likewise, does Nature simultaneously create bone and flesh and every other part? A single thing acting in a single, simple way would not be able to fashion such a variety of complex structures. 

Does not Nature in plants also possess productive powers just as she does in animals? Or shall we not say that in plants, too, the orderly process of growth and their very lives prove they are brought to perfection by orderly causes? It is evident, therefore, by this same reasoning, that the "natures" of plants also contain these visible productive powers. 

Let us then ascend from these specific examples to the one **Nature of the Earth**. This Earth-Nature generates everything that breathes and creeps upon its surface; with a much higher priority, it must contain the productive powers of all plants and animals. Otherwise, how could we explain the generation of things from **putrefaction**? <note>Referring to the ancient belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter. The author argues this isn't accidental but driven by the Earth's inherent formative powers.</note> (For the hypothesis of the **experimentalists** <note>Those who rely solely on physical observation and mechanical explanations, ignoring metaphysical causes.</note> is weak and useless.) How is it that different kinds of plants grow in the same place without human care? Is it not evident that this comes from the total Nature of the Earth, which contains the productive powers of all these things within herself? 

And proceeding in this way, we shall find that the Nature within each of the elements and the **celestial spheres** <note>The concentric shells of the heavens in ancient cosmology, each believed to be governed by a specific guiding intelligence or nature.</note> contains the productive powers of the animals which it contains.
