If we ascend to the nature of the universe itself, we may also inquire respecting this, whether it contains **forms** <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes or "blueprints" of all things in the Platonic tradition.</note> or not, and we shall be compelled to confess, that in this also the **productive and motive powers** of all things are contained: for whatever is perfected from inferior natures subsists in a more excellent and perfect manner from more universal natures. The nature of the universe, therefore, being the mother of all things, comprehends the productive powers of all things; for, otherwise, it would be absurd that art, imitating natural **reasons** <note>original: "reasons" (referring to the Latin *rationes* or Greek *logoi*), the rational principles or blueprints that guide the creation of a thing.</note>, should operate according to productive principles, but that nature herself should **energize** <note>to act or manifest power in the world</note> without reasons, and without inward measures. 

But, if nature contains productive principles, it is necessary that there should be another cause prior to nature, which is comprehensive of forms; for nature **verging to bodies** <note>turning its attention and activity toward physical matter</note> energizes in them, just as if we should conceive an artist verging to pieces of timber, and inwardly, by various operations, reducing them to a certain form: for thus nature, merged together with and dwelling in corporeal masses, inspires them with her productive powers and with motion; since things which are moved by others require a cause of this kind, a cause which is properly irrational indeed, that it may not depart from bodies, which cannot subsist without a cause continually residing with them, but containing the productive powers of bodies, that it may be able to preserve all things in their proper boundaries, and move every thing in a convenient manner. 

Nature, therefore, belongs to other things, being merged in, or coordinated with, bodies. But it is requisite that the most principal and proper cause should be **exempt** <note>meaning the cause is independent of and superior to the thing it creates</note> from its productions: for, by how much more the maker is exempt from the thing made, by so much the more perfectly and purely will he make. And, in short, if nature is irrational, it requires a leader. There is, therefore, something prior to nature, which contains productive powers, and from which it is requisite that every thing in the world should be suspended. Hence, a knowledge of generated natures will subsist in the cause of the world more excellent than the knowledge which we possess; so far as this cause not only knows, but gives **subsistence** <note>the act of bringing something into real, independent existence</note> to, all things; but we possess knowledge alone. 

But if the <term>demiurgic cause</term> <note>demiurgic cause: the Creator or "Divine Craftsman" who shapes the physical world according to eternal patterns.</note> of the universe knows all things, if he beholds them externally, he will again be ignorant of himself, and will be subordinate to a partial soul; but, if he beholds them in himself, he will contain in himself all forms, intellectual and <term>gnostic</term> <note>gnostic: relating to the capacity for spiritual or intellectual knowledge (from the Greek *gnosis*).</note>.

# INTRODUCTION TO

In the fifth place, things produced from an <term>immovable cause</term> <note>A cause that does not change or shift, providing a stable foundation for eternal things.</note> are immovable and without mutation; but things produced from a <term>movable cause</term> <note>A cause subject to change; anything it creates is temporary and will eventually pass away.</note> are again movable and mutable, and subsist differently at different times. If this be the case, all such things as are essentially eternal and immutable must be the progeny of an <term>immovable cause</term>; for, if from a <term>movable cause</term>, they will be mutable; which is impossible. Are not, therefore, the form of man and the form of horse from a cause, if the whole world subsists from a cause? From what cause, therefore? Is it from an <term>immovable</term> or from a <term>movable cause</term>? But if from a <term>movable cause</term>, the human species will some time or other fail; since every thing which subsists from a <term>movable cause</term> ranks among things which are naturally adapted to perish. We may also make the same inquiry respecting the sun and moon, and each of the stars: for, if these are produced from a <term>movable cause</term>, in these also there will be a mutation of <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or core "being" of a thing.</note>. But if these, and all such forms as eternally subsist in the universe, are from an <term>immovable cause</term>, where does the <term>immovable cause</term> of these subsist? For it is evidently not in bodies, since every natural body is naturally adapted to be moved. It therefore subsists proximately in <term>nature</term> <note>In this Neoplatonic view, "nature" is the lowest level of divine power that directly touches and shapes the physical world.</note>. But <term>nature</term> is irrational; and it is requisite that causes properly so called should be intellectual and divine. Hence, the <term>immovable causes</term> of these <term>forms</term> subsist primarily in <term>intellect</term>, secondarily in <term>soul</term>, in the third gradation in <term>nature</term>, and lastly in bodies. For all things either subsist apparently or unapparently, either separate or inseparable from bodies; and if separate, either immovably according to <term>essence</term> and <term>energy</term> <note>original: *energeia*. Here meaning the active operation or "output" of a thing's power.</note>, or immovably according to <term>essence</term>, but movably according to <term>energy</term>. Those things, therefore, are properly immovable, which are immutable both according to <term>essence</term> and <term>energy</term>, such as are <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Pure realities that can only be understood by the mind, existing beyond the reach of physical change.</note>; but those possess the second rank which are immovable indeed according to <term>essence</term>, but movable according to <term>energy</term>, and such are <term>souls</term>: in the third place, things unapparent indeed, but inseparable from the <term>phænomena</term> <note>The outward, visible appearances of the world.</note>, are such as belong to the empire of <term>nature</term>; and those rank in the last place which are apparent, subsist in <term>sensibles</term> <note>Physical objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, and are divisible: for the gradual subjection of <term>forms</term> proceeding as far as to <term>sensibles</term> ends in these.

In the sixth place, let us speculate after another manner concerning the subsistence of <term>forms</term> or <term>ideas</term>, beginning from demonstrations themselves. For **Aristotle** has proved in his <term>Last Analytics</term> <note>Now commonly known as the *Posterior Analytics*, Aristotle's famous work on logic and how we prove scientific truths.</note>, and all scientific men must

# THE PARMENIDES.

### VOL. III. D

...confess, that <term>demonstrations</term> <note>In this context, logical proofs that move from a general cause to a specific effect.</note> are entirely from things which have a priority of <term>subsistence</term> <note>A technical term meaning the way something exists or holds its place in reality.</note>, and which are naturally more honourable. But if the things from which demonstrations consist are universals, (for every demonstration is from these),—hence, these must be causes to the things which are unfolded from them. When, therefore, the astronomer says, that the circles in the heavens bisect each other, since every greatest circle bisects its like, whether does he demonstrate or not? For he makes his conclusion from that which is universal. But where shall we find the causes of this section of circles in the heavens which are more universal than the circles? For they will not be in bodies, since every thing which is in body is divisible. They must, therefore, reside in an <term>incorporeal essence</term> <note>A non-physical reality or "being" that does not have a body and cannot be divided.</note>; and hence there must be forms which have a subsistence prior to apparent forms, and which are the causes of subsistence to these, in consequence of being more universal and more powerful. Science, therefore, compels us to admit that there are universal forms, which have a subsistence prior to particulars, are more essential and more causal, and from which the very being of particulars is derived.

By ascending from motion we may also after the same manner prove the existence of ideas. Every body from its own proper nature is <term>alter-motive</term> <note>Moving only when acted upon by something else; lacking the power of self-motion.</note>, or moved by another, and is indigent of motion externally derived. But the first, most proper and principal motion is in the power which moves the <term>mundane wholes</term> <note>The major components of the physical universe, such as the planetary spheres.</note>: for he possesses the motion of a mover, and body the motion of that which is moved, and corporeal motion is the image of that which pre-subsists in this power. For that is perfect motion because it is <term>energy</term> <note>From the Greek "energeia," referring to the active, full expression of a thing's nature, rather than just potential movement.</note>; but the motion in body is imperfect energy: and the imperfect derives its subsistence from the perfect.

From knowledge also we may perceive the necessity of the same conclusion. For last knowledge is that of bodies, whether it be denominated sensible or imaginable: for all such knowledge is destitute of truth, and does not contemplate any thing universal and common, but beholds all things invested with figure, and all things partial. But more perfect knowledge is that which is without figure, which is immaterial, and which subsists by itself, and from itself; the image of which is sense, since this is imperfect knowledge, subsisting in another, and not originating from itself. If, therefore, as in motion, so also in knowledge and in life, that which participates, that which is participated, and that which is <term>imparticipable</term> <note>The "imparticipable" is the highest form of a quality that remains pure and untouched, acting as the source for the versions of that quality shared (participated) by lower things.</note>, are different...

For <term>matter</term> <note>The underlying "stuff" of the physical world which has no form of its own.</note> is one thing, the form which it contains another, and still different from either is the **separate form**. For God and Nature do not make things imperfect which <term>subsist</term> <note>A technical term for existing or having a foundation in reality.</note> in something different from themselves, and which have an obscure and *debile* <note>original: "debile"; meaning weak, feeble, or lacking strength.</note> existence, but have not produced things perfect, and which subsist from themselves; but by a much greater priority they have given subsistence to these, and from these have produced things which are participated by, and merged in, the **darkness of matter**.

But if it be requisite summarily to relate the cause that induced the **Pytha-goreans** and **Plato** to adopt the **hypothesis of ideas**, we must say, that all these visible natures, <term>celestial</term> <note>Relating to the heavens or the stars.</note> and <term>sublunary</term> <note>Literally "under the moon"; referring to the earthly realm where things are born, change, and die.</note>, are either from chance, or subsist from a cause. But that they should be from chance is impossible: for things more excellent will subsist in things subordinate, viz. <term>intellect</term> <note>In this context, a higher divine mind or pure consciousness.</note>, reason, and cause, and that which proceeds from cause. To which we may add, as **Aristotle** observes, that prior to causes according to <term>accident</term> <note>Things that happen by chance or are not part of a thing's essential nature.</note>, it is requisite that there should be things which have an **essential subsistence**; for the accidental is that in which the progressions of these are terminated. So that a subsistence from cause will be more antient than a subsistence from chance, if the most divine of things apparent are the progeny of chance. But if there is a cause of all things, there will either be many unconjoined causes, or one cause; but if many, we shall not be able to assign to what it is owing that the world is one, since there will not be one cause according to which all things are coordinated. It will also be absurd to suppose that this cause is irrational. For, again, there will be something among things posterior better than the cause of all things, viz. that which, being within the universe, and a part of the whole, operates according to reason and knowledge, and yet derives this prerogative from an irrational cause. But if this cause is rational and knows itself, it will certainly know itself to be the cause of all; or, being ignorant of this, it will be ignorant of its own nature. But if it knows that it is essentially the cause of the universe, it will also definitely know that of which it is the cause; for, that which definitely knows the one will also definitely know the other. Hence, he will know every thing which the universe contains, and of which he is the cause: and if this be the case, beholding himself, and knowing himself, he knows things posterior to himself. > i. e. “The <term>intellect of the Father</term> <note>In this mystical tradition, the "Father" represents the primary divine source, and his "intellect" is the divine mind that contains the blueprints for all of creation.</note> made a crashing noise, understanding with unwearied counsel <term>omniform ideas</term> <note>Patterns or "Forms" that contain every possible shape and variety of being.</note>. But with winged speed they leaped forth from one fountain: for both the counsel and the end were from the Father. In consequence, too, of being allotted an intellectual fire, they are divided into other intellectual forms: for the king previously placed in the multiform world an intellectual incorruptible impression, the vestige of which hastening through the world, causes it to appear invested with form, and replete with all-various ideas of which there is one fountain. From this fountain other immense distributed ideas rush with a crashing noise, bursting forth about the bodies of the world, and are borne along its terrible bosoms like swarms of bees. They turn themselves, too, on all sides, and nearly in all directions. They are intellectual conceptions from the paternal fountain, plucking abundantly the flower of the fire of sleepless time. But a self-perfect fountain pours forth primogenial ideas from the primary vigour of the Father.”

Through these things, says **Proclus**, the Gods have clearly shown where ideas <term>subsist</term> <note>To "subsist" here means to have a real, independent existence in the divine realm.</note>, who the divinity is that comprehends the one fountain of these, and that from this fountain a multitude proceeds. Likewise, how the world is <term>fabricated</term> <note>Constructed or crafted by the divine mind.</note> according to ideas; that they are motive of all <term>mundane systems</term> <note>The physical structures and laws of our world (the 'mundus').</note>; that they are essentially intellectual; and that they are all-various according to their characteristics.

If, therefore, he adds, arguments persuade us to admit the hypothesis respecting ideas, and the wise unite in the same design, viz. **Plato**, **Pythagoras**, and **Orpheus**, and the Gods clearly bear witness to these, we should but little regard <term>sophistical arguments</term> <note>Clever but fallacious reasoning, likely referring here to critics who deny the existence of universal Forms.</note>, which are confuted by themselves, and assert nothing scientific, nothing sane. For the Gods have manifestly declared that they are conceptions of the Father: for they abide in his intelligence. They have likewise asserted that they proceed to the fabrication of the world; for the crashing noise signifies their progression;—that they are omniform, as comprehending the causes of all divisible natures; that from fontal ideas others proceed, which are allotted the fabrication of the world, according to its parts, and which are said to be similar to swarms of bees; and lastly, that they are generative of secondary natures.

# THE PARMENIDES.

The oracles <note>This refers to the *Chaldaic Oracles*, a collection of mystical verses that Neoplatonic philosophers believed contained divine revelations about the structure of the universe.</note> say that the fountain of ideas <note>The "fountain" is the primary source or "womb" from which all logical patterns and forms emerge.</note> pre-subsists in the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Demiurge" is the Divine Craftsman or Creator who shapes the physical world according to eternal patterns.</note>; nor are these assertions discordant with each other, as they may appear to be to some. For it is not the same thing to investigate the one and total cause of mundane forms <note>Patterns that specifically belong to the physical, "earthly" world.</note>, and simply to contemplate the first unfolding into light of every series of ideas; but the comprehension of the former must be referred to the <term>demiurgus</term>, and of the latter to the intelligible order itself, of divine natures, from which the <term>demiurgus</term> is filled, and all the orders of an ideal essence. 

And, on this account, I think the oracles assert that ideas proceed with a crashing noise <note>The "crashing noise" is a metaphor for the powerful, sudden, and energetic manifestation of divine reality into the lower world.</note> from their intellectual fountain, and, being distributed in different places, burst about the bodies of the world, in consequence of the cause of mundane natures being comprehended in this fountain, according to which, all generated composite natures in the world are invested with form, conformably to the demiurgic will. But the forms subsisting in <term>animal itself</term> <note>Original Greek: *Autozōon*. This is the "Absolute Living Being," a high-level divine intellect that contains the blueprints for every kind of living creature.</note>, according to an intelligible bound, are neither said by Plato to be moved, nor to leap into bodies, but to impart essence <note>In this context, to "impart essence" means to give things their fundamental "what-ness" or nature just by existing, without needing to take an action.</note> to all things by their very essence alone. 

If, therefore, to exist through energy and motion is secondary to a making prior to energizing and being moved, it is evident that the ideas intelligibly and immovably established in <term>animal itself</term> are allotted an order more elevated than demiurgic ideas. And the <term>demiurgus</term> is fabricative of forms in a twofold respect; both according to the fountain in himself, and according to intelligible ideas: for there are the total causes of all things, and the <term>four monads</term> <note>The "four monads" here likely refer to the four primary classes of living beings described in Plato's *Timaeus*: the heavenly gods, birds, aquatic creatures, and land animals.</note>; but, thence originating, they proceed through the whole divine orders as far as to the last of things, so that the last and sensible images of these possess a certain similitude, more clearly of some, and more obscurely of others. 

He, likewise, who is capable of following the divine progressions will perceive that every sensible form expresses the <term>idioms</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, "idioms" are the unique, identifying characteristics or specific properties of a thing.</note> of all of them. For the immovable and the eternal in sensible forms are no otherwise present than from the first forms: for they are primarily eternal; and hence they communicate eternity to the consequent progressions in a secondary and third gradation. Again, that every form is a multitude, subsists according to a peculiar number, and is filled with its proper numbers, and that on this account a different form is referred to a different divine order to us unknown and ineffable,—this it receives from the summit of the intelligible and at the same time intellectual order, and from the forms which there subsist occultly, and ineffably: just as the power of

But to be entirely perfective of an imperfect nature, and to produce into energy the aptitude of subjects, comprehending the unfigured in figures, and the imperfect in perfection, is solely derived from perfective deity, and the forms which there appear. Again, so far as every form hastens to verge to itself <note>This refers to the concept of "reversion," where a thing turns back toward its divine source to find its own identity.</note>, and comprehends parts uniformly in itself, so far it bears an image of the summit of <term>intellectuals</term> <note>The "Intellectual" realm in Neoplatonism refers to the level of pure mind or intellect (Nous), which is above the physical world.</note>, and the <term>impartible subsistence</term> <note>Something that exists without being divided into parts; a unified, indivisible state of being.</note> of forms established according to that order. Again, so far as it possesses the power of giving form to matter, is filled with artificial fabrication pervading through nature herself, and evinces a wonder subtilty, and a production of forms according to reason, so far it receives the representations of <term>demiurgic ideas</term> <note>The "demiurgic" ideas are the blueprints used by the Divine Craftsman to build the physical universe.</note>. If, likewise, it assimilates <term>sensibles</term> <note>Physical objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> to <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Eternal truths or forms that can only be understood by the mind/intellect, not the senses.</note>, and separates the essences of them by mutations according to reasons, it is evident that it resembles the assimilative orders of forms, from which the divisible progressions of <term>mundane natures</term> <note>Mundane here means "belonging to the world" (from the Latin *mundus*), rather than "boring."</note> appear, which invest sensibles with the representations from intelligibles. Further still, if every form pervades to many things, though it be material, and bounds the multitude of them according to its proper form, must it not, according to this power, be referred to that order of Gods which governs with a liberated characteristic the allotments in the world, and draws to itself many portions of divine allotments in the universe? We may behold, therefore, an uninterrupted continuity of the whole series supernally proceeding from intelligible ideas as far as to the last of things, and likewise perceive what peculiarities sensibles derive from each order. For it is requisite that all secondary things should participate of the natures prior to them, and thus enjoy each, according to the order which they are severally allotted.

With respect to *what things there are ideas of, and what not*, I shall summarily observe, that there are ideas only of universal and perfect substances, and of whatever contributes to the perfection of these, as for instance of man, and whatever is perfective of man, such as wisdom and virtue; and consequently matter, particulars, parts, things artificial, evil and sordid natures, are excluded from the region of ideas.

# THE PARMENIDES.

To the question *what kind of beings ideas are*, we may answer with Xenocrates <note>Xenocrates (c. 396–314 BCE) was a student of Plato and the third leader of the Platonic Academy.</note>, according to the account of Proclus, that they are *the exemplary causes of things, which perpetually subsist according to nature.* They are *exemplars* <note>Exemplars are the perfect "blueprints" or original models in the divine mind from which all physical things are copied.</note>, indeed, because the final cause, or *the good*, is superior to these, and that which is properly the efficient cause, or the <term>demiurgic intellect</term> <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine "Craftsman" or Creator-Mind who shapes the universe using the Ideas as his guide.</note>, is of an inferior rank. But they are the exemplars of things *according to nature*, because there are no ideas of things unnatural or artificial: and of such natural things as are *perpetual*, because there are no ideas of changing particulars.

Lastly, *ideas are shared by material natures*, similar to the impressions made in wax by a seal, to images appearing in water or a mirror, and to *pictures*. For material species, on account of their union with matter, are like the impressions of a seal; but on account of their apparently real, but at the same time deceptive existence in the dark container of matter, they are similar to images in water, or in a mirror, or a dream; and they resemble *pictures* on account of their likeness, though very distant and faint, to the first ideas themselves. We may add too, as Proclus beautifully observes, that they derive their existence as *impressions* from the <term>mundane Gods</term> <note>Gods who oversee the physical laws and operations of the visible universe.</note>; their *apparent* existence from the <term>liberated Gods</term> <note>Divine powers that act as mediators between the physical world and the higher, purely spiritual realms.</note>; and their *likeness* to higher *forms* from the *supermundane* or *assimilative Gods* <note>Higher deities who create the similarities between the different levels of reality.</note>. And thus much for the first part of the dialogue, or the doctrine of ideas*.

But in order to have a summary view of the incredibly deep and lofty discussion which the second part contains concerning *the one*, it is necessary to observe, that by *the one itself* the Pythagoreans and Plato meant the first cause, which they very properly considered as perfectly <term>supereffential</term> <note>Existing above or beyond the very nature of "being" or "essence" itself.</note>, ineffable <note>Too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.</note> and unknown. For it is necessary that a many (multitude) should come after a one (unity): but it is impossible to conceive *being*² without a many, and consequently the cause of all beings must be free of many and beyond existence. And that this was really the opinion of the most ancient Pythagoreans, from

***

* See more concerning ideas in the first dissertation prefixed to my translation of Proclus on Euclid, in the notes to my translation of Aristotle's Metaphysics, and in the notes to this dialogue.

² If *being* were the same as *the one*, then "the many" (multitude) would be the same as *non-being*: for the opposite to the one is the many, and the opposite to *being* is *non-being*. Since *being*, therefore, is not the same as *the one*, it must come after *the one*; for there is nothing in all things more excellent than unity.

"So that it is necessary to assert that there are three principles; *that which is the subject of things (or matter), form, and that which is of itself motive, and invisible in power*. <note>original Greek: Ὡστ' αναγκα τρεις ειμεν τας αρχας, ταν τε εστω των πραγμάτων και ταν μορφω, και το εξ αυτȣ κινατικον και αορατον δυναμει</note> With respect to the last of which, it is not only necessary that it should have a subsistence <note>In this context, "subsistence" refers to a state of real, independent existence.</note>, *but that it should be something better than intellect*. <note>original Greek: το δε τοιοῦτον ὀν ου μονον ειμεν δει, αλλα και νοῳ τι κρεσσον</note> But that which is better than intellect is evidently the same with that which we denominate God." <note>original Greek: νοῳ δε κρεσσον εστι ὀπερ ονομαζομεν Θεον Φανερον</note> 

It must here however be observed, that by the word **God** we are not only to understand the first cause, but every God: for, according to the Pythagoric theology, every Deity, considered according to the characteristic of his nature, is superior to intellectual essence <note>This means that the Gods exist at a level of reality even higher than the highest form of thought or "Intellect."</note>. Agreeably to the above passage is that also of Brotinus, as cited by Syrianus <note>Syrianus was a Neoplatonist philosopher and the head of the Academy in Athens in the 5th century CE.</note> in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* (p. 102, b), who expressly asserts that the first cause "surpasses every intellect and essence both in power and antiquity." <note>original Greek: νȣ παντος και ȣσιας δυναμει και πρεσβεια ὑπερεχει</note> 

Again, according to the same Syrianus (p. 103, b), we are informed, “that the Pythagoreans called God *the one*, as the cause of union to the universe, and on account of his superiority to every being, to all life, and to all-perfect intellect. But they denominated him the measure of all things, on account of his conferring on all things, through illumination, essence and bound <note>In Platonic philosophy, "bound" (or limit) is the principle that gives specific shape, order, and definition to the chaos of "the infinite."</note>; and containing and bounding all things by the ineffable supereminence of his nature, which is extended beyond every bound.” <note>original Greek: Των θειων ανδρων ἐν μεν λεγοντων τον Θεον ὡς ενωσεως τοις ὀλοις αιτιον, και παντος τȣ οντος, και πασης ζωης, και νȣ τȣ παντελῶς επεκεινα. Μετρον δε των παντων ὡς πασι την ȣσιαν, και το τελος επιλαμποντα, και ὡς παντα περιεχοντα, και οριζοντα ταις αφραστοις αυτȣ, και παντος ὑπερηπλωνμεναις περατος ὑπεροχαις.</note>

This silence is, indeed, remarkably obvious in Hesiod <note>Hesiod (8th century BCE) was one of the earliest Greek poets, famous for his "Theogony," which describes the origins of the gods.</note>, when in his *Theogony* <note>A poem describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods.</note> he says:

->Truly, at the first, Chaos was generated—<-

That is, “*Chaos was the first thing which was generated*”—and consequently there must be some cause prior to Chaos, through which it was produced; for there can be no effect without a cause. Such, however, is the ignorance of the moderns, that in all the editions of Hesiod **generated** <note>original Greek: γενετο (geneto)</note> is translated **was** <note>original Latin: fuit</note>, as if the poet had said that Chaos *was the first of all things*; and he is even accused by Cudworth <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) was an English philosopher and leader of the Cambridge Platonists.</note> on this account as leaning to the atheistical system. But the following testimonies clearly prove, that in the opinion of all antiquity, *generated* was considered as meaning *was generated*, and not *was* simply. And, in the first place, this is clearly asserted by Aristotle in book 3, *On the Heavens* <note>original Latin title: de Coelo</note>. “There are certain persons (says he) who assert that there is nothing unbegotten, but that all things are generated. > "Aristotle (says he) ranks Hesiod among the first physiologists <note>A term for early Greek philosophers who studied "physis" or nature.</note>, because he sings Chaos was first generated. He says, therefore, that Hesiod in a particular manner makes all things to be generated, because that which is first is by him said to be generated. But it is probable that Aristotle calls Orpheus and Musæus <note>Orpheus and Musæus were legendary mythical poets and prophets of ancient Greece, often associated with the earliest mystical teachings.</note> the first physiologists, who *assert that all things are generated, except the first*.. It is, however, evident that those theologists, singing in fabulous strains, meant nothing more by *generation* than the procession of things from their causes; on which account *all of them consider the first cause as unbegotten*. For Hesiod also, when he says that *Chaos was first generated*, insinuates that there was something prior to Chaos, from which Chaos was produced. For it is always necessary that every thing which is generated should be generated from something. But this likewise is insinuated by Hesiod, that the first cause is above all knowledge and every appellation." (On the Heavens <note>original Latin: De Cælo</note>, p. 147.)

But these divine men not only called the first cause *the one*, on account of his transcendent simplicity, but likewise *the good*, on account of the superlative excellency of his nature; by the former of these appellations considering him as that principle from which all things flow, and by the latter as that supreme object of desire to which all things ultimately tend. And hence Plato, in his Republic, asserts that *the good is superessential* <note>Meaning "above essence" or "beyond being." This is a central concept in Neoplatonism: the ultimate source of reality is higher than reality itself.</note>; and Aristotle, in book 14 of the Metaphysics, chapter 4, alluding to Plato and the Pythagoreans, says, "that according to some, *the one* is the same with the good." Some say that the one itself is the good itself. <note>original Greek: 'Οι μεν φασιν αυτο το εν, το αγαθον αυτο ειναι.</note>

ineffable than all silence, and more unknown than all essence; that he is holy among the holies, and is concealed among the intelligible Gods.” <note>This quote describes the supreme principle of Neoplatonism—the One—which is so far beyond human understanding that it is "ineffable," meaning it cannot be expressed in words.</note>

Plato, too, in the *Republic*, that we may be enabled to gain a glimpse from analogy of this transcendent nature, compares him to the sun. For as the sun by his light not only confers the power of being seen on visible objects, but is likewise the cause of their generation, nutriment, and increase; *so the good, through superessential light, imparts being and the power of being known to every thing which is the object of knowledge.* <note>"Superessential" (or *hyperousios* in Greek) describes something that exists "beyond being" or above the level of traditional existence.</note> Hence, says Damascius <gloss>1 On First Principles <note>original Greek: Περι αρχων (Peri archon). Damascius was the last head of the Platonic Academy in Athens, writing in the 6th century CE.</note></gloss>, “this highest God is seen afar off as it were obscurely; and if you approach nearer, he is beheld still more obscurely; and lastly, he takes away the ability of perceiving other objects. He is, therefore, truly an incomprehensible and inaccessible light, and is profoundly compared to the sun: upon which the more attentively you look, the more you will be darkened and blinded; and will only bring back with you eyes stupefied with excess of light.”

And such is the doctrine of Plato and the Pythagoreans <note>The followers of Pythagoras, whose mathematical and mystical teachings heavily influenced Plato's later philosophy.</note> concerning the highest principle of things. But, according to the same divine men, the immediate progeny of this ineffable cause must be Gods; and as such must have a superessential subsistence. For what else prior to unities <note>In this context, "unities" (or Henads) are the first manifestations or "gods" that emerge directly from the ultimate One.</note> is it lawful to conjoin with *the one*, or what is more conjoined with a God subsisting according to unity, than the multitude of Gods? Besides, progressions are every where perfected through similitude <note>A central Neoplatonic law: a cause always produces something that resembles itself before it produces something different.</note> to their principles. For both nature herself, intellect, and every generative cause, leads and conjoins to itself similar natures, prior to such as are dissimilar. For as there can be no vacuum either in incorporeal or corporeal natures, it is necessary that every thing which has a natural progression should proceed through similitude. Hence, every cause must deliver its own form and characteristic to its progeny, and, before it generates that which is hypostatic <note>Related to the "hypostasis" or the underlying reality and substance of a thing.</note> of progressions far distant and separate from its nature, must constitute things proximate to itself according to essence, and conjoined with it through similitude. As nature, therefore, generates a natural number, soul one that is animal, and intellect an intellectual number, it is necessary that the first unity should produce from itself,

prior to every thing else, a multitude of natures characterized by unity, and a number the most of all things allied to its cause. And hence the fountain of universal good must produce and establish in beings *goodnesses* <note>In Neoplatonism, "goodnesses" (or *agathotetes*) refer to the divine unities or "Henads" that proceed from the First Cause to give order and divinity to the rest of existence.</note> naturally conjoined with himself; and these exalted natures can be no other than Gods.

But if these divine natures are alone superessential <note>Existing "above" or "beyond" being or essence.</note>, they will in no respect differ from the highest God. They must, therefore, be participated by beings; that is, each must have some particular being consubsistent <note>Existing together or inherently with something else.</note> with its nature, but yet so as not to lose its superessential characteristic. And hence every unity may be considered as the lucid blossom <note>The "blossom" (Greek: *anthos*) is a poetic technical term for the highest, most unified part of a soul or being that allows it to touch the divine.</note> or centre of the being by which it is participated; absorbing, as it were, in superessential light, and thus deifying the essence with which it is connected.

Nor let the reader imagine that this sublime theory is nothing more than the fanatic jargon of the latter Platonists, as is rashly and ignorantly asserted by Cudworth <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) was a leader of the Cambridge Platonists who, while admiring Plato, often criticized the more "mystical" interpretations of later followers like Proclus.</note>; for it is a doctrine as old at least as Timaeus the Locrian. For, in his book *On the Soul of the World*, after asserting that there are two causes of all things, intellect of such as are produced according to reason, but necessity of such as are produced by force, according to the powers of bodies, he adds—"that the former of these, that is intellect, is a cause of the nature of *the good*, and is called God, and is the principle of such things as are best." "Of these, one is of the nature of the good, and is called God, being the principle of the best things." <note>original Greek: Τουτων δε, τον μεν τας ταγαθω φυσιος ειμεν, θεον τε ονυμαινεσθαι, αρχαν τε των αριστων.</note> But according to the Pythagoreans, as we have abundantly proved, *the good* or *the one* is above essence and intellect; and consequently by intellect here we must not understand the first cause, but a deity subordinate to the first. Intellect, however, is (says he) of the nature of *the good*; but *the good* is superessential, and consequently intellect participates of a superessential nature. And when he adds that intellect is called God, he plainly intimates that every God (the first being excepted) partakes of a superessential nature.

<margin>¹ In the 5th book of the Manuscript Commentary on the Parmenides.</margin>
But to return to our inimitable dialogue: This second part consists of nine hypotheses; five of which consider the consequences which result from admitting the subsistence of *the one*, and the other four what must be the consequences if it were taken away from the nature of things. But as Plato in these hypotheses delivers the Eleatic method <note>The Eleatic school of philosophy, founded by Parmenides, focused on the nature of "Being" and used rigorous logical arguments to explore unity and change.</note> of reasoning, it is necessary to inform the reader that, according to Proclus¹, it was as follows:—Two

<meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of the dialectic method used in Plato's *Parmenides*. The previous page ended with "for it is a doctrine...", and although the catchword provided was "It", the text here resumes with the explanation of logical hypotheses.</meta>

->## INTRODUCTION TO THE PARMENIDES<-

hypotheses being laid down, viz. <note>original: "videlicet," meaning "that is to say" or "namely."</note> *if a thing is*, and *if it is not*, each of these may be tripled by considering in each *what happens*, *what does not happen*, *what happens and at the same time does not happen*: so that six cases will be the result. But since, *if a thing is*, we may consider itself either with respect to itself, or itself with respect to others; or we may consider others themselves with respect to themselves, or others with respect to that thing itself, and so likewise if a thing is not: hence, the whole of this process will consist of eight triads <note>A group or set of three. In Neoplatonic logic, these sets explore every possible relational outcome of a premise.</note>, which are as follows:—1. *If a thing is*, what happens to itself with respect to itself, what does not happen, what happens and at the same time does not happen. 2. *If a thing is*, what happens to itself with respect to others, what does not happen, what happens and at the same time does not happen. 3. *If a thing is*, what happens to others with respect to themselves, what does not happen, what happens and at the same time does not happen. 4. *If a thing is*, what happens to others with respect to that thing, what does not happen, what happens and at the same time does not happen. And the other four, which are founded on the hypothesis *that a thing is not*, are to be distributed in exactly the same manner as those we have just enumerated. Such (says Proclus <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was the last great head of the Platonic Academy in Athens; his commentaries are the primary source for the systematic Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato’s dialogues.</note>) is the whole form of the dialectic method <note>The highest form of philosophical inquiry for Platonists, which uses logic to ascend from the world of appearances to the understanding of first principles.</note>, which is both intellectual and scientific; and under which those four powers, the definitive and divisive, the demonstrative and analytic <note>These represent the four classical operations of logic: defining terms, dividing concepts into categories, proving truths, and tracing conclusions back to their premises.</note>, receive their consummate perfection.

In the *first hypothesis*, therefore, Plato considers *what does not follow to the one, considered with respect to itself and to others*. *In the second, what does follow*. *In the third, what follows and at the same time does not follow*. And this forms the first hexad <note>A grouping of six components; here, it refers to the first six logical results derived from the initial hypotheses.</note>. But in the *fourth hypothesis* he considers *what follows to others with respect to themselves, and what does not follow, what follows and at the same time does not follow*. In the *fifth*, *what follows to others with respect to the subject of the hypothesis, what does not follow, what follows and at the same time does not follow*. And so two hexads, or four triads, are by this means produced from the five hypotheses, *if the one is*. And the reader will easily perceive how each of the other four, which suppose *the one is not*, may form a triad: so that these four triads, in conjunction with the preceding four, will give the whole Eleatic <note>Named for the school of Parmenides of Elea, who focused on the nature of "The One" and the unchanging reality behind appearances.</note> or dialectic method complete.

->## THE PARMENIDES<-

It is likewise necessary to observe, that these hypotheses are derived from the triple division of *the one*, and the twofold division of *non-being*. For *the one* is either *above being*, or *in being*, or *posterior to being*. But *non-being* is either *that which in no respect is*, or *that which is considered as partly having a subsistence, and partly not*. This being premised, let the reader attend to the following beautiful account of these hypotheses from Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who provided systematic commentaries on Plato's works.</note> on Plato’s Theology, and from his admirable commentary on this dialogue.

The first hypothesis demonstrates by negations the ineffable supereminence of the first principle of things; and evinces that he is exempt from all essence and knowledge. But the second unfolds the whole order of the Gods. For Parmenides does not alone assume the intellectual and essential idiom <note>characteristic property or unique nature</note> of the Gods, but likewise the divine characteristic of their <term>hyparxis</term> <note>The "flower" or summit of an essence; its most fundamental, divine existence or "subsistence."</note>, through the whole of this hypothesis. For what other *one* can that be which is participated by *being*, than that which is in every being divine, and through which all things are conjoined with the <term>imparticipable one</term> <note>The absolute Unity (The One) that remains untouched and cannot be shared or divided by lower levels of reality.</note>? For, as bodies through their *life* are conjoined with *soul*, and as *souls* through their *intellective part* tend to *universal intellect* and the *first* intelligence, in like manner *true beings*, through the *one* which they contain, are reduced to a *separate union*, and are conjoined with the *first cause of all*.

But because this hypothesis commences from that which is *one being*, and establishes the summit of <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Realities that can only be grasped by the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses.</note> as the first after *the one*, but ends in an essence which participates of time, and deduces divine *souls* to the extremities of the divine orders, it is necessary that the third hypothesis should demonstrate by various conclusions the whole multitude of particular *souls*, and the diversities which they contain. And thus far the separate and incorporeal <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A term for an underlying reality or distinct level of existence.</note> extends.

But after this follows *that nature which is divisible about bodies and inseparable from matter*, which the fourth hypothesis delivers supernally <note>from a higher or divine origin</note> depending from the Gods. And the last *hypostasis* is the procession of matter, whether considered as one or as various, which the fifth hypothesis demonstrates by negations, according to its *dissimilar similitude to the first*. But sometimes, indeed, the negations are privations, and sometimes the separate causes of all productions. And that which is most wonderful of all, the

But each of the negations consequent to these is affirmative; the one paradigmatically <note>as an archetype or perfect pattern</note>, but the other iconically <note>as an image or representation</note>, or according to similitude. But there are four hypotheses besides these, which by taking away ***the one*** entirely subvert <note>undermine or destroy</note> all things, both such as truly are, and such as subsist in generation <note>the world of physical change and becoming</note>, and show that no being can any longer exist. ***The one***, therefore, being admitted, all things subsist even to the last <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A layer of reality or distinct level of existence.</note>; and this being taken away, essence itself is immediately destroyed.

The preceding mode of exposition (except in the second hypothesis) agrees with that of the great ***Plutarch*** <note>Referring here to Plutarch of Athens (died c. 431 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher, rather than the more famous biographer Plutarch of Chaeronea.</note>, preserved by ***Proclus*** in his commentary on this dialogue, and which is as follows:

The first hypothesis discourses concerning the first God. The second, concerning the first intellect, and an order entirely intellectual. The third, of the soul. The fourth, of material species. And the fifth, of formless matter. For these are the five principles of things. ***Parmenides*** <note>The central philosopher in Plato's dialogue of the same name.</note> in the mean time, after the manner of his own Pythagoreans, calls every separate substance, on account of its simplicity, by the common appellation of ***one***. But he denominates matter and corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> form ***different***, on account of their flowing nature and far distant diversity from divine essences: especially since these two do not so much subsist by themselves as through others, and are not so much causes as <term>con-causes</term> <note>original: "concauſes"; contributing or secondary causes that assist a primary cause.</note>, as it is asserted in the ***Timaeus*** and ***Phaedo*** <note>Two of Plato's most famous dialogues dealing with the creation of the world and the immortality of the soul.</note>. With great propriety, therefore, the three first hypotheses, which inquire how ***the one*** is related to itself and to others, are considered as treating of principal causes. The sixth hypothesis, therefore, proves that, if there is *not that which is one in beings*, i. e. if intelligible <note>the realm of pure thought and Forms, accessible only to the mind</note> has no real subsistence, but partly possesses and is partly destitute of being, that which is sensible <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> would alone exist in the order of things. For, if intelligible is taken away, that which is sensible must alone remain; and there can be no knowledge beyond sense. And this the sixth hypothesis demonstrates to be absurd. But the seventh hypothesis proves that, *if the one which beings contain* has no kind of subsistence, there can be no knowledge, nor any thing which is the object of knowledge, which this seventh hypothesis shows is foolish to assert. And again, *if this one partly subsists and is partly without subsistence*, as the sixth hypothesis feigns, other things will be similar to shadows and dreams, which the eighth hypothesis confutes as absurd. But *if this one has no kind of subsistence*, other things will be less than shadows or a dream, that is, nothing; which the ninth hypothesis represents as a monstrous assertion. Hence the first hypothesis has the same relation to those which remain, as the principle of the universe to the universality of things. But the other four which immediately follow the first, treat concerning the principles posterior to <note>coming after or lower than</note> *the one*. And the four consequent to these prove that, *one being taken away*, all that was exhibited in the four prior hypotheses must entirely perish. For since the second demonstrates that, *if that one subsists which is conjoined with being*, every order of soul must subsist; the seventh declares that, *if this one is not*, all knowledge, reason, imagination, and sense, must be destroyed. Because a line is the first continuous and divisible nature amongst magnitudes, hence it participates of an indivisible, that is, of a *point*. And this *point*, though it is allotted a superlinear <note>existing above or beyond the nature of a line</note> condition and is indivisible, yet it subsists in the *line*, is something belonging to it, and is the summit of the line. To which we may add, that many lines in a circle touch by their several points the centre of the circle. In like manner an intelligible and intellectual essence, because it is the first multiplied nature, on this account partakes of an excellent unity. **W**HEN we arrived at Athens from Clazomenia <note>A city on the coast of Ionia (modern-day Turkey), known for its philosophical tradition.</note>, the place of our abode, we fortunately met with Adimantus and Glaucus <note>Adimantus and Glaucon were the older brothers of the philosopher Plato.</note> in the forum: and Adimantus, taking me by the hand, I am glad to see you (says he), Cephalus; and if you are in want of any thing here, in which we are able to assist you, I beg you would inform me. Upon which I replied, I came for this very purpose, as being indigent of your assistance. Tell me, then (says he), what you are in want of. And I replied, What was your brother’s name? for I do not remember: as he was almost a child when I first came here from Clazomenia; and, since that circumstance took place, a great length of time has intervened. But his father’s name was, I think, Pyrilampes. Entirely so (says he), and my brother’s name was Antiphon. But what is it you principally inquire after? I replied, These my fellow-citizens are very philosophic, and have heard that this Antiphon was frequently present with one Pythodorus, the <term>familiar: a close friend or intimate associate</term> of Zeno, and that he treasured in his memory the discourses which Socrates, Zeno, and Parmenides had with each other, and which had frequently been heard by Pythodorus. Hence truly proceeding as far as to the last of things, and suspending all things from a paternal cause <note>The "paternal cause" refers to the primary, father-like creator or origin of the universe.</note>, and perfecting the conceptions of Socrates concerning these, he proceeds to the third problem, or the manner in which ideas are participated, again extending obstetric aid <note>A metaphor for teaching: like a midwife helping to give birth to a child, the teacher helps the student give birth to their own latent knowledge.</note>. For the mode of the discourse is every where **maieutic** <term>maieutic<note>Derived from the Greek word for midwifery; Socrates famously called his method of questioning "maieutics" because it brought truth out from within the soul.</note></term> or obstetric, and does not confute, and is **pirastic** <term>pirastic<note>From the Greek 'peirastikos,' meaning to test or probe; an exploratory style of argument meant to examine different possibilities.</note></term>, or explorative, but not vindicative. It differs, however, so far as at one time it proceeds from on high as far as to the last of things, and at another recurs downwards to assertions adapted to divine causes; according to each of these forms perfecting and elevating Socrates, and distinctly unfolding his conceptions respecting these particulars. Such, then, is the mode of the discourse, calling forth spontaneous conceptions, accurately expanding such as are imperfect, and elevating those that are able to follow them; truly imitating the paternal cause, which from the summit of all beings preserves, perfects, and draws upwards all things by the unknown powers which he contains. Let us now proceed to consider the mode in which forms or ideas are participated, following the divine Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers of antiquity, known for his deep commentaries on Plato.</note> as our leader in this arduous investigation.

The participations of intellectual forms are assimilated to the representations in a mirror; for as, in these, habitude and position cause the image of the person to be seen in the mirror; so, the aptitude of matter extending itself as it were to the Artificer <note>The "Demiurge" or divine craftsman who shapes the material world according to the eternal Forms.</note> of the universe, and to the inexhaustible abundance which he contains, is filled from him with forms. The participations are also assimilated to the impressions in wax. For ideas impart a certain vestige and impression of themselves; and neither is this impression the same with the seal by which it was produced, as neither is the form merged in matter the same with the immaterial and divine form from which it originated. But this latter mode differs from the former so far as it indicates a certain passive property in the recipient; for the mirror does not exhibit passivity sensibly, as the wax does in the latter instance. Hence some of the Platonic philosophers, considering matter as impassive <note>Meaning it does not change or suffer when receiving an image, just as a mirror is not changed by what it reflects.</note> in the participation of forms, assimilate it to a mirror, but call forms images and representations. Others again, considering matter as passive, say, that it is impressed like the wax by the seal, and call forms the *passions* of matter.

Forms also are said to be like the similitudes of icons <term>icons<note>From the Greek 'eikon,' meaning a likeness or image. In this context, the physical world is seen as a living portrait of the perfect, divine realm.</note></term>, whether effected by the painter’s, or the plastic, or any other art. For these forms, being fashioned by a divine artificer, are said to be similar to divine forms; and hence the whole sensible order is called the icon of the intelligible. But this assertion differs from the former, so far as this separates the maker from the exemplar;

It must, however, be observed, that each of these is imperfect considered by itself, and incapable of representing to our intellectual conceptions the whole truth respecting this participation. For, in the first place, consider, as to the mirror, that the countenance beheld in it turns itself towards the mirror, while, on the contrary, an intellectual cause beholds itself, and does not direct its vision to outward objects. If, too, the mirror appears to possess a communication of something, but in reality does not, (for the rays are reflected back to the countenance,) it is evident that this also is foreign from the participation of divine forms; for, as they are perfectly incorporeal, nothing can be separated from them and distributed into matter. <note>The mirror analogy fails because a reflection is a passive illusion, whereas a divine Form is an active, self-aware cause that doesn't actually "lose" pieces of itself to the matter it influences.</note>

In the second place, if we consider the impressions in wax, we shall find, that both that which impresses externally impresses, and that which is passive to the impression is externally passive; but form pervades through the whole of the subject matter, and operates internally. For nature fashions body inwardly, and not externally like art. And above all, in this instance, that which is participated approximates to that which participates. But it is requisite that divine forms should be exempt from all things, and not be mingled with any thing of a different nature. <note>The wax analogy fails because a seal is pressed onto the outside of the wax, but a divine Form shapes a thing from the inside out, like life growing within a seed.</note>

In the third place, let us consider the analogy from icons <note>original: "icons" - here referring to man-made images, such as paintings or statues.</note>, and we shall find this also deficient. For, in the first place, forms fashion the whole of the subject matter by which they are received, and this by an internal energy: and, in the next place, the exemplar and the maker are here separated from each other. Thus, the figure which is painted does not produce its likeness on the canvas, even though the painter should paint a resemblance of himself; for it is the soul which operates, and not the external figure, which is the exemplar; nor does that which makes, *assimilate* <note>To make something similar to or like itself.</note> that which is produced to itself; for it is soul which makes, and that which is produced is the resemblance of external form. But divine forms are at the same time paradigmatic <term>paradigmatic<note>From 'paradigm'; acting as the original model or perfect blueprint.</note></term> and demiurgic <term>demiurgic<note>From 'demiurge' (craftsman); meaning the Forms are not just models, but are the active forces that build and shape reality.</note></term> of their resemblances: for they have no similitude to the impressions in wax, but possess an efficacious essence, and a power assimilative of things secondary to themselves.

No one of these modes, therefore, is of itself sufficient to represent the true manner in which divine forms are participated. But, perhaps, if we can discover the most proper mode of participation, we shall see how each of these touches on the truth, at the same time that it falls short of the whole characteristic.

It is requisite, therefore, in order to this participation, to consider as the causes by which it is effected, the efficacious power of primary and divine forms, and the desire and aptitude of the natures which thence derive their formation. For neither is the fabricative and efficacious power of forms alone sufficient to produce participation; for they are every where similarly present, but are not similarly participated by all things. Nor is the desire and aptitude of the participants sufficient without the productive energy of forms; for desire and aptitude are of themselves imperfect. The prolific essence, therefore, of the demiurgic intellect exerts an

---

In the <term>intelligible world<note>The realm of pure ideas and eternal truths that can only be understood by the mind, not the physical senses.</note></term>, there exists that which is called the *just*, or the *beautiful itself*. Through these, things in our world may be said to participate in "wholes" rather than just "parts." For example, the <term>idiom<note>The 'idiom' refers to the unique, essential property or defining characteristic of a Form.</note></term> of the *beautiful* is found everywhere and in all things; however, in one place it is present intellectually, while in another it is present materially. 

It is evident that the ways more perfect things participate in these Forms are more abundant than those things further from perfection. Some things participate according to many powers, and others according to only a few. For instance, let the *beautiful itself* be defined as an *intellectual, vital form that causes symmetry*. Therefore, the "form" and *that which creates symmetry* are present in every beautiful thing, for this is the essential property of the *beautiful itself*; thus, every beautiful thing participates in that entire property. 

However, the *intellectual nature of the beautiful* is not present in all beauty, but only in the beauty belonging to the soul, for the beauty in the soul is uniform. Furthermore, its *vital nature* is not present in all beauty, but only in that which is celestial. Meanwhile, the mere *splendour of beauty* is seen in gold and in certain stones. Some things, therefore, participate in both the *intellectual and vital nature of the beautiful*; others participate in its vital nature separate from its intellectual nature; and others participate only in its outward appearance. 

More <term>immaterial natures<note>Things not made of physical matter, such as thoughts, souls, or mathematical truths.</note></term> receive more of these powers than material things. Secondary things, therefore, participate in both the "wholes" and "parts" of their proper <term>paradigms<note>An eternal, perfect model or blueprint in the divine mind which physical things attempt to copy.</note></term>. This is the proper way to speak to those who can look toward the incorporeal essence of forms. 

But to those who believe that "participation" is a physical or corporeal process, we must say that <term>sensibles<note>Physical objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note></term> are incapable of participating in either the wholes or the parts of ideas. Parmenides demonstrates this by leading Socrates to discover the most accurate way that forms are participated in. First, he shows they are not participated in as a "whole." Socrates suggests nothing prevents a whole form from being participated in, but Parmenides rejects this. He argues that if the same thing were in many separate things at once, then the thing itself would be separate from itself—which is the most absurd conclusion of all. 

For if a finger, or anything else that exists within other things—whether it is a physical part or a power—were in many separate things at once, it would be separate from itself. A physical power belonging to a subject would thus belong to many subjects and be separate from itself, existing as both one and many. Regarding a physical body, it is impossible for the whole of it to be in one place and simultaneously in another. It cannot be denied that many bodies may occupy one place when those bodies consist of pure, immaterial light (such as the celestial spheres that carry the planets), but it is impossible for the *same* body to be in many places at the same time. Therefore, it is impossible for a "whole" to be present in many subjects in a physical or corporeal way.

But, says <term>Proclus<note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (412–485 AD) whose commentaries on Plato are essential for understanding late antique philosophy.</note></term>, if you wish to see the accuracy of Plato’s language in a way suited to <term>theological speculation<note>Deep philosophical inquiry into the nature of the divine and the first principles of reality.</note></term>, you should divide the words and consider them as follows: Since forms first exist in the paradigm of intelligibles (as we learn in the *Timæus*), each of the primary forms will be *one*, and *being*, and a *whole*. Because they are such, it is impossible for the same thing to be in many separate things at once, except in an <term>exempt manner<note>To exist in an 'exempt manner' means to be the cause of something without being limited, contained, or diminished by the thing it creates.</note></term>. In this way, a form can be both "everywhere" and "nowhere," present with all things eternally without being mixed or diluted by them. For—

It concludes that while physical bodies cannot be in two places at once, divine Forms exist in an "exempt manner," allowing them to influence the material world without being confined by it.</summary>

it seems. Are you then willing to assert that one form is in reality divided, and that nevertheless it is still one? To that Socrates said, "By no means." For see (said Parmenides), whether upon dividing <term>magnitude|the abstract concept of size or "greatness"</term> ¹ itself, it would not be absurd that each of the many things which are great, should be great by a part of magnitude that is actually less than magnitude itself? "Entirely so," said Socrates.

***

¹ Parmenides, says <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Greek philosopher who wrote this commentary to explain the deeper metaphysical meanings in Plato's dialogues.</note> Proclus, wishing to show the absurdity of admitting that a <term>formal essence|the essential nature of an ideal Form</term> is <term>partible|capable of being divided into parts</term>, discourses concerning magnitude, equality, and <term>parvitude|smallness</term>, because each of these is observed in relation to quantity. But quantity does not have a part that is the same as the whole; for example, a part of a certain quality (like the heat of fire) seems to keep the same power as the whole, whereas a part of a quantity (like a gallon of water) is simply less than the whole. Therefore, in the cases of magnitude, equality, and smallness, he very properly disproves the ideas of those who say that Forms can be broken into parts. For, if these forms—which seem most likely to be divisible because they deal with size—cannot be divided, then by much greater reason other forms must be indivisible, such as "the just itself," "the beautiful itself," and "the similar itself." Parmenides groups these with magnitude to ask how they are shared by <term>sensibles|physical things we can perceive with our senses</term>. He focuses his demonstration on magnitude first. If we imagine magnitude can be physically divided, the part would be less than the whole. If a physical object becomes "great" by receiving only a *part* of Greatness, it would be called "great" by receiving something that is actually "smaller." This contradicts the rule that things which share in "the great" must be great, and those that share in "the small" must be small.

Let us however consider magnitude itself by itself, apart from physical division. Do we not say that it contains a multitude of powers and is not just one simple thing? But, if it has a multitude of parts, shall we say that each of its parts is "magnitude itself," or that each is less than the whole? If every part were the same as the whole "magnitude itself," we would have to divide it forever to infinity. But if magnitude is not made of smaller magnitudes, then the whole would be made of parts that don't match its nature. We must conclude that the "parts" of a Form like magnitude are powers that match the whole, but are not exactly what the whole is. For example, a spark of fire is still fire, but the power of a bonfire is greater than that of the spark; the fire is not made of "cold" parts, nor is a tiny spark as strong as the whole flame. Hence we must understand that magnitude itself has two types of power: one that allows incorporeal (spiritual or mental) things to surpass one another, and another that acts upon physical bodies. So, even though a Form has many powers, it never loses its <term>proper idiom|unique and essential character</term>. By thinking about "parts" and "wholes" in this intellectual way—rather than thinking of them like pieces of a physical object—we can avoid the logical traps that Parmenides is pointing out.

But what then? Can that which participates in a part of **equal** <gloss>1</gloss> itself, be equal to anything by this its part of equality, which is less than equality itself?

<gloss>1</gloss> **Magnitude itself** <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "Form" or "Itself" refers to the perfect, abstract version of a concept that exists beyond the physical world.</note> is the source of excellence and complete perfection for all things, whether that perfection is intellectual, vital, or exists within physical space. But **the equal** is the cause of harmony and proportion in all things. As we shall show in the additional notes to the *Timaeus* <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's famous dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note>, all mathematical and physical averages are derived from equality, and its ultimate goal is friendship and union. Since the <term>demiurgus|the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</term>, in decorating the universe, used all these mathematical bonds, we can safely conclude that the intellectual cause of these bonds is this "creator-style equality." Just as the <term>monad|the primary unit or "the One"</term> which exists in the creator gives life to every natural number, so too the equality found there generates all the "middle points" we see in our world. Even the equality in our own <term>dianoëtic|the capacity for discursive, logical reasoning</term> mind generates mathematical concepts. If this is true for mere images of things, it is even more true for the perfect intellectual Forms. Therefore, **Equality** is what gives order to all worldly things. It provides "co-ordination" to beings, just as **magnitude** provides "excellence" and <term>parvitude|the quality of being small or "smallness"</term> provides "subjection" (the state of being below or smaller). It appears that all things are shaped by this triad of forms—Magnitude, Equality, and Smallness—as they grant greatness to higher things, smallness to lower things, and a shared connection to those on the same level. Every series of things in the universe requires these three: **excellence, co-ordination,** and **subjection.**

Let us now see how Parmenides defeats the arguments of those who think that physical "equal" things share in the Form of Equality in a physical, bodily way. For, if any physical object shares only a *part* of Equality, it is obvious that it shares in something less than the whole. But if that were the case, the thing sharing in the "lesser" would no longer be lesser, but equal <note>This is a logical trap: if you become "equal" by taking a piece of "Equality" that is "less than" the whole, you are using something "small" to become "equal," which makes no sense.</note>. However, this shouldn't be; it is agreed that the Forms give their names to physical things. Therefore, something that shares in "the small" must be called smaller, not equal; and something that shares in "the equal" must be called equal, not smaller. If we look at Equality itself as an <term>incorporeal essence|a non-physical, spiritual reality</term>, we must say that while it is one thing, it contains within itself the causes of all types of equality: equality in weight, in size, in groups, in status, and in birth. Each of these specific examples is a type of **equal**, but each has a power and status lower than the "Whole Equality." Since every Form produces all the different versions of its power, there are many "equalities" contained under the one "Great Equality." We should not be surprised if all these smaller equalities are affected by "smallness" because all Forms communicate with one another. Even **magnitude** itself, because it has less power than some other Forms, shares in "smallness." Likewise, **smallness** itself, because it is greater than other forms, shares in "magnitude." Meanwhile, every physical thing shares in a Form only as it is in itself, and not in the way it mixes with others.

<meta>This page continues the logical puzzle from page 50 regarding how physical things "participate" in abstract Forms. Having discussed Magnitude (Greatness) and Equality, the dialogue now turns to Parvitude (Smallness).</meta>

## THE PARMENIDES.

It is impossible. But some one of us must possess a part of this small quantity; and that which is *small itself*¹ will be greater than this, this small quantity

---

<note>¹ **Smallness itself** (referred to here as <term>parvitude|the abstract essence of being small</term>) can be seen as the source of how all things are contained or "subjected" within their forms. It provides <term>impartibility|the quality of being impossible to divide</term> and a power that pulls everything toward a single point. 

Through this principle of "smallness" or "concentration," souls are able to move away from a life scattered among physical bodies and senses toward a more unified, undivided way of living. Because of this, physical bodies are compressed and held together by their indivisible causes; the entire world remains a single unit, with its life force converging at the center. From this concept, we derive things like the poles of the earth, the centers of circles, and points of contact where lines meet—things that have no physical width or "parts."

However, the current argument shows that it is impossible for physical, <term>sensible|things that can be perceived by the five senses</term> objects to "take a piece" of Smallness in a physical way. If Smallness itself had parts, the whole of Smallness would be "greater" than its part. This is a logical contradiction: how can the very essence of "Small" be "Great" or "Greater" than anything? 

Furthermore, if we were to take a piece away from "the Small" and add it to something else, that thing would technically have something added to it, making it larger, not smaller. Therefore, the Form of Smallness cannot be divided into pieces.

The philosopher Proclus mentions that his colleague, Pericles, interpreted this the same way. It is absurd to think Smallness can be sliced up. Proclus notes that some earlier scholars found this logic so difficult they thought the passage was fake. However, Parmenides uses these examples of adding and subtracting to show that trying to understand these abstract Forms as if they were physical, "corporeal" objects is a mistake.

In summary, Proclus argues that **Magnitude** (Greatness), **Parvitude** (Smallness), and **Equality** are all "impartible"—they have no physical parts and are entirely non-physical. Physical things are limited by <term>interval|physical space or extension</term>, but these abstract Forms are present everywhere at once, regardless of how big or small a thing is. They exist above space and "untemporally" (outside of time).</note>

<summary>This page concludes the argument that the Form of Smallness cannot be divided into parts, as it would lead to the logical contradiction of "Smallness" being "greater" than its parts. It establishes that Forms like Magnitude and Equality are non-physical, indivisible, and exist outside of time and space.</summary>
