"In what manner then, O Socrates," [asked Parmenides], "can**

Forms give the participation of themselves to created things? They do so in an instant, without being divided, and without needing any length of time to do so. Let no one, therefore, try to apply physical rules to the Forms—such as time, location, or physical division—nor should anyone imagine that Forms are made of parts or can be separated. Such things are very far removed from the non-physical simplicity of Forms, and from the purity of an indivisible essence that exists in eternity.

¹ The entire phrasing of these words, says <term>Proclus|A major Neoplatonic philosopher (412–485 AD) who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato</term>, is "excitative" and <term>maieutic|A 'midwife-like' method of teaching that helps a student give birth to their own ideas</term> of Socrates' thoughts. For this reason, Parmenides does not simply declare "physical things do not participate in Forms" like a debater seeking a quick victory. Instead, he pushes Socrates to discover for himself the most appropriate way that things "participate" in these abstract ideas. 

We have already noted that "whole" and "part" should not be understood as physical pieces, but in a way suited to non-physical, intellectual realities. Physical things participate in both the "whole" and the "parts" of a Form. For example, insofar as the <term>idiom|The unique, signature quality</term> of a Form flows down into every individual thing, that thing participates in the "whole." But, because secondary, physical things cannot hold the full power of their divine causes, they only participate in "parts." 

Thus, higher beings receive more power from the perfect <term>paradigm|The original pattern or model (the Form)</term>, while lower beings receive less. If there are beings elsewhere in the universe more perfect than humans, they would have a greater connection to the "Idea of Man" and possess more of its powers. 

Consider the "Lion": the <term>celestial|Heavenly or cosmic</term> Lion is a purely intellectual being, while the <term>sublunary|Earthly (literally 'under the moon')</term> lion is a physical, irrational animal. The heavenly one is closer to the true "Idea of a Lion" than the earthly one. Yet, the signature quality of that Idea reaches even down to mortal creatures; this shared connection is why earthly things "sympathize" with heavenly things. 

Proclus also uses the Moon as an example: the Moon seen in the heavens is a divinity, but the "Lunar Form" is also found here on Earth in certain stones. These stones possess a power belonging to the Moon’s order, as they may grow or shrink in harmony with the Moon's phases. Thus, a single quality flows from the highest Gods down to the lowest objects, passing through middle levels like <term>daemons|Spiritual intermediaries between gods and humans</term>. These "series" or chains of influence extend from the intellectual Gods to the heavens, and from the heavens down to the Earth, changing as they pass through the different elements. The higher parts of these chains participate more fully, and the lower parts less so, but the same signature quality binds the whole series together as one.

¹ From what has been already delivered (says <term>Proclus|A major Neoplatonic philosopher (412–485 AD) whose commentaries are essential for understanding how the later Academy interpreted Plato</term>) it is sufficiently evident that forms are not participated in a physical or "corporeal" manner; from which we may infer that they do not create physically, nor do they operate by pushing things around like the motions of bodies. But if this is the case, it is evident that the order of forms is non-physical. In the *Sophist* <note>original: *Sophista*</note>, therefore, it is shown that the **one** is non-physical; for, if it were a body, it would require something else to unite its parts. 

But it is here shown that **true being and intellectual forms** have an indivisible existence: and in the *Laws*, it is shown that the soul is shared by the parts of form, insofar as they do not participate in the form itself, but in its images; and images are like reflections or "parts" of their proper <term>paradigms|The original, perfect patterns or 'blueprints' of which physical things are mere copies</term>. For an image is to its paradigm as a part is to the whole. And if anyone, admitting this explanation, examines what has been already delivered concerning ideas, none of those impossibilities will follow which some of the ancients have considered as the inevitable consequences of the doctrine of ideas. 

For example, will it be impossible for the same thing to be in all things, if we admit that a non-physical and intellectual form—existing in itself and requiring no physical seat or place—is equally present to all things which are able to receive it? Will it be impossible that an essentially indivisible form, which exists beforehand as one, should be divided among those who participate in it and suffer a <term>Titanic divulsion|A reference to the Greek myth of the Titans tearing the god Dionysus into pieces; here it refers to the philosophical problem of a single idea being 'shattered' into many physical objects</term>? 

And is it not most true that whatever participates in **magnitude itself** (greatness) participates in the lesser? For magnitude in the participant, being divisible, is merely the image of magnitude itself; but the image is naturally less than the perfect pattern by a certain degree. In like manner, that which we call **equal** in the world of the senses is less than the power of the **equal itself**, and is nothing more than the image of perfection; but the equal itself is greater than this, insofar as it is more perfect in power. 

In short, with respect to each of these three forms, since they are distinct from the things that share in them, they measure the essence of those things and provide the reason why they are subordinate. According to their distinct excellence, each employs **magnitude itself**; according to their measuring power, the **equal itself**; and according to the gift of being subordinate, <term>parvitude|An archaic term for smallness</term> itself. All, therefore, cooperate with each other in the gifts which they grant to secondary natures. For, if magnitude itself grants a power which extends to all things, but smallness grants the quality of being a single unit, they are <term>connascent|Born together or inherently linked</term> with each other; since by pervading a great number of particulars in an indivisible way, they are indivisible to a greater degree: and both are equal in a greater degree, by being especially the measures both of themselves and others. 

There is nothing, therefore, absurd or impossible if "whole" and "part" are considered in a manner suited to the nature of forms; rather, all things follow logically according to the hypothesis. This is why Parmenides appears to continually ask Socrates how physical things participate in forms, and how "whole" and "part" are to be viewed in them—to elevate him to the most true understanding of the Ideas.

The doubt prior to this considered the participation of ideas as if it were a physical or corporeal process. Parmenides, therefore, ascends to a certain incorporeal reason. Looking at physical things, we must define this reason as physical, and we must assert that the mode of participation is indeed incorporeal, but possesses something in common with the participants. For if, along with incorporeal participation, we also considered the things participated in as perfectly separate from their participants, no doubt would remain concerning the participation. These two things produce the doubt: the idea of a physical mode of being present, and the possession of something common between ideas and their participants. As the proximate transition, therefore, is from bodies to natures, Parmenides evinces that physical reasons fall short of the perfection of ideas, which is primary and unmingled with its participants.

From hence it may be inferred, that, as form is that primarily which the multitude under it is secondarily, it neither communicates with this multitude according to name alone, nor is synonymous with it; and that it is not necessary again to investigate that which is common to form and its depending multitude. When, therefore, we consider the one in every form, we ought not to investigate it either <term>doxastically|Based on "doxa," or mere opinion and sensory perception</term> or <term>dianoëtically|Based on "dianoia," or discursive, step-by-step reasoning</term>: for these knowledges are not connate with <term>intellectual monads|The highest, most unified principles of pure intellect, which are indivisible and prior to all complexity</term>, which neither belong to the objects of opinion, nor to those of the dianoëtic part, as we learn from the sixth book of the *Republic*. But it is fit that we should survey the simple and uniform essence of forms through intellectual intuition. Nor must we conceive that the one in these subsists according to composition from the many, or by an abstraction from particulars: for the intellectual number of forms proceeds from *the good and the one*, and does not depart from a union and alliance adapted to the cause which gave it subsistence. Hence, Socrates in the *Philebus*, at one time calls *ideas* unities, and at another time monads. For, considered with relation to *the one*, they are *monads*, because each is a multitude, since it is a certain being, life, and intellectual form; but considered with relation to their productions, and the series to which they give subsistence, they are *unities*; for things posterior to them are multiplied, and from their <term>impartible essence|A reality that cannot be divided into parts; a whole that is present everywhere at once</term> become partible. For they are neither <term>connumerated|Listed or counted together as part of the same group</term> with their effects, nor do they give completion to their essence; since, if they subsisted in their productions, they could not be beheld as the principle of them, and as their prolific cause. He, therefore, who is willing to pass from these <term>sensibles|Physical objects perceived through the senses</term>, and every way divided natures, to forms themselves, must permit intellect instead of opinion to be the leader of the way, and must contemplate every form uncoordinated and unmingled with objects of sense; neither conceiving that they possess any <term>habitude|A specific relation or state of connection</term> with sensibles, nor surveying any common definition of essence between them and the many, nor, in short, any coordination of participants and the things which are participated. Parmenides, therefore, gradually evinces that primary <note>Forms</note> are expanded above divisible forms, and all that is mingled and connumerated with these, and this according to a wonderful transcendency of nature.

And here, what Socrates observes in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and the Forms</note> respecting the participation of forms, is worthy of admiration: for he there says, that he cannot yet strenuously affirm whether it is requisite to call this participation *presence*, or *communion*, or any thing else besides these. For, from the first doubt, it may be evinced that it is impossible for the participation to be *presence*, since neither the whole, nor certain parts of them, are able to be present with their participants. But, from this second doubt, we may confute those who contend that the participation is *communion*. If, therefore, there is any thing common to ideas and their participants, there will be a transition <note>original: "ad infinitum"</note> to infinity from the participants of that which is common to that which is common; and hence this latter doubt is different from the former. For the former was, that form is present with its participants, and is something belonging to them; but the latter, that form is different from its participant, but possesses an abundant communion with it. Hence, in the former, the argument proceeds from the inability of form being present, either according to the whole or a part of itself; but, in the latter, it no longer proceeds in a similar manner, but, from that which is common in form and its participant, again ascends to something else which is more common than the one form, and the many by which it is participated. He alone, therefore, can assign a scientific reason concerning the participation of forms, who takes away that which is corporeal in their being present, and removes that which is common from an incorporeal essence. For thus ideas will be incorporeally present with their participants, but will not be subdued by one relation towards them; that they may be every where, through their incorporeal nature, and no where, in consequence of being exempt from their participants. ->away exempt transcendency<- <note>This likely begins a new section of the commentary emphasizing the "exempt" or separate nature of Forms.</note> For it is requisite, indeed, that there should be communion, yet not as of things coordinate <note>things of the same rank or level</note>, but only so far as participants are suspended from ideas; but ideas are perfectly exempt from their participants. Whence union to things every way dissipated? Whence is a never-failing essence present with things perpetually generated, unless the incorporeal and all-perfect order of forms has a subsistence prior to these? Others again, of the antients, says **Proclus**, allied that which is common in particulars as the cause of the permanency in forms: for man generates man, and the similar is produced from the similar. They ought, however, at the same time to have directed their attention to that which gives subsistence to what is common in particulars: for, as we have before observed, true causes are exempt from their effects. That which is common, therefore, in particulars, may be assimilated to one and the same seal which is impressed in many pieces of wax, and which remains the same, without failing, while the pieces of wax are changed. What, then, is it which proximately impresses this seal in the wax? For matter is analogous to the wax, the sensible man to the type, and that which is common in particulars, and verges to things, to the ring itself. What else, then, can we assign as the cause of this, than nature proceeding through matter, and thus giving form to that which is sensible, by her own inherent reasons? Soul, therefore, will thus be analogous to the hand which uses the ring, since soul is the leader of nature; that which ranks as a whole of the whole of nature, and that which is partial of a partial nature. But intellect will be analogous to the soul which impresses the wax through the hand and the ring; which intellect fills that which is sensible through soul and the nature of forms, and is itself the true <term>Porus|A figure from Plato's Banquet representing 'Plenty' or 'Resource,' here used to describe the overflowing source of divine principles</term> \*, generative of the reasons which flow, as far as to matter. It is not necessary, therefore, to stop at the things common in particulars, but we should investigate the causes of them. For why do men participate of this peculiar something which is common, but another animal of a different something common, except through unapparent reasons? For nature is the one mother of all things; but what are the causes of definite similitudes? It is necessary, therefore, that there should be another cause of similars prior to similars; and hence it is necessary to recur from the things common in particulars to the one cause which proximately gives <term>subsistence|the state of having real, independent existence</term> to <term>sensibles|things that can be perceived by the senses</term>, and to which Parmenides himself leads us. If, therefore, we fashion certain ideas from these, we shall often make infinities, though it is requisite that ideas should be less numerous than their participants, the participants of each, at the same time, being many. Very properly, therefore, does Parmenides direct the mode of transition to ideas, as not being scientific, if it proceeds from the things common in sensibles; for it will always be possible to conceive different things common, and thus to proceed *to infinity* <note>original Latin: *ad infinitum*</note>. 1 The fourth problem concerning ideas is here considered, viz. what kind of beings they are, or in other words, where they subsist, whether in souls, or prior to souls. Socrates, therefore, being separated by Parmenides from physical forms, calls idea a *conception* belonging to the soul <note>original Greek: *noema psychikon*</note>, and defines the place of it to be soul. For the form in soul is one and incorporeal; and this dogma is not attended with the former difficulties. For this form is exempt from the many, and is not co-ordinate with them like the forms in matter, in consequence of being allotted a subsistence in soul. There is likewise nothing common between this form and the many; nor is it either according to the whole, or a part of itself, in its participants, so that it may be shown to be separate from itself, or to have a partible subsistence. Socrates, therefore, by adopting this dogma, avoids the above-mentioned doubts. But, says Proclus, when Socrates calls idea a *conception* (thought), we must not think that he asserts it to be that which is the object of intellectual vision <note>original Greek: *to nooumenon*</note> in the same manner as we call that which is apprehended by sense *sensible* <note>original Greek: "as we say the 'sensible' is that which is grasped by sense"</note>; but that intelligence itself understanding form, is here called a *conception*; being so denominated as a certain theorem and dogma ingenerated in souls, about **dogmatized and deiform concerns** <note>original Greek: "Thus it is called a 'thought,' being a kind of theorem and doctrine arising in souls about things that are established and deiform (god-like in form)."</note>. Looking to this essential reason we say, that the soul is all forms, and is the place of forms, not in capacity only, but in that kind of <term>energy|the state of being active or actualized; in Greek philosophy, "energeia" refers to the fulfillment of a potential</term>, through which we call one skilled in geometry a geometrician in energy, even when he does not geometrize, and which Aristotle accurately calls the prior form of being in energy. This, therefore, which is denominated a conception, as of posterior origin, is very properly said to be different from the essential reason of the soul: for it is more obscure than the many in sensibles, as being posterior and not prior to them. But the essential reason or form of the soul is more perfect, because the conception of posterior origin, or in modern language, *abstract idea*, has a less essence than the many, but the essential form more.

That it is not, however, proper to stop at conceptions of posterior origin, i. e. notions gained by an abstraction from sensible particulars, but that we should proceed to those essential reasons which are allotted a perpetual subsistence within the soul, is evident to those who are able to survey the nature of things. For, whence is man able to collect into one by reasoning the perceptions of many senses, and to consider one and the same unapparent form prior to things apparent, and separated from each other; but no other animal that we are acquainted with, surveys this something common, for neither does it possess a rational essence, but alone employs sense, and appetite, and imagination? Whence, then, do rational souls generate these universals, and recur from the senses to that which is the object of opinion? It is because they essentially possess the *gnostically* <note>The word "gnostically" here refers to the faculty of knowing or cognitive understanding.</note> productive principles of things: for, as nature possesses a power productive of sensibles, by containing reasons, or productive principles, and fashions, and connects sensibles, so as by the inward eye to form the external, and in a similar manner the finger, and every other particular; so he who has a common conception of these, by previously possessing the reasons of things, beholds that which each possesses in common. For he does not receive this common something from sensibles; since that which is received from sensibles is a *phantasm*, and not the object of opinion. It likewise remains within such as it was received from the beginning, that it may not be false, and a non-entity, but does not become more perfect and venerable, nor does it originate from any thing else than the soul. Indeed, it must not be admitted that nature in generating generates by natural reasons and measures, but that soul in generating does not generate by *animastic* <note>Relating to the "anima" or soul; specifically the vitalizing power of the soul.</note> reasons and causes. But if matter possesses that which is common in the many, and this something common is essential, and more essence than individuals; for this is perpetual, but each of those is corruptible, and they derive their very being from this, since it is through form that every thing partakes of essence,—if this be the case, and soul alone possesses things common which are of posterior origin (<term>common concepts of posterior origin <note>original Greek: hysterogenē koina</note></term>), do we not make the soul more ignoble than matter? For the form which is merged in matter will be more perfect and more essence than that which resides in the soul; since the latter is of posterior origin, but the former is perpetual; and the one is after, but the other generative and connective of the many. Further still: the universal in the many is less than each of the many; for by certain additions and accidents it is surpassed by every individual. But that which is of posterior origin <note>That is, a universal concept formed in the mind *after* (posterior to) observing many individual examples.</note> (i.e., universal abstracted from particulars) comprehends each of the many. Hence it is predicated of each of these; and that which is particular is contained in the whole of this universal. For this something common, or abstract idea, is not only predicated of that something common in an individual, but likewise of the whole subject. How then can it thence derive its subsistence, and be completed from that which is common in the many? For, if from the many themselves, where do we see infinite men, of all which we predicate the same thing? And if from that which is common in the many, whence is it that this abstract idea is more comprehensive than its cause? Hence it has a different origin, and receives from another form this power which is comprehensive of every individual; and of this form the abstract idea which subsists in opinion is an image, the inward cause being excited from things apparent. To which we may add, that all demonstration, as Aristotle has shown in his <term>Last Analytics|Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, a treatise on logic and scientific knowledge</term>, is from things prior, more honourable, and more universal. How, therefore, is universal more honourable, if it is of posterior origin? For, in things of posterior origin, that which is more universal is more unessential; whence <term>species|a specific category or type</term> is more essence than <term>genus|a broader classification or group</term>. The rules, therefore, concerning the most true demonstration must be subverted, if we alone place in the soul universals of posterior origin: for these are not more excellent than, nor are the causes of, nor are naturally prior to, particulars. If, therefore, these things are absurd, it is necessary that essential reasons should subsist in the soul prior to universals, which are produced by an abstraction from <term>sensibles|physical objects perceived through the senses</term>. And these reasons or productive powers are indeed always exerted, and are always efficacious in divine souls, and in the more excellent orders of beings; but in us they are sometimes dormant, and sometimes in <term>energy|the state of being active or actualized; from the Greek "energeia"</term>.

Form, therefore, uniformly *is*, and lives, and *intellectually energizes*; but with respect to its progeny, some participate of all these, others of more or less of them, and others of one idiom alone. Since also in forms themselves, their intellectual nature is derived from the first intellect, their life from imparticable, or the first life, their being from the first being, and *the one* which they contain from the unity which is beyond beings.

For the end of obstetrication <note>This refers to "midwifery," the famous Socratic method of helping others "give birth" to the knowledge already within their souls.</note> is the evocation of inward knowledge, but of contention, victory. If, therefore, Socrates by every doubt advances, and is perfected, and distinctly evolves his conceptions concerning primary forms, we must say that he is rather obstetricated than vanquished by Parmenides.

This being premised, let us see how the hypothesis of Socrates approximates to the truth, but does not yet possess the perfect. For he is right in apprehending that forms are intellectual and truly paradigms <note>A "paradigm" is an original model or perfect pattern that exists in the divine mind.</note>, and in defining their idiom <note>In this context, "idiom" means a unique, essential characteristic.</note>, by asserting that they are *established*; and further still, in admitting that other things are assimilated to them. For the stable and a perpetual sameness of subsistence are the idioms of eternally energizing forms. For, in the *Politicus* <note>Plato's dialogue "The Statesman."</note>, it is said that a subsistence according to the same, and after the same manner, belongs only to the most divine of all things; and the Eleatean guest <note>The "Eleatic Stranger," the main speaker in Plato's "Sophist."</note>, in the *Sophista*, defines the *being established* (<term>being established</term> <note>original Greek: *to histasthai*, meaning to stand still or remain fixed in being</note>) to be nothing else than a subsistence according to the same, and after the same manner. If, therefore, Socrates also says, that forms are *established*, but things established subsist according to the same and after the same manner, and things which thus subsist are the most divine of all things, it is evident that forms will be most divine. Hence, they will no longer be the conceptions of souls, but will be exempt from every thing of this kind. These things, therefore, are rightly asserted; and Socrates also very properly admits union in forms prior to multitude. For the words *in nature* (<term>in nature</term> <note>original Greek: *en tê phusei*</note>) manifest the one henad <note>original text "enad": a Neoplatonic term for a supreme, divine unity</note> or unity of forms. It is usual indeed with Plato to give the appellation of *nature* to intelligibles. For Socrates, in the *Philebus*, says, that a royal intellect, and a royal soul, subsist in the *nature of Jupiter* <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>; and Timæus says, “*the nature of animal itself being eternal*,” signifying by nature the monad <note>A "monad" is the primary unit or source of a series.</note> of intelligible ideas. Such, therefore, is that which is now called nature, viz. the one unity and comprehension of intelligible forms. And thus far, as we have said, Socrates is right.

However, as he only attributes a paradigmatic idiom to ideas, and does not assert that they also *perfect*, guard, and unite, in this respect he will appear to have yet imperfectly apprehended the theory concerning them. For every form is not only the paradigm of sensibles, but also gives subsistence to them; since if it were alone paradigmatic, another nature would be requisite, in order to produce and assimilate sensibles to forms, which would thus remain sluggish and unmoved, without any efficacious power, and resembling impressions in wax. Forms, therefore, produce and generate their images: for it would be absurd that the reasons in nature <note>The "logoi" or rational principles that govern the physical world.</note> should possess a certain effective power, but that intelligible forms should be deprived of it. Hence, every divine form is not only paradigmatic, but also *paternal*, and is by its very essence a cause generative of the many. It is also *perfective*: for it leads sensibles from the imperfect to the *perfect*, fills up their indigence, and brings matter, which is all things in capacity, to become that in energy which it was in capacity, prior to its becoming specific. Forms, therefore, contain in themselves this perfective power. But do they not also possess a *guardian* power? For whence is the order of the universe indissoluble, except from forms? Whence those stable reasons, and which preserve the one sympathy of wholes infrangible, through which the world abides for ever

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Socrates' "paradigm" theory of forms. On the previous page, Parmenides began challenging Socrates' idea that things "participate" in forms by being "similar" to them, leading into the famous "Third Man" argument or the problem of infinite regress.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>

# THE PARMENIDES.

If any thing, therefore, becomes similar¹ to a form, can it be possible that the form should not be similar to that which is assimilated to it, insofar as the assimilated nature is rendered perfect, without the loss of any form, except from stable <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "stable causes" refers to the unchanging, divine principles that remain fixed while their effects change.</note> causes? Again, the divisible and scattered nature of bodies is held together and connected only by a power that cannot be divided. For a body is, by its very nature, divisible, and it requires the connective power of forms. But, if *union* comes before this connection—because everything that connects must first be one and undivided—then form will not only be a creator, and possess a *guarding* and *perfective* power, but it will also be *connective* and a unifier of all secondary natures. Socrates, therefore, should not only have said that form is a *paradigm* <term>paradigm: an original model or perfect pattern</term>, but should also have added, that it *connects*, *guards*, and *perfects* the things made in its likeness; which Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato's "Timaeus," who describes the creation of the universe.</note> also teaching us, says, that the world was generated *perfect* and *indissoluble* through its likeness to the "all-perfect animal" <note>original: "animal itself". In Platonic thought, this refers to the Intelligible Living Being, the divine blueprint containing the forms of all living things.</note> itself.

<gloss>¹ Socrates, as we have before observed, was not accurate in asserting that ideas are paradigms alone, since they also generate, *perfect*, and guard sensible things <note>Physical things perceived by the senses.</note>; and that sensible things are resemblances alone of ideas, since they are generated and guarded by them, and from them derive all their perfection and duration. This being the case, Parmenides, in a truly divine manner, grants that forms are established as paradigms in nature; but Socrates having introduced "similitude" (likeness), and a participation based on likeness, in order to solve the first doubts concerning how things share in forms, Parmenides—desiring to show the primary and total cause of the paradigm and its freedom from any dependence on its copies—shows that if a sensible thing is similar to an intelligible <note>Something understood by the intellect rather than the senses.</note> form, it does not follow that the relationship is mutual. The intelligible form does not have to be "similar" to the sensible thing. If it were, then before we could have two things similar to each other, we would have to search for yet another form to be the cause of that similarity, and this would continue to infinity <note>original: "ad infinitum"</note>: for things similar to each other completely share in a certain something which is the same, and through this "sameness" within them, they are said to be similar. Hence, if it be granted that the participant and that which is participated are similar—or, in other words, the paradigm and its copy—there will be something else prior to them which makes them similar, and this will continue to infinity. To avoid this problem, Socrates should have said that "the similar" has two meanings: one where two similar things are joined together, and another where a subject is similar to its original archetype. In the first, similarity is seen in a shared ratio; in the second, the copy possesses the same form *from* the original, but not *alongside* it as an equal. This much may be said through logic and philosophical inquiry.</gloss>

But if we direct our attention to the many levels of forms, we shall find the great depth which they contain. For there are physical forms prior to sensible things, the forms in the soul prior to those, and intellectual forms preceding those in the soul; but there are no others prior to these. Intellectual forms, therefore, are paradigms alone, and are by no means similar to the things that come after them; but the forms in the soul are both paradigms and images. And insofar as they are images, both these forms themselves, and the things that come after them, are similar to each other, as they both draw their existence from the same intellectual forms. This is also the case with physical forms, which are similar to sensible things, insofar as both are images of the forms which are above them. But will not that through the participation of which similars become similars be *form itself*? Entirely so. Nothing, therefore, can be similar to *a form*, nor *a form* to any other. For in this case another *form* will always appear besides some particular *form*: and if this again should become similar to another, another would be required; and a *new form* would never cease to take place, as long as any *form* becomes similar to its participant <note>This is the famous "infinite regress" argument. Hence, then, other things do not participate of *forms* through similitude <gloss>¹</gloss>; but it is necessary to seek after something else through which they participate. So it seems.

We may also say, speaking theologically <note>In this context, "theologically" refers to the Neoplatonic study of the divine hierarchy and the nature of primary causes.</note>, that there is one order of forms in the mundane <term>mundane: belonging to the physical, material world</term> intellect, another in the demiurgic <term>demiurgic: relating to the "Demiurge," the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</term> intellect, and another subsisting between these, namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note> in participated but supermundane <term>supermundane: existing in a realm above the physical world</term> intellect, or, in other words, in an intellect consubsistent indeed with soul, but unconnected with body, and binding the forms in the mundane intellect with that intellect which is not consubsistent with soul, and is therefore called imparticipable <term>imparticipable: a divine principle that is "unshared" and remains pure, rather than descending into lower things</term>. To those, therefore, who begin downwards, we may say that the intellectual forms in the world and in soul are similar to each other, so far as all these are secondary to the assimilative <term>assimilative: the power that makes lower things resemble higher, divine models</term> or supermundane intellects, and are as it were sisters to each other. But to those who recur to imparticipable intellect, this can no longer be said. For the assimilative order has a middle subsistence; and hence it assimilates sensibles <term>sensibles: things that can be perceived by the physical senses</term> which are subordinate to it to intellectual forms, but not, the other way around <note>original: "vice versa"</note>, intellectuals to sensibles. For it is not lawful that what is secondary should impart any thing to that which is primary, nor that what is primary should receive any thing from what is secondary. That Parmenides, therefore, might indicate to Socrates these paradigms, which are indeed intellectual, but established in imparticipable intellect prior to assimilative intellects, he shows him that it is not proper that the habitude <term>habitude: the relationship or disposition of one thing toward another</term> of forms to sensibles should reciprocate: for this pertains to things secondary to an assimilative cause.

Such, then, are the doubts, both of which happen through the exempt essence <term>exempt essence: a nature that is transcendent and completely separate from the physical world</term> of *forms*, which exemption we consider so transcendent as to have no communication with secondary natures <note>secondary natures: the physical or material things that come after and depend upon the higher Forms</note>. For that which thus subsists is foreign from us, and is neither known by, nor is gnostic <note>gnostic: possessing knowledge of</note> of, us. 

But, if the exempt nature of *forms*, together with transcendency, is also present to all things, our knowledge of them will be preserved, and they will possess a formal knowledge of secondary natures. For if they are everywhere present to all things, we may then be able to meet with them, by only making ourselves adapted to the reception of them. And if they adorn all things, they comprehend intellectually the cause of the things adorned. It is necessary, therefore, that those who wish to guard these dogmas, should consider *forms* as unshaken and exempt, and pervading through all things. And here also we may see how this accords with the unrestrained nature of *forms*: for neither does that which is *demiurgic* <term>demiurgic: relating to the "Demiurge" or divine craftsman who shapes the universe</term> in them possess any habitude <note>habitude: a specialized relationship or binding connection to something else</note> to things secondary, nor is their unrestrained and exempt nature such as to be incommunicable with, and foreign from, *sensibles* <term>sensibles: things that can be perceived by the five senses</term>.

But here the divine conception of *Plato* is truly admirable, which previously subverts through these doubts all the confused and atheistical suspicion concerning divine *forms*; imitating in this respect intellect itself, which, prior to the shadowy subsistence of evils, gave subsistence to subvertive powers. That it is not proper, therefore, to make that which is generative in *forms* possessing any habitude to that which is generated, or that which is paradigmatic to consist in verging to that which is governed, *Parmenides* has sufficiently shown in what has been already delivered. For all habitude requires another collective and connecting cause, so that, prior to *forms*, there will be another form conjoining both through similitude; since habitude is of the similar, with relation to the similar. 

But that the exempt nature of *forms* is not sluggish and without providential energy, and is not foreign from things secondary, *Parmenides* indicates through these doubts. For, perhaps, some one, alone looking to the unrestrained nature of *forms*, may say that they neither know their participants <note>participants: the physical objects that "take part" in a Form's nature</note>, nor are known by us. Hence, he leads *Socrates* to an animadversion <note>animadversion: a focused mental observation or consideration</note> of the mode of the exempt power of divine *forms*. And how, indeed, he collects that *sensibles* are not known by them, will be afterwards manifest to us; but he wishes, first of all, to evince that we are not able to know them, assuming, for this purpose, in a manner perfectly divine, that the science which we possess pertains to human objects of scientific knowledge, but that divine science belongs to such as are divine. And this, indeed, appears to deprive us of the knowledge of divine natures. It is, however, true in a certain respect, and not according to one mode, but after one manner when philosophically, and after another when theologically, considered. For let the science which is with us pertain to our objects of scientific knowledge; but what prevents such objects from being images of divine natures? Why, also, is it wonderful that the science which is with us should be so called with relation to that which is with us the object of scientific knowledge, and should be conjoined with this? For it is <term>coordinate: being on the same level or rank of existence</term> to that with respect to which it is denominated. It may also, not as coordinate knowledge, but as that which is of an inferior order, be admitted to <term>intelligibles: eternal truths or realities that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</term> themselves. For coordinate knowledges of all things are of one kind, and those which are arranged according to a different order of things known, of another, and which either apprehend the nature of things subordinate in a more excellent manner, as opinion the nature of sensibles, or which apprehend things more excellent secondarily and subordinately, as opinion that which is the object of science. He, therefore, who possesses scientific knowledge, and he who opines rightly, know the same thing, but the one in a more excellent, and the other in a subordinate manner. Hence there is no absurdity that science should be denominated not with relation to the object of science among intelligibles, but with relation to that with which it is conjoined, and that it should apprehend the former not as coordinate, but in a secondary degree. Agreeably to this, Plato in his <note>Seventh Epistle: A letter attributed to Plato where he discusses the difficulty of expressing philosophical truths in writing and the "five stages" of knowledge.</note> Seventh Epistle says that the intelligible form is not known through science but through <term>intelligence: here, the direct and immediate vision of the mind (intellect), rather than logical reasoning</term>, or the direct and immediate vision of intellect. For scientific knowledge is of a more composite nature with respect to intellectual intuition; but intellect is properly the spectator of ideas: for these are naturally intellectual, and we every where know the similar by the similar; intelligibles indeed by intellect, the objects of opinion by opinion, and things scientific by science. It is by no means wonderful, therefore, that there should be no science of *forms*, and yet that another knowledge of them should remain, such as that which we denominate intelligence.

that the hearer should possess a *naturally good disposition*, and this in a remarkable degree, that he may be by nature a philosopher, may be astonished about an incorporeal essence <note>A reality that exists without a physical body or material form.</note>, and prior to things visible may always pursue something else and reason concerning it, and may not be satisfied with things present; and in short he must be such a one as Socrates in the Republic describes him to be, who *naturally loves the speculation of wholes* <note>The study of universal truths and the totality of existence rather than just individual parts.</note>. In the next place, he must be skilled in a multitude of particulars, not indeed in a multitude of human affairs, for these are trifling, and contribute nothing to a divine life, but in logical, physical, and mathematical theorems. For such things as our <term>dianoëtic: the faculty of discursive reason that thinks through arguments step-by-step</term> power is unable to survey in the Gods, we may behold in these as in images; and beholding we are induced to believe the assertions of theologists concerning divine natures. 

Thus if he wonders how multitude is contained in *the one*, and all things in the <note>impartible: that which cannot be divided into parts; a perfect unity.</note> impartible, he will perceive that the even and the odd, the circle and the sphere and other forms of numbers are contained in the <term>monad: the primary unit or the "One" from which all numbers originate</term>. If he wonders how a divine nature makes by its very essence, he will perceive in natural objects that fire essentially imparts heat, and snow coldness. And if he wonders how causes are every where present with their effects, he will behold the images of this in logic. For <term>genera: broad categories or "families" of things</term> are every where predicated of the things of which species are predicated, and the latter indeed with the former, but the former without the latter. And thus in every thing, he who is unable to look directly to a divine nature, may survey it through these as images. It is requisite, therefore, in the first place, that he should possess a naturally good disposition, which is allied to true beings, and is capable of becoming winged <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul grows wings as it ascends toward divine truth.</note>, and which as it were from other persuasions vindicates to itself the conceptions concerning permanent being. For as in every study we require a certain preparation, in like manner in order to obtain that knowledge which genuinely leads to being, we require a preceding purified aptitude. In the next place, skill, as we have said, in many and all-various theorems is requisite, through which he will be led back to the apprehension of these things; and, in the third place, alacrity <note>Eager readiness or cheerful speed.</note>, and an extension of the powers of the soul about the contemplation of true beings; so that from his leader alone indicating, he may be able to follow his indications.

Three things, therefore, are requisite to the contemplation of an incorporeal nature: a naturally good disposition, skill, and alacrity. And through a naturally good disposition indeed, faith in a divine nature will be spontaneously produced; but through skill the truth of paradoxical theorems will be firmly possessed; and through alacrity the amatory tendency <note>The "love" or "eros" that drives the soul toward beauty and truth.</note> of the soul to the contemplation of true being will be excited.

But the leader, says Proclus, of these speculations, will not be willing through a long discourse to unfold divine truth, but to indicate it with brevity, framing his language similar to his <term>intellections: acts of pure intellectual intuition or direct mental grasping of truth</term>; nor will he accomplish this from things known and at hand, but supernally, from principles most profoundly one. Nor again, will he so discourse as that he may appear to speak clearly, but he will be satisfied with indications. For it is requisite that mystical concerns should be mystically delivered, and that occult conceptions respecting divine natures, should not be rendered popular. <gloss>1</gloss> The discourse here proceeds to other doubts, one of which takes away from our soul the knowledge of true beings, while the other deprives divine natures of the knowledge of sensibles <note>Objects or things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>; through both of these, our progression from and return to divine natures are destroyed. Secondary and primary things also appear to be torn apart from each other—the secondary being deprived of the primary, and the primary failing to produce the secondary natures. The truth, however, is that everything is in all things in an appropriate manner; the middle and last types of wholes exist by their causes in the first things, which is why they are truly known by them, just as they exist within them; but primary things exist according to participation in those that are middle; and both of these in such things as are last. Hence souls also know all things in a manner suited to each: through images, they know things that come before them; but through causes, they know things that come after them; and in a shared and coordinated manner, they know the reasons or productive principles which they themselves contain. These doubts, therefore, follow the two prior ones concerning the order of ideas, because Socrates and everyone who admits that there are ideas must be led to this hypothesis through a causal and scientific knowledge of everything in the world. Hence those who deny that there are ideas also deny the providential care of intelligible things <note>The eternal, non-physical realities that can only be understood by the mind.</note>. Parmenides, therefore, proposes at present to show that by admitting ideas to be alone exempt <note>Existing independently and separately from the physical world.</note> from things, it must also necessarily be admitted that they are unknown, as there will no longer be any connection between us and them, nor any knowledge of whether they exist or not, whether they are participated in, and how, and what order they are assigned, if they are alone exempt, and are not, together with unrestrained energy, the causes of secondary natures. But for the consideration of this, the discourse pre-assumes certain axioms and common concepts; and, in the first place, that ideas are not entirely exempt, and do not exist by themselves without any connection with lower things. For how can this be possible, since both we and all other things depend upon them? For the place in which they exist is the intellect—not that it is a "place" as if they required a seat, in the same way as accidents <note>Properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like color.</note> require a substance for their support, or as material forms require matter. For the discourse no longer supposes them to be corporeal or physical, or conceptions of the soul, but prior to all these. For they are not in us, says Parmenides; nor are they coordinate with our conceptions.

You may say, then, philosophically with Proclus, that they are <term>exempt from</term> <note>Meaning they exist on a higher level and are not restricted by or contained within us.</note>, and are not in us; and that they are present every where, and are participated by us, without being <term>ingenerated</term> <note>Produced or born within.</note> in their participants. For they being in themselves, are proximate to all things for participation that are capable of receiving them. Hence, we participate them through the things which we possess, and this is not only the case with us, but also with more excellent natures, who possess in themselves essential images of ideas, and introducing these as <term>vestiges of paradigms</term> <note>Traces or footprints of the original models (the Ideas).</note> to ideas, they know the latter through the former. For he who understands the essence of these, knows also that they are images of other things, but knowing this, it is also necessary that by <term>intellections</term> <note>Acts of pure intellectual perception.</note> he should come into contact with the paradigms. But you may say, theologically, that the forms which are exempt from those that are intellectual, are perfectly established above our order. Hence, of intellectual forms, we perceive both in ourselves, and in sensibles, images; but the essence of intelligibles, through its profound union, is perfectly exempt both from us and all other things, being of itself unknown. For it fills Gods and intellects with itself; but we must be satisfied with participating intellectual forms in a manner adapted to the soul. Plato also manifests these things when he makes our life to be twofold, political and theoretical, and assigns us a twofold felicity; elevating the former life to the patronymic government of Jupiter, and the latter to the Saturnian order and a pure intellect. <note>An asterisk-like mark appears here in the text, possibly indicating a reference or footnote on a different page.</note> For from hence it is evident that he re-elevates the whole of our life, as far as to the intellectual kings: for Saturn subsists at the summit, and Jupiter at the extremity, of the intellectual order. <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "Saturn" represents pure, inward-looking contemplation, while "Jupiter" represents the creative, governing power of the universe.</note> But such things as are beyond these, he says in the *Phaedrus*, are the spectacles of souls divinely inspired and initiated in them as in the most blessed of all mysteries. So that thus the proposed axiom will be true, when considered as pertaining to a certain formal order. And thus much for the things.

With respect to the diction, says Proclus, the words **In what respect, O Parmenides?** <note>original Greek: πη δη ῶ Παρμενιδη;</note> are the interrogation of Socrates, vehemently wondering if intellectual form is unknown, and not yet perceiving the transition, and that Parmenides proceeds through the whole extent of forms till he ends in the first ideas. But the words **For how could it any longer subsist itself by itself?** <note>original Greek: πως γαρ αν αυτη καθ’ αυτην ετι ειη;</note> are asserted according to common conceptions.

Hence, through these three terms, *itself*, *by itself*, and *essence*, <term>Parmenides</term> unfolds the whole truth concerning these <term>forms</term> <note>The perfect, eternal patterns or "Ideas" of things that exist in the divine mind.</note>. It remains, therefore, separately in itself, and being participated in, does not become anything belonging to those who participate in it; rather, subsisting prior to them, it imparts to them as much as they are able to receive. It is neither in us (for we participate, not by receiving the Idea itself, but something else proceeding from it) nor is it generated in us, for it is entirely void of generation.

<gloss>1</gloss> This is the second axiom, says <term>Proclus</term> <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher whose massive commentary on this dialogue provides the bulk of this text's interpretation.</note>, contributing to the study of the object of inquiry. For the former axiom was that forms are by no means in us, but in themselves; but this second axiom is that <term>sensibles</term> <note>Physical things we can perceive with our five senses.</note> when named as relatives, are named so in relation to each other; and that <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Things that can only be understood by the mind or intellect, existing beyond the physical world.</note> are named in relation to each other, and not in relation to <term>sensibles</term>; and that <term>sensibles</term> are not named in relation to <term>intelligibles</term>. For, by those who are accustomed to consider these things more logically, it is well said that <term>universals</term> <note>General concepts, like "Beauty" or "Equality" in general.</note> ought to be referred as relatives to <term>universals</term>, but particulars to particulars; science simply considered to that which is simply the object of science, but a particular science to a particular object of science; things indefinite to the indefinite; such as are definite to the definite; such as are in capacity to things in capacity; and such as are in energy to things in energy. And of these things the logical and physical treatises of the ancients are full. If, therefore, in things universal and things particular, alternations cannot be admitted in comparing the one with the other, by a much greater reason it cannot take place in ideas and the images of ideas; but we must refer <term>sensibles</term> to <term>sensibles</term>, and <term>intelligibles</term> to <term>intelligibles</term>. These things, then, are perfectly true, if we consider each so far as it is that which it is, and not so far as it makes something, or is generated as something. For in this case, <term>sensibles</term> have the relation of things generated to <term>intelligibles</term>, but <term>intelligibles</term> have the relation of producing causes to <term>sensibles</term>; and as images, <term>sensibles</term> are related to <term>intelligibles</term>, but ideas, as <term>paradigms</term> <note>Original models or archetypes.</note>, are related to <term>sensibles</term>.

If, therefore, we assume dominion itself, it must be referred to servitude itself; but if we consider it as a <term>paradigm</term>, it must be referred to that which is similar to dominion itself; though we are accustomed, indeed, to call the Gods our lords, so that dominion there will be named with reference to servitude with us. This, however, is true because we participate in servitude itself, to which dominion itself has a preceding reference. because we participate of servitude itself. But that which is called dominion with us, with reference to servitude among us, is no longer also denominated with reference to servitude among ideas, because the being of servitude which is there does not subsist from that which is with us, but the very contrary takes place. For things which govern more excellent natures must also necessarily govern such as are subordinate, but not vice versa. <note>Parmenides is arguing that "Mastery" and "Servitude" in the divine world of Ideas relate only to each other, not to human masters or servants. Divine power governs divine things, while human power governs human things.</note>

But from all these doubts we learn what an idea truly so called is. From the **first doubt** we assume that it is incorporeal <note>Not made of physical matter.</note>; for if it were a body, neither the whole, nor a part of it could be participated. But from the **second doubt** we assume that it is not coordinate with its participants; for if it were coordinate <note>on the same level or rank</note>, it would possess something common, and on this account we must conceive another idea prior to it. From the **third doubt** we learn, that it is not a conception of essence, but essence and being; for otherwise all its participants would participate of knowledge. From the **fourth**, we collect that it is a paradigm <note>A perfect pattern or blueprint.</note> alone, and not an image also, as the reason or productive principle in soul, lest being similar to that which proceeds from it, it should introduce another idea prior to itself. From the **fifth**, we learn that intelligible idea is not directly known to us, but from the images of it. For science <note>In this context, "science" means certain, structured knowledge.</note> in us is not coordinate with it. And from the **sixth** we infer that it understands things which are secondary to it, and that it knows them by being itself their cause. Idea, therefore, truly so called, is an incorporeal cause, exempt from its participants, is an immovable essence, is a paradigm only and truly, and is intelligible to souls from images, but has a causal knowledge of things which subsist according to it. So that from all the doubts we derive one definition of idea truly so called. Hence, those that oppose the doctrine of ideas, should oppose this definition, and not assuming corporeal imaginations of them, or considering them as co-arranged with sensibles, or as unessential, or as coordinate with our knowledge, sophistically discourse concerning them. Let it also be observed that Parmenides says that ideas are Gods, and that they have their subsistence in deity; in the same manner as the <term>Chaldaean oracle</term> <note>A collection of mystical philosophical verses from the 2nd century, highly regarded by later Platonists.</note> also calls them the conceptions of the father: for whatever subsists in deity is a God. Lastly, we must be careful to remember that when we speak of relation as subsisting among ideas, we must remove from them mere, unessential habitudes <note>fleeting characteristics or temporary states.</note>: for nothing of this kind is adapted to the Gods. But we must assume sameness for habitude; and even prior to this sameness, the <term>hyparxis</term> <note>The deepest, most fundamental level of existence; the "flower" or "peak" of a being's essence.</note> of each in itself: for each is of itself first, and is both united to itself and to other things. Communion, therefore, according to participations characterizes the power of things which are said to be relatives in the intelligible world.

You will, however, find dominion and servitude peculiarly subsisting there. For what else pertains to despots, than to have absolute dominion over slaves, and to arrange every thing pertaining to them with a view to their own good? And what else is the province of slaves, than to be governed by others, and to minister to the will of their masters? Must not these, therefore, by a much greater priority, be found among forms which are arranged one under the other, and among which some are more powerful, and use those of a subordinate nature, but others are subservient, and cooperate with the powers of the higher orders of forms? Dominion, therefore, is <term>an employing power</term> <note>original: χρηστικη δυναμις (chrestike dynamis)</note>, and servitude a ministrant power. And both these subsist essentially among forms, and not casually, as in their images: for dominion and servitude among sensibles <note>Sensibles: things we can perceive with our five senses.</note>, are the last echoes, as it were, of dominion and servitude in the intelligible world.

But if you are willing not only to survey these two in forms philosophically, but also theologically, in the divine orders themselves, direct your intellectual eye to those intellectual and at the same time intelligible Gods, and to the forms which are suspended from them; and you will see how both these are adapted to that order of forms. For having primarily a middle subsistence, they rule over all secondary natures, but are suspended from the forms which are prior to them, and which are alone intelligible, energize with reference to their good, and are from them that which they are. For being first unfolded into light from them, they are governed by, and abide in, them; but they supernally rule over the essences and powers posterior to themselves. Hence, also, in the secondary orders, the more total govern the more partial, the more monadic, the more multiplied, and the exempt, the coordinated. Thus, for instance, in the demiurgic <note>Demiurgic: related to the "Demiurge," the divine craftsman or creator of the universe.</note> genera, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The Roman name for Zeus, used here to represent the primary creative god.</note> in Homer at one time issues his mandates to <term>Minerva</term>, at another time to <term>Apollo</term>, at another to <term>Hermes</term>, and at another to <term>Iris</term>; all of whom act in subservience to the will of their father, imparting their providential energies according to the demiurgic boundary. The angelic tribe, also, and all the better genera, are said to act as servants to the Gods, and to minister to their powers.

But, that dominion and servitude have an essential, and not a casual subsistence only, we may learn from the <term>Phaedo</term> <note>One of Plato's famous dialogues concerning the soul.</note>: for it is there said, that nature commanded the body to act the part of a slave, but the soul that of a master. If, therefore, these have a natural subsistence in the soul and body, it is nothing wonderful that we should refer dominion itself, and servitude itself, to divine forms, theologists employing these names as indications of the ruling and ministrant powers in the Gods; just as the paternal and maternal there subsist in one respect according to a divine idiom, and in another according to a formal cause, mere habitude <note>Habitude: a temporary state or relationship, as opposed to an essential quality.</note> having no subsistence in these, but prolific power, and an essence adapted to the Gods.

We ought not however, says Proclus, <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose extensive commentaries on Plato aim to harmonize the dialogue with a complex theological system.</note> to say, with some of the friends of Plato, that divine science does not know itself, but from itself imparts self-knowledge to other things. For every divine nature primarily directs its energy to itself, and begins its <term>idiom<note>original: "idion"; here meaning a specific, essential characteristic or property that defines a thing's nature.</note></term> from itself. Thus the cause of life fills itself with life, and the source of perfection produces itself perfect. Hence, that which imparts knowledge to other things, possesses itself prior to other things the knowledge of beings; since also the science which is with us being an image of science itself, knows other things, and prior to other things, itself. Or what is that which informs us what this very thing science is? And must not relatives belong to the same power? Knowing, therefore, the objects of science, it also knows itself, being the science of those objects. As the knowledge, however, of divine science is simple and uniform, so the object of its knowledge is single and comprehensive of all other objects of scientific knowledge. Science itself, therefore, is the cause of scientific knowledge to other things, and by a much greater priority, to itself. For it is an essence essentialized in the knowledge of itself and of being. For science there is not a habit, nor a quality, but a self-perfect <term>hyparxis<note>original: "hyparxis"; a technical term in later Greek philosophy referring to the fundamental existence, foundation, or "real being" of a thing.</note></term> subsisting from, and established in, itself; and by knowing itself, knowing that which is primarily the object of scientific knowledge, or that which is simply being. For it is conjoined with this, in the same manner as that which is intellect simply, to that which is simply intelligible, and as that which is simply sense, to that which is simply sensible. But the many sciences after science itself are certain <term>progressions<note>In Neoplatonism, the process by which the One unfolds or "flows out" into the many levels of reality.</note></term> of the one science conjoined with the multitude of beings, which the being of that one science comprehends. For being is many, and in like manner science. And that which is most characterized by unity in science itself, is united to the one of being, which also it knows; but the multitude in science itself knows the multitude of beings which being itself comprehends.

There are, however, knowledges more partial than this, some evolving one, and others a different object of knowledge. Some of these, also, are conversant with <term>generation<note>The physical world of change, birth, and decay, as opposed to the eternal world of the Forms.</note></term>, and the variety it contains; others investigate the whole of nature; and others contemplate supernatural beings. We ought not however, says Proclus, <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato, interpreting the dialogues as theological and mystical texts.</note> to pervert the name of science by introducing arts into the midst, and the ideas of these, to which the uses of a mortal life gave a being; for they are nothing more than <term>adumbrations<note>Faint sketches or shadows; in Platonic thought, physical objects and human arts are merely blurry shadows of the perfect "Forms" in the divine mind.</note></term> of true science. As, therefore, we say that there are ideas of things which contribute to the perfection of essence, but not of things proceeding from these, and alone subsisting accidentally in others, in like manner the arts being the images of the sciences have here their generation. But the sciences themselves are derived from the sciences which <term>presubsist<note>To exist beforehand; specifically, existing in the realm of Ideas before being reflected in the human mind.</note></term> among ideas; and through the former we are enabled to ascend to the latter, and become assimilated to intellect. However, as there it is necessary that there should be one science prior to the many, being the science of that which is truth itself, just as the many sciences have many truths for their objects (for the peculiar scientific object of every science is a certain truth) in like manner with respect to the sciences with us which are many, it is necessary to understand the one and whole form of science, which neither receives its completion from the many, nor is coordinated with them, but presubsists itself by itself. But the many sciences distribute the one power of science, a different science being arranged under a different object of knowledge, and all of them being referred to and receiving their principles from the one and entire form of science. The science, therefore, which is with us is very different from that which is divine; but through the former we ascend to the latter.

Exempt forms, therefore, are unknown by our science. All forms indeed, are only to be seen by a divine intellect, but this is especially the case with such as are beyond the intellectual Gods. For neither sense nor <term>doxastic<note>original: "doxastic"; relating to opinion or belief (doxa) rather than certain, scientific knowledge.</note></term> knowledge, nor pure reason, nor our intellectual knowledge, is able to conjoin the soul with those forms; but this can alone be effected through an illumination from the intellectual Gods, as some one speaking divinely says. Hence Socrates in the *Phaedrus*, as we have before observed, assimilates the survey of them to the mysteries, and calls the spectacles of them entire, tranquil, simple and happy visions. For the divided causes of these, and the powers which rule over them, are in the intellectual <term>Gods<note>In Neoplatonism, these are the divine beings associated with the realm of pure Mind or Intellect.</note></term>. But the ideas which are properly called <term>intelligible<note>Refers to the highest realm of reality, accessible only to the pure intellect, beyond the physical world.</note></term>, are established above all such divisions; they produce all things according to united and the most simple causes; and both their effective energy and knowledge are one, collected and uniform. Hence there the intelligible cause of the celestial <term>genus<note>A category or class of beings.</note></term> produces every thing celestial—Gods, angels, <term>daemons<note>Spiritual beings that act as intermediaries between gods and men; not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note></term>, heroes, souls—not so far as they are daemons or angels (for this is the peculiarity of divisible causes, and of divided ideas, of which the intellectual forms make a distribution into multitude), but so far as all these genera are in a certain respect divine and celestial, and so far as they are allotted an <term>hyparxis<note>A technical term for "essential existence" or the "innermost point of being."</note></term> united to the Gods; and in a similar manner with respect to each of the rest. Thus, for instance, the intelligible idea of every thing pedestrian and terrestrial cannot be said to rule over things, each of which is separated according to one form (for this is the province of things distributed from it into multitude), but it governs all things so far as they are of one genus. For things nearer to the One give existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> to all things in a more total and uniform manner.

As, however, we shall hereafter speak of this, let us rather consider the opinion of Plato concerning <term>providence<note>The care and guardianship exercised by the divine over the created world.</note></term>. The <term>Athenian guest<note>The main character in Plato's "Laws," often thought to represent Plato himself.</note></term>, therefore, in the *Laws* clearly evinces that there is a providence, where his discourse shows that the Gods know and possess a power which governs all things. But Parmenides at the very beginning of the discussion concerning providence evinces the absurdity of doubting divine knowledge and dominion. For to assert that the conclusion of this doubt is still *more dire* than the former, sufficiently shows that he rejects the arguments which subvert providence. For it is *dire* to say that divinity is not known by us who are rational and intellectual natures, and who essentially possess something divine; but it is still *more dire* to deprive divine natures of knowledge; since the former pertains to those who do not convert themselves to divinity, but the latter to those who impede the all-pervading goodness of the Gods. And the former pertains to those who err respecting our essence, but the latter to those who convert themselves erroneously about a divine cause.

But the expression still *more dire*, (<note>original: "δεινότερον" / deinoteron</note>) says Proclus, is not used as signifying a more strenuous doubt, in the same manner as we are accustomed to call those *dire* (<note>original: "δεινοὶ" / deinoi</note>) who vanquish by the power of language, but as a thing worthy of greater dread and caution to the intelligent. For it divulges the union of things, and dissociates divinity apart from the world. It also defines divine power as not pervading to all things, and circumscribes intellectual knowledge as not all-perfect. It likewise subverts all the <term>fabrication of the universe<note>The process by which the divine Mind shapes and orders the world.</note></term>, the order imparted to the world from separate causes, and the goodness which fills all things from one will, in a manner accommodated to the nature of unity. Nor less dire than any one of these is the confusion of piety. For what communion is there between Gods and men, if the former are deprived of the knowledge of our concerns? All supplications, therefore, of divinity, all sacred institutions, all oaths adducing the Gods as a witness, and the untaught conceptions implanted in our souls concerning divinity, will perish. What gift also will be left of the Gods to men, if they do not previously comprehend in themselves the desert of the recipients, if they do not possess a knowledge of all that we do, of all we suffer, and of all that we think though we do not carry it into effect? ## ...thing else? Certainly. If, therefore, any one possesses *science itself* <note>In Platonic thought, "Science itself" refers to the Form or perfect Archetype of Knowledge, existing eternally in the divine mind.</note>, will you not assert that no one possesses the most accurate science more than a God?
