---

<margin>1</margin> Parmenides, as Proclus beautifully observes, well knew what the wandering of the soul is, not only in the senses, imaginations, and <term>opinions</term> <note>opinions: *doxa*, or beliefs that lack the certainty of scientific knowledge</note>, but also in the <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>dianoëtic: relating to *dianoia*, the type of discursive reasoning that moves step-by-step through an argument</note> evolutions of arguments. Knowing this, therefore, and remembering the labours he had endured, he is afraid of again descending to such an abundant wandering; like another Ulysses, after passing through various regions, and being now in possession of his proper good, when called to certain similar barbaric battles, he is averse, through long experience, to depart from his own country, as remembering the difficulties which he sustained in war, and his long extended wandering. Having, therefore, ascended to reasoning from phantasies and the senses, and to intellect from reasoning, he is very properly afraid of a descent to reasoning, and of the wandering in the <term>dianoëtic</term> part, lest he should in a certain respect become oblivious, and should be drawn down to phantasy and sense. For the descent from intellect is not safe, nor is it proper to depart from things first, lest we should unconsciously abide in those of a subordinate nature. Parmenides, therefore, being now established in the port of intellect, is averse again to descend to a multitude of reasonings from an intellectual and simple form of energy. At the same time, however, he does descend for the sake of benefitting secondary natures; for the very grace <note>original: "charis" (χάρις)</note> itself is an imitation of the providence of the Gods. Such, therefore, ought the descents of divine souls from the intelligible to be, coming from divine natures, knowing the evils arising from wandering, and descending for the benefit alone of fallen souls, and not to fill up a life enamoured with generation <note>generation: the physical world of birth and decay</note>, nor falling profoundly, nor agglutinating <note>agglutinating: literally "gluing" or binding themselves too tightly to material life</note> themselves to the indefinite forms of life. I only add, that Ibycus, from whom Parmenides borrows his simile of a horse, was a Rheginensian poet, and is mentioned by Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations*, book 4; Pausanias in *Description of Greece: Corinth*, book 2; Suidas; and Erasmus in *The Adages*. There are also two epigrams upon him in the *Greek Anthology*.

<note>1</note> Parmenides, says Proclus, descending to the evolution of arguments, and to scientifically-discursive energies <term>scientifically-discursive energies: the mental process of reasoning through a chain of logic, rather than grasping a truth all at once through intuition.</term> from his intellectual place of survey, and from a form of life without, to one with habitude <term>habitude: a state of being or a specific relation to a subject.</term>, asks his participants whence he shall begin, and from what hypothesis he shall frame, his discourse; not suspending his intellect from their judgment; for it is not lawful that the energy of more excellent natures should be measured from that of such as are subordinate; but converting them to himself, and exciting them to a perception of his meaning, that he may not insert arguments in the stupid, as nature implants productive principles in bodies, but that he may lead them to themselves, and that they may be impelled to *being* in conjunction with him. For thus intellect leads souls, not only elevating them together with itself, but preparing them to assist themselves. He exhorts, therefore, his participants to attend to themselves, and to behold whence he begins, and through what media he proceeds, but does not seek to learn from them what is proper on the occasion. That this is the case is evident from hence, that he does not wait for their answer, but discourses from that which appears to him to be best.

<note>2</note> The one method of Parmenides assumes one hypothesis, and according to it frames the whole discourse, this hypothesis not being one of many, as it may appear to some, but that which is comprehensive of all hypotheses, and is prior to the many. For it unfolds all beings, and the whole order of things, both intelligible <note>intelligible: things known by the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses.</note> and sensible, together with the unities of them, and the one ineffable unity, the fountain of all these. For *the one* is the cause of all things, and from this all things are generated in a consequent order from the hypothesis of Parmenides. But perhaps, says Proclus, some one may ask us how Parmenides, who in his poems sings concerning true or the one being <note>original: "to hen on" (τὸ ἓν ὄν)</note>, calls *the one* his hypothesis, and says that he shall begin from this his proper principle. Some then have said that, Parmenides making *being* the whole subject of his discussion, Plato, finding that *the one* is beyond being and all essence, corrects Parmenides, and represents him beginning from *the one*. For, say they, as Gorgias and Protagoras, and each of the other persons in his dialogues, speak better in those dialogues than in their own writings, so, likewise, Parmenides is more philosophic in Plato, and more profound, than in his own compositions; since in the former he says, if *the one is*, it is not *one being*, as alone discoursing concerning *the one*, and not concerning *one being*, or *being characterized by the one*; and in the following hypotheses he says, if *the one is not*; and lastly, infers that if *the one is*, or is not, all things are, and are not. <term>*the one.*</term> <note>The "One" is the central concept of this dialogue. In this tradition, it represents the absolute first principle of the universe, which is so simple and pure that it is beyond all names or descriptions.</note> In answer to this it may be said that it is by no means wonderful if Parmenides in his poems appears to assert nothing concerning <term>*the one*</term>: for it is ineffable <note>ineffable: something that cannot be expressed in words.</note>, and he in his poems generates all beings from the first being; but he might indicate something concerning it, so far as this can be effected by discourse, in his unwritten conversations with Zeno. Very properly, therefore, does he call this business concerning <term>*the one*</term> his own <term>hypothesis</term> <note>hypothesis: here meaning a fundamental starting point or "supposition" used to build a logical argument.</note>. Proclus adds—if, however, it be requisite to speak more truly, we may say, with our preceptor Syrianus <note>Syrianus was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher and the teacher of Proclus; he is cited here as an authority on the text.</note>, that Parmenides begins indeed from <term>*one being*</term>; (for the <term>hypothesis</term>, *if the one is*, having the *is* together with <term>*the one*</term>, belongs to this order of things); but that he recurs from one being to <term>*the one*</term>, clearly showing that <term>*the one*</term>, properly so called, wills this alone, to be <term>*the one*</term>, and hastily withdraws itself from being. He also shows that <term>*one being*</term> is the second from this, proceeding to being through subjection <note>subjection: the process by which a higher, simpler principle "descends" or limits itself to become something more complex, like "existence."</note>, but that the <term>*one itself*</term> is better than the *is*, and that if it *is*, together with the *is*, it no longer remains that which is properly <term>*the one*</term>. Hence, it is true that Parmenides makes *true being*, or <term>*the one being*</term>, the subject of his <term>hypothesis</term>, and also, that through this <term>hypothesis</term> he ascends to <term>*the one itself*</term>, which Plato in the Republic denominates <term>unhypothetic</term> <note>unhypothetic: a principle that does not depend on any prior assumptions; the ultimate foundation of all truth.</note>: for it is necessary, says he, always to proceed through <term>hypotheses</term>, that ascending, we may at length end in the <term>unhypothetic one</term>; since every <term>hypothesis</term> is from a certain other principle. But if any one should make the <term>hypothesis</term> the principle, we may say to such a one, with Plato, that where the principle is unknown, and the end and middle also consist from things that are unknown, it is not possible that a thing of this kind can be science. <term>The one</term> alone, therefore, is the principle, and is <term>unhypothetic</term>; so that what is made the subject of <term>hypothesis</term> is something else, and not <term>*the one*</term>. But Plato ascends from this to <term>*the one*</term>, as from <term>hypothesis</term> to that which is <term>unhypothetic</term>. Whence also it appears that the manner in which Parmenides manages the discourse is admirable. For, if he had assumed the <term>unhypothetic</term> as an <term>hypothesis</term>, and that which is without a principle as from a principle, he would not have followed the method which says it is entirely necessary to consider what is consequent to the <term>hypothesis</term>. Or, if he had not assumed <term>*the one*</term> as an hypothesis, but some one of the things more remote from <term>*the one*</term>, he could not easily have made a transition to it, nor would he have unfolded to us spontaneously and without violence the cause prior to being. That <term>*the one*</term>, therefore, might remain <term>unhypothetic</term>, and that at the same time he might recur from a certain proper <term>hypothesis</term> to <term>*the one*</term>, he makes <term>*the one being*</term> the subject of his <term>hypothesis</term>, which proximately subsists <note>subsists: to have a specific type of existence or reality.</note> after <term>*the one*</term>, and in which, perhaps, that which is properly <term>*the one*</term> primarily subsists, as we shall show at the end of the first <term>hypothesis</term> of this dialogue. And thus he says that he begins from his own <term>hypothesis</term>, which is <term>*the one being*</term>, and this is, “ if the *one is*,” and transferring himself to the <term>unhypothetic</term>, which is near to this, he unfolds the subsistence of all beings from the unity which is exempt from all things. Whence, saying that he shall make his own one the subject of <term>hypothesis</term>, in evincing what things follow, and what do not follow, at one time as using <term>*the one*</term> alone, he demonstrates the *is*, employing affirmations; but at another time he assumes, together with <term>*the one*</term>, the conception of the *is*. where reasons as looking to *the one*, either unparticipated, or participated, that he may show that all things are through *the one*, and that separate from *the one*, they and their very being are obliterated.
<sup>1</sup> In the Introduction to this Dialogue we have spoken concerning the number, and unfolded the meaning of the hypothesis about *the one*; let us, therefore, with Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher whose extensive commentaries on Plato shaped the medieval and Renaissance understanding of these texts.</note>, discuss a few particulars respecting principle, that we may more accurately understand the nature of *the one*. The principle, therefore, of all beings and non-beings is called *the one*, since to be united is good to all things, and is the greatest of goods; but that which is entirely separated from *the one* is evil, and the greatest of evils. For division becomes the cause of dissimilitude, and a privation of sympathy, and of a departure from a subsistence according to nature. Hence the principle of wholes, as supplying all things with the greatest of goods, is the source of union to all things, and is on this account called *the one*. Hence, too, we say that every principle, so far as it is allotted this dignity in beings, is a certain <term>enad</term> <note>Original: "henad." In Neoplatonism, a henad is a supreme "unit" or divine unity that exists at the very top of the hierarchy of being.</note> or unity, and that what is most united in every order ranks as first, placing this principle not in parts, but in wholes, and not in some one of the many, but in the <term>monads</term> <note>A monad is a "single" or "solitary" unit; here it refers to the primary source or "leading" unit of a particular group or level of reality.</note> connective of multitude; and, in the next place, especially surveying it in the summits, and that which is most united in monads, and according to which they are conjoined with *the one*, are deified, and subsist without proceeding, in the one principle of all things.
Thus, for instance, (that we may illustrate this doctrine by an example,) we perceive many causes of light, some of which are celestial, and others sublunary; for light proceeds to our terrestrial abode from material fire, from the moon, and from the other stars, and this, so as to be different according to the difference of its cause. But if we explore the one monad of all mundane <note>mundane: belonging to the physical or visible world.</note> light, from which other lucid natures and sources of light derive their subsistence, we shall find that it is no other than the apparent orb of the sun; for this orbicular body proceeds, as it is said, from an occult and supermundane order, and disseminates in all mundane natures a light commensurate with each.
Shall we say then that this apparent body is the principle of light? But this is endued with interval, and is divisible, and light proceeds from the different parts which it contains; but we are at present investigating the one principle of light. Shall we say, therefore, that the ruling soul of this body generates mundane light? This indeed, produces light, but not primarily, for it is itself multitude: and light contains a representation of a simple and uniform subsistence. May not intellect, therefore, which is the cause of soul, be the fountain of this light? Intellect, indeed, is more united than soul, but is not that which is properly and primarily the principle of light. It remains, therefore, that *the one* of this intellect, its summit, and as it were flower, must be the principle of mundane light: for this is properly the sun which reigns over the visible place.

<term>*the one*</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, 'The One' refers to the absolute, first principle of all existence, which is beyond being and description.</note> will not be many? For how can it be? It is necessary, therefore,
->that<-

and, according to Plato in the *Republic*, is the offspring of <term>*the good*</term>; since every unity proceeds from thence, and every deity is the progeny of the unity of unities, and the fountain of the Gods. And as <term>*the good*</term> is the principle of light to <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Realities that can only be understood by the mind, rather than perceived through the physical senses.</note>, in like manner the unity of the solar order is the principle of light to all visible natures, and is analogous to <term>*the good*</term>, in which it is occultly established, and from which it never departs.

But this unity having an order prior to the solar <term>intellect</term> <note>The 'Nous' or Divine Mind; the level of reality where all eternal truths exist as a unified whole.</note>, there is also in <term>intellect</term>, so far as <term>intellect</term>, an unity participated from this unity, which is emitted into it like a seed, and through which <term>intellect</term> is united with the unity or deity of the sun. This, too, is the case with the <term>soul</term> of the sun; for this through <term>*the one*</term> which she contains, is elevated through <term>*the one*</term> of <term>intellect</term> as a medium, to the deity of the sun. In like manner, with respect to the body of the sun, we must understand that there is in this a certain echo as it were, of the primary solar <term>*one*</term>. For it is necessary that the solar body should participate of things superior to itself; of <term>soul</term> according to the life which is disseminated in it; of <term>intellect</term> according to its form; and of unity according to its <term>one</term>, since <term>soul</term> participates both of <term>intellect</term> and this <term>one</term>, and participations are different from the things which are participated. You may say, therefore, that the proximate cause of the solar light is this <term>*unity*</term> of the solar orb.

Again, if we should investigate the root as it were of all bodies, from which celestial and sublunary <note>Referring to the region under the moon, usually the Earthly realm of change and decay.</note> bodies, wholes and parts, blossom into existence, we may not improperly say that this is <term>*Nature*</term>, which is the principle of motion and rest to all bodies, and which is established in them, whether they are in motion or at rest. But I mean by <term>*Nature*</term>, the one life of the world, which being subordinate to <term>intellect</term> and <term>soul</term>, participates through these of generation. And this indeed is more a principle than many and partial natures, but is not that which is properly the principle of bodies; for this contains a multitude of powers, and through such as are different, governs different parts of the universe: but we are now investigating the one and common principle of all bodies, and not many and distributed principles. If, therefore, we wish to discover this one principle, we must raise ourselves to that which is most united in <term>*Nature*</term>, to its flower, and that through which it is a deity, by which it is suspended from its proper fountain, connects, unites, and causes the universe to have a sympathetic consent with itself. This <term>*one*</term>, therefore, is the principle of all generation, and is that which reigns over the many powers of <term>*Nature*</term>, over partial natures, and universally over every thing subject to the dominion of <term>*Nature*</term>.

In the third place, if we investigate the principle of knowledge, we shall find that it is neither <term>phantasy</term> <note>The power of imagination or mental representation.</note> nor <term>sense</term>; for nothing impartible <note>Indivisible; that which cannot be broken into parts.</note>, immaterial, and unfigured is known by these. But neither must we say that <term>doxastic</term> <note>Relating to 'doxa' or opinion, the lowest form of intellectual awareness.</note> or <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>Relating to 'dianoia' or discursive reasoning, where the mind moves step-by-step through a logical argument.</note> knowledge is the principle of knowledge; for opinion does not know the causes of things, and the <term>dianoëtic</term> power, though it knows causes, yet apprehends the objects of its perception partially, and does not view the whole at once, nor possess an energy collective and simple, and which eternally subsists according to the same. Nor yet is <term>intellect</term> the principle of knowledge: for all the knowledge which it contains subsists indeed, at once, and is intransitive and impartible. But if the knowledge of <term>intellect</term> was entirely without multiplication, and profoundly one, perhaps we might admit that it is the principle of knowledge.

knowledge. Since, however, it is not only one but various, and contains a multitude of <term>intellections</term> <note>Acts of pure intellectual perception or thought-forms within the Divine Mind.</note>; for as the objects of intellect are separated from each other, so also are intellectual conceptions. This being the case, <term>intellect</term> <note>The 'Nous' or Divine Mind.</note> is not the primary source of knowledge; rather, knowledge must be credited to the **one** of intellect. This "One" is what generates all the knowledge the intellect contains and all that is observed in the lower levels of existence. Because this unity is set apart from the "many," it serves as the principle of knowledge for them. It is not like the "sameness" found in the intellect, because sameness is simply the opposite of "difference" and is lower than <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or "being" of a thing.</note>. 

But the **one** transcends and holds together an intellectual essence. It is through this **one** that an intellect is a God, but not through "sameness" or "essence." In short, an intellect is not a God simply because it is an intellect—otherwise, even a partial or human intellect would be a God. The specific job of an intellect is to understand, contemplate, and judge beings; but the job of a God is to provide unity, to generate, to act with providence, and other things of this kind. 

Therefore, an intellect is a God by that part of itself which is *not* intellect (its unity), and it is a divine intellect by that part of itself which is *not* a God (its thinking capacity). This unity of the intellect knows itself insofar as it is intellectual, but it becomes "intoxicated with nectar" <note>A metaphor from Plato’s 'Symposium' and 'Phaedrus,' later used by Plotinus to describe the soul or intellect being filled with divine grace or the Absolute, transcending rational thought.</note> as the saying goes, and generates the whole of knowledge insofar as it is the "flower of intellect" <note>The 'anthos nou'—the highest, most divine spark of the mind that allows it to touch the absolute One.</note> and a <term>superessential</term> <note>Existing beyond the category of "being" or "substance."</note> one. 

Again, by investigating the source of knowledge, we have climbed back up to the **one**. We find this not only here but in everything else: <term>monads</term> <note>Primary, indivisible units that lead a specific group or "number" of things.</note> lead their respective groups, but the unities of those monads act as the true principles of things. Everywhere, the **one** is the beginning, and you may say about this principle what Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*:

> “a principle is unbegotten.”

For if no single total form can ever truly fail, then by an even greater necessity, the one principle of each must be preserved and remain forever. This ensures that every "multitude" (the many things of the world) can exist around that principle, originating from it in its own way. It is the same thing, therefore, to say "unity" and "principle," if a principle is defined as that which is most characterized by unity. Hence, he who speaks about every **one** is really speaking about principles. 

The Pythagoreans, therefore, thought it right to call every incorporeal essence **one**; but they called corporeal and divisible essences **other**. So, by considering the **one**, you will stay on track with the theory of non-physical realities and the unities that serve as principles. For all these unities exist within and are deeply united with each other; their union is far greater than the "sameness" found in regular beings. In regular beings, there is a mixing of forms, likeness, and participation; but the union of the Gods, being a union of unities, is much more uniform, beyond words, and transcendent. In this realm, *all are in all* <note>A Neoplatonic axiom meaning every divine principle contains every other principle within itself, though each maintains its own unique character.</note>, which does not happen in the realm of regular forms or ideas*; and their pure, unmixed nature and unique characteristics—which far surpass the diversity found in ideas—keep their natures from being confused and distinguish their unique powers. 

Hence, some of them are more universal, and others more specific; some are defined by staying still (permanency), others by moving forward (progression), and others by returning to their source (conversion). Some are generative (creating), others <term>anagogic</term> <note>From the Greek 'anagoge', meaning 'leading upwards'; powers that help souls return to the divine.</note> (leading things back to their causes), and others <term>demiurgic</term> <note>From the 'Demiurge', the creator god in the 'Timaeus'; refers to the power of world-building or craftsmanship.</note>; and, in short, there are different—

<note>This section describes the specific characteristics of different divine orders, namely: the connective (which holds things together), the perfective (which brings things to completion), the demiurgic (the creative or "craftsman" gods), the assimilative (which make lower things like higher things), and others. Though all these qualities exist within all gods, each god remains a distinct and separate entity.</note>

Indeed, Proclus adds, we obtain a knowledge of their union and characteristics from the natures by which they are participated: for, with respect to the apparent Gods <note>The "apparent" or visible gods refer to the celestial bodies like the sun and planets, which Neoplatonists viewed as the physical manifestations of divine souls.</note>, we say that there is one soul of the sun, and another of the earth, directing our attention to the apparent bodies of these divinities, which possess much variety in their essence, powers, and dignity among wholes. As, therefore, we apprehend the difference of incorporeal essences from sensible inspection <note>By looking at the physical world.</note>, in like manner, from the variety of incorporeal essences, we are enabled to know something of the unmingled separation of the first and <term>superessential</term> <note>Existing beyond the level of "being" or "essence"; the highest state of divinity.</note> unities, and of the characteristics of each; for each unity has a multitude suspended from its nature, which is either intelligible alone, or at the same time intelligible and intellectual, or intellectual alone; and this last is either participated or not participated, and this again is either supermundane <note>Existing beyond the physical world.</note> or mundane: and thus far does the progression of the unities extend. 

Surveying, therefore, the extent of every incorporeal <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A distinct, underlying reality or substance.</note> which is distributed under them, and the mutation proceeding according to measure from the occult <note>The hidden or secret source.</note> to that which is separated, we believe that there is also in the unities themselves <term>idiom</term> <note>A specific, unique characteristic or property.</note> and order, together with union: for, from the difference of the participants, we know the separation which subsists in the things participated; since they would not possess such a difference with respect to each other if they participated the same thing without any variation. And thus much concerning the subsistence of the first unities, and their communion with, and separation from, each other, the latter of which was called by the ancient philosophers, <term>idiom</term>, and the former, union, contradistinguishing them by names derived from the sameness and difference which subsist in essences. 

For these unities are <term>superessential</term>, and, as some one says, are flowers and summits <note>Metaphors for the most refined and highest aspects of divine reality.</note>. However, as they contain, as we have observed, both union and separation, Parmenides, discussing this, that he may supernally unfold all their progression from the exempt unity, the cause of all things, assumes as an hypothesis his own one. But this is *the one* which is beheld in beings, and this is beheld in one respect *as the one*, and in another as participated by being. He also preserves that which has a leading dignity, surveying it multifariously, but varies that which is consequent, that through the sameness of that which leads, he may indicate the union of the divine unities: for whichever of these you receive, you will receive the same with the rest; because all are in each other, and are rooted in *the one*. 

For as trees by their summits are rooted in the earth, and are earthly according to these, after the same manner, divine natures are by their summits rooted in *the one*, and each of them is an <term>enad</term> <note>Also spelled 'Henad'; a divine unity or a "One" that acts as a bridge between the Absolute One and the world of many.</note> and one, through unconfused union with *the one*. But through the mutation of that which is consequent, Parmenides at one time assumes *whole*, at another time *figure*, and at another something else, and these either affirmatively or negatively, according to the separation and <term>idiom</term> of each of the divine orders. And, through that which is conjoined from <term>enad</term> and what is consequent, he indicates the communion, and at the same time unmingled purity of each of the divine natures. Hence, one thing is the leader, but many the things consequent, and many are the things conjoined, and many the hypotheses.

Parmenides, also, through the hypothesis of the one being, at one time recurs to *the one* which is prior to the participated unities, at another time discusses the extent of the unities which are in beings, and at another time discovers that subsistence of them which is subordinate to being.

Nor must we wonder that there should be this union, and at the same time separation, in the divine unities. For thus also we are accustomed to call the whole of an intellectual essence impartible and one, and all intellects one, and one all, through sameness which is collective and connective of every intellectual <term>hypostasis</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "substance" or "underlying reality." In this context, it refers to the actual existence of an intellectual being.</note>. But if we thus speak concerning these, what ought we to think of the unities in beings? Must it not be that they are transcendently united? that their commixture cannot be surpassed? that they do not proceed from the ineffable <term>adytum</term> <note>original: "adytum"; refers to the innermost, most sacred part of a temple. Here, it metaphorically describes the hidden, unreachable source of the One.</note> of *the one*? and that they all possess the form of *the one*? Every where, therefore, things first possess the form of their cause. Thus, the first of bodies is most vital, and is similar to soul; the first of souls has the form of intellect; and the first intellect is a God. So that the first of numbers is uniform and <term>enadic</term> <note>Derived from the Greek word "henas" (unity). It means something that is characterized by being a single, unified entity.</note>, or characterized by unity, and is <term>superessential</term> <note>Existing beyond the category of "essence" or "being." It describes the highest divine state which is superior to existence itself.</note> as *the one*. Hence, if they are unities and number, there is there both multitude and union.

Again, the scope of this first hypothesis, as we have observed in the Introduction, is concerning the first God alone, so far as he is generative of the multitude of Gods, being himself exempt from this multitude, and uncoordinated with his offspring. Hence, all things are denied of this one, as being established above, and exempt from, all things, and as scattering all the idioms of the Gods, at the same time that he is uncircumscribed by all things. For he is not a certain one, but simply one, and is neither intelligible nor intellectual, but the source of the subsistence of both the intelligible and intellectual unities. For it is requisite in every order which ranks as a principle that <term>imparticipable</term> <note>A technical Neoplatonic term for a principle that remains pure and independent. It does not "participate" in or mix with the lower things it creates.</note> and primary form should be the leader of participated multitude. Thus, immaterial are prior to material forms. Thus, too, a separate life, unmingled, and subsisting from itself, is prior to the life which subsists in another; for every where things subsisting in themselves precede those which give themselves up to something else. Hence, <term>imparticipable soul</term>, which revolves in the <term>supercelestial place</term> <note>A reference to a realm described in Plato's "Phaedrus," located above the physical heavens, representing the highest level of truth and reality.</note>, is the leader, according to essence, of the multitude of souls, and of those which are distributed in bodies. And one, imparticipable intellect, separate, eternally established in itself, and supernally connecting every intellectual essence, precedes the multitude of intellects. The first intelligible also, unmingled, and uniformly established in itself, is expanded above the multitude of intelligibles. For the intelligible which is in every intellect is different from that which is established in itself; and the latter is intelligible alone, but the former is intelligible as in intellectuals. The imparticipable one, therefore, is beyond the many and participated unities, and is exempt, as we have before said, from all the divine orders. Such, then, is the scope of the first hypothesis, viz. to recur from the one being, or in other words, the first and highest being, to that which is truly the one, and to survey how he is exempt from wholes, and how he is connumerated with none of the divine orders.

can only be effected by exercising the mind logically, intellectually, and at the same time divinely. This is done so that we may be able to grasp the demonstrative power of Parmenides, follow his intuitive perceptions which cling to true beings, and recur—in a divinely inspired manner—to the ineffable and uncircumscribed <term>consensation</term> <note>A term used by the translator to describe a unified, intuitive grasping of a truth that transcends analytical thought; a "sensing together" of the divine.</note> of *the one*. For we contain within ourselves the images of the first causes, and we participate in the "total soul," the breadth of the intellect, and divine unity. 

It is necessary, therefore, that we should awaken these powers within us to understand the things proposed. For how can we draw near to *the one*, unless we awaken the *one* of our own soul, which acts as an image of the ineffable One? And how can we cause this "one" and <term>flower of the soul</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, this refers to the highest, most unified peak of the human soul, which is capable of connecting with the Divine.</note> to shine its light, unless we first act according to the intellect? For intellectual activity leads the soul to the tranquil activity of *the one* which we contain. 

And how can we perfectly obtain intellectual activity unless we proceed through logical concepts? Before we reach simple insights, we must use those that are more complex. Therefore, demonstrative power is required for our initial assumptions; intellectual energy is required for the investigation of beings (for the various levels of being are denied of *the one*); and a divinely-inspired impulse is needed to sense that which is exempt from all beings. We do this so that we do not unconsciously—through an aimless imagination—be led from "negations" into "non-being" and its dark, endless void. 

Let us, therefore, by awakening *the one* which we contain, and through this, causing the soul to come alive again, join ourselves with *the one itself*. Let us establish ourselves in it as if in a port, standing above everything intelligible in our nature, and dismissing every other activity, so that we may associate with it alone. We should, as it were, dance around it, leaving behind those activities of the soul that are concerned with secondary matters. The style of this discourse, then, must be logical, intellectual, and <term>entheastic</term> <note>From the Greek *entheastikos*, meaning "divinely inspired" or "full of God."</note>: for only in this way can the proposed hypothesis be understood in a proper manner.

In the third place, let us consider what "negations" are, and whether they are better or worse than "affirmations." To most people, affirmation appears more noble than negation; they say negation is a lack or "privation," while affirmation is the presence of a specific form or habit. For physical forms and things made of form, affirmation is indeed better than negation. It is necessary for a form to have its own characteristics present and for "privation" to be absent. In short, it is better for beings "to be" than "not to be," and affirmation is better than negation because "being" is the model for affirmation, while "non-being" is the model for negation. 

However, it is quite clear how Plato, in the <term>Sophista</term> <note>original: "Sophista"; Referring to Plato's dialogue *The Sophist*.</note>, says that *non-being* (by which he means *difference*) is related to being, and is not less than being. But since *non-being* has many meanings—one kind being "more excellent than being," another "equal to being," and a third being a "privation of being"—it is evident that we can observe three types of negations: 
1. One that is above affirmation.
2. One that is inferior to affirmation.
3. One that is, in a certain respect, equal to it. 

Therefore, affirmation is not always better than negation. When a negation speaks of that "non-being" which is *above* being (the Divine), then affirmation takes the second place. But since this higher non-being is also of two kinds—one being the "divine unities" (the immediate offspring of *the one*) and the other being the "ineffable principle of all things" (the One itself)—it is not counted along with

With any being, it is evident that to this latter affirmation is not by any means adapted, and that to the former negation more properly belongs than affirmation; though in a certain respect affirmation is adapted to this so far as it communicates with being. However, though nothing can be truly said of that non-being which is <term>uncoordinated</term> <note>Meaning something that does not sit on the same level or within the same classification system as ordinary existence.</note> with being, yet negation may be more properly asserted of it than affirmation; for, as affirmations belong to beings, so negations to non-being. In short, affirmation wishes to be conversant with a certain form; and when the soul says that one thing is present to another, and makes an affirmation, it adduces some of the kindred natures which it contains. But the <term>first cause</term> <note>In this context, the "first cause" refers to "the One," the absolute pinnacle of reality in Neoplatonic thought, which precedes even the concept of Being.</note> of all is above form, and it is not proper to introduce to it any thing belonging to secondary natures, nor transfer to it things adapted to us: for we shall thus deceive ourselves, and not assert what the first is. We cannot, therefore, in a becoming manner employ affirmations in speaking of this cause, but rather negations of secondary natures; for affirmations hasten to know something of one thing as present with another. But that which is first is unknown by the knowledge which is <term>connate</term> <note>Knowledge that is "born with" or natural to our level of existence.</note> with beings, and nothing can be admitted as belonging to, or present with, it, but rather as not present: for it is exempt from all composition and participation. To which we may add, that affirmations manifest something definite; for "non-man" is more infinite than "man." <note>This is a logical principle: the term "man" is limited to one species, but the term "not-man" encompasses everything else in the universe, making the negation "vaster" in scope.</note> The incomprehensible and <term>uncircumscribed</term> <note>Limitless; literally "without a circle drawn around it."</note> nature of the *one* is therefore more adapted to be manifested through negations: for affirmations may be said to vanquish beings, but negations possess a power of expanding from things circumscribed to the uncircumscribed, and from things distributed in proper boundaries to the indefinite. Can it, therefore, be said that negations are not more adapted to the contemplation of the *one*? For its ineffable, incomprehensible, and unknown nature can alone through these be declared, if it be lawful so to speak, to partial intellectual conceptions such as ours. Negations, therefore, are better than affirmations, and are adapted to such as are ascending from the partial to the total, from the coordinated to the uncoordinated, and from the circumscribed and vanquished form of knowledge to the uncircumscribed, single, and simple form of energy.

In the fourth place, let us consider how, and after what manner, negations are adapted to the first cause. They must not then be adapted as in things capable of receiving negation, but yet which do not receive it, as if we should say that Socrates is not white: for, in short, *the one* does not receive any thing, but is exempt from every being, and all participation. Nor, again, must negation be adapted to *the one*, as in that which in no respect receives negation, which possesses a privation of it, and is unmingled with form; as if any one should say that a line is not white, because it is without any participation of whiteness. <note>The author is distinguishing between saying "Socrates is not white" (he could be white, but isn't) and "a line is not white" (a line cannot have color by its very nature). The One is even further removed than the latter.</note> For that which is first is not simply <term>divulged</term> <note>Separated or pulled away.</note> from its negations; nor are these entirely void of communion with *the one*, but they are thence produced: nor can it be said that, as whiteness neither generates a line, nor is generated by it, so things <term>posterior</term> <note>Things that come after or are lower in the divine hierarchy.</note> to *the one* neither generate *the one*, nor are generated by it; for they thence derive their <term>subsistence</term>. <note>Their foundational existence or reality.</note> Nor yet must negation be applied according to that middle mode, in which we say, that things do not receive indeed, but are the causes to others in which they are inherent, of receiving affirmation; as, for instance, motion is not moved, but that which is in motion. And so both ways *the one* will be many, and not one. True. But it is necessary <note>This opening section appears to be a concluding fragment of a passage from Plato's dialogue before the commentator begins their explanation.</note>

are moved through it. And, in short, every <term>passion</term> <note>In this philosophical context, 'passion' refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing change, rather than an emotion.</note> is itself impassive; since, being simple, it either is or is not. But that which suffers, or the passive subject, is through passion a composite. Negations, therefore, are not after this manner denied of *the one*; for neither is *the one* ingenerated in any thing, but is the cause of all the affirmations, the negations of which we introduce to it; but it is by no means ingenerated in those things of which it is the cause. It may be concluded, therefore, that as *the one* is the cause of wholes, so negations are the causes of affirmations; whence such things as the second hypothesis affirms, the first denies. For all those affirmations proceed from these negations; and *the one* is the cause of all things, as being prior to all things: for, as soul, being incorporeal, produces body, and as intellect, by not being soul, gives <term>subsistence</term> <note>The act of existing or having a distinct reality.</note> to soul, so *the one*, being void of multitude, gives subsistence to all multitude, and, being without number and figure, produces number and figure; and in a similar manner with respect to other things: for it is no one of the natures which it produces; since neither is any other cause the same with its progeny. But if it is no one of the natures to which it gives subsistence, and at the same time gives subsistence to all things, it is no one of all things. If, therefore, we know all things affirmatively, we manifest *the one* negatively, by denying every thing of it; and so this form of negation is generative of the multitude of affirmations. Thus, the unfigured, when applied to *the one*, is not like that of matter, which is beheld according to a <term>privation</term> <note>The lack or absence of a quality that something should naturally have; here contrasted with the 'One' which lacks figure because it is beyond it, not because it is deficient.</note> of figure, but it is *that* which generates and produces the order which subsists according to figure.

With respect to matter, therefore, negations are worse than affirmations, because they are privations, but affirmations are participations of which matter is essentially deprived. But, with respect to beings, negations are conjoined with affirmations: and when applied to *the one*, they signify transcendency of cause, and are better than affirmations. Hence, negations of things subordinate are verified in causes posterior to *the one*. Thus, when we say that the soul neither speaks nor is silent, we do not assert these things respecting it as of stones and pieces of wood, or any other insensible thing, but as of that which is generative in an animal of both voice and silence. And again, we say that nature is neither white nor black, but uncoloured, and without interval. But is she without these in the same manner as matter? By no means: for she is better than the things denied. But she is uncoloured, and without interval, as generative of all-various colours and intervals. In the same manner, therefore, we say that the <term>monad</term> <note>The fundamental unit or primary principle from which numbers arise.</note> is without number, not as being subordinate to numbers and indefinite, but as generating and bounding numbers. I mean the first monad, and that which we say contains all the forms of numbers. All, therefore, that is denied of *the one*, proceeds from it: for it is necessary that it should be none of all things, that all things may be its offspring. Hence, it appears that Plato often denies of *the one* things which are opposite to each other, such as that it is neither *whole* nor *part*, neither *same* nor *different*, neither *permanent* nor *in motion*: for it is expanded above all habitude, and is pure from every <term>duad</term> <note>The principle of 'twoness' or duality, representing the first step away from unity toward complexity.</note>, being the cause of all the multitude of these, of twofold coordinations, of the first duad, and of all habitude and opposition. For nature is the cause of all corporeal oppositions, the soul of all vital causes, and intellect of the genera pertaining to soul. The cause, however, of all opposition is not itself opposed to any thing: for, if it were, it would be requisite that there should be some other cause of this opposition, and ***the one*** would no longer be the cause of all things. Hence, negations are generative of affirmations: those which are assumed in the first hypothesis of those which are investigated in the second: for whatever the first cause generates in the first hypothesis is generated and proceeds in its proper order in the second. And thus the order of the Gods subsisting from <term>exempt unity</term> <note>Unity that is "exempt" or set apart from the world of change and multiplicity.</note> is demonstrated.

But here, perhaps, some one may ask us whether we use negations through the imbecility of human nature, which is not able firmly to apprehend the simplicity of ***the one***, through a certain projection of intellect, and adhesive vision and knowledge? or whether natures better than our soul know ***the one*** negatively in an analogous manner? We reply, therefore, that intellect by its perceptions which are conjoined with forms, knows forms, and comprehends intelligibles, and this is a certain affirmative knowledge: for ***that which is***, approaches to ***that which is***, and intellect is that which it understands through the intellectual perception of itself. But, by an unity above intellect, it is conjoined with ***the one***, and through this union knows ***the one***, by not being that which is ***being***. Hence, it knows ***the one*** negatively: for it possesses a twofold knowledge, one kind as intellect, the other as not intellect; one as knowing itself, the other becoming inebriated, as some one says, and agitated with divine fury from nectar <note>The mention of "nectar" and "inebriation" is a metaphor for the state of divine ecstasy where the mind moves beyond rational thought to touch the divine.</note>; and one so far as it is, but the other so far as it is not. Much-celebrated intellect itself, therefore, possesses both a negative and affirmative knowledge of ***the one***. But if intellect, divine souls also, according to their summits and unities, energize enthusiastically about ***the one***, and are especially divine souls on account of this energy; but, according to their intellectual powers, they are suspended from intellect, round which they harmonically dance. According to their rational powers they know themselves, preserve their own essence with purity, and evolve the productive principles which they contain; but, according to those powers which are characterized by opinion, they comprehend and govern in a becoming manner all sensible natures. And all the other kinds of knowledge which they possess are indeed affirmative: for they know beings as they are; and this is the peculiarity of affirmation. But the enthusiastic energy about ***the one*** is in these a negative knowledge: for they do not know that the ***one is***, but that he ***is*** NOT, according to that which is better than the ***is***. The <term>intellection</term>, however, of that which is not, is negation. If, therefore, both divine souls and much celebrated intellect itself knew ***the one*** through negation, what occasion is there to despise the imbecility of our soul, earnestly endeavouring to manifest negatively its uncircumscribed nature? For nothing pertaining to the ***first*** is such as we are accustomed to know, i.e. a certain quality of a thing, as Plato says in his **second Epistle** <note>Plato’s Second Letter contains a famous passage stating that the nature of the "First King" cannot be described in words or known through the senses.</note>. [The One] will neither be a whole, nor possess parts, if *the one* is one. It will not.

<meta>catchword: If,</meta>

by our reasoning power <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>The 'dianoëtic' power refers to the discursive or logical mind that moves step-by-step, unlike 'Intellect' which sees truths all at once.</note> we understand mathematical objects, and just as by our intellectual part we know that which is intelligible, so by the "one" within ourselves we know *the One*.

Again, in the fifth place, let us consider whether Plato denies all things of *the one*, or, if not all, what those things are which he denies, and why he goes exactly this far. But first, it will be helpful to list all the specific things which the first hypothesis says *the one* is not. These appear in the following order:

*   It is not many.
*   It is neither a whole nor a part.
*   It has no beginning, middle, or end.
*   It has no boundary.
*   It is without figure <note>Meaning it has no shape or geometric form.</note>.
*   It is neither in another thing nor in itself.
*   It is neither in motion nor at rest.
*   It is neither the same nor different.
*   It is neither similar nor dissimilar.
*   It is neither equal, nor greater, nor lesser.
*   It is neither older nor younger.
*   It does not participate in any way in generation <note>The process of coming-to-be or being born.</note> or time.
*   It does not even participate in being.
*   It cannot be named and cannot be spoken of.
*   It is neither an object of opinion nor of science.

These, then, are briefly what the first hypothesis denies of *the one*. We now propose to investigate why these specific qualities were chosen. Proclus informs us that earlier philosophers were quite puzzled by this. Some believed that everything contained in the <term>ten categories of Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle’s classification of all things that exist: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and affection.</note> is covered by these negations. However, as Proclus rightly points out, those categories contain many other things that Parmenides does not mention here.

Others claimed these negations were grouped into the <term>five genera of being</term> <note>The fundamental classes of existence defined in Plato's 'Sophist': Being, Sameness, Difference, Motion, and Rest.</note>, namely *essence, sameness, difference, motion, and permanency*. Yet, more than just these are denied of *the one*—things like *figure, the whole, time, number, similarity*, and *dissimilarity* are also mentioned, and these are not considered "genera of being."

But Proclus says the most likely explanation comes from those who show that all these negations exist within the <term>monad</term> <note>The 'monad' here refers to the mathematical unit or the principle of number, which reflects the higher unity of the One.</note>. For the monad contains many things in a hidden way: it has the qualities of a whole, parts, and figures; it exists both in itself and in others because it is present in everything that comes from it. It is both still and moving—staying the same while it proceeds to create numbers—and even when it multiplies, it never leaves its own nature. One could show that other things belong to the monad in a similar way.

We can easily agree that these things exist in the monad, and that the monad is an imitation of the Intellect. Therefore, all these qualities are contained even more primarily and powerfully in the Intellect itself. These things are denied of *the One* specifically because the One is above the Intellect and above every intellectual essence. 

Proclus notes that Parmenides himself, in his poems about "true being," says that being contains the sphere, the whole, the same, and the different. Parmenides celebrates "true being" as being like a *perfect sphere*, equal in every direction from the center, and finding joy in its own stable existence. He also calls it perfectly whole and unmoved. 

So, all these qualities exist first in the Intellect; secondarily, like an image, in the monad; and thirdly, in the physical world. For the Intellect is an **intelligible sphere**, the monad is a **dianoëtic sphere** (of thought), and this world is a **sensible sphere** (of the senses), carrying within itself the images of the eternal Gods.

However, the supporters of this opinion still cannot explain why Parmenides chooses only these specific traits and no others. For neither are these

...specific things alone in the <term>monad</term> <note>The Monad refers to the principle of oneness or the first unit from which all numbers and things arise.</note>, but many others also may be found, such as the even and the odd, and each of the forms subsisting under these. Why, therefore, these alone from among all are assumed, they assign no clear reason. Our preceptor, therefore, Syrianus, says Proclus, is the only one we are acquainted with who perfectly accords with Plato in the knowledge of divine concerns. He therefore perceived, that all such things * as are affirmed in the second <note>The "second hypothesis" in the Parmenides explores what follows if the One exists and participates in being, leading to positive attributes.</note> are denied of *the one* in the first hypothesis; and that each of these is a symbol of a certain divine order; such as the many, the whole, figure, the being in itself and in another, and each of the consequent negations. For all things are not similarly apparent in every order of being; but in one multitude, and in another a different idiom <note>Here "idiom" means a unique characteristic or specific property.</note> of divine natures is conspicuous. For, as we learn in the *Sophist*, *the one being*, or, in other words, the highest being, has the first rank, *whole* the second, and *all* the third. And in the *Phaedrus*, after the intelligible Gods, an essence without colour, without figure, and without touch, is the first in order, *colour* is the second, and *figure* the third; and in other things, in a similar manner, an unfolding of different things takes place in a different order of being. If, therefore, all these things manifest the extent of the first being, but, according to Plato, *the one* is beyond all beings, with great propriety are these things alone denied of *the one*. How each of these is distributed in the divine orders, we shall know more accurately in the second hypothesis. It is apparent, therefore, what are the particulars which are denied of *the one*, and that so many alone are necessarily denied: for so many are the enumerated orders of true beings. Thus much, however, is now evident, that all the negations are assumed from the idiom of being, and not from the idiom of knowledge. For to will, and to desire, and every thing of this kind, are the peculiarities of vital beings; but to perceive intellectually, or <term>dianoëtically</term> <note>Dianoëtically refers to the use of discursive, step-by-step logical reasoning.</note>, or sensibly, is the idiom of gnostic <note>From the Greek 'gnostikos', meaning 'capable of knowing' or 'intellectual'.</note> beings. But these negations are common to all beings whatever. For the hypothesis was, *If the one is*, so many things will follow as negations of *the one*, that at last it may be inferred if *the one* is, this one is not, as being better than the *is*: for it is the recipient of nothing, which is consequent to the *is*. And it appears that those alone are the things which belong to beings, so far as they are beings; which the second hypothesis affirms, and the first denies; and we shall not find things common to all beings, except these. But, of these, the higher are more total, but the others more partial. Hence, by taking away the higher, Plato also takes away those in a following order, according to the hypothesis. He has, therefore, in a wonderful manner discovered what are the things consequent to being, so far as being, as he was willing to show that *the one* is beyond all beings.

But if any one should think that this hypothesis collects things impossible, he should call to mind what is written in the *Sophist*, in which the Eleatean guest examines the assertion of Parmenides concerning being, and clearly says that <term>for that which is truly one must be without parts</term> <note>original: αμερες γαρ δει το ὡς αληθως εν</note>. So that, this being granted, all the conclusions of the first hypothesis must unavoidably follow, as in every respect true, and as alone according with that which is truly *the one*. For it is absurd to admit that true being has a subsistence, and

not only true being, but also the truly equal, the truly beautiful, and every other form, but that the true one should no where subsist, but should be a name alone, though by this all beings are preserved and have a subsistence. But if it is, it is evident that it is not many: for it would not be the true one, if it were replete with any thing; since the many are not one. If, therefore, it is not many, again the whole of the first hypothesis will follow, this being assumed; and it is by no means proper to accuse it as asserting impossibilities.

Again, in the sixth place, let us consider concerning the order of the negations: for, if they originate supernally <note>Meaning "from above" or from the highest spiritual source.</note> and from things first, how does he first of all take away the many, and, in the last place, being, and even the *one itself*? *The one*, therefore, appears to us to be more venerable than multitude, and *being itself* as among beings is most venerable. But if they originate from things last, how, after the genera of being, does he assume the similar and dissimilar, the equal and unequal, the greater and the lesser? For these are subordinate to the genera of being. It is better, therefore, to say, that he begins supernally, and proceeds through negations as far as to the last of things. For thus also in the Phædrus, denying of the summit of the intellectual orders, things consequent to, and proceeding from it, he makes the <term>ablation</term> <note>The process of "taking away" attributes to describe a higher reality that transcends them.</note>, beginning supernally; in the first place, asserting that it is without colour, in the next place, without figure, and, in the third place, without contact. For here colour symbolically signifies that middle order of the intelligible and at the same time intellectual Gods, which is called by theologists <term>connective</term> <note>original: "synochike" ($\sigma\upsilon\nu\omicron\chi\iota\kappa\eta$)</note>; but *figure* indicates the extremity of that order, which is denominated <term>perfection-making</term> <note>original: "telesiurgic" ($\tau\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\sigma\iota\omega\rho\gamma\iota\kappa\eta$)</note> or the *source of perfection*; and *contact* signifies the intellectual order. In like manner here also the negations begin supernally, and proceed together with the series of the divine orders, of all which the *one* is the generative source. But that at the end he should take away the *one itself*, and being, is by no means wonderful. For, if we follow the whole order of the discourse, this will become most apparent. For it is immediately evident, that in affirmative conclusions it is requisite to begin from things most allied, and through these to evince things less allied, which are consequent; but in negative conclusions it is necessary to begin from things most foreign, and through these to show things less foreign, which are not consequent to the hypothesis. For it is requisite, says Plato, that those who use this method should begin from things most known. Hence he first denies *many* of the one, and last of all *the one that is*, which is by position most allied to *the one*, but is participated by essence, and on this account is a certain one, and not simply one. Hence it is necessary, since the conclusions are negative, that the beginning of all the hypothesis should be *not many*, and the end *not one*.

In the seventh place, let us consider what we are to understand by the *many*, which Plato first denies of *the one*. Some of the antients then, says Proclus, assert that multitude of every kind is here taken away from *the one*, because *the one* transcends all multitude, both intelligible and sensible. But these should recollect, that in the second hypothesis *the many* is affirmed. What sensible multitude then can we behold there? For all things are asserted of true beings, because *the one* is there equal to *being*. Others more venerable than these assert that *intellectual multitude* is denied of *the one*. For the first cause, say they, is one without multitude; intellect, *one many*;

<note>The text begins by completing a sentence from the previous page regarding the limits of things.</note> ...beginning are the bounds of every thing? How should they not?

<margin>*The one, therefore,*</margin>
soul, *one and many*, through its divisible nature, being in need of a link <note>original: "copula"</note>; body, *many and one*, as being a divisible nature characterized by a crowd of parts; and matter, *many alone*. This *many*, therefore—meaning the multitude found in the realm of the mind <term>intellectual multitude<note>A philosophical term for the way many distinct ideas exist together within a single mind or divine intellect.</note></term>—Parmenides removes from the first cause, so that the first cause may be "one" alone, and existing above the mind. It is proper, therefore, to ask those who disagree: what do they mean by "mind" <note>original: "intellect"</note>? For, if they mean that which is properly the mind, which is secondary to the <term>intelligible<note>The realm of pure forms or ideas that the mind thinks about; in this hierarchy, what is "thought about" is higher than the "act of thinking."</note></term>, then not only is the *one* beyond the multitude of the mind, but the "intelligible" is also beyond it, as being better than the mind itself. But if they call the whole of an "intelligible essence" the mind—as was the case with the followers of Plotinus <note>A famous philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who founded Neoplatonism; here the author suggests Plotinus's students were not specific enough about divine hierarchies.</note>—they are ignorant of the differences that exist among the Gods, and of how things are generated according to a specific measure. Other philosophers, therefore, more inspired <note>original: "enthusiastic"</note> than these, dismissing the things of the senses and not even admitting a multitude in the mind, say that before the numbers of the mind there are "intelligible monads" <note>Single, unified divine building blocks.</note>, from which every mental multitude and the many divided ranks of reality are unfolded into light. Plato, therefore, removes from the *one* that multitude which is "intelligible" (the realm of pure ideas), as that realm exists immediately after the *one*; but he does not yet remove the multitude of the "intellectual" (the realm of active thought). For it is not surprising that the *one* should be set apart from the multitude of the mind, since even the "intelligible monads" are ranked above that. And hence this discourse, being divine, returns to certain simpler causes. It is necessary, however, to understand that there are many ranks in the realm of pure ideas, and that three <term>triads<note>Groups of three divine principles often used in ancient theology to explain how the One becomes the Many.</note></term> are celebrated in them by theologists, as we shall show when we come to the second argument <note>original: "hypothesis"</note>. But, if this be admitted, it is evident that these must be the first and most basic multitude: for these, insofar as they are "many," exist only because of the *one*; and from these, the grouping of three proceeds from above all the way down to the very last things in the mental, supernatural, and physical worlds; and whatever is granted existence participates in this grouping of three. Hence, some of the ancients, climbing as far up as this rank, considered its highest point to be the same as the *one*. We must either, therefore, admit that the *many* which are now denied of the *one* exist according to this high "intelligible" multitude, or that they are the first multitude in the realms that are both intelligible and mental at the same time. Indeed, the "many unities" <note>Often called "Henads," these are the first sparks of individuality emerging from the One.</note> are not in the intelligible Gods, but in those immediately following them. For there is one unity in each intelligible group of three; but the multitude of unities is first visible in the first rank of the Gods who are both "intelligible" and "intellectual." Thus much, therefore, must now be admitted: that Plato sets the *one* apart from all the multitude of these unities, as he is the father of them and gives them their existence; and he does this by assuming from our shared human intuition <note>original: "common conceptions"</note> that the *one* is not many. But at the end of this argument, he even removes "intelligible multitude" itself from the *one*, joining the end of his thought with the beginning: for he there shows that the *one* is not *being* <note>The state of existing as a "thing."</note>, which is the characteristic of the intelligible order.

It is likewise necessary to observe that Plato does not think that the statement, "the one is not many," requires a formal proof or any confirmation of its truth; instead, he assumes it according to a common and natural understanding. For, in deep thoughts concerning the first cause of all things, it is especially necessary to awaken these common understandings; since all things are naturally arranged after the first cause, and without effort—both those things that act according to a mind, and those that act according to nature alone. ...therefore, is infinite<sup>5</sup> <note>The number 5 refers to a lost or separate footnote in the original text regarding the nature of the infinite.</note>, if it has neither beginning nor end? Infinite. And

---

should be the principle of all demonstration <note>In this context, "demonstration" refers to a logical proof or a mathematical-style deduction.</note>, and that common conceptions <term>common conceptions<note>Basic, self-evident truths that everyone agrees upon, such as "the whole is greater than the part."</note></term> should be the leaders of demonstrations, as also geometricians assert. But there is nothing more known and clear to us than that the *one* is not *many*.

<gloss>a</gloss> It is necessary, says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note>, that the first negation <note>A "negation" in this philosophy is a way of describing the Divine by saying what it is *not*, rather than what it is.</note> of the *one* should be that it is not *many*; for the *one* is first generative of the *many*; since, as we have before observed, the first and the highest multitude proceeds from the *one*. But the second negation after this is, that the *one* is neither a whole, nor has any part: for it gives subsistence <note>Takes on a form of existence or reality.</note> to this order, in the second place, after the first multitude. This will be evident from considering in the first place logically, that in negative conclusions, when through the ablation <term>ablation<note>The logical process of "taking away" or stripping away attributes to reach a fundamental truth.</note></term> of that which precedes we collect a negative conclusion, that which precedes is more powerful; but that when through the ablation of that which is consequent we subvert <note>Undermine or disprove.</note> that which precedes, that which is consequent; and, in short, that which by the subversion of itself takes away that which remains, whether it precedes or follows, is more powerful. 

Thus, if we say, "If there is not *being*, there is not *man*"; but also, "If there is not animal, there is not man": animal, therefore, is more universal than man. Let this then be one of the things to be granted; but another which must be admitted is as follows:—Every thing which is more comprehensive than another according to power, is nearer to the *one*. For, since the *one* itself *is*, if it be lawful so to speak, the most comprehensive of all things, and there is nothing which it does not ineffably contain, not even though you should adduce privation <note>The state of lacking something; even "nothingness" or "lack" is contained within the One’s scope.</note> itself, and the most evanescent of things, since, if it has any subsistence, it must necessarily be in a certain respect one;—this being the case, things also which are nearer to the *one* are more comprehensive than those which are more remote from it; imitating the uncircumscribed cause, and the infinite transcendency of the *one*. Thus *being*, as it is more comprehensive than life and intellect, is nearer to the *one*; and life is nearer to it than intellect. 

These two axioms being admitted, let us see how Parmenides syllogizes <note>Constructs a logical argument or syllogism.</note>. If the *one*, says he, is a whole, or has parts, it is many; but it is not many, as was before said: neither, therefore, will it be a whole, nor will it have parts. And again, If the *one* is not many, it is neither a whole, nor has parts. In both these instances, by the subversion of the many, *parts* also and whole are subverted. But our position is, that whatever together with itself subverted that which remains in things conjoined, is more powerful and more comprehensive; but that which is more comprehensive is nearer to the *one*. Hence, *many* is nearer to the *one* than parts and *whole*. For *parts* are *many*, but *many* are not entirely *parts*. So that the *many* are more comprehensive than *parts*, and are therefore beyond them. The *many*, therefore, first subsist in beings; and in the second place, whole and parts. Hence, the *one* produces the first by itself alone, but the second through the many. For first natures, in proceeding from their causes, always produce, together with their causes, things consequent. Since, therefore, the negations generate the affirmations, it is evident that the first generates such of these as are first, but the second such as are second. We may also see the geometrical order which Plato here observes: for that the *one* is not many, is assumed as an axiom, and as a common conception; but that it is neither a whole, nor has parts, is collected through this common conception. And again, that the *one* has neither beginning nor end, is demonstrated through the prior conclusion;

without figure <note>This refers to the "One" being formless and without geometric shape because it precedes physical reality.</note> $^6$, therefore, for it neither participates of the round $^7$ figure nor <note>Superscripts 6 and 7 refer to philosophical notes regarding the One's lack of boundaries and shape.</note>

clusion; and thus always in succession according to the truly **golden chain of beings** <note>original: "seira" — a famous Neoplatonic concept, inspired by Homer, describing a continuous link of existence from the highest god down to the lowest matter.</note>, in which all things are indeed from *the one*, but some immediately, others through one medium, others through two, and others through many. After this manner, therefore, it may be logically demonstrated that these *many* are prior to *whole and parts*.

If we wish, however, to see this in a manner more adapted to things themselves, we may say that the many, so far as many, have one cause, *the one*: for all multitude is not derived from any thing else than *the one*; since also, with respect to the multitude of beings, so far as they are intelligible, they are from being, but, so far as they are multitude, they subsist <note>To "subsist" means to have their foundation or existence in something else.</note> from *the one*. For, if multitude was derived from any other cause than *the one*, that cause again must necessarily either be one, or nothing, or not one. But if nothing, it could not be a cause. And if it was not one, not being one, it would in no respect differ from the many, and therefore would not be the cause of the many, since cause every where differs from its progeny. It remains, therefore, either that the many are without cause, and are uncoordinated with each other, and are infinitely infinite, having no *one* in them, or that *the one* is the cause of being to the many. For either each of the *many* is not one, nor that which subsists from all of them, and thus all things will be infinitely infinite; or each is indeed one, but that which consists from all is not one: and thus they will be uncoordinated with each other; for, being coordinated, they must necessarily participate of *the one*: or, on the contrary, that which consists from all is one, but each is not one, and thus each will be infinitely infinite, in consequence of participating no *one*: or, lastly, both that which consists from all and each must participate of *the one*, and in this case, prior to them, there must necessarily be that which is the source of union both to the whole and parts, and which is itself neither a whole, nor has parts; for, if it had, this again would be indigent of *the one*; and if we proceed to infinity, we shall always have the *one* prior to *whole and parts*. To this we may also add, that if there was another cause of the many besides *the one*, there would be no multitude of unities. If, therefore, there are many unities, the cause of this multitude so far as multitude is *the one*: for the primary cause of unities is *the one*, and on this account they are called unities. But the multitude of beings is from the multitude of unities; so that all multitude is from *the one*. But whole and parts belong to beings: for, though *whole* should be *the one being*, it is evident that, together with being, it is a *whole*, though it should be *the participated one*. This also entirely consubsists with being; and though it should be *being* alone, this is immediately **essence** <term>essence<note>Greek: *ousia*. In this context, it refers to the fundamental nature or substance of a thing that makes it what it is.</note></term>. If, therefore, whole and part are beings, either essentially or according to participation, these also will indeed be produced from *the one*, but from essence also, if whole and part belong to beings. Hence, *whole* is a certain being. For all such things as participate of essential wholeness, these also participate of essence, but not all such things as participate of essence participate also of wholeness. Thus, for instance, parts, so far as they are parts, partake of essence, but so far as they are parts they do not participate of wholeness. But if this be the case, essence is beyond essential wholeness. And hence, the essential whole participates of essence, and is not the same with it. Thus, also, if there is any wholeness which is characterized by unity, it participates of *the one*: a part however characterized by unity must indeed
