...one as possesses parts? How? Thus: If the term *it is* is spoken of *one being*, and the *one* is spoken of *being which is one*, and *essence* <note>original: "essence" (ousia)</note> is not the same as the *one*, but each belongs to that *same one being* which we have supposed, is it [not necessary that the one being should be a whole, and the parts of it the one and being?]

But after such a vision, what can language announce concerning this transcendent object? That it is perfectly indistinct and void of number. "And," as Damascius <margin>See *Excerpts*, p. 228.</margin> beautifully observes:

> "Since this is the case, we should consider whether it is proper to call *this* which belongs to it *simplicity* <note>original: απλοτης (haplotes)</note>; *something else, multiplicity* <note>original: πολλοτης (pollotes)</note>; *and something besides this, universality* <note>original: παντοτης (pantotes)</note>. For that which is intelligible is *one, many, and all*, so that we may triply explain a nature which is one. But how can one nature be *one and many*? Because *many* is the infinite power of *the one*. But how can it be *one and all*? Because *all* is the every-way extended energy of *the one*. Nor yet is it to be called an energy, as if it were an extension of power to that which is external; nor power, as an extension of existence <note>original: "hyparxis" (the essential foundation or "subsistence" of a thing)</note> abiding within; but again, it is necessary to call them three instead of one: for one name, as we have often testified, is by no means sufficient for an explanation of this order. And are all things then here indistinct? But how can this be easy to understand? For we have said that there are three principles following each other; namely: *father, power, and paternal intellect*. But these in reality are neither *one, nor three, nor one and at the same time three* <margin>Original Greek: "But these in reality are not one, nor three, nor one and at the same time three."</margin>. But it is necessary that we should explain these by names and concepts of this kind, through our poverty in what is adapted to their nature, or rather through our desire of expressing something proper on the occasion. For as we name this *triad one*, and *many*, and *all*, and *father, power, and paternal intellect*, and again bound, infinite, and mixed—so likewise we call it a monad <note>a single unit</note>, and the *indefinite dyad* <note>the principle of duality or "twoness"</note>, and a *triad*, and a paternal nature composed from both these. And just as we reject the former names as unable to harmonize with the things themselves after purifying our thoughts, we should likewise reject the latter for the same reason."

Now from this remarkable passage in particular, and from all that has been said respecting the intelligible triad, it follows that the Platonic trinity is totally different from the Christian trinity. This is because the former is a triad that comes after the first cause, who according to Plato is a principle transcendently removed from all multitude, and is not coordinated or existing together with any being or beings whatever.

A superficial reader indeed, who knows no more of Platonism than what he has gathered from Cudworth's *Intellectual System* <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a Cambridge Platonist who sought to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, will be led to think that the genuine Platonic trinity consists of *the first cause* (or *the good*), *intellect*, and *soul*, and that these three were considered by Plato as in a certain respect one. To such men as these, it is necessary to observe that a triad of principles distinct from each other is a very different thing from a *triad which may be considered as a whole*, and of which each of the three is a part. But *the good* or *the one* is, according to Plato, superessential <note>beyond the nature of being or essence</note>, as is evident from the first hypothesis of this Dialogue, and from the sixth Book of his *Republic*. It is impossible, therefore, that the good can exist together with *intellect* (which is even secondary to *being*), and much less with *soul* (which is subordinate to *intellect*). And hence *the good, intellect*, and *soul* do not form a single, co-existing triad.

Is it not necessary that the whole of it should be *one being*, but that its parts should be the *one* and *to be*? It is necessary. Whether, therefore, should we call each of these parts a part alone, or a part of the whole? Each should be called a part of the whole. That which is *one*, therefore, is a whole, and possesses a part. Entirely so. What then? Can each of these parts of one being—namely, the *one* and *being*—desert each other, so that the *one* shall not be a part of *being*, or *being* shall not be a part of the *one*? It cannot be. Again, therefore, each of the parts will contain both *one* and *being*, and each part will at least be composed of two parts; and, for the same reason, whatever part arises will always possess these two parts: for the *one* will always contain *being*, and *being* the *one*; so that two things will always be produced, and no part will ever be just one. Entirely so. Will not, therefore, *one being* thus become an infinite multitude? So it seems.

But proceed, and still further consider this. What? We have said that the one participates in essence <note>original: "essence" (ousia), referring to the fundamental nature or substance of a thing</note>, so far as it is being. We have said so. And on this account *one being* appears to be many. It does so. But what then? If we receive <term>dianoëtically</term> <note>dianoëtically: through the power of discursive reason or logical thought, as opposed to direct intuition</note> that "one" which we said participates in essence, and apprehend it alone by itself without that which we have said it participates in, will it appear to be one alone? Or will this also be many? I think it will be one. 

But let us consider another certain circumstance. It is necessary that its essence should be one thing, and itself another thing, if the *one* is not the same as essence, but rather participates in essence. It is necessary. If, therefore, *essence* is one thing, and the *one* another thing, the *one* is not different from *essence* simply because it is the *one*, nor is *essence* different from the *one* simply because it is *essence*; rather, they are different from each other through the quality of being *different* and *another*. Entirely so. So that the concept of *different* is neither the same as the *one* nor the same as *essence*. How could it be? What, then, if we should select from them—whether you choose *essence* and *different*, or *essence* and the *one*, or the *one* and *different*—should we not, in each selection, choose certain things which might very properly be called "both"? How do you mean? In this way: Is there not that which we call *essence*? There is. And again, that which we name the *one*? And this also. Is not, therefore, each of them named? Each. But what, when I say *essence* and the *one*, do I not speak of both of these? Entirely so. And if I should say *essence* and *different*, or *different* and...

And regarding *being* and *the one*, should I not perfectly, in each of these, pronounce both? 
Certainly. But can those things which are properly denominated "both," be both, and yet not two? 
They cannot. And can any reason be assigned why, of two things, each of them should not be one? 
There cannot. As, therefore, these two subsist together, each of them will be one. 
It appears so. But if each of them is one, and *the one* is placed together with them, by any kind of conjunction, will not all of them become three? 
Certainly. But are not three *odd*, and two *even*? 
How should they not be? But what then? Being two, is it not necessary that "twice" should be present? And being three, "thrice"; since twice one subsists in two, and thrice one in three? 
It is necessary. But if there are two and "twice," is it not necessary that there should be twice two? And if there are three and "thrice," that there should be thrice three? 
How should it not be? But what if there are three and "twice," and two and "thrice," is it not necessary that there should be thrice two and twice three? 
Entirely so. Hence, there will be the evenly even, and the oddly odd; and the oddly even, and the evenly odd. 
It will be so. If, therefore, this be the case, do you think that any number will be left which is not necessarily there? 
By no means. If, therefore, *the one* is, it is also necessary that there should be number <note>original: "¹"</note>. 
It is necessary.

***

¹ Parmenides, after the intelligible triads <note>In Neo-Platonic philosophy, "triads" refer to groupings of three divine principles or stages of reality.</note>, generates the intelligible and at the same time intellectual orders, and demonstrates, by subsequent conclusions, a continuous progression of the Gods. For the series and connection of the words with each other imitate the indissoluble order of things, which always joins the middle terms with the extremes, and through middle genera advances to the ultimate progressions of beings. 

As there are then three intelligible triads, consisting of *one being*, *whole itself*, and *infinite multitude*, so three intelligible and at the same time intellectual triads present themselves to our view: namely, *number itself*, *whole itself*, and the *perfect itself*. Hence, *number* here proceeds from *one being*; but that which is a *whole* proceeds from *whole itself* in intelligibles; and the *perfect itself* from *infinite multitude*. For in the intelligible triad, the *infinite* was omnipotent and perfect, comprehending all things, and subsisting as incomprehensible in itself. 

The *perfect*, therefore, is analogous to that which is omnipotent and all-perfect, possessing an intellectual perfection, and such as is posterior <note>meaning: following after or lower in the hierarchy</note> to primary and intelligible perfection. But *the whole*, which is both intelligible and intellectual, is allied to that which is intelligible, yet it differs from it so far as the latter possesses wholeness according to the *one union of the one being*; but the *one* of the former appears to be essentially a whole of parts characterized by unity, and its being a composite of many beings. 

But again, *number* must be considered as analogous to *one being*. For *one being* subsists among intelligibles occultly <note>meaning: hidden or in a unified, non-manifest state</note>, intelligibly, and paternally; but here, in conjunction with difference, it generates...

<summary>Parmenides argues that if "the one" and "being" exist, they form a pair (two), which inevitably generates the concepts of even, odd, and all subsequent numbers. The commentary explains this as a metaphysical progression from unified "intelligible" principles to more complex "intellectual" orders of reality.</summary>

But if number exists, it is necessary that the "many" should exist, as well as an infinite multitude of beings. Or do you think that number, though infinite in multitude, will also participate in essence <note>original: "essence" (ousia); the fundamental nature or "beingness" of a thing</note>? By all means, I think so. If, therefore, every number participates in essence, will not each part of number also participate in essence? Certainly. Essence, therefore, will be distributed through all things which are many, and will not desert any being, whether the least or the greatest; for how can essence be absent from any being? In no respect. Essence, therefore, is distributed as much as possible into the least and the greatest, and into all things in every way; it is divided more than all other things and possesses infinite parts. It is so. Its parts, therefore, are very many. Very many, indeed. But consider: is there any one of these which is a part of essence, and yet is not *one* part? But how can this be? But if it exists, I think it must always be necessary, as long as it exists, that it should be a certain "one"; it cannot possibly be nothing. It is necessary. *The one*, therefore, is present with every part of essence, deserting no part, whether small or great, or in whatever manner it may be characterized. It is so. Can *one being*, therefore, be a whole that exists in many places at once? Consider this diligently. I do consider it, and I see that it is impossible. It is divided, therefore, since it is not a whole; for it can be present with all the parts of essence in no other way than in a divided state. Certainly. But that which is divisible must necessarily be as many as its parts.

***

<margin>This commentary explains how the concept of "difference" generates number, which establishes the separation of forms and rational principles <note>original: "reasons" (logoi); the underlying principles or patterns of reality</note>.</margin> For *difference* first exhibits itself in this order, but exists among the "intelligibles" <note>original: "intelligibles"; things that can only be known by the mind/intellect, rather than the senses</note> as *power* and the *duad* <note>original: "duad"; the principle of "twoness" or duality</note>. And in this order, it is a maternal and prolific fountain. With great propriety, therefore, does Plato begin his negations of the *one* from the summit of this order; for the *many* exist here through that "difference" which divides *being* and the *one*. This is because the *whole*, which is denied of the *one*, is intellectual and not merely intelligible. The negation, therefore, asserts that the *one* is not a whole, which implies the affirmation must be: *the one is a whole*. For an *intelligible whole* is *one being*, but it is not *the one* itself. And he thus denies *the many* by saying, "The one is not many," the opposite of which is, *the one is many*. 

But the multitude of intelligibles, and not the *one*, is the immediate cause of the *many*. In short, the entirety of that which is intelligible is characterized by *one being*. For both *being* and the *one* are contained in this, and are naturally joined with each other; here, *being* is characterized by the *one* more than anything else. But when each of these—namely *being* and the *one*—proceeds into multitude, they become distant from one another and show a greater diversity of nature. Each is distributed into multitude through the prolific nature of "difference" itself. Thus, it is evident from this that the "intelligible-and-intellectual" orders proceed in a hierarchy analogous to the "intelligible triads." In the notes to the *Phaedrus*, it will be shown how Socrates leads us to this order of Gods.

When Parmenides, therefore, says that the <term>one</term> is both *moved and stands still*, by *motion* he indicates the vivific <term>hyparxis</term> <note>original: hyparxis; the essential existence or "subsistence" of a divine being</note> of the Gods, and the generative fountain of wholes; but by *permanency* coordinated with motion, he indicates that pure <term>monad</term> which contains the middle centers of the triad of *guardian deities*, or, in other words, one of the <term>Curetes</term> <note>Minor deities in Greek mythology who protected the infant Zeus/Jupiter; here used as a philosophical category</note> consistent with Rhea. For as *that which is in another* is causally more ancient than *that which is in itself*, so here that which is moved is more ancient than that which is *permanent*. Hence, according to the Greek theology, the Curetes are powers subordinate to Saturn, Rhea, and Jupiter, the parents of the intellectual order, and are contained in them.

# THE PARMENIDES

The one suffers what we have related above. How? Everything, in a certain respect, relates to everything else in this way: it is either the same as it or different; or if it is neither the same nor different, it will be a part of that to which it is related, or it will be a whole in relation to a part. It appears so. Is **the one**, therefore, a part of itself? By no means. It will not, therefore, be a whole with respect to itself, as if it were its own part. For that is impossible. But is **the one**, therefore, different from **the one**? By no means. It will not, therefore, be different from itself. Certainly not. If, therefore, it is neither different, nor a whole, nor a part with respect to itself, is it not necessary that it should be the same as itself? It is necessary. But what of that which exists elsewhere than in itself, subsisting in the **same**—

***

<note>The text below shifts from the translation of Plato's dialogue to a Neoplatonic commentary, likely by Proclus, explaining the divine archetypes represented by these logical terms.</note>

—which subsist around the *demiurgus* <note>original: "demiurgus"; the "Craftsman" or Creator-God in Platonic philosophy</note>, according to which he produces and preserves all things. Being exempt from his productions, he is firmly established in himself and separates his own kingdom from the united government of his father—all these are here revealed.

Hence, what Parmenides first demonstrates concerning the nature of **the one**—namely, that it is **the same as itself**—represents to us the monadic and paternal characteristic according to which Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> is the *demiurgus*. For the term **same** is a manifest sign of his proper or paternal *hyparxis* <note>original: "hyparxis"; the essential core or "subsistence" of a divine being</note>. For being one, and the transcendent *demiurgus* and father of all wholes, he establishes his own union within himself. This term also remarkably shows the uniform nature and the alliance of this deity with **bound** <note>The principle of limit or definition</note>. 

But his being **the same as others** is the illustrious benefit of prolific power, and of a cause proceeding to all things and pervading through all things without hindrance. For he is present to all things which he produces and is in all things which he adorns, pre-establishing in himself an essence that generates all wholes. Hence **bound** and **the infinite** <note>The principles of Limit and the Unlimited</note> exist in him in a creative manner; the former consisting in a sameness separate from **others**, and the latter in a power which generates **others**. 

The assertion also that **he is different from others** manifests his undefiled purity and his transcendence, which is exempt from all secondary natures. Therefore, by his never-ceasing to impart good, by his providence, and by his generating subordinate things, **he is the same as them**; for he is participated in by them and fills his progeny with his own providential care. But by his purity, his undefiled power, and his undeviating energies, he is separate from all wholes and does not coexist with others. 

Just as Saturn <note>Cronus</note>, the first king of the intellectual Gods, is granted a nature that does not lean toward matter through that pure monad or guard united to him (namely, the first of the *Curetes* <note>Minor deities who acted as guardians</note>); and as the life-giving goddess Rhea possesses her stable and undeviating power from the second of the guardian deities; so also the *demiurgic* intellect guards a transcendence separate from others and a union that withdraws itself from the multitude through the third monad of the *Curetes*, who are the leaders of purity.

### THE PARMENIDES

If "the one" is in itself, must it not necessarily be different from itself, since it has a subsistence <note>subsistence: a state of existing or being</note> elsewhere? It appears so to me. And in this manner *the one* appears to exist, being at the same time both in itself and in another. So it seems. Through this, therefore, it appears that *the one* is different from itself. It does so.

But if anything is different from another thing, is it not different from that which is different? Necessarily so. But are not all such things as are not "one" different from *the one*? And is not *the one* different from such things as are not "one"? How could it be otherwise? *The one*, therefore, will be different from other things. Different. But see whether *different* and *same* are not contrary to each other. How could they not be? Do you think, therefore, that *same* can ever be in *different*, or *different* in *same*? I do not.

<note>The following text is a commentary or footnote continuing from the previous page.</note>

Parmenides indicates this when he asserts that *the one* is *different from itself*. Just as the demiurge <note>original: "demiurgus"; the divine "craftsman" or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note> is the same as himself through paternal union, so he is separated from himself and his father according to this difference. From where, then, does Parmenides say that the demiurge derives this power? We reply: from being *in himself* and *in another*. For these things were united in the first father, but separate in the third. Hence, separation exists there according to cause, but in the demiurge it shines forth and unfolds his power into light. 

For Parmenides himself proves in the first hypothesis that the cause of division exists in a certain respect in the first father, when he says that everything which is in itself is in a certain respect *two* <note>original: "duad"</note>, and is *separated from itself*. But the "two" is there hidden, while here it exists more clearly, where all intellectual multitude is apparent. For difference is the offspring of the "two," which is firmly established there. This difference, therefore, separates the demiurgic intellect from the Gods prior to it, and also separates from each other the monads <note>monads: individual, indivisible units or primary beings</note> which it contains. 

Hence Parmenides, when he divides the signs of fabrication <note>fabrication: the act of creating or "building" the cosmos</note>, shows that the characteristics of the pure and divisive monads are in the middle of them, insofar as they are also in a certain respect included in the one creation of things. For the first of the conclusions demonstrates that *the one is the same as itself*; the second, that it is *different from itself*; the third, that it is *different from others*; and the fourth, that it is *the same as others*. This joins the divisive power with the paternal union and connects the providential cause of secondary natures with a superiority that remains separate from them. For in the Gods, it is necessary that union should exist before separation, and a purity unmixed with secondary things should exist before a providential care of them. Through this, the divinities, being everywhere, are also nowhere; being present to all things, they are exempt from all things; and being all things, they are no single one of their offspring.

I only add that the reader will find the theology concerning Saturn <note>original: "Saturn" (Cronus)</note>, delivered by Plato in perfect agreement with what has been asserted above of this deity, in the *Cratylus*, *Politicus*, and *Gorgias*; that concerning Rhea in the *Cratylus*; concerning Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter" (Zeus)</note> in the *Timaeus*, *Critias*, *Philebus*, *Protagoras*, and *Politicus*; and concerning the Curetes <note>Curetes: minor deities or armored dancers who protected the infant Zeus</note> in the *Laws*.

<meta>This page continues the dialectical investigation into the nature of "the one" and its relationship to "others" (things which are not one), specifically focusing on the concepts of sameness, difference, and similarity.</meta>

# THE PARMENIDES

If, therefore, *different* is never in *same*, there is no being in which *different* exists for any amount of time; for, if it existed in it during any time whatever, in that time *different* would be in *same*. Would it not be so? It would. But since it is never in *same*, *different* will never exist in any being. True. Neither, therefore, will *different* be in things which are not one, nor in *the one*. It will not. *The one*, therefore, will not be different from things which are not one by means of *different*, nor will things which are not one be different from *the one*. Indeed not. Nor likewise will they be different from each other, since they do not participate in *different*. For how can they? But if they are neither different from themselves, nor from *different*, must they not entirely escape from being different from each other? They must escape. 

But neither will things which are not one participate in *the one*; for if they did, they would no longer be *not one*, but in a certain respect one. True. Hence, things which are not one will not be a number; for they would not be entirely *not one* if they possessed number <note>In Platonic philosophy, number implies a collection of units, and thus a participation in "oneness."</note>. Certainly not. But what, can things which are not one be parts of one? Or would not things which are *not one* by this means participate in *the one*? They would participate. If, therefore, this is entirely *the one*, but those are *not one*, neither will *the one* be a part of things which are not one, nor a whole with respect to them, as if they were parts; nor, on the contrary, will things which are *not one* be parts of *the one*, nor yet wholes, as if *the one* were a part. They will not. 

But we have said that things which are neither parts nor wholes, nor different from each other, must be the *same* as each other. We have said so. Must we not therefore assert that *the one*, since it exists in this manner with respect to things which are not one, is the *same* as them? We must. *The one*, therefore, as it appears, is both different from others and itself, and the *same* as them and as itself. It appears from this reasoning to be so.

But is it also similar¹ and dissimilar to itself and others? Perhaps so.

<meta>This page continues the dialectical investigation into the nature of "the one" and its relationship to "others," specifically focusing on the concepts of difference, sameness, and the theological implications of these categories within the Platonic hierarchy.</meta>

<page-num>177</page-num>
# THE PARMENIDES

Since, therefore, it appears to be different from others, others also will be different from it. But what then? Will it not be different from others in the same manner as others are from it? And will this difference be neither more nor less? How could it be otherwise? If, therefore, it is neither more nor less, it must be different in a similar manner. Certainly. Will not that through which *the one* becomes different from others, and others in a similar manner from it, also be that through which both *the one* becomes the same as others, and others the same as *the one*? 

What do you mean? 

I mean this: Do you not agree that every name is the name of something? I do. But what then? Do you pronounce the same name often or only once? I pronounce it once. When, therefore, you speak that name once, do you name that specific thing to which the name belongs? And if you speak it often, do you not still name the same thing? Or, whether you pronounce the same name once or often, must you not necessarily always signify the same thing? 

But what then? Does not a "different" name belong to some specific thing? Entirely so. When, therefore, you pronounce this name, whether once or often, you do not assign this name to any other thing, nor do you name any other thing than that to which this name belongs. It must be so. But when we say that other things are different from *the one*, and that *the one* is different from others, even though we pronounce the name *different* twice, we still signify nothing more than the nature of that thing of which this is the name. Entirely so.

<note>The following section transitions from the dialectic of the dialogue to a Neoplatonic commentary on the divine hierarchy.</note>

...this order to the demiurgic <term>demiurgic: relating to the Demiurge, the divine "craftsman" or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</term> series, and from there to grant them a generation that proceeds according to order and measure.

As this order of Gods, therefore, according to the Greek theologians, makes sensible things <note>original: "sensibles"; things perceived by the senses</note> like intellectual things <note>original: "intellectuals"; things grasped by the mind or intellect</note>, and produces all things that come after it by imitating their causes, it is the primary cause of similarity <note>original: "similitude"</note> for things subordinate to itself. Hence, it is also the cause of dissimilarity <note>original: "dissimilitude"</note> which exists alongside similarity: for all things that participate in the similar must also necessarily participate in the dissimilar.

Similarity in this order also has an existence analogous to paternal causes and to those causes that turn things back toward their original principles. Dissimilarity, however, is analogous to prolific <note>original: "prolific"; life-giving or multiplying</note> causes, which preside over multitude and division. Therefore, similarity brings things together, while dissimilarity separates things as they proceed outward.

Parmenides sufficiently demonstrates that the specific characteristics <note>original: "idioms"</note> of these Gods proceed from the demiurgic monad <note>monad: the primary, indivisible "One" from which all numbers or beings originate</note> and the signs that exist there beforehand. For as he says, demiurgic sameness and difference are the causes of the similarity and dissimilarity of this order.

The reader will find the theology regarding this order delivered by Plato, in agreement with what is said here, in the *Politicus* (The Statesman), the *Laws*, the *Gorgias*, and the *Cratylus*.

If, therefore, *the one* is different from others, and others are different from *the one*, because they both experience the same quality of "difference," then *the one* will not experience something different from others, but rather the same as others. But is it not true that whatever experiences the same thing is, in a certain respect, *similar*? Certainly. In the same manner, as *the one* becomes different from others, everything becomes similar to everything else; for everything is different from all other things. It appears so. 

But is the similar contrary to the dissimilar? It is. And is not *different* contrary to *same*? This is also true. But it is likewise apparent that *the one* is both the same as and different from others. It is apparent. To be the same as others is a contrary state <note>original: "passion"</note> to being different from others. Entirely so. 

But *the one* appears to be similar insofar as it is different. Certainly. Therefore, insofar as it is *the same*, it will be dissimilar, because it experiences a state contrary to that which produces the similar. Or was it not the quality of "difference" that produced the similar? Certainly. Therefore, the quality of "sameness" will make it dissimilar; otherwise, it would not be the contrary of "difference." So it appears. 

*The one*, therefore, will be both similar and dissimilar to others: insofar as it is *different*, it will be similar; but insofar as it is *the same*, it will be dissimilar. That appears to be the case. 

And it is also affected in this way: How? Insofar as it experiences *sameness*, it does not experience variety; and by not experiencing variety, it cannot be dissimilar; and not being dissimilar, it must be similar. But insofar as it experiences *difference*, it will be varied; and being varied, it will be dissimilar. You speak the truth. 

Since, therefore, *the one* is both the same as and different from others—both in combination and in each state individually—it will be both similar and dissimilar to others. Entirely so. And will this not also be the case in relation to itself? Since it has appeared to be both different from and the same as itself, it follows that according to both these states, and according to each individually, it will appear to be both similar and dissimilar to itself. Necessarily so.

<note>The following is a commentary on the philosophical implications of "contact" in the text.</note>

partible <note>original: "partible" — capable of being divided into parts</note>, and all-perfect producing power of their father, and deducing it to subordinate beings. This contact, therefore, with and separation from inferior natures clearly represents to us a liberated idiom <note>original: "idiom" — here meaning a specific characteristic or property</note>. For *touching* indicates a providence allied to and coordinate with us; and *not to touch* indicates a transcendency exempt and separate from others. Hence these epithets admirably accord with the liberated genus of Gods, who are said to be at the same time conjoined with the celestial divinities, and expanded above them, and to proceed to all things with unrestrained energy. 

Hence the Fates, as we have shown in a note on the 10th book of the *Republic*, belong to this order; for they are said by Socrates to *touch* the celestial circulations. In the *Cratylus* also, the mundane *Core* or *Proserpine*, who governs the whole of generation, is said to *touch flowing essence*, and through this contact to have been called *Phersephatta*. To which we may add, that in the *Phaedo*, where we are taught what the mode is of the cathartic <note>original: "cathartic" — purifying</note> life of souls, Socrates says that the soul, when it is not conversant with the body, *passes into contact with being*; through all which Plato indicates that contact is the business of an inseparable providence and coordinate inspection; and that the negation of this is the employment of a dominion separate, unrestrained, and exempt from the natures that are governed.

These liberated Gods are the same with those which the Chaldeans call *azonic* <note>original: "azonic" — not bound to a specific zone or sphere</note>, and which according to them are *Serapis*, *Bacchus*, the series of *Osiris*, and of *Apollo*, as we are informed by Psellus in his exposition of Chaldaic dogmas. He adds, "they are called *azonic* because they rule without restraint over the zones, and are established above the apparent Gods."

But if it should be inherent in the whole, will it not either be extended equally through the whole of *the one* or surround *the one*? Plainly so. If smallness, therefore, is equally inherent in *the one*, will it not be equal to *the one*? But if it surrounds *the one*, will it not be greater? How could it not be? Can smallness, therefore, be equal to or greater than anything, and exhibit the properties of greatness <note>original: "magnitude"</note> and equality, rather than its own? It is impossible. Smallness, therefore, will not be inherent in the whole of *the one*; but if it is there at all, it must be in a part. Certainly. Nor yet again can it be in the whole of a part; for the same consequences would follow in the part of *the one* as in the whole of *the one*: for it would either be equal to or greater than the part in which it is inherent. It is necessary. Smallness, therefore, will not be inherent in any being, since it can neither be in a part nor in a whole; nor will there be anything small, except smallness itself. It does not appear that there will.

And because it is less, must it not also be fewer in number?

Indeed, we should say that all these are parts of a whole and of a unity; but that the *one*, together with its completion <note>original: "the end"</note>, is generated as *one* and as a whole. We should say so. But the completion, I think, must be generated last of all, and the *one* must be naturally generated together with this. So that the *one*—since it is necessary that it should not be generated contrary to nature—being produced together with the completion, will be naturally generated last among the others. *The one*, therefore, is younger than the others, but the others are older than *the one*. But what of this: must not the beginning, or any other part whatever of *the one*, or of anything else—if it is a single part and not multiple parts—must it not necessarily be one, since it is a part? *The one*, therefore, will possess the same age as the others, as (if it is not to be *the one* contrary to its own nature) it will be generated neither before nor after the others, but together with them. After this manner, therefore, *the one* exists and is generated. But what shall we say respecting its becoming older and younger than the others, and the others than *the one*; and again, that it neither becomes older nor younger? Shall we say that it exists in the same manner with respect to the term *becoming to be* as it does with respect to the term *to be*? Or otherwise? I am not able to say. 

But I am able to affirm this: however one thing may be older than another, it cannot exist in the state of *becoming older* except by that difference of age which it possessed as soon as it was born. Nor, on the contrary, can that which is younger exist in the state of *becoming younger* except by that same difference. For, when equal amounts are added to unequal things—whether they are units of time or anything else—they always cause them to differ by the same interval by which they were distant at first. How should it be otherwise? *That which is*, therefore, cannot exist in the state of *becoming to be*...

Is not to lose essence <note>original: "essence" (ousia); here meaning fundamental being or existence</note> the same as to perish? Entirely so. *The one*, therefore, as it seems, by receiving and losing essence, is generated and perishes. Necessarily so. But since it is both one and many, and exists in a state of becoming and perishing, when it becomes one does it cease to be many, and when it becomes many does it cease to be one? Entirely so. 

But, in consequence of becoming one and many, must it not be separated and collected? It must. And when it becomes dissimilar and similar, must it not be assimilated <note>made similar</note> and dissimilated <note>made different</note>? Certainly. And when it becomes greater, lesser, and equal, must it not be increased, diminished <note>original: "corrupted"; in this mathematical context, it refers to the decrease in size or value</note>, and equalized? It must be so. 

But when it moves from being in motion to standing still, and when from standing still it is changed into being moved, it is necessary that it should not exist in these two states at the same time. How could it? But that which before stood still and is afterwards moved, and was before moved and afterwards stands still, cannot experience these changes without a transition <note>original: "mutation"</note>. For how can it? 

But there is no time in which anything can neither be moved nor stand still. There is not. Yet it cannot be changed without a transition. It is not probable that it can. When, therefore, will it be changed? For it will be changed neither while it stands still, nor while it is moved, nor while it is in time. It will not. 

Is there, then, this strange thing in which it exists when it changes? What thing? *The sudden* <note>original: "to exaiphnes"; a pivotal Platonic concept describing the instantaneous moment of change that exists outside of chronological time</note>, or that which appears to spring forth unexpectedly. For *the sudden* seems to signify something from which a thing passes into each of these conditions. For while it stands still, it will not be changed from standing; nor while in motion will it be changed from motion. But that wonderful nature, *the sudden*, is situated between motion and rest; it exists in no time, and into this and from this, that which is moved passes into standing still, and that which stands still passes into motion. 

It appears so. *The one*, therefore, if it stands still and is moved, must be changed into each state; for only in this way will it experience both these conditions. But, in the act of changing, it will be changed suddenly; and when it changes, it will be in no time, for it will then neither stand still nor be moved. It will not. 

Will *the one* also be affected in this way with respect to other transitions? And when it is changed from *being* into the *loss of being*, or from *non-being* into *becoming to be*, does it not then become a medium between certain motions and rests? Nor yet are these "others" entirely deprived of *the One*, but they participate in it in a certain respect. In what respect? Because things different from *the One* are different because they have parts; for if they had no parts, they would be entirely one. Right. 

But we have asserted that parts belong to that which is a whole. We have. But it is necessary that a whole should be a single unit composed of many, and of this "one," the many are parts. If anything should be a part of many, among which it exists itself, it would doubtless be a part of itself (which is impossible), and a part of each one of the others, since it is a part of the total. For if it is not a part of one of these, it will be a part of the others, this one being excepted; and so it will not be a part of each one. And not being a part of each, it will be a part of no one of the many. And being a part of no one of the many, it is impossible that it should be anything belonging to all those things, of which it is neither a part nor anything else. 

So it appears. A part is indeed a part of this whole. Entirely so. If, therefore, other things have parts, they will also participate in a whole and in the One. Certainly. Furthermore, every part, whatever it may be, which is a part of the whole, is one part. It is so. Must not, therefore, those things which participate in *the one* participate in it while being different from *the one*? How could they not? Are not those things "multitudes" in which *the one* is not present? Multitudes, certainly. What then? If we were willing to take away the least possible quantity from these by our thinking <note>original: "cogitation"</note>, would it not be necessary that this quantity which is taken away should itself be a multitude, and not one, since it does not participate in *the one*? It is necessary.

Entirely so. And since every part becomes one, the parts will have bounds <note>original: "bounds"; limits or borders that define a thing's extent</note> with respect to each other and to the whole; and the whole will have bounds with respect to the parts. Perfectly so. It will happen, therefore, to things different from *the one*—as it appears both from *the one* and from their communicating with each other—that a certain different quality will arise in them. This quality provides them with a bound toward each other, while in the meantime, their own nature causes them to become essentially connected with infinity. It appears so. And thus things different from *the one*, both as wholes and according to their parts, are infinite and yet participate in bound.

Entirely so. It ought, therefore, to have, as the bond of *not to be*, *to be that which is not* <note>original: "For between μη ειναι (not to be) and ειναι ον (to be being), ειναι μη ον (to be not-being) must exist as a medium."</note>, if it is to truly be *not to be*: just as *being* ought to have as a bond *not to be that which is*—

not¹, so that it may be perfectly *that which is*. For in this way, in the most eminent degree, *being* will be and *non-being* will not be: *being* participating in essence <note>original: "essence" (ousia), meaning the fundamental nature or substance of a thing</note>, in order that it may *be being*; but participating in *non-essence*, in order that it may achieve *being non-being*, if it is to *be* perfectly. On the other hand, *non-being* must participate in *non-essence*, in order that it may not be that which is *not being*; but it must also participate in essence, in order that it may achieve *being non-being*, if it is to be perfectly *that which is not*. 

Most truly so. 

Since, therefore, *non-being* is present with *being*, and *being* with *non-being*, is it not necessary that *the one* also—since it is not—should participate in being, in order that it may not be? 

It is necessary. 

Essence, therefore, will appear to belong to *the one*, even if it is not. 

So it seems. 

And *non-essence* will also appear, since it is not. 

How could it not? 

Can anything, therefore, which is in a certain state, not be in that state unless it is changed from that condition? 

It cannot. 

Does not everything, therefore, signify a certain mutation <note>original: "mutation," meaning change or transformation</note> if it is at one time in a certain state and at another time not in that state? 

How could it not? 

Is mutation a motion, or what else do we call it? 

It is a motion. 

But has not *the one* appeared to be both being and non-being? 

Certainly. 

It has appeared, therefore, to be both *in this state* and *not in this state*. 

It has. 

*The one*, therefore, which is *non-being* appears to be moved, since it possesses a mutation from *being* into *non-being*. 

It appears so. 

But if it is nowhere among beings—as it is *not* in consequence of *not being*—it cannot pass from one place to another. 

For how could it? 

It will not, therefore, be moved by transition <note>original: "transition," referring to local motion or moving from place to place</note>. 

It will not. 

Neither will it revolve in the *same* <note>original: "same" (tauton), referring to the philosophical category of identity or a fixed point</note>: for it will never touch the *same*, since the *same* is a being. But it is impossible that *non-being* can reside in *any being*. 

Impossible. 

*The one*, therefore, which *is not*, cannot revolve in that in which it is not. 

It cannot. 

Neither will *the one* be altered from itself, either into *being* or *non-being*: for our discourse would no longer be concerning *the one* if it were altered from itself, but concerning something different from this one. 

Right. 

But if it is neither altered, nor revolves in the *same*, nor undergoes transition, is there any way in which it can be moved? 

How could there be?

But if it be moved, there is a great necessity that it should be altered; for, so far as anything is moved, it is no longer affected in the same manner as before, but differently. There is so. *The one*, therefore, since it is moved, is also altered. Certainly. But as again it is in no respect moved, it will be in no respect altered. It will not. Certainly not. *The one, therefore, which is not*, is both altered and not altered. It appears so. And thus *the one which is not* will be generated and dissolved, and will neither be generated nor dissolved. It will not.

But let us again return to the beginning, and see whether these things will appear to us in our subsequent discussion as they do now, or otherwise. It is necessary, indeed, so to do. Have we not already related, *if the one is not*, what ought to happen concerning it? Certainly. But when we say *it is not*, do we signify anything else than the absence of essence <note>original: "essence"; referring to *ousia* or true being/substance</note> from that which we say *is not*? Nothing else. Whether, therefore, when we say that anything *is not*, do we say that in a certain respect it is not, and that in a certain respect it is? Or does the term *is not* simply signify that it is in no respect anywhere, and that it does not somehow participate in essence, since it *is not*? It signifies, indeed, most simply. Neither therefore can that which *is not* be, nor in any other respect participate in essence. It cannot. But is to be generated and corrupted anything else than for this to receive essence and for that to lose essence? It is nothing else. That therefore with which nothing of essence is present, can neither receive nor lose it. How can it? *The one, therefore*, since it in no respect is, can neither possess, nor lose, nor receive essence, in any manner whatever. It is proper

It should be so. *The one which is not* will therefore neither be destroyed nor created, since it in no respect participates in essence <note>original: "essence" (ousia); here meaning fundamental being or substance</note>. It does not appear that it will. Neither, therefore, will it be in any respect altered; for if it suffered this change, it would be created and destroyed. True. 

But if it is not altered, is it not also necessary that it should not be moved? It is necessary. But that which in no respect *is*, we have likewise asserted, cannot stand still; for that which stands ought always to be in a certain *same* state or place? How could it not be? And thus we must assert that non-being neither at any time stands still nor is moved. Indeed, it does not. 

But likewise, nothing that belongs to beings is present with it; for if it were, it would participate in essence by participating in being. It is evident. Neither magnitude, therefore, nor <term>parvitude</term> <note>smallness</note>, nor equality, belongs to it. Certainly not. Neither will similarity or diversity, either with respect to itself or others, be present with it. It does not appear that they will. 

But what, can other things be in any respect present with it, if nothing ought to be present with it? They cannot. Neither, therefore, are similar things nor dissimilar things, nor the *same* nor the different, distinct from it. They are not. But what, can anything be asserted of it, or be associated with it? Can it be any certain thing, or "this" thing, or belong to "this" or "that"? Can it be with some other thing, or exist formerly, or hereafter, or now? Can science, or opinion, or sense, or discourse, or a name, or anything else belonging to beings, exist concerning that which is not? There cannot. *The one*, therefore, *which is not*, will not in any respect exist anywhere. So indeed it appears.

But let us again declare: *if the one is not*, what must happen to other things? Let us do so. In a certain respect, *others* ought to exist; for, unless *others* have a being, we cannot speak concerning them. True. But if discourse is about *others*, then *others* will be different; or do you not call *others* and *different* the *same*? I do. But do we not say that *different* is different from something different, and *other* is other than *another*? Certainly. With respect to *others*, therefore, if they are to be *others*, there must be something else from which they are different. It is necessary. But what will this be? For they will not be different from *the one*, since it does not exist. They will not. They are different, therefore, from each other; for this alone remains to them, or else they would be different from nothing. Right. According to multitudes, therefore, each—

Each is different from each; for they cannot be different according to *the one, since the one does not exist*. But each mass of these, as it appears, is infinite in multitude. And though anyone should assume that which appears to be the least, like a dream in sleep, on a sudden, instead of that which seemed to be *one*, many would rise to the view; and instead of that which is smallest, a quantity perfectly great with respect to the multitude distributed from it. 

Most right. 

But among these masses or heaps, others will be mutually different from one another, if they are *others and the one is not*. 

Eminently so. 

Will there not then be many heaps, each of which will appear to be one, but is not so *since the one is not*? 

*There will be so*. 

There will likewise appear to be a number of these, if each of these which are many is one. 

Entirely so. 

But the even and odd which are among them will not have a true appearance, *since the one will not have a being*. 

*They will not*. 

But likewise that which is smallest, as we have said, will appear to be with them; but this minimum will seem to be many things and great, with respect to each of the things which are many and small. 

*How should it not?* 

And every small heap will seem in the eye of opinion to be equal to many small heaps: for it will not appear to pass from a greater into a lesser quantity, before it seems to arrive at something between; and this will be a <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: "phantaſm"; an illusory appearance or mental image rather than a reality.</note> of equality. 

*It is likely to be so*. 

Will it not also appear to be bounded with respect to another heap, itself with respect to itself, at the same time neither having a beginning, nor middle, nor end? 

*How so?* 

Because, when anyone apprehends by the <term>dianoetic power</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic power"; the capacity for discursive reasoning or logical thought.</note> some one of these prior to the beginning, another beginning will always appear, and after the end another end will always be left behind: but in the middle there will always be other things more inward than the middle; and smaller, because each of them cannot receive *a single one, since the one is not*. 

*This is most true*. 

But everything which anyone may apprehend by the <term>dianoetic power</term>, must I think be broken to pieces and distributed; for the bulk will in a certain respect be apprehended without *the one*. 

*Entirely so*. 

But will not such a heap, to him who beholds it afar off and with a dull eye, necessarily appear to be one: but to him who with an intellectual eye surveys it near and acutely, will not each appear to be infinite in multitude, since it is deprived of *the one*, because it has no <term>subsistence</term> <note>original: "ſubſiſtence"; real existence or underlying reality.</note>? 

*It is necessary it should be so in the highest degree*.

<summary>Parmenides argues that if "the one" does not exist, the "others" can only appear as fragmented, infinite heaps that lack true unity, boundaries, or numerical properties like evenness and oddness. Without a unifying principle, any perceived "one" is merely a deceptive mental illusion that dissolves upon closer logical inspection.</summary>

Each, therefore, of the other things must appear both infinite and bounded, and both one and many, *if the one does not exist*, and if things other than *the one* have a real existence <note>original: "subsistence"; here meaning a state of being or underlying reality</note>. It must be so. Will they, therefore, also appear to be similar and dissimilar? But how? Since to someone who looks at these *others* from a distance, as if they were obscured in shadow, they all appear to be one, they will seem to experience the same qualities and to be similar. Entirely so. But to someone who approaches nearer, they will appear to be many and different; and because of the illusion <note>original: "phantasm"</note> of *diversity*, they will appear different from and dissimilar to themselves. It is so. These heaps <note>referring to the "many" without a unifying principle</note>, therefore, will necessarily appear to be both similar and dissimilar to themselves and to each other. Entirely so. Will they not also be the same as and different from each other, both in contact with and separate from themselves, moved with all possible motions, and in every way standing still? Likewise, will they not be both generated and destroyed <note>original: "corrupted"</note>, and yet neither of these? Indeed, they will appear to have all such qualities, which may be easily listed, if the *many* exist even though *the one does not exist*. All this is most true.

Once more, therefore, returning again to the beginning, let us state what must happen to things different from *the one*, *if the one does not exist*. Let us state it. Does it not, therefore, follow that these *others* are not *the one*? How could it be otherwise? Nor yet are they many; for, if they were many, *the one* would also be present within them. For if none of these things is "one," then all of them are nothing, so that there cannot even be "many." True. *The one*, therefore, not being present in these *others*, the *others* are neither many nor one. They are not. Nor will they even appear to be either one or many. Why not? Because these *others* cannot have any connection at all with things that do not exist, nor can any part of non-being be present with the *others*; for no part of anything exists within non-beings. True. Neither, therefore, is there any opinion of that which does not exist present in the others, nor any mental image <note>original: "phantasm"</note>; nor can that which does not exist become in any way the subject of an opinion for the others. It cannot. *The one*, therefore, *if it does not exist*, cannot be thought of by opinion to be any specific "one" among the others, nor yet "many"; for it is impossible to form an opinion of many without the concept of *the one*. It is impossible. *If the one*, therefore, *does not exist*, then the *others* have no real existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> at all; nor can *the one* or the *many* even be conceived of by opinion. It does not appear that they can. Neither, therefore, do similar or dissimilar things exist. They do not. Nor do the same or the different exist, nor things in contact, nor such <meta>catchword: such</meta>

# INTRODUCTION
### TO
# THE SOPHISTA <note>original: "Sophista," the Latinized title for Plato's dialogue "The Sophist."</note>.

---

**THE** following is the preface of Proclus¹ to this dialogue, as preserved in the Greek Scholia <note>Scholia: ancient grammatical or explanatory notes written in the margins of manuscripts.</note> on Plato, published by Ruhnkenius. “Plato not only calls a certain man a Sophist, but also applies the term to Love², Pluto, and Jupiter, and says that the sophistical art is all-beautiful; from which we may conjecture that the dialogue has a more noble purpose than it appears to possess. For, according to the great Iamblichus, its scope concerns the sublunary demiurge³ <note>sublunary demiurge: a divine creator or "craftsman" responsible for the physical world below the moon.</note>; since this Divinity is the maker of images and the purifier of souls. He is always separating souls from opposing arguments, acting as a transformer and a paid hunter of wealthy young men. While he receives souls coming from above that are full of creative principles, he takes from them a reward—namely, the creation of animals—in a way that is suited to the nature of mortals. This Deity gives himself to non-being because he creates material beings and embraces matter, which is a thing that is truly false. At the same time, however, he looks toward true being. He is also many-headed, casting forth many essences and lives through which he provides the variety found in the world of generation <note>generation: the process of coming into being in the physical world.</note>. This same power is likewise a magician, because he charms souls with natural reasons so that they are only with great difficulty torn away <note>original: "divulsed"</note> from the cycle of birth. For Love and Nature are also called magicians by some.”

¹ Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Italian scholar who translated Plato into Latin.</note>, who has provided a translation of this preface, attributes it to Proclus, and undoubtedly did so on good authority.
² This word is missing in Ruhnkenius’s edition and is supplied from the translation by Ficinus.
³ Namely, Pluto.

<summary>This introduction presents a Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato's "Sophist," arguing that the dialogue's true subject is not merely a human deceiver, but the "sublunary demiurge" (Pluto) who shapes the material world.</summary>

<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE SOPHIST</header>

on account of the sympathy and antipathy in things which have a natural existence. Now, therefore, Plato wishes to instruct us in an all-various sophist. For a philosopher is a sophist, as imitating the celestial and also the sublunary <term>demiurgus</term><note>original: demiurgus; the "craftsman" or creator deity who fashions the physical world.</note>: for the divisive art imitates the progression of things from the *one*, and the sublunary imitates the celestial demiurgus; and on this account he is a sophist. A sophist also among men is so called because he imitates great things: and hence Plato denominates the sophist "many-headed." The Elean guest is analogous to the super-celestial and exempt father of the creators of things, but his hearers are analogous to demiurgic intellections—one of these being analogous to the intellection of Jupiter, and the other to angelic intelligence, as being Mercurial and geometrical. And because fabrication proceeds from the imperfect to the perfect, on this account the Elean guest first converses with Theodorus, and afterwards turns himself to Socrates in particular."
Thus far Proclus.

Plato in this dialogue presents us with six definitions of a sophist; but as definition cannot be obtained without division—for the latter is the principle of the former—hence he divides the genus of the sophist by its proper differences, from which, in conjunction with genus, species is composed and defined.

# THE SOPHIST

<page-num>205</page-num>

He also shows, in accordance with what is presented in the *Parmenides* <note>One of Plato's most difficult dialogues, dealing with the nature of the "One" and "Being."</note>, that *being* is subordinate to the *one*. He enumerates five categories <note>original: "genera"</note> of *being*: *essence, sameness, difference, stability <note>original: "permanency"</note>, and motion*. He likewise teaches us that true *essence* belongs to incorporeal <note>Spiritual or non-physical</note> natures, while that which can be imagined belongs to corporeal <note>Physical or bodily</note> natures. He expresses indignation toward those who deny that there are forms superior to sensible objects <note>Things perceived by the senses</note>, and also toward those who argue that all things are either only permanent or only in motion. 

Besides all this, he discusses science and opinion, true and false discourse, and the function of verbs and nouns, insofar as they pertain to the discussion of *being*. He likewise observes that the sophist <note>A paid teacher of rhetoric in ancient Greece, often accused of using fallacious arguments</note> is hidden from our view because he is shrouded in the darkness of non-existence <note>original: "non-entity"</note>. Conversely, a philosopher is also not easily recognized because of the splendor of *being* with which he is surrounded:

> "For the eyes of ordinary souls," he says, "are unable to endure the sight of that which is divine." <note>original: "for the eyes of vulgar souls (says he) are unable to support the view of that which is divine."</note>

In order, however, to understand the most difficult <note>original: "abstruse"</note> part of this dialogue, it is necessary to refer the reader to our extensive Notes and Introduction to the *Parmenides*. For he whose mental eye has gained a glimpse of the inexpressible <note>original: "ineffable"</note> light of *super-essential unity* <note>A unity that exists above the level of basic existence or "being"</note> will more easily perceive the splendors of *being*.

I only add that Plato, in his dialogue, has given a most beautiful specimen of that part of his dialectic $^1$ called <term>division</term> <note>The process of defining a concept by dividing a genus into species</note>. This is a branch of the master science in which he and the most illustrious of his disciples were eminently skilled. By this method, they were enabled to discover all the connecting links in the vast series of existence and to ascend from the lowest things in the universe to the inexpressible principle of all things.

---

$^1$ For a full account of this master science, see the Introduction to the *Parmenides*.

**WE** have arrived, Socrates, according to our agreement yesterday, as good manners require, and have brought with us this guest. He is an Elean <note>A native of Elea, a Greek city in southern Italy</note> by birth, but very different from the associates of Parmenides and Zeno <note>Parmenides and Zeno were famous philosophers from Elea known for their difficult logical paradoxes</note>; he is, however, a great philosopher.

**SOCRATES.** Perhaps, therefore, Theodorus, according to the assertion of Homer¹, you are conducting a certain God, and not a stranger. For he says that both other Gods, and especially the deity of hospitality, are familiar with men who possess a sense of just shame, and that they inspect the insolent and the equitable conduct of men. So it may be that he who now follows you is one of those natures superior to man, who attends you in order to behold and confute us who dispute poorly, as being himself a certain god of refutation.

**THEODORUS.** This is not the manner of this guest, Socrates; he is more modest than those who are fond of contention. And he appears to me, being a man, not to be a God, but to be divine; for so I name all philosophers.

See the Apology for the Fables of Homer, volume 1, page 163 of this work. It is well observed by the Greek Scholiast <note>term: Scholiast; an ancient commentator or grammarian who wrote explanatory notes on classical texts</note> on this passage, that Socrates now—consistently with what he asserts in the *Republic*—reproves these verses of Homer, but in a milder manner, as a result of becoming an associate with the Elean guest.

**SOCRATES.** And you do well in calling them so, my friend. But indeed, the class <note>original: "genus"</note> of philosophers is not much more easily distinguished, I might say, than that of divinity. For those who are not falsely but truly philosophers appear—through the ignorance of others—to be of a many-sided nature. As they wander through cities and look down from above at the lives of those below, they appear to some to deserve no honor, while by others they are considered worthy of every honor. Sometimes they appear to be politicians, at other times Sophists <note>term: Sophist; a paid teacher of rhetoric and philosophy in ancient Greece, often criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments</note>; and sometimes, in the opinion of certain people, they are considered to be completely insane. I would gladly, therefore, inquire of our guest here, if it is agreeable to him, what his associates in Elea <note>note: A Greek colony in Italy, home to the "Eleatic" school of philosophy</note> think of these things, and what names they give them.

**THEODORUS.** What things do you mean, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** The Sophist, the politician, and the philosopher.

**THEODORUS.** What is the nature of the doubt about these that you would wish to have resolved?

**SOCRATES.** This: whether they consider all these to be one or two classes. Or, as there are three names, whether they also divide them into three distinct types <note>original: "genera"</note> and assign each name to its respective type.

**THEODORUS.** I do not think he will begrudgingly refuse to discuss these things. What do you say, Guest?

**GUEST.** Just as you say, Theodorus. I shall not refuse, nor is it difficult to inform you that they think these are three distinct types. But to define clearly what each of them is, is neither a small nor an easy task.

**THEODORUS.** You have perhaps, Socrates, happened upon questions similar to those we were asking our guest before we arrived here. He gave us the same answers then as he just gave you; for he said that he had heard enough of these questions and had not forgotten them.

**SOCRATES.** You ought, therefore, to gratify us, Guest, regarding our first question. But tell us this: are you accustomed to discuss what you wish to prove by yourself in a long speech, or by asking questions? I once heard Parmenides <note>note: A famous Eleatic philosopher known for his difficult and profound theories on the nature of being</note> employing the latter method while delivering beautiful arguments, when I was a young man and he was very elderly.

**GUEST.** If the person answering, Socrates, does so without difficulty and in a calm manner—

<page-num>209</page-num>
<header>THE SOPHIST.</header>

Regarding the matter which we now take upon us to investigate, it is by no means easy to understand what a <term>sophist</term> <note>original: "sophista"; a paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric in ancient Greece, often associated with deceptive reasoning</note> is. It appears to all men, however—and it is an ancient opinion—that whoever wishes to work through great things well should exercise himself in things that are small and easier before he attempts the greatest. Now, therefore, as we are of the opinion that the category of a <term>sophist</term> is difficult to investigate, I would advise, <term>Theætetus</term> <note>A young Greek mathematician and student of Socrates</note>, that we should first of all consider the method of this investigation in something easier, unless you are able to show a more efficient way.

**THEÆTETUS.** But I am not able.

**GUEST.** Are you willing, therefore, that by bringing forward a common thing, we should establish it as a <term>paradigm</term> <note>A model or pattern for comparison</note> for a greater thing?

**THEÆTETUS.** Yes.

**GUEST.** But what if we propose a thing well known and of a trivial nature, but which will contribute as well as anything to the understanding of greater things? For instance, a fisherman. Is he not known to everyone? And is it not likewise certain that he does not deserve much serious consideration?

**THEÆTETUS.** It is so.

**GUEST.** Yet I suspect he will furnish us with a method and a process of reasoning that is well-suited to our design.

**THEÆTETUS.** In that case, then, it will be well.

**GUEST.** Come then, let us begin from this: inform me whether we should consider a fisherman as one gifted with <term>art</term> <note>original: "techne"; a specialized skill, craft, or systematic knowledge</note>, or as one without art but possessing some other power.

**THEÆTETUS.** We must by no means consider him as being without art.

**GUEST.** But there are essentially two species of all arts.

**THEÆTETUS.** How so?

**GUEST.** Agriculture, and the care of every mortal body, together with the care pertaining to everything composite and <term>plastic</term> <note>In the sense of being molded or shaped, like pottery or sculpture</note>—which we call a <term>utensil</term>—and in conjunction with these the imitative power; all of these may be justly called by one name.

**THEÆTETUS.** How so? And by what name?

**GUEST.** When anyone afterwards brings into existence that which did not exist before, then we say that he who leads the process "makes," and that the thing led is "made."

<summary>The Guest and Theætetus begin their search for a definition of the Sophist by first applying their logical method to a simpler subject: the fisherman. They begin by categorizing all arts, specifically identifying the "productive" or "making" arts that bring new things into existence.</summary>

**THEAETETUS.** Right.
**GUEST.** But all the particulars which we just now mentioned possess a power adapted to this.
**THEAETETUS.** They do.
**GUEST.** In a summary way, therefore, we shall denominate them **effective** <note>original: "effective" (poietike); the art of making or producing something new</note>.
**THEAETETUS.** Be it so.
**GUEST.** But after this, the whole species of discipline and knowledge, together with the species of gain, contest, and hunting, may be called a certain **art of acquiring** <note>original: "art of acquiring" (ktetike); the art of obtaining things that already exist</note>, since no one of these fabricates anything, but procures things which are and have been—partly subjecting them to its power by words and actions, and partly conceding them to those by whom they are received.
**THEAETETUS.** They may be so called: for it is proper.
**GUEST.** Since all arts, therefore, consist either in acquiring or in effecting, in which of these, Theaetetus, shall we place the art of fishing?
**THEAETETUS.** Doubtless in the art of acquiring.
**GUEST.** But are there not two species of the art of acquiring? The one being a commutation <note>an exchange or trade</note> between those that are willing, through gifts, buying, and wages? But the other will be a **mancipation** <note>original: "mancipation" (cheirotikon); the act of taking possession by force or skill, literally "hand-taking"</note>, effected either by deeds or words.
**THEAETETUS.** It appears this must be the case, from what has been said.
**GUEST.** But what? Must not mancipation also receive a twofold division?
**THEAETETUS.** After what manner?
**GUEST.** The one being apparent, and wholly **agonistic** <note>original: "agonistic"; relating to open competition or combat, like an athletic or legal struggle</note>; but the other being occult <note>hidden or secret</note>, and wholly consisting in hunting.
**THEAETETUS.** Yes.
**GUEST.** It is likewise absurd not to give hunting a twofold division.
**THEAETETUS.** Inform me how.
**GUEST.** One member of the division consists of the inanimate, and the other of the animated kind.
**THEAETETUS.** Undoubtedly: for there are both these.
**GUEST.** How, indeed, is it possible there should not? And it is requisite that we should leave the hunting of inanimate things without a name—and that we should likewise dismiss the consideration of certain parts of the art of swimming, and other trifling things of this kind—and denominate

the other part, which is the hunting of living beings <note>original: "animated natures"</note>, the hunting of animals.
THEAETETUS. Be it so.
GUEST. But is it not rightly said that there are two types of animal hunting? One is the hunting of land animals <note>original: "the pedestrian kind"</note>, which is distinguished by many species and names; the other is the hunting of every swimming animal, which is called water-hunting.

THEAETETUS. Yes.

THEAETETUS. What do you mean? And how do you divide each?
GUEST. Anything that encloses and restrains something on all sides for the sake of trapping it is properly called a net.

GUEST. And do you call a bow-net, a <term>dictuon</term> <note>The <term>dictuon</term> was a larger and wider kind of net.</note>, a snare, or a casting-net anything other than nets?

THEAETETUS. We must.

# THE SOPHIST <note>original: "The Sophista"</note>

**THEAETETUS.** Let us pay no attention to the name: for this is sufficient.

**GUEST.** Of striking-hunting <note>original: "percutient-hunting," referring to hunting by wounding or hitting the prey</note>, therefore, one kind is, I think, nocturnal, being carried out by the light of fire; and for this reason, it happens to be called fire-bearing <note>original: "igniferous"</note>.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**GUEST.** But the other kind is diurnal <note>daytime</note>, and is carried out with tridents hooked on the ends of rods; the whole of this being hooked fishing <note>original: "aduncous fishing"</note>.

**THEAETETUS.** It is indeed so called.

**GUEST.** Of hooked-striking-fishing, therefore, that kind which is carried out by darting the tridents into the water from above is, I think, called by some "trident fishing."

**THEAETETUS.** So certain persons say.

**GUEST.** Only one species then, as I may say, remains.

**THEAETETUS.** What is that?

**GUEST.** A striking contrary to this, carried out indeed with a hook, but not randomly striking any part of the body—as in fishing with tridents—but piercing only the head and mouth of the fish, and drawing it upwards with rods and reeds. By what name, Theaetetus, shall we say this ought to be called?

**THEAETETUS.** By that of hooked fishing with rods <note>angling</note>: and we now appear to have accomplished that which we proposed to discuss.

**GUEST.** Now, therefore, you and I have not only agreed in giving a name to fishing, but we have likewise sufficiently explained the manner in which it is conducted. For, of the whole art, one half we said consisted in acquiring; and the half of this in manual subjugation <note>the art of taking possession by force or skill</note>; and again the half of this in hunting. Likewise, that the half of hunting consisted in the capture of animals; and that the half of the capture of animals was hunting in water. That again, of hunting in water, the downward division of the whole was fishing; that the half of fishing was striking; that the half of striking fishing was performed with a hook: and lastly, that the half of this consisted in drawing that which is below upwards; and that, deriving its name from this, it is called hooked fishing with rods.

**THEAETETUS.** This, therefore, has been in every respect sufficiently shown.

**GUEST.** Come then, let us endeavor according to this model <note>original: "paradigm"</note> to discover what a **sophist** is.

**THEÆTETUS.** By all means.
