**GUEST.** We said that one kind of image-making would be assimilative <note>original: "assimilative"; refers to making a likeness that is true to the proportions of the original</note>, and the other phantastic <note>original: "phantastic"; refers to making an appearance that only looks like the original from a certain perspective</note>, if it should appear that the false is truly false, and is a real thing among existing beings.

**THEÆTETUS.** We did say so.

**GUEST.** Is it not, therefore, apparent that we have now undoubtedly identified these two species?

**THEÆTETUS.** Yes.

**GUEST.** We must, therefore, again divide the phantastic species into two parts.

**THEÆTETUS.** How?

**GUEST.** One kind is that which is produced through external instruments, but the other is the illusion <note>original: "phantasm"</note> created when the producer uses their own person as the instrument of the effect.

**THEÆTETUS.** What do you mean by that?

**GUEST.** I mean when someone, by using their own body or voice, makes it appear similar to your body or your voice; this is specifically called imitation within the phantastic species.

**THEÆTETUS.** It is.

**GUEST.** Calling this "imitative," we will divide it further; but we will set aside the other part of the division, as we are now weary, and we will allow someone else to gather it together and give it a proper name.

**THEÆTETUS.** Let the part you speak of be divided, then, and let us dismiss the other.

**GUEST.** And indeed, Theætetus, it is right to think that this imitative part is also twofold; take notice of the reason why.

**THEÆTETUS.** Tell me.

**GUEST.** Of those who imitate, some do so knowing that which they imitate, while others do it without knowing it. Can we find any greater division than that between ignorance and knowledge?

**THEÆTETUS.** We cannot.

**GUEST.** Will not the example we just mentioned be an imitation performed by those endowed with knowledge? For a man who knows you can imitate your appearance.

**THEÆTETUS.** Undoubtedly.

# THE SOPHIST <note>original: "SOPHISTA"</note>

**GUEST.** But what shall we say regarding the form of justice, and, in short, regarding the whole of virtue? Do not many people, though they are ignorant, think that they know this? And while they imitate what seems to them to be the form of justice, do they not endeavor—both in words and works—to make it appear that justice is inherent in them?

**THEAETETUS.** Very many, indeed.

**GUEST.** Are they not, therefore, unsuccessful in their attempts to appear just, since they are not actually just in any respect? Or does the very opposite of this take place?

**THEAETETUS.** The very opposite takes place. <note>Meaning they often succeed in appearing just to others despite their ignorance.</note>

**GUEST.** I think, then, we must say that this imitator is different from the other: the one who is ignorant is different from the one who knows.

**THEAETETUS.** We must.

**GUEST.** From where, then, can anyone derive a name suited to each? Or is it evident that this is difficult? This difficulty exists because an ancient cause of the division of "genera" <term>general categories</term> into "species" <term>specific types</term> was unknown to our ancestors; thus, none of them attempted to make these divisions. On this account, they were necessarily lacking in specific names. But at the same time—though it may be a bold assertion—for the sake of distinction, we shall call the imitation which is based on mere opinion *doxomimetic* <note>original: "doxomimetic"; from the Greek 'doxa' (opinion) and 'mimesis' (imitation)</note>; but that which exists in conjunction with science <term>knowledge or certain understanding</term>, we shall call a certain "historic" imitation.

**THEAETETUS.** Let it be so.

**GUEST.** The first of these names, therefore, must be used: for a sophist was not found to be among those who possess scientific knowledge, but among the imitators.

**THEAETETUS.** Very much so.

**GUEST.** Let us then consider this *doxastic* <note>opinion-based</note> imitator—one who imitates based on opinion—as if he were a piece of iron, and see whether he is solid or whether he contains within himself a twofold nature.

**THEAETETUS.** Let us consider it.

**GUEST.** He is, therefore, very complex. For among sophists, one type is foolish, thinking that he knows the things which he only has an opinion about. But the form of the other—because he "rolls like a cylinder" in his discourse <note>a metaphor for someone who is slippery or evasive in debate</note>—is full of suspicion and fear that he is actually ignorant of those things which he pretends to know in front of others.

**THEAETETUS.** There are indeed both these kinds of sophists, as you have said.

<summary>The Guest distinguishes between imitators who act out of genuine knowledge and those who act out of mere opinion, further dividing the "opinion-based" sophists into those who are self-deluded and those who secretly fear their own ignorance.</summary>
<keywords>Sophistry, Justice, Virtue, Doxomimetic, Historic Imitation, Opinion vs. Knowledge, Classification of Sophists</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue of "The Sophist" (Sophista), finalizing the definition of the Sophist through the method of division.</meta>

<page-num>282</page-num>
<header>THE SOPHIST.</header>

**GUEST.** May we not, therefore, categorize one of these as a simple imitator and the other as an ironical imitator?
**THEAETETUS.** It is proper to do so.
**GUEST.** And again, shall we say that the genus <note>original: "genus"; here meaning the general class or category</note> of this is one or two?
**THEAETETUS.** See for yourself whether it is or not.
**GUEST.** I am considering it; and two types of imitators appear to me: one who employs irony publicly among the multitude and in long-winded <note>original: "prolix"</note> speeches; and the other who, in private and through short exchanges, compels the person conversing with him to contradict himself.
**THEAETETUS.** You speak most rightly.
**GUEST.** What, then, did we show the imitator to be who employs long-winded speeches? Did we show him to be a politician or a popular orator <note>original: "popular speaker"; likely referring to a demagogue</note>?
**THEAETETUS.** A popular orator.
**GUEST.** But what did we call the other—a wise man or a sophist?
**THEAETETUS.** To call him a wise man is impossible, since we have established that he is ignorant; but as he is an imitator of a wise man, he must evidently receive a similar name. And I now clearly understand that this character ought truly to be called one who is, in every respect, a real sophist.
**GUEST.** Shall we not, therefore, bind his name together, as we did before, connecting everything from the end back to the beginning?
**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.
**GUEST.** He, therefore, who compels those who converse with him to contradict themselves; who is part of the ironic genus; who is a belief-based <note>original: "doxastic"; from the Greek 'doxa' meaning opinion or belief rather than certain knowledge</note> imitator; who likewise belongs to the "fantastic" <note>original: "phantastic"; the art of creating appearances or illusions rather than true likenesses</note> genus, which proceeds from the representative art; who is defined as a human rather than a divine production; and who, by the artifice of his speeches, belongs to the wonder-working <note>original: "wonder-working"; referring to the creation of intellectual illusions or "magic" tricks with words</note> division—anyone who says that a real sophist is of this lineage and kinship <note>original: "consanguinity"</note> will, it appears, speak most truly.
**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

->THE END OF THE SOPHIST.<-

# INTRODUCTION
### TO
## THE PHÆDRUS.

---

<margin>\* In the Manuscript Scholia <note>original: "Scholiis MSS." - ancient or medieval commentaries</note> on the Phædrus.</margin>

**SOME**, says Hermeas \*, have endeavoured to show that this dialogue is concerning rhetoric, looking only to its beginning and end; others, that it is about the soul, since here especially Socrates demonstrates its immortality; and others, that it is about love, since the beginning and occasion of the dialogue originate from this. For Lysias had written an oration in order to prove that it is not proper to gratify a lover, but rather one who is not a lover; he being vehemently in love with Phædrus, but pretending that he was not. Wishing, therefore, to withdraw him from other lovers, he viciously <note>In this context, "viciously" means with flawed logic or immoral intent.</note> composed an oration, the design of which was to show that it is requisite rather to gratify one who is not a lover, than one who is. This gave occasion to Socrates to discourse concerning this intemperate love, together with temperate, divine, and enthusiastic love, because it is a love of this latter kind which should be embraced and followed. Others again assert that the dialogue is theological, on account of what is said in the middle of it. But, according to others, its subject is *the good*, because Socrates says that the super-celestial <note>original: "fuperceleftial" - referring to a realm beyond the physical heavens.</note> place has never been celebrated according to its merit, and that an uncoloured and unfigured essence <note>A reference to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas" which lack physical shape or color.</note> subsists there. And, lastly, others assert that it is concerning the beautiful itself. All these, therefore, form their opinion of the whole scope of the dialogue from a certain part of it. For it is evident that the discourse concerning the soul is assumed for the sake of something else, and also that concerning the first beauty: for Socrates ascends from other beautiful things to this, and to the

<summary>This page introduces the various historical interpretations of Plato's Phædrus, debating whether its primary subject is rhetoric, the soul, love, theology, the good, or beauty.</summary>

<page-num>286</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE PHAEDRUS</header>

super-celestial place. It is also evident that the discussions about love are to be referred to the lover. It must not, therefore, be said that there are many different goals; for it is necessary that all of them should be extended to one thing, so that the discourse may be, as it were, a single living being. In short, <term>Socrates</term> speaks concerning all-various beauty. Hence he begins from the visible beauty in the form of <term>Phaedrus</term>, with which <term>Lysias</term> was enamored as a result of falling away from the character of a true lover. But afterwards he proceeds to the beauty in speech and writing, of which <term>Phaedrus</term> is represented as a lover. From this he ascends to the beauty in the soul—namely, to the virtues and sciences—and from there, in his <term>recantation</term> <note>original: "palinode"; a poem or song in which the author retracts something said in a former one</note>, to the gods of the physical world. After which he ascends to the intelligible fountain of beauty itself, to the God of Love, and to the "Beautiful Itself" <note>The Platonic Form or Idea of Beauty</note>; from where he again descends through the art of division to the beauty in the soul, and in the virtues and sciences; and afterwards again to the beauty in speech, thus joining the end with the beginning.

In short, the whole intention of the dialogue may be divided into three parts, corresponding to three ways of life:
1. Into intemperate love, which is seen in the speech of <term>Lysias</term>;
2. Into temperate love, which is seen in the first discourse of <term>Socrates</term>;
3. And, in the third place, into divinely inspired love, which is seen in the recantation and in the last discourse of <term>Socrates</term>.

It may also be said that the lovers, the types of love, and the objects of love are analogous to these three lives. Hence, those who assert that the dialogue is about love do not deviate much from its design, since love is seen in relation to the object of love; and it is necessary indeed not to be ignorant of these related differences, since <term>Plato</term> himself does not provide random distinctions of love and its objects. However, it is evident that the primary goal of the dialogue is not love itself; for it discusses neither its essence nor its power, but rather discourses concerning its actions in the world and in souls. If <term>Plato</term> ever makes love the primary goal of a dialogue, he discusses its essence, power, and action. For example, in *The Banquet* <note>original: "The Symposium"</note>, where love is the leading object, he describes its middle nature and its rank, calling it a mighty <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "dæmon"; in Greek philosophy, a spirit or power intermediate between gods and men</note>, as it binds secondary natures to primary ones. But here, a discourse concerning the beautiful takes the lead, to which all things are raised up by love.

And here it is necessary to observe that the first existence of the beautiful—the primary object of this dialogue—is in the <term>intelligible intellect</term> <note>The highest level of reality in Neoplatonic thought, where the Forms exist</note>, the extremity...

This beauty too, as we have observed in a note on the *Parmenides*, is a vital intellectual form and the source of symmetry <gloss>1</gloss> to all things.

With respect to the persons of the dialogue, they are Lysias (or rather the oration of Lysias), Phædrus, and Socrates. Lysias and Phædrus are, as we have said, lovers of each other; but Socrates is the guardian <note>original: "curator"</note> of youth and the providential inspector of Phædrus, elevating him from the apparent and external beauty found in words to the beauty found in the soul and intellect. 

As some, however, have accused <gloss>2</gloss> the dialogue of having inflated language because of what is said in the recantation <note>The "recantation" refers to Socrates' second speech in the Phædrus, where he apologizes to the god of Love for his previous criticisms.</note>, it is necessary to observe that Socrates employs words adapted to the things themselves. For, as he discourses about objects that are hidden <note>original: "unapparent"</note> and unknown to the many, he accordingly uses an elevated style that accords with an intelligible and divine essence. Indeed, if human nature in its current degraded condition is capable of receiving divine inspirations, and if a part of the present dialogue was composed under such an influence, an accusation of this kind is certainly its greatest commendation.

Hence it is justly observed by Proclus <gloss>3</gloss>, "that Plato in this dialogue, being inspired by the Nymphs and exchanging human intelligence for a divine frenzy <note>original: "fury"; referring to the Platonic concept of 'divine madness' or inspiration.</note>—which is a thing far more excellent—delivers many secret doctrines <note>original: "arcane dogmas"</note> concerning the

***

<gloss>1</gloss> Symmetry, according to the most accurate and philosophical definition of it, is the dominion of that which is naturally *more* excellent over that which is naturally *less* excellent. Hence symmetry exists in a body when *form* conquers *matter*. Had Mr. Burke <note>Edmund Burke (1729–1797), whose famous treatise on aesthetics is here criticized by the author for lacking Platonic depth.</note> known and understood the above definition of beauty, he would not have given to the world such a crude work as his treatise *On the Sublime and Beautiful*.

# INTRODUCTION TO THE PHÆDRUS.

intellectual Gods, and many things concerning the liberated rulers of the universe, who elevate the multitude of mundane <note>original: "mundane," meaning gods belonging to the physical world or cosmos</note> Gods to the intelligible monads <note>original: "intelligible monads," referring to the primary, unified sources of being in Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, separate from the wholes which this universe contains. And still more does he deliver about the mundane Gods themselves, celebrating their intellections <note>original: "intellections," meaning acts of pure intellectual perception or thought</note> and fabrications about the world, their unpolluted providence, their government over souls, and other particulars which Socrates discloses in this dialogue according to a deific energy <note>original: "deific energy," meaning a divine or god-like power of inspiration</note>.”

I only add, that though there are frequent allusions in this dialogue to that unnatural vice <note>A reference to pederasty or same-sex relations, which were common in ancient Greek social structures</note> which was so fashionable among the Greeks, yet the reader will find it severely censured in the course of the dialogue by our divine philosopher. There can be no reason to fear, therefore, that the ears of the modest will be shocked by such allusions, since they are inserted with no other view than that they may be exploded <note>original: "exploded," meaning rejected or utterly discredited</note> as they deserve. But if, notwithstanding this, any one shall persist in reprobating certain parts of the dialogue as indecent, it may be fairly concluded, that such a one possesses the affectation of modesty without the reality; and that he is probably a bigot to some despicable and whining sect of religion, in which cant <note>Hypocritical or sanctimonious talk</note> and grimace are the substitutes for genuine piety and worth.

# THE PHÆDRUS.

---

## PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.
### SOCRATES AND PHÆDRUS.
### SCENE.—THE BANKS OF THE ILISSUS. <note>The Ilissus is a small river in Athens, often associated with local myths and religious sites.</note>

---

### SOCRATES.

**WHERE** are you going, my dear Phædrus, and where have you come from?

**PHÆDR.** From Lysias, the son of Cephalus, Socrates; but I am going for a walk outside the city walls. I have been sitting with him for a long time, indeed from very early this morning until now. But I was persuaded by Acumenus¹, who is a friend of yours as well as mine, to take some exercise, so I decided to go for a walk. He said that walking was less tiring and, at the same time, more healthful than running on the racecourse.

**Soc.** He speaks well on that subject, my friend. So, it seems Lysias was in the city?

**PHÆDR.** He was. He is staying with Epicrates in the house of Morychus, which is next to the temple of Olympian Zeus.

**Soc.** And what was he doing there? Or did Lysias perhaps provide you with a feast of orations <note>original: "banquet of orations"; a metaphor for a long, intellectual speech or essay</note>?

**PHÆDR.** You shall hear, if you have the leisure to walk along with me and listen.

---

¹ This Acumenus the physician is also mentioned by Plato in the *Protagoras*, and by Xenophon in the third book of the *Memorabilia* <note>original: "Sayings and Deeds of Socrates"; usually referred to today by its Latin title, Memorabilia</note>.

**SOCRATES.** But what, do you not think that I—to use a phrase from Pindar—would consider the account of your conversation with Lysias as a matter superior even to business?
**PHÆDRUS.** Go on then.
**SOCRATES.** Begin the account, then.
**PHÆDRUS.** And indeed, Socrates, hearing this is quite appropriate for you <note>Socrates acknowledges that he knew three specific things: the *amatory art* (the art of love), as he says regarding Diotima in the *Banquet*, "she taught me amatory affairs"; the *maieutic art* (the "midwife" art of bringing forth ideas), as he says in the *Theætetus*, "divinity has ordered me to act as a midwife"; and the *dialectic art* (logical discussion), as he says in the *Cratylus*, "for I know nothing except how to give and take words."</note>. For I do not know how it happened, but our discourse was about love. For Lysias, at the persuasion of a certain beautiful person—though not one of his lovers—had composed an oration on love, and in a very elegant manner. In the course of it, he asserts that one who is not in love ought to be favored rather than a lover.
**SOCRATES.** What a generous man! I wish he had likewise asserted that favor should be shown to the poor rather than the rich, the old rather than the young, and so on for all the rest. Then I myself, and many more of us, might be favored <note>It is scarcely necessary to observe that Socrates says this ironically.</note>. For then his discourse would have been both polite and publicly useful. I am so desirous <note>Socrates desires to hear because, from his amatory disposition, he vehemently wishes to act divinely and to save the youth.</note> of hearing his oration that even if you were to walk as far as Megara, and, like Herodicus <note>This Herodicus, as we are informed by Hermeas, was a physician who performed gymnastic exercises outside the city walls. He would start from a set distance, walk to the wall, and immediately turn back; by doing this repeatedly, he completed his exercise.</note>, turn back again the moment you reached the walls, I would not leave your side.
**PHÆDRUS.** What are you saying, most excellent Socrates? Do you think me such an idiot as to suppose myself capable of repeating, in the manner it deserves, a discourse which Lysias—the most skillful writer of the present age—spent a long time composing at his leisure? I am certainly very far from thinking I could do that, though I would rather be able to do so than possess a great quantity of gold.
**SOCRATES.** O Phædrus, if I do not know Phædrus, I have also forgotten myself; but neither of these is the case. For I well know that...

# THE PHAEDRUS.

He has not only heard the discourse of Lysias once, but he has desired him to repeat it often; and Lysias willingly complied with his request. But even this was not sufficient for Phaedrus; having at length obtained the book, he studied that which he mostly desired to see. Sitting down to peruse it very early in the morning, he continued his work until, becoming fatigued, he went out for a walk. By the dog <note>original: "by the dog" — a common Socratic oath, often associated with Anubis or Hermes</note>, it appears to me he committed it to memory, unless perhaps it was too long for that purpose. He then directed his course beyond the city walls so that he might meditate on this oration. Meeting, however, with one who was madly fond of discourse <note>Socrates refers to himself here</note>, he rejoiced on beholding him, because he would have a partner in his <term>corybantic fury</term> <note>A state of divine madness or religious frenzy, named after the Corybantes, the armed priests of Cybele</note>; and he asked him to walk on. But when that lover of discourse requested him to repeat the oration, Phaedrus feigned as if he were unwilling to comply; yet, though he pretended he did not want to be heard, he was at length compelled to give the account. I therefore entreat you, Phaedrus, that you will quickly accomplish all I desire.

**Phaedr.** Well then, I will endeavor to satisfy you in the best manner I am able; for I see you will not dismiss me until I have exerted my utmost abilities to please you.

**Soc.** You perfectly understand the truth regarding me.

**Phaedr.** I will therefore gratify you; but, in reality, Socrates, I have not learned the exact words of this oration by heart, though I nearly retain the sense of all the arguments by which he shows the difference between a lover and one who does not love; and these I will summarily relate to you in order, beginning from the first.

**Soc.** But show me first, my friend, what you have got there in your left hand.

<note>1. Not to hear once, but often, says <term>Hermeas</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Phaedrus</note>, manifests the unwearied labor of men regarding apparent beauty. The book here signifies that sensible beauties are images of images, just as the letters in it are primarily indicative of the soul, but secondarily of the reasons proceeding from the soul. A dog is dedicated to <term>Hermes</term>, and is the last vestige of the <term>Mercurial series</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the "series" or chain of beings and symbols descending from the god Hermes/Mercury</note>. As the present hypothesis, therefore, is about the oration of <term>Lysias</term>, and <term>Hermes</term> is the overseeing guardian of discourse, <term>Socrates</term> very properly swears by the dog. It may also be said that he thus swears as reverencing the lowest part of this divine order, and through it calling the overseeing <term>Hermes</term> himself as a witness.</note>

<note>2. The left hand here manifests that a rhetoric of this kind is extended to the worse, or in other words, the passive part of the soul; and that it does not pertain to the pure power and summit of [the soul].</note>

**SOCRATES:** ...hand, under your cloak: for I suspect that you have got the oration itself. And if this be the case, think thus with yourself respecting me, that I perfectly esteem you; but that, when Lysias is present, it is by no means my intention to listen to you. And therefore show it me.

**PHÆDRUS:** You ought to desist: for you have destroyed those hopes, Socrates, which I entertained respecting you; the hopes I mean of contesting with you <note>Phædrus hoped to recite the speech from memory to see if he could match Socrates's eloquence, but Socrates has caught him with the written text.</note>. But where are you willing we should sit, while we read?

**SOCRATES:** Let us, turning hither, direct our steps towards the river Ilissus: and afterwards, when you shall think proper to rest, we will sit down.

**PHÆDRUS:** And this will be very seasonable, as it appears, for I am at present without shoes <gloss>The state of being barefoot here signifies a readiness and a lack of excess, an aptitude for being led upward to higher truths. This was always the case with Socrates, but was true for Phædrus at this moment because he was about to be instructed by Socrates.</gloss>; but this is always the case with you. It will be easy, therefore, for us to walk by the side of the brook, moistening our feet; nor will it be unpleasant, especially at this season of the year, and this time of the day.

**SOCRATES:** Go on then, and at the same time look out for a place where we may sit down.

**PHÆDRUS:** Do you see that most lofty plane tree?

**SOCRATES:** Why, what then?

**PHÆDRUS:** For there, there is a cool shade, moderate breezes of wind, and soft grass, upon which we may either sit, or, if you are so disposed, lie down.

**SOCRATES:** Let us go then.

**PHÆDRUS:** But inform me, Socrates, whether this is not the place in which Boreas <note>The North Wind in Greek mythology.</note> is reported to have ravished Orithya from Ilissus.

---

<note>
The concealment of the book under Phædrus's garment signifies that this kind of rhetoric—which does not belong to the rational soul or the intellect, but rather to the opinion-based <term>doxastic</term> and imagination-based <term>phantastic</term> parts of the mind—is involved in darkness. It has fallen away from the light of true science because it deals with material concerns and human trifles.

The summer and midday are also suited to this spiritual re-elevation, following the saying of Heraclitus that "the soul that has a dry splendor is the wisest." Dipping the feet in the brook signifies touching the world of physical generation with the lowest and most humble powers of the soul (represented by the feet), while the rational soul contemplates that generation from above. The breezes represent the providential inspiration of the Gods, while the shade signifies an intellectual, hidden, and elevating power that is remote from the agitating world of the senses (which is represented by the bright light).
</note>

**SOCRATES.** It is reported so indeed.

**PHAEDRUS.** Was it not just here then? For the brooks hereabouts appear to be pleasing to the eye, pure and transparent, and very well suited for the play of young women.

**SOCRATES.** It was not, but two or three stadia <note>A stadium was a Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet; two or three stadia is about a third of a mile.</note> lower down, where we find the temple of Diana <note>original: Artemis</note> ¹, and in that very place there is a certain altar sacred to Boreas <note>The personification of the North Wind</note> ².

->**PHAEDRUS.**<-

---

¹ The Athenians, says Hermeas <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato</note>, established a temple of Rural Diana, because this Goddess is the watchful guardian of everything rural, and she restrains everything rustic and uncultivated. But the altars and temples of the Gods signify their assigned domains; just as you may also call the sun's altar and temple—and the temple of the soul of the sun—this physical body, or the visible solar orb. So, in this context, the domains and divine inspirations of the Gods in temples represent the "intelligible theory" <note>The philosophical study of universal truths</note>, which investigates universal principles through specific examples, and seeks true *being* through that which only appears to *exist*. The "temple" of this theory is the intellect itself.

² A twofold solution, says Hermeas, may be given for this myth; one is historical and more ethical, while the other elevates our understanding to "wholes" <note>Universal or cosmic principles</note>. The first is as follows: Orithyia was the daughter of Erechtheus and the priestess of Boreas; for each of the winds has a presiding deity, which the telestic art <note>The religious practice of sacred mysteries and rituals</note> religiously honors. The God Boreas was so favorable to Orithyia that he sent the north wind for the safety of the country; furthermore, he is said to have assisted the Athenians in their naval battles. Orithyia, therefore, becoming divinely inspired and possessed by her specific God, Boreas, no longer acted as a mere human (for living beings cease to act according to their own individual traits when possessed by higher causes). She died under this inspiring influence, and thus was said to have been "carried off" by Boreas. This is the more ethical explanation of the myth.

But the second explanation, which applies the story to universal principles, is as follows (and does not entirely disprove the first, for divine myths often use historical events to serve the teaching of universal truths): They say that Erechtheus is the God who rules over the three elements—air, water, and earth. Sometimes, however, he is considered the ruler of the earth alone, and sometimes as the presiding deity of Attica specifically. Orithyia is the daughter of this deity; she represents the fertile power of the earth, which is indeed linked with the name *Erechtheus*, as the breakdown of the name suggests: for it means *the fertile power of the earth flourishing and restored according to the seasons*. Boreas, meanwhile, represents the providence of the Gods shining down from above onto secondary natures. They symbolize the providence of the Gods in the world as Boreas because this Divinity blows from high places. Conversely, the "anagogic" <note>Upward-leading or elevating</note> power of the Gods is symbolized by the south wind, because this wind blows from low to high places; additionally, things situated toward the south are considered more divine. Therefore, the providence of the Gods causes the fertile power of the earth (or of the Attic land) to rise and move into the visible world.

Orithyia also, says Hermeas, may be said to be a soul * aspiring after things above, from the Greek word *orouo* <note>meaning to dart or rush forward</note>.

* This follows the "psychical" <note>Relating to the soul</note> method of interpreting myths. See the **General Introduction, volume 1,** of this work.

# THE PHAEDRUS

**PHAEDRUS:** I did not know that perfectly. But tell me, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Socrates, are you truly convinced that this mythological story ¹ is true?

**SOCRATES:** If I were to disbelieve it, as the "wise" men do, I would not be acting out of character. If I were then to speak like a clever scholar <note>original: "sophistically"</note>, I might claim that the North Wind, Boreas, blew Orithya off the nearby rocks while she was playing with Pharmacia. I would say that because she died in that manner, people claimed she had been carried off by Boreas—either from here or from the Hill of Mars <note>The Areopagus</note>. There is, after all, another version of the story that she was taken from that spot instead of this one. 

But for my part, Phaedrus, I think such interpretations are quite clever, yet they are the work of a man who is excessively curious, hardworking, and not altogether fortunate. This is for no other reason than because, once he has explained this myth, he is then forced to "correct" the appearance of the Centaurs <note>half-man, half-horse creatures</note> and the Chimera <note>a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, goat's body, and serpent's tail</note>. After that, a whole crowd of Gorgons <note>snake-haired monsters</note> and Pegasuses <note>winged horses</note> will overwhelm him, demanding similar explanations for their own monstrous 

---

<note>
...and *theo* <note>to run</note>, according to the Attic Greek custom of adding a letter at the end of a word (in this case, an omega). Such a soul is therefore "carried away" by Boreas blowing from above. If Orithya was thrown from a cliff, this is also fitting: for such a soul dies a "philosophic death" rather than a natural one. She abandons a *proairetic* life <term>proairetic: relating to the soul's own deliberate choice or will</term> even while her body remains alive. As Socrates says in the *Phaedo*, philosophy is nothing other than a preparation for death. In this sense, let Orithya represent the soul of Phaedrus, and Boreas represent Socrates, who "seizes" the soul and leads it toward this higher, deliberate death.

¹ Some believe that Socrates, in this passage, rejects the use of myths entirely. However, it is clear that he frequently uses and values myths. What he actually criticizes here are those "rational" explanations that reduce myths to mere historical accidents or material causes—like wind, earth, or air—which do not lead the mind toward true reality or divine matters. 

Therefore, Socrates asks: "If I were to explain this myth using only physical causes—claiming the wind simply blew a girl off a rock—would I not be speaking absurdly?" He calls this the method of the "wise" (meaning the physical scientists of his day), but he views it as shallow and based on guesswork. It fails because it looks only at natural forces and "vortices" (as mentioned in the *Phaedo*) rather than looking toward the soul, the intellect, and the Gods. 

When Socrates describes the person who does this as *very curious, hardworking, and not entirely happy*, he is referring to someone who is obsessed with material, sensory things. The Centaurs, Chimeras, Gorgons, and Pegasuses represent the chaotic powers that govern material nature and the earthly realm. For a proper guide on how divine myths should be interpreted, see the Introduction to the second book of the *Republic*.

* This refers to a life governed by her own individual will; in a "philosophic death," the soul instead aligns herself with the divine will.
</note>

He uses the story of Boreas and Orithya to illustrate how physical explanations fail to capture the deeper, spiritual meaning of such allegories.</summary>

natures, immense both in their number and their strangeness. If someone who does not believe in their literal meaning should try to reduce them to a probable sense, using a kind of rustic wisdom for the task, he would require a great deal of leisure time. As for me, I simply do not have the leisure for such an undertaking; and the reason is that I am not yet able, according to the Delphic precept, to know <gloss>1</gloss> myself. It seems ridiculous to me to speculate about things foreign to me while I am still ignorant of my own nature. Therefore, saying goodbye to such myths and being satisfied with the opinion I have just mentioned about them, I do not examine them. Instead, I examine myself, considering whether I am a wild beast <gloss>2</gloss>—something more complex and tangled than the monster Typhon, and far more raging and fierce—or whether I am a milder and simpler animal, naturally sharing in a certain divine and modest state. But, my friend, have we not arrived at our destination in the middle of our conversation? Is that not the oak tree to which you were leading us?

Now that we have arrived here, I for my part am disposed to lie down; but you, assuming whatever position you think most convenient, begin to read.

PHÆDRUS. Hear then.—“You are well acquainted with the state of my affairs, and you have heard, I think, that it is most conducive to my advantage for them to remain in this manner. For lovers, when their desires cease, repent of the benefits which they have bestowed; but there is no time in which it is proper for those void of love to repent of their kindness. Since they do not act from necessity, but voluntarily, and in the best manner regarding their own affairs, they do good as far as their circumstances will admit. 

Besides, lovers sometimes reflect on how negligently they have attended to their own concerns through love, what benefits they have bestowed to their own loss, and what labors they have undergone; they therefore think they have already conferred favors worthy of the objects of their love. But those void of love neither blame themselves for neglecting their affairs, nor complain of past labors, or disagreements with their family and friends, as being produced by some beloved object. So that, such mighty evils being removed, nothing else remains for them than to perform with willingness and alacrity whatever they think will be acceptable to the objects of their generous exertions. 

Besides, if it is said that lovers value the beloved party so highly because they love in the most eminent degree, and are always prepared, both in words and actions, to comply with the desires of their beloved—even if they should offend others by doing so—it is easy to see that this is not the truth. By persuading them to abstain from people like these, they cause them to abandon their friends. If, therefore, you consider your own advantage, you will be wiser than they are and will entirely disagree with their opinion. But those who are not your lovers, but who act in a becoming manner through virtue, will not envy your association with others. Instead, they will hate those who are unwilling to be your companions, thinking that you are despised by such people but benefited by your associates. So, there is much more reason to hope that friendship will be produced by this means than that enmity will arise from such a connection. 

Add to this that most lovers desire the possession of the body before they know the character <note>original: "manners"</note> or have tested anything else belonging to the beloved object. Consequently, it is uncertain whether they will still wish to be friends when the desire produced by love has faded. But for those who are without love—since from the beginning of their friendship they acted without regarding sexual pleasure <note>original: "venereal delight"</note>—it is probable that they will act with less sudden passion, but will leave their actions as lasting monuments of their conduct for the future. 

Besides, it will be more advantageous to you to be persuaded by me than by a lover. For love will represent you in such a light. It likewise compels the unfortunate to consider things as calamities which cause no trouble to others, and it obliges the fortunate to celebrate as pleasant things which are not truly deserving of delight. Therefore, it is much more proper to pity than to envy <note>original: "emulate"</note> lovers.

But if you will be persuaded by me, I will first associate with you without caring for present pleasure, but for the sake of future advantage. I will not be vanquished by love, but will maintain self-control. I will not excite severe enmity over mere trifles, but will indulge only a very little anger, and even then only slowly for great offenses. I will pardon involuntary faults and endeavor to turn you away from committing voluntary ones. For these are the marks of a friendship likely to endure for a very long period of time.

It is necessary, however, that you should receive no harm from your partner, but that some advantage should result for both of you. To me, it appears that I have said enough; but if you think anything should be added, tell me what it is.”

# THE PHÆDRUS

**SOCRATES.** Divinely indeed, my friend, so much so that I am astonished. And I am affected toward you in the same transcendent manner, Phædrus, as I watch you, because you appeared to me to be transported with delight while reading the oration. Since I considered you to be more skillful in such matters than myself, I followed your lead; and in following, I was agitated along with you—O divine head!—with a Bacchic fury <note>original: "bacchic fury"; a reference to the inspired madness or religious ecstasy associated with Dionysus/Bacchus</note>.

**PHÆDRUS.** Are you inclined to jest in this manner?

**SOCRATES.** Do I seem to you to be jesting, and not speaking seriously?

**PHÆDRUS.** You do not seem to be serious at all, Socrates. But, by Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter"; the Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods</note>, who presides over friendship, tell me truly: do you think any other Greek could say anything greater or more abundant on this subject?

**SOCRATES.** But what? Do you think a discourse ought to be praised by you and me simply because the composer has said what is sufficient? Should it not also be praised because he has artistically fashioned every word to be clear, well-rounded, and accurate? If it is necessary, this must be granted for your sake, for such skill is hidden from me because of my own insignificance. Therefore, I only paid attention to the composer's eloquence; as for the substance, I do not believe that even Lysias <note>A famous orator of the time known for his clear, plain style</note> himself would think he has done enough. Indeed, Phædrus, it seems to me—unless you disagree—that he has repeated the same points two or three times, as if he did not possess a great abundance of ideas on the subject. Or perhaps he simply did not care much about such things. Furthermore, he seems to me to be acting like a youth, showing off that he can express the same idea in different ways, and yet in each version, he claims to speak as well as possible.

**PHÆDRUS.** You are missing the point, Socrates. This oration possesses a wealth of thought in the highest degree. He has omitted nothing belonging to his subject that could be properly introduced. No one could ever speak more fully or more to the point on this same subject than he has done.

**SOCRATES.** I cannot agree with you there. The wise men and women of old, who have spoken and written on this subject, would refute me if I admitted that just to please you.

**PHAEDRUS:** Who are those ancient authors? And where have you heard better things than these?

**SOCRATES:** I do not sufficiently remember at present; but it is clear that I have somewhere heard of such things, perhaps from the beautiful Sappho <note>Sappho: A famous Greek lyric poet from Lesbos, known for her poems on love.</note>, or the wise Anacreon <note>Anacreon: A Greek lyric poet known for his songs about wine and love.</note>, or certain other writers. But from where do I derive this guess? Because, O divine man! finding my breast full of ideas, I perceive that I have something to say in addition to what has been already delivered, and this of no inferior quality. I well know, indeed, that I understand nothing about such things from myself, as I am conscious of my own ignorance. It remains therefore, I think, that I myself, like a vessel, should be filled with knowledge through hearing from the fountains of others; but that, through my dullness of understanding, I have forgotten how, and from whom, I received the information.

**PHAEDRUS:** You speak, most generous man, in the most excellent manner. For you cannot inform me—even if I should command you to do so—how and from whom you derived your knowledge; but you are able to accomplish what you speak of, since you possess more abundant and more excellent ideas than those contained in the speech of Lysias <note>Lysias: A famous orator in Athens known for his clear and persuasive style.</note>. And if you are but able to accomplish this, I promise you—after the manner of the nine Archons <note>Archons: The chief magistrates of Athens. Phaedrus refers to a tradition where they promised to dedicate a golden statue if they violated their oaths.</note>—to place a golden statue of equal size at Delphi, not only of myself, but also of you.

**SOCRATES:** You are of a most friendly disposition, Phaedrus, and truly "golden" yourself, if you suppose me to have asserted that Lysias was perfectly faulty, and that something better might have been said than the whole of his speech. For I do not think that this can ever happen, even to the worst of writers. But to the point in hand regarding this speech: Do you think that anyone who asserts that it is more proper to gratify one who does not love than a lover can have anything to say besides that assertion, if he omits to prove that he who is void of love is prudent, while the lover is not, and praises the one while blaming the other? I think that omissions of this kind are to be allowed, and even pardoned, in a writer; in such cases, it is not the invention <term>invention: In rhetoric, the process of finding arguments or "inventing" the subject matter.</term> of these discourses, but the elegance of the composition, which ought to be praised. But in things which are not necessary, and which are difficult to discover, I think that not only the composition, but also the invention, should be praised.

# THE PHÆDRUS

The first principle for those who intend to deliberate in a proper manner is to know the subject about which they consult; otherwise, they must inevitably wander far from the truth. However, most people are unaware that they do not understand the essence <note>original: "essence" (ousia); the fundamental nature or definition of a thing</note> of each particular thing. Consequently, at the beginning of their investigations, they do not bother to define what that essence is, acting as if they were already experts in such matters. But as their inquiry proceeds, they offer nothing more than probable arguments; thus, they end up agreeing neither with themselves nor with others.

Therefore, to ensure that you and I do not suffer from the very fault we condemn in others, we must establish a foundation for our inquiry. In deciding whether a friendship should be formed with someone who is not in love rather than with someone who is, we must first understand what love is and what power it possesses. We should mutually agree on a definition of love, and by keeping this definition in view and referring our discussion back to it, we can determine whether love is a source of benefit or harm.

It is obvious to everyone that love is a type of desire; yet we also know that those who are not "in love" still desire beautiful things. To distinguish a lover from a non-lover, we must recognize that there are two distinct governing and leading principles within each of us, which we follow wherever they lead. One is an innate <note>natural or inborn</note> desire for pleasure; the other is an acquired opinion <note>a developed judgment or conviction</note> that strives for what is best. Sometimes these two principles exist in harmony, but at other times they are in a state of conflict and discord, with one or the other gaining the upper hand.

When opinion is guided by reason toward what is best and achieves victory, that restraint is called temperance <note>original: "temperance" (sophrosyne); self-control or moderation</note>. But when desire irrationally lures us toward pleasure and gains dominion over us, that rule is called excess <note>original: "injury" (hubris); insolence or out-of-control passion</note>. This "excess" has many names, for it is multifaceted and consists of many types. Whichever of these forms is most prominent gives its name to the person it inhabits, and it is not a name that is graceful or honorable. For example, when the desire for food overcomes the rational pursuit of what is best and rules over other desires, it is called gluttony, and the person is called a glutton. Similarly, the desire that tyrannizes a person regarding intoxication, and leads them in that direction...

<sig>VOL. III. 2 R</sig>
<meta>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword for the next page is "its".</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues that any rational debate must begin with a clear definition of terms, specifically defining love as a form of desire that competes with the rational desire for what is best. He categorizes the conflict between innate pleasure-seeking and acquired reason, labeling the victory of the former as "excess" or "hubris."</summary>

Its possessor, wherever it pleases, evidently confers on him its own name. And it is sufficiently manifest what the sisters of these desires, and the names of those sister-desires, ought to be called when they rule with absolute power. But the reason for which all this has been said is now nearly evident; though it will certainly be clearer in every respect if stated plainly than if not. For the desire which, without reason, rules over the opinion tending toward what is right, and which draws it down toward the pleasure of beauty—being vehemently invigorated by its kindred desires for the beauty of the body—leads and subdues it. This desire, receiving a name from its own strength, is called Love <note>original: "Eros," implying a forceful, irrational passion</note>. But, my dear Phaedrus, do I appear to you, as I do to myself, to be suffering a certain divine passion?

PHAEDRUS. Indeed, Socrates, you possess a certain fluency of expression beyond what is usual for you.

SOCRATES. Hear me then in silence. For in reality, this place appears to be divine. If, therefore, during my discourse, I should be often hurried away by the inspiring influence of the Nymphs <note>The local deities of the stream and grove where they sit</note>, you must not be surprised. For the words which burst from me at present are not very far removed from dithyrambic verse <note>A passionate, wild, and rhythmic form of Greek poetry</note>.

PHAEDRUS. You speak most truly.

SOCRATES. But you are the cause of this. However, hear the rest; for perhaps the spirit that now possesses me may depart. But this will be taken care of by the divine. Let us, therefore, again direct our discourse to the young man. What that thing is, then, which was the object of our consultation, has been declared and defined. But looking toward this definition, let us consider what remains: what assistance or harm will properly happen to the boy who is gratified by a lover, and to the boy who is gratified by one who is not a lover.

It is necessary, then, that a man who is enslaved by desire, or who is in subjection to pleasure, should render the object of his love as agreeable to himself as possible. But to one who is diseased, everything is pleasant which does not oppose his disease; however, that which is better or equal to him is troublesome. Hence, the lover is never willing that the object of his love should possess anything more excellent than himself, or anything approaching an equality with himself; but rather that, as much as possible, the beloved should be inferior to and more needy than himself. # THE PHAEDRUS

Through ignorance, he may become inferior to the wise; through timidity, inferior to the bold; through inability to speak, inferior to the rhetoricians; and through dullness, inferior to the acute. When these—and far more numerous ills than these, according to the conceptions of the lover—are naturally inherent or are produced in the beloved object, the lover rejoices. He even endeavors to introduce further defects so that he may not be deprived of his desired pleasure. Hence, it is necessary that the lover should be envious of his beloved and should endeavor by all possible means to exclude him from associating with others through whom he might become a most excellent man. Thus, in reality, the lover is the cause of a mighty injury to his beloved. 

But the greatest injury he causes is that of depriving his beloved of the means of becoming eminently prudent. One becomes most prudent through divine philosophy, from which the lover is necessarily compelled to withdraw his beloved through the fear of being despised. Besides this, he is obliged to use a variety of other artifices so that his beloved, by becoming ignorant of everything, may place all his admiration upon the lover alone. In this way, the youth may become most acceptable to his lover, but most pernicious <note>original: "pernicious" meaning harmful or destructive</note> to himself. Thus, with respect to things relating to the rational part <note>The "rational part" refers to the soul's capacity for reason and intellect.</note> of the soul, an association with a lover is by no means advantageous, but rather prejudicial to the party beloved.

After this, it is necessary to consider how he who is compelled to prefer the pleasant to the good would take care of the body of his beloved if it were committed to his charge. Indeed, he would endeavor that it should not become firm and vigorous, but effeminate and soft; and that it should not be nourished in the pure light of the sun, but under the mingled shade. He would ensure the youth was educated without having any experience of manly labors and "dry sweats" <note>original: "dry sweats" refers to the physical exertion of the gymnasium or athletic training without the use of oils.</note>; but on the contrary, should be continually accustomed to a delicate and effeminate mode of living, adorned with foreign colors and ornaments for lack of his own proper decorations. He would ensure the youth was studious of everything else that follows from cares of this kind. All of these points, as they are unworthy of a longer narration, having been summarily defined, we shall proceed to what remains of our discourse. Enemies in battle and other great necessities will confidently assault such a body, but friends and lovers will be in fear for its safety. This point, being sufficiently evident, we shall dismiss. Besides, while he loves, he is pernicious and importunate <note>term: importunate; persistent to the point of annoyance</note>. And, lastly, when the time comes that he ought to repay the youth for his kindness, the lover receives a new ruler and patron within himself—namely, intellect and temperance, instead of love and fury. Thus becoming entirely changed, he deceives his once beloved object. And then the beloved, calling to mind the former actions...

**Socrates:** You, O Phædrus, have delivered a terrible, terrible discourse, and you have compelled me to utter the same.

**Phædrus:** But how so?

**Socrates:** The discourse has been foolish, and in a certain respect impious. And can anything be more terrible <note>original: "dire"</note> than this?

**Phædrus:** Nothing, if you speak the truth.

**Socrates:** What then? Do you not think that Love <note>For an account of Love considered as a Deity, see the notes on *The Banquet*.</note> is the son of Venus and a certain God?

**Phædrus:** So it is said.

**Socrates:** Yet this was neither acknowledged by Lysias, nor in your discourse, which was drawn out of you—as if by a magic spell—through my own mouth. But if Love is a God, or something divine (as is really the case), he cannot be in any respect evil; and yet in our discourse about him, he has been spoken of as evil. In this, therefore, we have offended against Love. Furthermore, our arguments, though polished, appear to have been very foolish; for though they asserted nothing sound or true, they boasted as if they did, and as if they would achieve something significant by winning the approval of some trifling, deluded men. It is necessary, therefore, my friend, that I should purify myself. There is an ancient purification for those who offend in matters regarding mythology, which Homer did not recognize, but which was known to Stesichorus. For Stesichorus, having been deprived of his sight because of his accusations against Helen, was not ignorant of the cause of his blindness like Homer was, but knew it because he was a musician <note>In this context, "musician" refers to a servant of the Muses, or a poet-philosopher.</note>. Consequently, he immediately composed the following lines:

->False was my tale; you never across the sea<-
->In beautiful ships did fly, Troy’s lofty towers to reach.<-

And thus, having composed a poem directly contrary to what he had previously published—which is called a recantation <note>original: "palinode"</note>—he immediately recovered his lost sight. I am, therefore, in this present instance wiser than both of these poets:

<margin>The following account is entirely mythological, concealing certain divine truths under the symbols of fable. But as this account of Stesichorus and the story of the *Iliad* is beautifully explained by Proclus in his commentary on Plato's *Republic* (page 393), I shall present the reader with the following summarized translation of his commentary.</margin>

> "Stesichorus <note>A Greek lyric poet</note>, who treated the entire story of Helen as a literal historical account and based his poetry on that assumption, quite rightly suffered the punishment for his folly—that is, his ignorance. But eventually, through the help of the Muses <note>original: "music"</note>, he is said to have recognized his error. Thus, by understanding the hidden meanings <note>original: "mysteries"</note> concerning Helen and the Trojan War, he recovered his sight. Homer, however, is said to have been blind not because of ignorance like Stesichorus, but because of a more perfect state of the soul. That is, he separated himself from physical beauty, fixed his understanding above all outward harmony, and stretched the intellect of his soul toward the hidden and true harmony of the universe. Therefore, he is said to have been blind because divine beauty cannot be perceived by physical eyes. For this reason, stories that lean toward tragedy claim Homer was blinded because he spoke ill of Helen. But in my opinion, these stories use Helen to represent all the beauty that exists within the world of physical change <note>original: "generation"</note>. Souls fight a perpetual battle over this beauty until the more intellectual souls, having defeated the more irrational parts of life, return to the place from which they first came. According to some, the cycle of their journey through physical forms lasts ten thousand years, since a thousand years make up one circuit, much like one year. For nine circuits—that is, nine thousand years—souls revolve around the world of physical change. But in the tenth, having conquered all the chaotic, 'barbaric' turmoil, they are said to return to their original heavenly homes."

I shall therefore observe, in answer to the followers of Van Dale, Fontenelle, and others who have endeavored to prove that the oracles of the ancients were nothing more than the tricks of fraudulent priests, that to suppose mankind should have been the dupes of such impositions for the space of three thousand years, would exceed the most extravagant fiction in romance. For how is it possible, even if these priests had been a thousand times more cunning and deceitful than they are supposed to have been, that they could have kept such a secret so impenetrable in every city and province where there were any oracles, as never to have given themselves the lie in any particular? Is it possible that there should never have been one man among them of so much worth as to abhor such impostures? That there should never have been any so inconsiderate as unluckily to discover all the mystery for want of some precautions? That no man should ever

# THE PHAEDRUS

...to us by a divine gift. For the predicting prophetess at Delphi, and the priestesses <note>The Pythia and other female oracles.</note> have explored the sanctuaries, subterranean passages, and caverns, where it is pretended they kept their machines? That they should never have had occasion for workmen to repair them? That only they should have had the secret of composing drugs proper to create extraordinary dreams? And, lastly, that they should have perpetually succeeded one another, and conveyed their machines and their juggling tricks to all those that were to follow them in the same employments from age to age, and from generation to generation, and yet no man have been ever able to detect the imposition?

Besides, who were these priests, that, as it is pretended, were monsters of cruelty, fraud, and malice? They were the most honorable men among the heathens \*, and such as were most esteemed for their piety and probity. They were sometimes magistrates and philosophers. Thus Plutarch † informs us in one of his treatises, that he was himself, to a very old age, the priest of Apollo of Delphi, and that he presided in this character over the oracle, the sacrifices, and all the other ceremonies of this deity for many years. Depraved as the age is, will anyone be hardy enough to assert that a man of such probity, of such gravity of manners, of so much penetration, learning, and judgment as Plutarch, was a cheat and an impostor by profession? That he was capable of speaking through a hollow image to counterfeit the voice of Apollo? Or of suborning a female to act the part of one possessed, when she was seated on the Tripos? <note>The three-legged stool upon which the Pythia sat to deliver oracles.</note> There is not surely anyone so lost to shame, so devoid of common sense as to make such an assertion.

Again, how could those clear and precise oracles have been produced by fraud, in which what was done in one place was foretold in another, as in that famous oracle which was delivered to the ambassadors of Croesus? This most stupid of kings, and most unfortunate of cooks, as he is justly called by Maximus Tyrius, in order to try the veracity of the oracles, had determined, it seems, in a secret part of his palace to do something to which no one should be privy but himself, and sent to the oracle of Apollo to tell him what he was doing. His messengers returned with the following answer:

-> I know the number of the grains of sand and the measure of the sea; <-
-> I understand the dumb, and I hear those who do not speak. <-
<note>original Greek: Οιδα δ' εγω ψαμμου τ' αριθμον και μετρα θαλασσης, Και κωφου συνιημι, και ου λαλεοντος ακουω.</note>

\* The pontiffs and other priests among the Greeks, as well as among the Romans, held the first rank of honor. They were usually taken from noble or patrician families. This we may learn from Aristotle in the third book of his *Politics*, chapter 10; from Cicero, *On Divination*, book 1, and *On the Laws*, book 2, where he speaks of Romulus and Numa; from Homer, *Iliad* 6, line 76, and Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 3, when they speak of Helenus; and from the latter also when he speaks of king Anius, *Aeneid* 3, line 80:

Croesus, it seems, was at the very time when this oracle was delivered boiling a lamb and tortoise together in a brazen vessel. This story is first related by Herodotus, *History* book 1, chapter 8, and after him by various other writers, both heathen and Christian; and among the rest by Basil, who, with the rest of the Church Fathers, says that the devil was the author of it. Now the fact is as certain as any in antiquity. Besides, it is not the only one of this nature: Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Dionysius Halicarnasseus, Strabo, Florus, etc., relate several instances of predictions having been verified in one place of what was doing in another. Plutarch, in the life of Paulus Aemilius and in that of Sylla, adds others also; but one especially that happened in the reign of Domitian, and of the truth of which he says no man doubted in his time. 

The circumstance, as related also by Augustine, book 2 of *The City of God*, chapter 24, was that a servant of one Lucius Pontius prophetically exclaimed, "I come a messenger from Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war.</note>; the victory, Sylla, is yours!" He afterwards added that the Capitol would be in flames. Having said this, he immediately left the camp, and the next day returned more rapidly and exclaimed that the Capitol had been burnt. And the Capitol, it seems, had in reality been on fire. Augustine adds that it was easy for the devil to foresee this and most rapidly to tell it. Indeed, such predictions must have been the effect of inspiration, either from divinity or from some of the <term>genera</term> <note>Classes or types of beings.</note> between divinity and man; and hence Augustine, very consistently with his religion, ascribed them to an evil <term>daemon</term> <note>In this context, a spirit or supernatural being, not necessarily "demonic" in the modern sense, though Augustine viewed them as evil.</note>. The Platonic reader, however, will easily account for most of them more rationally, as he *scientifically* knows that divination has *deity* for its origin; and that, when the persons inspired are worthy characters and the predictions beneficial, such inspiration cannot be the offspring of fraudulent spirits.

It is very justly indeed observed by Plutarch, in his treatise concerning the Pythian oracles, that with respect to cursory predictions, someone might foretell that a certain person should be victorious in battle, and he accordingly conquered; that such a city should be subverted, and it was accordingly destroyed; but, says he, *when not only the event is foretold, but how, and when, after what, and by whom it shall be effected, this is no conjecture of things which may perhaps take place, but a pre-manifestation of things which will absolutely happen.* 

<gloss>After Boethus had gone through these points, Serapion said: "The argument Boethus uses is just regarding those things spoken indefinitely and without specific conditions; if victory is foretold to a general, and he conquers; or the destruction of a city, and it is destroyed. But where not only the event is told, but also how, and..."</gloss>
<note>original: Τοιαυτα του Βοηθου διελθοντος ὁ Σεραπιων, δικαιον (εφη) το αξιωμα περι των ουτως λεγει Βοηθος αοριστως και ανυποθετως λεγομενων· ει νικη στρατηγω προειρηται, νενικηκεν· ει πολεως αναιρεσις, απολωλεν. Όπου δε ου μονον λεγεται το γενησομενον, αλλα και πως, και...</note>

privately and publicly, to the Greeks; but when they have been in a prudent <note>original: "prudent state," meaning a state of ordinary, rational sobriety as opposed to divine inspiration</note> state, they have been the cause of very trifling benefits, or indeed of none at all.

<note>original Greek: ποτε, και μετα τι, και μετα τινος, ουκ εστι εικασμος των ταχα γενησομενων, αλλα των παντως εσομενων προδηλωσις. — Translation: "The knowledge of when, after what, and with whom something will happen is not a mere guess of things that might occur, but a clear foretelling of things that will certainly come to pass."</note>

Should it be asked why such inspiration, if it once existed, no longer exists at present, I reply by repeating what I have said in my notes on *Pausanias* (Vol. 3. p. 251): that when those celestial cycles take place—mentioned in a note on the eighth book of the *Republic*—during which the parts of the earth exist according to nature, and this is accompanied by a gathering of proper *instruments*, *times*, and *places*, then divine illumination is abundantly and properly received. But when parts of the earth exist contrary to nature as they do at present (which has been the case ever since the oracles ceased), then as there is no longer a fitness of *places*, *instruments*, and *times*, divine influence can no longer be received. This is true even though the illuminations of divine natures continue immutably the same. As Proclus says: it is just as if a face stood in the same position, but a mirror at one time received a clear image of it, and at another, one that was obscure and weak <note>original: "debile"</note>, or indeed, no image at all. For, as the same incomparable man further observes, it is no more proper to refer the lack of divine inspiration to the Gods, than to accuse the sun of being the cause of the moon's eclipse, instead of the conical shadow of the earth into which the moon falls. The reader will find the theory of oracles scientifically explained in the place mentioned above.

<margin>The ancients did not consider divine madness to be disgraceful.</margin>

...none at all. And if we should speak of the Sibyl <note>A female prophet of the ancient world believed to be possessed by a deity.</note>, and others who have employed divine prophecy, rightly predicting many things to many people regarding the future, we would be too wordy, and at the same time only speak of that which is obvious to everyone. This indeed is worthy of being testified: that those ancients who gave names to things did not consider *mania* <note>original: "mania"; here meaning a state of divine possession or inspired madness.</note> as either base or disgraceful. For they did not connect the name of *mania* with that most beautiful art by which we are enabled to judge the future as if it were something harmful; rather, they gave it a name of this kind as something beneficial when it exists through a divine gift. 

But men of the present day, being ignorant of what is appropriate, have inserted the letter *t* and call it *mantike* <note>original: "μαντικη"; the Greek word for the art of divination.</note>, or the art of divining. Indeed, the investigations of the future by prudent men—which take place through observing birds and a variety of other tokens, proceeding from the reasoning part of the soul <note>original: "dianoëtic part"; the faculty of discursive reason or logical thought.</note> through human intelligence—they denominated "intellect" and *intellective opinion*. Moderners, however, through a reverence for the letter *o* <note>original: "ω" (omega).</note>, call this *augurial* <note>original: "oionistike"; pertaining to the practice of augury or reading omens.</note>, or pertaining to augury. By how much more perfect and honorable, therefore, prophecy is than augury, and the name and operation of the one than the name and operation of the other, by so much did the ancients testify...

<meta>This page continues the speech of Socrates regarding the nature of divine madness and begins the formal proof of the immortality of the soul.</meta>

# THE PHAEDRUS

<page-num>319</page-num>

That madness <note>original: "mania"</note> proceeding from divinity is more beautiful than the prudence which proceeds from men. Indeed, in the greatest diseases and labors to which certain persons are sometimes subject through the indignation of the Gods—as a consequence of ancient guilt—madness, when it takes place and predicts what they need, discovers a liberation from such evils by seeking refuge in prayer and the worship of the Gods. Hence, by obtaining purifications and the advantages of initiation through these means, it renders the person who possesses it free from disasters, both for the present and the future, by revealing a solution for present evils to the one who is properly "insane" and possessed by divinity.

But the third species is a possession and madness descending from the Muses. This, receiving a soul tender and solitary, rouses and agitates it with inspired <note>original: "Bacchic"</note> fury through songs and other types of poetry. Consequently, by adorning the countless actions of antiquity, it becomes the means of instructing future generations. But he who approaches the gates of poetry without the madness of the Muses¹, persuading himself that he can become a poet sufficiently through art alone, will be imperfect—both in himself and in his poetry. For the poetry produced by mere prudence <note>meaning: rational skill or technical craft</note> vanishes before that which is the offspring of divine madness.

These, then, are the many beautiful works arising from divine madness—and there are still more than these which I could relate if it were necessary. Therefore, we ought not to be afraid of madness; nor should any argument disturb us which tries to prove that we ought to prefer a "prudent" friend to one who is divinely agitated. For he who asserts this must also show, in order to win the argument, that love was not sent from the Gods for the benefit of the lover and his beloved. On the contrary, we must now demonstrate that a madness of this kind was sent by the Gods for the purpose of producing the greatest happiness. This demonstration will indeed be incredible to the unworthy, but to the wise, it will be an object of belief. It is necessary, therefore, in the first place, that by observing the passions and operations of the divine and human soul, we should understand the truth concerning the nature of each. Let this then be the beginning of the demonstration:

->**Every soul is immortal²: for that which is perpetually moved is eternal.**<-

***

¹ See the Note on the tenth book of the Republic, concerning the different kinds of poetry.
² Plato’s discourse here is, as it were, analytical. Thus, for instance, the end of man... <note>The note breaks off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Socrates argues that divine madness—specifically prophetic, initiatory, and poetic inspiration—is superior to human rationality, and begins a formal proof for the immortality of the soul based on its perpetual motion.</summary>
<keywords>divine madness, mania, Muses, poetic inspiration, immortality of the soul, Socrates, Plato, Phaedrus, purification</keywords>

--- Page 1665 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the nature of the soul and its inherent immortality, transitioning from the mechanics of motion to the soul's divine origins and memory.</meta>

# THE PHAEDRUS

But that which moves another and is moved by another, when it has a cessation of motion, has also a cessation of life. Hence that alone which moves itself, because it does not desert itself, never ceases to be moved; but this also is the fountain and principle of motion to other things which are moved. But a principle is unbegotten <note>original: "unbegotten"; meaning it has no beginning and was not created by something else</note>: for everything which is generated is necessarily generated from a principle, while the principle itself is incapable of being generated. For neither could it any longer be a principle if it was generated from an external cause. Since then it is unbegotten, it is also necessary that it should be incorruptible <note>original: "incorruptible"; meaning it cannot decay or be destroyed</note>: for, should the principle become extinct, it could neither renew its being from another, nor generate another from itself, since it is necessary that all things should be generated from that which is the principle. 

And thus the beginning of motion is derived from that which moves itself: and this can neither be destroyed nor generated. For, if this were admitted, all heaven and earth falling together must stop; nor could any force be found, whence being moved, they would be again generated. Since then it appears that a self-moving nature is immortal, he who asserts that this is the very essence and definition of soul will have no occasion to blush. For every body to which motion externally arrives is inanimate. But that to which motion is inherent from itself is animated; as if this was the very nature of soul. And if there is nothing else which moves itself except soul, soul is necessarily without generation, and immortal. And thus much may suffice concerning the immortality of the soul ¹.

---

<note>The following section appears to be a commentary or transition explaining the purpose of the dialogue.</note>

...is nothing else than felicity <note>original: "felicity"; meaning supreme happiness or blessedness</note>, and this is a union with the Gods; for Plato does not place felicity in external things. But the soul is conjoined with the Gods even in the present life, when, surveying the whole of sensible and celestial beauty, she acquires a reminiscence <note>original: "reminiscence"; the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul "remembering" knowledge it had before birth</note> of intelligible beauty. But her reminiscence must be of that which she once beheld: for reminiscence is of things which someone has either heard of or seen. But the soul formerly beheld this beauty, when she revolved in conjunction with her proper God. She must, therefore, be immortal: for if not, she would neither have revolved nor have recovered her memory. Hence he first speaks concerning the immortality of the soul, her idea, and what follows; and afterwards he discourses concerning that to which Love conducts us, namely, an intelligible essence, and divine beauty, simple, and unmoved.

¹ This part contains one of the strongest demonstrations possible of the immortality of the soul, as will be evident to everyone whose intellectual eye is not blinded by modern pursuits. But when Plato says "every soul," the reader must not suppose that the souls of brutes <note>original: "brutes"; meaning non-human animals</note> are meant to be included,
