<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's nature and immortality, transitioning from logical proofs to a mythological description of the soul's form.</meta>

# THE PHAEDRUS.

But regarding its idea¹ we must speak in the following manner: To give a perfect description of its nature would indeed be a task for

<margin>a narration</margin>

a god, and would require a long discourse; but to say what it resembles is a shorter task and within human capacity. Let it then be compared to the combined power of a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now, the horses and charioteers of the gods are all both good themselves and of good stock; but the condition of others is mixed. In our case, first of all, the ruler guides a pair of horses; and next, one of these horses is noble and good, and of similar origin, but the other is of opposite origin and opposite character. Therefore, the driving in our case is necessarily difficult and troublesome.

---

¹ By the "idea" of the soul, we are not to understand its heavenly archetype, but its internal form, and the disposition and, as it were, the shape of its power. By the "chariots of the Gods"—that is, of the worldly Gods and beneficial demons—we are to understand all the internal reasoning powers of their souls, which seek the knowledge of all things, and which can simultaneously contemplate higher truths and care for lower concerns. The horses signify the effectiveness and moving strength of these powers. 

However, the horses and chariots of "partial" souls (such as ours when separated from the body) are a mixture of good and evil. Our governing part is the intellect. The better horse represents spiritedness <note>original: "anger"; here referring to the 'thumos' or righteous passion</note>, and the worse horse represents desire. The wings are the uplifting or "reductory" powers <note>powers that lead the soul back to its source</note>, and specifically belong to the charioteer, or intellect. 

An immortal living being is composed of a soul and a celestial body; but a mortal living being is composed of a soul and an elementary body. For partial souls, like ours, have three vehicles: one ethereal, derived from the heavens; the second aerial; and the third this gross terrestrial body. 

Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> here signifies the head of that order of Gods which exists immediately above the worldly Gods and is called *apollytos* <note>original: απολυτος; meaning "liberated" or "unattached"</note>: for the term "mighty," as is well observed by <term>Proclus</term>, is a symbol of exempt supremacy. The twelve Gods, therefore, who are divided into four triads, are Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Vesta, Minerva, Mars, Ceres, Juno, Diana, Mercury, Venus, and Apollo. 
*   The first triad is **fabricative** (creative); 
*   The second is **defensive** (protective); 
*   The third is **vivific** (life-giving); 
*   The fourth is **reductory** (leading back to the divine). 

The chariots of these Gods are super-worldly souls, in which they are directly carried. By the "heavens," which the liberated and worldly Gods travel to contemplate, the author cannot mean the physical, visible heavens: for what blessed sights do these contain, or how can Gods be turned toward things that are lower than themselves? It is evidently, therefore, the "heaven" which <term>Plato</term> in the *Cratylus* defines as "sight directed to that which is above" <note>original: οψις ες το ανω</note>; it forms that order of Gods called by the <term>Chaldean Oracles</term> "intelligible and intellectual" <note>original: νοητος και νοερος</note>. 

There is a remarkable error here in the Greek text: instead of "celestial arch" <note>original: ουρανια αψιδα</note>, it should read "sub-celestial arch" <note>original: υπουρανια αψιδα</note>, as is evident from <term>Proclus</term> in *Platonic Theology*, page 217, who places particular stress upon the word "sub-celestial" as a reading universally acknowledged. Our journey is said to be difficult and hard because the motion of the better horse leans toward the intelligible realm, but the worse horse leans toward the world of the senses and physical birth; and because our soul is unable in this present life to simultaneously contemplate divine truth and act with divine foresight. By "ambrosia" is signified that power which keeps the Gods separate from the cycle of birth; by "nectar" is meant the unchanging nature of their caring energies, which extend even to the lowliest of things.

The commentary provides a Neoplatonic interpretation of the gods, their hierarchies, and the soul's struggle to ascend toward divine contemplation.</summary>

# THE PHAEDRUS

To describe the soul as it truly is would require a long and divine explanation; however, to describe it through a certain likeness is a task suited for human and shorter discourse. Let it then be compared to the combined power of a winged chariot and its charioteer. All the horses and chariots of the Gods are indeed good and made of good elements; but those of other beings are mixed. 

In the first place, our ruling part <note>original: "principal part"; referring to the Reason or Intellect</note> governs the reins of a two-horse chariot. In the next place, one of the horses is good and beautiful, and is composed of similar qualities; but the other is of a contrary nature and is composed of contrary qualities. For this reason, our journey is necessarily difficult and hard. 

We must now endeavor to explain why an animal is called either "mortal" or "immortal." Every soul takes care of everything that is inanimate and revolves around the whole of heaven, taking on different forms at different times. While the soul is perfect and winged, it travels on high and governs the entire universe. But the soul whose wings fail and fall away <note>original: "suffer a defluxion"</note> sinks downward until it encounters something solid that stops its descent. There, it takes on an earthly <note>original: "terrene"</note> body as its destined home, which appears to move itself through the power of the soul. This whole—the combination of soul and body—is called a living being and is given the name "mortal animal." 

The nature of an "immortal" being, however, cannot be understood by any rational deduction, unless we use a hypothetical or imagined description. This is because we have neither seen nor sufficiently understood God as an immortal being endowed with a soul and possessing a body naturally joined to that soul for all time. These matters, however, are as the Divine pleases. 

But let us now declare the cause for which the wings were cast aside and fell from the soul. It is of the following kind: the wings of the soul have a natural power to lift what is heavy up to the heights where the race <note>original: "genus"</note> of the Gods resides. Of everything connected to the body, the soul shares most in that which is divine. That which is divine is beautiful, wise, and good, and everything of a similar kind. The winged nature of the soul is especially nourished and increased by these things; but it loses its integrity and perishes through what is evil, base, and other such opposites. 

Likewise, Jupiter, the mighty leader in the heavens, driving his winged chariot, begins the divine procession, ordering and arranging all things with providential care. The army of Gods and demons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Greek philosophy, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note>, divided into eleven parts, follows him.

<summary>Socrates uses the allegory of the winged chariot to explain the soul's composition and its fall from the divine realm into a mortal body. He describes how the soul's wings are nourished by divinity and beauty but lost through evil.</summary>

his course; but Vesta <note>The goddess of the hearth, representing the stable center of the universe</note> alone remains in the habitation of the Gods. But each of the other Gods belonging to the twelve <note>The twelve Olympian deities</note> presides over the office committed to his charge. There are many, therefore, and blessed spectacles and processions within the heavens, to which the race of the blessed Gods is turned as each accomplishes the proper employment of his nature. But *will* and *power* are the perpetual attendants of their processions, for envy is far distant from the divine choir of Gods. 

But when they proceed to the banquet and the enjoyment of delicious food, they sublimely ascend in their progression to the sub-celestial arch. And, indeed, the vehicles <note>The chariots representing the souls</note> of the Gods, being properly adapted to the guiding reins and equally balanced, proceed with an easy motion; but the vehicles of other natures are attended in their progressions with difficulty and labor. For the horse participating in depravity <note>The "dark horse" of the soul, representing base desires</note> becomes heavy; and when he has not been properly disciplined by the charioteers, he leans and gravitates toward the earth. And in this case, labor and an extreme contest are proposed to the soul. 

But those who are called immortals, when they arrive at the summit, proceeding beyond the extremity of heaven, stand on its back; and while they are established in this eminence, the circumference carries them round, and they behold what the region beyond the heavens contains. But the super-celestial place has not yet been celebrated by any of our poets, nor will it ever be praised according to its dignity and worth. It exists, however, in the following manner—for we should dare to affirm the truth, especially when speaking concerning the truth: without color, without figure, and without contact, existing as true essence, it alone uses contemplative <gloss>¹</gloss> intellect, the governor of the soul; about which essence the genus of true science resides. 

As the rational power <note>original: "dianoëtic power," referring to the soul's capacity for discursive reasoning</note> of divinity revolves with intellect and immaculate science, so likewise the rational power of every soul, when it receives a condition accommodated to its nature, perceiving "being" <note>True reality as opposed to temporary appearances</note> through time, becomes enamoured with it. Contemplating truth, the soul is nourished and filled with joy, until the circumference, by a circular revolution, brings it back again to its original situation. But in this circuit, it beholds justice herself, it beholds temperance, and science herself: not the kind of science associated with the world of change <note>original: "generation"</note>, nor that in which one thing has a particular local residence in another (to which we give the name of "beings"), but—

<note>The text describes the soul's encounter with</note> that which is science in *true being*. And, besides this, contemplating and banqueting on other true beings in the same manner, again entering within the heavens, it returns to its proper home. But, when it returns, the charioteer, stopping his horses at the manger, presents them with ambrosia, and together with it, nectar for drink. And this is the life of the Gods.

But, with respect to other souls, such as follow divinity in the best manner, and become similar to its nature, they raise the head of the charioteer <note>The head of the charioteer is that unity of the soul which she participates from a divine unity, and which is, as it were, the very summit and flower of her essence.</note> into the super-celestial place; where he is borne along with the circumference. However, he is disturbed by the course of the horses, and scarcely obtains the vision of perfect realities. But other souls at one time raise, and at another time depress, the head of the charioteer: and, through the violence of the horses, they partly see indeed, and are partly destitute of vision. 

And again, other souls follow, all of them desiring the vision of this superior place: but from being unable to accomplish this design, they are carried round in a submerged condition, struggling against and rushing on each other, through a contention for precedence in their course. Hence the tumult, contest, and perspiration are extreme. And here, indeed, many become lame through the fault of the charioteers, many break many of their wings, and all of them, involved in mighty labor, depart destitute of the perception of reality; but after their departure they use a nourishment composed from opinion; because of which there is a great endeavor to behold where the *plain of truth* is situated. 

For, from a *meadow* of this kind, that which is best in the soul receives convenient nutriment; and from this the nature of the wing is nourished, by which the soul is enabled to ascend. And this is the law of Adrastia <note>original: Adrasteia; the Greek goddess of inescapable destiny or necessity</note>, that whatever soul attending on divinity has beheld anything of reality shall be free from damage, until another period takes place: and that if she is always able to accomplish this, she shall be perpetually free from the incursions of evil. 

But if, through an inability to accomplish this end, she has not perceived reality, and from some misfortune—being filled with oblivion and depravity—she becomes heavy and drowsy, breaks her wings, and falls again to the earth <note>The general cause of the soul's descent is her neglecting, as it were, the universal form of the world, diligently contemplating a certain portion of it only, and ardently desiring a partial mode of subsistence; imagination and her vegetable power strongly alluring her to such a condition of being.</note>, then this law prevents her in her first generation from <note>The text continues on the next page regarding the soul's incarnation.</note>

The law of destiny prevents the soul from being implanted in some brutal nature <note>original: "brute nature," referring to an animal body</note> during its first descent. Instead, it commands the <term>soul</term> which has seen the most of truth to inhabit the body of a <term>philosopher</term>, or of one who desires beauty; of a <term>musician</term>, or of one devoted to love $^1$. 

But it orders the <term>soul</term> whose perceptions rank in the second class to descend into a legitimate king, or a man dedicated to empire and war. It distributes a <term>soul</term> of the third order into the governor of a republic, or the ruler of a family, or the master of a trade. And again, it distributes a <term>soul</term> of the fourth rank into one engaged in gymnastic exercise, or in procuring remedies and taking care of the body. <term>Souls</term> of the fifth order it distributes into <term>prophets</term> and <term>mystics</term>. In the sixth, it makes a distribution into a poetic life. In the seventh, into a <term>geometrician</term> or <term>artificer</term> <note>original: "artificer," meaning a skilled craftsman or artisan</note>. In the eighth, into a <term>sophist</term> <note>original: "sophist," here meaning a professional teacher of rhetoric who prioritizes persuasion over truth</note> or a popular character. And in the ninth, into a <term>tyrant</term>. 

In all these cases, he who passes his life justly will afterwards obtain a better condition of being; but he who acts unjustly will pass into a worse state of existence. For no <term>soul</term> will return to its original condition until the expiration of ten thousand years $^2$, since it will not recover the use of its wings before this period—unless it is the <term>soul</term> of one who has practiced philosophy sincerely, or who, alongside philosophy, has...

---

$^1$ As there are principally nine <term>celestial souls</term>—namely, the <term>soul</term> of the world and the <term>souls</term> of the eight celestial spheres to which our <term>souls</term> are at different times assigned—souls receive nine different characters during their descent. The <term>philosophic genius</term> holds the first rank because it is naturally adapted to the investigation of everything human and divine. Since such a genius is studious of wisdom and truth, and the highest beauty exists within these, it is very appropriate that this rank includes the pursuit of beauty. We receive the image of beauty through sight and hearing; therefore, <term>Plato</term> connects the musician and the lover with this character: the former because of audible beauty, and the latter because of visible beauty. The next character is that of a king, who indeed provides a universal <term>providence</term> <note>original: "providence," meaning protective care or foresight</note> toward mankind, but whose contemplations are not as vast as those of the philosopher. The protective energies of those who follow are even more limited. When he places <term>prophets</term> and <term>mystics</term> in the fifth order, we must not suppose he means divine ones, but rather mercenary and common <term>prophets</term> who do not work through <term>science</term> and <term>art</term>, but through habit and chance.

---

$^2$ The numbers three and ten are called "perfect" because three is the first complete number <note>having a beginning, middle, and end</note> and ten is, in a sense, the sum of all numbers, as the following series is merely a repetition of the numbers ten contains. Since 10 multiplied by itself produces 100 (a plane number), and this multiplied by 10 produces 1,000 (a solid number), and since 1,000 multiplied by 3 forms 3,000, and 1,000 by 10 forms 10,000, <term>Plato</term> uses these numbers as symbols for the <term>purgation</term> <note>original: "purgation," the process of cleansing or purifying</note> of the <term>soul</term> and its restoration to its proper perfection and happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>. I say "as symbols," for we must not suppose this happens in exactly that many years, but rather that the <term>soul</term>'s restoration takes place in a complete and perfect manner.

loved beautiful forms. These, indeed, in the third period of a thousand years—if they have thrice chosen this mode of life in succession and have thus restored their wings to their natural vigor—shall, in the three-thousandth year, fly away to their original home. But other souls, having arrived at the end of their first life, shall be judged. And of those who are judged, some, proceeding to a subterranean place of judgment, shall there endure the punishments they have deserved. But others, in consequence of a favorable judgment, being elevated into a certain celestial place, shall pass their time in a manner suited to the life they lived in human form. 

And in the thousandth year, both kinds of those who have been judged, returning to the lot and selection of a second life, shall each receive a life agreeable to his desire. Here also the human soul shall pass into the life of a beast <gloss>1</gloss>, and from that of a beast again into a man, if it was first the soul of a man. For the soul which has never perceived the truth cannot pass into the human form. Indeed, it is necessary to understand man—defined according to his species—as a being who proceeds from the information of many senses to a perception gathered into one by the power of reasoning. 

But this is a recollection of what our soul formerly saw when in the company of the divine, when she was in a perfect state of being; it is when she looked down upon what we now consider to be realities and was raised upward to the contemplation of that which is truly real. On this account, the intellectual power <note>original: "dianoëtic power"; the capacity for discursive reasoning and logical thought</note> of the philosopher alone is justly winged. For the philosopher's memory perpetually clings as much as possible to those divine things, by attending to which even a God becomes divine. 

He who properly uses meditations of this kind, being always initiated into perfect mysteries, alone acquires true perfection. Such a person, being separated from human studies and pursuits and clinging to that which is divine, is accused by the common people of being insane; meanwhile, because he is filled with divine inspiration <note>original: "enthusiasm," from the Greek *enthousiasmos*, meaning "possessed by a god"</note>, his true state is hidden from the multitude. This entire discourse, therefore, which concerns the fourth kind of divine madness <gloss>2</gloss>, explains the means by which anyone, upon perceiving a portion—

But since he cannot accomplish this according to his wish, like a bird looking on high and despising inferior concerns, he is accused of being insane. This enthusiasm <gloss>¹ This person, moved by this enthusiasm, possesses that purification which the Platonic philosophers call *telestic* <note>pertaining to the sacred mysteries or rites of initiation</note>, because it is obtained by the exercise of mystic rites and gives perfection to the soul.</gloss>, therefore, is of all enthusiasms the best, and is composed of the best elements, both for the one who possesses it and the one who shares in it. He who is under the influence of this mania <note>divine madness or inspiration</note> when he loves beautiful objects is called a *lover*. 

For, as we have observed before, the soul of every man has by its nature perceived realities, or it could not have entered into the human form. But to recollect superior natures from objects of sense is not easy for all men; neither for those who were only engaged for a short time in the contemplation of those divine objects, nor for those who, in descending to this world, have been unfortunate. It is also difficult for those who, turning to injustice through certain associations, have become forgetful of the sacred mysteries which they once beheld. And hence but a few remain whose memory is sufficient for this exalted purpose. 

But these few, when they behold any likeness of heavenly <note>original: "supernal"</note> forms, are astonished and, as it were, carried away <note>original: "rapt"</note> beyond themselves. At the same time, they are ignorant of what this passion may be, because they do not possess a clear enough perception. Indeed, we behold no splendor in the earthly likenesses of justice, temperance, and whatever else is precious to the soul. Only a very few are able—and even for them it is difficult—to perceive through these dark instruments <note>the physical senses</note> and images the true nature <note>original: "genus"</note> of that which is represented.

...in conjunction with some other God; at the same time being initiated $^1$ in those mysteries which it is lawful to call the most blessed of all mysteries $^2$.

<meta>The catchword "And" indicates the start of the next section in the original text.</meta>

The souls are equal in number to the stars; that is, as we have observed in the Introduction to that dialogue, they are equal according to analogy, and not when considered as individual units <note>original: "monadically considered"</note>. Now, therefore, in conformity to what is asserted there, he says, "we together with Jupiter," as each soul recognizes its own specific God. For this is the happiness of the human soul: to revolve in conjunction with its proper deities, since it is not possible to pass beyond the Gods.

$^1$ The word <term>telete</term> <note>original: τελετη</note> or *initiation*, says Hermeas, was so named from *rendering the soul perfect* <note>original: παρα το τελεαν ψυχην αποτελειν</note>. The soul, therefore, was once perfect. But here in the material world it is divided and is not able to act <note>original: "energize"</note> wholly by itself. But it is necessary to know, says Hermeas, that *telete*, *muesis*, and *epopteia* <note>original: τελετη, μυησις and εποπτεια</note> differ from each other. *Telete*, therefore, is analogous to the preparation for purifications. But *muesis*, which is so called from "closing the eyes," is more divine. For to close the eyes in *initiation* means to no longer receive those divine mysteries through the senses, but with the pure soul itself. And *epopteia* is to be established in, and become a spectator of, the mysteries. See more on this interesting subject in my *Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries*.

$^2$ There is nothing from antiquity more celebrated than the mysteries, and especially the Eleusinian, though the leading details of this majestic institution are perfectly unknown to moderns, as I have shown in my *Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries*. One circumstance in particular of the highest importance has been grossly misrepresented by that most arrogant critic <note>original: "consummate sophist"</note> Dr. Warburton, in his *Divine Legation of Moses*. The circumstance I allude to belongs to that part of the mysteries called <term>epopteia</term> <note>original: εποπτεια</note>, or *inspection*. For here the Gods themselves became actually visible in splendid images to the eyes of the "epoptæ," or initiated inspectors. 

And this, in the first place, is evident from the following passage of Proclus, in a manuscript commentary on the first *Alcibiades*: "In the most holy of the mysteries, before the God appears, the impulses of certain terrestrial spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> become visible, alluring the initiated from undefiled goods toward matter" <note>original: Εν ταις ἁγιωταταις των τελετων, προ της θεου παρουσιας δαιμονων χθονιων τινων εκβολαι προφαινονται, και απο των αχραντων αγαθων εις την ὑλην προκαλουμεναι.</note>. And that by "the most holy of mysteries" he means the Eleusinian is evident from his sixth book *On the Theology of Plato*, page 371, where he expressly calls them by this name. 

He speaks even more clearly in his *Commentary on Plato’s Republic*, page 380: "In all initiations and mysteries, the Gods exhibit many forms of themselves and appear in a variety of shapes. And sometimes, indeed, a formless light <note>original: "unfigured light"</note> of themselves is held forth to the view; sometimes this light is shaped into a human form, and sometimes it proceeds into a different shape" <note>original: Εν απασι ταις τελεταις και τοις μυστηριοις, οἱ θεοι πολλας μεν ἑαυτων προτεινουσι μορφας πολλα δε σχηματα εξαλλαττοντες φαινονται· και τοτε μεν ατυπωτον αυτων προβεβληται φως, τοτε δε εις ανθρωπειον μορφην εσχηματισμενον, τοτε δε εις αλλοιον τυπον προεληλυθως.</note>. 

And we are informed by Psellus in a manuscript *On Spirits* <note>original: "Dæmons"</note> that this summoning of divine natures formed one part of the priestly office; though, says he, those who now preside over the mysteries are ignorant of the chant necessary for the summoning <note>original: Αλλ᾿ οἱ γε νυν της τελετης προεξαρχον, την μεν της κλησεως ουκ ισασιν επῳδην.</note>. This doctrine, too, of divine appearances in the mysteries is clearly confirmed by Plotinus, *Ennead* 1, book 6, page 55, and *Ennead* 9, book...

# THE PHAEDRUS

And these divine mysteries <note>original: "orgies," used here in the classical sense of "sacred rites"</note> were celebrated by us while we were perfect and free from those evils which awaited us in a succeeding period of time. We likewise were initiated in, and became spectators of, entire $^1$, simple, quietly stable $^2$, and blessed visions, resident in a pure $^3$ light; being ourselves pure, and liberated from this surrounding vestment, which we call the body, and to which we are now bound, like an oyster to its shell.

With these speculations, therefore, we should gratify our memory; for the sake of which, and through a desire of those realities which we once beheld, I have given such an extent to my discourse. But beauty, as we have said, shone upon us during our progressions with the Gods; but on our arrival here we possessed the power of perceiving it, shining most clearly <note>original: "perspicuously"</note>, through the clearest of our senses. For sight $^4$ is the most acute of all our bodily senses; though even through this, wisdom cannot be perceived. If indeed it could, what vehement love would it excite, by presenting to the eye some clear image of itself! And the same may be

---

<margin>Book 9, page 770. From all this we may collect how egregiously Dr. Warburton was mistaken when, in page 231 of his *Divine Legation*, he asserts that the light beheld in the mysteries was nothing more than an illuminated image which the priest had purified. "This," says he, "which was all over illuminated, and which the priest had thoroughly purified, was an image <note>original: αγαλμα (agalma)</note>." But, indeed, his whole account of this divine institution is absurd, false, and ridiculous in the extreme. I only add, that the preceding observations plainly show to what Plato alludes in this part of the dialogue, by his *simple and blessed visions resident in a pure light*, and that we can no longer wonder why the initiated are reported to have been called *happy*.</margin>

$^1$ Namely, perfect.
$^2$ By this Plato indicates the firm and permanent nature of intelligible realities <note>original: "intelligibles," referring to things known by the intellect rather than the senses</note>.
$^3$ He says this because the light here on earth is not pure, being mingled with the air.
$^4$ Plato now wishes to speak concerning the amatory character <note>the nature of a lover</note>, and to show how it is led back from sensible beauty <note>beauty perceived by the senses</note> to intelligible beauty. What he says, therefore, is this—that intelligible beauty shines forth in an intelligible essence, together with the spectacles which are there, and that from this beauty, sensible beauty is unfolded into light. For, as the light proceeding from the sun illuminates the whole sensible world, so beauty, originating from the realm of the intellect, pervades through the regions of sense. But he calls the sight the clearest of all the senses, because it is more acute than the rest. Hence, it is considered as analogous to fire by those who compare the senses to the elements. But its superior acuteness is evident from this, that when sound and that which is visible are produced together, as in the instance of thunder and lightning, we first see the lightning, and some time after the sound reaches our hearing. The reason of this is evident: for sight sees without time, or in an instant; but the other senses require time. Sight also is analogous to the intellect: for as the intellect sees all things indivisibly, so likewise does sight. For it directly sees the interval which reaches from here as far as to the heavens.

<summary>Socrates describes the soul's original state of purity and its vision of divine beauty before being "imprisoned" in the body. The commentary argues that sight is the highest sense because it most closely mimics the instantaneous perception of the intellect.</summary>

# THE PHAEDRUS

The same may be said of everything else which is the object of love. But now, beauty alone is granted the privilege of being the most visible and lovely of all things. Therefore, a person who has not recently descended to this world from the divine realm, or whose character has become corrupt, will not be quickly moved from this world to a vision of Beauty itself <note>The "Beautiful itself" refers to the Platonic Form of Beauty—the perfect, eternal essence of beauty that exists beyond the physical world.</note> by merely looking at physical objects that share the same name. Consequently, he does not feel reverence when he sees it; instead, surrendering himself to mere pleasure, he attempts to go about and procreate like a four-legged animal. By engaging in harmful behavior with others, he is neither afraid nor ashamed of pursuing pleasure that is contrary to nature.

But he who has been recently initiated into the mysteries—who was formerly a spectator of many blessed visions—when he beholds a god-like face that elegantly imitates beauty, or some incorporeal form, he is at first struck with horror <note>1</note> and feels something of that terror that once overcame him. However, upon further looking, he venerates it as a God. If he did not fear being thought completely insane, he would offer sacrifice to his beloved <note>2</note> as if to a holy statue or a God. 

As a result of looking at this beautiful object, he experiences a change in his feelings: a shivering and an unusual heat <note>3</note>, similar to the physical reaction produced by horror. For, receiving the flow of beauty through his eyes, he becomes warm, and this moisture waters the growth of his wings. Once heated, the parts of the soul where the feathers sprout begin to melt—parts which were previously hardened and compressed, preventing the vigorous growth of his plumage. But as this flow of nourishment...

---

<note>1 It is well observed by Hermeas <note>Hermeas was a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Phaedrus.</note> that it is necessary to understand what is said here in a vital and intellectual sense. Just as we are seized with astonishment when seeing certain physical things, we are similarly affected by the vision of the Gods. This is not the kind of terror that comes from seeing an approaching enemy, but a "better" kind of terror caused by the overwhelming abundance of the Gods. It is necessary, therefore, for the human soul to submit itself to the Gods and to the non-physical forms that surpass our power. The soul should be seized with a terror greater than human fear at the sight of them—not because they are cruel, dreadful, or hostile (for those are qualities of material and earthly things), but because they are divine. Plato, therefore, uses the word *horror* to mean the soul's awakening as it moves from physical objects to intellectual realities.</note>

<note>2 That is, he would sacrifice to "Intelligible Beauty" <note>The ultimate, non-physical source of all beauty.</note>, of which physical beauty is merely a representation, likeness, and image. taking place, the quill of the wing swells and endeavors to burst forth through the whole form of the soul; for the whole soul was formerly winged. Therefore, in this state, the entire soul becomes feverish and leaps upward. Just as infants are tormented by the friction and pain of their gums during the growth of their teeth, the soul is affected in the same way regarding the sprouting of its wings; it becomes subject to immoderate heat, irritation, and torment. 

When, therefore, the soul beholds the beauty of some human form, it imbibes the particles which flow from that beauty—which is why this feeling is called "desire" <note>original: "desire" (himeros), which Plato etymologically links to "flowing in" (ienai meros)</note>. The soul becomes watered and heated, ceases to be in pain, and rejoices. But when it is separated from this vision of beauty and becomes dry through heat, the orifices of the passages through which the feathers endeavored to sprout are closed, blocking the growth of the wing. These wings, being shut in together with desire and leaping about like a pulsating heart, strike against the pathways of their progression. 

Hence, the whole soul, being pierced on all sides, is agitated with fury and tormented; yet, through the memory of the beautiful, it again exults with delight. From the mixture of both these feelings, it is grievously tormented by the novelty of the passion and becomes confused and raging. While it is in this state of fury, it can neither sleep by night nor stay still anywhere by day; instead, it runs about agitated by desire wherever there is any probability of seeing the beautiful object. 

But upon beholding the beloved beautiful object and drawing in desire as if through a channel, the soul now frees what was previously enclosed. By this means, enjoying the benefit of "breathing" <note>Plato uses the metaphor of respiration to describe the relief of the soul's pressure</note>, it is liberated from its stings and birth-pangs. For the moment, therefore, it reaps the advantage of this most delicious pleasure. The soul is so charmed by this pleasure that it would never voluntarily depart from its allurements, nor does it value anything as much as this beloved beauty. It consigns its parents, brothers, and friends to oblivion. Furthermore, it considers the loss of its possessions through negligence to be of no consequence and perfectly despises those legal institutions and social decencies in which it formerly took pride. It is always prepared for every kind of servitude and subjection, provided it may be near to the object of its desire. For, besides reverencing that which possesses beauty, the soul finds that this beauty alone is the physician for its greatest diseases.

# THE PHAEDRUS

The present discourse is called by men "Love" <note>original: *Eros*</note>; but if you should hear how it is named by the Gods, you would probably laugh because of your youth. However, I think that certain followers of Homer <note>original: "Homerics"</note> assert, based on some hidden <note>original: "recondite"</note> verses, that there are two poems upon Love. One of these describes him as perfectly injurious and not very refined; but they celebrate him as follows:

->By men Love's *flying* called; but, forced to fly,<-
->He's named the *winged*, by the powers on high.<-

In these verses, it is partly lawful to believe, and partly not. This, however, is the cause and the passion of lovers. When anyone, therefore, who is an attendant of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus; here referring to souls who followed the king of the gods in the celestial procession.</note> is taken captive by love, such a person is able to bear the burden of this winged God with greater firmness. But those who are subservient to Mars <note>The Roman name for Ares; referring to souls characterized by a more spirited or aggressive nature.</note>, and revolve in conjunction with that deity, are different. When they are ensnared by love and think they are in any respect treated unjustly by their beloved, they are easily incited to slaughter, and are ready to destroy both themselves and the objects of their affection. And thus, everyone honors the God around whom he harmoniously revolves, and imitates that God's life as much as possible.

***

<note>Plato, says Hermeas, wishes to explain the origin of the name of Love—specifically, the passion generated in us by beauty. This passion is called by men *Love* <note>original: *Eros*</note> from the idea of "flowing inward" <note>original: *esros*</note>, but by the Gods it is called "winged" because it gives wings to the soul. Plato calls those who sing the verses of Homer "Homerics." He also calls the verses "hidden" to indicate the concealed, divine, and secret nature of the statement.</note>

<note>For all the gifts of Jupiter, says Hermeas, are firm, stable, and always exist in the same manner.</note>

<note>For Mars is the source of division and motion. But it is necessary to know this as a universal rule, says Hermeas: whatever is granted by any divinity is received according to the specific capability <note>original: "aptitude"</note> of the receiver. Thus, for instance, Venus bestows friendship and union; but since the light granted by the Goddess is mingled with physical matter, the receiver often corrupts her gift. Friendship then becomes adultery because it is received in a flawed way. Things are granted in one way by the Gods, but are received in another way by those who participate in them. Similarly, when different substances receive the sun's heat, one is melted like wax and another is hardened like clay; each receives what is given according to its own nature, even though the solar light itself remains the same. 

Hermeas adds that it may also be said, speaking more theoretically, that the "slaughter" attributed here to Mars signifies a tearing away from physical matter. This happens by rapidly turning away from the material world and no longer acting physically, but intellectually. For "slaughter," when applied to the Gods, can be said to be a turning away from lower things, just as slaughter in our world signifies the loss of the present life.</note>

In this manner, he lives through his first generation here on earth, associating with and conducting himself toward his beloved and others. Every person, therefore, chooses a love of beauty according to his own fashion. As if he considered his beloved to be a God for himself, he fashions and adorns that person like a statue, making them the object of his adoration and sacrifice. 

Those who are followers of Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, associated here with philosophy and leadership.</note> seek a soul belonging to this God as the object of their affection. Consequently, they consider whether the beloved is naturally philosophical and suited for command. When they find a beloved with such dispositions, they endeavor by all possible means to make him completely so. If they have not already begun to obtain what they desire, they strive anxiously for its possession through the incitements of love. They learn the means by which it may be acquired and investigate for themselves how to discover the nature of their own specific deity. They eventually find it by being compelled to look with intense focus toward their presiding God. 

When they become connected with that God through memory and are moved by a divine influence, they receive from him manners and pursuits, as far as it is possible for a human to participate in divinity. Because they consider the object of their love to be the cause of all this, their love becomes even more intense. If they draw their inspiration <note>original: "afflatus," meaning a divine breath or inspiration.</note> from Jupiter, then, like the female priests of Bacchus <note>The Maenads or Bacchantes, known for their religious ecstasy.</note>, they pour their enthusiasm into the soul of their beloved. By this means, they become as similar as possible to their ruling God. 

However, those who follow Juno <margin>Of the two divinities, Juno and Apollo, mentioned here, Hermeas says that the former converts all things through imperial power, and the latter leads all things to harmony and union.</margin> seek after a royal soul. When they have discovered such a person, they act toward them in every respect like the attendants of Jupiter. Similarly, the followers of Apollo, and of each of the other Gods, imitate their specific deities and seek a beloved who is naturally like themselves. Once they have found such a person, they use imitation, persuasion, and refined manners to lead their beloved toward the pursuits and the ideal of their particular God. They do not do this by employing envy or ungenerous malice toward the objects of their affection, but by striving to lead them to a perfect likeness of the God whom they particularly worship.

# THE PHÆDRUS

The willing desire and goal of true lovers—if they achieve what they pursue—is exactly as I have described. Thus, they become illustrious and blessed through the madness of love toward the beloved, once that beloved object is finally won.

But everyone who is enticed is captured in the following way. At the beginning of this fable <note>Socrates refers to his earlier allegory of the soul as a winged chariot.</note>, we assigned a triple division to every soul; we established two specific types belonging to the form of the horses, and we considered the charioteer as the third type. Let this division remain the same for us now. We said that one of the horses was good and the other was not. However, we have not yet explained the virtue of the good horse or the vice of the bad one; it is therefore appropriate that we should explain it now. The good horse, therefore, exists in a more beautiful...

***

<note>1</note> Socrates, having spoken concerning that love which exists according to righteousness, and also concerning that which exists according to a deviation from righteousness—and having, therefore, discussed the extremes—now wishes to speak about the middle ground: namely, temperate and intemperate love. 

As he speaks of the soul considered as associating with the body, he very properly gives it different horses. For, in proportion as the soul descends into the world of "generation" <note>The physical world of birth, change, and death.</note> and approaches these stormy realms, she receives a greater number of "garments" <note>A Neoplatonic term for the layers of the soul or subtle bodies acquired during its descent.</note>. Hence, he discourses concerning other horses: those that have a relationship to this physical body and share in its vital passions. 

For while the soul lives in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, beyond the physical.</note>, she has other horses characterized by *sameness* and *difference*. This is evident, for ancient theology gives horses even to the Gods themselves. Now, however, he considers different horses—namely, anger and desire—and calls his discourse concerning them a *fable*. He did not do this before when speaking of the horses of divine beings, or of the human soul itself when liberated from this earthly body. 

The reason for this, as Hermeas <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Phædrus.</note> beautifully observes, is because the soul is in this body as if in a *fiction*. For the entire visible body with which we are surrounded, and the whole visible order of things, is similar to a *fable*. Very properly, therefore, does Socrates—wishing to speak concerning the soul's relationship, proximity, or alliance to this body—call his discourse a fable. But he did not call what he said prior to this a fable, because the soul, while *living on high* with the Gods, had different horses. 

He also here calls the rational soul <term>hēniochikos</term> <note>original: ηνιοχικος</note>, meaning *of the nature of a charioteer*, and not <term>hēniochos</term> <note>original: ηνιοχος</note>, *a charioteer*, as he did previously. This signifies that the rational soul in the present body only imitates a charioteer. In speaking of the horses, too, he uses the word <term>hippomorpha</term> <note>original: ιππομορφα</note>, or *having the form of horses*, and not <term>hippoi</term> <note>original: ιπποι</note>, *horses*, as before. For the energies of the soul in conjunction with the body are not the same as when she is united with pure intellectual realities.

<note>2</note> The divine Plato, says Hermeas, distributes the parts of the soul into different parts of the body. Hence, considering intellect and the reasoning power as analogous to the ruler of a city, he establishes them in the brain; for the brain is spherical, and man is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>A "little world" that reflects the structure of the entire universe.</note>. He makes the brain, therefore, analogous to the heavens. In the next place, since anger is naturally more noble...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical description of the two horses of the soul from Plato's Phædrus, focusing on the physical and moral characteristics of the "noble" horse (representing spirit or anger) versus the "ignoble" horse (representing desire).</meta>

### THE PHÆDRUS.

<page-num>335</page-num>

The horse in a beautiful condition is upright and well-proportioned; it has a lofty neck, a somewhat aquiline <note>original: "hooked" or eagle-like</note> nose, a white color, and black eyes. It is likewise a lover of honor¹, along with temperance and modesty. It is the companion of true opinion; it does not need to be whipped and is governed only by verbal encouragement and reason. But the bad horse is crooked², multicolored <note>original: "various"</note>, rash in its movements, and stiff-necked.

***

<note>The following section provides a commentary on the symbolism used by Plato.</note>

The spirited part of the soul is more noble than *desire*. It is analogous to those in a city who fight for its defense and suppress whatever is disorderly and tumultuous; Plato calls these the *auxiliaries* <note>The warrior class in Plato's Republic</note>. Since anger also reproves and opposes desire, he places it in the heart so that it may be in the entrance-hall of reason, separated from the brain only by the interval of the neck. 

But the *desiderative* part <note>term: the part of the soul driven by physical appetite and desire</note>, being irrational and similar to the *mercenary* class and the common masses in a city, he places in the liver, like an ass at a manger. Anger, therefore, is more noble than desire because it is closer to reason; hence it has a better station, for it is arranged in a superior region of the body. 

He says, first, concerning anger (the good horse), that it is more beautiful and is shaped by forms—sometimes from the body, and sometimes from the character and the soul. He calls it *straight* because it follows the rules of reason; *well-articulated* (that is, of a distinct and pure nature, not mixed); and having its *neck lofty* (meaning it is always reaching upward and despising lower conditions). He also says it has an *aquiline nose*, indicating its royal nature; for a hooked or aquiline nose, says Hermeas <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Phædrus</note>, is always attributed by Plato to that which is royal and noble, as the aquiline shape is more elegant than a flat nose. He adds that it is *white* to the sight, indicating it is most splendid and shining with beauty. Its eyes are *black*, meaning they investigate profound things and wish to observe hidden and spiritual <note>original: "intelligible"</note> realities; for he refers to the unapparent as "black."

***

¹ Having described the physical advantages of the better horse, Plato now lists its spiritual qualities. Honor is the greatest of goods, as he says in the *Laws*; but nothing evil is truly honorable. For this reason, we also honor Divinity. The good horse, therefore, is a lover of honor; that is, it aspires after ideal form and the Good. But it also loves honor in conjunction with temperance; it possesses these virtues of the soul, performs its own proper duties, and refuses to be filled with the opposite vices. It is governed only by reason and encouragement because it is close to reason and aligns all the measures of its life with reason's standards.

² Plato here speaks concerning the worse of the two horses and mimics its confused nature. He no longer speaks first of the body and then of the soul, but mixes the order. In contrast to the noble horse, he says this one is *crooked*, which is characteristic of desire, for desire is like a wild beast. It is *various* (multicolored), an epithet suited to desire, which takes many forms and loves the crowd. It is *rash in its motions*, being driven by random impulses. He adds that it is *stiff*, indicating its resistant nature; *short-necked*, as it is lowly, living only for appetite and not aspiring to honor; *flat-nosed*, meaning it is vulgar, groveling, and not royal; of a *black color*, meaning it is dark and not clear or shining like the other; and *having gray eyes*, as it only has a superficial brightness and possesses only basic thoughts.

The second horse is short-necked, flat-nosed, black in color, and has gray eyes full of blood. He is the companion of injustice and arrogance; his ears are hairy and deaf, and he is hardly obedient to the whip or the spur. <gloss>The description of the horse's eyes being "full of blood" means he is closely tied to the world of physical generation and birth. He is the "companion of injury and arrogance" because his traits are the exact opposite of the first horse, who represents temperance and modesty. His "hairy and deaf ears" signify his disobedience and his tendency to hear without paying attention. Finally, he is "scarcely obedient to the whip and the spur" because he cannot be improved by simple encouragement or correction.</gloss>

When the charioteer <note>The charioteer represents the Reason or Intellect of the soul.</note> beholds the beloved's eye, it inflames the entire soul through the senses, filling it with the stings of desire and longing. At that moment, the horse that is obedient to the charioteer—as it always is—checks its own movements out of shame and restrains itself from leaping upon the beloved. 

However, the other horse cannot be held back by the charioteer’s spur or whip. He hurries forward violently, leaping and jumping, and forces both the charioteer and his fellow horse to rush toward the pleasures of sex. At first, both the charioteer and the good horse resist this violence, feeling indignant at being forced into such dreadful and lawless behavior. But eventually, when there seems to be no end to this affliction and they are driven by sheer force, they give in. They consent to do what they are told and allow themselves to be led toward the sight of the beloved’s radiant face.

When the charioteer sees this vision, his memory returns to the true nature of Beauty. He perceives Beauty once again, firmly established alongside Temperance in a pure and holy seat. <note>original: "seat" refers to the intelligible region—the realm of true forms—because the beauties found here on earth are not genuinely beautiful.</note> 

Because of this vision, the charioteer is terrified. Filled with awe, he falls backward, and is forced to pull back the reins with such intensity that both horses are thrown back onto their haunches. The good horse does this willingly, offering no resistance; but the rebellious horse resists with arrogant opposition, being extremely unwilling to comply. When they have moved further away, the good horse is so overcome by shame and astonishment that he drenches the entire soul with sweat. But the rebellious horse, once he is free from the pain of the bridle and the fall, can hardly catch his breath. Full of anger, he begins to insult the charioteer and his partner, accusing them of cowardice and of deserting their duty and...

Hence it sometimes happens that the soul of a lover follows its beloved with reverence and fear, and that the lover pays the beloved every kind of observance and attention as if he were equal to a God. This is not done with any hypocrisy, but because he is truly affected in this way. So, when the beloved happens to be naturally a friend, his friendship merges into one with that of his devoted lover.

If, therefore, in some former period of time, the youth has been deceived by his associates or by others asserting that it was shameful to be familiar with a lover, and has on this account rejected him; yet advancing age and the natural needs of life lead him to the companionship of love. For it was never decreed by fate either that the evil should be a friend to the evil, or that the good should not be a friend to the good. When, therefore, the youth admits his lover to an intimate familiarity, the benevolence of the lover astonishes the beloved. He perceives that all other friends and associates show no degree of friendship that can be compared with that of a friend who is divinely inspired. 

But when the lover continues to act in this manner for a long space of time, living with his beloved in close familiarity—frequently touching him in gymnastics and other social gatherings—then the fountain of that <term>effluxion</term> <note>original: "effluxion"; a flowing out or discharge of divine energy or beauty</note> which Jupiter, when enamored with <term>Ganymedes</term> <note>In Greek mythology, a beautiful Trojan prince carried off by Zeus (Jupiter) to serve as cupbearer to the gods</note>, denominated *desire*, begins streaming abundantly...

towards the lover, is partly infused into him, and partly through its exuberance flows forth externally. And as air, or a certain echo, when received by smooth and solid bodies, is again impelled to the place from which it proceeded; so this effluxion <note>original: "effluxion"; a flowing out or discharge</note> of beauty, flowing back again to the beautiful person through the eyes, as it is naturally adapted to penetrate into the soul and stimulate the avenues of the wings, now irrigates and excites them to shoot forth their feathers, and fills the soul of the beloved with love. 

Hence he loves, but is doubtful concerning what he loves; and neither knows what he suffers, nor is able to relate it. But just like an eye infected with the vision of another eye which is diseased, he is unable to assign the cause of his malady, and is ignorant that he beholds himself in his lover, as in a mirror. Hence, when his lover is present, he, like him, ceases to be in pain; but, when he is absent, he desires in the same manner as he is desired, possessing, instead of love, nothing more than an image of love <note>original: "anteros" or counter-love</note>; and he names it, and thinks that it is not love, but friendship. He desires, therefore, in a manner similar to his lover, though more feebly, to see, to touch, to kiss, to sit together; and, as it is reasonable to suppose, he performs all this afterwards with the greatest speed. 

Hence, in their most intimate associations, the intemperate horse <note>In Plato's allegory, the soul is a chariot pulled by two horses: one noble (reason/spirit) and one rebellious (appetite/lust).</note> of the lover calls on the charioteer, and tells him that he ought to be gratified with a small degree of pleasure as the reward of such mighty labors. But the same horse of the beloved has, indeed, nothing to say; but, bursting with tension and doubt, it embraces the lover, full of vehement benevolence towards him, and is prepared to comply in every respect with the desires of the lover. But the noble horse, together with the charioteer, resists this familiarity through reason and shame. 

If, therefore, the better parts of the reasoning power <note>original: "dianoëtic power"; the capacity for discursive or logical thought</note> obtaining the victory lead the lovers to an orderly and philosophic mode of conduct, then they pass through the present life with happiness and concord, subduing themselves, and adorned with modest manners; the vicious part of the soul being in subjection, and the virtuous part free. But, arriving at the end of the present life, they become winged and light, in consequence of being victors in one of the truly Olympic contests <margin>These contests are called Olympic, not from the mountain Olympus, but from Olympus, meaning heaven. But he who philosophizes truly becomes the victor in three such contests.</margin>; a greater good than which, neither human wisdom nor divine madness can confer upon man.

<summary>Socrates describes how the beloved catches the "infection" of love from the lover like a reflection in a mirror, leading to a struggle between the soul's base desires and its rational pursuit of a philosophical life.</summary>

# THE PHAEDRUS

human temperance, nor divine fury, can extend to man. But if they lead a more arrogant and unphilosophic life, though one still united with ambition, their intemperate horse <note>In Plato’s allegory, the "intemperate horse" represents the soul's irrational desires and appetites.</note> will perhaps lead their unguarded souls into intoxication or other lazy habits. This causes them to embrace those delights which the common people consider the most blessed of all pleasures, and keeps them constantly striving to satisfy their desires. They will, therefore, indulge in these delights, though only rarely, because the whole of their <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic"; referring to the capacity for discursive reason or logical thought.</note> nature does not consent to such enjoyments. 

These people will also live in friendship with each other, just like the philosophical lovers, through the outward flow of love, but with less intensity. They believe they should give and receive the greatest confidence from one another—a bond they feel would be unlawful to break, lest they become enemies instead of friends. When they eventually depart from their current bodies, they will not yet have grown wings, but they will be stirred to begin growing them; thus, they carry with them a significant reward for their "amatory fury" <note>The inspired state of being in love.</note>. For the law forbids those who have begun the celestial journey to enter into darkness or the subterranean path. Instead, because they led a bright and splendid life, the law decrees they shall be happy with each other during their travels; and when they eventually regain their wings, they shall do so together because of their love. 

Such, O young man, are the many divine benefits which the friendship of a lover will bring you. But the intimacy of a man who lacks this divine love—being mixed only with human restraint and dealing only in mortal, stingy concerns—will instead breed a sense of "illiberality" <note>A narrow-minded or ungenerous spirit.</note> in the soul of his companion, even though the common people mistake this for virtue. This will cause that soul to wander for nine thousand years, rolling aimlessly upon and under the earth.

***

In the first place, he subjects all the inferior powers of his soul to the intellect; in the second place, he obtains wisdom combined with divine fury; and in the third place, recovering his wings, he flies away to his kindred star. But if someone, through a naturally generous disposition, is inclined toward love but has not been philosophically or morally educated from the beginning, he may give in to physical pleasures after being captured by love. Because of this lapse, such a person cannot fully recover his wings; yet, because of the wonderful <term>anagogic</term> <note>original: "anagogic"; meaning "leading upward," specifically referring to the power of love to elevate the soul to spiritual heights.</note> power of love, he will be prepared to recover them eventually. Therefore, once he has cut away his lust over time and formed a virtuous friendship while retaining the sublimity of love, he will not be cast into the lowest regions of punishment after this life. Instead, he will be purified in the air until he has reached the highest degree of philosophy.

# THE PHÆDRUS

And thus, O beloved Love <note>Socrates is addressing the god Eros</note>, through the impulse of Phædrus, we have offered and extended to you a recantation, clothed in poetic figures and expressions in the most beautiful and best manner we are able to accomplish. Therefore, pardoning what we previously asserted, and gratefully <gloss>1</gloss> receiving our present discourse, continue to look kindly and favorably upon the amatory art <gloss>2</gloss> <term>amatory art: the skill or discipline of understanding love</term> which you have bestowed upon me. Do not take away or diminish this gift through avenging anger. Instead, grant that among those who are beautiful, I may be even more honored than I am at present. And if Phædrus and I have formerly said anything harsh against your divinity, grant that—by blaming Lysias as the author of that previous discourse—we may cease from all such claims in the future. Furthermore, graciously convert Lysias to the study of philosophy, like his brother Polemarchus, so that this lover of his <note>Referring to Phædrus, who was an admirer of Lysias's rhetoric</note> may no longer drift back and forth without any stability, as is currently the case, but may instead spend his life honorably in the future, dedicated to love and philosophical discussions.

**PHÆDRUS:** I join you in this prayer, Socrates, if it is indeed better that all this should happen to us. But for some time now, I have wondered at your discourse; it so far surpasses the one you delivered earlier that I am afraid Lysias himself will appear quite mediocre if he wishes to compete against another speech. In fact, just recently, a very prominent person in the government insulted him with this very label; throughout his entire accusation, he called Lysias nothing more than a "writer of speeches." Perhaps, therefore, Lysias will stop writing out of wounded pride.

**SOCRATES:** You hold a ridiculous opinion, young man, and you greatly misunderstand the intentions of your friend if you think him so extremely timid. Perhaps you actually believe that his critic spoke the truth in what he said against him?

PHAEDRUS: And indeed, very much so.

<note>1. According to Iamblichus and Hermeas, spirits <term>original: "dæmons"; here referring to intermediary spirits between gods and men</term> are signified by the grasshoppers in this fable. This is not surprising, since in the preceding part of this dialogue—which is full of allegory—something even more divine than spirits is implied by the horses of the Gods. Furthermore, the role assigned here to grasshoppers perfectly corresponds with the work that Plato, in the *Banquet*, attributes to benevolent spirits: they stand, as it were, over our heads, converse with each other, and meanwhile observe our affairs, disapproving of our evil deeds and commending the good. This is also confirmed by Hesiod in his *Works and Days*. Additionally, they receive divine gifts and deliver them to us, approach the Muses, and report our actions to the Gods. Because of this similarity, Iamblichus and Hermeas conclude with great probability that aerial spirits are represented here by grasshoppers. For just as these animals live perpetually singing and breathe in the air through this sound, so do beneficent aerial spirits live in the air by perpetually celebrating divine natures.</note>

<note>2. According to Hermeas, the interpretation of this passage by the divine Iamblichus is as follows: Socrates calls "men" those souls dwelling in the intelligible world <term>the realm of pure thought and forms, beyond the physical senses</term>. For souls, before they live a mortal life, abide on high in the intelligible realm, contemplating the Forms themselves alongside the celestial Gods. Thus, "men" existed before the Muses "had a being"—that is, before the celestial spheres and the physical world existed. The term "before" here does not signify a sequence in time, but rather a state of existence that is primary or fundamental <note>original: "prior to this apparent progression of the spheres"</note>. For the "birth" of the Muses represents their visible manifestation, proceeding from the Creator <term>original: "demiurgus"</term> into the physical world. Therefore, the Muses, the spheres, the physical world, the soul of the universe, and the individual souls of men all began their existence together. These souls, being newly born and remembering what they had seen in the intelligible realm, were reluctant to enter the cycle of physical birth. They were unwilling to eat and drink—meaning they did not wish to engage with physical opinions—because they possessed spiritual nourishment. Consequently, by "wasting away," they eventually "perished," which means they returned to the intelligible world.</note>

<note>* Namely, an unmanifested existence: for this is prior to a *manifested* existence, in the same way that every cause, simply by being a cause, is prior to its effect, even if they exist at the same time.</note>

Hence, by informing Terpsichore <note>The Muse of choral song and dance.</note> of those who reverence her in the dance^2, they render her favorable to them. ^1 He who lives according to the intellect, says Hermeas <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the Phaedrus.</note>, who is a lover of the Muses and a philosopher, desires to ascend again to the Gods. Consequently, he does not require the care of the body and of a physical life, but considers these as nothing, being desirous to be separated from them. For he meditates on death—that is, a departure from the present life—as he knows that the body molests and impedes the activities of the intellect. * First, that of the Gods; 
* Second, that of divine souls; 
* Third, the revolution of the celestial divinities—namely, of the seven planets and the fixed <note>original: "inerratic"</note> sphere—is called a dance; 
* Fourth, those who are initiated in the mysteries perform a certain dance <note>original: "Επειτα και ενταυθα οἱ τελουμενοι τοις θεοις χορειαν τινα αποτελουσιν εν τοις μυστηριοις" — "Then also here those being initiated to the gods perform a certain dance in the mysteries."</note>; 
* And finally, the entire life of a philosopher is a dance. 

Terpsichore, therefore, is the watchful guardian of all dancing. Who, then, are those who honor the goddess in the dance? Not those who dance well physically, but those who live well through the whole of their present existence, elegantly arranging their life and dancing in harmony <note>original: "symphony"</note> with the universe. Erato, says Hermeas, is named after Love <note>Greek: *Eros*.</note>, and from making the works of Love lovely, for she cooperates with Love. Calliope is named from the eye <note>original: "παρα την οπα" — "from the voice/eye"; Hermeas links her name to "beautiful voice" or "beautiful sight."</note>; and Urania presides over astronomy. Through these two goddesses, we preserve our rational part from being in subjection to our irrational nature. For, through sight surveying the order of the celestial Gods, we properly arrange our irrational part. And further still, through rhythms, philosophy, and hearing, we elegantly dispose of that part of ourselves which is disorderly and lacking in rhythm.

SOCRATES. Let us, therefore, consider what we lately spoke of: namely, in what manner anyone may both speak and write properly or improperly.

PHAEDRUS. By all means.

Is it not, therefore, necessary that he who is about to speak with propriety should possess a true <gloss>1</gloss> <term>dianoetic</term> <note>dianoetic: relating to the discursive reason or the process of thinking things through logically</note> perception of the subject of his discourse?

<note>
1 Plato here teaches how to write, and the method for writing and speaking well or ill. He makes the problem more universal and scientific after having referred the entire beginning of the discourse to the Muses and the Gods. Just as a distorted thing is judged by a rule, and that which is not straight is judged by the straight, so that which is false can only be accurately known by the truth. Hence, he says that in speaking or writing well, it is necessary that truth and a knowledge of the subject should lead the way. For he who does not know the truth of a thing speaks only by guesswork about it. 

Three things, therefore, are said to be present with those who speak or write: 
First, a knowledge of the truth. 
Second, an ability to make one thing many, which is the business of the <term>divisive method</term> <note>divisive method: the logical process of breaking a general concept down into its specific parts or species</note>. By this, we know the various meanings of the proposed subject—whether it has many meanings, whether the name applies to different things (homonymous) or the same thing (synonymous), whether it is a general category (genus) or a specific type (species), and so on. 
Third, the many must be collected into one, which is the business of the <term>analytic and definitive methods</term>. To be able to collect many things into one sentence is to provide the definition of a thing. 

Afterward, the composition and decoration of the speech must follow. These instruments of speaking and writing—namely, the nature and the essence, or the truth of a thing—ought to be known before everything else. For thus we shall know how we ought to proceed: whether through things that are true, or through things that merely resemble the truth. For he who does not know the truth, but only has an opinion about it (like those who practice popular rhetoric), will often persuade his hearers to the opposite of what he intends. 

Afterward, the philosopher relates how many benefits are derived from true rhetoric, and how many evils happen from that which is falsely named rhetoric.
</note>

<note>
2 There are three parts of rhetoric: *deliberative* <note>original: το συμβουλευτικον (to symbouleutikon)</note>, *forensic* <note>original: το δικανικον (to dikanikon)</note>, and *panegyric* <note>original: το πανηγυρικον (to panegyrikon)</note>. Regarding the goals of these three: justice is the goal of the forensic (legal); the good is the goal of the deliberative (political); and beauty (or honor) is the goal of the panegyric (ceremonial). 

In opposition, justice and injustice are the goals of the forensic; good and evil are the goals of the deliberative; and the beautiful and the base are the goals of the panegyric. A certain duality also appears in each: in forensic rhetoric, accusation and defense; in deliberative, exhortation and dissuasion; and in panegyric, praise and blame.
</note>

<summary>Socrates and Phaedrus begin to examine the requirements for effective speaking and writing, specifically whether an orator must know the actual truth of a subject or merely what is persuasive to an audience. The accompanying notes categorize the logical methods of rhetoric and its three primary branches: deliberative, forensic, and panegyric.</summary>

**SOCRATES.** The sayings of the wise, Phaedrus, are by no means to be despised, but we should rather consider the meaning of their assertions; and, consequently, we must not pass by what you have now said.

**SOCRATES.** Not yet; but consider when I should earnestly persuade you to do this by a discourse composed in praise of an ass, calling him a horse, and asserting that he is a most excellent animal, useful for domestic and military purposes, able to carry burdens, and adapted for a variety of other employments.

**PHAEDRUS.** This, indeed, would be perfectly ridiculous.

**SOCRATES.** Have we not therefore, my friend, reviled the art of speaking in a more rude <note>original: "rustic"</note> manner than is becoming? For the art itself will, perhaps, thus address us: "What madness <note>original: "delirium"</note>, O wonderful men, has invaded you? For I compel no one who is ignorant of truth to learn how to speak: but if anyone will take my advice, he will then only employ me when he has acquired the possession of truth. This, then, I assert as a thing of great consequence,

<summary>Socrates uses the humorous analogy of mistaking an ass for a horse to illustrate the danger of an orator who persuades a public ignorant of the truth to mistake evil for good. He argues that true rhetoric must be grounded in the knowledge of reality rather than mere popular opinion.</summary>

**PHAEDR.** I confess it, if our subsequent reasons prove that <term>rhetoric</term> <note>The art of effective or persuasive speaking or writing.</note> is an art. **PHAEDR.** By Jupiter, I am not perfectly acquainted with all of this. It is spoken and written about as an art mostly used in <term>judicial matters</term> and public speeches; but I have not heard that it extends any further.

**SOC.** What, have you heard of the <term>rhetorical art</term> which Nestor and Ulysses practiced at Troy, but have never heard about that of Palamedes? <note>Socrates is using the names of Homeric heroes to represent different styles of oratory.</note>

**PHAEDR.** By Jupiter, I have indeed heard about the orations of Nestor—unless you mean to suggest that Gorgias is a certain Nestor, or that Thrasymachus and Theodorus are a certain Ulysses.

**SOC.** Perhaps they may be; but let us drop any further talk about them. Instead, you inform me what litigants do in <term>judicial matters</term>: do they not contradict one another? Or shall we say they do something else?

**PHAEDR.** Nothing else.

# THE PHAEDRUS

SOCRATES: But are not their contradictions about what is *just* and *unjust*?

PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: But does not he who accomplishes this by art cause the same thing to appear to the same persons, whenever he pleases, at one time just, and at another time unjust?

PHAEDRUS: Of course.

SOCRATES: And in his oration, does he not cause the same things to appear to the city at one time good, and at another time *just* the contrary?

PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: And do we not know that the Eleatic Palamedes <note>Socrates is likely referring to Zeno of Elea, a philosopher famous for his paradoxes, whom he playfully compares to the mythical inventor Palamedes.</note> is reported to have been able by his art to cause the same things to appear to his hearers as both similar and dissimilar, one and many, and both standing still and moving?

PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: The art of contradiction, therefore, takes place not only in judicial matters and public speeches, but, as it appears, in everything which is the subject of discourse. It is a single art that enables us to make everything resemble everything else—at least among things capable of such resemblance—and to bring these resemblances to light, even when they are hidden or disguised by something else.

PHAEDRUS: What do you mean by that?

SOCRATES: My meaning will appear in the following inquiries: Does deception occur in things which differ much, or only a little, from each other?

PHAEDRUS: In things which differ only a little.

SOCRATES: But by making a transition through small steps, you will achieve a greater concealment while passing toward an opposite view than you would by a transition made in great leaps.

PHAEDRUS: How could it be otherwise?

SOCRATES: It is necessary, therefore, that he who intends to deceive another should accurately know the similarity and dissimilarity of things.

PHAEDRUS: It is necessary.

SOCRATES: Is it possible, then, for someone who is ignorant of the truth of a thing to judge the degree of similarity—whether great or small—that exists in other things?

PHAEDRUS: It is impossible.

<summary>Socrates argues that the art of rhetoric is a universal skill used to make things appear similar or contrary, noting that effective deception requires a precise knowledge of the truth to subtly lead an audience away from it.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Phaedrus, Zeno of Elea, Palamedes, rhetoric, deception, logic, similarity, justice, persuasion</keywords>
