**SOCRATES.** It is evident, therefore, that those who form opinions contrary to the truth of things, and who are deceived, are affected in this way through certain similarities <note>original: "similitudes"</note>.

**PHAEDRUS.** That is the case.

**SOCRATES.** Can a person who is ignorant about the nature of each particular thing skillfully <note>original: "artificially," meaning with technical skill or art</note> convey anything by moving through small steps toward its opposite, using similarities? Or can such a person avoid falling into error?

**PHAEDRUS.** He cannot.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, my friend, he who is ignorant of the truth and is led only by opinion will, it appears, produce a ridiculous and unskillful rhetoric.

**PHAEDRUS.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** Are you willing, then, to look at the speech of Lysias which you are carrying, and the one which we just delivered, to see what we said without technical skill and what was done according to the rules of art?

**PHAEDRUS.** I am willing above all things. For at the moment we are speaking in a trivial manner, as we lack sufficient examples.

**SOCRATES.** But indeed, as it seems, some arguments have been given—through the help of a certain good fortune—which have all the force of examples. These show that he who knows the truth will attract his listeners, even while he is joking in his discourse. And I consider, O Phaedrus, the local Gods to be the cause of this. Perhaps, also, the messengers <note>original: "interpreters"</note> of the Muses, singing over our heads, have inspired us with this ability; for I myself possess no skill ¹ belonging to public speaking.

**PHAEDRUS.** Let it be as you say; only make what you claim clear.

**SOCRATES.** Come then, read the beginning of Lysias's speech.

**PHAEDRUS.** "You are well acquainted with the state of my affairs; and you—"

¹ It was common for Socrates to deny that he possessed any invention of his own and to refer all things to the Gods. But there is, says Hermeas, a communion between us and the Gods, our soul being illuminated from that source both directly <note>original: "without a medium"</note> and through the middle classes of beings. Providence, therefore, says he, is twofold: for it is either that of the superior Gods themselves, or it occurs through the more excellent classes, such as angels, spirits <note>original: "dæmons," referring to intermediary spirits, not evil beings</note>, and heroes, and the local Gods. Socrates, therefore, attributes such an arrangement and management of words to the local Gods. But he signifies by the "singing over his head" the more excellent classes of beings who attend the Gods. For it is always necessary to call that which transcends us a "spirit" <note>original: "dæmon"</note>; as, for instance, the rational part is the spirit of the irrational part, and a God is the spirit of the intellect.

# THE PHAEDRUS

> "I have heard, I think, that it is most conducive to my advantage for things to remain in this manner. But it appears to me that I am not unworthy to be deprived of what I wish to obtain simply because I am not one of your lovers; for lovers, when their desires cease, repent of the benefits which they have bestowed."

**Socrates:** Stop there. Are we not then to show in what way he <note>Referring to Lysias, the author of the speech being discussed</note> is faulty, and in what respect he has acted without art?

**Phaedrus:** Certainly.

**Socrates:** Is it not, therefore, manifest to everyone that when we speak upon certain subjects we are unanimous in our conceptions, but when we speak upon others, we are discordant in our opinions?

**Phaedrus:** I think I understand what you say; but, notwithstanding this, speak more plainly.

**Socrates:** When anyone pronounces the name of iron or silver, do we not all understand the same thing?

**Phaedrus:** Entirely so.

**Socrates:** But when we pronounce the name of the *just* or the *good*, are we not of different opinions? And do we not doubt both with others and ourselves?

**Phaedrus:** Very much so.

**Socrates:** In some things, therefore, we agree in sentiments, and in others we do not.

**Phaedrus:** We do so.

**Socrates:** Where, then, are we more easily deceived? And in which of these is rhetoric able to accomplish the most?

**Phaedrus:** Evidently in those subjects about which we are dubious <note>original: "dubious"; meaning uncertain or wavering</note>.

**Socrates:** He, therefore, who is about to pursue the rhetorical art ought first of all to distinguish these in order; to consider the character of each species; and to perceive in what matters the multitude must necessarily be doubtful, and in what they are not.

**Phaedrus:** He who is able to accomplish this, Socrates, will understand a beautiful species <note>original: "species"; here meaning a specific class or form of knowledge</note>.

**Socrates:** Afterwards, I think, he ought not to be ignorant when he comes to particulars, but to perceive acutely to what genus <note>original: "genus"; the general category or classification</note> the subject of his future discourse belongs.

**Phaedrus:** What then?

He argues that a true rhetorician must systematically categorize subjects to understand where an audience can be easily persuaded or deceived.</summary>

**Socrates:** With respect to Love, shall we say that it belongs to things that are debated <note>original: "dubious"</note>, or to such as are not?

**Phaedrus:** To debated things, certainly.

**Socrates:** Do you think Love would permit you to assert what you have just claimed—that he is harmful both to the beloved and the lover—and then again, that he is the greatest of all goods?

**Phaedrus:** You put that in the best possible way.

**Socrates:** But inform me of this as well (for, due to my enthusiastic inspiration <note>original: "enthusiastic energy"</note>, I do not perfectly remember): did I define love at the beginning of my discourse?

**Phaedrus:** By Jupiter, you did, and in a most wonderful manner.

**Socrates:** Oh, how much more wise you make the Nymphs of Achelous <note>Achelous was a river god; Socrates suggests the local spirits inspired his speech</note> and Pan, the son of Mercury, appear to be regarding oratory than Lysias, the son of Cephalus! **Phaedrus:** If you like; though you will not find what you are looking for there.

**Socrates:** Read it anyway, so that I may hear it again.

**Phaedrus:** 
> "You are well acquainted with the state of my affairs, and you have heard, I think, that it is most beneficial for me if things remain this way. But it seems to me that I should not be denied what I wish to obtain simply because I am not one of your lovers. For lovers, when their desires fade, repent of the favors they have bestowed."

**Socrates:** He seems here to be very far from accomplishing what we are looking for. He tries to move through his discourse by starting not at the beginning, but at the end, in a contrary and backwards <note>original: "resupine," meaning lying on one's back or reversed</note> manner. He begins with what the lover—who has already stopped being a lover—says to his former beloved. Or perhaps, my dear Phaedrus, I am speaking to no purpose.

**Phaedrus:** But it is the conclusion, Socrates, which is the actual subject of his discourse.

**Socrates:** But what about the rest? Do not all the other parts of the discourse appear to be...

PHAEDRUS: But what is this "something"?

SOCRATES: That they are, in a certain respect, contrary to each other. For one kind of speech asserts that the lover should be gratified, and the other asserts that the person who is void of love <note>original: "he who is void of love"; referring to the non-lover</note> ought to be gratified.

PHAEDRUS: And it asserts this, indeed, most strenuously.

SOCRATES: I should have thought that you would have answered more truly, "and indeed furiously so." But what I inquire after is this—do we say that love is a certain mania <note>original: "mania"; here meaning a form of divine madness or inspired enthusiasm</note>, or not?

PHAEDRUS: A mania, certainly.

SOCRATES: But there are two species of mania: the one arising from human diseases, but the other from a divine transformation <note>original: "mutation"</note>, taking place in a manner different from established customs.

PHAEDRUS: Entirely so.

SOCRATES: But there are four parts of the divine mania, distributed according to the four divinities which preside over these parts. For we assign prophetic inspiration to Apollo; telestic <term>telestic</term><note>The "telestic" or mystic mania refers to the madness of religious rituals and initiations intended to purify the soul.</note> or mystic inspiration to Bacchus; poetic to the Muses; and the fourth, or amatory mania—which we assert to be the best of all—to Venus and Love. And I know not how, while we are representing the amatory passion through images, we perhaps touch upon a certain truth; and perhaps we are at the same time hurried away elsewhere. Hence, mingling together a speech <note>original: "oration"</note> that is not perfectly improbable, we have produced a certain fabulous hymn. With moderate abilities, we have celebrated your lord and mine, Phaedrus—namely Love, who is the watchful guardian of beautiful youths.

PHAEDRUS: And this was done in such a way that it was far from unpleasant to me, your listener.

SOCRATES: Let us, therefore, endeavor to understand how our discourse has passed from censure to praise.

PHAEDRUS: What do you mean by this?

SOCRATES: To me, we seem to have really been playing with respect to the other parts of our discourse. But I think that if anyone is able to comprehend, according to the rules of art, these two species which we have spoken of through a certain good fortune, he will not be an ungraceful person.

PHAEDRUS: What do you mean?

SOCRATES: By looking to one idea, he is able to bring together things that are scattered in every direction; so that, by defining each thing, he may always make manifest that which...

which he is desirous to teach: just as we acted at present with respect to our definition of Love, whether good or bad. For certainly our discourse by this means became more clear, and more consistent with itself.

PHÆDR. But what do you say respecting the other species, Socrates?

SOC. That this again should be cut into species according to its natural members; not by breaking any member like an unskillful cook, but, as in the previous discourse, perceiving the foam of the <term>dianoetic energy</term><note>original: "dianoëtic energy"; referring to the activity of the discursive reason or the power of thinking things through logically.</note> as one common species. But whether or not I properly name those who are able to accomplish this, God knows. But I have hitherto called them men conversant with <term>dialectic</term><note>The art of investigating or arriving at the truth through logical discussion and the classification of ideas.</note>. Tell me, therefore, by what name it is proper to call them, according to your opinion and that of Lysias. Or is this that art of speaking which Thrasymachus and others employing, became themselves wise in oratory, and rendered others such, who were willing to bestow gifts on them as if they had been kings?

PHÆDR. Those were indeed royal men, but yet not skilled in the particulars about which you inquire. But you appear to me to have properly named this species in calling it dialectic; but the rhetorical art appears as yet to have escaped us.

SOC. How do you say? Can there be anything beautiful which is destitute of these particulars, and yet be understood by art? If this be the case, it is by no means to be despised by me and you; but we must relate what remains of the rhetorical art.

PHAEDRUS: And there are many things, Socrates, which are recorded in books about the art of speaking.

SOCRATES: You have reminded me at a very opportune moment. For I think you would say that the introduction <note>original: "procoemium"</note> ought to be called the first part of the oration, and that things of this kind are the ornaments of the art.

PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: And, in the second place, a certain narration; and this is accompanied by testimonies. In the third place, the reasoning. In the fourth, probable arguments. And besides this, I think that a certain Byzantine—the best craftsman of orations—introduces confirmation and further proof.

PHAEDRUS: Do you not mean the illustrious Theodorus?

SOCRATES: I do. For he discovered how refutation <note>original: "confutation"</note>, both in accusation and defense, might not only take place, but also be strengthened. But why should we not introduce the most excellent Evenus the Parian? For he first discovered indirect declarations <note>original: "sub-declarations"</note> and the art of praising; and, according to the reports of some people, he delivered his rebukes in verse for the sake of assisting the memory. For he is a wise man. But shall we leave Tisias <margin>1. This Tisias is said by Cicero to have been the inventor of rhetoric.</margin> and Gorgias to sleep? They placed probabilities before realities and, through the strength of their discourse, caused small things to appear large and the large small; likewise, they made old things seem new and the new seem old. Besides this, they discovered a concise method of speaking and, conversely, an infinite lengthiness <note>original: "prolixity"</note> of words. When Prodicus once heard me relate all of this, he laughed and asserted that he alone had discovered what words this art required; he claimed it required neither few nor many, but a moderate quantity.

PHAEDRUS: You were, therefore, most wise, O Prodicus.

SOCRATES: But shall we not speak of Hippias? For I think that he will be of the same opinion as the guest from Elis.

PHAEDRUS: Why should we not?

SOCRATES: But what shall we say of the musical composition of Polus <margin>2. Polus was a disciple of Gorgias the Leontine. See the dialogue *Gorgias*.</margin>, who employed the doubling of words, a collection of maxims <note>original: "sentences"</note>, metaphors <note>original: "similitudes"</note>, and elegant names <note>original: "appellations"</note> in order to give splendor to his orations, according to the instruction which he had received from Lycimnion?

# THE PHAEDRUS

**PHAEDRUS.** But were not the orations of Protagoras, Socrates, of this kind?

**SOCRATES.** His style was indeed appropriate, and contained many other beautiful qualities besides. However, the Chalcedonian orator <note>original: "Chalcedonian orator" refers to Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, a famous sophist and rhetorician.</note> excelled in evoking pity by describing the hardships of poverty and the weaknesses of old age. He was also most skillful in stirring a crowd to anger and then, once they were enraged, calming them down again—as he put it—by "enchantment." He also highly excelled in creating and dismissing slanders, which could be used to great advantage. But everyone seems to agree on the conclusion of a speech, which some call the "recapitulation," while others give it a different name.

**PHAEDRUS.** Do you mean that the conclusion briefly reminds the listeners of everything that was said before?

**SOCRATES.** I do—and anything else you might have to say about this art of rhetoric.

**PHAEDRUS.** What I have to say is only minor and not worth mentioning.

**SOCRATES.** Let us, therefore, set aside these minor observations and instead look clearly at the specific ways in which the power of this art prevails, and under what circumstances it does so.

**PHAEDRUS.** Its power, Socrates, is most effective in public assemblies.

**SOCRATES.** It is indeed. But, my divine friend <note>original: "dæmoniacal man," a term Socrates uses to suggest someone possessed by a spirit or particularly inspired.</note>, do you also see—as I do—that the fabric of their arguments seems to have its threads coming apart?

**PHAEDRUS.** Show me what you mean.

**SOCRATES.** Tell me then: suppose someone approached your friend Eryximachus, or his father Acumenus <note>Eryximachus and Acumenus were well-known physicians in Athens.</note>, and said, "I know how to apply certain treatments to the body to make it hot or cold whenever I want. Furthermore, when I choose, I can induce vomiting or a bowel movement, along with many other similar effects. Because I know these things, I claim to be a physician and able to make anyone else a physician by teaching them this knowledge." What do you think the person hearing this should reply?

**PHAEDRUS.** What else could he say but ask whether the man also knows to *whom*, *when*, and to *what extent* each of these treatments should be applied?

<summary>Socrates and Phaedrus discuss the rhetorical techniques of famous sophists before Socrates uses a medical analogy to argue that true expertise requires knowing how and when to apply technical skills, not just possessing the skills themselves.</summary>

# THE PHAEDRUS

**Socrates:** If, therefore, he should say that he by no means understands all this, but that he who is instructed by him ought to do so and so; what then would be his answer?

**Phaedrus:** He would answer, I think, that the man was mad; and that, having heard from some book about things of this kind, or met with some remedies, he thought he might become a physician without knowing anything about the art.

**Socrates:** But what if anyone, addressing Sophocles and Euripides <note>Famous Athenian playwrights known for their mastery of tragedy.</note>, should say that he knew how to compose a long-winded discourse on a very trifling subject, and a very short one on a great occasion; and that when he pleased he could excite pity, and its contrary, horror and threats, and other things of this kind; and that by teaching these he thought that he delivered the art of tragic poetry?

**Phaedrus:** And these also, I think, Socrates, would deride him, who should fancy that a tragedy was anything else than the composition of all these, so disposed as to be adapted to each other, and to the whole.

**Socrates:** And I think they would not rudely <note>original: "rustically"</note> accuse him; but, just as if a musician should meet with a man who believes himself skilled in harmony because he knows how to make a chord sound sharp and flat, he would not fiercely say to him, "O miserable creature, you are mad"; but, as being a musician, he would thus address him more mildly: "O excellent man! It is necessary that he who is to be a musician should indeed know such things as these; but at the same time nothing hinders us from concluding, that a man affected as you are may not understand the least bit of harmony: for you may know what is necessary to be learned prior to harmony, without understanding harmony itself."

**Phaedrus:** Most right.

**Socrates:** In like manner, Sophocles would reply to the person who addressed him, that he possessed things previous to tragedy, rather than tragedy itself: and Acumenus <note>A famous Athenian physician and friend of Socrates.</note>, that the medical pretender understood things previous to medicine, and not medicine itself.

**Phaedrus:** Entirely so.

**Socrates:** But what if the sweet-speaking <note>original: "mellifluous"</note> Adrastus <note>Likely a reference to the legendary king or a contemporary orator noted for his persuasive speech.</note>, or Pericles, should hear those all-beautiful artificial inventions—concise discourses, metaphors <note>original: "similitudes"</note>, and other things which we said should be discussed in the light—do you think that they would...

<summary>Socrates argues that knowing the technical components of an art (like medicine, music, or tragedy) is merely a prerequisite and does not constitute mastery of the art itself. He uses these analogies to suggest that rhetoric requires more than just learning stylistic devices.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Phaedrus, Sophocles, Euripides, tragedy, harmony, music, Acumenus, medicine, Adrastus, Pericles, rhetoric, technical skill vs. art</keywords>

<page-num>358</page-num>
<header>THE PHAEDRUS</header>

would they be angry—as we were, through our lack of refinement <note>original: "rusticity"</note>—with those who wrote about and taught such things as if they were the same as rhetoric? Or rather, as being wiser than us, would they not instead reprove us? "It is not proper, Phaedrus and Socrates, to be angry with such characters; but you ought rather to pardon those who, being ignorant of dialectic <note>The art of logical discussion</note>, are unable to define what rhetoric is. Because of this ignorance, and because they possess a knowledge of the preliminary requirements of the art, they think they have discovered rhetoric itself. By teaching these preliminaries to others, they imagine they teach rhetoric in perfection. Yet, at the same time, they leave to the individual effort of their disciples the art of arranging each of these elements so as to produce persuasion, and of composing the whole oration, as if it were unnecessary for them to teach how to accomplish those goals."

PHÆDR. Such indeed, Socrates, does that art appear to be which these men teach and write about as rhetoric; and you seem to me to have spoken the truth. But how and from where shall we be able to acquire the art of true rhetoric and persuasion?

SOC. It is probable, Phaedrus, and perhaps also necessary, that perfection may be obtained in this as in other contests. For, if you naturally possess rhetorical abilities, you will become a celebrated orator by the assistance of science and practice; but if you are destitute of any one of these, you will be imperfect through that deficiency. However, the method employed by Lysias and Thrasymachus <note>Two famous teachers of rhetoric in ancient Greece</note> does not appear to me to demonstrate the true greatness of this art.

PHÆDR. But what method does, then?

SOC. Pericles, that most excellent man, appears with great propriety to have been the most perfect of all in the rhetorical art.

PHÆDR. Why?

SOC. All the great arts require continual meditation and a study of the sublime parts of nature. For an elevation of intellect and a perfectly effective power appear, in a certain respect, to proceed from this source. Pericles possessed this in conjunction with his naturally good disposition. For by meeting, I think, with Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that Mind (Nous) ordered the universe</note>, who possessed these qualities, Pericles was filled with elevated discourse. He came to understand the nature of intellect and of folly—subjects which Anaxagoras discussed at length—and from that source, he transferred to the art of speech whatever could contribute to its advantage.

<summary>Socrates argues that true rhetoric requires more than just technical preliminaries; it demands a philosophical understanding of nature and the intellect, as exemplified by the statesman Pericles.</summary>

<header>THE PHAEDRUS.</header>

PHAEDRUS: What do you mean by that?

SOCRATES: In a certain way, the method of the rhetorical art and the medical art is the same.

PHAEDRUS: How so?

SOCRATES: In both cases, it is necessary to make a systematic analysis <note>original: "distribution"</note>—of the nature of the body in one, and of the nature of the soul in the other. You must do this if you intend to use skill and art, rather than just routine and experience, to produce health and strength in the body by applying medicine and nourishment. Likewise, in the second case, you must do this if you wish to instill persuasion and virtue into the soul through reasoned argument and proper institutions.

PHAEDRUS: That seems very likely, Socrates.

SOCRATES: But do you think that the nature of the soul can be understood well enough without understanding the nature of the universe?

PHAEDRUS: If we are to trust Hippocrates <note>A famous ancient Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine"</note>, the successor of Asclepius <note>The Greek god of healing; original: "Æsculapius"</note>, even the nature of the body cannot be understood without this method.

SOCRATES: He speaks well, my friend. But in addition to the authority of Hippocrates, we must examine our own argument and see if it is consistent.

PHAEDRUS: I agree with you.

SOCRATES: Consider, then, what Hippocrates and true reason say about nature. Isn't it necessary, when thinking about the nature of anything, to first ask whether the subject we want to master—and teach others—is simple or complex <note>original: "multiform"</note>? And next, shouldn't we investigate its power? That is, what can it naturally do to other things, or how is it naturally acted upon <note>original: "passive"</note> by them? And if it has many forms, shouldn't we list them and examine each one, just as we did with the single form, to see its natural power to act or be acted upon?

PHAEDRUS: It seems we should, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Therefore, any method that proceeds without these steps is like the wandering of a blind man. But someone who works according to a true art should not be compared to the blind or the deaf. It is clear that whoever applies their speeches <note>original: "discourses"</note> to any art must accurately show the essence of the nature they are addressing; and this nature is, undoubtedly, the soul.

**PHAEDRUS:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Will not such a person, then, direct all their attention toward this goal: producing persuasion in the soul?

**PHAEDRUS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** It is clear, then, that Thrasymachus <note>A famous teacher of rhetoric and a character in Plato's *Republic*</note>—or anyone else who seriously studies the art of rhetoric—must first describe the soul with the greatest possible accuracy. **PHAEDRUS:** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** Secondly, he must show what the soul is naturally capable of doing to others, or what it is capable of experiencing <note>original: "suffering," meaning to be acted upon</note> from others.

**PHAEDRUS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Thirdly, having systematically categorized the different types of speeches and the different types of souls—along with the emotions that affect them—he should examine all the causes. He must match each type of soul to each type of speech, teaching which kind of soul will necessarily be persuaded by a particular kind of speech and why. Likewise, he must explain why a certain kind of soul will remain unpersuaded by those same speeches.

**PHAEDRUS:** Such a method of proceeding would, it seems, be most beautiful.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, anyone who acts in any other way will neither write nor speak skillfully <note>original: "artificially," meaning with technical skill/art</note> on this or any other subject. However, the writers on the art of rhetoric today (whom you yourself have heard) are crafty; they hide from us the fact that they actually possess a very beautiful knowledge of the soul. Until they both speak and write according to this systematic method, we will never be convinced that they write according to the true rules of art.

**PHAEDRUS:** What method do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** It is not easy to list the exact words that should be used for this. But, as far as I am able, I am willing to tell you how one ought to write if they desire to write according to the rules of art.

**PHAEDRUS:** Tell me then.

<meta>This page continues Socrates' explanation of how a true master of rhetoric must not only understand the theory of the soul but also possess the practical ability to recognize different types of people in real-time and apply the appropriate style of speech to persuade them.</meta>

<page-num>361</page-num>
<header>THE PHAEDRUS.</header>

...people of such a particular nature, as a result of certain arguments and for specific reasons, are easily persuaded to believe specific things. However, those who are naturally different are only persuaded with great difficulty through these same means. Therefore, once a person sufficiently understands all of this, they must be able to recognize these patterns happening in real-life situations. They must follow them with great speed through direct observation; otherwise, they will possess nothing more than the empty words they once heard from their teacher <note>original: "preceptor"</note>. 

But when he is truly able to say who will be persuaded by which arguments—and is sharp enough to perceive that the person standing before him is of the specific nature previously discussed, and can be moved by certain speeches to certain actions—then, at last, he will be a perfect master of this art. This occurs when, to his previous knowledge, he adds the skill of knowing when to speak and when to remain silent. He must know how to use (and when to avoid) brief speech, mournful or forceful language, and all the other techniques of rhetoric taught by his masters. But until this is accomplished, he cannot claim mastery. 

Anyone who fails in any of these areas—whether in speaking, teaching, or writing—and yet claims to speak with professional skill <note>original: "according to art"</note>, is defeated by the very person he is unable to persuade. But what then? (Perhaps a writer of speeches <note>original: "orations"</note> might ask us): "Does it appear to you, Phaedrus and Socrates, that the art of speaking is to be gained through this method, or is there another way?"

**PHAEDRUS:** It is impossible, Socrates, that it could be obtained any other way, although achieving it seems to involve a great deal of effort.

**SOCRATES:** You are right. And for that reason, we should examine all kinds of arguments thoroughly <note>original: "tossing upwards and downwards all discourses"</note> to see if an easier and shorter path to this goal presents itself. We do not want to wander aimlessly down a long and difficult road when we might have walked along a short and smooth one. If, therefore, you can offer any help based on what you have heard from Lysias <note>A famous orator and speechwriter in Athens</note> or anyone else, try to remember it and tell me.

**PHAEDRUS:** I would try if I could, but I cannot recall anything at the moment.

**SOCRATES:** Would you like me, then, to tell you what I once heard regarding these matters?

**PHAEDRUS:** Of course I would!

Soc. It is said, Phaedrus, that it is only fair to "speak for the wolf"—that is, to hear the other side of the story. <note>original: "to tell what is reported of the wolf." This refers to an ancient Greek proverb about hearing the defense before reaching a verdict.</note>

Soc. They say, then, that there is no need to praise or exaggerate these details in such a way, nor to derive our discussion from such lofty or distant abstract heights. For, as we said at the beginning of this discussion, anyone who intends to be sufficiently skilled in <term>rhetoric</term> does not need to possess the truth regarding *matters of justice and goodness*, or regarding *men* who are just and good, whether by nature or through education. For in the courts of law, no attention at all is paid to the truth of these things, but only to persuasion. And persuasion depends on what is "probable," which is what anyone speaking according to the rules of art should study. They argue that a speaker should never state the actual facts unless they seem probable; instead, in both accusation and defense, one should always introduce probabilities. In short, the speaker should pursue what seems likely and, if he speaks at length, he should say goodbye to the truth. For when this method is followed throughout a whole speech, it creates the highest perfection of the art.

Phaedr. You have accurately described the views held by those who are skilled in <term>rhetoric</term>, Socrates; for I remember that we briefly touched upon this earlier in our conversation. To those who make this their profession, this seems to be a matter of great importance. But you have certainly spoken harshly of <term>Tisias</term> himself. <note>original: "reviled Tisias." Tisias of Syracuse was one of the legendary founders of Greek rhetoric in the 5th century BCE.</note>

Soc. Then let <term>Tisias</term> himself tell us: does he define the "probable" as anything other than that which seems true to the common crowd?

Phaedr. What else could he call it?

Soc. Instead, the coward should claim that the daring man was not alone when he attacked him. Meanwhile, the daring man should deny there were others, asserting instead that he was alone when the alleged assault happened, while artfully asking the court: "How is it possible that a man as weak as I am could attack someone as strong as he is?" Then the other man, unwilling to admit his own cowardice, would try to invent some other false—

**PHÆDR.** This seems to be very well said, Socrates—if only it were actually possible for someone to complete such a difficult undertaking.

**Soc.** But even the attempt at noble <note>original: "beautiful"</note> goals is beautiful, as is enduring whatever may happen to be the result of our efforts.

Socrates’ story in this place is both allegorical and uplifting <note>original: "anagogic, or reductory"—referring to a spiritual process that leads the soul back to its divine origin</note>. <note>This section provides a Neoplatonic commentary on the myth of Theuth and Thamus.</note>

...a Mercurial soul, and at the same time a divine spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note>, relates their inventions to King Thamus. And though a man named Thamus once reigned in Egypt, yet in an anagogical sense <note>original: "anagogically" – an interpretation that leads the mind toward spiritual or divine truths</note> Thamus is a Mercurial divinity, either celestial or beyond the heavens <note>original: "supercelestial"</note>. But Ammon is that superior Jupiter who encompasses the Mercurial gifts. Lastly, invention belongs to natural instinct and conception, but judgment and discrimination belong to reason and perfect intelligence, which are far more excellent. Both, at the same time, belong to Jupiter Ammon; though, when taken separately, invention—which is, so to speak, the material form of art—must be referred to a spirit-like <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note> or human Mercury. However, judgment, use, and that which leads toward the final goal belong to Thamus, who is superior to both a human and a spirit-like Mercury. Although the narration seems to combine Thamus and Ammon into the same person, accurate reasoning is able to distinguish between them. They relate that the Egyptian Ibis was similar to a stork, that it had the shape of a heart, that it walked in a very uneven manner, and that it brought forth its eggs through its throat, just as Mercury delivers his offspring into the light. These and other Mercurial symbols signify wisdom, geometry, eloquence, and interpretation.

PHÆDRUS. Very true.

SOCRATES. For writing has this strange quality, which makes it truly similar to a painting. The creations of a painter stand there as if they were alive; but if you ask them a question, they remain solemnly silent. It is the same with written speeches: you would think they spoke as if they possessed some wisdom. But if you want to learn and you question them about what they say, they always tell you one and the same thing. 

Once a speech is written down, it is circulated <note>original: "rolled"</note> everywhere among those who understand it and even among those who have no business hearing it. It does not know who it should speak to and who it should ignore. And when it is misunderstood or unfairly criticized, it always needs its father <note>meaning the author</note> to help it. For a piece of writing cannot protect or defend itself.

PHÆDRUS. You seem to have stated this very correctly as well.

SOCRATES. But what? Shall we not consider another kind of speech, which is the 

<summary>Socrates argues that writing is an inferior imitation of living speech because it cannot answer questions, adapt to its audience, or defend itself without the author's help. He contrasts the "ancient" respect for truth—regardless of its source—with the "modern" obsession with the speaker's identity.</summary>

...the genuine brother of this—how it is legitimate, and how much better and more powerful its nature is than the other?

PHAEDRUS. What is this? And how do you say it is produced?

SOCRATES. That which is written in the soul of the learner along with true knowledge <note>original: "science," from the Greek *episteme*</note>, which is able to defend itself, and which knows to whom it ought to speak and before whom it ought to remain silent.

PHAEDRUS. You are speaking of the living and breathing <note>original: "animated"</note> speech of one who possesses knowledge, of which the written word may justly be called a mere image.

SOCRATES. Exactly. But answer me this as well: would a farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> who has any sense <note>original: "intellect"</note> take the seeds he values most, and from which he hopes for a harvest, and scatter them during the summer in the "gardens of Adonis" <note>The "gardens of Adonis" were shallow pots of soil used in festivals where seeds sprouted quickly but died just as fast because they had no deep roots. Socrates uses this as a metaphor for the superficiality of writing.</note>? Would he work with great effort and attention just to see them reach a beautiful peak in only eight days? Or would he only do that for the sake of a festival or for amusement? Instead, when he is serious about the business of farming, wouldn't he sow his seeds in proper soil and be perfectly satisfied if they reached full maturity <note>original: "consummation"</note> within eight months?

PHAEDRUS. He would certainly act that way, Socrates—sowing seriously at one time and for the sake of amusement at another.

SOCRATES. But should we say that a person who possesses the knowledge of things that are just, beautiful, and good has less sense than a farmer when it comes to the seeds he sows?

PHAEDRUS. Certainly not.

SOCRATES. Therefore, he will not with hurried and anxious effort write them in "black water" <note>referring to ink</note>, sowing them with a pen alongside spoken words. For in that form, it is impossible for the writing to defend itself through speech, and impossible for it to adequately present the truth.

PHAEDRUS. That would certainly not be right.

SOCRATES. Definitely not. Instead, it seems he will sow and write in the "gardens of letters" <note>meaning the written page</note> for the sake of amusement. When he writes, he builds up a store of memories for himself against the forgetfulness of old age, should he live to see it, and for the benefit of others who follow in his footsteps. He will take delight in watching his delicate offspring <note>original: "progeny," referring to his written ideas</note> grow...

<summary>Socrates compares writing to the "gardens of Adonis"—quick-growing but shallow—arguing that true knowledge is sown in the soul and takes time to mature. He concludes that a wise person uses writing only for amusement or as a memory aid for old age, rather than as a serious tool for teaching truth.</summary>

**PHAEDRUS.** You are speaking, Socrates, of a most beautiful diversion—not a lowly amusement—belonging to the man who is able to play with discourse, and who can <note>original: "mythologize"</note> weave stories about justice and the other subjects you mentioned.

**SOCRATES.** The specific details we came here to learn: we wanted to investigate the failure of *Lysias* <note>Lysias was a famous professional speechwriter whose work Socrates had been criticizing for being unorganized and lacking truth.</note> in the art of writing, and to examine which discourses are written with genuine skill <note>original: "art"</note> and which are not. **PHAEDRUS.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** But again, we must remember that no one can achieve perfection in the art of speaking—whether for teaching or persuading—until he is well acquainted with the truth of the subjects he speaks or writes about. He must be able to define the whole of a thing and, once defined, know how to divide it into its <term>species</term> until he reaches the <term>indivisible</term> <note>Socrates is describing the process of "Collection and Division": grouping things by their common nature and then breaking them down into their smallest logical parts.</note>. Furthermore, by using this method to examine the nature of the soul and discovering the <term>species</term> of discourse adapted to the nature of each person, he can then arrange and decorate his speech accordingly. He must offer complex and varied speeches to a soul characterized by variety, but simple speeches to a soul of a simple disposition.

**PHAEDRUS.** It appears to be so in every respect.

**SOCRATES.** But what shall we say to the question of whether it is honorable or shameful <note>original: "beautiful or base"</note> to speak and write speeches; and in what respect this work may be blameworthy or not? Perhaps what we said a little earlier is sufficient for this purpose.

**PHAEDRUS.** What was that?

**SOCRATES.** That if **Lysias**, or anyone else, has at any time written—or now writes—laws, either for private or public use, and in composing a political work thinks it contains great stability and clarity; this is shameful in a writer, whether anyone says so or not. For to be ignorant of the difference between true visions and the delusions of sleep, or between what is just and unjust, evil and good, cannot fail to be truly shameful, even if the entire common crowd <note>original: "the whole rout of the vulgar"</note> should join together in its praise.

**PHAEDRUS.** It cannot be otherwise.

**SOCRATES.** But consider the man who thinks that a written speech is largely for the sake of amusement. He considers no discourse, whether in prose or verse, to be deserving of great study in its composition or its recital—much like those <term>rhapsodists</term> who, without judgment or learning, recite verses just to be persuasive. 

In reality, he believes that even the best of those written works were created only to remind those who already know the subject. Instead, he believes that clarity, perfection, and serious value can only be found in discourses intended to teach; those delivered for the sake of learning, which are truly written in the soul, concerning what is just, beautiful, and good. He judges that discourses of this kind should be called his "legitimate offspring." First among these is the knowledge inherent in himself, if he should find it there, and after that, whatever offspring or brothers spring up in a proper way from that progeny of his own soul in the souls of others. To all other types of writing, he bids farewell. A man of this kind, **Phaedrus**, appears to be the sort of person you and I should pray to become.

**PHAEDRUS.** I perfectly desire and pray for the possession of what you speak of.

**SOCRATES.** We have, therefore, spoken enough about speeches in this playful manner. It only remains for you to tell **Lysias** that, as we descended with our intellects to the stream of the **Nymphs** and **Muses**, we heard certain voices. They ordered us to inform **Lysias**, and every other—

...writer of orations, likewise **Homer**, and any other who may compose either poetry alone <note>original: "naked poetry," referring to poetry without musical accompaniment</note>, or that which is adorned with song; and in the third place **Solon**, and all who may commit political laws to writing—if their compositions result from knowing the truth, and if they are able to defend their writings against the objections of adversaries who claim they can prove the dishonesty <note>original: "improbity"</note> of their discourses, then they ought not to be named after works of this kind, but from what they have written with serious purpose.

**PHAEDRUS.** But what will you do? For it is not proper that your own companion should be neglected.

**PHAEDRUS.** What?

**SOCRATES.** He appears to me to possess such excellent natural talents that his productions ought not to be compared with the orations of **Lysias**. Besides this, his character <note>original: "manners"</note> is more noble; so that it will be by no means wonderful if, when he is older, he should far surpass all the other boys who ever meddled with orations in those very speeches which are now the objects of his study. Or, if he should not be content with a pursuit of this kind, I think that a more divine impulse will lead him to greater attainments; for there is naturally, my friend, a certain philosophy in his intellectual <note>original: "dianoëtic," from the Greek "dianoia," meaning the power of discursive reason or the thinking mind</note>...

...prophetic <note>original: "ëtic"; in the context of the original Greek and Taylor's translation, this refers to the "prophetic" or "divine" potential Socrates sees in the young Isocrates</note> part of this man. **PHAEDRUS.** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** O beloved **Pan**, and all you other Gods who are residents of this place¹, grant that I may become beautiful within, and that whatever I possess externally may be friendly to my inward attainments! Grant, also, that I may consider the wise man as one who abounds in wealth; and that I may enjoy that portion of gold which no one but a prudent man is able either to bear or properly manage! Do we require anything else, **Phaedrus**? For to me it appears that I have prayed tolerably well.

**PHAEDRUS.** Pray also in the same manner for me: for the possessions of friends are common.

**SOCRATES.** Let us then depart.

¹ By **Pan**, and the other Gods, understand local deities beneath the moon <note>original: "sublunary"</note>. But **Pan** is named as if he were "all" <note>from the Greek *pan*, meaning "all"</note>, because he possesses the most ample sway in the order of local Gods. For, just as the Gods beyond the world <note>original: "supermundane"</note> are referred to **Jupiter**, and the celestial Gods to **Bacchus**, so all the local Gods and divine spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> of the earthly realm are referred to **Pan**.

# INTRODUCTION
->TO<-
## THE GREATER HIPPIAS.

---

**T**he purpose of this dialogue—which is called the *Greater Hippias* to distinguish it from another dialogue of the same name called the *Shorter* (or *Lesser*) *Hippias*—is to gradually reveal the nature of *the beautiful* as it exists within the soul. That this is its real purpose will be immediately clear when one considers that logical methods are suited to everything related to the soul, because the soul’s activities are naturally discursive <note>original: "discursive"; meaning the soul moves from one thought to another through reasoning, rather than grasping truth all at once</note>. However, these methods do not suit the intellect <note>In Platonic philosophy, "intellect" (*nous*) represents a higher level of reality than the "soul" (*psyche*)</note>, because the intellect’s vision is simple, unified, and immediate. Therefore, this dialogue is full of *trials* ¹ *and refutations, definitions and demonstrations, divisions, compositions, and analyses*; whereas the part of the *Phaedrus* that discusses beauty in its primary form contains none of these methods, because its character is "enthusiastic" <note>original: "enthusiastic"; here meaning divinely inspired or a state of spiritual ecstasy</note>.

However, it is important to note that when we say the dialogue’s purpose concerns beauty as it exists in the soul, we do not mean only the human soul, but the soul in general. In other words, it concerns that beauty which first exists in the "Soul of the Universe," which in Platonic terms is the monad <note>monad: the primary unit or single source from which a series or order is derived</note> of all souls, and is then passed down to all subsequent types of souls.

Mr. Sydenham ² has correctly observed that Plato hides the significance of his meaning in this dialogue behind a layer of humor and wit that runs through the entire work. The introductory part of the dialogue

---
¹ Trials and refutations, and definitions, and demonstrations, and divisions, both compositions and analyses. <note>original Greek: Πειραι και ελεγχοι, και ορισμοι, και αποδειξεις, και διαιρεσεις, συνθεσεις τε και αναλυσεις.</note>
² I regret that I could not include the entirety of his argument for this dialogue. However, since he was not deeply versed in Plato’s philosophy, he is mistaken on many points—especially regarding the purpose of the dialogue, which he believes concerns the highest or supreme beauty.

<summary>This introduction explains that the "Greater Hippias" explores the nature of beauty within the soul using logical and discursive methods, contrasting it with more intuitive or "inspired" works like the "Phaedrus."</summary>
<keywords>Greater Hippias, Plato, The Beautiful, soul, intellect, monad, Sydenham, logic, aesthetics</keywords>

<page-num>376</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE GREATER HIPPIAS.</header>

is purely ironical, and seems intended to use ridicule <note>original: "deriding"</note> to cleanse the sophists of their "twofold ignorance" <note>In Platonic philosophy, this refers to being ignorant but thinking that one actually knows the truth</note>. It exposes their love of profit, their **polymathy** <term>an accumulation of wide-ranging knowledge that is ultimately useless for the primary purposes of life</term>, and their complete lack of that true wisdom which leads to virtue and happiness. Mr. Sydenham also notes that the dramatic quality of this dialogue is so perfect that, if it only had a plot <note>original: "fable"</note>, it could be performed on stage by skilled comedians to great effect. He adds that the behaviors it portrays are so vivid <note>original: "highly picturesque"</note> that they would make an excellent subject for any moral painter. It seems some of the ancients placed it among the "anatreptic" <note>original: *anatreptic*; from the Greek *anatreptikos*, meaning "subverting" or "overturning" an opponent's argument</note> dialogues; however, I believe it should instead be ranked among those that are **pirastic** <note>original: *pirastic*; from the Greek *peirastikos*, meaning "testing" or "exploratory"</note> and **maieutic** <note>original: *maieutic*; from the Greek *maieutikos*, meaning "midwifery," referring to Socrates' method of helping others give birth to their own ideas</note>* in nature.

Should it be asked—since it is never explicitly stated in this dialogue—what *the beautiful in the soul is*, we reply that it is a living, rational form, and the cause of symmetry to everything within and lower than <note>original: "posterior to"</note> the soul. The accuracy of this definition will be obvious if we consider that the highest beauty is a living *intellectual* form—the source of harmony for all things that come after the "ineffable principle of all" <note>The "ineffable principle" refers to "The One" or "The Good," the ultimate source of reality in Neoplatonic thought</note>, as we have shown in the Notes on the *Parmenides*. Consequently, when the soul participates in this beauty, it preserves all its essential characteristics, except that its *intellectual* nature becomes *rational* through that participation.

---

* That is, among those dialogues which explore and act as a midwife to <note>original: "obstetricate"</note> the ideas within the soul.

<sig>3 C</sig>

# THE GREATER HIPPIAS.

## *PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.*

### SOCRATES AND HIPPIAS.

### SCENE¹.—THE LYCEUM.

### SOCRATES.

HIPPIAS, the elegant² and the wise! What a long time it has been since you last put in³ at Athens!

HIP. ———

---

¹ The scene of this dialogue is clearly the Lyceum, a structure of astonishing grandeur and beauty located a short distance from the city by the side of the River Ilisus. It was the largest and most magnificent of the three public buildings constructed at the state's expense for the purpose of bathing and gymnastic <note>original: "gymnic"</note> exercises. The other two were within the city, located conveniently for the use of ordinary citizens and businessmen. But this one was most frequented by men of larger fortune and more leisure, many of whom Socrates knew intimately. As we learn from Plato’s *Symposium*, it was his usual custom to go there with his friends and spend most of the day. The Sophists also frequented the same place whenever they came to Athens, as Isocrates mentions in his *Panathenaic Oration*; this is natural to assume, as the nobler part of the youth gathered there daily. These young men were extremely curious after knowledge and great admirers of philosophy, and the Sophists claimed to teach it, promising to make any man a philosopher for a set fee. To carry on this professional business, they traveled constantly like the Rhapsodists from city to city ("appearing quickly everywhere," <note>original: *tacheōs pantachē gignomenoi* (ταχέως πανταχῆ γιγνόμενοι)</note> says Isocrates) wherever philosophy and knowledge were respected; but they visited Athens most often, where, above all places, those intellectual ornaments were highly valued. —S.

² Hippias was known for his flamboyant clothing, as we shall see further on. Because this caught Socrates’ eye immediately upon meeting him, he addressed him first with this description. —S.

³ In this sentence, Socrates humorously uses a nautical term <note>original: "touched at"</note> to represent the life led by the Sophists as resembling that of sailors, who wander incessantly from port to port and never continue...

...continue long in one place. But possibly there is a further meaning; it may be intended to prepare us for observing that instability of Hippias himself—his notions and opinions—which is later to appear throughout the dialogue. This is an instability arising from his lack of the fixed principles of science, which are the only sure foundation of settled opinions. At the same time, there is a propriety in this expression coming from the mouth of an Athenian, to whom it must have been habitual; Athens being located near the sea, the Athenians being the principal merchants, and their state being the greatest maritime power then in the world. — Sydenham <note>original: "S." refers to the translator Floyer Sydenham.</note>

**HIPPIAS.** It is because I have not had leisure <note>Plato informs us as soon as possible about the character of his speakers. In this first speech by Hippias, the vain and boastful sophist and the formal orator both appear in a strong light, and prepare us at once for all which is to follow. — Sydenham</note>, Socrates. For you must know that the Eleans, whenever they have any public affairs to negotiate with any of the neighboring cities, constantly apply to me. They appoint me their ambassador for that purpose in preference to all others, because they trust me as the person most able to form a right judgment of what is argued and alleged by every city, and to make a proper report of it to them. My embassies <note>See Philostratus, page 495, Olearius edition. — Sydenham</note>, therefore, have been frequent to many of those powers; but most often, and regarding the greatest number of points as well as those of the highest importance, have I gone to Sparta to treat with the Lacedaemonians. This is the reason, then, in answer to your question, why I so seldom visit these parts.

**SOCRATES.** This is what it means, Hippias, to be a man truly wise and perfectly accomplished. For, being thus qualified, you have, in your private <note>Hippias is here represented as being both a sophist and an orator. To better understand this double character, and the many passages of Plato where these professions are mentioned, it may be useful to give a summary account of their rise and nature. Ancient Greek wisdom, or philosophy, in the earliest times of which any records remain, included physics, ethics, and politics. This lasted until the time of Thales the Ionian, who, giving himself up entirely to the study of Nature—her principles, elements, and the causes of various phenomena—became famous above all the ancient sages for natural knowledge. He led the way for a succession of philosophers called "Ionic" after their founder and first master. Devoted to the contemplation of things far removed from human affairs, these men all lived as isolated as possible from society. They revealed the secrets of nature only to a few select disciples who sought them out in their retreats and had a talent for the same complex inquiries, along with a taste for the same retired kind of life. As the fame of their wisdom spread, the curiosity of that whole inquisitive nation, the Greeks, was finally excited. This gave—</note> capacity, great—

---

<note>
The shift in Greek culture gave rise to a new profession or sect, very different from those speculative sages. A group of men—driven not by the love of wisdom, but by fame and glory—appeared in Greece. These were men of great natural talent, notable industry, and boldness. Assuming the name of Sophists <note>original: "Sophists" — a term that originally meant "wise person" but came to refer to professional teachers of rhetoric and virtue who charged fees.</note>—a title that had previously been highly honorable and given only to those believed to make mankind wiser, such as ancient poets, lawgivers, and the gods themselves—they undertook to teach all parts of philosophy in a short time through a few lessons. They offered this to anyone, regardless of their disposition or mental capacity, provided they were able to pay well for the instruction. 

In the same age as Thales lived Solon the Athenian, who chose to cultivate a different branch of philosophy. By applying himself chiefly to moral and political science, he became so skilled in those studies that he provided a new system of excellent laws for his country. From this, a lineage of politicians arose in Athens, students of law and the art of government. Through this succession, fueled by natural genius, good governance, commerce, and the wealth of the Athenians, great improvements were made in all the liberal arts. However, oratory <note>original: "oratory" — the art of public speaking.</note> flourished above the rest for one specific reason: the Athenians lived under a popular government, where the power to rule comes only through persuasion. 

Since eloquence was one of the primary tools of persuasion, and persuasion was the only way to gain and keep power, everyone ambitious for a high office or magistracy in the government studied to become an eloquent orator. Thus, the arts of rhetoric and politics were joined in the same individuals. Accordingly, we learn from the Attic writers of that time that the most popular orators in Athens were appointed as ambassadors, magistrates, commanders of armies, and leaders of the supreme administration of all civil affairs. See particularly Isocrates in his orations *On the Peace* and the *Panathenaicus*. <note>original: "Orat. de Pace, & Panathen."</note> 

In this dialogue, we see that the same spirit prevailed at Elis. In men of great ability, the dominant passion is more often ambition than greed. Therefore, those Sophists who excelled in quick thinking, breadth of knowledge, and ingenuity—such as Hippias—added the arts of popular oratory to their other accomplishments, and by those means entered the management of the state. This summarizes the matter for now; the rest of this short history, as far as it is necessary for our purpose, will appear at appropriate times. — Sydenham <note>original: "S."</note>
</note>

<note>
The Sophists did not believe it was their job to teach basic skills—they thought that task was beneath them. Instead, after a young man had completed a standard liberal education and finished the physical and mental exercises of youth, they would provide the "finishing touches." This meant qualifying him to speak persuasively on all subjects and to support either side of any debate with clever arguments. Through what was later called "sophistical" reasoning—often using fallacies to win arguments—they taught students how to influence listeners, silence opponents, and control all matters of public life. To gain these skills, the young gentleman would constantly follow his teacher everywhere, observing how they debated *concerning any entity* <note>original: "de quolibet ente"</note>—on whatever topic arose—and learning by degrees to imitate them. Because of this, what we translate as "tuition" or "teaching" is always called *associating with the young* <note>original: "συνεῖναι τοῖς νέοις" (syneinai tois neois)</note> in Plato. Another part of a <term>Sophist</term>'s occupation, quite distinct from the former though carried on at the same time, was to read lectures for a set price to each listener. These lectures, on subjects chosen at random, were essentially formal essays or "exhibitions" <note>original: "ἐπιδείξεις" (epideixeis)</note> designed for entertainment and show, rather than lasting instruction. A third branch of their trade, which they performed for free to gain fame and attract paying customers, was to answer any question proposed to them—much like the ancient Oracle at Delphi. In this passage, Socrates only mentions the two paid versions from which they earned their profit.—S. <note>"S." refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham, an 18th-century scholar.</note>
</note>

**HIPPIAS.** Strictly speaking, Socrates, I must admit that is the case. However, people are not used to giving such a meaning to the word *law*.

<page-num>387.</page-num>
<header>THE GREATER HIPPIAS.</header>

**SOCRATES.** Do you speak of men who know what law means, or of men who lack that knowledge?

**HIPPIAS.** I speak of the bulk of mankind—the masses.

**SOCRATES.** And are they the type who know the truth of things, this multitude?

**HIPPIAS.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** But those who possess that knowledge—the wise—hold that what is more beneficial is, in reality and according to the truth of things, more of a law to all men than what is less beneficial. Do you not agree with them on this?

**HIPPIAS.** I agree that, in reality, it is so.

**SOCRATES.** Is not the nature and the condition of everything exactly as those who truly understand the thing believe it to be?

**HIPPIAS.** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** Now, you say that for the Spartans, an education under you—a foreigner—and in a foreign style, would be more beneficial than being educated in the manner of their own country.

**HIPPIAS.** And I say what is true.

**SOCRATES.** And what is more beneficial is more of a law. You say this as well, Hippias.

**HIPPIAS.** I have admitted that this is the case.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, according to your account, having the sons of the Spartans educated under Hippias is more in accordance with the law; and their education under their fathers is more contrary <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to the law—assuming that they would receive truly greater advantages from you.

**HIPPIAS.** And indeed they would, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** It follows, then, that the Spartans violate the law by not giving you payments of money and by not entrusting their sons to your care.

**HIPPIAS.** So be it; for you seem to be arguing in my favor, and it is not my business to contradict <note>original: "controvert"</note> your argument.

**SOCRATES.** So we find that these Spartans are lawbreakers, my friend—and in the most important matter, too—even though they are thought to be the most devoted observers of the law. But, in the name of the Gods, Hippias, what kind of lectures <note>original: "dissertations"</note> are they for which they give you such high praise <note>original: "encomiums"</note>? And upon what topics do they take such great pleasure in hearing you speak <note>original: "harangue"</note>?

<note>
^1 The government <term>polity</term> of the Spartans was designed with the goal of making them a military people. For this reason, the mechanical and necessary arts were left to servants and slaves; only those liberal arts were admitted that contributed to military skill or prepared them for the hardships and strategies <note>original: "toils and the stratagems"</note> of war. However, philosophy and the sciences are said to have been completely excluded. Many passages from the ancient authors proving this are collected by the commentators on Aelian’s *Various History* <note>original: "Var. Hist."</note>, book 12, chapter 50, and by Nicholas Cragius in his previously cited treatise, book 3. Perhaps, however, this was only the case in appearance. It may be worthwhile to carefully examine and consider what Plato says on this subject in his *Protagoras*. —S. [Floyer Sydenham]
</note>

<note>
^2 The Spartans were no more famous for their contempt of grammar and mathematics than Hippias was for his skill in those sciences, as is shown in the shorter dialogue named after him. This third and final part of the introduction gains much grace from both these facts. Mentioning the sciences here in this way, with a mix of compliment and humor, seems to arise naturally from the character of the person Socrates is talking to and from the character of the people who are the current subject of their conversation. Plato uses such exquisite skill in the arrangement <term>economy</term> of his dialogues that whatever is brought up seems to fit in naturally. At the same time, all the circumstances harmonize; every detail helps carry out his primary or secondary goals, having been intentionally introduced for that purpose. —S. [Floyer Sydenham]
</note>

¹ This was the era of Athenian greatness. Because of the mildness of Solon’s laws, the limits they placed on the formidable power of a permanent senate, and the popular liberty they established, the people developed such a spirit—always the result of mild government, legal liberty, and a share of power—that Athens soon grew able to rival Sparta and to be her competitor for the leadership and management of the general affairs of Greece. If it makes no difference to you, therefore, I should be glad to be allowed to play the part of an objector in order to better master the subject.

HIPPIAS. Take the part of an objector, then. As I said just now, the point you inquire about is not very difficult <note>original: "knotty"</note>. I could teach you to answer questions much more difficult than this in such a manner that no one should ever be able to refute you.

I will try to be what he is to the best of my power, and in his person, I will begin to question you. Now, if he were in the audience when you delivered that lecture <note>original: "dissertation"</note> you spoke of concerning the beauty of manners, after he had heard it through and you had finished speaking, this point—relating to the beautiful—would be the very first thing on his mind to question you about. HIPPIAS. I shall answer: "It is by their having honesty."

SOCRATES. "Is not this honesty, then, a certain real thing?"

**Socrates.** An excellent answer, by the dog¹! <note>original: "by the dog"</note>, Hippias; and it is the kind of answer that cannot fail to be applauded. If I answer in this way, will I have answered the question asked of me? And will I have done so well enough that I cannot be refuted?

¹ In his dialogues, Plato has portrayed his hero with such minute detail that he seems not to have omitted even the smallest quirk of that great man's everyday conversation. We see a very remarkable instance of this here. It seems that Socrates, in common speech, often used to swear by animals. The various reasons given for his doing so, and the different criticisms leveled against him, can be found collected by Ménage in his notes on Laërtius (pages 92, 93); by Mr. Massieu in the first volume of *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles Lettres* (page 205); and by Mr. du Soul in his notes on Lucian (volume 1, page 556, Hemsterhus edition). This much is clear: the Cretans had a law or custom, introduced by Rhadamanthus, to use that very kind of oath specifically to avoid using the names of the Gods they believed in on every trivial occasion. See the authors cited by Olearius in his notes on Philostratus (page 257, note 22). The opinion of Porphyry, in his third book *On Abstinence from Animal Food* (section 16), is that the great Athenian philosopher followed the example of the old Cretan judge and lawmaker. Indeed, this is highly probable, because we find Socrates swearing by the exact same species of animals commonly invoked by the Cretans. The dog is named most frequently in the oaths of both, likely because it was a domestic animal and most often in sight while they were talking. See the commentator on Aristophanes' *The Birds* (line 521) and Suidas under the entry <term>Oath of Rhadamanthus</term> <note>original: Ῥαδαμάνθυος ὅρκος</note>.—S.

² The Greek is, "whether there is anything that is the beautiful itself" <note>original: ει τι εστιν αυτο το καλον</note>. Among the Athenian writers, the word for "if" (*ei*) often has the force of an interrogative adverb meaning "whether," just like the English word "if." This is one of the many idioms of our language that corresponds with those of ancient Athenian Greek. However, this idiom seems not to have been well known, or at least not observed here, by any of the translators; for they all interpret this part of the sentence in a conditional sense, treating "if" as a conditional conjunction. Nor does it seem to have been better understood by those old transcribers of the original manuscripts from which our editions of Plato are printed. Their ignorance on this point seems to have caused the errors in the text noted in the following two remarks.—S.

¹ <note>The Greek text is printed: "And I will say that if a beautiful maiden is a beauty, through which these things would be beautiful" <note>original: "Εγω δε δη ερω, ὁτι ει παρθενος καλη, καλον εστι δι᾿ ὁ ταυτ᾿ αν ειη καλα"</note>. But the meaning clearly requires us to remove the word "if" <note>original: "ει"</note> before "maiden," and to read "that a beautiful maiden is a beauty," etc. The person who added this word no doubt intended to make this sentence match the previous one; and so they completed the series of mistakes that arose gradually from ignorance of the Attic dialect used in the previous sentence—a mistake we blamed on the scribes in the previous note. This final mistake led to another, quite ridiculous one, made by Augustinus Niphus in a Latin treatise *On the Beautiful* <note>original: "De Pulchro"</note>. In the first part of that work, he intends to explain Plato's *Greater Hippias*. To do this, he feels it is necessary to first prove the excellence of some specific beauty, which he probably thinks best shows the perfection of the ideal pattern. For this purpose, he politely and gallantly makes the following argument, clearly based on the error mentioned in this note: "If the Princess Joan of Aragon is beautiful without a fault, then there must be something absolutely beautiful in nature. But no one can deny the faultless beauty of the Princess Joan; therefore, etc." To prove this last claim, he gives a long list of the princess's charms, including her mind and manners, as well as her golden hair, blue eyes, and dimpled chin, from head to foot. —S.</note>

<gloss>1</gloss> The Greek is printed as *hon sy epagē* <note>original: ὃν σὺ ἐπάγῃ</note>; and interpreted by all translators as: "That Heraclitus, whose testimony you cite," as if the word for "witness" (*martyra*) was implied after "cite." Whether this interpretation fits Plato’s words or not, it clearly contradicts the facts: for it was Socrates himself, not Hippias, who had just cited Heraclitus. However, if we assume Heraclitus was frequently cited by Hippias, the meaning might be: "He whose testimony you usually cite." Yet, changing the word *hon* ("whom") to *ho an* ("which/whatever") will, we believe, make better sense to any attentive reader. Heraclitus's saying—which he inferred by analogy from his comparison between apes and men—is a logical follow-up to what Hippias just admitted regarding the soup-pan and the maiden. Our learned readers will also notice the grammar is much more natural when the sentence is read: *Ē ou kai Hērakleitos tauton touto legei, ho an sy epagē* <note>original: Ἢ οὐ καὶ Ἡράκλειτος ταὐτὸν τοῦτο λέγει, ὃ ἂν σὺ ἐπάγῃ</note> — "Or does not Heraclitus say this very thing, which you would also infer?" — S. <note>The "S" refers to the editor/translator, likely Floyer Sydenham.</note>

<note>The following notes provide historical context on Greek dining and botanical translations.</note>

The ingredients, mixed together and often disrupting the usual order of cooking, were many of them served at the table in the very stewing pans in which they were made. See Aristophanes, *The Knights*, Act 4, Scene 1; Athenæus, Book 9, page 406; and Casaubon’s commentary on Athenæus, page 693. For this reason, those elegant people were very particular about the beauty of these pans or dishes. Their material seems to have been a kind of porcelain, and the form was not unlike our tureens. If any of our readers are curious enough to inquire into the composition of these soups, they may find some information by looking into Athenæus and Apicius Cælius, Book 5, Chapter 3. — S.

¹ In the Greek text, the word is *sykine* <note>original: συκινη; meaning "made of fig-wood"</note>. However, there is great reason to suspect that we should read *sykamine* <note>original: συκαμινη; meaning "made of sycamore-wood"</note>. The wood of the fig tree was found to be so unfit a material for making any domestic utensils that the Greeks, in common speech, metaphorically called whatever was useless "a fig-tree thing" <note>original: συκινον</note>. For this reason, Horace gives that wood the epithet "useless" <note>original: *inutile*; Satires, Book 1, Satire 8</note>. On the other hand, the wood of the sycamore tree—*sykamine*—is described by Theophrastus as "wood useful for many purposes" <note>original: ξυλον προς πολλα χρησιμον; *History of Plants*, Book 4, Chapter 2</note>. This is not even to mention the extreme bitterness of fig-tree wood to the taste and the offensiveness of its smoke when burning, which is worse than any other tree (see Plutarch, Volume 2, page 684)—qualities which suggest its scent and flavor would not be very agreeable. The change in this word is easily explained: the sycamore <note>original: συκαμινος or συκομορος</note> being the same as the "Egyptian fig-tree" <note>original: συκη Αιγυπτια</note>, it is probable that the Alexandrian Platonists, to illustrate the word *sykamine*, wrote *sykine* in the margin of their books. This later replaced the original word more easily because the fig tree was well known to be the most common tree in Attica. — S.

**SOCRATES.** I don't think he would be, Hippias. He would not have beaten me wrongfully if I had given him such an answer; rather, it seems to me I would have deserved it.

**HIPPIAS.** It seems so to me as well then, Socrates, if that is your own opinion.

**SOCRATES.** Shall I tell you why, in my own opinion, I would have deserved a beating if I had answered that way? Will you condemn me too without a trial <note>original: "trying the cause"</note>, or will you hear what I have to say?

---

<note>¹ The Greek is *ball’ es makarian* <note>original: βαλλ’ ες μακαριαν</note>. Various explanations of this proverb are given to us by Timaeus (in his *Platonic Lexicon*), Hesychius, Suidas, and others. However, none of them are satisfactory to us. Erasmus, with his usual sharp insight and wisdom, was the first—as far as we know—who discovered its most likely origin. Though, with his typical Socratic modesty, he only says, "It seems to be so." After reviewing the standard explanations, he offers his own: that the specific spot of ground where a large part of the Persian forces died in the Battle of Marathon—a deep marsh in which they sank and were overwhelmed—was called *Macaria*, as noted by Pausanias. Consequently, the Greeks used this proverb to express detestation when they cursed anyone: "Throw him into Macaria!"—the place where our hated enemies perished. See Erasmus’s *Adagia*, volume 2, century 1, number 98 <note>original: Adag. chil. ii. cent. 1. n. 98</note>. Schottus gives the same interpretation using the exact words of Erasmus, but, like many other learned commentators, without acknowledging his source. See *Commentary on Zenobius*, page 42 <note>original: Schol. in Zenobium</note>.—S.</note>
