**SOCRATES.** Let us consider it, however, for fear that we might be making a mistake on this point.

**HIPPIAS.** I agree we ought to do so.

**SOCRATES.** Observe then. Regarding what we call the becoming <note>original: "the becoming". In Greek philosophy, this refers to *to prepon*—the fitting, the appropriate, or that which is suitable to a specific context.</note>: is it not either something whose presence makes all things appear beautiful; or something which gives them the actual reality of beauty; or something which provides both $^1$, causing them not only to appear beautiful, but to actually be so?

**HIPPIAS.** I think it must be one or the other of these.

**SOCRATES.** Which of these, then, is "the becoming"? Is it that which only creates a beautiful appearance? For instance, when a man with a deformed body puts on clothes or shoes that fit him, he looks handsomer than he actually is. Now, if "the becoming" causes everything to look handsomer than it truly is, then it must be a kind of fraud or deception regarding beauty. It cannot be what we are searching for, Hippias. After all, we were inquiring what it is that makes all beautiful things beautiful. Just as $^2$, if we were asked what makes all great things great, we would answer that it is by "surpassing" other things of the same kind $^3$. That is how all things are great: even if they do not all appear great to us, they must necessarily be great if they surpass others. We say the same is true of the beautiful; it must be something that makes things beautiful, whether they appear so or not. But this cannot be "the becoming," because, according to your account, "the becoming" makes things appear more beautiful than they really are, thereby concealing the truth...

---

$^1$ A most egregious and gross blunder has corrupted the Greek text in this place; where we read "neither" <note>original Greek: ουδετερα (*oudetera*)</note>: instead of which we ought to read "both" <note>original Greek: αμφοτερα (*amphotera*)</note>: as will appear clearly in the course of the argument. Yet, gross as the blunder is, all the translators have followed it.—S. <note>original: "S." refers to the editor and translator Floyer Sydenham.</note>

$^2$ In the Greek we read: "just as that by which all great things are great, by the surpassing" <note>original Greek: ωσπερ ᾧ παντα τα μεγαλα εστι μεγαλα, τῳ ὑπερεχοντι (*hōsper hōi panta ta megala esti megala, tōi hyperechonti*)</note>. Stephens, in his annotations, says he would prefer if the word "by which" <note>original Greek: ᾧ (*hōi*)</note> were omitted. Similar passages can be found in Plato to justify the expression as it stands. But if it were necessary to make an alteration, we would surely suppose the error lies in the last words and read them as: "the surpassing something" <note>original Greek: το ὑπερεχον TI (*to hyperechon ti*)</note>. For in the sentence immediately following, where this comparison is used to define the term, Plato uses the same expression: "so we say also of the beautiful, by which all things are beautiful—what might it be?" <note>original Greek: ουτω δη φαμεν και το καλον, ᾧ καλα παντα εστι,—TI αν ειη (*houtō dē phamen kai to kalon, hōi kala panta esti,—ti an eiē*)</note>.—S.

$^3$ Magnitude itself—as we have shown in the notes on the *Parmenides*—is, according to Plato, the cause of transcendency <note>term: transcendency—the state of excelling or surpassing others in size or quality.</note> in all things.—T. <note>original: "T." refers to the Platonist translator Thomas Taylor.</note>

**HIP.** It is rather the case, Socrates, that in those points men are ignorant of what is beautiful.

**SOC.** But this would not be the case if those beautiful things had the appearance of beauty added to their reality. They would have this appearance if "the becoming" <note>original: *to prepon*, meaning the fitting or appropriate.</note> were the beautiful itself, and caused things—as you say it does—both to be and to appear beautiful, bestowing on them real and apparent beauty at the same time. Hence it follows that if "the becoming" is that by which things are made truly beautiful, then "the becoming" must be the "beautiful" which we are searching for, and not merely that by which things are made beautiful in appearance. But if "the becoming" is that by which things are made beautiful only in appearance, it cannot be the "beautiful" which we are searching for; for the true "beautiful" provides the reality of beauty. It is not in the power of the same thing to cause both the appearance and the reality—not only in the case of beauty, but in any other instance whatever. Let us choose now: which of these two shall we take for "the becoming"? That which causes the appearance of beauty, or that which causes the reality?

**HIP.** "The becoming," Socrates, I believe, must be that which causes the appearance.

**SOC.** Oh no, Hippias! Our discovery of the beautiful has fled away and escaped us. For "the becoming" has turned out to be something different from "the beautiful."

**HIP.** So it seems; and quite unexpectedly, too.

**SOC.** However, my friend, we must not give it up for lost. I still have some hope left that the nature of the beautiful may come forth into the light and show itself.

**HIP.** It will show itself with great clarity, Socrates, beyond doubt; for it is by no means difficult to find. I am positive that if I were to go aside for a little while and consider it by myself, I could describe it to you with an accuracy beyond anything ever so accurate.

**SOC.** Ah! Do not talk, Hippias, in such a confident tone. You see what trouble it has given us already; I fear it might grow angry with us and run away even further than before. But I talk idly; for I assume you will easily find it out when you are alone. Yet, in the name of the Gods, I beg you to make the discovery while I am still with you; and if it is agree— <meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence, continuing on the next page.</meta>

If it is agreeable to you, accept me as your companion in this search, just as you did before. We say, for example, that eyes are beautiful—not those that look as if they cannot see, but those that appear to have a strong faculty of sight and are useful for the purpose of seeing. Don't we?

**SOC.** And don't we also call the whole body beautiful based on its utility? One body might be beautiful for racing, another for wrestling. This applies to all animals too—such as a beautiful horse, rooster, or quail. The same applies to all sorts of household utensils and transport for traveling abroad, whether they are land vehicles or ships and barges for the sea. It also applies to musical instruments and the tools used in other crafts; to these, you may also add moral rules and laws. 

We call almost everything of this kind "beautiful" for the same reason: based on the purpose for which it was born, made, or established. We pronounce it beautiful according to how it is useful, for what purpose, and on what occasion. But something that is useless in every respect, we declare to be totally void of beauty. Do you not share this opinion, Hippias?

**HIP.** I do.

**SOC.** We are correct, therefore, in saying that above all things, the useful proves to be the beautiful.

**HIP.** Most certainly right, Socrates.

**SOC.** Now, isn't something that can perform or achieve an effect "useful" insofar as it has power and ability? Whereas something powerless and unable is "useless"?

**SOC.** But the profitable is that which effects or produces good.

tiful and chop it into pieces. You treat everything in nature that becomes the subject of your discussion in the same way, splitting and dividing it <gloss>1</gloss>. Consequently, you are unaware of the true magnitude of things <gloss>2</gloss>,

---

<gloss>1</gloss> It was Socrates's custom in conversation, whatever the subject might be, to rise to the consideration of the subject in general; to divide it into its various species; and to distinguish each species from the others by some specific character, in order to arrive at the definite and precise nature of the very thing in question.—S. <note>Referring to the translator/commentator, likely Floyer Sydenham.</note></gloss>

<gloss>2</gloss> According to the Platonic doctrine, all things in nature, distinguished into their various general and specific kinds, are the manifestation of universal form and beauty. To make this principle—which defines every part of nature—appear in a clearer light, the opposite principle, "infinitude" or the infinite, is presented here. Among the various descriptions of it given by the ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "physiologists"</note>, that of Anaxagoras is singled out from the rest; probably because it provides the strongest contrast. According to his doctrine, the infinite is—if we may use the expression—the most infinite of all; or, as Simplicius styles it, *infinitely infinite* <note>original: *απειρακιϛ απειρον* (apeirakis apeiron)</note>. A brief summary of this may be necessary to fully understand the passage before us.

Down to the time of Anaxagoras, all philosophers agreed on the doctrine of a single infinite, material principle of things. Pythagoras and his followers held this to be nothing more than a common underlying matter of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water), or the primary forms of nature; from the various combinations of these four, in different proportions, all other natural bodies are made. The disciples of Anaximander supposed it to have a form, though a vague and undefined one, out of which all opposites arose through separation. Others imagined the infinite to have some specific and distinct form, and these thinkers were further divided. For some, led by Thales, thought it was a watery fluid or moisture, filled with the seeds of all things; they believed everything was produced from some seed-like principle by development and expansion through the action of the fluid. In the opinion of others, such as Anaximenes and his school, it was a kind of air; through the thinning <note>original: "rarefaction"</note> and thickening <note>original: "condensation"</note> of this air, other large and uniform types of matter were produced throughout the universe, and by mixing, these created smaller composite things.

Such were the most ancient accounts of the material cause of things and their origin from the one infinite. But Anaxagoras forged a new path to the knowledge of nature. Denying the origin of things from any single infinite source—whether defined or undefined, formed or unformed; denying the existence of any primary or elementary bodies; and denying all essential change in nature, including any alteration in anything except what arose from local motion or the shifting of parts from one body to another—he taught that the particles <note>original: "corpuscula"</note>, or component parts of things, were always what they are at present. He argued that the forms of nature, though innumerable in their kinds, were composed of similar and uniform <note>original: "homogeneous"</note> parts. Furthermore, he taught that each of these minute bodies, though uniform with the whole of which it was a part, was itself composed of different and diverse <note>original: "heterogeneous"</note> parts, infinite in number; for there are no limits to smallness in nature. These infinitely small, diverse bodies were of all kinds, so that all things were, in some measure, present together everywhere. Each of those particles, apparently so uniform, contained all the various principles of things; and the predo- <note>The note continues onto the next page.</note></gloss>

---

<note>This note continues from the previous page, explaining Anaxagoras’s theory of matter.</note>

...the dominance of some one of these principles—that is, the quantity of it exceeding that of the rest—constituted the nature of each minute body. This fitted it for union with bodies of the same kind <note>original: "homogeneous"</note>, meaning other bodies where the same principle was predominant. Since all things are in perpetual motion—which first began and is continued by an active mind <note>Anaxagoras's concept of 'Nous' or Divine Intellect</note> that organizes all things—the dominance of each principle was continually fluctuating and changing. The destruction of the current dominant principle resulted in the dissolution of each temporary being, and a new dominance by some other principle resulted in the birth <note>original: "generation"</note> of what we call a new being. 

For instance, although every drop of water contains <term>air particles</term> <note>original: "aërial particles"</note> within it, as soon as these begin to predominate in any watery drop, it rises into the air. By receiving an increase of the <term>air principle</term> <note>original: "aërial principle"</note> there, it gradually becomes united to the air. Similarly, air refines into fire and thickens into water through the overpowering influence of one or the other of these neighboring principles, with which it has always maintained a hidden relationship. 

In the same way, the earthy particles accumulated in water produce mud, which gradually hardens into earth, then into various minerals, stones, and metals, according to the kind of earth predominant in each place through motion. These again crumble into common earth, from which all the various plants <note>original: "vegetable beings"</note> arise in a similar manner, nourished and increased by the accumulation of similar particles. They eventually fall and are dissolved again through the decay and reduction of those particles whose superior number and strength to resist others of a different kind had previously constituted that being. 

In the same manner, all parts of animals—whether muscular, membranous, bony, or otherwise—receive nourishment or suffer decay by the addition or subtraction of <term>similar particles</term> <note>original: "homogeneous particles"</note>. It will be easy for a thinking mind to follow nature acting in this method, according to <term>Anaxagoras</term>, through all things. 

The principles of things are thus made infinite, not only in number and minuteness, but because there is also a continuity of <term>homoiomeries</term> <note>original: "ὁμοιομερειαι" (homogeneous parts)</note>, or particles of the same kind, <term>connected by contact</term> <note>original: "ἁφη συνεχιζομεναι" (linked by touch)</note> throughout the universe. Every <term>homoiomery</term> <note>original: "ὁμοιομερια"</note>—that is, every kind of thing—is a natural body, infinite in size and infinitely divisible into parts that completely agree with their own kind. 

<term>Simplicius</term>—in his commentary on the <term>Physics</term> of <term>Aristotle</term>, to which invaluable storehouse of <term>ancient natural science</term> <note>original: "antient physiology"</note> we owe most of this note—draws the same conclusion. His words are these: 

"From the account now given, it is easy to understand that if everything is separated out of everything, and all things are in all things—not only the whole universe, but every individual part within it—it will be infinitely infinite, not only in the number of its parts, but also in size." <note>original Greek: "εκ των ειρημενων προχειρον συννοειν, οτι ει παν εκ παντος εκκρινεται, και παντα εν πασιν εστιν, ου μονον το παν αλλα και εκαστον, ου τω πληθει μονον αλλα και τω μεγεθει, απειρακις απειρον εσται"</note>

To venture it for once, however; tell me—is not each of us one person? And is not the state of being "one" a circumstance that accompanies our existence?

**HIPPIAS.** Without doubt.

**SOCRATES.** If each of us is one, then each of us must also be an odd number. Or do you think that "one" is not an odd number?

**HIPPIAS.** I think it is.

**SOCRATES.** Are we both "odd" when taken together, then, notwithstanding the fact that we are two people?

**HIPPIAS.** That is absurd, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** But taken both together, we are an even number. Is it not so?

**HIPPIAS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Now, because both of us together are even, does it follow from this that each of us individually is also even?

**HIPPIAS.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** There is not, therefore, such an absolute necessity—as you claimed just now—that whatever we both were together, each should be the same; and that whatever each of us was individually, the same we must both be together.

**HIPPIAS.** Not in cases such as these, I acknowledge; but it still holds true in the cases I listed before.

**SOCRATES.** That is enough, Hippias. I am satisfied with this acknowledgment: that it appears to be so in some cases, but in others it is different. For, if you remember how this present dispute arose, I said that the pleasures of sight and hearing could not derive their beauty from any circumstance which belonged to each but not to both; nor from any which belonged to both but not to each. Instead, I argued that their beauty was derived from something which they had belonging to both of them in common, and specifically to each individually. I said this because you had admitted that they were beautiful both together and each separately. From this, I drew the conclusion that they were indebted for their beauty to some essence <note>original: "some being"</note> whose presence always accompanied them both, and not to something that was lacking in either one. I still remain of the same mind. But answer me as if we were now beginning this last inquiry from the start. If pleasure through sight and pleasure through hearing are both supposed to be beautiful—both together and each individually—tell me, does not the cause of their beauty accompany both of them taken together, and also each considered separately?

**HIPPIAS.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** They are not beautiful, therefore—either of them—because of any quality that belongs to each one by itself. We cannot argue from the individual to the pair, nor can we infer what they both are together from what each is separately. So, we might claim that both of these pleasures are beautiful together according to our current <term>hypothesis</term> <note>original: "hypothesis" — a starting proposition or theory used as a basis for reasoning</note> of the beautiful; however, this theory will not support us in claiming that either one is beautiful on its own. **HIPPIAS.** So it appears.

**SOCRATES.** Shall we say then that both together are beautiful, but deny that each one is beautiful on its own?

**HIPPIAS.** What reason is there to think otherwise?

**SOCRATES.** This reason, my friend, as it seems to me: because we had assumed that certain qualities apply to things with this condition—that if they belonged to any two things together, they also belonged to each at the same time; and if they belonged to each, they also belonged to both. Or is there no reason why it should not be here as it is in numbers $^1$? Two numbers, taken together, may be even, even though each separately is perhaps odd or perhaps even. Or as it is in <term>magnitudes</term> <note>original: "magnitudes" — in this context, geometric measurements like the length of a line</note> $^2$; where two of them, though each is <term>incommensurable</term> <note>original: "incommensurable" — lacking a common measure; two lengths that cannot both be measured exactly by the same unit</note> with some third, yet both together may perhaps be commensurable with it, or perhaps incommensurable. $^1$ For instance: the two odd numbers, seven and three, together make the even number, ten; and the two even numbers, six and four, make that very same number. — <note>original: "S." refers to the translator/editor, likely Floyer Sydenham.</note>

So, whenever I return home and go inside, as soon as he hears me talking in this way, he asks me if I am not ashamed to speak with so much confidence about which professions and jobs are fine, or beautiful, or appropriate, when I have plainly shown myself to be so ignorant regarding beautiful things that I do not even know what the nature of beauty consists of. 

"And how can you judge," he says, "who has given a beautiful or fine speech, or who has done anything else in a handsome manner—and who has not—ignorant as you are of what the beautiful and handsome actually is? Since your mind is in such a state, is it even possible that you can think life is more desirable <note>original: "eligible"; in this context, it means worthy of being chosen or preferable.</note> to you than death?" 

Thus, I have had the misfortune, as I told you, to suffer insults <note>original: "obloquy"; meaning strong public criticism or verbal abuse.</note> and reproach from you, and to suffer insults and reproach from him as well. But, perhaps, it is necessary to endure all this. If I have received benefit or improvement from it, then there is no harm done. And I seem to myself, Hippias, to have been improved and benefited by the conversation of you both. For I think I now know the meaning of the proverb, "Beautiful things are difficult," <note>original: "Things of beauty are things of difficulty." This is a translation of the Greek proverb *chalepa ta kala*, which suggests that anything truly excellent requires great effort to achieve, understand, or maintain.</note> if I am not mistaken about myself.

# INTRODUCTION
### TO
# THE BANQUET.
---

**THE** composition, says Mr. Sydenham <gloss>1</gloss>, of this dialogue is of a unique style, and different from that of any other. For the principal part of it consists of oratorical speeches, spoken at a certain banquet or entertainment, by some of the company in their turns, upon a subject proposed by one of their number. The speakers are these six: Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus, Aristophanes, Agatho, and Socrates. Their several speeches are finely distinguished by different styles of oratory, and with great suitability <note>original: "propriety"</note> display the peculiar character of each speaker. 

The first of them, Phaedrus, was a young gentleman of the most noble <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> disposition—modest, sincere <note>original: "candid"</note>, and a lover of truth; refined, elevated, and heroic in his sentiments. He is the same person whose character Plato has drawn at length in the dialogue named after him. From that work, we also learn that he was a great admirer of Lysias the orator. Accordingly, the speech made by him in this Banquet strongly reflects the style of Lysias, as it is characterized by Plato <gloss>2</gloss> himself; the language being pure and elegant and the sentences <term>periods</term> <note>In classical rhetoric, a "period" is a complex sentence structured with several balancing clauses.</note> well-balanced and polished. However, he expresses the same sentiments over and over again in a variety of language; and where the sentiments are varied, they are void of all method or order in how they are arranged.

The next speech reported in the dialogue is that of Pausanias, who appears to have been a statesman or politician, and a great admirer...

of both the Spartan and the Athenian laws, and an enemy to all other systems of government and manners. The style of his oratory corresponds exactly with the character that Hermogenes gives us of the style used by Isocrates. He is clear and distinct, and divides his subject properly; he is generous with ornaments and perhaps too precise <note>original: "nice"</note> and accurate. He is broad and extensive in his sentiments, though not in his expression, and takes a long path of argument before reaching his point. 

We find him, however, free from those faults for which that critic justly reprimands Isocrates. In the speech of Pausanias, there is no lack of energy or tediousness, nor is he guilty of preaching or being didactic <note>instructive in a patronizing or overly formal way</note>—vices in oratory that usually accompany old age. In Isocrates, these faults were perhaps mainly due to that cause; it is certain that most of his surviving orations were composed in the decline of his life, and that in the latest of them, those blemishes are the most obvious. 

But at the time when the speeches reported in this dialogue were supposed to have been spoken, Isocrates was in the prime of both his age and his eloquence. Add to this that Pausanias here excessively adopts some of those small stylistic flourishes for which Isocrates was remarkable in his younger years; such as antitheses <note>original: "$\alpha\nu\tau\iota\theta\epsilon\sigma\epsilon\iota\varsigma$"</note>, or oppositions; parisons <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\rho\iota\sigma\omega\sigma\epsilon\iota\varsigma$"</note>, or parities, where one member of a sentence answers another in either sound or sentiment; and those merely verbal or literal similarities, such as adnominations <note>wordplay using words with similar sounds but different meanings</note>, alliterations, and the same beginnings or endings of two or more words near one another. 

Plato ridicules one of these ornaments, when improperly used, through mockery as soon as the speech of Pausanias is ended. This alone seems sufficient evidence that Plato, in framing that speech, purposely imitated the style of Isocrates. His intention in doing so, as seems probable from the beginning of the speech itself, was to contrast those two celebrated orators, Lysias and Isocrates. He intended to show Lysias as treating his subject in a general, vague, and indeterminate way—wordy in his language but lacking substance <note>original: "jejune in matter"</note>—while the other is shown as distinguishing and methodical, full of substance, and detailed in particulars, having studied the nature of his subject more distinctly, philosophically, and minutely. [He] had the same goal in mind when mentioning Isocrates near the end of his dialogue called *Phaedrus*. The speaker following Pausanias is Eryximachus, who was a physician. His speech matches his profession, as he takes a broader view of the subject. Beginning with the human body in both health <note>original: "sound"</note> and disease <note>original: "morbid state"</note>, he proceeds like a dedicated scientist <note>original: "thorough naturalist"</note>, tracing his examples through every part of nature—earth, air, and sky—all the way up to the divine. 

In our humble opinion, his style of speaking aligns with what the critic Hermogenes<gloss>¹</gloss> says about Pericles: that among all the ancient orators (meaning those before the time of Demosthenes), Pericles possessed the most *deinotēs* <note>original: "δεινοτης"</note>. This term refers to a speaker's weight or influence with their audience and their power to stir the passions. According to that critic, an orator’s true mastery consists in the quick and skillful use of general knowledge, or applying it at the right moment while handling a topic. This mastery is most obvious, he says, when the *ennoiai* <note>original: "εννοιαι"</note>—the thoughts and sentiments—are deep, unusual, and original, yet still impactful and powerful. 

Both this genuine and apparent mastery are visible in the only surviving speech by Pericles, which Thucydides included in his history. Both also seem to be used somewhat deliberately <note>original: "affectedly"</note> in Eryximachus's speech; we assume, therefore, that Plato wrote this speech to imitate Pericles’s style. 

After him speaks Aristophanes, the famous comic playwright. The same rich humor and lively, overflowing wit found in his surviving plays also define his speech in the *Banquet*. 

The next speech is given by Agathon, the host of the party. At this time, Agathon was a wealthy young man, generous, grand, and refined in his manners. He was widely admired for his physical beauty and praised by Plato in the *Protagoras* for his intelligence <note>original: "fine parts"</note> and naturally good character. His talent drew him toward poetry, especially tragedy. He was so successful in this field that he won the top prize over all his competitors in one of the annual playwriting contests held during the festival of Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine and theater</note>. It was on this occasion that he hosted the party for his friends which Plato has made famous forever in this magnificent dialogue. We have no...

<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

[This is the only] piece of his writing surviving <note>original: "extant"</note>; but it is very likely that the speech attributed to him here provides a fair representation of his style. The language used is extremely poetical, ornate <note>original: "florid"</note>, and full of metaphors. While the thoughts are wonderfully elegant, ingenious, and imaginative, they lack even the appearance of being based on truth.

The last speaker on the subject is *Socrates*, and his speech is in every respect worthy of the man. In all his conduct, he was modest and careful to avoid even the slightest bit of showing off. In all his conversation, he was concerned above all else with finding the truth in every subject,^1 and he made that his primary goal in all his disputes, inquiries, and research. Whenever he led a conversation, he began with things that were easy, common, and obvious, but gradually rose to speculations that were most difficult, sublime, and excellent. 

Consistent with this character, he delivers nothing in his speech as coming from himself. Instead, he introduces another person who takes on the authoritative <note>original: "magisterial"</note> air of a teacher, yet remains humble, gentle, and friendly. This person is *Diotima*, a lady who was highly respected at that time for her communication with the gods and her predictions of future events. 

The speech of *Socrates* contains the retelling of a conversation between himself and this prophetic lady. He puts the lessons he wishes to teach into her mouth to suggest <note>original: "insinuate"</note> that his speech was unquestionably true, worthy of being considered divinely inspired, and a source of knowledge about divine things. The eloquence of this speech illustrates the doctrine taught by *Plato* in his dialogues *Phaedrus* and *Gorgias*: that the person who best knows the truth of their subject and intends the well-being of those they are trying to persuade—the person who has the most knowledge of human nature and the various temperaments of men, and can therefore adapt their speech to the mood of their audience—is likely to be the most capable and best speaker. Other qualifications required to be an orator are relatively minor <note>original: "mean"</note> and, as far as the art of speaking is concerned, easily learned. 

The truth of this doctrine was soon after fully confirmed by *Demosthenes*. By forming himself according to the rules laid down by *Plato*, he became at once the most perfect patriot, politician, and orator of his age (and I had almost said of any age).

the stage—Alcibiades, a young nobleman of the highest rank in Athens, possessed of great natural and acquired talents, primarily in military matters, but of loose and thoroughly corrupt <note>original: "dissolute and thoroughly debauched"</note> manners. Being ambitious for power and a role in government too early, before he was prepared for them by knowledge and experience, he had for some time been a follower of Socrates. He saw that Socrates' eloquence and reasoning always triumphed over those of the Sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized by Socrates for prioritizing persuasion over truth</note>, and he hoped to acquire the same superior power of persuasion through Socrates' company and conversation. His goal was to use that power with the people to satisfy his own ambitious plans. 

He is introduced into the banquet room far from sober, and his behavior and speech (for he is invited by the company to give a speech) perfectly match his character. The subject he speaks on is supposedly, and in all appearance, unrelated to the topic discussed by the others—as his chaotic and unthinking state would suggest—but in reality, it is far from irrelevant. Plato has not only woven this into the design of this incomparable dialogue but has made it one of the most essential parts. Without it, the work would have been completely flawed in the purpose for which it was created.* 

These speeches, along with the conversation and events at the banquet, form the main part of this dialogue. They are presented not as a play but as a narrative. The introduction is partly narrative and partly dramatic, which makes it somewhat complex <note>original: "intricate"</note>. The dialogue opens with a conversation between only two people, Apollodorus and a friend of his, though others are present whom playwrights call "mute characters" <note>Characters who are present on stage but have no speaking lines</note>. At the very beginning, Apollodorus describes a short conversation he recently had with Glaucon <note>original: "Glauco"</note>. He tells his friend that he then gave Glaucon an account of what happened at the banquet hosted by Agathon <note>original: "Agatho"</note>. This account, repeated by him here, makes up the rest of the dialogue. He says it was told to him by Aristodemus, one of the guests, who began his story by recounting a short conversation between Socrates and himself, along with some other events leading up to the banquet. This same account, now given by Apollodorus to his friend and the company at that friend’s house, immediately introduces the story of that truly noble entertainment. <meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato’s dialogue "The Banquet" (The Symposium), moving from the characterization of Alcibiades to a summary of the various arguments about the nature of love presented by the different speakers.</meta>

<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

It is usually and very properly entitled, "Concerning Love," because the philosophical study <note>original: "speculation"</note> of love is its leading object.

With respect to the speeches, that of Phædrus treats the word *love* in a general sense, so as to include love toward persons of the same sex (commonly called friendship) as well as love toward persons of a different sex—specifically and prominently styled love. 

Pausanias distinguishes between love of the mind and love merely of the body, proving them to be affections of very different kinds because they produce very different effects. 

Eryximachus considers love as that universal principle in nature which attracts, unites, or associates one thing to another in a regular way. The effect of its operation is harmony or concord. It is that which also heals the breaches made by the opposite, disuniting, and dividing principle, which is the cause of irregular motions and of discord. 

Aristophanes treats love as other writers of comedy do, taking it only in the coarsest <note>original: "grossest"</note> sense of the word, as it refers to the passion common to humans and all brute animals. 

And Agatho talks about it in a vague manner without any determined or fixed meaning at all, taking it in various senses. Usually, he uses it to mean the refinement of that passion between the sexes, but sometimes for a great liking or attachment of the mind to any object. Then, all at once, he uses the word—like Eryximachus—to signify concord and harmony, not only between rational beings but even among the unthinking parts of nature. 

But when Socrates begins to speak upon the subject, he goes much deeper into it by degrees. In the first place, he establishes <note>original: "premises"</note> certain universal truths relating to love: that the object of it is beauty; the essence of it is desire; and its aim or end is the possession of beauty, or, if already possessed of it, the perpetuity of that possession. 

Next, he considers love as the desire for good; for whatever is beautiful is also good, so far as it is beautiful. Love, specifically so called, is part of that universal love or desire for good common to all beings, both intelligent and sentient. He considers this universal love, or desire for good, as the link between the eternal nature and the mortal—between the fullness of good and the total lack of it. 

He considers that the aim of this desire, according to a certain property of it observed before, is not only to enjoy good but to immortalize that enjoyment. The desire for immortality, therefore, is of necessity, he says, attached <note>original: "annexed"</note> to the desire for good, or the love of beauty. But personal immortality being impossible to be attained by any being whose nature is mor—

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato’s "Banquet," specifically summarizing Socrates’ speech (which recounts the teachings of Diotima). The text begins mid-word, completing the thought that all mortal beings seek immortality through procreation.</meta>

...mortal, every such being, prompted by nature, seeks to continue itself and its enjoyment of what is good in the only way possible: through the propagation of its species and the production of another being resembling itself—another "self"—to succeed it and to continue, as it were, the enjoyment of that same good. 

Therefore, the love of that beauty—which makes every animal most attracted to the beautiful members of its own kind—is accompanied by an instinct or natural desire to unite with it, and thus to generate another animal of the same species. From physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> beauty and that lower species of love regarding it, a person naturally proceeds further as their mind opens and improves. They attain a vision of that beauty which is seen only by the eye of the intellect: the character and disposition of a kindred mind. Fired with the love that attends the sight of this mental beauty, they are drawn to it. 

To this love is also joined, says Socrates, the desire of "generating"—of stamping one's own thoughts upon that other mind, and of raising and nurturing between them an intellectual offspring <note>original: "progeny"</note> of noble <note>original: "generous"</note> sentiments and beautiful ideas. By means of this union and this enjoyment—that is, through conversation that improves the understanding—the mind, he observes, rises higher. It reaches a point where it can view beauty in the subjects of the conversation themselves: first in virtuous pursuits, studies, and employments; and next in the sciences and every branch of knowledge. 

In the "embrace" of these various forms of beauty, the mind generates an offspring of the most beautiful and durable kind. The poet produces his immortal writings; the hero, through the force of his example, creates constant copies of his virtue; the founder of a state <note>original: "civil polities"</note>, through his institutions, initiates a long succession of patriotic actions; and the lawmaker creates wise and beneficial laws to bless future generations. 

But if the soul is endowed with a genius of the highest kind, it does not stop here, nor does it fix its attachment on any one of these mental excellencies or beauties in particular. The genuine lover of truth rises from these to the survey of that universal, original, and ideal <note>original: "exemplar"</note> beauty from which everything beautiful proceeds, both in the intellectual <note>original: "intelligible"</note> world and the world of the senses <note>original: "sensible"</note>. Plato calls the love and pursuit of this supreme beauty "philosophy"; and he attributes the birth and growth of true virtue to the "embrace" or enjoyment of this beauty, and to no other cause.

...offspring <note>Continuing from the previous page: "the mind generates an offspring..."</note> in the character of Socrates, as one who had been initiated into the mysteries of love—that perfection of virtue which such an initiation is capable of achieving. Mr. Sydenham <note>Floyer Sydenham (1710–1787), a renowned translator of Plato whose work was later completed by Thomas Taylor.</note>, therefore, was very unfortunately convinced to abandon his plan of publishing his translation of this speech; he was quite mistaken <note>original: "mistaekn"</note> in thinking that some part of it is so crude or indecent <note>original: "grossly indecent"</note> that it might offend virtuous people and encourage the wicked. For as will appear in our notes, this apparent indecency is introduced in accordance with the symbolism <note>original: "machinery"</note> of the ancient mysteries, with the sole purpose of purifying the reader from everything improper, and to free them, in short, from common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> love, by awakening the mind's eye to the vision of objects that are indescribably beautiful and truly divine.

<margin>¹ Modern interpreters, focusing on the more elevated part of Socrates' speech but ignoring its general direction <note>original: "drift"</note>, call this dialogue metaphysical or theological. Among the ancient Platonists, Albinus—acting as if he were primarily focused on the speech of Pausanias and relating all other speeches to it—calls it "political." —S. <note>The "S." likely refers to Sydenham.</note></margin>

The ancients, with good reason, generally rank this dialogue among those of the ethical <note>original: "ethic"</note> class¹; however, its character is of a mixed type—that is, partly narrative and partly dramatic. Its overall spirit <note>original: "genius"</note> is defined by its instructional <note>original: "didactic"</note> part: the speech of Socrates. The reasoning in his speech is entirely analytical, breaking love down into its core principles and tracing all beauty upward to the source from which it flows to every level of existence.

->*SCENE⁷.—Principally within the City of ATHENS.*<-

---

¹ Readers of Plato will notice that before each of his dialogues, the names of the speakers are listed. They are not organized by social rank or their importance to the dialogue—as is the custom with modern playwrights before their tragedies and comedies—but rather in the order in which they first appear. Since two or more people must appear together in every scene of conversation, they are named in the order in which they first speak. This follows the way characters were listed in the dramatic writings of the ancients.

² Apollodorus was a disciple of Socrates, but he had not been a student for very long at this time. His character in the dialogue is therefore appropriately defined by the intensity of his devotion to philosophy and his admiration for his master.

³ This friend is not mentioned by name. This fact alone has led some to imagine that Plato meant to represent himself as the friend of Apollodorus.

⁴ If this is the same Glaucon who was Plato's brother, and if Plato is the friend introduced here, it seems strange that Apollodorus would speak to Plato about his own brother as if he were completely unknown to him, only mentioning his name later as if by accident.

⁵ Aristodemus was a constant, humble follower of Socrates.

⁶ For the descriptions of all the following individuals, we refer to the first part of the preceding Introduction.

⁷ The conversation between Apollodorus and his friend—the only "present-day" dramatic part of the dialogue, as the rest is a narrative—seems to take place at this friend's house. This is as suitable a place as any for the long story Apollodorus had to tell, and the most appropriate place to visit him for that purpose. The road from Phalerum <note>original: "Phalerus," the port city of Athens</note> to Athens, a long walk, is fittingly made the setting for the conversation between Apollodorus and Glaucon. Apollodorus explains that he gave the same long recital to Glaucon during that walk. The brief conversation between Aristodemus and Socrates occurs in the street; by doing this, the sudden interruption of their talk fits the appropriateness of the setting. Finally, Agatho's house is the main setting for the most significant part of the work: the speeches given at the dinner party. —S. <note>This "S." refers to the editor/translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

### APOLLODORUS.

For it happened * a few days ago <note>original Greek: πρῴην (*proen*)</note>, as I was walking up to the city from my house in Phalerus <margin>Phalerus was a seaport town about four or five miles from Athens.</margin>, that an acquaintance of mine, who was going the same way, saw me a considerable distance ahead and called out to me. You man of Phalerus! Won't you wait a moment until I catch up to you?" So, I stopped and waited for him. 

As soon as he reached me, he said, "Apollodorus, I was just looking for you. I have a great desire to know exactly what happened in the conversation between Agatho, Socrates, Alcibiades, and the rest of the party at that dinner where the subject of their discussion was Love. I would be very glad if you could inform me what was said on that occasion. The person who gave me an account of it—which he heard from Phoenix, the son of Philippus—told me that you knew every detail. He also said that he himself did not claim to have a perfect or exact memory of the story. But first," he said, "tell me: were you yourself one of the guests?"

"It seems very clear," I replied, "that your source did not give you a very accurate account of the timing of that conversation, if you think it happened recently enough for me to have been there."

"I really did imagine so," he replied.

## THE BANQUET.

Glaucon? Do you not know that Agatho has not been in Athens for many years? It has not even been three years since I first became a follower of Socrates and began, as I have continued ever since, to observe and study all his words and actions every day. Before that time, I wandered here and there, wherever chance led me, imagining I was well-occupied, when in reality no person was in such a wretched state as I was. You are in that same state now, giving every study and every pursuit preference over philosophy.

"Stop scolding me," he said, "and tell me when that conversation took place."

"Before we were considered grown men," I replied. "It was at the time when Agatho brought his first tragedy to the stage and won the prize for it. It was the very next day after he and his chorus members <gloss>1</gloss> had offered the traditional sacrifice of thanks for his victory."

"Then it seems it was a long time ago," he said. "But who was it," he continued, "who related the conversation to you? Was it Socrates himself?"

"Not Socrates, by Zeus <note>original: 'Jupiter'—the 18th-century translator used the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note>," I replied; "but the same person who told it to Phoenix. <note>Interpretation of Apollodorus's character: The conclusion of it represents Apollodorus as a simple and sincere man, but with a kind of mental weakness that made him remarkably hasty, negligent of social graces, and prone to speaking thoughtlessly and without discretion. —S. <note>original: S. likely refers to the translator/commentator Floyer Sydenham</note></note>

<gloss>1</gloss> Socrates, in his ordinary way of life, accustomed himself to endure voluntary hardships. From this he gained an advantage: he suffered less than other men when called to bear hardships that were necessary. In the same way, the Cynics and Stoics—likely in imitation of Socrates—did many things for the sake of training <note>original Greek: askēseōs eneka</note>; that is, for the purpose of habituating their minds and bodies to endurance through practice. However, Socrates, unlike the Cynics, kept this consistent with a regard for the decencies of civil and social life, a proper compliance with custom, and conformity to fashion. He always readily relaxed his severity whenever, as on this occasion, he judged the practice of it to be unreasonable. This politeness distinguishes Socrates's manners from the savage rudeness of Aristodemus mentioned earlier. We cannot help but think that these two seemingly slight details in the description of these two people were mentioned by Plato so close together on purpose to make that distinction easier to notice. We learn from **Aelian**, in *Historical Miscellany, book 4, chapter 18*, that Socrates was accused—probably by the Cynics—of being fastidious and particular about his house, his bed, and his fine slippers. This confirms the truth of our observation in this note. —S.

He believes Plato failed to consider that Homer puts these words in the mouth of the god Apollo, who was a biased friend to the Trojans and consequently an enemy to Menelaus. Athenæus argues strongly against Apollo and Plato, using many examples from Homer to prove that Menelaus was no coward. In reality, however, he only proves himself to be a bitter enemy of Plato. To insult him, he misinterprets Homer, who used the word "soft" <note>original: μαλθακον</note> in that passage to mean nothing more than being "relaxed in strength" or "weak" <note>original: ανειμενον τη ισχυι, ασθενη</note>, as the ancient commentator <term>scholiast</term> correctly explains. However, a better critic than Athenæus—unless they were well-versed in Plato's unique writing style—might more fairly criticize him for the seemingly dull and long-winded nature of this side-discussion about the proverb. Indeed, if this were merely a tangent, that criticism would be valid. But Plato intended it as a functional part of the dialogue.

<meta>catchword: demus,</meta>

<note>
This note is highly important to this dialogue; it serves to guard the text against the misinterpretation to which it might be vulnerable from people of severe, sour, and spiteful tempers. It signifies that not everyone was worthy or properly qualified to partake, as it were, of the banquet Plato has provided. It points out for whom it was particularly improper to be present: the *tous malthakous* <note>original: τους μαλθακους</note>, or *molles* <note>original: Latin for "soft"</note>—the luxurious, or men of weak and effeminate minds and manners. In this sense, the word *malthakos* is often used; see especially Xenophon in *Memorabilia*, book 3, chapter 2, section 10, where it is applied to lustful love and opposed to that which inspires the sentiments of friendship. 

Homer, it is true, had a different meaning, such as we have explained before; and Plato uses a kind of catachresis <term>the use of a word in a way that departs from its traditional meaning</term> in adapting this passage to his purpose. But it was sufficient for him if it was applicable in any way. Some passage or other from Homer had to be introduced here to keep the reader's mind focused on it for some time. This observation holds true throughout all of Plato’s writings: whenever he cites a verse from any poet, especially from Homer, he does not do it—like writers of a lower class—to decorate the plainness of prose with fine scraps of poetry. Rather, his goal is always to strike the reader's mind more forcibly when conveying some important meaning, making it sink deeper into the memory; or else to prepare the reader for something significant that is to follow by introducing it with the solemnity of verse and the authority of the poet, which carried much weight in those days. —S. <note>“S.” refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>
</note>

Then, turning to me, he said, "Aristodemus, take your place next to Eryximachus." And immediately he ordered a servant to come and wash my feet <note>original: "wash my feet clean"</note>, so that I might take my place upon the couch. Just then the

---

¹ The original Greek reads: *And he said that the servant should wash me, so that he might lie down somewhere* <note>original: "Και εμε εφη απονιζειν τον παιδα, ινα που κατακεοιτο."</note>. The remarkable <term>enallage</term> <note>a grammatical shift from one person or tense to another</note>, or transition here—speaking of himself by switching from the first person ("me") to the third person ("he")—is not unusual in Plato’s writing, but it is too bold and would be a <term>solecism</term> <note>a grammatical mistake or intentional breaking of rules</note> in English. Translated as literally as possible, the sentence runs: "Immediately he ordered the [proper] servant to wash off [the dirt] from me, so that [he says] he may lie down somewhere." We have added the words in brackets to complete the sense. The first part of the sentence is narrative, while the latter part represents Agathon speaking. However, the word *ephē* (he said), having been used just before in a different sense, is omitted here, probably to avoid repetition. Henri Estienne <note>original: "Harry Stephens," a famous 16th-century printer and scholar</note>, not realizing this transition, had doubts about the correct reading of this passage. He tried, unnecessarily, to fix it by changing *katakeoito* (he might lie down) to *katakeoimēn* (I might lie down). The same learned printer and editor proposed a similar change in a passage of the *Euthyphro* where there is a similar transition, failing to observe this unique feature of Plato’s style, as Dr. Forster has wisely noted in his commentary on those five dialogues (page 328).—S. <note>“S.” refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

² In that refined age, luxury and an excess of delicate manners had become so common even among the brave Greeks that when they ate their evening meal (supper)—which was their main meal of the day, much like modern dinner—they did not sit on chairs, stools, or benches at the table like modern Europeans. Nor did they sit or lie on mats or carpets on the floor like some Eastern nations. Instead, their custom was to recline on sofas, couches, or day-beds. The heads of these couches were placed at the sides of a rectangular table and covered with cushions; the guests would then lean on their elbows. Therefore, it was necessary for Aristodemus to have his dirty feet washed before he was fit to lie on one of those sofas. Plato likely included this small detail to confirm the earlier description of Aristodemus's habits and to highlight how they contrasted with those of Socrates, who required no such ceremony because he had already washed.

"Let it be so then, if you think it best," said Agathon; "but let the rest of us, however, proceed to supper."

You know it is not my way to do so on these occasions. Immediately after this, he said, they went to supper, but Socrates was still missing. Agathon, therefore, would every now and <meta>then</meta>

---

Different from either of these is the case of Alcibiades, further on in the dialogue. For, as he comes in drunk and dirty, in the midst of his rowdy <note>original: "rakehelly"</note> rambles about the town, slippers are ordered to be brought to him, but not for his feet to be washed, as he was wearing shoes. Plato is so meticulous in his detail of every circumstance that may help to illustrate the characters of those persons he introduces. Whatever weight there is in this observation—be it great or small—the same amount of importance lies in the blunder committed by all the Latin translators, and by the Italian translator after them, in making Agathon order water to wash the hands of Aristodemus instead of his feet. In the same degree, praise is due to the judgment and accuracy of Monsieur Racine, who, in his translation of this dialogue into French, corrects this error. Although he might naturally be assumed to be prejudiced in favor of washing the hands before meals, according to both modern French fashion and ancient Greek custom, he correctly explains Agathon’s orders. He was no doubt aware that washing the feet of Aristodemus, not his hands, was a proper preparation for him to rest his legs upon the sofa <note>The "sofa" or couch used for reclining at a Greek symposium</note>. But Racine omits Agathon's reason for giving those orders, even though it is expressly mentioned by Plato; this was probably because he was unsure how to translate the words, being puzzled by the doubts raised about them by Stephens <note>Henri Estienne, also known as Stephanus, a famous 16th-century scholar and printer</note>, as mentioned in the preceding note.—S.

Agathon then began giving orders to his servants to call Socrates in; but I, said Aristodemus, constantly opposed it. At length Socrates, having stayed away, as usual, not very long, entered—around the time, at the latest, when supper was half finished.

Agathon then, who was reclining on the couch at the lower end of the table alone, said, "Come here, Socrates, and lie down by me; so that by being close to you, I may benefit from that wisdom $^1$, which you newly acquired in the porch. For it is plain that you found it and are in possession of it; otherwise you would never have stopped your search."

Socrates then, sitting down on the couch, said, "It would be well, Agathon, if wisdom were the kind of thing that could flow from those who have plenty of it into those who lack it, simply by sitting close to one another and being in contact—much like water flowing through a wool thread $^2$ from a fuller vessel into an emptier one..."

---

<note>The following commentary (signed "S.") was written by the translator, Floyer Sydenham, to explain the literary artistry of Plato's dialogue.</note>

...the alteration produced in him by studying that wisdom. And for the same reason, mention is made of the many admirers of that truly admirable man. But all these circumstances are made to appear simple and artless, the more irresistibly to achieve their intended effect upon the reader’s mind.

The short conversation which follows, between Apollodorus and his friend, continues this same purpose; but it goes to even greater lengths of praise in the character description given there of Socrates. Then comes a narration of some small details, occurring immediately before the celebrated banquet, serving to influence the reader’s mind with an idea of the excellence of the company assembled at Agathon’s. Of this kind is the extraordinary care which we see Socrates has taken with his person and dress, as a proper mark of respect to that assembly; and another of the same kind is the argument which he politely urges to Aristodemus, when he is persuading him to join the party.

The circumstances that follow—the profound meditation of Socrates on his way to Agathon’s, his stepping aside immediately upon arriving there, plainly with the design to finish his reflections, his staying away until supper was half over, and, during that stay, the conversation turning on Socrates as the principal person missing, together with the impatience of Agathon at his absence—are all designed on purpose to raise the expectation for the great figure Socrates is soon to make. They prepare the reader for the high part he is to play in a conversation where all the speakers shine in their individual characters, focusing on the finest and most interesting subject in human life: Love. —S.

We have information from a certain friend, a man of credit and truthfulness, that in some parts of Wiltshire a similar method is practiced for purifying water. They let it run down—in the manner we have described—along twisted wool, which they call "the twist." Cornarius says in his *Eclogae* <note>original: "Eclogæ," a collection of literary excerpts</note> that he cannot imagine what wool could have to do with the matter; therefore, he suggests that instead of the Greek word for "wool" <note>original Greek: εριου (*eriou*)</note>, we should read "pipe" or "instrument" <note>original Greek: οργάνου (*organou*)</note>, meaning a conduit pipe to convey water out of one full cistern into another. But by this alteration of the word, a very humorous part of the comparison is lost: the part representing wisdom streaming out of one man into another, as if by a strong transfer <note>original: "transpiration"</note> through their woolen cloth garments while they are in contact with one another.—S. <note>The translator, Floyer Sydenham</note>

$^1$ See the *Greater Hippias*.

$^2$ Socrates taught that outward things (the objects of the senses) were only images of those general ideas which are the objects of the mind or intellect. Like images in dreams, these sensory objects seemed to be the real things themselves. The Sophists of his time, on the other hand, agreed with the general public in maintaining that sensory objects were the only realities, and that those ideal things which Socrates praised as real and true were at best only shadows, outlines, or faint images of the former. Thus, each side seemed to the other to be in a dream, taking the image for the substance. Accordingly, it was debated between them who was the dreamer and who possessed the perception of a man whose mind was truly awake. See a passage to this effect in the *Theaetetus*. See also the fifth book of the *Republic*.—S.

$^3$ Plato used the word "wisdom" in two very different general senses. One was the philosophical sense, signifying the knowledge of nature, the principles of things, the science of the mind, or universal science. The other was the common sense; the word being at that time frequently used, as it is here, to signify excellence in any particular science or art—any knowledge or skill beyond common achievement. See the first part of Plato’s *Theages* and Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, book 6, chapter 7. Once this observation is made, it will be easy to determine which meaning is intended in every instance.—S.

$^4$ Those who were spectators at the performance of his tragedy.

I imagine, too, that many more of us are in the same condition, specifically those who were here at the entertainment yesterday. Consider, therefore, what way is the best to make drinking agreeable and easy for us."

Aristophanes then said, "It is a good proposal of yours, Pausanias, in my opinion, that we should by all means ensure ourselves an easy drinking session. For I am one of those who were 'well soaked' yesterday."

Upon hearing this, Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus, said, "Both of you are right. But I would be glad to be informed about one other person, and that is Agathon: in what condition of strength does he find himself regarding drinking?"

"I am by no means very strong at present myself either," said Agathon.

"It is lucky for us," said Eryximachus, "for me, and Aristodemus, and Phaedrus, and the rest of us here, if you 'stout men at the bottle' <note>Those with a high tolerance for alcohol</note> are unable to drink. For we are at all times weak in that respect. Socrates, indeed, I exclude; for he is equally well-qualified to drink or to leave it alone. Thus, he will be satisfied and ready to comply whichever course we take. Since none of the company, therefore, seems inclined to drink heavily, I may be less offensive, perhaps, if I speak the truth about this matter in plain terms. For I have been convinced myself, from the experience acquired in my profession <note>Eryximachus was a physician</note>, that hard drinking is usually attended with ill consequences. For this reason, I would neither choose to venture far in drinking myself, nor advise it to any other person, especially when burdened with the weight of the last night’s excess."

"As for me," said Phaedrus, addressing himself to Eryximachus, "I am accustomed to listen to your advice in everything, especially in what relates to your own profession; but now I find all the rest of the company are in the same agreeable mood."

This they all assented to, and agreed not to make the present meeting a drunken revel, but to drink, every man, just as much as might be agreeable to him.

<note>The following text is a lengthy commentary or footnote by the editor or translator, indicated by the asterisk.</note>

* It was customary with the ancients, at or after their feasts and banquets, to entertain their minds—without the laborious exercise of thinking—through those nobler senses which have a near affinity with the mind. They would regale their ears with vocal and instrumental music, and their eyes with spectacles that were either beautiful or wonderful. The performers and exhibitors in these several ways used to attend on these occasions.

Accordingly, in the banquet described by Xenophon, one of each kind of entertainer is introduced; the conversation begins only after they have all performed their parts. Plato has been accused of a lack of elegance and politeness because he did not follow the same method in his banquet, but instead dismissed the female musician so abruptly. Those who make this objection seem not to perceive the difference between the banquets described by these two excellent writers. Nor do they seem aware that they framed these, as well as others of their works, on different plans, even though they were on the same subjects. 

The guests at the entertainment given by Callias, as described by Xenophon, were a mixed company. They were composed partly of Autolycus and his friends, who either excelled in bodily exercises themselves or admired those skills in others. The rest were Socrates and his friends, whose abilities lay in the exercises of the mind. It was proper to entertain such a miscellaneous assembly in the usual manner. But the guests of Agathon were a select party who all had a high relish for the rational pleasures of conversation, good sense, wit, and humor. Every one of them probably expected to enjoy only those pleasures that evening, and to be able afterward to say to each other—as our poet Cowley <note>Abraham Cowley (1618–1667), an English poet</note> said to his friend Harvey:

> ->We spent it not in toys, in lust, or wine,<-
> ->But search of deep philosophy,<-
> ->Wit, eloquence, and poetry,<-
> ->Arts which I loved, for they, my friend, were thine.<-

It also seems as if Agathon had assembled them for that very purpose. He had held his grand feast the day before (as was the custom after a thanksgiving sacrifice), to which he had invited not only his friends and intimates but a crowd of acquaintances—everyone known to him. At that party, it appears they had drunk heavily and, consequently, conversed very little. 

Furthermore, at Callias’s entertainment, a proposal was made to furnish some talk by having each guest declare what he most valued in himself, and why. This gave rise to much pleasantry and many ingenious and shrewd sayings and repartees on various subjects. After this, Socrates alone gave a discourse of moderate length on the subject of Love, to allow time for short preparations being made outside for a play about Bacchus and Ariadne <note>A mythological play or "interlude" performed for the guests</note>. The whole event is short and ends early enough for some of the company to take their accustomed evening walk. 

But the conversation at Agathon’s had an air of solemnity and formality. It consisted of rhetorical speeches on a single subject, but so full and diverse in matter, and so long that they lasted until a very late hour of the night. A variety of other entertainments of a different kind would have been inconsistent, unnecessary, improper, and absurd.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham</note>

<sup>1</sup> <note>The following text is a lengthy commentary by the editor or translator explaining the history of Greek drama.</note> Ancient Greek tragedies were dramatic representations, each depicting a single event that was uncommon and important. These were chiefly events that had happened long before and were part of their mythical or ancient history. Because the whole of this history was not then recorded in any writings, but handed down through oral tradition, it was subject to much variety in the telling. This not only permitted the tragic poets great latitude in the choice of their fables, or mythical stories, to represent; but it also allowed room for much invention of their own, especially regarding the circumstances of things and persons, and what had happened prior to those signal events celebrated in their tragedies. 

It was necessary to inform the audience of these circumstances and prior accidents, which the poet made the foundation of his story, because they might possibly have heard those stories related with different circumstances; and they certainly would have been ignorant of details that were "unknown and untold" <note>original: *ignota indictaque*</note> or of the poet's own invention. This was the origin of prologues, in which the audience was given the necessary information. The prologue was spoken now and then in the person of some deity—the secret cause or leader of the great event about to be represented—but more frequently in the dramatic character of one of the actors in the drama. In either of these cases, the prologue made a part of the play itself. Sometimes the player spoke it in his own proper character as a performer, according to the modern custom; and very rarely, the author spoke it himself, appearing openly and professionally as the author, or had the player appear for him as his representative. 

An instance of this kind is the case cited here by Plato; and the reason why Euripides chose such a prologue for his *Melanippe* was probably this: he had, it seems, given great offense to the women of that age by drawing so many of his female characters as bad, and making their infamous actions so frequently the subject of his plays. But none of his characters, except that of Phaedra, were likely to be thought more injurious to the sex than this character of Melanippe. And in fact, so it proved; for we learn from Aristophanes in *Thesmophoriazusae* <term>original: Θεσμοφ.; a comedy by Aristophanes mocking Euripides for his depiction of women</term> that Euripides incurred the displeasure of women by no plays more than by these two. Therefore, when his *Melanippe* was to be brought upon the stage, his business was to deflect this criticism as well as he was able by an apology beforehand. Accordingly, as in his prologue to the *Hippolytus*, he had artfully made Venus take upon herself the whole blame for Phaedra's

Just as Phaedra's <note>Phaedra: A figure in Greek mythology known for her tragic and forbidden love for her stepson, Hippolytus</note> unhappy conduct was described, so in his prologue to the *Melanippe*—as appears by the line quoted here (for the prologue and the play are both lost)—Euripides humorously excuses and clears himself of blame. He declares, with an air of simplicity, that the plot of the play was already established before he began and that he had no hand in it. From this, one was meant to conclude that if Melanippe was a bad woman, he could not help it. The verse of Euripides seems to have been this:

->For the story I am about to tell is not my own.<-
<note>original: Εμος γαρ ουκ ὁ μυθος, ὁν μελλω λεγειν.</note>

Or, if the "for" <note>original: γαρ</note> was added by Plato to weave it into his own style, the verse probably was this:

->The story is not mine, which I am about to tell.<-
<note>original: Ὁ μυθος ουκ εμος εστιν, ὁν μελλω λεγειν.</note>

The intended application of this passage from the poet is as follows: Eryximachus, being a doctor and thus of a serious profession, thought it necessary for a man of his character to apologize in the same way for introducing such a proposal—namely, that Love should be the subject of discussion that evening. Such a proposal would seem much more appropriate coming from the youthful and handsome Phaedrus; therefore, Eryximachus is pleased to attribute the idea to him. In short, Plato himself, with his usual great skill, apologizes in this manner for making Love the subject of his dialogue. Because he always examines his subject from every possible perspective and thoroughly analyzes its nature, he could not avoid introducing here, among the rest of the speeches, those which seemed the most questionable. At the same time, by beginning like one of the prologues of Euripides and using a verse taken from it, he signals (to those acquainted with his style) his intention that this first speech of Eryximachus should be, or be taken for, the prologue to the dramatic entertainment that follows.—S.

The allegorical story, or fable, of the "Choice of Hercules" related in that dissertation is recorded by Xenophon; though, as he tells us himself, he did not use the pompous words of the original author, but wrote it in his own much more elegant, simple style. It will be necessary to add, in explanation of the above sentence from *Moschopulus*, that according to the Greek theologians, every Deity is the leader of a series which possesses his characteristic properties because they originate from him, and which extends to the very last of things. Every link of this series (the "golden chain of *Homer*") was very properly named by them after the same manner as its monad <note>monad: in this philosophical context, the primary unit or the divine source from which a series of related things begins</note>, or leader. This observation, when properly understood, is—as I have observed in my Notes on *Pausanias*—the true key to ancient mythology.—T. <note>“T.” refers to Thomas Taylor, the "Platonist" who completed Sydenham's translations.</note>

"I believe," said Socrates, "that none of us will object to your proposal. For I certainly never would, as I claim to have no knowledge of any subjects other than those concerning Love$^1$; neither would Agatho, nor Pausanias. Neither will Aristophanes, unquestionably, for his whole time is taken up with Bacchus and Venus <note>The Roman names for Dionysus (god of wine) and Aphrodite (goddess of love), as was common in English translations of this period.</note>. Nor, indeed, will any other person whom I see present. We, who sit at the end of the table and are to speak last, will have the disadvantage. However, if the earlier speakers speak well and fully to the point, we shall desire nothing more. Let Phaedrus then, with our best wishes to attend him, begin and deliver his <term>panegyric</term> <note>original: panegyric; a formal speech of high praise</note> upon Love."

To this, all the rest of the company consented and joined with Socrates in encouraging Phaedrus to begin. Now, Aristodemus did not perfectly remember everything said by each of the speakers; nor can I, indeed, remember all that he told me. But the speeches of those whom I looked upon as the most significant persons, and everything which I thought most worth remembering, I will endeavor to relate to you clearly.

He told me, then, that Phaedrus, complying with the request made to him, spoke first. He began somewhat in this way, saying:

Love is powerful$^2$ and wonderfully great, both on earth and among the Gods. Superior dignity belongs to him for many reasons, but especially regarding his origins. For being one of the eldest of the Gods, he said, is a circumstance that adds greatly to his honor. > ->First from the eternal council Love came forth,<-
> ->First of the Gods.—<-

Acusilaus says the same thing as Hesiod. It is agreed upon from so many different sources$^1$ that Love is among the most ancient of the Gods. And as he is of the highest antiquity in the nature of things, so is he the cause of the greatest good to humankind. For I know of no greater good for young persons, at their first setting out in life, than love—to the party beloved, if she has a worthy lover; or to the lover himself, if his mistress be worthy. This is because the leading principle that guides us toward right conduct in every circumstance of life cannot be inspired so effectively by family ties <note>original: consanguinity</note>, nor by honors, nor by riches, nor by anything else, as it is by love.

The principle I mean is the sense of shame that accompanies base conduct, together with a sense of honor in doing what is honorable. Without such a principle, no civil community or private person can accomplish anything great or noble. To confirm this, I assert that if a man in love is found committing a base action, or suffering shameful treatment from anyone through cowardice or without taking revenge, he is not in as much pain at being seen by his father, by his close friends, or by any...

The Gods paid a singular regard to this virtue of his, and rewarded with their choicest favors the regard he had shown to friendship by setting so high a value on the man who admired and loved him. For Aeschylus talks idly <note>meaning he speaks foolishly or incorrectly; original: "idly"</note> when he says that Achilles was the admirer of Patroclus; Achilles—whose excellence, though he was only in the dawn of manhood, surpassed not only Patroclus but all the other Grecian heroes. It is true that the Gods confer superior honors on all virtue where love and friendship provide the opportunity for its exercise; but they wonder more, approve more, and bestow greater rewards when the person who is *admired* feels the full force of friendship and affection for their *admirer*, rather than when the noblest acts of friendship are performed by the other party <note>Phaedrus argues that the Gods are most impressed when the younger, beloved partner (Achilles) sacrifices himself for the older lover (Patroclus)</note>. For the admirer has more of divinity in him than the person admired, being filled with the God who inspires and possesses him. 

For this reason, the Gods rewarded Achilles with a higher degree of happiness than they did Alcestis; for to her, they gave only a second life on earth, but to the hero, they assigned a mansion in the Islands of the Blessed. Thus I have performed my part in asserting that Love is the eldest in age and of the highest dignity among the Gods, and is uniquely the author of virtue and happiness for all humankind, both while they live and after they have departed.

Such, Aristodemus told me, was the discourse given by Phaedrus. After Phaedrus, several others spoke whose speeches, he said, he did not remember well. Omitting these, therefore, he next repeated the speech of Pausanias, who began like this:

## THE SPEECH OF PAUSANIAS.

In my opinion, Phaedrus, the subject was not presented to us fairly or distinctly when it was proposed in general terms that we should make speeches of praise <note>original: "encomiums," a formal expression of high praise</note> for Love. This, indeed, would have been correct if there were only one kind of Love, or if Love were of only one kind. But since the truth is otherwise, the better way is to first declare which Love it is our current business to praise. To put this matter on the right footing, I shall first distinguish the Love whose praises we ought to celebrate, and then do my best to celebrate them myself in a manner worthy of his divinity <note>original: "Deity"</note>. We all know that it is the role of Love to always attend upon Venus <note>original: "Venus," the Roman name for the Greek goddess Aphrodite</note>. If then there

<meta>This page continues the speech of Pausanias from Plato's Symposium. He begins by arguing that there is not just one "Love," but two distinct types, just as there are two distinct versions of the goddess Venus (Aphrodite).</meta>
