...if there were only one Venus, there would have been no occasion for more than one Love. But since there are two Venuses, there must of necessity be two Loves. For it is undeniable that there are two different goddesses,¹ each of whom is a Venus: one of them is the elder, who had no mother and was born only from Uranus (or Heaven), her father; she is called the **Celestial Venus**. The other is younger, the daughter of Jupiter and Dione; and to her we give the name of the **Vulgar Venus** <note>original: "vulgar Venus"; from the Greek *Aphrodite Pandemos*, meaning "Venus of all the people," representing common or physical attraction</note>. 

Agreeably to this account, it is proper to call that Love who attends on the latter Venus by the name of the **Vulgar Love**, and the other by the name of the **Celestial Love**. It is indeed our duty to honor all the gods with our praises; but we ought to distinguish each by his peculiar attributes as well as we are able, so that we may give each his due praise. For every action or operation is governed by this condition: the doing of it, considered simply in itself, is neither base nor honorable. For instance, every one of the things² we are now doing—drinking, singing, or conversing—is in itself a matter of indifference; it is the manner of doing it that determines the nature of the thing. Rightly performed, it is right and honorable; performed in a wrong manner, it is wrong and dishonorable. So—

¹ This distinction between the two Venuses, laid down by Pausanias as the foundation of his argument throughout his speech, is not a fanciful one of his own but is a part of ancient mythology. > “Now, whether in reality there be one Venus only, or whether there be two, a celestial Venus and a vulgar one, I know not: (for Jupiter also, whom I presume to be but one and the same being, has many surnames given him:) but this I know, that altars are raised, temples built, and sacrifices offered to each of these two Venuses distinctly; to the vulgar one, such as are common, trivial, and of little worth; to the celestial one, such as are more valuable, pure, and holy. Likewise, not every form of Love is generous or noble, or deserves high praise <note>original: "encomiums"</note>; rather, only that Love who encourages and drives men to love generously and nobly is worthy. The companion of the **Vulgar Venus** is a love that is truly common <note>original: "vulgar"; here meaning low-born or lacking in refinement</note>, allowing himself to be used in even the lowliest actions. It is this Love that inspires the petty and the worthless. 

Those who are the most addicted to this love are, first of all, the least inclined toward friendship. Secondly, they are more in love with the bodies than with the minds of those they pursue. Furthermore, they choose the silliest creatures they can find as the objects of their passion. Because they focus only on satisfying their passion through the physical act, they do not care how they achieve it—whether through dishonorable or honorable means. Consequently, in the pursuit and later in the enjoyment of their loves, they are equally ready to perform any action that presents itself, whether good or bad, without distinction. 

For the Love that inspires them is born of that younger Venus, in whose creation there is a mixture of the male and the female; because of this, she shares the qualities of both. But the other Love springs from the **Celestial Venus**—the goddess whose qualities are these: first, she does not share in the female nature, but only the male; therefore, she is the source <note>original: "parent"</note> of friendship. Second, she is older in age and a stranger to crude <note>original: "brutal"</note> lust. 

Because of this, those who are inspired by this love devote themselves to friendship, developing an affection for that which by nature possesses greater strength and intelligence. Now, it is easy to tell whether a man under the influence of love feels the genuine impulse of this noble affection. If he does, he does not focus his love on anyone who has not yet reached a maturity of understanding. 

By starting their love from this point in time, one may reasonably assume that both partners are qualified to live together throughout their lives as partners in all things. In such a case, the lover is not likely to act like one who—after discovering some childish mistake in the person he has chosen—exposes them, turns them into an object of ridicule, breaks his word and abandons them, and then attaches himself to a new partner. 

To prevent this, there ought to be a law that no man should choose someone who is too young for a life partner; this is because it is so uncertain how such a young person may turn out in the future, whether good or bad in either mind or body. Men of virtue, indeed, impose this <note>The text ends here; the catchword "this" indicates the start of the next page.</note> upon themselves...

...this should be a law. Furthermore, we should place a public restraint of this kind upon those common lovers <note>original: "vulgar lovers"; meaning those driven by base physical desire rather than intellectual connection</note>, just as we restrain them, as much as possible, from entering into romantic affairs with any women above the rank of servants <note>original: "rank of servitude"</note>. ->It is a loss of honor for the beautiful<-
->To yield and grant the lover's prayer.<-

But he said this only with a view toward lovers of this kind, seeing their premature haste and eagerness, as well as their ingratitude and injustice. For certainly no action governed by the rules of justice and decency can in any way deserve blame.

Now, the rules concerning love established in other states are easy to understand because they are plain and simple. However, our own laws—and those of Sparta—regarding this subject are complex and intricate. For in Elis <note>A region in the Peloponnese, home to Olympia</note> and among the Boeotians <note>A region in central Greece, whose people were often stereotyped by Athenians as being uncultured or "dull-witted"</note>, and in every other Greek state where the art of rhetoric <note>original: "arts of speaking"</note> does not flourish, the custom <note>original: "the law"</note> in such places absolutely makes it honorable to satisfy a lover. No person there, whether young or old, can mark such conduct with dishonor. I presume the reason for this law is to prevent the great trouble they would otherwise have in courting the beautiful and trying to win them through the art of oratory—an art in which they have no skill.

^1 It is remarkable that Xenophon, in his own *Banquet* <note>original: "Symposium"</note>, where he distinguishes between the virtuous friendship established among the Spartans and the lustful <note>original: "libidinous"</note> behavior authorized by fashion and common practice among the Boeotians and Eleans, cites this same Pausanias as someone who had confused them and given them equal praise. We cannot help but imagine that Xenophon, in citing Pausanias, is alluding to what was said at Agatho’s party. If our conjecture is true, that slight difference in circumstances confirms Plato’s account in the main and suggests it has at least some foundation in real fact.—S.

^2 The word *law* here, and wherever else it occurs in this speech from this point to the end, does not mean a written law or a specific legal prohibition. Instead, it refers to custom and fashion. But in Ionia, and many other places $^1$, and in all non-Greek countries <note>original: "barbarian countries"; to the ancient Greeks, a 'barbarian' was simply anyone who did not speak Greek</note> universally, the same conduct is mandated and held to be dishonorable. For the tyrannical governments under which the people of those countries live discourage that form of mutual love and bring it into disgrace. But the same fate in those countries attends philosophy—the love of wisdom—as it does the pursuit of physical training <note>original: "manly exercises"</note>. And the reason, I suspect, in all these cases is the same: it is not in the interest of the rulers for their subjects to be high-spirited or high-minded, nor to allow strong friendships or any other bonds of shared interest to form among them. These are the natural effects of love, as well as of those other studies and practices prohibited by tyrants.

Those who formerly ruled Athens as tyrants found this to be true. For the firm and stable friendship between Aristogiton $^2$ and Harmodius <note>The famous pair of lovers who assassinated the tyrant Hipparchus in 514 BC, becoming symbols of Athenian freedom</note> was the destruction of their tyranny. Thus we find that wherever the closer bonds of love and friendship are forbidden or discouraged, it is due to vice: to the ruler's lust for power and private interest, and to a lack of spirit, courage, and virtue in the subjects. On the other hand, wherever they are encouraged simply and without restriction, it is due to a smallness and laziness of soul in those who make the laws. 

But in our own state, the laws relating to this point are established on a better footing; though, as I said before, it is not obvious or easy to understand their meaning. For when we consider that among us it is considered honorable for men to profess their love openly, rather than to keep it a secret; and to fix their best affections on those who excel in intellectual achievements <note>original: "accomplishments of mind"</note>, even if they are inferior to others in outward beauty; we see that everyone highly favors and—

...applauds the lover, believing he is not involved in any schemes that are base or unsuitable for a man. In our society, success in love is considered an honor for the lover, while failure is a disgrace. The law grants the lover the freedom to do everything possible to achieve his goal. It even allows such strange actions to be praised in him—actions that, if a man were guilty of them in any pursuit other than love, or as a means of succeeding in any other goal, would surely earn him the harshest criticism from philosophers. 

For instance, if a man submitted to the things lovers usually do to win their beloved—such as begging humbly, making vows and oaths, staying awake all night at their doors, and voluntarily accepting a level of slavery no actual slave would endure—just to get money, a government position, or power, then both his friends and enemies would try to stop him. His enemies would mock him for his submissiveness and lack of dignity <note>original: "illiberality"; in this context, it refers to behavior unbecoming of a "liberal" or free-born citizen</note>, while his friends would warn him and feel ashamed for him. 

But in a lover, all of this is seen as charming. The law gives him free permission to do it without being judged, treating it as a highly praiseworthy task for him to undertake. But what is most extraordinary of all is that the gods, though they do not forgive perjury in any other case, excuse a lover for breaking an oath—at least, if the common opinion is true. For they say that oaths made in love are not binding. Thus, both gods and men grant all kinds of freedom to the lover, according to the laws of our city. 

Looking at it this way, one might imagine that in our society, not only is the lover’s passion honorable, but so is a favorable response from the beloved. But then we see the parents of beautiful young people appointing chaperones <note>original: "governesses"</note> and guardians over them, with strict instructions not to let them speak privately with their lovers. We see their peers and others of their own age criticizing them if they are reckless enough to do so, and the older generation does not stop these critics or tell them their judgments are unfair. From this perspective, one would think that we actually condemn the very things we otherwise seemed to approve of.

The vicious lover is he of the common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> sort, who is in love with the body rather than the mind. For he is not a lasting lover, being in love with a thing which is not lasting; since, with the flower of youth <gloss>1</gloss>—when that which he admired is gone—the lover himself also takes wing and flies away, shaming all his fine speeches and fair promises. But the man who is in love with his mistress's moral character—when her disposition and manners are settled in what is right—is a lover who stays for a lifetime, as he is united with that which is durable and abiding. 

Our law decrees accordingly that all lovers should be thoroughly and fairly tested; and that, after such a trial, the favors of the beloved should be bestowed upon some, while to others they should be constantly refused. It encourages, therefore, the lover to pursue, but bids the beloved party flee; by every kind of trial and every type of struggle <note>original: "combat"</note>, it reveals what kind of person the lover is, and what kind of person his beloved is. For this reason, the law deems it dishonorable, first of all, to be won quickly or easily, so that time may be gained; for time seems to be the fairest test of the truth of many things. Second, it is held dishonorable for the beloved one to be won by considerations of profit or power—whether she is mistreated or terrified and therefore yields through a lack of noble endurance, or whether she is flattered by riches or rank and does not despise such obligations. For none of these things appear fixed or durable; much less can they give rise to any noble <note>original: "generous"</note> friendship. There remains, then, only one way in which, according to our law, the beloved may honorably yield and consent to her lover’s passion. <meta>This page continues the speech of Pausanias from Plato’s *Symposium* (The Banquet). Pausanias is explaining the specific conditions under which it is considered honorable for a beloved person to yield to a lover, distinguishing between motives of material gain and the pursuit of virtue.</meta>

<page-num>466</page-num>
<header>THE BANQUET.</header>

...for his mistress is not considered flattery <note>original: "adulation"</note> by our law, nor is it looked upon as a matter of disgrace. On the other hand, there is only one other kind of service or compliance that is not disgraceful for the beloved <note>original: "the fair"</note>; and this is the service performed for the sake of virtue. 

It is a settled rule among us that whoever pays court or attendance to another, or yields any service or compliance in the expectation of improving in wisdom or any other branch of virtue through that person, is not guilty of servility or low flattery by such voluntary submission. Now, these two rules must align with one another and work toward the same end—the rule concerning lovers, and the rule concerning philosophy and every other part of virtue—in order to make it honorable for the beloved to comply with a lover’s passion. 

For when the lover and the beloved <note>The original text uses "mistress" and "her," reflecting the translator's choice to use 18th-century romantic language for the original Greek relationship between an older man and a youth.</note> come together, each bringing their own rule—the lover’s being that it is right to serve the beloved in any way, and the beloved’s being that it is right to provide any service or compliance to the person who improves them in wisdom and virtue—and when the one has the ability to teach and improve the other, while the other has a desire for instruction and self-improvement; then, and only then, by the meeting of all these necessary requirements, does it become honorable for the beloved to gratify the lover. 

Furthermore, in this specific case, it is no dishonor to the beloved to be deceived. However, in the case of compliance on any other terms, the beloved incurs shame whether they are deceived or not. For instance, if someone yields to a lover assuming he is wealthy in order to enrich herself, but is disappointed and gets nothing from her lover <note>original: "paramour"</note> because she eventually discovers he is poor, it is no less dishonorable to her. This is because such a person reveals her own heart and makes it clear that, for the sake of wealth, she would yield anything to anyone; and this is highly dishonorable and base. 

But if she yields to a lover imagining him to be a good man, with a view to her own improvement in virtue through his friendship, and is deceived upon finding him to be a bad man lacking virtue, her disappointment is still honorable to her. In this case, her own aims have also been revealed; it has become evident that, as a means to acquire virtue and to become better, she was ready to resign her all to any man. This is, of all things, the most generous and noble motivation. So entirely and absolutely honorable is it for the beloved to comply for the sake [of virtue].

<summary>Pausanias argues that yielding to a lover is only honorable if done to gain wisdom and virtue, rather than for wealth. He posits that even if a lover turns out to be a fraud, the beloved's intention to seek moral improvement remains a noble and virtuous act.</summary>

<gloss>1</gloss> These small ornaments of style were introduced into oratory and first taught by Gorgias. It is probable that he had observed them in the works of Homer, where every beauty and ornament of speech, great or small, is to be found. Isocrates, who had studied the art of oratory under Gorgias, seems to have received from him what his own mature judgment later rejected: the excessive and poorly-timed use of these superficial ornaments. The preceding speech by Pausanias, in imitation of Isocrates, is full of various kinds of these—some quite childish—which it was impossible for us to preserve or imitate when translating these passages into English. Although all languages allow for such devices, every language differs from others in the meanings of the words where these sounds occur. An instance of this appears in the passage now before us, where the Greek *Pausaniou de pausamenou* <note>original: "Παυσανιου δε παυσαμενου"</note>, translated accurately, runs thus: "When Pausanias had ceased speaking," that is, had ended his speech. But all similarity of sound would thus be entirely destroyed. Therefore, as it was necessary in this place to preserve it to some degree, however imperfectly, we found ourselves obliged here to make sense give way to sound. — S.

### THE SPEECH OF ERYXIMACHUS.

Since *Pausanias*, after starting so excellently well, ended his discourse incomplete <note>original: "imperfectly"</note>, it seems my duty <note>original: "a task incumbent on me"</note> to finish the argument which he began. For, in distinguishing two different kinds of Love, he made, I think, a very proper and just distinction. But that Love attracts us <note>original: "gives us an attraction"</note> not only to beautiful people <note>original: "persons"</note>, but to many other things besides; and that he dwells not only in human hearts, but also has his seat in other beings, in the bodies of all animals, and in the vegetable productions of the earth—in short <note>original: "in fine"</note>, that he lives throughout all nature—my own profession, medicine, has given me the opportunity <note>original: "occasion"</note> to observe. I have remarked how great and wonderful a god Love is, stretching his attractive power everywhere and reaching all things, whether human or divine. 

I shall first use medicine as an example, so that I may pay my first regards to my own profession. I say, then, that our bodies partake of this twofold love. For physical health and disease are similar <note>original: "bear an analogy"</note> to the two different dispositions of the soul mentioned by *Pausanias*. And as the body in a state of health and the body when diseased are in themselves very different from one another, so they love and long for very different things. The love in a healthy body is of one kind; the love in a diseased body is of another kind, quite different. Now, as *Pausanias* says, it is honorable to comply with a good lover but dishonorable to yield to one who is immoral <note>original: "vicious"</note>; so it is with respect to the body. Whatever is in a sound and healthy state, it is commendable and right to please; it is the physician's duty to do so, and the effective doing of it—

—sneezing <note>Continuing the sentence from the previous page: "When you have sneezed once or twice, even the most violent hiccups will stop."</note> comes upon a man in a fit of the hiccups, it puts an end to the disorder." Upon this general rule, no doubt, the present prescription of *Eryximachus* was founded. *Dr. G. E. ¹ The words used by *Plato* in this passage are even stronger, effectively meaning he "defines him as a physician." In *Plato's* day, preserving health through the proper use of the "non-naturals"—environmental and lifestyle factors such as sex, age, temperament, climate, and the seasons—was considered the most important part of medicine. Ancient Greek doctors reached a degree of accuracy in this area that was largely lost or neglected in later centuries. <term>non-naturals</term> — <note>An old medical term for things that affect health but are not part of the body itself, such as air, food, sleep, and exercise.</note>

For he must be able to reconcile those things in the body which are most at variance with each other $^1$, and to foster friendship and mutual love between them. The things most at variance are those that are the most contrary to one another, such as cold is to hot, bitter to sweet, dry to moist, and all others of that sort $^2$. Into these things, thus at variance, our ancestor Asclepius <note>original: "Æsculapius"</note> had the power to inspire a spirit of love and concord. As our friends the poets tell us, and as I believe, by framing the rules for doing so into a system, he was truly the founder of our art. 

So it is that medicine, in the manner I have described, is entirely under the direction and management of Love. The same is true of the athletic art $^3$ and the art of agriculture $^4$. That music is also governed by Love is evident to anyone who considers the nature of this art with even the least attention; and it is perhaps the very thing which Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of change and the unity of opposites.</note> meant to say, though his way of expressing himself is inaccurate and obscure. A good soil is improved by a fertilizer that matches its nature; a bad soil is improved by an opposite method of cultivation that alters its nature and condition. As for the metaphor, the same has always been used in agriculture to this day. We say that a certain soil "loves" a certain fertilizer, and that a tree, plant, or other vegetable "loves" and "delights in" a certain soil when they correspond to each other—when the nature of the one is suited to the other and helps it thrive and flourish.—S.

$^5$ The author of the treatise *On the World* <note>original: "Περι κοσμου" (Peri kosmou)</note>, printed among the works of Aristotle and usually attributed to him (though not with any certain authority), cites the following passage from the same Heraclitus, which may help illustrate this point: "You must connect the perfect and the imperfect, the agreeing and the disagreeing, the consonant and the dissonant; and from all things comes one, and from one come all things" <note>original Greek: "συναψιας ουλα και ουχι ουλα, συμφερομενον και διαφερομενον, συναδον και διαδον, και εκ παντων ἑν, και εξ ἑνος παντα"</note>. In this passage, by "the one from all things," he means the universe; and by "all things from one," he suggests the existence of all things from "the One," the indescribable principle of everything.—T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the translator.</note>

<summary>Eryximachus argues that the principle of Love (harmony between opposites) is the foundation of medicine, athletics, agriculture, and music, citing the philosopher Heraclitus's idea of "concord in disagreement."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Eryximachus, who is drawing a parallel between medicine (the harmony of bodily humours) and music (the harmony of sounds). He is refining the idea that harmony is the reconciliation of opposites.</meta>

<page-num>471</page-num>
<header>THE BANQUET.</header>

It is very absurd to say that any disagreement can find a place in harmony, or that the component parts of harmony can ever disagree. But perhaps his meaning was this: that things which are by their own nature disagreeing—that is, sounds, some shrill and others deep—are at length brought to an agreement by the musical art to compose harmony. For harmony cannot consist of shrill and deep sounds while they remain in disagreement, because harmony is consonance <note>original: "consonance," meaning a sounding-together or agreement of sounds.</note>, or a breathing together of sounds. Consonance is one kind of agreement, but it is impossible for any agreement to exist between disagreeing things as long as they disagree. It is no less impossible that things between which there is no agreement should at the same time harmonize together so as to produce harmony. 

As it is with sound, so it is with motion; the quick measures and the slow ones, which naturally disagree, are afterwards brought to agree together to compose rhythm. In both these cases <gloss>¹</gloss>, where things differ and are opposite to one another, it is the art of music which brings about the reconciliation and agreement, just as the art of medicine does in the former case <gloss>²</gloss>, inspiring them in the same manner with the spirit of love and concord. And thus musical science is the knowledge of those amorous conjunctions <note>The union or joining together of elements through the power of Love (Eros).</note> whose offspring are harmony and rhythm. 

Now, in the systems themselves, whether of harmony or of rhythm, there is no difficulty at all in knowing these amorous conjunctions, for here love is not distinguished into two kinds. But when the intention is to apply rhythm and harmony to the ears of an audience, then comes the difficulty. Then there is a need for a skillful artist, whether in composing the odes and setting them to music, or in making a right choice of those already composed and set <gloss>³</gloss>, and properly adapting them to the characters <note>original: "geniuses," meaning the natural dispositions or tempers.</note> of youth. For here that distinction takes place; here we must recur again to that rule of Pausanias: that it is right to gratify the decent, the well-ordered, and the virtuous,

<meta>This page continues the speech of Eryximachus from the Symposium. He is expanding his argument that the two types of Love—celestial and vulgar—exist not only in human relationships and music but also in the natural world, medicine, and the movements of the stars.</meta>

...gratify them for the sake of preserving their love, and to improve those who are still lacking in virtue. The Love that inspires these people is noble and celestial; it is the Love that attends the celestial Muse <note>Urania, the Muse of astronomy and celestial spheres</note>. But the other Love—the attendant of Polyhymnia <note>The Muse of sacred song; here Eryximachus associates her with a more common or "vulgar" inspiration</note> and the follower of any Muse at random—is of the vulgar kind. We must indulge this Love with caution whenever we do so, so that he may enjoy his own pleasures without introducing disorder and debauchery. 

This is a task of no less difficulty than it is in my own art <note>the art of medicine</note> to prudently manage the appetites for food, so as to permit the enjoyment of proper pleasures without the danger of disease. Thus, in the practice of music, medicine, and every other pursuit, whether human or divine, we must preserve both kinds of Love as far as we consistently can, for both are found in all things <gloss>¹</gloss>. 

The makeup of the yearly seasons is full of both. When those natural opposites I mentioned before—the hot and the cold, the dry and the moist—admit a sober relationship and a temperate mixture under the influence of the modest Love, they bring fair seasons, fine weather, and health to men, animals, and plants, doing harm to none. But when that Love who inspires lawless and ungoverned passion dominates the constitution of the season, he corrupts, injures, and ruins many of the beautiful forms of nature. For the typical results of this Love are plagues and other abnormal <note>original: "preter-natural"</note> diseases which strike animals and vegetables alike. Mildew, hailstorms, and blights are generated from the irregular state of the "amorous affections" in these elementary beings and the lack of moderation in their unions. The study of these amorous attractions and their resulting unions—viewed in relation to the positions of the heavenly bodies and the seasons of the year—is called astronomy.

...a mutual interaction between the Gods and mortals, are carried out with no other goal than to preserve the right kind of love and cure the wrong kind. Every form of impiety <note>disrespect for the divine</note> is the common result of not yielding to and satisfying the better, more orderly Love, and of not giving our primary attention to him—but rather to the other Love ¹—in everything we do concerning our parents, whether living or dead, and in everything relating to the Gods. In all such cases, supervising these Loves, nurturing the right one and curing the wrong one, is the work of divination <note>the art of discovering the will of the gods or the future</note>. 

Thus, divination is a skilled artist who knows how to create and encourage friendship and good communication between gods and men. She does this through her knowledge of which romantic passions in humans lead toward piety and justice, and which are the opposite and lead the other way. The power of Love is so broad, so dominant, and indeed so all-prevailing. This is true of all love in general; but it is most true of that Love who achieves his goals by attaining good things and enjoying them without ever exceeding the limits of temperance <note>self-control and moderation</note> or violating the laws of justice. 

For it is this Love who holds the greatest power over both human and divine natures; it is this Love who brings us every kind of happiness, allowing us to live in social harmony with one another and in friendship with those beings who are so much greater than ourselves: the Gods. It is possible that in the panegyric <note>a formal speech of praise; original: "panegyric"</note> I have made on Love, I may have missed many topics of his due praise, just as Pausanias did. ### THE SPEECH OF ARISTOPHANES.

"My intentions, Eryximachus, are to speak in a way very different, I assure you, from the way taken by you and Pausanias in your speeches. To me, men seem utterly insensitive to the power of Love. <meta>This page continues Aristophanes' famous "Origin of Love" speech from the Symposium. Having introduced his intent to explain why humans do not understand the power of Love, he now begins his mythological account of our original physical form.</meta>

<page-num>475</page-num>

In ancient times, there were three sorts <gloss>1</gloss>, or types, of the human race; not as at present, only two, male and female. There was then a third species besides, which partook of both the others; the name only of which species now remains, the species itself being extinct and lost. For then there actually existed and flourished hermaphrodites <note>original: "hermaphrodites"—here referring to androgynous beings who were physically both male and female</note>, who shared the characteristics of both the other species, the male and the female. But they have now become merely a name, a name of abuse and of reproach.

Next, the entire form of every individual of the human race was cylindrical; for their bodies, back and sides together, were everywhere, from top to bottom, circular. Every one had four hands, and the same number of legs. They had two faces each, upon their round necks, identical in every way; but these two faces belonged to only one head, on the sides of which these faces were placed, opposite to one another. Each had also four ears, and two sets of sexual organs.

From this description, it is easy to conceive how all the other parts of the human body were doubled. They walked upon whichever legs they pleased, on any side; and, as they walk now, upright. But when anyone wanted to go with speed, then, like gymnasts who, after pitching on their hands, throw their legs upward and bring them over to tumble themselves round, in the same manner did the people of those days, supported by their eight limbs alternately, roll along with great dispatch.

Now you are to know that these three species of the human race were exactly three in number, and their bodies made in such a form, for this reason: because the male kind was produced originally by the sun, the female rose from the earth, and the third, which partook of the other two, was the offspring of the moon;

---

> <gloss>1</gloss> Plato is so far from being a careless writer that he always has some concealed and important meaning, even in things apparently the most trivial and absurd. For what can be apparently more absurd than this account which Aristophanes gives of the changes which human nature has undergone? And yet it secretly suggests a very important truth: that kindred human souls, of both male and female characteristics, were in a more perfect state of existence united with each other much more profoundly than they can be in their present state. However, though it suggests a more perfect condition of being, yet it is by no means that of the soul in its highest state of happiness. For the *cylindric* bodies indicate its being still involved with, or *rolling* about, the realm of physical birth <note>original: "generation"—in Platonic philosophy, this refers to the material world of change, birth, and decay</note>, that is, the regions under the moon. Plato, therefore, probably indicates in this fable an *aerial* condition of being. For though the soul, while living there in a descending condition, is in reality in a fallen state, yet she is more perfect than when resident on the earth. Agreeably, and perhaps with allusion to this fable, which I doubt not is of greater antiquity than Plato, Pythagoras defined a friend to be *a man's other self.*—T. <note>The "T." refers to the translator, Thomas Taylor (1758–1835), a famous English Neoplatonist.</note>

...for the moon, you know, partakes of both the others, the sun and the earth. Therefore, the bodies of each kind were round, and they moved in a circular motion, resembling their celestial parents. Their force and strength were prodigious, and their minds were elevated and haughty; so they undertook to invade heaven. The same story is told of them that Homer relates of Ephialtus and Otus <note>Ephialtus and Otus were twin giants who attempted to storm Mount Olympus by piling mountains on top of one another</note>: that they set about raising a path up to the skies with the intention of attacking the gods.

Upon this, Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter"—the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note> and the other deities consulted together to decide what they should do to these rebels¹; however, they could not come to a determination about the proper punishment to be inflicted on them. They could not resolve to destroy them with thunderbolts, as they did the giants, for then the whole human race would be extinct; consequently, the honors paid to the gods by that race would vanish along with them, and their temples would fall into ruin. Yet, they could not allow those mortals to continue in their insolence. 

At length Jupiter, after much consideration of such a difficult case, said, "I have a plan by which the race of men may be preserved, and yet an end put to their insolence; for my device will greatly diminish their strength. I intend, you must know, to divide every one of them into two. By this means, their strength will be much weakened, and at the same time their number will be increased, which will be to our advantage and increase our honor. They shall walk upright upon two legs; and if any remains of insolence shall ever appear in them again, and they refuse to be quiet, I will divide them once more, each into two; and they shall go upon one leg, hopping." 

As he said this, he acted; he cut all the human race in two, just as people slice eggs² to preserve them in salt. The face, together with the half—

...half-neck of every half-body, he ordered Apollo to turn the face half-way around and fix it on the side where the body had been cut in half. His intention was that all people, by seeing the side where they had suffered the loss of half of themselves, might be brought to a sober way of thinking and learn to behave with more modesty. As for what remained to be done, he ordered Apollo to use his own healing art.

Accordingly, Apollo turned the face of every person toward the opposite of its former position. Drawing the skin together from all parts of the body—like pulling a drawstring purse—over what is now called the belly, toward a single opening, he tied it off at the middle of the stomach; this opening is now called the navel. He then smoothed most of the wrinkles in the skin after shaping the bones of the chest beneath it, just as shoemakers smooth the wrinkles in leather after stretching it over a wooden mold <note>original: "last" — a mechanical form shaped like a human foot used by shoemakers</note>. However, he left a few wrinkles on the belly and navel as a memorial of their ancient crime and punishment.

Once the entire human race had been split in two <note>original: "bisected"</note> this way, every person longed for their other half. When these halves happened to meet, they embraced and folded themselves in each other's arms, wishing they could grow together and be united. As a result, they both died from hunger and the other hardships naturally caused by their inactivity. If one of these halves died and left the other behind, the survivor immediately began searching for another partner. Whether they happened to meet the half of a "whole woman" (the half we now call a woman) or the half of a "whole man," they were constantly embracing.

<note>The following is a scholarly footnote by the translator regarding a difficult Greek passage.</note>

By looking at the phrase *with hairs* <note>original: "ταις θριξιν" (tais thrixin)</note> and considering the abbreviations common in old manuscripts, we made our conjecture even more likely (to ourselves, at least) by reading the latter part of the sentence this way: *"or, as those who cut eggs for pickling"* <note>original: "η, ωσπερ τα ωα τεμνοντες εις ταριχευσιν"</note>. We suppose these words were written in the margin in this manner: *"or as those who [cut] eggs for pickling"* <note>original: "ἡ ὥσπερ οἱ τα ωα τ. εις ταριχσιν"</note>, with the initial letter of the word *cutting* <note>original: "τεμνοντες"</note> standing for the whole word, as was usual in such cases. 

Thus, these last words were likely read aloud by some uneducated librarian to a new scribe (as was common for speed). The scribe, not paying attention to the meaning, easily mistook the abbreviated letters for the word *with hairs* <note>original: "ταις θριξιν"</note>. We know from the comic poet Alexis (as cited by Athenaeus, pages 57 and 60) and from Columella <note>Roman writers on food and agriculture</note> that it was customary for the ancients to salt and pickle eggs for preservation after boiling them hard and cutting them in two. Columella further tells us that they were sometimes hardened for that purpose in a brine heated over a fire. — S. <note>The "S" likely stands for the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

Previously, they had reproduced, not with one another, but with the earth, like grasshoppers. Jupiter carried out this plan; thus, he made the work of reproduction happen through both sexes together, with the female conceiving from the male. Now, in making this the sole way of reproducing, Jupiter had these goals in view: that, if a man should meet with a woman, they might reproduce together in their embrace, and the human race would thus continue. But if he met with another man, then both might find satisfaction in that union; and that, immediately ceasing from their embraces, they might apply themselves to business and turn their studies and pursuits to the other affairs of life. 

From all this, it appears how deeply mutual love is naturally implanted in the human race. It brings us back toward our original <note>original: "pristine"</note> form, joining us together and attempting to make one out of two, thereby healing the wounds of human nature. So it is that every one of us at present is but the <term>tally</term> <note>original: "tally" — a piece of wood or bone split into two matching halves used for identification or record-keeping</note> of a human creature; we have been cut like a flatfish <note>original: "polypus" — see the translator's note below regarding the Greek word "psetta"</note>, and out of one, two were made. 

Hence it comes that we are all in a continual search for our several counterparts to match with us. Accordingly, those men who are sections of that double form called the hermaphrodite <note>original: "androgynous"</note> are lovers of women; many men who are unfaithful to their wives <note>original: "rakes"</note> are of this species. On the other hand, those women who are addicted to the love of men are sprung from the same mixed race. But those women who are sections of the original all-female form are not much inclined toward men; their affections tend rather toward their own sex: these are the Sapphic lovers <note>original: "Sapphic lovers" — a reference to the poet Sappho of Lesbos, used here to describe lesbians</note>. 

In the same way, men who are sections of the all-male form follow other males. While they are children, being originally fragments of men, they love men and find the most delight in men's company and affection. Those children and youths who are of this sort are the best, as they are the most manly in their temper and disposition. Some people, I know, say they are shameless and impudent; but in this they wrong them. It is not impudence or a lack of modesty, but rather a manly assurance—accompanied by a manly temper and turn of mind—by which

They have naturally no inclination to marry and father children; they do so only to obey the laws, and would choose to live unmarried in a state of friendship. Such persons as these are indeed formed by nature for friendship alone, always embracing whatever is compatible with themselves. 

Now, whenever it happens that a man meets that very counterpart of himself—his "other half"—they are both struck with love in a wonderful manner. They recognize an ancient intimacy. They are strongly attracted together by a consciousness that they belong to each other, and they are unwilling to be parted or separated again, even for a very short time. Those pairs who, by free choice, live together throughout their lives are those who have met with this good fortune. Yet none of them are able to tell exactly what it is they want from one another. For it does not seem to be merely sexual intimacy <note>original: "the venereal congress"</note>. In all appearance, it is not merely for the sake of this that they feel such extreme delight in each other's company and seek it so eagerly when they are apart. It is evident that their souls long for something else which neither can explain. They can only give obscure hints of it through riddles <note>original: "ænigmas"</note>, and each party can only guess at the other's meaning, as if by intuition <note>original: "divination"</note>.

The cause of this desire in us all is this: our original <note>original: "pristine"</note> nature was such as I have described; we were once whole. The desire and pursuit of this wholeness of our nature—our becoming whole again—is called Love. For, as I said, we were anciently one. Considering this should encourage every man to promote the universal practice of piety <note>Religious devotion or reverence.</note> toward the gods, so that we may escape this misfortune and reach that better state, as it please Love to guide and lead us. Above all, let none of us act in opposition to this kind deity; no one opposes him except those who are at enmity with the gods. "You speak well, Phaedrus," said Agatho, "and nothing hinders me from beginning my speech. For I shall not lack <note>original: "want"</note> frequent opportunities to debate with Socrates again."

## THE SPEECH OF AGATHO.

I shall begin by showing in what way a speech of praise <note>original: "panegyric"</note> on Love ought to be made 1, and then proceed in that same way to make one myself. For none of those who have spoken before me have, in my opinion, truly celebrated the praise of Love; instead, they have made it their only business to congratulate humankind upon the good they enjoy through the generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note> of that god. For what he is in himself—he from whom all this happiness is derived—none of them has shown. Now, whatever the subject of our praise may be, there is only one right way to compose it: and that is by showing how excellent the nature is, and how good the actions or effects are, of the person or thing we are praising. It is in this way that we ought to make our speeches of praise on Love; praising, first, the excellence and absolute goodness of his own nature, and then his relative goodness to us in the blessings he bestows. According to this method, I take it upon myself, in the first place, to say—if I may be allowed to say it without offense to what is sacred and divine—that, though all the gods enjoy a state of blessedness, Love is blessed above all others, as he excels them all in beauty and in virtue. He must be the most beautiful for these reasons: first, because he is the youngest of the gods, my **Phaedrus**! Of this he himself gives us convincing proof by running away from **Old Age**, and outrunning him who is evidently so swift-footed. For **Old Age**, as you know, arrives and is with us sooner than we desire. Between **Love** and him there is a natural hostility <note>original: "antipathy"</note>: so that **Love** does not come anywhere near him 2; but makes his home with

1 The following speech abounds with wit; but it is a rambling and inconsistent kind of wit, without any fixed idea; it is very far from aiming at the truth. In the first place, he means (as **Socrates** later observes of him) that which is loved, rather than that which loves; that is, outward beauty, rather than the passion which it excites. Immediately he changes this idea for that of the passion itself. Then at once, without giving notice, he takes a flight to the first cause of orderly motion in the universe. And this he immediately confuses with the harmony of nature, the complete effect of that cause.

I must admit, therefore, that while I agree with **Phaedrus** in many of his other opinions, I cannot agree with him on this: that **Love** is older than **Saturn** and **Iapetus** <note>In Greek mythology, Saturn (Cronus) and Iapetus were Titans, the ancient generation of gods who preceded the Olympians.</note>. Of all the gods, I affirm, he is the youngest and enjoys perpetual youth. 

Accordingly, I contend that if any such events happened among the gods as **Hesiod** and **Parmenides** report, they were caused by the power of **Necessity** <note>original: "Necessity," or *Ananke*, a personification of the cold, unyielding laws of the universe that preceded the civilizing influence of Love.</note>, not by the power of **Love**. For had **Love** been with them, there would have been no castrations \*, no chains, and none of those many other acts of violence would have been committed or suffered among them. Instead, friendship and peace would have flourished in heaven, just as they do now and have always done since **Love** began his reign and became the chief among the gods. 

Thus, then, it appears that **Love** is young. Nor is he any less delicate or tender. But he lacks a poet, such as **Homer** was, to express in suitable terms how great his tenderness is. Now **Homer**, where he tells us that **Ate** (or **Mischief**) was a goddess of a subtle and fine frame, thus describes the tenderness and delicacy of her feet:

> The tender-footed Goddess shuns the ground;
> With airy step, upon the heads of men
> Sets her fine treading, and from head to head
> Trips it along full nimbly.—

The poet here provides fair proof, I think, of her tenderness: she walks on soft places rather than hard ones. I shall use the same argument to prove the tenderness of **Love**. For he neither walks on the ground, nor goes upon human heads (which, in truth, are places that are not altogether soft); instead, **Love** makes the softest places possible his path and his dwelling too. He fixes his residence in the characters <note>original: "manners"</note> and in the souls of gods and men. He does not settle in all souls indiscriminately; for if he happens upon anyone whose character is rough, away he marches, and takes up his residence in tender souls whose manners are the softest. 

Since, therefore, he refuses to touch anyone but the softest people, or any but their softest parts—both with his feet and all over his fine frame—he cannot be anything but extremely delicate and tender. Thus have we seen that **Love** is full of

For it would be impossible for him to diffuse himself through every part of us and penetrate into our innermost soul, or to make his first entry and his final exit unnoticed by us, if his substance were hard and resistant to the touch. But a clear proof of his yielding, easy, and pliant form is that gracefulness of person, which everyone acknowledges belongs to him in the highest degree: for ungracefulness and **Love** never agree but are always visibly at odds. 

That he excels in beauty of color is evident from his way of life, in that he is continually familiar with flowers, which are like himself. For **Love** does not reside in a body, or in a soul, or any other place where flowers never grew; or, if they did, where they have all fallen and the place is quite stripped of flowers <note>original: "deflowered"</note>. He never acts through compulsion or force himself, for compulsion or force cannot reach **Love**; nor does he ever force or compel others, for every being obeys the dictates and commands of **Love** freely and willingly. Where both parties are willing and each freely consents to the other, the laws—which are the "kings" of the city—say there is no injustice done. 

But not only does the perfection of justice belong to **Love**; he is equally endowed with consummate temperance. For to be superior to pleasure and to govern one's desires is everywhere called temperance. Now it is universally agreed that no pleasure is superior to **Love**; but, on the contrary, that all pleasures are his inferiors. If so, they must all be subjects and servants to **Love**, and he must rule and be the master. Having dominion thus over all pleasures and all desires, in—

In the other kind of creative power—the creation of animals—it is undeniably thanks to the wisdom of this deity that all living things owe their birth and production. Furthermore, regarding the works of the mechanical arts, do we not know that every artist who has Love for his teacher becomes eminent and illustrious, but that the artist whom Love does not inspire and animate never rises from obscurity? Archery, the art of healing, and the art of divination were the inventions of *Apollo* under the guidance of Love and the influence of his favorable power. So we see that the God of Wisdom himself was the disciple of the God of Love. Prompted by Love, the *Muses* invented the art of music, *Vulcan* <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and blacksmiths.</note> the art of working metals, *Minerva* <note>The Roman name for Athena, goddess of wisdom and weaving.</note> the art of weaving, and *Jupiter* <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note> the art of governing both gods and mortals. From the beginning of that era, the affairs of the gods were well settled; it began from the time when Love arose and intervened among them—specifically, the love of beauty, for disorder and deformity are by no means the objects of Love. Before that time, as I mentioned earlier, they say many sad and strange accidents befell the gods; it was when Necessity reigned and ruled over all things. But as soon as the charms of beauty gave birth to the God whom we celebrate, every good thing that blesses either gods or mortals rose with him. Thus, *Phaedrus*, in the first place, Love appears to me to be most excellent himself in beauty and in virtue; in the next place, he is the cause of similar excellencies in other beings. I feel inclined to write a verse or two on this subject, concerning the effects which Love produces:—

---

¹ This passage relies on the fact that the Greek word *poiesis* <note>original Greek: *ποίησις*</note>, which we have translated as "creative power," signifies not only making or creation, but poetry as well, just as the word *poietes* <note>original Greek: *ποιητὴς*</note> signifies both "creator" and "poet." Taking advantage of these different meanings, *Agathon* attributes *poiesis*, or creation, to each of the three kinds of Love mentioned in note 2, page 486, as the work or effect of each. To the first, he attributes poetry—an art which creates, as it were, or makes its own subject out of nothing real, but out of the mere imagination of the poet. To the next, he justly ascribes the making or generating of animals in a way peculiar to Nature; she begins from the smallest materials and collects all the rest by imperceptible degrees from all neighboring sources—forming and animating them all the while—and thus seems to create out of nothing as well. And Love, in the sense in which he uses the word last, he no less justly supposes to have the principal hand in making the most excellent works of every art, where the artist has his subject matter already created and lying all at once before him, and therefore apparently creates nothing but the form. —S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, the translator.</note>

It is he who frees us from reserve and strangeness, and who provides us with openness and intimacy. It is he who establishes social gatherings and assemblies like this one. In festive entertainments, in dances, and in feasts, he is the manager, the leader, and the founder; introducing courtesy and sweetness, banishing coarseness and wildness; spreading benevolence and kindness, and restraining malice and ill-will. He is favorable, gracious, and good to all: the admired wonder of wise men, and the heartfelt delight of the gods. He is the envy of those who do not possess him, and the prize of only those who are fortunate. He is the father of delicacy and tenderness, of elegance and grace, of attractive charms and amorous desires. He is observant of good and overlooks evil. In difficulties, in fears, in silent wishes, and in gentle conversation, he is the protector, the encourager, the patron, and the inspirer. Of both gods and men, all linked together, he is the beauty and the ornament: a guide to all that is good and lovely, the best and the most charming. It is the duty of everyone to follow him, joining in a chorus of praise or taking part in that sweet song sung by <term>Love</term> <note>original: "Eros"</note> himself, with which he softens the heart and soothes the mind of every god and mortal.—This is my speech, <term>Phaedrus</term>, which I dedicate to <term>Love</term>; a speech, partly playful and partly serious, such as the best of my poor abilities in wit and eloquence are able to provide.

I realized how ridiculous it was for me to claim to be an expert in matters of love and to agree to join you in giving <term>panegyrics</term> <note>panegyric: a formal public speech delivered in high praise of a person or thing</note> on Love, when at the same time I was completely ignorant of the matter. I did not even know the right way to praise anything. For I was so foolish¹ as to imagine that we should never say anything but the truth in our <term>encomiums</term> <note>encomium: a speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly</note> on any subject; I thought the real qualities of the subject were the materials we had to work with, and that the job of a <term>panegyrist</term> was simply to select the most beautiful and best of those real qualities and arrange them in the most skillful way. 

Because I was under this impression, I was confident that I would speak well on the subject, because I knew what praises could truthfully be attributed to Love. However, I now see that this is not the right way to deliver a <term>panegyric</term>. Instead, when we praise something, we are supposed to attribute every great and good quality to it, whether those qualities truly belong to it or not. ...doing, where it was possible for us; adapting these passages one to the other in the translation. But in one of the words, which is important for the humor, we found it nearly impossible. For the word *deinos* <note>original: δεινὸς</note>, here in <term>Homer</term>, means "terrible" or "frightful"; yet the same word as used here by <term>Plato</term> means "great," "weighty," or "powerful." Now in English, both these meanings cannot be fully and exactly expressed by the same single word. The word "formidable," however, though it would weaken the sense in <term>Homer</term>, may serve to express the allusion in <term>Plato</term> to <term>Homer’s</term> "terrific" usage. 

This double meaning of the word *deinos*, and the similarity in sound between "Gorgon" and "<term>Gorgias</term>"—or between "the Gorgon's head" <note>original: Γοργειη [κεφαλὴ]</note> and "the Gorgian head" <note>original: Γοργιειη</note>—seem to be humorous imitations of the style of <term>Agathon</term> and <term>Gorgias</term>, both of whom were fond of such puns and childish wordplay. It is necessary to notice some other words in this passage because <term>Stephens</term> <note>Henri Estienne, a famous 16th-century editor of Plato</note> suspected they might not be original—specifically the words "in the speech" <note>original: ἐν τῷ λόγῳ</note>. He likely imagined them to be a marginal note explaining the word "to speak" <note>original: λέγειν</note>. In truth, however, they are absolutely necessary to the sense; for "speech" <note>original: λόγῳ</note> here is contrasted with "action" <note>original: ἔργῳ</note>—referring to the actual sending forth and visibly presenting the head of <term>Gorgias</term>. Furthermore, omitting those words would lessen the impact of another <term>Gorgiasm</term> <note>a rhetorical device typical of the orator Gorgias</note> intended in the repetition of the words "to speak" <note>original: λέγειν</note>, "speech" <note>original: λόγῳ</note>, and "of speech" <note>original: λόγου</note>. — S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, the translator</note>

Whether these claims are false, it seems, is not considered important. For the proposal, it appears, was this: that each of us should compose a <term>panegyric</term> <note>panegyric: a formal public speech delivered in high praise of someone or something</note> which, by common consent, was to be accepted as a tribute to Love—not to compose a panegyric that actually describes Love or gives him the credit he truly deserves. I assume this is why you collect every possible topic of praise from all sides and attribute every kind of perfection to Love. You represent him and his actions in such a way that he cannot help but appear beautiful and good in the highest degree—at least to those who do not know him. He certainly could never be seen that way by those who actually understand him. In this way, the panegyric is made to sound fine and pompous. 

But for my part, I was completely unfamiliar with composing panegyrics in this manner, and it was in my ignorance that I agreed to be one of the speakers. Therefore, I only committed myself with my tongue; my mind was not a party to the agreement. <note>original: "Only with my tongue... did I engage myself: my mind was no party to the agreement." This is a famous reference to a line from Euripides' play *Hippolytus*: "My tongue swore, but my mind remains unsworn."</note> So, farewell to that promise, for I shall never give a panegyric in that style; indeed, I would not know how. However, I am ready to speak the truth concerning the subject proposed, if you wish to hear it and if I may be allowed to speak in my own way. I do not intend to set my speech in competition with any of yours and so <unclear>run</unclear> the risk of being rightfully laughed at. Consider, therefore, Phædrus—for <unclear>it</unclear> is your project—whether the kind of speech you can expect from <unclear>me</unclear> would be acceptable to you. "Instead of just being 'probable,'" said Socrates, "consider if it is not actually necessary that every being who feels desire should desire only that which he lacks. to a necessary degree. But how does it appear to you?

"You speak well," said Socrates. "I ask you then: can a man who is already large wish to be a man of large size? Or can a man who is strong wish to be strong?"

### THE SPEECH OF SOCRATES.

It is right and proper, Agatho, to follow the method you established: first, to declare what kind of being Love is, and then to show the effects he produces. I think the easiest way to carry out this plan is to present the entire doctrine to you in the same way and order in which I was questioned and taught on the subject by Diotima. 

She began with me when I was saying much the same things that Agatho just asserted: that Love was a deity excellent in goodness, and was also one of those who were fair and beautiful. She refuted me with the same arguments I used to refute Agatho, proving to me that Love, by my own account, was neither beautiful nor good. 

"What are you saying, Diotima?" I asked. "Is Love then an ugly and evil being?" 

"Hush," <note>original: "Soft"</note> she replied; "do not use such language! <note>The original "abusive language" here refers to speaking ill of a deity or blaspheming.</note> Do you imagine that every being who is not beautiful must necessarily be ugly?" 

"Without a doubt," I answered. 

"And do you conclude," she said, "that every being who is not wise must be ignorant? Do you not realize there is a middle ground between wisdom and ignorance¹?" 

I asked her what that could be. 

"To have right opinions," she said, "perceiving things as they really are, without being able to explain the reason why they are so. Do you not perceive," she continued, "that this is not the same as having science <note>In this context, "science" refers to *episteme* or certain, demonstrative knowledge.</note> or true knowledge? For how can there be science when the cause or reason for a thing remains unknown²? Yet it is not ignorance either; for that which—

To apply this to the case of Love: though you have agreed he is neither good nor beautiful, do not imagine he must therefore be ugly and evil; rather, he is something between those opposites." 

"Well," said I, "but he is acknowledged by everyone to be a powerful God, regardless." 

"By everyone who knows him, do you mean," she asked, "or by everyone who knows him not?" 

"By everyone universally," I replied. 

Upon this she smiled and said, "How, Socrates, could he be acknowledged as a powerful God by those who absolutely deny his divinity?" 

"Who are they?" I asked. 

"You yourself," she replied, "are one of them, and I am another." 

"Explain your meaning," I said. 

"My meaning is easy to be explained," she said. "For answer me this question: Do you not say that the Gods are, all of them, blessed and happy? Or would you dare to say of any one of the Gods that he was not a blessed and happy being?" 

"Not I, for my part," I said, "by Jupiter!" 

"By a happy being," she said, "do you not mean a being possessed of things fair, beautiful, and good?" 

"It is granted," I answered. 

"And you granted before," she said, "that Love, from his poverty <note>original: "indigence"</note> and lack of things good and beautiful, desired those things of which he was destitute." 

"I allowed it." 

"How then," she said, "can he be a God, if he is destitute of things fair, beautiful, and good?" 

"It appears," I said, "that he by no means can be." 

"You see then," she said, "that even in your own judgment, Love is no God." 

"What!" I said, "must Love then be a mortal?" 

"Far from that," she replied.

<note>This note explains that knowledge requires a rational foundation. In the Greek it runs thus: <term>αλογον γαρ πραγμα πως αν ειη επιστημη ;</term> <note>original Greek: "For how can a thing without reason be knowledge?"</note> Aristotle expresses the same meaning in the same concise way, thus: <term>μετα λογου γαρ η επιστημη.</term> <note>original Greek: "For knowledge is accompanied by reason."</note> (Nicomachean Ethics, Book 6, Chapter 6). Here, <term>logos</term> <note>original: "λογος", meaning reason or account</note> is the same thing that Plato in his *Meno* calls <term>logismos aitias</term> <note>original: "λογισμος αιτιας"</note>, which is the rational account of a thing, deriving it from its cause. For the cause (the formal cause) of every particular truth is some general truth, in which that particular is virtually included. Accordingly, in a perfect <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> we may see the truth of the conclusion virtually included in the truth of the major proposition. Nor can we properly be said to know any one truth until we see the whole of that higher truth in which the particular one is contained.—S.</note>

the immortal.—"But what specifically is he, Diotima?"—"A great spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note> ¹," she replied.

¹ The following excellent account of Love, which explains why Plato calls him a great spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note>, is from the manuscript commentary of Proclus on the *First Alcibiades*:

Different Gods have different properties: some are the creators of whole things, of the form of all beings, and of their essential beauty; others provide life and are the sources of its various types; others maintain the unchanging order and guard the unbreakable connection of things; and finally, others who are assigned a different power preserve all things through their beneficial actions. In the same way, every order of love is the cause for all things to turn toward divine beauty—leading back, joining, and establishing all secondary natures in what is beautiful, filling them from that source, and shining upon all things with the gifts of its light. 

For this reason, it is stated in *The Banquet* that *Love* is a great spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note>, because Love first demonstrates this kind of power within itself; it is the middle ground between the object of desire and the nature that desires, and it is the cause of lower things turning toward higher things. Therefore, the entire sequence of love, being positioned at the entrance to the cause of beauty, calls all things upward to this cause. It forms a middle path between the object of Love and the things that Love recalls. Thus, it establishes within itself the model for the entire spiritual <note>original: "dæmoniacal"</note> order, holding the same middle position among the Gods that spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> hold between divine and mortal natures. 

Since every sequence of love possesses this property among the Gods, we must consider its unified and hidden peak to be inexpressibly established in the highest orders of the Gods, joined with the first and most intelligible beauty. Its middle stage shines among the celestial <note>original: "supermundane"</note> Gods with an intellectual nature; its third stage possesses a distinct power among the independent <note>original: "liberated"</note> Gods; and its fourth stage is distributed in many ways throughout the world, producing many orders and powers and giving these gifts to different parts of the world. 

But after this unifying and first principle of Love, and after the three-part essence perfected from it, a vast variety of "Loves" shines forth with divine light. From these, the choirs of angels are filled with Love; and the groups of spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note>—filled with this God—attend on the Gods who are drawn back to intelligible beauty. Furthermore, the army of heroes, along with spirits and angels, are moved to participate in beauty with a divine, ecstatic frenzy <note>original: "bacchanalian fury"</note>. Finally, all things are excited, revived, and flourish through the influence <note>original: "influx"</note> of beauty. 

But the souls of those people who receive such inspiration, and who are naturally related to the God, constantly move toward beauty. They enter the realm of physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note> to benefit more imperfect souls and to provide for those natures that need to be saved. The Gods and their attendants, remaining in their proper states, benefit all lower natures and turn them toward themselves; however, the souls of men, by descending and entering the world of birth, imitate the beneficial providence of the Gods. 

Just as souls aligned with other Gods descend purely into the mortal regions to benefit the souls living there—some helping imperfect souls through prophecy, others through mystical ceremonies, and others through divine healing—so too do souls who choose a life of love follow the deity who presides over beautiful things, for the purpose of caring for noble <note>original: "well-born"</note> souls. From the beauty that is visible, they are led back to divine beauty, and together with themselves, they elevate those who are the objects of their love.

And this also divine Love primarily accomplishes in the realm of pure thought <term>intelligibles; things perceived by the mind rather than the senses</term>: for he unites himself to the object of love, extends the participants of his power toward it, and inserts in all things one bond and one indissoluble friendship with each other, and with beauty itself. Souls, therefore, possessed by love and sharing the inspiration derived from it—by using a pure spiritual body <term>undefiled vehicle; in Platonic thought, the soul's subtle or celestial "envelope"</term>—are led from visible beauty to the beauty of the mind, and make this the ultimate goal of their energy. Likewise, by kindling a light in more imperfect souls, they also lead these back to a divine nature, and are divinely moved together with them around the fountain of all-perfect beauty.

But those souls who, through a corrupt education <note>original: "perverse education," meaning a upbringing that misleads the soul</note>, fall away from the gift derived from above, yet are still granted a nature prone to love—these souls, through their ignorance of true beauty, are busily occupied with what is material and divisible. They are astonished by these material things because they do not understand the passion they are experiencing. Consequently, they abandon everything divine and gradually sink into impiety and the darkness of matter. They appear, indeed, to hasten toward a union with the beautiful, in the same manner as perfectly loving souls; but they are ignorant of the nature of that union, and instead drift toward a scattered life and into the "sea of unlikeness" <note>original: "sea of dissimilitude," a Platonic metaphor for the chaotic and unstable material world</note>. They are also joined with ugliness itself and the material lack of form. For how can material natures truly merge with one another? Or where can visible beauty be found pure and genuine, when it is thus mingled with matter and filled with the deformity of its physical subject? Some souls, therefore, genuinely share in the gifts of Love, while by others these gifts are corrupted. For just as according to Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> the downward flow of intellect produces mere cunning, and a distorted sharing of wisdom produces sophistry, so too the light of Love, when it meets a depraved recipient, produces a tyrannical and unrestrained life.

After this, in another part of the same admirable commentary, Proclus presents us, as he says, with some of the more secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> assertions concerning Love; and they are as follows:

> Love is neither to be placed among the first nor among the last of beings. Not among the first, because the object of Love is superior to Love itself; nor yet among the last, because the lover participates in Love. It is necessary, therefore, that Love should be established between the object of love and the lover, and that it should come after beauty, but before every nature that is filled with love. Where then does it first exist? How does it extend itself through the universe, and from which primary units <term>monads</term> does it spring forth?

> There are three foundational realities <term>hypostases</term>, therefore, among the intellectual and hidden Gods. The first is characterized by *the good*, meaning *the good itself*, residing in that place where, according to the oracle, the paternal source <term>monad</term> remains. The second is characterized by *wisdom*, where the first intelligence flourishes. The third is characterized by *the beautiful*, where, as Timaeus says, the most beautiful of intellectual beings resides. in the indescribable order <note>original: "ineffable order"</note> * of the Gods, I mean *faith, truth,* and *love.* And *faith* indeed establishes all things in good; but *truth* unfolds all the knowledge in beings; and lastly, *love* converts all things, and gathers them into the nature of beauty. This triad indeed proceeds from that point through all the orders of the Gods, and imparts to all things by its light a union with the realm of pure thought <term>intelligible itself</term>. It also unfolds itself differently in different orders, everywhere combining its powers with the unique characteristics <term>idioms</term> of the Gods. And among some it exists indescribably, incomprehensibly, and as a single unity; but among others, as the cause of connecting and binding; and among others, as endowed with a perfecting and forming power. Here again it exists intellectually and paternally; there, in a manner entirely moving, life-giving, and effective; here, as governing and assimilating; there, in a liberated and pure <term>undefiled</term> manner; and elsewhere, according to a multiplied and divided mode. Love, therefore, descends from the highest realms of thought to the concerns of the world, calling all things upward to divine beauty. Truth also proceeds through all things, illuminating all things with knowledge. And lastly, faith proceeds through the universe, establishing all things as a unity in what is good. Hence the oracles assert that all things are governed by, and remain in, these. And on this account they order practitioners of divine ritual <term>Theurgists</term> to join themselves to divinity through this triad. The objects of pure thought <term>intelligibles</term> themselves, indeed, do not require the medium of love, because of their indescribable union. But where there is a union and separation of beings, there also Love remains. For it is the binder and peacemaker of natures existing after and before itself; but it is the converter of lower things into higher ones, and the soul-elevating <term>anagogic</term> and perfecting cause of imperfect natures.

The oracles, therefore, speak of Love as binding, and residing in all things: and hence, if it connects all things, it also unites <term>copulates</term> us with the governments of spirits <term>dæmons; in Greek philosophy, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</term>. But Diotima calls Love a great spirit <term>dæmon</term>, because it everywhere fills up the middle ground between the one who desires and the object desired. And, indeed, that which is the object of Love claims for itself the first rank, but that which loves is in the third rank from the beloved object. Lastly, Love takes a middle position between each, gathering and collecting together that which desires and that which is desired, and filling subordinate natures from better ones. But among the intellectual and hidden <term>occult</term> Gods it unites the intellectual mind to the first and secret beauty by a certain life better than intelligence itself. Hence, the theologian of the Greeks <note>Likely referring to Orpheus</note> calls this Love blind; for he says "shepherding in his breast blind, swift Love:" <note>original Greek: ποιμαινων πραπιδεσσιν ανομματον ωκυν ερωτα</note>. But in natures that come after the highest realms of thought, it imparts by illumination a bond that cannot be broken to all things perfected by itself: for a bond is a certain union, but one accompanied by much separation. On this account the oracles are accustomed to call the fire of this Love a joiner <term>copulator</term>: for, proceeding from the highest intellectual mind, it binds all following natures with each other, and with itself. Hence, it joins all the Gods with divine beauty, and spirits <term>dæmons</term> with Gods; but it joins us with both Gods and spirits. In the Gods, indeed, it has a primary existence; in spirits a secondary one; and in individual souls an existence through a third progression from these principles. Again, in the Gods it exists beyond being <term>superessential</term>: for every class of Gods is beyond being. But in spirits it exists according to their essence; and in souls according to illumination. And this triple order appears similar to—

Through their intervention proceeds every kind of divination, and the priestly art relating to sacrifices, and the mysteries and incantations, along with the whole of divination and magic.
