the triple power of intellect. For one intellect exists as transcendent <term>imparticipable</term>, being exempt from all partial types; but another exists as shared <term>participated</term>, in which the souls of the Gods also share as a better nature; and another is produced from this within souls, which is, indeed, their perfection. And *Timaeus* himself signifies these three distinctions of intellect. That Love, therefore, which exists in the Gods must be considered as similar to transcendent intellect: for this is exempt from all the beings which receive and are illuminated by its nature. But daemonic Love is similar to shared intellect: for this is essential, and is perfected from itself, in the same manner as shared intellect resides most closely in souls. And the third Love is similar to intellect which exists as a habit, and which inserts an illumination into souls. Nor is it without reason that we consider Love as coordinate with this intellectual difference: for in the realm of pure thought <term>intelligible intellect</term> it possesses its first and hidden existence <term>hypostasis</term>: and if it leaps forth from there, it is also established there according to its cause. And it appears to me that *Plato*, finding that the realm of pure thought was called by *Orpheus* both Love and a great Daemon, was himself pleased to celebrate Love in a similar manner. Very properly, therefore, does *Diotima* call it a great daemon; and *Socrates* joins the discourse about Love with that concerning Daemons. For, as everything daemonic is suspended from the medium of love, so also the discourse concerning a daemonic nature is joined with that concerning Love, and is allied to it. For Love is a medium between the object of love and the lover; and a daemon is a medium between man and divinity. —T. <note>The "T" refers to Thomas Taylor, the translator and Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>

After they had finished supper, Poverty came begging because there was such an abundance of delicacies, and she lingered by the door. Just then, Plenty—intoxicated with nectar <gloss>1</gloss> (for wine <gloss>2</gloss> did not yet exist)—went out into the gardens of Jupiter. Burdened by the weight of the liquor he had drunk, he fell asleep <gloss>3</gloss>. Poverty, hoping in her need to have a child by Plenty, craftily lay down beside him and became pregnant with Love. 

Because of this, Love is the constant follower and attendant of Venus, having been conceived on the goddess's birthday. Also, because of his natural disposition, he is a lover of all beauty, and is all the more attached to Venus herself because she is beautiful. Now, since Love is the son of Plenty and Poverty, his life and circumstances are as follows: First, he is always poor. He is far from being fair or delicate, as most people imagine him; instead, he is rough, weathered, and dry. He goes barefoot, has no home, and sleeps on the bare ground without a roof over his head. He lies at doorsteps and in the streets, in the open air. In this way, he shares his mother’s nature, living in constant want. 

On the other hand, from his father’s side, he inherits very different qualities. This is why he is always scheming for what is good and beautiful. He is courageous, energetic, and quick to act—a master hunter, always inventing new tricks to catch his prey. He is deeply thoughtful and full of resources, spending his whole life philosophizing. He is powerful in magic and charms, and equally skilled in clever argument <term>sophistry</term>. By nature, he is not a mortal in the common sense...

all things, but is filled as far as it can be filled from *Plenty*, whose overflowing fullness ends in its dark and echoing <note>original: "rebounding"</note> seat. *Plato*, therefore, by calling *Love* the offspring of *Plenty* and *Poverty*, appears to understand its entire nature. For *Love*, understood as being the same as *Desire*, exists as the son of *Plenty* according to its existence within *Jupiter*; but according to its lowest form of existence, it is the offspring of *Matter*. For *Matter* also desires what is good, though her desire is extremely weak and fading. By describing *Poverty* becoming pregnant with *Love* at the birth of *Venus*, *Plato* secretly suggests <note>original: "occultly intimates"</note> that the divine abundance in the <term>Demiurge</term> (the Creator of the world) flows into matter in conjunction with the light of divine beauty.—T.

way of mortality, nor yet is he immortal in the same way as the immortal gods. Instead, sometimes within the same day, he lives and flourishes when he happens to be successful, and shortly afterward he dies; then, soon after that, he revives again because he shares his father's nature. Whatever abundance flows to him is continually slipping away, so that Love is never completely in a state of either wealth or total poverty.

Furthermore, he is positioned in the middle ground between wisdom and ignorance. The situation regarding wisdom is this: none of the gods pursue philosophy <note>original: "philosophize"</note> or desire to become wise, for they already are so. If there is any other being besides the gods who is truly wise, that being does not pursue philosophy either. On the other hand, the search for wisdom does not belong to the ignorant <gloss>¹</gloss>. For this is the very reason the state of ignorance is so miserable: although a person in this state is not beautiful, good, or wise, they believe they have no need for any kind of correction or improvement. Thus, those who are ignorant do not seek or desire that which they do not realize they lack.

"Then who are they, Diotima," I asked, "who pursue philosophy, if they are neither the wise nor the ignorant?"

"That is obvious," she said. "Even a child could see by now that they must be those who stand in the middle rank of existence, and Love is one of them. For wisdom is among the things of the highest beauty, and all beauty is the object of love. It follows, therefore, by necessity, that Love is a philosopher—a lover of wisdom—and as such, he stands between the expert in wisdom and the completely ignorant. This, like all the rest of his circumstances, is due to his parentage; he is born of a father who is wise and rich in all things, and a mother who is unwise and in want of all things.

Such, dear Socrates, is the nature of this <term>daemon</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, a 'daemon' is a spirit that acts as an intermediary between gods and humans, not an evil 'demon' in the modern sense</note>. But it is not at all surprising that you had other thoughts about the being you took for Love. Based on the description you gave of him yourself, you seem to have mistaken the *beloved* for the *lover*. I imagine it was because of this mistake that Love appeared so beautiful to you. For the object of love—that which is lovable—is truly beautiful and delicate, perfect, and completely blessed. But the subject who loves has a different nature, such as—"

"This, Socrates," she said, "is the next thing I shall do my best to teach you. It is already clear what kind of being Love is and who his parents were; and you yourself have asserted that his object is beauty. Now, what answer should we give if we were asked, 'O Socrates and Diotima! What do you mean when you say that beauty is the object of Love?' To put my question in simpler terms," she said, "what is it that the lover of beauty desires?"

"To possess that beauty," I replied.

"Your answer," she said, "leads to a further question: What will be the condition of the person who possesses that beauty?"

I told her I could not easily answer such a question.

"Suppose then," she said, "that we change the subject of the question. If we put 'the good' <note>The Greek term used here is *agathos*, referring to the ultimate moral or functional excellence.</note> in the place of 'beauty,' and someone were to ask you, 'Answer me, Socrates: what is it that the lover of good desires?'"

"To possess that good," I answered.

"And what," she asked me again, "will be the condition of the person who possesses that good?"

"This," I said, "is a question I can answer much more easily: that person will be happy."

"Correct," she said; "for it is by possessing good things that happy people are in that state of happiness they enjoy. There is no need to ask further, 'Why, or for what purpose, does a person wish to be happy?' The answer appears to be final and fully satisfactory."

"That is true, without dispute," I said.

"Now, do you think this wish and this desire," she asked, "are common to all people? Do you think that everyone wants to always possess good things? Or do you think otherwise?"

"I think exactly that," I replied; "such a wish is common to everyone."

"Well then, Socrates," she said, "must we not acknowledge that everyone is in love, seeing as the desires of everyone are always fixed on the same things? Or shall we say that some people are in love and others are not?"

"That thought," I confessed, "surprises me a little."

"Do not be surprised," she said; "for the reality is simply this: we take the name 'love,' which actually belongs to all love in general, and we apply it to only one particular kind of love that we have singled out from the others, while we distinguish the other types by different names."

"To help me understand your meaning more perfectly," I said, "can..."

"Can you not produce some other case parallel to this?" I asked.

"I can," she said. "The following case is parallel: Making or creating, as you know, encompasses many kinds of operations. For every cause by which anything passes from non-being into being¹ is a creation. Thus, all the operations and all the works executed through any of the arts are indeed so many creations; and all the artists and craftsmen are real creators, makers, or poets <note>original: 'poietai' (the Greek word for both 'makers' and 'poets')</note>."

"True," I said.

"And yet you know," she continued, "they are not all called 'poets' or 'makers,' but are distinguished by different names. Meanwhile, one particular kind of creation—that which is performed in meter through the Muse’s art—is singled out from the other kinds. The name 'poetry,' to which all types of creation have an equal right, is given to that form alone. For that alone is called 'poesy' or 'making,' and only the artists in this specific branch of creation are distinguished by the name of 'poets' or 'makers'."

"Perfectly right," I said.

"It is just the same in the case of Love," she said. "Universally, all desire for good things and all that longing for happiness found in every individual of humankind is the work of the mighty deity of Love, who subdues and governs the hearts of all through secret ways and stratagems. His followers <note>original: 'votaries'</note> in many various ways—such as those engaged in the pursuit of wealth, physical strength, or wisdom—are not said to be 'in love,' nor is the name of 'lover' granted to any of them. But we reserve the terms 'love,' 'lovers,' and 'being in love' only for those who are devoted to Love in one particular way and devote themselves to one certain species of love—even though these terms should be considered general and applicable in common to all the different kinds."

"In all appearance," I said, "you are entirely right."

She proceeded, however, to confirm the truth of what she had said in the following manner: "There is a saying," she continued, "that lovers are in search of their other half. But my teaching is that we love neither the half nor even the whole of ourselves, unless it happens, my friend, to be in some way or other **good**—

¹ *Being* does not here signify existence in general, but the particular form or essence of anything—the "being" what it is. Likewise, "non-being" just before does not signify absolute non-existence, but the non-being of some particular thing, or the absence of some form that is afterward introduced into existence. Accordingly, *creation*, immediately after, does not mean what is nowadays generally understood by that term—a making of something out of mere nothing—for Plato seems to have had no concept of that possibility. Instead, it is to be understood here as bringing a specific form or being into existence that did not exist before.—S. <note>The "S." identifies this note as belonging to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

For to conceive and to impregnate is to immortalize the species <note>original: 'kind'</note>: it is producing immortality out of an animal which is mortal. Hence, whenever that which is filled with procreative power approaches something beautiful, it smiles benignly; and through the delight it feels, opening and expanding itself, it breeds or procreates. But whenever it meets with something deformed or ugly, it grows morose, saddened, and contracts; it turns away, retreats, and does not procreate. Instead, restraining the swollen power within that is ready to burst forth, it carries the burden with distress. 

This is why those who are full of this power, and long to procreate, focus much of their creative energy upon that which is beautiful: it is because beauty frees them from those labor pains <note>original: "generative throes"</note> with which they struggle. This is only possible in one way: through procreation. By this process, a new living thing is constantly produced to take the place of the old one that has died. In no other way is life continued for any individual being, of whom we say that they are still living and call them the same person. For example, every man from infancy to old age is called the same person, even though he never has anything in him that remains the same; he is continually becoming a new man, having lost who he was in his hair, his flesh, his bones, his blood, and indeed his whole body. And this is true not only of his body, but also of his soul..."

<meta>This page continues Diotima’s explanation of how mortal beings achieve a form of immortality through constant change and replacement, transitioning from physical procreation to the pursuit of eternal fame.</meta>

<page-num>508</page-num>
<header>THE BANQUET.</header>

...so too does he undergo incessant change. His ways, his manners, his opinions, his desires and pleasures, his fears and sorrows—none of these ever remain the same in any person. Instead, new ones are generated and spring up within him while the former ones fade and die away. 

But a paradox much greater than any yet mentioned concerns knowledge. Not only do we acquire some new portions of knowledge <note>original: "portions of knowledge we acquire"</note> while losing others of which we were previously masters—never remaining the same persons regarding the sum of our current knowledge—but we also undergo a similar change in every specific piece of that knowledge. For what we call study <note>original: "meditation"</note> assumes that some knowledge has actually, in a sense, left us; indeed, forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivion"</note> is the departure of this knowledge. Study then raises up a fresh remembrance in our minds in the place of this departed knowledge, preserving and continuing for us in some manner that which we had lost, so that the memory—the likeness of the knowledge—seems to be the very same thing. 

Indeed, everything mortal is preserved only in this way: not by remaining absolutely the same forever, like divine things, but by leaving behind another in its place—a new being bearing its resemblance—when it departs, dies, or vanishes. By this natural design, Socrates, the body and every other thing that is naturally mortal shares in immortality. That which is naturally immortal, however, is immortal in a different way. 

Do not wonder, therefore, that all beings are by nature affectionately drawn toward their offspring. For this loving regard follows every being for the sake of immortality.

"These things, Diotima, wisest of women," I said, "are undoubtedly true." 

To which she replied, in the style of the most accomplished scholars <note>original: "sophists"</note>, "You may be assured, Socrates, it is the truth. Nor is it any less clear, from different examples, that immortality is the great aim and goal of all. For if you observe how the love of fame and glory works upon men, and what effect it has on their conduct, you would wonder at their folly in working so hard and suffering so much in pursuit of it—unless you consider the mighty power of that passion which possesses them: a zeal to become famous in future ages and to acquire a reputation that may last forever and be immortal. It is for this, more than for the sake of their families or friends, that they..."

"Do you think," she continued, "that Alcestis <note>A mythological queen who volunteered to die in place of her husband to save his life.</note> would have died for her husband Admetus to preserve his life? Or that Achilles <note>The hero of the *Iliad* who chose a short, glorious life over a long, obscure one.</note> would have died for his friend Patroclus to avenge his death? Or that your Athenian King, Codrus <note>A legendary king of Athens who sacrificed himself in battle because an oracle predicted that the city would fall if its king were not killed.</note>, would have died for his children's sake to secure the royal succession for them, had they not imagined their virtue would live forever in the memory of future generations <note>original: "posterity"</note>, as it actually does throughout all Greece to this very day? 

Rest assured, their conduct would have been quite different had they not been filled with this vision <note>original: "imagination"</note>. For all great actions have been performed with a view toward the immortality of virtue and the never-ending glory that accompanies it. This vision inspires and motivates the actors in proportion to their own personal worth and excellence. For they are governed by that universal passion: the desire for immortality. 

But though immortality is sought by all people, those with different temperaments seek it in different ways. In people of certain constitutions, the creative power <note>original: "generative power"</note> lies chiefly and prominently in their bodies. Such people are particularly fond of the opposite sex and seek intimacy primarily with women. They are easily enamored in the common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> way of love. By fathering children, they obtain the preservation of their names and a memory of themselves which they hope will be immortal—a happiness they believe will endure forever. 

In people of another nature, the faculties of creation are just as prominent, but they are of a mental kind. For there are those who are more prolific in their souls than in their bodies; they are full of the seeds of the kind of offspring that it is the specific nature of the human soul to conceive and produce. And what offspring is this? It is wisdom and every other virtue. Those who create the most, and who are parents to the most numerous progeny in this way, are the poets and other artists who are said to have been the inventors of their respective crafts. 

But by far the most excellent and beautiful part of wisdom is that which deals with the founding and proper ordering of cities and other human societies—a part of wisdom known by the names of temperance and justice. When a person's soul has been teeming with the seeds of this wisdom since youth (and it is the natural property of divine souls to teem in this way), as soon as he reaches maturity and those seeds are fully ripened, he longs to

sow them in the souls of others, and thus to propagate wisdom. In this state of mind, his entire purpose, I imagine, is to look around and search for beauty where he may create; for he can never create anything from what is ugly or unattractive. When he first encounters outward beauty—the beauty of the body—he welcomes and embraces it; however, he turns away from where he sees physical deformity, for his soul is full of love. But if, in his further and deeper search, he has the good fortune to encounter the inward and hidden beauty of a kind-natured and noble soul, he then completely attaches himself and remains close to the whole person in whom it is found—the combination of both soul and body.

He now finds in himself an ease and an abundance of expression when he engages this partner of his soul in conversations about virtue: how it is acquired; what constitutes a truly good character; what subjects should be studied; what arts should be learned; and how time should be spent to form such a character. Desiring, therefore, to shape and perfect the object of his love, he takes on the role of a teacher <note>original: preceptor</note>. Indeed, while he converses intimately with that which is beautiful, those seeds of wisdom with which he was previously pregnant <note>original: "big with"</note> burst forth spontaneously, and he creates. 

From that time forward, whether in the presence or absence of the beloved, his mind and memory become alert and active, and he readily shares all his intellectual store. Both "parents" then join in nurturing, raising, and cultivating the fruits of their love and intellectual companionship. As a result, a friendship of the firmest kind bonds such a pair; they are held together by a much stronger tie than those who share only biological children, as they have a common and shared interest in an offspring of their own making that is more beautiful and more enduring. 

Who would not choose to be the father of such children, rather than of mortals born from his body? Who, considering *Homer*, *Hesiod*, and other excellent poets with the admiration they deserve, would not wish for such a legacy <note>original: issue</note> as they left behind—a mental offspring that preserves their memory with the highest honor and secures for them an immortal fame? Among your own people, what honors are paid to the memory of *Solon* <note>An Athenian statesman and poet often credited with laying the foundations for Athenian democracy.</note>, who fathered *the Laws*! There are the names of many others, non-Greeks as well as Greeks, who have exhibited many noble actions to the world, and have thus given birth to all kinds of virtue! To men like these, temples have often been erected on account of such offspring; but never was any man honored in this way on account of his mortal, merely human children. In the <term>mysteries</term> <note>The Greek religious rites, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries, which involved secret knowledge revealed only to initiates.</note> of Love, <term>Socrates</term>, you may perhaps be initiated and advanced this far. ¹ But I doubt whether you are able to be perfected and to attain the <term>intuition</term> <note>original: "epopteia" — the highest stage of initiation where the initiate "sees" the truth directly.</note> of what is secret and inmost ², for which all the rest is merely an introduction, even if undertaken with a rightly disposed mind. However, she said, not wanting to lack readiness in giving you thorough information, I will do my best to lead you until we have reached the end. You must simply do your best to follow me.

Whoever enters upon this great matter in a proper manner, and begins according to a right method, must have been familiar with beautiful bodies from his earliest youth. Prepared by this acquaintance with beauty, he must—if his leader ³ leads him correctly—first fall in love with one particular beautiful person, and with her produce fine sentiments and beautiful discourse. He must afterwards consider that the beauty of outward form, which he admires so highly in his beloved, is sister to a beauty of the same kind found in others. If he can then pursue this physical beauty and trace it wherever it is to be found throughout the human species, he must lack <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword is "understanding."</note>

¹ We have here a pause, or break, more solemn and awe-inspiring than any other found in <term>Plato</term>. It is very appropriate here, as it fits the sublime and mysterious character of <term>Diotima</term>; it is also necessary to introduce, with greater solemnity, the very sublime and mysterious speculations that follow.—S. <note>S. refers to the scholar Floyer Sydenham.</note>

² Great consistency of character is observed here by putting a metaphor into the mouth of the prophetess. This metaphor is taken from the method of initiation into those religious <term>mysteries</term> which were held in the highest reverence at that time. To make this initiation perfect, three orderly steps or degrees were taken. The first was called <term>purgation</term> <note>Cleansing the soul of errors.</note>, the second <term>illumination</term> <note>Receiving the light of knowledge.</note>, and the third <term>intuition</term>; very few people were ever deemed worthy to be raised to this last stage. The method observed by <term>Diotima</term> in her initiation of <term>Socrates</term> into the mysteries of wisdom follows this same gradation. Her disproving of his supposed former notions (which are actually the preceding speeches in this dialogue) corresponds to the "purgative" part of religious initiation. Her following positive instructions in the true doctrine of Love correspond to the "illuminative" part. And the rest of her discourse, as she herself plainly indicates here, alludes to the final part of religious initiation: the "intuitive."—S.

³ That is, his <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daimon" — a guiding spirit or inner divine voice, not a "demon" in the modern evil sense.</note>.—T. <note>T. refers to the scholar Thomas Taylor.</note>

understanding not to conceive that beauty is one and the same thing in all beauteous bodies. With this conception in his mind, he must become a lover of all visible forms which are partakers of this beauty. In consequence of this general love, he must moderate the excess of that passion for one only female form which had hitherto engrossed him wholly; for he cannot now entertain thoughts extravagantly high of the beauty of any particular fair one—a beauty not peculiar to her, but which she partakes of in common with all other physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> forms that are beauteous. 

After this, if he thinks rightly and knows how to estimate the value of things justly, he will esteem that beauty which is inward, and lies deep in the soul, to be of greater value and worthy of more regard than that which is outward and adorns only the body. As soon, therefore, as he meets with a person of a beauteous soul and generous nature, even if they possess only a little superficial beauty, he is satisfied with this little. He has all he wants; he truly loves, and assiduously employs all his thoughts and all his care on the object of his affection. Searching his mind and memory, he draws forth and generates such notions of things—such reasonings and discourses—as may best improve his beloved in virtue. 

Thus he arrives, naturally, to view beauty in the arts <margin>1. The word used here by Plato is *epitedeumasi* <note>original: επιτηδευμασι</note>, by which he means to include all the particulars of right discipline: every study and every exercise recommended by ancient policy to the youth of good families; in a word, all the accomplishments formed by a liberal education. These may be reduced to three kinds: habits of polite behavior, knowledge of the liberal arts, and practice of the liberal exercises of the body. As these depend on principles of art and are acquired by study, we have used the words *art, study,* and *discipline* to translate Plato’s term as the most expressive of his meaning.</margin>, the subjects of discipline and study; and he comes to discover that beauty is congenial in them all. He now, therefore, accounts all physical beauty to be of mean and inconsiderable value, as being but a small and insignificant part of beauty. From the arts he proceeds further to the sciences, and beholds beauty no less in these <margin>2. The sciences meant here are those the Platonists termed "mathematical," as being the *mathemata* <note>original: μαθηματα</note>, or the learning they deemed a necessary preparation for the study of true philosophy. These were arithmetic, geometry, music theory, and astronomy. In these sciences, every step the mind takes is from beauty to beauty; for every new theorem discovered in any of these sciences is a new object of beauty to the mind.</margin>. Having seen this, and now considering within himself that beauty is manifold and various, he is no longer like a domestic servant who has developed a narrow affection for one specific child of the family. He is no longer a mean and small-minded slave to the beauty of any one particular thing—whether it be a person, an art, a study, or a practice. Instead, betaking himself to the vast sea of beauty and surveying it with the eye of the intellect, he gives birth to many beautiful and magnificent reasonings and <term>dianoëtic</term><note>original: "dianoëtic"; referring to the process of discursive reasoning or logical thought</note> conceptions in fruitful philosophy. Thus, being strengthened and increased, he finally perceives what that one science is which is so uniquely great as to be the science of such a uniquely great beauty.

But now, she continued, try to give me all the attention you are capable of. Whoever has been advanced this far in the mysteries of Love by a right and regular progress of contemplation, and is now approaching perfect intuition, will suddenly discover a beauty bursting into view that is astonishingly admirable. This is the very beauty toward which all his preceding studies and labors had been directed. The peculiar characteristics of this beauty are these: In the first place, it never had a beginning, nor will it ever have an end; it always exists and always flourishes in perfection, incapable of growth or decay. In the next place, it is not beautiful only when looked at in one way or seen in one light, while appearing ugly when viewed another way or in a different light. It is not beautiful only at certain times, or only in reference to certain circumstances; it does not become the opposite of beauty at other times or when circumstances change. Nor is it beautiful only in some places...

<gloss>Each of these sciences opens to her view some proportion or symmetry, some harmony or order, undiscovered before. Each different science seems a different world of beauty, still enlarging on the mind’s eye as her views become more and more extensive in the science. For proportion in arithmetic differs from proportion in geometry; musical proportion differs from them both; and the science of the celestial orbs—of their several revolutions, their mutual aspects, and their distances from each other and from their common center—is involved in each of those three different proportions and comprehends them all. — Sydenham</gloss>

places, or as it appears to some persons; while in other places, and to other persons, its appearance is the reverse of beautiful. Nor can this beauty, which is indeed no other than the beautiful itself, ever be the object of imagination; as if it had some face or hands of its own, or any other parts belonging to a body. Nor is it some particular reason, nor some particular science. It resides not in any other being—not in any animal, for instance; nor in the earth, nor in the heavens, nor in any other part of the universe. Instead, simple and separate from other things, it exists alone with itself, and possesses an essence eternally uniform. All other forms which are beautiful participate in <note>original: "participate of"</note> this; but they participate in such a manner that through their creation or destruction, this supreme beauty suffers no decrease, receives no addition, nor undergoes any kind of alteration. 

When a man begins to gain a sight of this supreme beauty by re-ascending from those lower beauties through the right way of Love, he must have almost attained his goal. Now, to go—or to be led by another—along the right way of Love is this: beginning from those beauties of lower rank, to proceed in a continual ascent, always proposing this highest beauty as the end. One must use the rest merely as so many steps in the ascent: proceeding from one to two, from two¹ to all beautiful bodies; from the beauty of bodies to that of souls²; from the beauty of souls to that of arts; from the beauty of arts to that of disciplines <note>original: "disciplines" (referring to branches of knowledge or sciences)</note>; until at length, from these disciplines, he arrives at that discipline which is the study of nothing other than that supreme beauty; and thus finally attains the knowledge of what is "the beautiful itself."

The ultimate object of desire to man is to live in beholding this consummate beauty. If you ever attain the sight of this, it will appear to be found neither in gold <gloss>1</gloss>, nor in magnificent attire, nor in beautiful youths or damsels. With such things, however, many of you are currently so entirely taken up, and so absolutely charmed by the sight of them, that you would rejoice to spend your whole lives, were it possible, in the presence of those enchanting objects, without any thoughts of eating or drinking, but feasting your eyes only with their beauty and living always in the bare sight of it. 

If this be so, what effect, do you think, would the sight of beauty itself have upon a man, were he to see it pure and genuine? Imagine if it were not corrupted and stained all over with the mixture of flesh, and colors, and much more of such perishing and fading trash, but if he were able to view that divine essence—the beautiful itself—in its own simplicity of form. Do you think, she said, that the life of such a man would be contemptible or mean; the life of the man who always directed his eye toward the right object, who looked always at real beauty, and was conversant with it continually? 

Do you not perceive, she said, that in beholding the beautiful with that eye <note>The "eye of the soul" or intellect</note> with which alone it is possible to behold it, thus, and thus only, could a man ever attain to generate, not the images or semblances of virtue (as he is not having his intimate commerce with an image or a semblance), but virtue that is true, real, and substantial, born from the converse and embraces of that which is real and true? Thus begetting true virtue, and bringing her up until she is grown mature, he would become a favorite of God...

For my own part, I make it my chief study to cultivate the art which Love teaches, and employ myself upon the subjects proper for the exercise of that art with particular attention; encouraging others to follow my example, and at all times, as well as now, celebrating the power and virtue of Love as far as I am able. This speech, Phaedrus, you may accept, if you are so pleased, as a panegyric <note>original: "panegyric" — a formal public speech delivered in high praise of someone or something</note> in praise of Love: or if you choose to call it by any other name, and to take it in any other sense, let that be its right name and its proper meaning.

### THE SPEECH OF ALCIBIADES.

Socrates having thus spoken, the rest praised his oration; but Aristophanes endeavored to say something, because Socrates in his speech had mentioned him. On a sudden, however, a loud knocking was heard at the door of the porch, together with the voices of intoxicated people and the sound of the pipe. Upon this, Agatho said to the servants, "See who is there; and if there is anyone among them fit for this company, call him in: if not, say that we are no longer drinking." Not long after this, the voice of Alcibiades, who was very much intoxicated, was heard in the court, asking where Agatho was and commanding to be led to him. The flute-player, therefore, and some other of his companions, brought him to Agatho and stood with him at the doors. He was crowned with a garland of ivy and violets, having many fillets <note>original: "fillets" — ribbons or headbands worn as a sign of honor or festivity</note> on his head, and exclaiming, "All hail, my friends! Either receive as your associate in drinking a man who is very much intoxicated, or let us depart after crowning Agatho alone, for whose sake we came. For I could not," says he, "be with you yesterday; but now I come with fillets on my head, so that I may crown the head of the wisest and the most beautiful person with my own, if I may be allowed to speak so. Do you, therefore, laugh at me..."

Do you look at me as if I am intoxicated? However, though you may laugh, I well know that I speak the truth. But tell me immediately whether I may come in to join him or not, and whether you all continue drinking or not? All the company, therefore, was in an uproar and ordered him to enter and seat himself. He did so, and called for Agatho. Agatho, therefore, came, led by his companions; and Alcibiades, at the same time taking off his fillets <note>original: "fillets"; decorative ribbons or headbands worn at festivals</note>, intended to crown him. He did not see Socrates, even though he sat right before him, but sat near Agatho, between him and Socrates; for Socrates had made way for him so that he might sit. 

Alcibiades, therefore, being seated, saluted and crowned Agatho. Then Agatho said, "Boys, take off the shoes of Alcibiades, so that he may recline as the third among us." Alcibiades said, "By all means," but asked, "Who is this third drinking companion of ours?" At the same time, turning himself around, he saw Socrates. Upon seeing him, he started and exclaimed, "O Hercules! <note>An exclamation of surprise or shock</note> What is this? Are you again sitting here to ensnare me? It is usual for you to appear suddenly where I least expected to find you. And now, for what purpose are you here? And why do you sit in this place, and not with Aristophanes, or with some other who is ridiculous and wishes to be so? Instead, you have contrived to sit with the most beautiful of the guests." 

Then Socrates said to Agatho, "See if you can assist me; for the love of this man is no small matter to me. Since the time I began to love him, I am no longer at liberty either to behold or speak to any other beautiful person. Does he not, as a result of emulating and envying me in amatory <note>original: "amatory"; relating to physical love or romance</note> affairs, contrive wonderful devices, and also revile me and scarcely keep his hands off me? See, therefore, that he does not do this now, but conciliate us; or, if he should attempt violence, assist me: for the mania of this man, and his amatory impulse, very much terrify me."

Alcibiades then said, "There is no occasion for any conciliation between you and me. I shall, however, at some other time take vengeance on you for these things. But now, Agatho," he said, "give me some of the fillets, so that I may crown the wonderful head of this man. I do this so he may not blame me for crowning you, but not him—the man who vanquishes all men in discourse <note>original: "discourse"; formal speech or debate</note>, not only recently as you have done, but at all times." 

At the same time, receiving the fillets, he crowned Socrates and seated himself. Being seated, he said, "Come, gentlemen, drink, for you appear to me to be sober. This, however, is not to be allowed; for it was agreed that we should drink. I therefore engage to be your..."

The satyr Marsyas. That your outward form, therefore, is similar to these, O Socrates, even you yourself will not deny; but that you also resemble them in other things, hear in the next place. You are insolent <note>original: "contumelious"</note>: or are you not? For, if you do not acknowledge it, I will bring witnesses. Are you not also a piper much more wonderful than Marsyas¹? For he charmed men through instruments, by a power proceeding from the mouth; and he also accomplishes this even now, when any one uses that melody <note>original: "modulation"</note>. For I call the melody of Olympus² that of Marsyas, because he instructed Olympus in it. That harmony, therefore, whether it is produced by a good piper, or by a bad female player on the pipe, alone captivates <note>original: "detains"</note> the hearers, and reveals—because it is divine—those who stand in need³ of the Gods and the mysteries. But you differ from that harmony in this respect only: that you effect this very same thing by mere words without instruments. 

We, therefore, when we hear some other person relating the discourse of another, though he that relates it should be a very good orator <note>original: "rhetorician"</note>, yet we pay, as I may say, no attention to it. But when any one hears you, or another person relating your discourses—even if the one repeating them is a bad speaker, and whether it is a woman, a man, or a boy who is the listener—we are astonished and possessed. I therefore, my friends, unless I should appear to be very much intoxicated, will tell you upon oath in what manner I have been affected by the discourses of this man, and how I am even now affected.

---

¹ A celebrated piper of Celaenae in Phrygia. He was so skillful in playing on the flute that he is generally considered the inventor of it. It is fabled of him that he challenged Apollo to a trial of his skill as a musician; and, being defeated, the God flayed him alive.

² Olympus was both a poet and a musician: he was the disciple of Marsyas and flourished before the Trojan war.

³ Proclus, in his manuscript commentary on the *First Alcibiades*, where he makes a division of musical instruments, observes that those of an exciting nature were most adapted to enthusiastic energy. Hence, says he, in the mysteries and in the greatest of mystic sacrifices, the pipe is useful: for they employ its moving power in order to excite the intellectual <note>original: "dianoëtic"</note> part toward divinity. <note>original Greek: 'Τα δη κινητικα προς ενθουσιαν οικειοτατα· διο δη και εν τοις μυστηριοις και εν ταις τελεταις χρησιμος αυλος· χρωνται γαρ αυτου τω κινητικω προς την της διανοιας εγερσιν επι το θειον.</note> Such, therefore, as were excited by the melody of the pipe in a very small degree may be supposed to be implied by those who "stand in need of the Gods and mysteries"; as the other machinery of the mysteries, in conjunction with the pipe, would necessarily produce that excitation which the pipe alone was, in people such as these, incapable of effecting.

For when I hear him, my heart leaps much more than the hearts of those who celebrate the mysteries of the Corybantes <note>Priests of the goddess Cybele whose rituals involved ecstatic dancing and loud music.</note>; and my tears flow because of his discourses. I also see many others affected in the same manner. But when I hear Pericles and other good rhetoricians, I think, indeed, that they speak well, but I suffer nothing of this kind; nor is my soul agitated with tumult, nor is it indignant, as if it were in a servile condition. 

But by this Marsyas <note>A satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest; here, Alcibiades compares Socrates’ speech to Marsyas’ flute-playing.</note> I am often so affected that it appears to me I ought not to live while I lead such a life as I do. You will not, Socrates, say that these things are not true. And even now I perceive that, if I were willing to listen to him, I could not bear it, but should be affected in the very same manner. For he would compel me to acknowledge that, being yet deficient in many things, I neglect myself, but attend to the affairs of the Athenians <margin>See the First Alcibiades.</margin>. By violence, therefore, restraining my ears, I depart from him, flying, as it were, from the Sirens <note>Mythological creatures whose song lured sailors to their destruction; Alcibiades flees Socrates to avoid being "enchanted" into staying forever.</note>, lest I should sit with him until I became old. 

From him alone, likewise, of all men, I suffer that which no one would think to be in me: to be ashamed of something. I am abashed before him alone. For I am conscious that I am unable to deny that what he exhorts me to do ought to be done; but when I depart from him, I am vanquished by the honor which I receive from the multitude. I therefore avoid and fly from him; and when I see him I am ashamed, in consequence of what I had consented to do. And often, indeed, it would be a pleasure to me no longer to see him among men; and yet again, if this should happen, I well know that I should be in a much greater degree afflicted; so that I am ignorant in what manner I should use this man. And from the melodies, indeed, of this satyr, both I and many others have suffered such things.

But hear from me how much he resembles such things as I shall compare him to, and what a wonderful power he possesses. For be well assured of this, that no one of you knows him; but I will reveal him, since I have begun to speak. You see then that he is disposed in a very amatory <note>original: "amatory"; meaning inclined toward love or attraction.</note> manner toward beautiful things; and that he is always occupied with and astonished by these. And again, he knows all things, and yet knows nothing <margin>Very few have penetrated the profound meaning of Socrates when he said that he knew nothing.</margin>; so that this figure of him is very Silenical <note>Resembling Silenus, the tutor of Bacchus, who was depicted as an ugly satyr but was said to be full of wisdom within.</note>; for he is externally invested—

He is invested with his outer appearance like a carved <term>Silenus</term> <note>original: "Silenus"; in Greek mythology, Silenus was a tutor to Dionysus, often depicted as a grotesque, drunken satyr, but whose statues sometimes contained small, beautiful figures of gods inside.</note>. He thinks that all these possessions are of no worth, and that we are nothing. He also passes the whole of his life among men in irony and jest; but when he is serious and is opened, I do not know whether any of you has seen the images which are within. Thinking too that he paid great attention to my beauty, I considered this as my gain and as a wonderfully fortunate circumstance. Thinking this—as prior to this I had never been with him alone without an attendant—I then dismissed my attendant and remained with him alone. It is necessary to narrate everything to you truly.

But now attend to me; and if I lie, you, <term>Socrates</term>, must refute me. I was with him, O my fellow guests—I alone with him alone—and expected that he would immediately speak to me in such a manner as lovers are accustomed to speak to the objects of their love in solitude; and I was delighted with the expectation. After this, I encouraged him to engage with me in gymnastic exercises, expecting that I should achieve something by this means. We engaged, therefore, in these exercises, and often wrestled together with no one else present. But what need is there to say more? I did not in the least accomplish my purpose. Not succeeding in this in any respect, it appeared to me that I should attack the man more vigorously, since it was my determination to ensnare him. Hear now, then, what happened. <margin>Proclus tells us in his Manuscript Commentary on the First Alcibiades, that there was an inscription in the Eleusinian grove forbidding the uninitiated to enter into the *adyta* <term>adyta: the innermost, secret sanctuaries of a temple</term> or secret recesses of the temple. Alcibiades, therefore, as he is about to relate a circumstance which—considered independently of the design with which it is mentioned—is indecent, very properly forbids the profane <note>original: "profane" — here meaning those who are not initiated into higher philosophical or spiritual truths.</note> to be auditors of it. For in this he follows the mysteries, in which, as I have shown in my Dissertation on them, page 123, the indecent was introduced. In the mysteries too, as exhibitions of this kind were designed to free the initiated from licentious passions by gratifying the sight, and at the same time vanquishing desire through the awful sanctity with which these rites were accompanied, so what is now related by Alcibiades is introduced by Plato in order to liberate his countrymen from an unnatural vice. So that it benefits the reader at the same time that it exalts the character...

...tude. Hence the former of these, through intense study, was of a sorrowful appearance; and the latter, when he began to recall his intellect from the senses and was impeded by his eyes, blinded himself. In short, all those who have made great discoveries in the regions of science have accomplished this by retiring from the body into the sublime tower of intellect. Hence Plato says in the *Phaedrus*, that the intellects of philosophers especially recover the "wings of the soul" because they are always attentive to divine concerns; and on this account, he at one time calls such philosophers divine, and at another, sons of the Gods. Hence too Aristotle says, in his *Problems*, that all who have excelled in any art have been melancholy <note>In the ancient sense: a temperament associated with deep thought and genius</note>, whether they were born such, or whether they became such by continued meditation.

Hence both he and his companion retreated with security; for scarcely was anyone attacked who conducted himself in this manner during battle, but the enemy pursued those who fled rapidly and in disorder.

There are many other things, indeed, in which <term>Socrates</term> <note>The famous Athenian philosopher (c. 470–399 BC)</note> is admirable, and for which he might be praised. In other pursuits, others perhaps may merit the same praise; but to resemble no man, neither among the ancients nor the moderns, is a circumstance worthy of all wonder. For such as <term>Achilles</term> <note>The legendary Greek hero of the Iliad</note> was, one might conjecture that <term>Brasidas</term> <margin><term>Brasidas</term> was a famous Spartan general, who, after many great victories obtained over Athens and other Grecian states, died of a wound at Amphipolis, which Cleon the Athenian had besieged.</margin> and others were also; and again, such as <term>Pericles</term> <note>The influential statesman of Athens' Golden Age</note> was, it may be said that <term>Antenor</term> and <term>Nestor</term> <note>Wise elders and advisors from Homeric legend</note> were as well. There are likewise others who may be compared with one another in the same manner. 

But such a prodigy is this man, both in his person and his discourses, that no one by searching will find any man who nearly resembles him, neither among those of the present age nor among the ancients. He can, therefore, only be said to resemble—both in himself and his discourses—those things to which I have compared him: namely, no one among men, but the <term>Silenuses</term> and <term>Satyrs</term> <note>Mythological figures associated with Dionysus; Silenuses were often depicted as wise but ugly old men, while Satyrs were wild, half-man, half-goat creatures.</note>. 

For I omitted to mention this before: his discourses are most similar to the <term>Silenuses</term> when they are opened. To someone willing to hear them, the discourses of <term>Socrates</term> will at first appear to be perfectly ridiculous. This is because the nouns and verbs he employs externally wrap his meaning in the guise of a mocking <term>Satyr</term>. He speaks of donkeys and their burdens, of blacksmiths, shoemakers, and tanners, and he always appears to say the same things using the same examples; so that every unskillful and ignorant man will ridicule his words. 

But he who beholds his discourses when they are opened, and penetrates into their depth, will find two things. First, he will find that these alone, of all other discourses, contain true intellect within them. Second, he will find that they are most divine, are filled with numerous images of virtue, and have a very wide reach—or rather, they extend themselves to everything that a man should consider if he intends to become truly worthy. 

These, then, are the things, my fellow guests, for which I praise and also for which I blame <term>Socrates</term>. I have likewise included the injuries he has done to me. Nor has he acted in this manner toward me alone, but also toward <term>Charmides</term> the son of <term>Glauco</term>, <term>Euthydemus</term> the...

<meta>catchword: son</meta>

# THE BANQUET

son of Diocles, and very many others; for he has deceived these, as if he had been their lover, when at the same time he rather became the beloved object himself. Hence, I caution you, Agatho, not to be deceived by this man, but, knowing what I have suffered, take care, and do not—as the proverb says of fools—become wise only through painful experience.

Aristodemus related that when Alcibiades had spoken this way, the freedom of his speech excited a general laugh, because he appeared to still have a romantic regard for Socrates. Socrates, therefore, said, "You seem to me, Alcibiades, to be sober; for, otherwise, you would not have attempted in so elegant and roundabout a manner to conceal the real reason you have said all these things. Nor would you have added that point at the end as if it were unrelated to the purpose; as if the intention of everything you said was not to drive a wedge between me and Agatho. For you think that I ought to love you and no other, and that Agatho ought to be loved by you, and by no one else. This <term>Satyric and Silenic drama</term><note>Socrates refers to the satyr-plays of Greek theater, which were ribald and mocking; he compares Alcibiades' speech to these performances.</note> of yours is not hidden from us, but is perfectly obvious. But, dear Agatho, may none of these contrivances of his succeed! Let us endeavor that nothing may separate you and me."

To this Agatho replied, "Indeed, Socrates, you appear to speak the truth; and I infer that he sits between you and me specifically so that he may separate us. He will, however, gain no advantage from this; for I will come and sit next to you."

"By all means," said Socrates, "come here and sit below me."

"O Jupiter!"<note>original: "O Zeus!"</note> Alcibiades exclaimed, "how much I suffer from this man! He thinks it is necessary to surpass me in everything. But, O wonderful man, allow Agatho, if no one else, to sit between us."

"It is impossible," said Socrates, "for you have praised me, and it is necessary that I should now praise the person sitting at my right hand. If, therefore, Agatho reclines below you, he certainly will not be praised by me until after he has praised me again. But stop, you <term>demoniacal</term><note>original: "daimonie." In this context, it means someone acting under a strange or divine impulse, often used as a term of exasperated endearment.</note> man, and do not envy my praise of the lad; for I very much desire to deliver a <term>eulogy</term><note>original: "encomium"; a formal speech of high praise.</note> on him."

"Excellent! Excellent!" said Agatho to Alcibiades. "There is no reason why I should stay here, but there is every reason that I should change my seat, so that I may be praised by Socrates."

"These things are typical," said Alcibiades. "When Socrates is present, it is impossible for any other to share the favors of the beautiful. And now observe how easily, and with what persuasive language, he draws this youth to him."

After this Agatho rose, so that he might sit by Socrates; but on a sudden—

<page-num>530</page-num>
<header>THE BANQUET.</header>

Then many revellers came to the gates, and, finding them open because someone had just gone out, they entered and seated themselves. Consequently, the room became full of tumult; and as there was no longer any order observed, everyone was compelled to drink a great quantity of wine. Aristodemus therefore said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others went home to get some sleep; but he himself slept there quite soundly, as the nights were long, and woke up about daybreak when the cocks were crowing. 

When he had risen, he saw that some of the guests were asleep and others had departed; but Agatho, Aristophanes, and Socrates were the only persons still awake, and they were drinking from a great bowl, passing it to the right. He also added that Socrates was discoursing with them; however, he did not recollect the exact details of the conversation because he was not present for the beginning of it, having been asleep. Nevertheless, the summary of it, he said, was this: Socrates compelled them to acknowledge that it was the talent of the same person to compose both comedy and tragedy, and that he who was by art a tragic poet was also a comic poet. 

When they had assented to these points—by compulsion rather than readily—Aristodemus said they fell asleep. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and afterwards, when it was already day, Agatho followed. But Socrates, once they were asleep, rose and went out, with Aristodemus following him as usual. And lastly, Socrates went to the Lyceum <note>A public meeting place and gymnasium in Athens, later famous as the site of Aristotle's school.</note> and, having washed himself as he would at any other time, conversed there the whole day, and finally went home in the evening to rest.

### THE END OF THE BANQUET.

# THE PARMENIDES.
### FROM THE MANUSCRIPT COMMENTARY* OF PROCLUS ON THAT DIALOGUE.
---

**THE** beginning of this admirable Commentary, which is dedicated to Asclepiodotus the physician, is as follows:—"I beseech all the Gods and Goddesses to lead my intellect to the proposed theory, and, enkindling in me the splendid light of truth, to expand my reasoning <term>original: dianoëtic; the soul's capacity for discursive or logical thought</term> power to the science of beings. I pray them to open the gates of my soul to the reception of the divine narration of Plato, and, conducting my knowledge to the most splendid of being as if to a port, to liberate me from an abundance of false wisdom and the wandering about non-beings. May they do this through a more intellectual converse with real beings, through which alone the eye of the soul is nourished and watered, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*. And may the intelligible Gods impart to me a perfect intellect; the intellectual Gods, an uplifting <term>original: anagogic; refers to the power that leads the soul upward from the material to the divine</term> power; the supermundane rulers, an energy indissoluble and liberated from material knowledge; and the governors of the world, a winged life;

---

<note>* Though I have already cited largely from this admirable Commentary, yet I rejoice in the opportunity which is afforded me of making the following additions from it. There is not, perhaps, among the writings of the ancients any one which, on the whole, is so well calculated to lead the lover of wisdom gradually to a knowledge of the most sublime, arduous, and blissful <note>original: felicitous</note> doctrines of the philosophy of Plato. Inestimably great are the benefits which I have derived from the study of it; and it is my earnest wish that the reader of these and the preceding extracts may be able to strengthen this testimony of its excellence by his own experience. For, if I may be allowed to prophesy, this Work—if not at present, then at some future period—will be the source of the greatest good to mankind. It will be admired and studied as it deserves, while the duration of writings of a different kind, though now so popular, will, when compared with the extent of this, be fleeting like that of morning dreams.</note>

<note>The following is a translation of the Greek text provided in the original document:</note>

I pray to all the gods and goddesses to guide my mind into the proposed contemplation, and by kindling a bright light of truth within me, to extend my understanding toward the very knowledge of true beings. May they open the gates of my soul for the reception of Plato’s divinely inspired guidance, and having anchored my knowledge in the most luminous part of existence, may they cause me to cease from much "opinion-wisdom" <note>original: "doxosophia," the pretense of wisdom</note> and from wandering around things that do not truly exist. May they do this through the most intellectual occupation with true beings, by which alone the eye of the soul is nourished and watered, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*. 

May they grant me: a perfect mind from the intelligible gods; a leading power from the intellectual gods; an activity free and released from material knowledge from the rulers who are over the whole of existence; a winged life from those who have been allotted the world; a true manifestation of divine things from the angelic choirs; a fulfillment of the inspiration from the gods from the good spirits; and a high-minded, solemn, and elevated condition from the heroes. 

In short, may all the divine orders prepare me perfectly for the participation in the most visionary and mystical contemplation of Plato, which he himself reveals to us in the *Parmenides* with a depth appropriate to the subject matter. This was unfolded by the most pure applications of him who truly shared in divine inspiration with Plato, and who became a companion <note>original: "homostoichos," meaning standing in the same rank or row</note> of divine truth, becoming our leader in this contemplation and of these divine [doctrines]...

Truly a high priest <note>hierophant</note> of these discourses. I would say that he came as a model of Philosophy to humanity for the benefit of souls here on earth—instead of statues, instead of temples, instead of the whole of her sacred rites—and as a leader of salvation for the people who exist now and for those who will be in the future.

### Page 37. *When we arrived at Athens from Clazomenia, etc.*

The Italian philosophers, says Proclus, being familiar with the contemplation of the forms of beings, concerned themselves very little with the philosophy of objects of opinion <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note>. However, the philosophers of Ionia <note>the coast of modern-day Turkey</note> paid little attention to the theory of intelligibles <note>abstract, eternal truths</note>, but minutely considered nature and the works of nature. Socrates and Plato, however, participating in both of these philosophies, brought perfection to the lower branch and revealed the more elevated one. 

Indeed, Socrates demonstrates this in the *Phaedo* when he says that he was formerly a lover of physiology <note>original: "physiology," here meaning the study of natural science and physical causes</note>, but that he afterwards returned to the study of forms and the divine causes of beings. Therefore, Plato appears to me to have indicated through this opening scene exactly what they demonstrate in their philosophy: the perfection of both the Ionic and Italian doctrines. 

What is wonderful in this, and explains the matters discussed here, is that those from Ionia come to Athens so that they may share in more perfect doctrines. However, those from Athens do not go to Italy for the same reason—to share in the Italian philosophy—but instead, while remaining in Athens, they communicate their own proper doctrines there. 

In the same way, those who are able to look at beings themselves will perceive that primary things are present everywhere with unhindered energy, reaching down to the very last of things through those that act as intermediaries. These last things are perfected through the intermediaries, and the intermediaries receive what is granted by the primary natures, while moving and converting the last things toward themselves. 

Therefore, let Ionia be a symbol of nature; let Italy be a symbol of an intellectual essence; and let Athens represent that which exists in the middle, through which awakened souls may ascend from nature to the intellect. This is why Cephalus says immediately in the Introduction that he came from Clazomenia to Athens to hear the discourses of Parmenides. He met Adimantus and Glaucon in the forum, and through them became acquainted with Antiphon. He then heard the discourses, which he related just as he had learned them from Pythodorus, who had heard them from Parmenides. Through this, it is also indicated

# ADDITIONAL NOTES

He who is to be led back to an **intelligible essence** <note>The realm of pure thought and being, beyond the physical world</note> ought, in the first place, to be awakened from the body and to flee from a communion with it; for the body is merely the habitation of the soul. In the next place, he should connect himself with the "allotment of Minerva" <note>Athena/Minerva represents divine wisdom and intellectual order</note> among the "wholes" <note>Universal or cosmic entities</note>. Through the participation in this allotment, it is no longer surprising that the soul should become a spectator of the first entities, and through these arrive at the inspection of the "unities of beings" <note>The Henads, or the ultimate units of reality</note>. 

But if you are willing to speak not only in this manner, but even more universally, you may say that the Gods who govern nature, and the various powers of material forms—who also contain the entirety of indivisible and sensible reasons—are suspended from the First Cause. Being illuminated by Minerva, they are converted toward the intellectual region and hastily withdraw themselves from the **mundane system** <note>The physical, worldly universe</note>; for this system is also said to be the "habitation" of the Gods which it contains. 

By this conversion, they are also led to the united multitude of beings, and there, through divine power, proceed to the **monad** <note>The singular, primary unit or "The One"</note> of all multitude. For what is said here by Plato affords an image of these things to those who are not entirely unacquainted with such speculations. Every physical form is lower than "multitude"; but the multitude above this is indeed what it is said to be—multitude—yet it also participates in a coordinated unity. But prior to this is the "exempt one," to which there is an ascent through the **duad** <note>The principle of "twoness" or duality, acting as a bridge between the One and the Many</note> as a medium. 

The departure, therefore, from Clazomenia <note>The home city of the travelers in the dialogue</note> demonstrates an energy exempt from physical reasons. The meeting with Adimantus and Glauco in the forum indicates the dominion of the duad in the united multitude. Finally, the association with Antiphon through these two indicates the return to their unity, by which they derive perfection and a fullness of divine goods. For in every order of Gods there is a monad and the dominion of the duad; the entirety of the distributed parts is joined with the monad through the united multitude and the duad it contains—which is the mother and, as it were, the root of this multitude.

These things, as I have said, afford an image of the Gods themselves and will present an abundance of concepts to those who are willing to follow the analogy. For you may observe that the Clazomenians are many, but that Adimantus and Glauco are two; and through these two, the many communicate with Antiphon, who is one. It is evident that everywhere the "multiplied" enjoys the monad through the duad; that secondary things are always suspended from the natures prior to them; and that

<header>ON THE PARMENIDES.</header>

All are extended toward the one Parmenidean intellect. For the Clazomenians <note>Residents of Clazomenae, a Greek city in Ionia</note> are in search of Adimantus and Glauco; these lead the Clazomenians to Antiphon; Antiphon fills them with the discourses of Pythodorus; and Pythodorus is the messenger of the conversation between Parmenides, Zeno, and Socrates. These two, in turn, are united to Parmenides and wish to adhere to his doctrine; Socrates, indeed, looks toward the multitude of forms, but Zeno unites this multitude, hastening toward *the one* itself. 

We may also contemplate their order as follows: Parmenides, Zeno, and Socrates preserve an image of the entire divine order, while those who follow are likened to the secondary types of beings. Pythodorus, indeed, may be ranked according to the highest level of daemons <note>term: daemons; In Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and men, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, announcing and transmitting to secondary beings those things that proceed from primary natures. For both these roles pertain to this highest level: the one as that which is filled, the other as that which fills. 

But Antiphon may be ranked according to the daemonic order itself. For this order uses appetite and impulses and, in short, assumes a secondary life. Hence, he is represented as skilled in the equestrian art <note>The art of horse-riding, symbolizing the control of the soul's lower impulses</note>. He, therefore, is filled by those who are first, but fills those after him with an anagogic <note>term: anagogic; leading the soul upward to divine things</note> conversation from more elevated natures. 

The Clazomenians are analogous to souls familiar with the world of generation <note>The physical world of birth and decay</note>, who require the assistance of nearby daemons, but all of them aspire after that which is on high and the participation in divine discourse. Hence, leaving their habitation—the body—they proceed from ignorance to intellectual prudence (for this is Athens <note>The city is allegorized as the state of wisdom</note>). In the first place, they are united to the daemons above them, to whom the forum and the duad <note>term: duad; the number two, representing division or plurality</note> pertain, and an ascent through the duad to the monad <note>term: monad; the number one, representing unity and the divine source</note>. 

In the second place, they are extended through these to certain angels and Gods; for all association and conversation between men and Gods, both when asleep and when awake, occurs through daemons, as Diotima says in *The Banquet* <note>original: "The Symposium"</note>. Again, therefore, according to another method, we may transfer the analogy from things to persons. It is necessary, prior to the mystic theory of the things themselves, to exercise our dianoetic <note>term: dianoetic; relating to the power of discursive reason or logical thought</note> power in these characters as if they were images. For the men immediately meeting with Adimantus and Glauco (the brothers of Antiphon) upon their arrival in Athens, provides an image of another theological concept: that ascending souls derive much assistance from good fortune, which aligns them with the proper things, in the proper place, and in the proper manner; and also that we

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the opening of Plato’s Parmenides, focusing on the symbolic meaning of the characters' meeting and the specific style of the dialogue's prose.</meta>

<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

These matters do not only require the gifts of good fortune in external things, but in the anagogic <note>original: "anagogic"; meaning "upward-leading" or spiritual elevation</note> energies of the soul. Hence Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* that a divine madness <note>original: "mania"</note> regarding the objects of love is given to the lover by the Gods with the greatest good fortune. And by tracing souls back from the intelligible realm, he says that different souls descend into bodies with different fortunes. Therefore, even before entering bodies, they experience the gifts of fortune; they are governed by it and led toward that which is suited to their nature. It is very appropriate, then, that returning souls are said here to be joined with the causes that bring them to perfection through a certain kind of fortune. 

You may also see how the hierarchy of the persons is preserved here: for they meet with Adimantus and Glaucon. Socrates demonstrates in *The Republic* that Glaucon was the more perfect of these men, for he says there that he always admired Glaucon's nature. Thus, if Adimantus was the inferior, it is very proper to say they met with Adimantus and Glaucon; for the imperfect is first connected with that which is more like itself, and through that, it participates in the more perfect.

The very first sentence also reveals the character of the dialogue; it is free of anything superfluous, and is accurate and pure. Indeed, concise, pure, and spontaneous language is suited to intellectual projections <note>The direct, intuitive grasp of truth by the mind</note>. Plato is not the only one to maintain this proper style of speech; Parmenides also does so in his poetry. Although the poetic form of composition usually employs metaphors, figures of speech, and tropes, Parmenides nevertheless embraces an unadorned, simple, and pure form of expression. This is evident from expressions such as, "being approaches being" <note>original Greek: εον γαρ εοντι πελαζει</note>; and again, "since they now exist together" <note>original Greek: επει νυν εστιν ὁμου</note>; likewise, "it is not right that there should be anything either greater or smaller" <note>original Greek: ουτε τι μειζον, ουτε τι βαιοτερον πελεν χρεων εστι</note>; and everything else of this kind. Consequently, his writing appears more like prose than poetic language. 

It is evident, therefore, in this introduction by Plato, first, that he has chosen a rapid form of speech, for this is suited to the subject matter itself. In the second place, he has focused on conciseness, combined with a forceful style that binds the speech together and quickly completes the thought. And, in the third place, he proceeds using only the most necessary words, cutting out all those details from the story that someone might sophistically add for the sake of mere ornament.

### Page 38. **And upon our begging him to relate the discourses, etc.**

The request of the Clazomenians <note>Residents of Clazomenae, a Greek city in Ionia; here interpreted as souls seeking higher knowledge</note> represents the genuine adherence of souls to their proper leaders. For souls can no otherwise obtain a union and revolve in conjunction with the Gods, than through these demons <note>original: "dæmons"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not evil entities</note>. But a knowledge of them, in the first place, precedes the request: for how can they make a request of those whose nature they are ignorant of, and also of the benefits of which they are the leaders? In the next place, a desire to participate in them follows. For it is necessary to aspire after the things of which we are in want, since without aspiring we shall not be ranked among those who are in need. 

But the unwillingness of Antiphon to comply presents us with an image of the hidden and inexpressible power of divine causes. For a divine nature, wherever it may be, is apprehended and known with difficulty, and is scarcely unfolded to souls, even when they genuinely receive its participation and a communion with it. For souls require to be accustomed to the divine splendor which divine demons exhibit to souls extended toward them, and hastening through them to perceive everything divine. But to souls firmly and stably receiving them, these demons expand and unfold divine truth. And this is the narration: an expanding and unfolding of things concealed, and an uplifting <note>original: "anagogic"; referring to the process of leading the soul upward to the divine</note> perfection imparted to souls from divine demons.

### Page 38. *Antiphon, therefore, said that Pythodorus related, etc.*

It appears to me, says Proclus, that the reduction of all the persons to Parmenides indicates much of the truth of the things themselves. For all the multitude and all the orders of beings are united around their divine cause. And this is indicated to the more sagacious by naming them in succession: Antiphon, Pythodorus, Zeno, Parmenides. 

The mention also of the Panathenaea <note>The greatest festival in Athens, held in honor of Athena</note> contributes to the whole design of the dialogue: for we learn from history that in the celebration of this festival the Athenians dwelt together. Again, therefore, here also the multitude is united and arranged together around the Goddess who presides over the city. But this was the end of the dialogue: to suspend all things from the *one*, and clearly to show that everything is derived from it. The assertion, too, that these men did not come to Athens merely for the city, but for the Panathenaea, is no small praise. They came, therefore, for the sake of the Goddess and the festival.

->P. 38. *That Parmenides was very much advanced in years, etc.*<-

An elderly man among the Greeks was limited by seventy years. Parmenides, therefore, was very elderly. But he was called an "old man" who passed beyond this decade. The countenance also of Parmenides was graceful throughout his life: for a certain elegance and venerableness descends from the soul in worthy men, and extends as far as to the body. These things, however, may be much more perfectly surveyed in the soul itself. Thus, for instance, the soul possesses the "elderly" quality from being full of intellect and science. For it is usual to call intellectual disciplines, and those which embrace the whole of nature, "hoary" <note>original: hoary; meaning white-haired or ancient</note>, as it is evident from the *Timaeus*, in which those souls are called "juvenile" who have no hoary discipline—namely, those who do not, according to their highest peak, participate in intellectual light. For blackness belongs to the worse, as whiteness belongs to the better coordination. 

But the soul is *beautiful and good in its aspect* <note>original: καλὴ δὲ καὶ ἀγαθὴ τὴν ὄψιν (kalē de kai agathē tēn opsin)</note>, as extending its eye to intelligible *beauty*, and to the *goodness* which gives subsistence to all things, and through the participation of which all things are *good*. We may still, however, more perfectly survey these things in the Gods, according to analogy. For where do the *elderly* and the *hoary* exist in such a manner as in them? These qualities are likewise celebrated by theologians among the paternal Gods. Where, also, are the *beautiful* and the *good*, such as they possess? Plato also, in saying unitedly *beautiful and good* <note>original: καλὸν κἀγαθὸν (kalon kagathon); a Greek ideal of gentlemanly perfection</note>, speaks in a manner most adapted to those natures in whom *the one and the good* are the same.
