### Page 38. *He likewise said that he met with them together with Pythodorus, etc.*

Let their meeting with Pythodorus be a symbol—to those who look toward divine paradigms <note>original: "paradigms"; refers to the eternal patterns or archetypes of things</note>—of the Gods first being revealed through angels, and within the order of angels. For a house is a symbol of the specific order or rank of each being. Furthermore, this meeting taking place "beyond the walls" <note>referring to the setting outside the city walls of Athens</note> signifies the exempt and incomprehensible nature of the Gods. Just as everyone appears collected in the house of Pythodorus—some from the city and others from elsewhere—so also the governors of the world and the intelligible Gods become apparent in angels, and are known by us through the essence of these angelic beings.

### Page 38. *Where also Socrates came, etc.*

Here we may perceive how Socrates, through a disposition that is naturally good in the extreme, earnestly follows these divine men. We see how he does not associate with sophists and the "wise" for the same reasons. He associates with the former <note>the sophists</note> in order to expose their ignorance and pride, but with the latter <note>the divine philosophers</note> in order to draw out their knowledge and intellect. 

Here, therefore, he becomes the leader of the lovers of philosophy; for all of them desire to hear, but they obtain their desire together with and through him. These things, as well as the previous points, are images of the Gods. Socrates was young—a young leader—with Plato almost repeating what he says in the *Phaedrus*: "The mighty leader Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter"; referring to Zeus</note> first proceeds, and the army of Gods and demons <note>original: "dæmons"; in the Greek sense of intermediary spirits, not evil beings</note> follows him." For intellect, being everywhere assigned a converting role, leads upwards, and together with itself converts the entire multitude that depends upon it. 

Socrates being young is also a symbol of the "youthfulness" celebrated in the Gods. For theology calls Jupiter himself and Bacchus "boys" and "young"; in short, theologians use these terms for the intellectual realm when compared with the intelligible and paternal realms <note>In Neoplatonism, "intellectual" (nous) is a younger or later stage of emanation than the "intelligible" (noetos) or "paternal" source</note>. ## Page 38. *Zeno himself read to them, etc.*

Plato here provides us with a wonderful indication of divine matters; and he who is not blind to analogies will see a sublime theory in these images. For, in the first place, the fact that Parmenides was not present at the beginning, but only when the discourse was finished, is a symbol of more divine causes revealing themselves to subordinate beings only after those beings have perfectly participated in the natures closest to them, but not before. 

Therefore, once Zeno’s discourse was completed, the great Parmenides appears; and together with him, Pythodorus and Aristotle <note>This refers to the character Aristotle in the dialogue, one of the "Thirty Tyrants," not the famous philosopher Aristotle.</note> enter. Of these two, the former is a follower of Zeno, but Aristotle is, in a certain respect, arranged alongside Parmenides; for he organizes the hypotheses together with him, doing nothing else but answering questions. 

But here Parmenides, as we have often said, is analogous to that which is everywhere first among divine natures—whether it be the "First Being," or the "Intelligible," or in whatever other way you may choose to name it. For this principle exists in all the divine orders and in each of the Gods. Hence, he fills all who hear him with divine conceptions, imitating that order which adorns all things: first, middle, and last. 

He gives perfection to Zeno, who represents the middle rank, drawing everywhere from that summit. But he perfects Socrates through both himself and Zeno, just as in the divine realm, the progression of the third rank occurs through both the first and middle natures. He also perfects Pythodorus, but not simply by himself alone; rather, he does so in conjunction with Zeno and Socrates. 

Finally, he gives perfection to Aristotle last of all, and from himself alone. For something is imparted from Parmenides even down to the very last state of being, to which the energy and power of Zeno do not reach. This is just as the creative production of the "First Being" naturally extends further than the production of "Life." 

Zeno is himself filled by Parmenides, but he fills Pythodorus in one way (as his disciple) and Socrates in another (as one who explores the truth alongside him). Pythodorus, too, is able to participate not only in Zeno’s wisdom but also in that of Socrates. For, in divine natures, the middle rank extends its energy to that which comes after it and proceeds through all things, imparting a mere aptitude to the last of its participants, which

It again perfects in conjunction with the natures immediately suspended from it. So that the former participation indicates the imperfect representation of first things, which it imparts by acting prior to secondary natures. But the second participation indicates a perfection of representation existing through things that are close by. And Socrates, who is the third, gives completion to the triad <note>A group of three; in Neoplatonism, reality is often structured in threes.</note> which pervades through all numbers, and exists analogous to the intellect which is there, or in whatever other way you may be willing to name it. 

Hence he first participates in the doctrines of Zeno, and is joined through him with Parmenides; just as among the Gods, the intellect in each is immediately filled with a certain divine life, but through this is united with the "intelligible" itself <note>The highest realm of pure being that can be grasped by the mind.</note> and its own proper *hyparxis* <term>hyparxis</term><note>original: hyparxis; the essential "subsistence" or the very summit of a thing's being.</note>. But Pythodorus, being arranged according to the "unfolding" genus <note>The class of beings that reveal or explain higher truths.</note>, is the disciple of Zeno and participates in the prolific doubts of Socrates. For the Gods give existence to angels from middle and third powers, and not from those that are first; for these first powers are the parents of Gods. 

And Aristotle <note>Referring here to the character in the dialogue, not necessarily the historical philosopher Aristotle, though the author draws a parallel.</note> is arranged by analogy to souls which, through a divine inspiration, are often joined with the most divine natures, but afterwards fall from this blessedness. For it is not surprising that a soul which is now divinely inspired <note>original: "entheastically disposed"</note> should again choose an atheistical and dark life. But he is filled from Parmenides alone; since among the Gods also, it is the property of those who are first to impart to souls of this kind a certain participation of divine light, through their excellence of power. 

Thus theologians call an intellectual life "Saturnian" <note>Related to Cronus/Saturn, representing the highest intellectual level.</note>, but not "Jovian" <note>Related to Zeus/Jupiter, representing the demiurgic or governing level.</note>, even though the ascent is through the mighty Jupiter. But just as Jupiter, being filled from his father and ascending to him as to his own proper intelligible, also elevates that which is below himself; in the same way souls, though they make their ascent together with Jupiter, yet that intellectual life fills the middle and third orders of them, and, in the last place, souls which act with divine enthusiasm regarding it. 

Nor should you wonder if divine natures have such an order with respect to each other, since you may also see in philosophers themselves how he who is more perfect among them is also more powerful and benefits a greater number. Thus Cebes or Simmias benefits himself alone, or someone else similar to himself; but Socrates benefits himself, and these men, and Thrasymachus. In the same way Parmenides, being more powerful, benefits even the one who has the least fitness among those who are assembled. But he reveals the obscurity of this participation by calling him the youngest of those present; which is a symbol.

The symbol of an imperfect habit <note>original: "habit"; here meaning a settled disposition or state of being</note>; and by adding that he afterwards became one of the thirty tyrants; from which we also justly considered him as analogous to those souls that once lived enthusiastically <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, "enthusiastically" refers to being filled with divine inspiration or "god-filled."</note>, and in conjunction with angels—just as he makes his entrance together with Pythodorus—but who afterwards fall from this power. For Pythodorus remains in his proper habits, so that he also partakes of another conversation <note>original: "conversation"; here meaning a way of life or social conduct</note>; just as the angelic tribe always remains wholly beneficent, and fills secondary beings with the participation of divine natures. 

But Aristotle, instead of a philosopher, becomes a tyrant. For souls which possess a life of this kind according to habit and not essentially, sometimes depart from this order and descend into the realms of generation <note>The material world of birth, change, and decay.</note>: for a tyranny is a symbol of the life in generation; since such a life becomes situated under the throne of Necessity, as a consequence of being led under passive, unstable, and disordered appetite. For Aristotle, having been one of the thirty tyrants that governed Athens, represents a gigantic and earth-born life, which rules over Minerval <note>Pertaining to Minerva (Athena), symbolizing wisdom and intellect.</note> and Olympian goods. 

When reason and intellect take the lead in such souls, then Olympian benefits and those of Minerva have dominion, and the whole life is royal and philosophic; but when the multitude—or in short, that which is worse and earth-born—holds the reins of empire, then the whole life is a tyranny. If, therefore, Plato says that Aristotle was one of the thirty tyrants, it will appear to be the same as if he had said that he is analogous to souls who at one time act enthusiastically, and at another rank among the earth-born race, and who, by submitting their life to those most bitter tyrants, the passions, become themselves tyrants over themselves. And perhaps the philosopher manifests through these things that it is not impossible for the same soul to evolve different lives, and at one time to philosophize, and at another to live tyrannically; and again to pass from a tyrannic to a philosophic life.

->P. 38. *If beings are many, it is necessary that the same things should be both similar and dissimilar, etc.*<-

Through these and the other arguments of Zeno, it is shown that it is impossible for "the many" to have an existence when deprived of *the one*. Beginning from here, we shall also find a concise way to the first principle of things. It is necessary, therefore, that there should either be many principles not participating in a certain "one," or that

### ON THE PARMENIDES.

There should be either one principle only, void of multitude, or many principles participating in *the one*, or one principle containing multitude within itself. But if there are many principles destitute of *the one*, all the same absurdities will occur as those Zeno’s arguments bring against people who assert that beings are many without *the one*. If there are many principles that participate in a certain "one"—that is, which have a certain unity existing alongside them—that participated unity must proceed to its participants from another "one" which has a prior existence. This is because every "one" that belongs to other things proceeds from that which is simply and purely one. 

But if there is one principle possessing multitude within itself, it will be a "whole" and will consist of the many parts or elements it contains. This would not be the truly "one," but rather a "passive one" <note>original: "passive one," referring to a unity that is composed of parts rather than being absolutely simple</note>, as we learn from the *Sophist* <note>original: *Sophista*, a dialogue by Plato</note>. Consequently, it would be neither simple nor self-sufficient—qualities which a first principle must necessarily possess. It is necessary, therefore, that there should be one principle of all things that is void of multitude. This much we may gather from all of Zeno's arguments.

We may also observe that Socrates again imitates his "paradigm intellect" <note>The ideal or divine model of intelligence</note>, expanding himself and his thoughts toward Zeno and calling forth Zeno's knowledge. For in the divine models of these men, subordinate beings suspend the whole of their energy from the middle natures; through an expansion of their own powers, they are filled from above with more perfect goods.

**P. 39. *Is it not then the sole intention of your discourses to prove by contesting, etc.***

Parmenides, establishing himself in *the one* and surveying the "monad" <note>The primary unit or source</note> of all beings, does not turn himself toward multitude and its scattered existence. Zeno, however, flees from multitude toward *the one* and seeks to take multitude away. The former (Parmenides) is like one who is already purified, elevated, and has set aside the multitude within himself. The latter (Zeno) is like one who is still ascending and in the process of laying aside multitude, because he is not yet entirely separated from it. 

Hence, "contention" <note>original: *to diamachesthai* (τὸ διαμάχεσθαι), meaning to fight it out or struggle through argument</note> is suited to Zeno. He does not yet possess a tranquil life free from obstacles; nor, as he opposes multitude, has he yet arrived at *the one* alone. But this contention, and this conclusion reached through many arguments ending in the same negative result, demonstrates to Socrates that the "many" do not exist separately from *the one*. For Plato compares the path—

Thus, in the *Republic*, he exhorts us to discourse about *the good* as if piercing through a battle, thinking it appropriate to speak of it in no other way than through negative conclusions. And here it is necessary, indeed, not to consider the word *contending* carelessly; but through this we should make it known that both in this place and in the *Republic*, *contention* is intended by Plato to signify *negations*. Just as each of the arguments of Zeno is self-perfect and demonstrates the conclusion, this is the characteristic of scientific power.

## **Page 40.** *Do you think that there is a certain form of similitude, etc.*

Parmenides leads all beings upward to the exempt "one being," or being itself. He withdraws his conceptions from that which is multiplied and distributed, moving toward the one monad <note>original: "monad"; a single, indivisible unit or principle</note> of the entire multitude of beings. The "many" <note>referring to those who believe only in the material or plural world</note>, on the contrary, give the multitude of beings precedence over intellect and union. They do not even consider being itself as the principle; instead, they assert that distributed multitude simply exists and progresses into being separately from being itself. 

It is evident that by thinking this way, they defame the doctrine of Parmenides. For while Parmenides is of the opinion that being should be considered as characterized by unity alone, separate from multitude, they on the contrary establish a multitude deprived of unity. However, it is indeed impossible that multitude should not participate in *the one*, for every multitude is composed of *the one*. All multitudes, therefore, and all the masses of bodies, are overcome by the participation of unity. 

Hence, if multitude requires *the one*, but *the one* has no need of multitude, it is better to call being *one* than to say the many exist alone by themselves, separate from the participation of *the one*. And Parmenides, indeed, by proving that being is one, also gives existence to the multitude of beings—not only to the multitude of sensible things <note>things perceived by the senses</note>, but likewise to the multitude of intelligible things <note>things understood by the intellect or spirit</note>. For in these, there is a divine number of all things united to each other. 

Empedocles also later perceived this, being himself a <term>Pythagorean</term> <note>a follower of the philosopher Pythagoras, who emphasized mathematics and the soul</note>. He calls the whole of an intelligible nature a "sphere," as it is united to itself, and asserts that it attracts to itself, through beauty, the beautifying and uniting God. For all things there, loving and desiring each other, are eternally united to each other. Their love is also intelligible, and their association and mixture are ineffable <note>too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note>. But the "many," being exiles from union and the monad of beings, and

It contrasts the unity of the intelligible realm with the fragmented perspective of those who prioritize material multitude.</summary>

--- Page 1892 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Parmenides, specifically discussing Zeno’s defense of Parmenides’ doctrine against those who favor the existence of "the many" without "the one."</meta>

<page-num>547</page-num>
<header>ON THE PARMENIDES.</header>

Throughout their lives, which are divisible and distributed, people are drawn down toward multitude, toward multiform opinions, toward indefinite fantasies, toward passive senses, and material appetites. They consider "the many" <note>The "many" refers to the plurality of individual things in the world.</note> as being separate from their union. They do not see how these many things are overcome by the coordinated monads <note>term: monad; a fundamental, indivisible unit that provides order to a group.</note> they contain, how indefinite things are subject to definite measures, and how scattered natures exist in sympathy and union through the participation in common traits. Not perceiving this, they wander from the truth and basely revile and deride the doctrine of Parmenides. 

Zeno, therefore, knowing they were affected in this way, becomes a corrector of the multitude, a leader guiding them from folly toward intellect, and a guardian of his teacher's doctrine. At first, he persuades them to return from these multitudes to the unities within the many, and to behold how this multitude—though tending toward infinity—is at the same time overcome by the monad of beings and held together by a certain unity it contains. However, he offers his persuasion by assuming a hypothesis pleasing to the common people: namely, the existence of a multitude deprived of unity. He does this because their assertion is easily proven wrong in that form; for if they had established "the many" alongside "the one," they would not yet be defeated by his arguments. Parmenides himself also demonstrates in his hypothesis that he is accustomed to showing that the same thing is both similar and dissimilar, doing so only by treating *the many* as separate from *the one*.

Zeno, therefore, as we have said, considers these "many" as being deprived of *the one* which approaches and is contained within them. Yet he does not consider intelligible things <note>term: intelligibles; things understood by the mind or intellect, rather than the senses.</note> alone, nor sensible things <note>term: sensibles; things perceived by the physical senses.</note> alone, but, in short, all such things as are said to be "many" in both the intelligible and sensible orders. For it is the task of a more perfect and primary science to extend the same method to all things of a similar form and to observe what is analogous in all things. Whether, therefore, there is an intelligible, sensible, intellectual, or dianoetic <note>term: dianoetic; relating to discursive reason or the step-by-step process of thought.</note> multitude, all of this is assumed here. 

Hence, it is necessary to discover how multitudes are nowhere to be found if they are deprived of *the one*. For, if they were deprived of *the one*, they would be at the same time similar and dissimilar. This is because things which do not participate in *one* and the same thing are dissimilar to each other; and yet, by this very fact, they share something with each other—namely, the fact that they do not participate in *the one*. But things which possess something common and the same are similar; so it would follow that the same things are both similar and dissimilar. If, therefore, the many exist without a participation in *the one*, then according to this one thing—their non-participation—

<summary>This page explains Zeno's philosophical defense of Parmenides, arguing that "the many" (plurality) cannot exist without "the one" (unity) because a lack of unity leads to logical contradictions, such as things being simultaneously similar and dissimilar.</summary>

--- Page 1893 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical analysis of the relationship between "the one" and "multitude," specifically focusing on the logical contradictions that arise when one attempts to conceive of a plurality without a unifying principle.</meta>

<page-num>548</page-num>
<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

Through the non-participation of *the one*, things will be both similar and dissimilar. That is, considered as possessing this non-participation in common, they will be similar; but considered as not possessing *the one*, they will be dissimilar. Because they are subject to this very thing—the non-participation of *the one*—they are similar. Thus, the same things are both similar and dissimilar. In short, the possession of "nothing in common" is itself common to them, and therefore the assertion undermines itself.

Indeed, the things shown to be both similar and dissimilar are further shown to be neither similar nor dissimilar. For if they do not participate in *the one*, they are, in short, not similar; this is because similar things are similar by the participation of a certain "one," as similarity is a form of oneness. Furthermore, if they do not participate in *the one*, this lack is common to them; but things that have something in common are, according to that very commonality, not dissimilar. Consequently, the "many" are neither similar nor dissimilar.

It is impossible, therefore, for a multitude to exist deprived of *the one*, because so many absurdities happen to those who adopt such a hypothesis. It is a terrible thing for a contradiction to occur; it is more terrible for this to happen with contraries <note>Contraries are opposites like "black" and "white" which cannot both be true, while contradictions are "A" and "not-A".</note>; and it is the most terrible of all things for both contraries and contradictions to follow from the assertion. By showing that the same thing is similar and dissimilar, we have gathered contraries; but by showing that the same thing is similar and not similar, and neither of these, we have gathered contradictions. For "similar" is a contradiction to "not similar," and "dissimilar" to "not dissimilar."

From this, we may also be able to prove that it is impossible for there to be many first principles. Regarding these many principles, do they participate in one thing, or not in one thing? If they participate, that which they participate in will be prior to them, and there will no longer be many principles, but one principle. But if they do not participate, they will be similar to each other because this non-participation is common to them; yet they will also be dissimilar insofar as they do not participate in a certain common "one." But it is impossible for the same things, in the same respect, to be both similar and dissimilar. In the same way, we may conclude that these many principles are neither similar nor dissimilar. However, if they were participants of a certain "one," we could not conclude that they are dissimilar according to the participation of this "one," but only that they are similar; and thus we shall overturn the existence of many first principles.

Through this method, therefore, Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea (c. 490–430 BC), a philosopher famous for his paradoxes designed to support Parmenides' doctrine that "all is one."</note> proves that it is impossible to separate the
->many<-

<meta>The text concludes mid-sentence, leading into a further discussion of the "many" on the following page.</meta>

It further applies this logic to prove that there can only be one first principle rather than many.</summary>

# ON THE PARMENIDES.

Many things proceed from *the one*, and the mind rises from this multitude to the monads <note>Monad: from the Greek *monas*, meaning a fundamental, indivisible unit or primary source.</note> of the many, so that we may perceive the nature of the unities that exist independently of things. For the monads that are coordinated with things are merely images of those that are uncoordinated and independent. 

But Socrates, driving the discourse toward the subject of Ideas <note>Forms or Ideas: the eternal, unchanging archetypes of all things in Platonic philosophy.</note>, and assuming that common properties have a subsistence <note>Subsistence: a self-contained existence or reality.</note> in and of themselves, surveys another kind of multitude within them. He thinks it proper that Zeno should also apply this method to the Forms, and demonstrate through them how the similar is dissimilar, and the dissimilar is similar. Shortly after, Proclus further observes the following:

Socrates, before he enters into the doubts involving the essence of Forms, asks Zeno whether he admits that Forms have a real existence, and whether or not he is among those who embrace this cause as he himself does; in short, he asks what opinion Zeno holds concerning them. For the Pythagoreans were observers of Forms; and Socrates himself demonstrates this in the *Sophist* <note>The *Sophista* or *Sophist* is a dialogue by Plato.</note>, calling the wise men in Italy "the friends of Forms." 

However, the one who especially honors and clearly establishes the reality of Forms is Socrates. Through his investigation into definitions, he discovered the nature of the things being defined, passing from these definitions (which act as images) to the formal causes themselves. He, therefore, first asks if Zeno also admits that there are Forms, and honors this essence of all things—an essence that exists from itself and is established in itself, requiring no other foundation. He characterizes this by the words *itself by itself* <note>original: *auto kath’ auto* (αυτο καθ’ αυτο)</note>, believing these words are properly suited to this essence. For they indicate the unmingled, simple, and pure nature of Forms. 

Thus, through the word *itself*, he signifies the simplicity of those things; but through the words *by itself*, he signifies their purity, unmingled with lower or secondary natures. Indeed, through the words *by itself*, he separates Forms from the qualities that are merely attributed to the many. For which among these qualities is truly *itself*? Since such a quality possesses its existence only in relation to subjects, is gathered from sensory perception, is the object of mere opinion, and is adapted to the conceptions of the imagination <note>original: *phantasy*</note>. But by the word *itself*, he separates Forms from that which is common in particular things and which can be defined: for this is contained in...

something different from itself, and exists together with matter; for this reason, it is also filled with internal change and is, in a certain respect, mortal through its connection with that which is material. By no means, therefore, must it be said that forms which exist by themselves—which are established on a sacred foundation and are immaterial and eternal—are the same as material forms of later origin, which are full of variety and shifting relationships. For the former are unmixed, undefiled, and simple; they are eternally established in the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Demiurge" or divine craftsman who fashions the universe.</note> of the universe. They possess their undefiled and pure nature from the inflexible deity that proceeds alongside the demiurgus, but their simplicity comes from the demiurgic intellectual essence, which is single and indivisible. As the <term>Chaldæan theologists</term> <note>Ancient Babylonian or Near Eastern sages whose mystical oracles influenced later Neoplatonism.</note> would say, it has a "fontal" or source-like existence. 

You may also say that the term *itself* separates the true Form from those conceptions derived from sensible objects <note>original: "ennoemata" (εννοηματα) — mental concepts or thoughts formed in the mind after perceiving physical things.</note>. For none of these mental concepts is the thing *itself*; since they merely correspond to the things they represent, they belong to and exist within other things. But the words *by itself* separate the Form from that which exists only in particular objects, or that which exists in something different from itself.

Neither, therefore, must we admit the opinion of those who say that an "Idea" is the same as the "common quality" found in many things. For Ideas exist prior to the common qualities found in sensible objects, and the latter derive their existence from the former. Nor must we agree with those who consider Ideas to be the same as the mental concepts we derive from physical objects. Those people, as a result of this mistake, ask why there are not also Ideas of individual people, or of things that are contrary to nature. In reality, the mental concepts of such things are entirely secondary to the particulars that trigger them; they exist in us, and not in the power that adorned the universe, in whom we say the Ideas reside. 

Nor yet must we admit the opinion of those who connect Ideas with <term>spermatic reasons</term> <note>original: "logoi spermatikoi" — the formative, "seed-like" principles or biological blueprints that govern the growth of natural organisms.</note>. For the "reasons" or productive principles found in seeds are imperfect, and those in nature which generate seeds lack conscious knowledge. But Ideas exist in "energy" <note>In the Aristotelian sense of "energeia" or active reality.</note>, always the same, and are essentially intellectual. If, therefore, we wish to define their unique character through things that are better known to us, we must take from "physical reasons" the quality of producing what they produce by their very being; but we must take from the "reasons of art" <note>The principles or designs used by a human craftsman.</note> the quality of being <term>gnostic</term> <note>Possessing conscious knowledge or intellect.</note> of the things they make, even though human arts do not create things simply by their very being. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of divine forms and their relationship to the Demiurge, following the previous analysis of the immovable and simple nature of the Gods.</meta>

<page-num>551</page-num>
<header>ON THE PARMENIDES.</header>

nature, being immovable, exists prior to things that are moved; being simple, it exists prior to composite things; and being separate, it exists prior to things which are inseparable from matter. On this account, Parmenides does not cease discoursing concerning them until, at the end of his arguments, he says that they are Gods; by this, he signifies all that we have previously observed.

With respect to the similar and the dissimilar, these exist primarily in the *demiurgus* <note>The "Demiurge" or divine craftsman/creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note>, or, to speak more clearly, they have in him a fontal <note>original: "fontal"; meaning acting as a fountain or primary source.</note> subsistence. This is because they exist more conspicuously in the assimilative Gods, and especially in the paternal Deities of that order, as is evident from the second hypothesis of this dialogue. But since the demiurge possesses the one fountain of these, the form of similitude is also contained in him, pre-existing in the one monad of ideas. The demiurge, therefore, is a monad <note>A "monad" refers to a singular, unified principle or ultimate unit.</note> comprehensive of many divine monads, which impart to each other their proper idioms <note>original: "idioms"; here meaning unique characteristics or essential properties.</note>: one, the idiom of purity; another, of an assimilative essence; and another of something else, according to which they are allotted their proper *hyparxis* <note>original: "hyparxis"; a Greek term referring to the essential "subsistence" or the very peak of a thing's existence.</note>. 

For it must not be thought that forms indeed pre-exist as the causes of things which are generated according to them, but that there is not a different idea by which generated natures become similar and dissimilar to those forms. Both similitude, however, and dissimilitude, are immaterial, pure, simple, uniform, and eternal essences. The former is collective, unifying, the cause of bound, and uniform; the latter is the source of division, internal change, and infinity. 

But the order of these ideas is neither in the most generic nor in the most specific of forms. For the most generic are such forms as are participated in by all beings, so that there is not anything whatever which does not exist from the participation of these—such as *essence*, *sameness*, and *difference*. These pervade all beings. For what is there void of *essence*? What is void of *difference*? What is void of *sameness*? Do not all things possess a certain *hyparxis*? And are they not essentially separated from other things, and do they not also communicate with them? If this be the case, this triad is the common cause of all beings. 

But the most specific ideas are such as are naturally adapted to be participated in by individual forms, such as *man*, *horse*, and *dog*, and each of this kind. For these immediately generate the monads in individuals—such as "man" in particular people, and "dog" and "horse" in the many—and in a similar manner each of the rest. But the forms which exist between these have indeed a very extended existence, but do not operate in all beings.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the nature of Forms and their participation in one another, specifically focusing on the relationship between similarity and difference.</meta>

<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

Thus, for instance, justice exists in souls, but not in wood and stones. Among these middle forms, therefore, similarity and dissimilarity must be ranked: for though they are shared by most things, they are not shared by all. As Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note> well observes, where can there be either similarity or dissimilarity among infinites?

->P. 40. *For if anyone should show that similar things themselves become dissimilar, etc.*<-

Forms are not to be considered as entirely unmixed or without communication with each other. Instead, each Form is exactly what it is, preserving its own distinct character <note>original: "idiom"</note> pure; at the same time, it participates in others without confusion. It does not become something belonging to those other Forms, but rather receives the character of that which it participates in, while imparting its own character to the other. 

Thus, for instance, "sameness" participates in "difference" without actually being difference, and "difference" participates in "sameness" insofar as they communicate with each other. In the same way, similarity and dissimilarity participate in each other; yet similarity is not dissimilarity, nor is dissimilarity similarity. Furthermore, insofar as one is similarity, it is not dissimilar; and insofar as the other is dissimilarity, it is not similar. 

The expression "insofar as" <note>original: "so far as"</note> is used in two ways. In the first place, it is used when one thing is always accompanied by another; for example, if someone should say, "Insofar as there is air, there is also light; and insofar as there is light, there is also air." But even admitting that there is illuminated air, air is not light, nor is light air. Rather, air is in light, and light is in air, because the parts of air and light are situated near each other, and there is no part of one where the other is not also seen. 

However, this expression is also used in a second way when it is applied to anything that always essentially introduces another thing; as when we say, "Man is a recipient of knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>." It is not true that light is in the air, or air in light, according to this second meaning, since air does not entirely and necessarily bring light with it in the same way we say the concept of "man" necessarily brings with it the concept of "a recipient of knowledge"; the essence of air is different from that of light. 

Similarity, therefore, participates in dissimilarity according to the first of these modes; for there is nothing belonging to it which does not participate in dissimilarity, and yet the being of the former is different from that of the latter. It does not participate in one part and not in another, since nothing prevents it from pervading through dissimilarity; nor is its indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> nature of such a kind that it participates in it in only one respect,

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato's Parmenides, specifically discussing the nature of incorporeal forms and Socrates' evolving understanding of their relationship.</meta>

respect, and in another remains unmingled with it. For the whole proceeds through the whole: similarity through dissimilarity, and in like manner dissimilarity through similarity. Not, indeed, that each, because it is what it is, participates in the other; rather, while it participates, it preserves its own essence pure. This, therefore, is the unique characteristic of incorporeal forms: to pervade one another without confusion; to be distinct from each other without separation; and to be more united than things that are fused together (because of their indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> nature); and yet to be more distinct from each other than things separated in the physical world, because of their unmingled purity.

Socrates, therefore, says Proclus, doubted whether forms exist in conjunction with each other. He called on Zeno to assist him in solving this doubt. Fearing that forms might be so mingled that "similarity itself" becomes "dissimilarity," he calls such a doctrine a *prodigy* <note>meaning a monstrous or unnatural thing</note> and rejects any such mixture. But again, suspecting that forms—through the union of intelligible realities—participate in each other in a certain way, he says he would *wonder* if anyone were able to show this to be the case, using the language of someone who has a suspicion. Finally, inferring that they may be both united and separated, he calls the person able to demonstrate this *admirable*. 

Here you see the order of intellectual ascent: for Socrates first denies; second, he has a suspicion of the truth; and third, he is firmly convinced of the truth through demonstration. His initial denial of the mixture of forms is not wrong, for in the way he first imagined it, they are indeed unmingled. Nor is his suspicion false, for in one respect they are able to participate in each other, and in another they do not communicate. His final conclusion is the most true: for they are both united with and separated from each other.

However, it is the soul which first divides those things that previously existed in the intellect in supreme union. This is true not only of our human soul, but also of the divine soul. <meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the nature of the soul's intelligence and its relationship to the divine intellect and the "Forms."</meta>

The soul possesses a collected energy of intellect that aspires after the perfection and simple form of intelligence contained within it. Consequently, the soul revolves around the intellect. Through the transitions of its projective energies, it divides the indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> nature of the Forms. It perceives the beautiful itself, the just itself, and every other Form separately, understanding all things by surveying them one at a time rather than all at once. 

In short, as the soul ranks in the third order from *the One* <note>The ultimate, simple source of all existence in Neoplatonic philosophy</note>, it properly possesses this kind of energy. For *the One* is alone and exists prior to all intellection <note>The act of understanding or thinking</note>. Intellect understands all things as a single whole, but the soul understands all things by surveying them one at a time. Therefore, division first exists in the soul. This is why theologians say that during the tearing apart <note>original: "lacerations"</note> of Bacchus, the intellect of the God was preserved undivided by the providence of Minerva <note>Athena</note>. 

The soul is that which is first distributed into parts, and it is to the soul that a division into seven parts first applies. It is, therefore, no longer surprising that while divine Forms exist united within the demiurgic <note>The "Demiurge" is the divine craftsman or creator-mind</note> intellect, our soul should approach them divisibly. Our soul surveys the first and most common Forms at one time, those of a middle nature at another, and finally the most specific and individual Forms. Since even a divine soul divides what is indivisible through its shifting connections and contacts, what should we say regarding a partial soul such as ours? Must it not, even more so, apprehend in a partial and divided way those things which actually exist together and within each other? It is, therefore, not at all surprising that our inquiries and answers grasp different Forms at different times, just as spoken language divides the single, simple conception of the soul and passes through the united thoughts of the intellect over time.

The Forms previously mentioned by Socrates are the most generic and common: namely, unity, multitude, similarity, dissimilarity, permanency, and motion. However, the Forms now presented to us are partly secondary to these and partly not. This is similar to how we speak of human virtue: we say it is partly subordinate to the soul and partly better than it. Insofar as virtue perfects the soul, it is better; but insofar as it is something belonging to and existing within the soul, it is subordinate. In the same way, the *good* <note>The good, considered here as existing among the Ideas/Forms, and not as that "Good" which is beyond all being <term>superessential</term> and the source of all things.</note>, the beautiful, and the just are partly more excellent than the Forms that produce essences, and are partly inferior to them. As far as they are most generic <note>original: "generic" — referring to the most universal categories of being</note>, these also communicate with them; but the latter are the primary causes of being to sensible things <note>original: "sensibles" — objects perceived by the senses</note>, and the former are the sources of their perfection. Justice proceeds as far as to souls, adorning and perfecting them, but the beautiful extends its illuminations even as far as to bodies. Hence Socrates in the *Phaedrus* says that beauty has the prerogative of being the most apparent and the most lovely of all things, but that the splendor of justice is not visible in the imitations of it which are here on earth. Again, the good perfects all things according to the peculiar essence of each. For the beautiful perfects according to the symmetry of form with respect to matter; and symmetry then exists when that which is naturally more excellent rules over that which is naturally inferior. According to this symmetry, therefore, the beautiful shines in bodies. But the good illuminates according to the perfect; and it is present to everything invested with form when it possesses perfection from nature. In this triad <note>A group of three related things; here, the Good, the Beautiful, and the Just</note>, therefore, the first is the good, the second the beautiful, and the third the just.

But that there are forms or ideas of these, and of all such as these—as, for instance, of temperance, fortitude, and prudence—we shall find by considering that every virtue, and every perfection according to virtue, assimilates us to a divine nature. By how much the more it is inherent in us, by so much the nearer do we approach to an intellectual life. If, therefore, the beautiful and the good, and every virtue, assimilate us to intellect, intellect will entirely possess the intellectual paradigms <note>original: "paradigms" — the perfect, original patterns or models in the divine mind</note> of these. For, with respect to the similar, when it is said to be similar to that which is more excellent, then that which is more excellent possesses that primarily which the subordinate nature, upon receiving it, becomes similar to. 

The forms of the virtues, therefore, must necessarily exist in intellect prior to the soul. Each of these, however, must be considered in a twofold respect: namely, as a divine unity and as an intellectual form. Thus, for instance, the "just" which exists in forms is not the same as that which exists in the Gods. For the former is one particular idea, is a part of another, and possesses intelligence proceeding as far as to souls; but the latter is a certain whole and proceeds in its providential energies as far as to the very last of things. It also originates from the first intellectual Gods, for there it is first apparent. But the former is an idea contained in the demiurgic <note>original: "demiurgic" — relating to the Creator or "Craftsman" of the universe</note> intellect. Thus also, with respect to the beautiful, that which exists as a form is different from that which is the unity of divine beauty. And

<sig>6</sig>

The energy of the latter, indeed, is directed to the Gods insofar as they are Gods, and first originates from the first intelligible <note>The "intelligible" refers to the highest realm of being that can be grasped by the intellect</note>; but the former is in ideas, and is beheld around ideas. And lastly, with respect to the good, one is essential, and the other, as we have before observed, is super-essential <note>original: "supereſſential"; meaning existing beyond or above the level of basic essence or being</note>.

->P. 42. *I mean hair, clay, and mud, or anything else which is vile and abject, etc.*<-

It is necessary, says Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) known for his systematic commentaries on Plato</note>, either that there should only be ideas of things which exist according to nature, or also of things which are contrary to these; and if only of things according to nature, that there should alone be ideas of things perpetual, or also of each of the things which are not perpetual. And if there are alone ideas of things perpetual, they must either be of such as are essential, or also of such as are un-essential. And if of the essential, they must either be alone confined to wholes, or also extend to parts; and if to wholes alone, either to such as are alone simple, or also to such as are composed from these. 

Such then being the division of ideas, we say, that of intellects proceeding from one intellectual essence it is not proper to establish paradigms <note>term: "paradigms" (original: "paradigms"); in Platonic philosophy, these are the perfect, eternal patterns or "Forms" of which physical things are mere copies</note>: for that of which there is a paradigm must necessarily be an image. But to call an intellectual essence an image is of all things the most absurd: for every image is the idol <note>original: "ειδωλον" (eidolon); a representation, phantom, or likeness</note> or resemblance of that of which it is the image; and the Elean guest <note>A character in Plato's dialogue, the *Sophist*</note> in the *Sophist* expressly names an idol *not true being*. If, therefore, every intellectual essence belongs to true being, it will not be proper to name it either an image or an idol. 

For, indeed, every intellectual nature is indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>, and its progression is achieved through sameness; because of this, secondary intellects exist in a state of union (without having fully departed) within those that are first, and are partially what the intellect which ranks as a whole is totally. But it is necessary in the image that dissimilarity should be mingled with similarity; through the latter of which the image is turned back toward its paradigm. In intellectual essences, therefore, there are not image and paradigm, but cause alone, and things proceeding from cause. Because of this, theologians, placing many fountains <note>meta: catchword: fountains</note> in the demiurgic <note>term: "demiurgic"; relating to the Demiurge, the divine "craftsman" or creator of the material world</note> intellect, assert that there is one of the multitude of ideas. Hence, not everything which proceeds from the demiurge proceeds according to a formal cause; but such things as make a more extended progression, and such as possess a divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> essence, these exist from an ideal cause. But the other

<page-num>557</page-num>
# ON THE PARMENIDES.

Fountains are generative of intellectual and divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "hypostases"; refers to underlying substances or individual realities in Neoplatonic philosophy</note>. We must not, therefore, establish in the intellect a paradigmatic cause of every intellectual essence, but only a cause which is characterized by unity and is divine.

In the next place, it is necessary to consider if there is a primary cause of souls within the forms, and whether there is one or many. But that there is, indeed, a certain <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monad"; a single, indivisible unit or source</note> of them in the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>original: "demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</note>, in which monad every number of souls is comprehended as a single unit, is evident from the nature of things and from the doctrine of Plato. For, if the soul is the first generated nature and that which is primarily divisible, it is necessary that the indivisible form should precede things that are divisible, and that the eternal should precede things which are in any way generated. 

And if, as time is to eternity, so is the soul to the intellect—but time is the image of eternity—it is also necessary that the soul should be the image of the intellect. And if in "Being" there is not only life, as Socrates says in the *Philebus*, but also soul, it is necessary to consider the soul which exists there as the <term>paradigm</term> <note>original: "paradigm"; the perfect original model or blueprint</note> of the multitude of souls proceeding from the intellect, and as comprehending, in the manner of a unity, both their order and their number. 

But if there is not just one form of rational souls alone, but there are also many forms after the one (since all of them are immortal), it is necessary that there should be a paradigm for each. Again, however, it is impossible that the proceeding multitude should be just as numerous as that which remains at the source; for progression increases quantity but diminishes power. We must therefore say that there is a monad in the divine intellect which is the paradigm of all souls, from which the multitude of them flows, and which unitedly comprehends the measure that limits their number. 

But with this monad, a second number is naturally linked, divided, and serves as a paradigm of divine souls. This contains the proper paradigm of each, and one form from which divine souls proceed first, and afterwards the multitude coordinated with each. Thus, from the paradigm of the soul of the sun, the divine soul of the sun first proceeds; in the next place, all such angelic souls as have a solar characteristic; in the third place, such as are of a <term>demoniacal</term> <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to "daemons," intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> rank surrounding the sun; and, in the last place, such as are partial souls. On this account, there are also coordinations of parts to wholes, and of attendants to their leaders; the one intellectual cause of them imparting union and connection to their progression. In like manner, also, the paradigm of the lunar soul first generates the divine soul around the moon, afterwards the angelic, then the demoniacal, and then that which is partial; and the...

The intellectual monad <note>original: "monad"; a fundamental, indivisible unity or "the One" from which all things in a series arise</note> comprehends the entire number of these. The same also takes place in other divine souls; for each has a separate idea <note>original: "idea"; here meaning a formal, eternal archetype in the divine mind</note>. However, the orders of angelic, demoniacal <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to "daemons," intermediary spirits between gods and men, not necessarily evil beings</note>, or partial souls which follow them, participate in that one idea. 

And just as the one monad of the paradigms <note>original: "paradigms"; the perfect patterns or models of things in the intelligible realm</note> of souls existing there gives subsistence to the one soul of the world, so the many monads produce the multitude of souls. The former monad comprehends the whole multitude uniformly, while the latter monads comprehend the measures of their own specific series. The demiurgic intellect <note>original: "demiurgic intellect"; the divine "Craftsman" or Creator-mind that shapes the universe</note>, therefore, primarily comprehends the forms of divine souls, which it generates first. Each of these forms is one and at the same time many, for it contains within itself the cause of the entire multitude of souls subsisting under it. 

Thus, every soul exists according to a certain proper paradigm, but not all souls participate in the same form in the same way. Ancient theologians, having the same conceptions on this subject, say that the total causes of souls—which generate the whole series of them—are different from the partial causes, through which they derive a separation according to species and a division into individual souls.

In the next place, with respect to irrational souls <note>original: "irrational souls"; the life-principles of animals or the non-reasoning parts of the psyche</note>, it is evident that there is also an intelligible paradigm for these, if we consider irrational souls to be all secondary lives that are divisible around bodies. From where, then, do these derive their perpetuity? It must necessarily be from a certain immovable and intellectual cause; and it appears that this is accomplished as follows:

Again, one monad and one idea must be arranged prior to these, whether it be called the "fontal" <note>original: "fontal"; meaning "source-like" or "fountain-like"</note> or "sensitive" nature, or by whatever other name you wish to call it. For it may be said that irrational souls derive their existence from the one demiurgic sense through a cognitive characteristic <note>original: "gnoſtic idiom"</note>, but through desire or appetite <note>original: "orexis"</note> they derive it from the highest or fontal nature, which exists prior to the multitude of natures. 

From these causes, therefore, the multitude of perpetual but naturally irrational souls proceeds. This multitude exists partially in eternal vehicles <note>original: "eternal vehicles"; the subtle, celestial bodies that carry the soul</note>, in which it is also established according to a certain number and the formal measure that exists there. For every perpetual multitude is bounded; and prior to every bounded multitude, there exists that which bounds and numbers it. These irrational souls also proceed from rational souls, or rather from the paradigms which they contain. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the hierarchy of forms and the origins of various types of souls and natural forces.</meta>

<page-num>559</page-num>
<header>ON THE PARMENIDES</header>

In the multitude of forms, the divine also generates this specific number of souls. Divine souls indeed, and those that are pure, preserve even their irrational nature undefiled. However, partial souls <note>Individual human souls as opposed to world-souls</note> employ irrational souls because they have a composite life; in some, the more excellent part holds dominion, while in others, it is frequently in a state of subjection. From these perpetual irrational souls, those that are mortal are assigned their generation. These mortal souls are also preserved according to their species through their intellectual paradigm <note>The eternal blueprint or ideal form</note>, but the individuals perish because they derive their existence from the junior Gods <note>original: *junior Gods*; referring to the lesser deities in the *Timaeus* who fashion the mortal parts of the soul</note>. This is because the irrational souls prior to these are generated from those celestial souls whose creative energy is intertwined with the monad <note>The primary, unifying principle</note> of their entire series. Therefore, souls that perish have a certain analogy to the divine causes from which they derive their existence, just as immortal souls relate to their formal causes.

In the third place, let us consider how we are to admit a paradigm of Nature. For we must not, as *Plato* says, establish forms of fire, water, and motion, yet deprive Nature—which is the source of these—of an intellectual cause. Theologists indeed place the fountain of Nature in the life-giving Goddess *Rhea*; for they say that immense Nature is suspended from the shoulders of the goddess. But, according to *Plato*, we must say that the form of Nature exists in the demiurgic intellect <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator mind</note>, and this form is the origin of every natural vehicle. *Timaeus* also says that the demiurge <note>The Creator</note> pointed out to souls the *nature of the universe* and the laws of fate. For within him exists the single nature of all things, as well as the understanding of those fatal decrees according to which he arranges and divides the universe. If it is the demiurge who speaks, he turns souls toward himself; but if this is the case, he also shows them the nature of the universe and the laws of fate as they exist within himself. 

Hence, the single form of Nature is found there; however, the souls that use this form also produce the specific natures that are inspired by them, and these perpetual natures in turn generate partial and temporary natures. It may be concluded, therefore, that the paradigm of natures collectively contains within the demiurgic intellect the total number of those things that have a perpetual existence. Furthermore, the distinct causes of perpetual natures are contained in *Vulcan* <note>Hephaestus</note>, who according to theologists is the creator of the form of the body alone. For from this divinity, every physical order and the multitude of natures immediately exist and are given life.

<page-num>560</page-num>
<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

In the fourth place, with respect to bodies, must we not admit that the single and total cause of these resides in the first <term>demiurgus</term> <note>original: "demiurgus"; the divine craftsman or creator of the universe</note>? This cause encompasses the entire number of bodies that are classified as "wholes" (such as planets or the universe itself). However, after this <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monad"; the primary, unified source</note>, must we not also admit that the distinct causes of bodies which are classified as "parts" exist within the creative cause of a physical nature? 

This must necessarily be the case: for he who encompasses the single form of the world is the first father of the universe; and those things which are produced through necessity must consequently be parts. These parts require the care and foresight of that power which crafts physical bodies. Besides, it is also evident that—just as we said regarding souls—it is necessary to assert here that there are intellectual and formal causes for divine bodies. This is because the "vehicles" <note>The subtle or ethereal bodies that carry a soul</note> of <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmons"; intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not to be confused with "demons" in a modern evil sense</note> and individual souls participate in these causes in a second and third degree of rank. 

Thus, for example, the form of the sun's body also generates the solar vehicles of daemons and individual souls; and therefore, as soul relates to soul, so does each vehicle relate to its proper celestial sphere. In short, since there is a multitude of divine causes, the causes of bodies must be seen as existing differently within different divinities. Thus, in Vulcan <note>The god of fire and craftsmanship, representing the formative power over matter</note>, the creator of the physical body, the distinct causes of bodies exist specifically as bodies. But in the generative principles of souls, they exist "psychically" (in the manner of a soul); and in Jupiter, the creator of all "wholes," they exist as living beings, deriving their <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; their fundamental reality or underlying substance</note> from him according to both their souls and their bodies.

It now remains for us to consider whether there is also a "form" for matter itself. Here, perhaps, it is necessary that—just as in souls, natures, and bodies, where creation does not begin with the imperfect—so too in matter, there must be a <term>paradigm</term> <note>original: "paradigm"; an ideal model or pattern</note> of matter that exists prior to that which is formless and fleeting. This paradigm would be, in a certain sense, a "form" characterized by a single boundary and permanence. This will also have a twofold origin: namely, from its own ideal model and from a divine cause alone. For every intellectual power produces in conjunction with the divine; but the divine acts by itself, reaching even down to those things which do not derive their existence from an intellectual form.

Having, therefore, considered the simple foundations of beings, let us direct our attention to the things composed of these—namely, animals and plants. There will be intellectual models for all of these; because not only the general category (genus) but also the specific type (species) of each completes the universe and makes it more similar to its original model. For the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and ideal forms</note> encompasses all such animals in an intellectual way.

He concludes that every species of plant and animal has a corresponding ideal form in the "intelligible world" that gives the universe its completeness.</summary>

<page-num>561</page-num>
# ON THE PARMENIDES

As the apparent world contains things sensibly, each of these is assimilated to a certain intellectual form. However, "Animal Itself"—or the extremity of the intelligible triad <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "intelligible triad" refers to Being, Life, and Intellect; "Animal Itself" represents the perfect model of all living things</note>—comprehends the causes of souls, bodies, and animals in a united and intelligible way. For, just as it contracts the entire number of ideas into a "tetrad" <note>original: "tetrad of ideas"; referring to the Pythagorean four, symbolizing the completion of the ideal world</note>, it also reassumes, according to union, the distributed causes of things. This includes things that are simple as well as those that are composite in the intellectual realm. 

In short, both the universal and the essential are derived from that source. For where else would things obtain their never-failing nature if there were no eternal cause? From where would that which is common, and which extends to a multitude of things, arise? Whatever is derived from the circular motion of the heavens is partial, since the motion of the heavens itself is, in a certain respect, partial. But it is impossible for a universal to be generated from something that is partial. 

Every form, therefore, of both plants and animals, exists according to a certain intellectual paradigm <note>term: paradigm; an eternal, perfect model or blueprint in the divine mind</note>. For everything generated, and everything that has any form of existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note>, derives its being from a cause. From where, then, do these visible forms come, and from what cause? Shall we say they come from a cause that is mutable? That is impossible. They must, therefore, derive their existence from an immovable cause, since they are perpetual. We say that an "intellectual" is a cause of this kind, for it abides perfectly in eternity. 

Shall we admit, then, that there are forms not only of species, but also of particulars? For instance, is there a form of Socrates, and of every individual—not just as a man, but as a specific individual? If this were the case, would not the mortal necessarily be immortal? For if everything generated according to an "Idea" is generated according to an immovable cause, and everything that exists according to an immovable cause is immutable in its essence, then Socrates and every individual of the human species would be established according to a perpetual sameness of essence. This is impossible. 

It is likewise absurd to think that an Idea should be the paradigm of something at one time, and not at another. For eternal being possesses whatever it possesses eternally. Hence, that which is a paradigm will either not possess form at all, or will always possess it, since it would be absurd to claim there is anything accidental among the Ideas. If, therefore, it is a paradigm, it is necessary that its image also be perpetual, for every paradigm is the paradigm of an image. But if it is essential at one time and not at another, it will also be a paradigm at one time and at another...

<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

Another note: besides, is it not necessary to be persuaded by Socrates, who says that we are led to admit the subsistence <note>original: "subsistence"; here meaning the independent existence or reality</note> of ideas so that we may have the "one" prior to the "many"? For, if there are ideas of particulars <note>individual, specific things</note>, there would be one prior to one—or rather, infinite ideas prior to finite things. Since sensible natures <note>things perceived by the senses</note> are finite, the ideas would be infinite. Nothing, however, can be more absurd than this: for things nearer to *the one* <note>the ultimate source or first principle in Neoplatonism</note> are more bounded in number than those that are more remote from it. And hence it appears that there can be no ideas of individuals. 

Since, however, everything which is generated is generated from a certain cause, we must also admit that there are causes of individuals. The <gloss>one</gloss> general cause is the order of the universe, but the many causes include the motion of the heavens, partial natures, the characteristic peculiarities of the seasons and climates, and the inspective guardians <note>spiritual or divine overseers</note> of these. For, when the cause is moved, it moves along with itself, in a certain respect, that which is generated from it. Hence, from the idioms <note>specific characteristics or properties</note> of the presiding causes, different appropriate figures, colors, voices, and motions are imparted to different animals. 

For generations vary in different places; partial natures not only proceed from the whole of nature, but also receive something from the idiom of seeds. They are fashioned by turning toward bodies and becoming, as it were, eminently corporeal <note>physical or material</note> by departing from their true selves. We see, therefore, that they do not exist from a paradigmatic cause <note>a cause that serves as a perfect model or "Idea"</note>: for it is not the same thing to exist from a cause as it is to be generated according to a paradigm. For "cause" is defined in many ways, only one of which is the paradigmatic.

Again, with respect to parts, shall we say that there are also ideas of these? Is there not only a paradigm of "man," but also of "finger" and "eye," and everything of this kind? Indeed, because each of these is universal and an essence, it exists from a certain stable cause; but because they are parts and not wholes, they are subordinate to an impartible <note>indivisible</note> and intellectual essence. For there is no absurdity in admitting that things which are not only parts but also wholes exist according to that essence; but it is absurd to admit this of things that are parts only. For the generation of wholes comes from that source, since the uniform exists prior to the multiplied, and the whole exists prior to the part. Will it not, therefore, be right to assert of all such things that their causes are not intellectual—for every intellect is impartible, and consequently wholes exist in it prior to parts, and indivisible natures prior to divisible ones—but that they are psychical <note>relating to the soul</note> and physical? For that which is primarily partible <note>capable of being divided</note> is in souls, and

After these in natures <note>original: "natures" refers here to the level of reality governed by the natural world, below the soul</note>. Here, therefore, there is a reason and form of finger and tooth, and of each of these. And the wholeness of these, indeed, exists beforehand in the intellect; but that which in the "one" also comprehends the multitude is found in souls. That which vitally distributes the "one" from the multitude is in natures; and that which makes a division accompanied by physical space <note>original: "interval"</note> is in bodies. In short, it must not be denied that there are definite demonic <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to intermediary spirits or powers, not "evil" demons</note> causes of these, as invocations upon the finger, eye, and heart prove; but of the wholes which encompass these parts, there are divine causes.

In the next place, let us consider accidents <note>term: "accidents" refers to non-essential qualities of a thing, like its color or size, which can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</note>. Do these then also have ideas <note>term: "ideas" or "forms"; the eternal, perfect archetypes of things in the divine mind</note>, or is there a twofold consideration regarding them? For some of them perfect and complete the essence of a thing, such as similarity, beauty, health, and virtue; but others exist within essences yet do not complete or perfect them, such as whiteness, blackness, and everything of this kind. 

Therefore, things which complete and perfect essences have primary exemplary <note>original: "paradigmatic"</note> causes; but things which are generated in bodies are indeed produced according to reason, and the temperament of bodies is not sufficient for their generation. Instead, form is derived inwardly from nature, yet they are not produced according to a specific, definite intellectual cause. For that which is essential, perfective, and common pertains to the forms; but that which is deprived of all these exists from some other cause, and not from the primary forms. 

For nature, receiving the order of forms as they proceed into physical matter <note>original: "corporeal masses"</note>, divides wholes from parts and essences from accidents—which before this were united and indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>—expanding these by her divisive powers. It is not indeed possible that things perfectly divided should immediately exist from things that are united, nor things most specific <note>original: "partial"</note> from those that are most common. Rather, a division must necessarily be produced from the lower state of the natures that exist in between. 

We must therefore admit that there is a cause of figure <note>term: "figure" refers to geometric shape</note> which is the fertile source of all shapes, and one monad <note>term: "monad" refers to the primary "one" or the fundamental unit from which all numbers or things of a certain class originate</note> of numbers which generates all numbers. Since even the monad we possess shows that it contains the even and the odd and all forms of numbers united within it, what then ought we to think concerning the Monad which is in the divine realm? Must it not be that it is uniformly the cause of all things, and that its infinite power also generates infinite number within us? Indeed, this must necessarily be the case, since the monad here proceeds as the image of that higher one.

In the next place, with respect to artificial things <note>original: "things artificial"; man-made objects</note>, shall we say that there are ideas—

# ADDITIONAL NOTES

What should we say of these? Socrates, indeed, in the *Republic*, does not refuse to speak of the "idea" of a bed and of a table. However, in that context, he calls the productive principle within the <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>original: dianoëtic; referring to the capacity for discursive reasoning or the "thinking-through" part of the mind</note> part of the artist an "idea." He says that this productive principle is the offspring of divinity because he believed that the capacity for art itself is granted to souls by the divine. 

For if it were claimed that the forms of these artificial objects exist in the divine intellect, would they pass into the sensible world immediately, or through nature as a medium? If they passed immediately, it would be absurd, since such a progression never occurs with other forms; rather, things that are closer to the intellect are the first participants in ideas. But if they pass through nature as a medium—because the arts are said to imitate nature—then nature would possess the forms of artificial things long before art does. Yet, all things generated by nature are alive and undergo the processes of birth and growth, provided they belong to things created in matter; for nature is a specific kind of life and the cause of living things. It is, however, impossible for a bed, or anything else produced by art, to live and grow. Therefore, artificial things do not have pre-existing ideas or intellectual paradigms for their existence.

If, however, someone wishes to call the sciences "arts," we must make the following distinction: regarding those arts that lead the soul back and make it like the divine intellect, we must admit there are ideas to which they align us. For a geometric figure and the mental understanding of that figure are similar, as are a number and the mental understanding of that number. We must admit, therefore, that there are ideas of arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy—not insofar as they are applied to practical, everyday purposes, but insofar as they are intellectual and contemplative of divine forms. 

For these sciences indeed connect us with the intellect when, like the "leader of the choir" <note>original: Coryphæan philosopher; referring to the lead philosopher described by Plato</note> in the *Theaetetus*, we study astronomy above the heavens, survey the intellectual harmony according to which the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>original: demiurgus; the "craftsman" or creator-god of the universe</note> generated souls and this universe, and contemplate that number which exists in all forms secretly and separately. We also contemplate the intellectual figure which is the source of all shapes, and according to which the Father of the Universe revolves the world and gives to each of the elements its proper shape. 

Of these sciences, therefore, we must establish that there are ideas, as well as of any other sciences that elevate souls to the intellect and whose assistance we require in returning to the <term>intelligible</term> <note>the realm of pure thought and divine reality</note>. But regarding those sciences that pertain to the soul while she is playing and occupying herself with mortal concerns and serving human needs, there are no intellectual forms; rather, the soul possesses a power in opi— <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "opinion."</note>

<summary>This page argues that while artificial objects like beds do not have divine "ideas," the theoretical sciences (arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy) do have archetypes because they elevate the soul toward the divine intellect.</summary>
