Opinion is the fruitful source of theorems and is naturally adapted to generate and judge such particulars. There are, however, by no means separate forms <note>Platonic Ideas</note> of the arts, or of artificial things. But it is not surprising that the causes of these should exist in demons <note>original: "dæmons"; here referring to intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, who are said to be the watchful guardians of arts and to impart them to men; or that they should also be symbolically present in the Gods. Thus, for instance, a certain demon of the order of Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> is said to preside over the brazier's art <note>metalworking</note> and to contain the form of this art; but the mighty Vulcan himself is said symbolically to fabricate the heavens from brass. In a similar manner, there is a certain Minerval <note>pertaining to Athena/Minerva</note> demon who presides over the weaver's art, while Minerva herself is celebrated as weaving the order of intellectual forms in a different and demiurgic <note>term: demiurgic; relating to the divine Creator or "craftsman" of the universe</note> manner.

In the next place, with respect to evil, must we say that there is such a thing as "evil itself," the idea of evils? Or shall we say that—just as the form of things endowed with interval <note>spatial extension</note> is indivisible, and the form of multiplied things is unitary—the paradigm <note>term: paradigm; a divine model or pattern</note> of evil things is actually good? For the assertion is by no means sane which admits that evil itself exists among the Ideas, lest we should be compelled to say that Divinity himself is the cause of those evils of which he contains the patterns; even though we, when we look to those patterns, become better than we were before. 

But if someone should say that the form of evils is good, we ask: is it good only in its essence, or also in its energy <note>active expression or operation</note>? For, if it were good in its essence alone, it would be productive of evil by its energy, which it is not lawful to assert. But if it is good in its energy also, it is evident that what is generated by it will be good. For the effect of beneficent power and energy is good, just as the effect of fire is hot. Evil, therefore, insofar as it is evil, is not generated according to a specific divine paradigm. Furthermore, if—as Parmenides also says—every Idea is a God, and no God (as we learn from the *Republic*) is the cause of evil, then we must not say that Ideas, being Gods, are the causes of evil. Since paradigms are the causes of the things of which they are patterns, it follows that no Idea is the cause of evil.

From all that has been said, we may summarily conclude that Ideas are of universal essences and of the perfections within them. For the good, the essential, and the perpetual are most suited to forms; the first of these (the good) proceeds from the First Cause, the second (the essential) from the highest Being, and the third (the perpetual) from Eternity, reaching down to the first order of forms. From these three elements, therefore, we may define which things are generated according to a specific paradigmatic intellectual cause, and which things exist from other principles.

# ADDITIONAL NOTES

...and not from an intellectual paradigm <note>original: "paradigm"; an eternal, perfect model or archetype in the divine mind</note>. For hair, though it should be a leading part, will not be there; for it has been shown that other things are there, and not parts. But clay is an indefinite mixture of two elements not subsisting according to a physical reason; since we are also accustomed to connect together ten thousand other particulars for our use. We do not, however, refer anything of this kind to a Form: for these works are either the offspring of art, or of a deliberative tendency toward things in our power. 

And as to mud, since it is a certain evil of that with which it subsists, it cannot subsist from Ideas, because, as we have shown, nothing evil is generated from that source. On this account, these things—because they are exits from and privations <note>original: "privations"; the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note> of Ideas—do not derive their origin from them. For darkness is a privation of light; but the sun, being the cause of light, is not also the cause of its privation. In like manner, Intellect, being the cause of knowledge, does not also give existence to ignorance, which is the privation of knowledge; and the Soul, being the supplier of life, does not also impart a privation of life. 

But if someone should say that Intellect, in knowing good, also knows evil, and on this account should place evil within Intellect, to this we must reply: there is no paradigm of evil in Intellect, but it possesses a *knowledge* of evil. This knowledge is the paradigm of all the knowledge of evil, and he who receives it is benefited. For ignorance is evil, but the knowledge of ignorance is not; rather, it is a single knowledge of both itself and of ignorance. For, if we speak this way, we shall neither introduce Ideas of evil things (as some Platonists have), nor shall we say that Intellect only knows things of a more excellent nature (as others have asserted). Instead, ranking between both views, we shall admit that it has a knowledge of evils, but we shall not introduce a paradigmatic cause for these, since such a cause would itself be evil.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into the nature of the "One" or the first principle, specifically exploring its relationship to the totality of existence as discussed in Plato's Parmenides.</meta>

<page-num>567</page-num>
# ON THE PARMENIDES.

Should we say that the one principle of all things is beyond all things? Or is it something belonging to all things, acting as the summit of the things that proceed from it? Furthermore, should we say that all things exist together with it, or that they are secondary to it and originate from it? 

If someone were to assert the latter, how can the principle be something external to all things? For, in short, "all" refers to that from which nothing is absent. Yet the principle is absent from that set, as it does not rank among the things it created. Therefore, all things are not simply secondary to the principle, but exist alongside it. 

Furthermore, all things must be considered as a collection of many finite things; for infinite things clearly cannot constitute a "whole" or "all." Nothing, therefore, will be external to "all things." For *allness* <note>original: παντοτης (pantotes)</note> is a specific boundary and enclosure, in which the principle is the upper boundary, and the final result of the procession <note>term: procession; the Neoplatonic idea of reality flowing outward from a single source</note> from the principle is the lower boundary. All things, therefore, exist together within these boundaries. 

Again, the principle is coordinated with the things that proceed from it; for it is called, and truly is, their principle. The cause is also coordinated with the things it causes, just as that which is first is coordinated with the things that follow it. But when many things exist in a single coordination, they are called "all"; so the principle is also among "all things." In short, we use the term "all things" for everything we conceive to exist in any way whatever; and we certainly conceive the principle to exist. Hence, we are accustomed to call the governor and the governed together "all the city," and the begetter and the begotten together "all the race." 

But if all things exist together with the principle, will the principle not be just one part of "all things," since it is included in that total sum? If so, the single coordination of all things—which we call "all"—would be without its own principle or cause, unless we wish to keep searching for causes forever in an infinite loop. 

It is necessary, however, that everything must either be the principle itself or come from the principle. All things, therefore, are either the principle or from the principle. But if the latter is true, the principle will not exist as part of "all things," but will be external to them, acting as the source of everything proceeding from it. If the former is admitted—that all things are the principle—then what would be the result that proceeds from "all things" as if from a source? Therefore, all things are neither the principle itself, nor are they entirely separate from the principle. <margin>For the principle, insofar as it is the principle, ranks among all things.</margin> Furthermore, all things are, in a certain respect, seen to exist in a state of multitude and a certain separation...

<summary>This page examines the logical paradox of the "First Principle" (the One): whether it sits outside the totality of existence as a separate cause, or whether it is the "summit" and part of the totality itself.</summary>

# ADDITIONAL NOTES.

For we cannot conceive of the whole without these. How, therefore, do a certain separation and multitude directly appear? Or are not all things everywhere in separation and multitude? But is *the One* the summit of the many, and *the monad* <note>original: "monad"; in this context, a single unit that contains a plurality within itself</note> the united subsistence of things which are separated from each other? And, still further, is *the One* more simple than *the monad*? 

In the first place, however, if this is said, every monad is number, though existing in a contracted state and in profound union; and thus the monad also is all things. And, in the next place, *the One* is not something belonging to *the many*; for if it were, it would give completion to *the many* in the same manner as any other individual thing. But however numerous the many are according to a certain division, *the One* will be just as numerous prior to that division, according to that which is in every way indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note>. For it is not *the One* in the sense of being the smallest possible thing, as Speusippus <note>A Greek philosopher and Plato's successor as head of the Academy</note> appears to say, but it is *the One* as all things. For by its own simplicity it approaches all things and makes all things to be one. 

Hence all things proceed from it, because it is itself all things prior to all. And just as that which has a united existence is prior to things which are separated from each other, so *the One* is many prior to *the many*. But when we expand every conception belonging to our nature to all things, then we do not describe all things in the same way, but in a triple respect at least: namely, *unically* <note>as a single unit</note>, *unitedly* <note>as a joined whole</note>, and in a *multiplied* manner. 

All things, therefore, are from *the One*, and with reference to *the One*, as we are accustomed to say. If then, according to a more usual manner of speaking, we call things which consist in multitude and separation "all things," we must admit that *the united*, and in a still greater degree *the One*, are the principles of these. But if we consider these two as "all things," and assume them in conjunction with all other things—according to their relationship <note>original: "habitude"</note> and coordination with them, as we have said before—we must then investigate another principle prior to all things. It is no longer proper to consider this higher principle as being in any way "all things," nor to categorize it alongside its offspring. 

For if someone should say that *the One*, though it is all things which have any kind of existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note>, yet is *One* prior to *all things*, and is more *One* than *all things*; since it is *One* by itself, but *all things* as the cause of all, and according to a coordination with all things—if this should be said, *the One* will thus be doubled, and we ourselves shall become doubled and multiplied in our attempt to understand its simplicity. For by being *the One*, it is all things in the most simple manner. At the same time, even if this should be said, it is necessary that the principle of all things...

# ON THE PARMENIDES.

The principle should be exempt from all things, and consequently, it should be exempt from the most simple *allness*, and from a simplicity that absorbs all things, such as that of *the One*. Our soul, therefore, prophesies that the principle which is beyond all things that can in any respect be conceived is uncoordinated with all things <note>meaning it does not exist in the same category or relationship as other things</note>. Neither, therefore, must it be called a principle, nor a cause, nor that which is first, nor prior to all things, nor beyond all things. By no means, therefore, must we celebrate it as "all things," nor, in short, is it to be celebrated or even recalled into memory. 

For whatever we conceive or consider is either something belonging to "all things," or is "all things" itself—even if, through analysis, we should ascend to that which is most simple. This simplicity is the most comprehensive of all things, being, as it were, the ultimate circumference—not of beings, but of non-beings. For among beings, that which has a united subsistence <note>original: "united subsistence"; refers to an existence where all parts are perfectly joined</note> and is perfectly without separation is the extremity, since every being is mingled from elements which are either *bound* and infinity, or the progeny of these. 

But *the One* is simply the last boundary of *the many*. For we cannot conceive anything more simple than that which is perfectly *one*. If we name it the "principle," the "cause," the "first," and the "most simple," these and all other things exist there only according to *the One*. But because we are not able to contract our thoughts into a profound union, we are divided about it; we predicate of *the One* the distributed multitude which is in ourselves—unless we despise these names also, because *the many* cannot be adapted to *the One*. 

Hence, it can neither be known nor named; for if it could, it would in this respect be *many*. Or, these things also will be contained in it according to *the One*. For the nature of *the One* is all-receptive, or rather all-producing, and there is not anything whatever which *the One* is not. Hence, all things are, as it were, evolved from it. It is, therefore, properly the cause, the first, the end, and the last, the defensive enclosure of all things, and the *one* nature of all things. This is not that nature which is found within things and proceeds from *the One*, but that which is prior to them—which is the most impartible <note>original: "impartible"; indivisible or incapable of being divided into parts</note> summit of all things whatever, and the greatest comprehension of all things which in any respect are said to have a being.

But if *the One* is the cause of all things and is comprehensive of all things, what ascent will there be for us beyond this also? For we do not strive in vain, extending ourselves toward that which is nothing. For that which is not even *one* does not exist according to the most accurate mode of speaking. From where, then, do we conceive that there is something...

<header>ADDITIONAL NOTES</header>

Is there something beyond *the One*? For *the many* <note>original: "the many" refers to the plurality of things in the universe</note> require nothing else than *the One*. And hence *the One* alone is the cause of *the many*. Hence also *the One* is entirely the cause, because it is necessary that the cause of the many should alone be *the One*. For it cannot be nothing; since nothing is the cause of nothing. Nor can it be *the many*: for so far as they are *many* they are uncoordinated; and *the many* will not be a single cause. But if there are many causes, they will not be causes of each other, because they are uncoordinated, and because of a progression in a circle, where the same things would be both causes and the things caused. Each, therefore, would be the cause of itself, and thus there would be no cause of the many. Hence it is necessary that *the One* should be the cause of the many, and it is also the cause of their coordination: for there is a certain conspiring coordination and a union with each other.

If, therefore, someone doubting this should say that *the One* is a sufficient principle, and should add as the highest point that "we do not have any conception or suspicion more simple than that of *the One*," and should therefore ask how we can suspect anything beyond the last suspicion and conception we are able to frame;—if someone should speak this way, we must pardon the doubt. For a speculation of this kind is, as it seems, inaccessible and immense. At the same time, however, from things more known to us we must extend the ineffable labor pains <note>original: "parturitions"; the soul's struggle to give birth to high truths</note> of our soul toward the ineffable shared sensation <note>original: "cosensation"</note> of this sublime truth. 

For, just as that which exists independently is in every respect more honorable than that which exists in a relationship <note>original: "habitude"; a state of being related to something else</note>, and the uncoordinated is more honorable than the coordinated—just as the theoretical life is higher than the political life, and Saturn, for instance, is higher than Jupiter <note>In Neoplatonic thought, Saturn represents the higher intellect and Jupiter the demiurgic or governing power</note>; being is higher than forms, and *the One* is higher than *the many*, of which *the One* is the principle—so, in short, that which transcends everything of this kind is more honorable than all causes and principles. It is not to be considered as existing in any arrangement or relationship; since *the One* is naturally prior to *the many*, that which is most simple is prior to things more composite, and that which is most comprehensive is prior to the things which it comprehends. 

So that, if you are willing to speak this way, *the First* is beyond all such opposition—not only the opposition found in coordinated things, but even that which arises from its existence as the first. *The One*, therefore, and the "united" are posterior <note>term: "posterior"; coming after or lower in the hierarchy of being</note> to the First: for these contain, in a causal way, a multitude as numerous as that which is unfolded from them. *The One*, however, is no less one—if indeed it is not more so—because separate multitude is posterior to it and not within it; and the united is no less united because it contracted in

# ON THE PARMENIDES.

One things are separated prior to separation. Each of these, therefore, is all things, whether according to their coordination or according to their own nature. But all things cannot be the primary things, nor the principle itself. Nor can one of them alone be the principle, because this "one" would be simultaneously all things according to *the one*; yet we would not have yet discovered that which exists beyond all things. To this we may also add that *the one* is the summit of *the many*, acting as the cause of the things proceeding from it. We may likewise say that we form a conception of *the one* according to a purified intuition <note>original: "suspicion"; here meaning a subtle mental apprehension or inkling</note> extended toward that which is most simple and most comprehensive. 

However, that which is most venerable must necessarily be incomprehensible by all conceptions and intuitions. Since in all other matters, that which always soars beyond our understanding is more honorable than that which is more obvious, it follows that what escapes all our intuitions will be the most honorable of all. But if this is the case, it is *nothing*. Let "nothing," however, be understood in two ways: one is better than *the one*, and the other is lower than sensible objects <note>original: "posterior to sensibles"; referring to the void or non-being at the bottom of the scale of existence</note>. If we also strive in vain while asserting these things, this "striving in vain" is likewise twofold: one falls into the ineffable <note>term: ineffable; that which cannot be expressed in words</note>, while the other falls into that which has no existence whatsoever. For *this latter* is also ineffable, as Plato says, but in the worse sense; whereas *the former* is ineffable in the better sense. 

If we search for a certain advantage arising from this, it is the most necessary advantage of all: that all things proceed from there as if from a sanctuary <note>original: "adytum"; the innermost, most sacred part of a temple</note>—from the ineffable, and in an ineffable manner. For things do not proceed from it in the way that *the one* produces *the many*, nor as *united* things become separated, but rather as the ineffable produces all things similarly and ineffably. 

But if, in asserting these things concerning it—that it is ineffable, that it is no one of all things, and that it is incomprehensible—we seem to contradict <note>original: "subvert"</note> what we say, it is proper to know that these are merely the names and words of our intellectual labor <note>original: "parturitions"; the "birth pangs" of the mind trying to grasp a difficult concept</note>. We are daringly and anxiously exploring it; standing in the vestibules of the sanctuary, we announce nothing that actually belongs to the ineffable itself. Instead, we signify the manner in which we are affected by it—our doubts and our disappointment. Even this is not expressed clearly, but through indications to those who are able to understand these investigations. We also see that our intellectual labors suffer these same difficulties regarding *the one*, and that they are similarly troubled and overturned. For *the one*, says Plato, if it exists, is not *the one*. But if it does not exist, no assertion can be applied to it; so that there can neither be a negation of it, nor can any name be given to it. For a name is not even a simple...

What then? Shall we investigate something else beyond the ineffable? Or, perhaps, indeed, Plato leads us ineffably through *the One* as a medium, to the ineffable beyond *the One*, which is now the subject of discussion; and this by an ablation <note>original: ablation; the process of stripping away or removing attributes to reach a core truth</note> of *the One*, in the same manner as he leads us to *the One* by an ablation of other things. For, that he gives to *the One* a certain position is evident from his *Sophist* <note>original: Sophista; one of Plato's dialogues</note>, where he demonstrates that it exists prior to being, itself by itself. But if, having ascended as far as to *the One*, he is silent, this also is becoming in Plato to be perfectly silent, after the manner of the ancients, concerning things in every respect unspeakable: for the discourse was, indeed, most dangerous, because it might fall on ignorant <note>original: idiotical; in the classical sense of "unskilled" or "uninitiated" rather than the modern insult</note> ears. 

Indeed, when discoursing concerning that which in no respect has any existence, he subverts his own assertions, and is fearful of falling into the "sea of dissimilitude" <note>a Platonic metaphor for the chaotic world of matter and difference</note>, or, rather, of an unexisting void. But if demonstrations do not agree with *the One*, it is by no means wonderful: for they are human and divisible, and more composite than is fit. Indeed, they are not even adapted to being, since they are formal—or rather, they are neither adapted to forms nor essences. Or, is it not Plato himself, who in his *Epistles* <margin>See the seventh Epistle of Plato.</margin> shows that we have nothing which is significant of form: no type, nor name, nor discourse, nor opinion, nor science? For it is intellect alone which can apprehend ideas by its projecting energies, which we cannot possess while busily engaged in discourse. 

If, therefore, we even act intellectually, since in this case our intellection <note>the act of understanding or mental processing</note> is characterized by form, we shall not be in harmony with *the united* and with being. And if at any time we are able to project a contracted intelligence, even this is unadapted and discordant with *the One*. If, also, we act according to the most profoundly united intelligence, and through this hiddenly perceive *the One itself*, yet even this is expanded only as far as to *the One*, if there is a knowledge of *the One*; for this we have not yet determined. At the same time, however, let us now apply ourselves to the discussion of things of such great importance, through indications and suspicions, being purified with respect to unusual conceptions, and led through analogies and negations, despising what we possess with respect to these, and advancing from things more dishonorable—

Shall we therefore say that the nature which we now investigate as the first is so perfectly ineffable <note>original: "ineffable"; meaning that which cannot be expressed in words</note>, that it must not even be admitted that it is thus ineffable? Rather, we should say that *the One* is ineffable because it escapes all composition of words and names, and all distinction between that which is known and that which knows. It is to be apprehended in the most simple and comprehensive manner. It is not "one" alone as a specific characteristic of a single thing, but as *one all things*, and one prior to all things—not a "one" that is merely a part of all things. These, indeed, are the "birth-pangs" <note>original: "parturitions"; a metaphor for the soul's labor in bringing forth divine ideas</note> of the soul, and are thus purified with respect to *the simply One*, and that which is truly the *one cause* of all things. 

In short, we form a conception of the One within us—which is the summit or "flower" of our essence—as being more proximate and allied to us, and more ready to lead us toward a suspicion of that which leaves all things behind. From a particular thing that is made the subject of a hypothesis, the transition is easy to that which is simply supposed; even if we cannot fully reach it, we are carried by the most simple part of ourselves to form a suspicion concerning that which is prior to all things. *The One*, therefore, is in one sense *effable* <note>expressible</note> and in another sense *ineffable*; but that which is beyond it is to be honored with the most perfect silence, and, prior to this, by the most perfect ignorance*, which despises all knowledge.

Let us, therefore, now consider, in the second place, how it is said to be perfectly unknown. For, if this be true, how do we assert all these things concerning it? We do not usually engage in much discussion about things of which we are ignorant. But if it is in reality uncoordinated with all things, and without any relation <note>original: "habitude"; a technical term for a relationship or disposition toward something else</note> to all things, and is nothing among all things—nor even *the One itself*—then these very characteristics constitute its nature. Besides, regarding its being unknown: do we either know that it is unknown, or are we ignorant of this? If we are ignorant of its being unknown, how can we say that it is perfectly unknown? And if we know this, then in this respect it is known. Or shall we say it is known that "the unknown is unknown"? We cannot deny one thing of another without knowing the subject of the negation; nor can we say that

It is not this or that, when we can in no respect reach it. How, therefore, can we deny things which we know of that of which we are perfectly ignorant? For this is just as if someone who was blind from birth should assert that heat is not in color. Or perhaps, indeed, he also will justly say that color is not hot. For he knows this by the touch; but he knows nothing of color, except that it is not tangible: for he knows that he does not know it. Such a knowledge, indeed, is not a knowledge of color, but of his own ignorance. 

And we also, when we say that the First <note>The "First" refers to the Neoplatonic concept of the Absolute or the One, the ultimate source of all existence.</note> is unknown, do not announce anything about it, but we confess the manner in which we are affected by it. For the non-perception of the blind man is not in the color, nor yet is his blindness in the color, but in him. The ignorance, therefore, of that of which we are ignorant is in us. For the knowledge of that which is known is in the one who knows, and not in the thing known. 

But if knowledge is in that which is known—being, as it were, its splendor—then someone might say ignorance is in that which is unknown, being as it were its darkness or obscurity, according to which it is unknown by, and is unapparent to, all things. He who says this is ignorant that just as blindness is a privation <note>term: privation; the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>, so likewise is all ignorance; and that as the invisible is, so is that of which we are ignorant and which is unknown. 

In other things, therefore, the privation of this or that leaves something else behind. For that which is incorporeal <note>term: incorporeal; having no physical body or substance.</note>, though invisible, yet is intelligible <note>term: intelligible; able to be understood by the intellect or mind rather than the physical senses.</note>. And that which is not intelligible by a certain intelligence leaves at the same time something else. But if we take away every conception and suspicion, we must say this also is perfectly unknown by us, regarding which we close every eye.

Nor must we assert anything of it, as we do of the intelligible—that it is not adapted to be seen by the eyes—or as we do of *the One*—that it is not naturally adapted to be understood by an essential and abundant intellection <note>term: intellection; the action or process of understanding; intellectual perception.</note>. For it imparts nothing by which it can be apprehended, and nothing which can lead to a suspicion of its nature. For neither do we only say that it is unknown (as if, being something else, it might naturally possess the quality of being unknown), but we do not think it fit to predicate <note>term: predicate; to state, affirm, or assert something about a subject.</note> of it either *being*, or *the One*, or *all things*, or *the principle of all things*, or, in short, *anything*. 

Neither, therefore, are these things its nature: namely, *the nothing*, *the being beyond all things*, *super-causal subsistence* <note>term: super-causal subsistence; an existence that stands above the chain of cause and effect.</note>, and *the uncoordinated with all things*. Rather, these are only ablations <note>term: ablations; the removal or taking away of attributes (negative theology).</note> of things that come after it. How, therefore, do we speak concerning it? Is it not true that, knowing these posterior things <note>original: "posterior things"; referring to effects or lower levels of reality that come after the first cause</note>, we despise them in comparison to the status, if I may speak this way, of that which is in every respect ineffable <note>term: "ineffable"; that which cannot be expressed in words</note>? For, just as that which is beyond some particular knowledge is better than that which is understood by such knowledge, so that which is beyond all suspicion <note>original: "suspicion"; here meaning a mental inkling, conception, or even the slightest grasp of a thought</note> must necessarily be most venerable. This is not because it is known to be so, but because it possesses this "most venerable" quality as it exists within us, and as a consequence of the way we are affected by it. 

We also call this a prodigy <note>original: "prodigy"; a marvel or wonder that defies the natural order</note>, because it is entirely incomprehensible to our thoughts. For it follows by analogy that if something which is unknown in a certain respect is superior to that which is known in every respect (due to its more excellent subsistence <note>term: "subsistence"; the mode in which something exists</note>), then that which is in every respect unknown must necessarily be acknowledged as supreme. 

However, it does not actually possess the "supreme," nor the "most excellent," nor the "most venerable" as inherent qualities; rather, these terms are our own confessions regarding that which entirely escapes all our conceptions and inklings. For by this very assertion—that we can form no suspicion of it—we acknowledge that it is most wonderful. If we were to suspect anything concerning it, we would then have to investigate something else prior to that suspicion, and we would either have to proceed to infinity in our search, or stop at that which is perfectly ineffable. 

Can we, therefore, demonstrate anything concerning it? And is that "demonstrable" which we do not even think fit to consider as a thing whose existence we can even guess at? Or, when we assert these things, do we not indeed demonstrate *concerning it*, but not *it* itself? For it contains neither the "demonstrable" nor anything else. 

What then? Do we not hold an opinion concerning these things which we now assert? But if there is an opinion of it, it must also be an object of opinion. Or shall we say we hold the opinion that it is *not* these things? For Aristotle also says that there is such a thing as true opinion. If, therefore, the opinion is true, the thing to which the opinion is adapted must also exist in a way that makes the opinion true. For an opinion is true because the thing itself exists. 

Yet, how can this be? How can that be true which is perfectly unknown? Or shall we say that this is true: that it is *not* these things, and that it is *not* known? Is it therefore truly false to say that it *is* these things, and that it *is* known? Or shall we say that these things are to be referred to privations <note>term: "privations"; the absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present</note>, and to that which in a certain respect is not, where there may be a falling away from the hypostasis <note>term: "hypostasis"; the underlying substance or real nature of a thing</note> of form? This is just as we call the absence of light "darkness." For if light did not exist, neither would there be any darkness. But to that which is never and in no respect a "being," nothing among beings can...

As Plato says, it is impossible to approach. Therefore, it is neither "non-being," nor, in short, "privation" <note>original: *privatio*; the absence or lack of a quality</note>; and even the expression *never in no respect* <note>original: το μηδαμη μηδαμως (*to medame medamos*)</note> is incapable of signifying its nature. For this very expression is a form of "being," and the act of signifying is something that belongs to the realm of beings. Likewise, even if we should form the opinion that it does not exist in any respect, the moment it becomes the object of our opinion, it belongs to the category of beings. 

Hence, Plato very properly calls that which "never and in no respect is" both ineffable <note>too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note> and incapable of being the subject of opinion. This is categorized as "worse" than what can be spoken of or thought about, in the same way that we say the Supreme is "better" than these things. What then? Do we not think, and are we not persuaded, that the Supreme exists in this way? Or, as we have often said, do these descriptions not simply express the way we are affected by it? 

We possess this opinion within ourselves, but it is therefore empty—much like our mental concept of a vacuum or the infinite. We form a phantastic <note>original: *phantastic*; relating to the imagination or "phantasy"</note> and fictitious opinion of these things as if they existed, even though they do not. It is just as if we were to judge the sun to be no larger than a sphere with a diameter of one foot; even though we think it, this is far from the truth. So, if we form any opinion concerning that which "never and in no respect is," or concerning the subject of these writings, the opinion is merely our own. The vain attempt at understanding exists within us; in grasping at it, we only think we are apprehending the Supreme. It is, however, nothing pertaining to us, so much does it transcend our conceptions. 

How, therefore, do we demonstrate that there is such an ignorance in us concerning it? And how do we say that it is unknown? We reply, in one word: because we always find that whatever is above knowledge is more honorable; so that what is above *all* knowledge, if it were to be found, would be found to be the most honorable of all. But it is sufficient for the demonstration to show that it *cannot* be found. 

We also say that it is above all things; because, if it were something known, it would rank among "all things." There would then be something common between it and all other things—namely, the quality of "being known." But there is a single coordination <note>a systematic arrangement or classification</note> of things in which there is something common; if it shared this, it would exist on the same level as all other things. Hence, it is necessary that it should be unknown.

In the third place, the "unknown" is inherent in beings just as the "known" is, though they are both present at the same time in a relative sense. Therefore, just as we say that the same thing is relatively large or small depending on what it is compared to, we also say that a thing is known or unknown with reference to different things. <meta>This page continues the philosophical analysis of the nature of the "One" and the "Unknown" within the context of Platonic and Neoplatonic metaphysics, specifically discussing the limits of human and divine knowledge.</meta>

# ON THE PARMENIDES.

Just as something that participates in two forms—the great and the small—is at the same time both great and small, so that which participates in both the known and the unknown is both of these. Thus, the "intelligible" <note>The realm of reality that can be understood by the mind but not perceived by the senses.</note> is unknown to the senses but is known to the intellect. For a higher reality will not be a "privation" <note>original: "privation"; a lack or absence of something.</note> while an inferior reality is a "form" <note>A formal structure or essence.</note>; since every absence or privation of this kind exists either in matter or in the soul. In contrast, all things are present in the intellect, and even more so, in a certain respect, in the intelligible realm. 

Unless, indeed, we define "privation" according to a more excellent way of existing. For example, we say that which is above form is "not form," and that which is "superessential" <note>original: "superessential"; existing beyond the category of "being" or "essence."</note> is "not being." In this sense, that which is truly unknown is "nothing," according to a transcendence that surpasses all things. If, therefore, *the One* is the last thing known among all things that are in any way known or suspected, then that which is beyond *the One* is primarily and perfectly unknown. It is so unknown that it does not even have an "unknown nature," nor can we approach it as we would approach something unknown; it is even unknown to us whether it is unknown at all. 

There is an all-perfect ignorance regarding it. We cannot know it as something known, nor as something unknown. Consequently, we are completely overturned because we are unable to reach it in any respect, because it is not even "one thing"—or rather, it is not even "that which is not one thing." Therefore, it is that which has no existence in any respect whatever; or it is even beyond this, since "this" is a negation of being, and "that which is not even one thing" is a negation of *the One*. 

But that which is not one thing—or, in other words, that which is "nothing"—is a void and a falling away from all things. We do not, however, think of the "ineffable" <note>original: "ineffable"; that which is too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.</note> in this way. Or shall we say that "nothing" is twofold: one being beyond all things, and the other being below all things? For *the One* is also twofold: *this* one being the extreme (such as the "one" of matter), and *that* one being the first (as that which is more ancient than being). 

So, with respect to "nothing" also, *this* nothing is that which is not even the "last one," while *that* nothing is that which is not even the "first one." In this way, therefore, that which is unknown and ineffable is twofold: *this* as not even possessing the slightest hint of existence, and *that* as not even being the first of things. Must we, therefore, consider it as that which is unknown to us? This is not paradoxical, for it will be unknown even to the highly-honored intellect, if it is lawful to speak this way. For every intellect looks toward the "intelligible," and the intelligible is either *form* or *being*. But might divine knowledge know it? Might it be known to divine knowledge superessentially? This knowledge, however, applies itself...

to *the one*, but that which we are now investigating is beyond *the one*. In short, if it is also known in conjunction with other things, it will also be something belonging to all things; for it would share the quality of being known with others, and to that extent, it would be categorized alongside them. Furthermore, if it is known, divine knowledge will comprehend it. It will, therefore, define it. Every boundary, however, ascends ultimately as far as *the one*; *but that principle is beyond the one*. It is, therefore, perfectly incomprehensible and invisible, and consequently is not to be grasped by any kind of knowledge. 

To this we may add that knowledge concerns things which can be known, such as beings, or things having a subsistence <note>original: "subsistence"; refers to the state of existing or having a distinct reality</note>, or things participating in *the one*. But this principle is beyond all of these. Furthermore, *the one* also appears to be unknown, if it is necessary that the thing known be one thing and the knower be another, even if both exist within the same entity. Thus, *the truly one* will not know itself, for it does not possess a certain duality. There will not, therefore, be within it a knower and a thing known. 

Hence, even a God—when considered according to *the one* itself alone and as being joined with *the one*—will not be united with that which is simple by means of duality. For how can the double be joined with the simple? But if he knows *the one* by means of *the one*, then the knower and the known will be *one*, and in each, the nature of *the one* will be revealed, existing alone and being *one*. So he will not be joined as one distinct thing with another distinct thing, or as a gnostic <note>original: "gnostic"; relating to knowledge or the capacity for knowing</note> subject with a known object, since this very thing is one alone; therefore, he will not even be joined according to the process of knowledge. 

Much more, therefore, is that which is not even *the one* unknown. But if *the one* is the last thing known, we know nothing of that which is beyond *the one*; so that this present discussion is useless. Or shall we say we know that these descriptions are unworthy to be asserted—if it is lawful to speak this way—of the *first hypothesis* <note>original: "first hypothesis"; likely referring to the first deduction in Plato's Parmenides regarding the absolute One</note>? For even now, not yet knowing the intelligible forms <note>original: "intelligible forms"; the eternal, non-physical archetypes of things</note>, we despise the images of their eternal and indivisible nature that exist within us, since these images are divisible and change in many ways.

But now we are ignorant of *the one*, which does not contract, but rather expands all things toward it;

And in us, simplicity itself consists of a relationship to the "all" which we contain, but it is very far from coming into contact with the all-perfect nature of *the One*. For *the One* and *the simple* in our human nature are only in the smallest degree what they are said to be, except insofar as they are a sign or indication of the divine nature that exists there. Thus, also, by assuming in the intellect everything that can be in any respect known or suspected, we think it appropriate to ascribe it as far as *the One*—if it is necessary to speak of things that are unspeakable and to conceive of things that are inconceivable. 

At the same time, we also think it appropriate to make that the subject of our hypothesis <note>original: "hypothesis"; here meaning a foundational philosophical assumption</note> which cannot be compared and is uncoordinated <note>original: "uncoordinated"; meaning it does not sit on the same level or in the same category as other things</note> with all things. It is so exempt <note>original: "exempt"; meaning set apart or transcending all categories</note> that it does not even possess the quality of being "exempt" in reality. For that which is exempt is always exempt from *something*, and is therefore not exempt in every respect, as it maintains a relationship <note>original: "habitude"</note> to that from which it is set apart, and, in short, precedes it within a certain shared order. 

If, therefore, we intend to make that which is truly exempt the subject of our hypothesis, we must not even suppose it to be "exempt." For, strictly speaking, its proper name will not be accurate when ascribed to *the exempt*; for in this case, it would simultaneously be part of a shared order. Thus, it is necessary even to deny this description of it. Likewise, negation is a certain type of sentence, and that which is denied is a certain thing; but that of which we are now endeavoring to speak is not "any thing." Therefore, it can neither be denied, nor spoken of, nor be in any way known. It is not even possible to deny the negation itself. What appears to us to be a demonstration of what we are saying is actually a perfect subversion of language and thought. What end, therefore, will there be to this discourse, except the most profound silence and an acknowledgment that we know nothing of that which it is not lawful—since it is impossible—to bring into the realm of knowledge?

May it not, therefore, be said by someone who ventures to make such inquiries: if we assert something concerning it based on things of a secondary nature, we see that the monad <note>original: "monad"; the primary unit or "the one" that leads a specific group</note> is everywhere the leader of its own specific number? For there is one first soul and many souls, one first intellect and many intellects, one first being and many beings, and one first unity and many unities. If this is the case, may it not be said in a similar manner that it is necessary for there to be one "Ineffable" <note>original: "ineffable"; that which cannot be expressed in words</note> and many "ineffables"? If this were admitted, it would be necessary to say that the Ineffable is ineffably prolific <note>original: "prolific"; meaning fruitfully creative or producing offspring</note>. It would, therefore, generate its own multitude. Or should we say that these and similar conceptions arise only from forgetting what has been asserted before?

This question indeed is not difficult to solve; for we have said before that all these things apply to that which is "nothing" in any respect because it is worse than all these <note>i.e., "nothingness" as a lack of being, like matter.</note>, but they apply to the First Principle because we admit it to be better than all these <note>i.e., "nothingness" as a transcendence of being, being "beyond" existence.</note>. For we deny things of both matter and *the one*, but in two different ways, in the manner mentioned above. This question then, as I have said, is easily solved.

Again, therefore, it may be asked: Does not something proceed from it to the things which are here? Or how indeed should this not be the case, if all things are from it? For everything participates in that from which it proceeds. For, if nothing else, it possesses from that source its very identity, breathing its proper principle and turning itself toward it as much as possible. Hence, too, must it not also be more like it, so that it will likewise be suited to participate in it, and will indeed participate in it? Is it as if it were hastening to be joined with it? Shall we, therefore, say that because this nature is arcane <note>original: "arcane"; meaning hidden, secret, or beyond the reach of human understanding</note>, it bestows a hidden participation on all things, through which there is something mysterious in every thing? For we acknowledge that some things are more hidden than others: *the one* more than *being*, *being* more than *life*, and *life* more than *intellect*. This continues in succession in the same manner—or rather, inversely. From matter up to a rational essence, these things exist according to the worse <note>referring to the lower, more material levels of reality</note>, but those according to the better, if it is lawful to speak this way. 

May we not say, however, that whoever admits this will also create a progression from the first principle, and a certain hidden order of things proceeding from it? In doing so, we would introduce all such "effable" <note>original: "effables"; things that can be expressed in words</note> qualities to the hidden realm, just as we have categorized them with the expressible. We would therefore create three monads <note>original: "monads"; primary, indivisible units or sources</note> and three numbers, rather than two: namely, the essential, the unical (that characterized by unity), and the arcane. Thus, we would admit what we formerly rejected—that is, a "multitude" within the hidden realm, and an order of things that are first, middle, and last. There would also be permanency, progression, and regression; in short, we would mix much of the expressible with the inexpressible. 

But if, as we have said, the terms *it* or *those* cannot be applied to that hidden nature—which we consider to be above both *the one* and *the many*—then nothing else besides *the one* must be admitted as coming before the many, nor should anything else be categorized with the many in the process of participation. Therefore, it is neither participated in, nor does it give any part of itself to its offspring; nor is every God "arcane" before being "one," just as a God is "one" before being "essence." 

May we not say, then, that the fact that language fails here proves this nature is arcane? It does this by conceiving of contradictions in every possible way based on things that come after it. And why is this surprising, since we are involved in similar doubts concerning *the one*? Indeed, is this not also the case concerning "being" and that which is *perfectly* united?

Thus also *the one* of the sun and *the one* of the moon are the truly real sun and moon. After this, he observes the following: Neither *the one* nor "all things" fully agrees with the nature of *the one*. For these concepts are opposed to each other and divide our understanding. ...abolish *the one* and the *simple*. But this is because we are divided, and look to *divided idioms* <note>original: "idioms"; here meaning specific properties or characteristics</note>. At the same time, however, aspiring after the knowledge of it, we connect all things together, so that we may thus be able to apprehend this mighty nature. But fearing the introduction of all multitudes, or contracting the peculiar nature of *the one*, and rejoicing in that which is simple and the first when speaking of the most ancient principle, we thus introduce *the one itself* as a symbol of simplicity; since we likewise introduce *all things* as a symbol of the comprehension of all things. 

But that which is above or prior to both, we can neither conceive nor name. And why is it wonderful that we should suffer these difficulties regarding it, since the distinct knowledge of it is <term>unical</term> <note>unical: existing as a single, indivisible unit; characterized by absolute oneness</note>, which we cannot perceive? We suffer other things of this kind regarding *being*. For, endeavoring to perceive *being*, we dismiss it, but run around its elements: limit and infinity. But if we form a more true conception of it—that it is a united plenitude of all things—in this case the conception of *all things* draws us down to multitude, and the conception of *the united* abolishes that of all things. 

Neither, however, is this yet wonderful. For, with respect to forms also, when we wish to survey any one of these, we run around its elements, and, striving to perceive its unity, we obliterate its elements. At the same time, however, every form is one and many; not indeed partly one and partly many, but the whole of it is, through the whole, a thing of this kind. Not being able, therefore, to apprehend this collectively, we rejoice in approaching it with a distribution of our conceptions. 

But always adhering to our ascent—like those who climb clinging with their hands and feet to things which extend us to a more <term>impartible</term> <note>impartible: indivisible; that which cannot be divided into parts</note> nature—we obtain, in a certain respect, a shared sensation within the distribution of that which is uniform. We despise this, therefore, in comparison to the collected apprehension of it, which we cannot obtain unless a certain vestige of collected intelligence in our nature is stirred. And this is the light of truth, which is suddenly enkindled, as if from the collision of flint stones. For our greatest conceptions, when exercised with each other, verge to a uniform and simple summit as their end, like the extremities of lines in a circle hastening to the center. And though even thus they exist indeed with distribution, yet a certain vestige of the knowledge of form which we contain is pre-excited; just as the equal tendency of all the lines in a circle to terminate in the middle affords a certain obscure representation of the center. After the same manner...

<summary>The author explores the paradox of human reason attempting to grasp the "One" or the "First Principle," noting that our minds naturally divide concepts into parts even when the reality is a single, indivisible whole. He uses the metaphor of lines in a circle meeting at a center to describe how diverse thoughts can point toward a unified truth.</summary>

<page-num>583</page-num>
# ON THE PARMENIDES
### 583

In the same manner, we ascend to being. In the first place, we do this by understanding every form that we encounter as distributed—not only as indivisible, but also as united—and this is achieved by merging (if it is appropriate to speak this way) the multitude within each form. In the next place, we must collect everything that has been separated and remove the boundaries. It is just as if we were making many streams of water into a single body of water; however, we must not understand that which is united from all things as a mere collection. Instead, we must conceive of that which exists prior to all things as the "form of water" that exists before the divided streams. Thus, we must expand ourselves toward *the One*, first collecting and afterwards dismissing what we have collected, for the sake of the super-expanded transcendency of *the One*.

As we ascend, therefore, shall we meet with it as something known? Or, wishing to meet with it as such, shall we instead arrive at the unknown? Perhaps we may say that both are true. For we meet with it from afar as something known; but when we are united to it from afar, passing beyond that part of our nature which is <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: "gnostic"; meaning "capable of knowing" or "intellectual"</note> of *the One*, we are then brought to *be* one. That is, we become unknown to ourselves instead of being a knower. This contact, as of one with one, is above knowledge; but the other kind of contact is as a knower with that which is known.

However, just as the crooked is known by the straight, so we form a conjecture of the unknown by the known. And this is indeed a mode of knowledge. *The One*, therefore, is known only so far as it does not admit of an intimate, approximating knowledge; it appears from afar as known and imparts a <term>gnostic</term> indication of itself. Unlike other things, however, the nearer we approach it, it is not more known, but, on the contrary, less known. Knowledge is dissolved by *the One* into ignorance, since, as we have observed before, where there is knowledge, there is also separation. But separation, <unclear>tend</unclear>ing toward *the One*, is enclosed in union; so that knowledge also is poured back into ignorance.

This is also what the analogy of Plato requires. For first we endeavor to see the sun, and we do indeed see it from afar; but the nearer we approach it, the less we see it. At length, we see neither other things nor the sun itself, the eye becoming spontaneously dazzled by its light. Is *the One*, therefore, in its proper nature unknown, even though there is something else unknown besides *the One*? *The One* indeed wills to be by itself, and with no other; but the unknown beyond *the One* is perfectly ineffable <note>original: "ineffable"; meaning "unspeakable" or "beyond description"</note>. We acknowledge that this principle neither knows nor is ignorant, but possesses a "super-ignorance" with respect to itself. Hence, by proximity to this, *the One*...

<summary>This page describes the Neoplatonic ascent to "the One," explaining that as the soul approaches the ultimate principle, intellectual knowledge must be abandoned in favor of a mystical union that transcends the distinction between knower and known.</summary>

The intellect itself is darkened: for, being very near to the immense principle—if it be lawful to speak this way—it remains, as it were, in the *adytum* <note>original: "adytum"; the innermost, most sacred shrine of a temple where only priests could enter</note> of that truly mystic silence. On this account, Plato, when speaking of it, finds all his assertions subverted: for it is near to the subversion of everything, which takes place regarding the First Principle. It differs from the First, however, in this: that it is *one* simply, and according to *the one*, it is also at the same time all things. But the First is above *the one* and all things, being more simple than both of these.

->P. 166. *Note. Such then is the intelligible triad.*<-

In order to convince the reader that the doctrine delivered here regarding the intelligible triad is not a fiction devised by the later Platonists, I shall present the following translation from the same excellent work by Damascius, *Concerning Principles* <note>original: "Περι αρχων" (Peri archon)</note>, in which the agreement of all the ancient theologians concerning this triad is most admirably demonstrated.

The theology contained in the Orphic rhapsodies <note>The "Orphic Rhapsodies" were a collection of sacred poems attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, central to ancient Greek mystery religions.</note> concerning the intelligible Gods is as follows: *Time* is symbolically placed as the one principle of the universe; but *Aether* and *Chaos* represent the two principles following this one. *Being*, simply considered, is represented under the symbol of an egg. This constitutes the first triad of the intelligible Gods. 

For the perfection of the second triad, they establish either a conceiving and a conceived egg as a God, or a white garment, or a cloud: because from these, Phanes <note>A primeval deity in Orphic tradition, often associated with light and the creation of the universe.</note> leaps forth into light. Indeed, they philosophize in various ways concerning the middle triad. Here, Phanes represents intellect. However, conceiving him beyond this as "father" and "power" adds nothing to the Orphic account. 

They call the third triad Metis as *intellect* <note>The original Greek text omits "as intellect" (Ως νους), but the author restores it for clarity.</note>, Ericapaeus as *power*, and Phanes as *father*. But should we not consider the middle triad according to the three-shaped God, while conceived within the egg? <note>The author notes that while this is not phrased as a question in the original Greek, the context requires it to be one.</note> For the middle always represents each of the extremes; as in this instance, where the egg and the three-shaped God exist together. Here you may perceive that the egg is that which is united; but the three-shaped and truly multiform God is the separating and discriminating cause of that which is...

intelligible. Likewise, the middle triad exists according to the "egg," which is as yet united; but the third <note>original: *to triton*; the Greek for "the third" was likely omitted in the source text</note> exists according to the God who separates and distributes the entire intelligible order. This is the common and familiar Orphic theology. 

However, the theology delivered by Hieronymus and Hellanicus <note>Hieronymus and Hellanicus were ancient historians or mythographers who recorded alternative versions of Orphic cosmogony</note> is as follows. According to them, *water* and *matter* were the first productions from which earth was secretly drawn forth. Thus, water and earth are established as the two first principles; the latter of these has a *dispersed* existence, while the former glues together and connects the latter. But they are silent concerning the principle prior to these two, regarding it as ineffable <note>too sacred or great to be expressed in words</note>. Because there are no illuminations or descriptions concerning him, his secret and ineffable nature is sufficiently proven by this silence. 

The third principle following these two—*water* and *earth*—and which is generated from them, is a *dragon*. This dragon is naturally endowed with the heads of a bull and a lion, but in the middle, it has the face of the God himself. They add, likewise, that he has wings on his shoulders and that he is called *undecaying Time* and *Hercules*. They also say that *Necessity* resides with him (which is the same as *Nature*) and incorporeal *Adrastia* <note>a goddess of inevitable fate or retribution</note>, who is extended throughout the universe and binds its limits in friendly conjunction. But, as it appears to me, they describe this third principle as being established according to essence, and they assert that it exists as both male and female for the purpose of showing the generative causes of all things.

I also find in the Orphic rhapsodies <note>the "Sacred Utterances" or poems attributed to Orpheus</note> that, by neglecting the first two principles along with the one principle who is passed over in silence, the third principle following the two is established by this theology as the original starting point. This is because this principle is the first to possess something expressible and suited to human discourse. 

In the former hypothesis, the highly revered and undecaying *Time*, the father of ether and chaos, was the principle. But in this version, *Time* is neglected, and the principle becomes a *dragon*. It likewise says that there was a triple offspring: moist ether, an infinite chaos, and cloudy, dark Erebus <note>the personification of darkness</note>. This delivers a second triad analogous to the first: this one being potential, just as the first was paternal. Hence, the third procession of this triad is dark Erebus; its paternal summit is ether (not according to a simple existence, but an intellectual one); and its middle is infinite chaos, considered as a progeny or procession. This chaos is described as "laboring with birth" because from these, the third intelligible triad proceeds. What then is the third intelligible triad? I answer: The egg; the duality of the natures of male and female...

That *Love* is to be placed as the third monad <note>original: monad; a single, indivisible unit or primary principle</note> of the intelligible order, considered according to its power to turn things back toward their source; for it is named this way by Orpheus in his rhapsodies. But *Earth* is placed as the first, being first established in a certain firm and essential permanency. And *Tartarus* is the middle, as it in some way excites and moves forms into their distribution. 

However, Acusilaus appears to me to establish *Chaos* as the first principle, as it is entirely unknown; and after this, two principles: *Erebus* as male, and *Night* as female. He places the latter for infinity, but the former for *bound* <note>The "Limit" and "Unlimited" are core Pythagorean/Platonic concepts</note>. From the mixture of these, he says that *Ether*, *Love*, and *Counsel* are generated, forming three intelligible <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: hypostases; distinct underlying substances or realities</note>. He places *Ether* as the summit; *Love* in the middle, according to its naturally middle existence; and *Metis* or *Counsel* as the third, which is the same as the highly-reverenced intellect. According to the history written by Eudemus, from these he produces a great number of other Gods. 

But Epimenides establishes *Air* and *Night* as the two first principles; he is clearly honoring in silence the one principle that exists prior to these two. From *Air* and *Night*, *Tartarus* is generated, forming—as it appears to me—the third principle, as a certain mixed temperature of the two. This mixture is called by some an <term>intelligible medium</term>, because it extends itself to both the summit and the end. From the mixture of these extremes with each other, an egg is generated, which is truly an <term>intelligible animal</term>: and from this again another progeny proceeds. 

According to Pherecydes of Syros, the three first principles are: *a Perpetually-abiding Vital Nature*, *Time*, and *an Earthly Nature*. One of these exists, as I conceive it, prior to the other two. But—

<margin>Heaven, Earth, etc. are much superior to the worldly <note>original: mundane</note> deities.</margin> Indeed, if this is not admitted, the <term>Theogony</term> <note>The "birth of the gods," specifically referring to Hesiod's poem</note> of Hesiod must be perfectly absurd and inexplicable. For why does he call Jupiter, in agreement with Homer, "father of gods and men" <note>original: πατηρ ανδρων τε θεων τε (patēr andrōn te theōn te)</note>? Shall we say that he means literally that Jupiter is the father of *all* the Gods? This is impossible; for he describes the generation of Gods who are the parents of Jupiter. He can, therefore, only mean that Jupiter is the parent of all the worldly Gods. His Theogony, when considered according to this explanation, will be found to be beautifully consistent and sublime. In contrast, according to modern interpretations, the whole thing is a mere chaos—more wild than the delirious visions of Emanuel Swedenborg <note>A 17th-18th century Swedish theologian known for his mystical visions</note>, and more disconnected than the filthy ranting of a street-preaching Methodist. I only add, that "earthly" <note>original: γηιν (gēin)</note> is erroneously printed as "earth" <note>original: γην (gēn)</note> in the excerpts by Wolfius.

He asserts that *Time* generates from its own offspring—*Fire, Spirit,* and *Water*—which signify, as it appears to me, the triple nature of that which is intelligible <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure thought or forms, existing beyond the physical senses</note>. But from these, distributed into five profound recesses, a numerous progeny of Gods is constituted, which he calls *five-times animated* <note>original: πεντεμυχος (pentemychos), literally "five-nooked" or "five-recessed"</note>; and which is, perhaps, the same as if he had said a *five-fold world* <note>original: πεντεκοσμος (pentekosmos)</note>. But with respect to the theology of the foreigners <note>original: "barbarians," used here in the classical sense to mean non-Greeks</note>, the Babylonians seem to pass over in silence the single principle of the universe. Instead, they establish two principles, *Tauthe* and *Apasoon*. They consider *Apasoon* as the husband of *Tauthe*, whom they name the mother of the Gods. From them, an only-begotten son, *Mooumis*, was produced; who, as it appears to me, is no other than the intelligible world deduced from two principles <note>That is, from bound and the infinite</note>. From these, another generation is derived: *Dache* and *Dachus*. Likewise, a third from these: *Kissare* and *Assorus*. From these again, three deities are produced: *Anus, Illinus,* and *Aus*. From *Aus* and *Dache*, a son called *Belus* is produced, who they say is the *creator* <note>original: "demiurgus," the craftsman or maker of the physical world</note> of the world. 

Regarding the *Magi* and all the *Aryan race*, as we are informed by *Eudemus*, some of them call the entire intelligible and united world *Place*, and some of them *Time*. From this, a *good divinity* and *an evil demon* are distributed; *Light and Darkness* existed prior to these, according to the assertions of others. However, both groups, after considering a nature that is not yet divided, consider that nature as having an existence which distributes the twofold arrangement of higher natures: one of which arrangements *Orosmades* <note>Ahura Mazda</note> presides over, and the other *Arimanius* <note>Ahriman</note>. 

The *Sidonians*, according to the same historian, place *Time, Desire, and Cloudy Darkness* before all things. They assert that from the mingling of *Desire and Darkness* as two principles, *Air* and a *gentle Wind* were produced. *Air* represents the summit of the intelligible triad; but the *gentle Wind*, raised and proceeding from this, is the vital prototype of the intelligible. And again, from both of these, the bird *Otus* (similar to a night raven) was produced; representing, as it appears to me, *intelligible intellect*. But as we find with—

Without the assistance of Eudemus <note>Eudemus of Rhodes, a pupil of Aristotle who wrote a history of theology</note>, the Phoenician mythology, according to Moschus, places *Ether* and *Air* as the two first principles. From these, the intelligible God *Oulomus* <note>original: Oulomos; likely representing the Phoenician 'Olam' or Eternity</note> was produced, who, as it appears to me, is the summit of the intelligible order. But from this God (yet proceeding together with him) they assert that *Chousorus* <note>original: Chouforus; corrected via the author's note below to Chousorus, the Phoenician artisan-god</note> was produced, being the first unfolding procession. And after this an *egg* succeeds, which I think must be called "intelligible intellect." But the unfolding *Chousorus* is "intelligible power," because this is the first nature which distributes an undistributed subsistence. 

Unless, perhaps, after the two principles *Ether* and *Air*, the summit is *one Wind*; but the middle consists of *two Winds*, the *south-west* and the *south*; for in a certain respect they place these prior to *Oulomus*. But *Oulomus* himself is intelligible intellect, and unfolding *Chousorus* is the first order after the intelligible series. And the *egg* itself is *heaven*; from the bursting of which into two parts, the sections are said to have become heaven and earth. 

But with respect to the Egyptians, nothing accurately is related of them by Eudemus. According to certain Egyptian philosophers among us, however, an unknown *Darkness* is celebrated in some Egyptian writings as the one principle of the universe, and this is *thrice pronounced as such*. But for the two principles after the first, they place *water* and *sand*, according to Heraïscus; but according to the more ancient writer Asclepiades, *sand* and *water*. From these, and after these, the first Kamephis <note>A creator deity in late Egyptian theology, often associated with Kneph or Amun</note> is generated. But after this a *second*, and from this again a *third*; by all which the whole intelligible distribution is accomplished. For thus Asclepiades determines. 

But the more modern Heraïscus says that the Egyptians, naming the third Kamephis after his father and grandfather, assert that he is *the Sun*; which, doubtless, signifies in this case "intelligible intellect." But a more accurate knowledge of these affairs must be received from the above-mentioned authors themselves. It must, however, be observed, that with the Egyptians there are many distributions of things according to union; because they unfold an "intelligible nature" into the characteristics, or peculiarities, of many Gods, as may be learned from those who are desirous of consulting their writings on this subject.

...in celebrating the intelligible triad <note>The "intelligible triad" refers to the first grouping of divine principles in Neoplatonism: Being, Life, and Intellect.</note>, and venerating in silence the ineffable principle of things, but may likewise behold the origin of the Christian trinity, its deviation from truth, and the absurdity, and even impiety, with which a belief in it is unavoidably attended. Consonant too with the above relation is the doctrine of the Chaldeans concerning the intelligible order, as delivered by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, in his *Conclusions according to the opinion of the Chaldean theologians*: "The intelligible coordination (says he) is not in the intellectual coordination, as Amasis the Egyptian asserts, but is above every intellectual hierarchy, imparticipably <note>term: imparticipably; existing in a way that cannot be shared or divided by lower levels of reality.</note> concealed in the abyss of the first unity, and under the obscurity of the first darkness." <note>original Latin: Coordinatio intelligibilis non est in intellectuali coordinatione, ut dixit Amasis Ægyptius, sed est super omnem intellectualem hierarchium, in abyssos primæ unitatis, et sub caligine primarum tenebrarum imparticipaliter abscondita.</note>

<margin>† That is: Intelligible Gods; Intelligible and at the same time Intellectual; Intellectual; Supermundane; Liberated or Supercelestial; and Mundane. <note>original Greek: Θεοι νοητοι, νοητοι και νοεροι, νοεροι, ὑπερκοσμιοι, απολυτοι sive ὑπερουρανιοι, et εγκοσμιοι.</note></margin>
But from this triad it may be demonstrated that all the processions of the Gods may be comprehended in six orders, namely: the *intelligible* order, the *intelligible and at the same time intellectual*, the *intellectual*, the *supermundane*, the *liberated*, and the *mundane* †. For the *intelligible*, as we have already observed, must hold the first rank, and must consist of *being*, *life*, and *intellect*—that is, it must abide, *proceed*, and *return*, and this super-essentially; at the same time, it is characterized, or exists principally, according to *being*. 

But, in the next place, that which is both *intelligible* and *intellectual* succeeds it, which must likewise be triple, but must principally exist according to *life*, or *intelligence*. And, in the third place, the *intellectual* order must succeed, which is *triply convertive* <note>term: convertive; referring to the "return" or "conversion" of an effect back toward its cause.</note>. But as, in consequence of the existence of the sensible world, it is necessary that there should be some demiurgic <note>term: demiurgic; relating to the Demiurge, the divine "craftsman" or creator of the physical universe.</note> cause of its existence, this cause can only be found in *intellect*, and in the last hypostasis <note>term: hypostasis; a distinct substance or individual reality within the divine hierarchy.</note> of the *intellectual triad*. For all forms in this hypostasis exist according to all-various and perfect divisions; and forms can only fabricate <note>original: "fabricate"; here meaning to create or shape the physical world.</note> when they have a *perfect intellectual separation* from each other. But since fabrication is nothing more than *procession*, the demiurge will be to the lower order of the Gods what *the One* is to the orders prior to the *demiurge*; and consequently, he will be that secondarily which the first cause of all is primarily.
