->Page 323: *It alone uses contemplative intellect, etc.*<-

**B**y the "governor of the soul" in this passage, a partial intellect <note>original: "intellectus partialis"; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to an individual intellect rather than the universal Divine Mind</note> is meant. For this intellect is established immediately above our essence; it elevates and perfects us, and it is that toward which we turn when we are purified through philosophy and join our own power of reasoning with its higher intelligence. 

This partial intellect is shared by all other nearby demonic <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to *daemons*, intermediary spirits between gods and humans in Greek philosophy, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> souls. It illuminates our own souls when we turn toward it and make our reason intellectual. In short, just as every individual soul is essentially dependent upon a certain guardian spirit, and every guardian spirit has a higher intellect above itself, every individual soul will likewise have this intellect ranked above it as an indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> essence. 

Therefore, the first to participate in this intellect will be a demonic soul, but the second will be the individual souls under its guidance, which is what makes them "partial" or individual. It also appears that the intellect immediately above every guardian spirit—insofar as it is a whole and a unity—is the intellect of the spirit that directly participates in it. However, it also contains the total number of souls under its care and their intellectual archetypes <note>original: "paradigms"</note>. 

Every individual soul, therefore, will have its own specific archetype as its indivisible essence. This archetype is contained within that higher intellect; the soul does not possess the entire intellect, but rather its specific part, just like the guardian spirit that serves as its leader. Hence, the "indivisible" part belonging to every individual soul may be accurately defined as the *Idea* of that soul. This Idea is contained within the one intellect that serves as the leader of the spiritual series under which every such soul is organized. Thus, it is true that the intellect of every individual soul is alone supernally <note>The text ends here, continuing the thought that the soul's highest part remains rooted in the divine realm.</note>

## P. 322. *Likewise Jupiter the mighty leader, etc.*

It is said by Plato<margin>This account of that divine order which was named by ancient theologians *intelligible* and at the same time *intellectual* is extracted from the fourth book of Proclus on the *Theology of Plato*.</margin> in the *Phædrus* that there are twelve leaders who preside over the universe, who govern all the worldly <note>original: "mundane"</note> Gods and all the companies of demons <note>original: "dæmons"; here referring to intermediary spirits, not evil entities</note>, and who sublimely march toward an *intelligible nature*. It is likewise asserted that Jupiter presides over these twelve Gods; he drives a winged chariot, distributes all things in order, and takes care of and leads the entire attendant army. First, he leads them to an *elevated place of speculation* <note>original: "speculation" here means "contemplation" or "vision"</note> within the heavens, and to those blessed contemplations and unfoldings <note>original: "evolutions"</note> of intelligible realities which it contains. Afterward, they proceed to that *subcelestial arch* which immediately <note>original: "proximately"</note> embraces the heavens and which the heavens contain. After this arch, they proceed into heaven and to the *back of heaven*. In this place, divine souls are said to stand, and, while they are carried along with the movement of the heavens, they contemplate every superior essence. But prior to the heavens, there is said to be *a place* called *supercelestial*, in which *true essence, the plain of truth, the kingdom of Adrastia* <note>Adrastia: a goddess of necessity or inevitable fate, often associated with the distribution of justice</note>, *and the divine choir of virtues* reside. It is asserted that by the intelligence of these unified realities <note>original: "monads"</note>, souls are nourished and benefited while they follow the revolution of the heavens.

And so much is asserted in the *Phædrus*, where Socrates clearly speaks as one moved by a divine impulse and touches on mystical matters. But it is necessary to consider, in the first place, what this *heaven* may be that Socrates speaks of, and in what order of beings it is placed. For, having discovered this, we may then con—

What then is that heaven to which Jupiter brings the Gods? If we call it the "sensible" heaven <note>The physical, visible universe perceived by the senses</note>, as some do, it would follow that the more excellent beings must naturally turn themselves toward subordinate things. For if Jupiter, that great leader in the heavens, is himself carried to this physical heaven and leads all the attendant Gods to it, he must himself be turning toward things inferior and secondary to himself. This would also be the case for all the deities and demons <note>original: dæmons; here meaning intermediary spirits or divine beings, not evil entities</note> who follow him. Yet, the same Socrates in the *Phaedrus* asserts that even a partial soul <note>An individual human soul, as opposed to a "total" or universal soul</note>, when in a perfect state, revolves on high and governs the universe. How, then, can the leaders of universal souls be turned toward this physical heaven and exchange their intellectual place of observation for a worse condition? These are the beings who preside over the universe through these souls, so that they may illuminate worldly natures with an absolute and liberated power! 

Besides, what blessed intellectual insights could the Gods obtain by contemplating this physical heaven? And what developments could there be there for the full knowledge of physical concerns? If this were the case, Plato must be condemned for creating a relationship of no value regarding the knowledge of the intelligible Gods <note>Gods existing in the realm of pure thought/intellect</note>. For the Gods perfectly know things existing in this physical region, not by turning toward them, but because they contain the causes of those things within themselves. Hence, as a result of knowing themselves, they likewise know and govern these physical concerns in a causal manner; they do not survey them by leaning toward the things being governed, but instead, through love, they turn subordinate natures toward themselves. 

It is not, therefore, lawful for the Gods—by whom all heaven is governed and who consider it worthy of their providential care—ever to exist under its revolution. Nor, indeed, is there any true happiness <note>original: beatitude</note> in the contemplation of things situated under the heavens. Nor are the souls who are turned toward a contemplation of this kind counted among the blessed or among those who follow the Gods; instead, they rank among those who exchange intellectual nourishment for the "food of opinion" <note>Uncertain or sensory knowledge rather than certain truth</note>. These are the ones Socrates represents as "lame souls" who have broken their wings and are in a submerged condition. How can we attribute this conversion toward the sensible heaven to the leading Gods? Besides, Socrates asserts that souls, standing on the back of heaven, are carried around by the celestial revolution. But *Timaeus* and the Athenian guest <note>The "Athenian guest" refers to the main speaker in Plato's *Laws*.</note> say that souls perform all things in the heavens through their own motions, and externally clothe bodies with their powers. They argue that because souls live their own life throughout the whole of time, they impart secondary powers of motion to bodies. How, then, can these descriptions agree with those who consider this "heaven" to be the physical, sensible sky? For souls do not contemplate and, as it were, dance around "intelligibles" <note>original: *intelligibilia*; these are the pure, non-physical forms or ideas that can only be understood by the mind.</note> as a result of the physical revolution of the heavens. Rather, it is through the unseen circular motion of the souls that the bodies themselves are carried around in a circle, and perform their revolutions around these souls. If anyone, therefore, should say that this is the sensible heaven, and that souls are simultaneously carried around with its physical revolutions—distributed according to its back, its depth, and its sub-celestial arch—it is necessary to admit that many absurdities will follow.

But if anyone asserts that the heaven to which Jupiter leads all his attendant Gods and demons is an <term>intelligible heaven</term> <note>A realm of pure thought or being, rather than physical space.</note>, he will explain the divine narrations of Plato in a manner agreeable to the nature of things, and will follow his most celebrated interpreters. For both Plotinus and Iamblichus consider this to be a certain <term>intelligible heaven</term>. And prior to these, Plato himself in the *Cratylus*, following the Orphic theogony <note>The "Orphic theogony" refers to the ancient mystical poems attributed to Orpheus concerning the genealogy of the gods.</note>, calls Saturn the father of Jupiter, and Heaven the father of Saturn. He explains the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator-God who fashions the physical universe.</note> of the universe through certain names, investigating the truth which those names contain. He describes the <term>Demiurgus</term> as one who possesses a divine intellect, but describes "Heaven" as the intelligence of the first intelligibles. For Heaven, he says, is *sight looking to things on high* <note>original: *οὐρανία* (ourania), which Plato etymologically links to *ὁρῶ τὰ ἄνω* (horo ta ano), "looking at the things above".</note>. And hence, Heaven exists prior to every divine intellect with which the mighty Saturn is said to be filled; it understands superior natures and whatever is situated beyond the celestial order. The mighty Heaven, therefore, is assigned a middle kingdom between the "intelligibles" (pure beings) and the "intellectuals" (thinking minds).

For, indeed, the celestial revolution in the *Phædrus* is *intelligence*, by which all the Gods and their attendant souls obtain the contemplation of intelligibles. For *intelligence* is the bridge between the intellect and the intelligible. In this middle ground, therefore, we must establish the whole of Heaven. We must assert that it contains the single bond of the divine orders; being, indeed, the father of the intellectual race, but generated by the...

The supercelestial place must be considered as existing before the kings <note>referring to the divine orders or "monarchs" of the celestial spheres</note> it is said to behold. We must also consider it as situated between the <term>supercelestial place</term> <note>the realm above the heavens, associated with pure intelligibles</note> and the <term>subcelestial arch</term> <note>the lower boundary of the celestial spheres</note>.

Again, therefore, if the supercelestial place is indeed that unparticipated and hidden genus of the intelligible Gods, how can we establish such a great divine multitude there, and one so clearly separated—namely, truth, science, justice, temperance, the <term>meadow</term> <note>a Platonic metaphor for the source of spiritual nourishment</note>, and Adrastia <note>the goddess of inevitable fate or divine law</note>? For neither are the fountains of virtues proper to the intelligible Gods, nor are separation and variety of forms. For those things which are primary and most characterized by unity extend the <term>demiurgic intellect</term> <note>the "craftsman" or creator mind that shapes the universe</note> of the whole toward an intelligible exemplar, and toward the comprehension of forms which exist there. 

But, in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates asserts that a partial intellect <note>an individual soul's mind, as opposed to the universal mind</note> contemplates the supercelestial place. For this (as it is beautifully said by our ancestors) is the governor of the soul. If, then, it is necessary to investigate the difference of intelligibles from this analogy: just as the demiurgic intellect is unparticipated, but that which is partial is participated; so it is with respect to that which is intelligible. The "intelligible" of the demiurge is the first model of the first intelligibles, but the "intelligible" of a partial intellect is the model of secondary intelligibles. These are indeed intelligibles, but they are granted an intelligible supremacy among the intellectual orders. 

However, if the supercelestial place is situated above the celestial revolution <note>the movement of the heavens</note>, but is inferior to the <term>intelligible triads</term> <note>the highest groupings of divine principles in Neoplatonism</note> because it is more expanded—for it is the plain of truth, yet it is not unknown, and is divided according to a multitude of forms, and contains a variety of powers, and the meadow there nourishes souls and is visible to their natures—then the first intelligibles illuminate souls with an inexpressible union, even while they remain unknown to those souls through ordinary intelligence. If this is the case, it is necessary that the supercelestial place should be situated between the intelligible nature and the celestial revolution. 

Furthermore, if Plato himself establishes "true essence" in this place, must he not consider this place as intelligible, and as participating in the first intelligibles? For, because it is essence, it is intelligible; but, because it is *true* essence, it participates in "being" itself. And if it contains within itself a multitude of intelligibles, it cannot be placed in the first triad. For "one being" is there, and not a multitude of beings. But if it possesses a varied life, which the *meadow* demonstrates, it is inferior to the second triad. For intelligible life is one and without separation. And because it shines with divided forms, all-various orders, and prolific powers, it is inferior to the third or all-perfect triad. But after the super-celestial place and Heaven itself, the sub-celestial arch is situated, which, as is evident to everyone, is placed under, and not *in*, the Heavens: for it is not called by Plato a *celestial*, but a *sub-celestial* arch. For the intellectual summit separates itself from the celestial kingdom; but the boundary of the intelligible and intellectual Gods is joined to, and in every way surrounded by, this kingdom. And this summit establishes the whole of intellect and the intellectual multitude, and (as Socrates says) the blessed transitions of the Gods. But the boundary alone limits the celestial series and provides the Gods with an ascent to Heaven. For when the Gods ascend to the banquet and delicious food, and to the fullness of intelligible good, they then proceed upward to the sub-celestial arch, and through this to the celestial revolution. 

Hence, if you assert that the sub-celestial arch perfects the Gods and turns them toward the whole of heaven and to the super-celestial place, you will not wander from the concepts of Plato. For the Gods are nourished with the intelligible—with the "meadow" and the divine forms which the super-celestial place contains. But they are replenished with this nourishment through the sub-celestial arch: for through this they participate in the celestial revolution. They revolve, therefore, through the sub-celestial arch; but they receive a vigorous intelligence from the celestial order, and they are replenished with intelligible goods from the super-celestial place. The first place is allotted to an intelligible summit <note>original: "intelligible summit," referring to the highest point of the divine hierarchy accessible to the mind</note>; the celestial revolution occupies the middle extent, and the subcelestial arch possesses the intelligible extremity. For all things are contained within this. Indeed, the intellect is endowed with a convertive power <note>the power to turn back toward its source</note>, but the intelligible is the object of desire. Divine intelligence fills up the middle; it perfects the conversions of divine natures and joins them with those that are first, while also making the desires for intelligible things apparent and replenishing secondary natures with preceding goods. And thus, I think we have sufficiently treated the order of these three.

Perhaps, however, someone may inquire why we characterize the whole progression of the "intelligible and at the same time intellectual" Gods according to this medium. Why do we call one of the extremes "supercelestial" and the other "subcelestial" based on their relationship to the middle? Why do we demonstrate that one has an exempt transcendency, while the other has a proximate and conjoined foundation <note>original: "hypobasis," meaning the underlying basis or lower stage of existence</note>? 

To this, we shall briefly answer that this entire genus of the intelligible and intellectual Gods connects both these extremes. To some things, it is the cause of conversion; to others, it is the cause of an unfolding into light and a presence extended to secondary natures. Therefore, just as we call all the intelligible Gods "paternal" and "unical" <note>original: "unical," meaning characterized by oneness or unity</note>—characterizing them from the summit and asserting that they are the boundaries of wholes, the fabricators of essence, the causes of perpetuity, and the authors of the production of form—in the same manner, we show that these middle Gods are the leaders of the bonds of wholes because of the medium they contain. 

For this entire middle order is life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note>, connective, and perfective. Its summit unfolds the impressions of the intelligibles and their ineffable union. Its termination converts the intellectual Gods and joins them with the intelligibles. Its middle leads this order as if toward a center and establishes the total genera of the Gods. For, through a tendency toward the middle, we also attribute to the extremes a relationship of transcendency and subjection, naming one "above" and the other "beneath" the middle.

Let us now consider the negations by which Plato celebrates this middle order of Gods. Those sacred genera—the connective, the perfective, and the paternal—belonging to those divine natures properly called "intellectual," are established immediately after the intelligible summit of all intellectuals. For this summit,

Being exempt from these, it also transcends all the intellectual Gods. For whatever every genus of Gods is to *the one*, those three orders following it are to this summit. Plato, therefore, names the celestial order—which connects wholes and illuminates them with intelligible light—*colour*; because the visible beauty of the heavens shines with all-various colours and light. Hence, he calls *that* Heaven "intellectual colour and light." For the light proceeding from *the good* <note>The "Good" refers to the ultimate principle or the One in Neoplatonism.</note> is, in the order above this one, unknown and hidden, dwelling in the inner sanctuaries <note>original: "adyta"</note> of the Gods; but it is revealed in this order, and from being hidden becomes visible. On this account, it is compared to colour, which is the offspring of light. Furthermore, if Heaven is "sight looking to things on high," according to the definition of Socrates in the *Cratylus*, then its intelligible aspect is very properly called colour, which is joined with sight.

The cause, therefore, of the intelligibles in *Heaven* is *without colour* and is exempt from them. For sensible colour is the offspring of the solar light. But the sub-celestial arch, which exists immediately after the celestial order, is called by Plato *figure*: for the "arch" itself is the name of a geometric figure. In this order, Parmenides also places intellectual figure; but he first attributes *contact* to the summit of the intellectuals, as is evident from the conclusions of the *Parmenides*. For, in the first hypothesis, when taking away *figure* from *the one*, he uses this as a middle point: that *the one* does not *touch* itself. *Contact*, therefore, first exists here, and exists here according to its cause. For of such things as the demiurge <note>The "demiurgus" or demiurge is the divine artisan or creator of the material world.</note> is the immediate cause, the father prior to him is the paradigmatic <note>The "paradigm" is the eternal blueprint or model.</note> cause. Hence, *contact* here is the paradigm of the liberated Gods. These three orders, therefore, are successive: namely, *colour*, *figure*, and *contact*. And the supercelestial place is essentially exempt from these. Hence, it is *without colour*, *without figure*, and *without contact*.

In the next place, let us consider the triad which is celebrated by Socrates as existing beforehand in the supercelestial place: namely, *the plain of truth*, *the meadow*, and *the nourishment <note>original: "aliment"</note> of the Gods*. *The plain of truth*, therefore, is intellectually expanded toward intelligible light and is illuminated with the splendours that proceed from there. But *the meadow* is the fertile power of life and of all-various reasons <note>original: "reasons" (logoi), referring to the formative principles or rational structures of reality.</note>; it is the gathering of the primary causes of life and the cause of the variety and the procreation of forms. For meadows in this sensible world are fertile with forms and productive powers, and

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "contain" indicates the start of the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page provides a Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato's Phaedrus, explaining why the supercelestial realm is described as being without colour, figure, or contact, and introducing the symbolic "plain of truth" and "meadow." It links these concepts to the hierarchy of the Gods and the progression from hidden divine light to visible form.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Phaedrus, Neoplatonism, Supercelestial Place, Plain of Truth, Meadow of Life, Intellectual Gods, Demiurge, Parmenides, Metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 1945 ---
<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Plato's Phaedrus, specifically interpreting the allegorical nourishment of the soul and the gods.</meta>

# ADDITIONAL NOTES ON THE PHÆDRUS.

The vessels contain water, which is a symbol of life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> energy. However, the nourishing cause of the Gods is a certain intellectual <note>original: "intelligible"</note> union. This union contains within itself the entire perfection of the Gods, filling them with vigor and power so that they may provide for lower <note>original: "secondary"</note> beings while maintaining an unchanging understanding of the highest principles. 

The Gods participate in these qualities in a unified way in the higher realms, but they experience them with more distinction as they descend through their various levels of being. Plato calls one kind of this spiritual food "ambrosia" and the other "nectar." Here, we may also observe that the charioteer <note>In Plato's allegory, the charioteer represents the rational part of the soul.</note>, who is nourished by intellectual realities, participates in the perfection shining from the Gods in a single, unified way <note>original: "unically"</note>. The horses <note>The horses represent the spirited and appetitive parts of the soul.</note>, however, participate in it separately: first through ambrosia, and afterwards through nectar. 

It is necessary for the horses to remain firmly and immovably fixed in the higher natures by means of ambrosia, but they must also provide for lower beings without changing their own essence through the power of nectar. This is because the ancients say that ambrosia is a solid food, while nectar is a liquid. Therefore, the nourishment of nectar signifies a form of divine providence that is unrestrained, unbreakable, and which reaches out to all things with perfect purity. On the other hand, the nourishment of ambrosia signifies that which is permanent and firmly established in the higher realms. 

From both of these, it is implied that the Gods are permanent while simultaneously reaching out to all things. Neither their steady energy—which does not turn toward lower things—is unproductive, nor is their productive power and progression lacking in stability. Instead, while remaining permanent, they move forward; and while being established in the highest natures, they provide for lower things with absolute purity.

->THE END OF THE THIRD VOLUME.<-

<summary>This page provides a Neoplatonic interpretation of the allegory of ambrosia and nectar in Plato's Phaedrus, explaining how the Gods maintain stability while providing for the material world.</summary>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>ON THE NATURE AND CONSTITUTION [OF LOGIC]</header>

# QUESTION II.
## Concerning the Subject of Logic.

In this question we will do three things: 1. We will expel extraneous matters. 2. We will establish the true subject. 3. We will explain certain things pertaining to it.

## ARTICLE I.
### Is the subject of Logic a "Being of Reason"? <note>original: "Ens rationis"; a concept that exists only in the mind, such as a fictional creature or a mathematical abstraction.</note>

<margin>Suarez, Metaphysical Disputations 54, section 1, number 5; and On the Soul, book 2, chapter 2, numbers 14, 15, and following.</margin>
I. CONCLUSION. A "being of reason" is not the subject of Logic. This is proven, first: Because a being of reason, as it is distinguished from other beings, is that which has no existence in reality, but only in the intellect. However, Logic does not deal with such a being; for it deals with definitions, propositions, and syllogisms, which are real beings—namely, spoken or written speech. Therefore, [it is not a being of reason].

It is proven, second: The subject of any science ought to be more noble than the science itself, because the whole science exists for the sake of the subject. However, Logic, which is a real habit <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition or quality of the mind</note>, is more noble than a being of reason. Therefore, [it is not the subject].

It is proven, third: The subject of a science must have real properties <note>original: "passiones"; attributes or characteristics</note> which are demonstrated concerning it. However, a being of reason does not have such properties. Therefore, [it is not the subject].

<margin>Smiglecius, Disputation 1, question 2, article 2.</margin>
II. CONCLUSION. The subject of Logic is not merely "second intentions." <note>original: "secundae intentiones"; abstract logical categories like "genus" or "species" applied to our first concepts of things.</note> This is proven, first: Because Logic deals with definitions, propositions, and syllogisms, which are "first intentions"—namely, real entities. Therefore, [it is not merely second intentions].

It is proven, second: Because second intentions are beings of reason, which Logic does not deal with for their own sake <note>original: "per se"</note>, but only incidentally <note>original: "per accidens"</note>, insofar as they serve the direction of the intellect. Therefore, [they are not the primary subject].

## ARTICLE II.
### What is the true subject of Logic?

<margin>Fonseca, Institutes, book 1, chapter 1; Coimbrans, question 1, preface, article 4.</margin>
III. CONCLUSION. The subject of Logic is **Reason**, insofar as it is directed in its operation. This is proven, first: Because Logic is the art of directing the act of reason; and the subject of an art is that which is directed by the art. Therefore, [it is Reason].

It is proven, second: Because everything Logic deals with refers to the direction of reason. For the definition directs the first operation [of the mind]; the proposition directs the second; and the syllogism directs the third. Therefore, [it is Reason].

<margin>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, part 1, question 1, article 7.</margin>
In this conclusion, by <term>Reason</term> we mean the reasoning power, not merely as an accidental quality of the soul, but as the principle of intellectual operations. By <term>Operation</term> we mean the three acts of the intellect: namely, apprehension, judgment, and discourse <note>original: "discursus"; the process of reasoning from one premise to another.</note>.

<summary>This page argues that the true subject of Logic is the human faculty of Reason as it performs its three operations (apprehension, judgment, and discourse), rather than abstract mental constructs or "beings of reason."</summary>
<keywords>Logic, subject matter, Being of Reason, second intentions, first intentions, Reason, operations of the intellect, apprehension, judgment, discourse, Suarez, Smiglecius, Fonseca, Thomas Aquinas</keywords>

# INTRODUCTION
### TO
## THE THEÆTETUS.

---

**T**he following very learned and admirable dialogue is on a subject which, to a rational being, is obviously of the utmost importance. For what can be more important to such a being than an accurate knowledge of things human and divine, practical and theoretical? And as such a knowledge cannot be obtained without science <note>original: "science"; here meaning "episteme" or certain, demonstrative knowledge</note>, the inquiry into what science is must consequently rank among those investigations that are the most useful and necessary to man.

As this dialogue is wholly of the maieutic <note>original: "maieutic"; referring to the Socratic method of "midwifery," or bringing ideas to birth through questioning</note> kind, Socrates, with admirable skill, acts the part of a midwife toward Theaetetus, one of the principal persons of the dialogue, in leading forth his conceptions concerning science into light. For this purpose, he, in the first place, asks him what science is. Theaetetus replies that science is geometry and arithmetic, together with other disciplines of this kind and the several arts. This answer is, however, rejected by Socrates, as by no means agreeing with the question; because, when asked what science is, he replies by enumerating how many sciences there are and on what subjects they are employed. 

In the next place, Socrates introduces the definition of Protagoras: that science is sense <note>original: "sense"; meaning sensory perception</note>. For Protagoras asserted that man is the measure of all things, and that everything was to every man exactly as it appeared to him. This doctrine was, indeed, founded in the philosophy of Heraclitus, of which the principal dogma was this: that nothing is permanent, but that all things are in a continual flux. Socrates, however, refutes this opinion because, if it were admitted, the perceptions of the intoxicated and insane, of those who dream, and of those whose senses are corrupted by disease, would be true simply because they appear to be so, though at the same time they are evidently false. From this—

<summary>This introduction establishes the Theaetetus as a dialogue seeking the definition of knowledge, beginning with Socrates' rejection of definitions based on specific disciplines or sensory perception.</summary>
<keywords>Theaetetus, Socrates, Protagoras, Heraclitus, maieutic method, epistemology, science, sensory perception, flux</keywords>

--- Page 1953 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument against the Protagorean idea that "man is the measure of all things," specifically addressing the distinction between sensory perception and true knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

hypothesis also, all men would be similarly wise, the opinions of the most illiterate in geometry would be as true as any geometrical theorems; and in the actions of human life the means of accomplishing any end would be indifferent <note>original: "indifferent"; meaning it would not matter which method one chose</note>, and consequently all deliberation and consultation would be vain¹.

In order to demonstrate that science <note>original: "science"; here meaning "episteme" or certain, demonstratable knowledge</note> is not the same as sense perception, Socrates, in the first place, obtains this admission from Theaetetus: that sense arises from the soul perceiving physical things situated outside itself through several organs of the body. And secondly, that one sense, or organ-based perception, cannot take notice of the object of another; for example, sight cannot see sounds, nor can hearing hear light and colors. Hence he infers that when we compare the objects of several senses together and consider certain things which are common to them all, this cannot be sense or organ-based perception, because one sense cannot consider the object of another. 

If there is anything common to both, the soul cannot perceive it by either organ. Thus, for instance, when we consider sound and color together and attribute several things to them in common—such as, in the first place, essence <note>the fundamental nature of a thing</note>, and in the next place, sameness in each with itself, and difference from the other; when we also consider that both of them are two, and each of them one—by what sense or organ does the soul perceive all these things which are common both to sound and color? It cannot be by the senses of sight or hearing, because these cannot consider each other’s objects; nor can any other bodily organ be found by which the soul may passively perceive all these and consider the objects of both those senses of sight and hearing. Hence, Theaetetus is led to confess that the soul does not perceive these things through the organs of any sense, but by itself alone without any bodily organ.

Theaetetus, therefore, being convinced that science is not sense perception, in the next place defines it to be "true opinion." This, however, is refuted by Socrates, because rhetoric also produces true opinion when its assertions are true, and yet rhetoric cannot produce science. For there never can be any science of—

---

<note>¹ This absurd opinion is very subtly opposed by Sextus Empiricus. If, he says, every imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; meaning an appearance or mental impression</note> is true, then the imagination that "not every imagination is true" will also be true, and so the assertion that "every imagination is true" will be false. <note>original Greek: Ει πασα φαντασια εστιν αληθης, και το μη πασαν φαντασιαν ειναι αληθη, κατα φαντασιαν ὑφισταμενον εσται αληθες· και ουτω το πασαν φαντασιαν ειναι αληθη γενησεται ψευδος.</note></note>

<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, Sextus Empiricus, epistemology, sense perception, true opinion, rhetoric, essence, sameness, difference, logic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical analysis of the nature of knowledge, specifically critiquing definitions of science provided by Theætetus and his contemporaries.</meta>

# THE THEÆTETUS

things which are perpetually in motion, and which exist differently at different times. Such, however, are human affairs with which orators are familiar, especially when they persuade their hearers to believe things about which they themselves are doubtful. After this, Theætetus adds the definition of Leucippus and Theodorus the Cyrenæan, that science <note>original: "scientia"; here meaning certain knowledge or systematic understanding</note> is true opinion in conjunction with reason; and therefore, that things which possess reason can be known, but by no means those which are deprived of it. This, however, is also refuted by Socrates, who shows that whether reason (*logos*) signifies external speech, or a progression through the elements of a thing, or a formal definition, science cannot simply be true opinion in conjunction with reason.

Though Socrates, therefore, refutes all these definitions of science as being erroneous, he does not inform us what science actually is. This would have been contrary to the character of the dialogue, which, as we have already observed, is entirely maieutic <note>original: "maieutic"; referring to the Socratic method of "midwifery," where the teacher helps the student give birth to their own ideas rather than providing answers</note>, and consequently can do no more than present us with the conceptions of Theætetus fairly unfolded into the light. As all these conceptions are found to be false, we must search elsewhere for an accurate definition of science.

What then shall we say science is, according to Plato? We reply that, considered according to its first existence, which is in the intellect, it is the *eternal and uniform intelligence of eternal entities*; but in partial souls, such as ours, it is a *dianoëtic perception* <note>original: "dianoëtic"; relating to the power of discursive reasoning or the step-by-step process of the mind</note> *of eternal beings*. It is, consequently, a perception that is neither eternal nor uniform, because it is transitive <note>original: "transitive"; moving from one thought to another rather than seeing all at once</note> and accompanied by the intervention of oblivion <note>original: "oblivion"; the state of forgetting or being unaware of the higher truths the soul once knew</note>.

<summary>This page concludes Socrates' refutation of Theætetus's definitions of science, explaining that the dialogue's purpose is "midwifery" rather than providing direct answers. It offers a Platonic definition of science as the intellect's perception of eternal truths, which in humans is limited by discursive reasoning and forgetfulness.</summary>

<keywords>Theætetus, Socrates, Plato, Leucippus, Theodorus the Cyrenæan, maieutic method, logos, dianoëtic perception, epistemology, nature of science</keywords>

# THE THEAETETUS

## PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE

->EUCLID <note>original: Euclid of Megara</note>, || SOCRATES,<-
->TERPSIO, || THEODORUS,<-
->And THEAETETUS.<-

---

**EUCLID.** Have you just now arrived, Terpsio, or has it been some time since you came from the country?
**TERPSIO.** I left the country a considerable time ago. I have been looking for you around the forum <note>The public marketplace and center of civic life</note> and wondered why I could not find you.
**EUCLID.** I was not in the city.
**TERPSIO.** Where were you then?
**EUCLID.** As I was going down to the harbor, I met Theaetetus, who was being carried from the military camp at Corinth to Athens.
**TERPSIO.** Was he alive or dead?
**EUCLID.** He was living, but could hardly be said to be so; he was in a very dangerous condition because of certain wounds. What is worse, he was afflicted with a disease while in the camp.
**TERPSIO.** Was it dysentery?
**EUCLID.** It was.

<note>1. This Euclid was a celebrated philosopher and logician of Megara. The Athenians having prohibited the Megarians from entering their city on pain of death, this philosopher disguised himself in woman’s clothes so that he might attend the lectures of Socrates. After the death of Socrates, Plato and other philosophers went to Euclid at Megara to shelter themselves from the tyrants who governed Athens.</note>
<note>2. This Theaetetus is mentioned by Proclus in his commentary on Euclid (Book 2, page 19), where he gives a short history of geometry prior to Euclid. Theaetetus is ranked by him among those contemporary with Plato who increased the number of geometrical theorems and made them more scientific.</note>

<summary>This introductory scene features a meeting between Euclid and Terpsio, where Euclid describes encountering a wounded and ill Theaetetus returning from war, setting the stage for the dialogue's narration.</summary>
<keywords>Theaetetus, Euclid of Megara, Terpsio, Socrates, Athens, Corinth, geometry, Platonic dialogue, Peloponnesian War context</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory dialogue between Terpsio and Euclid regarding the health of Theætetus and the origins of the recorded conversation with Socrates.</meta>

# THE THEÆTETUS

**TERPSIO.** What a man you speak of as being in such a dangerous condition!

**EUCLID.** A worthy and good man, O Terpsio; for I just now heard certain persons paying him very great honors <note>original: "encomiums"</note> for his conduct in the military.

**TERPSIO.** That is not surprising; indeed, it would be much more surprising if that had not been the case. But why was he not carried here to Megara?

**EUCLID.** He hastened home; for I both entreated and advised him to do so, though it was against his will. And besides this, while attending him on his journey, after I left him, I recollected and was filled with admiration for Socrates. Socrates often spoke prophetically about many things, and he did so regarding this man. For a little before his death, if I am not mistaken, he met with Theætetus, who was then a young man. After conversing with him, Socrates very much admired his character. Furthermore, when I came to Athens, Socrates related to me his discussions with Theætetus, which are very much worth hearing; he observed that Theætetus would necessarily become famous if he lived to adulthood. And it appears indeed that Socrates spoke the truth.

**TERPSIO.** But can you relate what those discussions were?

**EUCLID.** Not word-for-word, by Zeus <note>original: "by Jupiter"</note>; but as soon as I returned home, I committed the substance of them to writing. Afterwards, at my leisure, I wrote down nearly the whole of them by memory. Whenever I went to Athens, I asked Socrates about the specific details that I could not remember, and upon my return here, I made the necessary corrections; in this way, I have written down nearly the entire discourse.

**TERPSIO.** True. I have heard you say this before, and I have come here today specifically because I have been wanting to urge you to relate this discourse. What should hinder us from doing so now? I am in great need of rest, as I have just come in from the country.

**EUCLID.** I also accompanied Theætetus as far as Erineus <note>A village located between Megara and Athens.</note>; so rest will be pleasant to me as well. Let us go, therefore, and while we rest, a servant boy shall read to us.

**TERPSIO.** That sounds like a good plan.

**EUCLID.** This then is the book, O Terpsio. But I did not compose it as if Socrates were telling the story to me—though in reality he did—but rather as if he were speaking directly with the people he mentioned. He said these people were the mathematician <note>original: "geometrician"</note> Theodorus and Theætetus. That...

<summary>Euclid explains to Terpsio how he painstakingly recorded Socrates' past conversation with the brilliant young Theætetus, and the two men prepare to have the manuscript read aloud.</summary>
<keywords>Theætetus, Euclid, Terpsio, Socrates, Megara, Athens, memory, manuscript, Theodorus, geometry</keywords>

--- Page 1957 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory dialogue between Euclid and Terpsion, transitioning into the reading of the written account of Socrates' conversation with Theaetetus.</meta>

# THE THEAETETUS

So that we may not, therefore, be troubled during the reading with the frequent repetition of "I said," "He said," "He agreed," or "He denied," I have written the dialogue as if Socrates himself were speaking directly with them.

**TERPSION.** And that is not at all improper, Euclid.

**EUCLID.** Here, boy, take the book then and read.

**SOCRATES.** If, Theodorus, I cared more for those in Cyrene <note>A Greek colony in North Africa, the home of Theodorus.</note> than for anyone else, I would ask you about the people there—whether any young men have applied themselves to geometry or any other philosophical study. But as it is, I care less for them than for our own people, and I am more eager to know which of our young men are likely to become men of merit. I look out for such youths myself as much as I can, and I ask about them from others with whom I see the young men associating. You, certainly, have no small number of followers, and rightly so; for you deserve to be followed both for your general character and for your knowledge of geometry. If, therefore, you have met with any young man worth mentioning, I would be pleased to hear the details about him.

**THEODORUS.** Indeed, Socrates, it is entirely appropriate both that I should tell you, and that you should hear, what a remarkable youth I have met among your fellow citizens. If he were beautiful, I would be very afraid to mention him, lest I should seem to be in love with him. But as it is—and do not be offended with me—he is not handsome. In fact, he resembles you, having a flat nose and protruding eyes, though he has these features to a lesser degree than you do. You see, I speak freely to you. Know then, that of all the many young men I have worked with, I have never yet met one who possesses such a wonderfully good natural disposition. It is difficult to find someone who is so quick to learn <note>original: "docile"</note>, remarkably mild-tempered, and who also possesses a courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note> equal to anyone. Truly, I did not think such a person existed, nor do I see others with these combined qualities. For those who are sharp-witted, like this boy, and possess good memories, are for the most part also quick to anger; they are swept away impulsively like ships without ballast, being naturally frantic rather than brave. On the other hand, those who are more composed in their manners are often sluggish and forgetful when they apply themselves to their studies <note>original: "disciplines"</note>. But this young man approaches his studies and investigations in such an easy, steady, and effective manner, that it can be compared to the silent flow <note>original: "flux"</note>

**Theaetetus:** We should consider that.

**Socrates:** If we found that to be the case, should we not be persuaded by him? But if he were ignorant of music, should we not disbelieve him?

**Theaetetus:** True.

**Socrates:** Now, therefore, I think if we care at all about the similarity of our faces, we should consider whether he speaks as a painter or not.

**Theaetetus:** So it seems to me.

**Socrates:** Is Theodorus a painter, then?

**Theaetetus:** Not that I know of.

**Socrates:** But is he a geometrician <term>geometrician</term><note>A mathematician specializing in geometry; in Plato's time, this was considered a fundamental branch of philosophy.</note>?

**Theaetetus:** He is perfectly so, Socrates.

# THE THEÆTETUS

**Socrates:** Is he also skilled in astronomy, logic <note>original: "logistic"; the art of calculation or mathematical reasoning</note>, music, and the other disciplines that follow these?

**Theætetus:** He appears to be so to me.

**Socrates:** If, therefore, he says that we resemble each other in a certain part of our body, while at the same time praising or blaming this resemblance, it is not particularly worth our while to pay much attention to him.

**Theætetus:** Entirely so, Socrates.

**Socrates:** Take notice, therefore, my friend Theætetus; it is your business to demonstrate your character, and mine to observe it. For you should know that although Theodorus has praised many strangers and citizens in my hearing, he has never praised any one of them as much as he just now praised you.

**Theætetus:** That is good to hear, Socrates; but consider whether he might have been speaking jokingly.

**Socrates:** It is not usual for Theodorus to do so. Do not reject what has been granted by believing he spoke in jest, lest he should be compelled to testify to his words. For no one can object to what he said. Persist, therefore, confidently in what has been admitted.

**Theætetus:** It is proper, indeed, to do so, if it seems right to you.

**Socrates:** Tell me, then—do you learn geometry from Theodorus?

**Theætetus:** I do.

**Socrates:** Do you, likewise, learn things pertaining to astronomy, harmony, and mathematical calculation?

**Theætetus:** I endeavor to do so.

**Socrates:** For I also, my boy, endeavor to learn these things both from this man and from others who appear to me to understand anything of these subjects; but, at the same time, I am only moderately skilled in them. There is, however, a certain trifling thing about which I am in doubt, and which I wish to consider along with you and those who are present. Tell me, therefore: is learning not the process of becoming wiser in that which one learns?

**Theætetus:** Undoubtedly.

**Socrates:** And I think that the wise are wise because of their wisdom.

**Theætetus:** Certainly.

**Socrates:** But does "wisdom" differ in any respect from "science" <note>original: "science"; here used in the classical sense of *episteme* or certain, organized knowledge</note>?

**Theætetus:** In what way?

# THE THEÆTETUS

**SOCRATES:** Wisdom. Or are not those who have a scientific knowledge of anything also wise in that thing?

**THEÆTETUS:** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES:** Is, therefore, science <note>original: "science"; here meaning "episteme" or systematic knowledge</note> the same as wisdom?

**THEÆTETUS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** This, therefore, is what I am uncertain about; I am not able to sufficiently determine by myself what science is. Do we have anything to say to this? What do you say it is? And which of us can first give this information? He who errs, and is perpetually detected in an error, shall "sit as an ass," as the boys say when they play at ball. But he who is found to speak without error shall be our king, and shall order whatever he wishes us to answer. Why are you silent? Have I, O Theodorus, behaved in a rude <note>original: "rustic"</note> manner because of my love of conversation, and through my desire to make you discourse and become friends with each other?

**THEODORUS:** A thing of this kind, O Socrates, is by no means rude. But order one of these young men to answer you. For I am unaccustomed to this mode of discourse, and my age does not permit me to become accustomed to it now. But a thing of this kind is suited to these young men, and they will be greatly improved by it. For, in reality, youth is suited to every kind of improvement. But, as you began with him, do not dismiss Theætetus, but question him.

**SOCRATES:** Do you hear, Theætetus, what Theodorus says? I am of the opinion you will not disobey him. For you would neither be willing to do so, nor is it lawful for a young man to be unpersuaded by a wise man when he commands in things of this kind. Tell me, therefore, in a proper and candid <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> manner, what does science appear to you to be?

**THEÆTETUS:** It is right to comply, Socrates, since you command me. And if I err in any respect, you must correct me.

**SOCRATES:** We shall by all means do so, if we are able.

**THEÆTETUS:** It appears to me, then, that sciences are such things as anyone may learn from Theodorus, such as geometry and the other subjects which you just now listed. And besides these, the shoemaker’s art and the arts of other craftsmen; and that all and each of these are nothing other than science.

**SOCRATES:** Generously and bountifully, O friend, when asked by me concern—

# THE THEAETETUS

<margin>To define knowledge by naming specific arts is a mistake.</margin>
Knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> is, gives for an answer the name of any art. For he answers that there is a knowledge of a certain thing, when this is not what he was asked.

**THEAETETUS.** It seems so.

**SOCRATES.** And, in the next place, when he might have given a short and simple answer, he wanders immensely. As in the question concerning clay, a short and simple answer might have been given: that clay is earth mingled with moisture. At the same time, he should dismiss the consideration of all the different things that can be made of clay.

**THEAETETUS.** Now, indeed, Socrates, it appears easy to me. For you seem to ask about something that lately came into my mind as I was talking with your namesake here, Socrates <note>Referring to "Young Socrates," a student present at the dialogue</note>.

**SOCRATES.** What was that, Theaetetus?

**THEAETETUS.** Theodorus here has written a treatise on powers <note>In this context, "powers" refers to square roots</note>, concerning magnitudes of three and five feet. He demonstrated that they are not commensurable in length <note>original: "commensurable in length" — meaning they cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers; they are irrational numbers</note> to a magnitude of one foot. He proceeded through every number in this way as far as a magnitude of seventeen feet, and there he stopped his investigation. A thought occurred to me: since there appear to be an infinite multitude of these powers, we should endeavor to group them under one term, by which we may name all these powers.

**SOCRATES.** And was such a thing discovered?

**THEAETETUS.** It appears so to me. But you should also consider it.

**SOCRATES.** Speak then.

**THEAETETUS.** We divide all numbers into two types. One type is the number that can result from multiplying a number by itself <note>original: "equally equal"</note>; we compare this to a square figure and call it quadrangular and equilateral <note>These are square numbers like 4, 9, and 16</note>.

**SOCRATES.** And very properly so.

**THEAETETUS.** But those numbers which fall between these <note>Square numbers are 4, 9, 16, 25, etc. The numbers between them, which Plato calls "oblong," are 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, etc.</note>—such as three and five, and every number which cannot be formed by multiplying a number by itself <note>original: "evenly even"</note>, but is instead formed by a greater number multiplied by a lesser, or a lesser by a greater, and always has a longer and a shorter side—we compare to an oblong figure and call it an oblong number.

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus discuss how to provide a concise definition rather than a list of examples, using Theaetetus's mathematical discovery regarding square roots and "oblong numbers" as an analogy for finding a universal definition.</summary>

# THE THEAETETUS

**Socrates:** Most excellent. But what follows?

**Theaetetus:** Such lines as square an equilateral and plane number <note>original: "equilateral and plane number," referring to a square number like 4, 9, or 16</note>, we define to be **length**; but such as square an oblong number <note>original: "oblong number," a non-square number like 3, 5, or 6</note>, we define as **powers**. This is because they are not commensurate¹ in length to the others, but only to the planes <note>the areas</note> which are capable of being commensurable. And regarding solids, there is another similar classification.

**Socrates:** Best of men, my boys! It appears to me that Theodorus cannot be accused of giving a false account of your abilities.

**Theaetetus:** But indeed, Socrates, I am not able to answer you concerning **science** <note>original: "science," here meaning *episteme* or certain knowledge</note> as I am concerning length and power; though you appear to me to be inquiring after something of that kind. So, in that respect, Theodorus appears to be proven false again.

**Socrates:** But what of it? If he praised you for running and said he never met a youth who ran so swiftly, and afterwards you were defeated in a race by an adult who is a very rapid runner, do you think he would have praised you any less truly?

**Theaetetus:** I do not.

**Socrates:** And with respect to science—as I just said—do you think it is a trifling thing to find out what it is? Is it not, in every respect, an arduous task?

**Theaetetus:** By Jupiter, I think it is arduous in the extreme.

**Socrates:** Have confidence in yourself, then, and value what Theodorus said. Endeavor, by all possible means, to obtain a definition of other things and likewise of science, so as to know what it truly is.

**Theaetetus:** It appears we should do so, Socrates, for the sake of our own eagerness.

**Socrates:** Come then; for you explained the mathematical point just now in a beautiful manner. Endeavor to imitate your answer regarding "powers." Just as you comprehended those many different roots into one single species, try to comprehend the many different sciences into one single reason or definition.

**Theaetetus:** But know, Socrates, that I have often endeavored to accomplish this after hearing the questions you discuss. However, I can neither persuade myself that I can say anything sufficient on this occasion, nor have I heard anyone else discourse on it in the way you advise. And yet, I am unable to stop investigating it.

# THE THEÆTETUS

**Socrates:** You are tormented with the pangs of labor, friend Theætetus, not because you are empty, but because you are full.

**Theætetus:** I do not know, Socrates; but I am telling you what I am suffering.

**Socrates:** O ridiculous youth, have you not heard that I am the son of the generous, and at the same time severe, midwife Phænarete?

**Theætetus:** I have heard this.

**Socrates:** And have you also heard that I study the same art?

**Theætetus:** By no means.

**Socrates:** Know, however, that it is so; but do not betray me to others. For they are ignorant, my friend, that I possess this art; and because they are ignorant of this, they do not claim this regarding me. Instead, they say that I am a most absurd man, and that I cause men to doubt. Or have you not heard this?

**Theætetus:** I have.

**Socrates:** Shall I tell you the reason for this?

**Theætetus:** By all means.

**Socrates:** Consider everything pertaining to <term>midwives</term> <note>original: "midwives" — Socrates is introducing his famous "maieutic" method, comparing the delivery of ideas to the delivery of children.</note>, and you will easily understand what I mean. For you know that none of them deliver others while they themselves are still conceiving and bringing forth children, but only when they are no longer capable of conceiving.

**Theætetus:** Entirely so.

**Socrates:** But they say that Diana <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis, the virgin goddess of the hunt and childbirth.</note> is the cause of this; who, being herself a virgin, takes care of births. She does not, therefore, permit those who are barren to be <term>midwives</term>, because human nature is too weak <note>original: "imbecil"</note> to undertake an art in which it is inexperienced. Instead, she orders those to exercise this profession who, because of their age, are incapable of bearing children, thereby honoring their resemblance to herself.

**Theætetus:** It is likely.

**Socrates:** And is it not also probable and necessary that those who are pregnant, or not, should be better known by <term>midwives</term> than by others?

**Theætetus:** Entirely so.

**Socrates:** <term>Midwives</term>, likewise, by medicines and enchantments, are able to excite and alleviate the pangs of <term>parturition</term> <note>The act of giving birth.</note>, to deliver those who bring forth with difficulty, and to procure a <term>miscarriage</term> when the child appears to be abortive.

<summary>Socrates reveals to Theætetus that he practices a form of intellectual midwifery, inherited from his mother, which allows him to help others "give birth" to their ideas. He explains the divine precedent for this art through the goddess Diana, noting that midwives must have experience in childbirth but be past the age of bearing children themselves.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Theætetus, Phænarete, Diana, midwifery, maieutics, intellectual labor, childbirth metaphor</keywords>

**THEAETETUS.** That is true.

**SOCRATES.** But you should know that they pride themselves on this more than on cutting the umbilical cord. For do you think it belongs to the same art, or a different one, to tend to and harvest the fruits of the earth, and to know in what ground a specific plant or seed ought to be sown?

**THEAETETUS.** It is not likely that it does.

**SOCRATES.** It is not. But because of the unjust and ridiculous joining of men and women, which is called pandering <note>original: "bawdry"</note>, midwives—who are honorable women—avoid acting as matchmakers. They fear that by doing so they might be labeled as madams <note>original: "bawds"</note>, even though it is the proper role of legitimate midwives to arrange marriages correctly.

**THEAETETUS.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** Such, then, is the office of midwives; but it is less difficult than the part I have to play. For it does not happen to women that they sometimes give birth to illusions <note>original: "images"</note> and sometimes to realities. If it did, it would not be easy to tell them apart. If it were possible, distinguishing what was true from what was false would be the greatest and most beautiful of all tasks for a midwife. Or do you not think so?

**THEAETETUS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Now, my art includes all the other functions of midwifery, but it differs in this: it delivers men and not women, and it looks after their souls in labor <note>original: "parturient"</note>, not their bodies. # THE THEÆTETUS.

An answer to anything is truly objected against me, owing to my possessing nothing of wisdom. But the cause of this is as follows: Divinity <note>original: "the god" or "the divine power"</note> compels me to act as a midwife, but forbids me to generate. I am not, therefore, myself in any respect wise; nor is there any invention of mine of such a kind as to be the offspring of my soul. 

But of those who converse with me, some at first appear to be entirely void of discipline <note>original: "unlearned" or "ignorant"</note>, but all to whom Divinity is propitious, during the course of the conversation, make a wonderful proficiency, as is evident both to themselves and others. This likewise is clear: that they do not learn anything from me, but that they possess and discover many beautiful things in themselves—Divinity indeed, and I, being the cause of the midwife's office. 

But this is evident from hence: Many, in consequence of not knowing this, but believing themselves to be the cause, and despising me (perhaps through the persuasions of others), have left me sooner than was proper. After they have left me, through associating with depraved characters, they have become—as to what remains—abortive. Likewise, through badly nourishing what they have brought forth through my assistance, they have destroyed it, in consequence of preferring false things and images to that which is true. Lastly, they have appeared both to themselves and others to be unlearned. 

One of these was Aristides the son of Lysimachus, and many others; who, when they again came to me because they wanted my conversation and were affected in a wonderful manner, some of them my demonic power <note>original: "daimonion"; Socrates' internal guiding spirit or divine sign</note> restrained me from conversing with. But with others he permitted me to converse, who at length made a considerable proficiency. 

For those that associate with me suffer this in common with women in labor; they are tormented, and filled with doubt and anxiety, and this in a far greater degree than those in labor. This torment my art is able both to excite and appease. And such is the manner in which they are affected. 

But sometimes, O Theaetetus, I very kindly unite in marriage with others those who do not appear to me to be pregnant, as I know that they do not require my assistance; and (as I may say in conjunction with Divinity) I very sufficiently conjecture with whom it will be advantageous for them to be united. And many of these indeed I have delivered to Prodicus <note>A famous Greek Sophist and contemporary of Socrates</note>, and many others to wise and divine men. For the sake of this, O most excellent youth, I have been thus long-winded in relating these things to you. For I suspect, as you also think, that you are tormented in consequence—

consequence of being pregnant with something internally. Commit yourself, therefore, to me as being the son of a midwife, and as being myself skilled in what pertains to childbirth <note>original: "parturition"</note>. Endeavour, too, cheerfully to answer me what I shall ask you, and to the best of your ability. And if, in consequence of considering what you say, it shall appear to me that you have conceived a mere image and not that which is true, do not be angry with me—like women who are delivered of their first child—if I privately remove and throw it away. 

For many, O wonderful young man, are so affected towards me that they are actually ready to bite me when I throw aside any trifle of theirs. They do not think that I do this with a benevolent design; since they are very far from knowing that no divinity is malevolent to men, and that I do not perform anything of this kind through malevolence. But it is by no means lawful for me to admit that which is false and destroy that which is true. Again, therefore, from the beginning, O Theaetetus, endeavour to inform me what science <note>In this context, "science" refers to "episteme" or certain, systematic knowledge.</note> is; but by no means endeavour to speak beyond your ability. For if Divinity is willing and affords you strength, you will be able.

**Theaetetus:** Indeed, Socrates, since you thus urge me, it would be base for anyone not to offer what he has to say with the greatest alacrity. It appears then to me that he who has a scientific knowledge of anything perceives that which he thus knows; and, as it now seems, science is nothing else than sense <note>original: "sense" here refers to sensory perception.</note>.

**Socrates:** Well and generously answered, my boy: for it is requisite thus to speak what appears to be the case. But come, let us consider this together, whether this offspring is anything solid or vain. Do you say that science is sense?

**Theaetetus:** I do.

**Socrates:** You appear, indeed, to have given no despicable definition of science, but rather that which Protagoras <gloss>1</gloss> has given; though he has said the same thing in a somewhat different manner. For he says that man is the measure of all things: of beings so far as they have a being, and of non-beings so far as they are not. Have you ever read this?

THEAETETUS. That is very much the case.

THEAETETUS. It is.

Instead, through their movement <note>original: "lation," meaning local motion or change of place</note>, motion, and mixture with each other, all things become what we say they are, though we describe them incorrectly. For there is nothing that ever truly *is*, but everything is always in a state of generation, or *becoming*. In this, all the wise men of the past agree, except for Parmenides <note>Parmenides argued that true reality is changeless and unified; see Plato's dialogues *The Sophist* and *Parmenides*.</note>; namely, Protagoras, Heraclitus, and Empedocles. Among the poets, the leaders of each genre agree: Epicharmus in comedy, and Homer in tragedy. For when Homer calls the Ocean and mother Tethys the origin of the Gods, he is asserting that all things are the offspring of flux and motion. Or does he not seem to be saying this?

THEAETETUS: To me, he does.

SOCRATES: Who then can fight against such an army, led by Homer himself, without looking ridiculous?

THEAETETUS: It is not easy, Socrates.

SOCRATES: It is not indeed, Theaetetus. For this is a sufficient argument in favor of their claim: that motion gives things the appearance of being and of "becoming," while rest gives the appearance of non-being and perishing. For heat and fire, which create and govern other things, are themselves created from movement and friction. And these are forms of motion. Or are these not the origin of fire?

---

<note>The following is a commentary on the nature of the material world:</note>
Material imperfection cannot receive the whole of divine infinity at once; it can only partake of it gradually and partially, as if by drops in a momentary succession. Hence, the material world is in a continual state of flowing and formation, but never possesses real being. It is like the image of a tall tree seen in a rapid stream: it has the appearance of a tree without the reality. It seems to remain the same perpetually, yet it is continually renewed by the constant flow of the water.

Homer calls him the origin of the Gods because he gives birth to their movement into the physical universe. In short, he is the cause of every kind of motion—whether intellectual, mental <note>original: "psychical"</note>, or natural—for all secondary beings. Tethys, however, is the cause of the separation of the streams flowing from the Ocean, ensuring that each natural motion maintains its own purity. See more concerning these deities in the notes on the *Cratylus*.

SOCRATES. I will add further, regarding times of serenity and tranquility and all such states, that rest causes decay and destruction, while motion preserves. For Homer intended by this to signify nothing other than the sun; because, as long as the sun and its orbit are in motion, all things—both among the Gods and men—will exist and be preserved. But if the sun should stand still, as if it were bound, all things would be dissolved, and the proverb would come true: "all things would be turned upside down."
THEAETETUS. It seems to me also, Socrates, that Homer means what you say.
SOCRATES. In the first place, therefore, my excellent young man, consider the eyes in this way: that which you call a "white color" is not something external to your eyes, nor is it located inside your eyes; nor can you assign any specific place to it.

**THEÆ.** Not I, indeed.

**SOC.** What then? If Protagoras, or anyone else, should say to you, "O Theætetus, can anything become greater or more in any other way than by being increased?" How would you answer?

# THE THEAETETUS

<page-num>25</page-num>

What we have just now said is suspended on this principle:—That this universe is motion <note>original: "κίνησις" (kinesis)</note>, and that besides motion there is nothing. Likewise, that of motion there are two species; each of which is infinite in multitude, but one species has the power of acting, and the other of suffering <note>In this context, "suffering" means being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>. From the congress and mutual friction of these a progeny is produced, infinite in multitude, but twofold in species: one, indeed, being that which is sensible <note>term: sensible | things that can be perceived by the senses</note>, but the other sense, which always concurs and exists together with the sensible. And the senses, indeed, are named by us as follows: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and the touching of things hot and cold. Pleasures and pains, desires and fears, and innumerable other passions without a name, and an all-various multitude which are named, follow these. But to each of these the sensible genus is allied: namely, all-various colors to all-various sights; and in a similar manner, voices to hearings, and other sensibles are allied to other senses.

***

<note>The following is a commentary by the translator/editor.</note>

Plato here presents us with the substance of the atomical or mechanical philosophy, which asserted that the universe was produced by nothing else but the motion of indivisible particles, by means of which all things are generated and corrupted. It likewise asserted that all these sensible qualities which are noticed by the several senses—such as colors, sounds, flavors <note>original: "sapors"</note>, odors, and the like—are not things really existing external to us, but passions or sensations in us, caused by local motions on the organs of sense. 

This atomical philosophy, according to Posidonius the Stoic (as we are informed by Strabo <margin>If we are to believe Posidonius, the doctrine concerning atoms is ancient, originating from a Sidonian man named Moschus before the times of the Trojan war. Book 16.</margin>), is more ancient than the times of the Trojan war, and was first invented by one Moschus a Sidonian, or rather, if we prefer the testimony of Sextus Empiricus <margin>Against the Mathematicians, p. 367.</margin>, a Phoenician. This Moschus is doubtless the same person as that Moschus the physiologist <note>term: physiologist | in the ancient sense, one who studies "physis" or nature; a natural philosopher.</note> mentioned by Iamblichus <margin>With the prophets who were descendants of Moschus the physiologist and others, and with the Phoenician hierophants.</margin> in his *Life of Pythagoras*. For he there informs us that Pythagoras, during his residence at Sidon in Phoenicia, conversed with the prophets who were the successors of Moschus the physiologist, and was instructed by them. Hence it appears that this physiology was not invented either by Epicurus or Democritus.

Plato, as may be collected from his *Timaeus*, adopted this physiology: for he there resolves the differences of the four elements into the different geometrical figures of their insensible parts; and in so doing he likewise followed the Pythagoreans. However, he differed from the atomists in this (as I have observed in the Introduction to the *Timaeus*): he assigned commensuration and active fabricative powers to these insensible figures, which they did not; and he likewise differed from them in his arrangement of earth.

VOL. IV. E

# THE THEÆTETUS

What then is the intention of this discourse, **Theætetus**, with reference to what we said before? Do you understand what it is?

**THEÆTETUS.** Not very much, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** But see whether it can be completed in a certain way. For it intends to assert that all these things are, as we have said, in motion, and that there is both swiftness and slowness in their movements. So far as their motions are slow, they keep their motion in the same place and toward things nearby, and in this way they generate <note>original: "generate"; here meaning to produce a perception or a quality</note>. But the things generated in this way are slower. And again, so far as their motions are swift, they move toward things at a distance, and thus generate; but the things generated in this way are swifter. For they are carried along, and their motion naturally exists in lation <note>original: "lation"; a technical term for local motion or change of place</note>. 

When, therefore, the eye and anything commensurate to it generate by coming together, they produce whiteness and the sensation connected to it—which would never have been produced if either of them had been directed toward something else. Then, in that moment, while sight moves toward the eyes and whiteness moves toward that which helps generate the color, the eye becomes filled with vision; it then sees, and becomes not "sight" itself, but a seeing eye. Likewise, that which joined with the eye to generate the color becomes filled with whiteness, and is made not "whiteness" itself, but a white thing—whether it is wood or stone, or anything else that happens to be colored with that kind of color. 

We must conceive of other things in a similar manner, such as heat and hardness, and so on. We must understand that no one of these is essentially any one thing in itself; but, as we have already observed, all things of every variety are generated from motion through their congress <note>original: "congress"; the meeting or interaction of two things</note> with each other. Since, as they say, there is no stability in the idea that either the thing which acts or the thing which suffers <note>original: "suffers"; in the philosophical sense of being acted upon or receiving an impression</note> is any one thing on its own. For that which acts is nothing until it meets with that which is passive, nor is that which is passive anything until it meets with that which acts. For when that which meets and produces something falls upon another thing, it then makes the passive element apparent. 

So from all this, it follows as we said in the beginning: there is not any thing which is essentially one single thing, but it is always "becoming" something in relation to something else. Being itself is entirely absent from this process. Indeed, just now we frequently used the term *being*, compelled to do so by custom and ignorance; but, according to the assertions of the wise,
