<page-num>27</page-num>
# THE THEAETETUS

We ought not to attribute any quality to anything—either to another, to myself, to "this," or to "that"—nor should we call anything by any name that implies permanency. Instead, we should affirm, according to the laws of nature, that things are constantly being generated, made, corrupted, and changed. For if anyone asserts that things stand still, he may easily be proven wrong. It is necessary to speak this way both of things individually and of many things collected together; and in such collections, we categorize "man," "stone," and every animal and species. Do these ideas, O Theaetetus, seem pleasant to you, and are they agreeable to your taste?

THEAETETUS: I do not know, Socrates. I cannot tell whether you are asserting these things because you actually believe them, or if you are saying them merely to test me.

SOCRATES: Do you not remember, my friend, that I neither know any of these specifics myself, nor do I claim any of them as my own? I am "barren" of such ideas. <note>Socrates famously compared himself to a midwife who, though past childbearing age herself, helps others give birth to their own ideas.</note> Likewise, I act as a midwife for you. For this reason, I use these arguments like a charm and place before you the doctrines of various wise men so that you may taste them, until I can lead your own opinion <note>original: "dogma"</note> out into the light. Once I have brought it forth, I will then examine whether it appears to be empty and false, or fertile and true. Therefore, answer boldly and vigorously, in a proper and manly way, whatever you believe to be the truth regarding the things I shall ask you.

THEAETETUS: Ask then.

SOCRATES: Tell me again, then: is it your opinion that nothing has a fixed "being," but rather that "the good," "the beautiful," and everything we just listed are always in a state of "becoming"? <note>The distinction between "being" (permanent reality) and "becoming" (constant change) is central to Platonic philosophy.</note>

THEAETETUS: When I hear you explaining it in this way, the claim appears wonderful, and it seems that your arguments should be accepted.

SOCRATES: Let us, therefore, not overlook what remains. We must still speak concerning dreams, diseases, and especially insanity; likewise, we must consider whatever is seen, heard, or perceived in any other distorted way. For you know that in all these cases, the doctrine we just discussed—that "man is the measure of all things"—would seem to be easily proven wrong. In these states, the senses are more deceived than at any other time. In such cases, it is so far from being true that things are exactly as they appear to everyone that, on the contrary, nothing that appears to exist can be said to truly "be."

They begin to test this theory by considering how it accounts for sensory illusions in dreams and madness.</summary>

**THEAETETUS.** You speak with the greatest truth, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** What then, my boy, remains to be said by someone who asserts that sense perception is knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, and that things which appear to every person are, to that individual, exactly what they appear to be?

**THEAETETUS.** I am reluctant to reply, Socrates, since I do not know what to say; because just now, while I was speaking, you startled me. For, in reality, I cannot hesitate to admit that those who are insane or dreaming hold false thoughts, since some of the insane consider themselves to be Gods, and those who dream think they are flying like birds.

**SOCRATES.** Are you aware, then, of the doubt raised concerning these cases—especially concerning perceptions in sleep versus when we are awake?

**THEAETETUS.** What question is this?

**SOCRATES.** It is one I think you have often heard: by what arguments can anyone prove whether we are currently asleep and all our thoughts are dreams, or whether we are in a wakeful <note>original: "vigilant"</note> state and are actually speaking with each other?

**THEAETETUS.** Indeed, Socrates, it is difficult to see what arguments could prove this. For all the same characteristics seem to follow in both cases. Regarding our present conversation, nothing prevents us from imagining that we are merely dreaming that we talk to one another. Even when we dream that we are telling our dreams to others, the similarity to our waking conversation is quite wonderful.

**SOCRATES.** You see, then, it is not difficult to find reason for doubt, since it is uncertain whether our perceptions are dreams or waking realities. This is especially true since the time we spend sleeping is equal to the time we spend awake; in both states, our soul anxiously maintains that its current beliefs <note>original: "dogmas"</note> are the absolute truth. So, for an equal amount of time, we claim that one set of things is true, and then the other; we argue for the reality of each with equal intensity.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** The same logic applies to disease and insanity, except that in those cases, the time spent in those states is not equal to the time spent in health.

# THE THEAETETUS

**Theaetetus.** Right.
**Socrates.** What then? Shall truth be defined by the length or shortness <note>original: "multitude and paucity"</note> of time?
**Theaetetus.** That would indeed be very ridiculous.
**Socrates.** Do you have any other way to clearly show which of these opinions are true?
**Theaetetus.** It does not appear to me that I do.
**Socrates.** Hear, therefore, from me what those people will say who define appearances as being always true to those to whom they appear. For I think they will ask you this: "O Theaetetus, can something that is entirely different from another thing possess any power or quality that is the same as that other thing?" And must we not admit that a thing which is entirely different is not merely partly the same and partly different, but is wholly different?
**Theaetetus.** It is impossible for it to possess anything that is the same, either in power or in anything else, since it is altogether different.
**Socrates.** Must we not, therefore, necessarily admit that a thing of this kind is dissimilar?
**Theaetetus.** It appears so to me.
**Socrates.** If, therefore, anything happens to become similar or dissimilar to something else—whether to itself at a different time or to another object—must we not say that so far as it is similar, it is the "same," but so far as it is dissimilar, it is "different"?
**Theaetetus.** That is necessary.
**Socrates.** Have we not said before that there are many—indeed, an infinite number—of things which act <note>active factors in perception</note>, and an infinite number of things which are acted upon <note>original: "suffer"; the passive elements of perception</note>?
**Theaetetus.** Yes.
**Socrates.** And besides this, that when one thing is mingled with various other things, it does not produce the same results, but different ones?
**Theaetetus.** Entirely so.
**Socrates.** Shall we speak of you and me, and other things, in the same way? For instance, shall we say that Socrates when he is healthy is similar to Socrates when he is ill, or dissimilar?
**Theaetetus.** Do you mean to ask whether the whole of Socrates when ill is similar or dissimilar to the whole of Socrates when healthy?
**Socrates.** You understand me perfectly well. That is exactly what I mean.

**THEAETETUS.** I answer, then, that it is dissimilar and different.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, is it different because it is considered as dissimilar?

**THEAETETUS.** It must be so.

**SOCRATES.** And would you speak in a similar way regarding those who are asleep, and all the other cases we just discussed?

**THEAETETUS.** I would.

**SOCRATES.** But does not each of those things which are naturally capable of producing an effect <note>original: "effecting any thing"</note> use me as a different man when it acts upon me while I am sick, compared to when it acts upon me while I am well?

**THEAETETUS.** How could it be otherwise?

**SOCRATES.** And do we not produce different results from each encounter, with me being the patient <note>term: "patient" here refers to the person receiving the sensation or being acted upon</note> and that thing being the agent <note>term: "agent" refers to the object or force acting upon the person</note>?

**THEAETETUS.** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** But when I drink wine while I am well, it appears to me to be pleasant and sweet.

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** But, based on what we have granted, an agent and a patient produce sweetness and sensation, both being carried along together. And sensation, arising from the patient, causes the tongue to perceive; but sweetness, arising from the wine and moving toward the tongue, causes the wine both to be and to appear sweet to a healthy tongue.

**THEAETETUS.** We entirely agreed previously that these details exist in this manner.

**SOCRATES.** But when I drink wine while I am diseased, my tongue does not in reality receive it the same as before; for it now encounters something that is dissimilar.

**THEAETETUS.** It does.

**SOCRATES.** But Socrates, being affected in this way, and the act of drinking the wine again produce other things: a sensation of bitterness in the tongue, and bitterness produced and carried along in the wine. And the wine itself is not "bitterness," but "bitter"; and I am not "sensation," but "the one who senses" <note>original: "that which is sentient"</note>.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, I, perceiving in this way, never become anything else. For a different object produces a different sensation, which makes the perceiver varied and different. Nor does that which affects me in this way become a thing...

*THEAETETUS.* These things are so.

*SOCRATES.* Nor, indeed, am I such a person to myself, nor is that thing generated such a thing to itself.

*THEAETETUS.* Certainly not.

*SOCRATES.* But it is necessary that I should become aware of something when I perceive it; for it is impossible that I should be perceiving and yet perceive nothing. For it is impossible that a thing can be sweet and yet sweet to no one.

*THEAETETUS.* Entirely so.

*SOCRATES.* It remains then, I think, that we should mutually exist, if we exist at all; and if we are in the process of becoming, that we should be mutually in that state of <term>generation</term> <note>original: "generation"; here meaning the process of coming into being or changing</note>; since necessity binds our essence. But it does not bind it to any other thing, nor even to ourselves. It remains, therefore, that we are bound to each other. So that, if anyone says a certain thing exists, or is coming into being, it must be understood that it exists, or is becoming something, or of something, or to something. But it must not be said that it exists in itself, either as that which is, or that which is becoming. Nor must we allow this to be said, either by the thing itself or by any other, as the argument we have already discussed demonstrates.

*THEAETETUS.* Entirely so, Socrates.

*SOCRATES.* Since that which affects me belongs to me and not to another, do I not also perceive it, and not another?

*THEAETETUS.* Undoubtedly.

*SOCRATES.* My sense, therefore, is true to me. For it always belongs to my essence. And I, according to *Protagoras*, am a judge of things which have a being pertaining to myself—that they are—and of non-beings—that they are not.

*THEAETETUS.* It appears so.

*SOCRATES.* How then is it possible—since I am not deceived and do not falter in my <term>dianoetic</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic"; relating to the power of the intellect or discursive reason</note> part, either about things which exist or things in the process of becoming—that I should not possess scientific knowledge of the things which I perceive?

# THE THEAETETUS

Should appear to be not inferior in wisdom, either to any man or God? Or do you think that the Protagorean measure pertains less to Gods than to men?

**THEAETETUS.** I do not, by Jupiter <note>original: "by Jupiter" (a common Greek oath to Zeus)</note>. And I very much wonder at your question. For when we discussed in what manner it might be said that what appears to anyone is true to that person, it appeared to me to be perfectly well said; but now the very contrary has rapidly taken place.

**SOCRATES.** My dear boy, you are as yet a youth, and are therefore easily obedient to and persuaded by conversation. For to these things Protagoras, or anyone of his sect, would say: "O generous boys and aged men, you sit here together, conversing and calling on the Gods—concerning whom, whether they are or are not, I do not think it proper either to speak or write. Likewise, hearing the things which the multitude admit, these you assert: and among others, that it would be a terrible thing if every man did not far surpass every brute in wisdom. But you do not provide any demonstration or necessity that it should be so; you only employ probability. If Theodorus, or any other geometrician, should employ probability when practicing geometry, he would be considered unworthy of notice." Do you, therefore, and Theodorus consider whether you should admit persuasion and probable arguments when discoursing about things of such great consequence.

**THEAETETUS.** But, Socrates, both you and we should say that this would not be just.

**SOCRATES.** Now, however, as it appears from your discourse and that of Theodorus, another thing is to be considered.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely another thing.

**SOCRATES.** Let us, therefore, consider this: whether science <note>original: "science" (here meaning *episteme* or certain knowledge)</note> is the same as sense <note>original: "sense" (sensory perception)</note>, or different from it? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Do we then acknowledge that all such things as we perceive by seeing and hearing, we at the same time scientifically know? So that, for instance, shall we say that we do not hear the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarians" (non-Greek speakers)</note> when they speak, before we have learned their language? Or that, without this, we both hear them and at the same time know what they say? And again, whether...

# THE THEÆTETUS.

**SOCRATES.** When we are ignorant of letters <note>original: "letters" refers to the alphabet or basic elements of writing</note>, but look at them, shall we say we do not see them? Or shall we strenuously contend that we know them simply because we see them?

**THEÆTETUS.** We should say this, Socrates: that if we see and hear things, we know them through science <note>original: "scientifically"; here meaning certain or systematic knowledge</note>. In the case of sight, by perceiving the shape and color, we know the letters; and in the case of hearing, we at the same time both hear and know the high and low pitches of the sounds. However, we would say that we neither perceive nor know through sight or hearing what grammarians and interpreters teach about these things.

**SOCRATES.** Most excellently said, Theætetus. It is not worth while to oppose you on these points, so that you may continue to make such great progress. But consider also this other problem that arises, and see how it might be refuted.

**THEÆTETUS.** What is that?

**SOCRATES.** It is this: whether it is possible for a person to be ignorant of something that he has systematic knowledge of, while he still remembers it and preserves it in his mind. But I am being too wordy, it seems, in my desire to ask whether someone can fail to know something that he has learned and still remembers.

**THEÆTETUS.** But how is it possible he should not know it, Socrates? For otherwise, what you suggest would be a miracle <note>original: "prodigy"</note>.

**SOCRATES.** Am I, therefore, talking nonsense or not? Consider: do you not say that to see is to perceive, and that sight is a sense?

**THEÆTETUS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, does not he who sees something have a systematic knowledge of what he sees, according to our current argument?

**THEÆTETUS.** He does.

**SOCRATES.** Well then, do you not say that memory is something that exists?

**THEÆTETUS.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** But is it a memory of nothing, or of something?

**THEÆTETUS.** Of something, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not, therefore, a memory of those things which a person learns and perceives?

**THEÆTETUS.** It is of such things.

**SOCRATES.** And does a person ever remember that which he sees?

**THEÆTETUS.** He does remember it.

# THE THEAETETUS

We appear to have contradicted this meaning and to have delighted in doing so during our discussion. Although we have claimed not to be argumentative but wise, we are unaware that we are acting just like those clever debaters <note>original: "skilful men," likely referring to Sophists who used verbal tricks</note>.

THEAETETUS. I do not yet understand what you are saying.

SOCRATES. I will try to explain what I understand about these matters. We inquired whether anyone who has learned and remembers a thing does not have a scientific knowledge <note>original: "scientific knowledge" here refers to *episteme*, or certain, organized knowledge</note> of that thing. We showed that he who knows a thing, and remembers it with his eyes shut but does not see it, is simultaneously ignorant of it and remembers it. But we agreed that this is impossible. And so the Protagorean "fable" <note>original: "fable," used here to mean a philosophical theory or mythos</note> is destroyed, and at the same time yours is too—the one which asserts that science and sensory perception are the same.

THEAETETUS. It appears so.

SOCRATES. But I think, my friend, this would not be the case if the father of that theory were still alive; he would defend it vigorously. But now, since it is an orphan, we mock and insult it. Even the guardians whom Protagoras left behind—of whom Theodorus is one—are unwilling to help it. Therefore, for the sake of justice, we ourselves should venture to give it assistance.

THEODORUS. Indeed, Socrates, I am not one of the guardians of Protagoras's doctrine; rather, that should be said of Callias, the son of Hipponicus. We very quickly turned away from mere words to the study of geometry. Nevertheless, we shall be grateful to you if you assist this doctrine.

SOCRATES. You speak well, Theodorus. Consider, therefore, the assistance I shall provide. For he who does not pay attention to the power of words—by which we are usually accustomed to affirm or deny anything—must agree to consequences even more "dire" <note>original: "dire," meaning logically formidable or troublesome</note> than those we have just mentioned. Shall I tell you how, Theaetetus?

THEODORUS. Tell us both, then; but let the younger one answer. If he makes a mistake, it will be less disgraceful.

SOCRATES. I am speaking of a most difficult question, and I think it is this: **Is it possible that someone who knows a thing can be ignorant of the very thing he knows?**

THEODORUS. What shall we answer, Theaetetus?

THEAETETUS. I think it is not possible.

SOCRATES. But that is not the case if you admit that "to see" is "to know scientifically."

For how ought you to reply to that inevitable question, which, as it is said, is hidden in a well <note>original: "shut up in a well"; a reference to the proverb that truth lies at the bottom of a well</note>, if anyone should ask you, "O intrepid man, if you cover one of your eyes with your hand, can you see your garment with the covered eye?"

**THEAETETUS.** I think I should say, "Not with this eye, but with the other."

**SOCRATES.** Would you not, therefore, see and at the same time not see the same thing?

**THEAETETUS.** I should, in a certain respect.

**SOCRATES.** But he will say, "I neither ordered you to answer thus, nor did I ask in what respect you might be said to see, but whether, if you know a thing scientifically <note>original: "scientifically"; here meaning having certain or systematic knowledge (episteme)</note>, you also did not scientifically know it. But now you confess that while not seeing, you see; and prior to this you acknowledged that to see was to have scientific knowledge, and that not to see was not to know scientifically. Think what will happen to you from these admissions."

**THEAETETUS.** I think the very contrary to what we admitted will take place.

**SOCRATES.** But, perhaps, O wonderful youth, you will suffer many things of this kind if anyone should ask you whether it is possible to know scientifically in an acute or a dull manner, or when near but not at a distance, or vehemently and with remission <note>original: "with remission"; meaning with less intensity or more weakly</note>, and in ten thousand other ways. For an insidious man, armed with a shield and led to discussion for hire <note>A reference to a mercenary debater or Sophist who argues for victory rather than truth</note>, will—once you admit science and sense-perception to be the same—drive you toward hearing, smelling, and such other senses. There, detaining you, he will confute you and will not dismiss you until, having admired his exquisite wisdom, you are bound by him. And being thus brought into captivity and bound, you will be obliged to redeem yourself for a sum of money agreed upon by him and you. But you will perhaps say, "In what manner can Protagoras defend his opinions?" Shall we endeavor to say something else?

**THEAETETUS.** By all means.

**SOCRATES.** But all this which we have said in defense of him will, I think, be ineffectual. But, most sluggish Socrates, the truth is this: when by inquiry you consider any one of my assertions, if the person whom you are questioning..."

Do not, therefore, pursue my discourse in words only, but still in a clearer manner thus learn what I say. 

And in order to this, recollect what was said before: that to a sick man the things which he tastes appear and are bitter; but that to him who is well they are and appear to be the contrary. But it is not proper to make either of these the wiser on this account (for this is impossible); nor must it be asserted that he who is sick is an ignorant person because he entertains such opinions, and that he who is well is wise because he thinks differently; but that he is changed into a different habit <note>original: "habit" here means a state of being or disposition</note>. # THE THEAETETUS

The physician effects a change by medicines, and the sophist <note>original: "sophist"; here referring to a teacher of wisdom or rhetoric</note> by discourses. For no one can cause a person who thinks falsely to think truly afterwards. It is not possible for anyone to have an opinion of things which do not exist, or of things different from what he experiences. But the things which he experiences are always true to him. 

I think that a person who, through a depraved habit of soul, forms opinions of things allied to his own condition, may, through a good habit, be made to entertain opinions of different things. Some people, through ignorance, call these "true phantasms" <note>original: "phantasms"; mental images or appearances</note>. But I say that while some things are better than others, they are by no means more "true." 

Likewise, friend *Socrates*, I am far from calling wise men "frogs." Instead, I call those who are wise in matters pertaining to bodies, "physicians"; and in matters pertaining to plants, "husbandmen" <note>original: "husbandmen"; farmers or gardeners</note>. For I say that these men, when a plant is diseased, instill in it useful, healthy, and true sensations instead of depraved ones. In the same way, wise men and good rhetoricians cause things that are good to appear just to cities, instead of things that are base. For whatever things appear just and beautiful to each city are indeed just and beautiful to that city for as long as it thinks them to be so. 

But a wise man, instead of those particulars that are harmful to cities, causes advantageous things to both exist and appear to be just. In the same manner, a sophist who is able to discipline his students in this way is a wise man and deserves a great reward from those he instructs. And thus, some men are wiser than others, and yet no one entertains false opinions. 

This must be admitted by you, whether you are willing or not, since you yourself are the "measure of things." For this assertion is preserved in these arguments. If you have anything else you can urge against this from the beginning, urge it by providing opposing arguments. But if you prefer to do this through questioning, then begin to interrogate. For this method is not to be avoided; rather, it should be pursued above all things by anyone endowed with intellect. 

Act, therefore, in this manner, so that you do not behave unjustly while interrogating. For it is very absurd that a man who, by his own confession, applies himself to the study of virtue, should in his speech accomplish nothing but injustice. A person acts unjustly in this kind of debate when he does not distinguish between contending <note>original: "contending"; competitive arguing or debating for victory</note> and discoursing <note>original: "discoursing"; philosophical dialogue aimed at truth</note>. In the former, he jests and deceives as much as he can; but in the latter, he acts seriously and corrects the person with whom he speaks, pointing out only those errors by which the person was deceived, whether by himself or by his...

former discussions. If, therefore, you act in this manner, those who discourse with you will accuse themselves of their own confusion and perplexity, but not you. They will likewise follow and love you, but hate themselves; they will fly from themselves to philosophy so that, by becoming different from what they were, they may liberate themselves from their former habits. But if you act in a manner contrary to this—as is the case with the common people—the very opposite will happen to you. You will truly consider our assertion: that all things are in motion, and that whatever appears to anyone—whether to an individual or a city—is exactly what it appears to be. **THEODORUS.** But what? Will not *Theaetetus* follow you in your investigation much better than many who have long beards? <note>original: "long beards" — a reference to older men or those who affect the appearance of philosophers.</note>

For you do not dismiss him who engages with you until you have compelled him to wrestle with you in arguments, naked.

**SOCRATES.** You have most excellently, *Theodorus*, found a resemblance for my disease. But I am, indeed, more robust than these. For an innumerable multitude of *Heracleses* and *Thesuses*, who were very powerful in discourse, have contended with me and have been very much wearied; but, notwithstanding this, I have not in the least desisted; I am seized with such a dire love of this exercise. Do not, therefore, through envy, refrain from exercising yourself with me, and benefiting both me and yourself at the same time.

**THEODORUS.** I shall no longer oppose you. Lead me, therefore, wherever you please. For it is perfectly necessary that he who is proven wrong should endure this fatal destiny which you have knit; yet I shall not attempt to exert myself beyond what I promised you.

**SOCRATES.** This will be sufficient. But diligently observe this with respect to me: that I do not, through forgetfulness, adopt a childish <note>original: "puerile"</note> mode of discourse, so that we may not again be exposed to criticism.

**THEODORUS.** I will endeavor to do this, as far as I am able.

# THE THEAETETUS

**Socrates:** Let us, therefore, again resume this point which we discussed before. Let us see whether we properly or improperly reject the assertion of Protagoras that every person is self-sufficient in regard to wisdom. For Protagoras has granted us that some among the wise differ from others in respect to what is better and worse. Has he not?

**Theodorus:** Yes.

**Socrates:** If, therefore, he were present himself to acknowledge this, and we were not merely admitting it on his behalf, there would be no need to strengthen the point by revisiting the arguments in its favor. But now, since someone might consider us unauthorized defenders of his doctrine, it will be better to reach an agreement on this position in an even clearer manner. For it is of no small consequence whether this is true or not.

**Theodorus:** That is true.

**Socrates:** Therefore, let us obtain this agreement in the shortest way possible, not from other sources, but from his own assertions.

**Theodorus:** How so?

**Socrates:** In this way. Does he not say that what appears to any person is true to the person to whom it appears?

**Theodorus:** He does say so.

**Socrates:** Therefore, Protagoras, we are expressing the opinions of a man—or rather, of all men—when we say that there is no one who does not believe himself to be wiser than others in some respects, and others to be wiser than himself in other respects. In the greatest dangers, such as in war, or during diseases, or in storms at sea, do men not look to their leaders in each of these situations as if they were Gods? Do they not consider them their saviors, even though these leaders are superior in nothing else but knowledge? And in all human affairs, do not men seek out teachers and leaders—both for themselves and for other animals—whom they believe are capable of teaching and governing? In all these cases, what else can we say except that men believe that both wisdom and ignorance exist among them?

**Theodorus:** Nothing else.

**Socrates:** Do they not, therefore, think that wisdom is true <term>dianoetic energy</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic energy"; this refers to the active process of discursive reasoning or intellectual thought</note>, but that ignorance is false opinion?

**Theodorus:** Undoubtedly.

**Socrates:** What then, Protagoras, shall we assert? Shall we say that men always form true opinions, or that their opinions are sometimes true and sometimes false? From both these assertions, it follows that they do not always form true opinions, but rather both true and false ones. Consider, Theodorus, whether any of the followers of Protagoras—or you yourself—would argue that no one ever believes that someone else is ignorant or holds false opinions.

**Theodorus:** That would be incredible, Socrates.

**Socrates:** And yet the assertion that "man is the measure of all things" <note>original: *homo mensura*; the relativistic doctrine that truth is subjective to the individual</note> necessarily leads to this conclusion.

**Theodorus:** How so?

**Socrates:** When you judge something for yourself and then declare your opinion to me, then, according to the doctrine of Protagoras, your opinion is true for you. But regarding the rest of us, are we not allowed to be judges of your judgment? Or must we conclude that you always form true opinions? Is it not more likely that a countless multitude of men will continually oppose your opinions, believing that you judge and think falsely?

**Theodorus:** By Zeus <note>original: "By Jupiter"; the translator used the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods</note>, Socrates, as Homer says, there is indeed a "countless multitude" who would give me plenty of trouble on that front.

**Socrates:** What then? Are you willing to admit we should say that you hold a true opinion for yourself, but a false one to a countless multitude of other people?

**Theodorus:** That seems to be the necessary result of Protagoras's argument.

**Socrates:** But what about Protagoras himself? If neither he nor the general public believed that "man is the measure of all things"—and indeed, the public does not believe it—then wouldn't it follow that this "Truth" <note>Protagoras titled his book *Truth*</note> which he wrote is true for no one? Furthermore, if he believes it is true, but the majority of people do not agree with him, don't you see what follows? To the extent that the number of people who reject his theory is greater than the number who accept it, his theory is "not true" in a greater proportion than it "is true."

**Theodorus:** That must be the case, since according to his own logic, the reality of a thing depends on each person's opinion of it.

**Socrates:** In the next place, this situation will unfold in a most refined way. For Protagoras, according to his own theory, must admit that the opinion of those who disagree with him—those who believe he is wrong—is in some sense true, since he acknowledges that all men form true opinions.

**Theodorus:** Entirely so.

**Socrates:** Will he not, therefore, admit that his own opinion is false, if he grants that the judgment of those who think he is mistaken is true?

**Theodorus:** That is necessarily the case.

**Socrates:** But others will never admit that they themselves are mistaken; or do you think they will?

**Theodorus:** They certainly will not.

**Socrates:** Protagoras, however, based on what he has written, must acknowledge that their opinion is true.

**Theodorus:** It appears so.

**Socrates:** Based on everything Protagoras has asserted, it follows—or rather, he himself must grant—that when he admits that his opponent holds a true opinion, he is conceding that neither a dog, nor any man, is the measure of all things, nor of any single thing that he has not truly understood. Is it not so?

**Theodorus:** It is.

**Socrates:** Since, therefore, this "truth" is disputed by everyone, the "Truth" of Protagoras <note>Referring to Protagoras's book titled *Truth*</note> will not be true to anyone—not to anyone else, nor even to himself.

**Theodorus:** We are attacking my associate, Socrates, in a very aggressive manner.

**Socrates:** But it is unclear, my friend, whether or not we have strayed from the right path <note>original: "rectitude"</note>. For it is likely that he, being older than us, is also wiser. If he were to suddenly leap up and seize me by the shoulders, he would probably prove that I am talking nonsense <note>original: "delirious"</note> in many respects, and you as well for agreeing with me, and then he would immediately vanish. But I think it is necessary that we rely on ourselves as we are, and always say what appears to us to be the truth. And so, shall we say that anyone would grant us this: that one man can be wiser or more ignorant than another?

**Theodorus:** That appears to be the case to me.

Are things that are apparent exactly as they appear to everyone—namely, things that are hot, dry, sweet, and everything of this kind? And if it should be granted that in some things one person disagrees with another—as regarding things that are healthy <note>original: "salubrious"</note> or harmful—Protagoras would assert that not every woman, boy, or brute animal is capable of curing themselves by knowing what is healthy. Instead, he would say that in this case, if in any, one person differs from another in wisdom.
**Theodorus:** So it appears to me.
**Socrates:** Regarding political concerns, then—such as things beautiful and ugly <note>original: "base"</note>, just and unjust, holy and unholy—are the opinions that each city legally establishes for itself true for that city? And in these matters, is neither one individual nor one city wiser than another? But in determining what is advantageous or the contrary for a city, Protagoras would doubtless grant that one counselor is better than another, and that the opinion of one city is more true than that of another. Nor will he by any means dare to say that whatever a city establishes because it thinks it is advantageous to itself will actually be beneficial above all else. But cities, regarding what is just and unjust, holy and unholy, are willing to strenuously contend that none of these have naturally any essence <note>original: "essence of their own"; referring to objective reality independent of human opinion</note> of their own. Instead, they argue that what appears to be true to the community is true at the moment it appears, and for as long as it appears. And those who do not entirely follow the doctrine of Protagoras still conduct their wisdom in this manner. But for us, Theodorus, one discussion leads us into another—a greater one emerging from a lesser.
**Theodorus:** We are not, therefore, idle, Socrates.
**Socrates:** We do not appear to be so. And indeed, my friend <note>original: "O blessed man"</note>, I have often noticed—now as well as before—that those who have for a long time been occupied with philosophy appear to be ridiculous as public speakers <note>original: "rhetoricians"</note> when they go to courts of justice, and deservedly so.
**Theodorus:** Why do you assert this?
**Socrates:** Those who from their youth have been rolled like cylinders in courts of justice and similar places appear, when compared to those who have been raised in philosophy and such pursuits, like slaves educated among the free-born.
**Theodorus:** In what respect?

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the philosopher and the legal orator, focusing on the psychological effects of their respective lifestyles.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>
# THE THEAETETUS

**Socrates:** In this respect, these latter men—the philosophers—always, as you say, have an abundance of leisure. They peaceably conduct their discussions at leisure, just as we are doing now, engaging in a digressive conversation for the third time. Similarly, if any new question arises that pleases them more than the original subject of discussion, they are not at all concerned whether they speak briefly or at great length, provided they can attain the truth of reality. 

But the others—the legal orators—are always busily occupied when they speak; for the flowing water <note>original: "defluent water." This refers to the *clepsydra* or water-clock used in Athenian courts to limit the time allowed for speeches.</note> urges them on. They are not permitted to speak about whatever they desire; instead, their opponent imposes necessity upon them, following the "formula of the book" <note>The legal brief or formal indictment.</note> which must be followed strictly, and which they call the "affidavit" <note>original: "an oath respecting calumny." A preliminary oath taken by both parties in an Athenian lawsuit to certify they were acting in good faith.</note> of the plaintiff and defendant. Their speeches are always about a fellow slave, addressed to a master who sits holding the legal action in his hand. Their legal contests are never varied, but are always about the same narrow issues; often, their very lives are at stake. 

As a result of all these circumstances, these men become intense and sharp-witted. They know how to flatter the master with words to gain a favorable reality in the verdict. They do this because their souls are small and warped. Being in a state of "slavery" from childhood prevents the soul from growing and robs it of uprightness and liberty. It compels the soul to act in a distorted way, thrusting great dangers and fears upon tender young minds. Because they cannot endure these pressures while maintaining justice and truth, they immediately turn to falsehood and mutual injury, becoming bent and twisted. Consequently, with their <term>dianoetic</term> <note>The "dianoetic" part refers to the capacity for discursive reason or the intellect.</note> faculty in a diseased condition, they pass from youth to manhood believing they have made themselves skillful and wise. 

Such are men of that description, Theodorus. But would you like me to give you an account of the men who belong to our "choir" <note>A metaphor for the community of philosophers.</note>, or should we dismiss them and return to our main investigation, so that we do not digress too much, as we just cautioned?

**Theodorus:** By no means, Socrates. You observed very correctly that we, being members of the choir of philosophers, are not servants to our discourse; rather, our discourse is a servant to us, and it must wait upon our pleasure until we choose to finish it. For we have no judge or spectator presiding over us to criticize or govern us, as is the case with the poets in their competitions.

**Socrates:** Let us speak then, since it pleases you, about the <term>Coryphaei</term> <note>The "Coryphaei" were the leaders or most eminent members of the philosophical "choir."</note>.

<summary>Socrates contrasts the free, leisurely pursuit of truth by philosophers with the hurried, soul-warping pressures of legal orators who are constrained by time and the need to flatter judges. Theodorus agrees that philosophers are masters of their own time and discussion, unlike poets or lawyers.</summary>

# THE THEÆTETUS

<gloss>1</gloss> <note>The virtues are categorized into several levels: physical (natural temperaments shared with animals); ethical (habits and right opinions in children); political (reason governing the soul's lower parts); cathartic (purifying the soul from worldly attachments); or theoretic (where the soul devotes itself to pure intellect). Plato uses this last category to describe the "Coryphæan" or leading philosophers. Other virtues are discussed in the *Phaedo*.</note> For why should anyone speak of those who engage with philosophy in a corrupt or superficial manner? In the first place, the <term>Coryphæi</term> <note>original: Coryphæi; meaning the leaders or "head men" of a philosophical school</note>, from their youth, neither know the way to the marketplace, nor where the court of justice or senate house is situated, or any other public place of assembly belonging to the city. They likewise neither hear nor see laws or decrees, whether they are spoken aloud or written down. As for the ambitious efforts of their peers to obtain government offices, their political clubs, their banquets, and their rowdy parties accompanied by flute-players—they do not even dream of participating in such things. Whether something in the city has turned out well or ill, or what scandal has befallen someone because of their ancestors (whether male or female), these matters are more hidden from such a philosopher than—as the saying goes—how many <term>choes</term> <note>original: choes; an ancient Greek liquid measurement, roughly three quarts</note> of water the sea contains. Furthermore, he is even unaware that he is ignorant <gloss>2</gloss> <note>While the common person is ignorant of spiritual truths, the philosopher is "ignorant" of worldly gossip because his mind is focused on higher realities; this is a sign of intellectual excellence, not a lack of ability.</note> of all these trivial details. He does not avoid them to gain a reputation for being holy, but because in reality, only his body lives and resides in the city. His <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>original: dianoëtic; relating to the power of discursive reason or the thinking mind</note> part considers all these worldly affairs as trifling and worthless. He is carried away, as <term>Pindar</term> <note>A famous Greek lyric poet</note> says, in every direction: measuring the earth and what lies beneath it, studying the stars above the heavens, and thoroughly investigating the entire nature of every being in the universe, but never applying himself to anything that is close at hand.

**THEODORUS:** What do you mean by this, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** It is just like the story, Theodorus, of a certain clever and charming <term>Thracian</term> maidservant...

<meta>This page continues Socrates' description of the philosophical character, contrasting the philosopher's focus on universal truths with the common person's focus on mundane affairs.</meta>

# THE THEAETETUS

A witty and elegant Thracian maid-servant is reported to have said to Thales <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BCE), often considered the first Greek philosopher.</note>—when he fell into a well while studying the stars—that he was very eager to know what the heavens contained, but was ignorant of what was right before him and at his very feet. In the same manner, all those who are devoted to philosophy may be mocked. For, in reality, a person of this kind is not only ignorant of what his neighbor does, but he scarcely knows whether that neighbor is a human being or some other animal. 

However, what a human being is, and what a nature of this kind ought principally to do or endure, this he makes the object of his inquiry and earnestly investigates. Do you understand, Theodorus, or not?

**Theodorus:** I do; and you speak the truth.

**Socrates:** For in reality, my friend, when a man of this kind is compelled to speak (as I said before)—either privately with someone, or publicly in a court of justice, or anywhere else—about things right before his feet and in his view, he excites laughter not only in Thracian maid-servants but in the rest of the common people. Because of his lack of practical skill, he falls into wells and every kind of ambiguity. His terrible awkwardness causes him to be viewed as a clown <note>original: "rustic," implying an unrefined or socially ignorant person.</note>. 

For when he is in the company of slanderers, he has nothing reproachful to say, as he does not know any evil about anyone, because he has not paid attention to individuals. Consequently, having nothing to say, he appears ridiculous. But when he is in the company of those who praise and boast of others, since he is not only silent but openly laughs, he is considered insane. 

For when he hears praises given to a tyrant or a king, he thinks he hears some swineherd, shepherd, or herdsman being declared happy because he milks his flock abundantly; at the same time, he thinks that these rulers tend and milk the animals under their command in a more surly and treacherous manner. He believes it is inevitable that a ruler should become no less coarse and undisciplined through his occupation than a shepherd—the one being enclosed by city walls, and the other by a sheepfold on a mountain. 

Furthermore, when he hears someone boasting that he possesses ten thousand acres of land, or an even greater number, as if he possessed something wonderfully vast, it seems to the philosopher to be a very trifling thing, because he is accustomed to surveying the whole earth. Likewise, whenever someone celebrates the nobility of his family—demonstrating that he has seven wealthy grandfathers—the philosopher thinks that this is merely the praise of a dull mind which focuses on insignificant things.

<summary>Socrates describes the "philosopher's gaze," explaining how the pursuit of universal truths makes a thinker appear clumsy, socially ignorant, and unimpressed by wealth or power in the eyes of the public.</summary>

**THEODORUS.** If, Socrates, you could persuade all men to agree with what you say, as you have persuaded me, there would be more peace and less evil among men.

**SOCRATES.** But it is impossible, Theodorus, that evils should be destroyed; for it is necessary that there should always be something contrary to good. Nor can evils be established among the Gods; instead, they necessarily revolve around mortal nature and this place where we dwell. On this account, we ought to endeavor to fly from here to that higher place with the utmost speed. But this flight consists in becoming as much like the divine as possible. And this likeness is acquired by becoming just and holy, in conjunction with prudence <note>original: "prudence," meaning practical wisdom or spiritual insight</note>. 

But, O best of men, it is not altogether easy to persuade people that vice is to be avoided and virtue pursued for reasons other than those the common people adopt—namely, the desire to not seem wicked and to appear good. For these reasons are, as they say, the trifles <note>original: "nugacities," meaning trivialities or nonsense</note> of old women, as it appears to me. 

The truth, however, is as follows: Divinity is never in any respect unjust, but is perfectly just. And there is nothing more similar to God than a man when he becomes most just. It is in this area that a man's true skill—or his worthlessness and laziness—is revealed. For the knowledge of this is wisdom and true virtue; but the ignorance of it is a lack of education and clear wickedness <note>original: "improbity"</note>. 

Everything else which appears to be skill and wisdom is merely troublesome when it appears in political power, and is unrefined <note>original: "illiberal," meaning unworthy of a free person</note> when it appears in the mechanical arts. It will be by far the best, therefore, not to allow the man who acts unjustly, or who speaks or acts impiously, to be considered "skilled" because of his cunning. For a character of this kind will boast in his disgrace; he will not think of himself as a mere trifle or a "burden on the earth," but will consider himself the kind of man who is necessary for the preservation of a city. **THEODORUS.** Things of this kind, Socrates, are not unpleasant for me to hear. For, because of my age, I can easily follow you. But let us, if you please, resume our inquiry.

If someone were willing to strenuously assert that whatever appears to anyone is always what it appears to be to that person—and they were no less willing to assert this regarding justice—they might say that whatever a city establishes because it appears just to itself, is indeed just for as long as that law remains in effect. However, regarding what is *good*, no one is so bold as to argue that whatever a city establishes, believing it to be useful <note>original: "uſeful"; here meaning beneficial or advantageous</note> to itself, will actually be useful for as long as it is established—unless they were only talking about the mere *name* of "utility." **Socrates.** But does a city not consider the actual thing being named, and not merely the name itself?

**Theodorus.** Undoubtedly.

**Socrates.** And whatever it names as "useful," that is surely what it aims for in the business of legislation; it establishes all its laws to be as useful to itself as possible. Or does it establish laws while looking toward something else?

**Theodorus.** By no means.

**Socrates.** Does it, therefore, always accomplish its purpose, or is it often mistaken in its opinion?

**Theodorus.** I think it is often mistaken.

**Socrates.** If anyone were to inquire about every category of thing in which "the useful" consists, he would acknowledge this even more readily. **Theodorus.** Entirely so.

**Theodorus.** It is.

**Socrates.** "Shall we also say, O Protagoras, that he contains within himself a criterion of future things? And that such things as he thinks will happen, those things..."

**Socrates:** You speak to the purpose. But, with respect to the problem, we receive one tradition from the ancients (who concealed their meaning from the multitude in verse) that Ocean and Tethys <note>In Greek mythology, these are the primordial water deities, representing the source of all things.</note> are the generation of all other things, that all things are streams, and that nothing abides. What then shall we say to all these, my friend? For, proceeding by small advances, we have secretly fallen into the midst of both of them. And if we fly without resisting in any respect, we shall be punished like those in the *palaestrae* <note>original: *palæſtræ*; ancient Greek wrestling schools or gymnasiums.</note> playing a game with a line, who, when they are caught on both sides, are drawn in contrary directions. # THE THEAETETUS

If they appear to say anything to the purpose, we should draw ourselves together with them and endeavor to fly from the others. But if those who consider the universe as stable shall appear to have more truth on their side, we should fly to them from those who move even things immovable. And if it shall appear that neither of them assert anything sufficient, we shall become ridiculous by thinking that we—who are men of no importance—can say anything to the purpose when we only reprobate <note>original: "reprobate"; here meaning to criticize or reject</note> men who are very ancient and perfectly wise. Consider therefore, Theodorus, whether it is expedient to proceed into such a mighty danger.

THEO. Nothing ought to prevent us, Socrates, from considering what each of these men say.

SOC. Let us consider their assertions then, since you so earnestly desire it. It appears to me, therefore, that this speculation should commence from motion—I mean, what that motion is by which they say all things are moved. But what I wish to say is this: whether they say there is one species of motion, or, as it appears to me, two. Nor do I alone wish to know this myself, but I wish that you also may partake with me in this information, so that we may together be affected in a proper manner. Tell me, therefore, do you say a thing is moved when it changes one place for another, or is turned round in the same place?

THEO. I do.

SOC. Let this, therefore, be one species. But when anything abiding in the same place becomes old, or from being white becomes black, or from being soft becomes hard, or is changed by any other internal change, may not this be deservedly called another species of motion?

THEO. It appears so to me.

SOC. It is necessary, therefore, that there should be these two species of motion: namely, <term>alliation</term> <note>original: "alliation"; a philosophical term for qualitative change or alteration</note>, or internal change, and <term>lation</term> <note>original: "lation"; a philosophical term for local motion or change of place</note>.

THEO. Rightly said.

SOC. Having, therefore, made this division, let us now discourse with those who assert that all things are moved, and thus interrogate them: Do you say that everything is moved both ways—namely, according to lation and alliation—or that one thing is moved both ways, and another only in one way?

<summary>Socrates and Theodorus begin an investigation into the nature of motion, distinguishing between two types: change of place (lation) and change of quality (alliation).</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theodorus, Theaetetus, motion, lation, alliation, qualitative change, Greek philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 2007 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Theodorus regarding the Heraclitean doctrine of universal flux and its implications for perception.</meta>

<page-num>58</page-num>
# THE THEAETETUS

Theodorus: By Jupiter, I do not know what to say, but I think they would reply that everything is moved in both ways <note>original: "both ways" refers to the two types of motion previously discussed: change of place and change of quality</note>.

Socrates: Otherwise, my friend, things would appear to them to be both moving and standing still, and it would not be any more proper to assert that all things are moved than that they stand still.

Theodorus: Most true.

Socrates: Since, therefore, it is necessary that they should be moved, and that not one single thing should remain unmoved, all things will always be moved with every kind of motion.

Theodorus: It is necessary.

Socrates: Consider, likewise, this regarding their assertions—I mean concerning the generation of heat, or whiteness, or anything else. Do we not say that they assert that each of these is carried along, together with sensation, between the agent <note>the thing acting or the object</note> and the patient <note>the thing being acted upon or the perceiver</note>? And that the patient, indeed, is capable of sensation but has not yet become "sense" itself; while the agent is that which produces an effect but is not yet a "quality"? Perhaps, therefore, "quality" may appear to you to be an unusual name, and you do not understand me when I speak of these things collectively. Hear me, then, part by part. For the agent is neither heat nor whiteness in itself, but it becomes hot and white; and so it is with respect to other things. For do you not recollect that we observed before that nothing is any one thing essentially—neither that which is an agent, nor that which is a patient—but that from the meeting of both with each other, sensation and sensible things are generated, so that some things become certain qualities and others become sentient?

Theodorus: I recollect. For how is it possible I should not?

Socrates: As to other things, therefore, we shall omit the consideration of whether they speak in this manner concerning them or not. But let us attend only to this one thing for the sake of which we are now discoursing; and let us ask them: "Are all things moved, and do they flow as you say?" For is this not what they say?

Theodorus: Yes.

Socrates: Are they not, therefore, moved with both those motions which we enumerated, namely <term>lation</term> <note>original: "lation"; modern: local motion or change of place</note> and <term>alliation</term> <note>original: "alliation"; modern: alteration or change of quality</note>?

Theodorus: Undoubtedly; since it is necessary that they should be perfectly moved.

<summary>Socrates and Theodorus discuss the Heraclitean theory that all things are in a constant state of both physical motion and qualitative change, arguing that perception arises only from the interaction between an object and a perceiver.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theodorus, Heraclitus, flux, motion, lation, alliation, perception, agent, patient, quality</keywords>

--- Page 2008 ---
Socrates: If, therefore, things were only moving through space <note>original: "borne along"</note>, but were not internally changing, we might be able to describe the nature of these flowing things. Or what do you think?

Theodorus: I agree.

Socrates: But since even a "flowing white thing" does not remain white as it flows, but changes so that the whiteness itself is in flux and transitions into another color—and we cannot find it staying the same—can we correctly call it any specific color?

Theodorus: How is that possible, Socrates? How can we name whiteness, or anything else of that kind, if it is always slipping away even as we speak because it is in a state of constant flow?

Socrates: And what shall we say of the senses, such as seeing or hearing? Does anything in the act of seeing or hearing ever remain stable?

Theodorus: It should not, if it is true that all things are in motion.

Socrates: We must conclude, then, that a person no more "sees" than "does not see," nor uses any other sense more than they "do not use" it, since all things are moving in every possible way.

Theodorus: We must conclude that.

Socrates: Yet you and Theætetus said that perception <note>original: "sense"</note> is knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>.

Theodorus: We did.

Socrates: Therefore, when asked what knowledge is, our answer must be that it is no more "knowledge" than it is "not knowledge."

Theodorus: So it appears.

Socrates: This would be a fine "correction" to our answer! We wanted to prove that all things are in motion so that our definition of knowledge would seem correct. But it seems instead that if all things are in motion, every answer to every question is equally right. One could say a thing "is so" and "is not so," or if you prefer, that it is "becoming" <note>original: "in generation"</note> so, to avoid using words that imply standing still.

Theodorus: You are right.

Socrates: Except for this, Theodorus: we shouldn't even say "it is so" or "it is not so." For if we say "so," the thing is no longer moving; and if we say "not so," it is also a kind of standing still. Those who hold this theory of total flux need a new language, because currently they have no words to describe their view—unless perhaps the phrase "not even in this way" <note>original: "ουδ' ουτως" (oud' houtos)</note> might suit them best, as it is the most indefinite.

<summary>Socrates argues that if the theory of universal flux is true—meaning everything changes internally and externally at every moment—then language itself fails, and perception cannot be called knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theodorus, Theætetus, flux, Heracliteanism, epistemology, perception, constant change, nature of knowledge</keywords>

# THE THEAETETUS

**SOCRATES:** Do you say the same of the similar and the dissimilar, of the same and the different?

**THEAETETUS:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** But what about the beautiful and the ugly <note>original: "base"</note>, the good and the evil?

**THEAETETUS:** It appears to me that the soul principally considers the essence of these by comparing them with each other, reflecting within itself on things past and present with reference to those in the future.

**SOCRATES:** Take notice also of this: the soul perceives the hardness of a hard thing through the touch, and in a similar manner the softness of a soft thing; does it not?

**THEAETETUS:** It does.

**SOCRATES:** But their essence—what they are, their mutual opposition <note>original: "contrariety"</note>, and the nature of that opposition—the soul endeavors to distinguish by withdrawing into herself and comparing them with each other.

**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** Now, is the power of perceiving such sensations <note>original: "passions," referring to the way the soul is acted upon by external stimuli</note> that reach the soul through the body naturally present in both humans and animals as soon as they are born? And is reasoning about the essence and utility of these sensations only developed in those who achieve it with great difficulty, over a long period of time, through many specific experiences and through education <note>original: "discipline"</note>?

**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** Can we, therefore, grasp the truth through something by which we cannot grasp essence?

**THEAETETUS:** Impossible.

**SOCRATES:** But can anyone possess knowledge <note>original: "science," from the Latin *scientia*</note> of a thing when they do not grasp the truth of that thing?

**THEAETETUS:** How could he, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** Knowledge, therefore, does not reside in sensations, but resides in the reasoning process about them. For by this process, it appears, we may be able to reach essence and truth; but this cannot be achieved through sensations alone.

**THEAETETUS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** Can you, therefore, call sensation and knowledge the same thing, when there is such a great difference between them?

**THEAETETUS:** It would not be right to do so.

**Socrates:** But what name do you give to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, becoming hot, and becoming cold?

**THEÆTETUS:** I should give to all these the name of perception. For what other name can be given to them?

**Socrates:** Do you, therefore, call the whole of this "sense"?

**THEÆTETUS:** Necessarily so.

**Socrates:** But we said that this was not capable of touching upon truth, because it could not apprehend the essence <note>original: *ousia*; the fundamental nature or being of a thing</note> of a thing.

**THEÆTETUS:** It certainly cannot.

**Socrates:** Neither, therefore, can it touch upon science <note>original: *episteme*; here meaning certain knowledge or systematic understanding</note>.

**THEÆTETUS:** It cannot.

**Socrates:** Science, therefore, and sense, Theætetus, can never be the same.

**THEÆTETUS:** It appears, Socrates, they cannot.

**Socrates:** And now it becomes most eminently apparent that science is something different from sense. But we did not begin this conversation for the sake of finding out what science is *not*, but so that we might discover what it *is*. At the same time, we have advanced thus far as to be convinced that we must not seek for it in sense at all, but in that name which the soul possesses when it is occupied with beings <note>original: *ta onta*; things that truly exist</note>, itself by itself.

**THEÆTETUS:** But this, Socrates, is I think called *to opine* <note>original: *doxazein*; to form an opinion or belief</note>.

**Socrates:** You suspect¹ rightly, my friend. And now again consider from the beginning, obliterating all that has been already said, whether you can see more clearly, since we have proceeded thus far. And again tell me what science is.

**THEÆTETUS:** It is impossible, Socrates, to say that every opinion is science, because there are false opinions. But it appears that true opinion is science. And this is my answer. But if in the course of the inquiry it shall not appear to be so, as it does at present, I shall endeavor to say something else.

---

<note>¹ Socrates, in saying that Theætetus *suspects rightly*, indicates that he does not yet have a dianoetic <note>original: *dianoia*; relating to the discursive reason or the intellect's power to think through a problem</note> and scientific conception of the name in which science is to be found. For this name is *dianoia*, or the dianoetic power of the soul, whose very essence, as we have elsewhere observed, consists in reasoning scientifically. Hence he very properly says, "You suspect rightly" <note>original Greek: *orthos gar oiei*</note>. For his conception was nothing more than a vague conjecture or suspicion; at the same time, it was as accurate as could be obtained by mere suspicion.</note>

**THEÆTETUS:** But, Socrates, nothing else remains regarding any particular thing, except either knowing it or not knowing it.

SOCRATES: Is it not therefore necessary that he who forms an opinion should either form an opinion about things he knows something about, or about things he knows nothing about?

THEÆTETUS: It is necessary.

SOCRATES: Is it not likewise impossible that he who knows a thing should not know it, or that he who does not know it should know it?

THEÆTETUS: Undoubtedly.

SOCRATES: Therefore, does he who forms a false opinion regarding the things he knows, believe that these are not the things he knows, but something different from them—which he also knows at the same time? And though he knows both, is he ignorant of both?

THEÆTETUS: But this, Socrates, is impossible.

SOCRATES: Does he, therefore, think that the things he is ignorant of are certain other things that he is also ignorant of? And can he who knows neither Theætetus nor Socrates ever be persuaded to think that Socrates is Theætetus, or that Theætetus is Socrates?

THEÆTETUS: How could that be possible?

SOCRATES: Nor, again, can anyone think that the things he knows are the same as those he is ignorant of; or that the things he is ignorant of are the same as those he knows.

THEÆTETUS: For that would be monstrous.

SOCRATES: How then can anyone entertain false opinions? For it is impossible to form an opinion in any way other than these, since we either know or do not know all things. But in these scenarios, it seems in no way possible to form a false opinion.

THEÆTETUS: Most true.

SOCRATES: Should we, therefore, consider the object of our inquiry not by proceeding according to "knowing" and "not knowing," but according to "being" and "non-being"? <note>original: "being and non-being" refers to the ontological status of things—whether they exist or do not exist.</note>

THEÆTETUS: What do you mean?

SOCRATES: It is not a simple thing; because he who, with respect to anything, believes things which are not, must unavoidably believe falsely, in whatever manner the details pertaining to his <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic" refers to the capacity for discursive reason or the thinking mind.</note> part may exist.

THEÆTETUS: It is right that it should be so, Socrates.

SOCRATES: How then shall we answer, Theaetetus, if someone should ask us—and it is quite possible that what I am about to say might actually happen—"Can any man form an opinion <note>original: "opine"</note> about that which is not, whether it concerns actual beings or is considered by itself alone?" To this, it seems, we should reply that he thinks about that which is not when, in the act of forming an opinion, he does not think the truth. Or how should we put it?

THEAETETUS: In that manner.

SOCRATES: Does a thing of this kind, therefore, take place in any other context?

THEAETETUS: Of what kind?

SOCRATES: That someone sees something, and yet sees nothing at all?

THEAETETUS: But how could he?

SOCRATES: But if he sees one specific thing, he sees something which ranks among existing beings. Or do you think that "the one" <note>The concept of a single, unified thing.</note> does not rank among beings?

THEAETETUS: I do not think that.

SOCRATES: He, therefore, who sees one specific thing sees a certain being.

THEAETETUS: It appears so.

SOCRATES: And, therefore, he who hears a certain thing hears one specific thing, and thus a certain being.

THEAETETUS: He does so.

SOCRATES: And does not he also who touches a certain thing touch one specific thing, and that which has an existence, since it is a single thing?

THEAETETUS: This also is true.

SOCRATES: And does not he who forms an opinion think of one specific thing?

THEAETETUS: I grant it.

SOCRATES: He, therefore, who thinks of that which has no being thinks of nothing.

THEAETETUS: So it appears.

SOCRATES: But he who thinks of nothing does not form an opinion in any respect.

THEAETETUS: That is evident, it seems.

SOCRATES: It is impossible, therefore, to think of that which is not, either in relation to existing beings or as a concept by itself.

THEAETETUS: So it appears.

SOCRATES: To think falsely, therefore, is different from thinking of things which do not exist.

THEAETETUS: It appears that it is different.

<summary>Socrates argues that it is impossible to "think of nothing," concluding that false opinion cannot simply be the act of thinking about non-existent things, as thinking must always have an object.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, epistemology, false opinion, being vs. non-being, perception, logic</keywords>

# THE THEAETETUS. 69

SOCRATES. For false opinion is neither inherent in us in this manner, nor in the manner which we considered a little before.

THEAETETUS. It is not.

SOCRATES. Perhaps, therefore, we may define it as follows.

THEAETETUS. How?

SOCRATES. We say that a "foreign opinion" <note>original: "allodoxia"; a term for mistaking one thing for another</note> is a false opinion when someone, through a shift in their intellectual activity <note>original: "dianoëtic energy"; the process of discursive reasoning</note>, claims that one thing is actually something else. In this way, he is always forming an opinion about something that exists, but he mistakes one thing for another; and because he misses the mark regarding the object he is considering, he may be justly said to have a false opinion.

THEAETETUS. You now appear to me to have spoken with the greatest correctness. For when anyone thinks that something ugly is beautiful, or that something beautiful is ugly, then he truly holds a false opinion.

SOCRATES. It is evident, Theaetetus, that you look down on me and do not hold me in much awe.

THEAETETUS. In what respect?

SOCRATES. I do not think I appear to you to have fully grasped the nature of what is truly false. You didn't notice my point: when I asked whether the swift and the slow, the light and the heavy, or any other opposites, could ever become their own opposites. They remain what they are according to their own nature, even if they are attributed to things that are contrary to them. However, I will let this pass, so that your confidence is not bolstered in vain. But is it agreeable to you, as you say, that to have a false opinion is the same as "thinking foreign to the purpose"?

THEAETETUS. It is.

SOCRATES. It is possible, therefore, according to your opinion, for the intellectual power <note>original: "dianoëtic power"</note> to identify one thing as another, and not as the specific thing which it actually is ¹.

THEAETETUS. It is possible.

SOCRATES. When, therefore, the intellectual power does this, is it not necessary that it should be thinking about both of these things, or at least about one of them?

THEAETETUS. It is necessary.

SOCRATES. And, therefore, it must think about them either both together, or one after the other.

¹ This happens when the intellectual power turns itself toward the imagination, and as a result of this, produces false reasoning.

**THEAETETUS.** Most excellent.
**SOCRATES.** But do you define <term>dianoetic</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic energy"; referring to the process of discursive reasoning or thinking things through step-by-step</note> activity the same way I do?
**THEAETETUS.** How do you define it?
**SOCRATES.** As the discourse which the soul carries out within itself concerning the subjects it considers. I am explaining this to you like an unskilled person, but it seems to me that when the soul thinks discursively, it is doing nothing other than holding a conversation with itself <sup>1</sup>—asking questions and answering them, affirming and denying. But when it has reached a definition and asserts something without hesitation—whether it arrived there slowly or quickly—I call this <term>opinion</term> <sup>2</sup>. So, I define "to form an opinion" as "to speak," and I define "opinion" as a discourse addressed not to someone else, nor spoken aloud, but addressed to oneself. What do you call it?
**THEAETETUS.** I call it the same.
**SOCRATES.** Therefore, when anyone forms an opinion that one thing is another, he is saying to himself, it appears, that one thing is another.
**THEAETETUS.** Undoubtedly.
**SOCRATES.** Recall whether you have ever said to yourself that the beautiful is actually ugly <note>original: "base"</note>, or that the unjust is just. Or, to reach the heart of the matter, have you ever attempted to persuade yourself that one thing is definitely another thing? On the contrary, have you ever dared, even in your sleep, to say to yourself that even numbers are entirely odd, or anything else of that kind?
**THEAETETUS.** Certainly never.
**SOCRATES.** Do you think, then, that any other person—whether they are sane or insane—would seriously dare to say to themselves, and truly believe it, that a horse is necessarily an ox, or that two things are actually one thing?
**THEAETETUS.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, I do not.
**SOCRATES.** If, therefore, forming an opinion is a man speaking to himself, no one—while he speaks and thinks of two different things and touches upon both with his soul—will say and believe that one of them is the other. But we will dismiss this, if you

<sup>2</sup> Opinion is the conclusion of the dianoetic activity. See the *Sophist* <note>original: "Sophista"; a dialogue by Plato</note>.

<header>THE THEÆTETUS</header>

please, this word *the other*. For my meaning is this: that no one will think <note>original: "opine"</note> that the base is the beautiful, or anything else of this kind.

THEÆTETUS. You have my permission, Socrates, to dismiss this word; and the case appears to me to be as you say.

SOCRATES. He, therefore, who thinks of both these cannot think that one of them is the other.

THEÆTETUS. So it appears.

SOCRATES. And again, he who only thinks of one of these, but by no means the other, can never think that one of them is the other.

THEÆTETUS. True. For he would be compelled to touch upon that which he is not even thinking about.

SOCRATES. Neither, therefore, can he who thinks of both, nor he who only thinks of one of them, think "foreign to the purpose" <note>Socrates is arguing that if you know two things, or only one, you cannot confuse them in your mind.</note>. THEÆTETUS. It does not appear that it will.

SOCRATES. But, Theætetus, if this should not appear to be the case, we would be compelled to confess many things, and of an absurd nature.

THEÆTETUS. What are these?

SOCRATES. I will not tell you until I have endeavored to consider the matter in every possible way. For I should be ashamed, regarding this point about which we are in doubt, if we were compelled to confess what I am now suggesting. But if we discover the object of our search and become free from doubt, then we may speak concerning others as suffering these things, while we ourselves shall be raised beyond the reach of ridicule. But if we should be involved in inescapable doubts, and thus become dejected and filled with nausea, then, I think, we should permit our discourse to trample on us and use us as it pleases. Hear, then, whether I have found any path toward the object of our inquiry.

THEÆTETUS. Only speak.

SOCRATES. I shall now say that we were wrong to agree when we acknowledged that it was impossible for anyone to think that the things which he knows are things which he does not know, and thus be deceived. Instead, I say that this is, in a certain respect, possible.
