# THE THEAETETUS

**THEAETETUS.** Are you saying what I suspected might be the case when we made this assertion? For instance, if I know Socrates, but see another person at a distance whom I do not know, I might think it was Socrates, whom I do know. For what you are describing happens in a situation like that.

**SOCRATES.** Are we not, therefore, forced away from the hypothesis that caused us to admit that we are ignorant of things we know, at the very same time that we know them?

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** We must not, therefore, establish that hypothesis, but the following one; perhaps someone will agree with us in some respect, or perhaps they will oppose us. But we are now in a situation where it is necessary to examine the kind of reasoning that turns everything upside down. Consider, therefore, whether I am saying anything to the point. Is it possible for someone who was formerly ignorant of something to afterwards learn that thing?

**THEAETETUS.** It certainly is possible.

**SOCRATES.** And can he not also learn one thing after another?

**THEAETETUS.** Why should he not?

**SOCRATES.** Imagine for me, for the sake of an example, a <term>waxen image</term><gloss>1</gloss> inside our souls. In one soul, let there be a larger image, and in another a smaller one; in one, let it be made of purer wax, but in another of impurer and harder wax. In some souls, let the wax be of a moister kind, but in others, let it be sufficiently tempered <note>meaning properly balanced in consistency</note>.

**THEAETETUS.** I imagine it.

**SOCRATES.** We must say, then, that this is a gift of <term>Mnemosyne</term> <note>The Greek goddess of memory</note>, the mother of the <term>Muses</term> <note>The nine goddesses of the arts and sciences</note>. Whatever we wish to remember of the things we have seen, heard, or thought of, is impressed upon this wax like images made by a signet seal, by pressing itself into our senses and thoughts. Furthermore, we remember and know whatever is impressed in this waxen image as long as the figure remains; but when it is blurred or can no longer receive an impression, we forget and cease to know.

**THEAETETUS.** Let it be so.

***

<note>1</note> What is said here must not be understood literally; for Plato by no means believed that images are physically shaped by external objects within the soul. Rather, nothing more is meant here than that the soul either naturally possesses these images, or that, taking the opportunity provided by external movements and the experiences of the body, she creates forms within herself by her own inherent power.

<summary>Socrates introduces the famous "wax tablet" metaphor to explain how the soul receives and retains memories as impressions, exploring how learning and forgetting function within the mind.</summary>

# THE THEAETETUS

**SOCRATES:** Consider, therefore, whether he who knows these impressions, and attends to what he either sees or hears, can in this manner form a false opinion?

**THEAETETUS:** In what manner?

**SOCRATES:** With respect to what he knows, at one time believing that he knows it, and at another time that he does not know it. For we improperly granted earlier that it was impossible for this to happen.

**THEAETETUS:** But what do you say now?

**SOCRATES:** It is necessary to speak about these things in this way, defining them from the beginning: It is impossible that he who knows anything, and has a memory <note>original: "monument"</note> of it in his soul but does not currently perceive it, can believe it is something else which he also knows and possesses an image of, but does not perceive. 

And again, it is impossible that anyone can believe that what he knows is something which he does *not* know, and of which he does not possess an image. Or that what he does not know is something which he knows. 

It is likewise impossible for anyone to believe that what he perceives is some other sensory object different from what he perceives; or that what he perceives is something which he does not perceive; or that what he does not perceive is something else which he does not perceive; or that what he does not perceive is something which he *does* perceive. 

Nor, again, can anyone believe that what he knows and perceives—and of which he has a sensory image—is something else which he knows and perceives, and of which he similarly possesses a sensory image. Or that what he knows and perceives, and of which he possesses an image in a proper manner, is the same as that which he simply knows. Or that what he knows and perceives, and similarly retains, is that which he perceives. Or again, that what he neither knows nor perceives is the same as that which he simply does not know; or that what he neither knows nor perceives is the same as that which he does not perceive. 

For in all these cases, it is impossible to form a false opinion. It remains, therefore, that false opinion must occur in some things of this kind, if it has any existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> at all.

**THEAETETUS:** In what things, then? Tell me, so that I may see whether I can understand better from these examples. For at present, I do not follow you.

**SOCRATES:** In those things which a person knows, but believes they are certain other things which he knows and perceives; or which he does not know,

**SOCRATES.** Learn this, therefore, the first of the things which I wish to demonstrate to you: that it is possible for a man not to perceive that which he knows, and that it is likewise possible for him to perceive it.

**THEAETETUS.** True.

**THEAETETUS.** This also is true.

**SOCRATES.** See, then, if you can now follow me better. Socrates knows Theodorus and Theaetetus, but sees neither of them, nor is any other sense present with him respecting them. Can he ever in this case opine in himself that Theaetetus is Theodorus? Do I say anything of substance, or nothing?

**THEAETETUS.** You speak pertinently; for he cannot thus opine.

**SOCRATES.** This then was the first of those things which I said.

**THEAETETUS.** It was.

**SOCRATES.** But the second was this: that while I know one of you, but do not know the other, and perceive neither of you, I can never opine that he whom I know is the man whom I do not know.

**THEAETETUS.** Right.

**SOCRATES.** But the third was this: that while I neither know nor perceive either of them, I can never opine that he whom I do not know is some other person whom I do not know. And in a similar manner, think that you again hear all that was said above, in which I can never opine falsely respecting you and Theodorus—neither while knowing nor while ignorant of both, nor while knowing one and not knowing the other. And the same may be said respecting the senses, if you understand me.

**THEAETETUS.** I understand you.

I then endeavor to assign the proper impression of each person to my specific sight, trying to fit the visual image into its own footprint <note>original: "vestige"</note> so that recognition may occur. But if I fail in the attempt—much like someone putting their shoes on the wrong feet—I transfer the vision of each person to the wrong impression. I err by being affected in the same way as the eyes are by mirrors, where things on the right side are reflected back to the left. In that moment, "other-thinking" <note>original: "heterodoxy"; here meaning the mistaking of one thing for another</note> takes place, and I hold a false opinion.

**THEAETETUS.** I did not.

This leads Socrates to conclude that false opinion cannot simply be a mismatch between thought and sensory perception.</summary>

# THE THEÆTETUS

true definition, we should never be deceived in thought-based <term>dianoëtic: relating to the process of discursive reasoning or logical thought</term> conceptions themselves. But now, either there is no such thing as false opinion, or, if there is, a man may be ignorant of that which he simultaneously knows. And which of these options will you choose?

THEÆTETUS. You have proposed a difficult choice, Socrates.

SOCRATES. But it appears that reason will not permit both of these to be true at once. At the same time, however (for we must attempt all things), what if we should endeavor to cast aside our shame?

THEÆTETUS. How so?

SOCRATES. By being willing to say what it is to have a scientific knowledge of a thing.

THEÆTETUS. But why would this be considered impudent?

SOCRATES. You do not appear to understand that our entire discourse from the beginning has been an investigation of science <note>original: "episteme," often translated as "knowledge" or "scientific understanding"</note>, as if we did not already know what it is.

THEÆTETUS. I understand you.

SOCRATES. But does it not appear to be the mark of impudent people to try to show what it is to have scientific knowledge, while they are simultaneously ignorant of what science actually is? But, Theætetus, for some time now our speech has lacked precision. For we have ten thousand times employed the terms, "We know," and "We do not know," "We have scientific knowledge," and "We do not have scientific knowledge," as if we mutually understood one another, while all the while we are ignorant of what science is. Even at this moment, if you are willing, we are using the terms "to be ignorant" and "to understand," as if it were proper to use them while we are still destitute of the very definition of science.

THEÆTETUS. But in that case, Socrates, how will we be able to carry on the discussion?

SOCRATES. Not at all, while I remain as I am. But I might be able to if I were a professional debater <note>original: "contentious," referring to the Eristics who argued for victory rather than truth</note>. If such a person were present now, he would say that he abstained from using such terms, and he would severely rebuke us for the way I am speaking. But, since we are only ordinary men, are you willing for me to dare to say what it is to know scientifically? For it appears to me to be worth the effort.

THEÆTETUS. Dare then, by Jupiter <note>original: "Zeus"</note>. For you will certainly deserve to be pardoned for the attempt.

SOCRATES. Have you heard what people currently say it is to know scientifically?

# THE THEAETETUS

**THEAETETUS.** Perhaps so; but at present I do not remember.
**SOCRATES.** They say that knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> is a habit of the mind.
**THEAETETUS.** True.
**SOCRATES.** We, therefore, shall make a trifling alteration, and say that it is the *possession* of knowledge.
**THEAETETUS.** But in what way do you say this differs from the other?
**SOCRATES.** Perhaps in nothing. But when you have heard what appears to me to be the case, examine it together with me.
**THEAETETUS.** I will, if I can.
**SOCRATES.** To *possess*, therefore, does not appear to me to be the same as to *have* a thing. For example, if someone buys a garment, and, having the power of using it when he pleases, does not actually wear it, we should not say that he *has* the garment on him, but that he *possesses* it.
**THEAETETUS.** And very properly so.
**SOCRATES.** See then whether it is possible to possess knowledge in this manner, without "having" it at that moment: just as if someone had caught certain wild doves<sup>1</sup>, or other wild birds, and having constructed an aviary for them at home, should feed and nourish them. For in a certain respect we should say that he always *has* them, because he *possesses* them. Should we not?
**THEAETETUS.** We should.
**SOCRATES.** But in another respect we should say that he by no means *has* them in his hand, but rather that he has a power—since he has shut them up for his own use in an enclosure of his own—of taking and holding them when he pleases, and of again letting them go; and that he can do this as often as he likes.
**THEAETETUS.** Exactly so.
**SOCRATES.** Again, just as before we devised a sort of waxen model <note>original: "waxen figment"</note> in the soul, so now let us place a certain aviary in the soul containing all sorts of birds. Some of these fly in flocks, apart from others; but others again fly in—

---

<sup>1</sup> It is justly observed by Proclus, in his admirable Commentary on the first book of Euclid's Elements, page 3, that Socrates here, mingling the humorous with the serious, compares the various branches of knowledge <note>original: "sciences"</note> which are within us to doves. He also says that they fly away, some in flocks, and others separate from the rest. For the sciences that are more general contain within themselves many that are more specific; and those that are divided according to their type, touching on the objects of their knowledge, are separated from and not joined with each other, because they originate from different primary principles.

<summary>Socrates introduces the "aviary" metaphor to distinguish between possessing knowledge (having it stored in the mind) and having knowledge (actively using or grasping it). This replaces the earlier "wax tablet" model to better explain how one can possess information but still make mistakes.</summary>

**THEAETETUS.** Let it be so: but what follows?

**SOCRATES.** It is necessary to say that this receptacle is empty in children. In the place of birds, we must understand "sciences" <note>original: "sciences"; here meaning branches of knowledge or systematic learning</note>, and say that he who acquires a science and confines it in this enclosure has learned or discovered the thing of which he possesses the knowledge; and that this is what it means to have scientific knowledge.

**THEAETETUS.** Be it so.

**SOCRATES.** But again, consider what names should be used to express these actions: when someone wishes to hunt for these sciences, to take hold of them, to *possess* them, and afterwards to release them. Should we use the same names as we did at first when the sciences were first *acquired*, or different names? You will understand what I mean more clearly from what follows. **THEAETETUS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Suppose this art to be the hunting of the knowledge of all even and odd numbers.

**THEAETETUS.** I suppose it is.

**SOCRATES.** And I think that by this art, the arithmetician has the knowledge of numbers in his power and delivers them to others.

**THEAETETUS.** He does so.

**SOCRATES.** And we say that he who delivers this knowledge "teaches," while he who receives it "learns"; and he who holds it, because he possesses it in that enclosure we mentioned, "knows" it scientifically.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** But attend to what follows. Does not a perfect arithmetician know all numbers scientifically? For the knowledge of all numbers is in his soul.

**THEAETETUS.** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES.** Does not such a man sometimes count to himself internally, and sometimes count aloud externally, those things that have number?

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** But to "number" <note>original: "to number"; meaning to count or calculate</note> is considered by us as nothing else than the observation of the quantity of any given number.

**THEAETETUS.** It is so.

# THE THEAETETUS

**Socrates:** He, therefore, who has scientific knowledge, by speculating in this way, appears not to know—even though we have admitted that he knows every number. Do you hear these ambiguities?

**Theaetetus:** I do.

**Socrates:** When we compared sciences to the possession and hunting of doves, we said that hunting was twofold. One kind occurs prior to acquisition and exists for the sake of gaining possession; the other occurs after acquisition and possession, and exists for the sake of catching and holding in the hands things that were already possessed. In the same way, those sciences which someone had previously acquired through learning, and which he had known before, may be learned again by resuming and retaining the science of every particular thing he formerly possessed, but which he does not have immediately at hand in his <term>dianoetic</term> <note>original: "dianoëtic"; referring to the capacity for discursive reasoning or the thinking mind</note> part.

**Theaetetus:** True.

**Socrates:** For this reason, I just now inquired how names regarding these things were to be used—as when an <term>arithmetician</term> <note>a mathematician or one skilled in the theory of numbers</note> counts, or a <term>grammarian</term> reads. For, in either case, he who knows applies himself again to know for himself what he already knows.

**Theaetetus:** But this is absurd, Socrates.

**Socrates:** Shall we therefore say that the grammarian reads, or the arithmetician counts, things of which he is ignorant—even though we have granted that the one knows all letters and the other knows every number?

**Theaetetus:** But this is also irrational.

**Socrates:** Are you, therefore, willing for us to say that we are not at all concerned with how anyone might use the names "knowing" and "learning"? Since we have determined that it is one thing to *possess* science and another to *have* it, we must say that it is impossible for anyone not to possess that which he does possess. So, it will never happen that anyone does not know that which he actually knows; however, a false opinion may still be formed about that very thing. For it may happen that we mistake the science of one thing for the science of another when, hunting after one of our internal sciences, we erroneously catch some other science that flies past instead. This is like when someone believes that eleven things are twelve: for then, grasping the science of eleven instead of twelve, he takes a pigeon out of his aviary instead of a dove.

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between possessing knowledge (having it in the mind's "aviary") and actively having it in hand, explaining how one can make a mistake by "catching" the wrong piece of knowledge.</summary>

THEAETETUS. It is reasonable to suppose so.

SOCRATES. But when he catches that which he endeavors to catch, then he is free from falsehood and holds opinions that are true. In this manner, false and true opinion exist; and thus, none of the specific problems that disturbed us before will be an obstacle to us any longer. Perhaps, therefore, you agree with me? Or what will you do?

THEAETETUS. I agree with you.

SOCRATES. We are then now freed from the dilemma regarding a man knowing and at the same time not knowing a thing. For it will no longer happen that we shall not possess that which we do possess, whether we judge falsely or not. However, a more dreadful problem <note>original: "dire passion"</note> than this appears to me to present itself to our view.

THEAETETUS. What is that?

SOCRATES. If the exchange <note>original: "permutation"</note> of different branches of knowledge <note>original: "sciences"</note> should ever become false opinion.

THEAETETUS. But how?

SOCRATES. In the first place, is it not absurd that he who has the knowledge of anything should be ignorant of that very thing—not through ignorance, but through the knowledge of the thing itself? And in the next place, that he should judge this thing to be that, and that thing to be this? And is it not very irrational to suppose that when knowledge is present, the soul should know nothing, but should be ignorant of all things? For, following this logic, nothing hinders ignorance, when present, from enabling a man to know something, or causing blindness to see, if knowledge can ever make a man ignorant of anything.

THEAETETUS. Perhaps, Socrates, we have not properly introduced the birds. We only placed various kinds of knowledge <note>original: "sciences"</note> in the soul, but we ought at the same time to have placed various kinds of ignorance flying there in groups. Then, a man employed in "hunting" <note>original: "fowling"</note> would at one time catch knowledge and at another time ignorance about the same thing. Through ignorance he would hold a false opinion, but through knowledge he would hold the truth.

SOCRATES. It is by no means easy, Theaetetus, not to praise you. However, consider again what you have said. For let it be as you say. But he who catches ignorance, you will say, holds false opinions. Is it not so?

THEAETETUS. It is.

SOCRATES. But yet he will not think that he holds a false opinion.

# THE THEAETETUS

THEAETETUS. I propose that true opinion is science <note>original: "science"; here meaning certain knowledge or systematic understanding</note>. For to hold a true opinion is to be without error, and everything that proceeds from it is beautiful and good.

SOCRATES. Theaetetus, the man who leads others across a river, if asked about the depth of the water, will answer that the water itself will reveal its own depth. In the same way, if we move forward into our present subject and continue our inquiry, the very obstacle that hinders our passage may perhaps reveal the object of our search. But if we remain where we are, nothing will become clear.

THEAETETUS. You speak well; let us proceed and consider it.

SOCRATES. Is this not a matter that requires only brief consideration? For the whole of the legal art, and those who practice it, demonstrate that their art is not the same as science.

THEAETETUS. How so? And who are these practitioners?

SOCRATES. Those who excel all others in wisdom and who are called orators and lawyers. For these men persuade, but they do not teach by their art; they cause their hearers to form whatever opinion they please. Or do you think there are any teachers so skillful that they are able—in cases of robbery or other acts of violence—to sufficiently prove the truth of what happened in the short time allowed by a little water? <note>original: "a little water"; a reference to the clepsydra or water-clock used to time speeches in Athenian courts.</note>

THEAETETUS. I certainly do not think so; rather, these men persuade.

SOCRATES. But do you not agree that to persuade someone is the same thing as to cause them to form an opinion?

THEAETETUS. Undoubtedly.

SOCRATES. Therefore, when judges are justly persuaded regarding things that only an eyewitness can truly know, and not otherwise, is it possible for them to judge rightly? If they judge by report and hold a true opinion without having science, can they judge correctly even if we admit their judgment is sound?

THEAETETUS. I entirely believe they can.

SOCRATES. But, my friend, if true opinion, judgment, and science were the same thing, then even the most perfect judge could never hold a correct opinion without science. However, it now appears that each of these is something different.

THEAETETUS. I had forgotten, Socrates, what I heard a certain person say concerning science, but I remember it now. He said that true opinion in conjunction with reason <note>original: "reason"; likely translating the Greek 'logos', meaning an account, explanation, or rational justification</note> is science, but that without reason it is void of science. He argued that things cannot be known scientifically if there is no rational account for them, but that things which have a rational account can be known in this way.

<meta>The dialogue continues with Socrates examining the definition of science as "true opinion plus an account."</meta>

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus distinguish between "true opinion" and "science" by noting that lawyers can persuade judges of the truth without giving them firsthand knowledge. Theaetetus then introduces a new definition: that science is true opinion supported by a rational account.</summary>

# THE THEAETETUS

**Socrates:** How well you speak! But tell me how he divided things which may be scientifically known from those which cannot be so known, so that we may see whether you and I understand them in the same way.

**Theaetetus:** I do not know if I can discover for myself how he divided these; but I can follow along if another person explains it.

<margin>¹ Prodicus of Chios, imitating Leucippus, asserted that the elements of things are unknown because they are simple and therefore cannot be defined; however, composite things can be known since they can be defined.</margin>

**Socrates:** Hear, then, a dream in exchange for a dream. For I also seem to have heard from certain people that the first elements <note>original: "elements" refers here to the fundamental building blocks of matter or thought</note>, as it were, from which we and all other things are composed, cannot be rationally described. For they say that each of these can only be named by itself, but cannot be called anything else—neither that it "is" nor that it "is not"—because essence or non-existence would then be assigned to it. 

But it is necessary to add nothing if one speaks of a thing itself alone. For neither the term "this," nor "that," nor "each," nor "alone," nor any other such labels should be used, because these are applied to things in a circular fashion and are different from the things to which they are added. It is necessary, if possible, to speak of the thing itself, and if it has a proper definition, to state something regarding it without adding anything else. 

Now, however, none of these primary things can be made the subject of discourse; for they do not admit of anything other than a name. But the things composed from these elements are woven together, and just as they are woven, a discourse is produced from the weaving together of their names. For the connection of names is the essence of discourse. 

Hence, the elements themselves are ineffable <note>original: "ineffable"; meaning they cannot be expressed in words</note> and unknown, even though they are perceived by the senses. But "syllables" <note>original: "syllables" here refers to the combinations or complexes formed by the elements</note> are known and expressible, and may be understood through true opinion. Therefore, when anyone forms a true opinion of something without a rational explanation, his soul perceives the truth regarding it, but he does not truly *know* the thing; because he who is incapable of giving and receiving a rational explanation <note>original: "reason"</note> concerning a thing must be destitute of science <note>original: "science"; here meaning systematic, certain knowledge or *episteme*</note> regarding it. But when he receives a rational explanation, then he may be able to know all these things and acquire science in perfection. Have you heard this "dream" before, or is it something else?

**Theaetetus:** It is exactly that and nothing else.

<summary>Socrates presents a theory (the "dream") suggesting that fundamental elements are indefinable and only nameable, while their combinations (syllables) can be known through rational definition. This explores the relationship between simple components, complex structures, and the requirements for true scientific knowledge.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Theaetetus, Socrates, Prodicus of Chios, Leucippus, epistemology, elements and syllables, definition, rational explanation, ineffable, science vs. opinion</keywords>

**Socrates:** Is it, therefore, agreeable to you that we should establish science <note>original: "science"; here meaning "knowledge" or "systematic understanding"</note> to be true opinion in conjunction with reason?

**Theaetetus:** Very much so.

**Socrates:** Have we, therefore, Theaetetus, this very day detected that which many wise men in the past grew old investigating before they discovered it?

**Theaetetus:** To me, Socrates, what was just now said appears to be well said.

**Socrates:** And it is very fit it should be: for what science can there be without reason and right opinion? But one of the assertions does not please me.

**Theaetetus:** What is that?

**Socrates:** That which appears to be very elegantly said: that the elements of speech are unknown, but the category of syllables is known.

**Theaetetus:** Is this not correct?

**Socrates:** Take notice. For we have as the "hostages" <note>meaning the foundational examples or security for the argument</note> of our discourse those very paradigms <note>original: "paradigms"; examples or models</note> which the person who proposed this theory used when saying all that I have related.

**Theaetetus:** What are these paradigms?

**Socrates:** The things pertaining to letters—namely, elements and syllables. Or do you think that he who said what we have related spoke in this manner looking to anything else than these?

**Theaetetus:** To nothing else than these.

**Socrates:** Let us, therefore, taking these examples, examine them—or rather examine ourselves—to see whether we learn letters in this manner or not. In the first place, then, do syllables have a definition, while the elements do not?

**Theaetetus:** Perhaps so.

**Socrates:** To me, also, it very much appears to be so. If, therefore, anyone should ask you this regarding the first syllable of the word "Socrates"—O Theaetetus, what is *So*?—what would you answer?

**Theaetetus:** That it is *S* and *o*.

**Socrates:** You have, therefore, this definition of the syllable.

**Theaetetus:** I have.

**SOCRATES.** This, therefore, my friend, we have rightly asserted regarding science <note>original: "science"; here meaning "episteme" or systematic knowledge</note>.

**SOCRATES.** But have we rightly shown that a syllable is known, but an element is not?

**THEAETETUS.** It appears to me that we should say it is all the elements.

**THEAETETUS.** Undoubtedly.

**THEAETETUS.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** But what if he knows each, and yet, while knowing neither individually, he knows both together?

**THEAETETUS.** But this would be terrible and absurd, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** But if it is necessary to know each part if anyone is to know both, it is necessary that he who at any future time knows a syllable should previously know all the elements. **THEAETETUS.** And very suddenly, too.

**SOCRATES.** For we did not secure it well. Perhaps a syllable ought to have been defined not as the elements themselves, but as one specific form <note>original: "species"</note> produced from them, which is different from the elements.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so; and perhaps the matter works in this way rather than the other.

**SOCRATES.** We should consider this, therefore, and not in so weak <note>original: "effeminate"</note> a manner betray a great and venerable assertion.

**THEAETETUS.** We ought not, indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Let a syllable then, as we just now said, be one idea produced from several fitting elements, as much in letters as in all other things.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus debate whether a "syllable" (a whole) is simply the sum of its "elements" (parts) or a unique form emerging from them. They conclude that if the parts are unknowable, the whole must be as well, unless the whole is something distinct from its parts.</summary>

# THE THEAETETUS

SOCRATES. It ought not, therefore, to have any parts.

THEAETETUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. Because the whole of that which has parts must necessarily be all the parts. Or do you say that a whole which is produced from parts is one certain species <note>original: "species"; here meaning a distinct form or class</note> different from all the parts?

THEAETETUS. I do.

SOCRATES. But with respect to "the all" and "the whole," do you call each of these the same, or different?

THEAETETUS. I do not have anything clear to say; yet since you order me to answer with alacrity, I will venture to say that each of these is different.

SOCRATES. Your alacrity, Theaetetus, is right; but whether your answer is so, we must consider.

THEAETETUS. It is necessary.

SOCRATES. Does not the whole, therefore, differ from the all, according to your present assertion?

THEAETETUS. It does.

SOCRATES. But do "all things" and "the all" differ in any respect? As when we say one, two, three, four, five, six: or twice three, or thrice two, or four and two, or three and two and one, or five and one;—whether in all these do we say the same thing, or that which is different?

THEAETETUS. The same thing.

SOCRATES. Do we say anything else than six?

THEAETETUS. Nothing else.

SOCRATES. According to each mode of speaking, therefore, we find that "all" are six.

THEAETETUS. We do.

SOCRATES. Again, therefore, we do not say any one thing when we say "all things." <note>Socrates is arguing that the sum total of the parts is identical to the collection of the parts themselves.</note>

THEAETETUS. It is necessary.

SOCRATES. Do we say anything else than six things?

THEAETETUS. Nothing else.

SOCRATES. In things, therefore, which consist of number, we say that "the all" is the same as "all things."

THEAETETUS. So it appears.

<summary>Socrates leads Theaetetus through a logical exercise to determine if a "whole" is something distinct from the sum of its "parts," using the number six as a mathematical proof of their identity.</summary>

# THE THEAETETUS

**Socrates:** Should we not, therefore, say regarding these things, that the number of an acre is the same as an acre?
**Theaetetus:** We should.
**Socrates:** And in a similar manner, that the number of a stadium <note>original: "stadium"; a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet</note> is a stadium?
**Theaetetus:** Yes.
**Socrates:** And so regarding the number of an army, and an army itself, and all other such similar particulars? For every number, being an "all," is each of these particulars.
**Theaetetus:** It is.
**Socrates:** But is the number of each of these anything else than parts?
**Theaetetus:** Nothing else.
**Socrates:** Such things, therefore, as have parts consist of parts.
**Theaetetus:** It appears so.
**Socrates:** But it is acknowledged that all the parts are the "all," since every number is the "all."
**Theaetetus:** It is so.
**Socrates:** The "whole," therefore, is not derived from parts; for if it were, it would be the "all," because it consists of all the parts.
**Theaetetus:** It does not appear that it is.
**Socrates:** But does a part belong to anything else than to a "whole"?
**Theaetetus:** It belongs to the "all."
**Socrates:** You fight strenuously, Theaetetus. But is not the "all" this very thing—the "all"—when nothing is missing from it?
**Theaetetus:** It must be so.
**Socrates:** And is not, in the same manner, the "whole" that which it is when nothing is missing from it? And is it not true that whatever is in need of anything—because of this deficiency—is neither the "whole" nor the "all"?
**Theaetetus:** It now appears to me that the "whole" and the "all" do not differ from each other in any respect.
**Socrates:** Do we not say that the "whole" and the "all" are all the parts of that of which they are the parts?
**Theaetetus:** Entirely so.
**Socrates:** Again, therefore, so that we may resume what we attempted before,

<header>THE THEAETETUS</header>

**SOCRATES:** If a syllable is not the same as its elements, must it not necessarily follow that it does not have elements as parts of itself? Or, if it is the same as the elements, must it not be known in the same way they are?

**THEAETETUS:** It must.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, to avoid this conclusion, we must establish that the one is different from the other.

**THEAETETUS:** We must.

**SOCRATES:** But if elements are not parts of a syllable, can you name any other things that are parts of a syllable, yet are not its elements?

**THEAETETUS:** I would by no means agree, Socrates, that things which are not elements can be the parts of a syllable. For it is ridiculous to ignore the elements and go searching for other things.

**SOCRATES:** According to our current reasoning, then, Theaetetus, a syllable will be in every respect one particular <term>impartible idea</term> <note>original: "impartible idea"; an indivisible form or concept that cannot be broken down into smaller components</note>.

**THEAETETUS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** Do you remember, then, my friend, what we admitted a little while ago? We thought it was well said that there could be no rational explanation or definition of the "first things" <note>the primary elements or building blocks of reality</note> from which other things are composed. This is because each thing, when considered by itself, is not a <term>composite</term> <note>a thing made up of several parts</note>. We also said that neither the term "to be" nor the term "this" can properly be applied to such a thing, because these terms are treated as something different and foreign to the thing itself. Does not this very circumstance cause a thing to be <term>ineffable</term> <note>too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note> and unknown?

**THEAETETUS:** I do remember.

**SOCRATES:** Is there any cause other than this for a thing being uniform and indivisible? For I see no other cause.

**THEAETETUS:** It does not appear that there is any other.

**SOCRATES:** Will a syllable, therefore, be a <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning a specific form or type of being</note> of this kind, since it has no parts and is a single idea?

**THEAETETUS:** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** If, however, a syllable is made of many elements and is a certain "whole," and these elements are its parts, then syllables and elements must be known and described in the same way, since all the parts appear to be the same as the whole.

**THEAETETUS:** Very much so.

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus examine whether a syllable is merely the sum of its elements or a unique, indivisible "idea" that exists apart from its parts. They conclude that if a syllable is a single, partless entity, it must be as indefinable and "unknowable" as the primary elements themselves.</summary>

**SOCRATES:** But if a syllable is one indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> thing, then a syllable and an element are equally inexpressible <note>original: "ineffable"</note> and unknown. For the same cause renders them both so.

**THEAETETUS:** I cannot say otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** We must not, therefore, admit the assertion that a syllable is something known and expressible, while an element is the opposite.

**THEAETETUS:** We must not, if we are persuaded by this reasoning.

**SOCRATES:** But what if someone should assert the contrary? Would you not rather admit it based on those things you were conscious of when you first learned your letters?

**THEAETETUS:** What things are those?

**SOCRATES:** That you endeavored to learn nothing else than how to recognize the elements <note>In this context, "elements" refers to individual letters of the alphabet.</note> by your eyes and ears, each one by itself, so that their position—whether they were spoken or written—might not confuse you.

**SOCRATES:** And is learning to play the harp perfectly anything other than the ability to know which sound belongs to every string? For everyone agrees that these sounds should be called the "elements" of music.

**THEAETETUS:** It is nothing else.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, based on our experience with letters and syllables, if we were to draw a conclusion about other things, we would say that the category <note>original: "genus"</note> of elements provides a much clearer and more fundamental knowledge than that of syllables, especially for mastering any subject. And if anyone should say that a syllable is known, but that an element is naturally unknown, we would think he was joking, whether he meant to or not.

**THEAETETUS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** But, as it appears to me, there are still other ways to demonstrate this. However, we must not let these details make us forget our main goal: to investigate the claim that "reason" <note>original: "logos"</note> united with true opinion becomes the most perfect science <note>In this context, "science" refers to "episteme" or certain, systematic knowledge.</note>.

**THEAETETUS:** It is right, therefore, to consider this.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, inform me: what is the meaning of the word *logos*? For it appears to me to signify one of three things.

**THEAETETUS:** What are they?

SOCRATES: The first way to define it will be to make one's own mental conception <note>original: "dianoëtic conception"</note> apparent through the voice, using verbs and nouns; thus, the person's opinion is impressed upon the stream of breath flowing through the mouth, as if reflected in a mirror or in water. Does "logos" <note>original: "logos" - here meaning speech or discourse</note> not appear to you to be a thing of this kind?

THEAETETUS: It does; and we say that he who does this speaks.

SOCRATES: Cannot everyone do this—I mean, point out with more or less speed what appears to him regarding specific things—unless he is naturally deaf or dumb? And if so, it would follow that whoever holds a right opinion will always appear to hold it in conjunction with "logos"; thus, true opinion would never exist without science <note>original: "science" - here meaning "episteme" or certain knowledge</note>.

THEAETETUS: True.

SOCRATES: We must not, therefore, easily condemn the person who asserts that science is what we just mentioned, as if he said nothing of value. For perhaps this was not his full meaning; instead, he might have meant that when asked what a particular thing is, one should be able to answer the questioner by describing its basic elements.

THEAETETUS: How do you mean, Socrates?

SOCRATES: In the same way as Hesiod, when he speaks of a chariot as being composed of a hundred pieces of wood. I am not able to name them all, nor do I think you are. We would be satisfied if, when asked what a chariot is, we were able to say that it consists of wheels, an axle, the body-planking, the rims, and a yoke.

THEAETETUS: Entirely so.

SOCRATES: But he would perhaps think we are ridiculous—just as if we were asked your name and answered with a single syllable. He would acknowledge that what we say is true, but he would deny that we are grammarians, or that we possessed and spoke the grammatical definition of the name "Theaetetus" with expertise. He would likewise say that no one can speak scientifically about anything until he has reached a conclusion by going through all the elements, in conjunction with true opinion, as we observed before.

THEAETETUS: We did.

SOCRATES: In this manner, therefore, he would think we may possess a true opinion regarding the chariot; but that only he who is able to examine its essence through all its parts...

**SOCRATES.** Does anything, therefore, hinder the same person from being affected in the same manner regarding the second, third, and fourth syllable?

<header>THE THEÆTETUS.</header>

But likewise, if he has a flat nose and prominent eyes, shall I have a mental image of you any more than of myself, or any other person with such features?

SOCRATES. If I had met you yesterday, these distinct marks would remind me of you and cause me to form a correct opinion about you.

THEÆTETUS. Most true.

SOCRATES. Right opinion, therefore, regarding anything must be concerned with its "difference" <note>original: "difference"; here meaning the specific characteristics that distinguish one thing from all others</note>.

THEÆTETUS. It appears so.

SOCRATES. What then will be the consequence if "reason" <note>original: "logos"; here meaning a rational explanation or definition</note> is added to right opinion? For it would be ridiculous if someone should command us to form an opinion on exactly how a thing differs from other things.

THEÆTETUS. How so?

SOCRATES. Because, regarding things of which we already have a right opinion—specifically in how they differ from others—this person would be ordering us to *add* a right opinion of how they differ from others. And thus, like the spinning of a whip-top, or a pestle, or something similar, this command results in nothing being accomplished. It might more justly be called the command of a blind man; for it would order us to take hold of things we already possess, so that we might learn the very things we are already thinking. Thus, it would be perfectly similar to a command given to someone deprived of sight.

THEÆTETUS. Tell me what it is you just now asked.

SOCRATES. If someone, my boy, while ordering us to grasp "reason," should at the same time order us to *know*—rather than just have an opinion of—the difference, then "reason" would be a pleasant thing, and the most beautiful of all things pertaining to <term>science</term> <note>original: "episteme"; usually translated as "knowledge" in modern philosophy</note>. For to know is, in a certain respect, to possess <term>science</term>. Is it not?

THEÆTETUS. It is.

SOCRATES. When asked, therefore, what <term>science</term> is, he would essentially answer that it is "right opinion combined with the *knowledge* of difference." For, according to him, this is what it means to add "reason."

THEÆTETUS. It appears so.

<summary>Socrates argues that defining knowledge as "right opinion plus a rational explanation of difference" is circular and redundant, as it essentially defines knowledge using the word "knowledge" itself.</summary>

**Socrates:** But it is in every respect foolish for us, who are investigating knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, to say that it is "right opinion combined with knowledge," whether of difference or of anything else. Therefore, Theaetetus, neither sensation, nor true opinion, nor a rational explanation <note>original: "reason"</note> in conjunction with true opinion, can be defined as knowledge.

**Theaetetus:** It does not appear that they can.

**Socrates:** Are we, therefore, still pregnant and in labor, my friend, with any further ideas regarding knowledge, or have we brought everything forth?

**Theaetetus:** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, through your help I have already said more than I had within myself.

**Socrates:** Does not all this show, then, that my obstetric art <note>term: Socrates famously compared his method of questioning to midwifery, helping others "give birth" to their own ideas.</note> has delivered for us a result that is empty and does not deserve to be nurtured?

**Theaetetus:** Entirely so.

**Socrates:** If, therefore, after this you should endeavor to become pregnant with other ideas, and your endeavor should be successful, you will be full of better things because of the present discussion. But even if you should remain empty, you will be less troublesome to your companions, and more moderate and mild, because you will not think you know things which you do not actually know. For my art is able to accomplish this much, but nothing more. Nor do I know any of those secrets which are known, and have been known, to great and wonderful men. But this obstetric art was assigned to me and my mother by God <note>original: "divinity"</note>; she practiced it for women, and I for noble and beautiful youths. Now, however, I must go to the King's Porch <note>note: The Stoa Basileios, where Socrates was to face the preliminary hearing for his trial.</note> to answer the accusation of Melitus. But tomorrow morning, Theodorus, we will return here again.

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

# THE POLITICUS.

---

**A**s there is one end for which nature, or rather the author of nature, produced the parts of the human body, and another for which he formed the whole man, so likewise he directed an individual of the human species to one end, a family to another, and again a city and kingdom to another. And lastly, that is to be considered as the best end, for the sake of which he produced the whole human race. Let no one however think, that though there is a certain end <note>original: "finis"; the ultimate purpose or goal</note> of every partial association among mankind, yet there is none of the whole; and that though there is order in the parts of human life, yet there is confusion in the whole; or, in short, that though the parts possess union from being directed to one end, yet the whole is dispersed and unconnected: for, if this were admitted, parts would be more honorable than the whole; though the former exist for the sake of the latter, and not the latter for the sake of the former. 

Hence it is necessary that there should be a certain end of the human race, and that it should consist in those energies through which it may imitate as much as possible things supernal <note>heavenly or divine things</note>; by science speculating <note>original: "speculando"; observing or contemplating</note> things natural, human and divine; by prudence properly managing human affairs; and by piety cultivating and venerating divinity. An end, therefore, of this kind requires a twofold life, consisting both in action and contemplation, yet so constituted as that action may exist for the sake of contemplation, as that which is more excellent and divine.

Plato in this dialogue demonstrates that this end can alone be obtained by the human race, under the government of a king who possesses consummate probity <note>integrity and uprightness</note> and science. Hence employing a most accurate division which is

<summary>This introduction argues that just as individual organs serve the body, human societies exist for a higher purpose: the imitation of the divine through a balance of action and contemplation under a wise ruler.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Politicus, Statesman, teleology, contemplation vs action, monarchy, political philosophy, divine order</keywords>

<page-num>102</page-num>
# INTRODUCTION TO THE STATESMAN <note>original: "POLITICUS"</note>

Using the method of division, which is essentially necessary to definition and science—and in which Plato and his genuine disciples excelled to a transcendent degree—he Homerically <note>In the style of the poet Homer, who often called kings "shepherds of the people."</note> names a king the shepherd and caretaker <note>original: "curator"</note> of the human race. This king, too, he compares to a physician; since such a person, by imposing laws on both the willing and the unwilling, provides healthy remedies for his subjects. 

However, he more frequently calls such a governor and caretaker a "politician" <note>In this context, "politician" refers to a "statesman" or one skilled in the art of governing a city-state (polis).</note> rather than a king. By this, he signifies that the ruler will be so humane and mild that he will appear to be a fellow-citizen among the citizens. He will demonstrate that he is superior to them in justice, prudence, and knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> rather than in any other qualities. He likewise asserts that the man who far surpasses all others in justice and prudence is born a king, even if he should live the life of a private individual. 

It may also be gathered from his other dialogues that his opinion is that royal authority should be given to the older and more worthy individuals. A senate of these men should be the colleagues of the king, forming, as it were, a certain aristocracy—or a government of the most excellent men. Just as he proves in this dialogue that a royal government surpasses every other form, he likewise shows that a tyranny is the worst kind of dominion, since it governs neither by law nor intellect, but by unrestrained impulse and arbitrary will. 

As the next in excellence after a royal government, he praises an aristocracy, but condemns an oligarchy (the government of a wealthy few). He considers a popular government <note>A democracy.</note> as deserving praise in the third degree, provided it governs according to law. After this, he discusses the duty of a king and shows that it consists in providing those things necessary for the human race—especially those that contribute to its happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>. This involves prudently judging which arts are useful to this end in peace and war, and in public and private conduct, while exercising sovereign authority in conjunction with the senate.

With respect to what he says regarding the motion of the spheres and the kingdoms of Saturn and Jupiter, the mystic meaning of this symbolic <note>original: "fabulous"</note> narration will be explained in the notes on this dialogue.

<summary>This introduction defines Plato's ideal statesman as a "shepherd" or "physician" of the people and ranks forms of government, placing monarchy and aristocracy above democracy and tyranny.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Politicus, Statesman, kingship, aristocracy, tyranny, oligarchy, democracy, political science, Saturn, Jupiter</keywords>

## PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.

->SOCRATES, || A GUEST <note>Often referred to as the Eleatic Stranger</note>,<-
->THEODORUS, || And SOCRATES Junior.<-

---

->SOCRATES.<-

**I AM** greatly indebted to you, Theodorus, for making me acquainted with Theaetetus and this guest.

**THEODORUS.** Perhaps, Socrates, you will be indebted to me three times as much after these men have defined for you the statesman <note>original: "politician"</note> and the philosopher.

**SOCRATES.** Let it be so. But shall we say we have heard this from you, who are most skillful in reasoning and in matters pertaining to geometry?

**THEODORUS.** What is that, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** That we should consider each of these men as being of equal worth, even though they are further apart in value than can be measured by the proportions <note>original: "analogy"</note> of your mathematical art.

**THEODORUS.** By our God Ammon <note>An Egyptian deity often identified by the Greeks with Zeus</note>, Socrates, you have properly, justly, and promptly corrected me for my error in calculation! I shall speak with you about this at some other time. But as for you, guest, do not be weary in any way in gratifying us; please discuss for us, in order, either the statesman first, or, if it is more agreeable to you, the philosopher.

**GUEST.** We shall do so, Theodorus, as soon as we begin this discussion, and we shall not stop until we arrive at the end of it. But what ought I to do regarding Theaetetus here?

**THEODORUS.** About what?

**GUEST.** Shall we allow him to rest, and take in his place this younger Socrates here as our partner in the discussion? Or what do you advise?

THEODORUS: As you say, take Socrates <note>referring to Socrates Junior</note> in his stead; for, both being young men, they will easily be able to endure every kind of labor by taking turns resting.

I joined in a discussion with Theaetetus yesterday, and today I have heard him answering you; but neither of them has yet discussed things with the younger Socrates here. It is, however, proper that he should be considered. Let him then answer me some other time, but for now, let him answer you.

GUEST: Let it be so, Socrates. Do you hear this, Socrates Junior?

SOCRATES JUNIOR: I do.

GUEST: Do you, therefore, agree to what he says?

SOCRATES JUNIOR: Entirely so.

GUEST: It appears, therefore, that you will be no obstacle to our discussion; and perhaps it is necessary that I should be even less of an obstacle. But after defining a sophist <note>term: a paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric in ancient Greece, often associated with deceptive reasoning</note>, it is necessary, as it appears to me, that we should investigate the statesman <note>original: "politician"</note>. Tell me, therefore, whether this character should be placed among those who possess scientific knowledge. Or what shall we say?

SOCRATES JUNIOR: That he should.

GUEST: We must, therefore, divide the sciences into categories, just as we did in our investigation of the sophist.

SOCRATES JUNIOR: Perhaps so.

GUEST: But yet it appears to me, Socrates, that we should not divide them in the same manner.

SOCRATES JUNIOR: Certainly not.

GUEST: But in another way.

SOCRATES JUNIOR: So it seems.

GUEST: Who then can find the path to understanding the statesman? For it is necessary to find it, and, separating it from other things, to define it with one single idea. Then, marking the other branches with a different classification, we must lead our minds to understand that all sciences are contained within two primary species.

SOCRATES JUNIOR: I think, Guest, that this is your task, and not mine.

GUEST. But is not the science of a true king the "royal science"?

SOCRATES JUNIOR. Yes.

GUEST. And may not he who possesses this science—whether he is a private man or a ruler—be in every respect rightly called "royal," according to this art?

SOCRATES JUNIOR. He may, justly.

GUEST. And are not the manager of a household and a master the same?

# THE POLITICUS <note>original: The Statesman</note>

**Guest.** If we wish to divide the commanding branch of the intellectual science <note>original: "gnostic science," referring to knowledge-based or theoretical science</note> into parts, we should cut them accordingly.

**Socrates Junior.** According to what?

**Guest.** One part of it should be assigned to the categories of inanimate things, and the other to the categories of living beings. In this way, the whole will be divided into two parts.

**Socrates Junior.** Entirely so.

**Guest.** One part, therefore, we must set aside, and take up the other; and we must again divide that whole into two parts.

**Socrates Junior.** But tell me, which of these is to be taken up?

**Guest.** By all means, the part that rules over living beings. For it is not the duty of the royal science to command inanimate things, like the science of architecture <note>original: "architectonic science"</note>; but, being of a more noble nature, it always exercises its power over living beings and matters pertaining to them.

**Socrates Junior.** Right.

**Guest.** Regarding the birth and rearing of living beings, attention to the latter is confined to a single animal, but the care belonging to the former extends in common to the whole herd.

**Socrates Junior.** Right.

**Guest.** But we find that the focus of political science is not of a private nature, like that of an ox-driver or a groom; rather, it is similar to the attention paid by one who feeds horses and oxen in a herd.

**Socrates Junior.** This appears to be the case.

**Guest.** Therefore, regarding the rearing of living beings, shall we call the rearing of a flock "collective rearing" or "common nutrition"?

**Socrates Junior.** Both terms may be used in our discussion.

**Guest.** You have answered well, Socrates. And if you avoid being overly concerned with specific names, you will appear in your old age to be more wealthy in intellectual wisdom <note>original: "intellectual prudence"</note>. Let us, therefore, now do as you advise. But do you understand how someone, by showing that the rearing of a herd is twofold, will cause that which we are now investigating to be sought in two halves?

**Socrates Junior.** I am trying to follow you: and it appears to me that there is one kind of rearing for men, and another for brute animals.

<summary>The Guest and Socrates Junior use a process of logical division to define statesmanship, narrowing it down from a general intellectual science to the collective rearing of living beings, specifically humans.</summary>

GUEST. You have divided in every respect promptly and courageously. We must, however, to the utmost of our power, be careful that we do not suffer this error again.

SOCRATES JUNIOR. What error?

GUEST. That we do not take away one small part in opposition to many and great parts, nor take it away without identifying its specific form <note>original: "species"</note>, but always divide in conjunction with a specific form. For it is most ideal to separate the object of inquiry from other things immediately, if the separation is made correctly; just as you a little while ago hastily thought regarding division, because you perceived the discourse was tending toward mankind. Though indeed, my friend, it is not safe to divide with such thin subtlety. It is safer to proceed by dividing through the middle <note>original: "media"</note>; for in this way, we shall more readily encounter the true forms <note>original: "ideas"</note>. This entire method contributes to the objects of our investigation.

SOCRATES JUNIOR. How do you mean, Guest?

GUEST. I will endeavor to speak even more clearly, Socrates, because of the kindness of your nature. It is impossible, therefore, to demonstrate the things now proposed in such a way that nothing shall be lacking; yet we must endeavor to rise a little higher in our contemplation <note>original: "speculation"</note> for the sake of clarity.

SOCRATES JUNIOR. In what respect, then, do you say we have not just now divided correctly?

GUEST. In this respect: if anyone should attempt to give a twofold division to the human race <note>original: "genus"</note>, he would divide just as many people of the present day divide. For these people separate the Greek race apart from all others as one distinct thing; they then label all other kinds of men—which are innumerable, unmixed, and discordant with each other—by the single name of "Barbarians." Because of this one name, they mistakenly believe that this group is a single, unified race. 

But this is just as if someone, thinking that numbers should be divided into two types, should cut off ten thousand from all other numbers as if it were one specific type, and, giving one name to all the rest, should think that this remaining group becomes a separate and distinct type simply because of that name. He, however, will divide in a more beautiful manner—more according to the actual form and a proper twofold division—who cuts numbers into even and odd, or the human species into male and female. One should only separate the Lydians, or Phrygians, or certain other nations from all others when he is incapable of...

He argues that proper classification must follow natural "species" or forms, such as even and odd numbers or male and female.</summary>

**YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Yes.

**GUEST.** By dividing too hastily, we shall finish more slowly.

**YOUNGER SOCRATES.** What?

# THE POLITICUS <note>Also known as Plato's *Statesman*.</note>

**Socrates Junior.** You have answered me beautifully, as if you were discharging a debt; and you have added a digression as interest, completing your discourse.

**Guest.** Come, then, let us connect the beginning to the end by reviewing our discussion concerning the name of the political art.

**Socrates Junior.** By all means.

**Guest.** In the beginning, we asserted that one part of the cognitive science <note>original: "gnostic science"; the science of knowing or understanding</note> was of a commanding nature; and we said that the part of this science which issues commands on its own authority was similar to this. Again, we asserted that the rearing of animals was a part of this self-commanding science, and that this was a significant part. Likewise, we said that the rearing of herds was a species of the rearing of animals; and that the art of nourishing animals without horns specifically belongs to the art of feeding land-dwelling <note>original: "pedestrian"</note> animals. Again, it is necessary to combine at least three parts of this if one wishes to grasp it under a single name: the science of feeding a pure, unmixed genus. But a section from this, which alone remains and which feeds men—ranking them among the two-legged animals <note>original: "bipeds"</note>—is the part we are now exploring, which we call both the "royal" and the "political" art.

**Socrates Junior.** Entirely so.

**Guest.** Do you think, Socrates, that we have truly done as well as you say?

**Socrates Junior.** In what way?

**Guest.** I mean, has the subject we proposed been sufficiently discussed in every respect? Or has our investigation been particularly deficient in this: that it has provided a description of the thing, but one that is not perfectly finished?

**Socrates Junior.** What do you mean?

**Guest.** I will endeavor to explain my meaning more clearly.

**Socrates Junior.** Please do.

**Guest.** Since it has appeared that there are many types of herding <note>original: "pastoral"</note> arts, the political science is one of these, acting as the caretaker of one specific herd.

**Socrates Junior.** It is.

**Guest.** Our discourse defined this to be neither the rearing of horses, nor of any other beasts, but to be the common science of nourishing men.

He alone is skilled in the midwife's art <note>original: obstetric art</note> regarding birth and offspring. Furthermore, no one is better suited to comfort the herd through the kind of play and music that cattle can appreciate, or to soothe them with instruments or the voice. The same may be said of other animal shepherds, may it not?

**Younger Socrates.** That is quite right.

**Stranger.** How, then, will our argument regarding a king appear to be correct and complete? We have asserted that he alone is the shepherd and provider of the human herd, yet ten thousand others compete for that same office.

**Younger Socrates.** It would not be correct at all.

**Stranger.** Were we not right, then, to feel a certain fear a little while ago? We suspected that we might only be describing a "royal figure" rather than perfectly defining a political character. We cannot truly define him unless we identify those who are connected to this role—those who claim to be shepherds as well—and separate the king from them to show him in his pure form.

**Younger Socrates.** Our fear was indeed justified.

**Stranger.** This, therefore, Socrates, must be done by us, unless we intend to let our discourse fail at the very end.

<note>The substance of this fable is beautifully explained by Proclus, in his fifth book on the *Theology of Plato*, as follows:</note>

> "This universe is very properly said to have twofold lives, periods, and revolutions; one of these being Saturnian <note>Relating to the god Saturn (Cronus), representing a golden age of intellectual order.</note>, and the other Jovian <note>Relating to the god Jupiter (Zeus), representing the current age of material governance.</note>. According to the former of these periods, every good thing springs up spontaneously, and every living nature possesses a blameless and unwearied life. But the latter is the source of material error and of an abundantly changeable nature. For, as there is a twofold life in the world—the one hidden and more intellectual, the other more natural and visible—the one is bounded by providence, while the other proceeds in a disorderly manner according to fate. 
>
> Hence, this latter life, which is multiform and perfected through nature, is suspended from the Jovian order; but the former, which is more simple, intellectual, and hidden, is suspended from that of Saturn. This the Elean Guest clearly indicates by calling one of the circulations Jovian and the other Saturnian. Although Jupiter is also the cause of the hidden life of the universe, the supplier of intellect, and the leader of intellectual perfection, he leads all things upward to the kingdom of Saturn. Being a leader, together with his father, he gives existence to the whole mundane intellect <note>The "intellect of the world" or the cosmic mind.</note>. 
>
> Each of these periods—the visible and the hidden—participates in both these Gods; but the one is more Saturnian, and the other is in subjection to the kingdom of Jupiter. That the mighty Saturn is allotted the other kingdom of the Gods prior to him, the Elean Guest clearly proves in what he says before the fable: namely, that we have heard from many of the kingdom which Saturn obtained. So, according to this wise man also, Saturn is one of the royal Gods. 
>
> Therefore, as his father Heaven <note>Uranus.</note> contains the middle centers of the intelligible and intellectual Gods, Saturn is the leader of the intellectual orders. He supplies the whole of intellectual energy: first to the Gods; secondly, to the beings superior to man; and lastly, to partial souls such as ours, when they are able to extend themselves to the Saturnian 'place of survey' <note>A state of high contemplation.</note>. For this universe, and all the worldly Gods, perpetually possess this twofold life. They imitate the Saturnian intellection through hidden and intellectual energy, but the demiurgic <note>The "demiurge" is the creator or craftsman of the physical world.</note> intellect of Jupiter through providential attention to secondary concerns—and, in short, through the visible fabrication of things. 
>
> But partial souls <note>Individual human souls.</note> at one time act intellectually and consecrate themselves to Saturn, and at another time act according to the characteristics of Jupiter, providing for subordinate natures with unrestrained energy. When they revolve in a way analogous to these deities, they intellectually perceive intelligible things and bring order to sensible things, living both these lives in the same manner as the Gods and the more excellent beings. For their periods are twofold: one intellectual and the other providential. Their paradigms <note>The eternal patterns or models upon which the world is based.</note> also are twofold: of the one the—

<note>The following passage interprets the Greek myth of the "Age of Saturn" (Cronus) versus the "Age of Jupiter" (Zeus). In Neoplatonic philosophy, Saturn represents pure intellect, while Jupiter represents the "Demiurge" or the divine creator who organizes the physical world.</note>

...Saturnian intellect, and of the other the Jovian; since even the mighty Jupiter himself has a twofold energy: by intellect, indeed, adhering to intelligible realities, but by demiurgic fabrication <note>original: "demiurgic fabrication" — the act of a divine craftsman shaping the material world</note> adorning sensible things <note>things perceived by the senses</note>.

> "Since, therefore, the revolutions are twofold—not only in the universe as a whole but likewise in individual souls—in the Saturnian period, says the Elean guest, the generation of men is not from each other, as it is in the men we see today. Nor is it like the first man among us who is alone 'earth-born'; rather, in individual souls, this is the case with all of them. For they are led upwards from the lowest and earthly bodies, and they receive an invisible life while deserting a sensible one. 
>
> Neither do they grow toward old age, changing from younger to older; but on the contrary, they become more vigorous. They proceed intellectually in a path contrary to physical birth <note>original: "generation"</note>, and they dissolve, as it were, that variety of life which they made into a composite while descending into bodies. Hence, likewise, all the symbols pertaining to youth are present with those souls when they pass into such a condition of being; for they lay aside everything which clings to them from physical birth. 
>
> And when they are distributed around Saturn, and live the life which is there, he says fruits are produced in abundance from the trees, and many other things spring spontaneously from the earth. The inhabitants also are naked and without beds, and for the most part are fed while dwelling in the open air; for they possess a temperament of the seasons that cannot be destroyed. The grass, likewise, springing abundantly from the earth, supplies them with soft couches. 
>
> These and similar goods are what souls derive from this mighty deity, according to the Saturnian period. For they are filled from that source with life-giving <note>original: "vivific"</note> good, and gather intellectual fruits from the whole of reality, rather than seeking perfection and happiness <note>original: "beatitude"</note> for themselves through partial, individual efforts. For 'doxastic' <note>original: "doxastic" — relating to opinion or belief rather than certain knowledge</note> nourishment involves divided and material understandings; but intellectual nourishment consists of those understandings which are pure, indivisible, and spontaneous—which the word 'spontaneous' here obscurely signifies. 
>
> The fruits also granted from the earth signify the perfection of the fertile intellect of the Gods, which illuminates souls with a sufficiency from within themselves. For, through an ungrudging abundance of goods, the Gods are also able to grant happiness to lesser natures in a suitable measure. Therefore, they are neither clothed with garments—as they are when they enter into physical birth—nor do they overflow with the additions of worldly life. Instead, they are themselves pure, by themselves, free from all composition and variety. By exciting their own intellect, they are drawn by their intellectual father toward these divine benefits. They likewise participate in universal goods, being guarded by the intellectual Gods; and receiving from them the measures of a happy life, they pass the whole of their existence with ease. And lastly, establishing a sleepless and pure life in the creative powers of the intelligible realm, and being filled with intellectual fruits and nourished with immaterial and divine forms, they are said to live the life which belongs to the government of Saturn."

**GUEST:** There were then, and still will be, many records of ancient affairs; and among others, there is one extraordinary story concerning the dispute between Atreus and Thyestes <note>In Greek mythology, brothers who fought over the throne of Mycenae.</note>. **GUEST:** Not at all; I mean the change in the rising and setting of the sun and the other stars. For where they now rise, they then used to set; and they rose from the opposite direction. **SOCRATES JUNIOR:** We have heard that from very many.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR:** This is also one of the things said to have happened in the past.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR:** You speak most excellently. Tell it, then, and do not leave anything out.

**GUEST:** Listen, then. The Deity himself sometimes guides this universe in its movement and revolves it; but at other times he lets go of the reins of his government. This happens when the cycles of the universe have completed their allotted measure of time. Then, the world begins to turn back in the opposite direction of its own accord. It can do this because it is a living being <note>original: "animal"</note> endowed with wisdom by the one who first put it together, harmonizing all its parts into a whole. This movement in the opposite direction is naturally built into the world for the following reason.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR:** For what reason?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Guest and the Younger Socrates regarding the cosmic cycles of the universe and the nature of divine governance.</meta>

**GUEST.** To exist always in the same state, in a similar manner, and to be eternally the same, belongs only to the most divine of all things; the nature of the physical body does not belong to this divine order. Now, that which we call "heaven" and "the world" receives many blessed gifts from its creator <note>original: "producing cause"</note>. However, because it participates in the nature of a body, it cannot be entirely free from <term>mutation</term> <note>change or alteration</note>. Nevertheless, as far as it is able, it moves in the same place and in the same way with a single <term>lation</term> <note>original: "lation"; a technical term for local motion or "carrying" along a path</note>. For this reason, it is granted a circular motion, because that involves the smallest possible <term>mutation</term> of its movement. 

But almost nothing is able to rotate itself, except for that which leads all things that are moved <note>referring to the Soul or the Divine Mind</note>. And it is not permitted for this leader to move one way at one time, and in a different way at another. From all this, therefore, we must conclude that the world does not always rotate itself, nor is the whole of it always turned by God in two different and contrary directions. Nor, again, should we say that two specific Gods turn it whose wills are opposed to each other. 

Instead, we must assert what I just said, which is the only remaining possibility: at one time, the world is guided by a divine cause, receiving an externally granted life and a renewed immortality from the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note>. But at another time, when the Creator lets go of the reins of government, the world proceeds by itself. Being thus left alone for a time, it performs many millions of retrograde <note>backward-moving</note> revolutions; it does this because it is vast, perfectly balanced, and moves upon the smallest possible pivot <note>original: "accomplishes its progressions with the smallest foot"</note>.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Everything you have said appears to be very probable.

**GUEST.** From what has been said, we may now use logic to understand that circumstance which we previously called the cause of all wonderful things. For it is this very thing.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** What thing?

**GUEST.** That the circular motion of the universe is at one time performed as it is at present, and at another time in the opposite direction.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** But how is this the cause of all wonderful things?

**GUEST.** We must consider that this <term>mutation</term> is the greatest and most complete of all the celestial turnings.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** That is likely.

**GUEST.** It is proper, therefore, to think that the greatest changes then happen to us, the inhabitants of this world.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** That also is likely.

<summary>The Guest explains that the universe alternates between being guided by a divine Creator and moving independently in a reverse direction, a cosmic shift that causes profound changes for the world's inhabitants.</summary>

GUEST. But do we not know that the nature of animals sustains with difficulty great, numerous, and all-various changes <note>original: "mutations"</note>?

SOCRATES JUNIOR. Undoubtedly.

GUEST. Hence, the greatest deaths <note>original: "corruptions"</note> of other animals then necessarily take place, and very few of the human race remain.
