SOCRATES JUNIOR. What circumstance do you mean?

GUEST. That which takes place first of all: in whatever age a mortal animal is found, he is no longer seen advancing toward old age, but is changed back to the opposite, and naturally becomes, as it were, younger and more delicate. The white hairs of those more advanced in years then become black, and the cheeks of those that had beards become smooth; and thus each person is restored to the past flower of his age. The bodies, likewise, of those who were in the bloom of youth, becoming smoother and smaller every day and night, return again to the nature of a recently born child; and they are made like this nature, both in soul and body. And at length their bodies, rapidly wasting away, vanish. But the dead bodies of those who at that time died through violence were in like manner quickly and invisibly <note>original: "immanifestly"</note> decomposed.

SOCRATES JUNIOR. But what was then, O guest, the generation of animals, and in what manner were they produced from each other?

GUEST. It is evident, Socrates, that at that time there was no reproduction of one thing from another. But, as it is said that there was once an "earth-born race," this race was at that period restored back again from the earth. This information was delivered to us by our first ancestors, who lived immediately after the close of the last revolution. For they were public witnesses of the truth of our assertions, which at present are disbelieved—though improperly—by the common people. For I think this particular point ought to be attended to, as a logical consequence of the story. For, if old men returned to the nature of boys, it follows that those who were dead, but laid in

What is said regarding the "spontaneous life" of these men is asserted because Divinity himself fed them and was their guardian; just as men, who are of a more divine nature, are the shepherds of beasts, who are of a lower nature. Because men were fed by Divinity, there were no political systems, nor possessions of women and children <note>Plato suggests a communal existence without the private family structures of his own day.</note>. For all these people were restored to life from the earth, without having any recollection of former events. All such modern social structures were absent. The inhabitants also had fruits in abundance from oaks and many other trees, which did not grow through the help of agriculture but were spontaneously given by the earth. For the most part they went naked, slept without blankets, and lived in the open air. For the climate of the seasons was harmless <note>original: "innoxious"</note> to them. They had soft beds made of grass, which grew in generous abundance from the earth. 

And thus, Socrates, you have heard what the life of men was like under the reign of Saturn; but you yourself have seen what the condition of the present life is, which is said to be under Jupiter <note>The Greek god Zeus; representing the current age of human toil and self-governance.</note>. Are you able, and also willing, to judge which of these is the happier?

For after the time of all those people was finished and it was necessary for a change <note>original: "mutation"</note> to take place—and furthermore, when the entire earthly race was exhausted, as every soul had completed its allotted number of births and as many seeds had fallen on the earth as were destined for each soul—then the governor of the universe, letting go of the handle of his rudder, as it were, withdrew to his lookout point <note>original: "place of survey"</note> from which he contemplates himself.

All those Gods who govern specific regions, alongside the greatest spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note>, knowing what had now happened, again deprived the various parts of the world of their providential care. But the world, becoming inverted and conflicting with itself—being agitated by an impulse contrary to its beginning and end, and likewise creating a massive internal shock—produced once again a destruction of all kinds of animals. 

After these things, however, and after a sufficient length of time had passed, the tumult, confusion, and shocks ceased. The world, becoming tranquil and orderly again, proceeded in its usual course, maintaining a providential care and dominion both over itself and...

# THE STATESMAN <note>original: "THE POLITICUS"</note>

The world remembers, to the utmost of its power, the instructions of the creator <note>original: "demiurgus"</note> and father. At the beginning, therefore, it accomplished this more perfectly, but toward the end more negligently. The cause of this is the corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> form of its composition, which was nurtured alongside an ancient nature. For the world participated in much disorder before it arrived at its present orderly arrangement. From its composing architect, indeed, it possesses every good; but from its former habit, it retains all that atrocity and injustice which exist within the heavens. These qualities the world both possesses from that former habit and introduces into living beings. 

Therefore, when the world nourishes the animals it contains in conjunction with its governor, it produces small evils and mighty goods. But when it is separated from him, during the time immediately following his departure, it still conducts all things beautifully. As time passes, however, and as forgetfulness is generated within it, the quality of its former discord rules with greater force. At the final period of time, it loses its vigor <note>original: "deflorescent"</note>; producing few goods, but mixing in much of the temperament of things contrary to good, it reaches the danger of both itself and the beings within it being destroyed. 

Hence, that God who adorned the world, perceiving the difficulties under which it labors and anxious lest—being thus tempestuously agitated—it should be dissolved by the tumult and be plunged into the infinite sea of unlikeness <note>original: "dissimilitude"</note>, again resumes the helm. He adorns and corrects whatever is diseased and broken through the disordered motion of the former period, and renders the world immortal and ageless. 

This, therefore, is the end of the whole narration. This is sufficient to show the nature of a king to those who attend to what has been already said. For, the world being again turned toward the present path of creation <note>original: "generation"</note>, the progression of its age stopped, and it provided new things, the very opposites of what it provided before. For animals near to death, on account of their smallness, are increased. But bodies recently born from the earth, already gray-haired and dying again, descend into the earth; and all other things are transformed, imitating and following the condition of the universe. The imitation, likewise, of motion, creation, and nourishment, follows all things by necessity. For it is no longer possible for an animal—

By imitating and following the world through all the revolutions of time, we live and are born in different ways at different periods.

**Guest.** We sufficiently understand this, then: that the creation of a paradigm <note>term: A "paradigm" here refers to a model or pattern used as an example to explain a larger concept.</note> occurs when that which is the same in another separate <note>original: "divulged"</note> instance is rightly understood and applied to each case, producing one true opinion of both.

**Younger Socrates.** It appears so.

**Guest.** Should we wonder, then, if our soul—naturally experiencing the same thing regarding the elements of all things—is at one time firmly grounded in certain details by truth itself, and at another time wavers in other details regarding all things? And is it any wonder that when it thinks correctly in certain simple mixtures <note>original: "commixtions"</note>, it should again be ignorant of these very same things when they are transferred to the long and difficult "syllables" <note>note: Here, "syllables" is a metaphor for complex structures or combinations of ideas.</note> of reality?

**Younger Socrates.** There is nothing wonderful in this.

**Guest.** For how, my friend, can anyone who begins from a false opinion arrive at even the smallest part of truth and thus acquire wisdom?

**Younger Socrates.** Almost no one can.

**Guest.** If, therefore, these things naturally exist in this manner, you and I shall not err in any respect if we first endeavor to perceive the nature of the whole model in another small and partial example. After this, we can apply ourselves to the model of a king, which is the greatest

**Guest.** If, therefore, we take away political science, will not our investigation into the royal science <note>The art of kingship or statesmanship</note> be cast into doubt?

<summary>The Guest and Younger Socrates establish that the "art of measurement" must be divided into two types: relative measurement (comparing two things) and normative measurement (comparing a thing to the ideal "mean" or "appropriate" standard).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Guest and the younger Socrates regarding the methodology of dialectic and the purpose of their inquiry.</meta>

These men immediately group together things that differ widely from each other and consider them similar. Conversely, they do the exact opposite: they fail to divide things that are different into their proper parts. It is necessary that when someone first perceives a commonality among many things, he should not stop until he perceives all the differences within it that exist as distinct species <note>original: "species"; here meaning specific types or categories</note>. Again, when he perceives all kinds of differences among a multitude of things, he must not give up on this difficult task until he has enclosed all related things within a single similarity and comprehended them within the essence of a certain genus <note>original: "genus"; a general class or category</note>. Let this suffice regarding these details and concerning the concepts of deficiency and excess. We must only carefully observe that two types of measurement regarding these matters have been discovered, and we should remember what they are.

**Younger Socrates:** We will remember.

**Guest:** After this discussion, let us take up another point regarding the objects of our investigation and the overall purpose of this conversation.

**Younger Socrates:** What is it?

**Guest:** If someone were to ask us about the practice of students learning their letters—when they are asked what letters compose a word—should we say that the inquiry is made for the sake of that one word only, or so that they may become more skillful in everything pertaining to grammar?

**Younger Socrates:** Clearly, it is so that they may become more skillful in the whole of grammar.

**Guest:** What about our current situation? Is our inquiry regarding the politician undertaken more for the sake of understanding the politician himself, or so that we may become more skillful in every kind of philosophical discussion?

**Younger Socrates:** This also is evident: it is undertaken for the latter reason.

**Guest:** Indeed, no one with any intellect would be willing to investigate the art of weaving for its own sake alone. However, I think most men are unaware that there are certain perceptible similarities to things that are naturally easy to learn. There is no difficulty in making these clear when someone wishes to explain them to an inquirer—not just by pointing at physical objects, but by providing a rational explanation.

He emphasizes that while some things have physical examples, higher concepts require rational explanation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato's "Politicus" (The Statesman), specifically discussing the definition of a true ruler and the role of scientific knowledge versus written law.</meta>

<page-num>151</page-num>
# THE STATESMAN <note>original: THE POLITICUS</note>

The practitioner of the art of government is to be considered a political and royal character regardless of certain circumstances: whether they govern those who are willing or those who are stubborn; whether they rule according to written laws or without them; and whether they are rich or poor. We see a parallel in medicine: we call those who heal the body "physicians" regardless of whether they cure by surgery, cauterization <note>original: "burning"</note>, or any other painful treatment. It does not matter if the patient is cooperative or resistant, if the doctor follows medical texts or acts without them, or if the doctor is poor or rich. In all these cases, we say they are still physicians as long as they act according to their professional skill <note>original: "art"</note>—whether they are purging the body, thinning it down, or helping it grow—provided that their sole aim is the good of the body, restoring it from a worse to a better condition and maintaining that health. In this way alone, I believe, can we rightly define the standard for medical or any other form of government.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** That is very true.

**GUEST.** It follows, then, that a political system <note>original: "polity"</note> is only truly and rightly established when the governors are found to possess genuine scientific knowledge, and are not merely pretending to have it. This remains true whether they govern by laws or without them, whether they rule over the obedient or the rebellious, and whether they are rich or poor. None of these external factors are of any importance regarding the correctness of the government.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Beautifully said.

**GUEST.** Furthermore, it does not matter if they "purge" the city for its own good by putting certain people to death or banishing them; or if they reduce the population by sending out colonies like a swarm of bees; or if they increase the city's size by bringing in foreigners and making them citizens. As long as they use science and justice to make the city pass from a worse to a better condition to the best of their power, and preserve it in that state—only then, and by these definitions, can we say a political system is rightly established. Any other systems we have mentioned are not genuine or true political systems. We should say that those systems which imitate this ideal are reasonable and tend toward beauty, while those that do not imitate it tend toward ugliness by mimicking evil things.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Everything else you have said, Guest, seems to have been discussed sufficiently. However, it is not easy to accept your claim that it is necessary to govern without laws.

<meta>catchword: GUEST.</meta>

<summary>The Guest argues that true statesmanship is defined by the ruler's scientific knowledge and pursuit of the city's good, rather than by wealth, the consent of the governed, or adherence to written laws. He compares the statesman to a physician whose authority comes from their skill in healing, not from following a specific script.</summary>

# THE STATESMAN <note>original: "POLITICUS"</note>

GUEST. You have anticipated me a little, Socrates, by your question. For I was going to ask you whether you admit all these points, or whether you find any difficulty in anything that has been said. It is, however, evident that we now wish to inquire concerning the correctness of those who govern without laws.

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. <note>original: "SOC. JUN."</note> Undoubtedly.

GUEST. In a certain sense, it is evident that legislation belongs to the royal science <note>The art of ruling or statesmanship</note>; but it is best, not for the laws to prevail, but for a man who is royal in conjunction with prudence <note>Practical wisdom or "phronesis"</note> to rule. Do you know why?

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Inform me.

GUEST. Because law cannot—by attempting to grasp that which is most excellent and at the same time most accurately just for all men—always enjoin that which is best. For the differences between men and their actions, and the unceasing restlessness, as I may say, of human affairs, do not permit any art whatever to provide a simple rule for all things and for all time. Shall we admit these assertions?

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Undoubtedly.

GUEST. But we see that law nearly endeavors to accomplish this very thing. It acts like an arrogant and ignorant man who does not suffer anything to be done contrary to his own orders, nor allows anyone to ask whether it would be better to make some new regulation contrary to what he has ordained.

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. True. For the law does exactly as you say.

GUEST. But it is impossible for a thing which is simple <note>Inflexible or uniform</note> to prevail in matters which are never, at any time, simple.

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. It appears so.

GUEST. The cause, therefore, must be found out why it is necessary to establish laws, since law does not possess the greatest correctness.

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. Undoubtedly.

GUEST. Are there not, therefore, among us—as also in other cities—certain exercises for men who are gathered together, whether for racing or for anything else undertaken for the sake of competition?

SOCRATES THE YOUNGER. There are very many such exercises.

GUEST. Come then, let us again recall to our memory the mandates of those who preside over gymnastic exercises according to their art.

**Guest.** But I think that in a less precise way, he will establish laws for the multitude and for the general case—both written and unwritten—and such as are agreeable to the customs of the country.

**Younger Socrates.** Right.

**Guest.** Right indeed. For how, Socrates, can anyone attend sufficiently to individuals throughout their whole lives and accurately command what is adapted to each? **Younger Socrates.** It appears so, Guest, from what has been said.

**Guest.** Rather, my excellent young man, it appears so from what *will* be said.

**Younger Socrates.** What is that?

**Guest.** This: let us say to ourselves that if a physician or a gymnastics master intended to travel and be away from those under his care for a long time, and he thought that those exercising or those who are sick would not remember his instructions, he would want to write down notes <note>original: commentaries</note> for them. **Younger Socrates.** That he would certainly want to do so.

**Guest.** But what if the physician should return sooner than he expected?

**Younger Socrates.** These assertions cannot be contradicted.

**Guest.** Nor can these others.

**Younger Socrates.** Which assertions do you mean?

**Guest.** That no large crowd <note>original: "multitude"</note> can ever acquire that science by which a city is governed according to intellect. Instead, an upright government must be sought within a small number, a few, or even a single person. All other forms of government are to be considered merely as imitations, as we observed a little while ago.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It appears so.

**GUEST.** And shall we wonder, Socrates, that in such polities those evils should take place which we behold at present, and which will exist in the future, when they rest on the foundation of written mandates and long-established customs, and not on the firm basis of science? Or ought we not rather to admire how strong a thing a city naturally is? For, though cities have existed for an immense length of time in this condition, yet some of them have continued stable and have not been subverted. At the same time, many of them—like vessels sinking in the sea—have perished, do perish, and will perish through the depravity of the pilots and sailors, who are involved in the *greatest ignorance* respecting the *greatest concerns*. For though they know nothing about political affairs, yet they think their knowledge of the political science is the most clear of all scientific knowledge.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Most true.

**GUEST.** As, therefore, all these erroneous polities are full of difficulties, we should consider in which it is the least difficult and burdensome to live; for, though this is superfluous with respect to our present inquiry, yet perhaps universally we all do all things for the sake of this.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It is impossible it should not be necessary to consider this.

**GUEST.** Of three things, therefore, they say that one is remarkably difficult, and at the same time easy.

**SOCRATES JUNIOR.** What do you mean?

# THE POLITICUS

GUEST: No differently than I said before: that there are three <term>polities</term> <note>original: "polities"; systems of civil government or organized societies</note>—a <term>monarchy</term>, the government of a few, and the government of many. We mentioned these three systems at first in a general, unrefined manner.

YOUNG SOCRATES: We did.

GUEST: By dividing each of these in two, we shall produce six, while setting apart the "upright" or ideal system as a seventh.

YOUNG SOCRATES: How so?

GUEST: We must divide <term>monarchy</term> into the <term>royal</term> <note>rule by a king according to law</note> and the <term>tyrannic</term> <note>rule by a single person through force or whim</note>. Furthermore, we must divide the system governed by a small group into <term>aristocracy</term> <note>rule by the "best" or most virtuous few</note> and <term>oligarchy</term> <note>rule by a wealthy or powerful few</note>, which is a well-known distinction. Finally, we previously viewed the system governed by the masses as a single type and called it a <term>democracy</term>, but we must now establish it as twofold.

YOUNG SOCRATES: How so? In what way do we make this division?

GUEST: In the same way as the others, even though the name for both remains the same. The distinction between governing according to the laws and transgressing the laws is common to this and the other systems.

YOUNG SOCRATES: It is.

GUEST: When we were searching for the ideal, "upright" system, this distinction was not useful, as we showed earlier. But since we have set the ideal aside and have considered these other systems as the ones we must actually live with, we divide each of them based on whether they are legal or law-breaking.

YOUNG SOCRATES: That seems to follow from what has been said.

GUEST: Therefore, a <term>monarchy</term>, when joined with good written institutions—which we call laws—is the best of all the six systems. However, when it exists without law, it is grievous and the most burdensome to live under.

YOUNG SOCRATES: It appears so.

GUEST: Next, the system composed of "not many" <note>aristocracy or oligarchy</note> should be considered a middle ground, just as "a few" is a middle point between one and many. Finally, we should consider the system composed of many <note>democracy</note> as weak in all respects. Compared to the others, it is incapable of accomplishing either great good or great evil because authority in this system is divided into tiny portions among many people. Consequently, democracy is the worst of all the law-abiding systems, but it is the best of all the lawless ones. Where everyone is intemperate <note>lacking self-control or moral restraint</note>, it is best to live in a <term>democracy</term>; but where everyone is temperate, this system is the worst.

<summary>The Guest explains how the three basic forms of government (rule by one, few, or many) become six when distinguished by their adherence to law, concluding that democracy is the weakest but safest form of lawless government.</summary>

**YOUNGER SOCRATES.** How so?

**GUEST.** Those workmen first of all separate earth, stones, and many other things from the ore. But after this, substances remain that are allied to gold—honorable materials that can only be separated by fire—I mean brass, silver, and sometimes adamant <note>original: diamonds; likely referring to "adamas," a term for the hardest substances or impurities.</note>. These being separated with difficulty through melting <note>original: fusion</note>, only then allow us to see that which is called perfectly pure gold.

**YOUNGER SOCRATES.** That is indeed how those things are said to be done.

**GUEST.** In the same manner, we also appear now to have separated from the science of politics those things which are different, foreign, and unfriendly to it. We have left only those things which are honorable and allied to it. Among these remaining parts, we may rank the military and judicial arts, and that rhetoric <note>The art of persuasive speaking.</note> which communicates with the royal science by persuading men to act justly, and which, together with that science, governs the affairs of cities. If someone can successfully separate these from the core, he will reveal, naked and alone by himself, that true statesman <note>original: character</note> whom we are investigating.

<summary>The Guest compares the process of defining a true statesman to the refining of gold, arguing that false politicians must be stripped away like dross. He identifies military, judicial, and rhetorical arts as being closely related to, but distinct from, the core "royal science" of governing.</summary>

GUEST. But again, to what science shall we attribute the power of judging whether we should act toward certain people through persuasion or through a certain force; or, generally, whether we ought ever to employ either persuasion or force?

YOUNGER SOCRATES. What do you mean?

GUEST. My assertion is by no means common. For all the parts of virtue are usually said to be in harmony <note>original: "friendly"</note> with each other.

YOUNGER SOCRATES. It is indeed said so.

GUEST. Let us consider, therefore, with the greatest attention, whether this is so simple, or whether these virtues differ from one another more than anything else, despite being of a similar nature.

YOUNGER SOCRATES. Tell me how we are to consider this.

GUEST. In all such things as we call beautiful, it is proper to investigate them and categorize them into two contrary types <note>original: "species"</note>.

YOUNGER SOCRATES. You speak most clearly.

GUEST. Have you ever then either praised something yourself, or heard some other person praising sharpness and swiftness—whether in bodies or souls, or the movement of the voice, or in such imitations of these as are found in music and painting <note>original: "graphical imitations"</note>?

Guest: Do you also remember in what way praise is bestowed in each of these cases?

Socrates Junior: Not at all.

Guest: Shall we, therefore, be able to explain my thoughts on this to you in words?

Socrates Junior: What should stop us?

Guest: You seem to think such a thing is easy. Let us consider it, therefore, in <term>subcontrary genera</term> <note>Opposite categories or types that exist under a broader heading.</note>. For often, and in many actions, when we admire the swiftness, intensity, and sharpness of thought, body, or voice, we praise them, and at the same time use one of the names associated with courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>.

Socrates Junior: How so?

Guest: In the first place, we say a thing is sharp and vigorous, swift and manly, and similarly intense. Generally, we praise all these qualities by applying this common name to them.

Socrates Junior: We do.

Guest: But what about the opposite? Do we not often praise the qualities of quiet production in many actions?

Socrates Junior: Very much so.

Guest: Do we not, therefore, in praising these, say things contrary to what we said when praising the others?

Socrates Junior: How so?

Guest: We say that each of these is quiet and temperate. We admire these qualities when they occur in <term>cogitation</term> <note>Deep thought or reflection.</note>; but regarding actions, we admire what is steady <note>original: "flow"</note> and gentle; regarding the voice, we admire the smooth and the deep, all rhythmic motion, and the entirety of the arts <note>original: "the muse"</note> which use slowness at the right time. To all these, we give the name of moderation, and not of courage.

Socrates Junior: Most true.

Guest: But when both of these qualities occur at the wrong time, we then criticize each of them and call them by names that imply the opposite of praise.

Socrates Junior: How so?

Guest: When things appear to be sharp, swift, and hard at the wrong time, we then call them insolent and insane. But when they are deep and slow at the wrong time—

When these qualities flow slowly and softly, we call them timid and slothful. We find that these natures—fortitude and temperance <note>The Greek terms are *andreia* (courage/fortitude) and *sophrosyne* (moderation/temperance).</note>—are for the most part contrary to each other. **Socrates Junior:** In what way do you mean?

**Guest:** In all those particulars which we have just mentioned, and likely in many others. For I think that by praising certain things as their own—because of an alliance to their own nature—and blaming other things as foreign, they become very opposed to each other in many matters.

**Socrates Junior:** They appear to do so.

**Guest:** This difference, therefore, is merely a "sport" or minor friction between these types of virtue. However, a disease that is the most ruinous of all happens to cities regarding matters of the greatest consequence.

**Socrates Junior:** About what things?

**Guest:** About the entire way of life, as is likely. For those who are remarkably modest <note>original: "modest," here meaning those inclined toward quietness and moderation.</note> are always prepared to live a quiet life, attending privately to their own concerns. They are disposed to associate peaceably with both their fellow citizens and foreigners. However, through this love of peace—which is more ill-timed than is appropriate—when they pursue what they wish to accomplish, they secretly become weakened and cause the young men to be similarly affected. Hence, they are always subject to injuries; and in a short time, they, their children, and the entire city often decline by slow degrees from being free people to being slaves.

**Socrates Junior:** You speak of a severe and terrible suffering.

**Guest:** But what about those who lean more toward fortitude? Do they not incite the cities to which they belong to war? Through a more vehement desire for that kind of life than is becoming, they make many nations and powers hostile to their country. Thus, they either entirely ruin it or bring it into subjection to the enemy.

**Socrates Junior:** They do.

**Guest:** How is it possible, therefore, that we should not say that in these things both types <note>original: "genera"</note> are in the greatest degree opposed to each other?

**Guest.** Whether there is anything belonging to the constructive sciences <note>original: "synthetic sciences," referring to arts that combine different elements into a whole</note> which has any of its works—even the most humble—composed of things that are evil and yet useful at the same time? **Younger Socrates.** Undoubtedly.

**Guest.** The truly political science, therefore, according to nature, will never be willing for a city to be composed of both good and bad men. Instead, it is very evident that it will first of all test everything through education <note>original: "discipline"</note>. After this examination, it will commit the task of training to those who are able to instruct others and serve their needs, while the political science itself commands and presides. This is just like the art of weaving, which presides over the wool-combers and others who prepare the materials for weaving; it gives such orders to the preparatory workmen as it thinks will best contribute to the finished work it has in view.

**Younger Socrates.** Entirely so.

**Guest.** The royal science <note>The art of kingship or statesmanship</note> appears to me to do the very same. It permits those who instruct and educate others according to law to exercise and teach only that which, when blended correctly, will produce worthy character. But it punishes with death, exile, and the greatest disgrace those who are unable to share in fortitude, temperance, and such other things as tend toward virtue, but who instead—through a depraved nature—are violently driven toward impiety, insolence, and injustice.

**Younger Socrates.** This is said to be the case.

**Guest.** But those who wallow <note>original: "are rolled like cylinders"</note> in ignorance and a lowly spirit, it subjects to servile employments.

# INTRODUCTION
## TO
### THE MINOS.

---

**L**AW, considered according to its first existence in Deity, is justly defined by Plato to be a *distribution of intellect* <note>original: νου διανομη (nou dianome)</note>. As it originates, therefore, from deity, and is then shared by the human soul, its existence among men does not depend on arbitrary will or mutual agreements, but is truly an unfolding of one of those eternal ideas or forms which the soul essentially contains. He, therefore, who diligently attends to what is said by Plato in this dialogue, in his *Laws*, and in his *Republic* concerning law, will find that it is a true mode of governing. This mode directs the governed to the best end through proper means, establishing punishments for those who transgress and rewards for those who are obedient to this system. 

Hence, the institutions of princes—when they are not true and do not proceed toward the best end in a right path—are by no means laws, but merely decrees and edicts. For a work is frequently called "legitimate" because of law, "just" because of being legitimate, and "good, right, and true" because of being just; therefore, law is necessarily good and true. It also follows that law, properly so called, is eternal and perfectly unchangeable. For that which is changed by times, places, and opinions is not a law, but a mere custom or institute.

According to Plato, it also appears that there are four species of laws. The first of these are Saturnian—or, in other words, they exist in that deity who, according to ancient theologians, is the summit of the intellectual order. These laws are mentioned by Plato in the *Gorgias*, where Socrates says, "This was the law in the times of Saturn, and now also exists among the Gods." The second species are Jovian <note>relating to Jove or Jupiter</note>, and are indicated in the *Laws*, where the Athenian guest—

<summary>This introduction defines Plato's concept of law as an eternal, divine distribution of intellect rather than a human invention, distinguishing true law from mere political decrees. It begins to categorize law into four species, starting with the Saturnian and Jovian levels.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Minos, philosophy of law, intellect, Saturn, Jupiter, Gorgias, divine law, intellectual order</keywords>

<page-num>178</page-num>
# INTRODUCTION TO THE MINOS.

He says "that Justice follows Jupiter <note>original: Zeus</note>, being the avenger of those who desert the divine law." The third type of laws are fatal <note>meaning: pertaining to Fate or destiny</note>, as we learn from the *Timaeus*, where it is said that the Demiurge <note>The "Craftsman" or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note> "disclosed to souls the laws of Fate." And the fourth type are human. 

Since law, therefore, has a divine origin, all the illustrious framers of laws with the greatest propriety referred the invention of them to a Deity. Hence *Zoroaster*, when he delivered laws to the *Bactrians* and *Persians*, ascribed the invention of them to *Oromasis* <note>Ahura Mazda</note>; *Hermes Trismegistus*, the *Egyptian* legislator, referred the invention of his laws to *Mercury* <note>Thoth</note>; *Minos*, the *Cretan* lawgiver, to *Jupiter*; *Charondas*, the *Carthaginian*, to *Saturn*; *Lycurgus*, the *Lacedaemonian* <note>Spartan</note>, to *Apollo*; *Draco* and *Solon*, the *Athenian* legislators, to *Minerva* <note>Athena</note>; *Pompilius* <note>Numa Pompilius</note>, the *Roman* lawgiver, to *Egeria*; *Zamolxis*, the *Scythian*, to *Vesta* <note>Hestia</note>; and *Plato*, when he gave laws to the *Magnesians* and *Sicilians*, to *Jupiter* and *Apollo*.

<summary>This text categorizes laws into four types—divine, judicial, fatal, and human—and lists historical and mythical legislators who claimed their laws were divinely inspired.</summary>
<keywords>Justice, Jupiter, Demiurge, Fate, Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Minos, Lycurgus, Solon, Numa Pompilius, Plato, divine law, legal history</keywords>

# THE MINOS.

->PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.<-

->SOCRATES AND A COMPANION.<-
<note>original: "MINOS." While the title of the dialogue is Minos, the interlocutor is an anonymous friend; the historical Minos is discussed later in the text.</note>

---

->SOCRATES.<-

**WHAT** is law with us?
**COMPANION.** About what kind of law do you ask?
**SOC.** What is that by which one law differs from another law, according to this very quality: the essence of being law? Consider what I am asking you. I ask as if I were inquiring what gold is; and if you, in a similar manner, should ask me what kind of gold I am inquiring about, I would think you were not questioning me correctly. For gold does not differ from gold insofar as it is gold, nor does a stone differ from a stone insofar as it is a stone. In the same way, one law does not differ from another law; rather, all laws are the same. Each of them is equally law; one is not more of a law, and the other less. I ask you, therefore, about the whole of this very thing: what is law? If you have an answer ready, give it to me.
**COMPANION.** What else, Socrates, would law be than the things established by law? <note>original: "decrees" or "statutes"</note>
**SOC.** Does speech also appear to you to be the things which are spoken? Or sight the things which are seen? Or hearing the things which are heard? Or is speech one thing, and the things spoken another? Is sight one thing, and the things seen another? Is hearing one thing, and the things heard another? And so, is law one thing, and the things established by law another? Is this the case, or how does it appear to you?
**COMPANION.** This now appears to me to be the case.
**SOC.** Law, therefore, is not the same as the things established by law.

<summary>Socrates begins a philosophical inquiry into the nature of law, challenging his companion to define the essence of "law" itself rather than merely pointing to specific legal statutes or decrees.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Minos, definition of law, legal philosophy, essence vs. instance, Greek dialogue</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and a companion (referred to here as Minos) regarding the fundamental definition of law.</meta>

# THE MINOS

**MIN.** It does not appear to me that it is. <note>The companion is responding to a previous question about whether law is merely a decree.</note>

**SOC.** Let us consider what law might be in this way. Suppose someone should ask us about the things we just mentioned: since you say that visible things are seen by the sight, what is the "sight" by which they are seen? We would answer him that it is a sense which, through the eyes, reveals colors to us. And if he should ask us again, what is the "hearing" by which things are heard? We would reply that it is a sense which, through the ears, reveals sounds to us. 

In the same way, if he should ask us—since legal institutions are legally established by law—what is this "law" by which they are established? Is it a certain sense or a manifestation, in the same way that things which are learned are made manifest by science <note>original: "science" here refers to *episteme* or systematic knowledge</note>? Or is it a certain discovery <note>original: "invention"</note>, just as things are discovered? For example, healthy and harmful things are discovered by medicine, but the intentions of the Gods, as prophets say, are discovered by divination. For the art of divination is, for us, the discovery of such things. Is it not so?

**MIN.** Entirely so.

**SOC.** Which of these, then, should we especially presume law to be? Shall we say it consists of these dogmas <note>original: "dogma's" meaning settled opinions or formal tenets</note> and decrees?

**MIN.** It appears so to me. For what else can anyone say law is? So it appears that the whole of what you are asking about—that is, law—is the dogma of the city.

**SOC.** You call law, it seems, "political opinion."

**MIN.** I do.

**SOC.** And perhaps you are right; but perhaps we shall understand better by looking at it this way. Do you say that some men are wise?

**MIN.** I do.

**SOC.** And are the wise not wise by virtue of wisdom?

**MIN.** Yes.

**SOC.** What then? Are the just, just by virtue of justice?

**MIN.** Entirely so.

**SOC.** Are the law-abiding <note>original: "legitimate"</note>, therefore, also law-abiding by virtue of law?

**MIN.** Yes.

**SOC.** And the lawless <note>original: "illegitimate"</note>, are they lawless by a deprivation of law?

**MIN.** Yes.

<summary>Socrates leads his companion to define law as the "dogma of the city" or political opinion, while using analogies of sight, hearing, and medicine to question whether law is a form of discovery or a systematic science.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Minos, definition of law, political opinion, justice, wisdom, divination, legal philosophy</keywords>

<header>THE MINOS</header>

**Socrates:** And are those things that are legitimate also just?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** But are those that are illegitimate unjust?
**Minos:** Unjust.
**Socrates:** Are not justice and law, therefore, the most beautiful of things?
**Minos:** They are.
**Socrates:** And are not injustice and lawlessness the most base?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** And does not one of these preserve cities and everything else, while the other destroys and overthrows them?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** It is necessary, therefore, <term>dianoëtically</term> <note>original: "dianoëtically"; meaning to use the intellectual power of reasoning or logical thought</note> to consider law as something beautiful, and to seek it out as something good.
**Minos:** How could we not?
**Socrates:** Have we not said, then, that law is the "dogma" <note>original: "dogma"; here meaning a formal decree, opinion, or established principle</note> of the city?
**Minos:** We have said so.
**Socrates:** What then? Are not some decrees good, and others bad?
**Minos:** They are.
**Socrates:** Law, however, is not bad.
**Minos:** It is not.
**Socrates:** It is not, therefore, right to simply define law as the decree of the city.
**Minos:** It does not appear to me that it is.
**Socrates:** The claim, therefore, does not align with the truth if it implies that law could be a base or wicked decree.
**Minos:** It does not.
**Socrates:** Law, however, also appears to me to be a certain kind of opinion. And since it is not a "base" <note>original: "base"; meaning morally low or worthless</note> opinion, is it not evident that it must be a good opinion, if law is indeed opinion?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** But is not a "good opinion" actually a true opinion?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Is true opinion, therefore, the discovery of reality? <note>original: "discovery of being"; in Platonic philosophy, "being" refers to objective reality or the true nature of things</note>
**Minos:** It is.

<summary>Socrates leads Minos to conclude that law cannot simply be any decree made by a city, as laws must be inherently good and just. They determine that true law is not just an opinion, but the discovery of objective reality or "being."</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Minos, justice, law, dogma, dianoetic, true opinion, being, political philosophy</keywords>

<page-num>182</page-num>
# THE MINOS

**Socrates:** Law, therefore, is the discovery of being <note>original: "the discovery of being" (Greek: *tou ontos exeurosis*); in Platonic philosophy, this refers to the discovery of true reality or objective truth.</note>.

**Minos:** But, Socrates, if law is the discovery of being, how is it that we do not always use the same laws regarding the same things, since beings <note>meaning: objective realities</note> are discovered by us?

**Socrates:** Nevertheless, law *aims* to be the discovery of being; but men—as it seems—by not always using the same laws, are not always able to discover that which law aims for: namely, being. But come, let us see if it will become evident to us whether we always use the same laws, or different laws at different times; and if all of us use the same laws, or if different people use different laws.

**Minos:** But this, Socrates, is not difficult to know: that neither do the same people always use the same laws, nor do different people always use different laws. Thus, for example, it is not a law with us to sacrifice men—in fact, this is considered unholy—but the Carthaginians sacrifice men, as this is considered holy and legal with them. Some of them even sacrifice their sons to Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus; the author refers to the Carthaginian practice of child sacrifice to Ba'al Hammon.</note>, as perhaps you have heard. And not only do "Barbarian" <note>original: "Barbarian"; used here in the Greek sense to mean any non-Greek speaker.</note> men use laws different from ours, but also those in Lycia. And as for the descendants of Athamas ¹, what sacrifices do they perform, even though they are Greeks? You also know and have heard what laws we formerly used concerning the dead, cutting the throats of the victims before the dead body was carried out, and hiring women to wail at the sacrifices for the dead. And those even before these people buried the dead at home; but we do none of these things. Ten thousand other instances of this might be brought forward. For the evidence is very broad that we neither always think the same as ourselves, nor do men agree with each other.

**Socrates:** It is not at all surprising, my dear friend, if you are speaking correctly and this has simply been hidden from me. But as long as you state your opinion in a long speech, and I then do the same, we shall never, I think, come to an agreement. If, however, a common subject of inquiry is proposed, we shall perhaps reach an accord. If, therefore, you are willing, consider this with me by questioning me. Or, if it is more agreeable to you, answer my questions instead.

**Minos:** I am willing, Socrates, to reply to any question you may propose.

<note>¹ Athamas was the son of Aeolus and king of Thebes in Boeotia.</note>

<summary>Socrates argues that law is the pursuit of objective reality, while his companion counters by pointing out the vast diversity of legal and religious customs across different cultures and eras. They agree to proceed through a shared dialectic method of questioning rather than long individual speeches.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Minos, philosophy of law, cultural relativism, human sacrifice, Carthaginian customs, Greek burial rites, dialectic method, being vs. appearance</keywords>

# THE MINOS

<center>SOCRATES and MINOS</center>

**Socrates:** Come then. Do you think that just things are unjust, and unjust things are just? Or that just things are just, and unjust things are unjust?

**Minos:** I certainly think that just things are just, and unjust things are unjust.

**Socrates:** Is this opinion, therefore, held among all men, as well as here?

**Minos:** Yes.

**Socrates:** Among the Persians also?

**Minos:** And among the Persians too.

**Socrates:** But is this opinion always held?

**Minos:** Always.

**Socrates:** Are things which pull more <note>original: "attract more"; referring to the pull of gravity</note> thought by us to be heavier, while things which pull less are lighter? Or is it the contrary?

**Minos:** Not the contrary; things which pull more are heavier, and things which pull less are lighter.

**Socrates:** Is this the case, therefore, in Carthage and in Lycia?

**Minos:** Yes.

**Socrates:** Beautiful things, it seems, are everywhere thought to be beautiful, and base things to be base; but base things are not thought to be beautiful, nor beautiful things base.

**Minos:** That is so.

**Socrates:** As we may say, therefore, in all things, <term>beings</term> <note>original: "beings" (ontos); things that actually exist or are true in reality</note> are thought to exist, and not <term>non-beings</term> <note>original: "non-beings" (me ontos); things that have no basis in reality</note>, both with us and with all others.

**Minos:** It appears so to me.

**Socrates:** He, therefore, who wanders from <term>being</term> <note>the truth of what is</note> wanders from that which is <term>legitimate</term> <note>original: "legitimate" (nomimon); that which is according to the true law</note>.

**Minos:** Socrates, as you say, these things always appear legitimate both to us and to others. But when I consider that we never cease shifting laws back and forth <note>original: "transposing laws upwards and downwards"</note>, I cannot be persuaded by what you say.

**Socrates:** Perhaps you do not perceive that these things, even when shifted, continue to be the same. But consider them this way with me: Did you ever come across any book concerning the health of the sick?

**Minos:** I have.

**Socrates:** Do you know, therefore, to what art this book belongs?

**Minos:** I know that it belongs to the <term>art of medicine</term>.

<summary>Socrates argues that truth and justice are universal and objective, comparing the consistency of moral truths to the physical laws of weight and the professional principles of medicine.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Minos, justice, universal truth, ontology, being vs. non-being, legality, medical art, Carthage, Persia</keywords>

<header>THE MINOS</header>

**Socrates:** Do you, therefore, call those who are scientifically skilled in these matters "physicians" <note>original: "physicians"; here meaning medical doctors</note>?

**Minos:** I call them so.

**Socrates:** Now, do those who have scientific knowledge think the same things about the same subjects, or do some of them think differently from others about the same things?

**Minos:** It appears to me that they think the same things.

**Socrates:** Furthermore, do only the Greeks agree with other Greeks about things of which they have scientific knowledge, or do the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarians"; a term used by ancient Greeks to refer to all non-Greek speaking peoples</note> also agree with each other about such things, and also with the Greeks?

**Minos:** It is absolutely necessary that both Greeks and Barbarians who possess scientific knowledge should agree in opinion with each other.

**Socrates:** You answer well. Do they not, therefore, always agree?

**Minos:** Yes, always.

**Socrates:** Do not physicians also write down those things about health which they believe to be true?

**Minos:** Undoubtedly.

**Socrates:** Therefore, medical treatises and medical laws are the writings of physicians.

**Minos:** Medical things, certainly.

**Socrates:** In the same way, are geometrical writings also geometrical laws?

**Minos:** Yes.

**Socrates:** To whom, then, do the writings and established rules <note>original: "legitimate institutions"</note> concerning gardening belong?

**Minos:** To gardeners.

**Socrates:** Those laws, therefore, pertain to gardening.

**Minos:** They do.

**Socrates:** Are they not, therefore, the laws of those who know how to manage gardens?

**Minos:** How could they not be?

**Socrates:** And gardeners possess this knowledge.

**Minos:** Yes.

**Socrates:** But to whom do the writings and established rules concerning food belong?

**Minos:** To cooks.

<summary>Socrates leads Minos to agree that true laws are based on scientific knowledge and universal truths that remain consistent across different cultures, using medicine, geometry, and gardening as examples.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Minos, scientific knowledge, universal truth, medical law, gardening, expertise, Greeks and Barbarians</keywords>

# THE MINOS.

Socrates: Those, therefore, are cooking laws.

Minos: Cooking laws?

Socrates: And they belong, as it seems, to those who know how to manage the preparation of food.

Minos: Yes.

Socrates: But cooks, as they say, possess this knowledge.

Minos: They do possess it.

Socrates: Be it so. But who is responsible for the writings and legal institutions concerning the government of a city? Are they not the work of those who scientifically know how to govern cities?

Minos: It appears so to me.

Socrates: But do any others besides politicians and kings possess this knowledge?

Minos: They alone possess it.

Socrates: These writings, therefore, are political, which men call the writings of kings and good men.

Minos: You speak the truth.

Socrates: Therefore, those who possess scientific knowledge <note>original: "a scientific knowledge"</note> do not write differently about the same things at different times.

Minos: Certainly not.

Socrates: If, therefore, we see certain people doing this, shall we say that those who act in this manner are scientific or unscientific?

Minos: Unscientific.

Socrates: Shall we, therefore, say that whatever is right in every particular is legitimate, whether it pertains to medicine, cooking, or gardening?

Minos: Yes.

Socrates: But regarding what is not right, we no longer assert this to be legitimate.

Minos: No longer.

Socrates: It, therefore, becomes illegitimate.

Minos: Necessarily so.

Socrates: Hence, in writings concerning things just and unjust—and, in short, concerning the orderly distribution <note>original: "distribution of a city"; referring to the Greek concept of *nomos*, which implies both law and the "allotment" or "distribution" of resources and duties</note> of a city and the manner in which it ought to be governed—that which is right is a royal law. But that which is not right does not appear to be a royal law, because science <note>original: "science is wanting"; meaning the objective knowledge or expertise is missing</note> is lacking; for it is illegal.

<summary>Socrates argues that true law must be based on scientific knowledge and correctness; therefore, only "right" regulations can be considered legitimate royal laws, while incorrect ones are illegitimate.</summary>

# THE MINOS

**Minos:** It is.
**Socrates:** We have rightly, therefore, acknowledged that law is the discovery of reality <note>original: "invention of being"; in this context, Socrates argues that true law is not just a human whim but a discovery of objective truth</note>.
**Minos:** So it appears.
**Socrates:** Furthermore, we should also consider this: who is it that scientifically knows how to sow seeds in the earth?
**Minos:** The farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note>.
**Socrates:** Does he then sow the appropriate seeds in each type of soil?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** The farmer, therefore, is a good distributor of these things, and his laws and distributions in these matters are correct.
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** But who is a good dispenser of rhythms <note>original: "pulsations"</note> for melodies, and distributes what is appropriate? And whose laws in these matters, if he has any, are correct?
**Minos:** The laws of the flute-player <note>original: "piper"</note> and those of the harpist.
**Socrates:** He, therefore, who is most law-abiding <note>original: "legitimate"; meaning one who follows the technical rules or "laws" of his craft</note> in these matters is, in the highest degree, a flute-player.
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** But who, in the best manner, distributes nourishment to the bodies of men? Does not he do this who distributes that which is appropriate?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** The distributions, therefore, and the laws of this man are the best; and he who is most law-abiding regarding these things is the most excellent distributor.
**Minos:** Entirely so.
**Socrates:** Who is he?
**Minos:** The physical trainer <note>original: "instructor of children"; referring to the *paidotribes*, who managed the physical education and diet of youths</note>.
**Socrates:** Does he know how to feed the "flock" of the human body in the best manner?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** But who is he that feeds a flock of sheep in the best manner? What is his name?
**Minos:** A shepherd.
**Socrates:** The laws, therefore, of the shepherd are the best for the sheep.
**Minos:** They are.

<summary>Socrates uses analogies of farming, music, and physical training to argue that "law" is the correct distribution of what is appropriate by an expert in their field. He concludes that the best laws for any group—whether humans or animals—are those established by the most knowledgeable "shepherd" or leader.</summary>

**Socrates:** And those of the herdsman are for oxen?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** But which laws are the best for the souls of men? Are they not those of a king?
**Minos:** They are.
**Socrates:** You speak well. Can you, therefore, tell me who among the ancients was a good legislator regarding the laws of the pipes <note>original: "pipes" refers to the aulos, a woodwind instrument; Socrates is using a musical analogy for social harmony</note>? Perhaps you do not recollect. Are you, therefore, willing that I should remind you?
**Minos:** Perfectly so.
**Socrates:** Marsyas, then, and his beloved Olympus the Phrygian were of this description.
**Minos:** True.
**Socrates:** The harmony produced by the pipes of these men is most divine, and alone excites and unfolds those who stand in need of the Gods <note>See the speech of Alcibiades in *The Banquet* (The Symposium).</note>. It likewise alone remains to the present time as being divine.
**Minos:** These things are so.
**Socrates:** But who among the ancient kings is said to have been a good legislator, and whose legal institutions even now remain as being divine?
**Minos:** I do not recollect.
**Socrates:** Do you not know who they were that used the most ancient laws of the Greeks?
**Minos:** Do you speak of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, and Lycurgus the legislator?
**Socrates:** These institutions, however, have perhaps not been established for even three hundred years, or very little more than this. But do you know from where the best of their laws were derived?
**Minos:** They say, from Crete.
**Socrates:** Do they, therefore, of all the Greeks use the most ancient laws?
**Minos:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Do you know then who among these were good kings? I mean Minos and Rhadamanthus, the sons of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> and Europa, by whom these laws were framed.
**Minos:** They say, Socrates, that Rhadamanthus was a just man, but that Minos was rustic, morose, and unjust.

<header>THE MINOS.</header>

**Socrates:** You relate, O best of men, an Attic and tragical fable. <note>Socrates suggests the companion's negative view of Minos comes from Athenian theater rather than historical truth.</note>

**Minos:** Are not these things reported of Minos?

**Socrates:** They are not by Homer and Hesiod, whose authority is greater than that of all the tragic poets from whom you assert these things.

**Minos:** But what do they say about Minos?

**Socrates:** I will tell you, lest you as well as the many should be guilty of impiety. For there is not anything which is more impious than this; *nor is there anything of which we ought to be more afraid, than of offending against* THE GODS *either in word or in deed* <note>original: "This among many other passages must convince the most careless reader, that Plato was a firm believer in the religion of his country."</note>. And next to this we should be fearful of offending against divine men. We should however be very cautious, when we praise or blame any man, that we do not speak erroneously; and for the sake of this it is necessary that we should learn to know good and bad men. For divinity is indignant when any one blames a man similar to himself, or praises one dissimilar to him: but the former of these is the good man. Nor ought you to think that stones, pieces of wood, birds and serpents are sacred, but that men are not so: for a good man is the most sacred, and a depraved man the most defiled, of all things. 

Now, therefore, since Homer and Hesiod pass an <term>encomium</term> <note>a speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly</note> on Minos, on this account I thus speak, *lest you, being a man sprung from a man, should sin in what you say against a hero the son of* Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>. For Homer <note>Odyssey, book 19, verse 172, etc.</note>, speaking of Crete, that there are many men and ninety cities in it, says that among these is Gnossus, a great city in which Minos reigned, who for nine years conversed with the mighty Jupiter. This then is Homer's praise of Minos, which though short is such as he does not give to any one of his heroes. For that Jupiter is a <term>sophist</term> <note>original: "That is, one endued with wisdom; for this is the original meaning of the word."</note>, and that the art itself is all-beautiful, he demonstrates as well in many other places as here. For he says that Minos conversed nine years with Jupiter, and went to be instructed by him, as if Jupiter were a teacher of wisdom. That Homer, therefore, does not bestow this honor of being instructed by Jupiter on any other hero than Minos alone, must be considered as a wonderful praise. Ulysses also, in speaking of the dead <note>Odyssey, book 11.</note>, represents Minos judging with

On this account I say that Minos is praised by Homer beyond all other heroes. For the claim that he was the son of Jupiter and was instructed by Jupiter contains no ordinary level of praise. For the verse which says that Minos reigned nine years, and conversed with the mighty Jupiter, signifies that he was the associate of Jupiter; since *oaroi* <note>original Greek: οαροι</note> are discourses, and an *oaristis* <note>original Greek: οαριστης</note> is an associate in discourse. 

Hence, for nine years Minos went to the cavern of Jupiter, learning some things, and teaching others <note>This refers to Minos bringing the divine laws back to the people</note>, which during these nine years he had received from Jupiter. There are, however, some who imagine an *oaristis* to signify an associate of Jupiter in drinking and sport. But that those who think this way say nothing to the purpose may be inferred from this: although both the Greeks and Barbarians are numerous, there are none among them who abstain from banquets and the sports associated with wine, except the Cretans and the Lacedæmonians <note>The Spartans</note>, who were instructed by the Cretans. 

In Crete, too, this is one of the other laws which Minos established: that men should not drink with each other to the point of intoxication. And it is indeed evident that he made those things to be laws for his citizens which he thought to be beautiful. For Minos did not, like a base man, think one thing and do another different from what he thought; but his association with Jupiter was, as I have said, through discourse, in order to be instructed in virtue. Hence he established these laws for his citizens through which Crete is perpetually happy, and also Lacedæmon, from the time in which it began to use these laws, because of their being divine. 

But Rhadamanthus was indeed a good man, for he was instructed by Minos. He did not, however, learn the whole of the "royal art" <note>The art of kingship or governance</note>, but only that part of it which is of the administrative kind, and which possesses authority in courts of justice; and hence he is said to have been a good judge. <header>THE MINOS</header>

Having mentioned his name, he says <note>original: "he says" refers to the poet Hesiod</note> that he was the most royal of mortal kings, and that he reigned over many neighboring men, holding the scepter of Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter" (Zeus)</note>, with which he also governed cities. **MINOS.** On what account then, Socrates, did the report spread that Minos was an unlearned and morose man?

**SOCRATES.** For that very reason through which you, O best of men, if you are prudent—and every other man who intends to be celebrated—will be cautious never to offend a poet. For poets are able to achieve much regarding public opinion, both in praising men and blaming them. In this particular, therefore, Minos erred when he made war on this city <note>Athens</note>, in which there is much other wisdom, along with tragic and other poets of every description. 

But tragedy here is ancient; it did not originate, as is generally thought, from Thespis, nor from Phrynichus. If you consider it, you will find that it is a very ancient invention of this city. Tragedy is indeed, of all poetry, the most pleasing to the common people <note>original: "the vulgar"</note> and the most alluring. By applying ourselves to this art, we have taken vengeance on Minos for the tributes he compelled us to pay <note>A reference to the myth of the Minotaur and the Athenian tribute of youths</note>. In offending us, therefore, Minos erred; which is why, in reply to your question, he became infamous. 

The greatest proof that he was a good man, a friend to law, and a good "shepherd of the people" (as I have before observed) is that his laws are immutable <note>term: "immutable" — unchangeable; permanent</note>. This is because he truly discovered the truth concerning the government of a city.

**MINOS.** You appear to me, Socrates, to have discovered a probable reason.

**SOCRATES.** If, therefore, I speak the truth, do the Cretans—the citizens of Minos and Rhadamanthus—not appear to you to have used the most ancient laws?

**MINOS.** They do.

**SOCRATES.** These, therefore, were the best legislators of the ancients, and were also shepherds of men; just as Homer likewise says that a good general is the "shepherd of the people."

**MINOS.** Entirely so.

<page-num>191</page-num>
# THE MINOS

If a good legislator and shepherd of the body should ask us what those things are which, when distributed to the body, will make it better, we should answer well and briefly: they are nourishment and labor. The former increases the body's substance, and the latter exercises it, giving stability to the body.

**MINOS.** Right.

**SOCRATES.** If, therefore, after this, that good legislator and shepherd should also ask us what those things are which, being distributed to the soul, make it better, what shall we answer? How can we respond so that we are not ashamed of ourselves and of our age?

**MINOS.** I am no longer able to answer this question.

**SOCRATES.** It is, however, disgraceful to the soul of each of us if we should appear to be ignorant of things pertaining to our souls—in which good and evil are contained—while being knowledgeable in details pertaining to the body and to other things.

->THE END OF THE MINOS.<-

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

## THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES

---

The elevation and greatness of mind for which Socrates was so justly celebrated by antiquity are perhaps nowhere so conspicuously displayed as in this, his *Apology* <note>original: "Apology" here refers to a formal legal defense, not an expression of regret</note>. In a situation in which death itself was presented to his view, he neither deviates from the most rigid truthfulness, nor has recourse to any of those abject arts by which, in similar circumstances, pity is generally solicited and punishment sometimes averted. His whole discourse, indeed, is full of simplicity and noble grandeur; it is the energetic language of conscious innocence and offended worth.

The causes that led to this *Apology* were as follows: Aristophanes, at the instigation of Melitus, undertook to ridicule the venerable character of Socrates on the stage in his comedy, *The Clouds*. Once the way was opened to calumny and defamation, the fickle and licentious populace paid no reverence to the philosopher, whom they had previously regarded as a being of a superior order. When this had succeeded, Melitus stood forth to accuse him, together with Anytus and Lycon; the philosopher was then summoned before the tribunal of the Five Hundred <note>The Boule, or Council of 500, which handled the preliminary legal proceedings in Athens</note>. He was accused of making innovations in the religion of his country and corrupting the youth. But as both these accusations must have been obviously false to an unprejudiced tribunal, the accusers relied for the success of their cause on perjured witnesses and the envy of the judges, whose ignorance would readily yield to misrepresentation and be influenced and guided by false eloquence and fraudulent arts. That the personal enemies indeed of Socrates, vile characters, <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "racters" indicates the completion of the word "characters" on the following page.</note>

<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE APOLOGY</header>

Characters to whom his wisdom and his virtue were equally offensive should have accused him of making innovations in the religion of Greece is by no means surprising. However, that very many in modern times should have believed that this accusation was founded in truth, and that he endeavored to subvert the doctrine of polytheism <note>The belief in or worship of more than one god.</note>, is a circumstance which, by the truly learned reader, must be ranked among the greatest eccentricities of modern wit. 

For to such a reader, it will most clearly appear from this very *Apology* that Socrates was accused of impiety for asserting that he was connected in a very transcendent degree with a presiding demon <note>original: "dæmon"; in the Greek context, this refers to a tutelary spirit or divine voice, not an evil entity.</note>, to whose direction he confidently submitted the conduct of his life. For the accusation of Melitus—that he introduced other novel demonic natures—can admit of no other construction. Besides, in the course of *this* Apology, he asserts in the most unequivocal and solemn manner his belief in polytheism; and this is indubitably confirmed in many places by Plato, the most genuine of his disciples and the most faithful recorder of his doctrines. 

The testimony of Xenophon too on this point is no less weighty than decisive. "I have often wondered," says that historian and philosopher <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "Πολλακις εθαυμασα..." <page-num>198</page-num>
# INTRODUCTION TO THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.

...have made the great Socrates himself become the patron of their own shallow and distorted conceptions. But to return to the *Apology*.

Lysias, one of the most celebrated orators of the age, composed an oration in a labored and pathetic <note>original: "pathetic" here means "appealing to the emotions" or "evoking pity"</note> style, which he offered to Socrates to be delivered as his defense in the presence of his judges. Socrates, however, refused it, observing that a philosopher ought to be conspicuous for magnanimity <note>original: "magnanimity" refers to greatness of soul and courage</note> and firmness of soul. Hence, in his *Apology*, he paid no attention to the splendor of diction <note>term: the choice and use of words in speech or writing</note>, but trusted wholly to the intrinsic dignity of his sentiments. He contented himself with speaking to his judges as he used to do in common discourse, and with proposing questions to his accusers. Therefore, his defense was entirely the spontaneous effusion of his genius; simple and plain, yet vigorous and dignified.

Several persons who assisted in the court upon this occasion, besides Plato, drew up the *Apology* of Socrates. Among the rest, Xenophon compiled one from the account of Hermogenes, the son of Hipponicus, for Xenophon himself was not then at Athens. None of them survive today, however, except those of Plato and Xenophon. Of these, the first is in every respect worthy of the greatest disciple of Socrates; but the other presents us with an imperfect copy, because it was composed by a disciple who was absent. This imperfect copy, however, sufficiently proves that the substance of this *Apology* is accurate, no matter how much it may have been refined by passing through the hands of a writer like Plato.

It also notes that while several accounts of the trial were written, only those by Plato and Xenophon have survived.</summary>

# THE APOLOGY
### OF
# SOCRATES.

---

**I** do not know, O Athenians, how you may have been affected by my accusers. Indeed, because of them, I have almost forgotten who I am, so persuasively have they spoken; and yet, I may say, they have not uttered a single word of truth. 

But among the multitude of their false assertions, I am most surprised by this: their warning that you ought to beware of being deceived by me, as if I were an eloquent speaker. For they should be ashamed to make an assertion that will be immediately proven wrong by the facts—since in this very moment I shall appear to you to be by no means eloquent. This seems to me to be the height of impudence, unless they call a person "eloquent" simply for speaking the truth. If that is what they mean, I would indeed acknowledge myself to be a rhetorician <note>original: "rhetorician" — a teacher or practitioner of the art of persuasive speaking</note>, though not in the way they understand the term. 

They have not, as I said, asserted anything that is true; but from me, you will hear the whole truth. By Zeus <note>original: "by Jupiter" — the translator used the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods, Zeus</note>, O Athenians, you will not hear from me a discourse splendidly decorated with fine nouns and verbs, or polished in other ways like the speeches of these men. Instead, you will hear me speaking in such language as naturally occurs to me. For I am confident that what I say will be just, and none of you should expect it to be otherwise; for it would not be fitting for someone of my age to come before you like a young boy with a rehearsed speech. 

And, indeed, I earnestly request and beseech you, O Athenians: if you should hear me defending myself using the same terms and modes of expression which I am accustomed to use in the Forum <note>original: "Forum" — the Agora, or central public marketplace and meeting place in Athens</note>, at the money-changers' tables, and at the public banks, and in

<summary>Socrates begins his defense by addressing the Athenian citizens, warning them that his accusers have spoken persuasively but falsely, and requesting that the jury judge him on the truth of his words rather than his lack of polished oratory.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Athens, Apology, rhetoric, truth vs. eloquence, legal defense, Agora</keywords>

# THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.

<page-num>200</page-num>

—in other places, where many of you have heard me—that you will neither wonder nor be disturbed on this account. For the case is as follows: I now for the first time come before this tribunal, though I am more than seventy years old; and consequently, I am a stranger to the manner of speaking which is used here. Therefore, just as you would pardon me if I were actually a foreigner for using the language and the manner in which I had been educated, I now request—and justly so, it seems to me—that you allow my style of speech, whether it be better or worse. I ask you to focus only on this: whether I speak what is just or not. For this is the excellence of a judge, just as the excellence of an orator is to speak the truth.

In the first place, therefore, O Athenians, it is right that I should answer the first false accusations made against me and my first accusers, and afterwards the more recent accusations and the recent accusers. For many people have accused me to you for many years, asserting nothing true. I am more afraid of these than I am of <term>Anytus</term> <note>Anytus was a wealthy tanner and influential politician who was one of the three primary prosecutors of Socrates.</note> and his accomplices, though they are indeed powerful in persuasion. But those others are even more dangerous; having dealt with many of you since your infancy, they have persuaded you and accused me falsely. 

For they have said that there is a certain <term>Socrates</term>, a "wise man," who studies the heavens, explores everything under the earth, and who can make the weaker argument appear the stronger. These men, O Athenians, who spread this report are my most dreaded accusers. For those who hear it believe that people who investigate such things do not believe in the Gods. Furthermore, these accusers are numerous and have been accusing me for a long time. They also said these things to you at an age when you were most likely to believe them—when some of you were children or youths—and they accused me in my absence, with no one speaking in my defense. 

But the most irrational part of all is this: it is impossible to know or tell their names, unless one of them happens to be a comic <gloss>¹</gloss> poet. However, regarding all those who have persuaded you by using envy and slander, along with those who, having been persuaded themselves, then persuaded others—the method for dealing with them is very difficult. It is not possible to call them here before you to challenge them; instead, I must make my defense and refutation as if I were fighting with shadows, with no one there to answer me.
