# THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.

I have said that my accusers are twofold: some having accused me lately, and others formerly. I think it is necessary that I should answer the latter of these first; for you have heard these earlier accusers for a much longer time, and much more often, than you have heard those by whom I have been recently accused. Very well then. I must defend myself, O Athenians, and endeavor in this so short a space of time to remove from your minds the slander <note>original: "calumny"</note> which you have entertained for so long. I wish, therefore, that my defense may result in something better for both you and me, and that it may serve some more important purpose. I suspect, however, that this will be difficult, and I am not entirely ignorant of what that difficulty is. At the same time, let this end as God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> pleases. It is my duty to obey the law and to make my defense <note>original: "apology," from the Greek 'apologia,' meaning a formal legal defense rather than an expression of regret</note>.

Let us repeat, therefore, from the beginning what the accusation was—the source of that slander which Melitus relied upon when he brought this charge against me. Very well. What then do my accusers say? Their accusation must be formally read as if it were an indictment given under oath. It is this: **SOCRATES ACTS WICKEDLY, AND WITH CRIMINAL CURIOSITY INVESTIGATES THINGS UNDER THE EARTH AND IN THE HEAVENS. HE ALSO MAKES THE WEAKER ARGUMENT APPEAR THE STRONGER; AND HE TEACHES THESE THINGS TO OTHERS.**

Such is the accusation. You have seen these things yourselves in the comedy by Aristophanes <margin>See *The Clouds* by that poet, verse 112 and following, and verse 188.</margin>: for in that play, a character named Socrates is carried around, claiming that he walks on air and idly asserting many other trifles of that nature. I, however, know nothing at all about such matters. I do not say this to look down on such a science, if anyone actually is wise regarding those things—lest Melitus should charge me with that as a new crime—but because, O Athenians, I simply have no such knowledge. I call many of you as witnesses to this, and I ask those of you who have heard me speaking at any time—and there are many such people among you—to tell and declare to one another if you have ever heard me speak even a little about things of that kind. Neither is this true. This indeed appears to me to be a beautiful thing, if someone is able to instruct men, like Gorgias of Leontini, Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis. For each of these men, in the various cities they visit, has the power of persuading young men to join them. There is also another wise man, a Parian <note>A native of the island of Paros.</note>, who I hear has arrived here. It happened that I once met a man who spends more money on the Sophists <note>term: Sophists; professional teachers in ancient Greece who took fees for lessons in rhetoric, philosophy, and virtue.</note> than all others—I mean Callias, the son of Hipponicus. I therefore asked him, since he has two sons: "O Callias," I said, "if your two sons were two colts or calves, would we not hire someone to take care of them? Would we not pay someone to make them beautiful and ensure they possessed the good qualities natural to their kind? But now, since your sons are men, what master do you intend to have for them? Who is there that is scientifically knowledgeable in human and political virtue of this kind? For I think that you must have considered this, since you have sons. Is there such a person," I asked, "or not?" 

"There certainly is," he replied. 

"Who is he?" I asked. "And where is he from? And for how much money does he teach?" 

"It is Evenus the Parian," he said, "Socrates, and he teaches for five minae <note>original: five minæ (15l.); a mina was a unit of currency; the 15 pound sterling equivalent reflects the value at the time of this translation.</note>." 

And I indeed considered Evenus blessed if he in reality possesses this art and teaches so elegantly. I, therefore, would also glory and think highly of myself if I had a scientific knowledge of these things; but this, O Athenians, is certainly not the case.

Perhaps, however, someone may reply: "But, Socrates, what have you done then? Where did these slanders against you come from? For unless you had occupied yourself more strangely than others, and had done something different from the multitude, such a great rumor would never have been raised against you. Tell us, therefore, what it is, so that we do not pass a hasty sentence against you." 

The person who says these things appears to me to speak justly, and I will endeavor to show you what has caused me to receive this reputation and slander. Hear me, therefore; and though perhaps I shall appear to some of you to be joking, be well assured that I shall tell you the whole truth. For I, O Athenians, have acquired this name through nothing else than a certain wisdom. But of what kind is this wisdom? Perhaps it is human wisdom. For this, in reality, I appear to possess. Indeed, those whom I just now mentioned possessed perhaps more than human wisdom, which I do not know how to name: for I have no knowledge of it. And whoever says that I do, speaks falsely and makes this claim to slander <note>original: "calumniate"</note> me. You certainly know Chaerephon: he was my companion from youth, was a friend to most of you, and shared in your recent exile and return. <note>Referring to the democratic faction's exile during the reign of the Thirty Tyrants in 404 BCE.</note> You know, therefore, what kind of man Chaerephon was and how eager he was in all his undertakings. He once went to Delphi and had the boldness to consult the oracle about this very matter. Again, O Athenians, I beg you not to be disturbed: for he asked if there was anyone wiser than I am. The Pythian priestess <note>The priestess of Apollo who delivered the oracles.</note> answered that there was no one wiser. His brother can testify to the truth of these things for you, as Chaerephon himself is dead.

Consider now why I mention these things: for I am going to inform you how this slander against me arose. When I heard the answer of the oracle, I considered it like this: "What is the God saying? What is the hidden meaning <note>original: "obscurely signify"</note> of his riddle?" For I am not aware of being wise at all, either in a great or a small degree. What then does he mean by saying that I am the wisest? For he does not lie, as that is not permitted to him. 

For a long time, I was doubtful about what he could mean. Afterward, with considerable difficulty, I turned to the following method of investigating his meaning. I went to one of those who are reputed to be wise, so that there, if anywhere, I might disprove the prophecy and show the oracle, "This man is wiser than I am." 

While examining this man—there is no need to mention his name, but he was a politician—and while I observed him and talked with him, it happened, O Athenians, that this man appeared wise in the opinion of many other people, and especially in his own, but he was not actually wise. Afterward, I tried to show him that he only imagined himself to be wise, but was not. Because of this, I became hateful <note>original: "odious"</note> to him, and also to many others who were present. Departing,

Therefore, I reasoned with myself that I was wiser than this man. Hence, in this trifling particular, I appear to be wiser than him, because I do not think that I know things which I do not know. After this, I went to another of those who appeared to be wiser than him, and of him also I formed the same opinion. I am ashamed indeed, O Athenians, to tell you the truth; but at the same time it must be told. For, as I may say, almost all who were present would have spoken better about the things which these poets had composed. I discovered this, therefore, in a short time concerning the poets: that they did not achieve by wisdom that which they did, but by a certain genius and from enthusiastic energy, like prophets and those who utter oracles. Because they performed well in their specific craft, each one believed he was also very wise in other, more important matters. This error overshadowed the actual wisdom they did possess. I answered for myself and for the oracle that it was better for me to remain as I am.

I have nothing worth mentioning in either public or private affairs; instead, I am in great poverty because of my devoted service to the God <note>Socrates refers to his lifelong mission to test the Delphic Oracle's claim that he was the wisest man, which he viewed as a religious duty to Apollo.</note>.

Furthermore, the young people who follow me of their own accord—mostly those who have the most leisure time because they are the sons of the wealthiest citizens—enjoy hearing people being cross-examined by me. They often imitate me and try to test others themselves. In doing so, I believe they find a great many people who imagine they know something, but actually know little or nothing. As a result, the people they test become angry with me rather than with the young men. They say, "That Socrates is a most wicked man who corrupts the youth!" 

When someone asks them what I actually do or teach to corrupt them, they have nothing to say because they are ignorant. However, so they do not appear to be at a loss, they repeat the standard charges brought against all who study philosophy: that he "studies things in the sky and under the earth," that he "does not believe in the gods," and that he "makes the worse argument appear the better" <note>original: "makes the worse to be the better reason." This was a common accusation against Sophists, who were paid to teach the art of persuasion regardless of the truth.</note>. I believe they are unwilling to tell the truth—which is that they clearly pretend to be knowledgeable but actually know nothing. 

Therefore, since they are ambitious, forceful, and numerous, and they speak about me in an elegant and persuasive way, they have filled your ears with extreme slanders both in the past and now. Among these accusers, Melitus, Anytus, and Lycon have attacked me: Melitus is my enemy on behalf of the poets; Anytus on behalf of the craftsmen <term>artificers</term> and politicians; and Lycon on behalf of the orators. So, as I said at the beginning, I would be surprised if I could remove such a massive slander from your minds in such a short time. 

These things, O Athenians, are true. I speak to you without concealing or leaving out anything, whether great or small, even though I know well that I will make enemies by saying this. This very fact is proof that I am speaking the truth, that this is the slander raised against me, and that these are its causes. Whether you investigate these matters now or later, you will find them to be exactly as I have said. Regarding the specific charges my first accusers brought against me, let this be a sufficient defense <term>apology</term> to you.

Next, I shall try to respond to Melitus—that "good man and lover of his country," as he calls himself—and to my more recent accusers. Since they are different from the former accusers, let us look at their formal charges <note>original: "take the oath"; this refers to the sworn indictment or written charge brought by Melitus.</note>.

...worried about death and danger? For this, O Athenians, is truly the case: wherever a person takes a stand, thinking it to be best for them, or wherever they are stationed by a leader, there, as it seems to me, they ought to stay and face danger. They should not consider death or anything else more important than avoiding what is shameful <note>original: "base"</note>.

I would have acted disgracefully, O Athenians, if I had stayed at my post when the leaders you chose for me stationed me at Potidaea, Amphipolis, and Delium <note>These were three major battles in the Peloponnesian War where Socrates served as a hoplite (heavy infantryman).</note>—facing the danger of death like anyone else—but then deserted my post now. Now, when the Divine has ordered (as I believe and understand) that I should live my life practicing philosophy and examining myself and others, should I abandon my duty out of fear of death or anything else? 

That would truly be disgraceful. Then, someone might rightly bring me to a court of law <note>original: "judicature"</note> and accuse me of not believing in the gods, because I disobeyed the oracle <note>Referring to the Oracle at Delphi, which sparked Socrates's mission to find if anyone was wiser than he.</note> out of a fear of death, thinking I was wise when I am not. For fearing death, O Athenians, is nothing more than appearing to be wise without actually being so; it is pretending to know what one does not know. No one knows whether death might actually be the greatest possible good for a human being; yet people fear it as if they knew for certain it was the greatest of evils. 

And how is it possible that this should not be the most shameful kind of ignorance—to think one has knowledge of something they are actually ignorant of? In this, O Athenians, I perhaps differ from the majority of men. If I were to say I am wiser than someone else in any way, it would be in this: that because I do not have sufficient knowledge of the afterlife <note>original: "the things in Hades"</note>, I also do not pretend that I have this knowledge. But I do know that acting unjustly and being disobedient to a superior—whether God or man—is evil and shameful. I will never, therefore, fear and avoid things which, for all I know, may be good, more than those evils which I know to be evils. 

So, even if you should dismiss me now—refusing to be convinced by Anytus, who said that either I should never have been brought here in the first place, or that once I was here, it was impossible not to put me to death (telling you that if I escaped, all your sons would be corrupted by studying what Socrates taught them)—if, besides these things, you should say to me, "Socrates, we will not listen to Anytus this time; we will let you go, but only on this condition..."

<summary>Socrates argues that his commitment to philosophy is a divine mandate that he cannot abandon, comparing it to his military service. He asserts that fearing death is a form of false wisdom, as no one knows if death is actually a blessing or an evil.</summary>

...condition, that afterwards you no longer busy yourself with this investigation, nor practice philosophy <note>original: "philosophise"</note>, and if hereafter you are detected in so doing, you shall die—if, as I said, you should dismiss me on these terms, I should thus address you: 

"O Athenians, I honor and love you, but I obey God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> rather than you. As long as I breathe and am able, I shall not cease to practice philosophy. I will continue to exhort and point out the truth to any one of you I may happen to meet, speaking in my usual manner: 'O best of men, since you are an Athenian—a citizen of the greatest city and the most celebrated for wisdom and strength—are you not ashamed of being so focused on acquiring riches, glory, and honor in great abundance, while you bestow no care or consideration upon wisdom <note>original: "prudence*"</note> and truth, nor how your soul may exist in the most excellent condition?'"

And if any one of you should argue with me and say that these things are the objects of his care, I should not immediately dismiss him nor depart. Instead, I should interrogate, explore, and reason with him. If he does not appear to me to possess virtue, and yet pretends to possess it, I should reprove him as one who has little esteem for things of the greatest worth, but considers things of a vile and worthless <note>original: "abject"</note> nature to be of great importance. 

In this manner I should act toward anyone I might happen to meet, whether younger or older, a stranger or a citizen—but especially to citizens, because you are more closely allied to me. For be well assured that God commands me to act this way. And I think that a greater good never happened to you in the city than this, my obedience to the will of the Divine. 

For I go about doing nothing else than persuading both the younger and older among you neither to pay attention to the body, nor to riches, nor anything else before the soul. I urge you not to be so concerned for anything as how the soul may exist in the most excellent condition. I also say that virtue is not produced from riches, but riches from virtue—as are all other human goods, both privately and publicly. If, therefore, by asserting these things I corrupt the youth, then these things must be harmful <note>original: "noxious"</note>; but if anyone says that I assert anything other than these things, he says nothing of substance. In addition to this I shall say, O Athenians, that whether you are persuaded by Anytus <note>One of the primary accusers of Socrates.</note> or not, and whether you dismiss me or not, I shall not act otherwise, even though I should die many times over.

Do not be disturbed, O Athenians, but listen patiently to what I shall request of you; for I think it will be to your benefit to hear it. I am about to mention certain other things to you which might make you shout out in protest; however, please do not let that happen. 

Be well assured then: if you put me to death—being the kind of man I say I am—you will not injure me more than you injure yourselves. For neither Meletus nor Anytus can injure me; it is not in their power to do so. Indeed, I believe it is not in the nature of things <note>original: "not lawful"</note> for a better man to be truly harmed by a worse man. He may, perhaps, condemn me to death, or exile, or disgrace; and he or others may consider these to be great evils. I, however, do not think so. In my opinion, it is a much greater evil to act as he is acting now—attempting to put a man to death unjustly. 

Therefore, O Athenians, it is far from my intention to speak in my own defense (as some might think); rather, I speak for your sake, so that you do not sin against the gift of God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> by condemning me. For if you put me to death, you will not easily find another like me—though the comparison may sound ridiculous—whom God has attached to this city as if to a large and noble horse that has become sluggish because of its great size and needs to be stirred up by a gadfly <note>original: "a certain fly"</note>. 

In the same way, God seems to have attached someone like me to the city, so that I might never stop rousing, persuading, and reproving every one of you, staying by your side all day long wherever you are. Another man like me will not easily appear among you. Therefore, if you take my advice, you will spare me. 

Perhaps, however, you will feel annoyed—like people suddenly awakened from a deep sleep—and will strike out at me. If you are persuaded by Anytus, you might thoughtlessly put me to death. If that happens, you will spend the rest of your lives asleep, unless God sends someone else to look after you. 

You can understand that I am indeed such a person—one given to this city by God—from this evidence: it does not seem like natural human behavior for me to have neglected all my own affairs and my private interests for so many years, while always attending to your concerns—approaching each of you individually, like a father or an elder brother, to persuade you to the study of virtue. 

If I had gained any profit <note>original: "emolument"</note> from this behavior, or if I had received payment for exhorting you to these things, there might be some reason to claim I acted like other men. But now look: even my accusers themselves, who have so shamelessly slandered <note>original: "calumniated"</note> me in every other way...

Then, not through words but through deeds, I showed them—if the expression is not too blunt <note>original: "rustic"</note>—that I do not care about death at all. My only concern was that I should do nothing unjust or unholy. For the power of the Thirty, as formidable as it was, did not terrify me into committing an unjust act. When we left the Tholus, the other four went to Salamis and brought back Leon, but I simply went home. I might have been put to death for this, had that government not been quickly overthrown. Many of you can testify to these facts.

Do you think, then, that I could have survived for so many years if I had entered public life and acted as a good man should, supporting justice and making it my primary concern? Far from it, O Athenians; nor could any other man have done so. But throughout my whole life, whenever I have acted publicly, I have shown myself to be such a man. And I am the same in private: I will never yield anything to anyone that is contrary to justice—not even to those whom my accusers <note>original: "calumniators"</note> claim are my disciples. 

However, I have never been anyone’s teacher <note>original: "preceptor"</note>. But I never turned away anyone, young or old, who desired to hear me speak in my usual way. # THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.

It appears to me that I have now escaped <term>Meletus</term> <note>original: "Melitus"</note>; and not only have I escaped him, but it is perfectly evident that unless <term>Anytus</term> and <term>Lycon</term> <note>original: "Lyco"</note> had risen to accuse me, he would have lost his thousand <gloss>1</gloss> drachmas, since he did not receive even a fifth part of the votes on his side.

What, then, do I deserve to suffer or to pay, for not having remained silent during my life about what I have learned, but instead neglecting everything that the crowd values—riches, domestic concerns, military command, leadership in public assemblies, and other offices? I avoided the conspiracies and rebellions <note>original: "seditions"</note> which have happened in the city, believing that I was in reality a more honorable character than to depend on these things for my safety. I have not, therefore, devoted myself to those pursuits by which I could benefit neither you nor myself. Instead, my whole effort has been to benefit every individual in the greatest degree, striving to persuade each of you that he should pay no attention to any of his personal concerns before caring for himself—by which he may become a most worthy and wise man; that he should not attend to the affairs of the city before the city itself; and that attention should be paid to other things in a similar manner. 

What then, being such a man, do I deserve to suffer? Something good, O Athenians, if in reality you honor me according to my merit; and such a good as is appropriate for me to receive. What, then, is the reward that is suitable for a poor man who is a benefactor, and who requires leisure so that he may encourage you to virtue? # THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.

Perhaps you think, Athenians, that I was condemned because I lacked the kind of words that would have persuaded you—if I had thought it right to say and do whatever it took to escape punishment. Far from it. I was indeed condemned for a lack, but it was not a lack of words. Instead, it was a lack of audacity and impudence, and because I was unwilling to say the things you would have been most pleased to hear. I refused to weep and lament, or to do and say many other things that I consider beneath me, even though you are accustomed to seeing and hearing such behavior from other defendants. 

But I did not think then that I should do anything ungentlemanly <note>original: "illiberal" — meaning behavior not becoming of a free man</note> just to avoid danger, nor do I now regret defending myself in this way. I would much rather die after making this defense than live by behaving in that manner. In a court of law, just as in battle, neither I nor anyone else should try to escape death by any means possible. In battle, it is often obvious that a man could avoid death by throwing away his weapons and falling as a suppliant <note>original: "suppliantly converting himself" — turning toward pursuers to beg for mercy</note> before his pursuers. 

There are many other ways to escape death in dangerous situations, if one is daring enough to say or do anything. However, Athenians, escaping death is not the difficult part; escaping wickedness <note>original: "depravity"</note> is much harder, for it runs faster than death. Now I, being slow and old, have been caught by the slower runner (death). But my accusers, who are clever and quick, have been caught by the faster runner: wickedness <note>original: "improbity" — lack of integrity or honesty</note>. 

Now I depart, condemned by you to die. But they depart condemned by the truth to a reputation of wickedness and injustice. I accept this outcome, and so must they. Perhaps it was necessary for things to turn out this way, and I believe it is for the best.

Next, I wish to predict what will happen to those of you who have condemned me. I am now in that state where men are most likely to prophesy <note>The belief that people become prophetic at the moment of death can be traced back to the time of Homer and is undoubtedly an ancient idea.</note>—that is, when they are about to die. Additionally, a devastating plague struck Athens shortly afterward.</note> by dying in a

## THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.

...manner, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter" — the translator used the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods</note>, much more severe than mine has been. Instead, the finest and easiest way is not to silence others, but to behave in such a manner that you may become people of excellent character. This is my prophecy to those of you who condemned me.

But to those of you who voted for my acquittal, I would gladly speak about this affair while the officials are busy and before I am brought to the place where I must die. Stay with me for a little while, Athenians. For nothing prevents us from conversing with each other as long as we are permitted to do so; I wish to explain to you, as friends, the meaning of what has just happened to me. 

To me then, O my judges—and in calling you "judges," I use the title you truly deserve—a wonderful thing has happened. In the past, the prophetic voice of my divine spirit <note>original: "dæmon" — from the Greek *daimonion*, a divine inner sign or "voice" that Socrates claimed guided his actions</note> was constantly accustomed to speak to me. It would oppose me even in the most trivial matters if I was about to act improperly. But now, though these events have happened to me which you see—events which someone might think are the ultimate evils—the divine signal did not oppose me when I left home this morning, nor when I came up here to the place of judgment, nor when I was about to speak. In other situations, it frequently stopped me in the middle of a sentence, but in this entire affair, it has never opposed me in either word or deed. 

I will tell you what I believe to be the cause of this. This thing which has happened to me appears to be a good thing; those of us who think death is an evil are likely mistaken. I have great evidence for this: my accustomed signal would surely have opposed me, unless I were about to meet with something good.

death is good. For to die is one of two things. It is either to be as it were nothing <gloss>1</gloss>, and to be deprived of all sensation; or, as it is said, it is a certain change <note>original: "mutation"</note> and migration of the soul from this place to another. 

And if no sensation remains, but death is like a sleep uninterrupted by any dreams, then death will be a gain. For if anyone compares such a night as this—in which he sleeps so profoundly that he does not even see a dream—with the other nights and days of his life, and were to declare how many of them he had passed better and more pleasantly than this night, I think that not only an ordinary person, but even the Great King <note>The King of Persia, who was considered the most powerful and wealthy man of that era.</note> himself, would find so few that they could be easily counted. If, therefore, death is something of this kind, I say it is a gain; for then the whole of future time appears to be nothing more than a single night. 

But if, on the other hand, death is a migration from here to another place, and the claim is true that all the dead are there, what greater good, O my judges, can there be than this? For if someone arriving in the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note>, being liberated from those here who pretend to be judges, should find those who are true judges—those who are said to preside there, namely *Minos*, *Rhadamanthus*, *Aeacus*, and *Triptolemus* <note>In Greek mythology, these were legendary figures renowned for their justice who became the judges of the dead.</note>, and other demigods who lived justly—would that be a wretched <note>original: "vile"</note> journey? 

At what price would you not purchase a conversation with *Orpheus* and *Musaeus*, with *Hesiod* and *Homer*? Indeed, I would be willing to die many times if these things are true. For to me, the company will be wonderful when I meet *Palamedes*, and *Ajax* the son of *Telamon*, and any others of the ancients <note>original: "antients"</note> who died because of an unjust verdict. Comparing my own case with theirs will, I think, be a very pleasant occupation. 

But the greatest pleasure will consist in passing my time there, just as I have done here, in questioning and exploring who among them is wise, and who only fancies himself to be wise but is not. What would anyone not give, O my judges, for a conversation with the man who led that mighty army against *Troy* <note>Agamemnon</note>, or with *Odysseus* <note>original: "Ulysses"</note>, or *Sisyphus*, or ten thousand other men and women who could be mentioned? To converse and associate with these would be an immeasurable happiness <note>original: "inestimable felicity"</note>. Nor is my present condition the result of chance; rather, it is evident to me that to die now and be liberated from the affairs of life is better for me. For this reason, my accustomed signal <note>The "accustomed signal" refers to Socrates' *daimonion*, a divine inner voice or sign that warned him against taking actions that would be harmful to his soul.</note> did not oppose me in this matter. Nor am I very angry with those who accused and condemned me, even though their intention in doing so was to injure me; for this, they deserve to be blamed. 

However, I make this one request of them: punish my sons when they grow up if they cause you the same trouble <note>original: "molestation"</note> that I have. If they appear to you to pay more attention to riches or anything else than to virtue, and if they think they are something when they are actually nothing, then rebuke <note>original: "reprobate"</note> them as I do you. Criticize them for neglecting the care of things to which they ought to attend, and for imagining themselves to be of some consequence when they are of no worth. If you do these things, your conduct toward both me and my sons will be just. 

But it is now time to depart from here—for me to die, and for you to live. Which of us will arrive at a better <gloss>1</gloss> state, however, is completely unknown <note>original: "immanifest"</note> to everyone except to God <note>original: "Divinity"</note>.

---

<gloss>1</gloss> It is always good for a righteous man to die for his own sake; but it is often better for the community that he should live. Similarly, it is often better for a bad man to live than to die, so that his hidden <note>original: "latent"</note> vices may be brought out into the open; furthermore, a bad man is frequently an instrument in the hand of God to bring about good for others. Socrates, therefore, with as much accuracy as depth, says that only God knows whether it is better for him to die than for his accusers to live. This could only be determined by an extensive knowledge of the future <note>original: "futurity"</note>, and consequently could only be clear to the Divine.

# THE CRITO.

...and in the past, throughout your whole life, I have considered you happy because of your character <note>original: "manners"</note>, but even more so in your current misfortune, because you bear it so easily and calmly.

**Soc.** But it would be absurd, Crito, if a man of my age were to be resentful <note>original: "indignant"</note> when it is time for him to die.

**Cri.** And yet others, Socrates, who are just as old, have been resentful of their fate when they were caught in similar misfortunes, despite their age.

**Soc.** That is true. But why did you come to me so early?

**Cri.** I come, Socrates, bringing news that is not unpleasant to you, it seems to me, but is bitter and heavy to me and all your friends; news which I, especially, will find most difficult to bear.

**Soc.** What is it? Has the ship <note>See the *Phaedo*, near the beginning. The ship's return from a religious mission to Delos signaled the end of the stay of execution for prisoners.</note> come from Delos, the arrival of which means I must die?

**Cri.** Not yet; but it seems to me, based on what some people coming from Sunium <note>A cape at the southernmost tip of the Attic peninsula.</note> have reported, that it will arrive today. They left it there. From these messengers, it is clear it will be here today; and therefore, Socrates, it will be necessary for you to die tomorrow.

**Soc.** Well, may it be with good fortune, Crito; if it pleases the gods, let it be so. However, I do not think it will arrive here today.

**Cri.** What makes you think that?

**Soc.** I will tell you. For on the day after the ship arrives, or on the very day it arrives, the law says I must die.

**Cri.** The authorities <note>original: "Those that have power over these things"</note> say so.

**Soc.** Therefore, I do not think it will come today, but tomorrow. I conclude this from a certain dream I had tonight, just before you arrived; it seems you were very considerate <note>original: "very opportunely"</note> not to have disturbed me.

**Cri.** And what was this dream?

**Soc.** A certain woman, beautiful and lovely to look at, dressed in white robes, seemed to approach me and say, "On the third day from now, Socrates, you will reach fertile Phthia <note>Phthia was the home of the hero Achilles. Socrates interprets this quote from Homer's *Iliad* as a prophecy that his soul will "return home" to the afterlife in three days.</note>."

# THE CRITO.

**Cri.** What a strange dream, Socrates!

**Soc.** It seems clear enough to me, Crito.

**Cri.** Too clear, it seems. But, my dear <note>original: "blessed"</note> Socrates, please listen to me now and save yourself. For if you die, it will not be just one misfortune for me. Aside from losing a friend the likes of whom I will never find again, people who do not know us well will think that I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend my money, but that I neglected to do so. What could be more shameful <note>original: "base"</note> than such a reputation? It would make it look as though I value riches more than my friends. The majority <note>original: "multitude"</note> will never believe that you were unwilling to leave this place, even though we did everything we could to help you escape.

**Soc.** But why, my dear Crito, should we care so much about the opinion of the majority? The most reasonable men—whose opinions are the ones we should truly respect—will understand that these things happened exactly as they did.

**Cri.** Nevertheless, you see, Socrates, that it is necessary to pay attention to public opinion. Current circumstances show that the many can cause not just small evils, but nearly the greatest ones, if anyone is slandered by them.

**Soc.** I wish, Crito, that the many could indeed cause the greatest evils, for then they might also be capable of doing the greatest good—that would be ideal. But in reality, they can do neither. They cannot make a man wise, nor can they make him foolish <note>original: "destitute of wisdom"</note>; instead, they simply act at random.

**Cri.** That may be so. But answer me this, Socrates: are you worried about me and your other friends? Are you afraid that if you escape, informers <note>original: "calumniators"</note> will give us trouble for smuggling you out, and we will be forced to lose our property, pay a huge fine, or suffer some other punishment? If you fear anything like that, put it out of your mind. We are doing the right thing by taking this risk to save you—and even greater risks, if necessary. So please, listen to me and do not refuse.

**Soc.** I am considering these things, Crito, and many others as well.

**CRI.** It is agreed.

**CRITO:** We must not.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, even someone who is injured must not return the injury, as most people think, since one must never act unjustly.

**CRITO:** So it seems.

**SOCRATES:** What about this? Is it right to do harm <note>original: "evil"</note> to anyone, Crito, or not?

**CRITO:** It is not right, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** And what about this? Is it just to repay harm with harm, as most people say, or is it not just?

**CRITO:** Not at all.

**SOCRATES:** Because doing harm to people is no different from acting unjustly.

**CRITO:** That is true.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is never right to return an injury or to do harm to any person, no matter what harm you have suffered from them. But be careful, Crito, that in acknowledging this, you are not agreeing to something you do not truly believe. For I know that only a very few people hold or will ever hold this opinion. Those who believe this and those who do not have no common ground for counsel; they must inevitably look down on one another <note>original: "despise each other"</note> when they see each other’s decisions. Therefore, consider very carefully whether you agree with me and share this opinion, and whether we should start our discussion from this premise: that it is never right to do wrong, nor to return a wrong, nor to defend oneself against evil by returning evil. Or do you disagree and reject this starting point? This is what I believed then and what I still believe now; but if you have any other view...

We also say that he who is not obedient is triply unjust: first, because he is disobedient to his parents <note>original: "begetters"</note>; second, to those who educated him; and third, because, having promised to be persuaded by us, he neither obeys nor does he persuade us if we are doing something improperly. Yet, at the same time, we only propose—and do not fiercely command—him to do what we order. We leave him the choice of two things: either to persuade us <note>The Laws allow for legal dissent or efforts to change the law through reasoned argument.</note> or to obey our mandates; yet he does neither.

"And we say that you also, Socrates, will be vulnerable <note>original: "obnoxious"—in this context, it means liable to a charge or punishment rather than "annoying."</note> to these crimes if you carry out what you intend to do; and you will not be the least, but the most guilty of all the Athenians." 

If I should ask them the reason for this, they would perhaps justly reproach me by saying that I, more than the rest of the Athenians, promised to submit to all these conditions. For they would say, "Socrates, this is a great argument for us: that both we and the city were pleasing to you. You, especially of all the Athenians, would never have dwelt in it so constantly if it had not been particularly agreeable to you. For you never left the city for any of the public festivals <note>original: "spectacles"—referring to religious or athletic festivals outside of Athens, such as the Olympic Games.</note> except once, when you...

<meta>catchword: went</meta>

<summary>The personified Laws of Athens argue that Socrates has entered into a "social contract" by choosing to live in the city as an adult. They claim that by staying, he has implicitly agreed to obey the law or legally change it, making his escape an act of triple injustice.</summary>

"You never went to the Isthmian games <note>Ancient Greek athletic festivals held at the Isthmus of Corinth, second only to the Olympics.</note>, nor did you ever go anywhere else except on military expeditions. You never took any other journey like other men, nor had you any desire to see other cities or to become acquainted with other laws. We and our city were sufficient for you; you were so exceedingly attached to us, and so willingly consented to be governed by our commands. Besides, you have fathered <note>original: "procreated"</note> children in this city because you were pleased with it. 

"Furthermore, during this very trial <note>original: "judicial process"</note>, you could have been sentenced to exile if you had wished. You could have done then, with the city's consent, what you are now attempting to do without it. At that time, however, you carried yourself with dignity <note>original: "loftily"</note>, as one who would not be distressed if it were required that you should die; you said you preferred death to exile. But now you are neither ashamed of those claims, nor do you respect us, the Laws, since you are trying to destroy us. You are doing what the most wretched slave would do: attempting to run away in violation of the contracts and agreements by which you consented to be a member of this community. In the first place, therefore, answer us this: are we speaking the truth when we assert that you consented to be governed by us in reality, and not merely in words? Are we speaking the truth?"

What shall we say to these things, Crito? Can we say anything else than that we agree with them?

**CRI.** We must do so, Socrates.

**Soc.** "Are you not then," they will say, "violating these contracts and agreements you made with us? You did not consent to them out of necessity or through deception, nor because you were forced to decide in a short time. You had seventy years during which you could have left if you were dissatisfied with us, or if the contracts appeared unjust to you. Yet you preferred neither Sparta <note>original: "Lacedæmon"</note> nor Crete—which you are always saying are governed by good laws—nor any other city of the Greeks or non-Greeks <note>original: "Barbarians"</note>. Instead, you have been out of Athens less than the lame, the blind, and those with other physical disabilities. That is how much this city and we, the Laws, pleased you more than other Athenians. For who can be pleased with a city that has no laws? But now you are not abiding by your agreements. If you are persuaded by us, Socrates, you will abide by them and not make yourself a laughingstock by escaping from the city."

<summary>The Laws of Athens argue that Socrates has implicitly accepted a social contract by choosing to live in the city for seventy years, fathering children there, and declining the option of exile during his trial.</summary>

"Consider what advantage you or your friends would gain by breaking these agreements. It is quite obvious that if you escape from here, your friends will be put in danger of either exile <note>original: "banishment"</note> or the seizure of their property. As for yourself, if you retreat to any neighboring city, such as Thebes or Megara (for both are governed by good laws), you will be viewed, Socrates, as an enemy to their political system <note>original: "polity"</note>. Anyone who has any regard for their country will look upon you as a corrupter of the laws. 

"By doing this, you will also validate the opinion of your judges, who will appear to have been perfectly right to condemn you. After all, someone who corrupts the laws will certainly seem to be a corrupter of the young and the foolish. Will you then avoid these well-governed cities and people of the most refined character? If you do, will your life even be worth living? Or, if you go to these cities, will you not blush, Socrates, to speak about the same things you did here? Will you still claim that virtue, justice, legal institutions, and the laws should be a person’s highest priorities? Do you not think such conduct from Socrates would be deeply improper <note>original: "indecorous"</note>? You certainly must think so. 

"But perhaps, avoiding these cities, you will go to Thessaly <note>A region in northern Greece known in antiquity for its lawlessness and excessive lifestyle.</note> to stay with Crito’s friends. In that place, there is the greatest disorder and lack of restraint. Perhaps they will even enjoy hearing you tell the ridiculous story of how you escaped from prison by dressing yourself in a disguise <note>original: "apparatus"</note>—such as a leather skin or some other costume that escapees typically use—thus changing your usual appearance.

"Do you think no one will point out that you, an old man with very little time left to live, dared to cling to life with such shameful greed <note>original: "sordid avidity"</note> that you broke the highest laws? Perhaps no one will say this if you do not offend anyone. But if you do, Socrates, you will hear many things said about you that are beneath your dignity. You will live as a servant, subject to the whims of all men <note>original: "obnoxious, and in subjection to all men"</note>. And what will you do in Thessaly besides feast? You would be going to Thessaly as if you were merely traveling for a dinner party! And what would happen to those famous discussions of yours concerning justice and the other virtues? 

"But do you wish to live for the sake of your children, so that you may raise and instruct them? What then? By bringing them to Thessaly, will you educate them there? You would be making them foreigners <note>original: "stranger guests"</note> so they might 'benefit' from that status too. Or, if you do not do this but leave them here in Athens, will they be better raised and..."

<page-num>243</page-num>
<header>THE CRITO.</header>

"...Will your children be educated in your absence? For your friends will take care of them. Do you suppose, then, that your children will be cared for by your friends if you go to Thessaly, but that they will be neglected by them if you depart to the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note>? If indeed any benefit is to be gained from those who call themselves your friends, it is right to think they will not neglect them.

"But, Socrates, be persuaded by us, your nurturers. Do not prioritize your children, your life, or anything else over justice, so that when you arrive in the underworld, you may be able to justify all these actions to the rulers there. For if you act this way and break the laws, it will not be better, more just, or more holy for yourself or for any of your friends; nor will it be more advantageous to you when you arrive in the afterlife. As it stands, if you depart this life, you depart having been wronged not by us, the Laws, but by men. 

"However, if you escape so disgracefully—returning injury for injury and evil for evil, breaking your agreements and contracts with us, and harming those you should least of all harm (namely yourself, your friends, your country, and us)—then we will be angry with you as long as you live. Furthermore, in the next life, our brothers—the Laws who reside in the underworld—will not receive you kindly, knowing that you attempted, as far as you were able, to destroy us. Therefore, do not let Crito persuade you to follow his advice instead of ours."

Be well assured, my dear friend Crito, that I seem to hear these things just as those in a religious frenzy <note>original: "Corybantic fury"—referring to the ecstatic, rhythmic state of the worshippers of the goddess Cybele.</note> seem to hear the music of flutes. The sound of these words hums in my ears like bees, making me unable to hear anything else. You see, then, how I feel at this moment; and if you say anything to the contrary, you will speak in vain. However, if you think anything more should be done, tell me.

**CRITO:** But, Socrates, I have nothing further to say.

**SOCRATES:** Then stop here, Crito, and let us follow this course of action, since God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> persuades us to act this way.

# INTRODUCTION
->TO<-
## THE PHAEDO.
---

The following dialogue is as remarkable for its masterful composition as it is for the different effects its reading is said to have produced in the past. The arguments for the immortality of the soul contained within it are said to have driven <term>Cleombrotus</term> <note>Cleombrotus of Ambracia was a young man who reportedly jumped into the sea to reach the afterlife after reading this book.</note> to suicide, yet to have discouraged <term>Olympiodorus</term> <note>A 6th-century Platonic philosopher whose commentary on the *Phaedo* is a primary source for Neoplatonic thought.</note>, an eminent Platonic philosopher, from committing the same act. Indeed, it is not at all surprising that someone like Cleombrotus—who was ignorant (as his actions show) that the "death" so often emphasized in this dialogue is a philosophical death, not a natural one—should be led to an act that is, in most cases, a grave crime. However, this misunderstanding is not unique to Cleombrotus; I fear there are hardly any people today who realize that it is one thing for the soul to be separated from the body, and another for the body to be separated from the soul—and that the former is by no means a necessary consequence of the latter.

This philosophical death, or the separation of the soul from the body, which is one of the most important themes of the dialogue, is nothing other than the practice of the <term>cathartic virtues</term> <note>original: "cathartic virtues"; these are purifying practices intended to detach the soul's focus from physical sensations and passions.</note>, of which the reader will find a detailed explanation in the following notes. That these virtues are not mere inventions of the later Platonists, as some ignorant <term>verbalists</term> <note>Scholars who focus narrowly on grammar and literal definitions rather than deep philosophical meaning.</note> have recklessly claimed, is clear not only from the first part of this dialogue but also from the <term>Golden Pythagorean Verses</term>, which are certainly older than even the writings of Plato. One of the precepts in these verses states:

> "But abstain from the foods we mentioned, both in purifications and in the liberation of the soul, while exercising your judgment." <note>original: Αλλ' ειργου βρωτων, ων ειπομεν, εν τε καθαρμοις, Εν τε λυσει ψυχης κρινων·</note>

<meta>i.e. "Abstain"</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the *Phaedo*, distinguishing between the "natural death" of the body and the "philosophical death" (purification) of the soul. It defends the concept of purifying virtues as an ancient Pythagorean tradition rather than a later invention.</summary>
<keywords>Phaedo, Cleombrotus, Olympiodorus, immortality of the soul, philosophical death, cathartic virtues, Golden Pythagorean Verses, Plato, purification</keywords>

--- Page 2197 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato’s Phaedo, specifically expanding on the concept of "cathartic virtue" mentioned at the end of the previous page. It discusses the different arguments for the immortality of the soul found in the Phaedo versus the Phaedrus.</meta>

<page-num>248</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>
<sig>7</sig>

That is, "Abstain from the foods of which we have spoken in the **PURIFICATIONS** and **RELEASING** <note>original: "solution"; in this philosophical context, it refers to the "loosening" or detachment of the soul from the body's influence.</note> of the soul." The practice of cathartic virtue entirely consists in *purifying* the soul and liberating it from all attachment to the body, as far as the conditions of its union with the body will permit.

Regarding the arguments brought forward by Socrates in this dialogue, some—as will be shown in the notes—only demonstrate that the soul existed before the body and will survive its dissolution, but they do not prove that it has a *perpetual* existence. However, other arguments demonstrate with an unanswerable force that the soul is *truly immortal*. It may seem strange—and to those who are not deeply skilled in the philosophy of Plato, it undoubtedly will—that Socrates never introduces in any part of this dialogue the argument for the immortality of the soul which he adopts in the *Phaedrus*. That argument is drawn from the rational soul being the origin of motion, and it may be said to possess unbreakable <note>original: "adamantine"</note> strength. To answer this doubt, it is necessary to observe that in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates demonstrates the immortality of every rational soul—namely, the human, daemonic, and divine—but in the *Phaedo*, he demonstrates the immortality of the human soul alone.

But though some of the arguments in this dialogue are perfectly demonstrative, certain modern writers, through a lack of understanding, have not only attempted to invalidate them but have even imagined that Socrates himself, convinced of their insufficiency, suggests in the course of the dialogue the necessity of a divine revelation in order to obtain full conviction of this most important truth. As this is an opinion no less dangerous than it is erroneous, I shall present the reader with the passage that gave rise to it, and then reveal its true explanation from ancient sources.

About the middle of this dialogue, Simmias observes as follows:

> "Personally, Socrates, I am perhaps of the same opinion about these matters as you: that to know them clearly in the present life is either impossible or a thing very difficult to achieve. But to not examine what has been said in every possible way—or to give up before an exhausting investigation on all sides is finished—can only happen among lazy and weak-willed men. For in things of this kind, it is necessary either to learn or to discover the manner of their existence; or, if both of these are impossible, then by accepting the best of human reasons, and that which is..."

<summary>The author explains that the Phaedo focuses specifically on the immortality of the human soul, unlike the Phaedrus which covers all rational souls. He also begins to refute modern claims that Socrates believed human reason was insufficient to prove immortality without divine revelation.</summary>

<keywords>Phaedo, Phaedrus, Socrates, immortality of the soul, cathartic virtue, Simmias, divine revelation, Platonic philosophy, rational soul</keywords>

--- Page 2198 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's Phaedo, addressing modern criticisms and clarifying the philosophical arguments regarding the "divine reason" and "firmer vehicle" mentioned by Simmias in the dialogue.</meta>

<page-num>249</page-num>
<header>THE PHÆDO.</header>
<sig>VOL. IV. 2 K</sig>

...the most difficult to disprove, to venture upon this as on a raft, and sail in it through the ocean of life, unless someone should be able to be carried more safely and with less danger by means of a firmer vehicle, or a certain *divine reason.*" Here, in the first place, it must be observed that it is Simmias who speaks this way—an imperfect disciple of his great master, as is evident from many parts of this dialogue—and not Socrates himself. And, in the next place, though it should be urged that Socrates himself is here said by Simmias to have admitted that "to know these particulars<sup>1</sup> clearly in the present life is either impossible or a thing very difficult to obtain," it must be observed that Socrates speaks this way from a deep conviction that this sublime truth, the immortality of the soul, could not be fully understood by his listeners, who were very far from being masters in philosophy, and that this must be the case with the multitude in general. Hence, he says, it is either impossible or very difficult to obtain this knowledge. To the *multitude* it is impossible, and to the *few* very difficult, because it requires many preparatory disciplines and a genius naturally adapted to sublime speculations.

In the third place, by a *firmer vehicle*, or a *certain divine reason*, Socrates does not allude to a divine tradition, since this affords no higher evidence than that of opinion. It is well observed, therefore, by Olympiodorus, in his manuscript commentaries <note>original: "MS. Scholia"</note> on this dialogue, that by this <term>theios logos</term> <note>original: ϑειος λογος</note>, or *divine reason*, we must understand *self-beholding intellect*, which, agreeably to Plato's description of it in the *Phaedrus*, associates with Deity itself. <note>original Greek: Τις ὁ ασφαλεστερος, και ακινδυνότερος, και βεβαιοτερος, και ϑειος λογος; ου δηπου ὡς Φασιν ὁ ϑεοϑεν εκδοϑεις, δοξαστικος γαρ ὁ γε τοιουτος· αλλ’ εστιν ὁ ειρημενος αυτοπτικος νους, ὁ ϑεῳ τῳ οντι συνων, ὡς εν Φαιδρῳ. Translation: "What is the safer, less dangerous, more stable, and divine reason? Certainly not, as they say, a tradition given from the gods, for such a thing is based on opinion; but it is the aforementioned self-beholding intellect, which is associated with Being itself, as described in the Phaedrus."</note> In order however to understand what Olympiodorus means by *self-beholding intellect*, it is necessary to observe that there are four modes of knowledge which we are able to acquire in the present life. The first of these results from opinion, by which we learn *that* a thing is, without knowing the *why*; and this constitutes that part of knowledge which was called by Aristotle and Plato <term>paideia</term> <note>original: παιδεια</note>, or erudition; and which consists in moral instructions for the purpose of purifying ourselves from immoderate passions. But the second is produced by the sciences; in which, from establishing certain principles as hypotheses, we draw <note>original: "educe"</note> necessary conclusions, and arrive

---

<note><sup>1</sup> Namely, the particulars pertaining to the past and future existence of the soul.</note>

<summary>This page analyzes Simmias's metaphor of the "divine reason" as a raft for the soul, clarifying that Socrates views true knowledge of immortality as a difficult achievement involving "self-beholding intellect" rather than mere tradition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Phaedo, concluding the explanation of the four types of knowledge and the philosopher's direct intuition of truth, often called "divine reason." It also cites Plato's Seventh Letter to affirm his commitment to the soul's immortality.</meta>

<page-num>250</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE PHÆDO.</header>
<sig>8</sig>

## INTRODUCTION TO THE PHÆDO.

...at the knowledge of the *why* (as in the mathematical sciences); but at the same time, we are ignorant with respect to the principles of these conclusions because they are merely hypothetical. The third species of knowledge is that which results from Plato’s dialectic. In this, by progressing through all ideas, we arrive at the first principle of things and at that which is no longer hypothetical. We achieve this by dividing some things and analyzing others, and by producing many things from one thing and one thing from many. 

But the fourth species of knowledge is even simpler than this. It no longer uses analyses or compositions, definitions or demonstrations. Instead, by a simple and self-perceiving <note>original: "self-visive"</note> energy of intellect, it contemplates things themselves. Through intuition and direct contact, it becomes one with the object of its perception. This energy is the *divine reason* which Plato speaks of in the present passage. It far transcends the evidence of even the most divine revelation, since revelation is, at best, founded only on opinion, while this intuition surpasses even the undeniable certainty of science.

In short, it is evident from the *Phaedrus* and the tenth book of the *Republic* that Socrates, and consequently Plato, firmly believed in this most important truth. Furthermore, in the *Seventh Epistle* of Plato, there is the following remarkable passage: 

“It is proper indeed always to believe in ancient and sacred discourses, which announce to us that the soul is immortal, and that it has judges of its conduct, and suffers the greatest punishments when it is liberated from the body.” <note>original: πειθεσθαι δε ουτως αει χρη τοις παλαιοις τε και ἱεροις λογοις ἡ δη μηνυουσιν ἡμιν αθανατον ψυχην ειναι, δικαστας τε ισχειν, και τινειν τας μεγιστας τιμωριας, ὁταν τις απαλλαχθη του σωματος.</note> 

From this passage, we also learn that the immortality of the soul is a doctrine of the highest antiquity and that it was delivered in the sacred writings of the ancient Greeks <note>original: "heathens"</note>.

I shall only observe further that the character of Socrates, as exhibited in this dialogue, in the *Crito*, and in the *Apology*, is so transcendently great. It displays such a perfection of justice, fortitude, and piety that it may be considered a most splendid instance of the moral and intellectual excellence which human nature is capable of attaining. It is an example of consummate wisdom and virtue which will be imitated by the few in all future ages.

# THE PHÆDO.

---

## PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.

->ECHECRATES AND PHÆDO.<-

---

### ECHECRATES.

**W**ERE you present, Phædo, with Socrates on that day when he drank the poison in prison? Or did you hear an account of it from someone else?

**P<small>HÆDO</small>.** I myself, Echecrates, was present.

<margin>¹ Phlius was a city of the Peloponnese situated not far from the Isthmus. See <note>original: "Vid." (Latin: vide)</note> Strabo, Book 8; Pausanias in *Corinth*; and Stephanus on *Cities and Peoples* <note>original: "de Urb. et Pop." (Latin: De Urbibus et Populis)</note>.</margin>

**E<small>CHECRATES</small>.** What then was his discourse <note>original: "discourse" - here meaning his philosophical conversation</note> before his death? And how did he die? I should be very glad to hear the account. Hardly any of the Phliasian¹ citizens visit Athens now, and it has been some time since any stranger has arrived from there who could afford us any clear information about these particulars. Indeed, all that we heard was that he died by drinking poison, but the person who informed us of this had nothing further to say about the other details of his death.

**P<small>HÆDO</small>.** What! Did you not hear the manner in which he was tried?

**E<small>CHECRATES</small>.** Yes, someone related that to us. We wondered why, since his sentence was passed so long ago, he did not die until a considerable time afterward. What, then, Phædo, was the reason for this?

**P<small>HÆDO</small>.** A certain piece of fortune happened to him, Echecrates. For, on the day before his trial, the Athenians had just finished crowning the stern of the ship which they send every year to Delos. <note>This ship was sent on a religious mission to honor Apollo; while it was away, the city had to remain "pure," meaning no executions could take place.</note>

**E<small>CHECRATES</small>.** But what is the meaning of this?

<summary>Echecrates asks Phædo for a firsthand account of Socrates' final hours and death. Phædo explains that Socrates' execution was delayed because the ritual ship to Delos had been consecrated the day before his trial.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Phædo, Echecrates, Athens, Phlius, Delos, trial of Socrates, religious customs, Greek philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 2201 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Echecrates and Phædo, moving from the introduction into the specific reasons for the delay of Socrates' execution and Phædo's emotional state during the event.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>
<header>THE PHÆDO.</header>

**PHÆDO.** This is the ship, as the Athenians tell it, in which Theseus once carried the fourteen <note>original: "twice seven"</note> young children to Crete and saved both them and himself. The Athenians, it is reported, then made a vow to Apollo that if the children were saved, they would send a sacred procession to Delos every year. From that time on, they have regularly sent this mission to the god every year. As soon as the preparations for the sacred procession begin, the law requires the city to be purified. No one can be put to death by a public decree until the ship has reached Delos and returned to Athens. This sometimes takes a long time to accomplish when the winds delay their journey. The festival itself begins when the priest of Apollo crowns the stern of the ship. Now, as I told you, this happened on the day before the trial. Because of this, a long period of time passed for Socrates in prison between his sentencing and his death.

**ECHECRATES.** And what, Phædo, were the circumstances of his death? What did he say and do? Which of his friends <note>original: "familiars"</note> were with him? Or did the magistrates forbid anyone from seeing him, so that he died without his friends being present?

**PHÆDO.** Not at all; several friends—quite many, in fact—were there with him.

**ECHECRATES.** Please try to tell us all these details as clearly as possible, unless you have some business that prevents you.

**PHÆDO.** I am at leisure and will try to fulfill your request. Indeed, remembering Socrates—whether I am speaking myself or listening to others—is always the most pleasant thing in the world to me.

**ECHECRATES.** Truly, Phædo, others who hear you will feel the same way. Try to tell us every detail as accurately as you can.

**PHÆDO.** I was there myself, and I was strangely moved. I did not feel the pity one might expect when present at the death of a close friend. To me, Echecrates, this man seemed blessed when I considered his behavior and his words, and his fearless <note>original: "intrepid"</note> and noble death. It seemed to me that he did not go down to the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note> without a divine destiny, and that even there he would be in a happy state, if that can ever be said of anyone. For this reason, I was not at all moved...

**ECHECRATES.** How could I not?

**PHÆDO.** He, therefore, was remarkably affected in this way; and I myself, and the others, experienced great distress and confusion.

**PHÆDO.** I will try to relate the whole story to you from the beginning. We were in the constant habit of visiting Socrates—myself and several others—meeting in the morning at the courtroom <note>original: "the place where he was tried"</note>, for it was very near to the prison. There we waited every day until the prison was opened, talking among ourselves, for it did not open very early in the morning. However, as soon as we were admitted, we went to Socrates and generally spent the entire day with him. 

On that particular day, we met together earlier than usual; for the evening before, as we left the prison, we heard that the ship from Delos had returned <note>The return of the sacred ship from Delos marked the end of a religious period during which Athens was prohibited from carrying out executions. This meant Socrates' death sentence would now be carried out.</note>. We decided, therefore, among ourselves to come very early in the morning to the usual place. We met as planned, but when we arrived, the jailer <note>original: "goaler"</note> who used to attend to us told us to wait and not enter until he called for us. "For," he said, "the Eleven Magistrates <note>The 'Eleven' were the officials responsible for the prison and the administration of the death penalty in Athens.</note> are now removing Socrates' chains and announcing to him that he must die today." 

But not long after this, he returned and ordered us to enter. When we went in, we found Socrates just freed from his shackles, and *Xanthippe* <note>original: "Xantippe"</note>—you know her—was sitting by him, holding one of his children. As soon as *Xanthippe* saw us, she began to cry out in distress, saying the things women usually say in times of grief: "Socrates," she said, "this is the last time your friends will speak to you, or you to them." 

But Socrates looked toward *Crito* and said, "*Crito*, let someone take her home." Upon this, some of *Crito’s* servants led her away as she beat her chest and wept bitterly. 

Then Socrates, sitting upright on the bed, drew up his leg and, stroking it with his hand, said, "What a *wonderful* thing this is, my friends, which people call the *pleasant* and the *agreeable*! For throughout my life, the same dream has frequently come to me. In the past, I assumed the dream was encouraging and urging me to do what I was already doing, much like how spectators cheer on runners in a race. I thought that by telling me to practice music, it meant I should work at philosophy—for philosophy is the highest form of music. 

But now, since my sentence has been passed and the festival of the God <note>Apollo</note> has delayed my execution, I felt it was necessary to reconsider. If the 'music' the dream so often urged me to practice was actually the common kind <note>such as poetry or song</note>, I should not resist its promptings but rather comply with them. I thought it would be safer not to leave this life before I had purified myself by composing verses and obeying the dream.

***

¹ Socrates says that perhaps the philosopher will not destroy himself, for this is not lawful. The text demonstrates this through two arguments: one is mythical and Orphic <note>Based on the teachings of Orpheus, a legendary Greek prophet and musician whose followers believed in the soul's imprisonment in the body.</note>, while the other is dialectic <note>original: "dialectic" — a method of logical argument through dialogue.</note> and philosophical. 

But before we consider the text, says Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his commentaries on Plato.</note>, let us show by appropriate arguments that suicide is not lawful. The Divine possesses twofold powers: anagogic <note>original: "anagogic" — from the Greek meaning "leading upward," referring to powers that elevate the soul.</note> and providential. The providential powers, which care for secondary things <note>Lower forms of existence, like the physical body.</note>, are not hindered by the anagogic powers, which are directed toward higher things; rather, the Divine acts through both at once. In like manner, nothing prevents a philosopher—since he is an imitator of Divinity (for philosophy is an assimilation to the Deity)—from acting at once cathartically <note>original: "cathartically" — referring to spiritual purification or "cleansing" the soul from bodily passions.</note> and with a providential care for lower natures. For there is nothing great in living purely when separated from the body after death; but while one is held in the body, it is noble to be intent on purification. 

The second argument is this: just as a divine nature is always present to all things, and some things participate in it more or less through their own aptitude or inaptitude, so too it is necessary that the soul should be present to the body and should not separate itself from it. Thus, in the *Theaetetus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues concerning the nature of knowledge.</note>, the "leader" philosopher <note>original: "Coryphæan philoſopher"</note> is represented as not knowing where the marketplace <note>original: "Forum"</note> is located, and even being ignorant of his own ignorance regarding physical details; and he is this way while still in the body. 

The third argument is as follows: it is necessary that a voluntary bond should be voluntarily dissolved, but that an involuntary bond should be dissolved by an involuntary means, and not in a random manner. Hence, physical life, being involuntary <note>We do not choose to be born or for our biological systems to function.</note>, must be dissolved by an involuntary end—that is, by a natural death. However, the life of passions within us, which exists according to choice or free will, must be dissolved by a voluntary solution—that is, through purification or the exercise of the purifying virtues.

Regarding the text, it shows through two arguments (as we have observed) that suicide is not lawful. Of these, the mythical argument, according to Olympiodorus, is as follows: according to Orpheus, there are four governments. The first is that of Heaven, which Saturn <note>original: "Saturn" — the Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus, who overthrew his father Uranus.</note> received...

At the same time as he spoke these words, he withdrew his leg from the bed and placed it on the ground; and afterward, he continued to speak with us in a fitting
->posture,<-

cutting off the genitals of his father <note>In Greek mythology, Saturn (Cronus) castrates his father, Heaven (Uranus).</note>. After Saturn, Jupiter reigned, who hurled his father into Tartarus. And after Jupiter, Bacchus reigned, who they say was torn to pieces <note>original: "lacerated"</note> by the Titans through the schemes of Juno. It is also said that the Titans tasted his flesh, and that Jupiter, being enraged, hurled his thunderbolts at them; and that from the ashes of their burnt bodies, humanity was created <note>original: "generated"</note>. 

Suicide, therefore, is not proper—not, as the text seems to say, simply because we are in a certain bond within the body (for this is obvious, and he would not have called it a secret or "arcane" teaching), but because suicide is not lawful since our body is Dionysiacal. For we are a part of Bacchus, if we are composed from the ashes of the Titans who tasted his flesh. Socrates, therefore, fearful of disclosing this secret narration because it pertained to the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refers to the secret religious rites of ancient Greece, such as the Eleusinian or Orphic mysteries.</note>, adds nothing more than that we are in the body as if in a prison secured by a guard. But the interpreters, when the mysteries were declining and almost extinct due to the establishment of a new religion <note>A reference to the rise of Christianity displacing Neoplatonism.</note>, openly disclosed the fable.

But the allegory of this fable, says Olympiodorus, is of the same kind as when Empedocles asserts that the intelligible and sensible worlds were generated according to parts. This does not mean they were produced at different times, for they always exist; rather, it means our soul at one time lives according to the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" world refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms.</note>, and then the intelligible world is said to be generated for us. At another time, it lives according to the sensible world <note>The "sensible" world refers to the physical realm perceived by the senses.</note>, and then the sensible world is said to be generated. 

Likewise, in the teachings of Orpheus, those four governments do not exist at one time and then not at another, for they always are. Instead, they obscurely signify the levels of the virtues, through which our soul contains the symbols of all virtues: the theoretic and cathartic, the political and ethical. For the soul either acts according to the theoretic virtues—the pattern of which is the government of *Heaven* (and for this reason Heaven receives its name <term>from beholding the things above</term> <note>original: "παρα του τα ανω ὁραν"</note>)—or it lives "cathartically" <note>Referring to the "cathartic" or purifying virtues that cleanse the soul of material attachments.</note>, the pattern of which is the kingdom of Saturn. For this reason, Saturn is named as a *pure intellect* <note>original: "pure intellect, through beholding himself"</note>, <term>as if he were a 'pure-mind' because he beholds himself</term> <note>original: "ὁιον ὁ κορονους τις ὠν δια το ἑαυτον ὁραν". This is a Neoplatonic etymological pun on the name "Kronos" (Saturn) and "koros" (purity) combined with "nous" (mind).</note>. Hence, he is said to devour his own offspring, as he turns his focus back upon himself. 

Or, the soul acts according to the political virtues, the symbol of which is the government of Jupiter; hence Jupiter is the demiurge <note>The "demiurge" is the divine craftsman or creator of the physical universe.</note>, as he acts upon secondary natures. Finally, the soul lives according to the ethical and physical virtues, the symbol of which is the kingdom of Bacchus; hence he is torn to pieces, because these lower virtues do not consistently follow one another.

But Bacchus being torn apart by the Titans signifies his progression into the lowest levels of existence; for the Titans are the creators of these material things, and Bacchus is the unified source <note>original: "monad"</note> of the Titans. This was brought about by the schemes of Juno because this goddess is the guardian who watches over motion and progression. For this reason, in the *Iliad*, she continually urges Jupiter to pay providential attention to secondary things.

Then Bacchus (Dionysus) succeeded Jupiter; they say that by the plot of Juno, the Titans around him tore him to pieces and tasted his flesh. Jupiter, becoming angry, struck them with lightning, and from the soot of the vapors rising from them, matter was formed from which humans were created."</note>

<gloss>1</gloss> Socrates and Cebes are here speaking about two different kinds of death: Cebes refers to a physical death, while Socrates refers to a voluntary or chosen death.
