natures. Bacchus <note>Also known as Dionysus, the god of wine and religious ecstasy.</note> also, says Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator.</note>, presides over generation <note>original: "generation"; referring to the cycle of birth and physical existence.</note>, because he presides over life and death. He presides over life because he presides over generation; but he presides over death because wine produces an ecstatic <note>original: "enthusiastic"; meaning divine inspiration or being filled with a god.</note> energy, and at the time of death we become more inspired, as Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note> testifies along with Homer; for Homer became prophetic when he was dying. Tragedy and comedy are also associated with Bacchus: comedy because it represents the playfulness of life, and tragedy because of the calamities and death within it. Therefore, comic writers do not rightly accuse tragic writers of being un-Dionysian when they claim that these things do not belong to Bacchus. Furthermore, Jupiter <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus.</note> hurled his thunderbolts at the Titans, the thunder representing a "conversion" or turning back: for fire moves upward. Jupiter, therefore, turns them back to himself. And this is the mythical argument.

But the logical and philosophical argument is as follows: the Gods take care of us, and we are their property. Therefore, it is not right to release ourselves from life; instead, we should turn ourselves toward them. If it were true either that we belong to the Gods but they do not care for us, or that we do not belong to the Gods at all, it might be reasonable to free ourselves from the body. But since neither of these is true, it is not right to break our bonds.

On the other hand, it could be argued that suicide is necessary according to Plato. First, he states here that a philosopher will *perhaps* not commit suicide unless God sends some great necessity, such as the present situation <note>Referring to Socrates' own impending execution.</note>; the word *perhaps* suggests that suicide might sometimes be necessary. Second, Plato admits that suicide may be appropriate for the virtuous person, the average person, and the common or wicked person. It is for the virtuous person in this context; for the average person, as in the *Republic*, where he says suicide is necessary for those afflicted with a long and incurable disease, as such a person is useless to the city—since Plato intended for his citizens to be useful to society rather than just to themselves. Finally, for the common person, as in the *Laws*, he says suicide is necessary for someone possessed by incurable passions, such as being in love with his mother, committing sacrilege, or anything similar.

Furthermore, it could be argued on the authority of Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD).</note> that suicide is sometimes necessary, and also on the authority of the Stoics, who identified five rational reasons for suicide. As Olympiodorus says, they compared life to a banquet and claimed that it is necessary to end life for the same reasons that end a banquet. A banquet is ended either by a great and unexpected necessity, such as the sudden arrival of a friend; or it is ended when intoxication occurs; or when the food served is spoiled <note>original: "morbid"</note>. Additionally, it is ended when there is a lack of necessities for the feast, or because of obscene and vulgar language. In the same way, life may be ended in five ways. And, in the first

<header>THE PHAEDO:</header>

suicide, and yet that a philosopher should be willing to follow one who is about to die?—What (he says), Cebes, have not you and Simmias heard your close friend Philolaus <note>1</note> speak concerning things of this kind?—We have heard him.

<note>The following section uses the metaphor of a "banquet" to describe the conditions under which a life may be honorably ended.</note>

In the first place, as at a banquet, it may be dissolved through some great necessity, as when a man sacrifices himself for the good of his country. In the second place, just as a banquet is ended through intoxication, it is likewise necessary to end life through a delirium following the body; for a delirium is a physical intoxication. In the third place, as a banquet is ended when the food placed on the table is diseased <note>original: "morbid"</note>, so too it is necessary that life should be ended when the body suffers under incurable diseases and is no longer capable of serving <note>original: "ministrant"</note> the soul. In the fourth place, as a banquet is ended through a lack of things necessary for the entertainment, so suicide is appropriate when the necessities of life are missing. For these necessities are not to be accepted from corrupt <note>original: "depraved"</note> characters; since gifts from the defiled are small, and it is not proper for a man to pollute himself with them. And, in the fifth place, as a banquet is ended because of foul <note>original: "obscene"</note> language, so likewise it is necessary to end life when compelled by a tyrant to speak of secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> things, or things belonging to the religious mysteries. This is what a certain female Pythagorean is said to have done. For, being compelled to tell why she did not eat beans, she said, "I may eat them if I tell." And afterwards, being compelled to eat them, she said, "I may tell if I eat them"; and at length she bit off her tongue, as it is the organ of speech and taste.

What then shall we say? For the discussion has been brought to a contradiction. And how can it be admitted that suicide is unlawful? Or, may we not say that a liberation from life is not necessary as far as it pertains to the body, but that it is rational when it contributes a greater good to the soul? Thus, for instance, suicide is lawful when the soul is injured by the body. Just as it is unholy not to give assistance to a friend when he is being whipped, but if he is whipped by his father, it is not appropriate to assist him; so here, suicide is unlawful when committed for the sake of the body, but rational when committed for the sake of the soul, since this is sometimes advantageous to it.

I only add that, according to Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and Neoplatonist author.</note>, it is said in the secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> discourses concerning the return of the soul, "that the wicked in this life resemble those who fall upon smooth ground, and who cannot rise again without difficulty; but that souls departing from the present life with the stains of guilt are to be compared to those who fall from a high and steep place, from where they are never able to rise again." <note>original Latin: "Nam in arcanis de animæ reditu disputationibus fertur, in hac vita delinquentes similes esse super æquale solum cadentibus, quibus denuo sine difficultate præsto sit surgere: animas vero ex hac vita cum delictorum sordibus recedentes, æquandas his, qui in abruptum ex alto præcipitique delapsi sunt, unde facultas nunquam sit resurgendi." See Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 13.</note> Suicide, therefore, is in general unlawful, because it is not proper to depart from life in an unpurified state.

"But I," says Socrates, "speak based on what I have heard; and what I have heard I will not selfishly <note>original: "enviously"</note> hide from you. For what else could such a person be more properly doing until the sun sets?" <note>Referring to the Athenian custom of carrying out executions at the end of the day.</note>

For I heard from Philolaus <note>A distinguished Pythagorean philosopher.</note> some time ago, when he lived with us, and from others as well, that it was not right to do such a thing; but I never heard anything clear on the matter from anyone."

"Prepare yourself, then," says Socrates, "for perhaps you may be satisfied on this point. It remains the same even for those who would be better off dead than alive; though,

...nor look back when going to a temple, nor cut wood on the road. By the second of these rules, he shows that we should not divide or cut life short, for life is a journey. By the first, he points to the meditation on death. For the life of the future state is sacred, since our true father and homeland are there. He says, therefore, that whoever lives a purifying <note>original: "cathartically"</note> life should not turn back—that is, should not cut off that life of purification. 

Cebes met Philolaus in Boeotia, for he spent time with him in Thebes. Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato.</note> also notes that it was the Pythagorean custom to live communally, sharing all possessions, and adds the following: 

"If, therefore, anyone among them was found unfit for philosophy, they led him out with his property, built a cenotaph (an empty tomb), and mourned for him as if he were dead or had gone on a long journey. But a man named Cylo, having joined them and experienced this rejection, set fire to the school. All the disciples were burned to death except two: Philolaus and Hipparchus. Philolaus then came to Thebes to perform funeral rites for his deceased teacher. He also performed them for Lysias, who was buried there, and after whom Plato named a dialogue titled *Lysis, or Concerning Friendship*." <note>original Greek: Ει τις ουν ανεπιτηδειος ευρεθη προς φιλοσοφιαν, εξηγον αυτον μετα της ουσιας, και κενοταφιον εποιουν, και ωσπερ περι αποιχομενον αποδυροντο. # THE PHAEDO

Perhaps it seems strange to you that it should be better for some men to die, yet unholy for those same men to benefit themselves by suicide—and that they ought instead to wait for someone else to act as a benefactor <note>original: "benefactor" here refers to someone who brings about their death, such as the executioner or the divine will</note> on this occasion.

Then Cebes, laughing gently, said in his own dialect, "Zeus knows that!" <note>The original notes that Cebes speaks in his own tongue, likely the Boeotian dialect of Greek. The text uses "Jupiter," the Roman equivalent of Zeus.</note>

"For this indeed," says Socrates, "appears to be irrational; and yet, perhaps, it is not so, but has a certain reason on its side. For the discourse which is delivered about these matters in the secret teachings <note>original: "arcana"</note> of the mysteries—*that we are placed as if in a certain prison secured by a guard, and that it is not proper for anyone to free himself from this confinement and make his escape*—appears to me to be a statement of great importance and not easy to understand. But this appears to me, Cebes, to be well said: that the Gods take care of us, and that we, who are men, are one of the possessions belonging to the Gods. Or does this not seem to be the case to you?"

"It does to me," says Cebes.

"Would you not, therefore, if any one of your servants <note>Footnote 1</note> should destroy himself, when you had not signaled that you were willing for him to die—would you not be angry with him? And if you had any punishment available, would you not discipline him?"

"Entirely so," he says.

"*Perhaps*, therefore, it is not irrational to assert that a man ought not to kill himself before God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> lays him under a certain necessity <note>Footnote 2</note> of doing so, such as the one I am subject to at present."

"This, indeed," says Cebes, "appears to be reasonable. But that which you said just now, Socrates—that philosophers would very readily be willing to die—appears to be absurd, if what we have asserted is consistent with reason..."

<note>
1 How can we use human affairs, says Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato.</note>, to guess that things pertaining to the Gods work in a similar way? For the Gods are not like us; they do not suffer or have passions. May we not say that he compares them by analogy, but in terms of governance and management? For it is evident that the patterns <note>original: "paradigms"</note> of every worldly divine care are already contained within the Gods. But reconciliation and vengeance must be understood to take place in a very different way in the Gods. For the former is the rising of their own light when the darkness of guilt is cleared away; and the latter is a secondary form of divine care that punishes a soul that has turned away.
</note>

<note>

But of that necessity which is externally good, the pattern is the will of Fate granting primary <note>original: "precedaneous"</note> goods; and of that which is externally evil, the bestowing of things that are violent, unnatural, and destructive.

...that Divinity <gloss>1</gloss> takes care of us, and that we are one of his possessions; for it is illogical to suppose that the wisest men should not be distressed when departing from that service in which they are cared for by the Gods, who are the best of rulers. For such a person will by no means think that he shall be better cared for when he becomes free. On the other hand, someone who lacks intellect might perhaps think that he should flee from his master, not considering that one ought not to flee from a good master, but should by all means remain in his service. Therefore, he would leave his master in a most illogical manner. But he who is endowed with intellect will desire to live forever with one who is better than himself. And thus, *Socrates*, it is reasonable that the opposite of what you just said should be true: for it is proper that the wise, when about to die, should be sorrowful, but that the foolish should rejoice.

*Socrates*, therefore, upon hearing this, seemed to me to be pleased with the reasoning of *Cebes*; and looking upon us, he said, "*Cebes* never allows anything to pass without investigation, and is by no means willing to immediately admit the truth of an assertion."

"But indeed," says *Simmias*, "*Cebes*, O *Socrates*, appears to me to say something relevant now. For with what purpose can men, truly wise, flee from masters who are better than themselves, and, without any...

---

<gloss>1</gloss> Everything naturally provides for things beneath it; but the Gods exert a providential energy <note>original: "energy" here refers to *energeia*, or the active expression of their nature</note> prior to all things, and according to their <term>hyparxis</term> <note>original: "hyparxis"—a Neoplatonic term referring to the essential core or "summit" of a being's existence</note>. For each God is a *goodness*, because the highest God is *the Good* itself, and providence is the active expression of goodness, which imparts essential good. Divinity, too, may be said to take care of man because he makes man better; but man "cultivates" Divinity because he is made better by him. 

Observe also that just as in the universe, the intellect that exists after the Gods is first directed back to them, so likewise in us, the *intellect* is extended toward Divinity, but *ignorance* turns away from a divine nature. By "intellect" here, however, we must understand not only that which is <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: "gnostic"—relating to knowledge or the ability to perceive truth</note>, but also that which is <term>orectic</term> <note>original: "orectic"—relating to desire, appetite, or the soul's impulse toward an object</note> or desiring, both in the universe and in us. For the intellect possesses both desire and knowledge because it is the "first animal" <note>In Neoplatonism, the "First Animal" refers to the intelligible world which contains the archetypes of all living things</note>. This being admitted, we shall no longer be troubled by the doubt of whether <term>orectic</term> (virtue) is better than <term>gnostic</term> (science/knowledge) perfection; or, in other words, whether virtue is better than science. For the one is not perfect without the other.

Should it be asked how the Gods are our "masters," since a *master* usually considers his own good rather than the good of his servant (which is how a master differs from a *governor*); and should it also be asked, "What good can the Gods get from man?" we reply with the philosopher <term>Olympiodorus</term> <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a famous commentary on the Phaedo</note> that the Gods make all things primarily <note>original: "precedaneously"</note> for their own sake, and they are excellent in proportion to how much they are independent of other things. But they *govern* through a certain relationship with us; and the more we subject ourselves to them, the more we participate in them, by giving ourselves up to them and neglecting that which is merely our own.

(Crito says) that this would be your answer; but he urged me to do this, as I mentioned some time ago. "Let him do so," says Socrates; "but I am desirous of offering to you, as my judges, the reason why it seems to me that a man who has truly spent his life practicing philosophy should quite rightly be confident when he is about to die, and should possess good hopes of obtaining the greatest advantages after death. In what manner this takes place, Simmias and Cebes, I will endeavor to explain:

Those who engage with philosophy in the right way seem to have hidden from others that their entire study is nothing else than how to die and be dead <gloss>*</gloss>. If this is true, it would certainly be absurd if those who have made this alone their study through their whole life should be distressed when it arrives—a circumstance upon which they have previously bestowed all their attention and labor." 

But here Simmias said, laughing, "By Zeus <note>original: Jupiter</note>, Socrates, you make me laugh, though I am very far from desiring to do so at present. For I think that the multitude, if they heard this, would consider it well said regarding philosophers; and that men of the present day would perfectly agree with you that philosophers should in reality desire death, and that they are by no means ignorant that men of this description deserve to suffer death." 

"And indeed, Simmias, they would speak the truth, except in claiming that they are not ignorant of it. For both the manner in which true philosophers desire to die, and how they are worthy of death, is hidden from them. But let us say farewell to such people," he said, "and discourse among ourselves. To begin, do you think that death is anything?" 

Simmias replied, "Entirely so." 

"Is it anything else than a release of the soul from the body? And is not this what death is <gloss>²</gloss>—for the body to be released from the soul and to exist separately by itself, and likewise for the soul to be released from the body and to exist essentially [by itself]?"

<note>
* It is well observed by Olympiodorus that *to die* <note>original Greek: apothneskein</note> differs from *to be dead* <note>original Greek: tethnanai</note>. For the "cathartic" <note>term: a philosopher practicing spiritual purification</note> philosopher dies as a consequence of meditating on death; but the "theoretic" philosopher is *dead* as a consequence of being separated from the passions.

² Plato beautifully defines death to be a separation of the body from the soul, and of the soul from the body. For, regarding souls that are enamored with the body, the body is indeed separated from the soul, but the soul is not separated from the body because it is still joined to it through habit or alliance. It is from this attachment that those shadowy ghosts <note>original: phantaſms</note> are produced that wander about graveyards.
</note>

If these physical senses are neither accurate nor clear, the rest certainly cannot be: for all the others are, in a certain respect, more defective than these. <note>
...soul; and the theoretic, ideas—since no one is in reality a philosopher who does not have a knowledge of all things. But they differ in this: the political philosopher deals with pleasures and pains, for he attends to the body as an instrument, and his goal is not the total removal of the passions, but their moderation. However, the cathartic <note>referring to a "purifying" stage of philosophy</note> and theoretic philosophers treat the body as a minor distraction, so that it may not become an impediment to their activities; their goal is a complete liberation from the passions.

<note>
¹ Plato says that there is no truth in the senses because they do not truly "know." This is because physical sensation <note>original: "passion"</note> is mingled with their knowledge since it is obtained through physical media. Intellect is said to know accurately because that which understands is the same as the thing being understood. Besides, the senses cannot withstand the intensity of sensible objects. For instance, the eye cannot bear to look at something that is perfectly white. For sensible objects, when they are extreme, destroy the senses. 

Sense, however, may be said to be always true and accurate when compared with "assimilative knowledge," such as looking at images in mirrors. Therefore, when Aristotle says that sense is the principle of science, it must not be considered the producing cause, but rather as something that stirs the soul to a recollection of universal truths. It performs the office of a messenger or herald by exciting our soul to develop the sciences. The poets who assert that the senses know nothing accurately are Parmenides, Empedocles, and Epicharmus.
</note>

Is the truest nature of these perceived through the service of the body? Or shall we not rather say, that whoever among us prepares himself to think *rationally* <term>original: "dianoëtically"; refers to the soul's power of discursive reasoning</term> in the most excellent and accurate manner about each particular object of his study, such a person will come the nearest possible to the knowledge of each? — Entirely so. — Will he not, therefore, accomplish this in the purest manner, who applies himself to each through his *rational* <term>dianoëtic</term> power to the highest degree, neither employing sight in conjunction with his *rational activity* <note>original: "dianoëtic energy"</note>, nor dragging in any other sense along with his reasoning; but who, exercising a *rational*...

---

<margin>
$^1$ The activity <note>original: "energy"</note> of our soul, as we have observed before, is threefold: it either turns itself toward subordinate things, obtaining a knowledge of and organizing them; or it turns toward itself, acquiring a knowledge of itself; or it turns toward natures more excellent than its own. Socrates, therefore, having shown that the philosopher is willing to die by turning away from subordinate things (because he flees from and despises the body), and having shown this by a turning toward himself (because he attends to the body no further than extreme necessity requires), now also shows that he is willing to die by a turning toward more excellent things. For he wishes to know the Ideas; but it is impossible for the soul to know these while acting through the body, or having the body communicate with it in the investigation of them. For if sense-perception possesses something <term>impartible</term> <note>indivisible; perceived as a single whole</note>, as is evident from the unified nature of its perception—for it knows, for instance, all at once that a particular thing is white and not black, since if it knew this in a divisible way, it would be as if I perceived one part of a thing and you perceived another*—much more, therefore, does the rational soul perceive <term>indivisibly</term>. It differs from sense, however, in this: sense knows, but does not know that it knows, because it does not turn back upon itself (since neither the body, nor things that exist only in the body, can turn back upon themselves). But the rational soul knows both <term>sensibles</term> <note>objects perceived by the senses</note> and itself: for it knows that it knows. If this is the case, the soul will not accept the body, the senses, or the instruments of sense as partners in its investigation if it wishes to know things accurately.
</margin>

<margin>
* For these divisible <note>original: "partible"</note> perceptions would never produce a perception of that which is white as a single thing.
</margin>

So it is said that *we can never truly and in reality acquire wisdom through the body.* For nothing but the body and its desires cause wars, uprisings, and conflicts of every kind. All wars arise from the pursuit of wealth, and we are forced to acquire riches for the sake of the body, becoming slaves to its care. Because of all this, we have no time for the practice of philosophy. 

But the worst of all these evils is that even if we occasionally find leisure from the body's demands and turn our attention to the study of something, it invades our investigations from every side. It causes such agitation and confusion, and pushes us so violently, that its presence prevents us from perceiving the truth. Instead, it is clearly shown to us that if we are ever to know anything purely, we must be set free from the body and look at things with the soul alone. 

And then, as it seems, we shall obtain the object of our desire—that which we claim to love, namely wisdom—after we are dead, as our argument shows, but certainly not¹ while we are alive. For if it is impossible to know anything purely while joined with the body, one of two consequences must follow: either we can never possess knowledge, or we must obtain it after death. For then the soul will exist on its own, separate from the body, but never before that happens. And while we live in the body, it seems we will come closest to knowledge only if we avoid association and communication with the body as much as possible (except for what absolute necessity² requires), and if we do not let ourselves be filled with its nature,

<meta>This page continues Socrates' argument that true virtue is based on wisdom rather than the mere exchange of one pleasure or pain for another. It also introduces a detailed Neoplatonic commentary on the different levels or "gradations" of virtue mentioned in Plato's works.</meta>

<page-num>273</page-num>
<header>THE PHAEDO</header>

...in one word, true virtue exists with wisdom, whether pleasures and pains, and everything else of this kind, are present or absent. But if these are separated from wisdom and merely exchanged for one another, such virtue does not deserve to be called even a shadowy sketch; in reality, it is slavish and possesses nothing healthy or true. But that which is in reality true virtue¹ is a purification from all such things; and temperance and justice,

---

¹ The first of the virtues are the physical virtues, which are common even to animals. These are mixed with the physical temperaments and are for the most part contrary to each other—or rather, they pertain to the animal nature. Or it may be said that they are illuminations from reason when it is not blocked by a poor temperament, or that they are the result of activities in a former life. Plato speaks of these in the *Politicus* <note>original: "Politicus"; also known as the *Statesman*.</note> and the *Laws*. 

The ethical virtues, which are above these, are produced by habit and a certain right opinion; these are the virtues of children who are well-educated. These virtues are also found in some animals. They also transcend physical temperaments and, for this reason, are not contrary to each other. Plato presents these virtues in the *Laws*. However, they belong at the same time to both reason and the irrational nature. 

In the third rank above these are the political virtues, which belong to reason alone, for they are scientific <note>original: "scientific"; here meaning based on systematic knowledge or *episteme*.</note>. But they are the virtues of reason organizing the irrational part of the soul as its instrument: through prudence, it organizes the <term>gnostic</term> <note>original: "gnostic"; the power of knowing or cognition.</note> faculty; through fortitude, the <term>irascible</term> <note>original: "irascible"; the spirited or emotional part of the soul.</note> power; and through temperance, the <term>desiderative</term> <note>original: "desiderative"; the desiring or appetitive part of the soul.</note> power. All parts of the irrational nature are organized through justice. Plato speaks much of these virtues in the *Republic*. These virtues also follow one another in a sequence. 

Above these are the <term>cathartic</term> <note>original: "cathartic"; from the Greek *katharsis*, meaning purifying or cleansing.</note> virtues, which belong to reason alone. They involve the soul withdrawing from external things toward itself, casting aside the senses as useless, suppressing the activities of those senses, and liberating the soul from the bonds of physical existence <note>original: "generation"; the material realm of birth and decay.</note>. Plato particularly presents these virtues to us in this dialogue [the *Phaedo*]. 

Prior to these, however, are the <term>theoretic</term> <note>original: "theoretic"; meaning contemplative or relating to the intellectual vision of truth.</note> virtues, which belong to the soul as it introduces itself to natures superior to itself. This happens not only gnostically (through knowledge), as one might think from the name, but also <term>orectically</term> <note>original: "orectically"; from the Greek *orexis*, meaning through desire, appetite, or internal drive.</note>. For the soul hastens to become, as it were, intellect instead of soul; and intellect, as we have previously noted, possesses both desire and knowledge. These virtues are the reverse of the political: while political virtues act upon subordinate things according to reason, these act upon more excellent things according to intellect. Plato presents these virtues in the *Theaetetus*.

According to Plotinus, there is also another level of the virtues beyond these: the <term>paradigmatic</term> <note>original: "paradigmatic"; relating to the ultimate models or divine patterns in the universal mind.</note> virtues. Just as our eye is different from the light that illuminates it when it is first struck by solar light, but later becomes united with it and takes on a "solar form," so too is our soul. At first, it is illuminated by intellect and acts according to the theoretical virtues; but afterward, it becomes that which is illuminated and acts uniformly according to these ultimate models. It is the job of philosophy to make us "intellect," but it is the job of <term>theurgy</term> <note>original: "theurgy"; divine action or ritual intended to unite the soul with the divine.</note> to unite us to <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibles"; purely intellectual or divine realities.</note> so that we may act according to these ultimate models. Just as we know physical bodies when we possess physical virtues (since the subjects of such virtues are bodies)...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the various levels of virtue mentioned in Plato's Phaedo. It focuses on the distinction between the physical, ethical, political, cathartic (purifying), theoretic (contemplative), and paradigmatic (model) virtues, drawing heavily on the commentary of the Neoplatonist philosopher Olympiodorus.</meta>

<page-num>274</page-num>
### THE PHAEDO

Justice, fortitude, and prudence itself, are each of them a certain purification. And those who instituted the mysteries for us appear to have been by no means ordinary people.

For by possessing the ethical virtues, we know the fate of the universe, because fate is concerned with irrational lives. For the rational soul is not under the control of fate, and the ethical virtues deal with the irrational parts of our nature. According to the political virtues, we know worldly affairs; and according to the cathartic <term>purifying virtues that separate the soul from the body</term>, we know things beyond the world. By possessing the theoretic virtues, we know intellectual things; and from the paradigmatic <term>virtues existing as divine models in the Mind of the Creator</term>, we know intelligible natures. 

Temperance also pertains to the ethical virtues; justice to the political, because of social contracts; fortitude to the cathartic, by not leaning toward matter; and prudence to the theoretic. Observe, too, that Plato calls the physical virtues "servile" because they can exist in servile souls. However, he calls the ethical virtues "shadowy sketches" <note>original: "σκιαγραφιαι" (skiagraphiai); an ancient technique of outline painting or illusion</note>, because their possessors only know *that* the actions of such virtues are right, but do not know *why* they are so. 

It is also well-observed here by Olympiodorus that Plato calls the cathartic and theoretic virtues those which are, in reality, true virtues. He also separates them in another way: the political virtues are not "telestic" (meaning they do not pertain to the mystic ceremonies), but the cathartic and theoretic virtues are telestic <term>initiatory or belonging to the sacred mysteries</term>. 

Hence, says Olympiodorus, the cathartic virtues are named from the purification used in the mysteries; but the theoretic virtues are named from perceiving divine things <note>original: "απο του τα θεια οραν" (apo tou ta theia oran)</note>. On this account, he agrees with the Orphic verses, which say:

->The soul that uninitiated dies,<-
->Plunged in the blackest mire in Hades lies.<-

For initiation is the "Bacchic mystery of the virtues" <note>original: "τελετη γαρ εστιν ἡ των αρετων βακχεια" (teletē gar estin hē tōn aretōn bakcheia)</note>. Olympiodorus also further observes that by the "thyrsus-bearers," Plato means those who act according to the political virtues, but by the "Bacchuses" <note>meaning the true initiates of the god Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, he means those who exercise the cathartic virtues. For we are bound in matter like the Titans <note>In Orphic myth, the Titans represent the fragmented, material nature that tore apart the god Bacchus</note> because of the great divisibility of our nature; but we rise from the dark mire as Bacchuses. Hence, we become more prophetic at the time of death; and Bacchus is the overseeing guardian of death, because he is likewise the guardian of everything pertaining to the Bacchic sacred rites.

It is also necessary to observe here that all the virtues exhibit their proper characters—these being everywhere common, but existing in a way appropriate to each level. For the characteristic property of fortitude is not declining toward lower things; of temperance, a turning away from an inferior nature; of justice, an energy that is proper and adapted to one's being; and of prudence, the choosing of good things and the rejection of evil. 

Observe too, with Olympiodorus, that all the virtues exist in the Gods. For many Gods, he says, are adorned with these names, and all goodness originates from the Gods. Likewise, before there are beings like ourselves who only sometimes participate in the virtues, it is necessary that there should be natures that always participate in them. In what order, therefore, do the virtues first appear? Shall we say they begin in the soul's nature? For virtue is the perfection of the soul; and choice and pre-selection are the activities and projections of the soul. Hence, the Chaldean Oracles <note>A collection of mystical oracular utterances from the 2nd century AD</note> join "fontal virtue" <term>virtue as a primary source</term> with the "fontal soul"—or, in other words, with the soul existing according to its primary cause. But may it not also be said that the virtues naturally desire to bring orderly arrangement to disorder? If this is admitted, they must originate from the demiurgic <term>the creative or world-building</term> order.

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of virtues, distinguishing between ethical, political, and the higher "true" virtues of purification and contemplation. It links these philosophical concepts to the Orphic mysteries and the god Bacchus, suggesting that true virtue is a form of initiation that frees the soul from its "Titanic" material nature.</summary>

May we not say that through the purifying virtues, considered according to their primary existence in Jupiter the Creator <note>original: demiurgus</note>, he is enabled to remain in his usual state, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*? Furthermore, according to ancient theologians, he ascends to the tower of Saturn.

¹ It is necessary, says Olympiodorus, that logical <note>original: dialectic</note> concepts should either begin from divine riddles <note>original: ænigmas</note>, unfolding the secret truth which they contain; or that they should become established in them as in a harbor, and rest in the demonstrations of them; or that they should accomplish both of these. Olympiodorus further observes that what is said here mirrors the mystic and worldly cycle of souls. For these souls, he says, fleeing from an indivisible and Bacchic life <note>Bacchic: here referring to a state of divine, unified consciousness</note>, and acting according to that which is <term>Titannic</term> <note>Titannic: referring to the Titans, who represent the fragmentation of the soul into the material world</note>, become shackled and imprisoned. However, by remaining in punishment and attending to themselves, they are purified from <term>Titannic</term> defilements. Passing from a scattered existence into a unified one, they become "Bacchuses"—that is, whole and perfect, according to the Bacchus who remains in the higher realms. 

In the mysteries too, says Olympiodorus, popular purifications first take the lead; in the next place, such as are more secret <note>original: arcane</note> than these; in the third place, stable states of being <note>original: συστασεις (systaseis)</note> are introduced; in the fourth place, initiations with the eyes closed <note>original: μυησεις (muesis)</note>; and, in the last place, a direct inspection of the things themselves <note>original: εποπτειαι (epopteiai)</note>. "In the sacred rites, the public purifications took the lead; then after these, the more secret ones; after these, the stable states of being were received; then the initiations; and finally, the direct visions" <note>original: ότι εν τοις ἱεροις ἡγουντο μεν αἱ πανδημοι καθαρσεις· ειτα επι ταυταις απορρητοτεραι· μετα δε ταυτας συστασεις παρελαμβανοντο· και επι ταυταις μυησεις· εν τελει δε εποπται</note>. 

Hence, he says, the ethical and political virtues are analogous to the visible, public purifications; but those purifying virtues which reject everything external are analogous to the more secret purifications. The activities <note>original: energies</note> which are theoretical concerning intellectual things are analogous to the states that remain stable; but the narrowing of these activities into the indivisible is analogous to the initiations with eyes closed; and the simple, intuitive perceptions of simple forms are analogous to <term>epoptic</term> vision <note>epoptic: the highest stage of initiation, involving direct "seeing" of truth</note>, or an inspection of the things themselves.

Olympiodorus further observes that the goal of the mysteries is to lead souls back to that end from which, as a starting principle, they made their first descent; and in which also Bacchus established them, seating them on the throne of his own father—or, in other words, in the entirety of that life of which Jupiter is the source. He, therefore, who is initiated, necessarily dwells with the Gods, according to the goal of the initiating deities. But the greatest and most mystical sacrifices <note>original: τελεται (teletai); also meaning initiations</note>, he says, are twofold: the one here on earth, being certain preparations; and the other hereafter. The latter also, he adds, are in his opinion twofold: some taking place regarding the <term>pneumatic vehicle</term> <note>pneumatic vehicle: the "spirit" body or subtle envelope of the soul</note>, as here they occur regarding the "shelly" physical body <note>original: περι τον οστρεινον (peri ton ostreinon); referring to the physical body as a shell</note>, and others regarding the <term>luciform vehicle</term> <note>luciform vehicle: the "body of light" or radiant vehicle of the soul</note>. 

For there are three gradations of mystic as well as of philosophic ascent. For philosophers are led back to their original condition in the three-thousandth year, as it is said in the *Phaedrus*; and a <term>chiliad</term>, or a thousand, signifies a perfect and periodic life cycle. Therefore, he who is uninitiated, as he remains most remote from his proper end, lies in the mud <note>original: mire</note> here, and much more so there; for he is merged in the impurity of matter.

It explains that the soul's descent into matter is a "Titannic" fragmentation that must be cured by returning to a unified "Bacchic" state.</summary>

...whoever arrived there, purified and initiated, would dwell with the Gods. For, as it is said by those who write about the mysteries,

> "The thyrse-bearers ¹ are many,
> But the Bacchuses have always been few."

In my opinion, these few are none other than those who philosophize correctly; and so that I may be ranked among their number, I shall leave nothing untried, but exert myself in every possible way. But whether my efforts will be properly directed, and whether I shall accomplish anything when I arrive there, I shall know clearly and very soon, if it pleases the Divinity, as it seems to me. And this," he said, "Simmias and Cebes, is my apology ², why—upon leaving you and the rulers of this present life—I should not be distressed or indignant, since I am persuaded that I shall there meet with masters and companions no less good than those here. This is indeed incredible to many; but if my apology has more influence with you than it had with the Athenian judges, it will have a good effect."

***

¹ The thyrse <note>A staff topped with a pine cone, carried by followers of Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, says Olympiodorus, is a symbol of material and fragmented <note>original: partible</note> creation, because of its broken <note>original: divulged</note> continuity, which is why it is also called a Titanic plant. For it is held before Bacchus instead of his father's scepter, and through this, they call him into a fragmented nature. Besides, he says, the Titans are thyrse-bearers; and Prometheus hid fire in a reed—whether by this we are to understand that he draws celestial light down into the realm of birth <note>original: generation</note>, or drives the soul into the body, or calls forth divine illumination (which is entirely uncreated) into the material world. Therefore, Socrates, following the Orphic tradition, calls the masses "thyrse-bearers," as they live according to the Titanic nature. Olympiodorus further adds that he who lives "Bacchically" now rests from his labors, is set free from his bonds, and leaves behind his prison—or rather, his restricted life; and such a person is a purifying <note>original: cathartic</note> philosopher. Some, he says, prefer philosophy—such as Porphyry and Plotinus and many other philosophers—but others prefer the priestly <note>original: hieratic</note> discipline, or the discipline involving sacred ceremonies, such as Iamblichus, Syrianus, Proclus, and all the priestly philosophers. Plato, however, knowing that much may be said on both sides, unites these arguments into one by calling the philosopher a "Bacchus."

² The defense <note>original: apology</note> of Socrates is twofold: one addressed to the Athenian judges, and the other to his most sincere companions. The first argues for the safety of the "animal"—that is, the combination of soul and body—while the other argues for the separate and true life of the soul. The first is a mixture of knowledge <note>original: science</note> and opinion, while the second is a mixture of pure intellect and knowledge. The first arises from the civic life, but the second from the purifying life. And while the first shows that the death visible and known to everyone is good, the second asserts this of the *true* death, which is known only to philosophers.

When Socrates had finished speaking, Cebes resumed the conversation and said, "Socrates, the other things you have said seem well-argued to me. However, what you claimed about the soul will make many people skeptical. They think that when the soul is released from the body, it no longer exists anywhere. They believe that on the very day a man dies, his soul decays and perishes immediately upon being freed from the body. They fear that as it departs, it is dispersed like wind or smoke, flies away, and exists no longer. For if the soul remained a distinct essence collected within itself, and was liberated from those evils you just listed, there would be a great and beautiful hope, Socrates, that what you have said is true. But it will perhaps require significant proof and conviction <note>original: allurement and faith</note> to be persuaded that the soul still exists after a man dies, and that it possesses a certain power and intelligence <note>original: prudence</note>."

"You speak the truth, Cebes," said Socrates. "But what should we do? Are you willing for us to discuss these details—whether it is likely that this is the case for the soul, or not?"

"Indeed," said Cebes, "I would listen to your opinion on this subject with great pleasure."

"I do not think," Socrates answered, "that anyone who heard this discussion—even if he were a comic poet <note>A reference to Aristophanes, who mocked Socrates in the play *The Clouds* for 'pondering the sun' and other abstract matters</note>—could say that I was wasting time or discussing things not suited to my current circumstances. If it is agreeable to you, then, and since it is necessary to investigate these details, let us consider whether the souls of dead men survive in Hades, or not."

<note>
Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato</note> thought that each of the arguments in the *Phaedo* demonstrated the immortality of the soul. But, as Olympiodorus rightly observes, Iamblichus said this because he was acting through an inspired intellect <note>original: "energizing according to intellect enthusiastically"</note>, which, he says, was usual for him.

Proclus, or rather Syrianus <note>Proclus’s teacher</note>, as we learn from Olympiodorus, concludes that life and death are generated from each other because life is a joining together and death is a coming apart. But these are opposites, and opposites change into each other. The text shows that opposites change into each other in three ways. First, through induction <note>generalizing from specific examples</note>. Secondly, from the processes of birth themselves and the paths that lead to them: for if the processes change into each other—for instance, turning white changes into turning black—then the end results must also change into each other (that is, the white into the black). Thirdly, because nature would be impaired if one of two opposites changed into the other but the second did not change back; eventually, the process would fail because there would be nothing left for the remaining state to change into. Just as if someone awake changed into a sleeping state, but a sleeper never changed back into an awake state, the "Sleep of Endymion" <note>In Greek myth, the beautiful youth Endymion was granted eternal sleep by Zeus so that he would never age or die</note> would occur; for not only he, but all things, would eventually be asleep. Endymion, however, is said to have slept perpetually because he devoted himself in solitude to the study of astronomy. Hence, too, he is said to have been beloved by the moon.

It is likewise necessary to observe that Plato here speaks of things which are strictly opposites; and that, if he also mentions relative terms, these also change into each other through their participation in opposites.
</note>

Does it not become better from having been worse? And if it becomes more just, must it not have been produced <note>original: "generated"</note> from what was more unjust? 

"How could it be otherwise?"

"We have then," Socrates said, "sufficiently established this: that everything is produced in this way—that is, opposites from opposites." 

"Entirely so."

"But what about this: is there anything between these two opposites that acts as an intermediate state <note>original: "middle subsistence"</note>? Since all opposites come in pairs, are there two processes of generation—one from the first to the second, and another from the second back to the first? For example, between a greater and a lesser thing, there is increase and diminution; hence we say that the one is increased, while the other is diminished." 

"That is true," he said.

"And must it not be the same for being separated and mingled, for being cooled and heated, and for everything else in the same manner? Even though we sometimes do not have specific names for every individual process, must they not in reality always work this way—being generated from each other and being subject to a mutual cycle where each turns into the other?" 

"Entirely so," he said.

"What then," Socrates asked, "is there anything opposite to being alive, just as sleeping is the opposite of being awake?" 

"Entirely so," he replied. 

"And what is this opposite?" 

"To be dead." 

"Are these not, therefore, produced from each other, since they are opposites? And since they are two, are there not two processes of generation between them?" 

"How could there not be?" 

"I will, therefore," said Socrates, "tell you about one of these pairs <note>original: "conjunctions"</note> I have just mentioned and what its processes are; you tell me about the other. I say that one of these is *sleeping* and the other is *waking*. From sleeping, waking is produced, and from waking, sleeping. The processes for these are, on the one hand, falling asleep, and on the other, being woken up. Have I explained this clearly enough or not?" 

"Perfectly so." 

"Now," he said, "you inform me in a similar way concerning life and death. Do you not say that *living* is the opposite of *being dead*?" 

"I do." 

"And that they are produced from each other?" 

"Certainly." 

"What then is produced from that which is alive?" 

"That which is dead," he said. 

"But," Socrates asked, "what is produced from the dead?" 

"We must admit," he replied, "that it must be the *living*." 

"Therefore, Cebes," Socrates said, "living things and living people are produced from the dead." 

"It appears so," he replied. 

"Our souls, then," Socrates continued, "exist <note>original: "subsist"</note> in Hades <note>In Greek mythology, Hades is the underworld; here, Socrates uses it to mean the realm where souls dwell between lives.</note>." 

"So it seems." 

"Is not, therefore, one of the processes of generation between these two obvious? For the process of dying is, I think, sufficiently clear; is it not?"

"Entirely so," he said.

"What then shall we do? Shall we not provide a contrary process of birth <note>original: "generation"</note> in its turn, or shall we say that nature is defective and imbalanced in this particular? Or is it necessary to assign a specific contrary process of birth *to the state of being dead*?"

"Entirely so," he said.

"But what is this process?"

"*To be restored back to life again.*"

"But," Socrates said, "if there is such a thing as reviving, will not this revival be a birth from the dead into the living?"

"Perfectly so."

"This, then, is agreed upon by us: that the living are produced from the dead no less than the dead from the living. Since this is the case, it is a sufficient argument to prove that the souls of the dead must necessarily exist somewhere from which they may again be born."

"It appears to me, Socrates," he said, "that this must necessarily follow from what we have admitted."

"Notice then, Cebes," he said, "that we have not made these concessions without reason, as it appears to me. For if things, when produced, did not always replace one another by revolving as if in a circle, but instead birth followed a straight line <note>original: "right line"</note>—proceeding from one thing only into its opposite without ever returning to the other or making a turn—you know that all things would eventually possess the same form, would be affected by the same condition <note>original: "passion"</note>, and would cease to be produced at all."

"What do you mean?" he asked.

"It is not at all difficult to understand what I am asserting," Socrates replied. "It would be just as if there were such a thing as falling asleep without ever returning to a wakeful state produced from a sleepy condition. You know that eventually everything would resemble the story of Endymion <note>In Greek mythology, Endymion was a beautiful youth granted eternal sleep by Zeus so he would never age or die.</note> and would nowhere be seen, because everything else would suffer the same fate that happened to him: namely, being laid to sleep forever. And if all things were mixed together without ever being separated again, the theory of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) argued that originally "all things were together" in a chaotic mixture until "Mind" (Nous) set them in order.</note> would soon be proven true; for everything would be piled together in a single heap. In the same way, my dear Simmias, if all things that possess life were to die, and after they were dead remained in that lifeless form and did not revive again, would it not be inevitable that everything would eventually be dead and nothing would be left alive? For if living beings are produced from other things, yet those living beings die, how could it be otherwise? Must not all things eventually be extinguished by death?"

"It appears to me, Socrates," Cebes said, "that it cannot be otherwise; and in my opinion, you speak the perfect truth."

"To me, Cebes," Socrates said, "it seems to be so more than anything else..."

Instead, there really is such a thing as coming back to life again; the living are born from the dead; the souls of the dead continue to exist <note>original: "have a subsistence"</note>; and the condition of the good after this life will be better than it is now, but the condition of the wicked will be worse.

---

<note>The following sections consist of extensive scholarly commentary and footnotes by the translator, Thomas Taylor, explaining the Neoplatonic interpretation of the text.</note>

* Socrates, having shown from the cycle of life and death that the soul remains after its separation from the body, now shows—by arguing that learning is actually recollection—that the soul existed before it entered the body. By combining both these positions, one can conclude that the soul lasts for a much longer time than the body. However, the philosopher Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note> informs us that Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist</note> believed each of these arguments independently proved the immortality of the soul. For, he says, if life and death always arise from one another, the soul is eternal; and if learning is recollection, the soul must live forever. By uniting both arguments, he concludes that the soul is neither created nor can it be destroyed. However, as Olympiodorus correctly observes, neither argument (nor even both together) proves that the soul is immortal, only that it exists for a certain time before and after the body. Therefore, Plato, realizing he had not yet fully proven his point, introduces other arguments; only the fifth argument properly proves the immortality of the soul based on its own essential nature.

Since the discussion is now about recollection, and memory is closely related to recollection, while forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivion"</note> is the opposite of memory, let us define what these three things are based on their names. Recollection, therefore, is the renewal of memory, as its name indicates. But memory is the permanence of the intellect. And forgetfulness is, in a way, a certain dimness of the sight. For just as dimness is an obstacle to physical sight, so forgetfulness is a dimness of our knowledge—the "sight" of our mind. 

Memory, which is the permanence of the intellect, is seen first in the Pure Intellect, since it is a stable collection of knowledge. This is just as "eternity" <note>original: "the ever"</note> is the stability of being, and "immortality" is the stability of life (for it is a life that cannot be extinguished). In the same way, memory is the stability of knowledge. Because our soul does not possess infinite power regarding its knowledge—even though it does regarding its life—forgetfulness eventually intervenes. Thus, recollection acts as a kind of rebirth of knowledge. 

Memory first exists in the Pure Intellect because that intellect always understands and remains within itself. Secondly, it exists in divine souls, which possess thoughts that move from one subject to another <note>original: "transitive intellections"</note> and do not know all things simultaneously outside of time. Thirdly, it exists in our human souls, where forgetfulness also occurs. Memory is like eternity, always staying the same; but recollection is like time, because it moves from one thought to another.

As Socrates uses recollection to show that the soul existed before the body, the following Platonic arguments in defense of the soul's pre-existence are offered for the serious consideration of—

---

-> * Recollection is the renewal of memory. <note>original Greek: Ἀνάμνησις ἐστι ἀνανέωσις μνήμης.</note> <-
-> † Memory is the permanence of the intellect. <note>original Greek: Μνήμη δὲ μονὴ τοῦ νοῦ.</note> <-
-> ‡ Forgetfulness is like a certain dimness of the eyes. <note>original Greek: Λήθη δὲ οἷον λήμη τις.</note> <-

it is necessary that we must have learned the things which we now call to mind in some former period of time. But this is impossible, unless our soul existed <note>original: "sub-sisted"</note>

---

<note>This extensive footnote by the translator, Thomas Taylor, continues from the previous page, providing commentary from Neoplatonic sources like Olympiodorus to support the theory of recollection.</note>

...the reader. Unless the soul then had a being prior to her connection with the present body, she never would be led to search after knowledge. For if the objects of her investigation were things which she had never before been acquainted with, how could she ever be certain that she detected them? Indeed, it would be as impossible on this hypothesis for the soul to know anything about them, even when she perceived them, as it would be to tell the meaning of the words of an unknown language upon hearing them pronounced. 

The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, in order to subvert this consequence, have recourse to an "intellect in capacity" <note>original: "intellect in capacity"; refers to the mind as a "blank slate" with the potential to learn</note>, which is the passive recipient of all forms. The doubt, however, still remains: For how does this intellect understand? For it must either understand the things which it already knows, or things which it does not know. 

But the <term>Stoics</term> assert that "natural conceptions" are the causes of our investigating and discovering truth. If, therefore, these conceptions are "in capacity" <note>potential</note>, we ask the same question as before; but if they are "in energy" <note>original: "in energy"; meaning in an active or realized state</note>, why do we investigate things which we already know? 

Lastly, the <term>Epicureans</term> affirm that "anticipations" <note>original: "anticipations"; translating the Greek *prolepseis*</note> are the causes of our investigations. If they say that these anticipations exist distinctly, investigation must be vain; but if they exist indistinctly, why do we seek after anything besides these anticipations? Or, in other words, why do we seek after distinct knowledge, of which we have no anticipation?

Again, there are countless instances of persons who are terrified of certain animals—such as cats, lizards, and tortoises—without knowing the cause of their terror. Thus the nephews of Berius, says <term>Olympiodorus</term> <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note>, who were accustomed to hunt bears and lions, could not endure the sight of a rooster. The same author adds that a certain apothecary could look undisturbed at asps and snakes, but was so exceedingly frightened by a wasp that he would run from it crying aloud, paralyzed with terror. Thus too, he says, Themison the physician could apply himself to the cure of every disease except <term>hydrophobia</term> <note>rabies</note>; but if any person only mentioned this disease, he would be immediately agitated and suffer in a manner similar to those afflicted with the malady. Now, it is impossible to assign any other satisfactory cause for all of this than a recollection of having suffered through these animals in a prior state of existence.

Furthermore, infants are not seen to laugh for nearly three weeks after their birth, but pass the greatest part of this time in sleep; however, in their sleep they are often seen both to laugh and cry. But how is it possible that this can happen in any other way than through the soul being agitated by the whirling motions of the animal nature, and moved in accordance with the passions which it had experienced in another life? 

Besides, our looking into ourselves when we are endeavoring to discover any truth proves that we inwardly contain truth, though it is concealed in the darkness of oblivion. The delight, too, which attends our discovery of truth sufficiently proves that this discovery is nothing more than a recognition of something most eminently allied to our nature—something which had been, as it were, lost in the interval of time between our former knowledge of the truth and the recovery of that knowledge. For the perception of a thing perfectly unknown and unconnected with our nature would produce terror instead of delight; and things are pleasing only in proportion as they possess something known and familiar <note>original: "domestic"</note> to the natures by which they are known.

Upon this, Cebes said laughing, "Try, O Socrates, to persuade us to the contrary, as if we were afraid—or rather, as if we were not afraid. Although, perhaps there is a 'child' within us who might dread such things; him, therefore, we should try to persuade not to be terrified of death as if it were a boogeyman."

...through passing into contact with things of this kind? — Entirely so. — But when the soul contemplates anything by itself, it departs toward that which is pure, eternal, and immortal, and which possesses a consistent existence. Being allied to such a nature, the soul perpetually becomes united with it whenever it exists alone by itself and whenever it is permitted to obtain such a union. Then, too, it rests from its wanderings and perpetually exists in a similar state regarding those eternal natures, as it is in contact with them. This state <note>original: "passion"; here meaning a condition or experience of the soul rather than an emotion</note> of the soul is called wisdom <note>original: "prudence" or *phronesis*</note>. — You speak, Socrates, beautifully and truly in every respect. — To which category of things, then—those mentioned before and those mentioned now—does the soul appear to you to be more similar and related? — It appears to me, Socrates, that anyone, even the most unlearned <note>original: "indocile"</note>, must admit as a consequence of this reasoning that the soul is both totally and universally more similar to that which exists perpetually the same, than to that which does not. — But to which is the body most similar? — To the other category.

But consider also the following: since the soul and body exist together, nature commands that the one should be servant and obey, but that the other should rule and possess authority. In consequence of this, which of these appears to you to be similar to a divine nature, and which to a mortal nature? Or does it not appear to you that the divine nature is essentially adapted to govern and rule, but the mortal to be governed and be servant? — To me, it does. — To which, therefore, is the soul similar? — It is manifest, Socrates, that the soul is similar to the divine, but the...

¹ Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote commentaries on Plato.</note> here inquires why Plato calls *wisdom* <note>original: "prudence"</note> a *condition* <note>original: "passion"</note> of the soul. To this he replies that all the virtues are conditions. For it is evident, he says, that things which participate in something are "affected" by it. Because of this, even *Being*, when considered as participating in *the One*, is said by Plato to "suffer" or be passive to *the One*. Since the soul participates in the wisdom that exists in the intellect (or, in other words, intellectual wisdom), he calls wisdom a condition of the soul. "But consider, Cebes," says he, "whether from everything we have said, these conclusions follow: the soul is most like that which is divine, immortal, intelligible <note>intelligible: that which can be understood by the mind/intellect, rather than perceived by the physical senses</note>, uniform, and indissoluble, and which always exists in the same way. The body, on the other hand, is most like that which is human, mortal, lacking in intellect, multiform, dissoluble, and which never remains the same. Can we, my dear Cebes, offer any arguments to show that this is not the case?"

"We cannot."

"What then? As a result of all this, shouldn't the body naturally dissolve quickly, while the soul, on the contrary, remains entirely indissoluble, or at least something very close to it?" 

"How could it be otherwise?" 

"Consider then," says he, "that when a person dies, the visible part—the body—remains in the visible world. Even though we call it a corpse <note>original: "dead body subject to dissolution, ruin, and dissipation"</note>, it does not immediately rot or fall apart. It stays intact for quite a while. If the person dies with a healthy or graceful body, it retains its beautiful form for a long time. For example, when a body is preserved and buried in the way the Egyptians bury their dead, it remains almost entirely whole for an incredible amount of time. Even if some parts of the body decay, the bones, nerves, and similar parts are preserved so well they are almost immortal, so to speak. Is it not so?"

"Certainly."

"Can the soul, then—which is invisible and departs to another place like itself, a place noble, pure, and invisible, namely to Hades <note>Pluto, says Olympiodorus <note>Olympiodorus the Younger (c. 495–570 AD) was a philosopher who wrote commentaries on Plato's works</note>, is celebrated as wise and good because he gives back to souls the virtue and knowledge they lost in the physical world. Can the soul, I say—since it is naturally of this kind—simply blow away and perish as soon as it is freed from the body, as many people claim? 

This is certainly far from the case, my dear Cebes and Simmias. Instead, it is far more likely to remain intact if it is liberated in a pure state, carrying nothing of the body with it. This happens if the soul has not willingly associated with the body during life, but has instead avoided it and gathered itself into itself, making this practice its constant meditation. Indeed, certain shadowy phantoms of souls appear—the images produced by souls that have not been purely liberated from the body, but which still participate in the nature of visible things; and for this reason, they become visible. 

— It is very reasonable to suppose so, Socrates.

— It is reasonable indeed, Cebes. Likewise, these are not the souls of the worthy, but of the depraved, who are forced to wander around such places. In this way, they suffer the punishment for their former evil conduct. They are forced to wander in this way until, driven by the desire for the physical nature <note>original: "corporeal nature"</note> that still clings to them, they are once again bound to a physical body.

They are bound, however—as is only fitting—to the same types of behaviors they practiced in this life. 

— But what do you say these behaviors are, Socrates?

— For example, those who were addicted to gluttony, arrogant insults, and drunkenness, and who did so without any fear of the consequences, shall enter into the forms of asses and similar brutes. Or do you not think it is fitting that they should?

— You speak in a manner that is perfectly appropriate.

— But shouldn't we say that those who held injustice, tyranny, and plunder <note>original: "rapine"</note> in the highest regard shall enter into the forms of wolves, hawks, and kites? Or where else can we say such souls go?

— Into forms of that kind, certainly (says Cebes).

— It will, therefore, be obvious where the rest of the souls go, each according to the similarities of the behaviors they practiced.

— That is obvious (says he); for how could it be otherwise?

— Therefore (says Socrates), aren't the happiest among these—and those who go to the best place—the ones who have studied civic and social virtue <note>original: "popular and political virtue"</note>? This is what people call temperance and justice, which is developed through habit and practice, but without philosophy or true understanding <note>original: "intellect"</note>.

— But how are these the most happy?

— Because it is likely that these souls will again migrate into a social and mild species of this kind, such as bees, wasps, or ants, <note>Note: The text ends mid-sentence; the word "ants" is provided by the catchword from the original printer to indicate the start of the next page.</note>

The lovers of learning well know that when philosophy takes their soul under its protection, it finds the soul tightly bound and glued <note>original: "agglutinated"</note> to the body. The soul is forced to observe things through the body as if through a prison cell, instead of viewing reality through its own nature. Beyond this, the soul is steeped in every kind of ignorance. Philosophy also sees the terrible nature of this imprisonment: it is created by desire, so that the person who is bound actually helps to keep themselves imprisoned. 

Therefore, as I said, lovers of learning know that philosophy, finding the soul in this state, gently tries to encourage it and break its chains. It does this by showing that looking at things through the eyes is full of deception, and the same is true for hearing and the other senses. Philosophy persuades the soul to pull away from these deceptive messages and to use the senses only when absolutely necessary. It urges the soul to gather and collect itself into its own center. And besides this, philosophy teaches the soul to trust nothing but itself, with...

# THE PHAEDO.

...with respect to what the soul understands, when it exists by itself, regarding that which also has a real existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note> by itself. It should not consider anything to have a true being if it is perceived <note>original: "speculates"</note> through other means—such as the senses—or if it exists only within other things. Finally, things of that sort are sensible [perceived by the senses] and visible; but what the soul itself perceives is intelligible [known by the mind] and invisible. 

The soul of a true philosopher, therefore, believing that he should not resist this liberation <note>original: "solution"</note>, avoids pleasures, desires, griefs, and fears as much as possible. He considers that when someone is intensely delighted, terrified, pained, or filled with desire, they do not merely suffer the obvious evils one might imagine—such as illness or the loss of wealth <note>original: "consumption of wealth"</note> from indulging those desires. Instead, they suffer the greatest and most extreme of all evils, and they do so without even realizing it.

— But what is this evil, Socrates? (says *Cebes*).

— It is that the soul of every person is forced, whenever it feels intense pleasure or pain about something, to believe that the object causing this feeling is most real and true—even though it is not. These objects are almost always visible things. Is that not right?

— Entirely so.

— In this state of emotion <note>original: "passion"</note>, then, is the soul not bound to the body in the strongest way?

— In what manner?

— Because every pleasure and pain, as if armed with a nail, fastens and rivets the soul to the body. It causes the soul to become physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> and fills it with the belief that whatever the body claims is true. Because the soul shares the same opinions as the body and finds joy in the same things, it is forced to adopt the same habits and lifestyle <note>original: "manners" and "nourished"</note>. It becomes so affected by this that it can never pass into the afterlife <note>original: "Hades," referring to the unseen realm of the dead</note> in a pure state. Instead, it always departs full of a physical nature. Thus, it quickly falls back into another body; it is sown like a seed and reborn <note>original: "engendered"</note>. Finally, because of this, the soul is deprived of a divine, pure, and uniform companionship.

— You speak most truly, *Socrates* (says *Cebes*).

For these reasons, therefore, O *Cebes*! those who are truly lovers of learning are self-controlled <note>original: "moderate"</note> and brave, and not for the reasons the general public <note>original: "multitude"</note> claims. Or do you think they do?

— Not at all; it would be impossible.

— But the soul of a philosopher reasons in this way. He does not think that philosophy should free him from the body only for him to surrender himself back to pleasures and pains once he is free, which would only result in him being again bound...

...bound to the body, and will undertake a task that is impossible to finish, like re-weaving the web of Penelope. <note>original: "reweaving a certain web of Penelope." In Greek mythology, Penelope avoided suitors by weaving a burial shroud by day and unweaving it at night. Socrates uses this as a metaphor for the soul being trapped in a cycle of physical attachment.</note> Instead, the soul seeks tranquility regarding these passions. By following the guidance of reason and staying focused on it, the soul contemplates what is true, divine, and beyond mere opinion. Nourished by such contemplation, the person believes they should live in this manner while they are alive. Then, when they die, they believe they will depart to a kindred essence—to a nature like their own—and be liberated from the burdens <note>original: "maladies"</note> of human nature. With such nourishment, O Simmias and Cebes, the soul has no reason to fear that upon its liberation from the body, it will be torn apart, blown away by the winds, and vanish into nothingness, no longer having a real existence <note>original: "subsistence"</note>.

When Socrates had said this, a long silence followed. Socrates seemed to be reflecting on what had been said, as did most of us. However, Cebes and Simmias were talking quietly with each other. Finally, Socrates looked at them and asked, "What is it? Do you think my arguments have not been sufficiently proven? There are still many doubts and suspicions that could be raised if someone were to investigate them thoroughly. If you are talking about something else, I have nothing to say. But if you are doubting the points we just discussed, do not hesitate to speak up and review what has been said, especially if you think the argument could be better explained. And please, include me in your discussion again if you think my help would be beneficial."

Upon hearing this, Simmias said, "To be honest, Socrates, we have both been troubled by doubts for some time. We have been encouraging each other to ask you about them, because we want to hear them resolved. However, we were afraid of starting a debate that might be unpleasant for you, given your present circumstances <note>Simmias refers to the fact that Socrates is scheduled to be executed by sunset.</note>."

When swans perceive that it is necessary for them to die, they sing not only as they usually do, but then more than ever; they rejoice that they are about to depart to that Deity <note>Apollo</note> in whose service they are engaged. 

But men, because they themselves are afraid of death, wrongly accuse the swans and assert that they sing out of grief because they are distressed by death. These men do not consider that no bird sings when it is hungry or cold, or is suffering from any other ailment <note>original: "malady"</note>—neither the nightingale, nor the swallow, nor the lapwing, all of which are said to sing lamenting through distress. But it appears to me that neither these birds nor the swans sing through sorrow. In my opinion, swans are prophetic, as they belong to Apollo; because they foresee the good things that Hades <note>The Greek underworld or the afterlife</note> contains, they sing and rejoice at that time more remarkably than at any preceding time. 

I consider myself a fellow servant of the swans and sacred to the same Divinity. I possess a prophetic power from our common master no less than they do, nor shall I be more distressed than the swan in being freed from this present life. Therefore, it is proper that you should both speak and ask about whatever you please, as long as the Eleven magistrates <note>The "Eleven" were the Athenian officials responsible for prisons and the execution of the death sentence.</note> will permit it. 

"You speak excellently well," says Simmias; "and as you give me permission, I will tell you both what my doubts are, and how far Cebes does not accept what has been said. However, failing to examine what has been said in every possible way—or giving up before an exhausting investigation on all sides is finished—is the behavior of lazy and weak <note>original: "effeminate"</note> men. For in matters of this kind, it is necessary to either learn or discover the nature of how things truly exist. Or, if both of these are impossible, then one must take the best and most difficult to disprove of human arguments <note>original: "reaſons"</note> and, venturing upon this as if on a raft, sail through the ocean of life—unless someone should be able to be carried more safely <meta>catchword: safely,</meta>...

...travel more safely and with less danger by means of a firmer vehicle <note>original: "vehicle"—referring to the Neoplatonic "soul-vehicle" or *ochêma*, a subtle body that carries the soul</note>, or some *divine reason*¹. Therefore, I will not be ashamed to ask questions, given the admission you just made; nor will I blame myself later for not speaking what I am thinking right now.
