"And perhaps, my friend," said Socrates, "you are right. But tell me, in what way did it not seem sufficiently proven?"

"In this way," he replied; "because someone could say the same thing about harmony, a lyre, and its strings: for instance, that harmony is something invisible, incorporeal, beautiful, and divine in a well-tuned <note>original: "modulated"</note> lyre. But the lyre and its strings are physical bodies; they are of a corporeal nature, made of parts, earthly, and related to that which is mortal. Therefore, when someone has either broken the lyre or cut and snapped the strings, a person might argue from the same reasoning as yours that the harmony must still exist and cannot have been destroyed. For it would be impossible for the lyre to still exist when the strings are broken (since the strings themselves are of a mortal nature), and yet the harmony—which is innate and related to that which is divine and immortal—should perish before the mortal body itself. They would argue that the harmony must still be somewhere, and that the wood and strings must rot away <note>original: "ſuffer putrefaction"</note> before the harmony can be affected. For I think, Socrates, that you yourself have also realized this: we often consider the soul, in the highest sense, to be a kind of 'tuning' <term>temperament</term> <note>In ancient medicine and philosophy, "temperament" referred to the balance or "tuning" of the body's primary qualities</note> of hot and cold, moist and dry, and similar qualities, which our body is composed of and by which it is held together."

---

<gloss>¹ See the Introduction to this Dialogue.</gloss>
<gloss>* Harmony exists in three ways <note>original: "triple ſubſiſtence"</note>. First, there is harmony itself; second, there is that which is primarily harmonized and is so according to its whole being; and third, there is that which is secondarily harmonized and only partially shares in harmony. The first type must be assigned to the intellect, the second to the soul, and the third to the body. This third type is perishable because it exists within a physical subject. However, the other two are imperishable because they are not made of parts, nor are they dependent on a physical subject. Therefore, Simmias argues incorrectly here because he is only looking at the third type of harmony. In reality, the rational soul is like a musician, while the living body is like tuned strings; for the soul has an existence separate from the body, whereas the body's 'tuning' cannot exist without the musical instrument itself.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue in Plato's Phaedo, where Simmias has just proposed that the soul might be a "harmony" of the body's physical elements—a balance that ceases to exist when the body is damaged.</meta>

<page-num>300</page-num>
# THE PHAEDO

...that the soul is the harmony of all these parts when they are beautifully and moderately balanced with each other. If, therefore, the soul is a kind of harmony, it is obvious that when our body suffers from either tension or relaxation <note>original: "intension or remission"—musical terms referring to the tightening or loosening of strings</note> through diseases and other illnesses, the soul must necessarily perish immediately, even though it is of a most divine nature. This would happen in the same way that other harmonies perish, whether they exist in musical sounds or in the crafted works of artisans. Meanwhile, the remaining parts of each person's body must endure for a long time, until they are either burned or rot away. Consider, then, what we shall say to this argument, if someone should think that because the soul is the proportional mixture <note>original: "temperament"</note> of things existing in the body, it is the first thing to perish in what we call death.

Socrates, looking at us and laughing as he was often accustomed to do, said, "Simmias speaks fairly. If any of you is more ready <note>original: "prompt"</note> than I am, why does he not reply to these objections? For he seems to have presented this case quite well. However, it seems to me that before we make our reply, we should first hear from Cebes and know what his objection to our discourse is. This will allow some time to pass so that we may deliberate on what we shall say. Afterward, upon hearing the objections, we may either agree with them if they seem to assert anything appropriate <note>original: "becoming"</note>, or, if they do not, we can defend the argument we have already delivered. But," he said, "tell me, Cebes, what is it that disturbs you so much that it causes your disbelief?"

"I will tell you," said Cebes. "Your argument seems to me to still be in the same state, and to be subject to the same objection we mentioned before. I will not deny that the assertion that our soul existed before it entered this present form is a very refined <note>original: "elegant"</note> kind, and—if it is not too much to say—has been sufficiently proven. But that it still remains after we are dead does not appear to me to have been clearly proved. Nor do I agree with Simmias’s objection that the soul is not stronger and more lasting than the body, for it appears to me to be much more excellent than all of those. 'Why then,' my reason asks, 'do you still disbelieve? Since you see that when a man dies, the weaker <note>original: "imbecil"</note> part still remains, does it not seem necessary to you that the more lasting nature should be preserved during this period of time?' Consider, therefore, whether I shall say anything to the purpose in reply. For I, like Simmias, it seems, need to use a certain analogy <note>original: "similitude"</note>; for to me these—"

<meta>catchword: these</meta>

<summary>Simmias argues that if the soul is a "harmony" of the body, it must perish when the body's physical balance is disrupted by disease, while Cebes adds that even if the soul existed before birth, its continued existence after death remains unproven.</summary>

--- Page 2250 ---
<meta>This page continues the counter-argument from the previous page. Here, Cebes (through Simmias) introduces the famous "weaver analogy" to challenge the idea that the soul's survival through several bodies proves its immortality.</meta>

<page-num>301</page-num>

# THE PHAEDO

These arguments seem to be made in the same way as if someone were to speak about an elderly weaver who had died. He might claim that the man has not yet perished, but perhaps still survives somewhere. As proof for this assertion, he might show a garment <term>vestment</term> woven by the weaver, which the man used to wear and which is still safe and intact. 

If he were to ask someone who did not believe him which is more lasting—the nature <term>genus</term> of a man or that of a garment meant to be used and worn—the person would reply that the nature of man is much more lasting. He might then think it was demonstrated that the man is, by even stronger reasoning, preserved, since the object with the shorter lifespan has not yet perished. 

But I do not think, Simmias, that this is actually the case. Consider what I am saying, for anyone would see that someone who argues this way is speaking foolishly. This weaver, having woven and worn out many such garments, died *after* many of them were gone, yet I believe he died *before* the last one. Despite this, it cannot be inferred that a man is more fragile <note>original: "viler or more imbecil"—meaning lower in value or weaker in physical constitution</note> than a garment. 

I think the soul, in relation to the body, follows this same comparison. Anyone who makes this point seems to me to speak in a very reasonable manner. By this, I mean that the soul is of a lasting nature, while the body is more feeble <note>original: "debile"</note> and less durable. 

I would say that each soul wears out many bodies, especially if it lives for many years. If the body flows away like a stream <note>This refers to the philosophical idea that the physical body is in a constant state of flux and change</note> and is dissolved while the man still lives, then the soul must perpetually re-weave that which is worn out and consumed. It would follow that when the soul finally perishes, it would be wearing its last "garment" and would vanish just before that final body does. 

Once the soul has perished, the body would then show its inherent weakness <note>original: "imbecility"</note>. It would rapidly rot and be completely dissolved. Consequently, based on this reasoning, we should not yet be persuaded to believe with confidence that our soul exists somewhere after we are dead. 

For suppose someone were to grant even more than you have, and admit not only that our soul existed before we were born into this life, but that nothing prevents some souls from continuing to exist after death. They might exist in some future period, be born often, and perish again—for the soul is naturally strong enough to preserve itself through frequent births. Yet even if we grant all this, it might still follow that the soul would eventually tire...

<summary>Cebes uses the analogy of a weaver and his cloaks to argue that even if a soul survives several bodies, it might eventually wear out and perish, leaving the final body to rot.</summary>

...through those many generations, but that, upon finishing its course, in one of these deaths, it will entirely perish. No one can say that this specific death and dissolution of the body—the one that also brings about the destruction of the soul—can be known for certain, for it is impossible for any of us to perceive it. If this is the case, however, it follows that anyone who feels confident and hopeful about death is being foolishly confident, unless he can demonstrate that the soul is perfectly immortal and undecaying. Otherwise, it is necessary that a person about to die should always fear for his soul, lest in the death which is at hand, he should entirely perish through its separation from the body.

When we heard them speak in this manner, we were all very deeply unsettled <note>original: "disagreeably affected"</note>, as we later admitted to each other. Although we had been strongly persuaded by the previous discourse, they now seemed to disturb us and cast us into a state of disbelief. This was done in such a way that it not only caused us to doubt the arguments already presented but also any that might be stated afterward. We feared that either we were not capable judges of anything, or that the subjects themselves were simply unworthy of belief.

**Echecrates.** By the Gods, Phaedo, I can easily forgive you for feeling that way. Even now, as I listen to you, I cannot help but say to myself: "In what arguments can we believe any longer?" For the discourse of Socrates, which a little while ago seemed so incredibly credible, has now fallen into disbelief. The assertion that our soul is a certain <term>harmony</term> <note>In this context, Simmias argued that the soul is a "harmony" or "tuning" of the body's physical elements, meaning it would vanish if the body were destroyed.</note> gained my agreement both now and always in a wonderful way. Now that it has been mentioned, it recalls to my memory that I once held that same opinion. Thus, I am once again completely in need of some other reason—starting from the very beginning—which might persuade me that the soul of a dead man does not die along with the body. Tell me, therefore, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, how Socrates continued the discourse. Did he seem troubled by these objections, as you admit you were? Or, on the contrary, did he answer them with ease? Did he defend his doctrine sufficiently, or in a flawed manner? Relate all these details to us as accurately as you can.

**Phaedo.** Indeed, Echecrates, I have often admired Socrates, but never more than at that moment. That he should be able to say something...

# THE PHAEDO

His reply was perhaps not surprising; but I especially admired, first of all, the pleasant, kind, and wonderful way he received the young men’s discourse. Next, I admired how acutely he perceived how we were affected by their objections. Lastly, I was impressed by how well he cured our distress and called us back—as if we were soldiers fleeing and defeated—causing us to join him in following and considering the argument.

**Echecrates.** But how did he do this?

**Phaedo.** I will tell you. At that time, I happened to be sitting at his right hand on a low seat near his bed, while he sat much higher than I did. Stroking my head and smoothing the hair that hung on my neck—for he used to play with my hair sometimes—he said, "Tomorrow, Phaedo, you will perhaps cut off these beautiful locks <note>Cutting one's hair was a traditional sign of mourning.</note>." 

"It seems so, Socrates," I replied. 

"But you will not," he said, "if you will take my advice." 

"Why not?" I asked. 

"Because," he said, "both you and I ought to cut off our hair today if our argument dies and we are unable to bring it back to life. Indeed, if I were you and I found that the argument had escaped me, I would take an oath like the Argives <note>The inhabitants of Argos once swore not to let their hair grow until they had won back a lost territory.</note>: I would never let my hair grow until, by winning the debate, I had defeated the objections of Simmias and Cebes." 

"But," I said, "it is said that even Hercules was not a match for two at once." 

"Then call upon me," he said, "as your Iolaus¹ while the light of day still lasts." 

"I call upon you then," I said, "not as Hercules calling upon Iolaus, but as Iolaus calling upon Hercules." 

"It makes no difference," he replied.

"But first, we must be careful that we are not influenced by a certain passion." 

"What passion?" I asked. 

"That we do not become haters of reason <note>original: 'misologists'</note>," he said, "in the same way that some people become haters of men <note>original: 'misanthropists'</note>. For no greater evil can happen to anyone than to become a hater of reason. But a..."

<meta>This page continues Socrates' explanation of "misology"—the hatred of reasoning—comparing it to "misanthropy," the hatred of people. He warns that both arise from a lack of skill or knowledge when dealing with people or arguments.</meta>

<page-num>304</page-num>

# THE PHAEDO

A hatred of reason and a hatred of mankind are both produced in the same manner. For misanthropy <note>The hatred of human beings.</note> is produced in us by trusting someone too much without skill or judgment, and considering him to be a man who is true, sincere, and faithful. Then, in the course of a short acquaintance, we find him to be corrupt and unfaithful; and we find this to be the case again with another person. 

When someone often suffers this disappointment—especially from those he considered his most intimate companions and friends—at length, after being frequently hurt, he hates all men and thinks that there is no sincerity in anyone. Or have you never noticed that this happens?

"Entirely so," I said.

"But is this not shameful?" he asked. "And is it not evident that such a person attempts to deal with men without possessing the art <note>The "art" here refers to the skill or knowledge of human nature.</note> regarding human affairs? For if he dealt with them skillfully, he would think—as is really the case—that very good or very bad men are few in number, and that the greater part of mankind are those who exist somewhere in between."

"How do you mean?" I asked.

"In the same way," he said, "as with things very small and very great. Do you think that anything is rarer than to find an extremely large or an extremely small man, or dog, or anything else? Or, again, anything excessively swift or slow, beautiful or shameful, white or black? Do you not perceive that the extremes of all these are rare and few, but that the things existing between them are abundant and many?"

"Entirely so," I said.

"Do you not think, then," he said, "that if a contest of wickedness <note>original: "improbity"—lack of honesty or moral integrity.</note> were proposed, those who hold the first rank among the shameful would be found to be very few?"

"It is reasonable to think so," I said.

"It is indeed," he said. "But in this respect, arguments are not exactly like men (for I shall now follow you as the leader); but they are similar in this: when someone, without possessing the skill belonging to reasoning, believes that a certain argument is true, and shortly after it appears to him to be false—as it is sometimes one and sometimes the other—the same thing happens to him regarding different arguments. 

This is particularly the case with those who are familiar with contradictory arguments. For these people, as you know, think they have finally become very wise, and that they alone perceive that there is nothing sound <note>OCR original: "found"—likely a transcription error for "sound."</note> and stable either in things or in reasoning. Instead, they believe everything is whirled up and down, as if caught in the river Euripus <note>The Euripus Strait in Greece is famous for its powerful and unpredictable currents that change direction many times a day.</note>, and does not remain in any one condition for any length of time."

<summary>Socrates explains that "misology" (hatred of logic) arises when a person repeatedly trusts flawed arguments, leading them to believe that no objective truth exists. He compares this to misanthropy, where a lack of judgment leads a person to hate all of humanity after being disappointed by a few.</summary>

"...any portion of time whatever."

"What you say is perfectly true," I said.

"Then, Phaedo," he said, "would it not be a pitiable state if, when a certain reasoning is true, firm, and capable of being understood, someone should fall away from it and be filled with doubt? This might happen because he has heard arguments that seem true at one time and false at another—even though the reasoning itself remains the same. Instead of blaming himself and his own lack of skill, he eventually grows frustrated and shifts all the blame from himself to the reasoning itself. Thus, he would pass the rest of his life hating and slandering reason, and would be deprived of the truth and the knowledge of reality <note>original: "science of things"</note>."

"By Zeus!" <note>original: "By Jupiter"</note> I said. "Such a person would be miserable indeed."

"First, then," he said, "we should be very careful not to admit the opinion that no reasoning appears to be valid. Instead, we should much rather think that we are not yet in a healthy condition, and that we ought to vigorously and cheerfully study how to become well. This indeed ought to be the case for you and the others for the sake of the rest of your lives; but for me, it is for the sake of death itself. 

There is a danger at this moment that I might not behave philosophically, but instead act like those who are completely unskilful and argumentative. For when such people dispute any particular point, they are not at all concerned with the actual truth of the matter; they are only anxious that what they have established may appear true to the people present. I seem to differ from them only in this respect: I am not concerned that my discourse may appear true to those who are present (except perhaps by chance), but that it may appear to be true, above all, to myself. 

For I reason this way, my dear friend—and see how self-interested <note>original: "fraudulent"</note> I am being—that if my assertions are true, it will be a beautiful circumstance to be convinced of their truth. But if nothing remains for the dead, I shall at least have the advantage of being less troubled by my present condition than others before I die. This ignorance of mine will not continue long (for it would be bad if it did), but will shortly be resolved <note>original: "dissolved"</note>. 

And being thus prepared," he said, "Simmias and Cebes, I shall now return to the discourse. But if you would be persuaded by me, pay no attention to the person of Socrates; instead, be much more concerned with agreeing with the truth. If I should appear to you to assert anything true, accept it; but if this should not be the case, oppose me with all your might, for fear that..."

But to begin, he says: "First, remind me of what you have said, in case I have forgotten it. For I think Simmias distrusted our argument and was afraid that the soul—even though it is more divine and beautiful than the body—might perish before it, because it exists only in the form of harmony <note>The "harmony" theory suggests the soul is a byproduct of the body's physical components, like music from a lyre.</note>. "I was wonderfully convinced by that argument then," said Cebes, "and I still firmly hold the same opinion now."

"But," Socrates said, "it is necessary, my Theban guest <note>referring to Simmias, who was from Thebes</note>, that you think differently if you still hold the opinion that harmony is something composite—meaning it is made of parts—and that the soul is a kind of harmony made from the elements stretched through the body. "Certainly not, Socrates," he said.

"Then do you see," Socrates replied, "that you are being inconsistent when you say that the soul existed before it entered a human form and body, but also claim it was composed of things that did not yet exist? For harmony is not like the soul in the way you are imagining. The lyre, the strings, and the un-tuned sounds all exist *before* the harmony; harmony is the last thing created and the first thing to be destroyed <note>original: "dissolved"</note>. How, therefore, can your current argument agree with your previous one?"

"It cannot at all," said Simmias.

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of the idea that the soul is a "harmony" of the body's parts. Socrates argues that if all souls are equally "souls," they must be equally "harmonized," which would make the existence of moral differences (virtue and vice) impossible under this theory.</meta>

...more in quantity, or more or less intensely <note>original: "vehemently"</note> and in greater or lesser quantity, a soul than another?—By no means, he says.

Consider then, he says, by Jupiter <note>original: "by Jupiter," a common Greek oath referring to Zeus</note>, is it truly said that one soul possesses intellect and virtue and is good, but that another is foolish and vicious and is bad?—It is truly said.

Among those, therefore, who establish the soul as a harmony, what can anyone call virtue and vice in the soul? Will he call the one harmony and the other discord? And will he say that the one—that is to say, the good soul—is harmonized and, as it is a harmony, possesses another harmony within itself? But will he say that the other is discord and does not contain within itself another harmony?

I do not know what to reply, says Simmias; but it is manifest that he who establishes this theory would make some such reply.

But it has been granted, he says, that one soul is not more or less a soul than another. And this is nothing other than to confess that one harmony is not more intense <note>original: "vehemently"</note> or greater in quantity, nor less intense or less in quantity, than another harmony. Is it not so?—Entirely so.

But that which is neither more nor less a harmony is neither more nor less harmonized. Is it not so?—It is.

But can that which is neither more nor less harmonized participate more or less in harmony¹? Or does it participate equally?—Equally.

The soul, therefore, since it is not more or less a soul than another, is not more or less harmonized.—It is not.

But since it is in this state, it will participate in neither more discord nor more harmony.—By no means.

And again, in consequence of this condition <note>original: "passion," here meaning a state or attribute</note>, can one soul participate more in vice or virtue than another, since vice is discord but virtue is harmony?—It cannot.

But rather, Simmias, according to right reason, no soul will participate in vice if it is a harmony; for surely a harmony which is perfectly such can never participate in discord.—It certainly cannot.

Neither, therefore, can the soul, which is perfectly...

---

¹ As every rational soul is an incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note> harmony separate from a subject, it does not admit of variations in intensity <note>original: "intensions and remissions"</note>; and, therefore, one rational soul is neither more nor less a harmony than another, so far as each is *essentially* harmony. One soul, however, may be more similar to the pure Intellect, or to harmony itself, than another, and, so far as it is more similar, it will be more of a harmony in its *energy* <note>meaning its active expression or function</note>. Hence, virtue may be considered as the concord, and vice as the discord, of the rational and irrational nature; the former being produced by the rational part harmonizing the irrational part, as a result of being a more energetic harmony; and the latter arising from the irrational part being unharmonized by the rational part, because in this case the essential harmony of the soul is more dormant than active. The reasoning of Socrates, therefore, does not apply to that harmony which is separate from the body, but to that which is inseparable from the body.

<summary>Socrates uses logic to show that if the soul is merely a "harmony" of the body, then all souls must be equally good, as a perfect harmony cannot contain discord (vice). This challenges Simmias's suggestion by showing it cannot account for the existence of human wickedness.</summary>

Therefore, if anyone wishes to discover the cause by which everything is generated, destroyed, or exists, they ought to discover how it may best exist, or be acted upon, or perform anything else. Consequently, it is proper that a man should consider nothing else—either about himself or others—except what is most excellent and best. But it is necessary that he who knows the best should also know what is inferior <note>original: "subordinate"</note>, since there is one and the same science for both. Reasoning this way with myself, I rejoiced, thinking I had found a teacher in Anaxagoras <note>See a lengthy extract from the work of Anaxagoras to which Plato refers here, in the notes on the first book of my translation of Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*.</note> who would instruct me in the causes of things according to my own ideas. Because the bones are suspended in their joints, the nerves—by stretching and relaxing—enable me to bend my limbs as I do now. It is through this cause that I sit here in a bent <note>original catchword: "inflected"; meaning curved or bent at an angle</note> position.

...bent position—and again, if he should assign other similar causes for my conversation with you, such as voice, air, hearing, and a thousand other such details, while neglecting to provide the true cause: which is that since the Athenians thought it better to condemn me, I have also thought it better and more just to sit here, and, by staying, endure the punishment they have ordered for me. But to call such things "causes" is extremely absurd. Indeed, if someone were to say that without having things like bones and nerves and other parts of my body, I could not do what I choose to do, he would be speaking the truth. But to claim that I act as I do *because* of these things, and that I act with this <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellect"; the rational mind or *nous*</note> but not based on a choice of what is best, would be a statement full of extreme laziness. For this would be the result of failing to distinguish by <term>division</term> <note>original: "division"; the logical method of categorizing things to find their true definition</note> that the true cause of a thing is very different from the necessary conditions without which a cause could not act. 

And this indeed seems to me to be the case with the majority of people, who, as if fumbling in the dark, give things names that are far from the truth, calling things "causes" when they are not. Thus, one person places a <term>vortex</term> <note>original: "vortex"; a whirling motion of the heavens proposed by some early philosophers to explain why the earth stays in place</note> around the earth, created by the movement of the stars, and so makes the earth stay fixed in the center; another places air under the earth, as if it were a support for a broad trough. 

But they neither investigate the power by which things are currently arranged in the best possible way, nor do they think this power possesses any <term>divine strength</term> <note>original: "dæmoniacal strength"; here meaning a supernatural or spiritual power, not "demonic" in the modern sense</note>. Instead, they imagine they have found some "Atlas" who is stronger and more immortal than such a power, and who does more to hold all things together. They do not believe that "the Good" and "the Fitting" actually bind and support anything. 

As for me, I would gladly become the student of anyone who could show me how a cause of this kind operates. But since I have been deprived of this opportunity—having neither discovered it myself nor learned it from another—are you willing, Cebes, for me to show you the path I took in my "second voyage" to find the cause? <meta>This page continues Socrates' explanation of his intellectual shift. Having found physical explanations of the world's "causes" unsatisfying, he describes how he turned toward a more abstract, rational method of investigation.</meta>

"It appeared to me, therefore," says Socrates, "afterward, when I was exhausted with such speculations, that I ought to take care lest I should be affected in the same way as those who attentively watch an eclipse of the sun. I perceived something of this kind in myself, and I was afraid lest my soul should be perfectly blinded by looking at things with the eyes of my body, and by trying to grasp them by means of the various senses. 

Hence, I considered that I ought to take refuge in <term>rational arguments</term> <note>original: "reasons" (Greek: *logoi*); Socrates is moving from physical observation to the study of definitions and logical concepts</note>, and in them survey the truth of things. This, therefore, is the method I have adopted: I always establish the argument that I judge to be the most valid as my starting point, and whatever appears to me to be consistent with this, I fix upon as true—both concerning the cause of things and everything else. But whatever is not consistent, I consider to be untrue. However, I wish to explain what I am saying to you in a clearer manner, for I think that you do not understand me at present."

I shall return again to those ideas that are so celebrated; beginning from these, and laying down as a starting point that there is a certain 'Beautiful itself,' existing by itself; and a certain 'Good' and 'Great,' and so on for all the rest. If you permit me to do this, and allow that such things have a real existence, I hope that I shall be able to demonstrate this cause to you and discover that the soul is immortal."

"But consider," says Socrates, "the things that follow from these, and see whether you will then likewise agree with me. For it appears to me that if there be anything else beautiful, besides the 'Beautiful itself,' it cannot be beautiful for any other..."

<meta>This page continues Socrates' explanation of "causes." He moves from his dissatisfaction with physical explanations to his own theory, which suggests that things possess qualities because they "participate" in abstract Forms or Ideas.</meta>

<page-num>317</page-num>

...no other explanation than that it participates in <term>the beautiful itself</term> <note>original: "the beautiful itself"; refers to the Platonic "Form" or "Idea" of Beauty—the perfect, abstract essence of beauty that exists beyond the physical world</note>; and I would speak in the same way of all things. Do you admit such a cause?

"I admit it," he says.

"I do not, therefore," says Socrates, "any longer recognize or understand those other *wise* causes. If anyone tells me why a certain thing is beautiful and offers as a reason either its vivid color, its shape, or something else of this kind, I dismiss those other hypotheses—for in all others I find myself confused. Instead, I maintain for myself, simply, without artifice, and perhaps even foolishly, that nothing else causes it to be beautiful than either the presence of, or participation in, or however else one might describe the communication of that 'beautiful itself.'

For I cannot yet affirm exactly how this takes place, but only this: that all beautiful things become beautiful through beauty itself. It appears to me safest to answer both myself and others in this way. Adhering to this, I think I can never fall, but that I shall be secure in answering that all beautiful things are beautiful through beauty itself. Does it not also appear so to you?"

"It does."

"And that great things, therefore, are great, and larger things are larger, through <term>magnitude</term> <note>original: "magnitude" (greatness); the abstract Form of size</note> itself? And smaller things are small through smallness itself?"

"Certainly."

"Therefore, you would not agree if someone said that one person is larger than another 'by a head,' and that the one who is smaller is smaller by that very same thing—the head. Instead, you would testify that you meant nothing else than this: regarding everything great, one thing is greater than another by nothing other than greatness, and it is through this that it is greater. Likewise, the smaller is smaller through nothing else than smallness, and it is through this that it is smaller. 

For I think you would be afraid that if you said someone is greater or smaller 'by a head' <note>Socrates is pointing out a logical contradiction: if a "head" is a small thing, it is paradoxical to say it is the "cause" of someone being "great" or tall</note>, you would contradict yourself. First, you would be asserting that the greater is greater and the lesser is smaller by the very same thing; and second, you would be saying that the greater is greater by a 'head,' which is a small thing. It is absurd to suppose that anything which is great can become so through something which is small. Would you not be afraid of all this?"

"Indeed I would," says Cebes, laughing.

"Would you not also," says he, "be afraid to say that ten things are more than eight by 'two,' and that this is the cause ten exceeds eight, rather than by <term>multitude</term> <note>original: "multitude"; the abstract Form of number or many-ness</note> and through multitude? <page-num>318</page-num>
<header>THE PHÆDO.</header>

...is two <term>cubits</term> <note>an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> long is larger than one that is only one cubit, because of "the half" rather than because of <term>magnitude</term> <note>the abstract Form of "Greatness" or "Size"</note>? For the risk of error is indeed the same.

"Absolutely," he said.

"But what about this? If one is added to one, will the addition be the cause of them becoming two? Or if one is divided and two are produced, would you not be afraid to name 'division' as the cause? Indeed, you would shout aloud that you know no other way for anything to exist than by participating in the unique essence of whatever it participates in. In these cases, you can assign no other cause for them becoming two than their participation in the <term>duad</term> <note>original: "duad"; the abstract Form of 'twoness'</note>; and it is right that all things about to become two should participate in this, just as whatever is about to become one must participate in <term>unity</term> <note>original: "unity"; the abstract Form of 'oneness'</note>.

But you would say goodbye to these divisions, additions, and other such <term>subtleties</term> <note>original: "subtilties"; here meaning overly clever or distracting logical puzzles</note>, leaving them to be used in debate by those who are wiser than yourself. And fearing—as the saying goes—your own shadow and your own lack of skill, you would stick to this safe hypothesis and answer in the way I have described. 

But if anyone should challenge this hypothesis, you would refrain from answering him until you had considered the consequences resulting from it, and whether they were consistent or contradictory to one another. Then, when it is necessary for you to provide a reason for the hypothesis itself, you will do so in a similar way: by proposing another hypothesis—one that appears to be the best among the higher principles—until you arrive at something sufficient. At the same time, you will by no means confuse things by mixing them together, as argumentative people do, when you discuss the starting principle and the consequences arising from it—at least if you wish to discover anything about true reality. 

For such people probably pay no attention to this. Because of their 'wisdom,' they are quite capable of mixing everything together while still remaining pleased with themselves. But you, if you are truly a philosopher, will act, I think, in the way I have described."

Both Simmias and Cebes said, "You speak most truly."

**ECHECRATES.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Phædo, they agreed with good reason! For he seems to me to have explained this wonderfully clearly, even to someone with only a small amount of intelligence.

**PHÆDO.** And so indeed, Echecrates, it appeared in every respect to everyone who was present.

**Socrates:** If I remember correctly, after they had granted all this and acknowledged that each of the several <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here referring to the Platonic Forms or Ideals, the perfect abstract versions of qualities like Beauty or Greatness</note> was a real thing, and that other things participating in these Forms received their names from them, he then questioned them as follows: "If you agree that these things are so, when you say that Simmias is taller than Socrates, but shorter than Phædo, are you not asserting that both <term>magnitude</term> <note>greatness or largeness</note> and <term>parvitude</term> <note>original: "parvitude"; smallness</note> are present in Simmias?"

"I am."

"And yet," Socrates said, "you must admit that the fact of Simmias surpassing Socrates does not actually exist in the way the words seem to imply. For Simmias is not naturally meant to surpass Socrates simply because he is Simmias, but because of the greatness which he possesses. Nor, again, does he surpass Socrates because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates possesses smallness in relation to Simmias’s greatness."

"*True.*"

"Nor, again, is Simmias surpassed by Phædo because Phædo is Phædo, but because Phædo possesses greatness in relation to the smallness of Simmias."

"*It is so.*"

"Simmias, therefore, is labeled as both small and great, being situated in the middle of both. He shows his smallness by being surpassed by the greatness of Phædo, and his greatness by surpassing the smallness of Socrates." 

And at the same time, laughing gently, Socrates said, "I seem to have spoken with all the precision of a legal document <note>original: "precision of an historian"; Socrates is joking about how overly technical and dry his logical definitions have become</note>; but, nonetheless, it is as I say."

He agreed.

"But I have mentioned these things so that you might reach the same opinion as myself. For it appears to me, not only that 'Greatness' itself is never willing to be both great and small at the same time, but also that the greatness within us never desires to accept what is small, nor to be surpassed. Instead, it is willing to do one of two things: either to fly away and withdraw when its opposite, 'the small,' approaches it, or to perish when it arrives. What it is unwilling to do is to stay, receive smallness, and thus become something different from what it was. 

In the same way, I myself, having received and endured smallness, remain exactly who I am—I am still small. But that which is 'Great' does not dare to be small. In like manner, the 'smallness' which resides in us is never willing to become great or to be great. For then, my friend, we spoke concerning things which possess contraries, calling the contraries by the names of the things in which they reside; but now we speak of the actual things <note>referring to the Forms or Essences</note> which give their names to the objects residing in them. And we should never be willing to assert that these contraries receive an origin from one another." And at the same time, looking at Cebes, he said, "Did anything which has been said by this person disturb you also?"

"Indeed," says Cebes, "it did not; and at such a time as this, there are not many things which can disturb me."

"We frankly, therefore," says Socrates, "agree to this: that a contrary can never become contrary to itself."

"Entirely so," says Cebes.

"Entirely so."

Whatever things are occupied by the <term>Idea</term> <note>original: "idea"; refers to the Platonic Form—the perfect, eternal template of a concept</note> of three must not only be three, but also odd. — "Entirely so." — To a thing of this kind, therefore, we assert that an Idea contrary to that form, through which it becomes what it is, will never approach. — "It cannot." — But it becomes what it is through the odd, does it not? — "Certainly." — But is not the contrary to this the Idea of the even? — "It is." — The Idea of the even, therefore, will never enter into three things. — "Never." — Are not three things, therefore, <term>destitute</term> <note>original: "destitute"; in this context, it means "devoid of" or "lacking"</note> of the even? — "Destitute." — The <term>triad</term> <note>original: "triad"; the number three</note>, therefore, is an odd number. — "It is."

The things which I mentioned then are defined as follows: they are things which, though they are not the opposite of a particular nature themselves, still do not admit that which is opposite to them. For example, the triad in this instance, though it is not the opposite of "the even," still does not receive the even for that very reason: for it always brings with it that which is the opposite of the even. In the same way, the <term>duad</term> <note>original: "duad"; the number two</note> never admits the odd, and fire never admits cold, and so on for many other examples. 

But see if you would define it this way: not only does an opposite not receive its opposite, but also that any nature which brings an opposite with it to whatever it approaches, will never receive the opposition of the thing it introduces. But let us recollect again, for it will not be useless to hear it repeated often. Five things will not receive the form of the even; neither will ten things, which are the double of five, receive the form of the odd. This <note>original footnote 1: "That is, the double."</note>, therefore, though it is itself contrary to something else <note>original footnote 2: "That is, the half."</note>, yet will not receive the form of the odd. Nor will the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialter"; a ratio of one and a half, or 3:2</note>, nor other things of this kind, such as the half and the third part, ever receive the form of the whole, if you follow and agree to these consequences. — "I most strongly," says he, "follow and agree to them."

[...that the soul, when] death approaches it, should perish. For it follows from what has been said that the soul does not admit death, and of course, it will never be dead. This is just as we said: the number three will never be even, nor will the "odd" itself ever be even. Similarly, fire will never be cold, nor will the heat that is essential to fire ever become cold.

But someone might say: "What prevents the 'odd' from being destroyed when the 'even' arrives, rather than just refusing to become even?" We cannot argue against someone making this objection by claiming the "odd" is not destroyed, because "the odd" is not inherently indestructible. If we had already agreed that the "odd" was indestructible, we could easily counter the objection by saying that when the "even" approaches, the "odd" and the number "three" would simply depart. We could argue the same way about fire, heat, and other things, could we not?

"Entirely so," said Cebes.

"And therefore, since we have agreed that whatever is immortal is also indestructible, it must follow that the soul—being immortal—is also indestructible. If this is not admitted, we will need other arguments to convince us."

"But there is no need for that," he replied. "For it is hardly possible that anything else could be free from <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "corruption"; here meaning decay, dissolution, or the state of being destroyed</note> if that which is immortal and eternal is subject to being broken apart."

"I believe," said Socrates, "that the Divine, and the <term>Form</term> <note>The "Forms" are Plato's concept of perfect, eternal patterns of which all physical things are mere copies.</note> of life itself, and anything else that is immortal, must be admitted by everyone to be entirely free from destruction."

"By Zeus!" <note>original: "by Jupiter"; the translator used the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note> he said, "all men must acknowledge this, and I believe the Gods would acknowledge it even more."

"Since, therefore, that which is immortal is also incorruptible, will the soul not be indestructible, seeing as it is immortal?"

"It is absolutely necessary."

"When, therefore, death attacks a man, his mortal part, it seems, dies; but the immortal part departs safe and uncorrupted, withdrawing itself from death."

"It appears so."

"The soul, therefore, O Cebes," he said, "will be immortal and indestructible more than anything else ¹; and our souls will, in reality, exist in <term>Hades</term> <note>The Greek underworld or the realm of the dead.</note>."

"Therefore, Socrates," he said, "I have nothing further to object to these arguments, nor any reason why I should doubt their reality. But if Simmias, or anyone else present, has anything to say, they would do well not to remain silent."

"But it is only right, my friends," Socrates said, "to consider that if the soul is immortal, it requires our care and attention, not only for the present time—which we call a lifetime—but also with a view toward the whole of time. It now appears that anyone who neglects the soul subjects themselves to a most terrifying danger. For if death were the end of the whole person, it would be an unexpected stroke of luck for the wicked to be liberated from the body and from their own wickedness along with their soul at the same time. 

But now, since the soul is shown to be immortal, there is no other escape from evil and no other safety for it except to become as good and as wise as possible. strives <gloss>1</gloss> to lead each soul to a specific place where it is necessary for them all to be gathered. After they have been judged, they must proceed to Hades together with their leader <note>In Greek mythology and Platonic thought, this is the "daimon" or guardian spirit assigned to a person at birth.</note>, who is ordered to conduct them from this world to that one. But after receiving the assignments proper to their condition and staying there for the necessary time, another leader brings them back here again after many long periods of time. 

The journey, therefore, is not as Telephus claims it to be in the writings of Aeschylus. For he says that a simple path leads to Hades, but it appears to me that the path is neither simple nor singular. If there were only one way, there would be no need for guides, nor could anyone ever wander from the right road. But now the path appears to have many forks and confusing turns; I infer this from our own holy and legal funeral rites. The soul, therefore, which is properly adorned with virtue,

---

follows its guide and is not ignorant of its present circumstances. However, since there are also natures joined with the "superessential unities" <note>original: "superessential unities"; a Neoplatonic term for the highest, most divine aspects of reality that exist beyond being itself</note>, it is necessary that there should be a certain middle class of beings. This class is neither directly attached to the Deity, nor does it fluctuate at different times between better and worse; instead, it is always perfect and never departs from its own virtue. It is unchanging, yet it is not joined to the superessential. This entire class is called "daimoniacal" <note>original: "dæmoniacal"; referring to daimons or spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and humans</note>. 

There are also different classes of daimons, for they are ranked under the gods who govern the world. The highest of these exists according to the *One* of the Gods, which is called a unifying and divine class of spirits. The next exists according to the intellect that depends on the Deity and is called "intellectual." The third exists according to the soul and is called "rational." The fourth exists according to nature and is called "physical." The fifth exists according to the body and is called "body-formed." And the sixth exists according to matter and is called "material." 

Alternatively, as Olympiodorus adds, some of these are celestial, others ethereal, others aerial, others aquatic, others terrestrial, and others subterranean. This division is clearly derived from the different parts of the universe. Furthermore, "irrational" spirits originate from the governors of the air, which is why the Oracle says:

->driving the aerial, terrestrial, and aquatic dogs.<-
<note>original: "περιων ελατηρα κυνων χθονιων τε και υγρων"</note>

Our guardian spirits, however, belong to that order of spirits which is organized under the Gods who preside over the ascent and descent of souls.

...those who are accustomed to speak about it imagine, as I am convinced from a certain person’s account.

"How is this, Socrates?" asks Simmias. "For I myself have also heard many things about the earth, and yet perhaps not these specific details that you believe. I would therefore be glad to hear you describe them."

"Indeed, Simmias," he says, "the 'art of Glaucus' <note>A Greek proverb referring to a very difficult or specialized skill, named after a famous metalworker or perhaps a legendary diver.</note> does not seem to me to be necessary in order to relate these details. But to prove their truth seems to me to be an undertaking beyond what the 'art of Glaucus' can accomplish. Besides, I myself am perhaps not able to achieve this; and even if I knew how, the time I have left to live, Simmias, seems by no means sufficient for the length of such a discussion. However, nothing hinders me from informing you what I am convinced is the truth regarding the form of the earth and the regions it contains."

"And this information," says Simmias, "will be sufficient."

"I am convinced, therefore," says he, "in the first place, that if the earth is in the middle of the heavens and is spherical in shape, it has no need of air or any other such physical necessity to prevent it from falling. Instead, the perfect uniformity of the heavens themselves and the equilibrium of the earth are sufficient causes for its support. For that which is perfectly balanced, when placed in the center of a uniform environment, cannot move more or less in one direction than another; but, existing on all sides in a similar state, it will remain free from any leaning. This is the first thing of which I am convinced."

"And quite rightly so," says Cebes.

"Furthermore," he says, "I believe that the earth is remarkably <note>original: "prodigiously"</note> large; and that we...

***

...consequently this must also be true of the earth. It is likewise evident that the earth is in the middle. For, if the universe is spherical, it exists around a center. The parts of the universe, therefore, which qualify as "wholes" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "wholes" refer to the major elemental spheres (like the sphere of fire or air) or celestial bodies.</note> will also exist around centers, and consequently this will be the case with the earth. Let it, however, be admitted that it exists around a center; but how is it evident that it exists at the center of the universe? We reply that if it is the densest <note>original: "most gross"</note> of all bodies, it will be the lowest of them. For the most refined <note>original: "attenuated"</note> of bodies, being able to pass through each other, occupy the higher places according to their degree of refinement, while the earth occupies the lower.

<margin>* That the earth is very large, says Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, is evident from the Atlantic island <note>A reference to the legend of Atlantis.</note> being larger than both Asia and Libya. It is likewise evident because the highest points of secondary things tend to resemble the extremities of the things above them; so that the summit of the earth must be refined and transparent <note>original: "attenuated and pellucid"</note>, similar to the most precious stones and metals.</margin>

...who dwell in places extending from Phasis <note>The Phasis is a river in modern-day Georgia, considered by the Greeks to be the eastern limit of the world.</note> to the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, the western limit of the ancient world.</note>, inhabit only a certain small portion of it around the Mediterranean Sea, like ants or frogs around a marsh. I am also convinced that there are many others elsewhere who dwell in many similar places. For I am persuaded that everywhere around the earth there are many hollow places of various forms and sizes into which water, mist, and air flow together. 

However, the earth itself—which is of a pure nature—is situated in the pure heavens where the stars are located, and which most of those accustomed to speaking about such matters call <term>æther</term> <note>original: "æther"; the "fifth element" or the pure, upper air of the gods.</note>. The places we inhabit are nothing more than the dregs of this pure earth, or cavities into which its dregs continually flow. We are ignorant, therefore, of the fact that we dwell in the cavities of this earth, and we imagine instead that we inhabit its upper parts. It is just as if someone dwelling at the very bottom of the sea should think that he resided on its surface; and, beholding the sun and the other stars through the water, should imagine that the sea is the heavens. But through laziness and weakness... <note>The text continues on the next page, likely explaining how we are unable to reach the true surface of the earth.</note>

---

...metals. And lastly, this is evident from the depth of the hollows in which we dwell and the height of the mountains; for these show that the <term>spheric superficies</term> <note>spherical surface</note> of the earth is larger than what is generally considered its surface. On this summit of the earth, therefore, the true heavens are visible. They are also seen closely, and not through <term>æther</term> alone, but with more beautiful eyes. According to Ammonius Hermeas—whom Olympiodorus calls the *Interpreter*—the stars themselves, as I have observed before, are not seen by us here; rather, we see only their "inflammations" in the air. And perhaps, he says, this is the meaning of that assertion by Heraclitus: "measures being kindled and measures being extinguished." For he certainly did not say this of the sun itself, but of the sun in relation to us.

Olympiodorus further observes that there is a triple division of the earth according to the three Saturnian deities <note>The sons of Saturn (Kronos): Jupiter (Zeus), Neptune (Poseidon), and Pluto (Hades).</note>: Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto. For to these, as Homer says, heaven and earth are common. But if they are common, it is evident that these two are divided among them. Hence, in the heavens, the <term>inerratic sphere</term> <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note> belongs to Jupiter; from there, as far as the sphere of the sun, belongs to Neptune; and the remaining part of the heavens belongs to Pluto. If there is also a division of the earth according to the universe, it must be divided into celestial, terrestrial, and middle. For the "Olympian earth" is honored as well as that which is strictly terrestrial. There must, therefore, be a certain middle earth. Likewise, if there is a division of the earth according to that of a living animal—for the earth is an animal—it must be divided into the head, middle parts, and feet.

It is also beautifully observed by Olympiodorus that each of the elements shares the <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>A 12-sided geometric solid.</note> in common, as a preparation for becoming a sphere. Hence, he says, the earth has the cubic form from itself, water the <term>icosahedric</term> <note>20-sided</note>, air the <term>octahedric</term> <note>8-sided</note>, and fire the pyramid (tetrahedron); but the <term>supermundane Gods</term> <note>Gods existing beyond the physical world.</note> impart the dodecahedron to all of them as a preparation for "intellectual participation," which is sphericity, or the receiving of a spherical shape.

And this also happens to us in the same way as the instance mentioned above, because of our weakness and laziness, which make us incapable of ascending to the highest point of the air. For otherwise, if anyone could reach its summit, or—growing wings—could fly there, he would be seen emerging from here. Just as fish, emerging from the sea into our world, see what our region contains, in the same way he would behold the various details belonging to the summit of the earth. 

Furthermore, if his nature were strong enough for such an elevated survey, he would know that the heavens he saw there were the *true* heavens, and that he was perceiving the true light and the true earth. For this earth where we live, the stones it contains, and the entire region of our home are all corrupted and eaten away, just as things in the sea are corroded by salt. Nothing of value <note>original: "worthy of estimation"</note> grows in the sea, nor does it contain anything perfect; instead, there are caverns and sand, and immense quantities of mud and filth wherever there is earth. The contents of the sea cannot be compared in any way with the beauty of the various things in our place of residence. 

But those upper regions of the earth will appear to be even more excellent than these where we live. For, if it is appropriate to tell you a beautiful myth <note>original: "fable"</note>, it is well worth hearing, Simmias, what kind of places exist on the upper earth, situated under the heavens.

Hence, whatever grows in this earth grows according to its nature—including trees, flowers, and fruits. Furthermore, its mountains and stones possess a similar perfection and transparency, and are made beautiful through various colors. The stones so highly valued by us in this place where we live are but small fragments of these, such as <term>sardin-stones</term> <note>original: "sardin-stones"; a reddish-brown gemstone now called sard or carnelian.</note>, jaspers, emeralds, and others of this kind. In our world, these elements cause filth and disease to the stones, the earth, the animals, and the plants found among us. But this pure earth is adorned with all of these, as well as with gold, silver, and other similar materials. Others dwell around the air as we do around the sea; others reside in islands which the air flows around, and which are situated not far from the mainland. In a word, what water and the sea are to us regarding their utility, the air is to them. But what the air is to us, <term>ether</term> <note>original: "æther"; in ancient cosmology, the pure "fifth element" that fills the space of the universe above the terrestrial sphere.</note> is to the inhabitants of this pure earth. 

Furthermore, the seasons there are endowed with such an excellent balance that the inhabitants are never troubled with disease and live much longer than those who dwell in our regions. They surpass us in sight, hearing, wisdom, and every faculty of this kind, just as much as air excels water in purity—and ether excels air. Besides this, they have groves and temples of the Gods in which the Gods truly dwell. They also have oracles, prophecies, and direct perceptions of the Gods, and similar associations with them. They see the sun, moon, and stars as they really are; and in every other respect, their happiness is of a corresponding nature.

This is how the whole earth naturally exists, along with the parts situated around it. But the circumference of the earth contains many places within its cavities. Some of these are deeper and more extended than the region we inhabit. Others are deeper, indeed, but have a narrower opening than our own dwelling place. There are also certain parts which are less deep, but broader than ours. 

All of these are perforated into one another in many places under the earth through narrower and broader avenues. They have passages of communication through which a great quantity of water flows into the different hollows of the earth, as if into bowls. Besides this, there are immense volumes of ever-flowing rivers under the earth, consisting of hot and cold waters. There is also a great quantity of fire—mighty rivers of fire—and many rivers of wet mud, some of which are purer and others more muddy. For example, in Sicily, there are rivers of mud that flow before a stream of fire, which is itself a flaming torrent.

From these sources, various places are filled, into which each river flows at specific times. But all of these move upward and downward, like a suspended vessel situated within the earth. Through its unique nature, this suspended vessel is one of the earth's chasms—the greatest of all, and completely perforated through the entire planet. Regarding this, Homer¹ thus speaks:

->Far, very far, where beneath the earth is found<-
->A gulf, the most profound of every depth:<-

which he and many other poets elsewhere call Tartarus². All rivers flow together into this chasm, and from it, they flow upward again. Each river takes on the qualities of the earth through which it passes. The reason why they all flow into and out of this chasm is that the moisture can find neither a bottom nor a base. Consequently, it rises and fluctuates up and down; the same is true for the air and spirit³ surrounding it. They follow this moisture, both when they are driven toward the more remote parts of the earth and when they move toward the regions where we live. Just as in breathing the flowing breath is constantly exhaled and inhaled, so too that spirit, rising with the moisture, creates violent and massive winds during its entrance and exit. Therefore, when the water is pushed and flows into the place we call "downward," the rivers flow through the earth into various channels and fill them, much like people pouring liquid into another vessel...

Because of this, he says, we have a celestial Tartarus where Heaven hid his children, a Saturnian Tartarus where Saturn hid his, and a Jovian <note>relating to Jove or Jupiter</note> version of this kind, which is <term>demiurgic</term> <note>original: "demiurgic"; referring to the Demiurge, the artisan-like figure responsible for fashioning and maintaining the physical universe.</note>.

Also, because the earth is a living animal, it must naturally "breathe," creating certain back-and-forth flows through its inhalations and exhalations. Furthermore, its "light-bearing" <note>original: "luciform"; referring to a luminous, ethereal body or vehicle of the soul.</note> part must be its primary vehicle, while its physical bulk is its visible part. Therefore, it requires a middle or "airy" vehicle to nourish and move more refined substances through its varied motions.
· Olympiodorus further observes that Tartarus and the Earth (which is joined with Heaven) are overseen by Typhon, Echidna, and Python. These form a certain <term>Chaldaic triad</term> <note>A grouping of three entities or principles significant in Chaldean Oracles and theology.</note>, acting as the protective guardians of all disordered creation.

...the water which they have drawn. When this water, departing from there, is driven here, it again fills the rivers on the earth. Once filled, these rivers flow through channels and through the earth; and after they have individually passed through the passages open to each, they create seas, lakes, rivers, and fountains. Then, flowing back from these places underground—some winding through longer and more numerous areas, others through shorter and fewer—they plunge back into Tartarus. Some enter much deeper than the point from which they were drawn, while others enter less deeply; however, the inflows of all these rivers are deeper than the points where they flow upward. 

The outflows of some rivers are in the opposite direction to their inflows, while in others, both flow in the same direction. There are some rivers that circle the earth entirely, winding like snakes once or many times around it; after descending as far as possible, they are again discharged from each side until they reach the center, but they never go beyond it. From either side, the ground slopes upward toward the center for both these streams.

There are many other great and diverse rivers, but among this abundance, there are four primary streams. The greatest of these, which flows in a circle around the outermost part of the entire earth, is called the Ocean. Opposite to this and flowing in the contrary direction is the Acheron. This river flows through other deserted places and under the earth, emptying its waters into the Acherusian marsh, where many souls...

---

¹ The four rivers mentioned here, according to Olympiodorus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator (c. 495–570 AD).</note> (following the "Interpreter," Ammonius Hermeas <note>A 5th-century philosopher and teacher of Olympiodorus.</note>), represent the four elements in Tartarus. Of these, the Ocean is water; Cocytus (or rather, the Styx) is earth; Pyriphlegethon is fire; and Acheron is air. Styx is opposed to Pyriphlegethon, just as cold is to heat, and Acheron is opposed to the Ocean, as air is to water. This is why Orpheus* also calls the Acherusian lake "aerial" <note>original: "Διο και Ορφευς την Αχερουσιαν λιμνην αε̈ριαν καλει" — "For this reason, Orpheus also calls the Acherusian lake aerial," implying it is composed of the element of air.</note>. However, Olympiodorus notes that the actual positions of the rivers do not match this interpretation. The Ocean is first and in the highest place. Below it is the Acheron. Below that is Pyriphlegethon, and in the lowest place is Cocytus. Furthermore, they are all called "rivers," even though the elements are different. Therefore, he says it is better to consider the various assignments and locations of souls as having a fourfold division based on depth. Before considering the places, we should consider their divine characteristics: the defining nature of the Ocean; the purifying <term>cathartic</term> nature of the Acheron; the punishment through heat in Pyriphlegethon; and the punishment through cold in Cocytus.

...where the souls of the dead pass. Staying there for certain destined periods of time—some longer, others shorter—they are eventually sent back to be reborn as animals. 

The third river bursts forth in the middle, and near its source it falls into a vast region burning with intense fire. It creates a lake larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From there it moves in a circle, turbulent and miry; winding around the earth, it reaches the edges of the Acherusian marsh but does not mix with its water. After many rotations under the earth, it flows into the deeper parts of Tartarus. This is the river which is called Pyriphlegethon <note>original: "Pyriphlegethon" — from the Greek for "fire-blazing."</note>, and its streams send off branching rivers to various parts of the earth. 

Opposite to this is the fourth river, which first falls into a place described as dreadful and wild, colored entirely a deep blue <note>original: "azure"</note>. This is called the Styx, and the streams flowing into it form the Stygian marsh. After falling into this marsh and gaining terrible powers from its water, the river sinks under the earth and winds around in a direction opposite to Pyriphlegethon, eventually meeting it at the Acherusian marsh from the opposite side. The water of this river also does not mix with any other; instead, it circles around and plunges into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. According to the poets, the name of this river is Cocytus <note>original: "Cocytus" — from the Greek for "wailing" or "lamentation."</note>.

Because these things are naturally arranged this way, when the dead arrive at the place where their guardian spirit <note>original: "dæmon" — in Greek philosophy, a *daimon* is a guiding spirit or lesser deity assigned to a person at birth.</note> leads each of them, they are first judged. This judgment applies to those who have lived in a proper, pious, and just manner, as well as those who have not. 

Those who appear to have lived an average life proceed to the Acheron. They board the vehicles ¹ prepared for them and arrive at the Acherusian lake. There they live until they are purified; having suffered punishment for any wrongs they may have committed, they are set free. Afterward, each receives a reward for their good deeds according to what they deserve. However, those who appear to be incurable because of the greatness of their crimes—either because they have committed many major acts of sacrilege, many illegal killings, or other similar things of this kind—

kind—these, a destiny adapted to their guilt hurls into Tartarus, from which they will *never* <gloss>*</gloss> be discharged. But those who are found to have committed curable, yet serious crimes—such as those who, in a fit of anger, have been guilty of any violence against their father or mother and have lived the remainder of their lives repentant for the offense, or who have become murderers in any other similar way—it is necessary for them to fall into Tartarus. 

But after they have fallen and have lived there for a year, the waves hurl them out of Tartarus: the murderers into the Cocytus <note>original: "Cocytus"—the river of wailing.</note>, and the violators of fathers and mothers into the Pyriphlegethon <note>original: "Pyriphlegethon"—the river of fire.</note>. When they are carried along by these rivers and arrive at the Acherusian marsh, they cry out and call upon those whom they murdered or injured. If they can persuade them to do this, they depart and find an end to their suffering; but if they are unable to accomplish this, they are carried back again into Tartarus, and from there back into the rivers. They do not cease from suffering this until they have persuaded those they injured to forgive them, for this punishment was ordained for them by the judges. 

But those who appear to have lived most excellently in regard to holiness—these are they who, being freed and released from these places within the earth as if from a prison, shall arrive at the pure habitation on high and dwell on the *ethereal* earth <gloss>‡</gloss>. Among these, those who are sufficiently purified by philosophy shall live without bodies through the whole of the time to come, and

***

<gloss>*</gloss> The reader should not imagine that the word *never* implies an infinite duration here. The Divine does not punish the soul as if influenced by anger, but rather like a skilled doctor <note>original: "physician"</note>, for the sake of healing the diseases <note>original: "maladies"</note> the soul has contracted through guilt. We must say, therefore—as Olympiodorus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato in the 6th century AD.</note> well observes—that the "incurable" soul is punished *eternally*, meaning for the duration of its "eternity," which is its specific period of existence. "For in reality," he says, "souls that have offended to the highest degree cannot be sufficiently purified in a single cycle, but are continually in a state of life within Tartarus; and this period is what Plato calls eternity."

<gloss>‡</gloss> Observe here that those who have lived a holy and blameless life without the study of philosophy will, after death, dwell on the summit of the earth; their bodies will consequently consist of the most rarefied <note>original: "attenuated"</note> air. Those who have practiced philosophy in a "political" or civic sense, says Olympiodorus, will live in the heavens with light-like <note>original: "luciform"</note> bodies. And those who are perfectly purified will be restored to the realm beyond the physical world <note>original: "super-mundane"</note> without bodies at all.

...will arrive at dwellings even more beautiful than these, which are not easy to describe, nor is the time we have left sufficient for such a task.

But because of these matters we have related, Simmias, we should do everything we can to participate in virtue and wisdom <note>original: "prudence"</note> during this life. For the reward is beautiful, and the hope is great. To insist, indeed, that these things are exactly as I have described them is not the mark of a man of reason. But to assert that either these things or something very much like them are true regarding our souls and their habitations—since our soul appears to be immortal—this is, I think, both fitting and worth the risk for anyone who believes in its reality. For the risk is a noble one <note>original: "the danger is beautiful"</note>; and it is necessary to soothe ourselves with such thoughts as if with enchantments. It is for this reason that I have told the story <note>original: "fable"</note> you have just heard. 

Because of these things, a man should be confident about his soul if, in this life, he has said goodbye to the pleasures and ornaments of the body as things foreign to his nature and of little value. Instead, he has earnestly devoted himself to learning <note>original: "disciplines"</note> as things of far greater consequence. Having adorned his soul not with borrowed ornaments but with its own proper jewels—namely, temperance, justice, courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>, freedom, and truth—he awaits his journey to the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note>, ready to depart whenever Fate calls upon him. You, therefore (he said), Simmias and Cebes, and the rest of you gathered here, will each depart at some time in the future; but

"…to myself, to my family, and to yourselves, even if you do not promise me anything right now. But if you neglect yourselves and are unwilling to live according to what has been said both now and in the past—as guiding principles <note>original: "vestiges of direction"</note> for your journey—you will achieve nothing, even if you make many solemn promises right now. 

"We shall take care, therefore," Crito said, "to act as you desire. But how would you like to be buried?" 

"Just as you please," Socrates replied, "if you can only catch me and I do not escape your pursuit." 

At the same time, laughing gently and addressing us, he said, "I cannot convince Crito, my friends, that I am the Socrates who is now talking with you and organizing <note>original: "methodizes"</note> every part of this discussion. Instead, he thinks I am the one he will soon see lying dead, and so he asks how he should bury me. But as for that long discourse I just gave you—in which I argued that after I have drunk the poison, I will no longer remain with you but will depart to the happiness of the blessed <note>original: "felicities of the blessed"</note>—I seem to have said all this to him in vain, even though I said it to comfort both you and myself. 

"Therefore," he continued, "promise Crito on my behalf exactly the opposite of what he promised the judges for me. For he promised them that I would not run away; but I want you to guarantee that when I die, I will *not* stay with you, but will depart and leave you entirely. This way, Crito may more easily endure this separation and will not be distressed when he sees my body either burned or buried, as if I were suffering some terrible misfortune. I do not want him to say at my funeral that Socrates is being laid out, or carried out, or buried. For you can be sure of this, excellent Crito: to speak improperly is not only a fault in our speech, but it also harms our souls with a kind of evil. Instead, you should be confident and say that it is only my body that is being buried—and you may bury it in whatever way is pleasing to you and which you think best fits our laws."

When he had said this, he rose and went into another room to wash himself, and Crito followed him; but Socrates told us to wait for him. We waited, therefore, discussing and reflecting among ourselves on what had been said. Sometimes we spoke about his death and how great a calamity it would be for us, sincerely feeling that we, like children deprived of their father, would spend the rest of our lives as orphans.
