...his family (for he had two small children and one who was almost a man), and the women of his household also came to see him. But once he had spoken to them in Crito's presence and given them the final instructions <note>original: "injunctions"</note> he thought appropriate, he ordered the children and women to leave, and he himself returned to us.

It was now near sunset, for he had been away in the bathing room for a long time. When he returned from washing, he sat down but did not say much after that. Then the servant of the Eleven <note>The "Eleven" were the magistrates in Athens responsible for the supervision of prisons and executions.</note> entered. Standing near him, he said, "Socrates, I do not see in you the same reaction I have noticed in others. Usually, they are angry with me and curse me when, following the orders of the magistrates, I inform them that they must drink the poison. But, on the contrary, I have found you to be the most noble, gentle, and best man who has ever come to this place. Therefore, I am certain you are not angry with me, but with those responsible for your current situation—you know whom I mean. So now (since you know what I came to tell you), farewell, and try to bear this necessity as easily as you can."

Then, bursting into tears, the man turned away and left. Socrates watched him go and said, "Farewell to you too; we will do as you advise." 

Turning to us, he said, "How courteous that man is! During the entire time I have been here, he has visited and often talked with me, proving himself to be the kindest of men. And now, how sincerely he weeps for me! But Crito, let us obey him. Have someone bring the poison if it has been ground <note>original: "bruised"; refers to the crushing of hemlock seeds or roots into a drinkable form.</note>; if not, let the man whose job it is grind it himself."

"But Socrates," Crito said, "I think the sun is still over the mountains and has not yet set. I have known others who waited until very late to drink the poison after being told to do so—those who have eaten and drunk well and enjoyed the company of their loved ones. Therefore, do not be in such a hurry; there is still enough time."

To this Socrates replied, "Crito, those men act quite appropriately in doing as you described—for they believe they gain something by doing so. Likewise, it is appropriate for me *not* to act that way. For I do not think I will gain anything by drinking it later, except perhaps making myself...

Then Crito, hearing this, signaled to the boy standing near him. The boy left, and after staying away for some time, he returned with the man who was to administer the poison, who carried it already prepared in a cup. When Socrates saw the man, he said, "Very well, my friend; but what am I supposed to do? For you are the expert in these matters."

"You have nothing else to do," the man replied, "but to drink it and walk around until your legs feel heavy, and then lie down. That is how it will take effect." At the same time, he handed the cup to Socrates. 

Socrates took it—and truly, Echecrates, he did so with great cheerfulness. He did not tremble, nor did his color or expression change in the slightest. Instead, as was his habit, he looked the man straight in the eye with a steady, bull-like gaze <note>original: "bull-like aspect" — This phrase translates the Greek *tauredon*, referring to Socrates's characteristic way of looking at people with a direct, intense, and slightly lowered brow.</note>. "We only prepare <note>original: "bruise"</note>," the man replied, "as much as we think is sufficient for the dose."

"I understand," said Socrates. "But it is surely both right and proper to pray to the gods that my journey from this world to the next may be a fortunate one. This is what I pray for; may it be so." And as he finished speaking, he drank the poison quite easily and cheerfully. 

Up until this point, most of us were able to hold back our tears reasonably well. But when we saw him drinking, and realized he had finished the cup, we could no longer restrain ourselves. As for me, despite my violent efforts to stop them, the tears flowed in torrents. I covered my face with my cloak and mourned my own misfortune. I was not weeping for him, but for my own fate, considering what a companion I was losing. Crito, unable to hold back his tears, had already stood up and moved away before I did. And Apollodorus, who had been weeping the entire time, began to cry out so bitterly that he broke the spirits of everyone present—except Socrates. 

Upon seeing this, Socrates exclaimed, "What are you doing, my dear friends? I sent the women away primarily so they wouldn't create a scene like this!"

<note>The following passage is a translation of the Greek commentary provided in the original text, which explains the symbolic meaning of ancient Athenian funeral rites through a Platonic lens.</note>

What certain Athenian ancestral customs regarding the deceased symbolize:
*   **Closing the eyes** signifies the ceasing of outward activity and the turning of the soul toward its internal life.
*   **Placing the body on the ground** serves as a reminder of how the soul may be united with the whole of existence.
*   **Washing the body** represents purification from the realm of "generation" <note>original: "γενεσεως" (geneseos) — refers to the cycle of physical birth and material existence</note>.
*   **Anointing with oil** signifies being drawn away from the "mire of matter" and invoking divine inspiration.
*   **Cremation** (burning the body) signifies leading the soul upward toward the indivisible realm.
*   **Placing the remains in the earth** signifies the soul's union with <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "νοητοις" (noëtois) — the realm of pure, abstract ideas or Forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note>.

### THE END OF THE PHAEDO.

<summary>The text concludes with a high tribute to Socrates's character and provides a philosophical interpretation of traditional funeral rites as symbols for the soul's liberation from the body.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the introduction to Plato's dialogue *Gorgias*, specifically drawing from the commentary of Olympiodorus. It sets the historical and theatrical stage for the debate between Socrates and the famous rhetorician Gorgias.</meta>

VOL. IV.
2 Y

# INTRODUCTION

### TO

## THE GORGIAS.

---

**IT** is necessary in the first place, says Olympiodorus¹, to investigate the <term>dramatic apparatus</term> <note>The setting, background, and theatrical context of the dialogue.</note> of the dialogue; in the second place, its purpose; in the third place, its structure; in the fourth place, the characters and the symbolism they represent; and in the fifth place, (a point investigated by many, though it does not deserve much discussion and was not doubted by older scholars), for what reason Plato introduces Gorgias here, given that he did not actually live at the same time as Socrates.

The <term>dramatic apparatus</term> is as follows: Gorgias of Leontini came from Sicily as an ambassador to the Athenians to discuss an alliance and the war against the Syracusans. He was accompanied by Polus, who delighted in <term>rhetoric</term> <note>The art of persuasive speaking.</note>; and he stayed in the house of Callicles, the public orator of the Athenians. This Callicles was also delighted by skilled rhetoricians, but he made pleasure the ultimate goal of life and deceived the Athenians by always addressing them in the style of Demosthenes: “What do you wish? What shall I write? In what can I gratify you?” Gorgias, therefore, demonstrated his art and so captivated the Athenian people that they called the days in which he performed *festivals* and his rhetorical phrases *lamps*. Consequently, Socrates—perceiving that the people were being deceived and being capable of doing good for all the youth—formed the plan of saving the souls of both the Athenians and Gorgias himself. Therefore, taking with him Chaerephon the philosopher (who is mentioned by Aristophanes), they went to the house of Callicles, and there their conversations and investigations of <term>theorems</term> <note>Philosophical principles or logical propositions.</note> took place.

---

¹ In his manuscript *Scholia* <note>original: "Scholia"; meaning "commentaries" or "explanatory notes".</note> on this Dialogue.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's *Gorgias* from the perspective of the commentator Olympiodorus, transitioning from the historical background of the characters to an analysis of the dialogue's central purpose and philosophical framework.</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE GORGIAS</header>

But he went with Chaerephon, and did not go alone, so that he might show how men of science <note>In this context, "scientific" refers to those possessing systematic philosophical knowledge.</note> conducted themselves and discussed matters. And this concludes our discussion of the <term>dramatic apparatus</term> <note>The setting and background details.</note> of the dialogue.

With respect to its scope, it has appeared to be different to different people. For some say that Plato’s design was to discuss rhetoric, and they title it “Gorgias, or On Rhetoric”; but they do so improperly, for they characterize the whole work based only on a part. Others say that the dialogue is concerning justice and injustice, showing that the just are happy and the unjust are unfortunate and miserable. Likewise, they argue that the more unjust a man is, the more miserable he becomes; that in proportion as his injustice is extended by time, he becomes even more miserable; and that if his injustice were immortal, he would be the most miserable of all. These people also derive the scope of the dialogue from only one part—namely, from the arguments against Polus. Others say that its scope is to speak concerning the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>original: demiurgos; the "craftsman" or creator of the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note>. But these also gather the scope from a single part, because the <term>demiurge</term> is mentioned in the fable at the end of this dialogue. These, however, speak absurdly and far from the purpose. We say, therefore, that its scope is to discuss the *principles which lead us to political happiness*.

Since we have mentioned principles and a <term>polity</term> <note>A form of government or a civil constitution.</note>, let us speak concerning principles universally, and concerning political happiness, and also what the principles of political science are. The principles of every thing are six:
1.  **Matter**, as wood is to a carpenter.
2.  **Form**, like the writing table, or something of this kind.
3.  **The Producing Cause**, such as the carpenter himself.
4.  **The Paradigm**, the model to which he directs his <term>phantasy</term> <note>The imagination or mental representation of the ideal form.</note> when he makes the table.
5.  **The Instrument**, perhaps the saw or the axe.
6.  **And the End**, the purpose for which it was made.

The common people, therefore, and the rhetoricians—not looking toward the truth—say that *the matter* of political science is the physical body which is preserved; *the form* is luxury; *the producing cause* is rhetoric; *the paradigm* is a tyranny; *the instrument* is persuasion; *and the end* is pleasure. Such are their assertions. We, however, say that the *matter* is the soul—and not just the rational soul, but that which consists of three parts <note>The "tripartite soul," consisting of reason, anger (spiritedness), and desire.</note>—for it imitates a <term>polity</term>. And just as in cities there are governors, soldiers, and mercenaries, so, within us, there is—

---

* i.e., Of reason, anger, and desire.

It introduces a six-fold framework for analyzing these principles, contrasting a superficial, pleasure-oriented view of politics with a philosophical one centered on the tripartite soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's *Gorgias*, specifically analyzing the dialogue's structure through the framework of the "four causes" (matter, form, efficient, and final) and the three parts of the soul.</meta>

<page-num>347</page-num>
<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

Reason is like a governor; anger is like a soldier, acting as a middle ground and obeying reason, while commanding and organizing the mercenaries—which represents desire. The *subject matter*, then, is the soul viewed as divided into three parts. For the political character seeks to experience anger and desire only regarding appropriate things and at appropriate times. Just as the lowest string of a musical instrument harmonizes with the highest and produces the same note, though it is more acute <note>The author is referring to an octave relationship, where two strings produce the same musical tone at different pitches.</note>, desire is joined with reason in the same way. 

But the *form* consists of justice and temperance. The *efficient cause* <note>original: producing cause</note> is a life of philosophy. The *model* <note>original: paradigm</note> is the world. For the political philosopher organizes everything in imitation of the universe, which is filled with perfect order. According to Plato, this universe is "order" (*kosmos* <note>original: κοσμος</note>) and not "disorder" (*akosmia* <note>original: ακοσμια</note>). Manners and discipline are the *tools* <note>original: instrument</note>. And the *goal* <note>original: end</note> is the good. 

It should be noted, however, that the "good" is twofold: one part applies to us in this life, while the other we will possess in the life to come¹. Therefore, *political good* belongs to us in the present, while *contemplative good* <note>original: theoretic good</note> will be our share in the next life. Consequently, the discussion with Gorgias concerns the *efficient cause*; the discussion with Polus concerns the *formal cause*; and the discussion with Callicles concerns the *final cause*. It is not surprising if all these elements seem to be present in each section. For the efficient cause contains the others, and the others contain all: there is a certain connection among them, and they influence one another. However, they take their primary classification from whichever element is most prominent.

Thus, the division of the dialogue becomes clear. It is divided into three sections: the conversation with Gorgias, the one with Polus, and the one with Callicles. It is also necessary to observe that justice and temperance are specifically called the "form" of political science. One must understand that while all virtues contribute to political happiness <note>original: felicity</note>, these two are especially important. For this reason, Plato always mentions them, as they are often neglected by men. People desire to know the other two virtues—though they do so imperfectly, falsely, and under incorrect names. For instance, they might say, "That man is prudent; he knows how to get rich." They speak similarly of courage <note>original: fortitude</note>, yet they ignore justice and temperance. However, there is a need for these virtues, as they extend through all...

---

¹ Although a few people are able to practice the *contemplative* <note>original: theoretic</note> as well as the *political* virtues in this life, we can only possess the good of the former in perfection in the hereafter. For an accurate account of these virtues, see the Notes on the *Phaedo*.

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on the parts of the soul and begins an analysis of the five characters in the *Gorgias* as allegories for different states of the soul and types of knowledge.</meta>

<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

the parts of the soul. For just as a person in a city who performs his own work and gives every man his due is said to be just, in the same way, justice rules in the soul when reason, anger <note>original: "anger" - here referring to *thymos*, the spirited or courageous part of the soul</note>, and desire each perform the specific function suited to them. If this is the case, then temperance exists in the soul when each part does not desire things that are foreign to its nature.

Next, it is worth investigating the number and the symbolic roles of the characters. Five characters are introduced: Socrates, Chaerephon, Gorgias, Polus, and Callicles. Of these, Socrates represents the intellectual and scientific faculty; Chaerephon represents right opinion; and Gorgias represents distorted opinion. Gorgias was not entirely defeated by injustice, but he was hesitant about whether he should be persuaded or not. Polus, however, represents injustice and those who are solely driven by ambition. Finally, Callicles represents a swinish nature <note>A "swinish nature" refers to a person driven entirely by base physical appetites and pleasures.</note>—one that is a lover of pleasure. 

Some people question why there are three orators but only two philosophers, and why the number of orators is "indivisible" <gloss>1</gloss> while the number of philosophers is "divisible." We argue, however, that this is not actually the case. Socrates represents the **monad** <gloss>2</gloss> <term>monad</term> <note>In Pythagorean and Neoplatonic philosophy, the "monad" refers to a fundamental, indivisible unit of unity.</note> looking toward the **One** (divinity). Divinity (or the One) is simple and produced from nothing else. Thus, the hymn to him says: "From whom all things emerge into light; but you alone do not exist for the sake of anything <gloss>3</gloss>." Chaerephon also represents a monad, but one that is material and inseparable from physical matter; Socrates, by contrast, represents the separate, pure monad. Because lower natures do not progress to higher ones (or higher to lower) without a middle ground, Chaerephon occupies a middle position. Consequently, it is his duty to transmit the qualities that the two extremes possess.

It now remains to ask why Plato mentions Gorgias. First, I say there is nothing strange about a writer recording unknown men and showing them in conversation with each other. Secondly, we know that Socrates and Gorgias were contemporaries. Socrates lived during the third year of the 77th Olympiad <note>Approximately 469 BCE.</note>, and Empedocles the Pythagorean, who was the teacher of Gorgias, lived at the same time. To this we may add that Gorgias wrote a treatise concerning Nature...

<gloss>2</gloss> The "monad" is the unified existence of a separated multitude, but "the One" is the very peak of that multitude.
<gloss>3</gloss> From whom all things emerge into light; but you alone do not exist for any other cause. <note>original: Εξ οὑ παντα πεφην'· συ δ' ουδενος ουνεκα μουνος.</note>

...inelegant <note>This fragment likely concludes a sentence from the previous page discussing a specific historical event or artistic performance.</note>, in the 84th Olympiad <note>An Olympiad is a period of four years; the 84th Olympiad began in 444 BCE.</note>; so that this was twenty-eight or a few more years before Socrates. Besides, Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, says that Socrates, when he was a very young man, met with Parmenides, who was then very advanced in years, and found him to be a most profound man. But Parmenides was the teacher <note>original: "preceptor"</note> of Empedocles, who was the teacher of Gorgias. And Gorgias lived to a great age; for, according to history, he died in the 109th year of his life. So, these two men lived at about the same time.

I shall only observe, in addition to what Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator on Plato.</note> has said, that Plato does not condemn all orators, but only those who strive to persuade their hearers to embrace whatever they please, whether it be good or bad, false or true—such as Lysias the Theban, Tisias, and Gorgias. But, in the *Phaedrus*, he prefers Pericles and Isocrates to all the other orators because they combined eloquence with philosophy. He also adds that a legitimate orator ought to understand the underlying reasons for things, the laws of morality <note>original: "manners"</note>, the power of words, and the different dispositions of men. He suggests that the orator should know how to compose words adapted, as much as possible, to the specific character <note>original: "genius"</note> of his hearers; and that he should not be so anxious that what he says may be pleasing to men, as he is that it may be acceptable to the Divine <note>original: "Divinity"</note>.

# THE GORGIAS

---

## *PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE*

| | | |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| CALLICLES | || | CHAEREPHON <note>original: "CHÆREPHO"</note> |
| SOCRATES | || | GORGIAS |

->And POLUS<-

---

### CALLICLES

In this way, Socrates, they say one should join a battle or a fight <note>Callicles is playfully using a proverb about arriving late to a conflict, implying Socrates has missed the main "action."</note>.

### SOCRATES

But have we, as the proverb goes, arrived after the festival? Are we late?

### CALLICLES

And a very elegant festival it was! For just a little while ago, Gorgias gave us a long and beautiful demonstration.

### SOCRATES

But Chaerephon here, Callicles, was the cause of our being so late; he forced us to spend our time in the marketplace <note>original: "forum"</note>.

### CHAEREPHON

It does not matter, Socrates. I can fix the problem, as Gorgias is a friend of mine. He will give us a demonstration whenever you like—either now or at some future time.

### CALLICLES

What is this, Chaerephon? Does Socrates really want to hear Gorgias?

### CHAEREPHON

That is exactly why we have come here.

### CALLICLES

Then come to my house whenever you like. Gorgias is staying with me and will perform for you whatever you wish to hear.

### SOCRATES

That is kind of you, Callicles. But would he be willing to talk with us now? I want to ask the man what the power of his art is, and what exactly it is that he claims to teach. As for the other things you mentioned, he can show us those some other time.

<meta>This page continues the opening dialogue of the *Gorgias*. Socrates and Chaerephon have just arrived at the home of Callicles to meet the famous orator Gorgias. Socrates has expressed his desire to understand the nature of Gorgias's art (rhetoric).</meta>

<page-num>351</page-num>

<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

**CALLICLES.** There is nothing like asking<sup>1</sup> him yourself, Socrates: for this is one of the things which he demonstrated. He just now promised everyone in the house that he would answer any question that might be asked of him.

**SOCRATES.** You certainly speak well. Ask him, therefore, Chaerephon <note>original: "Chærepho"</note>.

**CHAEREPHON.** What must I ask him?

**SOCRATES.** Ask him what he is.

**CHAEREPHON.** How do you mean?

---

<sup>1</sup> Rhetoric, says Olympiodorus <note>Olympiodorus the Younger (c. 495–570 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher known for his commentaries on Plato.</note>, is twofold; one being an art, and the other a skill. It is worth while, therefore, to inquire: for what reason is skill not considered an art? It is rightly observed in the *Phaedrus* that whoever intends to speak about anything should first define it, and afterwards teach it; for he who does not do this must necessarily go completely astray. For instance, in investigating whether the soul is immortal, we ought not immediately to show that it is immortal; but, prior to this, we should make a division and say that the soul is not one thing, but many things. For there is both a rational and irrational soul; and there is also a vegetative soul <note>original: "plantal soul"</note>—which is why we also say that plants "live." We say, then, that the rational soul is both immortal and not immortal. It is not immortal if we consider "immortal" to mean an existence that is eternal and unchanging <note>original: "subsistence perpetual and uniform"</note>; but it is immortal both in its essence and its activity <note>original: "energy"</note>.

Again, the definition of art is twofold. For art is a method proceeding in an orderly path in conjunction with imagination <note>original: "phantasy"</note>. Olympiodorus adds "in conjunction with imagination" in order to distinguish it from nature. For nature also proceeds in an orderly way, but without imagination. Again, art is a system of conclusions, practiced together toward a certain end that is beneficial to some of the purposes of life. According to the first definition, therefore, rhetoric (when falsely so-called) may be termed an art. For it proceeds in an orderly path: first, arranging the introduction <note>original: "proem"</note>; and afterwards the status or condition <note>original: "καταστασις" (katastasis)</note>, and what follows after this. But it is not an art according to the second definition, since this can only apply to true rhetoric, which explains the causes of what it asserts. Indeed, not only is false rhetoric called an art according to the first definition, but also *cookery* and *hairdressing*. For cooking is not the task of just any random person, but of one who possesses skill and proceeds in a specific way. In the same way, hairdressing involves a knowledge of ointments and knows how to style the hair. Therefore, the rhetoric which does not know how to explain the cause of what it asserts, but speaks on both sides—that is, both the true and the false—is not an art. For an art is that which has one good goal. But true rhetoric, which exists within a political context, is an art. For just as a rational physician knows how to cure an eye disease <note>original: "ophthalmy"</note>, so does the practitioner who relies only on experience <note>original: "empiric"</note>. But the former, who also acts according to art, can explain the causes of what he does, which the experiential practitioner cannot. Again, if someone should ask how art differs from science, since art also explains causes, we reply that science produces the knowledge of things whose existence is eternal and unchanging, but art produces the knowledge of things that are in flux. Shall we say, therefore, that the natural philosopher <note>original: "physiologist"</note> is not scientific because he investigates things that are material and in flux? By no means; for his investigation is not merely of material things, but he refers them to universal principles and explores the underlying reality <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> of universal physical natures. Thus, Plato condemns <note>original: "reprobates"</note> false rhetoric, not true rhetoric.

<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

**SOCRATES.** Just as, if he happened to be a craftsman of shoes, he would answer you that he was a shoemaker. Or do you not understand what I say?

**CHAEREPHON <note>original: "Chærepho"</note>.** I do; and I will ask him. Tell me, Gorgias, did Callicles here speak the truth when he said that you promised to answer whatever should be asked of you?

**GORGIAS.** He spoke the truth, Chaerephon: for I just now made this promise; and I say that no one has asked me anything new for many years.

**CHAEREPHON.** You will, therefore, answer easily, Gorgias.

**GORGIAS.** We shall put this to the test, Chaerephon.

**POLUS.** Do so, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>: but if you please, Chaerephon, talk with me instead. For Gorgias appears to me to be tired, as he has just now discussed many details.

**CHAEREPHON.** But what, Polus, do you think that you can answer better than Gorgias?

**POLUS.** What does it matter, as long as you are answered sufficiently?

**CHAEREPHON.** It is of no consequence; but, since you are willing, answer me.

**POLUS.** Ask.

**CHAEREPHON.** I ask you then: if Gorgias were knowledgeable in that art¹ in which his brother Herodicus is skilled, by what name might we justly call him? Might we not call him the same as his brother?

**POLUS.** Entirely so.

**CHAEREPHON.** Therefore, by calling him a physician, we would name him correctly?

**POLUS.** We would.

**CHAEREPHON.** But if he were skilled in 그 art in which Aristophon, the son of Aglaophon, is skilled—or his brother—what should we then rightly call him?

---

¹ There are two kinds of rhetoric, says Olympiodorus; but of these the categories <note>original: "genera"</note>, the goals, and the methods are different. For the category of true rhetoric is art; but that of false rhetoric is mere skill <note>term: "skill" (original: "experience" or "knack") refers to a practical ability gained by trial and error rather than a scientific understanding of principles.</note>. Again, the goal of the true is the good; but the goal of the false is persuasion, regardless of whether the thing one is persuaded to do is good or bad. And again, the method of the true is to know the powers of the soul; but the method of the false is not to know them. Systematic <note>original: "Doctrinal"</note> faith is also the method of the true; but "credible" faith <note>note: faith based on what seems plausible rather than what is proven</note> is that of the false. For the geometrician wishes to persuade, but in a demonstrative way, and not from mere plausibility, as the rhetorician does. Therefore, just as the medical art promotes health through different remedies, so different types of rhetoric proceed through different forms. Just as a knife is not of itself either good or bad, but is beneficial or the contrary to the person who uses it; so rhetoric is not of itself beautiful, but is beneficial to the person who uses it.

**POLUS.** Evidently, a painter.

**CHAEREPHON <note>original: "Chærepho"</note>.** But now, since he is skilled in a certain art, what can we properly call him?

<margin>¹ Experience <note>original: "πείρα" (peira)</note>, says Olympiodorus, differs from skill <note>original: "εμπειρία" (empeiria)</note>. For skill is asserted of actions, but experience refers to artificial things in a partial way. And again, experience is concerned with specific things, but skill with things that are more universal. Skill, therefore, does not produce art if skill deals with subordinate things; for, if it did, superior natures would be produced from inferior ones. But it may be asked, "Do we not arrive at skill from experience, and at art from skill?" We reply that experience, indeed, contributes to skill, and skill to art; but they are not the producing causes. This, however, takes place because we possess the cognitive principles <note>original: "gnoſtic reaſons"</note> of things and are stimulated by sensory objects. Therefore, just as he who makes sparks appear that have long been hidden in ashes is not said to have created light, but to have made it manifest; and in the same way, he who cures an eye of an inflammation <note>original: "ophthalmy"</note> does not produce light, but contributes to its presence in the eye: so the principles within us require something that may cause us to remember <note>original: "recollect"</note>. For we are like a sleeping geometer <note>original: "geometrician"</note>. Thus, skill is not the effective cause.</margin>

**POLUS.** O Chaerephon! There are many arts among men which are skillfully discovered through experience¹. For experience causes our life to proceed according to art, but lack of experience according to chance <note>original: "fortune"</note>. **GORG.** I will give you a specimen; and such a one that you will say you never heard a shorter discourse.

**GORG.** It is.

**SOC.** And is not music, therefore, concerned with the production of melodies?

**GORG.** Yes.

**GORG.** Undoubtedly.

**GORG.** It is.

**SOC.** And, indeed, other arts, Gorgias, will function <note>original: "subsist"</note> in this same manner. For each of them will be concerned with the speech that is used regarding the particular subject of which each is the art.

**GORG.** It appears so.

**SOC.** Why, then, do you not call these other arts "rhetorical," since they are concerned with speech, and yet you call this specific art which deals with speech, "rhetoric"?

**GORG.** Because, Socrates, the knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> of all other arts is concerned, as I might say, with manual work and similar activities. However, no part of the rhetorical art is manual, since all its action and authority exist through speech <note>original: "discourses"; from the Greek *logoi*</note>. **GORG.** Yes.

**SOC.** I think that, regarding all the arts, some are primarily focused on action and require very little speech. **GORG.** You understand my meaning very well, Socrates.

**GORG.** You are right, Socrates, and you understand me perfectly.

<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

**GORG.** I have heard it; but why do you say this?
**SOC.** Because those craftsmen <note>original: "artificers"</note> will immediately present themselves to you, who are celebrated by the author of this song; namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the physician,

were sung at entertainments, and were called <term>scolia</term> <note>original: "σκολια"</note>. They mostly consisted of short verses and were sung by the few guests who were most skilled in music. These *scolia* were primarily used by the Athenians, though they were known throughout Greece, where several famous writers of *scolia* lived, such as Anacreon of Teos, Alcaeus of Lesbos, Praxilla of Sicyon, and others. Their subjects <note>original: "arguments"</note> were varied; some were humorous and satirical, others romantic, and many were serious. Serious ones often contained a practical moral lesson <note>original: "sentence"</note> or advice, like the one Plato cites here. At other times, they praised the famous deeds of great men.

I believe all lovers of antiquity will appreciate this additional information from the manuscript annotations <note>original: "Scholia"</note> of Olympiodorus on this dialogue, as it is not found in any other writer.

Olympiodorus notes that Plato allowed music in his *Republic*—not popular music, but the kind that refines the soul. He adds the following: "The ancients especially used music at their banquets, since banquets excite the passions. A choir was formed. If they danced from the left side to the right, this was called a *progression* (<term>proodos</term> <note>original: "προοδος"</note>). If they moved to the left, it was an *epode* (<term>epodos</term> <note>original: "εποδος"</note>). If they moved to the middle, it was called a *mesodos* (<term>mesodos</term> <note>original: "μεσοδος"</note>). Again, if they turned backward toward the right, it was called a *strophe* (<term>strophe</term> <note>original: "στροφη"</note>). To the middle was again a *mesodos* (<term>mesodos</term> <note>original: "μεσοδος"</note>). Toward the far left, it was an *antistrophe* (<term>antistrophe</term> <note>original: "αντιστροφη"</note>). Stesichorus also mentions these. These movements were symbolic, imitating the motions of the heavens. For motion from left to right is western, while motion from right to left is eastern. Similarly, those who began the song, those in the middle, and those who finished the dance secretly represented the Earth. The Earth is a *beginning* because it is the center; it is a *middle* because of its position; and it is an *end* as the sediment <note>original: "dregs"</note> of the universe. When the music paused, they used branches of myrtle. One person would take it and sing, but instead of passing it to the person next to them, they passed it to the person opposite. Then that person passed it back to the first, and then to the second, and this back-and-forth passing was called *scolia* <note>The word implies "crooked" or "winding"</note>. This is why this part is called a *scolion*." 

<note>original Greek: Μαλιστα τοινυν εν τοις συμποσιοις μουσικη εκεχρηντο· επειδη τα συμποσια διατεινει εις παθος κινησα· χορος ουν εγενετο... (The Greek text provided is the source for the preceding English translation of Olympiodorus’s commentary on banquets, choral movements, and the passing of the myrtle branch.)</note>

Information similar to the above may be found in the Greek annotations on Hephaestion, but it is by no means as complete.

<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

...gymnastics instructors, and those who train men to fight with weapons. Instead, I believe we should blame those who do not use these skills properly. 

The same may be said of the rhetorical art. A rhetorician <note>original: "rhetorician"; a professional speaker or teacher of persuasion</note> is able to speak against all men and about every subject. In short, he can persuade the crowd regarding whatever he pleases more effectively than any other person. Nevertheless, we should not think less of physicians or other professionals <note>original: "artificers"; skilled craftsmen or practitioners of a trade</note> just because rhetoricians have this power. The art of rhetoric, like the arts of combat, should be used justly. In my opinion, if someone becomes a rhetorician and then acts unjustly using this power and skill, it is not right to hate the teacher or expel them from the city. The teacher imparted that knowledge for just purposes, but the student applied it to the opposite. It is only fair, therefore, to hate, banish, and punish <note>original: "flay"; literally to strip the skin off, used here as a metaphor for severe punishment or public shaming</note> the one who misuses rhetoric, rather than the one who taught it.

**Soc.** I think, Gorgias, that you are experienced in many debates. You have likely noticed that it is difficult for people to end a discussion on the topics they are trying to debate by simply defining terms, learning from one another, and teaching themselves. Instead, if they disagree about something, and one says the other is not speaking correctly or clearly, they become resentful. They think the criticism is spoken out of spite and a desire for victory, rather than from a genuine interest in examining the topic of the discussion. Some, indeed, leave in a shameful manner after they have insulted others—saying and hearing such things about one another that the audience feels disgusted for even stooping to listen to such men. 

But why am I saying all this? Because you now appear to me to be saying something that is not entirely consistent with what you first said regarding the art of rhetoric. I am afraid, therefore, to refute you, lest you should think that I am not speaking out of a passionate desire to find the truth of the matter...

**SOC.** Will you understand me once I have answered? For rhetoric, according to my doctrine, is an image <note>original: "eidolon" or a phantom/likeness</note> of a part of politics.

**GORG.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Socrates, I do not even understand what you are saying myself.

**SOC.** That is likely, Gorgias, for I have not yet spoken clearly. But Polus here is young and sharp <note>original: "acute"</note>.

**GORG.** Never mind him; inform me how it is you say that rhetoric is an image of a part of politics.

**GORG.** Undoubtedly.

**GORG.** I do.

**GORG.** You speak the truth.

**SOC.** I say that this kind of thing happens to both the body and the soul. It causes both the body and the soul to appear to be in a good condition, when at the same time they are not.

**GORG.** These things do take place.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 373. Socrates is elaborating on his theory that rhetoric is not a true "art" but a form of "adulation" (flattery). He has just introduced the idea that there are arts for the body and arts for the soul. Catchword from previous page: "justice."</meta>

<page-num>374</page-num>
<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

...medicine. But within the art of politics, I establish legislation as the counterpart to physical training <note>original: "gymnastic"</note>, and justice as the counterpart to medicine. These pairs communicate with each other because they deal with the same subjects: medicine connects with physical training, and justice connects with legislation. However, they still differ from one another in certain respects. 

Since there are these four arts that always provide remedies while seeking what is best—one pair curing the body and the other curing the soul—the power of adulation <note>original: "adulatory power"; the practice of flattery or telling people what they want to hear to gain favor</note> perceives this. I do not say it "knows" this, but rather it guesses it. By dividing itself into four parts and slipping under each of the true arts, it pretends to be the art it has mimicked. It is not at all concerned with what is actually best; instead, it always uses what is pleasant to hunt after foolish people and deceive them, making itself appear to be of great value. 

Cookery, therefore, hides under the guise of medicine and pretends that it knows the best food <note>original: "aliment"</note> for the body. If a cook and a physician were to compete before children—or before men as foolish as children—to decide which of them truly understood good and bad nutrition, the physician would starve to death <note>original: "die through hunger"</note>. This is what I call adulation; and I say, Polus, that such a thing is base <note>original: "base"; meaning morally low, shameful, or lacking in virtue</note>. I say this to you because it focuses on what is pleasant without any regard for what is best. 

Furthermore, I do not call it an art, but rather a "knack" or a skill, because it lacks a rational basis <note>original: "no reason"</note> by which it can show the true nature of the things it introduces. Therefore, it is unable to explain the cause of each thing it does. I refuse to call any irrational thing an "art." If you have any doubts about these things, I am willing to explain my reasoning to you. 

The flattery found in cookery is, as I have said, hidden under medicine. In the same way, the deceptive art of cosmetics <note>original: "the allurements of outward form"</note> is hidden under physical training. This practice of cosmetics is harmful, deceptive, ignoble, and unrefined <note>original: "illiberal"</note>. It deceives people through artificial shapes and colors, by smoothing the skin and appealing to the senses, causing people to chase after a borrowed beauty while neglecting their own natural health, which is achieved through physical training. 

So that I may not be long-winded <note>original: "prolix"</note>, I wish to explain it to you in the manner of geometricians (for perhaps you can follow me now): the art of cosmetics is to physical training as cookery is to medicine. Or rather, it is like this: the art of cosmetics is to physical training as sophistry <note>original: "the sophistic"</note> is to legislation; and cookery is to medicine as rhetoric is to justice.

# THE GORGIAS.

To whom does the government which he now possesses belong? He was born of a woman who was the slave of Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas. According to justice, Archelaus was himself the slave of Alcetas, and, if he had been willing to act justly, he would have served Alcetas as a slave; according to your doctrine, he would have been happy. But now, by committing the greatest crimes, he has become miserable to a wonderful degree. 

For, in the first place, he sent for his master and uncle, as if he intended to restore the government which Perdiccas had taken from him. After entertaining them and getting both him and his son Alexander—who was Archelaus's uncle and nearly his equal in age—drunk, he threw them into a cart. Causing them to be taken away by night, he murdered both of them by cutting their throats. And though he has committed these crimes, he is ignorant that he has become most miserable, and he does not repent of his conduct. 

Shortly after, he was unwilling to care for and restore the government to his brother, the legitimate son of Perdiccas, a boy of about seven years of age who had a just right to the throne. By doing so, he would have been happy. Instead, throwing the youth into a well and suffocating him there, he told the boy's mother, Cleopatra, that he fell into the well and died while chasing a goose. This man, therefore, having acted more unjustly than anyone else in Macedonia, is the most miserable—not the most blessed—of all the Macedonians. And perhaps every one of the Athenians, starting with you, would rather be any other Macedonian than Archelaus.

**Soc.** At the beginning of our conference, Polus, I praised you because you appeared to me to be well-instructed in rhetoric, but to have neglected the art of discourse <note>original: "art of discourse"; referring to dialectic, or the philosophical method of seeking truth through question and answer rather than persuasive speech</note>. And now, without providing any further proof, this is the kind of speech by which even a boy might "convince" me. In your view, I am now proven wrong by this story for having said that he who acts unjustly is not happy. But how is that so, my good man? For indeed, I did not grant you any of the details which you mention.

**Pol.** You are simply unwilling to admit them. For the matter appears to you exactly as I say.

**Soc.** My dear friend! You are attempting to refute <note>original: "confute"; to prove an argument wrong</note> me in a rhetorical manner, like those who are thought to refute others in courts of justice. For there, some appear to defeat others when they produce many respected witnesses for what they say; but the one who opposes them might only produce one single witness...

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the one who is acted upon experiences exactly what the person performing the action produces. <note>original: "A passion, therefore, of such a kind is in that which is struck, as the striker produces." In this context, "passion" refers to the passive state of being acted upon.</note>
**POLUS:** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES:** If, therefore, anyone burns something, is it not necessary that something should be burned?
**POLUS:** Undoubtedly.

**POLUS:** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES:** And will not the same reasoning apply if anyone cuts? For something will be cut.
**POLUS:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** And if the cut is large or deep, or causes pain, will the thing being cut not be cut with the same kind of wound that the cutter makes?
**POLUS:** It appears so.

**POLUS:** I do grant it.

**POLUS:** Necessarily, Socrates, it is to suffer something.
**SOCRATES:** Must it not, therefore, be caused by some <term>agent</term>?
**POLUS:** Undoubtedly. It is caused by the one who punishes.
**SOCRATES:** But does the person who punishes correctly not punish justly?
**POLUS:** Yes.
**SOCRATES:** Does he act justly, or not, by doing so?
**POLUS:** Justly.
**SOCRATES:** Must it not follow, then, that the person who is punished—as a consequence of that punishment—suffers justly?
**POLUS:** It appears so.
**SOCRATES:** But is it not acknowledged that all just things are beautiful? <note>original: "beautiful" translates the Greek *kalon*, which denotes moral excellence, nobility, or being "fine."</note>
**POLUS:** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES:** Of these two, therefore, the one performs the action, and the other (the one who is punished) experiences that which is beautiful.
**POLUS:** Yes.

**POLUS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** But what is that skill which frees one from disease? Is it not medicine <note>original: "the medicinal"</note>?

**POLUS:** Necessarily so.

**SOCRATES:** And what is it that frees one from corruption and injustice? If you cannot answer this question with the same ease <note>original: "facility"</note>, consider it this way: where, and to whom, do we take those who are sick in body?

**POLUS:** To physicians, Socrates.

<summary>Socrates argues that because injustice is the most shameful human condition but not the most physically painful, it must be the most harmful, making it the greatest of all evils. He then begins an analogy to identify the "medicine" for a corrupt soul.</summary>

# THE GORGIAS.

**SOCRATES:** But where do we take those who act unjustly and live without self-control <note>original: "intemperately"</note>?

**POLUS:** As you say, to the judges.

**SOCRATES:** And is it not, therefore, so that they may be punished?

**POLUS:** I agree.

**SOCRATES:** Don’t those who punish correctly, then, do so by applying a form of justice?

**POLUS:** It is clear that they do.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the skill <term>art</term> <note>In this context, "art" refers to a systematic craft or branch of knowledge.</note> that acquires money frees someone from poverty; the medical skill <note>original: "medicinal art"</note> frees someone from disease; and punishment frees someone from lack of self-control and injustice.

**POLUS:** So it appears.

**SOCRATES:** Which of these, then, do you consider to be the most beautiful <note>The Greek term used here, *kalon*, implies both aesthetic beauty and moral excellence or nobility.</note>?

**POLUS:** Which things are you asking about?

**SOCRATES:** Making money, the medical skill, and punishment.

**POLUS:** Punishment, Socrates, is far superior.

**SOCRATES:** Since it is the most beautiful, does it not then also produce either great pleasure, or a benefit <note>original: "advantage"</note>, or both?

**POLUS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** Is it, then, pleasant to be treated by a doctor? And do those who are being cured enjoy it?

**POLUS:** I do not think they do.

**SOCRATES:** But it is beneficial to be cured, is it not?

**POLUS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** Because it frees one from a great evil; therefore, it is beneficial to endure the pain in order to become healthy.

**POLUS:** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES:** In that case, is the person who is cured by a doctor the happiest regarding their body, or should that be said of the person who has never been sick at all?

**POLUS:** Clearly, it is the one who has never been sick.

**SOCRATES:** For, as it seems, being freed from a disease is not true happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>; rather, happiness consists in never having had the disease in the first place.

**POLUS:** That is true.

<summary>Socrates argues that while punishment is a beneficial "medicine" for an unjust soul, true happiness belongs to the person who never commits injustice at all, rather than the one who is punished and "cured" of it.</summary>

**SOCRATES:** But what about this? Which of these two men is more miserable: he who has a diseased body, or he who has a diseased soul?

**POLUS:** He who has a diseased soul.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not, then, the man who is cured by a doctor and freed from disease, or he who is not cured and remains sick?

**POLUS:** He who is not cured, it seems to me.

**SOCRATES:** Does it not follow, then, that suffering punishment is a release from the greatest of all evils—wickedness <note>original: "depravity"</note>?

**POLUS:** It does.

**SOCRATES:** For punishment produces a sound mind, makes men more just, and acts as the medicine for wickedness <note>original: "depravity"</note>.

**POLUS:** It does.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, he is happiest who has no vice in his soul, since vice appears to be the greatest of evils.

**POLUS:** That is evident.

**SOCRATES:** But undoubtedly, he ranks in the second level of happiness <term>felicity</term> <note>original: "felicity"; refers here to a state of blessedness or intense happiness.</note> who is freed from vice.

**POLUS:** It is likely.

**SOCRATES:** And this is the person who is cautioned, corrected <note>original: "reproved"</note>, and who suffers punishment.

**POLUS:** He is.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, he lives in the worst possible way who is full of injustice and is never freed from it.

**POLUS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** Isn't this exactly the kind of man who, having committed the greatest wrongs and practiced the most extreme injustice, manages to ensure that he is never corrected, restrained in his behavior, nor punished? This is just like you said of Archelaus <note>Archelaus I was a King of Macedon whom Polus previously cited as a "happy" man despite his many crimes; Socrates is now refuting this.</note>, and other tyrants, public speakers <term>rhetoricians</term>, and powerful noblemen.

**POLUS:** It seems so.

**SOCRATES:** For the behavior of these men, my dear friend <note>original: "O best of men"</note>, is almost exactly like someone afflicted with the most serious diseases who prevents doctors from treating <note>original: "inflicting on him the punishment of"</note> his bodily ailments. He fears being burned <note>Referring to cauterization, a common ancient medical practice.</note> or cut <note>Referring to surgery.</note> like a child, because these procedures are painful. Or does it not appear so to you?

**POLUS:** It does.

**SOCRATES:** And this is because he is ignorant, it seems, of the nature of health and the excellence of a healthy body. Based on what we have agreed, it seems those who escape punishment also do something similar, Polus. They look only at the painful nature of it, but are blind to its benefits. They are ignorant of how much more miserable it is to live with a soul that is not healthy, but is instead corrupt, unjust, and unholy, than it is to live with a diseased body.

He should be the first to accuse himself and all his close friends <note>original: "familiars"</note>, sparing neither himself nor them, but using rhetoric for this very purpose: so that by making the crimes known <note>original: "manifest"</note>, they may be freed from the greatest of evils, injustice. **POLUS:** This must indeed be the case.

--- Page 2348 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page where Callicles begins his famous "might makes right" rebuttal to Socrates. Callicles argues that Socrates has merely played a verbal trick on the previous speaker, Polus, by confusing social convention with natural law.</meta>

<page-num>399</page-num>
<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

Indeed, I do not praise Polus for granting you that doing an injury is more shameful than suffering one. Because of this concession, he was blocked by you in his argument and had nothing left to say, since he was ashamed to say what he really thought. For in reality, Socrates, you lead the discussion toward these troublesome and popular claims while you pretend to be searching for the truth—claims that are not noble by nature, but only by law. For the most part, nature and law are contrary to each other. Therefore, if anyone is ashamed and does not dare to say what he thinks, he is forced to contradict himself. 

But you, seeing through this subtle trick, act dishonestly in your discussions. For if someone claims that things according to law are also according to nature, you privately ask if natural things belong to law. In this current dispute about doing injury and being injured, when Polus spoke of what is more shameful according to nature, you followed what is more shameful according to law. By nature, everything that is worse—such as being injured—is also more shameful. But by law, it is worse to do an injury. 

For to suffer injury is not the experience of a man, but of some slave for whom death is better than life—someone who, when injured and disgraced, is unable to defend himself or anyone else under his care. But I believe that those who establish the laws are the weak men <note>original: "imbecil," which in this context refers to a lack of physical or political power rather than a lack of intelligence</note> and the masses. Therefore, they establish laws with an eye toward themselves and their own advantage, and they distribute praise and blame with the same goal. They also terrify the more powerful men—those who are capable of possessing more than others—by claiming that wanting to surpass others in possessions is shameful and unjust. They say that trying to have more than others is to "act unjustly." 

In my opinion, these weak men are satisfied with having an equal share because they are of an inferior nature. Thus, to try to possess more than the masses is, according to law, unjust and shameful; and they call this "committing an injury." But I believe nature herself shows that the better man should possess more than the worse, and the more powerful more than the weak. She demonstrates in many places—among other animals and in entire cities and families of men—that justice should be established so that the superior rule over and possess more than the inferior. For by what kind of justice did Xerxes <note>Xerxes I, the King of Persia who led a massive invasion of Greece in 480 BCE</note> wage war against Greece? Or his father <note>Darius the Great</note> against the Scythians? Or the ten thousand other examples of this kind that might be adduced? <note>original catchword: "adduced ?"</note>

<summary>Callicles argues that Socrates' idea of justice is a mere social construct created by the weak to restrain the strong, asserting that "natural justice" allows the superior to rule and possess more than the inferior.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Callicles' argument from the previous page, where he contends that social laws are merely conventions created by the weak to restrain the strong. He is now transitioning to his argument that "natural justice" dictates that the superior should rule the inferior.</meta>

...brought forward? <note>original: "adduced"</note> But I think that they do these things according to the nature of justice, and indeed—by Jupiter—according to the law of nature. This is perhaps not according to that law which we establish when we shape the best and strongest of our fellow-citizens—taking them from their childhood like young lions and enslaving them with spells and charms. Meanwhile, we claim that equality should be preferred and that this is what is honorable and just.

Trampling underfoot our written codes, magical tricks, charms, and laws that go against nature, he would rise up and reveal himself as our master instead of our slave; and in that case, natural justice would shine out. It appears to me that Pindar also proves the truth of what I assert in the verses where he says that "Law is the king of all mortals and immortals," and that law "carries out what is most just through violence and with a mighty hand." He adds, "I infer this from the deeds of Hercules, who drove away the oxen of Geryon without paying for them." ¹ He says something very close to that, for I do not remember the verses perfectly. 

He says, then, that Hercules drove away the cattle of Geryon <note>In Greek mythology, the tenth labor of Hercules was to steal the cattle of the triple-bodied giant Geryon</note> without having either purchased them or received them as a gift—as if it were naturally just for the property of the weaker and inferior to belong to the better and more excellent. Such, then, is the truth of the matter. You will realize this is so if, setting aside philosophy, you turn your attention to more important things. 

For philosophy, Socrates, is a charming <note>original: "elegant"</note> thing if one dabbles in it moderately while young. But if one spends more time on it than is appropriate, it ruins the man. Even if a man has a naturally good character but continues to philosophize late into life, he will inevitably lack the skills a man needs if he wants to be honorable, successful, and famous. For such men are ignorant of the laws of the city and of the types of arguments one must use when dealing with human contracts, both in public and private life. They are also completely inexperienced in human pleasures and desires—in short, they do not understand the ways of men. Therefore, when they engage in any private or political undertaking, they make themselves look ridiculous. Just as, in my opi—

<meta>This page continues Callicles’ speech to Socrates. Callicles argues that while philosophy is a useful part of a young man’s education, it becomes embarrassing and even dangerous for a grown man, as it prevents him from participating in public life and achieving political greatness.</meta>

<page-num>401</page-num>
<header>THE GORGIAS</header>

...opinion <note>original: "nion," continuing from "excellent" on the previous page</note>, politicians are ridiculous when they meddle with your disputations and arguments. For that saying of Euripides applies here: “Each person shines in this pursuit and hastens toward it, spending the greater part of the day so that he may excel himself <gloss>¹</gloss>.” But whatever a man is inferior at, he avoids and slanders; while he praises that in which he excels out of self-love, thinking that in this way he is praising himself. 

But I believe it is most right to participate in both of these. It is certainly fine to participate in philosophy for the sake of education, and it is not shameful for someone to philosophize while they are young. But it is a ridiculous thing, Socrates, for a man to still be philosophizing when he is advanced in years. I feel the same way about those who philosophize as I do about those who stammer and play. When I see a boy—for whom it is still appropriate to speak this way—stammering and engaged in play, I am pleased. His conduct appears elegant and noble <note>original: "liberal," meaning befitting a free-born citizen</note>, and proper for the age of a child. But when I hear a small child speaking with perfect clarity, it seems unpleasant to me; it offends my ears and strikes me as unbefitting a free person. 

Conversely, when someone hears a grown man stammering or sees him engaged in play, the man appears ridiculous, unmanly, and deserving of punishment. I feel exactly the same way about those who continue to philosophize. When I see philosophy in a young man, I am delighted; it appears becoming, and I consider that young man to be noble. But when I find a youth who does not philosophize, he appears to me to be base <note>original: "illiberal"</note>, as one who will never think himself worthy of any beautiful or generous thing. 

However, when I behold a man advanced in years still philosophizing and not yet freed from philosophy, such a person, Socrates, appears to me to require punishment. For this man—as I just said—inevitably becomes effeminate, even if he was born with the best disposition. This happens because he avoids the heart of the city and the marketplace <note>original: "forum"</note> where, as the poet says, men become truly famous. Instead, concealing himself from public view, he passes the remainder of his life whispering in a corner with three or four boys; he never utters anything noble, great, or significant. Now, Socrates, I feel quite fairly and friendly toward you. It seems that the same thing is now happening to me...

However, I will tell you frankly what is truly noble and just according to nature: anyone who intends to live properly should allow their desires to grow as large as possible and never restrain them. Instead, they should be prepared to serve these great desires through courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note> and intelligence <note>original: "prudence"</note>, always satisfying them with whatever they require. 

I realize, however, that this is not possible for the masses. This is why they criticize people like those I have mentioned—they hide their own weakness behind a mask of shame. They claim that lack of restraint <note>original: "intemperance"</note> is shameful because it makes men of a superior nature feel like slaves. Because they are unable to satisfy their own pleasures, they praise temperance and justice out of their own laziness. 

In reality, what could be more shameful or harmful than temperance for men who were born the sons of kings, or who are naturally capable of seizing power as a tyrant or a ruler <note>original: "dynasty," meaning a powerful political faction or narrow oligarchy</note>? Why would such men, who have the right to enjoy every good thing without any obstacle, choose to impose a master upon themselves—specifically, the law, the opinions of others, and the criticism of the masses? How could they not be miserable under the supposed "beauty" of justice and temperance? After all, these virtues would force them to give no more to their friends than to their enemies, even while they hold supreme authority in their own city. 

But the truth is, Socrates—the truth you claim to pursue—is this: luxury, lack of restraint, and total liberty, when backed by the right resources, are what constitute true virtue and happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>. Everything else—these social refinements, these agreements made against nature—are nothing but human trifles <note>original: "nugacities"</note> and are completely worthless.

**SOC.** You are attacking this argument in a very bold way, Callicles. You are openly saying what others certainly think but are afraid to say. ---

<note>
<sup>1</sup> *Euripides* (in his play *Phrixus*) says that to live is to die, and to die is to live. When the soul comes here, just as she gives life to the body, she also shares in a certain loss of life; but this is an evil. Therefore, when separated from the body, she truly lives. She "dies" here because she participates in a lack of life, as the body becomes the cause of evils. For this reason, it is necessary to master the body.

The meaning of the Pythagorean <note>original: "Pythagoric"</note> fable introduced here by Plato is as follows: We are said to be dead because, as noted before, we share in a lack of true life. The tomb which we carry around with us is the body, as Plato himself explains. "Hades" refers to the "unseen" <note>original: "unapparent"</note>, because we are situated in darkness, with the soul being in a state of slavery to the body. The jars <note>original: "tubs"</note> are the desires, named either because we hurry to fill them as if they were jars, or because desire persuades us that it is beautiful. 

The "initiated"—those who have perfect knowledge—pour into a solid jar, for their jars are full; in other words, they possess perfect virtue. But the "uninitiated"—those who possess nothing perfect—have jars full of holes <note>original: "perforated"</note>. Those who are slaves to desire always wish to fill it and become more inflamed; for this reason, they have leaky jars that are never full. The "sieve" represents the rational soul mixed with the irrational soul. The soul is called a "circle" because it seeks itself and is sought by itself; it finds itself and is found by itself. However, the irrational soul imitates a straight line, since it does not turn back on itself like a circle. Therefore, by using the image of a sieve, Plato signifies the rational soul in subjection to the irrational soul. The water is the flow of nature; for, as *Heraclitus* says, "moisture is the death of the soul."
</note>

In the same way, he called those who are stupid or lacking in intellect "uninitiated." He further said that the undisciplined and leaky nature of that part of the soul where the desires are located was like a leaky jar <note>original: "pierced tub"</note>, because of its insatiable greed. But this man, Callicles, showed—directly contrary to your view—that among those in the underworld <note>original: "Hades," which the text notes comes from the Greek word *aeides*, meaning "the invisible"</note>, the most miserable were these "uninitiated" ones. The sieve, therefore, as my source told me, represents the soul. He compared the soul of the foolish to a sieve because, just as a sieve is full of holes, their soul is unable to hold anything due to their lack of faith <note>original: "incredulity"</note> and their forgetfulness. These claims might indeed be considered quite strange in some respects, but they illustrate what I want to show you. I wish I could persuade you to change your opinion: that instead of choosing a life of insatiable and undisciplined greed, you would choose a life of moderation—one that is satisfied and abundantly filled with what is already present. 

But can I persuade you at all? Will you change your mind and say that the moderate are happier than the undisciplined? Or will I fail to persuade you, and will you refuse to change your opinion even if I tell you many more stories <note>original: "fables"</note> of this kind?

**CAL.** You have spoken more truly now, Socrates.

**SOC.** But come, I will show you another image from the same school of thought <note>original: "gymnasium"</note> as the one I just showed you. Consider whether you would speak in this way concerning the life of a temperate man versus an undisciplined man. Imagine two men who each have many jars <note>original: "tubs"</note>. The jars belonging to one of them are intact and full—one with wine, another with honey, a third with milk, and many others filled with various other things. Each of these liquids is rare and difficult to obtain, procured only with great labor and difficulty. 

Suppose, then, that this man whose jars are full no longer needs to draw any liquid or worry about them; as far as they are concerned, he is at rest. Now imagine the other man. He can also procure these liquids, though with difficulty, but his vessels are leaky and broken. He is compelled to fill them constantly, both day and night; if he does not, he suffers the most extreme pain. Since this is how each of them lives, will you still say that the life of the undisciplined man is happier than that...

**CAL.** They are certainly different, O most wise man.

**SOC.** Is courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note> also different from pleasure?

**CAL.** Undoubtedly.

**SOC.** Come, then, let us remember these points: that Callicles of Acharnae <note>An ancient district, or "deme," of Athens.</note> said that the pleasant and the good are the same, but that knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> and courage are both different from each other and from the good; and that Socrates of Alopeke <note>The Athenian district where Socrates was from.</note> did not agree with these things. Or did he agree with them?

**CAL.** He did not agree.

**SOC.** But I think that Callicles will not agree with himself either, once he looks at himself correctly. For tell me, do you not think that those who are doing well are in an entirely opposite state to those who are doing poorly?

**CAL.** I do.

**SOC.** If these states are opposites, then, must they not necessarily exist in the same way as health and disease? For, certainly, a person is not healthy and diseased at the same time, nor is he freed from both health and disease at the same time.

**CAL.** What do you mean?

**SOC.** Take any part of the body you like—for instance, the eyes. Consider whether a man can suffer from an eye disease <note>original: "ophthalmy"</note>.

**CAL.** Undoubtedly.

**SOC.** He certainly is not healthy if his eyes are diseased at the same time.

**CAL.** By no means.

**SOC.** But what then? When he is cured of the eye disease, is he then also robbed of the health of his eyes? Finally, is he freed from both at the same time?

**CAL.** Not in the least.

**SOC.** For I think that would be remarkable <note>original: "wonderful"</note> and absurd. Would it not?

**CAL.** Very much so.

**SOC.** Instead, I think he will gain one and lose the other in turn.

**CAL.** I agree.

**SOC.** And will he not, therefore, gain and lose strength and weakness in a similar way?

**CAL.** Yes.

**SOC.** And speed and slowness?

I mean, should we adopt the life you urge upon me—engaging in "manly" pursuits like public speaking, practicing rhetoric, and managing politics in the way you do? Or should we dedicate ourselves to a life of philosophy, and examine how it differs from that other way of life? Perhaps, then, as I just said, it is best to make a distinction between them; and once we have defined the two and agreed...

# THE GORGIAS.

...agreed with each other to consider, if these two ways <note>original: "species"</note> of life exist, how they differ from each other and which of them ought to be pursued. But perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying.

**Cal.** I do not.

**Soc.** Then I will speak to you even more clearly. **Cal.** I do agree.

**Soc.** Then come, agree with me on what I said to these men earlier, if I seemed to you then to be speaking the truth. I said that cooking did not appear to me to be an art, but a mere skill <note>original: "skill"; Socrates uses the term *empeiria*, meaning a "knack" or "routine" derived from experience rather than a systematic science or *techne*.</note>; and I said that medicine is an art. For I said that medicine considers the nature of what it cures and the causes of the things it does, and it is able to give a rational account of each of these. But I said that cooking proceeds toward pleasure in a totally unscientific <note>original: "inartifically"</note> way, focusing all its attention there. It does not consider in any respect the nature or the cause of pleasure, but is entirely irrational. It calculates nothing, so to speak, but depends wholly on habit and skill, merely preserving the memory of what usually happens, by which it is able to provide pleasures.

In the first place, then, consider whether you think these things have been sufficiently explained, and whether there are also certain other practices of this kind regarding the soul. Do some of these depend on art and pay careful attention to what is best for the soul, while others neglect this—just as cooking does with the body—and focus only on the soul’s pleasure and how it may be obtained? Do these practices fail to consider which pleasures are better or worse, attending to nothing else but gratification alone, regardless of whether it is beneficial or harmful? 

To me, Callicles, it appears that such things do exist; and I say that a thing of this kind is "flattery," whether it concerns the body, the soul, or anything else where pleasure is diligently pursued without any regard for what is better or worse. But do you hold the same opinion as we do regarding these things, or do you oppose them?

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between "arts," which are based on a rational understanding of nature and causes (like medicine), and "knacks" or "skills," which merely seek to provide pleasure through experience (like cooking). He argues that practices that aim only at the soul's pleasure without considering its well-being are forms of "flattery."</summary>

You assert that I can neither help myself, nor any of my friends or family, nor save myself from the greatest dangers. Instead, you say I am at the mercy <note>original: "obnoxious"; in this older sense, it means being liable to or vulnerable to someone else's power.</note> of anyone’s arbitrary will, like those who have lost their legal rights. You suggest—with what I'll call the youthful passion of your argument—that I might be struck in the face, stripped of my property, expelled from the city, or even killed, which you call the ultimate injustice. And according to your doctrine, to be in such a situation is the most shameful of all things. 

But according to my doctrine (which has indeed been often mentioned, yet there is no reason why it shouldn't be repeated), I do not say, Callicles, that being struck in the face unjustly is the most shameful thing. Nor is it most shameful for my body to be wounded or my purse to be cut <note>original: "purse... to be cut"; a reference to "cutpurses" or thieves who would slash a bag hanging from a belt to steal money.</note>. Instead, I say that to strike and wound me and my family unjustly is a thing more shameful and worse. I maintain that to defraud, enslave, break into a house, and, in short, to injure me and my property in any way, is more shameful and dishonorable for the person who does the injury than for me, the one who is injured. Or will he avoid being injured only if he has acquired the power of not being injured?

**CAL.** It is evident that he will not be injured if he has acquired the power.

Why do you not answer me this question, Callicles: whether...

CAL. It does follow.

CAL. This also is true.

SOC. It remains, therefore, that the only person who would be a friend worth mentioning to such a ruler is one who, because they share similar manners, would praise and blame the same things as the tyrant, and be willing to be governed and subject to the one who rules. Such a person in this city will be able to accomplish great things, and no one will injure him with impunity <note>Without being punished or suffering consequences.</note>. Is it not so?

CAL. Yes.

**Soc.** If, therefore, any young man in this city should think to himself, “How can I accomplish great things and avoid being harmed by anyone?” this, it seems, must be the way: from his youth, he must immediately accustom himself to like and dislike the same things as his master, and make himself as similar to the ruler as possible. Is it not so?

**Cal.** Yes.

**Soc.** Will it not follow, then, that such a man will avoid being harmed and, as you say, will be able to accomplish great things in the city?

**Cal.** Entirely so.

**Soc.** But will he also be able to avoid acting unjustly? Or will that be impossible if—since the governor is unjust—he has made himself similar to him so he can have power? I think the very opposite will happen: such a person will become highly capable of acting unjustly without being punished for it. Won't he?

**Cal.** It appears so.

**Soc.** Therefore, won't he suffer the greatest evil of all by having his soul corrupted and depraved through his imitation of his master and the power he gains?

**Cal.** I do not know why you are always twisting the conversation back and forth, Socrates. <note>original: "upwards and downwards"</note> Do you not know that the man who is imitated can, if he pleases, kill or seize the property of the one who does not imitate him?

**Soc.** I know it, my dear Callicles, unless I am deaf; I have heard this often from you, from Polus, and from nearly everyone in the city. But listen to me in return: yes, he may indeed kill whomever he pleases, but because he is a depraved character, he may kill someone who is worthy and good.

**Cal.** And is that not a terrible thing to endure?

**Soc.** Not to a man possessed of true understanding <note>original: "endued with intellect"</note>, as our argument shows. Or do you believe a person should strive to live as long as possible, and devote himself only to those arts which keep us safe from danger—like that <term>rhetoric</term> <note>The art of persuasive speaking, which Callicles argues is necessary for political survival and legal defense.</note> used in the law courts, which you urged me to practice?

**Cal.** I certainly do, by Jupiter, and I gave you good advice.
