**Soc.** But tell me, my excellent friend, does the skill of swimming also seem to be a noble thing to you?

**Cal.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, it does not.

**Soc.** And yet, this skill also saves men from death when they fall into a danger that requires it. But if this seems like a small thing to you, I will mention a greater one: the art of piloting a ship. This not only saves lives, but also bodies and possessions from extreme danger, just like rhetoric. Yet this art is modest and plain; it is not haughty or draped in grand ornaments as if it had accomplished something extraordinary. 

Even though it achieves the same results as the legal art, if it brings someone safely from Aegina to here, it demands, I think, only two <term>obols</term> <note>original: "oboli"; small ancient Greek coins</note>. If it brings them from Egypt or the Black Sea <note>original: "Pontus"</note>—even if it demands a larger sum because of the great benefit it has conferred by saving those I just mentioned (ourselves, our children, our wealth, and our wives) and bringing them safely to port—this fee is usually only two <term>drachmas</term> <note>original: "drachms"; silver coins worth six obols each</note>. 

The man who possesses this art and performs these tasks steps off the ship and walks near the sea and the vessel in a simple outfit. He reasons with himself, I think, that it is uncertain which of his passengers he has truly helped by preventing them from drowning, and whom he may have actually harmed. He knows that the bodies and souls of those who leave his ship are in no way better than they were when they first boarded. 

He will, therefore, reason that it is not as if a man afflicted with great and incurable physical diseases is lucky not to have drowned; such a man is actually miserable for having escaped death, and the pilot has provided him no real benefit. He also knows that if someone suffers from many incurable diseases in that which is more honorable than the body—namely, the soul—such a person ought not to live. He knows he will not benefit such a man, whether he saves him from the sea, or from a court of justice, or from anything else. He knows that it is not better for a corrupt man to live, because he must necessarily live badly. 

For this reason, it is not the custom for a pilot to be arrogant, even though he saves us. Nor, my wonderful friend, is it usual for an inventor of machines <note>original: "artificer of machines"</note> to be boastful, even though he is sometimes able to save a multitude of people, no fewer than those saved by a general, a pilot, or anyone else. For sometimes he saves entire cities. Do you think he is to be compared with a lawyer? Though, if he

If an engineer <note>original: "artificer of machines"</note> were to speak as you do, Callicles, praising his own profession, he would overwhelm you with words. He would argue and call on you to consider that you ought to be makers of machines, as if everything else were of no consequence. He would certainly have enough to say on the matter. 

But you, nevertheless, would despise him and his art. You would call him a "mechanic" <note>original: "maker of machines"</note> as a way to insult him. You would not be willing to give your daughter to his son in marriage, nor would you want his daughter for your own son. Yet, if you consider the reasons why you praise your own profession, with what justice can you despise the engineer and the others I have just mentioned? 

I know you will say that your profession is better because it deals with better things. But, my good man <note>original: "O blessed man"</note>, see whether being "noble and good" is something other than merely saving lives or being saved. Instead, he should leave those matters to the care of God <note>original: "Divinity"</note> and believe what the women say: that no one can avoid fate. 

Afterward, he should consider how he may spend the rest of his life in the most excellent way. SOC. And, indeed, it would only be proper to provide a benefit before receiving payment if their claims were true. For men, I think, do not act unjustly because they are slow runners, but because they are characterized by injustice. Do they not?

SOC. If, therefore, someone could actually remove this—I mean, injustice—would it not follow that there would be no reason to fear that he would suffer injustice in return? SOC. Hence, it appears there is nothing shameful <note>original: "base"</note> in taking money for giving advice about other things—for instance, regarding building or other technical arts.

SOC. But with respect to this specific action—I mean, how a person may be made into the best of men, and how he may govern his own family or the city in the most excellent manner—it is considered shameful to withhold advice unless money is given to the adviser beforehand. Is it not so?

...after they had received it from their father. This law $^1$, therefore, regarding mankind existed under Saturn; it always was, and still is, established among the Gods.

<note>The following commentary is likely by the translator or based on the Neo-Platonist Olympiodorus, explaining the symbolic meaning of the Greek gods.</note>

The ancients very properly called these "Gods," and viewed them as existing forever in a most wonderful and deep union with each other and the First Cause; yet, even in this union, they maintain their own distinct essence from that of their ineffable <term>too great or extreme to be expressed in words</term> cause.

But these mighty powers are called a *golden chain* by the poets because of their connection to one another and their incorruptible nature. You might call one of these powers *intellectual*; a second, *life-giving* <note>original: "vivific"</note>; a third, *healing* <note>original: "Pæonian," referring to Paean, the physician of the gods</note>, and so on. The ancients, wishing to explain these to us through names, described them symbolically. For this reason (says Olympiodorus in his manuscript commentary on the *Gorgias*), we should not be troubled when we hear names like "the power of Saturn," "the power of Jupiter," and similar titles, but instead explore the things to which they allude. 

For instance, by a "Saturnian power" rooted in the First Cause, understand a pure intellect. This is because *Kronos* <note>original: <term>Κρονος</term></note>, or Saturn, is *pure intellect* <note>original: <term>κορος νους</term></note>—that is, *the pure one* <note>original: <term>ὁ καθαρος</term></note>. Because of this, those who are pure and virginal are called *maidens* <note>original: <term>κοραι</term></note>. On this same basis, the poets* say that Saturn swallowed his children and later brought them back into the light. This is because the intellect turns back toward itself, seeks itself, and is itself what it seeks. However, he brings them forth again because the intellect not only seeks and creates, but also produces results in the light and provides benefit. For this reason, he is also called *crooked-counseled* <note>original: <term>αγκυλομητις</term></note>, or *inflected counsel*, because a bent or inflected shape turns back toward itself. Furthermore, as there is nothing chaotic or new in the intellect, they represent Saturn as an old man who moves slowly. This is why astrologers say that those who have Saturn well-placed in their birth chart <note>original: "nativity"</note> are prudent and gifted with intellect.

Furthermore, the ancient theologians called life by the name of Jupiter, giving him two names: *Dia* <note>original: <term>δια</term></note> and *Zena* <note>original: <term>ζηνα</term></note>. These names signify that he gives *life through himself*. They also claim that the sun is pulled by four horses and is eternally young. This represents his power, which moves the whole of nature under his control, his four seasonal changes <note>original: "fourfold conversions"</note>, and the strength of his energies. They say the moon is pulled by two bulls: two because of her waxing and waning <note>original: "increase and diminution"</note>, and *bulls* because, just as these animals plow the ground, the moon governs all the parts surrounding the earth.

Plato says, therefore, that Jupiter and Neptune received their shares of governance from Saturn. Since Plato is composing a philosophical story rather than a political one, he does not claim (as the poets do) that they took Saturn’s kingdom by force, but rather that they divided it. What, then, does "receiving law from Saturn" mean? We reply that law is the distribution of intellect; and as we have already noted, Saturn represents intellect. Therefore, law is derived from that source.

Again, mundane <term>earthly or worldly</term> natures, says Olympiodorus, are triple; for some are celestial, others terrestrial,

$^1$ Neither *was* nor *will be* can be said of a divine nature: for *was* refers to the past and no longer *is*, and *will be* is incomplete and does not yet exist. Nothing of this kind can be thought of regarding Divinity. Since Plato introduces this as a story <note>original: "fable"</note>, he uses the term *was*; but because the story is philosophical rather than poetic, he also uses the word *always*.

* This is claimed by Hesiod in his *Theogony*.

<meta>This page continues the Neo-Platonic commentary on the myth of the judgment of souls in Plato’s Gorgias, transitioning from the nature of the gods (Saturn and Jupiter) to the symbolic meaning of the three realms—celestial, terrestrial, and the "middle" realms—governed by Jupiter, Pluto, and Neptune.</meta>

<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

...Gods; namely, that the man who has passed through life in a just and holy manner, when he dies, departing to the islands of the blessed, shall dwell in all [happiness]. 

<margin>
Namely, the planets are distributed into different spheres and are not all contained in one sphere like the fixed stars.
</margin>

[There are] earthly <note>original: "terrestrial"</note> realms, and others between these—namely, the fiery, aerial, and aquatic. And of these, Jupiter possesses the celestial, Pluto the earthly, and Neptune those in between. Again, through these descriptions, the powers presiding over these different aspects of nature are signified. For this reason, Jupiter has a sceptre, as a symbol of the judicial power; but Neptune has a trident, as the ruler over the triple nature of the middle realms; and Pluto has a helmet, representing the obscure or hidden. Just as a helmet conceals the head, so this power (Pluto) belongs to things that are unapparent <note>The name Pluto was often associated with "wealth" (ploutos) hidden underground, or the invisibility of the afterlife</note>. 

Nor should it be thought that philosophers worship stones and images as divine things. Rather, since we live according to our physical senses, we are not able to reach an incorporeal <term>having no physical body</term> and immaterial power directly. Therefore, images are devised to help recall divine natures to our memory; by seeing and reverencing these, we may form a mental conception of those bodiless powers. 

This is also what the poets mean when they say that Jupiter, by mingling with Themis <note>The goddess of divine law and order</note>, fathered three daughters: Equity, Justice, and Peace. Equity, therefore, reigns in the unchanging <note>original: "inerratic," referring to the fixed stars</note> sphere: for there, the same motion continues perpetually and in the same manner, and nothing there is divided. But Justice rules in the planetary spheres: for here there is a separation of the stars; and where there is separation, justice is necessary so that a harmonious distribution may be made according to what is deserved. And Peace reigns over earthly <note>original: "terrestrial"</note> natures, because conflict exists among them; and where there is conflict, peace is necessary. For here, there is a conflict between the hot and the cold, the moist and the dry. 

Hence, the poets say that Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> wandered on the sea by the will of Neptune. By this, they signify that the life of Odysseus was neither purely earthly nor yet celestial, but somewhere between the two. Since Neptune is the lord of these "middle" natures, they say that Ulysses wandered through the will of Neptune because he was assigned to Neptune's realm. In the same way, they speak of the sons of Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, regarding the specific assignments <note>original: "allotments"</note> of each. For we say that he who has a divine and celestial way of life <note>original: "polity"</note> is the son of Jupiter; that he who has an earthly way of life is the son of Pluto; and that he is the son of Neptune whose life or assignment is between these two. 

Again, Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> is a certain power presiding over physical bodies; and hence he says of himself in Homer:

->*All day I fell ....*<-

This is because his attention to bodies is perpetual. On this account, he is also said to operate with bellows <note>original: *ἐν φύσαις ἐργάζεται*</note>, which is a play on words meaning "within natures" <note>original: *ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐν ταῖς φύσεσι*</note>. For this power leads nature forth to care for physical bodies. Since Plato mentions the islands of the blessed, punishment, and a prison here, let us explain what each of them is. Geographers say that the islands of the blessed are located in the ocean, and that souls who have lived well depart there. This, however, is absurd, for souls would then live a stormy life. What then shall we say? The solution is this: Philosophers compare the life of men to the sea because it is turbulent, productive, bitter, and laborious. But it is necessary to know that islands are raised above the sea, being more...

During the reign of Saturn, and even more recently while Jupiter held the government, the judges were living people judging other living people. They passed judgment on the very day a person was about to die. As a result, they judged poorly. Because of this, Pluto and the guardians of the islands of the blessed went to Jupiter. They informed him that people were arriving in their realms who were unworthy, regardless of whether they were the ones making accusations or the ones being accused.

Currently, judgments are handled badly because those being judged are judged while they are 'clothed'—that is, they are judged while they are still alive. Many," he said, "whose souls are wicked are dressed in beautiful bodies, come from noble families, and are wealthy. When their conduct is judged, many witnesses appear on their behalf, testifying that they have lived righteous lives. Consequently, the judges are distracted by these things. At the same time, the judges themselves are also 'clothed' while they judge; before their soul can see clearly, it is hidden behind a veil of eyes, ears, and the entire body¹." Philosophers are of the opinion that the earth is full of caverns, like a pumice stone, and that it is perforated all the way to its very center. They also believe that there are different places around the center, along with certain fiery, cold, and death-bringing <note>original: "Charonian," referring to Charon, the ferryman of the dead</note> powers, as the gases rising from the earth prove. This final place is called Tartarus. Therefore, it is necessary to understand that souls who have lived wickedly remain in this place for a certain time. They are punished in their <term>pneumatic vehicle</term> <note>In Neo-Platonic thought, this is a "spirit-body" made of subtle matter that the soul inhabits between physical incarnations</note>; for those who have sinned through the sweetness of pleasure can only be purified through the bitterness of pain.

Furthermore, souls that are cast into Tartarus no longer move, for it is the center of the earth, and there is no place beneath it. If they were to move, they would begin to ascend again, since every direction away from the center is "upward." Thus, that place serves as a prison for spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note> and the powers that rule over the earth. Figures like Cerberus <note>The three-headed dog guarding the underworld</note> represent these spiritual powers.

...advance from the imperfect to the perfect. When the fable, therefore, says that the judges were living judges of the living—judging on that very day in which anyone happened to die—and that as a consequence of this they judged poorly, this signifies that we human beings judge poorly, but divine judges judge well. For they know who ought to be sent to Tartarus <note>the deep abyss used as a dungeon of torment and suffering for the wicked</note> and who should go to the islands of the blessed. The fable, therefore, looking at our human judgment and beginning from a state of imperfection, says that formerly they judged poorly; but, proceeding toward perfection, it says that now they judge justly. Jupiter does not accomplish this on his own, but at the request of Pluto, because subordinate natures align themselves with superior natures.

Again, let us show what is meant by the judges being formerly in bodies, but now "naked." Here again, the fable makes a division and calls us from the more imperfect state to the perfect. It is necessary to know, therefore, that our life is obscurely represented by this, both in our present state of existence and in the life to come. In this life, both we and those we judge are in bodies, and therefore deception occurs. Because of this, by judging through our own biases <note>original: "judging passively"</note>, we do not send a corrupt person to Tartarus as someone who is miserable, but, on the contrary, we send them to the islands of the blessed. But in another life, both the judges and those who are judged are naked <note>stripped of the physical body and social status</note>.

$^1$ Prometheus, says Olympiodorus, is the overseeing guardian of the descent of rational souls. To exert a *providential energy* <note>the ability to plan and look forward</note> is the work of the rational soul, and its first task is to know itself. Irrational natures, indeed, only perceive through "percussion" <note>original: "percussion" refers to physical impact or reacting only to direct sensory stimuli</note> and know nothing until they are pushed; but the rational nature is able to know what is useful before receiving information from another. Hence, *Epimetheus* <note>whose name means "after-thought"</note> is the overseeing guardian of the irrational soul, because it only knows through physical impact and not before it. 

Prometheus, therefore, is that power which presides over the descent of rational souls. But fire signifies the rational soul itself; because, just as fire tends to move upwards, so the rational soul pursues higher things. But you will ask: Why is this fire said to have been stolen? Because that which is stolen is moved from its proper place to a foreign one. Since the rational soul is sent from its proper home on high down to earth, as if to a foreign region, the fire is said to be stolen for this reason. 

But why was it hidden in a reed? Because a reed is cavernous <note>original Greek: συριγγωδης (syriggōdēs)</note> and therefore signifies the flowing body <note>original Greek: το ρευστον σωμα (to rheuston sōma)</note> in which the soul is carried. But why was the fire stolen against the will of Jupiter? Again, the fable speaks in the language of myth: both Prometheus and Jupiter desire the soul to stay on high, but as it is necessary for the soul to descend, the fable creates specific details suited to the characters. It represents the superior character, Jupiter, as unwilling, for he wishes the soul to always remain on high; but the inferior character, Prometheus, compels her to descend. 

Jupiter, therefore, ordered *Pandora* to be made. And what is she but *the irrational soul* \*, which is characterized as feminine? For, just as it was...

...it was necessary that the soul should descend to these lower regions. However, because the soul is incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note> and divine, it was impossible for her to be joined with a body without a middle layer; therefore, she becomes united with the physical body through the "irrational soul." This irrational soul was called **Pandora**, because each of the Gods bestowed a particular gift upon it. This signifies that the light and influence which earthly natures receive come through the celestial bodies <note>the stars and planets</note>.

¹ Asia is in the east, while Europe has a more western location. Eastern parts correspond to heavenly natures because of their light, while Europe corresponds to earthly natures because of its "curvature" <note>likely referring to the density or downward tilt of the material world</note>. Through these two regions, Asia and Europe, a heavenly and an earthly system of government <note>original: "polity"</note> are signified. There is also a middle system, which Plato indicates through the relationship between these two extremes. For, having spoken of a heavenly and an earthly government, he also reveals that which exists in the middle; just as he previously mentioned those sent to the Islands of the Blessed and those cast into Tartarus, he also reveals the existence of souls characterized by a middle way of life.

Next, in order to understand what is meant by the **meadow** and the **roads** where the judgment takes place, it is necessary to observe that the ancients call the realm of "generation" <note>the physical world of birth and death</note> "moist," both because of its flowing, changing nature and because mortal life flourishes here. The place of judgment, therefore, is said to be in the aether <note>the upper atmosphere or divine air</note>, just beyond the regions below the moon; this is called a "meadow" because of its moisture and diversity.

* The irrational soul is an *immaterial body*, or, in other words, *vitalized extension*—similar to the geometric shapes we imagine in our minds. The celestial bodies are of this same nature.

<meta>This page continues Socrates' description of the afterlife from Plato’s Gorgias. He argues that just as the physical body retains its scars and characteristics immediately after death, the soul also retains the marks of its earthly habits and passions when it stands before the judges of the underworld.</meta>

<page-num>454</page-num>
<header>THE GORGIAS.</header>

...they are separated from each other, each of them keeps its own characteristics <note>original: "habit"</note>, almost exactly as they were when the person was alive. The body clearly retains its own nature, appearance, and the marks of its experiences. So, for instance, if someone’s body was naturally large while they were alive, or became so through nourishment <note>original: "aliment"</note>, or both, that person's body will also be large when dead. If they were corpulent, the body will be corpulent when dead; and so it is with other things. And if someone while living was careful to grow their hair long, the hair of their dead body will also be long. Again, if someone while living had been flogged and kept the marks of the blows on his body as scars from whips or other wounds, his dead body is also seen to preserve those same marks. And if the limbs of anyone were broken or distorted while he lived, these will also be visible when he is dead. In short, whatever the condition of a person’s body was while living, that will be its condition entirely, or for the most part, for a certain time after death.

The same thing, Callicles, seems to me to happen regarding the soul: everything is clearly visible in the soul after it is stripped of the body—both its natural qualities <note>See note 1</note> and those passions which the person acquired in their soul through their various pursuits. When, therefore, they come to the judge <note>See note 2</note>—those from Asia going to Rhadamanthus—Rhadamanthus stops them and examines the soul of each, not knowing who it belongs to. Often, he takes hold of the soul of the Great King <note>Referring to the King of Persia</note>, or of any other king...

---

<note>1. We must not think from this, says Olympiodorus <note>a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, that vice is natural to the soul. For, since the soul is incorporeal and immortal, if it naturally possessed vice, vice also would be immortal, which is absurd. By the term *from nature*, therefore, Plato means the soul living in connection with base things, so that vice is, as it were, integrated into its essence <note>original: "coeffentialized"</note>, with the soul becoming a servant to the physical temperaments of the body. The soul, therefore, suffers punishment for this because, being self-moving and connected with anger, desire, and certain bodily temperaments, she does not harmonize these and lead them to a better condition by her own self-moving power. For, just as a physician properly punishes <note>original: "scourges"</note> someone who has an eye inflammation <note>original: "ophthalmy"</note>—not because he suffers from the disease, but because he has touched and irritated his eyes and has not followed the rules set by the physician—in the same way, the Creator <note>original: "demiurgus"</note> punishes souls for not using their self-moving power to subdue the passions that were given to them for their own good. It is necessary that these passions should be conquered and used for a good purpose, not a bad one.</note>

<note>2. Plato here presents us with a myth <note>original: "fable"</note>, but he does not allow it to be merely poetic; he also adds logical demonstrations. This is the unique characteristic of philosophical myths. See the general Introduction to this work.</note>

...or powerful ruler <note>original: "potentate"</note>, he sees nothing healthy in such a soul. Instead, he sees that it has been severely whipped and is full of scars caused by the lies and injustices imprinted on it by its various actions. Everything in it is twisted ¹ through falsehood and arrogance, and nothing is straight because the soul was raised without truth. He also sees that through power, luxury, and a lack of self-control <note>original: "intemperate conduct"</note>, the soul is full of ugliness and shame. Upon seeing a soul in this condition, he immediately ² sends it into custody with disgrace; where, once it arrives, it will—

¹ For when the soul is polluted and wounded by the passions, nothing in it remains straight.

² Again, Olympiodorus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator</note> observes the following: It is necessary to know that souls that have sinned moderately are punished for only a short time and are purified before they ascend. When I say they "ascend," I do not mean in a physical location, but in their quality of life. For Plotinus says that the soul is raised up not by its feet, but by its way of living. However, souls that have committed the greatest crimes are immediately sent to Tartarus <note>the deepest abyss of the underworld used as a place of punishment</note>. Plato uses the word "immediately" <note>original Greek: *euthys* (ευθυς)</note> to mean "swiftly," as a straight line is the shortest distance between two points. 

It is worth questioning here why Plato says these souls are "always" judged and never purified. Does their punishment never end? If a soul is always punished and never experiences good, she remains forever in vice. But the purpose of punishment is to achieve some good. Therefore, it is not right for the soul to remain forever in a state contrary to its nature; it should eventually move toward a natural, healthy condition. If punishment does not benefit us or lead to a better state, it is inflicted in vain. Neither God nor nature does anything in vain.

What, then, should we understand by the word *ever*? We reply as follows: There are seven spheres—the Moon, the Sun, and the other five planets—but the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: "inerratic"</note> make up the eighth sphere. The lunar sphere completes its revolution most quickly, in thirty days. The Sun is slower, taking a year. Jupiter is even slower, taking twelve years. Saturn is slower still, taking thirty years. Because of these different speeds, the stars rarely align <note>original: "conjoined"</note> in their revolutions. 

For example, the spheres of Saturn and Jupiter align every sixty years. Since Jupiter completes a circuit in twelve years and Saturn in thirty, when Jupiter has made five revolutions, Saturn will have made two (since 2 x 30 = 60, and 12 x 5 = 60). Therefore, their cycles align every sixty years. Souls, therefore, are punished for periods like these. 

However, the seven planetary spheres only align their cycles with the sphere of the fixed stars over many tens of thousands <note>original: "myriads"</note> of years. This vast period is what Plato calls "for ever" or "all time" <note>original Greek: *ton aei chronon* (τον αει χρονον)</note>. Souls that have killed their fathers or mothers, or committed similar crimes, are punished *for ever*—meaning for the duration of this immense cosmic cycle. But suppose someone asks: "If a soul guilty of such a crime dies today, and sixty months, or years, or days later, the alignment of the seven planets with the fixed stars should take...

...for a man who has great power to act unjustly to live his life justly. Yet there are a few such men. They have existed both here and elsewhere, and I believe there will be worthy and good men in the future who will possess the virtue of justly managing the responsibilities entrusted to them. Aristides, the son of Lysimachus, was a person of this character and was very famous among the Greeks. But most powerful rulers <note>original: "potentates"</note>, my excellent friend, are bad men.

As I said, therefore, once Rhadamanthus takes a soul into his custody, he knows nothing else about it—neither who the person was nor where they came from. He only knows that it is a corrupt soul. Seeing this, he sends it to Tartarus <note>the deepest abyss of the underworld used as a place of punishment</note>, marking at the same time whether it appears to be curable or incurable. Once the soul arrives there, it suffers the punishments it deserves for its offenses. 

Sometimes, however, Rhadamanthus sees a soul that lived a life of truth—whether it is the soul of a private citizen or of anyone else. But I say, Callicles, that he especially admires the soul of a philosopher who minded his own business and did not get entangled in the many distractions of life. In such cases, Rhadamanthus is filled with admiration and sends the soul to the Islands of the Blessed. Aeacus does the same. Both judge while holding a rod¹ in their hands. But Minos acts as the supervisor; he is the only one who sits with a golden² sceptre, just as Homer's Ulysses³ describes seeing him:

> ->He holds a golden sceptre in his hand,<-
> ->And issues laws to the dead.<-

Therefore, Callicles, I am convinced by these stories. I am considering how I might appear before my judge with my soul in the healthiest possible condition. Therefore, leaving behind the honors sought by the masses and focusing on the truth, I will try to live as well as I can in reality—and to die that way too when the time comes. I call upon all other people, and I urge you as well, to choose this life and this struggle instead of the one you have chosen,

Out of so many arguments, while others are refuted <note>original: "confuted"</note>, this one alone remains unshaken: that we ought to be more afraid of doing an injury than of suffering one; and that a man ought, above all else, to strive not to *appear* good, but to *be* good in reality, both in private and in public. And further, all flattery <note>original: "adulation"</note>—whether toward oneself or others, and whether toward a few people or a crowd—must be avoided; and rhetoric, like every other action, must always be used for the sake of justice. Therefore, let yourself be persuaded by me and follow me to that place where, once you arrive, you will be happy both in life and in death, as my argument shows. Allow anyone to despise you as a fool and to heap disgrace upon you if they wish. And, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, you should confidently allow him to strike you that shameful blow. For you will suffer nothing terrible if you are truly honorable and good and practice virtue. 

Afterward, once we have trained ourselves together in this way, we can then turn our attention to political matters if it seems necessary, or deliberate on whatever we please, for we will then be better qualified to deliberate than we are now. For it is shameful, in our current state, to boast of ourselves with youthful arrogance <note>original: "juvenile audacity"</note>, as if we were some—

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

## THE PHILEBUS.

**THE** goal of this dialogue is to discover what constitutes the highest good <note>original: "chief good"</note> for humanity. To accomplish this in the most thorough way, the work is divided into twelve parts.

In the first part, Plato introduces the subject of discussion: namely, what the "good" of man is, and whether wisdom or pleasure contributes more toward achieving it.

In the second part, he explains the nature of a life focused on pleasure <note>original: "voluptuous life"</note> as well as a life led according to wisdom. This is done to determine which of the two contributes more to true happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>, and whether a third way of life might exist that is better than either of them. If such a life is found, he seeks to see whether pleasure or wisdom is more closely related to the perfection of that life.

In the third part, he demonstrates how this discussion should be conducted, showing that categorization <note>original: "division"</note> and definition must come before logical proof <note>original: "demonstration"</note>.

In the fourth part, he describes the requirements of the "good" and shows that neither wisdom nor pleasure alone constitutes the highest good of man.

In the fifth part, he examines the nature <note>original: "genus"</note> of pleasure and wisdom. He also explains those two great categories of reality—*limit* <note>original: "bound"</note> and *the infinite*—which are the principles next in rank to the unspeakable <note>original: "ineffable"</note> cause of all things. From these two principles, he identifies that which is "mixed" and suggests the cause of this mixture.

In the sixth part, because those categories reveal certain sparks of knowledge, he begins a comparison between pleasure and wisdom.

In the seventh part, he explains the cause of the mixture more extensively and continues the comparison more clearly.

In the eighth part, with the principles and categories now explained, he investigates

their differences; he inquires what pleasure and pain consist of, which among these are properly produced from feelings <note>original: "passion"; here referring to the state of being affected by external stimuli</note>, and how many parts they contain. In the ninth part, he investigates what knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> properly consists of and, having divided it, shows that a certain "third life" <note>A life combining both intellect and pleasure</note> presides over wisdom, and wisdom over pleasure. In the tenth part, it is shown how pleasure and wisdom are mingled together, and that our human good consists in a combination of this kind. In the eleventh part, he inquires what it is in that composition—by the power of which—happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> is produced; in this part, both our human good and the "Good" itself become clear. And, in the twelfth and last part, all the kinds of good which are worth pursuing as ends are listed in order, according to the relative value of each of them to man.

> “The subject of this dialogue,” says Mr. Sydenham <note>Floyer Sydenham (1710–1787), a scholar whose translations of Plato were later completed by Thomas Taylor.</note>, “is introduced by stating the different opinions of Socrates and Philebus concerning the nature of that good wherein the happiness of man is to be found; opinions which, it seems, they had just before severaly declared. Philebus, a man strongly convinced by the doctrine of Aristippus <note>Aristippus of Cyrene, a contemporary of Socrates who taught that pleasure is the highest good.</note>, had asserted that this good was pleasure—meaning pleasurable sensation, or pleasure felt through the outward senses. On the other hand, Socrates had supposed the supreme <note>original: "sovereign"</note> good of man to be placed in the mind, and in the activities <note>original: "energies"</note> of the mind on intellectual subjects. Philebus, in support of his own assertion, had been lecturing <note>original: "haranguing"</note> for a long time in the style of the Sophists, until he found his spirits and imagination—or perhaps his supply of plausible arguments—quite exhausted. He had, therefore, requested his friend Protarchus, a young gentleman who appears to have been a follower of Gorgias <note>A famous Greek rhetorician and Sophist.</note>, to take up the controversy and carry it on in his place. Protarchus had consented and committed himself to do so. Immediately upon this agreement, at this very point in time, the present dialogue begins: accordingly, it is carried on chiefly between Socrates and Protarchus. But as Philebus is the principal person whose opinion opposes that of Socrates, and as no higher role is given to Protarchus than that of an assistant <note>original: "accessary"</note> or second to Philebus in this intellectual combat, the dialogue before us—very properly and consistently with the rule which Plato seems to have followed in naming his dialogues—is given the name of *Philebus*.”

This admirable dialogue is filled with some of the most important principles <note>original: "dogmas"</note>

By those who are capable of distinguishing wholes from parts, it may be gathered from what is said here that the intellect does not share the same rank as the first cause of all. For, if our intellect is the image of the first intellect, and the good of our whole life is not to be defined by this alone, it necessarily follows that the cause of good is established above intellectual perfection. *The Good*, therefore, or the ineffable principle of things, has a super-intellectual existence <note>original: "subsistence"; in Neoplatonic terms, this refers to a mode of being that transcends rational thought.</note>, in agreement with what is asserted in the Sixth Book of the *Republic*.

I shall only add, as Mr. Sydenham <note>Floyer Sydenham (1710–1787), a scholar whose translations and notes Thomas Taylor often incorporated.</note> well observes, that the apparent form of this dialogue is *dramatic*; its nature <note>original: "genius"</note> is *didactic* <note>intended to teach, particularly in having moral instruction as an ulterior motive.</note>; and the reasoning is, for the most part, *analytical*.

<note>The following text, in a smaller typeface, is a translator's note (attributed to Thomas Taylor, indicated by "—T.") that appears to continue from the previous page.</note>

We might reply that there is a pleasure in knowledge because it shares in "appetite" <note>original: "participation of appetite"</note>. To feel pleasure when we grasp an object of knowledge comes from the adoption of desire. But to the other question, we may reply that the investigative power is analogous to the <term>orectic</term> <note>From the Greek *orexis*, referring to the faculty of desire, appetite, or reaching out for something.</note> power. For investigation, being as it were a cognitive <term>orexis</term> (appetite), is a way to a certain end, just as desire hurries toward a specific thing. But the possession of the object of desire is analogous to knowledge, which is the possession of truth.

Again, the vital and the desiring powers are not the same. For "life" is also attributed to knowledge, since knowledge moves, and that which knows is moved—which is the defining characteristic of life. However, the knower is moved when they investigate, not when they have arrived at the goal that knowledge represents.

Again, "good" is attributed to both knowledge and desire: for knowledge is beneficial and is the cause of union with the object of knowledge. But the "good" of desire is, as it were, practical <note>original: "practic"</note>; we wish not just to know it, but to be affected by it. We embrace it closely and cannot endure to have it at a distance. But we can endure the object of knowledge even at a distance, for we wish to know it, not to *be* it. 

What, however, shall we say desire is? It is not "common good," since that also pertains to knowledge. Nor is it something unknown, for desire exists together with knowledge. It is, therefore, a certain good that is known. Hence, it moves the perceiver from within themselves. This is "the beautiful," since desire, considered according to its common meaning, is nothing else than love—though love is an intense desire. For the difference between "more" and "less" produces no change in the type of thing it is; intensity alone makes it "strenuous." 

Furthermore, pleasure is the companion of desire, but pleasure is "apparent beauty." For apparent good is kind and lovely to all animals. But might the beautiful be related to the good in the following way? In the first place, the Good is "above idea" <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, the ultimate "Good" or "The One" is beyond all forms, definitions, or "ideas."</note>, but things existing within forms are more closely related to us. The Good is the formal object of desire, but the beautiful is the formal object of love—just as being is the formal object of knowledge. 

Desire, however, differs in kind from love. If desire is understood generally, it extends to one common good. But if the goals are different, the powers that hurry toward them must also be different. For the connection which, according to its specific nature, is called friendship, **philia** <note>original: φιλια</note>, and which creates a union with the good, is one thing, and the power which harmonizes with this must be called desire or longing, **ephesis** <note>original: εφεσις</note>. But the power which, driven by need, urges the masses is another; this kind of thing is called love or passion, **eros** <note>original: ερως</note>, and it hurries toward the beautiful. —T.

**Soc.** And will you, Protarchus, take up the debate as I have just now stated it?

**PROT.** I must, out of necessity.<sup>1</sup> For Philebus, our side's champion, is tired and has given up.

**Soc.** Now it is right and proper for us to discover, by every possible means, the full power and meaning of both those hypotheses; and we must not stop until we have resolved the dispute between them.

**PROT.** I agree with you; we must.

**Soc.** Let us also agree on this as well.

**PROT.** On what?

**Soc.** That each of us<sup>2</sup> should strive to explain what state and what condition<sup>3</sup> of the soul is able, according to our different hypotheses, to provide a happy life for every person. Is it not our business to do so?

---

<sup>1</sup> Necessity is threefold: it is either "self-perfect," connecting with *the good*; or "material," which involves lack and weakness; or it is that which is directed toward a goal, such as sailing for the sake of profit. According to Proclus.—T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the translator and Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>

<sup>2</sup> The Greek of this sentence, in all editions of Plato, is <term>each of them</term> <note>original: "αὐτῶν ἑκάτερος"</note>. However, all translators interpret it as if they read <term>each of us</term> <note>original: "ἡμῶν ἑκάτερος"</note> in the manuscripts; this reading clearly fits the meaning of the passage and makes it easier to understand. In the printed version, the word <term>them</term> <note>original: "αὐτῶν"</note> must refer to the <term>arguments</term> <note>original: "λόγων"</note>, which is a more distant reference that was implied rather than stated. "Each of the arguments" would then mean that the *argument should strive*, but to say that an argument "strives" is a style too metaphorical and bold for a prose writer.—S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, a co-translator of Plato's works.</note>

<sup>3</sup> In the Greek, this is <term>a state and an affection</term> <note>original: "ἕξιν καὶ διάθεσιν"</note>. All the differences between a <term>state</term> <note>original: "ἕξις"</note> and an <term>affection</term> <note>original: "διάθεσις"</note> are accurately explained by Aristotle in his *Categories*, chapter 8, and in his *Metaphysics*, book 4, section 19. In the sentence now before us, the difference between them is this: <term>an affection of the soul</term> <note>original: "διάθεσις ψυχῆς"</note> is the soul's present but temporary condition; a <term>state of the soul</term> <note>original: "ἕξις ψυχῆς"</note> is the soul's permanent condition. Thus we say of a man that he is in a "joyous state of mind" when the joy he feels has lasted for some time and is likely to continue. But of a man whose soul has just felt joy, we say that he is "seized" (meaning affected suddenly) with joy. And similarly, we say that the mind is in a "thoughtful state" when it has been thinking for some time and is not easily distracted; but when a thought arises suddenly within us while in an unthinking state of mind, or amidst wandering fancies, we say that a thought "strikes" us—that is, it suddenly affects our mind. It must not be ignored, however, that <term>state</term> <note>original: "ἕξις"</note> and <term>affection</term> <note>original: "διάθεσις"</note>, which we have here translated as *state* and *affection*, usually mean *habit* and *disposition*. But the connection between their usual meaning and the meaning they have in this passage will appear by considering that as the soul acquires certain habits of acting through frequently repeated acts of the same kind—for she is fixed in a certain state through frequent impressions made on her where she is passive, or through frequent energies of her own where she is active;

<summary>Protarchus takes over the defense of pleasure from Philebus, and Socrates proposes that they define the specific condition of the soul that leads to a happy life. The accompanying scholarly notes distinguish between different types of necessity and clarify the Greek terminology regarding temporary versus permanent mental states.</summary>

**PROT.** Certainly it is.

**Soc.** Well then: You say that the "Good" is the state of rejoicing; we say it is that of understanding and thinking correctly.

**PROT.** True.

**Soc.** But what if some other state should appear, one that is better than both of these, but more closely related to pleasure? Would we not both be refuted in that case, and be forced to give the preference to a life that offers the stable possession of those very things in which you place human happiness? However, at the same time, it must be agreed that a life of pleasure would be found more desirable than a life of knowledge or intellect. <note>original: "intellection"</note>

**PROT.** Without a doubt.

**Soc.** But if that better state of the soul should appear to be more closely related to knowledge, in that case, knowledge would be found to have the advantage over pleasure, and pleasure would have to yield. Do you not agree with me that these things are so? Or how else would you describe it?

**PROT.** I must admit, they seem to be exactly as you represent them.

**Soc.** But how do they seem to Philebus? What do you say, Philebus?

**PHIL.** To me, pleasure seems—and will always seem—to be superior, no matter what it is compared with. And you, Protarchus, will eventually be convinced of it yourself.

**PROT.** Since you have resigned the management of the debate to me, you can no longer be the master of what should be granted to Socrates and what should not.

**PHIL.** You are right. But regardless, I have done my duty; and I here call the Goddess herself <note>Philebus refers to Aphrodite, whom he associates with the divine power of Pleasure.</note> to witness it.

**PROT.** We too are witnesses of the same, and can testify to your making the assertion which you have just made. But now, Socrates, as for that investigation which is to follow after what you and I have agreed upon—whether Philebus is willing to consent or however he may feel—let us try to go through with it and bring it to a conclusion.

**Soc.** By all means, let us do so. Let us begin with that very Goddess who, according to Philebus, is called *Venus*, but whose true name is *Pleasure* ¹.

**PROT.** Perfectly right.

**Soc.** The fear ² which I always have within me concerning the proper names of the Gods is no ordinary kind of fear; it surpasses the greatest dread. Therefore, in the present case, regarding *Venus*, I would choose to call her by whatever name is most pleasing to her. But as for *pleasure* ³, I know well how varied and complex a thing it is. And as I just said, we ought to begin with this, by first considering and inquiring into the nature of pleasure. For although we hear it called by a single name, as if it were one simple thing, it actually assumes all sorts of forms, even such as—

---

¹ <note>original: "Why is Pleasure, says Olympiodorus, a Goddess..."</note> Why does Philebus consider *Pleasure* a Goddess? The philosopher Olympiodorus asks if it is because pleasure is the object of all desire and an ultimate goal. But why is *Venus* a Goddess? Is it because she is "lovely"? Perhaps they are both called Goddesses because they are involved in the reproduction of animals—the one as a presiding power, the other as a driving passion. Why was *Pleasure* not considered a Goddess by the ancient Greek theologians? Proclus says it is because pleasure is neither a primary <note>original: "precedaneous"</note> good, nor immediately beautiful, nor does it hold a middle ground between the two. However, we must note that according to Iamblichus, *Pleasure* is indeed a Goddess, and she was recognized in temples by Proclus of Laodicea.

Again, none of the ancient writers say that *Venus* is the same thing as *Pleasure*. Why is this? Perhaps it is because *Venus* represents the power of "joining together" (copulation), and while a certain pleasure follows that act, that pleasure can often be associated with things that are ugly or deformed. *Venus*, however, is beautiful—both the divine Venus and the one found in nature. In theology, the specific character of *Venus* is different from that of <term>Euphrosyne</term> <gloss>Delight</gloss>. —T.

² <note>original: "Why does Socrates, says Olympiodorus, so much venerate the names of the Gods?"</note> Why does Socrates show such deep respect for the names of the Gods? Olympiodorus suggests it is because, in ancient times, specific things were consecrated to match specific divine natures, and it is wrong to change what should remain fixed. Or, it could be that names are naturally suited to the nature of the Gods (as discussed in Plato’s *Cratylus*), or that these names are "spoken images" <note>original: "vocal images"</note> of the Gods, as Democritus believed. But how does a virtuous man "fear" the Gods? It is either a proper respect for divine justice, or a form of deep veneration rather than a terrifying dread. I will only add that this passage proves Socrates believed in the existence of divine beings who are the direct offspring of the unspeakable first cause of all things—in other words, he was a polytheist. —T.

³ <note>original: "Pleasure subsists together with motion..."</note> Pleasure exists alongside motion (or activity), for it is its constant companion. The "motion" of the intellect is an unchanging activity; the motion of the soul is a changing activity; and the motion of an animal is a reactive <note>original: "passive"</note> activity. However, the motion of a plant is pure reaction. —T.

\* That is, by none of the Greek theologians.

**PROT.** What are you saying, Socrates? Do you imagine that anyone who has asserted that pleasure is "the good" would ever admit your point? Do you think they would let it pass unchallenged that only some pleasures are good, while others are evil?

**PROT.** What do you mean?

**SOC.** I mean that if I were to imitate you and argue in your style—daring to claim that two things which are most unlike are actually the most similar—I would be saying exactly what you are saying. ¹ The meaning and logic require a small change in the Greek copies of Plato. Instead of "the similar ones" (Greek: *tas homoias* <note>original: τας ὁμοιας</note>), we should read "similarities" (Greek: *tas homoiotētas* <note>original: τας ὁμοιοτητας</note>) or rather "similes" (Greek: *ta homoia* <note>original: τα ὁμοια</note>). Similes of the kind meant here are called "the Socratic ones" (Greek: *ta Sōkratika* <note>original: τα Σωκρατικα</note>) by Aristotle in his *Art of Rhetoric*, book 2, chapter 20 (Du Vall edition). They are called this because Socrates used them so often. These are not like poetic similes, where the imagination scans all of nature to find superficial resemblances. Nor are they like an orator’s historical examples, used to prove a doubtful fact by matching it with past events. Instead, they are the kind an expert in dialectic chooses from everyday subjects to prove an uncertain point through its analogy to a truth that is obvious, clear, and easily accepted. However, nothing in the following text mentions "similar pleasures," and the phrase "the similar ones" (*tas homoias*) cannot belong to any previous noun except "pleasures" (Greek: *hēdonas* <note>original: ἡδονας</note>). **SOC.** <note>The OCR lists "POL." here, but the context and catchword indicate this is Socrates speaking.</note> Regarding wisdom <note>original: "prudence"</note>, knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, and intellect <note>original: "intelligence"</note>, and all those other things which I said were "good" at the start of our conversation—when I was asked what kind of thing "the good" was—must I not acknowledge that these have the same characteristics as the things you celebrated?

We have found that pleasures are many and various; likewise, branches of knowledge are also many and diverse. However, let us not hide the difference between your definition of "the good" and mine, Protarchus. Instead, let us dare to lay it out fairly and openly before us both. In this way, we can discover—if a close examination reveals anything—whether pleasure or wisdom should be declared the chief good of humanity, or perhaps some third thing that is different from both. After all, I assume we are not competing simply to see if my theory or yours wins the argument; rather, we should both be striving to support whatever has the truth on its side.

**PROT.** This is certainly our duty.

**SOCRATES:** The "wonders" you’ve just mentioned regarding "the one and the many," Protarchus, are clichés <note>original: "hackneyed in the mouths of the vulgar"</note>. By general consensus, such examples have been set aside and are no longer worth mentioning. They are viewed as childish, easy objections that only get in the way of a real discussion. It is now generally agreed that we shouldn't use the parts or limbs of a single object as an example of "the one and the many." Why? Because once a person being questioned admits that all these parts are that *one* thing—and thus "many" at the same time—the questioner just laughs at them. They are mocked for being forced into such ridiculous absurdities—claiming that a single *one* is an *infinite multitude*, and that an *infinite multitude* is only *one*.

**PROTARCHUS:** In that case, Socrates, what other examples do you mean—ones that aren't clichés and aren't yet settled by everyone?

perishable. As for the "ones" of this second type, it has been agreed, as I just said, to reject them as unworthy of a serious debate. The "ones" I am referring to are concepts such as "man," "ox," "beauty," and "the good." When these *henads* <note>original: "henads" — units or fundamental unities</note> ^1, or things like them, are proposed as subjects for debate, they deserve serious attention. When people try to divide any one of these into "many," much doubt and controversy arises.

**PROTARCHUS:** On what points exactly?

**SOCRATES:** First, whether we should believe that such *monads* <note>original: "monads" — from the Greek *monas*, meaning a single, indivisible unit</note> possess true, objective existence. And finally, whether we should imagine each monad is dispersed and spread out among an infinite number of created things—thereby turning from one into many—or whether it remains entirely itself, separate and apart from that multitude ^3. Of all these ideas, the most impossible might seem to be that one and the same thing...

^1 Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century philosopher and commentator on Plato.</note> says that Plato calls the highest points of "Forms" *monads* and *henads*. He calls them *henads* in reference to the specific group of things they lead, but *monads* in reference to the ultimate reality beyond existence. Or, we might say there are two types of highest points: those characterized by *essence* and those characterized by *unity*, as discussed in the *Parmenides* <note>Another of Plato’s dialogues.</note>. This reveals the ignorance of Cudworth <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a philosopher who argued against atheism.</note>, who, in his book *The Intellectual System* (p. 555), wrongly considers the doctrine of *henads* (derived from the "First One" or "the One itself") to be a later invention of the Neoplatonists. —T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the primary translator.</note>

^2 This second question assumes the first question has already been decided in favor of these monads having real existence. For if universal concepts are held to be merely names invented to describe imaginary fancies, it is a waste of time to ask how they stay stable; stability is a property of real beings only—unless that stability is just as imaginary as the things themselves. The Greek sentence here <note>original: "πως αυ ταυτας, μιαν ἑκαστην ουσαν αει την αυτην, και μητε γενεσιν μητε ολεθρον προσδεχομενην, ὁμως ειναι βεβαιοτητα μιαν ταυτην"</note> must be flawed. To make good sense of it, it is necessary to make a small alteration or two—reading "to have" instead of "to be," and "itself" instead of "this." In translating this passage, we have assumed it should be read that way. We believe the intended meaning is: "It must seem strange that distinct beings—which were not created by one another but are all equally eternal and independent—should nevertheless share the same nature of 'unity' and the same property of 'stability.'" —S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, a co-translator.</note>

^3 In the Greek, we read "itself apart from itself" <note>original: "αυτην αυτης χωρις"</note>. But it is presumed that we ought to read "itself by itself, separately" <note>original: "αυτην εφ’ αὑτης χωρις"</note>. —S.

<meta>This page continues Socrates' explanation of the "Promethean gift," a method of philosophical inquiry known as dialectic. The commentary at the bottom of the page, continuing from the previous page's footnote, provides a Neoplatonic interpretation by the philosopher Olympiodorus regarding how the "One" (unity) relates to the "Many" (multiplicity).</meta>

<page-num>478</page-num>
<header>THE PHILEBUS.</header>

The men of ancient times, who were better than we are and lived closer to the Gods, passed down this tradition to us—that those beings said to exist forever derive their essence from "the one" and "the many," and therefore have both limit <note>original: "bound"</note> and infinity innate <note>original: "connatural"</note> within them. Since things are constituted this way, we ought to assume there is one single idea in everything around us and search for it; for since it is there, we will surely find it if we look. 

Once we have found it, we must next look for two, if only two follow; otherwise three, or some other number. Again, we must examine each of these numbers in the same way, until a person finally perceives not only that the "one" they started with is both one, many, and infinite, but also discovers exactly how many parts it contains. A person should never jump to the idea of the infinite and apply it immediately to any number before they have fully discovered the specific, definite number that lies between the infinite and the one. But having completed—

->***<-

place, it consists of both the kinds <note>original: "genera"</note> of being and a single characteristic <note>original: "idiom"</note>. Fourthly, this characteristic is multiplied along with the "many," but there is a certain indivisible <note>original: "impartible"</note> peak in all the many. Fifthly, this peak is a unified form, but there is also something within it above form. And sixthly, this peak is at once the "unified" but not "the One" <note>The "One" refers to the ultimate, absolute principle in Neoplatonism</note> itself. Furthermore, as all things arise from the one and the many, it is necessary that these two principles are arranged before all things; the former being the cause of unity for all things, and the latter the cause of multiplicity <note>original: "multitude"</note>. They must also clearly be secondary to the first cause; for that is at *once* the cause of all things.

Again, in the furthest extremes of things, an infinite multiplicity is seen, but at the summit a monad <term>monad: a single, fundamental unit from which all numbers or things proceed</term> exists beforehand, according to every form. But an infinite multiplicity would not be produced unless an infinite power was presumed to exist in the monad that generates it. Nor would every individual within those infinites be limited unless "limit" <note>original: "bound"</note> extended to the very last of things. This progression exists through all appropriate middle steps <note>original: "media"</note>, from the monad to infinite multiplicity. 

First, this is seen in multiplicity that can be shared <note>original: "participated"</note>. For the progression does not go immediately from *the one* to the infinite, but to two and three, and the following numbers. Next, the progression of physical bodies is of this kind, for there is no void <note>original: "vacuum"</note> within its variety. Thirdly, the generative power of the monad, being both one and many, creates all things at once according to its whole self; secondary things always follow those that came before.

Furthermore, says Olympiodorus, the method of division <note>the process of breaking a general concept down into its specific species</note> proceeds alongside the progression of forms. It does not break the continuity of what is subordinate, nor does it introduce a void, but proceeds through all the middle steps from the one to the infinite. The task of the method of division is:
1. To place the *one* everywhere before the many.
2. To place the finite before infinite multiplicity.
3. To always define according to quantity, putting the smaller number before the larger.
4. To omit no number of things that complete the progression.
5. To select—

The commentary outlines the Neoplatonic rules for dividing forms and the philosophical relationship between the descent (progression) and ascent (conversion) of the soul.</meta>

<header>THE PHILEBUS.</header>

Once we make this discovery, we should finish our search and let go of all those specific numbers into the realm of the infinite, bidding them farewell. The Gods, as I said before, have granted us the ability to consider things in this way—to learn them and teach them to one another. But the "wise" men of today take any single unit <note>original: "monad"</note> they find and divide it into many parts more abruptly than they should, and with more rambling too, since they never reach a logical end. Immediately after the single unit, they jump straight to infinity, skipping over all the intermediate numbers. It is the specific mention of these intermediate numbers—or the lack thereof—that distinguishes fair dialectical debates like ours from those that are merely argumentative and sophistical.

PROT. Part of what you say, Socrates, I think I understand reasonably well. However, I would like to hear you explain the meaning of some things you have just said in even simpler terms.

---

<note>The following is a commentary note by the translator, Thomas Taylor, likely expanding on the Neoplatonic views of Olympiodorus.</note>

...numbers adapted to respective forms; the <term>triadic</term> <note>a grouping of three</note>, for instance, or the <term>hebdomadic</term> <note>a grouping of seven</note>, to Minerva <note>the Roman name for the goddess Athena</note>, and in a similar manner for all the rest. Different numbers emerge according to different forms; likewise, among the Gods, there are different numbers according to different Divinities. Even among single units <note>original: "monads"</note> themselves, one progression is unitary <note>original: "monadic"</note>, like that of the Monad; another is twofold <note>original: "dyadic"</note>, like that of the Dyad; and it continues similarly with the rest. Therefore, there is not a simple division of all things into two. 

Sixthly, one should divide through forms, but not through form and negation as Aristotle suggests; for no number is produced from a form and its denial. 

Seventhly, to bring every single unit into division in its proper order, whether it belongs to the realm of limit <note>original: "bound"</note> or to the realm of infinity—for each is present everywhere. 

Ninthly <note>The original text skips the eighth point.</note>, to produce things that are divided into opposites according to their contrast <note>original: "antithesis"</note>, whether certain middle points <note>original: "media"</note> are discovered or not. 

Tenthly, do not leave these middle points in the breadth <note>original: "εν τω πλατει" (en tō platei)</note>. 

Eleventhly, to assign different numbers appropriately to different levels of reality <note>original: "orders"</note>, such as the number twelve for natures beyond this world <note>original: "supermundane"</note>, and the number seven for the intellectual realms. 

Twelfthly, to see where smaller numbers are more excellent and where they are secondary, and to do the same for larger numbers. For the <term>decad</term> <note>a group of ten</note> of this world is secondary to the <term>duodecad</term> <note>a group of twelve</note> of the realm beyond; but the intellectual <term>hebdomad</term> <note>a group of seven</note> is superior to it.

Furthermore, the "analytic art" <note>the process of breaking things down from effects back to causes</note> is secondary to the "divisive art" <note>the process of dividing a general genus into specific species</note>. The latter comes from a cause, while the former comes from a sign. The divisive art surveys lower things from a high perspective, while the analytic art looks upward at higher things from below. The divisive art does not stop at anything perceived by the senses, but the analytic art requires the senses at first. Thus, the divisive art gives existence and creates, nearly forming the entire essence of the procession <note>the unfolding of reality from the Divine source</note>. In contrast, the analytic art converts things back; it allows that which has proceeded to leave behind its lower nature and adhere to a more excellent nature. For this reason, progression is more essential than conversion, and is therefore more excellent. So, the process of proceeding is superior to the process of returning, and the essential is superior to the upward-leading <note>original: "anagogic"</note>. However, regarding the descent of the soul, since progression here is a falling away from better natures, the ascent (which corresponds to conversion) is better than progression or descent.—T.

<header>THE PHILEBUS.</header>

SOC. Everything I have said, Protarchus, is clearly demonstrated in the study of letters <note>In this context, "letters" refers to the alphabet and the foundations of grammar.</note>. You can easily understand my meaning through these, which you have been taught since childhood.

PROT. How is it demonstrated in letters?

SOC. The voice that issues out of the human mouth may be considered a single general thing, yet it allows for an infinite number of articulations—not only across all humanity but also within every individual person.

PROT. Without doubt.

SOC. Now, we do not become knowledgeable in speech or articulate sound simply by knowing its infinite variety or its singular nature. Instead, knowing how many parts it is naturally divided into, and what those parts are—this is what makes any of us a grammarian, or someone skilled in grammar.

PROT. Most certainly.

SOC. And furthermore, the way a person becomes skilled in music is exactly the same.

PROT. How so?

SOC. Musical sound*, which is the subject matter of this art, may be considered in itself as one general thing.

PROT. Without dispute.

---

* In the Greek, the term used here, as well as just before (where this translation uses the word <term>voice</term>), is *phone* <note>original: "φωνη"</note>. In the previous instance, it signified articulated vocal sound, or <term>speech</term>; here it signifies the musical sound of the voice, or <term>vocal music</term>. We see then that Plato considers the human voice to be a common genus <note>A general category</note> divisible into these two types or species. It is expressly described this way by Nicomachus (in *Manual of Harmonics*, page 3, Amsterdam edition) in these words: "Those [writers concerning music] who came out of the Pythagorean school said that of the human voice [in general], as of one genus, there are two species. One of these two they properly named <term>continuous</term>, the other <term>discrete</term>." <note>original: "Της ανθρωπινης φωνης οἱ απο του Πυθαγορικου διδασκαλειου δυο εφασκον, ὡς ἑνος γενους, ειδη ὑπαρχειν· και το μεν συνεχες ιδιως ωνομαζον· το δε διαστηματικον."</note> These two technical terms he afterward explains by showing us that the <term>continuous</term> is that voice which we utter in speaking and in reading (which Aristoxenus and Euclid therefore termed <term>logical voice</term> <note>original: "φωνη λογικη"</note>), and that the <term>discrete</term> is the voice issued out of our mouths in singing (and therefore termed <term>melodic voice</term> <note>original: "φωνη μελωδικη"</note>). In this latter case, every single sound is distinguished by a certain or measured tone of the voice. The same division of the voice is laid down, and a similar account of it is given, by Aristoxenus in *Elements of Harmonics*, pages 8 and 9, Amsterdam edition.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to Thomas Sydenham, who began the translation of Plato's works later completed by Thomas Taylor.</note>

---

¹ Unison <note>original: "homotony"</note> of sound occurs when a string of a musical instrument, having the same degree of tension as a similar string of another, yields the same musical tone when played with it. It also occurs when two different voices utter the same musical sounds at the same time, where neither is higher or lower than the other. In both cases, the sameness of the sound is also termed homophony <note>original: "ὁμοφωνία"</note>. This is because the term "voice" <note>original: "φωνη"</note> is metaphorically attributed to all musical instruments (see Nicomachus, pages 5 and 6); conversely, "tone" is metaphorically attributed to the human voice, modulated by the will in the trachea, or "rough artery" <note>original: "aspera arteria"</note>. This natural wind instrument, aptly named the windpipe in English, receives any degree of tension it is capable of at the pleasure of the mind while it transmits air breathed out from the lungs. Similarly, the repetition of the same tone from a single human voice, or from a single string <note>original: "monochord"</note>, is termed a monotony. — S.

² An interval is the distance (or difference in position <note>original: "κατα τοπον"</note>) between any two musical sounds—between one that is high <note>original: "acute"</note> and another that is relatively low <note>original: "grave"</note>—however near or remote they may be from each other on a musical scale. Depending on the closeness of these two sounds, the interval is mathematically described as small or great—that is, short or long. Thus, different musical intervals, like any other distances from place to place, essentially differ from one another in magnitude or length. All other variations of intervals are founded upon this essential difference.

³ The bounds of each interval are those two musical sounds from which a direct step or transition is made to the other. In the most ancient musical scale, which consisted of only seven sounds produced by seven strings of different lengths, there were three principal sounds: the *hypate* <note>original: "ὑπατη"; the physically "highest" string on the lyre, which produced the lowest pitch.</note>, the lowest; the *nete* <note>original: "νητη"</note>, the highest; and the *mese* <note>original: "μεση"</note>, the middle sound between them. We consider these three the principal sounds because the first and easiest division of any quantity—whether it is continuous or discrete <note>Consisting of distinct, unconnected parts.</note>—is into two equal parts or halves. Therefore, the most distinguishable points or bounds of any quantity, regardless of how it is later subdivided, are the two extremes and the middle. Accord-

⁴ A "system" is a composition of three or more musical sounds; or (what amounts to the same thing) it is a range or extent that includes two or more intervals. The general varieties of these systems are laid down by Aristides (page 15 and following). However, in his definition of a system (as it is printed), an important error deserves notice. For we read there: <term>more than two</term> <note>original Greek: <term>πλειόνων ἢ δυοῖν</term></note>; instead of which we ought to read <term>two or more</term> <note>original Greek: <term>δυοῖν ἢ πλειόνων</term></note>, or else <term>more than one</term> <note>original Greek: <term>πλειόνων ἢ ἑνός</term></note>. The error probably arose from some manuscript copy of Aristides happening to be difficult to read in this place. We suppose the transcriber consulted Baccheius, who in his definition of a system uses the words <term>more than two</term> <note>original Greek: <term>πλειόνων ἢ δυοῖν</term></note>. These words are actually correct in Baccheius because he applies them to <term>musical sounds</term> <note>original Greek: <term>φθόγγων</term> (phthongoi)</note>, agreeing with our first definition; but they would be wrong in Aristides, who is speaking not of sounds, but of <term>intervals</term> <note>original Greek: <term>διαστημάτων</term> (diastemata)</note>, agreeing with our second definition. On the many diversities and variations to be made in such a large field of systems are founded those many different forms, figures, or modes of harmony, or types of tunes (the Greek writers call them <term>forms</term> <note>original Greek: <term>εἴδη</term></note>, <term>figures</term> <note>original Greek: <term>μορφαί</term></note>, <term>patterns</term> <note>original Greek: <term>σχήματα</term></note>, <term>modes</term> <note>original Greek: <term>тρόποι</term></note>, and <term>tones of harmony</term> <note>original Greek: <term>τόνοι ἁρμονίας</term></note>). According to Aristides (page 25), the general kinds of these are the Doric, the Phrygian, and the Lydian. If this is true, all other modes are to be considered subordinate to these three; indeed, some seem to be intensifications <note>higher pitches</note>, others to be relaxations <note>lower pitches</note>, and others to be mixtures of those more moderate and simple forms.—S.

Aristoxenus and Euclid mean, by the term "harmony," that kind of melody called enharmonic. Plato and Aristotle, when they speak of "harmony" in the singular without adding a specific description, mean the concept now commonly expressed by the word "music." This is probably because music was the first discovered of those sciences—as well as the first invented of those arts—that were anciently grouped together under one general idea and termed "music." But when these same great philosophers speak of "harmonies" in the plural, they mean those different forms or modes of harmony whose specific differences depend on the different systems, or on the different order of those systems, from which they are composed. **PROT.** Excellently well, O Philebus, has Socrates spoken in what he has now said, at least as it appears to me.

**PHIL.** It appears so to me as well. But how does all this speech of his concern our controversy? What was its purpose or drift?

**Soc.** I will do that as soon as I have gone through the little yet remaining of the subject on which I have been speaking. For, as the man who applies himself to the consideration of any kind of things whatever ought not, as I have said, to throw his eye at once upon the infinite, but upon some definite number in the first place; so, on the other hand, when a man is obliged to set out from the infinite, he ought not to move up immediately to the "one," but to some certain number, in each of whose "ones" a certain multitude is contained; and thus gradually rising from a greater to a smaller number, to end in one.
