<gloss>This note refers to a suspected error in some manuscript copies of Plato, suggesting that the words "of voice" <note>original: φωνῆς</note> and "not indeed" <note>original: μὲν οὐ</note> should be followed by "being" <note>original: ὄντα</note>. Combined, these words closely resemble "vowels" <note>original: φωνέντα</note>, a term that fits the context of the sentence and the language of ancient grammarians. —S.</gloss>

¹ These were called *semi-vowels* <note>original: ἡμίφωνα</note> by the old grammarians; because, in their very formation by the organs of speech, they are necessarily accompanied by the voice just enough to give a half-vocal sound, without the full aid of any vowel. —S.

² The Greek grammarians list eight of these semi-vowels. —S.

³ Socrates, by expressing himself this way regarding the general name of this third sort of letters—as if the name were then newly given to them at Athens—seems to disapprove of it. Perhaps the ancient term *consonants* <note>original: σύμφωνα</note>—a term applied by the newer grammarians to *semi-vowels* <note>original: ἡμίφωνα</note> as well as to *mutes* <note>original: ἄφωνα</note>—was, in his judgment, properly applicable only to those letters which produce no sound at all on their own. For mutes, as they are called, cannot be pronounced even imperfectly or obscurely (as semi-vowels can) without the help of some vowel or some perfectly vocal sound. —S.

⁴ In the Greek: *voiceless and soundless* <note>original: ἄφθογγα καὶ ἄφωνα</note>—evidently meaning those letters that are neither vowels nor semi-vowels. It seems, therefore, that by *voice* <note>original: φωνὴ</note> Plato meant a perfect and clear vocal sound, such as we utter when pronouncing a vowel alone; and by *sound* <note>original: φθόγγος</note> he meant that imperfect and obscure sound of the voice made while forming and pronouncing a semi-vowel without a vowel's help. Now, if this is true, then the printed version of the passage mentioned in note 3 on the preceding page may be justified. Aristotle, however, who treats this subject in his *Poetics* (chapter 20), does not recognize such a distinction between *voice* <note>original: φωνὴ</note> and *sound* <note>original: φθόγγος</note>. He attributes an *audible vocal sound* <note>original: φωνὴ ἀκουστή</note> to semi-vowels no less than to vowels. He states the difference between these two types of letters as follows: the voice, in uttering the vowels, proceeds *without any striking* <note>original: ἄνευ προσβολῆς</note>—that is, it does not hit against any parts of the mouth (the upper organs of speech) so as to be blocked in its free exit. But the expression of semi-vowels is *with a striking* <note>original: μετὰ προσβολῆς</note>; the voice in uttering them strikes against the mouth and meets with some degree of resistance. By this striking, the sound is indeed articulated; but by the resistance, as the passages through the mouth are narrowed, the sound becomes weaker and diminished—except when it is in a syllable, where a vowel will always assist the delivery by giving the voice a free passage into the air. Aristotle is undoubtedly right in attributing a *vocal sound* <note>original: φωνὴν; Latin: vocem</note> to a semi-vowel on its own; but his learned commentator Victorius is equally right in describing this vocal sound as *obscure, thin, and meager* <note>original: obscura, tenuis, & exilis</note>, since it is only half of the full vowel sound. Plato may fairly be allowed to distinguish this half-sound by a particular name. —S.

¹ *The desirable*, says Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonic philosopher and commentator</note>, proceeds from the "intelligible father" <note>the highest principle or source in this philosophical system</note>; the *sufficient* comes from power; and the *perfect* comes from the "paternal intellect." In reality, however, perfection is the third stage from essence, because the middle stage is life. But if this is true, it is clear that *the end* <note>the goal or "telos"</note> is different from *perfection*; for perfection is the last stage, but the end is the first, toward which essence, life, and intellect—and therefore all things—converge. So, in every form, the *end* will be the summit and the thing that holds the whole together; but *perfection* will be the third stage, existing after essence and life, for it is necessary for a thing to exist and to live before it can become *perfect*.

Furthermore, *the perfect* is subordinate to <note>original: "spread under"</note> *the sufficient*, just as *the full* is subordinate to *the overflowing* <note>original: "super-full"</note>, and *the sufficient* is subordinate to *the desirable*. This is because things, when they are full, excite desire. The *primary* end is likewise above *the desirable*, *the sufficient*, and *the perfect*. That end is simple and beyond words <note>original: "ineffable"</note>; and for this reason, Socrates does not say it is composed of these elements, but rather that these elements possess an indefinite portion of *the Good*. It is better, however, to call the unified collection <note>original: <term>συναιρεμα</term> (synairema), meaning a contraction or gathering together</note> of these three a "portion of the good," though this is unnamed. For *the Good* is all things, not just these three; nor is it only the end, but it is truly all things prior to everything else. Besides, the end currently being considered is knowable, so there must be another end more general <note>original: "common"</note> than this one.—T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the translator</note>.

\* That is, from the peak of the intelligible order.—See the *Parmenides* <note>Another dialogue by Plato</note>.

---

¹ Proclus, in his *Platonic Theology*, p. 132, observes that Plato here—following the theology of his own country—establishes two principles that exist after *the One*. According to Philolaus <note>a Pythagorean philosopher</note>, the nature of beings is constructed from things that are *limited* and things that are *infinite*. If beings, therefore, exist <note>original: "subsist"</note> from limit and the infinite, it is clear that these two must exist prior to all beings; in other words, they must be "superessential" <note>original: "superessential"—a term for realities that exist above or beyond the level of being or essence</note>. 

Because *limit* and the *infinite* are beyond essence, Socrates correctly says that "God has displayed them." Their emergence from the highest God is beyond words; they should be thought of as mysterious revelations from him rather than his "products." Mr. Sydenham <note>Floyer Sydenham, an earlier translator</note>, because he was unfamiliar with the sublime theology of the Greeks, completely misunderstood the deep meaning of this passage. His translation reads: "The Gods, we said, have shown us the infinite of things, and also their bound." The actual Greek text is: "We said somewhere, I think, that God has shown the infinite of beings, and also the limit." <note>original Greek: "τὸν θεὸν ἐλέγομεν που, τὸ μὲν ἄπειρον δεῖξαι τῶν ὄντων, τὸ δὲ πέρας"</note>

Should it be asked, says Olympiodorus <note>a late Neoplatonist commentator</note>, why the two elements *limit* and *infinity* are superior to that which is "mixed" (since these two are the principles of being), we reply that these principles must be viewed as universal orders that are simpler than the mixture. Secondary principles emerge from these two within the "first mixture"; these are secondary to the mixture in the same way that raw elements are always subordinate to the objects composed from them.

Furthermore, there is no perfect separation in the "second order"*: for the creation of form first belongs to Intellect, and the "First Intellect" is pure intellect. Because of this, Iamblichus says that the "monads of forms" exist within this—meaning by "monads" that which is undivided within every form. For this reason, it is "intellectual" as it exists among intellectual beings, and it is the cause of the essence of form, just as the second order is the cause of life, and the third is the cause of how form is crafted among intellectual beings.

Additionally, the "egg" <note>the Orphic Egg, symbolizing the origin of the universe</note>, the "paternal intellect," and "occult number"—in short, whatever is third after the *limit*—each represents the "third God" according to theologians. Consequently, each of these is the same as that which is "mixed" from limit and infinity.

Finally, the single principle that gives existence to all things and is their ultimate goal contains the "final cause" as something superior to the "producing cause"; for *hypostasis* <note>term: the fundamental reality or substance of a thing</note> is achieved through goals. The "First Principle" is both of these according to *the One*. The two principles, *limit* and *infinity*, divide these roles: *limit* exists according to the final goal, and *infinity* exists according to the producing cause.

---

* The reader must remember that the "intelligible order" consists of *being, life,* and *intellect,* and that each of these is divided into three parts. See the notes on the *Parmenides*.

**SOC.** Let us take these for *two* of the species of things; and for a third, let us take that which is composed of those two mixed together. But I deserve, I think, to be laughed at for pretending to distinguish things this way and to list their various species.

**PROT.** Why so, my good friend?

**SOC.** A fourth kind appears to have been omitted by me.

**PROT.** Tell me, what is it?

**SOC.** Consider the cause of that mixture—the combination of the first two. Beside those three species, mark down this cause¹ as a fourth.

**PROT.** Will you not also need a fifth species as a cause of disunion and separation?

**SOC.** Perhaps I may; but not, I believe, at present. However, should there be an occasion for it, you will pardon me if I go in pursuit of a fifth life <note>original: "life" — likely referring to a fifth category or class of existence being discussed</note>.

**PROT.** Certainly.

**SOC.** Of these four species, then, let us first divide the three. We can see that two of these—when both are divided and their divisions separated—are each of them "many." Then, gathering together the "many" of each and uniting them again, let us try to understand in what manner each of them is, at the same time, both one and many.

**PROT.** If you would only express your meaning more plainly, I might, perhaps, understand it.

**SOC.** I mean, then, that the two species I propose we consider now are the same ones I mentioned at the first: one of them is the *infinite*, and the other is the *limit* <note>original: "bound"</note>. I will attempt to show that the *infinite* is, in some manner, many; and let the *limit* wait for a while.

**PROT.** It shall wait.

Again, Socrates establishing that which is mixed as a certain cause of union, the cause of separation is also investigated. This cause, however, will be the *difference* which exists after the intelligible <note>original: "intelligible" — referring to the realm of pure thought or forms accessible only to the intellect</note>, as we learn from the *Parmenides* <note>another of Plato's dialogues focusing on the nature of "The One"</note>. For the intelligible is united alone. But it would be better to make *the One* the cause of all things; *limit* <note>original: "bound"</note> the cause of union; *infinite* the cause of separation; and the *mixture* <note>original: "mixt"</note> that which participates in both. Observe, too, that "the more" and "the less" are everywhere, but in the realm of intelligibles, they exist according to a superior and inferior degree of power. — T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the translator and commentator</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Protarchus from the *Philebus*. Socrates is leading the discussion toward defining the "infinite" (the boundless) by looking at qualities that fluctuate in degree, such as heat and cold.</meta>

<page-num>496</page-num>
<header>THE PHILEBUS.</header>

**SOC.** Give me your attention now. I admit that what I want you to consider is a difficult and uncertain matter. Consider it, however. First, regarding the "hotter" and "colder" in things, see if you can think of any limit <note>original: "bound"</note> to them. Or would not the "more" and the "less," existing within these classes of things, prevent any end from being fixed to them as long as they are present? For if they ever reached a definite end, their very existence <note>original: "beings"</note> would then be brought to a close as well.

**PROT.** That is certainly true.

**SOC.** And when we speak of one thing being colder or hotter than another, we are constantly attributing "more" and "less" to them.

**PROT.** Very much so.

**SOC.** Reason then constantly suggests to us that the *hotter* and the *colder* have no end; and being without an end, they are altogether *boundless*.

**PROT.** I am strongly inclined to agree with you on this point, Socrates.

**SOC.** You have answered well, my friend Protarchus; and you have rightly reminded me that the words *strongly* (which you just mentioned) and *faintly* have the same power as the *more* and the *less*. For wherever they are present, they do not allow anything to be *exactly so much* <note>original: "just so much"</note>. Instead, by infusing either the more *intense* or the more *relaxed* <note>original: "remiss"</note> into every action, they always produce in it either the *more* or the *less*, while the *exactly so much* flies away and vanishes before them. For, as we just observed, if they did not drive away the *exactly so much*—or if they permitted it and the *moderate* to enter the realms of the *more* and the *less*, or the *intense* and the *relaxed*—these very qualities would cease to exist in their own nature. Because if they admitted the *exactly so much*, the hotter and the colder would disappear. For the *hotter*, and likewise the *colder*, is always advancing forward and never stays in the same spot; but the *exactly so much* stops and remains still, having finished its progress. Now, according to this reasoning, the hotter must be *boundless*, and so must the colder.

**PROT.** So it appears, Socrates. But as you rightly said, these things are not easy to grasp. However, repeating questions about them again and again might show that the questioner and the respondent are in reasonably good agreement about them.

**SOC.** You are right, and we should try to do so. But for now, to avoid lengthening the discussion...

<summary>Socrates argues that qualities like "hotter" and "colder" are inherently boundless because they always exist in degrees of "more" or "less." He contrasts this with "exactly so much," which represents a fixed limit that ends the progression of these qualities.</summary>

Instead of lengthening this argument by listing every infinite thing, consider whether we may take this as the defining characteristic of the nature of all infinites.

**PROT.** What characteristic do you mean?

**SOC.** Anything that appears to us to be increasing or diminishing, or that admits of intensity and relaxation <note>original: "remission"</note>, or the "too much," and all other such attributes, we should refer to the category <note>original: "genus"</note> of the infinite. We should collect all of these into one group, just as we said before—that we ought to assemble and combine things that were divided and separated as well as we can, labeling them all with the mark of a single nature. Do you remember?

**PROT.** I remember it well.

**SOC.** Now, consider everything that rejects those attributes and admits only their opposites. First, there is the equal and equality; after the equal, there is the double, and every other ratio <note>original: "relation"</note> that one number bears to another, or one measure to another. In summing these up and referring them to the limit <note>original: "bound"</note>, don't you think we would be doing the right thing? Or what do you say?

**PROT.** Perfectly right, Socrates.

**SOC.** Well: but what about the third thing, which is made up of and consists of the other two? What characteristic shall we assign to this?

**PROT.** I presume you will show it to me.

**SOC.** A god indeed might, if any of the gods will listen to my prayers.

**PROT.** Pray, then, and look for the answer.

**SOC.** I am looking; and I think, Protarchus, that some god has now become favorable to us.

**PROT.** What do you mean? And by what sign do you know it?

**SOC.** I will tell you in plain words: but follow them closely.

**PROT.** Only speak.

**SOC.** We mentioned just now the hotter and the colder; did we not?

**PROT.** We did.

**SOC.** To these, then, add the drier and the moister; the more numerous and the fewer; the swifter and the slower; the larger and the smaller; and whatever else we previously ranked under the single heading of things that admit of the nature of the "more" and the "less."

**PROT.** You mean the infinite.

**SOC.** I do. Now, mingle together with this what we spoke of next—the category <note>original: "race"</note> of the limit <note>original: "bound"</note>.

**PROT.** What category do you mean?

**SOC.** Those things which we did not gather together under one heading (as we should have done), in the same way we gathered together the category of the infinite. But perhaps you will now do what was then omitted. When both sorts are gathered and viewed together, the category of the limit will then become clear.

**PROT.** What things are you speaking of? And how are they to be gathered?

**SOC.** I speak of that nature which includes the "equal" and the "double," and whatever else puts an end to the conflict between opposites. By introducing number, it makes them proportional to one another and brings them into harmony.

**PROT.** I understand your meaning to be that, from the blending <note>original: "commixture"</note> of those two, a certain result <note>original: "progeny"</note> will arise within every one of their classes.

**SOC.** You understand me correctly.

**PROT.** Describe, then, the results of these blendings.

**SOC.** In sickness, does not the right blending of those two produce the *recovery of health*?

**PROT.** Entirely so.

**SOC.** And regarding high and low pitches <note>original: "the acute and the grave"</note>, and fast and slow tempos—which are all "infinite" in their range—does not the other category, when introduced among them to create limits, constitute the perfection of all music <note>original: "the Muse's art"</note>?

**PROT.** Certainly so.

**SOC.** And in weather that is excessively cold or hot, does not the entrance of that other kind remove the excess—the extreme and the infinite—creating in their place not only moderation and measurement, but also balance and a proper relationship between their measures?

**PROT.** Without dispute.

**SOC.** And do not favorable seasons, and all their beautiful productions, arise for us from this: the mixture of things that are infinite with things that have a limit?

**PROT.** Doubtless.

**SOC.** I will refrain from mentioning a thousand other things—for instance, strength and beauty, which accompany bodily health, and the many noble excellencies within the soul. For Venus <note>Socrates uses the goddess of love and beauty to represent the divine principle of order and harmony.</note> herself, my good Philebus, observed lawless lust and every kind of vice reigning everywhere. Seeing that the love of pleasure in all men was boundless and their desires insatiable, she established a law and an order, setting limits <note>original: "bounds"</note> to pleasure and desire. You claimed this was done to diminish and impair pleasure, but I maintain that, on the contrary, it preserved pleasure from decay. And you, Protarchus, what do you think of it?

**PROT.** For my part, I am entirely of your mind, Socrates.

**SOC.** I have shown you those three categories <note>original: "kinds"</note>, then, if you understand my meaning.

**PROT.** I suppose I partly do. By one of those three, I assume you mean the infinite; by the second sort, you mean that which serves as the limit in all beings. But I do not yet have a clear grasp <note>original: "strong apprehension"</note> of what you mean by the third sort.

**SOC.** That is because the sheer variety <note>original: "multitude"</note> of that third category has overwhelmed you. Yet, the infinite also appeared to contain many different types; but since they were all marked by the characteristics of "more" and "less," they were clearly seen to be a single category.

**PROT.** True.

**SOC.** Then, as for the limit: that category did not contain many types, nor did we find any difficulty in accepting that its nature is one.

**PROT.** How could we?

**SOC.** It was not at all possible, indeed. Therefore, consider the "offspring" <note>original: "progeny"</note> of those first two categories—everything brought into existence through the proportions <note>original: "measures"</note> that are created in the immoderate when limits are set upon the infinite. In summing all these results together and viewing them as a single group, you should understand this to be the third category.

**PROT.** I understand you.

**SOC.** Now, besides these three, we must further consider what that fourth category is. As we examine it together, see whether you think it necessary that everything brought into existence must have some cause for its production.

**PROT.** I think it is; for without a cause, how could anything be produced?

---

¹ This is evidently a metaphor taken from the competitions common at that time between dramatic poets during the festivals of Bacchus, for the glory of being the best in their art. For the Greeks of those days had an ambition to excel in the musical entertainments of the mind as well as in the athletic <note>original: "gymnic"</note> exercises of the body. To inspire them with that ambition, competitions in poetry and music, as well as in athletics, were established by their legislators; and the contenders in either kind were alike termed <term>agonistai</term> <note>original: αγωνισται</note>, or "combatants." The metaphorical combatants meant by Protarchus are Mind and Pleasure. —S.

² In continuing the metaphor taken from theatrical contests, Protarchus compares himself to a member of the chorus in a tragedy or comedy, and Socrates to the <term>koryphaios</term> <note>original: κορυφαιος</note> or <term>chorēgos</term> <note>original: χορηγος</note>, the leader of the whole band. In the choral songs, it was the office of the leader to guide the vocal music, keeping it in time and tune with the instruments; and in the dialogue scenes, whenever the chorus took part, their leader spoke alone for them all. —S.

**SOCRATES:** You must be obeyed, Protarchus. Indeed, there is nothing difficult in your requests. But, in asking you to which of the two previously mentioned categories <term>The categories of the "Infinite" and the "Limit" discussed earlier.</term> intellect and science <note>original: "science" here refers to *episteme*, or systematic, certain knowledge.</note> were to be referred—when I was exalting, as *Philebus* says, the subject of my question—the joke I intended to soften its seriousness actually confused your thoughts, I see, in all earnestness.

**PROTARCHUS:** Completely so, I confess, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** And yet it was an easy question. For on this point, there is an agreement and harmony among all the wise—who thereby bring honor to themselves—that *Intellect is king of heaven and earth.* And what they say is perhaps <gloss>1</gloss> well said. But let us, if you are willing, consider the nature of this category <note>original: "genus"</note> more fully, and not in such a brief manner.

**PROTARCHUS:** Examine it in whatever way you think best, without worrying about the length of the inquiry; for its length will not be at all unpleasant to us.

**SOCRATES:** Well spoken. Let us begin, then, by proposing this question.

**PROTARCHUS:** What is it?

**SOCRATES:** Shall we say that the power of an irrational force governs all things in the whole universe, by chance and at random? Or shall we, on the contrary, agree with our ancestors and predecessors in affirming that a certain wonderful intellect and wisdom orders all things together and governs throughout the whole?

**PROTARCHUS:** There is no comparison between these two views, Socrates. What you just mentioned—the idea of random chance—is, in my opinion, impious. But to hold that Intellect arranges all things in a beautiful order is consistent with the view we have of the world, of the sun and stars, and of the entire rotation of the heavens. For my own part, I would never speak or think otherwise on this subject.

**SOCRATES:** Is it then your pleasure that we join our voices with those of the ancients and openly declare that belief to be our own? Should we do this without being content to merely repeat the words of others to avoid personal risk, but rather being resolved to take every risk together and share in whatever consequences follow?

# THE PHILEBUS.

**SOCRATES:** ...should we fear the criticisms of some great and formidable man when he asserts that in the universe as a whole there is no order <note>original: "no order." The person alluded to here is likely Critias, one of the "Thirty Tyrants" of Athens. He was an atheist philosopher and politician who argued that gods and cosmic order were human inventions. A fragment of his poetry on this subject is preserved by the philosopher Sextus Empiricus.</note>?

**PROTARCHUS:** How could I do anything but agree with you on this?

**SOCRATES:** Attend now to the argument that we must consider next.

**PROTARCHUS:** Please, propose it.

**SOCRATES:** In the bodies of all animals, we discover that fire, water, and air must naturally be part of their composition; and we clearly see the earth, which gives support to the other ingredients in their physical frame—just as sailors say when they are tossed about in a thunderstorm at sea and finally spot land.

**PROTARCHUS:** True; and indeed, we are being tossed about in these discussions, and we are completely at a loss for a harbor to anchor in.

**SOCRATES:** Let us proceed then. Concerning each of those elementary ingredients in our physical frame, understand this.

**PROTARCHUS:** Understand what?

**SOCRATES:** That the amount of each element within us is small and insignificant. Nowhere in any part of our bodies do we have any element that is completely unmixed and pure, nor does the element within us possess a power worthy of its true nature. Take one of them as an example by which you may judge all the rest. In some sense, there is fire within us; there is also fire in the universe <note>original: "Fire in some manner there is in us; fire there is also in the universe." Socrates is highlighting the difference between "wholes" (the vast elements of the universe) and "parts" (the tiny amounts in individual bodies). In Platonic thought, the "whole" is the cause and sustainer of the "part."</note>.

**PROTARCHUS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Now, the fire within our own makeup is weak and inconsiderable. But the fire in the universe is remarkable for its vast quantity, for the beauty it displays, and for every power and quality that belongs to fire.

**PROTARCHUS:** That is perfectly true.

**SOCRATES:** Well then: is the fire of the universe created, fed, and ruled by the fire inside us? Or, on the contrary, do my fire, and yours, and that of every other living thing, receive their existence, support, and governing laws from the fire of the universe?

<summary>Socrates argues that the four elements (fire, water, air, earth) within the human body are merely small, weak fragments of the vast, pure elements found in the universe. He suggests that our individual physical elements are dependent upon and governed by these universal "wholes."</summary>

**PROTARCHUS:** You are perfectly right.

**PROTARCHUS:** It is obvious that we must.

**SOCRATES:** Since we acknowledge, Protarchus, that these four categories <note>original: "genera." # THE PHILEBUS.

[Socrates:] ...belong there are beings of that fourth sort—causes that produce souls, build up bodies for those souls to dwell in, and heal those bodies when they are diseased; causes, also, which create and frame other compositions and repair them when they are impaired. These are causes to every one of which we gave a particular name, signifying a particular kind of wisdom or skill. Since, I say, we are persuaded of these things, we surely cannot think that the whole heaven—in the larger parts of which are the same four categories <note>original: "genera"</note>, and these in an incorrupt and pure state—can have any other cause than a nature which is full of contrivance and design, and in whom all the most beautiful and noble things unite.

**PROTARCHUS:** It would not be at all reasonable to think it could be otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** If this is then absurd, we may more confidently assert, as a consequence of our reasoning, that in the universe there is—as we have repeated several times—a great quantity of the **infinite** and a sufficient amount of **limit** <note>original: "bound"</note>. Besides these, there is a **cause**, neither small nor mean, which, by mixing them properly together, organizes and regulates the years, the seasons, and the months—a cause which, with the greatest justice, we may call **wisdom** and **intellect**.

**PROTARCHUS:** With the greatest justice, indeed.

**SOCRATES:** But further, **wisdom** and **intellect** could never exist without a soul. <note>That is, soul exists alongside wisdom and intellect. If this is the case, it is evident that when Plato in the *Timaeus* speaks of the "generation" of the soul by the *demiurge* (the divine craftsman), whom he expressly calls *intellect*, he does not mean a production that happens in time, but an "eternal procession" from a cause. In the same way, what he says there about the "generation" of the universe should be understood. Therefore, those who claim that the world, according to Plato, was produced in time are mistaken. —Thomas Taylor</note>

***

<note>In the Greek of this passage we read: *psychen te parechon kai soma skian empoioun* (providing a soul and creating a shadow for the body). Marsilio Ficino translates the last two words of this as: "*dum imprimit umbram*" (while it impresses a shadow). But since this is obscure, an error in the Greek manuscripts was rightly suspected by later translators, Cornarius and Serranus. Cornarius proposes reading *hygeian* (health) instead of *skian* (shadow); Serranus imagines we should read *somaskian* (physical exercise) as one word. Grynaeus and Bembo never attempt to correct the printed Greek, even where it is obviously wrong. Monsieur Grou took the easy way out by not translating the last two words at all. However, all the difficulty vanishes if, instead of *skian* (shadow), we read *skenos* (a tabernacle or tent)—a word used metaphorically by the Pythagoreans to signify the human body, as it is only a temporary dwelling for the soul. See Timaeus the Locrian in several passages, and a fragment of Ocellus the Lucanian, *On Law*, in Stobaeus's *Physical Selections*, chapter 16. See also Aeschines the Socratic, page 128, Horrei edition; the Greek index of which will provide the learned reader with examples of the same metaphor used by several Greek writers in succeeding ages. —Sydenham</note>

**PROTARCHUS:** Very true.

**PROTARCHUS:** We shall not fail to remember both of them.

**PROTARCHUS:** In my opinion, Socrates, you are very right; but let us see if we can show these truths in an even clearer light.

**PROTARCHUS:** What things do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** A lack <note>original: "want"</note> of food causes a disruption in the animal body’s system and, at the same time, causes the pain of hunger.

**PROTARCHUS:** True.

**SOCRATES:** And food, by repairing that disruption <note>original: "filling up the breach"</note>, produces pleasure.

**PROTARCHUS:** Right.

**SOCRATES:** A lack of drink also interrupts the circulation of the blood and fluids <note>original: "humours"; in ancient medicine, the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that were believed to regulate health and temperament</note>, bringing about decay <note>original: "corruption"</note> along with the pain of thirst. However, the power of a liquid—in moistening and replenishing the parts that have dried up—yields a pleasure. Similarly, an unnatural, suffocating heat that breaks down the structure of the body's parts gives a painful sensation; but a cooling down—a refreshment agreeable to nature—affects us with a sense of pleasure.

**PROTARCHUS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** And the thickening <note>original: "concretion"</note> of the bodily fluids through cold, which is contrary to their nature, causes pain; but a return to their original state of fluidity and a restoration of the natural circulation produces pleasure. Consider, then, whether you think this general explanation is correct regarding that kind of being which I said was composed of "the infinite" and "limit" <note>original: "bound"</note>. My point is that when any beings of that kind naturally possess a soul, their path toward decay <note>original: "corruption"</note> or a total breakdown is accompanied by pain. Conversely, their movement toward existence—the gathering together of all those particles that make up the nature of such a being—is attended by a sense of pleasure.

**PROTARCHUS:** I accept your account of this whole matter; for, it seems to me, it bears the stamp of truth.

**SOCRATES:** These sensations, then, which affect the soul only through the body, let us consider as one species of pain and pleasure.

**PROTARCHUS:** Let it be so.

**SOCRATES:** Consider now the feelings of the soul herself, in the expectation of—

**PROTARCHUS:** Tell me what it is.

***

$^1$ In the Greek text of this passage, instead of the singular participle *gignomenon* (happening), which would only agree with the word "body," we should read the plural *gignomena*, which agrees with the two preceding nouns, "soul" and "body," coupled together. This follows a standard rule in both Greek and Latin grammar. The words of this sentence, when placed in their grammatical order, are: "By the soul and the body being moved together, happening together in one experience—this movement, etc." <note>original Latin/Greek: "Τῳ κοινῃ κινεισθαι την ψυχην και το σωμα, κοινῃ γιγνομενα εν ένι παθει,---ταυτην την κινησιν κ. τ. λ."</note> If the editor Henri Estienne <note>Stephens</note> had recognized this, he would not have adopted the incorrect changes to the text made by Janus Cornarius. —S. <note>The "S." refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

---

$^1$ We cannot imagine for what purpose this compliment to Protarchus is introduced here, unless it is by way of a simile: to represent the dignity and excellence of the matters previously discussed; and, by reminding Protarchus of his illustrious birth, to signify to him that just as he should not fall short of the standards of his ancestors, so also should no new matters be brought up if they fall short in weight and value of those which preceded them. Perhaps an intimation is also given by Plato to his readers that one of the subjects of inquiry just mentioned by Socrates—the one concerning opinions—immediately related to that other concerning pleasures, specifically as to their truth or falsehood. In the Greek of this passage, it is probable that the printed reading <term>κείνου του ανδρός</term> <note>original: "of that man"</note> is erroneous; and that Plato wrote <term>κλειτου ανδρος</term> <note>original: "of an illustrious man"</note>. However, in later ages, a reader of some manuscript copy of this dialogue—where instead of <term>κλειτου</term> (illustrious) was written <term>κλεινου</term> (renowned)—collated it with another manuscript copy where he found <term>κλειτου</term> written. He might have written <term>του</term> (the) in the margin of the first copy, opposite to the syllable <term>νου</term>, where perhaps a new line began. Afterwards, a transcriber of this copy included <term>του</term> into the text of his own transcript just before <term>ανδρος</term> (man), supposing it to be a word accidentally omitted. Finally, when <term>κλεινου του ανδρος</term> was discovered to be a grammatical error in Greek syntax, <term>κλεινου</term> (a very uncommon word) was easily changed into <term>κείνου</term> (that), and the construction was thus corrected. — S. <note>This note by the translator Sydenham explains a complex theory of how the Greek text might have been corrupted by scribes over centuries.</note>

All the translators of Plato into other languages rightly suppose this sentence to be incomplete at its beginning. **Protarchus:** I do.

**Socrates:** And besides this: if we suppose that opinions in general possess attributes and qualities, shouldn't we also agree on whether pleasure and pain are simply what they are in themselves, or if they too can take on certain qualities?

**Protarchus:** It is evident that we should.

**Socrates:** But it is easy enough to see that these also allow for the addition of certain qualities. For we agreed a while ago that some pleasures and pains are great and others are small, and that each type can vary in its vehemence and its intensity <note>original: "intension"</note>.

**Protarchus:** Very true.

**Socrates:** And if the quality of "evil" is added to either a pleasure or an opinion, shall we not say that the opinion becomes evil, and the pleasure becomes evil in the same way?

**Protarchus:** Without doubt, Socrates.

**Socrates:** And what if correctness <note>original: "rectitude"</note>, or the opposite of correctness, is added to any of them? Shall we not say that the opinion *is right* if correctness is in it? And shall we not ascribe the same quality to *pleasure* under the same conditions?

**Protarchus:** We must, by necessity.

**Socrates:** And if we are mistaken about the object of our *opinion*, must we not acknowledge in such a case that our *opinion* is erroneous and not right, and that we ourselves are not right to hold such an opinion?

**Protarchus:** Certainly we must.

**Socrates:** But what if we find that we are mistaken about the object of our *grief* or of our *pleasure*? Should we still give to this *grief* or this *pleasure* the title of *right*, or *good*, or any other honorable name?

**Protarchus:** We certainly cannot, if there is a mistake involved in the pleasure.

**Prot.** Very true.

**Soc.** But if he were alone, this very thing would remain a thought within him; he might continue walking, keeping that same thought in his mind for a long time.

**Prot.** Undoubtedly.

**Soc.** Well now: does this matter appear to you in the same light as it does to me?

**Prot.** How is that?

**Soc.** In this case, the soul seems to me to resemble a book.

**Prot.** How so?

**Soc.** Memory, coinciding with the senses, along with the feelings <note>original: "passions"</note> of the soul that accompany both memory and current sensations, seem to me to join together in writing sentences within our souls at that time. When this internal scribe writes what is true, then true opinions and true sentences are produced within us. But when our scribe writes what is false, then what we think and what we say to ourselves is contrary to the truth.

**PROT.** Who is he?

**Soc.** An engraver <note>In other translations of Plato, this figure is often called a "painter" (zōgraphos), representing the faculty of the imagination that turns verbal thoughts into mental pictures.</note>, who follows after the scribe; he engraves within the soul images of those thoughts, statements, and sayings.

**Soc.** It happens when a person separates what they think and say to themselves—concerning what they see or perceive through any other outward sense—from the actual sensation they have of it. They then view, somehow within themselves, the image of that thought and of that statement. Or do you think no such thing is ever produced within us?

**PROT.** Nothing is more certain.

**Soc.** Now, the images of true thoughts and true statements—are they not true? And the images of those which are false, are they not themselves also false?

**PROT.** Undoubtedly.

**Soc.** Now, if we have concluded correctly so far, let us proceed to consider one further point.

**PROT.** What is that?

**Soc.** Whether all operations of this kind, as they are naturally performed within our souls, regard only things present and things past, but not things to come; or whether any of them refer to the future as well.

**PROT.** The difference in time makes no difference in these matters.

**Soc.** Did we not say before that pleasures and pains of the soul alone arise in us before those pleasures and pains which affect the body? In this way, we feel anticipatory <note>original: "antecedent"</note> joy and grief in the prospect of things to come in the future.

**PROT.** Very true.

**Soc.** Those writings, then, and those engravings which we just agreed are performed within us—do they respect only the past and the present time? Do they have no concern for the future?

**PROT.** They are very much concerned with the future, and primarily so.

**Soc.** In saying this, do you mean that all these things are expectations of the future; and that we are all, throughout our lives, full of expectations?

<summary>Socrates introduces the metaphor of the "engraver" (imagination) who turns the "scribe's" thoughts into mental images and explains that these internal processes create expectations, allowing us to feel pleasure or pain regarding the future.</summary>

**PROT.** That is exactly what I mean.

**Soc.** Now then, since we have agreed this far, answer this further question.

**PROT.** What is it?

**Soc.** Is a man who is just, pious, and entirely good not beloved by the Divine?

**PROT.** Undoubtedly.

**Soc.** And what of the unjust and entirely bad man? Is not the opposite true of him?

**PROT.** How could it be otherwise?

**Soc.** Now, as we just said, every man is full of many expectations.

**PROT.** True.

**Soc.** There are sayings written within every one of us, which we call "expectations." <note>Socrates is connecting the "internal scribe" mentioned on the previous page to the concept of hope. These "sayings" are the internal thoughts we have about what might happen in the future.</note>

**PROT.** There are.

**Soc.** And there are also fantasies <note>original: "phantasies"; refers to the mental images produced by the internal "engraver" or "painter" mentioned previously.</note> engraved within us. For instance, a person often sees—in their imagination—plenty of money flowing toward them, and consequently, many pleasures surrounding them. They see a mental image of themselves, engraved within their own mind, as being highly delighted.

**PROT.** That is often the case.

**Soc.** Regarding these "engravings," shall we say that good men—because they have the favor of the Divine—generally have those that are true, while bad men generally have those of the opposite kind? Or shall we deny it?

**PROT.** It cannot be denied.

**Soc.** Bad men, then, also have pleasures engraved within them, but these are of the false kind.

**PROT.** No doubt about it.

**Soc.** Therefore, wicked men mostly delight in false pleasures, while good men delight in pleasures that are true.

**PROT.** It must necessarily be so.

**Soc.** According to this account, there are false pleasures in the souls of men; though in a most ridiculous way, they imitate—and would gladly pass themselves off as—true pleasures. There are also pains with these same qualities.

<summary>Socrates argues that a person's moral character determines the truthfulness of their hopes and mental images, concluding that good people experience true pleasures while wicked people experience false ones.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates and Protarchus discuss how mental images and expectations can be true or false. # THE PHILEBUS.

**PROT.** Such pleasures and such pains there certainly are.

**SOC.** Can a man who indulges his imagination <note>original: "fancy"</note> at random, and accepts opinions of any kind whatsoever, not always really <gloss>1</gloss> think and believe that some things exist which neither exist now nor ever did, and sometimes even things that never will exist?

**PROT.** Certainly.

**SOC.** And isn't it the false appearances and perceptions of these unreal things that produce false opinions in him and cause him to think falsely? Is that not the case?

**PROT.** It is.

**SOC.** Well then: should we not say that the pleasures and pains felt by those bad men correspond to the case of false opinions?

**PROT.** What do you mean?

**SOC.** Might a man who pursues and embraces pleasure at random—pleasure in general, of any kind—not always really feel delight from things that do not exist, and sometimes from things that never existed, and often—perhaps most frequently—from things that will never happen?

**PROT.** This must necessarily be granted.

**SOC.** Shouldn't the same be said of fears, desires, and all similar feelings—that these are also sometimes false?

**PROT.** Certainly.

**SOC.** Now then: can we say that opinions are bad or good in any sense other than whether they turn out to be false or true <gloss>2</gloss>?

**PROT.** In no other way.

**SOC.** And I would think that we perceive pleasures to be "bad" for no other reason than that they are false.

**PROT.** Quite the opposite, Socrates. For hardly anyone would blame falsehood for the evils brought on by pain and pleasure; since many great evils come to them from other sources.

This is clear from a sentence shortly after regarding a man *really* delighted with thoughts of *unreal things*. **SOC.** We will speak of pleasures that are evil because of the harm they cause shortly, if we still think it necessary. But now we must speak of a multitude of pleasures felt by us and frequently arising within us—pleasures that are false in yet another way. This other way of considering pleasure might be useful to us in forming a right judgment of its various kinds.

**PROT.** By all means let us speak of these, if any such pleasures exist.

**SOC.** And there are such, Protarchus, in my opinion. But as long as this opinion remains unexamined, it is impossible for it to become certain or incontestable.

**PROT.** Fairly said.

**SOC.** Now, therefore, let us advance to this other argument, like champions entering the ring <note>original: "combat"</note>.

**PROT.** Let us proceed then.

**SOC.** We said, if we remember, a little while ago, that as long as the body's needs—which we call "desires"—remain unsatisfied, the body is affected in a way that is distinct and different from the soul.

**PROT.** We remember that this was our position.

**SOC.** In such a case, the part within us that desires would be the soul, wishing for her body to be in a state opposite to its current condition; and the part that felt uneasiness or pain from that condition would be the body.

**PROT.** That is how things would be with us.

**SOC.** Now put these things together and consider the result.

**PROT.** Tell me what it is.

**SOC.** In such a case, it turns out that pains and pleasures are placed side by side; and together, side by side, there arise in us a feeling of emptiness and a desire for its opposite, fullness. This is what we have just shown.

**PROT.** It is indeed apparent.

**SOC.** Has this not also been said? And does it remain a point settled between us by agreement?

**PROT.** What?

**SOC.** That pain and pleasure both allow for "the more" and "the less," and that they both belong to the class of the unlimited <note>original: "infinites"; referring to the Greek *apeiron*, things that have no inherent limit and can increase or decrease indefinitely</note>.

**PROT.** It was so said and agreed.

**SOC.** Is there not, then, some way in which we may judge pain and pleasure rightly?

**PROT.** What way, and what do you mean?

**SOC.** In judging them, are we not accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note>, in every case, to try them by these marks: which of them is the greater and which is the smaller; which of them has <note>original: "hath"</note> the nature of its kind most fully; and which is more intense than the other—whether we are comparing a pain with a pleasure, one pain with another, or one pleasure with another?

**PROT.** Such comparisons are often made, and from these comparisons we are accustomed to form our judgment and our choice.

**SOC.** Well now: in the case of physical sizes <note>original: "magnitudes"</note>, does not the distance of visible objects—some of which are seen far away and others near—render their real sizes uncertain, obscuring the truth of things and producing false opinions? And does not the same thing hold true regarding pains and pleasures? Is not the same effect produced by the same means in this case also?

**PROT.** Much more intensely <note>original: "feelingly"</note>, Socrates.

**SOC.** But in this case, it happens in a way opposite to what occurred in the case mentioned a little while ago.

**PROT.** What happens, you say?

**SOC.** In that previous case, the true and false opinions we held imparted their own qualities of truth and falsehood to the pains and pleasures that accompanied them.

**PROT.** Very right.

**SOC.** But in the case I am speaking of now, the pains and pleasures are viewed from far off and near; they are continually changing [their appearance based on their distance], and being set in comparison with one another. [It happens that] the pleasures [at hand], when compared with the [remote] pains, appear greater and more intense [than they really are]; and the pains, compared with the pleasures, [have an appearance] that is quite the opposite.

**PROT.** Such appearances must necessarily arise by these means.

**SOC.** Therefore, as far as the pains and pleasures appear smaller or greater than they really are, if you separate this appearance from the reality—this false appearance of what neither of them actually is—and take it by itself, you will not say that

**PROTARCHUS:** What do they mean?

This is how we should view them, especially if we consider their other harsh principles. Next, you will hear what pleasures I consider to be true pleasures. Then, by comparing both accounts, we can discover the nature of Pleasure and judge her relative value.

**PROTARCHUS:** Well said.

**SOCRATES:** Let us then follow them as our allies, wherever their strictness <note>original: "austerity"</note> leads us. I suppose they would begin their argument with a general principle, asking us something like this: if we wanted to understand the nature of any specific quality—for example, the nature of "hardness"—would we not understand it better by examining the hardest things, rather than by looking at a diverse variety of things that are less hard? Now, Protarchus, you must answer these strict people as if you were answering me.

**PROTARCHUS:** By all means. My answer to them is this: it is better to examine those things that are harder than all others.

**SOCRATES:** In the same way, then, if we want to know the nature of pleasure in general, we should not consider a multitude of small or minor <note>original: "mean"</note> pleasures, but only those which are called extreme and intense <note>original: "exquisite"</note>.

**PROTARCHUS:** Everyone would agree that your argument is true.

**SOCRATES:** Don’t the pleasures that are most accessible to us—those we often call the greatest—belong to the body?

**PROTARCHUS:** There is no doubt about it.

**SOCRATES:** Are the bodily pleasures felt by people suffering from diseases greater than the pleasures of the same kind felt by those in good health? Now, let us be careful not to make a mistake by answering too quickly.

**PROTARCHUS:** What is the danger of making a mistake?

**SOCRATES:** Perhaps we might be tempted to favor those who are healthy.

**PROTARCHUS:** Probably we would.

**SOCRATES:** But what about this: aren't the most intense pleasures those preceded by the strongest desires?

**PROTARCHUS:** That cannot be denied.

**SOCRATES:** Don't people suffering from fevers, or diseases similar to fevers, feel more thirsty than others? Don't they shiver more from the cold? And don't they suffer more from the other ailments the body is subject to? Aren't their needs more urgent? And don't they feel greater pleasure when those needs are satisfied¹? Or shall we deny that all this is true?

**PROTARCHUS:** A mixed kind of sensation, Socrates, seems to arise from this ailment, sharing in both pain and pleasure.

**SOCRATES:** However, I did not bring up this last subject for the sake of Philebus <note>Philebus is the character for whom the dialogue is named, who represents the view that pleasure is the highest good.</note>. I brought it up because we would never be able to settle the point we are currently discussing unless we examined these mixed pleasures and others that depend on them. Let us proceed, therefore, to consider those that are related to them.

**PROTARCHUS:** Do you mean those that share in both pleasure and pain because they are blended together <note>original: "commixture"</note>?

**SOCRATES:** That is exactly what I mean. Of these mixed feelings, then, some belong to the body and are generated there. Others belong to the soul and reside there. We will also find pleasures mixed with pains where both the soul and the body have a share. Now, even though these mixtures are composed of opposites <note>original: "contraries"</note>, they are sometimes called only "pleasures," and in other cases, only "pains."

**PROTARCHUS:** Please explain yourself more fully.

**SOCRATES:** When a person—whether they are healthy <note>original: "in a sound state"</note> or in declining health—feels two opposite sensations at the same time; such as when someone chilled with cold is warming themselves, or sometimes when someone overheated is cooling down. They do this, I suppose, with the goal of enjoying one sensation and being delivered from the other. In such cases, what is called the "bitter-sweet"—because of the difficulty of driving away the "bitter" part—causes an internal struggle and a violent clashing of opposite qualities and sensations.

**PROTARCHUS:** What you have said is perfectly true.

**SOCRATES:** Are not some of these mixed sensations composed of pain and pleasure in equal proportion? And in others, is not one of them stronger <note>original: "predominant"</note>?

**PROTARCHUS:** Without a doubt.

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus examine "mixed" sensations, such as the relief of an itch, where pleasure and pain coexist. They conclude that these sensations can occur in the body, the soul, or a combination of both, often resulting in a "bitter-sweet" internal struggle.</summary>

**SOCRATES:** Among those sensations where there is an excess <note>original: "overplus"</note> of pain, I include the condition called the itch and all other such irritations. This occurs when only a slight scratching or movement is applied—just enough to scatter the fluids <term>humours</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "humours" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to regulate health and temperament.</note> on the surface, but not enough to reach the bubbling and swelling of the fluids deep within. In this state, a person often applies heat to the painful parts out of impatience, and then—not knowing which way to turn—tries the opposite extreme. By doing this, they trigger incredible pleasures first, then the opposite sensation in their internal parts, compared to the pains felt on the outside. These sensations are still mixed with pleasures, depending on whether the fluids are driven outward or inward. By violently scattering the disease-causing matter <note>original: "morbific matter"</note> where it has gathered, or by forcing it together from where it was scattered, pleasures and pains are triggered at the same time and arise side by side.

**PROTARCHUS:** This is very true.

**SOCRATES:** Now, whenever a larger amount of pleasure is mixed in, the smaller amount of pain causes only a slight discomfort—just enough to tickle. On the other hand <note>original: "το δ’ αυτης ἡδονης" (of the pleasure itself); the translator suggests reading "το δ’ αυ της ἡ" (but on the other hand...).</note>, a great excess of pleasure spreading through the body causes the whole frame to convulse. It sometimes causes involuntary movements, changes the color of the face, alters the person's posture, and changes their breathing. Within the soul, it creates ecstatic states <note>original: "transports"</note> expressed through wild shouting.

**PROTARCHUS:** Exactly so.

**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, a friend, a person in this state is likely to say of himself—and others will say of him—that he is "dying" from an excess of pleasure. From then on, he is completely focused on chasing these same pleasures. This is especially true if he lacks self-control <note>original: "intemperate"</note> and is less governed by wisdom <note>original: "prudence"</note>. He calls these pleasures the greatest and considers the man who spends his whole life enjoying them, as much as possible, to be the happiest of all.

**PROTARCHUS:** Socrates, you have described this exactly as the majority of people experience it and think about it.

**SOCRATES:** But all of this, Protarchus, relates only to those pleasures mixed with...

<summary>Socrates describes how physical ailments like itching create "mixed" sensations where pain and pleasure are felt simultaneously, often leading lacking self-control to pursue these intense but unhealthy states as the "highest" form of happiness.</summary>

...pains as arise solely in the body, in its surface parts and interior parts alternately. And as to those feelings of the soul which meet with a contrary condition of the body—when pleasure in the mind is mixed with pain in the body, so that both are ingredients in one experience—we spoke of those before. Such cases include a desire for fullness <note>original: "fulness"</note> while feeling a sense of emptiness in the body; when hope provides delight, while the physical emptiness causes pain. We did not, indeed, consider them at that time as evidence for our current point; but we now say that in all those cases (and the number of them is infinite) where the condition of the soul is different from that of the body, a mixture of pain and pleasure happens to be produced.

**PROTARCHUS:** I believe you are perfectly right.

**SOCRATES:** Among the mixtures of pain and pleasure, there is a third kind remaining that we have not yet mentioned.

**PROTARCHUS:** What kind is that?

**SOCRATES:** Those cases where pleasures and pains arise frequently in the soul itself—entirely apart from the body—and are mixed together.

**PROTARCHUS:** In what cases do we say these mixtures are found?

**SOCRATES:** Anger, fear, desire, and grief <note>original: "lamentation"</note>, love, jealousy <note>original: "emulation"</note>, and envy, and all other such passions of the soul—do you not suppose them to give pain and uneasiness to the soul?

**PROTARCHUS:** I do.

**PROTARCHUS:** I certainly have.

**SOCRATES:** But have you noticed the state of your soul when watching a comedy? Do you realize that there, also, we feel pain mixed with pleasure?

**PROTARCHUS:** I do not perfectly understand that.

**SOCRATES:** It is not at all easy, Protarchus, at such a time to understand what mixed passions possess the soul in every case of that kind.

**PROTARCHUS:** Not at all easy, I believe.

**SOCRATES:** However, let us consider what our feelings are at that time—and all the more carefully because of their obscurity—so that we may be able to discover with greater ease what mixture there is of pain and pleasure in other cases.

**PROTARCHUS:** Speak on, then.

**SOCRATES:** Regarding the passion known by the name of envy: will you classify it as a sort of pain in the soul, or something else?

**PROTARCHUS:** As a sort of pain.

**SOCRATES:** And yet the man who envies another will plainly appear to be delighted by the evils that befall his neighbor.

**PROTARCHUS:** Clearly so.

**SOCRATES:** Now, ignorance is an evil; and so is what we call a lack of sense.

**PROTARCHUS:** Undoubtedly.

**SOCRATES:** From these premises, you may perceive the nature of ridicule and the ridiculous.

**PROTARCHUS:** You must tell me what it is.

**SOCRATES:** Every particular vice takes its name from some particular bad habit in the soul. But total vice—the habit of wickedness in all respects—is the direct contrary of that habit which the Delphic inscription <note>The inscription at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi: *Gnothi Seauton*, or "Know Thyself."</note> advises us to acquire.

**PROTARCHUS:** Do you mean the habit of knowing oneself, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** I do. And the contrary to this advice of the oracle would be not to know oneself in any respect at all.

**PROTARCHUS:** Certainly it would.

**SOCRATES:** Try now to divide this ignorance of ourselves into three kinds.

**PROTARCHUS:** How, you say, should this be done? For I am not able to do it myself.

**SOCRATES:** Do you wish for me to make this division in your stead?

# THE PHILEBUS.

**PROTARCHUS:** I not only say it, but I desire you to do so.

**SOCRATES:** Well then: whoever is ignorant of himself, must he not be ignorant in one of these three respects?

**PROTARCHUS:** What three?

**SOCRATES:** First, regarding external possessions: in imagining himself wealthier than he really is.

**PROTARCHUS:** There are many people who suffer from this sort of ignorance.

**SOCRATES:** Yet even more numerous are those who imagine themselves handsomer, nobler in their posture, or blessed with some other physical advantage to a higher degree than they actually are.

**PROTARCHUS:** Very true.

**SOCRATES:** But by far the greatest number, I presume, are those who are mistaken about themselves regarding the third kind of excellence—that which belongs to the soul—by fancying themselves possessed of more virtue than they truly have.

**PROTARCHUS:** Nothing is more certain.

**SOCRATES:** Among the virtues and excellencies of the soul, is not wisdom the one that the majority of mankind claims with the greatest earnestness? And is it not the one about which they are most argumentative, stubborn, and full of false notions?

**PROTARCHUS:** Evidently so.

**SOCRATES:** Now, anyone who says that ignorance and error in any of these respects are evils would be telling the truth.

**PROTARCHUS:** Quite right.

**SOCRATES:** But we must make still another division of this self-ignorance, Protarchus, if we wish to discover the odd mixture of pain and pleasure in that "mirthful envy" <note>original: "mirthful envy"; Socrates is defining the specific emotion felt when watching comedy—a blend of the pain of envy and the pleasure of laughter.</note> which is excited by comedy.

**PROTARCHUS:** Into what two sorts do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** For those who foolishly hold such false opinions of themselves, it necessarily happens—as it does to all men in general—that strength and power attend some, while the fate of others is quite the contrary.

**PROTARCHUS:** It must be so.

**SOCRATES:** According to this difference between them, distinguish those...

<page-num>539</page-num>

# THE PHILEBUS.

...ignorant persons into two sorts. For all those whose self-ignorance is accompanied by weakness, and by a lack of power to get revenge on those who laugh at them, you may justly say that they are vulnerable to ridicule, and you may properly call their characters "ridiculous." But as for the others, who have the power to take their revenge, if you were to say that these people are to be dreaded—as being powerful and hostile—you would be giving a very accurate account of them. For such ignorance, when armed with power, is capable of doing great mischief; it is not only hostile and harmful to everyone within its reach, but the same is true of all its forms and representations. However, self-ignorance without strength or power is to be ranked among things that are ridiculous, and is a proper object of laughter.

**PROTARCHUS:** There is much truth in what you say. But I do not yet clearly perceive what mixture of pain and pleasure exists in our feelings on such occasions.

**SOCRATES:** You must, in the first place, understand the nature of envy in these cases.

**PROTARCHUS:** Explain it to me then.

**SOCRATES:** Is not sorrow, on some occasions, felt unjustly? And is it not the same with joy and pleasure?

**PROTARCHUS:** No doubt about it.

**SOCRATES:** There is neither injustice nor envy in rejoicing at the evils that befall our enemies. <note>Socrates is drawing a distinction between "just" joy (at an enemy's downfall) and the "unjust" joy of envy.</note>

**PROTARCHUS:** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES:** But if at any time, when we see an evil happening to our friends, we feel no sorrow—if, on the contrary, we rejoice at it—are we not guilty of injustice?

**PROTARCHUS:** Without dispute.

**SOCRATES:** Did we not say that it was an "evil" for any person to be ignorant of themselves?

**PROTARCHUS:** We did, and rightly so.

**SOCRATES:** If any of our friends have a false conceit <note>original: "conceit"; in this context, it means a deluded or excessively favorable opinion of oneself.</note> of their own wisdom, or of their own beauty, or of whatever else we mentioned when we divided self-ignorance into three kinds, is not this conceit an object of ridicule when it is accompanied by powerlessness and weakness? But an object—

# THE PHILEBUS.

...of hatred, if power and strength <gloss>¹</gloss> are joined with it? Or do we deny what I just now said—that having such a false opinion, if it is not hurtful to others, is an object of ridicule?

**PROTARCHUS:** You said what is entirely true.

**SOCRATES:** And do we not acknowledge this false conceit <note>original: "conceit," here meaning an erroneous self-opinion or notion</note> to be an evil, as it is built on ignorance?

**PROTARCHUS:** Most heartily.

**SOCRATES:** Do we feel delight or sorrow when we laugh at it?

**PROTARCHUS:** It is plain that we feel delight.

**SOCRATES:** Did we not say that whenever we feel delight from the evils that happen to our friends, it is envy which causes that unjust delight within us?

**PROTARCHUS:** It must be envy.

**SOCRATES:** Our reasoning then shows that when we laugh at what is ridiculous in a friend, mixing delight with envy in this way, we mix together pleasure and pain. For we acknowledged long ago that envy gives uneasiness and pain to the soul, and we have admitted that laughing yields delight. Now, in these cases, both of them arise at the same time.

**PROTARCHUS:** True.

**SOCRATES:** We see, then, from the conclusion of our argument, that in mournful spectacles—and no less in comedies, not only as they are acted on the stage but as they are presented to us also in the tragedy and comedy of real life and in a thousand intermediate occurrences—pains and pleasures are blended together.

**PROTARCHUS:** It would be impossible, Socrates, for a man not to acknowledge this, no matter how zealous an advocate he might be for the opposite side.

**SOCRATES:** When we entered on this subject, we proposed to consider anger, desire, and grief; fear and love; jealousy and envy; and other such passions of the soul. We promised ourselves that we would find in them those mixed feelings which we have been speaking of again and again; did we not?

**PROTARCHUS:** We did.

**SOCRATES:** Do we perceive that we have already finished everything relating to grief, envy, and anger?

**PROTARCHUS:** We perceive it clearly.

**SOCRATES:** But there is much yet remaining.

**PROTARCHUS:** Very true.

**SOCRATES:** For what reason, principally, do you suppose it was that I explained to you the mixed feeling which a comedy causes in us? Do you not realize that it was to show myself able to explain to you—with much more ease—the similar mixture of pain and pleasure in fear, in love, and in the other passions? I hoped that after you had seen the truth of it in one instance, you might excuse me from the necessity of proceeding to the rest, or of lengthening out the argument any further. I wanted you to accept it as a truth, without limitation or exception, that the body without the soul, and the soul without the body, and both together likewise, are full of a sense of pleasures mingled with pains in many things which affect them separately or jointly. Say, then, whether you will dismiss me now, or make it midnight before we finish. But I imagine that, after I have added a few things more, I shall obtain my dismissal from you; for I shall be ready to give you a full account of all these things tomorrow. At present, however, I am desirous of proceeding to what remains on this subject, so that we may come to a decision on the point in controversy, as *Philebus* has commanded <note>original: "enjoined"</note> us.

**PROTARCHUS:** You have spoken well, O Socrates; and as to what remains, go through with it in whatever way is agreeable to yourself.

**SOCRATES:** Well then: after the mixed pleasures, we are to proceed, by a kind of natural necessity, to the several pleasures which are unmixed and pure.

**PROTARCHUS:** Perfectly well said.

**SOCRATES:** I shall endeavor to explain the nature of these to you by adapting for my own use—with a little alteration—what is said of them by others. For I do not entirely believe those persons who tell us that all pleasure consists merely in a cessation from uneasiness and pain. But, as I said before, I make use of these persons as witnesses to confirm this truth—that there are some things which seem to be pleasures, but are by no means so in reality. I also use them to show that there are other pleasures—many and great in the imagination—which are accompanied by pains, but at the same time provide relief from greater pains amid the distresses of the body and of the soul.

**PROTARCHUS:** But what pleasures are those, O Socrates, which a man would be right to suppose are "true" pleasures?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates begins to distinguish "pure" pleasures from the "mixed" pleasures discussed previously. He is now defining what constitutes absolute beauty in shapes and colors.</meta>

<page-num>542</page-num>

# THE PHILEBUS.

**SOCRATES:** The pleasures produced in us by seeing beautiful colors and beautiful figures; many pleasures of smell, and many others arising from hearing sounds; in short, whatever pleasures we feel from perceiving the presence of anything whose absence we do not notice, or which at least causes us no pain—all these are unmixed and pure.

**PROTARCHUS:** How do you explain this general statement, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** The meaning is not immediately obvious, but we must try to make it clear. By "beautiful figures," I do not mean—as most people would suppose—the beauty of living forms or their statues. Instead, I mean the straight and the round: lines and circles, whether in flat surfaces <note>original: "surfaces" referring to rectilinear plane figures like triangles or rectangles</note> or in solid objects <note>original: "solids" referring to three-dimensional shapes like cubes or spheres</note>. I am referring to the kinds of shapes fashioned by a turner's lathe or a carpenter's tools using rules and squares. For the figures I mean—if you follow me—have no relative beauty <note>Beauty that depends on how well a thing functions or how it compares to others</note> like those other forms; they are, by their own nature, always absolutely beautiful. Beholding them gives us certain unique pleasures, not at all like the pleasures triggered by any kind of motion. As for colors, I mean those that possess the same quality of absolute beauty and yield pleasures of a specific nature. Do we understand these things? Or what do we say to them?

---

<note>original: "Of pleasures, says Olympiodorus..."</note> According to the philosopher Olympiodorus, pleasures that cause intense agitation are those accompanied by pain. Only "energetic" pleasures are pure, seen when a perfect living being is actively functioning. Furthermore, pure physical pleasures include things like seeing balanced light; pleasures of the soul result from contemplating pure ideas; and pleasures belonging to both body and soul include things like health, where the soul rejoices in a movement that starts in the mind and descends to the body. —T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the translator</note>

<note>original: "That is, rectilinear plane figures..."</note> These include straight-lined shapes like triangles and rectangles, as well as circles. —S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, who began this translation</note>

<note>original: "Such as pyramids and cubes..."</note> Examples include pyramids, cubes, spheres, cylinders, and cones. —S.

<note>original: "The parts of every mathematical simple figure..."</note> The parts of every simple mathematical figure are all similar and can be measured by the same standard. In contrast, the beauty of animals arises from the proportions of different, unequal parts, which are measured by how well they serve their biological purpose. —S.

<note>original: "Such as the beautiful colours of many flowers..."</note> Examples include the colors of flowers or a clear morning sky. This is different from the color of a person's complexion or skin, which is only "relatively" agreeable because it indicates health or purity of blood in that specific species. —S.

**PROTARCHUS:** I am trying, Socrates, to understand your full meaning, but please go on and explain the whole of it thoroughly.

**SOCRATES:** Regarding sounds, I am referring to those that are smooth, clear, and resonant <note>original: "canorous"—meaning melodic or ringing</note>, which produce a pure and simple melody ¹. These are not beautiful in relation to any other sounds, but are musical in and of themselves. I am speaking of these and the inherent <note>original: "connatural"—existing as a natural part of something</note> pleasures that accompany them.

**PROTARCHUS:** I certainly agree that such pleasures exist.

**SOCRATES:** The pleasures we feel from certain scents are, admittedly, of a less "divine" kind than the pleasures of sound I just mentioned. However, because they are equally pure and do not necessarily involve any pain, I categorize them all together. For in any pleasure where we find this quality of being entirely free from pain, I contrast it with those other pleasures that are mixed with distress. Now, if you notice, we have already identified two different types of pleasure.

**PROTARCHUS:** I see that.

**SOCRATES:** To these, let us now add the pleasures found in the mathematical sciences. We should include these unless we believe that such pleasures must be preceded by a "thirst" or painful desire to learn them, or that once they are enjoyed, they create a new thirst for more, so that the entire process of learning is accompanied by discomfort.

**PROTARCHUS:** I do not think such discomfort is necessary at all.

**SOCRATES:** Well, then, suppose that after we have fully mastered these sciences, we happen to lose some part of that knowledge through forgetfulness. Do you see any distress arising from that?

**PROTARCHUS:** Not from the nature of the knowledge itself. However, when that knowledge is needed for some practical use in life, a person might feel distressed at having lost it because it would have been useful.

**SOCRATES:** But at this moment, my friend, we are only concerned with the feelings that arise in us from the nature of the knowledge itself, regardless of how useful it might be for calculation or measurement.

**PROTARCHUS:** You are right then to say that in mathematical knowledge, we often forget things without it causing us any inherent pain.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue as Socrates transitions from identifying pure pleasures (like those of math and science) to analyzing their metaphysical categories—specifically whether they belong to the "boundless" or the "measured" genus.</meta>

<page-num>544</page-num>
<header>THE PHILEBUS.</header>
<meta>catchword: Soc.</meta>

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must acknowledge that these pleasures—the pleasures of science <note>original: "science"—referring here to knowledge or systematic study</note>—are unmixed with pain. However, these pleasures do not belong to the common crowd <note>original: "vulgar multitude"</note>; they are enjoyed only by a very few.

**PROTARCHUS:** That must certainly be acknowledged.

**SOCRATES:** Now that we have distinguished fairly well between pure pleasures and those rightly called impure, let us add another distinction. Intense <note>original: "vehement"</note> pleasures lack moderation and measure. On the other hand, gentler pleasures possess measure and are moderate. 

Qualities like greatness, intensity, and their opposites—as well as how often or rarely they repeat—belong only to pleasures of the "boundless" category <note>original: "boundless genus"—referring to the *apeiron*, or that which lacks inherent limits and is defined by "more or less"</note>. This category is constantly changing in its amount and movement through both the body and the soul. Conversely, pleasures that do not experience these variations belong to the opposite category; they are connected to everything that possesses symmetry.

**PROTARCHUS:** Perfectly right, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Besides these classifications, we should distinguish pleasures in another way.

**PROTARCHUS:** How?

**SOCRATES:** We should consider whether the purity and simplicity of pleasures reveal what true pleasure is, or whether the truth of pleasure is better known from its intensity, quantity, size, and abundance.

**PROTARCHUS:** What is your goal, Socrates, in suggesting we consider this?

**SOCRATES:** I want to ensure we overlook nothing that might clarify the nature of pleasure and knowledge. I want to discover whether some kinds of each are pure while others are impure. By examining what is pure and simple in both, you, I, and this whole group may more easily form a correct judgment.

**PROTARCHUS:** Very well said.

**SOCRATES:** Well then, let us consider all the things we commonly call "pure" in the following way. But first, let us choose one of them as an example to study.

**PROTARCHUS:** Which one would you like us to choose?
