# THE SECOND ALCIBIADES

---

->*PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE*<-

->SOCRATES, ALCIBIADES.<-

->SCENE.—*The path to the* TEMPLE *of* ZEUS <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>¹<-

---

->SOCRATES.<-

**A**LCIBIADES! Are you going to the temple to offer your prayers to the God?

ALCIBIADES. Your guess is perfectly right, Socrates.

---

¹ In Athens, there were two buildings built in honor of Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>. One of these was a most magnificent temple called the Olympium <note>The Olympion, one of the largest temples in the ancient world.</note>, situated in the lower city. The other was only a small shrine in the upper city <note>The Acropolis</note>, dedicated to <term>Zeus the Savior</term> <note>original: Ζευς ὁ σωτηρ (Zeus ho soter)</note>, and located next to another shrine dedicated to <term>Athena the Savior</term> <note>original: Αθηνα ἡ σωτειρα (Athena he soteira)</note>, the protector of Athens. Both these shrines stood at the entrance of the treasury—likely one on each side—acting as guardians of the public money. This treasury was located at the back of the beautiful temple of Athena <note>original: "Minerva"</note> known as the Parthenon. 

If Socrates had met Alcibiades on the ascent leading first to the Parthenon and then to the shrines behind it, there would be no reason for him to assume Alcibiades was going to pray to Zeus rather than to Athena, the patron deity of Athens. However, Plato’s use of the masculine article <term>the</term> <note>original: τον (ton)</note> before the noun <term>God</term> <note>original: θεον (theon)</note> prevents us from thinking that Athena was intended here. In Athens, while Athena was referred to as <term>the Goddess</term> <note>original: ἡ θεος (he theos)</note> by way of eminence, Zeus was called either simply <term>God</term> or <term>the God</term>, as the supreme deity. 

In addition to this, we should note that in the shrine of Zeus in the upper city, he was worshipped in a specific role: as the protector of his followers during dangers from which they had already escaped. This is suggested by his title "Savior" and is clearly proven by the play *Plutus* by Aristophanes (Act 5, Scene 2) and the speech of Lycurgus against Leocrates (pages 168 and 253 in Taylor's edition). Now, there is no evidence that Alcibiades had recently escaped any great danger or was going to offer a thanksgiving sacrifice, as was common on such occasions. From all this, we can reasonably conclude that the scene of this dialogue takes place on a street leading to the Temple of Olympian Zeus in the lower city. —S. <note>“S.” likely refers to the translator/commentator Thomas Sydenham.</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates begins to categorize human states of mind. He previously established that insanity is the opposite of a sound mind; now, he leads Alcibiades through a logical exercise to determine if "understanding" and "lack of understanding" are mutually exclusive categories, similar to health and sickness.</meta>

**ALC.** I am.
**SOC.** Come, then, let us consider what sort of men these are. You have admitted that there are men who lack <note>original: "want"</note> understanding, men who do not lack it, and other men, you say, who are insane.
**ALC.** True.
**SOC.** Furthermore; are there not some men in a good state of health?
**ALC.** There are.
**SOC.** And are there not others in a bad state of health?
**ALC.** Certainly.
**SOC.** These, then, are not the same men as those.
**ALC.** Not at all.
**SOC.** Tell me now, are there any men who are in neither of those states?
**ALC.** Certainly none.
**SOC.** For every man must necessarily <note>original: "of necessity"</note> either *have* good health, or *lack* good health.
**ALC.** I think so too.
**SOC.** Well: do you think the same way regarding the possession of understanding and the lack of understanding?
**ALC.** How do you mean?
**SOC.** Do you think it is necessary$^1$ that a man should either *have* or *lack* a good understanding? Or is there, besides these, some third and middle state in which a man neither *has* nor *lacks* a good understanding?
**ALC.** There certainly is not.
**SOC.** Every man, then, must necessarily be in either one or the other of those two conditions.
**ALC.** So it seems to me.

$^1$ In all the printed editions of the Greek, we read here: *Dokei soi hoion te einai* <note>original Greek: Δοκει σοι οἱον τε ειναι</note>, which means, "Do you think it is possible," etc. And Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius (1500–1558), a German humanist translator</note>, as if he found this reading in the Hessenstein manuscript, translates it into Latin as: *Videtur tibi fieri posse* <note>original Latin: "It seems to you possible to happen"</note>, etc. Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin</note> and Stephens <note>Henri Estienne (1528–1598), the famous printer whose pagination is still used for Plato today</note> translate it as if they had read in their manuscripts: *Dokei soi dein einai* <note>original Greek: Δοκει σοι δειν ειναι</note>, meaning, "Do you think that a man ought to be," etc. Neither of these readings can be correct, because they both make this logical <note>original: "dialectical"</note> question seem foolish as well as irrelevant; and because either of them ruins the argument. To make the conclusion in the next sentence of Socrates logical and final, we must read it here as: *Dokei soi anankaion einai* <note>original Greek: Δοκει σοι αναγκαιον ειναι</note>, meaning "Do you think it is necessary," as we have assumed in this translation. The necessity of making this correction <note>original: "emendation"</note> in the Greek text was also seen by Dacier <note>André Dacier (1651–1722), a French classical scholar</note>, as appears from his French translation.—S. <note>This "S" refers to Thomas Sydenham, the 18th-century translator.</note>

<header>THE SECOND ALCIBIADES.</header>

**SOC.** Do you remember admitting that insanity is the opposite of a sound mind?
**ALC.** I do.
**SOC.** And do you remember admitting this also: that there is no middle or third state where a person neither *has* nor *lacks* <note>original: "wants"</note> a good understanding?
**ALC.** I admitted that as well.
**SOC.** But how can two different things be the opposite of the same thing?
**ALC.** That is not possible at all.
**SOC.** Therefore, a lack of understanding and insanity are likely the same thing.
**ALC.** It appears so.
**SOC.** If we then declared that all fools were madmen $^1$, we would be speaking correctly, Alcibiades.
**ALC.** We would.
**SOC.** First, consider those your own age—if any of them happen to be fools, as indeed many are—and some of your elders too; we must declare all of them to be madmen. For consider: do you not believe that in this city there are only a few wise men, but a multitude of fools, whom you call madmen?
**ALC.** I am of that opinion.
**SOC.** Can you imagine, then, that we could live with any ease or comfort in a city filled with so many madmen? Would we not have suffered from them long ago? Would we not have been hit, pelted, and faced all the other mischief that madmen are accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to commit? But consider, my good friend, whether our actual situation is different.
**ALC.** What then is the truth of the matter, Socrates, regarding the masses? For it is not likely to be what I just now imagined.

---

$^1$ The Stoic philosophers adopted from Socrates their famous paradox that "all fools are mad" <note>original Greek: παντας τους αφρονας μαινεσθαι</note>. This is an accurate observation made by Cicero in his *Tusculan Disputations* <note>original: Tuscul. Disputat. l. iii. § 5</note>. Dr. Davis, in his notes on that work, proves its accuracy by referring to this specific passage in Plato.—S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, the 18th-century translator</note>

**SOC.** I don't think it is so myself. But we should consider it in a way like this.
**ALC.** In what way do you mean?
**SOC.** I will tell you. We assume that there are some men who are unwell; do we not?
**ALC.** Certainly we do.
**SOC.** Do you think it necessary, then, that every man who is unwell must have the gout, or a fever, or an inflammation of the eyes <term>ophthalmy</term>? Do you not think that a man might be ill with something else, without suffering from any of those specific diseases? For we suppose that diseases are of many various kinds, and not just those few.
**ALC.** I suppose they are.
**SOC.** Do you not think that every inflammation of the eyes is a disease?
**ALC.** I do.
**SOC.** And do you think, therefore, that every disease is an inflammation of the eyes?
**ALC.** Not at all. Yet I am still at a loss as to what you mean.
**SOC.** But if you will give me your attention as we consider the matter together, we shall come close to finding the truth.
**ALC.** I am giving you, Socrates, all the attention I am capable of.
**SOC.** Did we not agree that every inflammation of the eyes was a disease, though not every disease is an inflammation of the eyes?
**ALC.** We did.
**SOC.** And I think we were right to agree. For all people who have a fever have a disease; however, not everyone who has a disease has a fever. Likewise, they do not all have the gout, nor do they all have an inflammation of the eyes. Every condition of this kind $^2$ is a disease; but those whom we call physicians say that diseases differ in their effects on the human body. For

---

$^1$ We have no single word in our language to denote that disease of the eyes called by the Greek physicians *ophthalmia* <note>original: ὀφθαλμία</note>, the word used here by Plato. They meant by it a watery inflammation of the eyes, or a discharge of fluids onto them, which in Latin is called *lippitudo* <note>original: "lippitudo," meaning eye-soreness or bleary eyes</note>.—S.

$^2$ That is, every persistent physical illness; whether the whole body suffers from it throughout, as in a fever; or whether it is located in a specific organ or part used for movement, as in the gout; or a part used for sensation, as in an inflammation of the eyes. Plato is always incredibly precise and often, as he is here, scientifically sound in his choice of metaphors and examples—which he only uses when necessary to illustrate his subject. In this style of writing on intellectual or abstract subjects, we know of no writer who is his equal.—S.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 592, where Socrates uses the analogy of various diseases to explain that although "folly" (lack of understanding) manifests in different ways—such as madness or simple-mindedness—it remains a single category of mental deficiency, just as different crafts (like shoemaking or sculpting) all fall under the category of "workmanship."</meta>

<page-num>593</page-num>
<header>THE SECOND ALCIBIADES.</header>

Not all diseases are alike, nor are they all accompanied by the same symptoms; rather, each operates with a power peculiar to itself, and yet they are all still diseases. It is just the same with respect to workmen; for we agree that some men are workmen, do we not? ¹

**Alc.** Certainly we do.

**Soc.** Such as shoemakers, smiths, sculptors <note>original: statuaries</note>, and a great multitude of others whom it is unnecessary to list individually. All of these have different types of workmanship divided among them, and they are all workmen. However, they are not all smiths, nor shoemakers, nor sculptors indiscriminately all at once. In the same way, folly is divided among men. Those who have the largest share of it, we call madmen; those who have a slightly smaller portion, we call senseless and stunned ²; but if we choose to speak of these in gentler terms, some of us say they are "magnanimous" ³ <term>great-souled</term>; others call them simpletons; and others again call them harmless, inexperienced in the world, or speechless ⁴. You will also find, if you reflect, many other names given to them besides these. But they are all comprised under the general term of folly or lack of understanding. There is, however, a difference between them, just as one art differs from another, or one disease from another. Or does the case seem different to you?

**Alc.** To me, it seems exactly as you represent it.

**Soc.** This point, therefore, being settled, let us return to where we were. For it was proposed, I think, at the beginning of our inquiry, to be

² In the Greek, the word is *embrontetous* <note>original: εμβροντητους</note>, literally translated as "thunder-stricken." The effect of lightning (when accompanied by thunder), and indeed of all celestial or electrical fire, is to stupify—at least for a time—whatever animal it strikes.—S.

³ This euphemism <term>a mild or indirect word used in place of one considered too harsh</term> is applied jokingly or in good humor to men who lack sense or understanding in the common affairs of human life. ## THE SECOND ALCIBIADES.

...we have considered which kinds of men lacked <note>original: "wanted"</note> understanding, and which were men of good understanding. For it was agreed that there were some of each sort. Was it not?

**Alc.** It was so agreed.

**Soc.** Then, do you suppose that those people have a good understanding who know how they should act and what they should say?

**Alc.** I do.

**Soc.** And what people do you consider to be lacking in understanding? Are they not those who are ignorant in both those cases?

**Alc.** These very people.

**Soc.** Then will these people, who are ignorant of what they should do and what they should say, both say and do what they should not, without even being aware of it?

**Alc.** It appears so.

**Soc.** Well then, Alcibiades, I said that Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus famously cursed his sons to die by each other's hands, a prayer born of madness and rage rather than "good understanding."</note> was this sort of person. And you may find many in our own times who, though they are not seized with sudden anger as he was, yet pray for things that are harmful to themselves; they do not suspect any evil in them, and imagine they are nothing but good. Oedipus, indeed, as he did not wish for anything good, did not imagine the thing he prayed for to be good either. But there are some others whose minds are in a state quite contrary to that of Oedipus. For in my opinion, if the God to whom you are going to offer your prayers should appear to you and—before you had even made any petition to him—should ask you: "Would your desires be satisfied with you becoming tyrant <term>a despotic or absolute ruler</term> of Athens?" And if you held this favor cheap, and thought it no great gift, he should add further: "And tyrant of all Greece?" And if he should perceive that you still deemed it too little for you, unless you were tyrant¹ of all Europe, he should promise you that also; and not merely promise, but make you so immediately on the spot, if you were in a hurry to have all the Europeans acknowledge Alcibiades, the son of Clinias, for their lord and master—in this case, it is my opinion that you would walk away full of joy, as if the greatest good had befallen you.

**Alc.** I believe, Socrates, that I would; and so would any other man whatever, if he had met with such an adventure.

***

¹ The word *tyrant*, everywhere in Plato's writings, signifies a despotic or absolute monarch.—S.

**Soc.** You would not, however, accept absolute power <note>original: "absolute dominion"</note> over the estates and persons of all the Greeks and barbarians <note>In the ancient world, "Barbarians" referred to anyone who did not speak Greek.</note> together, on the condition of giving your life in exchange for it.

**Soc.** You see, then, how dangerous it is either to recklessly accept power when offered, or to wish and pray for it yourself. A man may suffer great harm, or even the total loss of his life, by possessing it. In confirmation of this, we could mention many people who longed for tyranny <term>absolute power or rule by a single person who is not bound by law</term> and labored to obtain it, as if some great good were to be enjoyed from it; but having obtained it, they were forced to part with their very lives due to plots and conspiracies intended to deprive them of power. 

Indeed, I suppose it cannot have escaped your own hearing what happened just yesterday: Archelaus, the tyrant of the Macedonians, was murdered by his favorite. This favorite was no less fond of the tyranny than the tyrant was of him. He imagined that by obtaining the tyranny himself, he would be made a happy man; but after he had held that power for only three or four days, he was, in his turn, secretly murdered by others who had conspired against him. 

Amongst our own fellow citizens also, you see—for we have not heard this from the report of others, but have been eyewitnesses of it ourselves—that of those who succeeded in their ambition to command our armies, some were banished¹, and still live in exile from the city to this day; others lost their lives²; and even those who seem to have fared the best, having gone through many terrifying dangers³ in their campaigns...

And yet, despite the evidence of these and many other similar cases, it is rare to find a person who would refuse these "gifts of fortune" if they were offered, or who would refrain from praying for them if they could be obtained through prayer. Few men would reject even a tyranny <term>absolute rule by a single person, often obtained by force</term> if it were offered to them, or the chief command of an army, or many other things which often bring more mischief than benefit to the possessor. And to me, Alcibiades, it seems probable that some wise man or other—happening to be acquainted with certain persons who lacked understanding and observing them to pursue and pray for things that it would be better for them to remain without, but which appeared good to them—composed a common prayer for their use <gloss>1</gloss>. > Sovereign of Nature! grant us what is good,
> Whether or not it is the subject of our prayers;
> And from your petitioners, whatever is evil,
> Though we supplicate for it, still turn away.

Now, in this prayer, it seems to me that the poet says what is right, and that whoever makes use of it runs no risk. But if you have anything to say against it, speak your mind.

**SOC.** The man who clears you of any intent to have acted in that manner,

---

<note>
The part of Orestes' story alluded to here is well-known to those familiar with Greek literature from the *Libation Bearers* <term>original: Χοηφόροι (*Choephoroe*)</term> by Aeschylus, the *Electra* by Sophocles, and the *Electra* by Euripides. For the story of Alcmæon, we refer the reader to the ancient commentaries <term>original: "Scholia"</term> on Homer's *Odyssey*, book 11, verse 326 <note>original: "lib. xi. v. 326"</note>; or to Servius's commentary on Virgil's *Aeneid*, book 6, verse 445 <note>original: "lib. vi. v. 445"</note>. It is told in more detail by Apollodorus in book 3, chapters 6 and 7 <note>original: "lib. iii. cap. 6 and 7"</note>. 

However, in case some readers are unfamiliar with the history of ancient Greece, they should know that Orestes and Alcmæon committed the terrible crime of murdering their own mothers. They did this out of a mistaken sense of family duty and an ignorance of the limits of what one owes a father. 

Orestes was the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra. His mother, while his father was away at the siege of Troy, had an affair with Aegisthus, Agamemnon's first cousin <note>original: "cousin-german"</note>. When her husband returned home after the destruction of Troy, she and her lover murdered him. This was later avenged by his children; for Orestes, at the encouragement of his sister Electra, killed the adulterous couple together. 

Alcmæon was the son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle. This woman betrayed her husband into a situation where he was certain to lose his life. Knowing how she had acted and predicting the outcome, he ordered his son Alcmæon to avenge his death by killing Eriphyle. 

In neither of these cases cited here by Plato does there appear to be any malice in the young princes against their mothers; there was no spirit of revenge for personal injuries done to them, no greed for wealth or power—in short, no selfish passion or appetite at all. Their only intention was to perform what they imagined was a duty to their fathers, by carrying out a type of justice on their mothers that was not theirs to execute. It appears that both of these unhappy princes committed such an unnatural act because of mistaken ideas about duty, justice, and honor—that is, through a lack of moral wisdom or true foresight <note>original: "prudence"</note>. We believe, therefore, that Plato's point in this passage is to prove—using these tragic examples of the fatal effects of ignorance regarding the laws of nature and reason—the necessity of studying moral science to act rightly and be happy.—S.
</note>

**ALCIBIADES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** Observe then, if you can, how we proceed in this argument. You call some men wise and others foolish.

**ALCIBIADES.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Don't you call the many "foolish" and the few "wise"?

**ALCIBIADES.** Just so.

**SOCRATES.** And don’t you give these different labels <note>original: "epithets"</note> to these two types of people because of something in which they differ?

**ALCIBIADES.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Would you call a man wise who knows how to lecture <note>original: "harangue"</note> the people on those subjects of debate we mentioned, but does not know what advice is the best in general, or what is best for the present occasion?

->[This note continues from the previous page, discussing a missing phrase in the Greek text]<-

...wanting the words "it seemed to us" <note>original: εδοκει ἡμιν</note>; unless Plato purposely omitted them, thinking it unnecessary to repeat them after they had been expressed in the question immediately preceding. There remains yet another fault in this sentence: the word "us" <note>original: ἡμας</note>, a word which the grammatical construction by no means admits. If our conjectural correction of this sentence, which we now offer to the learned, should appear to be a just one, it will appear at the same time, on examination, that all the faults in the printed version are owing originally to a mere *transposition* of some of the words while copying it. This is an error frequently found in ancient manuscripts, and the cause of those many additional errors, in both printed and written copies, which were afterwards committed with the intention of "correcting" the first error. The proposed reading is this: "Therefore, if someone does what he knows, and it follows that he knows what is beneficial, [or 'it follows that he has knowledge of the best,' as Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian scholar who translated Plato into Latin</note> and Grynaeus <note>Simon Grynaeus (1493–1541), a German scholar and theologian</note> seem to have read], it seemed to us that it would be profitable for the state and for himself." <note>original: Ουκουν, καν μεν πραττη ἁ τις οιδε, παρεπεται δε ειδεναι το ωφελιμον, [οτ παρεπεται δε ἡ του βελτιστου επιστημη, as Ficinus and Grynæus ſeem to have read,] εδοκει ἡμιν, λυσιτελουντως εξειν τη πολει, και αυτον αὑτῳ.</note> — **S.** <note>The "S." refers to the translator and commentator Thomas Sydenham.</note>

It clearly refers to the passage mentioned in the last note. The sense of it must therefore be the same as that one. To express this sense exactly, we believe we should read it as follows: "But if ignorance [of the beneficial follows], the opposite of these things..." <note>original: ’Εαν δ’ αγνοια [sc. του ωφελιμου παρεπεται], ταναντια τουτων, κ. τ. λ.</note>. And, in the same way, if a man has acquired what is called "great learning" and many skills <note>original: "arts"</note> but lacks this specific knowledge, and is driven along by all those other things, will he not meet with—and quite deservedly—a very stormy <note>original: "tempestuous"</note> voyage? All the difficulty vanishes with this slight rearrangement and an easy change of "not before" <note>original: μὴ πρότερον</note> to "more violently" <note>original: λαβρότερον</note>—a word perhaps mistaken by the scribe to whom it was read, because he was not as thoroughly well-versed in the language of Homer as a man must be before he can everywhere understand the language of Plato. it will not be long <gloss>1</gloss> before he perishes. So, I think that the verse where the poet speaks of someone to disparage them is very applicable to such a person:

> He knew much, and had skill in many things;
> But whatever things he knew, he knew them poorly.

**ALC.** How, Socrates, does this verse of the poet relate to what we are speaking about? To me, it seems nothing to the purpose.

**Soc.** It is very much to the purpose. But you must know that almost all poets write enigmatically <note>riddle-like or in puzzles</note>, and this poet especially so. For it is the nature of poetry in general to use enigmatic language, and it is not for any ordinary person to understand it. But when, in addition to this difficulty, that enigmatic poetic genius takes hold of a man who is reluctant to share his knowledge—unwilling to tell us plainly what he means and desiring to hide his wisdom from the world <gloss>2</gloss> as much as possible—it becomes extremely difficult to find the real meaning of any such poet. For you certainly cannot think that Homer <gloss>3</gloss>—as divine a poet as he was—could be ignorant of how impossible it was for a man who possessed any knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> at all not to know it well. But I suppose he expresses himself enigmatically by using, instead of the word *evil* <gloss>4</gloss>, the phrase *to know*.

<gloss>1</gloss> In the Greek, "not a long life of the gods." Stephens <note>Henri Estienne, a famous 16th-century printer and scholar</note> proposes that "life of the gods" should be read for the last two words. We accept his proposal of reading "life," but suspect the correct reading of the very last word is actually "lives." — S. <note>The "S." refers to Floyer Sydenham, the 18th-century translator of this text.</note>

<gloss>2</gloss> From this passage, it appears what opinion either Plato himself or other learned men of his time held regarding Homer as a philosopher. For he represents the great poet as possessing profound knowledge which he thought proper and prudent to hide from the masses. Therefore, he made the discovery of it difficult on purpose, so that only those whose nature led them to philosophy—and whose wealth allowed them to follow it—might be able to discover it in his writings. — S.

<gloss>3</gloss> We see that the ancient poem titled *Margites* (named after its hero and containing the verse cited above) is expressly attributed to Homer by Plato here. It is also attributed to him by Aristotle in his *Poetics* (Chapter 4) and in his *Nicomachean Ethics* (Book 6, Chapter 7). For information on which ancient writers agreed or disagreed with this opinion, see Fabricius’s *Greek Library* <note>original: "Fabricii Bibliothecâ Græcâ"</note>, book 2, chapter 2, section 24. — S.

<gloss>4</gloss> In the Greek phrase "instead of the evil," we suspect the right reading to be "instead of the noun EVIL," just as "instead of knowing" refers to the infinitive and original verb "TO KNOW." — S.

<summary>Socrates quotes a poem (attributed here to Homer) to argue that knowing many things is useless, or even harmful, if one knows them "ill." He explains that poets often hide deep philosophical truths behind riddles and wordplay to ensure only the wise can uncover them.</summary>

the derivative words, *badly* <note>original: "ill"</note>, and *he knew*¹. If we then use the two proper root words, a sentence is formed in plain prose that expresses the poet’s meaning: *He was knowledgeable and skilled in many things, but to know all those things was an evil to him.* It is evident then, that if much knowledge was an evil to him, the knowledge he had was worthless, and he himself was a worthless person—assuming any credit is due to the conclusions of our previous arguments.

**ALC.** And I think they deserve that credit, Socrates; for I could hardly believe any other rational conclusions if I denied these.

**Soc.** And you are right to think so. But in the name of Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, let us continue. You see how great the difficulties are in the subject we are discussing; you also see the nature of those difficulties. It seems to me that you share in them yourself, as you never stop changing your mind over and over again on this subject—discarding the opinions you previously embraced so passionately and no longer remaining in the same mindset. If the god to whom you are going to pray should appear to you now, after all our conclusions, and ask you—before you had even made a request—whether your desires would be satisfied if you obtained any of those kingdoms <note>original: "dominions"</note> mentioned at the start of our argument, or if he should leave it to you to name what you wished for, how do you think you could best use this opportunity? Would you accept one of the offered grants, or would you name something else you wanted?

**ALC.** By the gods, Socrates, I wouldn't know what to say to such a proposal. Truly, I think it would be rash for me to give any final answer at all. Great caution is absolutely necessary in such a case to prevent a person from praying unintentionally for evil things while imagining them to be good—and from doing as you said, soon afterward taking back his choice and praying to be delivered from what he had previously prayed to receive.

---

¹ We have here an example of Plato’s unusual skill in philosophical or universal grammar. It is evident not only from his deriving the adverb *kakos* <note>original: ΚΑΚΩΣ</note>, meaning "badly" or "ill," from the noun *kakon* <note>original: ΚΑΚΟΝ</note>, meaning "evil," but also from his deriving *epistato* <note>original: ΗΠΙΣΤΑΤΟ</note>, meaning "he knew" (a verb in the indicative mood), from the infinitive or most general verb form *epistasthai* <note>original: ’ΕΠΙΣΤΑΣΘΑΙ</note>, meaning "to know." This shows a much deeper theory of words as parts of speech. See James Harris’s *Hermes* <note>A famous 1751 treatise on universal grammar</note>, book 1, chapters 11 and 8.—S. <note>Presumably the translator, Floyer Sydenham</note>

**Soc.** Didn't the poet I quoted at the start of this discussion know more than we do, when he asked Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note> to protect us from evil, even if we were the ones asking for it?

**Alc.** Indeed, I think so.

**Soc.** Therefore, Alcibiades, the Lacedaemonians <note>term: people from Sparta</note>—either because they admired and imitated this poet, or perhaps because they had independently considered the matter the same way—offer a prayer similar to his, both in private and in public. They ask the gods to grant them whatever good things are also beautiful; and they were never heard to pray for anything more than that. As a result, no people have been more prosperous than they have up to now. And if they have not succeeded in everything, it was not because they prayed wrongly; rather, I assume the gods have the choice to either grant a man what he asks for or send the exact opposite. I’d like to tell you something else about this that I once heard from some elderly men—that during the conflicts between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians, it so happened that whenever they fought a battle by land or sea, our city was always unsuccessful and could never achieve a single victory. The Athenians, troubled by these failures and unsure of what plan to use to end their pressing misfortunes, held a council and decided that their best course of action would be to send messengers to Ammon <note>term: The Oracle of Ammon, located in an Egyptian oasis, was dedicated to the god Amun, whom the Greeks identified with Zeus.</note> and consult him on what to do. They also asked him why the gods always give victory to their enemies, the Spartans, rather than to them—even though, as they said, "Of all the Greeks, we offer the gods the greatest number of sacrifices, and the finest of their kind; and though we, more than any other people, have decorated their temples with offerings hung within them; and in honor of the gods have conducted the most solemn and the

---

¹ <note>The oracle of Ammon was highly celebrated for the truth of its predictions. In ancient times, it was consulted by Hercules and Perseus. Long afterward, it was consulted by Croesus when he was planning to stop the advance of Cyrus’s armies in Asia. We learn how much the Romans revered it from the ninth book of Lucan. And from this passage in Plato, as well as from the biographies of Lysander, Cimon, and Alexander in Plutarch, it appears that among the Greeks of those days, it was as popular and trusted as any of their own oracles. —**S.**</note>

...most costly, and have paid the gods more money than all the rest of the Greeks combined. Meanwhile, the Lacedaemonians <note>term: Spartans</note>, the Athenians said, never care about any of these things. On the contrary, they worship the gods in such a casual manner that their sacrifices usually consist of animals with physical flaws; in every other way, the Athenians claimed, the Spartans are far inferior to us in honoring the gods—even though the wealth they possess is no less than ours. 

When the ambassadors had finished speaking and had asked the Oracle what they should do to end their current misfortunes, the prophet gave no answer other than this (for undoubtedly the god would not allow more). Sending for the Athenian ambassadors, he spoke these words: "This is what Ammon says: he says that he prefers the pious prayers <note>original: "addresses"</note> of the Lacedaemonians to all the sacrifices of all the Greeks." 

The prophet spoke these words and nothing more. Now, it seems to me that by "pious prayers," the god means only that specific prayer of theirs. And it is indeed far superior to the prayers of any other people. For the rest of the Greeks, after they have either led oxen with gilded horns to the altar or brought expensive offerings and gifts to hang in the temples, pray for whatever they happen to want, whether it is actually good or evil. Therefore, when the gods hear these impious prayers, they do not accept their costly processions, sacrifices, and gifts. 

So it seems to me that great caution and thought are required on this subject: what is appropriate to say to the gods, and what is not. You will also find sentiments in Homer similar to those I have been expressing. He tells us that the Trojans, on a certain night when they were camped outside the city walls,

> Sweet fragrant <note>original: "odorif'rous"</note> smoke; yet by the Gods
> Rejected, and the savory taste refused.
> For strong aversion in their holy minds
> Was rooted, against Troy's doomed <note>original: "devoted," meaning marked for destruction</note> towers,
> Against the injurious power of Troy's proud king,
> And against the Trojan people, who withheld

It was of no benefit, therefore, it seems, for them to sacrifice or to offer presents to the Gods whom they had made their enemies. For the divine nature, I assume, is not of such a kind as to be seduced by presents, like those whose trade it is to make the most of their money and who do not care by what means they are enriched. Besides, we argue very foolishly in our complaints to the Gods if we think to get the better of the Lacedaemonians <note>term: Spartans</note> by such arguments. For it would be a sad thing indeed if the Gods regarded our presents and our sacrifices and not the disposition of the soul when a religious and just man addressed them. 

In fact, in my opinion, they have much more regard for the soul than they have for those pompous processions and costly sacrifices. For nothing prevents any people, whether private individuals or civil states, from being well able to pay the Gods such a tribute every year, even if they have sinned against the Gods and against men ever so greatly. But because the Gods cannot be bribed, they disdain all that outward worship, as the divine Oracle says, and as the Prophet of the Gods also says. It seems, therefore, that justice and prudence are honored above all things by the Gods—and by men too, at least those who have good sense and understanding. Now, the prudent and the just are simply those who know what behavior and what speech is proper to use in our interactions, whether with gods or with men. But I would be glad to hear from you what your thoughts are on this subject.

---

...of that poet. Plato is forced to take this sentence quite out of its poetic meter here because he is relating it only at second hand; he is repeating what Homer said, whereas Homer himself puts the narration immediately into the mouth of the Muse. For the same reason, we have given a prose translation of it. In the preceding line, as well as in those which follow, Plato was able to preserve the meter while he only changed the indicative verbs into infinitive forms. — S. <note>likely Thomas Sydenham, the translator</note>

**ALC.** For my part, I am of the same opinion as you, Socrates, and the Oracle. And indeed it would ill become me to vote against the judgment of the God.

**SOC.** Do you not remember that you acknowledged you were much at a loss concerning prayer? You feared you might unintentionally pray for evil things, imagining them to be good.

**ALC.** I do remember it.

**SOC.** You perceive then, that it is not safe for you to go and make your prayer at the temple as you intended, lest your addresses should happen to be impious, and the God, hearing them, should wholly reject your sacrifice—and you perhaps should draw some further evil upon your own head. It seems to me, therefore, that your best way is to be quiet. Because of your "magnanimity" <note>Socrates is likely using this term ironically here to mean "high-minded pride" or "presumption."</note> (that fairest of names given to folly), I suppose you would not be willing to use the Spartan <note>original: "Lacedæmonian"</note> prayer. It is necessary, therefore, that a man should wait until he has learned what disposition he ought to have toward the Gods and toward men.

**ALC.** But, Socrates, how long will it be before that time comes? And who is he that will instruct me? For I should be very glad, I think, to see that man and to know who he is.

<margin>ᵃ Iliad. book 5. line 127.—S.</margin>
**SOC.** It is he who cares for you. But as Homerᵃ says of Minerva <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note>, that she removed the mist from before the eyes of Diomedes,

> That he might clearly see, and distinguish
> Gods from men, ——

so must he, in the first place, as it seems to me, remove from your soul the mist that now happens to surround it; and after that, he will apply those medicines by which you will clearly distinguish good from evil. For at present, I think you would not be able to do so.

**ALC.** Let him then remove that mist, or any other obstruction that he pleases; for he will find me readily disposed to follow any of his prescriptions, whoever the man is, if by those means I may become a better man than I am at present.

**SOC.** It is wonderful to consider how greatly he is disposed toward making you so.

**ALC.** Until that time, therefore, I think it is the better way to delay my sacrifice.

**SOC.** You think correctly. For it is a safer way than to run such a great risk.

**ALC.** It is undeniable, Socrates. In the meantime, however, since you seem to have advised me well, I shall place this crown¹ around your brow. And we shall offer crowns² and all other customary offerings to the gods when I see that day arrive. It will not be long before it arrives, if it please the gods.

**SOC.** Well, I accept this; and I would take pleasure in seeing the time come when you yourself³ have received something else in return for your gift to me. And just as Creon, when Tiresias—showing him his crown [of Gold]—said it had been given to him [by the Athenians] in honor of his knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> as the first offerings <note>original: "first-fruits"</note> of [their]⁴ victory obtained over the enemy, is made to say by Euripides:

---

¹ All those who went to the temples with the intention of petitioning the gods for any particular favor carried crowns or garlands with them, and they wore these while they were praying. It was because Alcibiades held such a crown in his hand that Socrates, meeting him, correctly guessed where he was going.—S.

² The learned Archbishop Potter, in his *Greek Antiquities* <note>original: "Archæolog. Græc."</note> book 2, chapter 4, very accurately observes that crowns and garlands were some of the gifts offered to the gods by their petitioners to obtain some future benefit. From the passage now before us, we infer that the very same crowns or garlands worn by those petitioners during their prayers in the temples were usually taken off their own heads at their departure and placed on the heads of the divine statues. From there, the priest later took them and hung them on the side walls of the temple. Plato here shows Alcibiades giving Socrates the very honor he had intended for the statue of Jupiter. By this, we assume he meant to signify that whoever could teach wisdom and virtue, as Alcibiades supposed Socrates could, was to be esteemed and honored as a godly man.—S.

³ In the Greek: "But I would gladly see you yourself receiving something else in return for the things given by you." <note>original: "αλλο δε [f. αλλο τι] αντι των παρα σου δοθεντων ηδεως ιδοιμι δεξαμενον εμαυτον."</note> In this sentence, we have no doubt that the last word is a corrupt reading and was written by Plato as "himself" or "yourself" [heauton]. For we cannot understand how a man who has received a gift can be said to make a return for it by his own receiving of another gift from the same or any other person.—S.

⁴ In this sentence, we have translated all the words enclosed in brackets from Euripides to make this passage from Plato clearer to those who have not read the *Phoenician Women* <note>original: "Phænissæ"</note> by that poet, the tragedy from which it is taken.—S.

# INTRODUCTION

## TO

### THE EUTHYPHRO.

---

**THE** whole of the *Euthyphro* of Plato, says Marsilio Ficino <note>original: "Ficinus"; Ficino was a 15th-century Italian scholar whose Latin translations of Plato were foundational for later readers like Taylor</note>, is employed in refutation. For this reason, some Platonists have called this dialogue, as well as the *Euthydemus* and *Greater Hippias*, "elenctic" <term>Refutative; a style of Socratic questioning aimed at cross-examining an opponent's claims to expose contradictions</term>. However, as Ficino justly observes, while Socrates refutes the false opinions which Euthyphro held regarding holiness, he presents certain traces <note>original: "vestiges"</note> of the truth to those who investigate it. 

We may conclude, therefore, from this dialogue and the *Gorgias*, that holiness, according to Plato, is that part of justice which attributes to Divinity that which is its own. But as man is a composite being <note>Referring to the Platonic view of humans as a combination of body and different levels of soul</note>, and the different parts of his composition were produced—according to Platonic theology—from different divinities, perfect piety will consist in consecrating to each deity that part of us which he immediately gave. 

Once this definition is established <note>original: "premised"</note>, what Plato says here and elsewhere respecting holiness will become clear. Hence, when it is said that holiness is that which is beloved by Divinity, it is true; but it is beloved by Divinity because it is holiness, and it is not holiness simply because it is beloved by him. Likewise, because it is beloved by him, it may indeed be "lovable," but it is not beloved merely because it has the capacity to be loved. For the holy is not in every respect the same as "that which may be beloved"; since the essence of holiness does not consist in being the object of love, but rather in retribution <note>In the sense of giving back what is due</note> and devotion.

Again, when it is said that holiness is that which serves <note>original: "ministrant to"</note> the operations of Divinity, this is also a true statement. This is because holiness serves the "conversion" <note>In Platonic terms, the "turning back" or returning of the soul toward its divine source</note> to Divinity of that which we receive from him. And the work of Divinity...

<meta>catchword: is</meta>

<summary>This introduction outlines the purpose of the Euthyphro, defining holiness (piety) as a form of justice toward the divine and exploring the "Euthyphro dilemma"—whether something is holy because the gods love it, or if they love it because it is holy.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Euthyphro, Marsilio Ficino, holiness, piety, justice, elenctic, Socrates, Platonic theology, Euthyphro dilemma</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's Euthyphro, specifically exploring the Neoplatonic interpretation of holiness and sacrifice, drawing on the philosopher Porphyry.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

is to produce, convert, purify, illuminate, and perfect. Hence it is beautifully observed by Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note>, “that being joined and made like <note>original: "conjoined and assimilated"</note> to the highest God, we should offer the elevation of ourselves to him as a sacred sacrifice; for thus we shall celebrate him and procure our own salvation.” He adds, “In the soul’s contemplation, therefore, of this Divinity, unattended by the passions, the sacrifice to him receives its completion; but his offspring <note>original: "progeny"</note>, the intelligible gods <term>In Neoplatonism, these are divine realities that can only be understood by the intellect, rather than the senses</term>, are to be celebrated vocally by hymns*.” Lastly, when it is said that holiness is the science of requesting from and giving to the gods, this likewise is true, though it is not a perfect definition of sanctity. For he who properly prays to Divinity will request him to impart that by which he may be enabled to offer himself to him in the most acceptable manner.

---

* For the sake of the Platonic reader, I will give the whole of this very beautiful passage <note>original: Taylor provides a long excerpt in Ancient Greek from Porphyry's "De Abstinentia," lib. ii. p. 165, 4to. 1767</note>:

> “Let us also sacrifice, but let us sacrifice in such a manner as is proper, offering different sacrifices to different powers. To that God, indeed, who is above all things—as a certain wise man says—neither burning incense <note>original: "fumigating"</note> nor consecrating anything perceptible to the senses <note>original: "sensible"</note>. For there is nothing material which is not immediately impure to an immaterial nature. Hence, neither is external language suited to him, nor even internal language when it is defiled by any passion of the soul; but we should adore him in pure silence, and with pure thoughts concerning him. It is necessary, therefore, that, being joined and made like him, we should offer the elevation of ourselves to Divinity as a sacred sacrifice; for thus we shall celebrate him and procure our own salvation. In the soul’s contemplation, therefore, of this Divinity, unattended by the passions, the sacrifice to him receives its completion; but his offspring, the intelligible gods, are to be celebrated vocally by hymns. For to each of the gods, the first fruits are to be sacrificed of what he imparts to us, and through which he nourishes and preserves us. As, therefore, the farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> offers his first fruits from handfuls of grain <note>original: "fruits"</note> and acorns, so also we should sacrifice from beautiful thoughts concerning the gods, giving thanks for those things of which they have imparted to us the contemplation, and that, through the vision of themselves, they truly nourish us, associating with and appearing to us, and shining upon us for our salvation.”

<summary>This page discusses the Neoplatonic definition of holiness as an internal spiritual elevation and sacrifice to God, supported by a lengthy quote from Porphyry regarding how to worship both the supreme God and the "intelligible gods."</summary>

# THE EUTHYPHRO

---

->*PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE,*<-
->EUTHYPHRO, SOCRATES.<-

---

### EUTHYPHRO.

**WHAT** new circumstance has happened, Socrates, that you have left your discussions in the Lyceum and are now waiting about the King's Porch $^1$? For surely you do not have a lawsuit <note>original: "action"</note> before the King, as **I** do.

**Soc.** The Athenians, Euthyphro, do not call it a lawsuit, but an indictment <note>original: "accusation"</note>.

**EUTH.** What do you say? It seems someone has indicted you. For I would not think that you would be the one accusing another.

**Soc.** Indeed, I would not.

**EUTH.** Has another, then, indicted you?

**Soc.** Certainly.

**EUTH.** Who is he?

**Soc.** I do not know the man very well, Euthyphro, for he appears to me to be young and unknown. But I think they call him Meletus; he is from the district <note>original: "town"</note> of Pitthos. You might remember a Meletus of Pitthos who has long hair, a thin beard, and a hooked <note>original: "aquiline"</note> nose.

**EUTH.** I do not remember him, Socrates. But what is his indictment against you?

**Soc.** What is it? Not a trivial <note>original: "ignoble"</note> one, it seems to me. For it is no

<margin>
$^1$ The King's Porch <note>The *Stoa Basileios*</note> was a place on the right side of the Kerameikos <note>A district of Athens</note> where the second of the nine archons <term>One of the nine chief magistrates of Athens</term>—who was titled "the King"—presided for a term of one year. See Pausanias in *Description of Greece* <note>original: "Attic. lib. i."</note> Book 1, p. 5, and Meursius in *Attic Lectures* <note>original: "Attic. Lect. lib. vi. c. 27"</note> Book 6, ch. 27.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' ironic praise of Meletus, the young man who has brought the indictment against him. Socrates is explaining to Euthyphro that Meletus claims to know how the youth are being corrupted and who is corrupting them.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>THE EUTHYPHRO.</header>

no small matter <note>original: "no despicable thing"</note> for a young man to be so knowledgeable about a matter of such importance. For he knows, or so he says, how the youth are being corrupted, and who it is that corrupts them. He seems to be quite a wise man; and seeing my ignorance, and viewing me as someone who corrupts his peers, he has accused me before the city, as if appealing to a mother. Because of this, he seems to me to be the only citizen who has started off on the right path. For it is right to prioritize the youth first, so that they may develop the best possible character; just as it is reasonable for a good farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> to first take care of the young plants, and only after that the others. In this same way, Meletus will perhaps first weed us out—those who "corrupt the blossoms of youth," as he puts it—and afterward he will surely turn his attention to those of an older age. Thus, he will become the cause of the greatest and most numerous benefits to the city. This is what one might expect to happen from someone who makes such a beginning.

**Euth.** I wish it were so, Socrates; but I fear that the opposite will happen. For, in reality, it seems to me that by trying to injure you, he is beginning to hurt the city from its very foundation—the Vestal hearth <gloss>¹</gloss> itself. But tell me, what specifically does he say you do to corrupt the youth?

**Soc.** The things he accuses me of, my dear man <note>original: "O wonderful man"</note>, must seem absurd when you hear them. He says that I am a maker of gods; and he has brought this accusation against me on the grounds that I introduce new gods and do not believe in the ancient ones.

**Euth.** I understand you, Socrates; it is because you say that a divine sign <gloss>²</gloss> <note>original: "dæmoniacal power"</note> is always present with you. Therefore, he has brought this accusation against you as someone who introduces innovations in religious matters, knowing well that the common people are always ready to believe these kinds of slanders. Indeed, they mock me as if I were crazy whenever I say anything in a public assembly concerning the gods and foretell future events for them—even though I have never predicted anything that did not come true. At the same time, however, they are jealous of all of us who are like this. But indeed it is...

---

<gloss>¹</gloss> The hearth, among the Greeks, was the place of the household gods, of whom Vesta <note>Hestia</note> was the chief. Therefore, "to begin from the Vestal hearth" was a proverbial expression used when speaking of starting with what is most excellent and sacred.

<gloss>²</gloss> This perfectly matches what we have cited from Xenophon in the Introduction to the *Apology of Socrates*. <note>This refers to the *daimonion*, the "internal voice" or "divine sign" that Socrates claimed guided his actions.</note>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Socrates and Euthyphro outside the court. <page-num>7</page-num>
<header>THE EUTHYPHRO.</header>

...not fit to pay any attention to them; but we should still go on in our own way.

**Soc.** But, dear Euthyphro, to be ridiculed is perhaps a trifling thing. For the Athenians, as it appears to me, are not very much concerned whether or not a man is skillful in anything, so long as he is not a teacher of his wisdom. But they are indignant with anyone whom they think makes others like himself, whether this is from envy, as you say, or from some other cause.

**Euth.** In regards to this situation, therefore, I am not very eager to test how they might feel toward me.

**Soc.** For perhaps you present yourself only rarely and are not willing to teach your wisdom; but I fear that, through my love of humanity <note>original: "philanthropy"</note>, I might seem to disclose too freely to every man whatever I possess—not only without taking a reward but even willingly paying one, if anyone is willing to listen to me. As I just said, if they were only going to ridicule me, as you say they do to you, there would be nothing unpleasant about spending the time in a court of justice, jesting and laughing. But if they are in earnest, how this affair may end is unclear <note>original: "immanifest"</note>, except to you diviners <term>diviners: people who predict the future or interpret the will of the gods</term>.

**Euth.** Perhaps, however, Socrates, the matter will amount to nothing; you will plead your case successfully, and I believe I shall win mine as well.

**Soc.** But what is this case, Euthyphro, that you have to plead? Are you the defendant or the plaintiff?

**Euth.** I am the plaintiff <term>plaintiff: the person who brings a legal case against another in a court of law</term>.

**Soc.** Whom are you prosecuting?

**Euth.** Someone who makes me appear insane for prosecuting him.

**Soc.** What? Are you pursuing a fugitive <note>original: "one that flies"</note>?

**Euth.** He is far from being a fugitive, for he is very advanced in years.

**Soc.** Who is he?

**Euth.** My father.

**Soc.** Your father? My dear man! <note>original: "O best of men!"</note>

**Euth.** He is, indeed.

**Soc.** But what is the crime, and of what do you accuse him?

**Euth.** Of murder, Socrates.

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Socrates and Euthyphro outside the court. Euthyphro has just revealed that he is at court as a plaintiff, and Socrates is about to learn who Euthyphro is prosecuting.</meta>

<page-num>8</page-num>
<header>THE EUTHYPHRO.</header>

**Soc.** Good Hercules! The majority of people, Euthyphro, will not understand how this could ever be right. For I do not think it is the business of just any ordinary person to make such an accusation with correctness <note>original: "rectitude"</note>, but only of someone who has made very great progress in wisdom.

**Euth.** Very great indeed, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Socrates.

**Soc.** Is it one of your relatives who has been killed by your father? Though it certainly must be so; for you would not prosecute your father for the murder of a stranger.

**Euth.** It is ridiculous, Socrates, if you think it makes any difference whether the person killed is a stranger or a relative, and are not convinced that this alone ought to be considered: whether the person who committed the murder did it justly or not. If he acted justly, he should be let go; but if unjustly, he should be prosecuted, even if he shares your home and your table. For you become equally defiled with him if you knowingly associate with such a person and do not purify both yourself and him by bringing him to justice. 

But to inform you of the facts: The deceased was one of our hired laborers <term>original: "farmers" — likely referring to a "pelates" or a dependent day-laborer</term>, who rented a piece of land from us when we lived at Naxos. This man, having one day drunk too much wine, was so overcome with rage against one of our slaves that he killed him. My father, therefore, ordered him to be thrown into a pit with his hands and feet bound, and immediately sent a messenger here to consult one of the interpreters of religious matters <note>original: "interpreters of sacred concerns"</note> on what he should do with him. In the meantime, he neglected the prisoner and left him without food <note>original: "sustenance"</note> as a murderer whose life was of no consequence; as a result, he died. Hunger, cold, and the weight of his chains killed him before the person my father had sent returned. 

Because of this, my father and the rest of my relations are angry with me. They are upset because, for the sake of a murderer, I accuse my father of murder—an act which they say he has not committed. And even if he had, they think that since the dead man was himself a murderer, I ought not to be concerned for his fate. For they say it is impious for a son to prosecute his father for murder; so little do they know how the divine nature feels about piety and impiety.

**Soc.** But, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Euthyphro, do you think you possess such an accurate knowledge about divine affairs, and how things holy and impious are circumstanced, <meta>catchword: circumstanced,</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>
<header>THE EUTHYPHRO.</header>

...given these circumstances, and things having happened as you say, are you not afraid that in prosecuting your father you might be committing an impious act?

**EUTH.** My profession, Socrates, would be of no use to me, and Euthyphro would be no different from any other man, if I did not accurately know all such details.

**Soc.** O remarkable Euthyphro, it will therefore be an excellent thing for me to become your disciple. Before the outcome of my trial <note>original: "determination of my process"</note>, I will let Melitus know that I have always considered the knowledge of divine matters to be of the greatest importance. Now, since he says I am guilty of acting recklessly and introducing innovations regarding divine beings, I have become your student. 

Therefore, I shall say: "Melitus, if you acknowledge that Euthyphro is wise and has the right perspective on such affairs, then you should think and judge the same of me. But if you do not hold this opinion, then bring him, my teacher <note>original: "preceptor"</note>, to court before you bring me. He is the one who corrupts older men—meaning me and his own father; me by his teaching, and his father by correcting <note>original: "reproving"</note> and punishing him." And if he is not convinced by me, but continues his prosecution or accuses me instead of you, I will have to say the very same things at the trial that I have already pointed out to him.

**EUTH.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Socrates, it would be so! And if he attempts to accuse me, I think I will find his weak spot, and he would be called to account in a court of justice long before I would.

**Soc.** And I, my dear friend, knowing these things, desire to become your disciple. I am convinced that no one—not even Melitus himself—dares to look you in the face, even though he sees through me so accurately, simply, and easily that he has accused me of impiety. 

Now, therefore, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, tell me what you just firmly claimed to know clearly: what kind of thing do you assert holiness <note>In Greek philosophy, "holiness" or "piety" (hosiotēs) refers to what is religiously correct or pleasing to the gods.</note> to be, and also unholiness, both regarding murder and other things? Is not holiness always the same in every action? And again, is not unholiness—which is the exact opposite of holiness—always consistent with itself? Does not everything that is unholy possess one certain essential character <note>original: "idea," referring to the Platonic concept of a "Form" or universal essence</note> of unholiness?

**EUTH.** Certainly, Socrates.

**Soc.** Tell me, then, what do you say holiness is, and what is unholiness?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Euthyphro justifies his decision to prosecute his father for murder. He claims that his deep knowledge of divine matters allows him to act with certainty, despite the concerns Socrates raised about potential impiety.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>

->### THE EUTHYPHRO.<-

**EUTH.** I say, therefore, that holiness is exactly what I am doing now: namely, to prosecute anyone who acts unjustly, whether it involves murder, sacrilege, or any other similar crime. It does not matter if the offender is a father, a mother, or anyone else; failing to prosecute such a person is impious. For look, Socrates, I will give you a great legal proof that this is the case—a point I have also mentioned to others—which is that it is right not to spare an impious man, whoever he may be. 

For men are firmly convinced that Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note> is the best and most just of the gods, and yet they acknowledge that he put his father in chains because he unjustly swallowed his children. They also acknowledge that Cronus <note>original: "Saturn"</note> castrated <gloss>¹</gloss> his own father <note>Uranus</note> because of other similar actions. Yet, these men are angry with me because I am prosecuting my father for acting unjustly. In this way, they say things that contradict themselves in what they say about the gods and about me.

**SOC.** Is this the reason, Euthyphro, that I am being brought to trial <note>original: "to the bar"</note>? Is it because when anyone asserts things of this kind about the gods, I find them painful to accept? Is this why, as it seems, someone calls me an offender? Now, if these things also seem true to you, who are well-acquainted with such matters, then it seems we must also accept them. For what else can we say, since we admit that we know nothing about such things? But tell me, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, the god who presides over friendship: do you really believe that these things actually happened?

---

> ¹ Regarding the meaning of "bonds" and "castrations" when applied to divine beings, see page 141 of the *Introduction to the Second Book of the Republic*. I shall only observe here, along with Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, that Plato believed all such stories will be condemned by the common people <note>original: "multitude"</note> and the foolish because they do not understand their secret <note>original: "arcane"</note> meaning; however, he believed they would suggest wonderful insights <note>original: "conjectures"</note> to the wise. 
>
> Therefore, although he does not approve of this way of telling myths, he thinks we should be persuaded by those ancients who were the descendants of the gods and investigate their hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> ideas, as is evident from what he says in the *Timaeus*. Consequently, although he rejects the "bonds of Cronus <note>original: "Saturnian bonds"</note>" and the "castrations of Uranus <note>original: "Heaven"</note>" when speaking with Euthyphro and the audience of his *Republic*, he does allow for other secondary "bonds" concerning the mighty Cronus <note>original: "Saturn"</note> and Hades <note>original: "Pluto"</note> in his *Cratylus*, where he investigates names philosophically. 
> 
> Therefore, Plato is by no means ridiculing the religion of his country in what he says here, as some modern writers have claimed. Rather, he accepts such stories with pain because he knew well that they would only be impiously misunderstood by, and were far beyond the comprehension of, the common people.

**EUTH.** Yes, Socrates, and I can tell you things even more wonderful than these, which the general public knows nothing about.

**SOC.** So, do you really believe that the gods *in reality* go to war with each other, and that there are terrible enmities and battles among them, along with many other such details as the poets describe? Our temples are decorated with artistic representations of these stories, and during the Great Panathenaea <note>An ancient Athenian festival held every four years to honor the goddess Athena.</note>, a robe <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "veil"; specifically the *peplos*, a ceremonial garment woven by Athenian maidens for the goddess.</note> covered in these kinds of diverse patterns is carried up to the Acropolis. Must we say, Euthyphro, that these things are true?

**EUTH.** Not only these things, Socrates; but as I just said, I can tell you many other things about divine matters if you wish. I know that when you hear them, you will be astonished.

**SOC.** I wouldn't be surprised. But you can tell me these things later when you have more time. For now, however, try to tell me more clearly what I just asked you. You see, my friend, you have not yet sufficiently answered my question about what holiness is. You have only told me that what you are doing now is holy—namely, prosecuting your father for murder.

**EUTH.** And I spoke the truth, Socrates.

**SOC.** Perhaps so. But, Euthyphro, don't you also say that many other things are holy?

**EUTH.** I do.

**SOC.** Remember, then, that I did not ask you to teach me one or two examples from among many holy things. I asked you for the *form itself* <note>original: "form itself" (Greek: *eidos*); the essential nature that makes something what it is.</note> by which all holy things are holy. For you said that unholy things are unholy because of one *idea* <note>original: "idea" (Greek: *idea*); Socrates is seeking a universal definition, not just a list of examples.</note>, and holy things are holy because of another. Do you remember?

**EUTH.** I do.

**SOC.** Teach me, then, what this very "idea" is. I want to look at it and use it as a *standard* <note>original: "paradigm" (Greek: *paradeigma*).</note> so that I may say that whatever action of yours—or anyone else's—is of this kind is holy, and whatever is not of this kind is unholy.

**EUTH.** If that is what you want, Socrates, I will tell you.

**SOC.** I do want it.

**EUTH.** That, therefore, which is dear to the gods is holy, but that which is not dear to them is unholy.

**SOC.** About what subjects, then, would a disagreement arise where we could not rely on a certain standard <note>original: "criterion"</note>? What would make us become enemies and be enraged with each other?

**EUTH.** Certainly.

**SOC.** Dogs also are benefited by the hunter’s art, and oxen by that of the livestock farmer, and all other things in a similar way. Or do you think that "care" is meant to harm that which is cared for?

**EUTH.** Not I, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"; the translator used the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods.</note>.

**SOC.** But it is for their advantage, then?

**EUTH.** How could it not be?

**SOC.** Is holiness, therefore—since it is a care of the gods—a benefit to the gods?

...to the gods, and does it make the gods better? And do you admit this: that when you perform any holy act, you make one of the gods better?

**EUTH.** Certainly not, by Jupiter! <note>original: "by Jupiter"; a common oath referencing Zeus, the king of the Greek gods.</note>

**SOC.** Nor do I think that you are saying this, Euthyphro; it is certainly quite the opposite. **EUTH.** And you were right to think so, Socrates, for I am not saying any such thing.

**SOC.** Very well. But what kind of care for the gods would holiness be?

**EUTH.** That kind of care, Socrates, which slaves provide to their masters.

**SOC.** I understand. It would then be a certain kind of service <note>original: "subserviency"; here meaning the act of serving as an assistant or subordinate.</note> to the gods, as it seems.

**EUTH.** Entirely so.

**SOC.** Can you tell me then, regarding the art that serves physicians: what work does it help to accomplish? Do you not think it serves to produce health?

**EUTH.** I do.

**SOC.** And what about the art that serves shipbuilders <note>original: "shipwrights"</note>? What work does it help to accomplish?

**EUTH.** Clearly, Socrates, it helps build a ship.

**SOC.** And isn't the art that serves architects <note>In ancient Greece, architects were "master builders" who oversaw construction.</note> used for the building of houses?

**EUTH.** Yes.

**SOC.** Tell me then, my good man: regarding the art that serves the gods, what work does it help to accomplish? For it is clear that you know, since you say you have a knowledge of divine matters far beyond that of other men.

**EUTH.** And I speak the truth, Socrates.

**SOC.** Tell me then, by Jupiter, what is that "all-beautiful" work which the gods produce by using our service?

**EUTH.** They are many and beautiful things, Socrates.

**SOC.** Army generals also accomplish many beautiful things, my friend; but at the same time, you can easily say what the main thing is they achieve—namely <note>original: "viz."; an abbreviation for the Latin *videlicet*, meaning "that is to say" or "namely."</note>, victory in battle. Can you not?

**EUTH.** How could I not agree?

**SOC.** Farmers <note>original: "husbandmen"</note> also, I think, accomplish many great things; but at the same time, the primary thing they produce is food <note>original: "aliment"</note> from the earth.

**EUTH.** Entirely so.

**SOC.** Of the many great things the gods accomplish, what is the main one?

**EUTH.** I told you a little while ago, Socrates, that learning exactly how all these things work <note>original: "subsist"</note> is a difficult task. But I will tell you simply this: if someone knows how to say and do things that please the gods through prayer and sacrifice, those things are holy. These actions protect both private homes and cities. But the opposite of what is pleasing to the gods is impious <note>original: "impious"; meaning unholy or lacking reverence.</note>, and these things undermine and destroy everything.

**SOC.** If you had wanted to, Euthyphro, you could have answered the essence of my question much more briefly. But it is clear that you are not really willing to teach me. For just now, when you were close to the point, you backed away. If you had answered, I might have already learned from you what holiness is. But now (since the questioner must follow wherever the person being questioned leads), what do you say holiness is? Do you say it is a kind of knowledge <note>original: "science"; from the Greek 'episteme', meaning a systematic body of knowledge or skill.</note> of sacrifice and prayer?

**EUTH.** I do.

**SOC.** Is sacrifice not the offering of gifts to the gods, and prayer the requesting of something from them?

**EUTH.** Very much so, Socrates.

**SOC.** From this, it follows that holiness is the knowledge of asking from and giving to the gods.

**EUTH.** You have understood what I said very well, Socrates.

**SOC.** That is because I am very eager for your wisdom, my friend, and I am paying close attention to it, so that nothing you say is wasted. But tell me, what is this service <note>original: "subserviency"</note> to the gods? Do you say it consists of asking from them and giving to them?

**EUTH.** I do.

**SOC.** Wouldn't it follow, then, that to ask correctly is to ask them for the things we need?

<summary>Euthyphro defines holiness as the knowledge of how to please the gods through prayer and sacrifice. Socrates refines this definition into a kind of "trading" relationship where humans give gifts to and request favors from the divine.</summary>

**EUTH.** What else can it be?

**SOC.** And again, does giving correctly not consist of giving the gods, in our turn, the things they need from us? For it would not follow the rules of any skill <note>original: "conformable to art"; Socrates argues that every specialized skill or "art" must have a specific, logical purpose.</note> to give someone things they do not need.

**EUTH.** You speak the truth, Socrates.

**SOC.** Holiness, then, Euthyphro, must be a kind of business transaction <note>original: "mercantile art"; a trade or commercial exchange.</note> between gods and men.

**EUTH.** Let it be called a business, if you like to call it that.

**SOC.** But it does not please me unless it is true. Tell me, then: what benefit do the gods get from the gifts they receive from us? For the benefit we get from their gifts is obvious to everyone, since we have no good thing that they did not give us. But how are they benefited by what they receive from us? Or do we have such an advantage in this trade that we receive every good thing from them, while they receive nothing from us?

**EUTH.** But do you really think, Socrates, that the gods are benefited by what they receive from us?

**SOC.** Then what is the point, Euthyphro, of these gifts of ours to the gods?

**EUTH.** What other use do you think they have, except for honor, reverence, and—as I just said—gratitude?

**SOC.** Holiness, then, Euthyphro, is what is acceptable to the gods, but not what is profitable to them or beloved by them?

**EUTH.** I think it is, above all things, what they love most.

**SOC.** Then holiness, it seems, is once again defined as that which is dear to the gods.

**EUTH.** Precisely so.

**SOC.** By making these claims, can you wonder that your argument does not seem to stand still, but wanders away? And can you accuse me of being the *Daedalus* <note>In Greek mythology, Daedalus was a legendary inventor whose statues were said to be so lifelike that they would walk away if not tied down.</note> who makes them wander, when you yourself far surpass *Daedalus* in skill and make your own statements go around in a circle? Or do you not see that our argument, revolving again, has come back to the same place? For you must remember that earlier in our discussion, "the holy" and "that which is dear to the gods" did not seem to be the same thing to us, but were different from each other. Or do you not remember?

**EUTH.** I do.

**SOC.** Now, therefore, do you not see that you are saying holiness is that which is beloved by the gods? But is this anything other than that which is dear to the divine?

**EUTH.** It is nothing else.

**SOC.** Either we did not conclude correctly before, or, if we did, our current position is wrong.

**EUTH.** It seems so.

**SOC.** Therefore, we must consider again from the beginning what holiness is. For I will not willingly run away like a coward before I have learned this. Do not look down on me, but give me your full attention and tell me the absolute truth. For if any man knows it, you do; and I will not let you go—just as Menelaus held onto the shape-shifting Proteus <note>original: "Proteus"; in Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god who changed shapes to avoid answering questions. One had to hold him tight until he returned to his true form to get the truth.</note>—until you have told me. 

Because if you did not clearly know what is holy and what is unholy, you would never have attempted to accuse your elderly father of murder for the sake of a day laborer <note>original: "hireling"; this refers to the worker whose death caused the legal dispute between Euthyphro and his father.</note>. You would have been too afraid of acting wrongly, fearing the anger of the gods and the judgment of men. But now I know well that you clearly *assume* <note>Plato here very properly uses the word *oiei* (οἴει), meaning "you assume" or "you suppose," because Euthyphro—suffering from "double ignorance" (being ignorant of his own ignorance)—had nothing more than a vague *notion* of the nature of holiness rather than true knowledge.</note> that you have knowledge of what is holy and what is its opposite. Tell me, therefore, most excellent Euthyphro, and do not hide from me what you think it is?

**EUTH.** It will have to be at some other time, Socrates; for now I am in a hurry, and it is time for me to leave you.

**SOC.** What are you doing, my friend? By leaving, you throw away the great hope I had of learning from you what things are holy and what are not. I hoped to free myself from the accusations of Meletus <note>original: "Melitus"; the primary accuser who brought Socrates to trial for impiety.</note> by showing him that I had become wise in divine matters through Euthyphro. I could have shown him that I would no longer speak recklessly or introduce strange new ideas <note>original: "novelties"; Meletus accused Socrates of inventing new gods and corrupting the youth.</note> out of ignorance, and that I would live a better life from now on.
