# INTRODUCTION

### TO

# THE MENO¹.

**T**HIS Dialogue has always been justly titled "Concerning Virtue." For the true subject of it is the nature and origin of virtue. The question, indeed, proposed to Socrates by Meno at the very beginning of the Dialogue, is a different one: "How is virtue acquired?" But Socrates immediately waives <note>original: "waves"</note> the question and draws the conversation toward an inquiry into "what virtue is," as this is necessarily required before inquiring into "where it comes from." 

However, from the result of the reasoning, we shall perceive that both of these questions can be answered together. We shall be convinced that no one can know the nature and essence of virtue without knowing the fountain from which it is derived; and whoever knows what this source is cannot fail to know, at the same time, what that is in which virtue consists. For, if we attend closely to the steps or gradual advances made in these inquiries through the course of this Dialogue, we shall discover that virtue consists in a certain kind of knowledge and a certain kind of power, taken together. The capacity for both of these exists in the human soul, as it partakes of a divine intellect, whose essence is its own object, and whose activity <note>original: "energy"; here referring to the Neoplatonic concept of *energeia* or actualized operation</note> is the contemplation of itself and the government of the universe. That kind of knowledge, therefore, which belongs to virtue is the knowledge of true good; and that kind of power in the soul, through which, joined to that knowledge, a man is virtuous, is the power of the

<summary>This introduction identifies the core theme of the "Meno" as the nature and origin of virtue, arguing that virtue arises from a combination of knowledge and power derived from the divine intellect.</summary>

intellect over the inferior part of the soul—the imagination and the passions. The gradual progress made toward this discovery shapes the structure of this divine dialogue. The first step is to show that virtue, though it seems to be a very complex idea made up of many different virtues that belong to different types of people, is actually just one simple idea. It is called by different names only because the specific subjects it acts upon, or the specific goals it aims for, differ from one another. 

In the next step, we find that this idea includes power and government. To this account, the author immediately adds <note>original: "subjoined"</note>, by way of explanation, these restrictions: power must be well and wisely exercised, and government must be well and justly administered. Here, then, we discover that the "Well," the "Wisely," and the "Justly" are essential to the idea of virtue. 

Next, we proceed through some obscurity; for here we see only with the help of a metaphor. This metaphor seems to be introduced merely as a comparison to illustrate a point already made clear: the wholeness, or rather the oneness, of the idea of virtue. The metaphor is taken from physical shape <note>original: "outward figure"</note>. The definition of a shape is that it is a "bound"—the boundary or limit of solid bodies. This suggests to every student or serious reader of Plato that virtue itself is a "bound" <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "bound" (or *peras*) is the principle of order and limit that gives form to the formless.</note>; that intellectual virtue is the bound of things within the mind, and that practical virtue is the bound of human actions and manners¹. 

We then move a step further in the same manner, guided only by the light of a metaphor. This metaphor is taken from "corpuscular philosophy" <note>The theory that the world is made up of minute physical particles or "corpuscles."</note>, which was then newly made popular by Protagoras (who had learned it from Democritus) and by Gorgias (who had learned it from Empedocles). Here, Socrates pursues the inquiry of this dialogue under the pretense of giving a definition of color, according to the doctrines of this philosophy which Meno had studied. Color, he says, is caused by "effluvia" <note>original: "effluvia"; particles or flows emitted from the surfaces of objects.</note> from the surfaces of bodies entering the pores of the eyes. These pores are exactly shaped to receive such particles; by this means, those particles, being proportionate

To prevent this impression, we should observe that, just as Pythagoras used to illustrate mental concepts using mathematical numbers, Plato frequently illustrates them using the principles of geometry, and also through sensory images or physical objects. Perhaps these two methods of illustration are the easiest and clearest ways through which we can first be led to conceive of purely abstract things, which are the objects of the intellect.—**S.** <note>Floyer Sydenham, the original translator and commentator.</note>

with these pores, become the objects of sight. Thus the philosopher plays with the prejudices of Meno, a disciple of the sophists <note>The Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece often criticized by Plato for teaching rhetoric and persuasion rather than absolute truth.</note>, and therefore not a proper subject for his instruction. He introduces, with the stated goal of only satisfying Meno’s curiosity, a point which seems very foreign to the subject and not at all necessary to illustrate his meaning. 

But to his own friends and followers, who were acquainted with his doctrine and were then near him, he thus enigmatically <note>original: "ænigmatically"</note> suggests that virtue and vice are, as it were, the "colors" of human actions; that by the light of the mind we are able to distinguish them; that the science of virtue is as natural to the human understanding as the perception of outward objects is to the physical eye; that the mental eye is exactly suited to its objects; and that all truth in general—and moral truth in particular, the present subject—is equal in scope to the mind. 

The next advance we make discovers to us that virtue consists in a love and desire of true good and true beauty, which necessarily follows from the knowledge of what is truly good and truly beautiful. It is impossible to keep from loving what appears beautiful, or desiring what appears good. And having already found that the idea of virtue includes power and governance, we find that the whole idea of virtue is the power of preserving or of recovering true good and beauty, known to be such, and loved and desired because they are known. 

The next step brings us to the end of our journey in this inquiry concerning virtue, by showing us that the knowledge of all truth—and consequently of true good and beauty—is innate <note>original: "connatural"</note> to the soul of man. This is so because her origin is divine and her essence is immortal. Now, the demi-urgic intellect <note>original: "demi-urgic intellect"; This refers to the "Creator" or "Craftsman" mind that Plato describes in other dialogues as fashioning the universe.</note>, the source of the soul's being, is immortal and divine, and truth resides there eternally as the stable and unchanging object of the intellect. Plato, therefore, in proving to us (as he does in this part of the dialogue by an undeniable example) that the soul of man naturally agrees with and embraces truth when it is fairly presented to her and shown in a clear light, proves to us at the same time that she participates in this eternal intellect and truth.

This concludes the first part, which is about one-half of the dialogue. In the latter half, the inquiry into the nature of virtue is resumed, but in a different way. For Meno, having here pressed for the consideration of his first question—"how virtue is acquired"—Socrates, in pretending to finally give in to this inquiry, brings us around by another road to the end, which he

<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

## INTRODUCTION TO

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Plato himself had the goal all along of teaching “what virtue is.” Here it is suggested, through a geometrical puzzle <note>original: "enigma," referring to the scene in the Meno where Socrates teaches a slave boy geometry to demonstrate innate knowledge.</note>, first that not every soul is capable of virtue; that a certain predisposition is required; and that the parts of the soul must be well-proportioned to each other in their natural structure. This is so that the whole man may, through virtue, be made **completely smooth and round** <note>original: *totus teres atque rotundus*, a Latin phrase from the poet Horace describing a person who is self-reliant and polished, like a smooth sphere that external things cannot cling to.</note>. In the next place, we find that virtue does not consist in any particular virtuous habit or habits of the soul—whether intellectual or moral—but in the wise <note>original: "prudential"</note> use and exercise of them. From this, it follows that virtue is not acquired by mere practice or habit alone. Third, we find that virtue does not consist merely in a good disposition without it being well-cultivated; consequently, it does not come by nature alone. Fourth, it does not consist in any particular science or sciences; therefore, it is not acquired by learning and is not to be taught in the ordinary method of instruction or discipline. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As a preparation for this part of the inquiry, a new character is introduced into the Dialogue: **Anytus**. He is a great enemy of the Sophists <note>The Sophists were itinerant teachers in ancient Greece who charged fees to teach rhetoric and virtue, often criticized by Socrates for prioritizing persuasion over truth.</note> and is eager to be thought of as a politician. He is a necessary person to show that neither the professional men of wisdom (the Sophists) nor the recognized men of virtue (the leaders who preserved the Athenian state through their good government) were fit masters or teachers in the science of virtue. At length, by the help of all these negative conclusions, we find what virtue positively consists of: true wisdom. This wisdom is not only derived originally from the divine mind by participation but is also inspired immediately by it through continual communication. However, this presupposes a necessary foundation or fit subject for receiving this wisdom: a soul well-disposed by nature, cultivated by right discipline, and strengthened by constant care and attention. But as the first two requirements—a good natural disposition and a proper upbringing—depend on Divine Providence, and as the last—the constant practice of virtue—depends on divine assistance, all these cooperating causes of virtue are summed up by Plato at the conclusion of this Dialogue in one phrase: **divine allotment** <note>original: *ϑεία moῖρα* (theia moira)</note>. This is the portion given to men who are justly called divine.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This should be enough for now to explain the subject and outline the parts of this Dialogue. Whatever is currently lacking in clarity or completeness, we shall endeavor to illustrate and expand upon in the notes. The goal and design of the Dialogue is to encourage men—who are naturally well-disposed and prepared by the basics of a good education—to the diligent cultivation and improvement of their minds by think-

<summary>This page outlines Plato’s argument that virtue is not simply innate, learned, or habitual, but is a form of wisdom granted by "divine allotment" to those with a well-prepared soul. It also introduces Anytus as a character used to demonstrate that neither politicians nor Sophists can effectively teach virtue.</summary>

teaching and reasoning. This intent is clear, first, from the unusual warmth and zeal with which Socrates is portrayed in the second half of the Dialogue, as he presses for an inquiry into lost knowledge and strives to discover hidden truths. The same intent is also evident from the extensive time spent recounting many unfortunate examples of high-ranking Athenian youths neglecting virtuous studies; this long list is so wordy <note>original: "prolix"</note> that it can have no purpose other than to discourage us from following their example. 

But the Dialogue's true direction is best shown by the effect its central doctrine—previously explained—must naturally have on every teachable and open mind. For, if the human mind shares in a divine intellect and everything that belongs to its essence; if truth has descended from Heaven into human souls, and if Divinity itself is present there, ready to share more and more heartfelt knowledge of divine and eternal things with every soul that retreats within itself; then who would not wish to go there? Who would not seek that sacred silence—the silencing of the passions—and that sacred solitude—the absence of all physical imagination—that "flight of the alone to the alone" <note>original Greek: *phygē monou pros monon*</note>, to enjoy the presence and conversation of the divine, solitary principle of all things? 

In keeping with Plato’s intent, and because the audience consisted of both strangers and Socrates’ friends and followers (as was typical where these conversations occurred), the Dialogue is framed as an inquiry. Socrates uses leading questions throughout to both provoke and assist the search, occasionally dropping hints about his deeper meaning. Meno is portrayed simply as a humble student of the Sophists <note>itinerant teachers of rhetoric and virtue</note>, and he does not dare to argue like his teachers. Meanwhile, Anytus is shown as an enemy to all philosophical debate. There is not even a hint of conflict throughout the entire Dialogue. Nevertheless, the classification of Plato’s Dialogues by Thrasyllus (and later Albinus) led them to categorize it as <term>Peirastic</term> <note>meaning "probing" or "testing," a category of dialogues intended to test a person's knowledge or character</note>, simply because they did not know where else to place it more accurately. Its outward form is purely dramatic, and the character of Anytus as shown here provides a clear preview of the role he would soon play in accusing Socrates and bringing him to a public trial as a criminal.

<note>¹ This is the same Meno mentioned by Xenophon in his account of the expedition of Cyrus the Younger <note>original: "Anabasis"</note> as one of the generals of the Greek allied army. Plutarch, in his *Life of Phocion*, relates that Meno commanded all the cavalry. It is certain from Xenophon's account that he had the command of the forces sent from Thessaly. Near the end of the second book of that incomparable history mentioned above, the elegant and faithful writer, having already given us an instance of Meno's baseness, presents us with a full-length portrait of him, the features of which are hateful. But at the time of his conversation with Socrates recorded in this dialogue, he was so young that his mind and true character could not yet have appeared openly or been known to the world. He first became prominent in the expedition with Xenophon while he was still in the flower of his youth; but he was soon taken prisoner and brought to Artaxerxes, by whose orders he was put to a lingering and shameful <note>original: "ignominious"</note> death, not as an enemy soldier but as a criminal <note>original: "malefactor"</note>. Some slight hints, however, appear even in this dialogue, giving us a sketch of his turn of mind, as will be observed in their proper places.</note>
<note>² Enough has been said of this man in the introduction to this dialogue to prepare the reader for his appearance and the role he plays there.</note>
<note>³ The following circumstances, considered together, show that the scene is set in the Lyceum. First, it was the place ordinarily frequented every day by Socrates with his disciples and followers. Next, it was the place of resort for all strangers, especially the young and noble such as Meno was, to see the Athenian youth exercise themselves and to hear the <term>Sophists</term> <note>Sophists: paid teachers of philosophy and rhetoric in ancient Greece</note>, if any happened to be at Athens, dispute and harangue. See the note on the scene of the *Greater Hippias*. Lastly, it cannot be supposed that Socrates should meet with Anytus, his enemy, at any place other than a public one, free to all men.—S. <note>This "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note></note>

# THE MENO.

### MENO.

**CAN**¹ you tell me, Socrates, whether virtue² can be taught; or whether it is acquired, not through teaching, but through practice and habit;

<note>¹ The reader will notice that this is a very abrupt way to begin a conversation, especially with a stranger known only by his name and reputation. What makes it even more remarkable is that a young person, having just reached adulthood, would address an old man in his seventieth year—venerable for his known wisdom and a long life of virtue—in such a manner. Some may think that Plato intended here to portray the arrogant familiarity of wealthy young men with poor educations in how they address those they consider inferior in terms of wealth. Such a thought perhaps has some foundation in truth. But Plato’s primary purpose in beginning the dialogue with an impertinent question from Meno is, as appears plainly from Socrates' reply, to show the arrogant claims of the sophists <term>sophists: professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized for prioritizing rhetorical skill over absolute truth</term>, and particularly Gorgias, who took it upon themselves to answer every philosophical question proposed to them. Meno had been used to this behavior in his own country; and Socrates had, long before this, acquired a distinguished reputation for his superior skill in philosophical debates. Meno, therefore, who saw no difference between Socrates and the sophists, attacks him directly without the ceremony of an introduction. He asks a "point-blank" question on one of the most difficult subjects in all of philosophy. He presumed that Socrates was sitting in the Lyceum <note>original: "Lycæum," a public gymnasium and garden in Athens where philosophers gathered</note> like one of the sophists, ready to answer all such questions. The only other dramatic dialogue of Plato which begins this abruptly is the *Minos*. There is the same kind of appropriateness in both. The only difference is that in the *Minos*, a dialogue between Socrates and a sophist, Socrates is the questioner; in the *Meno*, he is the person questioned. —S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note></note>

<note>² Many years before the time of this dialogue, Socrates had held a debate with Protagoras on this very point: whether virtue could be taught. That dispute was recorded by Plato in a dialogue named after that great sophist. The question was then debated before a large audience of sophists and their followers, as well as the friends and disciples of Socrates himself. The debaters, however, came to no agreement. The result of their conversation was only that Protagoras, the "prince of sophists," was generous enough to praise the great philosopher, saying that "he should wonder if Socrates in time did not become famous for his wisdom." This praise from a sophist—who was as renowned for his philosophical knowledge as he was respected for his age (being about 75 years old at the time)—increased Socrates’ reputation among the sophists. It is probable that these men spread the fame of that debate throughout all of Greece. It seems, therefore, that Meno, an admirer of the sophists who was raised by one of their disciples, wanted to hear Socrates himself speak on that celebrated subject of former debate. Accordingly, meeting Socrates in a convenient place, he attacks him at once with a question on that very point. We may observe, however, that Meno here states the question in a more thorough manner than it was considered in the debate between Socrates and Protagoras; he specifically mentions all the other ways, besides teaching, in which it was ever supposed that virtue was attainable. So this dialogue, *The Meno*, though perhaps not as entertaining as *The Protagoras*, is more comprehensive and provides a wider field for thought. —S.</note>

...or whether it comes neither by practice nor by teaching, but is present by nature in those who possess it; or does it come to them in some other way?

**SOCRATES:** Meno, you Thessalians have long been eminent among the Greeks<margin>1</margin>. You have long been admired for your superior skill in horsemanship<margin>2</margin> and famed for the great wealth you possess<margin>3</margin>. But I think you have now acquired no less a reputation for wisdom<margin>4</margin>. Among your people, the fellow citizens of your friend Aristippus<margin>5</margin> of Larissa have distinguished themselves quite a bit in this regard. Now, this is entirely the work of Gorgias. For in his travels, when he came to their city, he won over the chiefs of the Aleuadian family<margin>6</margin> (one of whom is your friend Aristippus), and indeed all those of the highest status in the other states of

---

1 The Thessalians were the most ancient inhabitants of Greece. From time to time, they sent out colonies from their own country, Thessaly, and spread themselves by degrees over all the rest of Greece, as we are told by the ancient geographers.—S.

2 The people who lived in Thessaly had the reputation of being the best horsemen and, in war, the best cavalry in the world. See Suidas under the entry <note>original: "Ἱππεῖς λευκοθώρακες," meaning "White-armored cavalry"</note>. This was due to their breeding of excellent horses, which were valued everywhere as the best for both service and beauty, as can be seen in the <note>original: "Ζευξὶς," Zeuxis</note> and the <note>original: "Ερωτες," Erotes (or 'The Amores')</note> of Lucian, and in a note to *The Greater Hippias*. This valuable breed of horses was favored by the soil of their country, which was partly mountainous and partly well-watered by fine rivers running through the middle of spacious and open plains.—S.

3 In Plato’s time, these people had grown very rich but were thought to have acquired their wealth mostly through very unjust means—by fraud, theft, and by kidnapping and selling free men as slaves. For these crimes, they were infamous throughout the rest of Greece. See Xenophon, *Memorabilia*, book 1, chapter 2, section 24.—S.

4 Referring to the superficial wisdom taught by the sophists <term>sophists: paid teachers in ancient Greece who focused on rhetoric and persuasion, often criticized by Socrates for lacking true moral foundations</term>.—S.

5 This Aristippus was a man of the highest rank and power in the city of Larissa. We find here that he had been influenced by the sophistry of Gorgias; and it may justly be inferred from his mention here that he himself had influenced Meno with these same ideas. However, it seems highly improbable that he is the same Aristippus mentioned by Aristotle at the beginning of the third book of his *Metaphysics*, for the latter was a professional sophist. The profession of a sophist was no more appropriate for men of high birth and status than the profession of a traveling quack doctor or a traveling stage actor is for us today. See Plato in the *Protagoras*.—S.

6 This was the noblest family in Larissa. They were descended from Aleuas, one of the kings of Thessaly from the lineage of Hercules, and were at this time the oligarchic <term>oligarchic: a form of government where power rests with a small, elite group</term> tyrants of their country. Meno is complimented here by the seemingly honorable mention of his friend, who we assume was also his direct instructor. At the time this dialogue takes place, Gorgias was over ninety years old and Meno was a very young man.—S.

Thessaly, to be the admirers of his wisdom¹. From him, you Thessalians learned the habit of answering any question whatever with an undaunted and noble confidence—the kind, indeed, that is appropriate for those who have a thorough knowledge of the subject proposed to them. For he² likewise offered himself to be freely questioned by any of the Greeks who wished to ask him anything, on any point the questioner might choose; and he never refused an answer to anyone’s question. But we here in Athens, my friend Meno, are in quite the opposite condition. Among us there is a dearth, as it were, of wisdom; it seems to have forsaken our country and fled to yours. So, if you were to take it into your head to propose the question you asked me to anyone here, every one of us would laugh and say, "My friend and stranger, you must think me wonderfully wise to know whether virtue is something that can be taught, or by what other means it is attained:

---

¹ The great reputation of Gorgias appears to have first arisen in Thessaly. For as Philostratus says in the introduction to his *Lives of the Sophists*: <note>original: "ἦρξε της αρχαιοτερας [fc. σοφιστικης] Γοργιας ὁ Λεοντινος εν Θετταλοις," meaning "Gorgias of Leontini was the leader of the older [sophistic art] among the Thessalians"</note>. Indeed, Thessaly was the most suitable of all places for Gorgias to display his art and thereby acquire a reputation. For his art was the art of deluding through sophistical oratory and sophistical argumentation; these are the most effective and successful tools that can be used for the purpose of deceiving. If, therefore, the people of Thessaly were as they are described, Gorgias could not have failed to find a multitude of followers and admirers there. In fact, these people became such experts in the art of deceiving, and so famous for practicing it, that every clever or skillful act of deceit was proverbially called a "Thessalian sophism" <note>original: "Θετταλον σοφισμα"</note>. In Athenaeus, page 308, Myrtilus, the sophist of Thessaly, is called a "cunning and crafty wrestler in disputation" <note>original: "Θετταλον παλαισμα"</note>; or, as Eustathius explains the term, "subtle in refuting any argument" <note>original: "Θετταλος ελεγκτικος"</note>. The same author, on page 11, jokingly calls this same Myrtilus a "Thessalian cheat" <note>original: "Θετταλον σοφισμα"</note> (in his manner of arguing).

² Plato, in his dialogue named *Gorgias*, introduces this great father and prince of <term>sophists</term> <note>Sophists: Professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments to win debates.</note> by relating that he had just then, at a private house, challenged any of the company to question him on whatever point they pleased, and had undertaken to answer all sorts of questions. This appears to have been usual for him. For Philostratus reports that when he came to Athens, he had the confidence to present himself in the middle of the theatre and say to the whole assembly, "Propose" <note>original: "Προβαλλετε," meaning "suggest a topic"</note>, referring to any argument for him to speak on. This agrees with the account given of him by Cicero at the beginning of his second book *On the Ends of Good and Evil* <note>original: "de Finibus"</note>, that he was the first who ever dared "to demand the question in a public assembly" <note>original: "in conventu poscere quaestionem"</note>; that is, as <term>Tully</term> <note>Tully: A common historical name for the Roman orator Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> says, "to invite anyone to name the subject they wished to hear about" <note>original: "jubere dicere quâ de re quis vellet audire"</note>.—S.

Now, Meno, this is exactly my own situation. I suffer from the same lack of knowledge on this matter, and I confess that I am totally ignorant regarding the essence of virtue. How, then, could I say what qualities belong to something that is completely unknown to me? Do you think it is possible for a man who has no idea who Meno is to know whether Meno is honorable, wealthy, or generous—or whether he is the opposite of all those things? Do you think that is possible?

MENO. I do not. But in all seriousness, Socrates, do you really not know what virtue is? And are you giving me permission to take home such a description of you, and to report this about you in my own country?

SOCRATES. Not only that, my friend, but also this: I have never met anyone, anywhere, whom I thought was a master of such knowledge.

MENO. Did you never meet Gorgias, then, while he was staying in this city?

SOCRATES. I did.

MENO. And did you think he knew nothing about the matter?

SOCRATES. I don't remember perfectly, Meno, and so I cannot say for certain what I thought of him then. But perhaps not only did he understand the nature of virtue, but you also know what he used to say on the subject. Remind me, then, what explanation he gave of virtue; or, if you would rather not, give me your own definition, for I assume you agree with his opinion.

MENO. I do.

SOCRATES. Then let’s leave him out of the conversation, especially since he isn't here. But tell me, Meno, what you yourself think virtue is. Share your knowledge freely, so that I may be happy to be proven wrong for saying that I never met a man who knew what virtue was—especially if it turns out that both you and Gorgias are so well acquainted with its nature.

MENO. Whatever you might imagine, Socrates, it is not at all difficult to tell you what you want to know. First, to give an example of the

**MENO.** Regarding the virtue of a man, nothing is easier to tell than that a man’s virtue consists in his ability to manage affairs of state, and, in managing them, to be of service to the public and to his friends, to harm his enemies, and to guard, at the same time, with vigilance and caution, against any harm that might arise from those enemies in their turn. Then, if you would know what the virtue of a woman is, it is easy enough to list the particulars: it is to manage the affairs of her family well, to carefully keep everything in the house safe, and to listen with obedience <note>original: "hearken with due observance"</note> to her husband. Another kind of virtue belongs to a child, which is different for a girl than for a boy; so is it likewise for the elderly. And if you choose to proceed further, the virtue of a free man is one thing, and that of a slave is another thing. There are many more virtues of all sorts, so that one cannot be at a loss to say what virtue is. For in every action, and in every stage of life, with reference to every kind of business, a specific virtue belongs to each person; and in vice also, I suppose, Socrates, there is the same relative difference and the same variety.

**SOCRATES.** I think myself much favored by Fortune, Meno; for, when I was only in search of one virtue, I have found, it seems, a whole swarm of virtues hiving in your mind. But, to pursue this analogy <note>original: "similitude"</note> taken from bees: Supposing, Meno, I had asked you what the nature of a bee was, and you had told me that bees were many and various, what would you have answered me if I had demanded of you further, whether you called them many and various, and differing one from another, in respect of their being bees; or whether you thought they differed not in this respect, but with regard to something else, such as beauty, or size, or some other accidental thing of a similar kind? What answer would you have made to such a question?

**MENO.** I should have answered thus: that so far as they were bees, in this respect they differed not at all from one another.

**SOCRATES.** Suppose, then, that I had afterwards said: Tell me, therefore, Meno, concerning this very nature of bees, in respect of which they do not differ, but all agree and are alike; what do you say it is? Should you have had any answer to give me to this question?

**MENO.** I should.

**SOCRATES.** Just so is it with the virtues. Many indeed are they, and of various kinds; but they all agree in one and the same idea <note>Socrates uses "idea" here in the Platonic sense, meaning the "Form" or essential nature that makes something what it is.</note>; through their agree—

...aspect in which they are, all of them alike, <term>virtues</term>. This idea the man, who is asked the question which I have asked of you, ought to have in his mind's eye when he answers it; and, copying from this idea, he should provide a description of <term>virtue</term>. Do you not understand the meaning of what I say?

MENO. I think I understand it reasonably well. But I do not grasp it as fully as I would like.

SOCRATES. Consider it this way then. Do you think this way concerning <term>virtue</term> alone—that the <term>virtue</term> of a man is one thing, the <term>virtue</term> of a woman another thing, and so on for other respective <term>virtues</term>, as if they are all different? Or do you have the same way of thinking regarding the <term>health</term>, <term>size</term>, and <term>strength</term> of the body? Do you think the <term>health</term> of a man is one thing, and the <term>health</term> of a woman is something different? Or is the same concept of <term>health</term> present everywhere, wherever <term>health</term> exists, whether it is in a man, or in whatever subject it is found?

MENO. The <term>health</term> of a man and the <term>health</term> of a woman, I think, are equally and alike <term>health</term>—one and the same thing.

SOCRATES. Do you not think the same way with regard to <term>size</term> and <term>strength</term>; that a woman, if she is strong, is strong according to the same principle, and with the same <term>strength</term>, which allows us to call a strong man "strong"? By "the same strength" I mean this: that whether <term>strength</term> is in a man or in a woman, when considered simply as <term>strength</term>, there is no difference. Or do you think that there is any difference between one <term>strength</term> and another?

MENO. I think there is none.

SOCRATES. And do you think, then, that any difference will be found in <term>virtue</term>, insofar as it is <term>virtue</term>, whether it is in a child or in an elderly person, in a woman or in a man?

MENO. This case of <term>virtue</term>, Socrates, seems somehow not to be exactly parallel with those other examples.

SOCRATES. Why? Did you not tell me that the <term>virtue</term> of a man consisted in his well-managing of <term>civil affairs</term>, and that of a woman in the well-managing of her <term>household</term>?

MENO. I did.

SOCRATES. I ask you, then, whether it is possible to manage any affairs well—whether <term>civil</term> or <term>domestic</term>, or any other affairs whatever—without a <term>prudent</term> and a <term>just management</term>?

MENO. By no means.

SOCRATES. If, then, the management of these things is just and prudent, must not the managers manage with justice and with prudence?

MENO. They must.

SOCRATES. Therefore, both of them require the same things to qualify them as good managers—both the woman and the man—namely, justice and prudence.

MENO. It appears they do.

SOCRATES. And how is it in the case of a child, or that of an old man? Can they ever be good if they are <term>dissolute</term> <note>original: "dissolute"; lacking in morals or self-restraint</note> and dishonest?

MENO. By no means.

SOCRATES. But only by being sober and honest?

MENO. Certainly.

SOCRATES. All people, therefore, who are good, are good in the same way; for they are good by possessing the same qualities.

MENO. It seems so.

SOCRATES. Now, if virtue were not the same thing in all of them, they would not be good in the same way.

MENO. They would not.

SOCRATES. Since, therefore, virtue is the same thing in all of them, try to remember and tell me: what was the definition given by <term>Gorgias</term> <note>A famous Greek Sophist and teacher of rhetoric who was Meno's teacher</note>, which seems to be the same definition you would give yourself?

MENO. What else is it but the ability to govern men? If you are searching for the one thing that is the same in all people who have virtue.

SOCRATES. That is exactly what I am searching for. But is this then the virtue of a child, Meno? And is it the virtue of a slave to be able to govern his master? Do you think he is still a slave when he is the one governing?

MENO. I think he is then certainly no longer a slave, Socrates.

SOCRATES. Nor is it appropriate, my friend, that he should be. Consider this further as well: you say it is virtue to be able to govern. Should we not immediately add the word *justly* and say, "to govern *justly*"? For you would not say that to govern unjustly is virtue.

MENO. I think we should. For justice, Socrates, is virtue.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates challenges Meno’s definition of virtue. Meno has just suggested that virtue is the "ability to govern men," but Socrates has pointed out that this definition cannot apply to children or slaves, as they are not meant to govern.</meta>

<header>THE MENO.</header>

SOCRATES. Is it virtue in general, Meno, or some specific virtue?

MENO. What do you mean by this distinction?

SOCRATES. I mean nothing different than how anything else is distinguished. For example, if you like, consider "roundness." I would say of roundness that it is a *specific* shape, and not simply and absolutely "shape" itself. I would express myself in that way because there are other shapes besides the round one.

MENO. You would be right to say so. And indeed, to tell the truth, I not only call justice a virtue, but I say that there are other virtues besides it.

SOCRATES. Tell me, what are these other virtues? Just as I would list for you, if you asked me, other shapes besides the round; you should list for me, in the same way, other virtues besides justice.

MENO. Well then; I think courage is a virtue, and <term>temperance</term> <note>original: "temperance"; the quality of moderation or self-restraint</note> is another, as are wisdom, <term>magnanimity</term> <note>original: "magnanimity"; the virtue of being high-minded or generous in spirit</note>, and a great many more.

SOCRATES. Once again, Meno, we have run into the same problem as before. We have found many virtues while searching for only one—though we have arrived at them in a different way this time. But we are still unable to find the one virtue that remains the same through all of these.

MENO. Because I am not yet able, Socrates, to grasp the kind of virtue you are looking for—that one essence in all of them—in the way I can with other things.

SOCRATES. That is likely; but I will do the best I can to help us move forward in our inquiry. You already understand, to some extent, that this principle applies to everything. For if someone had asked you what "shape" was (the thing I just mentioned) and you had said it was "roundness," and if he then asked you (using the same distinction I made concerning justice) whether roundness was "shape" or just a *specific* shape, you would answer that it was a specific shape.

MENO. Without any doubt.

SOCRATES. And wouldn't you answer that way because there are other shapes besides the round?

MENO. For that very reason.

SOCRATES. And if he were to ask you further what those other shapes were, would you tell him?

Do not deal with me in this way. ---

$^1$ Our senses are always drawing us toward a <term>multitude</term> <note>original: "multitude"</note>; which, when viewed only as a variety, belongs only to physical and outward things. But as soon as any multitude, or "many," are considered together and understood through one idea, they become objects of the mind. They are then both "one" and "many," because the mind is now working alongside our senses and imagination. To this way of considering things—this grasping of the many into one—Socrates here tries to lead Meno. He does this in the same way he leads Theaetetus elsewhere: by using mathematical objects, which Meno’s mind was already used to. This is the easiest step for him, and perhaps naturally the first step toward reaching universal ideas, which are purely mental. For the mind first opens itself to numbers; from there, it proceeds to figures as the boundaries of physical bodies, and is at first sight delighted with mathematical shapes. If the mind is afterwards taught the mathematical sciences, then as its powers open more and expand, it easily learns to see the "many in one." For instance, it can see the properties of all triangles contained within the idea of a triangle itself. The mind has the same comprehensive view of the circle, the square, the pentagon, and all other figures. Meno was well acquainted with these mathematical figures, and Socrates used this foundation to propose that he consider the nature of "figure" in general—that one thing in which all figures agree and are the same. — S. <note>original: "S."; this refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

$^2$ For example, <term>rectilinear</term> <note>original: "rectilinear"; consisting of straight lines</note> figures are the opposite of circles, because the entire perimeter of a circle is a curved line. — S.

**MENO.** But, Socrates, this is weak and silly.

**SOC.** How so?

**MENO.** According to your account, shape <note>original: "figure"</note> is that which always accompanies color.

**SOC.** Well?

**MENO.** But if someone were to reply that they did not know what color was, and were equally at a loss concerning both color and shape, what would you think of the answer you had given to their question?

**SOC.** Me? I would think that I had answered truthfully. And if my questioner happened to be one of those "wise men"—those professional debaters and arguers—I would tell him $^1$ that I had spoken; and that, if I had not spoken correctly, it was his business to take up the argument and refute what I had said. But if two parties, such as you and I here, were inclined to have a discussion as friends and in a friendly way, their answers to each other's questions ought to be made in a gentler manner and be more rational. Now, it is perhaps more rational that an answer should not only be truthful, but also be expressed in terms mutually understood by the person asking the question. Accordingly, I shall now attempt to give you that kind of answer. For tell me: do you not call a certain thing an "end," speaking of it as a "boundary" or "limit"? For by all these words I mean the same thing. Prodicus <note>A famous sophist known for his precise distinctions between similar-sounding words.</note>, indeed, might possibly argue with us about it, but you would use these expressions interchangeably: that such a thing is "bounded," or that it has an "end." This is all I mean; I am not looking for subtle arguments or precise distinctions.

---

<note>original: "S."</note> Socrates describes shape by its inseparable quality—that is, a circumstance which, though accidental or not necessarily part of its essence, actually always accompanies it: the presence of color. He here claims that he would be satisfied with such a description of virtue if it identified any circumstance that always attended it—as if we described virtue as "that which always accompanies wisdom."

$^1$ Socrates, when conversing with the sophists, never used an instructive method of teaching <note>original: "λογον διδασκαλικον" (logon didaskalikon)</note> to deliver his doctrine, because they, imagining themselves already sufficiently knowledgeable and wise, were not willing to learn. Nor did he ever take the truly dialectical way <note>original: "λογον διαλεκτικον" (logon dialektikon)</note> with them, because they were not concerned about truth in any argument, and because they either did not have, or would not acknowledge, any first principles from which to argue. Instead, he always disputed with them in their own way, through contentious arguments <note>original: "δια λογων εριστικων" (dia logon eristikon)</note>, refuting them using their own admissions and reducing the answers they gave to his questions to absurdities.

**MENO.** Well; there is something which I call an "end" <note>In the sense of a limit or boundary.</note>: and I think I understand what you mean.

**SOC.** Don't you and Gorgias believe that certain effluvia <note>original: "effluvia"; internal particles or vapors that flow out of physical objects</note> flow out from bodies, according to the doctrine of Empedocles?

**MENO.** We strongly hold to that doctrine.

---

[...disagreeably affect] the olfactory nerves, where the specific sense of smell is thought to be located. We will soon see how the ancient Corpuscularians <note>original: "Corpuscularians"; early scientists who believed matter was made of small particles or "corpuscles"</note>, whose system was more consistent and simpler than that of the moderns, extended the power of these effluvia to all the other outward senses. — S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

$^1$ Empedocles was a Pythagorean philosopher from Agrigentum in Sicily. He wrote a poem in three books titled *On Nature*, based on the principles of Pythagoras. Although Pythagoras, the great founder of the Italic sect, applied himself chiefly to the study of the mind—which he saw as the governing principle in nature and the only way to truly understand nature—he also philosophized about the physical and material <note>original: "corporeal"</note> parts of the universe. He did not believe the elements were irregular and infinite, as the Atomic and Atheistic philosophers imagined. Instead, he believed they were formed by rules of number and measure, being the work of a cosmic mind. Plato, in his *Timaeus*, introduced a Pythagorean (after whom the dialogue is named) to tell us the measures and proportions of these elements. For now, it is enough to say that these are the four things generally considered ever since to be the elements of nature: fire, air, water, and earth. On this foundation, Empedocles built his poem, explaining all the appearances of the natural world through the combination and motion of these four elements. The ancients considered his poetry equal to that of Homer in its versification. He seems to have been a celebrated poet before he became a philosopher. Although it does not appear that he revealed <note>original: "divulged"</note> any Pythagorean secrets in this poem, his fellow members of that sect (who were all strictly united in fellowship) expelled him from their society upon the publication of his poem. They were fearful of the precedent, as no writings had ever been published by any Pythagorean until then. At the same time, they made a law that from then on, no poet should ever be admitted as a member of their body. — S.

$^2$ Empedocles differed from the ancient Atomic philosophers because he believed all natural bodies, and even their smallest parts, were composed of the four elements as long as they remained part of those bodies. Now, since air and fire—two of those four—are active elements always in motion, and since all compound bodies are more or less porous, he supposed a constant flow <note>original: "efflux"</note> of fire-like <note>original: "igneous"</note> and air-like <note>original: "aërial"</note> particles out of those bodies through pores (whether straight or winding) that were sized for their exit. To replace these departed particles and maintain the body's structure, he supposed a constant influx of fresh air and fire from the outside. These would unite with their matching elements within the body, becoming ingredients in the frame of the compound or mixed bodies they entered. He believed these incoming streams were almost pure elements, as pure as the surrounding environment <note>original: "circumambience"</note>. However, he supposed the particles streaming out of bodies were impure, mixed or combined with watery <note>original: "aqueous"</note> particles and various types of earthy ones, depending on the nature of the body...

# THE MENO.

**SOC.** And do you not believe there are certain pores <gloss>1</gloss>, into which and through which those effluvia <note>original: "effluvia"; particles or vapors flowing out of physical objects</note> pass?

**MENO.** Certainly.

**SOC.** And that some of those effluvia <gloss>2</gloss> are adapted to some of these pores, while others are either smaller or larger than the pores?

->**MENO.**<-

---

He held the union of the four elements in compound bodies to be so intimate, and the particles of different elements to adhere so closely to one another, that none pass out as pure as they entered. Instead, every particle of the subtler and lighter elements, in departing, carries along with it some particles of the grosser and heavier elements, earth and water. Now, this is obvious to the sight in moist bodies that are strongly heated by an external fire acting on them; that is, in bodies into which so great a number of fire-like <note>original: "igneous"</note> particles have entered that they tend to cause the dissolution of those bodies. For here we see the watery particles, pregnant with air and fire, issuing forth and ascending in the form of steam and vapor. 

We may reasonably conclude that earthy particles are combined with them from the different colors of those steams or vapors. For the steam which arises from pure heated water always has the same uniform color. The difference in the color of steams or vapors must, therefore, be derived from the different kinds of earthy particles—or, as the chemists love to express it, the different salts—in those liquids and moist bodies from which the diverse colored steams or vapors arise. 

Similar appearances may be observed in the perspiration of animal bodies when they suffer a higher degree than usual of internal <note>original: "intestine"</note> heat; that is, when the fire-like particles within are put into intense motion and set loose through violent exercise of the body. We may then see the perspired moisture, by catching it on linen, to be tinged with the color of those salts which are constantly separated from the blood by the kidneys and thrown off in urine. 

It may perhaps not be irrelevant to note here that Empedocles, and the rest of the ancient elementary physiologists <note>original: "physiologers"; early scientists who studied the physical laws of nature</note>, attributed this difference of earth or earthy salts—from which they supposed all bodies derive their different colors—to different mixtures of the four elements constituting those very minute earthy particles. The purely earthy part of these is the residue <note>original: "caput mortuum"; a Latin term used by early chemists to describe the worthless remains left after distillation or heating</note> of the chemists, if this is indeed elementary pure earth. 

From this, the Corpuscularians <note>original: "Corpuscularians"; thinkers who believed the world was made of tiny physical particles or "corpuscles"</note>, by similar reasoning, drew this conclusion: that as bodies appeared to derive their different colors from the different kinds of earth which made up the bulk of their composition, the colors which reached our eyes were the finest earthy particles of those bodies. These were combined with particles of elementary fire—the essence of light, which is uncolored by itself—continually streaming forth in effluvia too minute for the eye to discern their shapes, and visible only in the form of color.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator and commentator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

---

...were large enough for the passage and release of their own effluvia <note>original: "effluvia"; the particles or vapors flowing out of physical bodies</note>, as well as for the admission and reception of other particles from the outside to take their place. However, this was not enough to explain the different types of sensation that occur in the various senses of living creatures, caused by the action and effect of the particles from other bodies sent toward them. They supposed, therefore, that the pores of the sensory organs were exactly the right shape and size for these external particles. Not all of those pores were suitable for all particles indiscriminately; that would be impossible, unless the souls of animals had the power to change the pores of their sensory organs at will to receive every kind of particle. In that case, all animals would be like Milton’s angels—entirely eye and entirely ear—and would be able to feel any kind of sensation in any part of their bodies at will. 

But the hypothesis of those natural philosophers <note>original: "phyſiologers"</note> we are discussing was this: that the organs of each sense had their pores specifically shaped to admit only the particles belonging to that sense, and no others. The eye, for instance, received the particles that create color; the ear, those that create sound; and the other sense organs were constructed in a similar way. Therefore, the different kinds of particles that could not enter—because they were either too large for the pores or shaped differently—passed by, while the particles that were too small passed through without affecting the sense at all. — **S.** <note>The "S" refers to the translator and commentator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

> As when the traveler, in dark winter’s night,
> Intent on journey, kindles up a light,
> The moon-like splendor of an oil-fed flame;
> He sets it in some lantern’s horny frame. <note>Lanterns were often made with thin, translucent sheets of animal horn instead of glass.</note>
> Calm and serene there sits the tender form,
> Screened from rough winds, and from the wintry storm.
> In vain rude airs assault the gentle fire:
> Their forces break, disperse, and they retire.
> Fences secure, though thin, the fair enclose;
> And her bright head she lifts amid her foes.
> Through the straight pores of the transparent horn
> She shoots her radiance, mild as early morn.
> Forth fly the rays; their shining path extends;
> Till, lost in the wide air, their lessening luster ends.
> So when the fire, fresh lighted from on high,
> Sits in the circling pupil of an eye;
> Over it, transparent veils of fabric fine
> Spread the thin membrane, and defend the shrine;
> The subtle flame enclosing, like a mound,
> Safe from the flood of humors <note>original: "humours"; the various fluids found within the eye</note> flowing round.
> Forth fly the rays, and their bright paths extend;
> Till, in the wide air lost, their lustres end.

We say this on the supposition that he agreed with Timaeus, a philosopher of the same sect, who—if Plato represents him rightly—accounted for vision in the same way. <margin>The following is a continuation of a note from the previous page explaining the ancient theory of vision.</margin>

...issuing from [the eye] are, in the darkness of night, extinguished by the air, which is then void of that element. However, as soon as the air is filled with light from the return of day—light whose essence is the same pure element of fire—the rays of light issuing from the eye unite themselves to their kindred element outside. Being in motion themselves, they put into that same motion those particles of outward light with which they are united. In this manner, rays of light are extended from the eye to all bodies within a certain distance, wherever the eye directs the motion of its own rays. 

These rays of light, thus extended to the surface of those bodies, meet there with the finest **effluvia** <note>original: "effluvia"; fine particles or vapors flowing out of a body.</note> issuing from them. These are particles of the same element of fire, mixed and colored with particles of the other elements carried with them out of the same bodies; a mixture or composition that the chemists call **oil** <note>In early chemistry, "oil" or "sulfur" was often used to describe the flammable or colorful principle in matter.</note>. These effluvia naturally unite themselves with the rays of light falling on the surfaces of those bodies from which they are emitted, as they are mostly of the same nature. Thus, those rays of light—which are pure and uncolored by themselves—now take on the color of these effluvia. Being reflected back from bodies (into which the streaming effluvia prevent them from entering), they communicate their color as they return to all those continuous particles of light between the object and the eye. They form continued colored rays reaching back to the eye, whose **pores** they enter. 

Modern philosophers <note>A reference to 17th and 18th-century scientists like Isaac Newton.</note> account for color through the different **refractions** <note>The bending of light as it passes through different mediums.</note> of the rays of light reflected. — S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

¹ Just as color is explained this way, sound was thought to be air violently forced out of a struck body, propagating its motion by continually repeated "strokes" through the air until it reached the ear—in the same way color moves along rays of light to the eye. Odors were considered the subtle, oily **effluvia** of bodies, released along with air and thus mixing with the element of air to be conveyed to the organ of smell. From moist bodies applied to the palate, juices were expressed—a thicker "oil"—which immediately entered the pores of the organ of taste. The causes of heat and cold were thought to be **sulphurous** and **nitrous** particles <note>Early scientific terms for chemicals associated with heat/combustion and cold/saltpeter.</note> of a body or the surrounding air, penetrating the pores of the skin and affecting the sense of feeling with those different sensations. — S.

**MENO.** There are people who imagine that things which are indeed evil are advantageous; and there are those who know them to be harmful.

**SOCRATES.** Do you think those who imagine such evil things to be advantageous actually know that the evil things are evil?

**MENO.** I do not think that at all.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not evident, then, that such people do not desire evil things—since they do not know the nature of the things they desire—but rather, they desire things which they imagine to be good, but which in reality are evil? **MENO.** I must admit, such people seem to be desiring good things.

**SOCRATES.** But what about the others—those who desire things that are evil, as you say, and who at the same time know that evil things are harmful to the owner? Do they know that they themselves will be harmed by those evil things if they possess them?

**MENO.** It is clear that they must know it.

**SOCRATES.** But do they not know that those who receive harm are in a bad state <note>original: "evil plight"</note>, to the extent that harm has come to them?

**MENO.** They must know this as well.

**SOCRATES.** And do they not also know that those who are in a bad state are unhappy as well?

<note>original: "1"</note> We learn from Xenophon (in *The Expedition of Cyrus* <note>original: "Expedit. Cyri"</note>, book 2) that the dominant passion in Meno's soul was the love of money; that his desire for honors and power in the state was secondary to that other master passion. He regarded power and honor only as the means of accumulating wealth. In the passage before us, therefore, it seems as if Plato meant to slyly and indirectly show us this strong feature of Meno's character; or rather, as if Socrates intended, in his usual humorous manner, to show Meno a true picture of himself.

<note>original: "2"</note> In the more ancient times of Greece, whenever men famous for their birth or status in life traveled from one Greek state or kingdom to another, or crossed the sea to Asia to observe the manners of other people or to learn the policy of other governments (and they seldom traveled for any other reason), they were always nobly entertained at the house of some great man in every country they visited. Persons of lower rank, whenever they traveled—which they rarely did—were everywhere treated courteously at the public expense. In the former case, that of private entertainment, not only did the noble host himself become entitled to the same hospitable reception from his guest if he should ever return the visit; but the rights of mutual hospitality also passed down to the descendants of both parties. Meno, it seems, had this connection with the Persian monarch, likely being descended (as was his friend Aristippus) from one of the ancient kings of Thessaly. However that may be, his family’s nobility is clear from his appointment to command the forces his country sent to assist Cyrus in his youth. This explains the passage now before us. Its beauty arises from the contrast seen here between Meno's high rank, which should naturally produce a noble spirit, and his shameful greed—a passion of the lowliest souls. — S. <note>This "S." likely refers to Thomas Sydenham, the 18th-century translator.</note>

No one would seek to know what they already know, because they have the knowledge already and have no need to look for it. Nor could anyone seek for what they are ignorant of, because they would not even know what they were searching for.

**MENO.** Do you not think, then, Socrates, that this way of reasoning is fair and correct?

**SOCRATES.** I do not.

### STROPHE.

> $^2$ When the soul has been stained by the guilt of lesser crimes,
> Not deserving sharp pains forever;

> If she regrets her guilt with sorrow,

> Then the ninth year sends the soul back to the light,
> And to former objects here on earth:
> Through death, she loses sight of these again;
> Again she is reborn to life.
> $^3$ At length, having well endured two trials,

> Or a sage, deeply learned in profound wisdom;
> Or a hero, spreading peace through his prowess.

$^1$ That is, ends its present life and begins a new life. For as Plato justly observes in his *Phaedo* <note>original: "Phædo"</note>, life and death succeed each other alternately throughout nature. In the passage now before us, however, the ending and beginning again of the human soul may be understood in different ways. The most obvious meaning is the breakdown of the body it inhabits and its departure into the seeds of a new body, which it then brings to life and gradually shapes to fit its own character and disposition. This meaning is consistent with the verses cited immediately after from Pindar.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to Floyer Sydenham, the 18th-century translator.</note>

$^2$ In translating this fine fragment of Pindar which Plato has preserved for us, we felt it necessary to paraphrase quite extensively to make it clear to an English reader. This is partly due to the conciseness of Pindar's style and partly because the ideas are taken from ancient mythology, with which people today are less familiar. However, we have stuck closely to the meaning of the original, completing the imagery only from that same mythology without adding any new thoughts or conceits <note>original: "concetti"</note> of our own.—S.

### EPODE.

> Through goodness, wisdom, and virtue, she is truly great;
> And greatly deserving of high advancement;
> Freed from the body, winged and swift,
> She freely ascends to the purest sky;
> To never live on earth again, and never die again.
> Among the gods in starry brightness,
> Seen far and wide throughout nature,
> She makes her home;
> Taking her heavenly throne,
> Having grown into a godlike state of being,
> An immortal demi-god.
> From then on, through the rest of time,
> In religious hymns and holy verses,
> Mortals below shall lift their songs <note>original: "lays"</note>,
> To praise the immortal demi-god;
> Who, freed from earthly impurities <note>original: "dross"</note>,
> And every element of the coarse physical body,
> Could climb to intellectual bliss in a heavenly seat.

Since the soul is immortal, has been born many times, and has seen everything that exists here on earth, in the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note>, and everywhere else, there is nothing she has not learned. It is no wonder, then, that she is able to remember what she previously knew about virtue and all other things. Because everything in nature is interconnected, and because the soul has previously known everything, there is nothing to stop a person who has recalled (or, as people usually say, "learned") just one thing from rediscovering all his former knowledge and everything else on his own—provided he is courageous and does not give up during his search. For all inquiry and learning is simply recollection $^1$ <note>original: "reminiscence"</note>. Therefore, we should not listen to that clever but deceptive <note>original: "sophistical"</note> way of reasoning mentioned earlier; believing it would only make us lazy. Consequently, the lazy and those who are opposed to...

$^1$ For a defense of recollection <note>original: "reminiscence"</note>, which Plato rightly considers one of the most important doctrines of philosophy, see the notes on the *Phaedo* <note>original: "Phædo"</note>.—T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the co-translator.</note>

...taking pains, delight to hear it. But this other way of thinking, which I have just now described to you, makes men diligent, sets them to work, and encourages them to inquire. And as I believe it to be true, I am willing, with your assistance, to inquire into the nature of virtue.

MENO. With all my heart, Socrates. But do you say this absolutely—that we do not learn anything, and that all which we call learning is only recollection <note>original: "reminiscence"</note>? Can you teach me to understand that this doctrine is true?

SOCRATES. I pointed out to you before how full of craftiness you are, O Meno. And, to confirm my observation, you now ask me if I can teach you—I, who say that there is no such thing as teaching, but that all our knowledge is recollection—just so that I may appear to directly contradict myself.

MENO. Not so, Socrates, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>. I did not express myself in those terms with any such design, but merely from habit and the common usage of that expression. But if you can prove to me in any way that your doctrine is true, please do so.

SOCRATES. This is by no means an easy task. However, for your sake, I am willing to try and do my best. Call over to me one of your many servants <note>original: "attendants"</note>, whichever you please, so that I may prove the truth of what I say through him.

MENO. I will, gladly. You there, come here.

SOCRATES. Is he Greek <note>original: "Grecian"</note>, and does he speak the Greek language?

MENO. Perfectly well. He was born in my own household.

SOCRATES. Pay attention now, and observe whether he appears to recollect things from within himself, or to learn anything from me.

MENO. I shall.

**Boy.** It is so, Socrates, for certain.

**Socrates.** Well, what do you think, Meno? Has this boy, in his answers, given any opinion other than his own?

**Meno.** None other; he has given his own opinion only.

**Socrates.** And yet, just a little while ago, as we both observed, he had no knowledge of the matter proposed and did not know how to give a correct answer.

**Meno.** True.

**Socrates.** But those very opinions, which you acknowledge to be his own, were in him all the time, were they not?

**Meno.** They were.

**Socrates.** Therefore, in a man who is ignorant, there are true opinions concerning the very things of which he is ignorant.

**Meno.** It appears there are.

**Socrates.** Those opinions, then, are stirred up again in the mind of that boy, just as dreams are. And if he were frequently questioned about these things, and by many different people, you may be assured he will eventually know them with as much certainty as any man.

**Meno.** Indeed, it seems so.

**Socrates.** Will he not then know them without being taught, having only been asked questions, and recovering the lost knowledge from within himself?

**Meno.** He will.

**Socrates.** And this recovery of knowledge from within ourselves—is this not what we call reminiscence <note>The Greek term is *anamnesis*. Socrates uses this demonstration to argue that the soul is immortal and "remembers" truths it knew before birth.</note>?

**Meno.** Without doubt.

**Socrates.** And this knowledge, which he now has, must he not have acquired it at some point, or else always possessed it?

**Meno.** Certainly.

*The greater always contains the lesser.* <note>original: "Omne majus continet in se minus."</note>—Proclus, in his commentary on the first book of the *Elements*, admires Euclid because the noble theorem introduced here by Plato—which relates only to right-angled isosceles triangles <note>A triangle with a 90-degree angle and two sides of equal length.</note>—was extended by Euclid to all right-angled triangles, whether scalene <note>A triangle where all three sides have different lengths.</note> or isosceles. We heartily join with him in this admiration, but could wish that the original theorem of Pythagoras had been added as a corollary <note>A proposition that follows naturally from one already proved.</note> to that truly admirable proposition, the 47th <note>Proposition 47 of Euclid’s *Elements* Book I is the Pythagorean Theorem: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.</note>.—S. <note>The "S." refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham (1710–1787).</note>

**Socrates.** Now, if he always possessed this knowledge, then he was always a person of knowledge. But if he first received it at some specific time, was it not in his current life? That is, unless someone has taught him the science of geometry. I ask you because you ought to know, since he was born and raised in your household.

**MENO.** I am certain that no one has ever taught him those sciences.

**Socrates.** And yet he holds those opinions which he has just now declared, does he not?

**MENO.** It appears, Socrates, that he must.

**Socrates.** If, then, he had this knowledge within him <gloss>2</gloss>, not having acquired it in this present life, it is clear that at some other time he had learned it and actually possessed it.

**MENO.** It appears so.

**Socrates.** And was that time not, then, when he was not yet a human being?

**MENO.** Certainly.

**Socrates.** If true opinions exist in him at both these times—the time when he is <gloss>3</gloss> and the time when he is not a human being—and if these opinions, when awakened and stirred by questions <gloss>4</gloss>, rise up into knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, then must his soul not have been well-equipped with this understanding <gloss>5</gloss> throughout all time? For it is clear that in every age he either is, or is not, a human being.

**MENO.** By all appearances, it must be so.

By "hypothetically," I mean in the same manner as geometricians often treat a question. For instance, when they are asked about a certain geometrical figure $^1$—whether it is possible for such a particular triangle (Fig. 13) to be inscribed $^2$ (Fig. 14) in a particular circle. A geometrician would answer: "I do not yet know $^3$ what kind of triangle this is $^4$. # THE MENO.

...down therefore these two hypotheses clearly, I can tell you what will follow in each of these cases¹ regarding the inscribing of that triangle within the circle—whether it is impossible or possible. We shall take the same approach in our inquiry concerning virtue: since we do not know what it is or what qualities it has, we shall propose a hypothesis about it. Based on that hypothesis, we will consider whether it can be taught or not. 

Let us state the question this way: Assuming virtue is one of those things belonging to the soul, should virtue, according to this hypothesis, be taught or not? In the first place, it is either a different kind of thing from knowledge, or it is the same kind of thing as knowledge. Based on each of these hypotheses, let us inquire whether virtue is or is not to be taught—or, as we recently phrased it, "recalled to mind" <note>Socrates refers here to his theory of "recollection," the idea that learning is actually the soul remembering knowledge it possessed before birth</note>. Whichever of these expressions we use, let it make no difference to us. The question, then, is whether virtue is something that is taught. Now, is it not clear to everyone that a person is taught nothing other than knowledge?

MENO. It seems so to me.

SOCRATES.

¹ In stating the question, it must be assumed as obvious that the given side of the triangle is not greater than the diameter of the given circle. For if it were greater, no such question could even be proposed; the absurdity or impossibility of the task would be too plain. It also seems that this given side is intended to be the diameter of the circle to be drawn, by using the midpoint of this side as the center. Only in this way can the circle properly be said <term>to be drawn around or about the given side</term> <note>original: "περιτεινεσθαι περι την δοθεισαν γραμμην"</note>. 

If this is granted, then in the first case (the possible one), the angle of the triangle opposite the given side must be either (fig. 15) a right angle or (fig. 16) an obtuse angle. In the other (impossible) case, that angle must be (fig. 17) acute. If the angle is assumed to be a right angle, then the circle drawn will be <term>circumscribed</term> <note>original: "περιγραφομενον"</note> about the triangle, and the triangle may also <term>be inscribed</term> <note>original: "εγγραφεσθαι"</note> within an equal given circle; for every angle of it would touch the circumference of that circle.

# THE MENO.

SOCRATES. If virtue, therefore, is a certain kind of knowledge, it is evident that virtue is to be taught.
MENO. Undoubtedly.
SOCRATES. We have quickly finished this part of the inquiry; and have fairly come to this conclusion: that if virtue is the same kind of thing as knowledge, it is to be taught; otherwise, it is not.
MENO. Very true.
SOCRATES. Next, it seems that we should consider whether virtue is knowledge or something different from knowledge.
MENO. I think we ought to consider this next.
SOCRATES. Well now, shall we suppose that virtue is something which is good? Shall we stick with this hypothesis, establishing it as a certainty that virtue is something good?
MENO. By all means.
SOCRATES. Now, if there is also any other good separate from knowledge, then perhaps virtue might not be a certain kind of knowledge. But if there is no sort of good which is not included under knowledge, then the suspicion that virtue is a kind of knowledge would be a justified suspicion.
MENO. What you say is true.
SOCRATES. But further: is it not through virtue that we are good?
MENO. It is.
SOCRATES. And if we are good, then we are advantageous <note>In this context, "advantageous" means beneficial, useful, or profitable to oneself and others</note>. For all things that are good are advantageous, are they not?
MENO. They are.
SOCRATES. Virtue, then, is something advantageous too.

Similarly, Greek historians say a wall is *stretched around* <note>original: *περιτεινεσθαι* (periteinesthai)</note> a camp or a city when the wall surrounds and encloses it, even if no tent or house should touch the wall. But we think Plato’s meaning is put beyond dispute by the word *to fall short* <note>original: *ελλειπειν* (elleipein)</note>, which does not apply to a triangle that touches the circle at every one of its angles. It is compatible only with a triangle where at least one angle falls short of the circumference of that circle (fig. 16) drawn around it. *To fall short* <note>original: *ελλειπειν*</note> is also the opposite of *to exceed* <note>original: *ὑπερβαλλειν* (hyperballein)</note>. In the latter case supposed by Plato, where the whole triangle cannot be contained within the circle (fig. 17) drawn about the given side, the angle which is opposite this side must be an acute angle; the sides that form this angle would have to extend beyond the circumference of the circle to meet and form that angle.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham, who provided these technical geometric explanations</note>.

_MENO._ It is likely, Socrates, that in that case this would be done.

ANYTUS. And what persons, Socrates, do you mean?

SOCRATES. You surely know that I am speaking of those who are called sophists <term>Sophists: Professional teachers in ancient Greece who traveled from city to city, teaching various subjects—including rhetoric and virtue—for a fee.</term>¹.

ANYTUS. By Hercules! <note>original: "O Hercules!"</note> Do not speak so shamefully, Socrates. May none of my relatives, friends, or acquaintances, fellow-citizens, or foreign guests, ever be seized with such madness as to go and be ruined by those men. For those men are the ruin and corruption of all who follow them.

SOCRATES. What are you saying, Anytus? Are these the only people among those claiming to know something beneficial to humankind who are so different from everyone else? Do they not only fail to improve what is put into their hands—as other craftsmen do—but actually corrupt and spoil it? And do they think it right to openly demand fees for doing so? I do not know how I can believe your account. For I know of one man in particular, Protagoras, who earned more wealth from his wisdom than Phidias—famous for his beautiful sculptures—and any ten other sculptors <note>original: "statuaries"</note> combined. What you tell me is a marvel. If cobblers <note>original: "menders of old shoes"</note> and tailors <note>original: "menders... of old clothes"</note> could not go a month without being publicly exposed if they returned clothes or shoes in worse condition than they received them—and would soon starve if they did—how is it that Protagoras could corrupt and spoil his followers for over forty years without being discovered by all of Greece? He was nearly seventy years old when he died, having spent forty of those years practicing his profession. Throughout all that time, he maintained a high reputation that continues even to this day. And it was not only Protagoras who met with this success, but many others as well; some who lived before him, and some who are flourishing today. Now, should we suppose that they knowingly deceived and corrupted the youth, as you say they did? Or should we suppose they did so without realizing it themselves? Should we consider such men—whom some call the wisest of mankind—to be so completely out of their senses?
