### THE MENO.

**ANYTUS.** They are far from being insane, Socrates. Rather, it is the youth who are insane for giving them money to corrupt them. Even more so are their relatives for entrusting them to the guidance of such men. But the most insane of all are those cities that allow such men to enter and do not drive away and banish every man—whether foreigner or citizen—who sets up such a profession.

**SOCRATES.** Has any of the sophists ever done you any harm, Anytus? Or why else are you so angry with them?

**ANYTUS.** By Zeus! <note>original: "by Jupiter"; the English translator used the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods</note> I have never interacted with one of them myself, nor would I allow anyone belonging to me to do so.

**SOCRATES.** You have no experience at all with those men, then.

**ANYTUS.** And I never desire to have any.

**SOCRATES.** How then could you know if there is any good or any harm in their teaching, when you have no experience with it at all?

**ANYTUS.** Easily enough. For I know what sort of fellows they are, whether I have had any experience with them and their teaching or not.

**SOCRATES.** Perhaps you have the gift of prophetic insight <term>Divination: The practice of seeking knowledge of the unknown or future by supernatural means; Socrates is being sarcastic here.</term>, Anytus. Otherwise, I would wonder how you could know what they are like based on your own account. But we were not asking who Meno might go to in order to become a bad man; if you wish, let those be the sophists. Now, tell us about those others. Do a kindness to this family friend <note>original: "hereditary friend"</note> of yours by directing him to the people in this great city he can go to in order to become eminent in that virtue I described to you just now.

**ANYTUS.** But why did you not direct him to such persons yourself?

**SOCRATES.** I have already told you which people I imagined were the teachers of these duties. But, as you inform me, I happen to have said nothing useful.

**ANYTUS.** There is perhaps some truth in that.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is now your turn to tell him which of the Athenians he should go to. Name anyone you choose.

**ANYTUS.** Why does he need to hear the name of any one man? Among the honorable and virtuous men of Athens, there is not one—the first he meets—who would not make him a better man than the sophists would, if he will only listen and be observant.

# THE MENO.

**SOCRATES.** But did these men of honor and virtue become so on their own, without having learned from anyone else how to be what they are? And are they able to teach others what they themselves were never taught?

**ANYTUS.** I assume they learned from those who went before them—men of similar honor and virtue. Or do you not think that our city has produced many excellent men?

**SOCRATES.** I believe, Anytus, that in this city there are men who are excellent in political affairs, and that there have been others no less excellent before them. But were they good teachers of that political excellence? This is the actual subject of our current debate: not whether men of honor and virtue can be found in this city now or in the past, but whether virtue can be taught at all. This is what we have been considering and inquiring about for a long time. In pursuing this inquiry, we have arrived at this question: did those excellent men, whether of the present or former days, know how to impart or pass down to others that virtue in which they themselves excelled? Or is it impossible for a person to pass down or impart virtue, and for men to receive it from one another? This is what Meno and I have been examining for a long time. Consider the question now in this way, based on your own argument. Would you not say that Themistocles <gloss>1</gloss> was a man of virtue?

**ANYTUS.** I would; and I would say he was the most virtuous of all men.

**SOCRATES.** And wouldn't you then say that if any man could teach his own virtue to another, Themistocles would have been a good teacher?

**ANYTUS.** I suppose he would have been, if he had intended to teach it.

**SOCRATES.** But do you suppose he did not want others to be made men of honor and virtue, and especially his own son? Or do you imagine that he maliciously and intentionally withheld from his son that virtue in which he himself excelled? Have you never heard that Themistocles taught <gloss>2</gloss> his—

<header>THE MENO.</header>

# THE MENO.

**SOCRATES.** Anytus seems to me to be angry, Meno. And I am not at all surprised at it. For, in the first place, he supposes that I spoke ill of those persons I mentioned; and then he considers himself¹ to be like them. Now if this man should ever come to know what it means to truly speak ill of others, he will cease to be angry; but at present, he is ignorant of it. Tell me then, and answer now: are there not among us men of honor and virtue?

**MENO.** Certainly there are.

**SOCRATES.** But are these men willing to offer themselves to the youth to teach them virtue? Do they profess to be teachers of it? Or do they agree that virtue is a thing which can be taught?

**MENO.** No, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, Socrates, they do not. For you may hear them sometimes maintaining that it can be taught, and at other times that it cannot.

**SOCRATES.** Shall we say then that these men are teachers of virtue, when they have not settled even this point—whether virtue can be taught or not?

**MENO.** I think we should not, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Well; but what do you say of those sophists <term>Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece who traveled from city to city, charging fees to teach various subjects, including rhetoric and "virtue."</term>, the only persons who claim to teach virtue? Do you think that they are the teachers?

**MENO.** It is for this reason, Socrates, that I especially admire **Gorgias**; because you will never hear him making any such claims, or taking such a role upon himself. On the contrary, he laughs at the others whenever he hears them promising to teach men to be virtuous; he believes the role of a sophist is only to make men great orators and powerful speakers.

**SOCRATES.** You do not think then that the sophists are the teachers of virtue either?

**MENO.** I know not what to say to this, Socrates. They have the same effect on me as they have on most other people; sometimes I think they are, and sometimes I think they are not.

**SOCRATES.** Do you know that not only you and those others who are experienced in public affairs sometimes think that virtue is acquired through teaching, and sometimes that it is not? Do you know that the poet **Theognis** is of the same mind, and speaks in exactly the same way?

**SOCRATES.** In his *Elegiacs* <gloss>1</gloss>; where he says,

> ->Always mix with men who are great through virtue,<-
> ->And let your happy seat be placed near theirs;<-
> ->Always be a companion at their table and bowl,<-
> ->And always bend your soul to what delights them.<-
> ->For goodness shall be caught through sweet contagion,<-
> ->And virtue will be taught by living manners.<-
> ->But the company of bad men is the school of folly,<-
> ->Where wisdom, taught backward, makes one a fool.<-

> ->If the wise could impart their wisdom to fools;<-
> ->If understanding could be infused by art;<-
> ->Or if right thought could be driven into the mind;<-
> ->For this, how often would great rewards be given?<-

That is, they would be given to those men who were complete masters of this skill. And again he says,

<gloss>1</gloss> An elegiac verse, strictly speaking, is a pentameter—a verse consisting of four feet and two half-feet, equally divided: two feet and a half making the first part of the verse, and two feet and a half the latter. However, very few poems were ever written purely in this meter. Those verses were commonly called elegiac where hexameter and pentameter verses were used alternately, such as the verses quoted here by **Plato**. They are found in that collection of the verses of **Theognis** still in existence today, under the title *Gnomai Elegiakai* <note>original: "Γνωμαι ελεγιακαι," meaning "Elegiac Maxims"</note>, beginning at verse 33. One would imagine, from Meno's last question and this answer from Socrates, that Theognis wrote some other poems in a different meter. **Fabricius** <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a German classical scholar.</note> accordingly says that *Gnomai* were written by Theognis in 2,800 verses of heroic measure, and cites **Suidas** <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> as his authority for this. We assume that he read this in some manuscript or old edition of Suidas, but in **Kuster’s** <note>Ludolf Küster (1670–1716), a German philologist.</note> edition we read "elegiac" and not "heroic." — S. <note>The "S." refers to the translator, likely Sydenham.</note>

**MENO.** I think what you say is true.

**SOCRATES.** But we agreed before that a thing for which neither teachers nor students can be found is not a subject of teaching and cannot be taught.

**MENO.** We were agreed in this.

**SOCRATES.** Now, there appear to be no teachers of virtue anywhere.

**MENO.** Very true.

**SOCRATES.** And if there are no teachers of it, then there are no students in it either.

**MENO.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** Virtue, therefore, must be a thing which cannot be taught.

**MENO.** It seems so, if we have considered the matter rightly. And because of this, Socrates, I am led to wonder whether any truly good men are ever to be found, and if there are, by what means they became so.

<header>THE MENO.</header>

Therefore, we ought to apply ourselves and search for someone who, by some reliable means, would make us better men. I say this regarding our current inquiry, in which we have been foolish enough not to realize that human affairs are not managed rightly and well solely under the guidance of knowledge <note>original: "science" (Greek: *epistēmē*), meaning systematic knowledge or certain understanding</note>. Or, if we will not admit that, then at least we must admit that they are not guided by knowledge alone, but also by something else. Perhaps the way in which men actually become good has escaped us.

**MENO.** How so, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you. We correctly agreed that good and virtuous men must also be beneficial to us, and that it is impossible for it to be otherwise. Isn't this true?

**MENO.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** And should we not also admit that they are beneficial to us because they manage our affairs correctly?

**MENO.** Without doubt.

**SOCRATES.** But it seems we were wrong to assume that it is impossible for a man to manage affairs correctly unless he is wise <note>original: "prudent"</note>.

**MENO.** What do you mean now by the word "correctly"?

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you what I mean. If a man who knew the way to Larissa <note>A major city in ancient Thessaly</note>, or anywhere else you like, were to lead others he had promised to guide there, wouldn't he guide them well and correctly?

**MENO.** Without doubt.

**SOCRATES.** And what if a man undertook to do this who only had a *correct opinion* about the way, but had never been there himself and had no certain knowledge? Wouldn't he also guide them correctly?

**MENO.** To be sure.

**SOCRATES.** And as long as he had a correct opinion about the way—the same way the other man knew for certain—he wouldn't be a worse guide at all. Even if he were only guessing correctly <note>original: "surmising justly"</note> rather than knowing clearly, he would be just as good as the man with perfect knowledge.

**SOCRATES.** Right opinion, therefore, regarding right action, is not at all a worse guide than certain knowledge <note>original: "science" (Greek: *epistēmē*), referring to systematic or certain knowledge</note>. **MENO.** In this respect, however, Socrates, it is; for he who has a perfect knowledge of his goal would always attain it, but the man who had only a right opinion of it would sometimes attain it and sometimes would not.

**SOCRATES.** What do you mean? Wouldn't the man who had a right opinion always attain his goal, as long as he held that right opinion?

**MENO.** It appears to me that he must. And therefore I wonder, Socrates—this being the case—for what reason systematic knowledge is so much more valuable than right opinion, and indeed in what way they differ from each other at all.

**SOCRATES.** Do you know now why you wonder? Or shall I tell you?

**MENO.** By all means, tell me.

**SOCRATES.** It is because you never attentively considered those statues <note>original: "images"</note> made by Daedalus <note>A mythical Greek inventor and craftsman; his statues were said to be so lifelike they could move on their own</note>. But perhaps you have none of them in your country.

**MENO.** Why is it that you speak of these statues now?

**SOCRATES.** Because these, if they are not fastened down, run away from us and become fugitives; but if they are fastened, they stay with us.

**MENO.** Well, and what then?

**SOCRATES.** To have in one's possession any of his works while they are loose and unfastened is like being the master of a runaway slave; it is a matter of little value because it is not permanent. But when fastened and secured, they are things of great value, for indeed they are works of great beauty. But you ask why I speak of these statues. I answer: it is with a view toward true opinions. For true opinions also, so long as they stay—

---

¹ In the Greek, *aitias logismō* <note>original: αιτιας λογισμω</note>, meaning "by a rational account of the cause"; or by proving how and from what cause it is that they are true. The cause of every truth is some other truth, higher and more general, in which it is included. To those who have considered the method naturally used by the mind in reasoning (commonly but incorrectly called the "art of reasoning"), this will be clear from this fact: a proposition is an opinion of the mind expressed in words which affirm or deny that one thing belongs to another. If the proposition—that is, if the opinion—is true, it allows for a rational proof. All rational proof consists in showing or displaying some general truth, or true proposition, in which the proposition to be proved is essentially included. In syllogistic reasoning (the only way of reasoning upward, or tracing any truths from their causes), that truth or true proposition which is more general than the proposition to be proved is called the "major proposition" for that reason—because it is of larger scope or more general than the conclusion (the proposition to be proved). It contains within it the truth of that conclusion, along with many other truths that are side-by-side with one another and all subordinate to, or less general than, the major proposition itself. In the same way, the truth of this major and more general proposition is to be traced out and deduced from another proposition that is even more general, and so on until we arrive at some self-evident truth. This self-evident truth is apparently the cause from which the truth of those other, less general propositions is deduced, which gradually and in order lead the mind up to it—the reason why they are true. If many subordinate truths arise out of one and the same general truth, they all equally depend on it; thus, through this general truth, they are all connected together, like the side-by-side chains mentioned as a metaphor (though regarding another subject) by Plato in his *Ion* <note>original: "Io"</note>, all hanging from the iron ring at the top that is attached to a magnet. — S. <note>likely the translator, Thomas Sydenham</note>

<summary>Socrates explains that right opinions are unstable and "slip away" unless they are tethered by a rational understanding of their cause, a process he identifies as "recollection." This anchoring is what distinguishes certain knowledge from mere opinion, making the former more valuable and permanent.</summary>

---

¹ This sentence, along with the one immediately before it, seems to be the right key to understand that part of the conversation between Socrates and his friends where he was generally thought to hide <note>original: "dissemble"</note> his great knowledge. We find him here disclaiming knowledge of things that are not the proper objects of knowledge, but only of imagination and opinion; and such are almost all the subjects even of philosophical conversation. We also find him at the same time openly declaring, with great seriousness rather than irony, that he knew the different nature of those two judgments of the soul: certain knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> and opinion. One of these comes from the mind, the other from the senses. Now, if all certain knowledge depends on knowing its own principle, and if this principle is the mind, and if the human soul shares in that mind, it follows that the human mind, knowing itself, knows how it differs from the lower faculties of the soul. It knows how its own judgment of things (which is certain knowledge) differs from theirs (which amounts to no more than mere opinion). It follows that the mind knows what certain knowledge is, and consequently knows what falls short of it. It also follows that the mind knows which objects belong to certain knowledge and which belong to opinion; it holds and contemplates the former within itself, while rejecting and disclaiming the latter as not belonging to its domain. Accordingly, we shall find that Socrates—who knew his true self, his mind—never pretended, as ignorant people often do, to know things that cannot be known; nor, on the other hand, did he pretend not to know the nature of the human mind, its principles, or its objects, so far as they are shared with individual minds by the universal mind. —S. <note>Floyer Sydenham, the translator</note>
² That is, in distinguishing certain knowledge from right opinion. —S.
³ This is because right opinion mainly concerns things perceived by the senses <note>original: "sensibles"</note>; but certain knowledge concerns things understood by the intellect <note>original: "intelligibles"</note>. —T. <note>Thomas Taylor, the philosopher/editor</note>

...but also by means of right opinion. And since neither of these is in men by nature—neither knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> nor right opinion—or do you think that either of them comes by nature?

**MENO.** Not I.

**SOCRATES.** Since, then, they do not come by nature, it is not by nature that men could have been good and virtuous.

**MENO.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** Now, seeing that virtue does not come by nature, we should next consider if it comes through teaching.

**MENO.** To be sure we should.

**SOCRATES.** Did it not appear to both of us that if virtue was wisdom, then it came through teaching?

**MENO.** It did.

**SOCRATES.** And that if virtue came through teaching, then virtue would be wisdom?

**MENO.** Very true.

**SOCRATES.** And that if there were any teachers of virtue, virtue would in that case be a thing that came through teaching; otherwise not?

**MENO.** Just so.

**SOCRATES.** But we have agreed that there were no teachers of it.

<note>
Just here, in all the Greek editions, these words are added: *neither are they acquired* <note>original: "ουτ' επίκτητα"</note>. This part of the sentence is apparently false: for knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> and right opinion are both acquired; knowledge through teaching, and right opinion through other external means. But even if it were true regarding right opinion, and even if the word *acquired* <note>original: "επίκτητα"</note> meant in this place *acquired through teaching*, it would be irrelevant to this part of the argument and premature. Socrates is here proving only this: that virtue does not come from nature. He proves this by showing that all men who act rightly and well do so either from knowledge or from right opinion, neither of which principles of action men have from nature. It is not until afterward that he proves virtue is not acquired through teaching. With great judgment, therefore, Janus Cornarius, in his translation, took no notice of those two words. In his *Selections* <note>original: "Eclogæ"</note>, he has with great probability suggested that the words *but acquired* <note>original: "αλλ' επίκτητα"</note> were an ancient commentary <note>original: "scholium"</note> written in the margin, and by subsequent transcribers—as happened frequently—incorporated into the main text. Afterward, the word *but* <note>original: "αλλ'"</note> was changed into *nor* <note>original: "ουτ'"</note> by some later copyist who was not attending to the course of the argument, but only to the conclusion. The necessity of this omission is so clear that we wonder not so much at the insight of Cornarius in seeing it, as at the blindness of Henri Estienne <note>original: "Stephens"</note> in not seeing it, but expressly denying it. — S.
</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Socrates and Meno are evaluating whether virtue is a form of knowledge (referred to here as "science") or if it stems from another source, since they have concluded it cannot be taught.</meta>

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>->THE MENO.<-</header>

**MENO.** True.

**SOCRATES.** We are agreed, therefore, that virtue does not come through teaching, and that virtue is not wisdom.

**MENO.** Certainly so.

**SOCRATES.** But we also agreed that virtue was something good.

**MENO.** True.

**SOCRATES.** And that whatever manages affairs rightly is something good and useful to us.

**MENO.** We clearly did.

**SOCRATES.** And that affairs are managed rightly by only two things: true opinion and knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>. By possessing either of these two, a man becomes a good leader and guide. Whatever results from luck <note>original: "fortune"</note> is not the effect of human conduct. But so far as a man has a role in managing things rightly, it is only through one of these means: true opinion and knowledge.

**MENO.** I think so.

**SOCRATES.** Now, since virtue does not come through teaching, it is not the result of knowledge.

**MENO.** It appears that it is not.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, of the only two things that are good and useful for a person's correct conduct, we have eliminated one from the discussion, having agreed that knowledge is not the means by which public <note>original: "civil"</note> affairs are administered and managed rightly.

**MENO.** I think it is not.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, it was not through any wisdom, nor by being wise, that such men governed the state—men like <term>Themistocles</term> <note>A famous Athenian politician and general who led the Greeks against the Persians</note> and the others whom <term>Anytus</term> <note>An influential Athenian politician and one of the men who later brought charges against Socrates</note> just now mentioned. For this very reason, they were not capable of making others like themselves, because it was not knowledge that made them who they were.

**MENO.** The case, <term>Socrates</term>, seems to be as you describe it.

**SOCRATES.** If, then, it is not knowledge, it follows that it must be the other remaining option—namely, right opinion—through which public affairs are managed correctly by our statesmen and politicians. In terms of wisdom, these men are not at all superior to the oracle singers and divine prophets. For these people also say many true things but have no real knowledge of anything they say.

**MENO.** I suspect this is the case.

**SOCRATES.** Now, Meno, don't those men deserve to be called divine, who either speak or act correctly in many matters of great importance without any rational <note>original: "intellectual"</note> knowledge of the subjects they are dealing with?

**MENO.** They certainly do.

**SOCRATES.** We should rightly call those men divine whom we just mentioned: the oracle singers, the prophets, and all who are inspired by the Muses. And we should say that politicians are no less divine than these; they are just as much enthusiasts <note>In this context, someone who is "possessed" or "inspired" by a god</note>, divinely inspired and possessed by the Divinity, when their speeches correctly guide many great affairs, even though they have no real knowledge of the subjects they are talking about.

**MENO.** We certainly should.

**SOCRATES.** And similarly, Meno, you know that women call men of virtue "divine men." And the Lacedaemonians <note>Another name for the Spartans</note>, when they praise any man of virtue, are used to saying of him that he is a "divine man."

**MENO.** And they seem to speak justly too, Socrates. And yet, perhaps Anytus <note>One of the men who later brought Socrates to trial; he has been listening to this conversation with growing frustration</note> here is offended by what you say.

**SOCRATES.** I am not concerned about that. We shall have a conversation with him, Meno, at another time. But if, during this entire conversation, we have pursued our inquiries and reasoning correctly, then virtue comes neither by nature nor through teaching. Instead, to those who possess it, it must come as a divine gift <note>original: "portion or allotment"</note>, without the person having any rational understanding or true knowledge of it—unless there should be found among the politicians someone capable of making another man a good politician. But if there were such a person, he could almost be said to be among the living what Homer tells us <term>Tiresias</term> <note>A famous blind prophet in Greek mythology</note> is among the dead. For Homer, speaking of him and of the others in <term>Hades</term> <note>The Greek underworld</note>, says:¹

truth and substance of things, compared with shadows $^1$, in respect of virtue.

**MENO.** What you say, Socrates, seems to me to be perfectly right.

**SOCRATES.** From this reasoning then, Meno, it appears to us that those who possess virtue have it as a divine gift <note>original: "portion or allotment"</note> to them. But we will only reach certainty on this point when, before inquiring by what means virtue comes to men, we first set about searching for what the <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing</note> of virtue is. — But it is now time for me to go somewhere else. And since you are now convinced of the truth of these conclusions—the result of our inquiries—go and persuade your friend Anytus to believe them as well. For he may thus be softened and become milder; and by persuading him, you might possibly do a great service to your country. <note>Anytus was one of the primary accusers who eventually brought Socrates to trial and execution. Socrates suggests that if Anytus understood virtue better, he might be less hostile to philosophy.</note>

***

$^1$ It is easy to see that this is a metaphor taken from the simile used here regarding Tiresias and the rest of the ghosts in Hades; or, it is an application of the simile to the subject it illustrates, using terms that apply literally to the simile but metaphorically to the subject. For the application of the simile is this: just as all the other ghosts in Hades are compared to Tiresias, so are men who only have "right opinion"—but lack scientific principles—compared to men of true <term>science</term> <note>original: "science"; here meaning systematic, certain knowledge (Greek: *episteme*)</note>, who understand those principles. In the simile, the common herd of ghosts are unreal, insubstantial shades or shadows compared with Tiresias, who is, in relation to them, real substance. In the subject being compared to this simile, men of right opinion are like shadows when compared with men of real science. The accuracy of this comparison depends on these doctrines of Plato: that matters of opinion are objects of the imagination, while matters of science are objects of the mind or intellect; that all objects of the imagination are only images of things perceived by the senses; and that these sensible objects are themselves but the shadows of "intelligible" things—the true objects of the intellect. —S. <note>The "S" likely refers to Thomas Sydenham, the translator and commentator.</note>

<note>Since the same question is discussed in this dialogue—though not as fully as in the *Meno*—namely, whether virtue can be taught, a lengthy introduction is unnecessary. I shall only observe that the liveliness and variety of the characters, the humor and pleasantry of Socrates, the simplicity and nobility of the narratives, and the knowledge of antiquity it displays are beauties as obvious as they are matchless. For an account of Protagoras, that leading sophist <term>sophist: a paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric in ancient Greece, often criticized for prioritizing persuasion over truth</term>, see the *Theaetetus*.</note>

### ASSOCIATE.

**W**HERE do you come from, Socrates? Or is it not obvious that you have been out hunting after the beauty of Alcibiades? For when I saw him recently, the man appeared beautiful to me. I say "the man"—for between ourselves, Socrates, he can certainly be called that now, since his beard is beginning to appear.

**SOCRATES.** What of it? Do you not actually praise Homer <note>original: "Homer³"; referring to the 10th book of the *Odyssey*, where Homer describes the god Hermes taking the form of a young man whose beard is just beginning to grow, the most charming age of youth</note>, who says that the age of a young man when his beard first begins to grow is the most delightful? And that is exactly the age Alcibiades has reached now.

<note>Prodicus was a sophist from the island of Cos who flourished around 396 BC. His pupils included the playwright Euripides, Socrates, the politician Theramenes, and the orator Isocrates. He charged his audience to hear him speak, which led some ancient writers to mention the "fifty-drachma lectures" of Prodicus. Among his many writings, he composed a famous story in which Virtue and Pleasure are introduced attempting to win over the hero Hercules.</note>

**ASSOCIATE.** But are you not coming from him right now? And how is the young man disposed toward you?

**SOCRATES.** He seems to be well-disposed toward me, especially today; for he said many things in my defense, and I have only just now left him. However, I want to tell you something very strange: though he was present, I did not pay attention to him, and I even forgot to look at him.

**ASSOCIATE.** What great event happened to both of you, then? For you could not have met with any other person as beautiful in this city.

**SOCRATES.** I did, however—and with one far more beautiful.

**ASSOCIATE.** What are you saying? Was he a citizen or a stranger?

**SOCRATES.** A stranger.

**ASSOCIATE.** Where did he come from?

**SOCRATES.** From Abdera <note>Abdera was a Greek city-state on the coast of Thrace, famous for being the home of Protagoras and Democritus.</note>.

**ASSOCIATE.** And did this stranger seem so beautiful to you that he surpassed the beauty of the son of Clinias <note>The "son of Clinias" refers to Alcibiades, a prominent and handsome Athenian statesman and a frequent companion of Socrates.</note>?

**SOCRATES.** How could it be otherwise, my friend <note>original: "O blessed man"; a common Socratic form of address (*o makarie*) used ironically or affectionately</note>? Must not the wisest person always appear to be the more beautiful?

**ASSOCIATE.** Do you come to us now, Socrates, from some wise man?

**SOCRATES.** I do indeed—from the wisest man currently living, if you consider Protagoras to be the wisest.

**ASSOCIATE.** What are you saying? Has Protagoras arrived here?

**SOCRATES.** He has been here for these three days.

**ASSOCIATE.** And have you just now been with him?

**SOCRATES.** I have; and I have both spoken and heard many things.

**ASSOCIATE.** Won't you recount this conversation to us, then? If nothing prevents you, please sit here; this boy will give you his seat.

**SOCRATES.** I will certainly tell you the story, and I will thank you for listening to it.

**ASSOCIATE.** And we shall thank you for the narration.

**SOCRATES.** Then there will be mutual thanks. Listen, then: This morning, while it was still dark, Hippocrates—the son of Apollodorus and the brother of Phason—knocked very hard at my gate with his staff. As soon as it was opened, he rushed into my bedroom, crying out in a loud voice, "Socrates, are you asleep?" Recognizing his voice, I said, "Is that Hippocrates? Do you bring any news?" "None," he replied, "except what is good."

"The education which I shall receive from Protagoras," he said, "seems to me to be exactly that kind of thing."

"...what you now intend to do? Or is it hidden from you?"

"About what?"

"That you are about to entrust your soul to the care of a man who, as you say, is a <term>sophist</term> <note>original: "sophist"; a traveling teacher in ancient Greece who reached philosophy, rhetoric, and virtue for a fee.</note>. If you are ignorant of this, you don't even know to whom you are delivering your soul, nor whether you are handing it over to something good or bad."

"But I think I know," he said.

"Tell me then, what do you think a sophist is?"

"I think," he replied, "as the name implies, that he is someone knowledgeable in matters of wisdom."

"But," I replied, "the same thing could be said of painters and architects—that they are also knowledgeable in matters of wisdom. If someone were to ask us in what specific ways painters are knowledgeable, we would answer him that their wisdom consists in the creation of images; we would reply in a similar way regarding other professions. But if someone should ask, 'In what specific matters is a sophist wise?' what should we answer? Of what art is he the master?"

"Socrates, he is the master of the art that enables men to speak eloquently."

"Perhaps," I said, "we are speaking the truth, yet we are not being specific enough. This answer requires another question: in what subject does a sophist make men eloquent? For example, doesn't a harpist also enable those he instructs to speak about the subject he knows—namely, playing the harp? Isn't that right?"

"It is."

"So be it, then. But about what subject does a sophist make men eloquent? It is obvious that it must be about things of which he has knowledge."

"That is likely."

"What, then, is that subject about which the sophist is knowledgeable and which he teaches to others?"

"By Zeus <note>original: "By Jupiter"; the translator uses the Roman name for the Greek king of the gods.</note>," he replied, "I can no longer tell you."

After this, I said, "Do you realize, then, the danger to which you are going to expose your soul? If you were going to risk your body's health—putting it in a good or bad condition—wouldn't you carefully consider whether or not to take that risk? Wouldn't you call your friends and relatives to consult with them? And wouldn't you take more than one day to think the matter over? 

Even though you value your soul far more than your body—and your happiness or unhappiness depends on whether your soul is in a good or bad state—you have not asked for advice from your father, your brother, or any of us, your companions, about whether you should entrust your soul to this stranger. Instead, having heard of his arrival only yesterday evening, you come here the next morning before daybreak. You have not considered whether it is appropriate to entrust yourself to him, and you are..."

...prepared to use not only all your own wealth for that purpose, but also the wealth of your friends, as if you already knew that you must by all means associate with Protagoras—whom, as you say, you neither know nor have ever spoken to. "Is a sophist, then, Hippocrates, a kind of merchant or retailer of the things that nourish the soul?"

"By studies <note>original: "disciplines"; here meaning branches of knowledge or subjects of instruction</note>," I replied. "But we must take care, my friend, lest the sophist deceives us while he praises what he sells, just as merchants and retailers do regarding food for the body. For they are ignorant of whether the goods they trade are healthy or harmful <note>original: "salubrious or noxious"</note> to the body, yet they praise everything they sell. Those who buy these goods are equally ignorant, unless the purchaser happens to be a physical trainer <note>original: "master of gymnastic"</note> or a physician. 

In the same way, those who carry studies from city to city, hawking and selling them to those who wish to buy, praise everything they sell. Yet perhaps some of these people too, my excellent young friend, may be ignorant of whether what they sell is beneficial or harmful to the soul. The same may be true for those who buy from them, unless the purchaser happens to be a 'physician of the soul.' 

If, therefore, you have scientific knowledge of what among these is good or bad, you may safely buy studies from Protagoras or anyone else. But if not, see, my dear friend <note>original: "O blessed youth"</note>, whether you are not putting your most precious concerns at extreme risk. For there is much greater danger in buying knowledge <note>original: "disciplines"</note> than in buying food. Someone who buys meat and drink from a food merchant <note>original: "victualler"</note> can carry them away in separate containers. Before he takes them into his body, he can keep them in his house and call in someone skilled in such matters to advise him on what should be eaten and drunk, what should not, and how much and when it is proper to eat and drink; so there is no great danger in buying provisions. 

Knowledge, however, cannot be carried away in a separate container. Instead, it is necessary that the person who buys a lesson receives and learns it directly in his soul, departing either harmed or benefited. Let us, therefore, consider these things with those who are older than we are, for we are too young to settle a matter of such great importance. Let us now...

Now, however, let us go where we intended and hear the man; and after we have heard him, let us also consult with others. For not only is Protagoras there, but Hippias of Elis and Prodicus too, I think, along with many other wise men.

Having agreed on this, we went on. But when we entered the porch, we stopped to discuss something that had occurred to us along the way. So that the matter might not remain unfinished, and that we might enter the house once it was resolved, we stood talking in the porch until we reached an agreement. It seems to me that the porter, who was a <term>eunuch</term> <note>At this time, wealthy households often employed eunuchs as doorkeepers or attendants</note>, heard us; because of the great number of sophists visiting, he was angry with anyone who came to the house. 

When we knocked at the gate, he opened it and, seeing us, said, "Ha, ha! More sophists. He is busy." At the same time, grabbing the gate with both hands, he slammed it shut with all his might. We knocked again, and without opening the gate, he said, "Didn't you hear me tell you he's busy?" 

"But, my good man," I said, "we aren't here to see Callias, nor are we sophists. Don't worry; we have come because we want to see Protagoras. Please announce us to him." 

Even so, the man was very reluctant to open the gate for us. Eventually, however, he opened it, and when we entered, we found Protagoras walking in the vestibule of the porch. Many people followed him: on one side was Callias, the son of Hipponicus, and his maternal half-brother; Paralus, the son of Pericles; and Charmides, the son of Glaucon <note>original: "Glauco"</note>. On the other side of him were Xanthippus, the other son of Pericles; Philippides, the son of Philomelus; and Antimocrus of Mende <note>original: "the Mendæan"; Mende was a Greek city in Chalcidice</note>. Antimocrus was the most famous of all Protagoras's disciples and is studying the art in order to become a professional sophist himself. 

The majority of those following behind to listen were strangers whom Protagoras brings with him from the various cities he passes through. He charms them with his voice like a modern Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek musician whose music was so powerful it could charm all living things</note>, and they follow his voice, spellbound. Some of our own countrymen were also in this chorus <note>original: "choir"; used here to describe the synchronized group of followers</note>. Seeing this group, I was delighted to observe how careful they were not to get in Protagoras’s way as he walked. Whenever he turned around, along with his inner circle, his listeners would part to the right and left in a graceful, orderly way, always falling back into their places beautifully behind him. He sent Clinias to be educated by Ariphron. However, before six months had passed, Ariphron—not knowing what to do with him—returned him to Pericles. I could also mention many others to you who were good men themselves but never made anyone else better, whether their own relatives or strangers. 

Therefore, Protagoras, looking at these examples, I do not believe that virtue can be taught. However, when I hear you claiming otherwise, I waver. I suspect you may have a point because I believe you are skilled in many things, and that you have learned much from others and discovered much yourself. > "There was a time, then, when the gods existed alone ^1, but mortal species <note>original: "genera"</note> did not yet exist. When the destined time for their creation <note>original: "generation"</note> arrived, the gods fashioned them within the earth by mixing together earth, fire, and the elements that are blended with these two. When they were about to bring them into the light of day, they commanded Prometheus and Epimetheus ^2 to distribute various powers to each kind and to adorn them in a way suited to their nature. But Epimetheus requested of Prometheus that he might distribute these powers himself: 'And,' he said, 'you can inspect my distribution.' Having thus persuaded him, he began the distribution. In his distributing, he gave to some strength without speed, and he adorned the weaker <note>original: "imbecile"</note> with speed. Some he armed; but giving to others an unarmed nature, he devised some other power for their safety. For those whom he made small in body, he either enabled them to fly away with wings or gave them a home underground <note>original: "subterranean habitation"</note>; but those whom he increased in size, he preserved by their very bulk. Thus, maintaining a balance <note>original: "equalizing"</note>, he distributed other traits, taking care that no species <note>original: "genus"</note> should be completely wiped out <note>original: "deprived of the means of preservation"</note>.

These same coverings served as natural <note>original: "spontaneous"</note> beds for each animal when they went to rest. Beneath their feet, he also added protective coverings <note>original: "arms," likely referring to hooves or claws</note>, and in other cases hair and tough, bloodless skin. Epimetheus was not very wise, and he ignorantly bestowed all his powers on irrational animals; but the human race still remained unequipped by him. Prometheus, therefore, came to him while he was hesitating and examined the distribution he had made. He saw that the other animals were well provided for, but that man was naked, unshod, without a bed, and unarmed. But the fated day had now arrived, on which it was necessary for man to emerge from the earth into the light. 

Prometheus, therefore, being uncertain what means of safety he could find for man, stole the technical wisdom <note>original: "artificial wisdom"</note> of Vulcan <note>Roman name for Hephaestus, god of fire and smithing</note> and Minerva <note>Roman name for Athena, goddess of wisdom and weaving</note> <gloss>¹</gloss>, along with fire. Since it was impossible to possess or use this wisdom without fire, he gave it to man. Through these means, therefore, man gained the wisdom needed for survival <note>original: "wisdom pertaining to life"</note>. He did not, however, have political wisdom, for that remained with Jupiter <note>Roman name for Zeus</note>. Prometheus was no longer permitted to ascend to the citadel, the home of Jupiter <gloss>²</gloss>. 

Furthermore, the guards of Jupiter were terrifying. Prometheus, therefore, secretly entered the shared dwelling of Minerva and Vulcan where they practiced their arts. By stealing the art of fire from Vulcan and the art of craftsmanship from Minerva, he gave them to man; and from this comes the abundance <note>original: "fertility"</note> of human life. But afterward, as the story goes, Prometheus was punished for his theft because of Epimetheus's mistake. 

Because man shared in a divine portion, he was the only animal who—through this kinship with the divine—believed in the gods and attempted to establish altars and statues to them. Next, through his skill, he began to distinguish and articulate sounds into words and

Because of this, they were destroyed by wild beasts, as they were everywhere weaker <note>original: "imbecile"</note> than them. The art of craftsmanship <note>original: "fabricating art"</note> was indeed a sufficient aid to them for finding food, but it was inadequate for the war against wild beasts; for they did not yet possess the political art, of which the military art is a part. They sought, therefore, to gather themselves together and to save themselves by building cities for this purpose. 

When, however, they were thus collected in a group, they injured each other because they did not possess the political art; so that, being scattered again, they were once more destroyed by the beasts. Jupiter <note>Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods</note>, therefore, fearing for our race, lest it should entirely perish, sent Hermes <note>The messenger of the gods</note> and ordered him to bring Shame and Justice to men, so that these two might be the ornaments and the bonds of cities, and the promoters of friendship. Hermes, therefore, asked in what manner he should give Shame and Justice to men. "Should I," he said, "distribute these as the other arts are distributed?" For the arts are distributed as follows: one man who possesses medical skill is sufficient for many private persons, and it is the same for other craftsmen. "Should I, therefore, implant Shame and Justice in men in this way? Or shall I distribute them to all?"

"To all," said Jupiter, "and let all be partakers of them. For cities will not exist if only a few participate in these, as they do in the other arts. Proclaim also this law in my name: that he who is incapable of partaking in Shame and Justice shall be put to death as a plague <note>original: "pest"</note> to the city."

"Thus, Socrates, and for this reason, both others and the Athenians think that only a few should be consulted when they discuss building or any other craft. And if anyone unskilled in these affairs offers to give advice, they do not allow him, as you say; and it is reasonable, as I say, that they should not. But when they proceed to a consultation concerning political virtue, the whole of which consists of justice and temperance, they very properly permit every man to speak; because it is right that every person should partake of this virtue, or there can be no cities. <meta>This page continues Protagoras’s argument to Socrates that civic virtue is not an innate gift but a quality that must be shared by all and can be taught through education and social pressure.</meta>

<page-num>118</page-num>

# THE PROTAGORAS.

[...regarding any] other art of which he is ignorant, those who hear him either laugh at or are angry with him, and his friends warn him as if he were insane. But in justice and other civic <note>original: "political"</note> virtues, even if it is known that a certain person is unjust, if he tells the truth about his own character before the public, they think he is insane for not hiding his wrongdoing. They say that all men should claim to be just, whether they are or not; and they believe that he who does not pretend to be just must be mad. It is as if it were necessary for everyone to share in justice in some way, or else no longer be considered human.

I say these things to show that every man <gloss>is</gloss> quite rightly allowed to give his advice concerning this virtue, because everyone is thought to have a share in it. But next, I will try to show you that people do not believe this virtue arises from nature or by chance, but that it can be taught and acquired through study. 

No one gets angry with another person for those defects which they believe arise from either nature or lack of skill; nor does anyone warn, teach, or punish those with such defects to make them different than they are. On the contrary, people pity them. For instance, who would be so mad as to criticize the deformed, the small, or the diseased? I believe people realize that these things—namely, those traits which are beautiful and their opposites—happen to men by nature and luck <note>original: "fortune"</note>. 

On the other hand, when people believe someone possesses certain vices because they neglected study, habit, and learning, then they become angry, they warn, and they punish. Among these vices are injustice, impiety, and in short, everything that is contrary to civic virtue. Since this type of virtue is obtained by study and discipline, people are angry with and warn anyone who neglects to acquire it. 

For if you are willing, *Socrates*, to consider what the punishment of the unjust is intended to achieve, this very thing will teach you that men believe virtue can be acquired. For no one endowed with reason <note>original: "intellect"</note> punishes a person who has acted unjustly simply because he has so acted; anyone who acts in that manner punishes like a wild animal, irrationally. But he who tries to punish with reason does not punish for the sake of past guilt (for what has been done cannot be undone), but for the sake of preventing future injustice, so that neither the offender himself nor any other who sees him punished will act unjustly again. Anyone who holds this view must be convinced that virtue can be taught, for punishment is inflicted for the [sake of deterrence].

<summary>Protagoras argues that civic virtue must be practiced by everyone for society to function and that the practice of punishment proves virtue is something learned and taught rather than a natural trait.</summary>

...sake of turning others from guilt. Therefore, everyone who punishes, whether privately or publicly, holds this opinion. Therefore, your fellow citizens are quite right to allow the metalworker <note>original: "brazier"</note> and the shoemaker to give advice on political matters; and, as it appears to me, Socrates, it has been sufficiently demonstrated to you that they consider virtue as a thing which may be taught and acquired.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;However, there still remains the doubt you raised concerning famous <note>original: "illustrious"</note> men: specifically, why they teach their sons and make them wise in skills that can be learned from teachers, but do not make them better than others in the very virtue for which they themselves are renowned. To resolve this doubt, Socrates, I will no longer use a myth <note>original: "fable"</note>, but a logical argument. Consider it this way: is there not one thing which all citizens must share if a city is to survive? Your doubt is solved through this one thing, and in no other way. For if this one thing exists—which is not the skill of the architect, the metalworker, or the potter, but is <term>justice</term>, <term>temperance</term>, and <term>holiness</term>, and, in short, human <term>virtue</term>—if this is the thing that everyone must share, and alongside which every person should learn and do whatever else they wish (but by no means without it); or if anyone who does not share in it must be taught and punished (whether boy, man, or woman) until punishment makes them better; and if someone who remains disobedient after being taught or punished is banished from the city or put to death as incurable; if this then is the case, and those famous men teach their children other things but not this, consider how strange it would be for them to become excellent men. For we have shown that they believe <term>virtue</term> can be taught both in private and in public. Since it can be taught, do you really think that fathers teach their children other things where ignorance carries neither death nor a penalty, but that in the very things where the penalty for ignorance is death, exile, or the confiscation of their property—in short, the ruin of their entire families—they fail to teach them?

...nor use their greatest efforts to ensure they acquire them? You must realize, Socrates, that fathers begin with their children when they are very young and continue to teach and advise them as long as they live. For as soon as a boy understands what is said to him, his nurse, mother, <term>tutor</term> <note>original: "pedagogue"; in Ancient Greece, this was a household slave who escorted the child and supervised their conduct</note>, and the father himself strive to the utmost to ensure the boy develops the most excellent character. They teach and point out to him, in every word and deed, that this is just and that is unjust; that this is beautiful and that is shameful <note>original: "base"</note>; and that this is holy and that is unholy. They tell him he should do certain things and not others. If the boy is easily persuaded, they feel they have succeeded; but if not, they force him into the right shape <note>original: "rectitude"</note> with threats and blows, as if he were a piece of wood that had become warped and bent. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Next, they send him to schoolmasters, and they command these teachers to pay far more attention to the boys’ character <note>original: "morals"</note> than to their reading and harp-playing. The teachers likewise look after the children; and when the boys have learned their letters and are able to understand what they read, the masters give them the works of the best poets to read instead of spoken advice, and they force them to memorize them. They do this because these poems contain many warnings and many stories, praises, and tributes to famous men of the past, so that the boy may be eager to imitate them and desire to become a similar person. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The music teachers <note>original: "masters of the harp"</note> do much the same; they focus on <term>self-control</term> <note>original: "temperance"</note> and ensure that the boys do not fall into any bad habits. Furthermore, when they have learned to play the harp, the teachers introduce them to the works of other great lyric poets, singing them to the accompaniment of the harp. They force these rhythms and harmonies to become familiar to the boys' souls, so that by becoming gentler, more orderly, and more harmonious, they may be more capable in both speech and action. For every human life requires rhythm and harmony. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Beyond this, they send them to physical trainers <note>original: "masters of exercise"</note> so that their improved bodies may usefully serve their rational minds <note>original: "the rational part of the soul"</note>, and so that they are not forced into cowardice during war or other activities because of a weak or poorly conditioned body <note>original: "the depravity of their bodies"</note>. These things are done by those who are most able to do them, and the most able are the wealthiest. Their sons begin their education at the earliest age and continue it for the longest time. But when they finally leave their teachers, the city then compels them to learn the laws and to live according to their model <note>original: "paradigm"</note>, so that they do not...

Even the person who appears to you to be the most unjust among those raised within our laws and civilization is actually just—a practitioner of justice—if he is compared to men who have had no education, no courts of justice, no laws, nor any necessity compelling them to care for virtue. However, it is easy to find teachers for those who are completely ignorant. 

The same is true for virtue and everything else. We should be grateful if someone even slightly surpasses us in helping us advance in virtue. I believe I am one of those people; I believe I understand better than other men what contributes to the beautiful and the good, and that I am worthy of the fee I receive for my instruction—and indeed, worth even more than I receive, which is also the opinion of my students. 

Because of this, I use a specific arrangement for payment: when someone has finished learning from me, if he is willing, he pays the sum of money I require. But if he is not, he may go to a temple and swear an oath as to how much my lessons <note>original: "disciplines"</note> were worth, and he deposits that sum for me.

"But it is easy, Socrates," he said, "to answer this question: virtue is one single thing, and the specific qualities you have brought forward are the parts of it."

"But tell me," I said, "are they parts in the same way that the mouth, nostrils, eyes, and ears are parts of the face? Or are they parts like the parts of a gold bar, which do not differ from each other or from the whole, except in being larger or smaller?"

"It seems to me, Socrates, that the parts of virtue have the same relationship to the whole as the parts of the face have to the whole face."

"In that case," I said, "do different men receive different parts of virtue? Or is it necessary that he who receives one part must possess all the parts of virtue?"

"By no means," he said; "since many men are brave, but unjust; and others again are just, but not wise."

"Then," I said, "are these qualities—namely wisdom and courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>—actually parts of virtue?"

"Certainly, most of all," he replied; "and the greatest of all the parts is wisdom."

"And," I asked, "is each of these parts distinct from the others?"

"Yes."

"Does each of them also have its own unique function <note>original: "power"; from the Greek *dynamis*, meaning the specific capability or effect of a thing</note>, in the same way that the parts of the face do? For instance, the eye is not like the ears, and its function is not the same; nor do any of the other parts resemble each other, nor are their functions the same, nor are they similar in any other respect. Is it therefore the same with the parts of virtue, so that one does not resemble the other, either in itself or in its function? Is it not obvious that this is the case, since it matches the example <note>original: "paradigm"</note> we have introduced?"

"It is exactly like that, Socrates," he said.

And I replied, "Therefore, no other part of virtue is quite like knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, nor like justice, nor like courage, nor like temperance <note>original: "temperance"; refers to self-control or moderation</note>, nor like holiness <note>original: "sanctity"</note>."

"It is not," he said.

"But come," I said, "let us consider together what kind of thing each of these is. First, is justice a specific thing, or is it nothing at all? To me, it certainly seems to be something. But what does it seem to be to you?"

"That it is also something," he said.

"What then? If someone should ask you and me, 'Protagoras and Socrates, tell me about this very thing you have just named—justice—is it itself just or unjust?' I would answer him that it is just. But what would you say? Would your answer be the same as mine or not?"

"The same," he replied.

"I therefore would say to the questioner that justice is a thing that is 'just' by its very nature. And wouldn't you also assert the same?"

"Yes," he said.

But there are other things, such as the parts of the face, in which one part is similar to another. So, even if you were to refute these points in this way, and even if you believe all things are similar to each other, it is still not right to call things "similar" just because they possess a *certain* degree of similarity. By the same token, it is not right to call things "dissimilar" <note>original: "dissimilars"</note> just because they have some differences, as long as they retain even a small amount of similarity.

And wondering at this, I said to him, "Do 'the just' and 'the holy' appear to you to be so distantly related that they possess only a small degree of similarity to each other?"

"Not entirely so," he said. "But then again, I do not view them in the same way you seem to."

"Well," I replied, "since these points do not seem to be agreeable to you, we will set them aside and consider this other thing you said. What do you call 'folly'? Do you not say that 'wisdom' is its perfect opposite?"

"To me, it appears to be so," he said.

"And when men act rightly and profitably, do they then appear to you to act temperately <note>original: "temperately"; from the Greek *sōphronōs*, meaning with self-control or soundness of mind</note>, or do they act temperately when they act in the opposite way?"

"They appear to me," he said, "to act temperately when they act rightly and profitably."

"And do they not act temperately by means of temperance?"

"That is necessary."

"Therefore, do those who act wrongly not act foolishly? And in acting that way, do they not act without temperance?"

"I agree with you," he said, "that they do."

"Acting foolishly, therefore, is the opposite of acting temperately."

He said it was.

"Are not things done foolishly, then, done through folly? And are things done temperately not done through temperance?"

He granted it.

"If, then, anything is done through strength, is it not done strongly? And if through weakness, weakly?"

"So it appears."

"And if anything is done with swiftness, is it not done swiftly? And if with slowness, slowly?"

He said it was.

"And if anything is done in the same manner, is it not done by the same quality? And if in an opposite manner, by the opposite quality?"

He granted it.

"Come then," I replied, "is there something called 'the beautiful'?"

He admitted there was.

"And is there anything opposite to this except 'the ugly' <note>original: "the base"</note>?"

"There is not."

"But what about this? Is there something called 'the good'? And is anything opposite to this except 'the evil'?"

"There is not."

"Is there also something called a 'high pitch' <note>original: "acute"</note> in the voice?"

He said there is.

"And is anything opposite to this except the 'low pitch' <note>original: "the grave"</note>?"

"There is not," he said.

"Therefore," I replied, "for every one of these opposites, there is only one opposite, and not...

"And that which is done in an opposite way is done by opposite qualities."

He admitted it.

"We also granted that what is done foolishly is done in a manner opposite to that which is done temperately."

He said we did.

He agreed that it was.

"And did we not also say that there is only one opposite for any one thing?"

"Which therefore of these positions, Protagoras, shall we reject? That which says there is only one opposite to one thing, or that in which it is asserted that wisdom is different from temperance? That each is a part of virtue, and that—besides being different—both they and their powers are dissimilar, in the same way as the parts of the face? Which of these shall we reject? For both of them cannot be harmoniously <note>original: "musically"; Socrates often uses musical metaphors to describe logical consistency</note> maintained, since they do not accord or harmonize with each other. For how can they accord if it is necessary that there should only be one opposite for any one thing, and not more than one? Yet to folly, which is one thing, both wisdom and temperance have appeared to be opposites. Is it so, Protagoras, or not?"

He acknowledged that it was so, but very unwillingly.

"Will not, therefore, temperance and wisdom be one thing? And again, prior to this, it appeared to us that justice and holiness <note>original: "sanctity"</note> were nearly the same thing. But come," said I, "Protagoras, let us not grow weary, but consider what remains. Does it then appear to you that a man who acts unjustly is wise because he acts unjustly?"

"I, Socrates," he said, "would be ashamed to acknowledge this, though it is asserted by many men."

"Whether then shall we address ourselves to them, or to you?"

"If you are willing," he said, "speak first to this assertion of the many."

"But it makes no difference to me, if you only answer whether these things appear to you to be true or not; for I especially direct my attention to the argument itself. It may, however, perhaps happen that I shall examine <note>original: "explore"</note> both myself as the questioner and the one who answers."

At first, therefore, Protagoras began to act with some self-importance <note>original: "assume some consequence"</note> (for he was reluctant to discuss this matter and said it was difficult); but afterwards he submitted to answer.

"Suppose it does," he said.

"But," I replied, "does this happen if they succeed <note>original: "do well"</note> while acting unjustly, or if they fail?"

"If they succeed."

"Do you then say that certain things are good?"

"I do."

"Therefore," said I, "are those things good which are beneficial <note>original: "advantageous"</note> to people?"

"By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>," he said, "they are; and I also call some things 'good' even though they are not beneficial to people."

And Protagoras, when he said this, appeared to me to be irritated, uneasy, and reluctant to answer. Seeing him in this condition, I cautiously and gradually questioned him; and I said, "Protagoras, do you speak of things which are beneficial to *no one*, or of those which are in *no respect* beneficial? And do you call such things as these 'good'?"

"By no means," said he; "but I know many things which are useless to humans—foods and drinks, medical potions, and ten thousand other things; and I also know some things which are beneficial to them. There are likewise some things which are not at all profitable to humans but are beneficial to horses; some which are beneficial to oxen only, and others to dogs. Others again are beneficial to none of these, but to trees; and others which are good for the roots of trees but deadly <note>original: "pernicious"</note> to their blossoms. Thus, for instance, dung is beneficial to the roots of all trees when spread upon them; but if you were to throw it on their branches and shoots, you would destroy them all.

So too, oil is an excellent thing for all plants, but it is very harmful <note>original: "most hostile"</note> to the hair of all animals except humans. For it is beneficial to the hair of a human and to the rest of his body. 'Good' is such a diverse and multifaceted thing that this very substance, oil, is good for the external parts of the human body, but is most harmful to his internal organs. And for this reason, all physicians forbid the sick from using oil—or at least only permit them to use it in a very small amount, just enough to offset the bad smell of the food they eat."

It appeared to all that this was what ought to be done. And Protagoras, indeed, was not very willing to comply; but at the same time, he was compelled to consent to ask the questions, and that when he had questioned sufficiently, he would in his turn answer with brevity.

And now you appear to me not to understand that this word "difficult" was perhaps not meant by Simonides in the way you understand it. It is like the word <term>terrible</term> <note>original: δεινος (*deinos*); this Greek word can mean "terrible" or "formidable," but also "clever," "powerful," or "wonderful." Socrates is teasing Protagoras about the need for linguistic precision.</note>, concerning which Prodicus continually corrects me. Whenever I am praising you or anyone else, and I say that..."

<meta>This page continues the debate between Socrates and Protagoras regarding the interpretation of Simonides’ poem. Socrates has just suggested that Prodicus (an expert in synonyms) might distinguish between "being" and "becoming" to resolve the poem's apparent contradictions.</meta>

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>THE PROTAGORAS.</header>

Protagoras is a wise and *skillful* <note>original: $\delta\epsilon\iota\nu\omicron\varsigma$ (*deinos*), a word that can mean both "clever/skillful" and "terrible/dreadful."</note> man, and he asks me if I am not ashamed to call excellent things *dreadful* <note>original: $\delta\epsilon\iota\nu\omicron\varsigma$</note>. For "the dreadful," he says, signifies something bad. Because of this, no one says *dreadful riches*, nor *dreadful peace*, nor *dreadful health*; but everyone says *dreadful disease*, and *dreadful war*, and *dreadful poverty*, as if that which is *deinon* is *bad*. Perhaps, therefore, the inhabitants of Ceos and the poet Simonides understood the word *difficult* <note>original: $\chi\alpha\lambda\epsilon\pi\omicron\nu$ (*chalepon*)</note> to mean either "that which is bad," or something different from what you conceive it to mean. 

Let us therefore inquire of Prodicus (for it is only fair to ask him the meaning of words used by Simonides): What, Prodicus, does Simonides mean by the word *difficult*? 

— "He meant bad," said he. 

— "For this reason, then," I replied, "he blames Pittacus for saying that it is *difficult* to *continue* to be good, just as if he had heard him saying that it is *bad* to continue to be good." 

— "But what else, Socrates," said he, "do you think Simonides intended, other than to blame Pittacus because he did not know how to distinguish terms correctly, since he was a *Lesbian* <note>A person from the island of Lesbos.</note> and educated in a barbarous language?" <note>To an Athenian like Socrates, the Aeolic dialect of Lesbos sounded "barbarous" or unrefined.</note> 

— "Do you hear Prodicus, Protagoras?" I said. "And do you have anything to say to these things?" 

— "This is very far from being the case, Prodicus," said Protagoras. "For I know well that Simonides meant by the word *difficult* not that which is *bad*, but that which we and others mean by it: namely, a thing that is not easy, but is accomplished through much labor." 

— "But I also think," I replied, "that Simonides meant this, and that Prodicus knows it too. He is only joking and wants to see if you can defend your assertion. For that Simonides did not mean anything bad by the word *difficult* is strongly confirmed by what he adds immediately after; for he says that 'Divinity alone possesses this honorable gift.' He certainly does not say that it is *bad* to continue to be good and then add that Divinity alone possesses this, attributing such a 'bad' honor to Divinity alone. If that were the case, Prodicus would have called Simonides a *profligate* <note>original: "a profligate, and not a divine man"; someone utterly immoral.</note> rather than a divine man." 

"But I wish to tell you what Simonides appears to me to have understood in this verse, if you think it proper to test my poetical skill. Or, if you prefer, I will listen to you."

<meta>This page continues Socrates' response to Protagoras regarding the poem by Simonides. Socrates begins to explain his own interpretation of the verse, using a humorous and ironic argument about the true nature of Spartan philosophy.</meta>

<header>THE PROTAGORAS.</header>

...me to do it. I will endeavor, then, said I, to explain to you my conceptions regarding this verse.

Philosophy is very ancient among the Greeks, particularly in Crete and Lacedaemon <note>Lacedaemon is the ancient name for the city-state of Sparta.</note>; and there are more sophists there than in any other country. They dissemble, however, and pretend that they are unlearned, so that it may not be obvious that they surpass the rest of the Greeks in wisdom (just as Protagoras has said regarding the sophists). Instead, they want to appear to excel only in military skill and bravery, thinking that if their real character were known, all men would pursue the same path of wisdom. 

But now, by concealing this, they deceive those who "Laconize" <note>To "Laconize" meant to imitate the customs of the Spartans (who lived in Laconia), such as being brief in speech or tough in lifestyle.</note> in other cities. For there are some people who, in imitation of the Spartans, scar their ears, wear cords for belts, love severe exercise, and wear short garments, as if the Lacedaemonians surpassed the other Greeks in only these outward things. But the Lacedaemonians themselves, when they wish to speak freely with their own sophists and grow weary of conversing with them in private, expel these "Laconian" imitators and then discourse with their sophists without admitting any strangers to their conversations. Neither do they allow any of their young men to travel to other cities—just as the Cretans do not—lest they should unlearn what they have been taught. 

In these cities, there are not only men of profound education, but women also. You may know that what I assert is true, and that the Lacedaemonians are disciplined in the best manner in philosophy and discourse, from the following circumstance: If anyone wishes to converse with even the lowest of the Lacedaemonians, he will at first find him, for the most part, apparently unimpressive in conversation. But afterwards, when a proper opportunity presents itself, this same "lowly" person, like a skillful javelin-thrower <note>original: "jaculator," a Latin-derived term for a thrower of darts or javelins.</note>, will hurl a sentence worthy of attention—short and pithy <note>original: "contorted"; here Socrates refers to the "Laconic" style of speech that is tightly wound and pointed.</note>—so that the one who converses with him will appear to be no better than a child. 

That to "Laconize," therefore, consists much more in philosophizing than in the love of exercise is understood by some of the present age and was known to the ancients. They were persuaded that the ability to utter such sentences as these is the mark of a perfectly learned man. Among the number of those who were thus persuaded were Thales the Milesian, Pittacus the Mitylenaean, Bias the Prienean, our own Solon, Cleobulus the Lindian, Miso the Chenean, and the seventh of these is said to be Chilo the Lacedaemonian. All these were followers...

<meta>This page continues Socrates' analysis of the poem by Simonides, focusing on the connection between Spartan (Laconic) brevity and the wisdom of the Seven Sages.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>
<header>THE PROTAGORAS.</header>

...imitators, lovers, and disciples of Spartan <note>original: "Lacedæmonian"</note> education. Anyone can see that their wisdom was of this kind: short sentences uttered by each of them that were worth remembering. These men also assembled together and dedicated the first fruits of their wisdom to Apollo, writing in the Temple of Apollo at Delphi those sentences which are celebrated by all men, namely: "Know yourself" and "Nothing in excess" <note>original: "Nothing too much"</note>. But why do I mention these things? To show that the style of philosophy among the ancients was a certain Laconic brevity of speech.

The saying which is attributed to Pittacus <note>Pittacus of Mytilene was one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> in particular, and which is celebrated by the wise, is this: "It is difficult to remain good." Simonides, therefore, being ambitious for wisdom, knew that if he could disprove this saying and triumph over it like a famous athlete, he himself would be celebrated by the people of his own time. In opposition to this saying, and with a view to gaining renown, he composed the whole of this poem, as it appears to me. Let us all, however, consider together whether what I assert is true.

In the first place, the very beginning of the poem would indicate that its author was insane if he—wishing to say that it is difficult to become a good man—had afterwards inserted the particle *indeed* <note>original: $\mu\epsilon\nu$ (men); a Greek particle often used to emphasize a word or set up a contrast.</note>. For this would appear to have been inserted for no purpose. Unless, perhaps, it should be said that Simonides, in what he says, is arguing against the saying of Pittacus; and that when Pittacus asserted that it is difficult to *remain* good, Simonides disputed this and said it is not difficult to remain so. Rather, it is difficult *indeed*, O Pittacus, to *become* a good man and to be *truly* good. 

For he does not use the word *truly* as if there were some men who are *truly* good and others who are good in name but not in truth (for this would have been stupid and unworthy of Simonides). Instead, it is necessary to consider the word *truly* as a <term>hyperbaton</term>¹ <note>original: "hyberbaton"</note> in the verse. We must imagine Pittacus speaking as if there were a dialogue between him and Simonides, with Pittacus saying, "O men, it is difficult to remain good," and Simonides answering, "Pittacus, your assertion is not true; for it is not difficult to be truly good, but to *become* so—in hands and feet and mind, shaped like a blameless square <note>A "blameless square" is a metaphor for a person of perfect integrity and balanced character.</note>."

---

¹ A <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>original: "hyberbaton"</note> is a rhetorical figure and signifies the shifting of words out of their normal grammatical order.
