<meta>This page continues Socrates' analysis of a poem by Simonides, specifically debating the distinction between "becoming" good and "being" (or remaining) good, in opposition to the sage Pittacus.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>THE PROTAGORAS.</header>

And thus it appears that the particle *indeed* is introduced for a reason, and that the word *truly* is rightly added at the end. All that follows also shows that this is the meaning of the passage. There are many sentences in this poem, each of which could be proven to be well-written, for it is composed with great elegance and accuracy. To prove this in detail, however, would take up too much time. Instead, let us briefly consider the overall form and intent of the poem, so we may show that its primary design is to refute that saying of Pittacus. For a little later the poet says the following: 

"It is *indeed truly* difficult to become a good man; yet for a certain time it is possible *to be* so. But once one *has become* a good man, to continue in this state and *to be* a good man (as you say, O Pittacus <note>Simonides is addressing Pittacus's claim that it is difficult to remain good, arguing instead that for a mortal, it is actually impossible to stay perfectly good forever.</note>) is impossible. For this is not a human trait; rather, Divinity alone possesses this honorable gift. A man who is overwhelmed by an unexpected calamity cannot remain free from vice."

Who, then, does an unexpected calamity overwhelm in the steering of a ship? Clearly not an unskillful person <note>original: "idiot"; from the Greek *idiotes*, meaning a private person or a non-expert rather than the modern insult.</note>, for the unskillful person is always overwhelmed. Just as one might throw to the ground a person who is standing upright, but can never throw down someone who is already lying prostrate, an unexpected calamity may sometimes overwhelm a skillful man, but never one who is already unskillful. 

A mighty storm bursting over the head of a pilot may render him unable to use his skill; bad seasons may ruin a farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note>; and similar logic may be applied to a physician. A good man may indeed become a bad man. This is also confirmed by another poet, who says, "A good man is sometimes bad, and sometimes worthy." But it is not possible for a bad man to *become* bad, because he is already and necessarily so. 

So, when an unexpected calamity overwhelms a skillful, wise, and good man, it is impossible for him not to become wicked. But you, Pittacus, say that it is difficult to *remain* good. The truth, however, is this: it is indeed difficult, though possible, *to become* good; but it is impossible *to remain* good. For every man who acts well is good, but he is bad if he acts poorly. What then is a "good action" regarding literature? And what makes a man excellent in literature? Clearly, it is being disciplined in it. What

<meta>This page continues Socrates' analysis of Simonides’ poem, moving from the analogy of a ship’s pilot to that of a physician to explain how "goodness" and "badness" relate to knowledge and expertise.</meta>

<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>THE PROTAGORAS.</header>

Does a good action likewise make a good physician? Evidently, it is the learning of the art of curing the sick. For a good physician cures properly¹, but a bad one improperly <note>original: *kakos de kakos*; literally "a bad [one cures] badly"</note>. Who is it, then, that becomes a bad physician? Evidently, the man who is first a physician, and secondly a good physician; for such a man is capable of becoming a bad physician. But those of us who are ignorant of the medical art can never, by acting poorly, become "bad physicians"; nor, being ignorant of architecture, can we become "bad architects," or anything else of this kind. For if someone does not first become a physician, it is evident that he cannot be a "bad" physician either. 

Thus, a good man may sometimes become a bad man, whether due to time, labor, disease, or some other circumstance—for the only truly bad action is to be deprived of knowledge <note>original: "science"; here meaning *episteme*, or systematic expertise</note>. However, a bad man can never *become* bad, for he is always so. If he is to *become* bad, it is necessary that prior to this he must have been good. 

So, these verses of Simonides tend toward this point: that it is not possible to be a good man in a way that is perseveringly or permanently good. However, it is possible to *become* a good man, and for this same good man to then become a bad man. Furthermore, those whom the gods love are, for the most part, the best men. All these things are said in opposition to Pittacus <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>, as the following verses show even more clearly. For he says:

> "Therefore, I shall not search in vain and hope for that which cannot be found: namely, a man nourished by the fruits of the earth who lives a blameless life and is perpetually good."

Afterwards he adds, "I will tell you when I have found him." So vehemently, throughout the whole poem, does he attack the saying of Pittacus. He also adds:

> "I willingly praise and love the man who does nothing dishonorable <note>original: "base"</note>; and the gods themselves are not able to contend with necessity."

And this, likewise, is said in opposition to Pittacus. For Simonides was not so unlearned as to say that he praised those who "willingly" did nothing bad, as if there were some people who committed dishonorable actions willingly. For I am nearly certain of this: that no wise man believes any person errs voluntarily, or acts dishonorably and wickedly by choice. Rather, he well knows that all those who act dishonorably and wickedly do so involuntarily. But—

<meta>This page continues Socrates' detailed line-by-line interpretation of Simonides’ poem. Socrates is arguing that Simonides was not claiming that he "willingly" praises those who do no wrong, but rather that he "willingly" offers this praise himself, even when forced by circumstances to honor those who are imperfect.</meta>

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>THE PROTAGORAS.</header>

Simonides does not speak as if he said that he praises the man who does not *willingly* do wrong, but he applies this word "willingly" to himself. For he thought that a worthy and good man is frequently compelled to love and praise certain people. Thus, for instance, it often happens that a man has an unnatural <note>original: "monstrous"; here meaning cruel or failing in parental duty</note> father, or mother, or country, or something else of this kind. Wicked characters, therefore, when anything of this nature happens to them, are in the first place glad to see it. In the next place, they blame and everywhere broadcast the wickedness of their parents or country, so that they may not be accused of having neglected them, or fall into disgrace for their neglect. Hence, they blame their parents or country to an even greater degree, adding intentional hatred to unavoidable hostility. 

But the worthy man conceals the faults of his parents or country. If any unjust conduct has led him to be enraged with them, he acts as a mediator to himself, reconciling himself to them and forcing himself to love and praise his own family. I also think that Simonides himself frequently praised and was the eulogist <note>original: "encomiast"</note> of a tyrant or some other such character, and did this not willingly, but by compulsion. This, then, is what he says to Pittacus: “I, O Pittacus, do not blame you because I am someone who loves to find fault; for I am satisfied if a man is not wicked, nor entirely useless <note>original: "indolent"</note>, since I know that a sane man benefits his country. Nor will I find fault, since I am not a lover of slander <note>original: "detraction"</note>. For the number of fools is infinite, so that he who delights in blaming will never run out of material. All things, indeed, are beautiful in which nothing shameful is mixed.” 

His meaning in this, however, is not as if he had said "all things are white in which no black is mixed" (for this would be very ridiculous), but he intends to signify that he accepts a middle ground <note>original: "mediocrity"; in the classical sense of the 'Golden Mean' or moderate excellence</note>, so as not to blame it. “And I do not seek,” says he, “a man perfectly blameless, or expect to find him among those who gather the fruits of the wide-bosomed earth; for I will tell you if I ever find such a person. So, on this account, I shall praise no one as perfect. But I am satisfied with a man of moderate excellence who does no evil, and I love and praise all such as these.” 

Here, too, he uses the dialect of the Mitylenaeans <note>The people of Mitylene on the island of Lesbos, where Pittacus lived</note> as if speaking to Pittacus and saying, “I willingly praise and love all these.” But here it is necessary to consider the word "willingly" as connected with the words “who does nothing shameful,” and to separate it from the verse in which he says, “There are also those whom I unwillingly praise and love. You, therefore, O Pittacus, I should never have blamed,

"Do so, O Hippias," said Alcibiades, "but let it be at another time. For now, it is only fair to focus on how Protagoras and Socrates agree with each other. For it seems to me that a conversation about poetry is very much like the banquets of lowly and unrefined <note>original: "vile and rustic"</note> men. Because these people lack education, they are unable to converse with each other while drinking using their own voices and their own words. Instead, they treat flute-players as guests of honor, hiring a 'foreign voice' (namely <note>original: "viz."/videlicet</note>, the sound of flutes) at great expense, and they socialize through that sound. 

But when noble, good, and well-educated men feast together, you will see neither flute-players, nor dancers, nor singers. Instead, they are capable of conversing by themselves without these trifles and playful distractions. They speak in their own voices and listen to one another in turn in a proper manner, even if they have drunk a considerable amount of wine. In the same way, conversations like this—when held between men such as we claim to be—require no outside voice and no poets. It is impossible to ask a poet what he meant by what he wrote, and those who quote them often attribute different interpretations <note>original: "conceptions"</note> to them without being able to prove the poet's real meaning. Wise men, therefore, say goodbye to such discussions <note>original: "conferences"</note> and instead converse with each other directly, testing one another's skill through their own discourse. It seems to me that you and I ought rather to imitate..."

Discussions of this kind—by setting aside the poets and talking directly with each other—allow us to test our own understanding of the truth. Then Socrates may converse with someone else, or anyone else in the company who is willing may carry on the discussion." 

Protagoras, it seemed to me, was ashamed because of what Alcibiades said. After Callias and nearly everyone else present urged him, he finally agreed to the debate and asked me to question him so that he might answer.

I then said to him, "O Protagoras, do not think that I am talking with you for any other purpose than to discuss those things about which I am constantly in doubt. A reference to Homer’s Iliad (Book 10, line 224), emphasizing the value of collaboration in thinking.</note> For as human beings, we are all more capable in every action, word, and thought when we are together. But if someone thinks of something by himself, he immediately searches for someone to share it with, and from whom he may find confirmation until he reaches his goal. 

It is for this very reason that I would rather converse with you than with anyone else. I believe that you, better than all other men, can distinguish the truth about things that a good person should consider, especially concerning virtue. For who else can do this besides you? You not only consider yourself to be a worthy and good man—whereas some others are personally worthy but unable to make others so—but you are both worthy yourself and able to make others good. You have such confidence in yourself that, while others hide this skill, you openly proclaim yourself to all the Greeks to be a <term>sophist</term> <note>original: "sophist"; here used in its original sense of a professional teacher of wisdom, before the term acquired its modern negative connotation of using clever but false arguments.</note>. ...qualified to set a price on his own instructions. Is it not appropriate, therefore, to ask you to consider these matters, and to question and converse with you concerning them? There is no reason why this should not be done.

You said before that these were not just names for the same thing, but that each name referred to its own distinct reality. You also observed that all of these are parts of virtue—not in the same way that pieces of gold are similar to each other and to the whole mass of which they are parts, but rather like the parts of a face. The parts of a face are different from the whole and from each other, and each possesses its own specific function. Tell me if these things still seem the same to you as they did then, or if you now think differently. I will not hold it against you if you speak differently now, for I would not be surprised if you said those things earlier just to test me.

"But, Socrates," he replied, "I still say that all of these are parts of virtue. However, four of them may rightly be considered somewhat similar to each other, while courage differs greatly from the rest. You can see that what I am saying is true by this: you will find men who are extremely unjust, unholy, intemperate, and ignorant, yet who are nonetheless remarkably brave."

"Stop," I said, "for what you say deserves to be examined. Do you call brave men 'daring' men, or something else?"

"I do," he replied, "and I also say they are the ones who rush headlong into things that the majority of people are afraid to approach."

"Tell me then: do you say that virtue is something beautiful <note>original: "beautiful." In this context, the Greek word *kalon* implies something that is both morally noble and aesthetically beautiful.</note>, and that you are a teacher of it because it is a beautiful thing?"

"Yes," he said, "it is a most beautiful thing—unless I have lost my mind."

"Then," I asked, "is one part of virtue shameful and another part beautiful? Or is the whole of it beautiful?"

"The whole of it," he replied, "is as beautiful as it can possibly be."

"Do you not know, then, that there are some people who boldly dive into wells?"

"I know that divers do so."

It does not end with these things; hear what follows. I say then, that if this is the case, your claim is ridiculous when you say that frequently, even though a person knows that evil things are evil, he still does them (even though he has the power to avoid doing them), because he is led astray and overwhelmed <note>original: "astonished"</note> by pleasure. And again, you say that a person, knowing what is good, is not willing to do it because he is overcome by immediate pleasure. 

It will become clear that these claims are ridiculous unless we stop using so many different names, like *pleasant* and *disagreeable*, or *good* and *evil*. Since it appears there are only these two things, we must also call them by two names: first, *good* and *evil*, and second, *pleasant* and *disagreeable*. Having admitted this, we will say that a man, knowing things to be evil, does them anyway. If someone should ask us why he does them, we must say: "Because he is overcome." "By what?" he will ask us. But we are no longer allowed to say "by pleasure," for we have given pleasure another name: "the good." We must, however, answer him and say that he does it because he is overcome. "By what?" he will say. "By the good," we must say, by Zeus! <note>original: "Jupiter." Early Modern translators often used Roman names for Greek gods.</note> 

If the person questioning us is arrogant, he will laugh and say, "You are saying something ridiculous when you claim that someone does evil, knowing it is evil (and that he should not do it), because he is overcome by the good." For he will ask, "Is he overcome because the good in him is not strong enough <note>original: "worthy"</note> to overcome the evil? Or is it because it *is* strong enough?" We will clearly say in reply that it is because the good was not strong enough. Otherwise, the person we say is subdued by pleasure would not have made a mistake. But perhaps he will ask, "Why is the good in such a person not strong enough to overcome the evil? Or the evil to overcome the good? Is it for any other reason than that one is greater and the other is smaller? Or that one is more and the other is less in number?" Do we have any other cause to assign than this? It is evident, therefore, he will say, that this thing called "being overcome" is actually receiving greater evils in exchange for smaller goods. So much for those details.

...they are unpleasant as a result of being conquered by pleasures—specifically, by pleasures that are not worthy of winning. And what other reason could there be for a pleasure being "unworthy" compared to pain, other than the difference in their scale—that is, when they become larger or smaller, or more or less numerous? For if someone should say, "But Socrates, immediate pleasure differs greatly from future pleasure and pain," I would reply by asking: Does it differ in any way other than in pleasure and pain? It is just as if a man skilled in weighing were to collect pleasant and painful things together and place both those which are near and those which are far in the scales, to determine which are more numerous. For if you weigh pleasures against pleasures, the greater and more numerous must always be chosen; but if you weigh pains against pains, the fewer and the smaller must be selected. Likewise, if you weigh pleasures against pains, and the unpleasant things are outweighed by the pleasures—whether those that are near are outweighed by those that are far, or those that are far by those that are near—we must choose the weightier side. They will say that they are. 

If, therefore, our well-being consisted in this—namely, in choosing and acquiring great masses while rejecting and avoiding small ones—what would be the safety of our lives? Would it be the art of measurement, or the power of sight which judges based on appearances? Or would the latter deceive us and involve us in error, often compelling us to judge the same thing differently at different times, changing our minds regarding our actions and our choices of things great and small? 

In contrast, the art of measurement would make this illusion <note>original: "phantasm"</note> void. By manifesting the truth, it would cause the soul to be at rest by remaining grounded in reality, and it would preserve our life. I then said, "Tell me, my friends—regarding this point—are not all actions that contribute to living well and pleasantly both noble <note>original: "beautiful" (Greek: *kalon*), which implies moral excellence and nobility as well as aesthetic beauty</note> and beneficial? And is not a noble deed both good and beneficial?" 

They granted this. 

"If, therefore," I said, "the pleasant is good, then no one who knows or believes that other things are better than what he is currently doing—and is able to do them—will continue to do those things when he has the power to do what is better. Therefore, when a man is 'conquered by himself' <note>original: "inferior to himself," referring to the concept of *akrasia* or the lack of self-control</note>, it is nothing other than ignorance; and when he is 'master of himself' <note>original: "superior to himself"</note>, it is nothing other than wisdom."

To this, all of them agreed.

"But what do you say? Do you define ignorance as having a false opinion and being deceived about matters of great importance?"

To this, likewise, all of them agreed.

"Does it not then follow," I said, "that no one willingly moves toward what is evil, or toward what they believe to be evil? For it seems it is not in human nature to choose things one considers evil instead of pursuing things one considers good. And when it is necessary to choose one of two evils, no one will choose the greater if it is in his power to choose the lesser." 

All of these points were agreed upon by all of us. 

"What then," I said, "do you call 'dread' and 'fear'? Is it what I would say it is—an expectation of evil—whether you use the word fear or dread?" 

It appeared to Protagoras and Hippias that dread and fear were exactly this; but Prodicus argued that dread was an expectation of evil, while fear was not. 

"That makes no difference, Prodicus," I said. "What matters is whether our previous conclusion is true. Is there, then, any man <meta>catchword: willing</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues that since pleasure is good and pain is evil, no one knowingly chooses the "worse" path unless they are ignorant of the true "measurement" of pleasure and pain. This establishes the Socratic paradox that no one does evil willingly.</summary>

## THE PROTAGORAS.

Is a person willing to turn toward things they dread, when they have the power to turn toward things they do not dread? Or is this impossible, based on what we have already agreed? For we have agreed that a person thinks the things they dread are evil, and that no one willingly goes toward or accepts things they consider evil. 

All of them agreed to this as well.

"This being admitted," I said, "now, Prodicus and Hippias, let Protagoras here defend the correctness of his first answer. At that time, he said that there were five parts of virtue, and that none of them resembled the others, but each had its own specific power. I am not pressing him on that point right now, but I am talking about what he said afterward: namely, that four of these parts might be considered similar to one another, but that one of them—courage <note>original: "fortitude" (Greek: *andreia*)</note>—differed greatly from the rest. 

He also said this could be seen from the following fact. He said, 'Socrates, you will find men who are most unholy, most unjust, most self-indulgent <note>original: "intemperate"</note>, and most undisciplined, but who are at the same time exceptionally brave. This shows that courage is very different from the other parts of virtue.' 

At that time, I was immediately surprised by your answer. My surprise has only grown since I have discussed these matters with all of you. I therefore asked him this: did he define brave men as 'bold' men? He said he did, and also called them 'impetuous' <note>original: "impetuous" (Greek: *iteoi*), here meaning those who are ready to rush headlong into danger</note>. Do you remember, Protagoras, that this was your answer?"

"I do," he said.

"Tell us, then," I said, "in what way are the brave 'impetuous' according to you? Is it in the same things that the timid <note>original: "timid" (Greek: *deiloi*), referring to the cowardly</note> attempt?"

"It is not," he said.

"Then it must be in different things?"

"Yes."

"But do the timid engage in bold attempts while the brave engage in things that are 'dreadful'?"

"That is what the common people say, Socrates."

"You are right," I replied. "However, I am not asking that. I am asking: in what way do you say the brave are impetuous? Is it in things they consider dreadful, or in things that are not dreadful?"

"But," he said, "as you just showed, it is impossible for a person to go toward what they think is dreadful."

"You are right about that too," I replied. "So, if this has been correctly demonstrated, no one goes toward things they think are dreadful, since we have found that being 'conquered by oneself' is actually just ignorance."

He acknowledged this.

"Nevertheless, all men—both the timid and the brave—engage in things they feel confident about. Consequently, both the timid and the brave pursue the same things."

"But surely, Socrates," he said,

"But," I asked, "is it a noble <note>original: "beautiful" (Greek: *kalon*), meaning morally honorable or fine</note> thing or a shameful <note>original: "base" (Greek: *aischron*), meaning morally ugly or disgraceful</note> thing to engage in war?"

"A noble thing," he said.

"If, therefore, it is a noble thing, we have already agreed above that it is a good thing. For we have acknowledged that all noble actions are good actions."

"You speak the truth," he said, "and this has always appeared to be the case to me."

"Right," I said. "But which of the two do you say is unwilling to engage in war, even though it is a noble and good thing?"

"The cowardly," he replied.

"If, therefore," I said, "it is noble and good, is it not also pleasant?"

"That is granted," he said.

"Are the cowardly, therefore, unwilling to proceed toward that which is nobler, better, and more pleasant, even when they know it to be so?"

"But," he said, "if we agreed to that, we would destroy what we acknowledged before." <note>referring to the previous argument that no one willingly chooses what they know to be bad or less good</note>

"But what about the brave man? Does he not engage in that which is nobler, more excellent, and more pleasant?"

"It is necessary to acknowledge that he does," he said.

"In short, then, the brave do not have any shameful fears when they are afraid; nor when they are bold, are they shamefully daring."

"True," he said.

"But if their daring is not shameful, does it not follow that it is noble daring?"

He agreed.

"And if their boldness is noble, is it not also good?"

"Yes."

"On the contrary, are not the cowardly, the rash, and the insane shamefully afraid and shamefully bold?"

He agreed they were.

"But are they shamefully and wickedly bold because of anything other than ignorance and a lack of training <note>original: "want of discipline"</note>?"

"That is so," he said.

"What then? Do you call this thing that makes the cowardly act cowardly 'cowardice' <note>original: "timidity"</note> or 'courage' <note>original: "fortitude"</note>?"

"Cowardice," he said.

"But have not the cowardly appeared to be what they are because of their ignorance of what is truly fearful?"

"Entirely so," he said.

"They are cowardly, therefore, because of this ignorance."

He acknowledged it.

"But you have granted that the thing that makes them cowardly is cowardice."

He said he had.

"Then will not the ignorance of what is fearful and what is not fearful be cowardice?"

He agreed.

"But," I said, "courage is the opposite of cowardice."

"It is."

"Will not, then, the wisdom of what is fearful and what is not fearful be the opposite of the ignorance of these things?"

To this also he agreed.

"But is not the ignorance of these things cowardice?"

He agreed to this with great difficulty.

"Therefore, the wisdom of what is fearful and what is not fearful is courage, since it is the opposite of the ignorance of these things."

And I said, "Why, Protagoras, do you neither agree with nor deny what I say?"

"Finish the argument yourself," he said.

"Right away," I replied. "Let me only first ask you if it still seems to you, as it did before, that there are certain men who are very ignorant and yet very brave?"

"You still seem very anxious, Socrates, for me to answer you. I will therefore satisfy you; and I say that, based on what we have already granted, it seems to me impossible that this should be the case." <note>Protagoras finally concedes that courage requires knowledge, meaning one cannot be both ignorant and truly brave.</note>

"But," I said, "I am not asking you all these details for any other reason than because I wish to consider how the matters pertaining to virtue exist, and what virtue itself is. For I know that once this becomes clear, the subject that has been the focus of our long discussion will be revealed—I, indeed, asserting that virtue cannot be taught, and you asserting that it can. And it seems to me that the conclusion of our arguments, as if it were a person, mocks and ridicules us; and if it had a voice, it would address us like this:"

> "You are acting absurdly, Socrates and Protagoras! You, Socrates, asserted in the earlier part of your discourse that virtue cannot be taught. Yet now you are eager to contradict yourself by trying to show that all these things—namely justice, temperance, and courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>—are knowledge <note>original: "science" (from Latin *scientia*, meaning a systematic body of knowledge)</note>. By this line of reasoning, virtue would clearly appear to be something that can be taught. For if virtue were anything other than knowledge, as Protagoras tries to prove it is, it clearly could not be taught. But now, if it should appear to be knowledge, as you, Socrates, are eager to conclude, it would be wonderful if it could *not* be taught. On the other hand, Protagoras at first admitted that it could be taught, but now, on the contrary, he seems to be trying hard to make virtue appear to be anything other than knowledge; and thus it would be the sort of thing that is least capable of being taught."

"Therefore, Protagoras, seeing all these points tossed back and forth in such terrible confusion, I am extremely eager for them to become clear. And I wish that we, by continuing to discuss these things, might discover what virtue is—and then examine it again to see whether it can be taught, or whether it can—"

# INTRODUCTION

### TO

# THE THEAGES.

---

**TO** understand the purpose of this dialogue, it is necessary to observe that wisdom is of two types: one is absolute, and the other is conditional. Absolute wisdom is that which is simply called "wisdom" without any further qualification. Conditional wisdom, however, is not called wisdom on its own, but rather a specific kind of wisdom. 

The first of these—absolute wisdom—is defined as the knowledge of things that are the subjects of <term>science</term><note>In this context, "science" refers to *episteme*, or certain, unchanging knowledge of universal truths, rather than modern empirical science.</note>. These subjects are things that possess a necessary, eternal, and unchanging existence, such as those radiant causes and principles of things found in a divine intellect. Plato calls these **ideas**, and Aristotle ¹ calls them "the most honorable things by nature." 

Conditional wisdom, on the other hand, is common to all arts and crafts; the peak or perfection of any art is called a certain kind of "wisdom." Of all the arts that possess this conditional wisdom, the most important is **political wisdom**, which all other arts serve. This is known as both the political and the "royal" discipline. Its subject is the city, its goal is the common good, and all other arts are its servants.

Because this political wisdom—the subject of this dialogue—forms an important part of virtue as a whole, Socrates indicates that it can only be obtained through a **divine destiny**. This is consistent with what he argued in the *Meno*.

¹ Aristotle, in his *Nicomachean Ethics*, defines wisdom in its absolute sense as: "Knowledge, the intellect of the most honorable things by nature, and the intellect of first principles." <note>original Greek: Η σοφία ἐστιν ἡ ἐπιστήμη, καὶ νοῦς τῶν τιμιωτάτων τῇ φύσει, καὶ νοῦς τῶν ἀρχῶν.</note>

<meta>catchword: divine (ϑεία)</meta>

<summary>This introduction distinguishes between absolute wisdom (knowledge of eternal truths) and conditional wisdom (mastery of arts), identifying political wisdom as the highest form of the latter and a gift of divine destiny.</summary>
<keywords>Theages, Plato, Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Meno, Socrates, political wisdom, divine destiny, ideas, science, virtue</keywords>

(<term>Divine destiny</term> <note>original Greek: *theia moira*</note>), without which all the endeavors of the most accomplished masters are useless; and he confirms this through various examples.

This conversation, according to Dacier <note>André Dacier (1651–1722), a French classical scholar and translator of Plato</note>, took place in the year that the Athenians were defeated at Ephesus by Tissaphernes <note>A Persian soldier and statesman</note>. This was the fourth year of the 92nd Olympiad, and 407 years before the birth of Christ <note>The original text erroneously lists 470; 407 BC is the historically accepted date for the 92nd Olympiad</note>. Plato, being twenty years of age, was then the disciple of Socrates.

## DEMODOCUS

I want, Socrates, to speak with you in private about certain things, if you are at leisure. If you are not, unless your business is of great importance, please make leisure for my sake.

**Soc.** I am indeed at leisure, and very much at your service. You have my permission, therefore, to speak, if you wish to say anything.

**Dem.** Would you be willing, then, for us to retire from this place into the porch of <term>Zeus the Liberator</term> <note>original: Jupiter Eleutherius. This was a famous portico, or covered walkway, in the Athenian marketplace (Agora) dedicated to Zeus as the protector of freedom.</note>, which is very near?

**Soc.** If you please.

**Dem.** Let us go then, Socrates. All plants—everything produced from the earth—as well as animals and man, appear to exist in the same manner. For with plants, the process is easy for those of us who cultivate the earth: that is, to prepare everything prior to planting, and the planting itself. But when that which is planted becomes alive, the attention the plant requires is great and very difficult. 

The same thing also appears to take place regarding men. I judge other matters based on my own affairs. For with my son here, the "planting"—or the procreating, or whatever else it may be necessary to call it—was the easiest of all things. However, his education is difficult and causes me to be in continual fear for him. 

Much could be said regarding other things, but the desire he now possesses terrifies me. It is not an ignoble desire, certainly, but it is dangerous. For he desires, Socrates, as he says, to become a wise man. It seems to me that certain commoners <note>original: "plebeians," likely referring to fellow citizens from the same local district or deme.</note> of the same age as him have been coming to this city and repeating...

...repeating certain discourses they have heard, have disturbed him deeply. He is eager to emulate them, and for some time now he has been troublesome to me, believing it is right for me to support him and pay a sum of money to one of the **sophists** <note>original: "sophists"; itinerant teachers in ancient Greece who taught subjects like rhetoric, philosophy, and virtue for a fee.</note> who might make him a wise man. I am not really concerned about the expense, but I believe the goal of his pursuit will lead him into significant danger. 

Until now, I have held him back by soothing him; but since I am no longer able to do this, I have thought it best to comply with his wishes, lest by frequently associating with others without my guidance he should be corrupted. This is why I have come here for this very purpose: to place him with someone who is recognized as a sophist. Our meeting with you is therefore a fortunate circumstance; since I am about to engage in affairs of this kind, I wish very much to consult you about them. If you have any advice to give regarding what you have heard from me, it is both lawful and proper for you to give it.

**Soc.** Counsel, Demodocus, is said to be a sacred thing. If anything else is sacred, then this consultation certainly is. For it is not possible for a person to consult about anything more divine than the **erudition** <term>erudition</term> <note>Learning or education, specifically the depth of knowledge acquired through study.</note> of himself and those who belong to him. 

First, then, you and I should agree on exactly what it is we are consulting about. Otherwise, I might understand it to be one thing while you think it is another. Then, after disagreeing throughout our conversation, we would both look ridiculous—I for giving advice and you for requesting it—without agreeing on a single thing.

**DEM.** You seem to me, Socrates, to speak rightly, and it is proper to do as you say.

**Soc.** I speak rightly, and yet perhaps not entirely, since I am considering a change in one small detail. I am thinking that perhaps this youth does not desire what we think he desires, but something else. If something else is the object of his wishes, we will act absurdly by consulting about something different. Therefore, it seems best to me to begin by inquiring of him what it is he desires.

**DEM.** It does indeed seem best to do so, as you say.

**Soc.** But tell me, what is the name of this fine youth? What must we call him?

### THE THEAGES.

**DEM.** His name, Socrates, is Theages.

**Soc.** You have given your son, O Demodocus, a beautiful and sacred name. <note>The name Theages is derived from the Greek words for "God" (*theos*) and "guide" (*agein*), suggesting someone led by the divine.</note> But tell us, O Theages, do you say that you desire to become a wise man, and do you think it is right that your father should find a man who, by associating with you, may make you wise?

**THEA.** I do.

**Soc.** But do you call those men wise who are scientifically knowledgeable, in whatever subject they possess this knowledge; or do you call those wise who do not possess scientific knowledge? <note>In this context, "science" or "scientific knowledge" refers to *episteme*, meaning a specialized skill, craft, or body of expertise rather than modern laboratory science.</note>

**THEA.** I call the scientific wise.

**Soc.** What then? Has your father not taught and instructed you in those things in which others here are instructed who are the sons of respectable fathers; namely, letters, playing the harp, wrestling, and other exercises?

**THEA.** He has.

**Soc.** Do you think, then, that there is still a certain science <term>science</term> <note>original: "science"; here meaning a specific branch of knowledge or a practical art.</note> lacking, which it is proper for your father to pay attention to for your sake?

**THEA.** I do.

**Soc.** What is it? Tell us as well, so that we may satisfy you.

**THEA.** My father also knows what it is, Socrates, for I have often mentioned it to him. But he deliberately says these things to you as if he did not know what I desire; for in other things also he similarly opposes me, and is not willing to place me with anyone.

**Soc.** But all that you have said to him until now has been said without witnesses. Now, therefore, make me a witness, and before me say what the wisdom is which you desire. For come now, if you should desire that wisdom by which men steer ships, and I should ask you, "O Theages, what is the wisdom which you lack, for which you blame your father as being unwilling to place you with a man through whom you might become wise?" what answer would you give me? What would you say this wisdom is? Is it not that of piloting?

**THEA.** Yes.

**Soc.** But if you desired to be wise according to that wisdom by which they drive chariots, and afterwards blamed your father, upon my asking you what this wisdom is, what answer would you give me? Would you not say it is the charioteering art?

**Thea.** It is not.

**Soc.** For this is music.

**Thea.** Certainly.

"...before you leave us; for I have heard the accustomed divine signal." At this, he stayed; and after remaining with us for a while, he rose again to depart and said, "Socrates, I am going." Furthermore, you can also learn from many people in Sicily what I predicted regarding the destruction of the army <note>original: "destruction of the army." This refers to the disastrous Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) during the Peloponnesian War.</note>. As for past events, you may hear about them from those who witnessed them; but you can now test the divine signal <term>original: "dæmoniacal signal." Socrates refers to his 'daimonion,' a spiritual voice that warned him against certain actions.</term> to see if it says anything relevant to the present. For Sannion, the son of Calus, has gone to join the army; and as he was leaving, I heard the divine signal. He has now gone with Thrasyllus <note>Thrasyllus was chosen as a general alongside Thrasybulus in the fourth year of the ninety-second Olympiad (roughly 409 BCE). — Dacier.</note> to wage war immediately against Ephesus and Ionia. I believe he will either die or meet some great misfortune, and I fear greatly <note>Indeed, the Athenians were defeated at Ephesus (Xenophon, Book I). I have told you all these things because this divine power has complete influence over the interactions of those who associate with me. It is opposed to many people, and those whom the divine power opposes cannot benefit from associating with me; therefore, it is not possible for me to spend time with them. With many others, however, the power does not prevent me from speaking, yet they are not all helped by associating with me. But those whose conversations with me are favored by the power of the divine signal are the ones you have noticed: for in a short time, they make great progress. Among these, some retain this advantage with firmness and stability. Many others, however, advance in a wonderful way as long as they are with me, but when they leave me, they are once again no different from other men. Aristides—the son of Lysimachus and grandson of Aristides <note>Aristides "the Just," a famous Athenian statesman.</note>—once experienced this. By associating with me, he made very great progress in a short...

<summary>Socrates explains that his ability to teach or benefit others is governed by his "divine signal," which permits or forbids his associations and allows him to predict future misfortunes.</summary>

<header>THE THEAGES.</header>

<margin>¹ This grandson of Thucydides was a rival to Pericles in the Athenian government.</margin>
...time; but afterwards he sailed from here in order to take part in a military campaign. When he returned, he found Thucydides—the son of Melesias and grandson of the famous Thucydides¹—spending time with me. This Thucydides had argued with me during a meeting just the day before. 

When Aristides saw me, he greeted me, and after we had spoken for a while, he said, "Socrates, I hear that Thucydides has a very high opinion of himself regarding certain matters and is angry with you, as if he were someone truly remarkable." 

"That is true," I replied. 

"But what?" he asked. "Does he not realize how insignificant <note>original: "what a slave he was." Aristides uses the term "slave" metaphorically to describe an intellectually or morally undeveloped state before meeting Socrates.</note> he was before he started spending time with you?" 

"By the gods, it seems he does not," I said. 

"But Socrates," he replied, "something ridiculous has happened to me." 

"What is that?" I asked. 

"It is this," he said. "Before I went off to join the army, I was able to hold a conversation with anyone, whoever they might be. I didn't seem inferior to anyone in an argument, and I even sought out the company of the most sophisticated <note>original: "elegant." Here meaning refined or intellectually polished.</note> men. But now, on the contrary, I avoid anyone I perceive to be learned, because I am so ashamed of my own lack of knowledge <note>original: "vileness." Aristides is being self-deprecating about his current intellectual state.</note>." 

"Tell me," I said, "did this ability leave you suddenly or gradually?" 

"Gradually," he replied. 

"When did you have it?" I asked. "Was it present while you were learning something from me, or did it happen in some other way?" 

"I will tell you, Socrates," he said, "something that sounds incredible, by the gods, but it is true. As you know, I never actually learned anything specific from you. However, I made progress <term>original: "proficiency." In this context, it means intellectual or spiritual growth.</term> just by being near you. I improved even if I was only in the same house as you, even if we weren't in the same room. But my progress was even greater when I was in the same room with you. I also felt that I improved much more when I looked at you while you spoke, rather than looking away. But I made the most progress by far when I sat right next to you and touched you. Now, however," he said, "that entire state of mind <note>original: "habit." Referring to his acquired skill or intellectual condition.</note> has completely vanished."

So, Theages, that is what it is like to associate with me. If it pleases the Divine <note>original: "divinity." Socrates refers to the divine force or his 'daimonion' that governs his interactions.</note>, you will make great and rapid progress; but if the Divine is not pleased, you will not. Think about it, then. Wouldn't it be safer for you to be taught by someone who has total control over the benefit they give to others, rather than by me? I may benefit someone, or I may not—it all depends on how it happens.

<header>THE THEAGES.</header>

**THEAGES:** It seems to me, therefore, Socrates, that we should act in this way: let us test this divine power <term>original: "dæmoniacal power." This refers to Socrates' *daimonion*, a "divine sign" or inner voice that he claimed warned him against certain actions.</term> by spending time together. If it is favorable to us, the best results will follow; but if it is not, let us immediately discuss what should be done—whether we should seek out someone else to study with, or attempt to appease the divine power that stays with you through prayers, sacrifices, or any other means taught by our seers <note>original: "diviners." Ancient Greek practitioners who interpreted the will of the gods through rituals.</note>.

**DEMODOCUS:** Do not oppose the young man any longer, Socrates, in these matters; for Theages speaks well.

**SOCRATES:** If it seems right to act this way, let us do so.

# THE LACHES.

---

### THE PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.

->LYSIMACHUS²,    ||   NICIAS³,<-
->MELESIAS,       ||   LACHES⁴,<-
->The Sons of LYSIMACHUS and MELESIAS, and SOCRATES.<-

---

¹ We have already noted, in the introduction to the *Parmenides*, that the energy of dialectics is threefold: it either exists through opposing arguments, unfolds the truth on its own, or refutes falsehood on its own. Since the purpose of the present dialogue is to refute the false opinions of Laches and Nicias concerning courage <note>original: fortitude</note>, and thus to free them from double ignorance <note>A Platonic concept where one is not only ignorant of the truth, but is also unaware that they are ignorant.</note>, the reader must not expect to find a precise definition of courage here. However, as the reader will undoubtedly be anxious to obtain this definition, I shall present the enlightened insights of the divine Iamblichus <note>original: Jamblichus; a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> on this subject.

Courage, considered according to its most essential existence, is an unchanging intellectual power and a most vigorous intellectual energy; or, in other words, it is a consistency and stable habit of the intellect within itself. The types of courage seen in life will be of this kind, whether they are considered as existing by themselves or as providing strength to the firm stability of reasoning. From these, those types of courage proceed which are seen in the passions, concerning terrifying things and their opposites, and in fear and boldness. These generously resist pleasure and pain, and always preserve the same correct opinions and balanced, moderate behaviors. Along with these, many types of courage arise from passion, reason, and free choice, through which human life gains a vigor of action that cannot be defeated. This vigorous energy also voluntarily performs whatever is morally noble <note>original: "beautiful" (Greek: *kalon*), meaning what is fine or honorable</note> and chosen for its own sake; for the sake of the good, it endures all labors and dangers. It also cheerfully and readily gives itself to things that appear to be difficult, boldly faces and contemplates death, and easily bears pain and calamity of every kind.

This dialogue is thought to have been written shortly after the defeat of the Athenians at Delium <note>A battle in 424 BCE during the Peloponnesian War</note>, which occurred in the first year of the 89th Olympiad.

² The son of Aristides the Just.
³ The general of the Athenians.
⁴ Another Athenian general.

### LYSIMACHUS.

**Y**ou have seen, Nicias and Laches, this man demonstrating how to fight in armor¹; and indeed, we did not tell you at the time why Melesias and I invited you to see him. But now we will tell you, for we think it is right to speak freely with you. There are, indeed, some people who laugh at matters of this kind; if anyone consults them, they will not say what they truly think. Instead, they try to guess what the questioner wants to hear and speak contrary to their own actual opinion. However, we believe that you are qualified to judge and that you will plainly say what you think. Therefore, we have made you our partners in this deliberation. 

The matter I have been introducing at such length is this: these are our sons. That youth, the son of Melesias, is called Thucydides, named after his grandfather; and this one, who is mine, is called Aristides, after my father. We have decided that we should pay as much attention to them as possible. We do not want to act as many people do, who, when their children become boys², allow them to do as they please; instead, we are now beginning to take all the care of them that we can. 

Seeing that you also have children, we thought that you especially must have considered how they may be educated so as to become the best of men. If, however, you have not frequently paid much attention to this, we now remind you that it is not proper to be negligent about it, and we call upon you to deliberate with us concerning the education of children. As for why we have been led to think this way, Nicias and Laches, you should hear it, even though the story may be somewhat long-winded.

Melesias and I share a single table, and these boys eat with us. As I told you at first, we shall speak freely to you. Both of us are able to tell these youths many noble deeds performed by our fathers, both in war and peace, during the time they managed the affairs of their allies...

...and deeds done for the city; but we cannot tell them of any great deeds of our own. This fills us with shame, and we blame our fathers for letting us live in luxury <note>original: "delicately"</note> when we became boys, while they were busily employed in the affairs of others. We point this out to these youths, telling them that if they neglect their own development and do not listen to us, they will become dishonorable <note>original: "ignoble"</note>; but if they apply themselves, they may soon be worthy of the names they carry.

They say they will obey us; so we are considering what kind of learning or study will help them become the best possible men. Because of this, someone recommended to us that the young men should learn how to fight in armor, calling it a noble skill <note>original: "discipline"—here meaning a field of study or training</note>. He also praised the man you just saw performing and advised us to see him too. So, we thought it was right to invite you along, so that you could not only watch with us but also give us your advice—if you are willing—on how we should care for our children. These are the matters we want to discuss with you. Now, it is your turn to give your opinion on this training: whether it seems proper to learn it or not, and whether you know of any other studies or pursuits worthy of praise for young men. Finally, tell us what kind of education you plan to provide for your own children.

**NICIAS:** Lysimachus and Melesias, I certainly praise your intention <note>original: "conception"</note> and am ready to join you in this discussion. I believe Laches here is also ready to do the same.

**LACHES:** You are right, Nicias. What Lysimachus just said about his father and the father of Melesias seems very well said—both against them and against us, and against all who are involved in politics. For the same things often happen to them: as he said, their children and household matters are neglected and ignored. These things, Lysimachus, you have said well. But I am surprised that you would ask us for advice on the education of youth and not ask Socrates here. For, in the first place, he is our fellow citizen; and second, he is always busy investigating exactly what you are looking for: what kind of training or pursuit is best for young men.

**Lysimachus:** What do you say, Laches? Does Socrates here pay attention to matters of this kind?

**Laches:** Most certainly, Lysimachus.

**Nicias:** I can also confirm this with just as much confidence as Laches. For recently, he introduced me to a stranger named Damon—a student <note>original: "disciple"</note> of Agathocles—to teach my son music. He is a most agreeable <note>original: "acceptable"</note> man, not only for his musical skill but also for other qualities that make him a fit companion for young men like these.

**Lysimachus:** Indeed, Socrates, Nicias, and Laches—I, and those of my own age, no longer have much acquaintance with younger people because we mostly stay indoors due to our advanced years. But, son of Sophroniscus, if you have any advice for the benefit of your fellow citizen here, it is only right that you share it. **Sons of Melesias and Lysimachus:** Yes, Father, it is the same man.

**Lysimachus:** By Hera <note>original: "Juno"</note>, it is good, Socrates, that you bring honor to your father, who was the best of men. From now on, your interests shall be mine, and mine shall be yours.

**Laches:** And truly, Lysimachus, you must not let this man go. I have seen him elsewhere, bringing honor not only to his father but also to his country. During the defeat at Delium $^1$, he retreated <note>original: "retired"</note> alongside me. I can assure you that if the others had conducted themselves as he did, our city would have stood firm and would not have suffered such a disaster <note>original: "ruin"</note>.

**Soc.** Regarding these things, *Lysimachus*, I will try to give you whatever advice I am able, and to do all that you request. It is not inferior to any other exercise, nor does it require less effort; and at the same time, this exercise and horsemanship <note>original: "equestrian skill"</note> are especially suitable for a gentleman <note>original: "liberal man," meaning a free citizen of high status</note>. Furthermore, this training is an advantage in battle itself, when it is necessary to fight in formation with many others. But it is most beneficial when the ranks are broken, and when it is necessary in single combat either to pursue a resisting enemy or to repel an attacker while retreating. Since this is the case, it is evident that he will apply himself to those noble skills and studies that follow, which are well worth a man's time to learn and study, and of which this training is the first step. We may also add this—which is no small addition—that this knowledge will make every man significantly more daring and brave in battle than he was before. **LAC.** But it is difficult, *Nicias*, to claim that any <term>training</term> <note>original: "discipline"</note> is not worth learning, for it seems good to know all things. Indeed, regarding this art of using weapons, if it truly is a skill—as those who teach it claim, and as *Nicias* asserts—then it is necessary to learn it. But if it is not a real skill, and those who promise to teach it are deceiving us, or if it is a skill but not of much value, why should we learn it? 

I say these things because I look at it this way: if it were of any real value, I believe it would not have been hidden from the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedæmonians"</note>, who care for nothing else in life but to seek and study how they may surpass others in war. And even if this art were hidden from them, it could not have been hidden from the teachers of it; they would know that the Spartans, more than any other Greeks, pay attention to things of this kind. They would also know that anyone renowned for these skills would accumulate much wealth from the Spartans and from others, just as a tragic poet does when he is renowned among us. Indeed, a person who thinks he can compose excellent tragedies does not wander out of Attica <note>The region surrounding and including Athens.</note>...

The other details about the man are not worth telling, but the outcome of this trick of using a scythe-headed spear shouldn't be overlooked. For while he was fighting, his scythe got caught in the rigging of the enemy's ship. *Stesileus* pulled to loosen it, but he couldn't get it free, and the two ships began to pass each other. Meanwhile, he was pulled along by the ship while still holding his spear. But as the enemy ship steered away and began to pull him overboard because he was still holding the spear, he let it slide through his hands until he was only holding it by the very end. 

The crew of the merchant vessel laughed and shouted at him being dragged by his own spear and at the ridiculous sight he made. Finally, someone threw a stone that landed right at his feet on one of the rowers' benches, and he dropped the spear. At that point, those on the <term>trireme</term> <note>original: "three-banked galley"</note> could no longer hold back their laughter, seeing that scythe-headed spear dangling from the enemy ship. Perhaps, therefore, this art may be of some use, as *Nicias* says; however, those are the specific events I witnessed. **MEL.** What do you mean?
**Soc.** Perhaps what I mean will be clearer this way: it doesn't seem to me that we have yet agreed on what exactly we are consulting and examining <note>original: "speculate"</note>. **NIC.** Weren't we, Socrates, considering whether or not young men should learn to fight in armor?
**Soc.** Exactly, Nicias. But when someone considers a remedy for the eyes—whether or not it is proper to apply it—do you think the consultation is about the remedy, or about the eyes?
**NIC.** About the eyes.
**Soc.** In the same way, when someone considers a bridle for a horse—whether it should be used and when—he will be consulting about the horse, not about the bridle.
**NIC.** True.
**Soc.** To put it simply: when anyone considers one thing for the sake of another, his consultation is really about the primary goal, and not about the secondary thing used to reach it¹.

I contemplate at the same time both the speaker and what is being said, observing how they fit and harmonize with each other. This is not because he is harmonized according to the melody of the lyre or other instruments of play, but because in reality he has tuned his own life. Such a person lives in concord with himself in both words and deeds—not according to the <term>Ionic</term>¹, or <term>Phrygian</term>, or <term>Lydian</term> harmony, but according to the <term>Dorian</term>, which is the only truly Greek harmony.

Therefore, when such a man speaks, he makes me rejoice and seem to be a lover of words, so eagerly do I receive what he says. I have not yet, indeed, had any experience with the words of Socrates, but it seems I have experienced his deeds in the past. There, I found him to be a man worthy of noble speech and complete liberty of expression. If, therefore, he is such a man, I will consult him, and I shall most willingly be questioned by him and not be reluctant to learn from him. **LACHES.** That is what I say.

->Swiftly they pursue and flee in every direction.<-

And for this very reason, Homer praises <term>Aeneas</term> himself for being skilled in fleeing, saying that he was an expert in the art of retreat.

**LACHES.** And quite rightly so, <term>Socrates</term>. For in that passage, Homer is talking about chariots, and you are talking about the <term>Scythian</term> cavalry. Their cavalry fights in that way, but the Greek infantry <note>original: "infantry of Greece"</note> fights as I described—by holding their ground.

**SOCRATES.** Except perhaps for the <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>The Spartans</note>, Laches. But once the Persian ranks were broken, the Spartans rallied <note>original: "rallied and fought like cavalry"</note> and won that battle.

**LACHES.** That is true.

**SOCRATES.** For this reason, I said I was the cause of your poor answer, because I did not ask the question well. I wanted to ask you not only about those who are brave in the infantry, but also about those who are brave in the cavalry and in every kind of warfare. 

Furthermore, I meant to ask not only about those who are brave in battle, but also those who show courage in dangers at sea, in illness, in poverty, and in politics. I also meant to include those who are strong in struggling against desires or pleasures—whether by facing their attacks or by retreating from them. For some men, Laches, show their bravery in these situations as well.

**LACHES.** Very much so, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** All of these people, then, are brave. However, some possess courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note> when facing pleasures, others in pain, others in their desires, and others in their fears. Meanwhile, I think others show cowardice <note>original: "timidity"</note> in these very same areas.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Laches. Laches has just suggested that courage is a "certain endurance of the soul." Socrates is now testing this definition by asking whether all forms of endurance can be considered courage.</meta>

<page-num>196</page-num>
<header>THE LACHES,</header>
<sig>4</sig>

# THE LACHES

**SOCRATES.** Do you then say that a thing of this kind is beautiful, even though it is bad and harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note>?

**LACHES.** That would not be right, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, you do not acknowledge such endurance as this to be <term>courage</term> <note>original: "fortitude"</note>, since it is not beautiful; and courage is beautiful.

**LACHES.** That is true.

**SOCRATES.** According to your argument, then, "prudent endurance" will be courage.

**LACHES.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** Let us see then in what way this endurance is "prudent." Is it prudent in all things, both great and small? For instance, if someone has the endurance to spend his money wisely, knowing that he shall be enriched by spending it, would you call him a brave man?

**LACHES.** By Zeus <note>original: "By Jupiter"; Laches would have sworn by the Greek gods, though the translator used the Roman equivalent</note>, certainly not!

**SOCRATES.** And what if a physician had a son, or some other patient, ill with an inflammation in his chest? If the patient should request him to give him something to eat or drink, but the physician stubbornly persisted in denying his request, would you call this endurance courage?

**LACHES.** I would not.

**SOCRATES.** But what about in war? Here is a man of endurance who is willing to fight. He wisely reasons with himself that others will come to his aid, that he is fighting against enemies who are fewer and more weak <note>original: "despicable"</note> than those on his own side, and furthermore, that he has the advantage of the terrain. Will you say that this man, who endures with such prudence and advantage, is braver than the man in the opposing army who is willing to stand his ground and endure?

**LACHES.** The man in the opposing army, Socrates, seems the braver to me.

**SOCRATES.** And yet the endurance of that man is more "imprudent" than the other's.

**LACHES.** That is true.

**SOCRATES.** Will you say, then, that a man who holds his ground in a horse-riding contest because he has <term>skill in horsemanship</term> <note>original: "equestrian science"</note> is less brave than the man who holds his ground without such skill?

**LACHES.** To me, it seems that he is.

<summary>Socrates challenges Laches's definition of courage as "prudent endurance" by showing that we often consider people who take "imprudent" risks to be braver than those who act with calculated advantages. This creates a logical paradox, as Laches previously agreed that courage must be a noble or "beautiful" quality, while imprudence is generally seen as bad.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Laches, courage, fortitude, prudence, endurance, military ethics, horsemanship</keywords>

**SOCRATES.** And will you also say the same of a slinger, or an archer, or of anyone else who persists <note>original: "endures"</note> in any other art?

**LACHES.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** And what about those who are willing to go down into a well and persist in swimming there, even though they are not skilled in this activity or in anything else of this kind—will you say that such men are braver than those who are skilled in these things?

**LACHES.** What else can one say, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** Nothing, if that is what he thinks.

**LACHES.** But I do indeed think so.

**SOCRATES.** And yet, Laches, such men encounter danger and persist more foolishly <note>original: "imprudently"</note> than those who do this with professional skill <note>original: "art"</note>.

**LACHES.** So it appears.

**SOCRATES.** Didn't we previously conclude that shameful <note>original: "base"</note> and foolish boldness and endurance are harmful <note>original: "noxious"</note>?

**LACHES.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** But <term>fortitude</term> <note>The Greek term *andreia* is usually translated as "courage" or "manliness"</note> was acknowledged by us to be something beautiful.

**LACHES.** It was acknowledged.

**SOCRATES.** But now, conversely, we are saying that this shameful and foolish endurance is fortitude.

**LACHES.** So it appears.

**SOCRATES.** Do you think we are speaking well then?

**LACHES.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"; Laches would have sworn by the Greek gods, though the translator used the Roman equivalent</note>, Socrates, I don't think we are.

**SOCRATES.** In your own language, therefore, Laches, you and I are not <term>Dorically harmonized</term> <note>The Dorian mode was a musical scale associated with strength and tradition. Socrates is using a musical metaphor to say their words and their actions (their "works") do not match</note>: for our works do not accord with our words. For someone, it seems, might say that we participate in fortitude in our deeds; but not, I think, in our words, if he were to hear us speaking now.

**LACHES.** What you say is very true.

**SOCRATES.** What then? Does it seem good <note>original: "beautiful"</note> to you that we should be in this condition?

**LACHES.** By no means.

**SOCRATES.** Are you willing, therefore, that we should agree <note>original: "yield our assent"</note> to what we said?

**LACHES.** To which statement of ours do you refer?

<summary>Socrates leads Laches into a logical contradiction: Laches admits that unskilled people who take risks are "foolish," yet he previously claimed they were "braver" than skilled professionals. This forces them to realize that their definition of courage is inconsistent and out of harmony.</summary>

**SOCRATES.** To that which commanded us to endure. If you are willing, then, let us persevere in our inquiry and endure, lest courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note> itself should mock us for not bravely investigating what it is—if indeed endurance itself is often courage.

**LACHES.** I, indeed, Socrates, am ready to stand my ground, though I am not used to such conferences. But a certain stubbornness <note>original: "pertinacity"</note> drives me against what has been said, and I am actually indignant that I am so incapable of expressing my thoughts. For I seem to myself to know what courage is; but I don't know how it just now escaped me, so that I cannot grasp it in words and say what it is.

**SOCRATES.** But a good hunter <note>original: "huntsman"</note>, my friend, ought to run after the beast he hunts and not abandon <note>original: "remit"</note> his pursuit.

**LACHES.** He certainly should.

**SOCRATES.** Are you willing, then, for us to call Nicias to join this hunt, so that we may see if he is in any way more wise <note>original: "sagacious"</note> than we are?

**LACHES.** I am willing; why shouldn't I be?

**SOCRATES.** Come then, Nicias, please your friends and help them in their doubts during this discussion, if you have any power to do so; for you see how we are stuck <note>original: "embarrassed"</note>. Tell us, then, what you think courage is, free us from this doubt, and confirm with an argument what you believe it to be.

**NICIAS.** For some time now, Socrates, it has seemed to me that you haven't defined courage well; for you aren't using that which I have heard you argue so effectively.

**SOCRATES.** What is that, Nicias?

**NICIAS.** I have often heard you claim that every one of us is good at those things in which he is wise, but bad at those of which he is ignorant.

**SOCRATES.** By Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>, what you say is true, Nicias.

**NICIAS.** If, therefore, a brave man is a good man, he is clearly a wise man.

**SOCRATES.** Do you hear that, Laches?

**LACHES.** I do, but I don't really understand what he's saying.

**SOCRATES.** But I think I understand him, and he seems to be calling courage a kind of wisdom.

**LACHES.** What kind of wisdom, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** Won't you ask him that yourself, then?

**LACHES.** I will.

**LACHES.** You are right to question him, Socrates; let him tell us what kind of wisdom it is.

**NICIAS.** I say then, Laches, that it is the knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> of things that are fearful <note>original: "dreadful"</note> and things that inspire confidence <note>original: "daring"</note>, both in war and in all other matters.

**LACHES.** How absurdly he speaks, Socrates!

**SOCRATES.** Why do you say that, Laches?

**LACHES.** Why? Because wisdom is separate from courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>.

**SOCRATES.** Nicias does not say so.

**LACHES.** He does not indeed, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter"</note>; and therefore he is talking nonsense <note>original: "raves"</note>.

**SOCRATES.** Let us therefore teach him and not insult <note>original: "revile"</note> him.

**NICIAS.** He is not insulting me; but it seems to me, Socrates, that Laches is eager to make it look like I am saying nothing of value, simply because that was just the case with him.

**NICIAS.** He does indeed say something, yet it is not true.

**SOCRATES.** How so?

Instead, he shifts back and forth <note>original: "he is rolled upwards and downwards"</note>, hiding his own confusion. **LACHES.** Consider this then, Socrates, yourself.

**SOCRATES.** I shall do so, my good man <note>original: "O best of men"</note>. Do not think, however, that you are to be excluded from this discussion; listen and consider what is being said.

**LACHES.** Let it be so, if that seems right.

**SOCRATES.** It certainly does. And you, Nicias, tell us again from the beginning—for you know that at the start of our conversation we considered courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note> to be a part of virtue.

**NICIAS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Didn't you also answer then that it was a part of virtue, along with other parts which, taken together, are called virtue?

**NICIAS.** How could I say otherwise?

**SOCRATES.** So, do you recognize the same things as parts of virtue that I do? Besides courage, I include temperance, justice, and other similar qualities as parts of virtue. Don't you agree?

**NICIAS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Listen then, for we are in agreement on these points. But let us consider what is meant by "terrible" things and "daring" things, so that we don't have different opinions about them. We will tell you what we think of them; if you don't agree, you can correct us. We believe that "dreadful" things are those that cause fear, while "daring" things—those that can be faced boldly—are those that do not cause fear. However, neither past nor present evils cause fear; only expected ones do. Fear, after all, is the expectation of a future evil. Does it seem that way to you too, Laches?

**LACHES.** Very much so, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Then listen to our claim, Nicias: dreadful things are future evils, while daring things are future goods—or at least, they are not evils. Do you agree with this, or do you have another view about these things?

**NICIAS.** I agree with that.

**SOCRATES.** And do you call the knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> of these things courage?

**NICIAS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Let us then consider one more thing to see if we still agree.

**NICIAS.** What is that?

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page, where Socrates and Laches were defining "dreadful" and "daring" things as future evils and future goods. Socrates now challenges Nicias to consider whether knowledge (science) can be limited only to the future.</meta>

<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>THE LACHES.</header>

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you. For it appears to me and Laches that regarding whatever things there is knowledge <note>original: "science" — here meaning a systematic body of knowledge or a craft</note>, there is not one knowledge of the past, by which we know how it was made; another for the present, by which we know how it is being made; and another for that which is not yet made, by which we know how it might and will be made in the most excellent <note>original: "beautiful"</note> manner. Instead, knowing all of these is the task of the same science. 

Thus, for instance, regarding what is healthy <note>original: "salubrious"</note> at all times, there is no other science than medicine; medicine, being one and the same, sees what has been, what is, and what will be healthy. Agriculture works in a similar way regarding things that grow out of the earth. Likewise, in matters of war, you yourselves can testify that the science of military command <note>original: "commanding an army"</note> provides most excellently for all things, including what will happen in the future. For this art does not think it right to be subservient to divination <note>original: "divination" — the practice of seeking knowledge of the future through supernatural means</note>, but instead to preside over it, as the general better knows what is happening and what will happen in war. The law also commands this: that the diviner shall not command the general, but the general shall command the diviner. Shall we assert these things, Laches?

**LACHES.** We must assert them.

**SOCRATES.** But what about you? Do you agree with us, Nicias, that it is the task of the same science to possess a knowledge of the same things, whether they are considered as past, or as present, or as future?

**NICIAS.** I do; for that is how it appears to me, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Is not, therefore, my friend <note>original: "O best of men"</note>, courage <note>original: "fortitude"</note>, as you say, the science of things terrifying and encouraging <note>original: "dreadful and daring"</note>?

**NICIAS.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** But it has been acknowledged that terrifying things are future evils, and encouraging things are future goods.

**NICIAS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** But the same science has a knowledge of things past, present, and future.

**NICIAS.** It has.

**SOCRATES.** Courage, therefore, is not only the science of things terrifying and encouraging: for it not only has a knowledge of future goods and evils, but also of those that are past and present—in short, it surveys all things like the other sciences.

<meta>catchword: NICIAS.</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues that any true field of knowledge must cover the past, present, and future equally. He concludes that if courage is the "science" of good and evil, it cannot be limited only to future fears and hopes.</summary>

**NICIAS.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** You have, therefore, Nicias, only defined for us in your answer a third part of courage <note>original: "fortitude" — the Greek term is *andreia*, commonly translated today as courage</note>, even though we asked you what courage is in its entirety. And now, it seems, according to your argument, courage is not only the knowledge <note>original: "science" — here meaning a systematic body of knowledge or understanding</note> of things that are fearful and those that inspire confidence <note>original: "dreadful and daring"</note>, but essentially the knowledge of almost all goods and evils, and in short, of all things, in whatever manner they might exist. Is this what you have decided, or what do you say, Nicias?

**NICIAS.** It appears that way to me, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Does such a virtue as this seem to you, my dear friend <note>original: "O blessed man" — a polite, sometimes ironic, Socratic form of address</note>, to be lacking in any respect, if it knows all good things—and how they have been, are, and will be produced—and knows the same regarding evil things? And do you think that a person is lacking <note>original: "indigent of"</note> in moderation <note>original: "temperance"</note>, or justice, or piety, if they alone possess the caution required for things that are fearful and things that are not, regarding both gods and men? One who also knows how to obtain what is good, and how to interact in a proper manner with others?

**NICIAS.** You seem to me, Socrates, to be onto something.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, Nicias, what you have just proposed will not be a part of virtue, but the whole of virtue itself.

**NICIAS.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, we previously said that courage was only one of the parts of virtue.

**NICIAS.** We did say so.

**SOCRATES.** But what we have just said does not appear to describe a mere part of virtue.

**NICIAS.** It does not.

**SOCRATES.** We have not, therefore, Nicias, discovered what courage is.

**NICIAS.** It does not appear that we have.

**LACHES.** And yet, my dear Nicias, I really thought you would have discovered it, considering how much you looked down on me when I was answering Socrates. Because of that, I had great hope that you would have found the answer through the wisdom of Damon <note>Damon was a famous Athenian music theorist and a sophisticated intellectual advisor to Pericles; Nicias was known to consult him</note>.

**NICIAS.** How wonderful indeed, Laches, that you should think it a matter of no importance that you just now appeared to know nothing about courage. Instead, your only concern is that I also might appear to be as ignorant as yourself. It seems you are satisfied if I, as well as you, am ignorant of things that a man who wishes to be of any importance ought to understand. You therefore appear to me to be acting, in reality,
