...in a human way, because you are not looking at yourself at all but at others. I believe, however, that I have spoken reasonably well on this subject. Once I have reached a firm conviction about these matters, I will teach you without any ill-will <note>original: "envy" — here meaning a refusal to share knowledge or a begrudging attitude</note>; for you seem to me to be in great need of instruction.

**LACHES.** You are indeed wise, Nicias. However, I advise Lysimachus and Melesias here to say goodbye to you and me when it comes to the education of young people. But do not dismiss Socrates, as I said from the beginning; I would do the same if my own children were old enough.

**NICIAS.** I agree with you; if Socrates is willing to take the boys <note>original: "lads"</note> under his care, no one else should be sought. **LYSIMACHUS.** That is fair, Nicias, especially since I am willing to do many things for him that I would not be very willing to do for many others. What do you say then, Socrates? Will you agree to our request and take charge of these boys so they may become people of the finest character?

**SOCRATES.** It would certainly be a terrible <note>original: "dreadful"</note> thing, Lysimachus, to be unwilling to try to help them become as worthy as possible. If I had appeared knowledgeable <note>original: "skilful"</note> in our previous discussion while the others did not, it would be right to call on me specifically for this task. But since we are all equally stuck in doubt, which of us should be chosen over the others? To me, it seems that none of us should be preferred. Since this is the case, consider whether my advice seems right: I say, gentlemen—since this conversation is just among ourselves—that we should all together look for the best teacher, first for ourselves (for we need one), and then for these boys, sparing no expense or effort. I do not advise staying in the state we are in now. And

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

# THE LYSIS.

---

**W**HEN Socrates, says Ficino <note>original: "Ficinus," the Latinized name of Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Italian scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin.</note>, disputes with the sophists <term>Sophists: professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized by Socrates for prioritizing clever rhetoric and persuasion over the pursuit of absolute truth.</term> and their followers, he refutes false opinions and suggests, rather than directly teaches, those that are true. This is evident from the *Euthydemus*, *Protagoras*, *Meno*, *Hippias*, *Euthyphro*, and *Lysis*. But where he discourses with his disciples, and those who were anxious to be instructed, he explains and teaches, as is evident from many of the preceding dialogues. In this dialogue, therefore, in which he debates concerning friendship among the disciples of the sophists, he is more focused on refuting false opinions than on demonstrating those that are true.

But, so that we may take a brief <term>original: "cursory"</term> view of the contents of the *Lysis*: in the first place, Socrates rebukes those who misuse the power of love and, under the pretext of friendship, serve low desires <note>original: "base lust".</note>. In the second place, he warns those who, looking no higher than physical beauty, think themselves worthy to be loved for this alone. And, in the last place, he indicates to the wise <term>original: "sagacious"</term> a certain path by which friendship may be investigated and discovered. Again, while Socrates ironically mocks Hippothales and Ctesippus, he indicates that they were captivated by unworthy love. And, while in their presence he prepares youth for moral discipline, he advises lovers how they should live together, and what kind of attachment they should feel for each other. Having instructed lovers in the second part of the dialogue, he then instructs those who are the objects of love;

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<summary>This introduction by Marsilio Ficino explains that the "Lysis" is a dialogue focused on refuting false ideas about friendship. It outlines Socrates' goals: to critique superficial attraction based on physical beauty and to guide students toward a more virtuous understanding of love.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Marsilio Ficino, Lysis, friendship, sophists, moral discipline, Hippothales, Ctesippus, Platonic love</keywords>

--- Page 2779 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's "Lysis," specifically continuing the description of how Socrates instructs the youth in moral discipline and the nature of attachment.</meta>

<page-num>212</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE LYSIS.</header>

...and, by a long series of inductive reasoning, he teaches that friends should seek out wisdom and prudence. These qualities make up the true beauty of the soul, rather than the shadowy form of the temporary body. In the third place, he refutes several opinions, starting with that of Solon <note>Solon (c. 638–558 BC) was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet.</note>, who said that those who are loved are the "friends"; for these loved ones often hate those who love them. He adds that lovers alone are not the only ones called friends either, because they are frequently the objects of hatred by those they pursue. From this, he concludes that mutual goodwill should be the true definition of friendship.

Next, he critiques Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC) was a Greek philosopher who proposed that the universe was composed of four elements joined by "Love" and separated by "Strife."</note>, who believed that any kind of similarity is enough to create friendship. However, the similarity found in many professions shows this to be false, as shared interests more frequently generate envy and hatred than friendship. Lastly, the assertion of Hesiod and Heraclitus is brought forward: that opposites <term>original: "dissimilars"</term> are friendly to each other. That they are not, however, is clear from the fact that hatred and love—being opposites—will never be friendly, nor will a just man and an unjust man be friends. 

If it should be argued that a thing sometimes desires its opposite—such as the dry desiring moisture, or the hot desiring the cold—the answer is that in this case, the thing does not love its contrary for its own sake. Instead, it seeks to restore its own balance through that opposite. For something that is abnormally <term>original: "preternaturally"</term> hot is brought back to its proper balance <term>original: "temperament"</term> through cold. Thus, it does not love the cold, but through the cold it desires a state suited to its own nature.

Having refuted these assertions, Socrates—as if inspired <term>original: "prophesying"</term>—introduces an opinion of his own. He says that there appear to be three categories <note>original: "genera," a Latin term for types or classes.</note> of things: the good, the evil, and that which is neither good nor evil. Because of their fundamental difference, the evil cannot be a friend to the good; furthermore, because of their injustice, the evil are actually harmed by other evil people. Therefore, they cannot be mutual friends. It is likewise impossible for one who is neither good nor evil to love the evil, for evil is harmful <term>original: "noxious"</term> and is always accompanied by hatred. It remains, therefore, that friendship must exist between the good and the good, or between that which is "neither" and the good. 

But here, certain objections arise which Socrates introduces openly, though he hints at the solutions more subtly <term>original: "occultly"</term>. First, the good is similar to the good; but it was previously argued (in opposition to Empedocles) that similar people are not necessarily friends. It must be observed, however, that it was not claimed that similar people are never friendly, but rather it was denied that every kind...

<meta>catchword: kind</meta>

<summary>This page outlines Socrates' refutation of various ancient theories on friendship, including those of Solon, Empedocles, and Heraclitus, before proposing his own theory involving the categories of good, evil, and the neutral.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Lysis, friendship, Solon, Empedocles, Heraclitus, opposites attract, similarity, moral philosophy, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

--- Page 2780 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato’s "Lysis," concluding a refutation of various philosophical views on friendship before defining Plato's own distinction between friendship and love.</meta>

<page-num>213</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO THE LYSIS.</header>

...no kind of similarity <note>original: "similitude"</note> is sufficient to produce friendship. Again, when it is objected—in the second place—that the good man is self-sufficient and therefore does not desire another, is without love, and consequently is not the friend of the good, it must be observed that this absurdity does not follow from the doctrine of Plato. Instead, it arises from the assertions of Empedocles and Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus (c. 535–475 BC) was a Greek philosopher known for his belief that change is the fundamental essence of the universe.</note> when they are considered only superficially. In their views, the desire found in love is not clearly distinguished from friendship. Since desire is a state of lack—for it always moves toward something it does not possess—it follows from their doctrine that friendship is always accompanied by desire. To admit this, however, would be to confuse friendship with love. But, according to Plato, they are different because they are directed toward different goals: for friendship tends toward the good, and love tends toward the beautiful.

In short, friendship, when considered in relation to humanity, is a union among virtuous characters arising from a similarity of disposition and pursuits. Love is also a union between the lover and the beloved; but it differs from the union of friendship in this: the former is inseparable from a state of lack <term>original: "indigence"</term>, from which it also originates. On the other hand, friendship arises from a state of fullness <term>original: "plenitude"</term>, which it always possesses in proportion to the perfection it holds. In the friendships of the most virtuous men, this union is not entirely without desire and is consequently accompanied by some sense of want; but this is because the object of their friendship, in this case, is not the highest good. Therefore, friendship with divinity is the only union in which a perfect fullness is produced, desire dies, and lack is unknown.

The character of this dialogue, like that of the *Theaetetus*, is maieutic <term>maieutic: referring to the Socratic method of "intellectual midwifery," where Socrates helps others give birth to their own ideas through questioning</term>, and the concepts brought forth here—for which Socrates acts as the midwife—are ultimately unsuccessful <term>original: "abortive"</term> in reaching a final definition, just as they are in that other work.

<meta>catchword: THE</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the introductory analysis of the "Lysis," distinguishing Plato's view of friendship (based on fullness and the good) from love (based on lack and beauty), and noting the dialogue's inconclusive, "midwifery" style.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Lysis, friendship vs. love, self-sufficiency, Empedocles, Heraclitus, maieutic method, plenitude and indigence</keywords>

**While** I was walking from the Academy straight toward the Lyceum—which is actually outside the city walls, though very close to them—I arrived at the gate near the Panopis fountain. There I met Hippothales, the son of Hieronymus, and Ctesippus of Paeania, along with other young men who were gathered together with them. 

Hippothales, seeing me approaching, said, "O Socrates, where are you going, and where have you come from?"

"I have come from the Academy," I replied, "and I am heading straight to the Lyceum."

"Won't you come join us?" he asked. "It would be worth your while."

"Where do you want me to go," I replied, "and who among you am I to join?"

"Over here," he said, showing me a certain enclosure and an open gate opposite the wall. "Here we, and many other very worthy people, spend our time."

I then asked him, "What is this place, and what do you occupy yourselves with?"

"It is a Palaestra <term>A wrestling school or gymnasium where young men trained in athletics and gathered for conversation.</term>," he replied, "newly built; but we spend most of our time in discourse, which we would be happy to share with you."

"You do well," I said. "But who is the teacher in that place?"

"Your associate and admirer," he said, "Miccus."

"By Zeus!" <note>original: "By Jupiter"</note> I said, "he is no ordinary man, but a sufficiently great sophist <term>A professional teacher of philosophy, rhetoric, and virtue.</term>."

"Are you willing, then," he asked, "to follow me, so that you may see those who have gathered there?"

"But first of all, I would gladly hear..."

...for what purpose I am to enter, and who that beautiful person is.

"To some of us, Socrates," he said, "he does not appear to be beautiful."

"But what does he appear to you to be, O Hippothales? Tell me this."

And I said, "O Hippothales, son of Hieronymus, you no longer need to inform me whether you love or not; for I know that you not only love, but that you are far advanced in love. For, while I am worthless and useless in other matters, the divine has given me the ability to very quickly recognize a lover and the person they love."

And on hearing this, he blushed even more than before. 

Ctesippus therefore said, "You are being modest, Hippothales, because you blush and refuse to tell Socrates the name of your beloved. But you will do nothing but praise him if Socrates stays with you for even a short time. As for our ears, Socrates, they are completely filled and even made deaf by the name of Lysis. And when Hippothales has been drinking heavily, it is easy for us to imagine, even when we are woken from sleep, that we hear the name of Lysis. And the things which he relates concerning him in prose, though bad <note>original: "dire"</note>, are not the worst part, except when he overwhelms us with his poems and other writings. And what is still more dreadful is when he sings of his love with a wonderful voice, which we are forced to endure. But now that you ask him, he blushes."

"This youth then, it seems," I said, "is Lysis. But I only guess this; for I do not actually know him from hearing his name."

"They very seldom call him by his own name," he said, "but he is still called by his father’s name because his father is a man who is very well known. But I know well that you are far from being unacquainted with the appearance of the youth, for he may be sufficiently known from that alone."

I then said, "Tell me, whose son is he?"

"He is the son of Democrates," he said, "who is the eldest son of Axoneus."

"So be it then, Hippothales," I said, "now that you have found this noble and youthful love. But come, show <note>original: "evince"</note> to me the things which you have shown to these people, so that I may see whether you know what a lover ought to say regarding the objects of his love, either to himself or to others."

"Are you questioning anything he claims, Socrates?" he asked. "But do you deny that you love him, as he says?"

"I do not," he replied. "But I maintain that I do not compose anything, either in prose or verse, with a view to my love affairs <note>original: "amours"</note>."

"He is not well," said Ctesippus, "but is delirious and insane."

Upon this, I said, "O Hippothales, I am not requesting to hear any verses, nor any song, which you may..."

"Absolutely, by the gods," Ctesippus said. "But it is actually quite ridiculous that he is a lover—paying far more attention to the youth than anyone else—yet has nothing original to say. Wouldn't even a child see how silly this is? He just repeats what the whole city already says about Democrates <note>Lysis' father</note>, and Lysis the grandfather, and all his ancestors—their wealth, their stables of horses, and their victories in the Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean games <note>These were the three other major athletic festivals in Ancient Greece, alongside the Olympics</note>. And beyond these, he speaks of things even more common. He recently related to us, in a poem, a story about how Hercules was once a guest—namely, how an ancestor of Democrates and Lysis hosted Hercules because they were related, both being descendants of Jupiter <note>Original: Zeus</note> and the daughter of the local ruler. These are the kinds of stories that even old women sing about! He celebrates many other similar details, Socrates, and these are the things he forces us to listen to him reciting and singing."

Upon hearing this, I said, "Oh, foolish Hippothales! Before you have even won, you are writing and singing a victory song <note>Original: *encomium*, a speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly</note> for yourself."

"But I don't write or sing these things for myself, Socrates," he replied.

I answered, "You might not think so."

"What do you mean?" he asked.

"These poems," I said, "are really all about you. For if you win over such a beloved person, your words and songs will be an ornament to you—a tribute to yourself as a conqueror for having made such a fine catch. But if you fail in this regard, then the greater the praises you have heaped on your beloved, the more you will seem to have lost something truly beautiful and good, and you will look even more ridiculous. 

Therefore, my friend, anyone wise in the affairs of love will not praise his beloved until he has actually won him, because he is cautious about how it might turn out. Besides, you must realize that beautiful people are filled with pride and vanity when they are praised and glorified. Don't you think this is the case?"

He replied, "I do."

"Doesn't it follow, then, that the more [insolent they become...]"

"What kind of a hunter, therefore, would he seem to be to you, who would drive wild beasts out of their hiding places and increase the difficulty of catching them?"

Nor did he deserve to be noticed for his beauty alone, but because he was also worthy...

I turned to Lysis and said, "Lysis, what you have asserted appears to me to be true; I mean that if we have considered this rightly, we will not have wandered from the truth in any respect. But we will proceed no further in this way, for that line of reasoning seems to me to be as difficult as a rough road. Instead, I think it is necessary to proceed along the path we have just entered, examining the claims of the poets; for to us, they are like the fathers and leaders of wisdom. Regarding those who are friends, the poets say—and not badly—that divinity makes them friends by leading them to each other. I believe they put it this way:

->God always leads like to like,<-
->And makes them known to each other.<-
<note>original: "Likeness to likeness, God for ever leads, / And makes it known." This refers to a common Greek proverb found in Homer's *Odyssey*.</note>

Or have you not encountered these verses?" "I have," he said. "Have you also come across the writings of the wisest men, which say that 'the similar is always necessarily a friend to the similar'? These are the men who discourse and write about nature and the universe." <note>Socrates is referring to the Pre-Socratic natural philosophers, such as Empedocles, who argued that "like attracts like" in the physical world.</note>

He replied, "What you say is true."

"So, do they speak well or not?"

"Perhaps they do," he said.

I replied, "Perhaps half of this is true, and perhaps the whole thing is. But we do not fully understand them. It seems to us that the closer a wicked <note>original: "depraved"</note> man gets to another wicked man, and the more frequently they associate, the more hostile <note>original: "inimical"</note> they become; for the wicked man will act unjustly. It is impossible for those who commit and suffer injury to be friends. Is it not so?"

He replied, "It is."

"On this account, half of this saying cannot be true, since the wicked are similar to each other in their wickedness."

"True."

"But it appears to me that the poets mean that only the good are similar and are friends to each other. They suggest that the wicked—as is often said of them—are never similar, not even to themselves, but are erratic and unstable. Surely, a person who is inconsistent and at odds with himself can never be similar to another, nor can he become another's friend. Or does it not appear so to you?"

"It does," he said.

"Therefore, my friend, it seems to me that those who say 'the similar is a friend to the similar' are obscurely hinting at this: that only he who is good is a friend to the good, but he who is wicked can never arrive at true friendship, either with the good or..."

<summary>Socrates examines the poetic and philosophical idea that "like attracts like," concluding that since the wicked are unstable and harmful even to themselves, only the good can truly be "similar" and thus capable of friendship.</summary>

...the wicked. Does this also appear to you to be the case? — It does. — So, we have now found those who are friends; for our discussion suggests to us that those who are worthy are friends. — It certainly seems that way to me, he said. — And to me as well, I replied. But even so, there is something difficult about this matter. Come then, by Zeus <note>original: "Jupiter," the Roman equivalent of the Greek god Zeus</note>, and look at what I suspect to be the case. A person who is similar, insofar as he is similar, is a friend to another who is similar, and such a person is useful to the other. Or rather, let's look at it this way: Is any kind of "similar" person of any advantage to another "similar" person? Or can he do any injury to his like that he does not already do to himself? Or can he suffer anything from his like that he does not also suffer from himself? But how can things like these, which are not able to provide any assistance to each other, be loved by each other? — They cannot. — And how can someone who does not love be a friend? — In no way. — But perhaps the similar is not a friend to the similar; rather, the good is a friend to the good insofar as he is good, and not insofar as he is similar. — Perhaps so. — But consider this: isn't a person who is good, insofar as he is good, sufficient to himself? — Yes. — And someone who is self-sufficient does not lack <term>indigent</term> anything, because he possesses sufficiency. — Undoubtedly. — And he who lacks nothing will not love anything. — He will not. — But he who does not love will not be a friend. — Certainly not. — How, then, will the good be friends to the good? They neither desire each other when they are apart (for they are self-sufficient when alone), nor do they need each other when they are together. By what means could these people hold each other in high esteem? — By none, he said. — And those who do not hold each other in high esteem will not be friends. — True. — Consider then, Lysis, how we are being deceived. Are we mistaken about the whole thing? — But how? he asked. — I once heard someone claim—and I remember it very well now—that the similar was hostile to the similar, and the good to the good. And the person who argued this cited Hesiod <gloss>1</gloss> as a witness, who says, "The potter is hostile to the potter, the singer to the singer, and the beggar to the beggar." And it seemed to him that all other things necessarily exist in this same way; that those things most similar to each other were filled with the highest degree of envy, rivalry, and hatred, while those most dissimilar were joined in friendship. ...was of the opinion that the poor man was necessarily a friend to the rich, and the weak to the strong, for the sake of help. In the same way, the sick man was a friend to the physician; and everyone who was ignorant loved and was a friend to the person endowed with knowledge. He even added something still more impressive: that a person is so far from being a friend to someone similar to himself, that the exact opposite takes place. For that which is most contrary is especially a friend to its opposite. Everything desires a nature of this kind, rather than that which is similar. Thus, the dry desires the moist; the cold, the hot; the bitter, the sweet; the sharp <note>original: "acute"</note>, the dull <note>original: "obtuse"</note>; the empty <note>original: "void"</note>, the full; and the full, the empty. The same thing happens in all other cases. For opposites provide nourishment <note>original: "aliment"</note> to each other, but similar things do not benefit from each other in any respect. 

And indeed, my friend, the man who asserted these things appeared to be a refined <note>original: "elegant," meaning clever or sophisticated</note> man, for he spoke well. But how does he appear to us to have spoken?

"Shall we say, therefore, that the contrary is especially a friend to the contrary?"

"Entirely so."

"That may be so," I replied, "O Menexenus; but isn't this absurd <note>original: "prodigious," here meaning strange or monstrous in logic</note>? And won't those all-wise men who are skilled in contradiction <note>Socrates refers to the Eristics, philosophers who argued for the sake of winning rather than finding truth</note> gladly rise up against us immediately and ask: 'Is friendship not the exact opposite of hatred?' What shall we say in answer to them? Is it not necessary to acknowledge that their assertion is true?"

"It is necessary."

"Will they therefore say that an enemy is a friend to a friend, or that a friend is a friend to an enemy?"

He replied, "They will say neither of those things."

"But is the just person a friend to the unjust, or the temperate to the intemperate, or the good to the bad?"

"It does not appear to me that this is the case."

"But," I replied, "if anyone is a friend to another based on contrariety, it is necessary that these people should also be friends."

"It is necessary."

"It doesn't appear so."

Pay attention, lest we are deceived. For we shall abandon the assertion that a friend becomes the friend of a friend, and that like is a friend to like; for we have already said this is impossible. But at the same time, let us consider the following, lest what is now being asserted should deceive us. Do we not say that the medicinal art <note>original: "medicinal art"; referring to the practice or science of medicine</note> is a friend for the sake of health? — Yes. — And therefore that health is a friend? — Entirely so. — If then it is a friend, it is for the sake of something. — It is. — But it is the friend of something, based on what we have agreed to before. — Entirely so. — Will not that thing, in turn, be a friend for the sake of another friend? — Yes. — Is it not therefore necessary that by proceeding this way, we should reject what we have said and arrive at a certain principle, which is not referred to another friend, but brings us to that which is the **first friend** <note>In Greek, the *proton philon*, or the ultimate object of love/desire</note>, and for the sake of which we say all other things are friends? — It is necessary.

This then is what I am saying: we should be cautious lest we are deceived by all those other particulars which we claim to be friends for the sake of the first friend, and which are, as it were, certain images of it; while, in the mean time, this first friend is truly a friend. For we should consider: that which anyone greatly esteems (as, for instance, a father sometimes esteems his son), he honors before all other things. But a man of this kind, because he highly esteems his son, will also highly esteem something else on his son's account. Thus, for instance, if he perceives that his son has drunk hemlock <note>A highly poisonous plant used in ancient Greece for executions; Socrates implies here its use in a situation requiring an immediate antidote</note>, he will greatly value wine, because he thinks that this will save his son. Or will he not? — Undoubtedly, he replied. — Will he not therefore also highly value the vessel which contains the wine? — Entirely so. — But will he then esteem the earthen cup, or three cups of wine, as much as his son? Or is the case actually this: the whole of the effort in an affair of this kind does not regard those things which are procured for the sake of something else, but rather that for the sake of which all such things are procured. 

Nor is the assertion which we frequently make true—that we greatly value gold and silver; for in this case, that which we highly esteem is that for the sake of which gold and all other preparations are procured. Shall we not say so? — By all means. — The same thing, therefore, may be said regarding a friend. Therefore, being overcome by their persistence—and because it seemed to us that since they had been celebrating at the feast of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurial feast"; the Hermaea, a festival in honor of the god Hermes, who was the patron of athletes and gymnasiums.</note> they would be difficult to deal with—we ended the conversation. 

At the same time, after they had departed, I said to Lysis and Menexenus, "We have become ridiculous—I, an old man, and you two boys. For those who have just left us will say that we think of ourselves as friends (for I count myself as one of you), yet at the same time we have not yet been able to discover what a 'friend' actually is."

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

## THE CHARMIDES.

---

**T**wo things should be noted in the <note>original: "exordium"</note> opening of this Dialogue, which transfer love from physical to non-physical form. First, the assertion of Socrates that nearly all young men appear beautiful to him. This is as if he had said that he did not stop at the beauty of a single body, but ascended to the common beauty of the entire species. 

Just as we ascend from the beauty of an individual to that which is common to the species, and from this to that beauty which is <note>original: "uncoordinated with the many"</note> independent of the multitude and is a non-physical form existing by itself; so, by what is said here, we are advised to pass from the love of an individual form to the love of that which is common, and from this to the love of the ideal form, which resides in the intellect as its natural home. 

The second thing deserving of notice is that Socrates orders the soul of Charmides to be exposed to view. By neglecting the form of the body, we should instead look upon the natural beauty of the soul and diligently strive to obtain beauty for the soul if it is found to be lacking. It is for good reason that this encouragement toward <term>temperance</term> <note>The Greek term "sophrosyne," often translated as temperance, self-control, or moderation.</note> begins with the beauty of the body. Physical beauty is nothing more than a harmony and agreement of the physical parts, which corresponds to temperance within the soul.

Plato, in the *Cratylus*, explains the name of temperance as signifying a certain safety and preservation of <term>prudence</term> <note>The original term is "phronesis," often translated as practical wisdom or mindfulness.</note>. He considered all truth to be naturally inherent in the soul; consequently, by looking deeply into herself, the soul will discover every truth. However, she is hindered from this turning back toward herself by an immoderate love of the body and physical natures. Therefore, temperance is necessary in the first place. By temperance, the darkness of <note>original: "perturbations"</note> emotional disturbances is expelled, the intellect becomes more serene, and it is abundantly lit up with the brilliance of divinity.

<vocab>Charmides, Socrates, Plato, Cratylus, temperance, incorporeal form, ideal form, intellect, prudence, divinity, exordium</vocab>

<summary>This introduction explains that the dialogue uses physical beauty as a stepping stone to understanding the beauty of the soul and the virtue of temperance. It argues that temperance is necessary to clear the mind of physical distractions so the soul can recognize the truth within itself.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Plato, Charmides, temperance, sophrosyne, physical beauty, ideal form, intellect, Cratylus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's dialogue "The Charmides," focusing on the philosophical definition of temperance and its relationship to the soul, body, and other virtues.</meta>

<page-num>240</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

But as Socrates intends to discuss temperance, he advises Charmides to look into himself. For the work of this virtue is to turn the soul toward itself. It is stated in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's later dialogues concerning the nature of the physical world and the human soul.</note> that all our affairs succeed when the soul is in harmony with itself and in agreement with the body. The Pythagoreans also claim that if the soul wisely governs not only its own motions but also those of the body, the result will be a long life for the body and perpetual health for both. To this, Socrates adds something even more remarkable: that the <term>Magi</term> <note>Ancient Persian priests and practitioners of wisdom.</note> promise immortality to bodies through their verses. We also learn from Plato, in the *First Alcibiades*, that the magic of Zoroaster was nothing other than the worship of divinity. Socrates observes, however, that the soul and body are protected from death not only by magical verses but also by philosophical reasoning and temperance. Furthermore, because a speech intended to persuade listeners toward temperance requires power granted by the divine and logic produced by philosophy, Plato calls such a discussion a "magical incantation."

Next, Socrates often asks what temperance is, yet neither Charmides nor Critias provides an accurate definition. One suggests something that is not properly temperance but rather its byproduct, while the other suggests something that belongs more to prudence. Consequently, Critias defines temperance as a specific <term>science</term> <note>original: "science"; in this context, it refers to a branch of knowledge or "episteme."</note> that knows both itself and all other sciences, but remains ignorant of the actual objects of those sciences. However, this is false because the truth of any knowledge consists in a specific agreement and connection between the knower and the thing being known. Additionally, knowledge cannot be fully understood unless it is clear what knowledge itself is; and this cannot be achieved without a knowledge of its object. 

But as Critias shifts the discussion from temperance to prudence, Socrates asserts that prudence—or the knowledge of good and evil—holds the highest authority regarding <term>beatitude</term> <note>The state of supreme happiness or the highest human good.</note>. This is because it demonstrates the most excellent goal and the means that lead to it, and because all arts and pursuits benefit us when governed by it, but lead to our harm when it is neglected. Finally, Socrates teaches us that nothing is more difficult to define or to acquire than temperance. It is extremely difficult to define because it is so closely combined with the other virtues, serving as their harmony <note>original: "consonance."</note>; and it cannot be obtained without

<meta>catchword: without</meta>

...without great difficulty, because from the moment our souls are united with our bodies, we are prone to intemperance, and from our infancy, we drink deeply from the poisoned cup of pleasure.

For the benefit of the student of Plato, as this dialogue is <term>pirastic</term> <note>original: "pirastic"; from the Greek "peirastikos," meaning a style of questioning used to test, probe, or try a person's knowledge.</note>, I shall conclude this Introduction with the following admirable observations from Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who sought to synthesize Greek philosophy with spiritual practice.</note>, in which the nature of temperance is beautifully explained:

> “Every virtue looks down upon that which is mortal and embraces that which is immortal; but this is the goal of temperance in a very remarkable degree. It despises those pleasures which fasten the soul to the body as if by a nail and establishes itself, as Plato says, on holy foundations. For how is it possible that temperance should not make us perfect, since it removes from us everything that is imperfect and driven by passive emotions? You may know that this is the case by attending to the fable of Bellerophon <note>A hero of Greek mythology best known for slaying the Chimera.</note>, who, fighting in alliance with moderation, destroyed the Chimera and every beastly, wild, and savage tribe. For, in short, the uncontrolled rule of the passions does not allow men to be truly human, but drags them down to that which is irrational, beastly, and disordered. But that excellent order, which keeps pleasures within definite limits, preserves families and preserves cities, according to the assertion of Crates. Furthermore, in a certain respect, it approaches the form of the gods. Perseus, therefore, journeying to the highest good of temperance with Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> as his leader, cut off the head of the Gorgon. This appears to me to represent desire pulling men down toward material matter and turning them into stone through a fullness of dull and foolish passions. Self-restraint regarding pleasure, therefore, as Socrates says, is the foundation of virtue; and temperance appears to be the crowning jewel of all the virtues, as Plato also asserts. And, as I say, this virtue is the fortification of our most beautiful habits. Hence, I shall confidently and strongly assert, as a thing truly acknowledged, that the beauty of temperance extends through all the virtues, that it brings them together in a single harmony, and that it provides them with symmetry and a proper balance with one another. Such then being the nature of temperance, it creates an opportunity for the planting of the other virtues, and when they are planted, it grants them a stable security.”

**Y**esterday, when I returned in the evening from the army, I gladly went back to my usual activities, as I had been away from them for some time. I entered the <term>Palaestra</term> <note>original: "Palæstra"; a Greek wrestling school or gymnasium where men gathered for physical training and conversation.</note> of Taurean Neptune, which is opposite the royal temple <note>Likely the *Stoa Basileios* or Royal Colonnade in Athens.</note>. Here I met many people, some of whom were unknown to me, but most of whom I knew. As soon as I was seen entering so unexpectedly, people from all sides immediately congratulated me from a distance. 

But Chaerephon, as if he were out of his mind, leaped from the middle of the crowd and ran toward me. Taking me by the hand, he said, "O Socrates, how did you survive the battle?" For a short time before we left, there was a battle at <term>Potidaea</term> <note>A city in northern Greece; the Battle of Potidaea (432 BC) was one of the catalysts for the Peloponnesian War.</note>, which those present had only just heard about. I answered them, saying, "It is as you see." 

"Indeed," he said, "a report was spread here that a very fierce battle had taken place, and that many of those we know had died in it." 

I replied, "You were told the truth." 

"But," he asked, "were you in the thick of the battle?" 

"I was," I said. 

"Sit down here," he said, "and tell us about it; for we have not yet heard the whole story clearly." 

At the same time, he led me along and sat me down near Critias, the son of Callaeschrus <note>Critias was a wealthy Athenian who later became the leader of the "Thirty Tyrants."</note>. Once seated, I greeted Critias and the others, and related the affairs of the army as they asked me. Some asked one thing, and others another. When we had discussed those matters enough, I asked them in turn about the state of philosophy—how it was faring at

...at present; and whether there were any young men who were remarkable for wisdom, or beauty, or both. 

Critias then, looking towards the gate and perceiving certain young men entering and teasing each other, with another crowd following behind them, said, "It appears to me, Socrates, that you will immediately have an answer to your question regarding beautiful youths. For those who are now entering are the forerunners and admirers of one who seems to be the most beautiful of all at the present time. And it appears to me that he is just now entering." 

"But who is he?" I replied; "and whose son is he?"

"Perhaps you know him," he said, "(though he was very young when you left this place); I mean, perhaps you know Charmides, the son of our uncle Glaucon <note>original: "Glauco"</note>, and my cousin."

"I certainly know him, by Zeus <note>original: "by Jupiter"</note>," I replied, "for he was not to be overlooked even then, though he was only a boy; but now I imagine he must be almost a young man."

"You will immediately know," he said, "both his age and the qualities he has acquired." And at the same time he was speaking, Charmides entered. 

Therefore, my friend, you should not pay any attention to my opinion. For I am truly a white rule <note>original: "white rule"; the Greek Scholiast on Plato notes that this expression refers to someone whose judgment is indistinct or neutral. Just as a white carpenter's rule leaves no visible mark on white stone, Socrates claims his judgment of beauty is useless because he finds almost everyone beautiful.</note> with respect to those who are beautiful, since nearly all young men appear beautiful to me. But even to me, he then appeared wonderful, both because of his stature and the beauty of his body. All the rest seemed to be in love with him; they were so astonished and disturbed when he entered. Many other lovers also followed among those behind him. 

Regarding the men, this was less surprising; but I also paid attention to the boys and saw that none of them looked at anyone else but him—not even the smallest among them—but the eyes of all were fixed on him as if he were a statue. 

And Chaerephon <note>original: "Chærepho"</note> calling to me, said, "What do you think of the youth, Socrates? Is he not a beautiful person?"

I replied, "Beyond measure."

"But," he said, "if he were willing to strip for exercise, he would seem to you to have a plain face, because his body is so very beautiful." 

And this claim by Chaerephon was confirmed by all the rest. I then said, "By Heracles <note>original: "By Hercules"</note>, you speak of an unconquerable man, if only one small thing further belongs to him..."

"What is that?" said Critias. 

I replied, "If his soul is naturally in a good condition. It is, however, appropriate, Critias, that it should be so, as he is a member of your family."

"But," he replied, "he is also very beautiful and good in this respect."

"Why then," I said, "do we not expose *this* <note>Socrates is referring to Charmides' soul.</note> naked to our view and contemplate it before his physical form? For since he is so inwardly beautiful, he will surely be willing to converse."

"Very much so," said Critias, "since he is a philosopher and—as it appears both to others and himself—very poetic."

I replied, "This beauty, friend Critias, comes down to you from your distant ancestor, Solon <note>Solon (c. 630–560 BCE) was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet; he was a relative of both Critias and Plato.</note>. But why do you not call the youth over and introduce him to me? For it would not disgrace us to talk with him, even if he were younger than he is, while you are present as his cousin and guardian."

"You are right," he said, "and we will call him." At the same time, he turned to the person following him and said, "Call Charmides, and tell him that I wish to put him under the care of a physician because of the illness <note>original: "infirmity"</note> he has lately complained about."

Critias then said to me, "Charmides has recently complained of a heaviness in his head when he gets up in the morning. What is to stop you from pretending to him that you know a remedy for this headache?"

"Nothing," I replied, "just let him come."

"But he is coming," he said. 

Which was indeed the case, and it caused much laughter. For each of us who were sitting together was so eager to sit near Charmides that we pushed our neighbors aside; eventually, we forced some of those sitting at the ends to stand up, while others fell off their seats onto the ground. He came and sat between me and Critias. I then said to myself, "My friend, I am now confused, and the confidence I had earlier—that I could easily talk with Charmides—has failed me." 

When Critias told him that I was the person who knew a remedy for his disease, he stared at me as if I were someone extraordinary <note>original: "prodigious"</note> and drew near as if he intended to ask me a question. Then everyone in the Palaestra <note>original: "Palæstra"; a public place for wrestling and exercise, serving as a social hub for Athenian men.</note> immediately gathered around us. When, O noble man, I saw the beauty of his form through his garments, I was set on fire by the sight and was no longer myself. I also thought that Critias was very wise in matters of love <note>original: "amatory affairs"</note> when he said, speaking of a beautiful boy but using a metaphor, that I should be careful: for if a fawn comes opposite to a lion, a piece of its flesh will be taken...

...taken away; for he seemed to me like someone captured by such an animal. At the same time, when Charmides asked if I knew a remedy for his headache, I hardly knew how to answer. 

"What is it?" he asked. 

I replied that it was a particular leaf, but that a certain incantation <note>An incantation is a series of words said as a magic spell or charm.</note> must be used with the medicine. If someone used the incantation along with the leaf, the medicine would restore them to perfect health; but the leaf alone would be of no use without the incantation.

He then said, "I will write down this incantation from you."

I replied, "Will you do this whether I persuade you to or not?"

Laughing, he said, "I will, if I am persuaded by you, Socrates."

"So be it," I replied. "And do you actually know my name?"

"I do, unless I am mistaken," he said. "For there is plenty of talk about you among people my age, and I remember you associating with Critias when I was a boy."

"Good," I replied. "I will now tell you more freely what the incantation is. Just a moment ago, I was unsure how to explain its power to you. For this incantation, Charmides, is such that it cannot make the head well on its own. It is perhaps like what you have often heard good physicians say when someone comes to them with diseased eyes. They say that they must not try to cure the eyes alone, but that it is necessary to cure the head at the same time <note>original: "Viz. Not only the head, but the whole body must be cured, when the eyes are diseased from an internal cause."</note> if they intend to bring the eyes into a good condition. 

And furthermore, they say it would be very foolish to think of curing the head without treating the whole body. Because of this reasoning, they turn their attention to the health of the entire body and try to cure the part along with the whole. Have you heard them say this, and is it not the case?"

"Entirely so," he replied.

"Does it therefore seem to you that they are right, and do you accept this doctrine?"

"Most certainly," he said.

When I heard him praise this method of treatment, I took courage, and my confidence was revived. I said, "Such, then, Charmides, is the power of this incantation. He also said, “The Greek physicians correctly claim the same things as I now claim. But Zamolxis,” he said, “our king, who is a god, says that just as it is not proper to attempt to cure the eyes without the head, nor the head without the body, so it is also not proper to cure the body without the soul. He says the reason why many diseases are unknown to the Greek physicians is because they are ignorant of the whole, to which attention ought to be paid. For when the whole is not in good health, it is impossible for a part to be healthy. For everything,” he said, “originates from the soul—both the good and the evil—and flows from there into the body and the whole man, just as fluids flow from the head to the eyes. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul's ailments should be healed first and most importantly, so that the head and the whole body may be healthy.” 

But he said, O blessed youth, “that the soul was cured of its ailments by certain incantations; and that these incantations were beautiful words <note>original: "beautiful reasons." In this context, Socrates refers to rational philosophical discourse that brings order to the mind.</note>, from which temperance <note>original: "temperance" (Sophrosyne). This is a central Greek virtue meaning self-control, moderation, and a healthy, balanced mind.</note> was generated in souls.” He further added, “that once this was present and established, it was easy to provide health both to the head and the rest of the body.” 

Having therefore taught me the medicine and the incantations, he said, “Let no one persuade you to cure their head with this medicine if they have not first presented their soul to be cured by you with the incantation. For the mistake of the present time regarding men,” he said, “is that certain people try to be physicians without a knowledge of temperance and health.” And he very earnestly ordered me to take care that no rich, noble, or beautiful person ever persuaded me to do otherwise. I therefore swore to him that I would not, and so I must obey him, which I am determined to do. 

And indeed, if you are willing, according to the foreigner's command, to present your soul first of all to be charmed by the incantations of the Thracian, I will apply the medicine to your head; but if not, I cannot help you in any respect, my friend Charmides.

Critias, hearing me speak this way, said, “This headache, Socrates, will be a benefit to the youth, if he is compelled to improve his <term>dianoëtic</term> <note>Dianoëtic refers to the part of the soul or mind responsible for discursive reasoning and logical thought.</note> part through his head. I can indeed assure you that Charmides not only excels beyond all his peers in the form of his body...”

But you say this is temperance. Or do you not?—Entirely so, I replied.—Know then, said he, that Charmides appears to be by far the most temperate of those who exist at present; and that, as far as his age permits, he is not inferior to anyone in everything else.—And I replied, It is only right, O Charmides, that you should excel all others in all such things. And again, there is the same renown on his mother's side: for no one of those who dwell on the continent <note>referring to Asia Minor</note> is said to surpass your uncle Pyrilampes in beauty and grandeur, as often as he goes as an ambassador to the Great King <note>The King of Persia.</note>, or to some other inhabitant of the continent. Indeed, his whole family is in no way inferior to any other. It is likely, therefore, that being the offspring of such people, you should be the first in all things. 

Hence, O beloved son of Glaucon, with respect to your visible form, you appear to me to disgrace none of your ancestors. And if you are naturally endowed with all that is sufficient for the possession of temperance <note>original: "Sophrosyne," meaning moderation, self-control, and a healthy mind.</note> and the other virtues, according to the assertion of Critias here, then your mother, O dear Charmides, brought you forth blessed. The case, then, is this: if temperance is present within you, as Critias says it is, and if you are sufficiently temperate, you will no longer require the incantations of either Zamolxis or the Hyperborean Abaris¹, but the medicine for the head should be administered to you immediately. But if you are in any way lacking <note>original: "indigent of."</note> in this, the incantation must precede the medicine. Inform me, therefore, whether you agree with Critias and affirm that you sufficiently participate in temperance, or whether you are deficient in this respect.

He answered me with dignity. He said, "It is not easy either to admit or reject the topics of our current investigation. For," said he, "if I were to claim that I am not temperate, it would be absurd to say such a thing about myself; at the same time, I would be proving that Critias and many others—who believe I am temperate—have spoken falsely. On the other hand, if I were to claim that I *am* temperate, I would be praising myself, which might cause offense. Therefore, I do not know how to answer you."

To this I replied, "You seem to me to speak well, Charmides. I think we should consider together whether or not you possess the quality I am inquiring about. That way, you won't be forced to speak against your will, and I won't carelessly return to discussing the medical art <note>original: "medicinal art." Socrates is referring to the physical cure for a headache he mentioned earlier, contrasting it with the "incantation" of philosophy.</note>. If you agree, I would like to examine this matter with you; but if you don't, we can drop it."

"It is the most agreeable thing in the world to me," he said. "Please continue the inquiry in whatever way seems best to you."

"This seems to me the best way to consider the subject," I replied. "It is clear that if temperance <note>original: *sophrosyne*, a complex Greek term meaning temperance, moderation, or self-control.</note> is present within you, you must have some opinion about it. If it is truly a part of you, it must produce some awareness of itself, from which you would form an opinion of what it is and what qualities it possesses. Don't you think so?"

He replied, "I do think so."

"And don't you also think," I said, "that since you know how to speak Greek, you can also tell me what you think temperance is?"

"Perhaps so," he said.

"So that we may guess whether it is within you or not, tell me: what is temperance, in your opinion?"

At first, he hesitated and was not entirely willing to answer. But eventually, he said that temperance seemed to consist of doing everything in an orderly manner—walking and talking quietly in public, and acting similarly in everything else. "In short," he said, "the thing you are asking about seems to me to be a certain quietness." <note>original: *Hesychia* (quietness) signifies, in this context, a steady and leisurely way of doing things.</note>

I replied, "You speak well. People do say, Charmides, that quiet people are temperate. But let's see if there is any truth to that. Tell me, isn't temperance something beautiful?"

He replied, "Absolutely."

In the art of grammar, is it most beautiful <note>original: "beautiful." The Greek word *kalon* implies both aesthetic beauty and moral nobility or excellence.</note> to write similar letters swiftly or slowly?

—Swiftly.

—But what with respect to reading? Is it most beautiful to read swiftly or slowly?

—Swiftly.

—And is it also by far more beautiful to play on the harp rapidly, and to wrestle with speed, than quietly and slowly?

—Yes.

—And does not the like take place in boxing <note>original: "pugilistic"</note> and pancratiastic <note>original: "pancratiatic"; refers to the pancratium, an ancient Greek sport combining wrestling and boxing</note> contests?

—Entirely so.

—And with respect to running and leaping, and all other works of the body, are they not beautiful when performed with vigor and rapidity; but when performed slowly, with difficulty, and quietly, are they not shameful <note>original: "base"</note>?

—It appears so.

—It appears to us, therefore, I replied, that with respect to the body, not the quiet, but the most rapid and the most vigorous actions are the most beautiful. Is it not so?

—Entirely so.

—But did we not say that temperance is something beautiful?

—Yes.

—Not quietness, therefore, but speed will be more in keeping with temperance with respect to the body, since temperance is beautiful.

—It seems so, said he.

—What then, I replied, is a readiness to learn <note>original: "docility"</note> more beautiful than being slow to learn <note>original: "dulness"</note>?

—It is.

—But readiness to learn, I said, is to learn swiftly; and slowness to learn is to learn quietly and slowly.

—It is.

—And is it not more beautiful to teach another swiftly and energetically <note>original: "vehemently"</note>, than quietly and slowly?

—Yes.

—And which is the more beautiful: to recollect and commit things to memory quietly and slowly, or energetically and rapidly?

—He replied, energetically and rapidly.

—And with respect to sagacity <note>original: "sagacity"; here meaning quick-wittedness or practical wisdom</note>, is it not a certain sharp energy, and not a quietness of the soul?

—True.

—Does it not therefore follow, that it is most beautiful in the art of grammar, in the art of playing on the harp, and in everything else, to understand what is said in the most rapid, and not in the most quiet manner?

—Yes.

—And again, in the investigations and deliberations of the soul, it does not appear to me that he who deliberates and discovers in the most quiet manner, and with difficulty, is worthy of praise, but rather he who does this easily and rapidly.

—To this also he assented.

—Hence, I replied, in all things, both pertaining to the soul and the body, such as are performed with speed <note>original: "celerity"</note> and vigor appear to be more beautiful than such as are performed slowly and quietly.

—It appears so, said he.

Neither would it follow from this that temperance consists of acting quietly rather than with vigorous and rapid energy—whether in walking, reading, or anything else. He replied, "It does not seem to me that such a city is well-governed."

"But," I said, "if a city is temperate, it is well-governed."

"Undoubtedly," he replied.

"Therefore, for a man to do only such things for himself, and to 'manage his own affairs' in that literal way, will not be temperance."

"It doesn't seem that it would be."

"The person, therefore, who said that temperance is a man 'doing things pertaining to himself' was speaking obscurely, as I just mentioned. For he was not so foolish as to mean that his words should be taken literally. Or did you hear some foolish person assert this, Charmides?"

"Not at all," he said, "since he seemed very wise to me."

"Then it seems to me that he proposed this as a riddle, because it is difficult to know what it really means for a person to 'handle his own business'."

"Perhaps so," he said.

"Can you, then, tell me what it means to 'handle one's own business'?"

He replied, "By Zeus, I do not know. But perhaps it is possible that even the person who said it did not know what he meant."

I am fearful that, while I think I know something when I actually do not, I might be unaware of my own ignorance. And now I say that I am doing this—that is, examining the argument—principally for my own sake, but perhaps also for the sake of my other friends. — "Very much so, Socrates," he replied.

— "Be bold, therefore," I said, "my friend <note>original: "O blessed man"</note>, and give your opinion in answer to the question. Do not worry whether it is Critias or Socrates who is being refuted. Instead, pay attention to the argument itself, considering what the result will be when either of us is proven wrong."

— "I shall do so," he replied; "for you seem to speak well."

— "Tell me then," I said, "what you say regarding temperance."

— "I say then," he replied, "that this alone, of all other sciences, is both the science of itself and of other sciences."

— "Will it therefore," I said, "be the science of ignorance <note>original: "science of ignorance"</note>, since it is the science of knowledge?"

— "Entirely so."

—"Therefore, if there is anything that is the double of other doubles and of itself, it would be the double of itself only by being half of itself. For nothing can be a 'double' except by being the double of a 'half.'"

We would likewise possess all our vessels and instruments, along with our garments, shoes, and all the conveniences and necessities of life, more skillfully <note>original: "artificially"</note> constructed than they are now, because we would employ true craftsmen. For with temperance as our guard, it will not allow ignorance to interfere or cooperate with us. But that we shall act well and be happy as a result of acting scientifically—this, friend Critias, I am not yet able to understand."
—"But indeed," he replied, "you will not easily find any other goal for acting well, if you despise acting scientifically."

> ¹ Socrates here refers to Homer's well-known description of the two gates of dreams, of which the following explanation is given by Porphyry, as preserved by Macrobius in *The Dream of Scipio* <note>original: "Somn. Scip."</note>, chapter 3. "All truth," he says, "is hidden <note>original: "latent"</note>; but the soul sometimes sees it when she is a little liberated by sleep from the duties of the body. And sometimes she extends her sight, but never perfectly reaches the object of her vision. Hence when she sees, she does not see it with a free and direct light, but through an intervening veil, which the layers of darkening nature draw over her eye. This veil, when in sleep it allows the sight to extend as far as the truth, is said to be of horn, whose nature is such, from its thinness <note>original: "tenuity"</note>, that it is transparent to the sight. But when it dulls the sight and repels it from the vision of truth, it is said to be of ivory, which is a body so naturally dense that, however thin it may be scraped, it cannot be penetrated by the visual rays."

"Of this one," said he, "and another."
"What other?" I replied. "Do you speak of the man who, besides knowing future events, knows everything past and present, and is not ignorant of anything? For let us admit that there is such a man; for I think you will not say that anyone lives more scientifically than this man."
"Certainly not."
"But this also should be added: Which of the sciences makes him happy? Or do all the sciences similarly produce this effect?"
"By no means," said he.
"But which most eminently accomplishes this? Is it that by which a man knows things past, present, and to come? And will it therefore be the <term>science of chess</term> <note>original: "chefs"; likely referring to the Greek game of *petteia*, similar to draughts or chess</note>?"
"But why of chess?" he replied.
"Will it then be the <term>logiſtic ſcience</term> <note>the art of calculation or mathematical logic</note>?"
"By no means."
"Shall we say it is the science by which health is procured?"
"Rather so," said he.
"But is it," I replied, "especially that science by which we know some particular thing?"
"It is that," said he, "by which we know good and evil."
"O you rascal <note>original: "vile man"; Socrates uses this ironically as Critias finally hits the point</note>," I replied, "some time since you led me round in a circle, concealing from me that to act well and be happy did not consist in living scientifically, and were not produced by the possession of all the other sciences, but are effected by one science alone, which enables us to know good and evil. And if, O Critias, you were willing to take away this science from the other sciences, would the medicinal science no less produce health, that of the leather-worker shoes, and that of the weaver garments? And would the pilot's art no less prevent us from perishing in the sea, and the military science from being killed in battle?"
"No less," said he.
"But, friend Critias, this science, by which we know good and evil, being taken away, each of these other sciences will no longer operate beneficially."
"True."
"But this science, as it seems, is not temperance <note>original: "sophrosyne"</note>, but that science whose employment is to benefit us: for it is not..."

"Don't you see, then, Critias, that I was right to be afraid earlier, and that I was right to blame myself because I saw nothing useful regarding temperance? In the context of this dialogue, the "incantation" or "charm" is a metaphor for the philosophical conversation itself, which Socrates claims can heal the soul.</note> which I learned from a Thracian, if it is a thing of no worth and I have spent so much labor in learning it to no purpose.

I also believe, as far as I am concerned, that nothing hinders me from being daily enchanted by you, for as long as you think it necessary."

"So be it," said Critias. "But, Charmides, if you act in this manner, it will be proof to me that you are temperate, because you will present yourself to Socrates to be enchanted and will not desert him for any reason, whether great or small."

"I shall follow him," he said, "and not desert him. For I would be acting in a terrible manner if I did not listen to you, who are my guardian <note>original: "tutor"</note>."

# INTRODUCTION

->TO<-

## THE LESSER HIPPIAS.

---

**In** this dialogue, Hippias the sophist <note>original: "sophist" (a professional teacher and rhetorician in ancient Greece, often depicted as a foil to Socrates)</note> plays the more prominent of the two secondary roles; for this reason, the dialogue takes its name from him $^1$. Its brevity, compared to the other dialogue between Socrates and the same sophist <note>This refers to the *Greater Hippias*, which is longer and focuses on the nature of beauty.</note>, has led to it being called *The Lesser Hippias*.

The title prefixed to it in all editions of Plato—*Concerning Lying <note>original: "περι ψευδους" (peri pseudous)</note>*, or untruth—is clearly inadequate because it only describes part of the subject matter. This is true unless the word "lying" is understood in the sense used by a recent writer $^2$, who relates it to every aspect of human behavior. However, since this is not the standard meaning of the word, we have ventured to change the title. We have provided one that we believe covers the entire subject and, using as few words as clarity requires, shows its true nature. For in this dialogue, a point is argued which has been long—

---

$^1$ See the latter part of the Prologue. — **S.** <note>The initial "S." likely refers to the translator Floyer Sydenham (1710–1787), who translated several of Plato's dialogues.</note>

$^2$ Mr. Wollaston in his *Religion of Nature Delineated* <note>William Wollaston (1659–1724) was an influential English philosopher who argued that morality is based on the "truth" of things.</note>: in that work, this very clever and learned man suggests that error, or straying from what is right in moral actions, consists of "acting a lie." That is, acting as if the nature of the person or thing involved in our action were different from what it actually is. In plain English, and in agreement with the language of the Platonists, this is the same as acting with inconsistency and impropriety; or, as the Stoics <note>An ancient Greek school of philosophy that taught that virtue is based on knowledge and living in harmony with divine Reason.</note> prefer to say, acting contrary to nature—both our own nature and the nature of other things. — **S.**

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Plato's dialogue *The Lesser Hippias*, specifically completing the sentence from the previous page regarding the "long-debated" controversy over the nature of human error.</meta>

<page-num>272</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION TO</header>

the subject of much controversy: “whether error in the will depends on error in judgment.” Socrates takes the affirmative side of the question. His goal in doing so is to prove the necessity of informing the understanding in moral truths—that is, of acquiring moral science—along with the necessity of maintaining the "governing part" within us in full power over our inferior parts—that is, of acquiring habits of virtue. The philosopher suggests that through a lack of this knowledge, and of this power or virtue, man is either led blindly or driven inevitably into evil. This design is executed in three parts.

The first part concerns words. In this section, it appears through inductive reasoning <note>original: "inductional reasoning"</note> that all untruth is caused either by some ignorance in the mind (that is, a lack of knowledge in those things which are the subjects of our affirmations or denials) or by some passion of the soul—the desire for glory, for instance. These factors prompt us to speak untruths or lies, either deliberately and by design, like Hippias, or inadvertently and rashly, like Achilles.

The second part concerns actions. It proceeds with the same way of reasoning by induction to prove that all error in acting arises from either ignorance or weakness. We see that in every purely physical action, and also in the energies or works of every art, when blamable faults are committed, the cause is either a lack of skill to design well or a lack of ability to execute.

In the final part—which is by far the shortest, but for which the other two are intended merely to prepare us, according to Plato's usual manner—the reasoning is analytical. It proves that in dishonest or bad men, the understanding is either unenlightened by science, or overpowered and blinded by passion, or else suffers in both ways. Therefore, along with the ignorance or powerlessness of mind under which they labor, they labor at the same time under a necessity of doing ill. They can be freed from this necessity only by inward light and strength—that is, by knowledge and virtue. Here we find the <term>wise man who is master of himself</term> <note>original: "Sapiens sibique Imperiosus"</note> described by Horace in a beautiful passage of his seventh Satire, the second book. We have paraphrased the portion that relates immediately to our purpose here:

> Your master does, himself, some master serve;
> Some impulse sets in action every nerve.
> Think not the puppet in his own command;
> His strings are guided by another’s hand.

->Who then is free?—who not by passion fooled,<-
->In every motion is by reason ruled.<-
->To all but reason he, superior, still<-
->Moves but as bids him his own better will.<-

Consistent with this is the doctrine of the Stoics, derived immediately, it seems, from this dialogue of Plato: "that only the wise man is free." The fifth Satire of Persius <note>Persius (34–62 AD) was a Roman poet whose Satires often explored Stoic philosophy.</note> serves as a lively commentary on this maxim. However, because this is a philosophical paradox, Plato employs great skill in introducing a truth into the mind that our own consciousness seems to contradict. For who is there—not under outward restraint and only influenced by internal motives—who does not think himself free? 

Our subtle philosopher therefore argues based on the supposition that bad men possess freedom of the will. By arguing this way, he proves an absurdity: "that those who do evil intentionally are better men than those who do evil without intending it." The consequence of this is that the argument proceeded from a false premise. It demonstrates that no one does evil with a clear-sighted and distinct view, and that in bad men, the will is not truly free. This much seems necessary for uncovering the hidden style, design, and method of this dialogue. A more explicit and—

***

¹ Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> also, the most ancient Platonist of any whose writings still remain, proves that only the mind or intellect is truly free. He argues that, therefore, liberty of the will in man—or his having actions in his own power, <term>self-governance</term> <note>original Greek: το αυτεξούσιον</note>—resides only in a soul whose inward operations follow the leading of the intellect or mind, <term>in a soul acting according to the mind</term> <note>original Greek: εν ψυχη κατα νουν ενεργουση</note>. And at the end of his argument, he concludes: <term>The soul, therefore, becomes free through the government of the mind; pursuing thus, without impediment or hindrance, her way to good</term> <note>original Greek: Γίνεται ουν ψυχη ελευθερα δια νου, προς το αγαθον σπευδουσα ανεμποδίστως</note>. Plotin. Enn. vi. l. viii. c. 5, 6, and 7. 

Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note> also, the oldest extant interpreter of Aristotle, defines the essence of man’s freedom as being governed <term>according to reason and judgment</term> <note>original Greek: κατα λογον τε και κρισιν</note>, by the judgment of his own reason; and in acting <term>according to a rational impulse</term> <note>original Greek: κατα λογικην ορμην</note>, from rational motives, or as he is prompted and excited by reason. See his treatise <term>On Fate</term> <note>original Greek: Περι ειμαρμενης</note>, § 14, and 23, London edition; and Aristotle himself, *Metaphysics*, book 9, chapter 5. 

Epicurus seems to have been the first who imagined human liberty to consist in acting without any motives at all, or at least independently of any. To account for this wild way of acting, he supposes that uncertain and unaccountable "swerving" of atoms, or their deviation from the ordinary course of nature, for which he is justly criticized by Cicero in many parts of his philosophical works. Yet this notion, or fancy, of Epicurus concerning the liberty of the will, absurd as it is, has been adopted by some modern writers of great reputation—though without his, or indeed any other clever invention, to avoid the absurdity.—S. <note>The "S." likely refers to the scholar Floyer Sydenham, who translated several Platonic dialogues in the 18th century.</note>

**W**hy is it, Socrates, that you are so silent, when Hippias here has been lecturing so excellently and at such length? Why do you not join the rest of the audience in praising his lecture <note>original: "dissertation"</note>; or, at least, raise some objections to it, if there was anything in it of which you disapproved? All the company has also left, and we are alone—we, who should claim a special right to share in all philosophical discussions.

<note>* The conversation recorded here was held immediately after Hippias had finished the performance or public reading of that lecture of his, which he highly praised himself in the larger dialogue of his name (*Greater Hippias*), and it takes place upon the same ground that had been the scene of his lecture. This is clear from several details. In the first place, Eudicus, who is mentioned there as the patron of Hippias and the promoter of that performance in particular, plays the same role in this dialogue. He opens it with a tone of triumph over Hippias's success, which was evident from the applause given to him by his audience. Whenever he speaks afterward, he adopts the tone and style of a patron—the kind who is a humble and ignorant admirer. It is probable that he stayed behind as one of the last of the assembly specifically for the opportunity of inviting and leading the orator to his house to feast together after his triumphant performance, as is the custom in modern times on similar occasions. Furthermore, it appears from that passage of the *Greater Hippias* mentioned earlier that Socrates, along with any of his philosophical friends he chose, was to be part of the audience at his intended lecture at the particular request of Hippias. ...a question or two about a subject he has just been discussing, taken from Homer. For I have heard your father, Apemantes, say that Homer's *Iliad* was a finer poem than his *Odyssey*, and that it surpassed it in excellence just as the virtue of Achilles surpassed the virtue of Ulysses <note>Ulysses is the Latin name for the Greek hero Odysseus.</note>. He said those two poems were intentionally composed to honor those two heroes: the *Odyssey* to show the virtues of Ulysses, and the *Iliad* those of Achilles. Regarding this specific point, then, I would be glad—if it pleases Hippias—to ask his opinion: what he thinks of those two individuals, and which of them, in his judgment, was the better man. For his presentation <note>original: "exhibition"</note>, besides covering a great variety of other topics, displayed much learning regarding the poets, and particularly Homer.

**EUDICUS:** There is no doubt that Hippias, if you propose a question to him, will condescend to give an answer. Will you not, Hippias, answer any question Socrates proposes to you? Or what other course will you take in this matter?

**HIPPIAS:** <gloss>¹ The usual method of Plato in his dialogues is to reveal the character of each person in their opening lines—a technique worthy of imitation by all dramatic poets. The most striking feature of Hippias’s character is vanity, or the desire for false and empty applause. Accordingly, it is shown in a strong light here at the very start of the dialogue. Furthermore, there is a specific reason for displaying it at the beginning of this particular dialogue: the display of Hippias’s vanity, and the influence that vanity had on his conduct, forms a material part of the subject and design. —S. <note>“S.” likely refers to Floyer Sydenham, the 18th-century translator of this edition.</note></gloss> I would take a shameful course indeed, Eudicus, if I were to decline

---

<note>This note continues from the previous page, discussing the historical and dramatic context of the dialogue.</note>

...find in this dialogue. For, not to insist on the improbability that Socrates would have been present without such a special invitation, it accounts for Socrates and his friends staying behind out of politeness to Hippias, who probably had escorted and introduced them to the place appointed for the presentation. That Socrates was accompanied by some of his followers in philosophy at this time is clear from Eudicus's first speech; at its conclusion, he addresses Socrates in the plural, referring to him and his friends. One more argument proving that Hippias's presentation—which provided the occasion for this dialogue—is the same one promised in the *Greater Hippias*, arises from the nature of the lecture <note>original: "dissertation"</note> itself. The characters of the heroes in Homer's *Iliad* were depicted in the presentation he had just given, as we learn from the following dialogue. It appears from the subject, title, and introduction of the promised lecture that a description of those very characters made up a significant part of it. These are all remarkable instances of Plato's exact fidelity to the dramatic circumstances of his dialogues, if they are true; or of his accuracy and exquisite judgment in adapting them to one another and to probability, if they are fictional. —S.
