...answering any question put by Socrates; I, who never fail to attend the Olympic games; and, leaving the privacy of home, constantly present myself in the temple there to give lectures <note>original: "dissert"</note> before the general assembly of the Greeks upon any of the subjects which I have ready for presentation <note>original: "exhibition"</note>, chosen by the audience; and to answer any question which any man shall think fit to ask.

**SOCRATES:** You are in a fortunate state of mind, Hippias, that every time the Olympic festival returns, you can <gloss>¹</gloss> proceed to the temple with a soul so full of eagerness and hope through your consciousness of wisdom. I would be very surprised if any of the athletic contestants on that occasion marched to the engagement with even half the security and confidence in the powers of his body that you, according to your own account, have in the abilities of your mind.

**HIPPIAS:** I have good reason, Socrates, to maintain such confidence. For since the time when I first competed for a prize in the trials of skill at the Olympics, I have never met a man who was my superior in any contest I engaged in.

**SOCRATES:** The reputation of your wisdom, Hippias, will be a fine monument of glory to your family and country. But what do you say to our question concerning Achilles and Ulysses? Which of the two, do you think, was the better man, and in what respects? For among the multitude of people who were inside, thronging about you during your presentation, I missed hearing some part of what you said; and, though I was desirous of asking you to repeat it over again, I suppressed that desire because of the size of the crowd and because I did not want to interrupt your lecture. But since we are now fewer... <note>original: "reduced"</note>

---

<note>¹ That is, when he was going to engage in those voluntary debates or competitions between the Sophists <note>Sophists were professional educators and rhetoricians in ancient Greece</note> to prove which of them could give the finest presentation. The decision regarding these seems to have been left to that "judicious" audience of theirs, the common people, who delivered their verdict—we assume—in their usual way: by giving a more or less loud roar of applause in proportion to how much they were pleased with each of the combatants in these side-battles. For, while it is certain that these made no part of those solemn contests or competitions at the Olympic festival according to its original institution, we do not suppose them to be among those added later, such as the competitions in the liberal arts and sciences. It is more probable that the Sophists, with a view of spreading their fame wider, gave these lectures for free to the public on these occasions, using the most popular of the presentations they usually gave for private audiences.—S.</note>

...to such a small number, and since Eudicus here encourages me to ask you, please give me a precise and clear account of what you said then about those two heroes, and what distinction you made between their characters.

**HIPPIAS:** Well, Socrates, I am willing to inform you more precisely and clearly than I did in my public lecture <note>original: "exhibition"</note> what my thoughts are concerning those heroes and others as well. I say then, that Homer made Achilles superior in virtue to all the Greeks who were at the siege of Troy, Nestor superior in wisdom, and Ulysses superior in cunning.

**SOCRATES:** Ah, Hippias! Will you grant me one more favor? That is, not to laugh at me if I am slow in understanding <note>original: "apprehending"</note> what you say and bother you with frequent and repeated questions. Will you try, on the contrary, to give me mild and gentle answers?

**HIPPIAS:** Since I make a profession of instructing others in the knowledge of these very things that you are asking about—and I believe that knowledge is so rare that it deserves to be well-paid for—it would be unfair and dishonorable of me, Socrates, not to excuse your ignorance and give a mild answer to your questions.

**SOCRATES:** That is very fairly and honorably spoken. You should know then, that when you said Homer made Achilles superior in virtue, I seemed to understand your meaning, just as I did when you told me his Nestor was made superior in wisdom. But when you further said that the poet had made Ulysses superior in cunning, I must confess the truth to you: I am entirely ignorant of what you mean by that. Perhaps I might understand your meaning better through your answer to this question: Is not cunning also part of the character of Achilles, as drawn by Homer?

**HIPPIAS:** Not at all; rather, he is the height of simplicity. For in the ninth book of the *Iliad*, where Achilles and Ulysses are shown in conversation together, Achilles, addressing Ulysses, speaks like this:

> -> * Son of Laertes, descendant of Zeus! <note>original: "progeny of Jove"</note> <-
> -> Subtle is your wit, Ulysses, and your brain... <-

In these verses, we see the character of each of those heroes: we see Achilles as sincere and straightforward, and Ulysses <note>original: "Ulyſſes"</note> as deceptive and cunning. For Achilles is made the speaker of these verses, and they are spoken to Ulysses.

**HIPPIAS:** Exactly so, Socrates. And accordingly, Homer has made Ulysses a man of that very character in many places, both in the *Iliad* and in the *Odyssey*.

**SOCRATES:** It seems then that Homer was of the opinion that the man of truth was a character different from the man of falsehood.

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly, Socrates. How could it be otherwise?

**SOCRATES:** And are you of the same opinion yourself, Hippias?

**HIPPIAS:** Most certainly. For it would be a terrible consequence to have those two opposite characters confused.

**SOCRATES:** Then let us leave Homer out of the question, as it is impossible for us to ask him what he had in mind when he wrote those verses. But, since you appear to support and defend his view, and to hold the same sentiments that you attribute to him, please answer for both the poet and yourself.

**HIPPIAS:** I will do so. Ask any question you think appropriate—only keep it brief.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hippias. Socrates is questioning Hippias's definition of a "cunning" or "false" person, specifically focusing on whether such a person acts out of capability and knowledge rather than ignorance.</meta>

<page-num>280</page-num>
<header>THE LESSER HIPPIAS.</header>

**SOCRATES:** Is it a kind of inability to perform certain actions—like the kind that sick men suffer from? Or do you mean men who have the ability and power for some performance or another?

**HIPPIAS:** I mean men who have powers—and very strong ones, too—for many purposes, but particularly for deceiving others.

**SOCRATES:** It seems then, according to your account, the cunning are men of strong power and ability. Are they not?

**HIPPIAS:** They are.

**SOCRATES:** Is it through folly and a lack of understanding that they are cunning and deceitful? Or is it through artfulness and a certain kind of understanding?

**HIPPIAS:** Through artfulness in the highest degree and a depth of understanding.

**SOCRATES:** They are men of good understanding then, it seems.

**HIPPIAS:** They have no lack of understanding, by Jupiter! <note>The original text uses "by Jupiter," a standard translation of the Greek oath "by Zeus."</note>

**SOCRATES:** Since they have understanding then, are they ignorant of what they are doing? Or do they know it?

**HIPPIAS:** They know well enough what they do. And it is because of this very knowledge that they are so wicked.

**SOCRATES:** With this knowledge which they have mastered, then, can they be lacking in discipline or skill? Or do they possess it in abundance?

**HIPPIAS:** They have discipline and skill more than sufficient for their purpose—which is to deceive.

**SOCRATES:** Hold on a moment; let me recap everything you have said. You assert that men of falsehood are men of ability, understanding, knowledge, and skill—at least in those subjects in which they deceive.

**HIPPIAS:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** And you assert that men of sincerity and men of falsehood are different kinds of people, with characters completely opposite to one another.

**HIPPIAS:** I stand by that assertion as well.

There are four causes for moral evil. The first is some disorder in the body, obscuring the light of the mind or obstructing the operation of its faculties. Another is some defect in the natural powers of the understanding. A third is a lack of science <note>original: "science" — here meaning systematic knowledge or learning</note>, and the fourth is a lack of virtuous habit and practice. — S.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hippias. Socrates is refining the definition of a "deceiver" by establishing that deception requires the actual ability and knowledge to perform the act, rather than being a result of ignorance or weakness.</meta>

<page-num>281</page-num>
<header>THE LESSER HIPPIAS.</header>

# THE LESSER HIPPIAS.

**SOCRATES:** Well then; it seems that according to your account, some among those who possess ability and skill are deceitful men.

**HIPPIAS:** Most true.

**SOCRATES:** When you say that deceitful men possess ability and skill in certain areas, do you mean they are capable of deceiving whenever they wish to? Or do you think they lack <note>original: "want"</note> the ability to deceive?

**HIPPIAS:** I think they have the ability for that purpose.

**SOCRATES:** To sum up the whole matter then: deceitful men are those who have the skill and ability to deceive.

**HIPPIAS:** Right.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, a person who lacks the ability or skill to deceive cannot be a liar or a deceiver.

**HIPPIAS:** Very right.

However, all the editors have given it the wrong meaning by incorrectly printing "ara" <note>original: $\alpha\rho\alpha$, a particle meaning 'then' or 'consequently'</note> instead of "âra" <note>original: $\tilde{\alpha}\rho\alpha$, a particle used to introduce a question</note>. All the translators were misled in this, as in most other places, by the errors in the printed Greek text. — S. <note>This refers to Thomas Sydenham, the 18th-century translator whose notes are included in this edition.</note></margin>

<margin>² That is, the absence of any external obstacle. In the common use of the words "power" and "liberty," only the absence of external obstacles and hindrances is considered. — S.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** ¹ Is a man able to do what he wants if he can use his ability whenever he chooses—assuming he isn't prevented by disease or some ² other similar obstacle? I mean it in the same way you are able to write my name whenever you choose. Don't you say that every person who has that same kind of power in other matters is "able"?

**HIPPIAS:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** Tell me now, Hippias; are you not well-versed in numbers and calculations?

**HIPPIAS:** Perfectly well, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** If a man were to ask you, "How much is three times seven hundred?" wouldn't you answer that question perfectly and very quickly, if you chose to do so?

**HIPPIAS:** I certainly would.

**SOCRATES:** And that is because your ability and skill are excellent in subjects of that kind.

**HIPPIAS:** True.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Hippias. Socrates is narrowing down his argument: if someone is a "skilled" liar, they must first have the knowledge and ability to know what the truth is, so they can intentionally avoid it.</meta>

<page-num>282</page-num>
<header>THE LESSER HIPPIAS.</header>

**SOCRATES:** Do you excel in ability and skill only? Or is your virtue¹ equal to your ability and skill regarding the same subjects—that is, numbers and accounts?

**HIPPIAS:** It is, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** You are perfectly capable, then, of speaking the truth on these subjects, are you not?

**HIPPIAS:** So I imagine.

**SOCRATES:** But what about this: are you not equally capable of speaking untruths on the same subject? Answer me now, Hippias, as you did before, with a generous freedom and openness. If a man were to ask you, "How much is three times seven hundred?" would you not be the person most capable of deceiving others? Could you not consistently give false answers on that subject, if you were constantly inclined to present falsehood as truth and never give a correct answer? Or would someone unskilled in calculations be better at deceiving than you are? Might² not an ignorant person, however much they wanted to keep giving false answers, occasionally happen to stumble upon the truth out of sheer ignorance? But you, who have the skill, if you also had the desire to deceive, would you not always and invariably give the wrong answer?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly; the case is exactly as you represent it.

**SOCRATES:** Now, as for the man who is thoroughly dishonest, is he a deceiver in other cases only, but not in numbering and computing? Would he not deceive others when numbers and calculations were the points in question?

**HIPPIAS:** By Jupiter, he would.³

**SOCRATES:** Let us suppose, then, Hippias, that there is a certain person who is a false man, or a deceiver, regarding the subject of numbers and calculations.

**HIPPIAS:** Very well.

**SOCRATES:** What kind of person must he be? In order to be a deceiver, must he not, as you yourself just now acknowledged, have the ability to deceive?

***

<note>¹ Socrates here refers to justice, particularly the part known as truthfulness <note>original: "veracity"</note>. — Sydenham</note>
<note>² In the original Greek here, we certainly ought to read "than the ignorant man" <note>original: ἢ ὁ μεν αμαθης</note>, and not simply "or" <note>original: ἢ</note> as it has been printed and translated until now. — Sydenham</note>
<note>³ Numbers and accounts are the primary areas where dishonest people commit fraud and deception. — Sydenham</note>

For, regarding any other man who lacked those abilities, you admitted—if you remember—that such a person would never be a good deceiver.

**Hip.** I remember; we agreed on this.

**Soc.** Was it not just proved that you yourself were capable in the highest degree of deceiving others with false information on the subject of numbers and calculations?

**Hip.** We agreed on this too.

**Soc.** And are you not also capable in the highest degree of giving true information on the same subject?

**Hip.** Certainly.

**Soc.** ¹ Therefore, one and the same person has abilities beyond other men to give either false or true information on the subject of numbers and calculations; and the good arithmetician is this person.

**Hip.** Without doubt.

**Soc.** Who, then, *Hippias*, appears to be the man of falsehood ², and the deceiver regarding numbers and calculations? Is it anyone other than the good arithmetician? For he is the one who is most capable. And this same man is also the true accountant.

¹ In the original, both parts of this sentence are erroneously made into questions by all the editors, as we understand it; they are translated as such by *Serranus* and *Bembo*. The other versions in this place agree with ours. — S. <note>original: "S." likely refers to the translator, Floyer Sydenham.</note>

² *Aristotle* observes that *Plato* here makes use of a paralogism <note>a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</note>, or a sophistical way of arguing. For by "false" <note>original: ψευδης (pseudes)</note>, or a man of falsehood, *Plato* (Aristotle says) means a man "capable of speaking untruths" <note>original: δυναμενος ψευδεσθαι (dynamenos pseudesthai)</note>; whereas the word properly signifies a man "who is prone to and chooses such false words, not for any other reason but for the sake of the falsehood itself, and who creates such notions in others" <note>original: ευχερης και προαιρετικος των τοιουτων [sc. ψευδων] λογων, μη δι' ἑτερον τι, αλλα δι' αυτο, και ὁ αλλοις εμποιητικος των τοιουτων λογων</note>. See *Aristotle's Metaphysics*, book 5, chapter 29. It is true that such a man is the subject of the present dispute between *Socrates* and *Hippias*; but it is an innocent piece of sophistry, since it is not employed for the purpose of deceiving anyone, but only for discovering the truth; it turns into just reasoning when the conclusion is later drawn from all the examples listed. *Aristotle* does not condemn *Plato* as being guilty of arguing unfairly or of swapping one sense of a word for another; but as he discusses the various meanings of the words "false" and "falsity" in that chapter of his *Metaphysics*, he produces this passage from *Plato* as a singular example of an improper use of the term "false" when applied to a person. — S.
